Type: proof
Title: Proof of [REF:thm:network-flow-recast-transport]
Relation: proof_of=unit-9d11c55afe9b88102407
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right); \qand := \quad\text{and}\quad
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof of [REF:thm:network-flow-recast-transport] ]
 We now construct a transport problem according to the minimum cost network flow problem, as demonstrated in [REF:fig:transport-from-network-flow] .

 For every vertex \(i \in V\), we construct a consumer, which demands
 \[
 \sum_{k: \pqty{i, k} \in E} \overline{m}_{ik} - b_i.
 \]

 For every edge \(\pqty{i, j} \in E\), we construct a supplier, which produces \(\overline{m}_{ij}\) units.

 We set the costs to be
 \[
 c_{ij, i} = 0 \qand c_{ij, j} = c_{ij}.
 \]

 Let the flow from \(ij\) to \(j\) be \(x_{ij}\), and the (remaining) flow from \(ij\) to \(i\) be \(\overline{m}_{ij} - x_{ij}\). (This gives the transport conservation for the suppliers.)

 We notice that the total flow into consumer \(i\) is given by
 \[
 \sum_{k: \pqty{i, k} \in E} \pqty{\overline{m}_{ik} - x_{ik}} + \sum_{k: \pqty{k, i} \in E} x_{ki}
 \]
 and we want this to be equal to the demand at \(i\). This then gives the equality
 \[
 \sum_{k: \pqty{k, i} \in E} x_{ki} + b_i = \sum_{k: \pqty{i, k} \in E} x_{ik},
 \]
 giving the conservation of flow in the original network flow problem.

 For any solution \(x_{ij}\) to the transport problem, the cost is given by
 \[
 \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} c_{ij} x_{ij}
 \]
 which gives identical costs.
\end{proof}

Label: optim-unit-0073

Content:
\begin{theorem}[Optimality Conditions for Transport Problem] 
 If, for some feasible \(\pqty{x_{ij}}\), and we have dual variables \(\vb*{\lambda} \in \RR^n\), \(\vb*{\mu} \in \RR^m\) such that for all \(i \in \bqty{n}\) and \(j \in \bqty{m}\), we have
 \[
 c_{ij} \geq \lambda_i + \mu_j
 \]
 and
 \[
 \pqty{c_{ij} - \pqty{\lambda_i + \mu_j}} x_{ij} = 0
 \]
 then \(\pqty{x_{ij}}\) is optimal.
\end{theorem}
label: optim-unit-0073

Relation: proof_of=unit-30cfbc6e6411a050f52f
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{proof}
 The Lagrangian is given by
 \begin{align*}
 L\pqty{\pqty{x_{ij}}, \vb*{\lambda}, \vb*{\mu}} &= \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} c_{ij} x_{ij} - \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_i \pqty{\sum_{j = 1}^{m} x_{ij} - s_i} - \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \mu_j \pqty{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_{ij} - d_j} \\
 &= \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \pqty{c_{ij} - \lambda_i - \mu_j} x_{ij} + \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_i s_i + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \mu_j d_j.
 \end{align*}

 Dual feasibility is guaranteed by \(c_{ij} - \lambda_i - \mu_j \geq 0\), i.e. \(c_{ij} \geq \lambda_i + \mu_j\). The second condition gives complementary slackness. Using [REF:thm:optimality-condition-lp] (Optimality Conditions for Linear Programs), we may conclude \(\pqty{x_{ij}}\) is optimal.
\end{proof}

embedding_text:
Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Network Flow > The Transport Algorithm > The Transport Algorithm
Type: prose
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
The transport algorithm maintains a spanning-tree basis of \(n+m-1\) cells in the balanced complete bipartite problem. Zero-flow basic cells may be needed in degenerate cases. An entering nonbasic cell creates a unique cycle; add and subtract the same amount alternately around it. Use an anti-cycling pivot rule when degeneracy occurs. The main steps are:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If \(c_{ij} \geq \lambda_i + \mu_j\) for all \(\pqty{i, j}\), then the current solution is optimal and the algorithm stops.
 \item If \(c_{ij} < \lambda_i + \mu_j\) for some \(\pqty{i, j}\), then select that edge and find edges in the current flow that forms a cycle with it.
 \item Increase the flow in the new edge \(x_{ij}\), until some flow in the cycle reaches zero.
 \item Re-calculate the dual variables and repeat this process.
\end{enumerate}

Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut > Maximum Flow
Type: definition
Title: Maximum Flow Problem
Label: optim-unit-0076
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{definition}[Maximum Flow Problem] 
 For a finite graph \(G=\pqty{V,E}\) with distinct source and sink and finite nonnegative capacities \(c_{ij}\) on its edges (the capacities of each edge), the maximum flow problem is to maximise \(\delta\), the flow, subject to constraints
 \begin{itemize}
 \item outgoing flow from vertex \(1\):
 \[
 \sum_{j: \pqty{1, j} \in E} x_{1j} - \sum_{i: \pqty{i, 1} \in E} x_{i1} = \delta;
 \]
 \item incoming flow to vertex \(n\):
 \[
 \sum_{i: \pqty{i, n} \in E} x_{in} - \sum_{j: \pqty{n, j} \in E} x_{nj} = \delta;
 \]
 \item flow conservation at vertex \(i \neq 1, n\):
 \[
 \sum_{j: \pqty{i, j} \in E} x_{ij} = \sum_{j: \pqty{j, i} \in E} x_{ji};
 \]
 \item capacity constraint: for all \(\pqty{i, j} \in E\),
 \[
 0 \leq x_{ij} \leq c_{ij}.
 \]
 \end{itemize}
\end{definition}
label: optim-unit-0076

 \[
 \phi_i \pqty{x} = \sum_{j: \pqty{i, j} \in E} x_{ij} - \sum_{j: \pqty{j, i} \in E} x_{ji}
 \]

 +1, &\qif i = 1, \\
 -1, &\qif i = n, \\
 0, &\qotherwise.
 \end{cases}
 \]
 then the problem became maximising \(\delta\), subject to constraints
 \[
 \phi_i \pqty{x} - b_i \delta = 0
 \]
 for all \(i\), and \(0 \leq x_{ij} \leq c_{ij}\).
\end{notation}

Label: optim-unit-0078

Content:
\begin{definition}[Cut of a Graph, Capacity of a Cut] 
 A cut of a graph \(G = \pqty{V, E}\) is a partition of \(V\) into two sets, \(\pqty{S, V \setminus S}\).
 
 The capacity of the cut is the sum of the capacities crossing the cut
 \[
 C\pqty{S} = \sum_{\substack{i \in S \\ j \in V \setminus S \\ \pqty{i, j} \in E}} c_{ij}.
 \]
\end{definition}
label: optim-unit-0078

\begin{theorem}[Maximum Flow is Upper Bounded by \(C\pqty{S}\)] 
 Let \(\pqty{x_{ij}}\) be a feasible flow with flow value \(\delta\). For any cut \(\pqty{S, V \setminus S}\) such that \(1 \in S\) and \(n \in V \setminus S\), we have
 \[
 \delta \leq C\pqty{S}.
 \]
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}
 For \(A, B \subseteq V\) (not necessarily disjoint), we define
 \[
 f_x \pqty{A, B} = \sum_{\substack{i \in A \\ j \in B \\ \pqty{i, j} \in E}} x_{ij}.
 \]

 Note that
 \[
 C\pqty{S} \geq f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S}
 \]
 since \(c_{ij} \geq x_{ij}\).

 We sum up the flow constraint for all \(i \in S\), which gives
 \begin{align*}
 \sum_{i \in S} \phi_i \pqty{x} &= \sum_{i \in S} \pqty{\sum_{j: \pqty{i, j} \in E} x_{ij} - \sum_{j: \pqty{j, i} \in E} x_{ji}} \\
 &= \sum_{i \in S} b_i \delta \\
 &= \delta
 \end{align*}
 and hence
 \begin{align*}
 \delta &= f_x \pqty{S, V} - f_x \pqty{V, S} \\
 &= f_x \pqty{S, S} + f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S} - f_x \pqty{S, S} - f_x \pqty{V \setminus S, S} \\
 &= f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S} - f_x \pqty{V \setminus S, S} \\
 &\leq f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S} \\
 &\leq C \pqty{S}.
 \end{align*}
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{definition}[Path, Augmenting Path] 
 A undirected path is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k\), satisfying \(\pqty{v_{i - 1}, v_i} \in E\) or \(\pqty{v_i, v_{i - 1}} \in E\) for all \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, k\).

 An augmenting path is a path such that, for every \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, k\), at least one of the following holds:
 \begin{itemize}
 \item forward edge with non-optimal flow: \(\pqty{v_{i - 1}, v_i} \in E\) and \(x_{v_{i - 1} v_i} < c_{v_{i - 1} v_i}\);
 \item reverse edge with positive flow: \(\pqty{v_i, v_{i - 1}} \in E\) and \(x_{v_i v_{i - 1}} > 0\).
 \end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
 If an augmenting path exist, we could increase the flow along that path by increasing the flow of forward edges by \(\epsilon\) and decreasing the flow of backward edges by \(\epsilon\), for sufficiently small \(\epsilon > 0\), without violating constraints.

\begin{theorem}[Maximum Flow is Minimum Cut]

 \delta^{\ast} = \min \set{C \pqty{S}}{S \subseteq V, 1 \in S, n \in V \setminus S}.

embedding_text:
Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut > Minimum Cut and Augmenting Paths
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8fee2068d8da9d1daae7
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \qand := \quad\text{and}\quad; \set := \left\{#1\mid #2\right\}
Content:
\begin{proof}
 It suffices to produce a set \(S\) such that \(C\pqty{S} = \delta^{\ast}\).

 If a flow \(x\) is optimal, then \(x\) cannot have augmenting paths from \(1\) to \(n\). Define
 \[
 S = \Bqty{1} \cup \set{i \in V}{there exists augmenting path from 1 to i}
 \]
 and observe \(1 \in S\) while \(n \notin S\). For this set \(S\), sum up the flow constraints of \(S\),
 \[
 \delta^{\ast} = f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S} - f_x \pqty{V \setminus S, S}.
 \]

 Notice that any \(i \in S\), \(j \in V \setminus S\) and \(\pqty{i, j} \in E\) must satisfy that \(x_{ij} = c_{ij}\) (otherwise we could extend an augmenting path to \(j\)); and similarly for any \(i \in S\), \(j \in V \setminus S\) and \(\pqty{j, i} \in E\) must satisfy that \(x_{ji} = 0\). Hence,
 \[
 f_x \pqty{S, V \setminus S} = C\pqty{S} \qand f_x \pqty{V \setminus S, S} = 0
 \]
 hence
 \[
 \delta^{\ast} = C\pqty{S}.
 \]
\end{proof}

Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut > The Ford--Fulkerson Algorithm
Type: prose
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
The Ford--Fulkerson Algorithm arising from [REF:thm:max-flow-min-cut] augments the augmenting paths from \(1\) to \(n\), and is described as follows.

\begin{itemize}
 \item Start from a feasible flow \(\pqty{x_{ij}}\), say the trivial flow with all zeros.
 \item While we can find an augmenting path between \(1\) and \(n\), augment by the minimum residual capacity on the selected residual path, increasing forward flows and decreasing reverse flows.
 \item When there are no augmenting paths, return the current flow and the cut of residual-reachable vertices; their values agree, proving optimality. 
\end{itemize}

It could be tedious to list all possible paths, so if at one point one fails to find an augmenting path between \(1\) and \(n\), it could be useful to stop and attempt to construct a cut with the same capacity as the flow, at which point we could stop.

embedding_text:
Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut > The Edmonds--Karp Algorithm and Convergence of the Ford--Fulkerson Algorithm
Type: prose
Local macros: \abs := \left|#1\right|; \bigO := \mathcal{O}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
One unsatisfying thing about the Ford--Fulkerson algorithm is it is not very obvious how this is related to the simplex algorithm. Indeed, the Ford--Fulkerson algorithm works relatively differently, in the sense that it does not necessarily jump to extreme points -- and hence convergence is not necessarily guaranteed (thought it is guaranteed to improve). In the case where all capacities are integral (in which case all increases are also integral) or rational (in which we could just scale the problem to be integral), it is guaranteed to converge after finitely many steps.

The Edmonds--Karp algorithm which augments the path in order of distance (i.e., finding such paths by breadth-first search), guarantees for the convergence of the algorithm in \(\bigO\pqty{\abs{V} \abs{E}^2}\) time.

Course: Optimisation: Convexity, Duality, Linear Programming and Network Flows
Section: Applications of Linear Program > Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut > Duality of Maximum Flow and Minimum Cut
Type: prose
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \qand := \quad\text{and}\quad; \qif := \quad\text{if}\quad; \qotherwise := \quad\text{otherwise}
Content:
We have discussed a lot about duality of problems in this course, and it is very tempting to prove that maximum flow corresponding to minimum cut is a duality problem. (This is also suggested by our two-part theorem proof.) However, it is not immediately clear how minimum cut can be a linear programming problem.

Recall the notation
\[
 b_i = \begin{cases}
 +1, &\qif i = 1, \\
 -1, &\qif i = n, \\
 0, &\qotherwise.
 \end{cases}
\]
and the primal becomes maximising \(\delta\), subject to
\[
 \sum_{j: \pqty{i, j} \in E} x_{ij} - \sum_{j: \pqty{j, i} \in E} x_{ji} = b_i \delta.
\]
and
\[
 0 \leq x_{ij} \leq c_{ij}.
\]

We introduce dual variables \(y_i\) for each vertex \(i\) for the equality constraints, and introduce slack variables \(s_{ij} \geq 0\) for each edge with corresponding dual variables \(z_{ij}\). Then, the Lagrangian of the primal problem is therefore (since \(\delta\) is to be maximised)
\begin{align*}
 L\pqty{\delta, \pqty{x_{ij}}, \pqty{s_{ij}}, \pqty{y_i}, \pqty{z_{ij}}} &= \pqty{-\delta} - \sum_{i \in V} y_i \pqty{\phi_i \pqty{x} - b_i \delta} - \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} \pqty{c_{ij} - x_{ij} - s_{ij}} \\
 &= \pqty{-1 + \sum_{i \in V} y_i b_i} \delta - \sum_{i \in V} y_i \pqty{\sum_{j: \pqty{i, j} \in E} x_{ij} - \sum_{j: \pqty{j, i} \in E} x_{ji}} \\
 &\phantom{=} \hspace{5em} - \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} c_{ij} + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} x_{ij} + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} s_{ij} \\
 &= \pqty{-1 + \sum_{i \in V} y_i b_i} \delta - \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} y_i x_{ij} + \sum_{\pqty{j, i} \in E} y_i x_{ji} \\
 &\phantom{=} \hspace{5em} - \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} c_{ij} + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} x_{ij} + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} s_{ij} \\
 &= \pqty{-1 + \sum_{i \in V} y_i b_i} \delta + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} \pqty{- y_i + y_j + z_{ij}} x_{ij} \\
 &\phantom{=} \hspace{12em} + \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} s_{ij} - \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} c_{ij}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the dual feasible set is given by
\[
 \sum_{i \in V} y_i b_i = 1 \qand z_{ij} \geq y_i - y_j \qand z_{ij} \geq 0.
\]

Notice the first constraint reduces to
\[
 y_1 - y_n = 1
\]
where \(1\) is the source vertex and \(n\) is the sink vertex. With this, the dual function is given by
\[
 -\sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} c_{ij}
\]
and the dual problem is, hence, to minimise
\[
 \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} z_{ij} c_{ij}
\]
subject to constraints
\begin{align*}
 y_1 - y_n &= 1 \\
 z_{ij} &\geq y_i - y_j \\
 z_{ij} &\geq 0.
\end{align*}

Notice that to minimise this, since all the capacities are non-negative, we always take
\[
 z_{ij} = \max \Bqty{0, y_i - y_j}
\]
and the dual objective is now minimising
\[
 \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} \max \Bqty{0, y_i - y_j} c_{ij}
\]
subject to \(y_1 - y_n = 1\).

To note this relation with the minimum cut problem, note that a cut \(\pqty{S, V \setminus S}\) assigned with \(y_i = 1\) for \(i \in S\) and \(0\) for \(i \in V \setminus S\), we have the constraint translates to \(1 \in S\) and \(n \in V \setminus S\), and
\[
 \sum_{\pqty{i, j} \in E} \max \Bqty{0, y_i - y_j} c_{ij} = \sum_{\substack{\pqty{i, j} \in E \\ i \in S \\ j \in V \setminus S}} c_{ij} = C\pqty{S}
\]
is indeed the capacity, so the minimum of the dual objective function is at most the minimum cut. There exists an optimal potential with values in \(\{0,1\}\).

Content:
\begin{proof}
Shift the potentials so \(y_n=0\), \(y_1=1\), and clip all potentials to \([0,1]\).
Clipping cannot increase \(\max(0,y_i-y_j)\). For \(0<t<1\), put
\(S_t=\{i:y_i>t\}\). This is a source--sink cut and
\[
\int_0^1 C(S_t)\,dt
=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}c_{ij}\max(0,y_i-y_j).
\]
Indeed each edge contributes for an interval of thresholds of length
\(\max(0,y_i-y_j)\). Some threshold cut therefore has capacity no larger than
the dual objective. Together with the reverse inequality above, this proves equality
and gives an optimal zero--one potential.
\end{proof}

In problem (i), we may write the path in the form \(y = y\pqty{x}\), with \(a \leq x \leq b\). Then its length is given by
\[
 L \bqty{y} = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + y'^2} \dd{x}.
\]

We can find the length of a parametrised curve similarly in (ii) and (iii).

This is a functional, which is a map from a function to a number, and the goal is to find the choice of the function \(y\pqty{x}\) that minimises this functional. We will develop tools in this course to determine minima/maxima of functionals.

Title: Stationary Point
Label: variation-unit-0002
Local macros: \RR := \mathbb{R}; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{definition}[Stationary Point] 
 
 We say a point \(\vb{a} \in \RR^n\) is a stationary point of \(f\), if
 \[
 \pqty{\grad f} \pqty{\vb{a}} = \vb{0},
 \]
 where the gradient is given by
 \[
 \grad f = \pqty{\pdv{f}{x_1}, \pdv{f}{x_2}, \ldots, \pdv{f}{x_n}}.
 \]
\end{definition}
label: variation-unit-0002

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Calculus on \(\RR^n\)
Type: prose
Local macros: \abs := \left|#1\right|; \contClass := C^{#1}; \diag := diag; \norm := \left\lVert#1\right\rVert; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \transpose := ^{\mathsf{T}}
Content:
We may also Taylor expand a function about a point, having
\[
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} = f\pqty{\vb{a}} + \sum_{i} \pqty{x_i - a_i} \pqty{\nabla_i f} \pqty{\vb{a}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i, j} \pqty{x_i - a_i} \pqty{x_j - a_j} H_{ij} \pqty{\vb{a}} + o\pqty{\norm{\vb{x} - \vb{a}}^2},
\]
where the Hessian matrix is given by
\[
 H_{ij} = \pdv{f}{x_i}{x_j}.
\]

Since \(f\) is \(\contClass{2}\), \(H_{ij} = H_{ji}\). From now on, we simplify the notation with \(\vb{a} = \vb{0}\) by a translation to the origin. Under the summation convention, at a stationary point, we have
\[
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} - f\pqty{\vb{0}} = \frac{1}{2} x_i H_{ij} x_j + o\pqty{\abs{\vb{x}}^2}.
\]

Recall that we may diagonalise \(H_{ij}\), since it is symmetric, and we may rotate the coordinates under the transformation
\[
 x_i = R_{ij} x'_{j}.
\]

Then the new Hessian matrix will be transformed as
\[
 \vb{H}' = \vb{R}\transpose \vb{H} \vb{R} = \diag(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n)
\]
and the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(\vb{H}\). Note that since \(\vb{H}\) is real, symmetric, all the eigenvalues are therefore real.

After diagonalisation, the quadratic form will be diagonalised as
\[
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} - f\pqty{\vb{0}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_i x_i'^2 + o\pqty{\abs{\vb{x}}^2}.
\]

Therefore, we have the following result.

Section: Calculus on \(\RR^n\)
Type: example
Title: Finding and Classifying Stationary Points
Label: variation-unit-0007
Local macros: \RR := \mathbb{R}; \functiondomain := #1:#2\to #3; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \tr := tr
Content:
\begin{example}[Finding and Classifying Stationary Points] 
 
 Consider the function \(\functiondomain{f}{\RR^2}{\RR}\), given by
 \[
 f\pqty{x, y} = x^3 + y^3 - 3xy.
 \]

 We find the gradient as
 \[
 \grad f = \pqty{3 x^2 - 3y, 3 y^2 - 3x},
 \]
 and note
 \[
 \grad f = \vb{0} \iff x^2 = y and y^2 = x.
 \]

 This then solves to \(\pqty{x, y} = \pqty{0, 0}\) or \(\pqty{x, y} = \pqty{1, 1}\).

 Now, looking at the Hessian matrix, we have
 \[
 \vb{H} = \begin{pmatrix}
 6x & -3 \\ -3 & 6y
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \]

 The determinant and the trace are therefore given by
 \[
 \det \vb{H} = 9 \pqty{4xy - 1}, \quad \tr \vb{H} = 6 \pqty{x + y}.
 \]

 At \(\pqty{x, y} = \pqty{1, 1}\), \(\det \vb{H} = 27 > 0\) and \(\tr \vb{H} = 12 > 0\). Therefore, \(\pqty{1, 1}\) is a local minimum, and
 \[
 f\pqty{1, 1} = -1.
 \]

 At \(\pqty{x, y} = \pqty{0, 0}\), \(\det \vb{H} = -9 < 0\). Therefore, \(\pqty{0, 0}\) is a saddle, and
 \[
 f\pqty{0, 0} = 0.
 \]

 We may calculate the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors as
 \[
 \lambda_1 = -3, \quad \vb{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}
 1 \\ 1
 \end{pmatrix}
 \]
 and
 \[
 \lambda_2 = 3, \quad \vb{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
 1 \\ -1
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \]

 Therefore, \(\pqty{0, 0}\) is a local maximum along the line parallel to \(\vb{e}_1\) (\(y = x\)), while it is a local minimum along the line parallel to \(\vb{e}_2\) (\(y = -x\)).

 But note \(f\) does not have a global maximum or minimum -- we can make \(x\) and \(y\) very large (but of the same sign), and \(f\) increases/decreases without bound.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0007

\begin{definition}[Convex Set] 
 
 A set \(S \subseteq \RR^n\) is convex, if for any \(\vb{x}, \vb{y} \in S\) and \(t \in \ccintv{0}{1}\), we have
 \[
 t \vb{x} + \pqty{1 - t} \vb{y} \in S.
 \]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Graph of Function] 
 
 Let \(f\) be a function with domain \(\dom\pqty{f} \subseteq \RR^n\), i.e., \(\functiondomain{f}{\dom\pqty{f}}{\RR}\). The graph of \(f\) is the surface
 \[
 z = f\pqty{\vb{x}}
 \]
 in \(\RR^{n + 1}\), with coordinates \(\pqty{\vb{x}, z}\). A chord of \(f\) is a line segment joining \(2\) points of its graph.
\end{definition}

Content:
\begin{examples}[Convex Functions] 
 
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item The function \(f\pqty{x} = x^2\) is strictly convex, since
 \[
 \bqty{\pqty{1 - t} x + ty}^2 - \pqty{1 - t} x^2 - t y^2 = - t \pqty{1 - t} \pqty{x - y}^2 < 0
 \]
 for \(t \in \oointv{0}{1}\), \(x \neq y\).

 \item The functions \(f\pqty{x} = e^x\) and \(g\pqty{x} = e^{-x}\) are strictly convex.
 
 \item The function \(f\pqty{x} = \abs{x}\) is convex but not strictly convex: to show it is not strict, take for example \(x = 1\) and \(y = 2\), because some chords lie on the graph.
 \end{enumerate}
\end{examples}

Title: First Order Condition
Label: variation-unit-0012

Content:
\begin{theorem}[First Order Condition] 
 
 If \(f\) is differentiable, then [REF:eq:convex-condition] is equivalent to
 \begin{equation}
 \forall \vb{x}, \vb{y} \in \dom\pqty{f}: f\pqty{\vb{y}} \geq f\pqty{\vb{x}} + \pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{x}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{x}} 
 \end{equation}

 Geometrically, this means that the graph of \(f\) lies on or above any tangent plane, as shown in [REF:fig:convex-fn-tangents] for the one-dimensional case.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ that [REF:eq:convex-condition] implies [REF:eq:first-order-condition] ]
 Let
 \[
 h\pqty{t} = \pqty{1 - t} f\pqty{\vb{x}} + t f\pqty{\vb{y}} - f\pqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}}.
 \]

 Then note that
 \[
 h'\pqty{0} = - f\pqty{\vb{x}} + f\pqty{\vb{y}} - \pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{x}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{x}}
 \]
 which is the difference of two sides in [REF:eq:first-order-condition] .

 But note that by definition,
 \[
 h'\pqty{0} = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{h\pqty{t} - h\pqty{0}}{t} = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{h\pqty{t}}{t}.
 \]

 But note that [REF:eq:convex-condition] gives that \(h\pqty{t} \geq 0\) for all \(t \in \oointv{0}{1}\), and hence \(h'\pqty{0} \geq 0\), giving [REF:eq:first-order-condition] .
 
\end{proof}

Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \dom := dom; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \vdot := \cdot
Content:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ that [REF:eq:first-order-condition] implies [REF:eq:convex-condition] ]
 In this direction, note that [REF:eq:first-order-condition] implies that
 \begin{align*}
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} &\geq f\pqty{\vb{z}} + \pqty{\vb{x} - \vb{z}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{z}} \\
 f\pqty{\vb{y}} &\geq f\pqty{\vb{z}} + \pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{z}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{z}}
 \end{align*}
 for all \(\vb{x}, \vb{y}\) and \(\vb{z} \in \dom\pqty{f}\).

 Taking a linear combination, we have
 \[
 \pqty{1 - t} f\pqty{\vb{x}} + t f \pqty{\vb{y}} \geq f\pqty{z} + \bqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y} - \vb{z}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{z}}.
 \]

 We now choose \(\vb{z} = \pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}\), which implies [REF:eq:convex-condition] .
\end{proof}

Relation: proof_of=unit-491c34826a0467b5d7f3
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \vdot := \cdot
Content:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ that [REF:eq:first-order-condition-alternative] implies [REF:eq:first-order-condition] ]
 We let \(\vb{z} = \pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}\).

 Then we have
 \begin{align*}
 f\pqty{\vb{y}} - f\pqty{\vb{x}} &= \bqty{f\pqty{\vb{z}}}_{t = 0}^{t = 1} \\
 &= \int_{0}^{1} \dd{t} \dv{t} f\pqty{\vb{z}} \\
 &= \int_{0}^{1} \dd{t} \pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{x}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{z}}.
 \end{align*}

 Hence,
 \[
 f\pqty{\vb{y}} - f\pqty{\vb{x}} - \pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{x}} \vdot \grad f\pqty{\vb{x}} = \int_{0}^{1} \dd{t} \Bqty{\pqty{\vb{y} - \vb{x}} \vdot \bqty{\grad f\pqty{\vb{z}} - \grad f \pqty{\vb{x}}}}.
 \]

 Replace \(\vb{y}\) with \(\vb{z}\) in [REF:eq:first-order-condition-alternative] gives that \(t \Bqty{\cdots} \geq 0\) (by using that \(\vb{z} = \pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}\)), and hence \(\Bqty{\cdots} \geq 0\).

 Hence, the integral is non-negative, and [REF:eq:first-order-condition] holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Second Order Condition] 
 
 If \(f\) is \(\contClass{2}\), then [REF:eq:convex-condition] is equivalent to all eigenvalues of the Hessian \(\vb{H} \pqty{\vb{x}}\) is non-negative, for all \(\vb{x} \in \dom\pqty{f}\). In other words, the Hessian is positive semi-definite.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}
For a convex \(C^2\) function and any direction \(v\),
\(f(x+hv)+f(x-hv)-2f(x)\ge0\). Divide by \(h^2\) and let \(h\to0\)
to obtain \(v^TH(x)v\ge0\). Conversely, along any line segment let
\(g(t)=f(x+t(y-x))\). Then \(g''(t)=(y-x)^TH(x+t(y-x))(y-x)\ge0\),
so \(g'\) is nondecreasing and \(g\) is convex. Its convexity inequality proves
convexity of \(f\) on the convex domain.
\end{proof}

Title: Using Second Order Conditions
Label: variation-unit-0016
Local macros: \dom := dom; \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \pmqty := \begin{pmatrix}#1\end{pmatrix}; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \set := \left\{#1\mid #2\right\}; \tr := tr
Content:
\begin{example}[Using Second Order Conditions] 
 Consider the function \(f\pqty{x, y} = \flatfrac{1}{xy}\), and \(\dom\pqty{f} = \set{\pqty{x, y}}{x > 0, y > 0}\). The Hessian is given by
 \[
 \vb{H} = \frac{1}{xy} \pmqty{\frac{2}{x^2} & \frac{1}{xy} \\ \frac{1}{xy} & \frac{2}{y^2}},
 \]
 and we have
 \[
 \det \vb{H} = \frac{3}{x^4 y^4} > 0
 \]
 and
 \[
 \tr \vb{H} = \frac{2}{xy} \pqty{\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2}} > 0.
 \]

 This means the eigenvalues of \(\vb{H}\) are strictly positive in \(\dom\pqty{f}\), and hence \(f\) is strictly convex.

 Note that if we take the domain to be
 \[
 \dom\pqty{f} = \set{\pqty{x, y}}{xy > 0},
 \]
 it seems like \(f\) would still be convex -- but that is not the case, because \(\dom \pqty{f}\) is not convex, and hence \(f\) is not convex.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0016

Content:
\begin{definition}[Legendre Transform] 
 
 The Legendre Transform of \(\functiondomain{f}{\dom\pqty{f} \subseteq \RR^n}{\RR}\) is
 \[
 \legendre{f} \pqty{\vb{p}} = \sup_{\vb{x} \in \dom \pqty{f}} \bqty{\vb{p} \vdot \vb{x} - f\pqty{\vb{x}}}
 \]
 with its domain as \(\dom \pqty{\legendre{f}} = \set{\vb{p} \in \RR^n}{the supremum exists and is finite}\).
\end{definition}

Section: Legendre Transform > Definition and Properties
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-bce7adc8d95c2985ae79
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \dom := dom; \legendre := {#1}^{*}; \oointv := (#1,#2); \pqty := \left(#1\right); \vdot := \cdot
Content:
\begin{proof}
 Let \(\vb{p}, \vb{q} \in \dom \pqty{\legendre{f}}\), and \(t \in \oointv{0}{1}\). We note that
 \begin{align*}
 \sup_{\vb{x} \in \dom \pqty{f}} \Bqty{\bqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{p} + t \vb{q}} \cdot \vb{x} - f\pqty{\vb{x}}} &= \sup_{\vb{x} \in \dom \pqty{f}} \Bqty{\pqty{1 - t} \bqty{\vb{p} \vdot \vb{x} - f\pqty{\vb{x}}} + t \bqty{\vb{q} \vdot \vb{x} - f \pqty{\vb{x}}}} \\
 &\leq \pqty{1 - t} \sup_{\vb{x} \in \dom \pqty{f}} \pqty{\vb{p} \vdot \vb{x} - f\pqty{\vb{x}}} + t \sup_{\vb{x} \in \dom \pqty{f}} \pqty{\vb{q} \vdot \vb{x} - f\pqty{\vb{x}}}.
 \end{align*}

 Since the right-hand side is finite, so must be the left-hand side, and hence \(\pqty{1 - t} \vb{p} + t \vb{q} \in \dom \pqty{\legendre{f}}\). In particular, the previous inequality also showed that
 \[
 \legendre{f} \pqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{p} + t \vb{q}} \leq \pqty{1 - t} \legendre{f} \pqty{\vb{p}} + t \legendre{f} \pqty{\vb{q}}
 \]
 so \(\legendre{f}\) is indeed convex.
\end{proof}

 F_{\vb{p}} \pqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \pqty{\vb{y}}} &= f\pqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}} - \vb{p} \vdot \pqty{\pqty{1 - t} \vb{x} + t \vb{y}} \\

Content:
\begin{corollary}[Legendre Transform of convex functions] 
 
 If \(f\) is convex and differentiable, then any stationary point of \(\vb{p} \vdot \vb{x} - f \pqty{\vb{x}}\) (which is a concave function, by [REF:prop:dot-product-convex] ) is a global maximum occurring at \(\vb{x} \pqty{\vb{p}}\) given by solving
 \begin{equation}
 \grad f\pqty{\vb{x}} = \vb{p}.
 
 \end{equation}

 Hence, we have
 \[
 \legendre{f} \pqty{\vb{p}} = \vb{p} \vdot \vb{x} \pqty{\vb{p}} - f\pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{\vb{p}}}.
 \]
\end{corollary}
label: variation-unit-0020

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Legendre Transform > Definition and Properties
Type: example_set
Title: Legendre Transforms for \(n = 1\)
Label: variation-unit-0022
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \RR := \mathbb{R}; \dom := dom; \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \legendre := {#1}^{*}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{examples}[Legendre Transforms for \(n = 1\)] 
 
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Consider the quadratic \(f\pqty{x} = \frac{1}{2} a x^2\) for \(a > 0\). \(f\) is strictly convex, and [REF:eq:legendre-transform-of-convex-function] holds if and only if \(x = \flatfrac{p}{a}\). Hence,
 \[
 \legendre{f} \pqty{p} = \frac{p^2}{a} - \frac{p^2}{2a} = \frac{p^2}{2a}.
 \]
 
 This is indeed convex, with domain \(\RR\).

 \item Consider the function \(f\pqty{v} = - \sqrt{1 - v^2}\) defined for \(-1 < v < 1\). This is a semi-circle and is convex. [REF:eq:legendre-transform-of-convex-function] holds if and only if \(p = \flatfrac{v}{\sqrt{1 - v^2}}\). This gives the solution
 \[
 v = \frac{p}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}
 \]
 for \(p \in \RR\). Hence,
 \[
 \legendre{f} \pqty{p} = \frac{p^2}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}} = \sqrt{1 + p^2},
 \]
 and this is defined for \(p \in \RR\).

 [REF:fig:graph-legendre-one-dimensional-2] are the graphs for the two functions.

 \item Let \(f\pqty{x} = cx\) for \(c > 0\). This is a convex function, but not strictly convex. The domain is given by \(\dom\pqty{f} = \RR\), and note
 \[
 px - f\pqty{x} = \pqty{p - c} x.
 \]

 If \(p \neq c\), the supremum of this is infinite (since \(x\) can be arbitrarily large in both directions). This supremum only exists for \(p = c\), and hence
 \[
 \legendre{f}\pqty{p} = 0
 \]
 only defined for \(p = c\), i.e. \(\dom \pqty{\legendre{f}} = \Bqty{c}\).
 \end{enumerate}
\end{examples}
label: variation-unit-0022

\begin{theorem}[Biconjugacy on the original open convex domain] 
 
Let \(f\) be differentiable and convex on a nonempty open convex set \(D\).
Then \(f^{**}(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). This statement does not assert
that the effective domains of \(f\) and \(f^{**}\) are identical.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}
For every \(p\), the definition gives \(f^*(p)\ge p\cdot x-f(x)\), hence
\(f^{**}(x)\le f(x)\). Choose \(p=\nabla f(x)\). The supporting inequality
\(f(z)\ge f(x)+p\cdot(z-x)\) for all \(z\in D\) shows
\(f^*(p)=p\cdot x-f(x)\), proving the reverse inequality.
No inverse or differentiability of \(\nabla f\) is needed.
\end{proof}

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Legendre Transform > Application of Legendre Transforms in Thermodynamics
Type: prose
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
An important application of Legendre transforms is in thermodynamics.

Consider a system made of many molecules (say \(10^{23}\)). We are concerned with the macroscopic behaviour of the system, i.e., involving length scale \(\gg\) separation of molecules.

In thermal equilibrium, we may describe the macroscopic physics of the system by just a few quantities: total energy \(E\), volume \(V\), temperature \(T\), pressure \(p\), and perhaps some others.

An isolated system is one which is simply not interacting with anything else, for example a gas in a vacuum flask.

For a simple compressible system with fixed particle number and composition, in thermal equilibrium, macroscopic physics in gas in a vacuum flask is fully specified by two quantities, \(E\) and \(V\). However, microscopically, this is far away from the description in microscopic physics (since we need to specify the position, velocity, orientation, etc. of each microscopic molecule). Therefore, there is some number of \(\Omega \pqty{E, V}\) of microscopic configurations that ``look identical'' macroscopically, at the scale of
\[
 \Omega \sim 10^{10^{23}}
\]

Section: Legendre Transform > Application of Legendre Transforms in Thermodynamics
Type: example
Title: Legendre Transforms for Temperature -- Helmholtz Free Energy
Label: variation-unit-0029
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Legendre Transforms for Temperature -- Helmholtz Free Energy] 
 Now, we forget [REF:eq:temperature] (for temperature). Consider the Legendre Transform of \(E\pqty{S, V}\) with respect to \(S\), with parameter \(T\). Call this \(-F\), i.e.,
 \[
 -F \pqty{T, V} = \sup_{S} \Bqty{TS - E \pqty{S, V}}.
 \] 

 We may show that the stability of equilibrium state implies that \(E\) is convex, with respect to \(S\). Now, [REF:eq:legendre-transform-of-convex-function] maximises for \(S\pqty{T, V}\) satisfying [REF:eq:temperature] , and
 \[
 F\pqty{T, V} = E - TS
 \]
 is called the Helmholtz Free Energy.

 Note [REF:eq:fundamental-thermodynamic-relation] implies that
 \[
 \dd{F} = - S \dd{T} - P \dd{V}
 \]
 and hence
 \begin{align*}
 S &= - \pqty{\pdv{F}{T}}_{V}, \\
 P &= - \pqty{\pdv{F}{V}}_{T}.
 \end{align*}

 In Part II, we will see that \(F\) is useful when considering an non-isolated system in equilibrium with an environment and temperature \(T\), for example gas in an uninsulated box.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0029

    \[
        F\pqty{T, V} = E - TS
    \]

    Note \autoref{eq:fundamental-thermodynamic-relation} implies that

        \dd{F} = - S \dd{T} - P \dd{V}
    \]

Label: variation-unit-0030

Content:
\begin{example}[Legendre Transforms for Pressure -- Enthalpy] 
 Similarly, we forget [REF:eq:pressure] (for pressure). Consider the Legendre Transform of \(E\pqty{S, V}\) with respect to \(V\) at fixed \(S\), with parameter \(-P\). We call this \(-H\), i.e.,
 \[
 -H \pqty{S, P} = \sup_{V} \Bqty{-PV - E\pqty{S,V}}
 \]

 Similarly, applying [REF:eq:legendre-transform-of-convex-function] maximises for \(V\) satisfying [REF:eq:pressure] , and
 \[
 H\pqty{S, P} = E + PV
 \]
 is called the enthalpy. It is very useful in chemistry.

 Now, [REF:eq:fundamental-thermodynamic-relation] implies that
 \[
 \dd{H} = T \dd{S} + V \dd{P}
 \]
 and hence
 \begin{align*}
 T &= \pqty{\pdv{H}{S}}_{P}, \\
 V &= \pqty{\pdv{H}{P}}_{S}.
 \end{align*}
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0030

Section: Legendre Transform > Application of Legendre Transforms in Thermodynamics
Type: example
Title: Legendre Transforms for Both -- Gibbs Free Energy
Label: variation-unit-0031
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Legendre Transforms for Both -- Gibbs Free Energy] 
 Finally, we may take the Legendre transform of \(E \pqty{S, V}\) with respect to both \(S\) and \(V\) with parameters \(T, -P\), and call this \(-G\). Equivalently, with the same admissible thermodynamic states,
\(G(T,P)=\inf_V(F(T,V)+PV)=\inf_S(H(S,P)-TS)\).
These identities follow by taking the infimum of \(E-TS+PV\) successively in its two variables; a smooth equilibrium formula requires that the infimum be attained. We have
 \[
 -G \pqty{T, P} = \sup_{S, V} \Bqty{TS - PV - E \pqty{S, V}}
 \]
 and applying [REF:eq:legendre-transform-of-convex-function] , we have the maximum of \(S\pqty{T, P}\) and \(V\pqty{T, P}\) gives both of [REF:eq:temperature-pressure] . Hence, \(G\) is given by
 \[
 G\pqty{T, P} = E - TS + PV
 \]
 is called the Gibbs free energy.

 Using [REF:eq:fundamental-thermodynamic-relation] gives
 \[
 \dd{G} = -S \dd{T} + V \dd{P}
 \]
 and hence
 \begin{align*}
 S &= - \pqty{\pdv{G}{T}}_{P}, \\
 V &= \pqty{\pdv{G}{P}}_{T}.
 \end{align*}
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0031

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Constraints and Lagrange Multipliers > Motivation
Type: prose
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \RR := \mathbb{R}; \functiondomain := #1:#2\to #3; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \vdot := \cdot
Content:
Consider a smooth surface \(S\) in \(\RR^3\). If we have \(\functiondomain{f}{\RR^3}{\RR}\), how do we determine the maximum/minimum of \(f\) on \(S\)?

(A real-life example might be \(S\) is a hill, and \(f\) is the temperature scalar field, and we want to find which points on \(S\) are hottest/coldest.)

Let \(\pqty{u, v}\) parameterise \(S\), i.e., let
\[
 S: \quad \vb{x} = \vb{x} \pqty{u, v}
\]

We would like to optimise \(f\pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{u, v}}\).

But this is straightforward -- \(f\) is now effectively in terms of \(u\) and \(v\), so we want
\begin{align*}
 0 &= \pdv{u} f\pqty{\vb{x}} = \pqty{\grad f} \vdot \pqty{\pdv{\vb{x}}{u}}, \\
 0 &= \pdv{v} f\pqty{\vb{x}} = \pqty{\grad f} \vdot \pqty{\pdv{\vb{x}}{v}}.
\end{align*}

Recall from Vector Calculus that the set
\[
 \Bqty{\pdv{\vb{x}}{u}, \pdv{\vb{x}}{v}}
\]
are linearly independent vectors tangent to \(S\). In other words, we have just shown [REF:prop:max-min-of-function-on-surface] for a parametrisation of \(S\).

Content:
Assume the constraint is regular: \(\nabla g(x_0)\ne0\). Otherwise the multiplier equation need not capture every constrained stationary point.

In practice, we don't always have a nice explicit parametrisation \(\vb{x}\pqty{u, v}\) of \(S\), and more commonly, \(S\) is determined more implicitly of the form
\[
 g\pqty{\vb{x}} = 0
\]
where \(g\) is some other function on \(\RR^3\). This equation is called an constraint, and the problem is to optimise \(f\) subject to the constraint \(g = 0\).

So [REF:prop:max-min-of-function-on-surface] is equivalent to
\[
 \grad f\pqty{\vb{x}_0} = \lambda \grad g\pqty{\vb{x}_0}

Title: Lagrnage Multiplier, Easier Example
Label: variation-unit-0037
Local macros: \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Lagrnage Multiplier, Easier Example] 
 Consider an open rectangular box with dimensions \(\pqty{x, y, z}\) (with the \(xy\) surface missing for the top). We want to minimise its surface area \(A\) subject to a constraint of fixed volume \(V = \flatfrac{L^3}{2}\).
 
 Mathematically,
 \[
 A = 2z \pqty{x + y} + xy
 \]
 with constraint
 \[
 xyz = \frac{L^3}{2}.
 \]

 A direct method could be eliminating the constraint by doing
 \[
 z = \frac{L^3}{2xy}
 \]
 and hence
 \[
 A = \frac{L^3}{x} + \frac{L^3}{y} + xy.
 \]

 Hence, \(A\) is stationary if and only if
 \[
 0 = \pdv{A}{x} = - \frac{L^3}{x^2} + y,
 \]
 and
 \[
 0 = \pdv{A}{y} = - \frac{L^3}{y^2} + x
 \]
 and hence \(x = y = L\), with \(z = \flatfrac{L}{2}\), and \(A = 3 L^2\).

 For \(x,y,L>0\), AM--GM gives \(L^3/x+L^3/y+xy\ge3L^2\), with equality exactly at \(x=y=L\); this certifies the global minimum.

 Using Lagrange multipliers, we consider the function
 \[
 \phi\pqty{x, y, z, \lambda} = A\pqty{x, y, z} - \lambda \pqty{xyz - \frac{L^3}{2}}.
 \]

 First, we look at
 \[
 0 = \pdv{\phi}{z} = 2\pqty{x + y} - \lambda xy,
 \]
 and this gives \(\lambda = \flatfrac{2 \pqty{x + y}}{xy}\).

 With respect to \(x\),
 \[
 0 = \pdv{\phi}{x} = 2z + y - \lambda yz = 2z + y - \frac{2 \pqty{x + y} z}{x} = \frac{y}{x} \pqty{x - 2z}.
 \]
 
 Hence, \(x = 2z\) or \(y = 0\), but we reject \(y = 0\) since it cannot satisfy the constraint.

 By symmetry, considering the \(y\) derivative gives \(y = 2z\).

 Finally, differentiating with respect to \(\lambda\), we have
 \[
 0 = \pdv{\phi}{\lambda} = -xyz + \frac{L^3}{2}
 \]
 recovering the constraint, so \(z = \flatfrac{L}{2}\) and \(x = y = L\).
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0037

Content:
The unrestricted Hessian in \((x,\lambda)\) does not classify the constrained
extremum. At a regular constrained stationary point use
\(d^T\nabla_x^2(f-\lambda g)d\) for tangent vectors \(d\), with
\(\nabla g\cdot d=0\). Indeed, for a feasible curve \(x(t)\), differentiating
\(g(x(t))=0\) twice and using \(\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g\) gives
\((f\circ x)''(0)=x'(0)^T\nabla_x^2(f-\lambda g)x'(0)\).
Definiteness of this restricted form supplies the usual sufficient local tests.

The main advantage of this method is it works even when the constraint is very complicated to solve explicitly (and often simpler even if the constraint can be solved).

Title: Optimising Quadratic Form
Label: variation-unit-0038
Local macros: \RR := \mathbb{R}; \abs := \left|#1\right|; \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Optimising Quadratic Form] 
 
 We find the minimum of the quadratic form on \(\RR^n\)
 \[
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} = x_i A_{ij} x_j
 \]
 on the surface \(\abs{\vb{x}}^2 = 1\), the unit sphere.

 We have
 \[
 \phi\pqty{\vb{x}, \lambda} = x_i A_{ij} x_j - \lambda \pqty{x_i x_i - 1}.
 \]

 Differentiating w.r.t. \(x_i\), we have (using product rule and removing a factor of 2) that
 \[
 0 = A_{ij} x_j - \lambda x_i.
 \]

 Differentiating w.r.t. \(\lambda\) recovers \(\abs{\vb{x}}^2 = 1\).

 We see that the stationary points are going to be the normalised eigenvectors of \(\vb{A}\) (which we would assume to be symmetric), and the value of the Lagrange multiplier would be the eigenvalue.

 At a stationary point,
 \[
 f\pqty{\vb{x}} = x_i A_{ij} x_j = \lambda x_i x_i = \lambda,
 \]
 so the eigenvalues of \(\vb{A}\) are the values of \(f\) at the stationary points, and the minimum of \(f\) is given by the lowest eigenvalue of \(\vb{A}\).

 Alternatively, we may use a rotation to diagonalise \(\vb{A}\) (which is what we did in Vectors and Matrices). Or, we could consider the ratio
 \[
 \Lambda\pqty{\vb{x}} = \frac{f\pqty{\vb{x}}}{g\pqty{\vb{x}}} = \hat{x}_i A_{ij} \hat{x}_j = f\pqty{\hat{\vb{x}}}
 \]
 where \(\hat{\vb{x}} = \flatfrac{\vb{x}}{\abs{\vb{x}}}\), so optimising \(f\) for \(\hat{\vb{x}}\) is equivalent to optimising \(\Lambda\) for \(\vb{x}\), unconstrained.

 Using the quotient rule,
 \begin{align*}
 0 &= \pdv{\Lambda}{x_i} \\
 &= \frac{1}{g} \pqty{\nabla_i f - \frac{f}{g} \nabla_i g} \\
 &= \frac{2}{g} \pqty{A_{ij} x_j - \frac{f}{g} x_i} \\
 &= \frac{2}{g} \pqty{A_{ij} x_j - \Lambda x_i},
 \end{align*}
 and we recovered the eigenvalue equation again!
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0038

Title: Optimising Information Entropy
Label: variation-unit-0039
Local macros: \Bqty := \left\{#1\right\}; \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Optimising Information Entropy] 
 What probability distribution \(\Bqty{p_1, \ldots, p_n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i = 1}^{n} p_i = 1\) maximises the ``information entropy''
 \[
 S = - \sum_{i = 1}^{n} p_i \log_2 p_i?
 \]

 We define
 \[
 \phi\pqty{p_1, \ldots, p_n, \lambda} = - \sum_{i = 1}^{n} p_i \log_2 p_i - \lambda \pqty{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} p_i - 1}.
 \]

 Hence, differentiating with respect to \(p_i\) gives
 \[
 0 = \pdv{\phi}{p_i} = - \log_2 p_i - \frac{1}{\log 2} - \lambda.
 \]

 This means that all \(p_i\)s are equal at the extremum. By the constraint,
 \[
 0 = \pdv{\phi}{\lambda} = 1-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i,
 \]
 so \(p_i = \flatfrac{1}{n}\) for all \(i\), and
 \[
 S_{\max} = \log_2 n.
 \]
For completeness, take \(p_i\ge0\) and \(0\log_2 0=0\). The function
\(h(p)=-p\log_2p\) is continuous on \([0,1]\) and strictly concave, since
\(h''(p)=-1/(p\ln2)<0\) for \(p>0\). Jensen's inequality gives
\(\sum_i h(p_i)\le n h(1/n)=\log_2 n\), including boundary distributions
by continuity. Equality requires the uniform distribution.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0039

\begin{definition}[Differentiability Classes] 
 For \(\Omega \subseteq \RR^n\), we define
 \begin{align*}
 \contClass{k} \pqty{\Omega} &= \set{\functiondomain{y}{\Omega}{\RR}}{y is k times continuously differentiable}, \\
 \smoothClass \pqty{\Omega} &= \set{\functiondomain{y}{\Omega}{\RR}}{y is smooth (infinitely differentiable)}
 \end{align*}
\end{definition}

 A functional is a map

 \]
 i.e. \(F\) maps a function to a number. More generally, a functional can take inputs of the form \(\pqty{f_1, \ldots, f_n}\) and output a number.

Section: Functionals and Euler--Lagrange Equations
Type: prose
Local macros: \RR := \mathbb{R}; \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \ccintv := [#1,#2]; \contClassSymb := \mathcal{C}; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \smoothClass := C^\infty
Content:
An important case is when \(\Omega = \ccintv{\alpha}{\beta} \subseteq \RR\), and \(\contClassSymb = \smoothClass \pqty{\Omega}\), and
\[
 F\bqty{y} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f\pqty{y \pqty{x}, y' \pqty{x}, x} \dd{x}
\]
for some smooth function \(f\) (with three arguments). We could generalise \(f\) to depend on other derivatives, but this is the most important example.

Our question is, which \(y \in \contClassSymb\) optimises \(F\)?

Let \(y_\epsilon=y+\epsilon\eta\), where \(\eta\) is an admissible smooth variation.
The first variation is the directional derivative
\[
\delta F[y;\eta]=\left.\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\epsilon}F[y+\epsilon\eta]\right|_{\epsilon=0}
=\int_\alpha^\beta(f_y\eta+f_{y'}\eta')\,\mathrm dx
=\int_\alpha^\beta\left(f_y-\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}f_{y'}\right)\eta\,\mathrm dx
+[f_{y'}\eta]_\alpha^\beta.
\]
This follows by differentiation under the integral and integration by parts.
The finite increment is \(F[y+\epsilon\eta]-F[y]=\epsilon\delta F[y;\eta]+o(\epsilon)\).
Fixed endpoint values give \(\eta(\alpha)=\eta(\beta)=0\). At a free endpoint,
vanishing of the boundary term for arbitrary endpoint variation requires the natural
boundary condition \(f_{y'}=0\). These are conditions for stationarity.

\begin{definition}[Functional Derivative]

Section: Functionals and Euler--Lagrange Equations
Type: theorem
Title: Euler--Lagrange stationarity criterion
Label: variation-unit-0043
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Euler--Lagrange stationarity criterion] 
Assume \(f\in C^2\) near the graph \((y,y',x)\), with \(y\in C^2([\alpha,\beta])\).
Allow all smooth compactly supported variations in the interior and impose boundary
conditions that make \([f_{y'}\eta]_\alpha^\beta=0\) for every admissible variation.
Then \(y\) is stationary if and only if
\(f_y-\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}f_{y'}=0\). Every differentiable local extremum
is stationary; the converse requires additional hypotheses.
\end{theorem}
label: variation-unit-0043

Content:
\begin{proof}
At a local extremum, the derivative of \(\epsilon\mapsto F[y+\epsilon\eta]\)
at zero vanishes. If the continuous Euler--Lagrange residual were nonzero at a point,
a nonnegative smooth bump supported where it has one sign would give a nonzero
first variation. Thus stationarity forces the residual to vanish. Conversely a zero
residual and vanishing boundary term give zero first variation.
\end{proof}

Type: prose

Content:
We write \(y = y\pqty{x}\), for \(x_A \leq x \leq x_B\), subject to constraints \(y\pqty{x_A} = y_A\), and \(y\pqty{x_B} = y_B\). In this case, we have the length functional satisfies
 \[
 L\bqty{y} = \int_{x_A}^{x_B} \sqrt{1 + \pqty{y'}^2} \dd{x}.
 \]

 We have \(f = \sqrt{1 + \pqty{y'}^2}\), and in particular, \(\pdv*{f}{y} = 0\). [REF:eq:euler-lagrange] implies that \(\pdv{f}{y'}\) is a constant, so
 \[
 \frac{y'}{\sqrt{1 + \pqty{y'}^2}}
 \]
 is constant. Hence, \(y'\) is constant, and \(y = mx + c\) is some straight line.

 Then \(m\) and \(c\) are fixed by the boundary conditions.

But by doing this, we excluded certain types of curves (which do not satisfy the vertical line test). So we consider another parametrisation.

Section: Functionals and Euler--Lagrange Equations > Geodesics of the Euclidean Plane > Use arbitrary parameter \(t \in \ccintv{0}{1}\).
Type: prose
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \flatfrac := \frac{#1}{#2}; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \qqtext := \quad\text{#1}\quad
Content:
We have \(t = 0\) at \(A\), \(t = 1\) at \(B\), and \(x = x\pqty{t}\), \(y = y\pqty{t}\). Then we have
\[
 L\bqty{\vb{x}} = \int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}\pqty{t}^2} \dd{t} \qqtext{where} \dot{\vb{x}} = \pqty{\dv{x}{t}, \dv{y}{t}}.
\]

The boundary conditions are \(x\pqty{0} = x_A\), \(x\pqty{1} = x_B\), and similar for \(y\). We have
\[
 f = \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2},
\]
and [REF:eq:euler-lagrange] on \(x\) imposes that
\[
 \dv{t} \pdv{f}{\dot{x}} - \pdv{f}{x} = 0.
\]

So \(\pdv{f}{\dot{x}}\) is some constant \(c\), and hence
\[
 \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}} = C
\]
for some constant \(C\). Similarly,
\[
 \frac{\dot{y}}{\sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}} = S
\]
for some constant \(S\). Note \(C^2 + S^2 = 1\), so let \(C = \cos \theta\), \(S = \sin \theta\) for some \(\theta\).

If we switch to use arc length \(l\) as a parameter,
\[
 \dv{l}{t} = \sqrt{\pqty{\dv{x}{t}}^2 + \pqty{\dv{y}{t}}^2} = \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}.
\]

Then
\[
 \dv{x}{l} = \flatfrac{\dv{x}{t}}{\dv{l}{t}} = \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{{\dot{x}}^2 + {\dot{y}}^2}} = \cos \theta
\]
and similarly \(\dv*{y}{l} = \sin \theta\).

So \(x = x_A + l \cos \theta\), \(y = y_A + l \sin \theta\) which is a completely arbitrary straight line.

Content:
\begin{proof}
 We have
 \begin{align*}
 \dv{f}{x} &= \pdv{f}{x} + \pdv{f}{y} y' + \pdv{f}{y'} y'' \\
 &= \pdv{f}{x} + y' \pqty{\pdv{f}{y} - \dv{x} \pdv{f}{y'}} + \dv{x} \pqty{y' \pdv{f}{y'}}.
 \end{align*}

 If [REF:eq:euler-lagrange] holds, we have
 \[
 \dv{x} \pqty{f - y' \pdv{f}{y'}} = \pdv{f}{x},
 \]
 and if \(\pdv*{f}{x} = 0\), we have \(f - y' \pdv*{f}{y'}\) is constant indeed.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Fermat's Principle
Label: variation-unit-0048
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Fermat's Principle] 
 We find the path of a light ray in the \(\pqty{x, z}\) plane where the refraction index is
 \[
 n\pqty{z} = \sqrt{a-bz},\quad a,b>0,\quad z<a/b.
 \]

 Assume our path is parameterised by \(x\), where \(x_A = \alpha \leq x \leq \beta = x_B\).

 We have
 \begin{align*}
 P\bqty{z} &= \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} n\pqty{z} \sqrt{1 + \pqty{z'}^2} \dd{x} \\
 &= \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f\pqty{z, z'} \dd{x}.
 \end{align*}

 So using the First Integral, we have
 \[
 k = f - z' \pdv{f}{z'} = \frac{n\pqty{z}}{\sqrt{1 + \pqty{z'}^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{a - bz}{1 + \pqty{z'}^2}}
 \]
 for some constant \(k\). So
 \[
 \pqty{z'}^2 = \frac{b}{k^2} \pqty{z_0 - z}
 \]
 for
 \[
 z_0 = \frac{a - k^2}{b}.
 \]

 Hence,
 \[
 \frac{z'}{\sqrt{z_0 - z}} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{b}{k^2}},
 \]
 and integration gives
 \[
 z = z_0 - \frac{b}{4k^2} \pqty{x - x_0}^2
 \]
 which is a parabola.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0048

Content:
\begin{example}[Brachistochrone Curve] 
 
 Suppose a bead slides on a frictionless wire in a vertical plane. What shape of the wire minimises the time for the bead to fall from rest at some point \(A\), to a lower point \(B\) (horizontally displaced)?
 
 We choose axes such that \(A\) is the origin. We use Conservation of Energy to see
 \[
 \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + m g y = 0,
 \]
 and hence
 \[
 v = v \pqty{y} = \sqrt{- 2 g y}
 \]

 Hence, the time functional is given by (for a curve parameterised by \(x\))
 \begin{align*}
 T &= \int_{A}^{B} \frac{\dd{l}}{v} \\
 &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2g}} \int_{A}^{B} \frac{\sqrt{\dd{x}^2 + \dd{y}^2}}{\sqrt{-y}},
 \end{align*}
 and in other words,
 \[
 T \propto \int_{0}^{x_B} \frac{\sqrt{1 + \pqty{y'}^2}}{\sqrt{-y}} \dd{x}.
 \]

 Let
 \[
 f = \frac{\sqrt{1 + \pqty{y'}^2}}{\sqrt{-y}}.
 \]

 Note there is no \(x\) dependence, so we have
 \[
 f - y' \pdv{f}{y'} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pqty{-y} \pqty{1 + y'^2}}}
 \]
 is a constant.

 So
 \[
 \pqty{-y} \pqty{1 + y'^2} = 2c
 \]
 where \(c > 0\) is some positive constant (due to squaring).

 If we substitute \(y = -c \pqty{1 - \cos \theta}\) for \(\theta \geq 0\) and \(x = x \pqty{\theta}\), this reduces to
 \[
 \dv{x}{\theta} = \pm c \pqty{1 - \cos \theta}.
 \]
 
 Hence, \(x = c \pqty{\theta - \sin \theta}\) (choosing the positive solution), using \(x = 0\) at \(y = 0\) for initial conditions. These equations define an inverted cycloid.

 To require the curve to pass through \(\pqty{x_B, y_B}\), this fixes \(c\) and the value of \(\theta\) at \(B\).
\end{example}

Assume the functional constraint is regular at the candidate: there exists an
admissible variation \(\eta\) such that \(DP[y](\eta)\ne0\).
The multiplier equations below are necessary stationarity conditions, not a
sufficient test for a constrained minimum or maximum.

To optimise a functional \(F\bqty{y}\) subject to a functional constraint \(P\bqty{y} = c\), some constant, we can introduce a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\), and optimise the new functional
\[
 \Phi_\lambda \bqty{y} = F\bqty{y} - \lambda \pqty{P\bqty{y} - c}.
\]

If we optimise with respect to \(y\), we have
\[
 \fdv{F}{y} - \lambda \fdv{P}{y} = 0,
\]
and optimising with respect to \(\lambda\), we have
\[
 P\bqty{y} = c.
\]

Label: variation-unit-0050
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \ccintv := [#1,#2]; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example} 
 We determine the \(y\pqty{x}\) that minimises
 \[
 \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{2} \pqty{y'}^2 \dd{x}
 \]
 subject to the constraint
 \[
 \int_0^1 y(x)\,\mathrm dx=1
 \]
 in the class of smooth functions on \(\ccintv{0}{1}\) with \(y\pqty{0} = y\pqty{1} = 0\). We have
 \begin{align*}
 \Phi_\lambda \bqty{y} &= \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{2} y'^2 \dd{x} - \lambda \pqty{\int_{0}^{1} y \dd{x} - 1} \\
 &= \int_{0}^{1} \pqty{\frac{1}{2} y'^2 - \lambda y} \dd{x} + \lambda.
 \end{align*}

 Let \(f = \frac{1}{2} y'^2 - \lambda y\). Euler--Lagrange Equation gives
 \[
 0 = \pdv{f}{y} - \dv{x}\pdv{f}{y'} = -\lambda - y'',
 \]
 and integrating twice gives
 \[
 y = - \frac{1}{2} \lambda x^2 + Ax + B
 \]
 for some constant \(A, B\).

 Boundary conditions on \(y\) give \(B = 0\) and \(A = \frac{1}{2} \lambda\). The constraint gives us
 \[
 1 = \int_{0}^{1} y \dd{x} = \bqty{- \frac{1}{6} \lambda x^3 + \frac{1}{2} \pqty{\frac{1}{2} \lambda} x^2}_{0}^{1} = \frac{\lambda}{12}
 \]
 so \(\lambda = 12\), and \(y_*(x)=6x(1-x)\).
 This is the unique global minimiser. Indeed, any admissible competitor is
 \(y_*+h\), with \(h(0)=h(1)=0\) and \(\int_0^1h\,dx=0\). Integration by parts gives
 \(\int_0^1 y_*'h'\,dx=-\int_0^1y_*''h\,dx=12\int_0^1h\,dx=0\).
 Thus \(F[y_*+h]-F[y_*]=\tfrac12\int_0^1h'^2\,dx\ge0\), with equality only for \(h=0\).
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0050

Type: example
Title: Sturm--Liouville using Lagrange Multiplier
Label: variation-unit-0053
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \fdv := \frac{\delta #1}{\delta #2}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Sturm--Liouville using Lagrange Multiplier] 
 We optimise
 \[
 \Phi_{\lambda} \bqty{y} = F\bqty{y} - \lambda \pqty{G\bqty{y} - 1}.
 \]

 We verify that the boundary term indeed vanishes in \(\var{\Phi_{\lambda}}\).

 Therefore,
 \begin{equation}
 
 \fdv{F\bqty{y}}{y\pqty{x}} - \lambda \fdv{G\bqty{y}}{y\pqty{x}} = 0
 \end{equation}
 and we have
 \[
 \fdv{F\bqty{y}}{y\pqty{x}} = 2 \sigma y - \dv{x} \pqty{2 \rho y'} = 2 L y
 \]
 where we define the operator \(L\) to be
 \[
 L = - \dv{x} \pqty{\rho \dv{x}} + \sigma.
 \]

 We also have
 \[
 \fdv{G\bqty{y}}{y\pqty{x}} = 2 w y.
 \]

 Hence, [REF:eq:euler-lagrange-sturm-liouville] reduces to
 \begin{equation}
 
 L y = \lambda w y
 \end{equation}

 [REF:eq:eigenvalue-problem] with the boundary conditions \(y\pqty{\alpha} = y\pqty{\beta} = 0\) is an eigenvalue problem: only for discrete \(\lambda\) does there exist a non-trivial solution (eigenfunction) \(y\pqty{x}\). This will be studied in Methods in more detail, and \(w\) is called a weight function.

 Note this is a linear problem: if \(y \pqty{x}\) fixes this, then so does \(C y \pqty{x}\). Therefore, our constraint of \(G\bqty{y} = 1\) fixes a normalisation of \(y\). Then putting \(y\) back into our functional, using integration by parts gives
 \begin{align*}
 F\bqty{y} &= \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} y L y \dd{x} + \bqty{\rho y y'}_{\alpha}^{\beta} \\
 &= \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \lambda w y^2 \dd{x} && by [REF:eq:eigenvalue-problem] \\
 &= \lambda G\bqty{y} \\
 &= \lambda
 \end{align*}
 so the solution of our problem must be the lowest eigenvalue.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0053

\begin{example}[Sturm--Liouville using Unconstrained Optimisation] 
 Define
 \[
 \Lambda \bqty{y} = \frac{F\bqty{y}}{G\bqty{y}},
 \]
 and we would like to optimise \(\Lambda\).

 We have (using chain rule)
 \begin{align*}
 0 &= \fdv{\Lambda}{y} \\
 &= \frac{1}{G} \pqty{\fdv{F}{y} - \frac{F}{G} \fdv{G}{y}} \\
 &= \frac{2}{G} \pqty{L y - \Lambda w y}
 \end{align*}
 and the minimal value of \(\Lambda\) is indeed the lowest eigenvalue of the Sturm--Liouville problem.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0054

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Constrained Variation of Functionals > Geodesics on a Surface, Function Constraints
Type: example
Title: Geodesics on a Surface
Label: variation-unit-0055
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \fdv := \frac{\delta #1}{\delta #2}; \grad := \nabla; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \qand := \quad\text{and}\quad
Content:
\begin{example}[Geodesics on a Surface] 
 Let \(\vb{x} \pqty{t}\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 1\) be a curve on \(S\), with
 \[
 \vb{x} \pqty{0} = \vb{x}_{A} \qand \vb{x} \pqty{1} = \vb{x}_{B}.
 \]

 We want to optimise the length functional
 \[
 L\bqty{\vb{x}} = \int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2} \dd{t}
 \]
 subject to a constraint given by a function
 \[
 g\pqty{\vb{x}\pqty{t}} = 0.
 \]

 Assume the surface is regular, \(\nabla g\ne0\), and the curve has nonzero speed.
 To do this, we use a Lagrange multiplier function \(\lambda\pqty{t}\): let
 \[
 \Phi\bqty{\vb{x}, \lambda} = L \bqty{\vb{x}} - \int_{0}^{1} \lambda \pqty{t} g\pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{t}} \dd{t}.
 \]

 Taking the functional derivative w.r.t. \(\lambda\) gives
 \[
 0 = \fdv{\Phi}{\lambda} = - g \pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{t}} \eqno{(\ast)}
 \]
 recovering the constraint; taking the functional derivative w.r.t. \(x_i \pqty{t}\) gives
 \[
 0 = \fdv{\Phi}{x_i \pqty{t}} = - \lambda \nabla_i g\pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{t}} - \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}}. \eqno{(\dagger)}
 \]

 We want to eliminate the Lagrange multiplier function \(\lambda\). The trick is to differentiate \((\ast)\) w.r.t. \(t\), giving
 \[
 0 = \dot{x}_i \pdv{g}{x_i}
 \]
 and hence
 \[
 \frac{\dot{x}_i \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} = 0.
 \]

 Taking another derivative gives
 \[
 \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}} \pdv{g}{x_i} + \frac{\dot{x}_i \dot{x}_j \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}{x_j}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} = 0.
 \]

 Using \((\dagger)\), we have
 \[
 \lambda\pqty{t} = \frac{\dot{x}_i \dot{x}_j \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}{x_j}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2} \pqty{\grad g}^2}
 \]

 Now, dividing by \((\dagger)\) by \(\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}\) gives
 \[
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}} + \frac{\dot{x}_j \dot{x}_k \pqty{\pdv{g}{x_j}{x_k}}}{\pqty{\grad g}^2 \pqty{\dot{\vb{x}}}^2} \nabla_i g = 0.
 \]

 This is the equation for the geodesics on the surface, and we solve this along with \((\ast)\) which is the constraint that the curve lies on the surface.

 If we re-parameterise to use arc length as a parameter, we have
 \[
 \dv{l} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} \dv{t},
 \]
 and our equation now becomes
 \[
 \dv[2]{x_i}{l} + \frac{1}{\pqty{\grad g}^2} \dv{x_j}{l} \dv{x_k}{l} \pdv{g}{x_j}{x_k} \nabla_i g = 0.
 \]
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0055

    Taking the functional derivative w.r.t. \(\lambda\) gives
    \[
        0 = \fdv{\Phi}{\lambda} = - g \pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{t}} \eqno{(\ast)}
    \]
    recovering the constraint; taking the functional derivative w.r.t. \(x_i \pqty{t}\) gives
    \[
        0 = \fdv{\Phi}{x_i \pqty{t}} = - \lambda \nabla_i g\pqty{\vb{x} \pqty{t}} - \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}}. \eqno{(\dagger)}
    \]

    We want to eliminate the Lagrange multiplier function \(\lambda\). The trick is to differentiate \((\ast)\) w.r.t. \(t\), giving
    \[
        0 = \dot{x}_i \pdv{g}{x_i}
    \]
    and hence
    \[
        \frac{\dot{x}_i \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} = 0.
    \]

    Taking another derivative gives
    \[
        \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}} \pdv{g}{x_i} + \frac{\dot{x}_i \dot{x}_j \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}{x_j}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} = 0.
    \]

    Using \((\dagger)\), we have
    \[
        \lambda\pqty{t} = \frac{\dot{x}_i \dot{x}_j \pqty{\pdv*{g}{x_i}{x_j}}}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2} \pqty{\grad g}^2}
    \]

    Now, dividing by \((\dagger)\) by \(\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}\) gives
    \[
        \frac{1}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} \dv{t} \pqty{\frac{\dot{x}_i}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}}} + \frac{\dot{x}_j \dot{x}_k \pqty{\pdv{g}{x_j}{x_k}}}{\pqty{\grad g}^2 \pqty{\dot{\vb{x}}}^2} \nabla_i g = 0.
    \]

    This is the equation for the geodesics on the surface, and we solve this along with \((\ast)\) which is the constraint that the curve lies on the surface.

    If we re-parameterise to use arc length as a parameter, we have
    \[
        \dv{l} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\dot{\vb{x}}^2}} \dv{t},
    \]
    and our equation now becomes
    \[
        \dv[2]{x_i}{l} + \frac{1}{\pqty{\grad g}^2} \dv{x_j}{l} \dv{x_k}{l} \pdv{g}{x_j}{x_k} \nabla_i g = 0.
    \]
\end{example}

Type: prose

Content:
Consider a system of \(N\) particles in three-dimensional space. The positions \(\vb{x}_1, \vb{x}_2, \ldots, \vb{x}_N\) of the particles correspond to a single point
\[
 \pqty{\vb{x}_1, \vb{x}_2, \ldots, \vb{x}_N}
\]
in a \(3N\)-dimensional space. This space is called configuration space. Of course, it is possible (and often useful) to use non-Cartesian coordinates, and the notation we use is
\[
 \vb{q} = \pqty{\vb{q}_1, \vb{q}_2, \ldots, \vb{q}_N}
\]
for this space.

Type: definition
Title: Lagrangian, Action
Label: variation-unit-0058
Local macros: \bqty := \left[#1\right]; \dimL := \mathsf L; \dimM := \mathsf M; \dimT := \mathsf T; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{definition}[Lagrangian, Action] 
 We define the Lagrangian
 \begin{equation}
 
 L \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t} = T - V
 \end{equation}
 and the action of a path \(\vb{q}\pqty{t}\) in the configuration space between \(\vb{q}_{A}\) and \(\vb{q}_{B}\) is
 \[
 I \bqty{\vb{q}} = \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L \pqty{\vb{q}\pqty{t}, \dot{\vb{q}} \pqty{t}, t} \dd{t}
 \]
 which has dimension \(\dimM \dimL^2 \dimT^{-1}\) (which has the same dimension as \(\hbar\) in quantum mechanics -- this is not a coincidence).
\end{definition}
label: variation-unit-0058

Title: Lagrangian for One Particle in a Potential
Label: variation-unit-0060

Content:
\begin{example}[Lagrangian for One Particle in a Potential] 
 We take \(N = 1\) and \(\vb{q} = \vb{x}\) in Cartesian. Then we have
 \[
 T = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\vb{x}}^2
 \]
 and assume \(V = V \pqty{\vb{x}, t}\), in particular with no dependence on \(\dot{\vb{x}}\). Then we have
 \[
 L = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\vb{x}}^2 - V \pqty{\vb{x}, t}.
 \]

 [REF:eq:euler-lagrange] reduces to
 \[
 \pdv{V}{x_i} + \dv{t} \pqty{m \dot{x}_i} = 0
 \]
 which gives
 \[
 m \ddot{\vb{x}} = - \grad V,
 \]
 a familiar result we met in Dynamics and Relativity for conservative forces!
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0060

Content:
\begin{proposition}[Time Independence leads to Conserved Energy] 
 
 If \(L\) has no explicit \(t\)-dependence, then there is a first integral of the form
 \[
 L - \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{q}_i \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} = - E,
 \]
 where \(E\) is a constant.
\end{proposition}
label: variation-unit-0061

embedding_text:
Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Principle of Least Action (Hamilton's Principle)
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-2fdce7059bc3a95ce047
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{proof}
 Consider the total derivative with respect to \(t\). We have
 \begin{align*}
 \dv{L}{t} &= \dv{t} L\pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t} \\
 &= \pdv{L}{t} + \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \pqty{\pdv{L}{q_i} \dot{q}_i + \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} \ddot{q}_i} \\
 &= \pdv{L}{t} + \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{q}_i \pqty{\pdv{L}{q_i} - \dv{t} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i}} + \dv{t} \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{q}_i \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i}.
 \end{align*}

 By the Euler--Lagrange equations, the term in the brackets vanishes, and hence
 \[
 \dv{t} \pqty{L - \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{q}_i \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i}} = \pdv{L}{t}.
 \]

 If \(L\) has no explicit \(t\)-dependence, the right-hand side reduces to zero, as desired.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{example}[Conserved Energy in Conservative Forces] 
 If \(V = V\pqty{\vb{x}}\) from above, we have
 \begin{align*}
 -E &= \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\vb{x}}^2 - V\pqty{\vb{x}} - \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{x}_i m \dot{x}_i \\
 &= - \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\vb{x}}^2 - V\pqty{\vb{x}} \\
 &= - \pqty{T + V}.
 \end{align*}

 So \(E\) is the total energy of the particle.
\end{example}

Consider particles in two-dimensions, using usual polar coordinates \(\vb{q} = \pqty{r, \phi}\). The kinetic energy is therefore given by
\[
 T = \frac{1}{2} m \pqty{\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\phi}^2}.
\]

Assume that we have a central potential \(V = V\pqty{r}\). Then the Lagrangian is given by
\[
 L = \frac{1}{2} m \pqty{\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\phi}^2} - V\pqty{r}.
\]

Type: example
Title: Conserved Angular Momentum
Label: variation-unit-0063
Content:
\begin{example}[Conserved Angular Momentum] 
 Euler--Lagrange equations gives for \(\phi\), that
 \[
 \pdv{L}{\phi} - \dv{t} \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} = 0,
 \]
 and with no explicit dependence on \(\phi\), a first integral gives
 \[
 \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} = constant,
 \]
 and hence writing this out gives
 \[
 m r^2 \dot{\phi} = constant,
 \]
 or more commonly seen, the angular momentum per unit mass \(h\) is conserved
 \[
 r^2 \dot{\phi} = h.
 \]
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0063
latex:
\begin{example}[Conserved Angular Momentum]\label{variation-unit-0063}
    Euler--Lagrange equations gives for \(\phi\), that
    \[
        \pdv{L}{\phi} - \dv{t} \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} = 0,
    \]
    and with no explicit dependence on \(\phi\), a first integral gives
    \[
        \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} = \text{constant},
    \]
    and hence writing this out gives
    \[
        m r^2 \dot{\phi} = \text{constant},
    \]
    or more commonly seen, the \emph{angular momentum} per unit mass \(h\) is conserved
    \[
        r^2 \dot{\phi} = h.
    \]
\end{example}

Content:
Another conservation result can be seen from no explicit \(t\) dependence, which gives conserved energy in the form
\[
 E = \dot{r} \pdv{L}{\dot{r}} + \dot{\phi} \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} - L = \frac{1}{2} m \pqty{\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\phi}^2} + V.
\]

We could use this instead of finding the Euler--Lagrange equation for \(r\). As seen in Dynamics and Relativity, eliminating \(\dot{\phi}\), we have
\[
 \frac{1}{2} m \dot{r}^2 + V_{eff} \pqty{r} = E
\]
for the effective potential
\[
 V_{eff} \pqty{r} = \frac{m h^2}{2 r^2} + V\pqty{r}.
\]

Content:
\begin{definition}[Hamiltonian] 
 The Hamiltonian \(H \pqty{\vb{q}, \vb{p}, t}\) is defined as the Legendre transform of \(L\) w.r.t. \(\dot{\vb{q}}\), i.e.
 \begin{equation}
 
 H \pqty{\vb{q}, \vb{p}, t} = \sup_{\dot{\vb{q}}} \bqty{\vb{p} \vdot \dot{\vb{q}} - L \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t}}.
 \end{equation}
\end{definition}
label: variation-unit-0064

\begin{example}[Hamiltonian for One Particle in a Potential] 
 In \(N = 1\), \(\vb{q} = \vb{x}\), we have
 \[
 L = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\vb{x}}^2 - V \pqty{\vb{x}, t}.
 \]

 We have by [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] ,
 \[
 p_i = \pdv{L}{\dot{x}_i} = m \dot{x}_i
 \]
 and
 \[
 \vb{p} = m \dot{\vb{x}}
 \]
 is the momentum of the particle. Using [REF:eq:hamiltonian] , we have
 \[
 H = \vb{p} \vdot \frac{\vb{p}}{m} - \pqty{\frac{\vb{p}^2}{2m} - V} = \frac{\vb{p}^2}{2m} + V
 \]
 is the total energy.
\end{example}

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Principle of Least Action (Hamilton's Principle) > The Hamiltonian and Hamilton's Equations
Type: example_set
Title: Two-Dimensional Central Potential
Label: variation-unit-0066
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{examples}[Two-Dimensional Central Potential] 
 Recall we have
 \[
 L = \frac{1}{2} m \pqty{\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\phi}^2} - V\pqty{r}
 \]
 with \(\vb{q} = \pqty{r, \phi}\).

 From [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] , we have
 \[
 p_r = \pdv{L}{\dot{r}} = m \dot{r},
 \]
 and
 \[
 p_{\phi} = \pdv{L}{\dot{\phi}} = m r^2 \dot{\phi}.
 \]

 So
 \[
 \dot{r} = \frac{p_r}{m}
 \]
 and
 \[
 \dot{\phi} = \frac{p_\phi}{m r^2}.
 \]

 Then we have from [REF:eq:hamiltonian] that
 \[
 H = p_r \dot{r} + p_\phi \dot{\phi} - L = \frac{p_r^2}{2m} + \frac{p_\phi^2}{2 m r^2} + V\pqty{r}
 \]
 is indeed the total energy of the particle.
\end{examples}
label: variation-unit-0066

embedding_text:
Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Principle of Least Action (Hamilton's Principle) > The Hamiltonian and Hamilton's Equations
Type: prose
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
The Hamiltonian is the energy function associated with this Lagrangian; its identification with physical kinetic plus potential energy holds for the natural mechanical systems considered above. It is given by
\[
 H = \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \dot{q}_i \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} - L,
\]
but since \(H = H\pqty{\vb{q}, \vb{p}, t}\), we would have \(\dot{\vb{q}}\) eliminated in favour of \(\vb{q}, \vb{p}\) and \(t\), using [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] .

Therefore, the Hamiltonian is conserved if \(\pdv*{L}{t} = 0\).

We can now `forget' about the Lagrangian formalism, and write the equations of motion in terms of \(H\).

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-2e7e193a4a3892f4dc92
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{proof}
 We have
 \begin{align*}
 \pqty{\pdv{H}{p_i}}_{\vb{q}} &= \dot{q}_i + \sum_{j = 1}^{3N} p_j \pdv{\dot{q}_j}{p_i} - \sum_{j = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_j} \pdv{\dot{q}_j}{p_i} \\
 &= \dot{q}_i
 \end{align*}
 by [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] .
\end{proof}

embedding_text:
Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Principle of Least Action (Hamilton's Principle) > The Hamiltonian and Hamilton's Equations
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-e21969d6651dccbbd4e8
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{proof}
 We have
 \begin{align*}
 \pqty{\pdv{H}{q_i}}_{\vb{p}} &= \sum_{j = 1}^{3N} p_j \pdv{\dot{q}_j}{q_i} - \pdv{L}{q_i} - \sum_{j = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_j} \pdv{\dot{q}_j}{q_i} = - \pdv{L}{q_i}
 \end{align*}
 by [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] .

 By Euler--Lagrange Equations, we have
 \[
 - \pdv{L}{q_i} = - \dv{t} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} = - \dot{p}_i
 \]
 again by using [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] .
\end{proof}

Content:
The Euler--Lagrange equations are second-order ODEs in a \(3N\)-dimensional configuration space with coordinates \(\vb{q}\). In contrast, Hamilton's equations are first-order ODEs in a \(6N\)-dimensional space with coordinates \(\pqty{\vb{q}, \vb{p}}\).

Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: definition
Title: (Spatial) Symmetry of the Action
Label: variation-unit-0074
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{definition}[(Spatial) Symmetry of the Action] 
 We say the smooth map \(\vb{Q}\) is a symmetry of the action if and only if for all curves \(\vb{q} \pqty{t}\) and starting/end times \(t_A, t_B\), we have
 \begin{equation}
 
 \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L\pqty{\vb{q}^{\ast} \pqty{t}, \dot{\vb{q}}^{\ast} \pqty{t}, t} \dd{t} = \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L \pqty{\vb{q} \pqty{t}, \dot{\vb{q}} \pqty{t}, t} \dd{t}.
 \end{equation}
\end{definition}
label: variation-unit-0074

Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: prose
Local macros: \abs := \left|#1\right|; \bigO := \mathcal{O}; \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
Consider a \(1\)-parameter family of such maps, labelled by say a parameter \(s\), i.e.,
\[
 \vb{Q} = \vb{Q} \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t, s}
\]
and assume \(\vb{Q} = \vb{q}\) if \(s = 0\).

For \(\abs{s} \ll 1\), we may Taylor expand \(\vb{q}^{\ast}\) for small \(s\), giving
\begin{equation}
 
 \vb{q}^{\ast} = \vb{q} + s \pqty{\pdv{\vb{Q}}{s}}_{s = 0} + \bigO \pqty{s^2}.
\end{equation}

Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: theorem
Title: Noether's Theorem, Version 1
Label: variation-unit-0075
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Noether's Theorem, Version 1] 
 
 If there exists an \(1\)-parameter family of (spatial) symmetries of the action (i.e., continuous symmetry of the action), then any solution of the Euler--Lagrange equations has a conserved quantity (i.e. a first integral) of the form
 \[
 \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} \pqty{\pdv{Q_i}{s}}_{s = 0} = constant.
 \]
\end{theorem}
label: variation-unit-0075

        \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} \pqty{\pdv{Q_i}{s}}_{s = 0} = \text{constant}.
    \]

Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-3ec14e5c552fced4f152
Content:
\begin{proof}
Put \(\eta_i=\left.\partial_sQ_i\right|_{s=0}\) and
\(p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\). Action invariance for every subinterval,
differentiated at \(s=0\), gives the pointwise identity
\[
0=\sum_i\left(L_{q_i}\eta_i+p_i\dot\eta_i\right)
 =\sum_i(L_{q_i}-\dot p_i)\eta_i+
 \frac{d}{dt}\sum_i p_i\eta_i.
\]
On an Euler--Lagrange solution the first sum vanishes, so the claimed quantity
is constant. Smoothness sufficient to differentiate the action is assumed.
\end{proof}

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: example
Title: Conservation of Conjugate Momentum
Label: variation-unit-0076
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right)
Content:
\begin{example}[Conservation of Conjugate Momentum] 
 Suppose \(L\) does not depend on \(q_1\) (for example, a central force does not depend on orientation). Then consider
 \[
 \vb{Q} = \pqty{q_1 + s, q_2, q_3, \ldots, q_{3N}}.
 \]

 Hence,
 \[
 q^{\ast}_1 = q_1 + s, \quad q^{\ast}_2 = q_2, \quad \ldots, \quad q^{\ast}_{3N} = q_{3N},
 \]
 while all the velocities remain identical. But \(L\) does not depend on \(q_1\), so this is indeed a symmetry of the action.

 By [REF:thm:noether-thm-ver-1] (Noether's Theorem), this gives rise to a conserved quantity
 \[
 \pqty{\pdv{Q_i}{s}}_{s = 0} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} = \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_1} = p_1
 \]
 which is the conjugate momentum, as in [REF:eq:conjugate-momentum] .
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0076

Course: Variational Principles: Convexity, Mechanics and the Calculus of Variations
Section: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
Type: example
Title: Conservation of Total Momentum
Label: variation-unit-0077
Local macros: \pqty := \left(#1\right); \vdot := \cdot
Content:
\begin{example}[Conservation of Total Momentum] 
 Consider coordinates \(\vb{q} = \pqty{\vb{x}_1, \vb{x}_2, \ldots, \vb{x}_N}\) where \(\vb{x}_i\) are in Cartesian. Assume \(L\) only depends on \(\vb{x}_i\) via their pairwise differences \(\vb{x}_i - \vb{x}_j\). Let the map be
 \[
 \vb{Q} = \pqty{\vb{x}_1 + s \vb{a}, \vb{x}_2 + s \vb{a}, \ldots, \vb{x}_N + s \vb{a}}
 \]
 where \(\vb{a}\) is a constant vector (i.e. spatial translation). Then we have
 \[
 \vb{x}^{\ast}_i - \vb{x}^{\ast}_j = \vb{x}_i - \vb{x}_j
 \]
 and hence
 \[
 L \pqty{\vb{q}^{\ast}, \dot{\vb{q}}^{\ast}, t} = L \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t}
 \]
 so [REF:eq:symmetry-of-action] holds. This means there is a conserved quantity of the form
 \begin{align*}
 \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} \pqty{\pdv{Q_i}{s}}_{s = 0} &= \vb{a} \vdot \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \pdv{L}{\dot{\vb{x}}_i} \\
 &= \vb{a} \vdot \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \vb{p}_i \\
 &= \vb{a} \vdot \vb{P}
 \end{align*}
 where \(\vb{P}\) is the total momentum of the system. This holds for arbitrary vectors \(\vb{a}\), hence \(\vb{P}\) must be conserved.

 The invariance of physical laws under spatial translations implies conservation of momentum.
\end{example}
label: variation-unit-0077

title: Conservation of Total Momentum

Type: example
Title: Conservation of Total Angular Momentum
Label: variation-unit-0078
Local macros: \RR := \mathbb{R}; \cross := \times; \pqty := \left(#1\right); \unitv := \widehat{\mathbf{#1}}; \vdot := \cdot
Content:
\begin{example}[Conservation of Total Angular Momentum] 
 We work in Cartesian again \(\vb{q} = \pqty{\vb{x}_1, \vb{x}_2, \ldots, \vb{x}_N}\), and let \(R\) be a rotation in \(\RR^3\) acting on individual \(\vb{x}_i\)s to give \(\vb{q}_R\). Suppose \(L\) is invariant under rotations, then
 \[
 L\pqty{\vb{q}_R, \dot{\vb{q}}_R, t} = L \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t}.
 \]

 We consider \(\vb{Q} = \vb{q}_{R\pqty{s}}\), where we rotate through an angle \(s\) about some fixed unit vector \(\unitv{n}\).

 For infinitesimal \(s\), we have
 \[
 R\pqty{s}\vb{x}=\vb{x}+s\unitv{n}\cross\vb{x}+O(s^2),
 \]
 so
 \[
 \pqty{\pdv{\vb{Q}}{s}}_{s = 0} = \pqty{\unitv{n} \cross \vb{x}_1, \unitv{n} \cross \vb{x}_2, \ldots, \unitv{n} \cross \vb{x}_N}.
 \]
 
 By Noether's Theorem,
 \begin{align*}
 \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \sum_{a = 1}^{3} \pdv{L}{\pqty{\dot{x}_i}_a} \pqty{\unitv{n} \cross \vb{x}_i}_{a} &= \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \vb{p}_i \vdot \pqty{\unitv{n} \cross \vb{x}_i} \\
 &= \unitv{n} \vdot \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \vb{x}_i \cross \vb{p}_i \\
 &= \unitv{n} \vdot \vb{L}
 \end{align*}
 where \(\vb{L}\) is the total angular momentum of the system. Since \(\unitv{n}\) is arbitrary, \(\vb{L}\) must be conserved.

 The invariance of physical laws under rotations implies conservation of angular momentum.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}[Noether's Theorem, Version 1, with Boundary Term] 
 If [REF:thm:noether-thm-ver-1] has the condition of [REF:eq:symmetry-of-action] changed such that
 \begin{equation}
 
 \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L \pqty{\vb{q}^{\ast}, \dot{\vb{q}}^{\ast}, t} \dd{t} = \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t} \dd{t} + \bqty{s K \pqty{\vb{q}, \dot{\vb{q}}, t}}_{t_A}^{t_B}+O(s^2)
 \end{equation}
 for small \(s\), for some \(K\), then there is a conserved quantity of the form
 \[
 \sum_{i = 1}^{3N} \pdv{L}{\dot{q}_i} \pqty{\pdv{Q_i}{s}}_{s = 0} - K.
 \]
\end{corollary}
