embedding_text:
Course: Introduction to Abstract~Algebra
Section: Friday, 7 December 2018 > RSA Continued
Type: prose
Content:
The real security of RSA is the fact that it is very hard to factor large numbers, so long as we can choose our initial primes in a good manner. This involves determining if a number is prime, which is suprisingly nontrivial. There are a couple of ways to do this. One is due to Fermat:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Take $n$ and hope it's prime.
\item if $n$ is prime, then for any $a \in Z$ where $(a,n) = 1$ then $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$.
\item Suppose on the other hand that $n$ is composite. Take $0 \leq a \leq n$ and evaluate $a^{n-1} \pmod{n}$. If you get something other than $1$, you know that $n$ isn't prime, and you call $a$ a Fermat witness. If you do get $1$, then you don't know that it's not prime, and you call $a$ a Fermat liar since it lies to you that $n$ is prime, like a little liar.
\item Repeat this process a bunch of times. If you keep getting $1$, then maybe $n$ is prime after all.
\end{enumerate}
This is a probabalistic test for how likely it is that $n$ is prime. How good of an estimate this is relates to how many liars there could be. For ``most'' $n$, at most half of the numbers in the range $0 < a < n$ are liars, so the chance of picking $k$ liars is around $(1/2)^k$. We should qualify what ``most $n$'' actually means. In fact, there exist $n$ called Carmichael numbers, which have the terrible property that any $a$ which is relatively prime to $n$ is a Fermat liar. This means that if you choose such an $n$ your kinda screwed if you use this test.

Content:
\begin{proof}[Forward direction]
Suppose that $p$ is a sum of squares. If $x \in Z$ then $x^2 \equiv 1$ or $0$ modulo $4$, which we check by squaring all $\bar{x} \in Z/4Z$. Since $p$ is the sum of two squares, $p$ is either $0$, $1$, or $2$ modulo $4$, and since $p$ is odd it must be $1 \pmod{4}$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Reverse Direction]
Assume that $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. First, let's construct $R = Z[i]$ and $N(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$. We claim that $p$ is nor a prime element in $R$, so there exist $x,y$ such that $p$ divides $xy$ but neither one individually. We know that $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ so $4$ divides $p-1$. Consdier $(Z/pZ)^\times \cong Z_{p-1}$. Then there exists an $n \in Z$ such that $\bar{n}$ has order $4$ in $(Z/pZ)^\times$. Then if $\abs{\bar{n}} = 4 \pmod{p}$ then $\abs{\bar{n}^2} = 2 \pmod{p}$ so $\bar{n}^2 = -1 \pmod{4}$ and $p$ divides $n^2 + 1$. In the Gaussian integers, then we know that $p$ divides $n^2 + 1 = (n-i)(n+i)$ but $p$ does not divide $n \pm i$.

Note that $R$ is a PID, which implies that all irreducible elements are prime, so $p$ is not irreducible in $R$, o there exist $x,y \in R$ such that $x,y \notin R^\times$ but $xy = p$. Recall that $N(p) = p^2 = N(x)N(y)$, and we know that $N(x),N(y) \not= \pm 1$. Then both are either $+p$ or $-p$. We can write $x$ as $a+bi$, so $N(x) = a^2 + b^2 = p$.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Label: d:group@c1
Content:
\begin{definition} 
A group is an ordered pair $(G,\ast)$ where $G$ is a set and $\ast$ is a binary operation on $G$ (a function $\ast:G\times G\to G$) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(G0)] Closure. For all $a,b\in G$, $a\ast b\in G$. (This is built into ``$\ast$ is a binary operation $G\times G\to G$''.)
\item[(G1)] Associativity. For all $a,b,c\in G$, $(a\ast b)\ast c=a\ast(b\ast c)$.
\item[(G2)] Identity. There exists $e\in G$ with $e\ast a=a\ast e=a$ for all $a\in G$.
\item[(G3)] Inverses. For each $a\in G$ there exists $a^{-1}\in G$ with $a\ast a^{-1}=a^{-1}\ast a=e$.
\end{enumerate}
The group is abelian (commutative) if in addition $a\ast b=b\ast a$ for all $a,b\in G$. We usually drop $\ast$ and write $ab$, and write $1$ (or $e$) for the identity.
\end{definition}
label: d:group@c1

Label: r:axiomstatus@c1
Content:
\begin{remark} 
A pair $(S,\ast)$ that satisfies (G0) and (G1) but not necessarily (G2),(G3) is a semigroup; with (G2) added it is a monoid. So a group is exactly a monoid in which every element is invertible. The single hardest axiom to verify in practice is associativity (G1); the easiest to disprove a group with is the failure of one inverse (G3) or non-closure (G0).
\end{remark}
label: r:axiomstatus@c1

\begin{proof}
Suppose $e$ and $f$ both satisfy (G2). Then $e=e\ast f$ (since $f$ is an identity, acting on the right of $e$) and $e\ast f=f$ (since $e$ is an identity, acting on the left of $f$). Hence $e=e\ast f=f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $b$ and $c$ both invert $a$, so $a\ast b=b\ast a=e$ and $a\ast c=c\ast a=e$. Then
\[
b=b\ast e=b\ast(a\ast c)=(b\ast a)\ast c=e\ast c=c,
\]
using (G2), the inverse property of $c$, associativity (G1), the inverse property of $b$, and (G2) again. Hence $b=c$.
\end{proof}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-d8d49a1fd5d316184952
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) By definition $a^{-1}$ is the unique element with $a\ast a^{-1}=a^{-1}\ast a=e$. Reading the equations $a^{-1}\ast a=a\ast a^{-1}=e$ the other way says precisely that $a$ is an inverse of $a^{-1}$. By uniqueness (Proposition~ [REF:p:invunique@c1] ), $(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$.

(b) Compute directly, using associativity to regroup:
\[
(ab)(b^{-1} a^{-1})=a\big(b\,b^{-1}\big)a^{-1}=a\,e\,a^{-1}=a\,a^{-1}=e,
\]
\[
(b^{-1} a^{-1})(ab)=b^{-1}\big(a^{-1} a\big)b=b^{-1}\,e\,b=b^{-1} b=e.
\]
So $b^{-1} a^{-1}$ is a two-sided inverse of $ab$; by uniqueness it equals $(ab)^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

Title: Cancellation laws
Label: p:cancel@c1
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Cancellation laws] 
Let $G$ be a group and $a,b,c\in G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Left cancellation) If $ab=ac$ then $b=c$.
\item[(b)] (Right cancellation) If $ba=ca$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular the equations $ax=b$ and $xa=b$ have unique solutions $x=a^{-1} b$ and $x=ba^{-1}$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:cancel@c1

Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) Left-multiply $ab=ac$ by $a^{-1}$: $a^{-1}(ab)=a^{-1}(ac)$, so $(a^{-1} a)b=(a^{-1} a)c$, i.e. $eb=ec$, i.e. $b=c$. (b) Symmetric: right-multiply $ba=ca$ by $a^{-1}$ to get $b(aa^{-1})=c(aa^{-1})$, so $b=c$. For $ax=b$, left-multiply by $a^{-1}$ to get $x=a^{-1} b$; this is a solution since $a(a^{-1} b)=(aa^{-1})b=b$, and it is the only one by left cancellation.
\end{proof}

Label: r:genassoc@c1
Content:
\begin{remark}[Generalized associativity] 
For $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n\in G$ the product $a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ is unambiguous: any way of inserting parentheses to evaluate it gives the same element. So we may drop all parentheses in finite products. The proof is an induction on $n$ reducing every parenthesization to the standard left-nested one $(\cdots((a_1a_2)a_3)\cdots)a_n$ using only (G1).
\end{remark}
label: r:genassoc@c1

Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > The group axioms: identity, inverses, and cancellation
Type: method
Title: Is $(S,\ast)$ a group? A four-step checklist
Content:
\begin{method}{Is $(S,\ast)$ a group? A four-step checklist}
Check the axioms in order, and stop at the first failure.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Closure (G0). Is $a\ast b\in S$ for all $a,b\in S$? Look for outputs that escape $S$ (e.g.\ a quotient leaving $Z$, a product hitting a forbidden value).
\item Associativity (G1). Is $(a\ast b)\ast c=a\ast(b\ast c)$? Standard ops ($+,\cdot$ on numbers, function composition, matrix product) are associative for free; for an exotic $\ast$ you must expand both sides symbolically.
\item Identity (G2). Solve $e\ast a=a$ (and $a\ast e=a$) for a single $e$ that works for every $a$.
\item Inverses (G3). For a generic $a$, solve $a\ast x=e$ (and $x\ast a=e$) for $x\in S$. If even one element has no inverse in $S$, it is not a group.
\end{enumerate}
Recognition / how to disprove. To prove a group you must verify all four. To disprove a group you need exactly one explicit counterexample to one axiom: a single pair leaving $S$ (kills G0), a single bad triple (kills G1), a proof no $e$ exists (kills G2), or a single element with no inverse (kills G3). Always name the witness explicitly.
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $(Z,+)$ is a group
Content:
\begin{wex}{$(Z,+)$ is a group}
Show that the integers under ordinary addition form an abelian group.
\wrec The operation is the standard $+$, so closure, associativity, and commutativity are inherited from arithmetic; only the identity and inverses need a named witness. This is the checklist applied to a ``known'' operation, where steps 1--2 are immediate.
\wsol
Run the four steps.
(G0) For $a,b\inZ$, $a+b\inZ$: the sum of two integers is an integer. Closed.
(G1) Addition of integers is associative: $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$ for all $a,b,c$.
(G2) Take $e=0$: $0+a=a+0=a$ for all $a\inZ$. Identity exists.
(G3) Given $a\inZ$, take $x=-a\inZ$: $a+(-a)=(-a)+a=0$. Inverse exists, and $-a$ is indeed an integer.
Commutativity: $a+b=b+a$. So $(Z,+)$ is an abelian group.
Check. Solve $5+x=2$: by Proposition~ [REF:p:cancel@c1] , $x=(-5)+2=-3\inZ$, and $5+(-3)=2$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is a group}
Show that the integers under ordinary addition form an abelian group.
\wrec The operation is the standard $+$, so closure, associativity, and commutativity are inherited from arithmetic; only the identity and inverses need a named witness. This is the checklist applied to a ``known'' operation, where steps 1--2 are immediate.
\wsol
Run the four steps.
(G0) For $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$, $a+b\in\mathbb{Z}$: the sum of two integers is an integer. Closed.
(G1) Addition of integers is associative: $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$ for all $a,b,c$.
(G2) Take $e=0$: $0+a=a+0=a$ for all $a\in\mathbb{Z}$. Identity exists.
(G3) Given $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, take $x=-a\in\mathbb{Z}$: $a+(-a)=(-a)+a=0$. Inverse exists, and $-a$ is indeed an integer.
Commutativity: $a+b=b+a$. So $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is an abelian group.
\textit{Check.} Solve $5+x=2$: by Proposition~\ref{p:cancel@c1}, $x=(-5)+2=-3\in\mathbb{Z}$, and $5+(-3)=2$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $(Z/(n)Z,\cdot)$ is NOT a group
Content:
\begin{wex}{$(Z/(n)Z,\cdot)$ is NOT a group}
Show that $Z/(n)Z$ (residues mod $n$, $n\ge 2$) under multiplication of classes is not a group.
\wrec The candidate identity is $\bar1$, and we must check (G3) for every class. The trigger: any structure containing an ``absorbing'' element (here $\bar0\cdot\bar a=\bar0$) cannot have that element invertible, because its products never reach the identity. Disprove via one failing inverse.
\wsol
The operation $\bar a\cdot\bar b=\overline{ab}$ is well defined, closed, associative, and has identity $\bar1$ (since $\bar1\cdot\bar a=\bar a$). So $(Z/(n)Z,\cdot)$ is a commutative monoid. It fails (G3) at $\bar0$:
for any $\bar x\inZ/(n)Z$, $\bar0\cdot\bar x=\overline{0\cdot x}=\bar0\ne\bar1$ (here $\bar0\ne\bar1$ because $n\ge2$). So $\bar0$ has no inverse, and $(Z/(n)Z,\cdot)$ is not a group.
Check (concrete, $n=6$). In $Z/(6)Z$: $\bar0\cdot\bar x=\bar0$ for every $\bar x\in\{\bar0,\dots,\bar5\}$, never $\bar1$. Moreover $\bar2,\bar3,\bar4$ also fail: e.g.\ $\bar2\cdot\bar x$ runs through $\bar0,\bar2,\bar4,\bar0,\bar2,\bar4$ as $x=0,\dots,5$, never $\bar1$ (because $\gcd(2,6)=2\nmid 1$). The units are exactly $\bar1,\bar5$, so deleting non-units gives the genuine group $(Z/(6)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar5\}$.
\end{wex}

Show that $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ (residues mod $n$, $n\ge 2$) under multiplication of classes is not a group.
\wrec The candidate identity is $\bar1$, and we must check (G3) for \emph{every} class. The trigger: any structure containing an ``absorbing'' element (here $\bar0\cdot\bar a=\bar0$) cannot have that element invertible, because its products never reach the identity. for any $\bar x\in\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $\bar0\cdot\bar x=\overline{0\cdot x}=\bar0\ne\bar1$ (here $\bar0\ne\bar1$ because $n\ge2$). So $\bar0$ has no inverse, and $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},\cdot)$ is \emph{not} a group.

Type: example
Title: $a\ast b=a+b+ab$ on $R$: identity $0$, but $-1$ has no inverse
Content:
\begin{wex}{$a\ast b=a+b+ab$ on $R$: identity $0$, but $-1$ has no inverse}
On $R$ define $a\ast b=a+b+ab$. Decide whether $(R,\ast)$ is a group, and whether $(R\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ is.
\wrec The clean trick is the factorization $a\ast b=(1+a)(1+b)-1$, which turns $\ast$ into ordinary multiplication after the shift $a\mapsto 1+a$. Recognition: whenever an exotic operation can be rewritten as $f(a)f(b)$ for a bijection-like $f$, transport the question to a familiar group/monoid. The forbidden value will be the preimage of $0$.
\wsol
Set up the shift. Let $u=1+a$, $v=1+b$. Then
\[
a\ast b=a+b+ab=(1+a)(1+b)-1=uv-1,\qquadso 1+(a\ast b)=(1+a)(1+b).
\]
(G0) Closed on $R$: $a\ast b\inR$.
(G1) Associativity: $1+\big((a\ast b)\ast c\big)=(1+(a\ast b))(1+c)=(1+a)(1+b)(1+c)$, symmetric in the grouping, so $(a\ast b)\ast c=a\ast(b\ast c)$. Associative.
(G2) Identity $e$: need $a+e+ae=a$, i.e.\ $e(1+a)=0$ for all $a$, forcing $e=0$. Check: $a\ast0=a+0+0=a$. Identity is $0$.
(G3) Inverse of $a$: need $x$ with $(1+a)(1+x)=1+0=1$, i.e.\ $1+x=\dfrac1{1+a}$, so $x=\dfrac1{1+a}-1=\dfrac{-a}{1+a}$. This requires $1+a\ne0$, i.e.\ $a\ne-1$.
At $a=-1$: $(-1)\ast x=-1+x-x=-1\ne0$ for all $x$, so $-1$ has no inverse. Hence $(R,\ast)$ is not a group.
On $R\setminus\{-1\}$ the map $a\mapsto 1+a$ is a bijection onto $R\setminus\{0\}=R^\times$, and it carries $\ast$ to multiplication. Since $(R^\times,\cdot)$ is an abelian group, so is $(R\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$: closed (if $a,b\ne-1$ then $(1+a)(1+b)\ne0$ so $a\ast b\ne-1$), identity $0$, inverse $\dfrac{-a}{1+a}$.
Check. Take $a=2$: $x=\dfrac{-2}{3}$, and $2\ast(-\tfrac23)=2-\tfrac23+2\cdot(-\tfrac23)=2-\tfrac23-\tfrac43=2-2=0$. Correct.
The transport of structure is exactly the commuting square
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
(R\setminus\{-1\})\times(R\setminus\{-1\}) \arrow[r, "\ast"] \arrow[d, "(1+\,\cdot\,)\times(1+\,\cdot\,)"'] & R\setminus\{-1\} \arrow[d, "1+\,\cdot\,"] \\
R^\times\timesR^\times \arrow[r, "{(u,v)\mapsto uv}"'] & R^\times
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes, all groups. Top-left: the Cartesian product $(R\setminus\{-1\})\times(R\setminus\{-1\})$, where pairs of inputs for the operation $\ast$ live. Top-right: $R\setminus\{-1\}$, the group under $\ast$ whose group structure we are establishing. Bottom-left: $R^\times\timesR^\times$, pairs of nonzero reals, i.e.\ inputs for ordinary multiplication. Bottom-right: $R^\times$, the abelian group of nonzero reals under multiplication. All four are abelian groups (the bottom row is classical; the top row is what we are proving).
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal: the operation $\ast$, sending $(a,b)$ to $a\ast b=a+b+ab$. Bottom horizontal: ordinary multiplication $\cdot$, sending $(u,v)$ to $uv$. Left vertical: the map $(1+\,\cdot\,)\times(1+\,\cdot\,)$, sending $(a,b)$ to $(1+a,1+b)$; it is a bijection $(R\setminus\{-1\})^2\to(R^\times)^2$. Left then bottom: first shift each factor to get $(1+a,1+b)$, then multiply to get $(1+a)(1+b)$. These are identical by the factorization $1+a+b+ab=(1+a)(1+b)$, which is just the elementary algebraic identity $(1+a)(1+b)=1+a+b+ab$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram encodes the algebraic reason why $(R\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ is a group: the shift $a\mapsto 1+a$ is an isomorphism from $(R\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ to $(R^\times,\cdot)$. Every group axiom for $\ast$ can be read off from the diagram by transporting it from $R^\times$ through the bijection. The proof that $(R,\ast)$ fails to be a group is also recorded: $a=-1$ maps to $0$, which is the missing element of $R^\times$.

\end{dgx}

Title: Using cancellation to solve $axb=c$ for $x$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Using cancellation to solve $axb=c$ for $x$}
In any group $G$, solve $a\,x\,b=c$ for $x$ in terms of $a,b,c$, and prove the solution is unique.
\wrec This is the equation-solving corollary of cancellation (Proposition~ [REF:p:cancel@c1] ): isolate $x$ by peeling off the outer factors with their inverses, respecting the side each sits on. Trigger: an equation with the unknown sandwiched between known group elements; multiply on the matching side and use associativity, never division.
\wsol
Start from $axb=c$. Left-multiply by $a^{-1}$:
\[
a^{-1}(axb)=a^{-1} c\ \Longrightarrow\ (a^{-1} a)xb=a^{-1} c\ \Longrightarrow\ xb=a^{-1} c.
\]
Now right-multiply by $b^{-1}$:
\[
(xb)b^{-1}=(a^{-1} c)b^{-1}\ \Longrightarrow\ x(bb^{-1})=a^{-1} c b^{-1}\ \Longrightarrow\ x=a^{-1} c\,b^{-1}.
\]
Existence: substitute back, $a\,(a^{-1} c b^{-1})\,b=(aa^{-1})c(b^{-1} b)=c$. Uniqueness: if $axb=ax'b$ then left-cancel $a$ and right-cancel $b$ to get $x=x'$. So $x=a^{-1} cb^{-1}$ is the unique solution.
\textit{Check (in $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$).} Solve $r\,x\,s=r^2$. Here $a=r$, $b=s$, $c=r^2$, so $x=a^{-1} c\,b^{-1}=r^{-1} r^2 s^{-1}$. Now $r^{-1}=r^3$ and $s^{-1}=s$, hence
\[
x=r^3\,r^2\,s=r^{5}s=r^{5-4}s=r\,s=rs.
\]
Verify: $r(rs)s=r^2 s^2=r^2$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Socks--shoes in a nonabelian group ($S_3$ and $D_8$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Socks--shoes in a nonabelian group ($S_3$ and $D_8$)}
Verify $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1} a^{-1}$ concretely, and show that the ``naive'' $a^{-1} b^{-1}$ is wrong, in a nonabelian group.
\wrec Proposition~ [REF:p:invlaws@c1] (b) is forced by associativity, but the order reversal only matters when $ab\ne ba$. Trigger: any time you invert a product in a noncommutative setting (permutations, matrices, dihedral symmetries), reverse the factors. Test the law against a case where reversing changes the answer.
\wsol
In $S_3$ (compose right-to-left). Let $a=(1\,2\,3)$, $b=(1\,2)$.
First $ab$: apply $b$ then $a$. $1\xrightarrow{b}2\xrightarrow{a}3$, $2\xrightarrow{b}1\xrightarrow{a}2$, $3\xrightarrow{b}3\xrightarrow{a}1$. So $ab=(1\,3)$, a transposition, hence $(ab)^{-1}=(1\,3)$.
Now $b^{-1} a^{-1}$: $b^{-1}=(1\,2)$, $a^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)$. Apply $a^{-1}$ then $b^{-1}$: $1\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}3\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}3$, $2\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}1\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}2$, $3\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}2\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}1$. So $b^{-1} a^{-1}=(1\,3)=(ab)^{-1}$. Law confirmed.
The wrong order $a^{-1} b^{-1}$: apply $b^{-1}=(1\,2)$ then $a^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)$: $1\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}2\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}1$, $2\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}1\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}3$, $3\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}3\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}2$. So $a^{-1} b^{-1}=(2\,3)\ne(1\,3)$. The naive order fails, exactly because $S_3$ is nonabelian.

In $D_8$. Let $a=r$, $b=s$, so $ab=rs$. Since $(rs)(rs)=r(sr)s=r(r^{-1} s)s=s^2=1$, the element $rs$ is its own inverse: $(rs)^{-1}=rs$. Socks--shoes gives $b^{-1} a^{-1}=s^{-1} r^{-1}=s\,r^3$. Reduce $sr^3=r^{-3}s=r s$ (using $sr=r^{-1} s$ thrice, equivalently $sr^k=r^{-k}s$). So $b^{-1} a^{-1}=rs=(ab)^{-1}$. Consistent.
Check. In both groups we recovered $(ab)^{-1}$ on the nose, and in $S_3$ the reversed and naive orders gave genuinely different permutations $(1\,3)$ vs $(2\,3)$, dramatizing why order reversal is mandatory.
\end{wex}

Title: The square--root subtlety: cancellation does not give $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The square--root subtlety: cancellation does not give $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$}
In a group, deduce from $x^2=e$ together with $xy=e$ what $y$ must be, and contrast with trying to ``cancel a square.''
\wrec Cancellation removes a matched factor from both sides; it does not let you halve an exponent. Trigger: students write $x^2=y^2\Rightarrow x=y$ by ``cancelling,'' which is false in general. Use cancellation only as Proposition~ [REF:p:cancel@c1] licenses it.
\wsol
From $xy=e$, no extra multiplication is needed: $xy=e$ already says $y=x^{-1}$ by uniqueness of inverses. If also $x^2=e$, then $x^{-1}=x$, so $y=x$.
Now the contrast: $x^2=y^2$ does not imply $x=y$. In $Z/(8)Z$ under $+$ (so the group operation is addition, and ``$x^2$'' means $x+x=2x$): $2\cdot\bar1=\bar2$ and $2\cdot\bar5=\overline{10}=\bar2$, so $2\bar1=2\bar5$ but $\bar1\ne\bar5$. The reason: cancelling the $2$ would require multiplying by an ``inverse of doubling,'' which is not a group element. Cancellation (Proposition~ [REF:p:cancel@c1] ) only cancels the same group element $a$ appearing on the same side, as in $ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$; it never cancels a repeated factor that equals the variable.
Check. In $Z/(8)Z$, $\bar1+\bar1=\bar2=\bar5+\bar5$ indeed, yet $\bar1\ne\bar5$: so $2x=2y$ is consistent with $x\ne y$, and ``cancelling the $2$'' is illegitimate. By contrast, legitimate cancellation cancels a fixed group element on a fixed side: from $\bar3+\bar1=\bar3+\bar5$ left cancellation of $\bar3$ would give $\bar1=\bar5$; since $\bar1\ne\bar5$, the premise must be false, and indeed $\bar3+\bar1=\bar4\ne\bar0=\bar3+\bar5$. No contradiction arises -- the legitimate law is never violated.
\end{wex}

For a finite group the entire operation is a multiplication (Cayley) table. Below is the Klein four-group $V_4=\{e,a,b,c\}$ with $a^2=b^2=c^2=e$ and $ab=c$, $bc=a$, $ca=b$ (all commuting).

 
\begin{tabular}{c|cccc}
$\ast$ & $e$ & $a$ & $b$ & $c$\\\hline
$e$ & $e$ & $a$ & $b$ & $c$\\
$a$ & $a$ & $e$ & $c$ & $b$\\
$b$ & $b$ & $c$ & $e$ & $a$\\
$c$ & $c$ & $b$ & $a$ & $e$\\
\end{tabular}

Content:
\begin{method}{Reading the group axioms off a Cayley table}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Closure (G0): every entry of the body lies in $\{e,a,b,c\}$ -- no new symbols appear.
\item Identity (G2): some row equals the column header and its column equals the row header. Here the $e$-row reads $e\,a\,b\,c$ and the $e$-column reads $e\,a\,b\,c$, so $e$ is the identity.
\item Inverses (G3): the identity $e$ appears in every row and every column. Here $e$ sits on the diagonal of each, so each element is its own inverse ($x^{-1}=x$).
\item Latin square (necessary for a group, helps spot errors): each element appears exactly once per row and once per column (cancellation laws in tabular form). Check: every row and column is a permutation of $e,a,b,c$.
\item Associativity (G1): not visible at a glance; must be checked separately (or inherited from a known model). For $V_4$ it follows from $V_4\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$.
\end{enumerate}
Recognition. Use a Cayley table whenever $|G|$ is small: it certifies G0, G2, G3 and the cancellation/Latin-square property visually, leaving only associativity to argue.
\end{method}

Title: Confirming $V_4$ is an abelian group from its table
Content:
\begin{wex}{Confirming $V_4$ is an abelian group from its table}
Use the table above to verify all axioms except associativity, confirm commutativity, and read off each inverse.
\wrec Apply the table-reading method: closure (no stray symbols), identity (header-matching row/column), inverses (where $e$ occurs), Latin-square (cancellation), and symmetry across the diagonal (abelian). Associativity is the one axiom the table cannot show, so cite the model $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$.
\wsol
Closure: all $16$ body entries are among $e,a,b,c$. Yes.
Identity: row $e$ is $e\,a\,b\,c$ and column $e$ is $e\,a\,b\,c$; so $e\ast x=x\ast e=x$. Identity $=e$.
Inverses: $e$ appears at positions $(e,e),(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$ -- once in every row/column -- so $e^{-1}=e$, $a^{-1}=a$, $b^{-1}=b$, $c^{-1}=c$.
Latin square: row $a$ is $a\,e\,c\,b$ (a permutation of $e,a,b,c$); rows $b,c$ likewise; columns likewise. So left/right cancellation hold.
Abelian: the table is symmetric across the main diagonal -- e.g.\ entry $(a,b)=c=(b,a)$, $(b,c)=a=(c,b)$, $(a,c)=b=(c,a)$. So $\ast$ is commutative.
Associativity: inherited from $V_4\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$ via $e\mapsto(0,0)$, $a\mapsto(1,0)$, $b\mapsto(0,1)$, $c\mapsto(1,1)$, where the operation is coordinatewise addition mod $2$ (associative).
Check. Test one associativity instance directly against the table: $(a\ast b)\ast c=c\ast c=e$ and $a\ast(b\ast c)=a\ast a=e$. Equal, as the model predicts.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A defective table: spotting the broken axiom
Content:
\begin{wex}{A defective table: spotting the broken axiom}
Decide whether the following table on $\{e,a,b,c\}$ defines a group:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\ast & e & a & b & c\\\hline
e & e & a & b & c\\
a & a & b & c & e\\
b & b & c & e & a\\
c & c & a & a & b
\end{array}
\]
\wrec Run the table-reading checklist and stop at the first violated condition. Trigger: a proposed finite operation -- always test the Latin-square property first, since a repeated entry in a row or column instantly kills the cancellation laws, which every group satisfies (they follow from (G1)--(G3)).
\wsol
Closure: all entries in $\{e,a,b,c\}$. OK.
Identity: row/column $e$ match the headers, so $e$ is an identity. OK.
Latin square: examine row $c$: it reads $c,a,a,b$ -- the symbol $a$ appears twice and $e$ does not appear at all. Two failures follow:
(i) $e$ is missing from row $c$, so there is no $x$ with $c\ast x=e$: element $c$ has no right inverse, violating (G3).
(ii) The repeat $c\ast a=a=c\ast b$ with $a\ne b$ violates left cancellation, which a group must satisfy.
Either observation alone shows this is not a group.
Check. In a genuine group every row is a permutation of the elements (rearrangement theorem); row $c=(c,a,a,b)$ is not a permutation, confirming the defect without even testing associativity.
\end{wex}

Title: Why the table cannot show associativity, and a diagram for cancellation
Content:
\begin{remark}[Why the table cannot show associativity, and a diagram for cancellation]
The Latin-square property is equivalent to both cancellation laws but is strictly weaker than being a group: there exist Latin squares (``quasigroups'') that are not associative. The cancellation law $ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$ is exactly the statement that left translation $L_a:x\mapsto ax$ is injective, which on a finite set forces it to be a bijection -- this is the rearrangement theorem. As a commuting square, the inverse map intertwines left and right translations:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=6em]
G \arrow[r, "L_a:\,x\mapsto ax"] \arrow[d, "(\cdot)^{-1}"'] & G \arrow[d, "(\cdot)^{-1}"] \\
G \arrow[r, "R_{a^{-1}}:\,y\mapsto y a^{-1}"'] & G
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four copies of the same group $G$, arranged at the four corners of the square. The top-left and top-right are $G$ viewed as a set of inputs before inversion; the bottom-left and bottom-right are $G$ viewed as the set of outputs after inversion.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal: left translation $L_a$, the map $x\mapsto ax$, acting on $G$ from the left by the fixed element $a$. Bottom horizontal: right translation $R_{a^{-1}}$, the map $y\mapsto ya^{-1}$, acting from the right by $a^{-1}$. Left vertical: the inversion map $(\cdot)^{-1}$, sending $x$ to $x^{-1}$. Right vertical: the same inversion map $(\cdot)^{-1}$, sending $ax$ to $(ax)^{-1}$. All four maps are bijections of $G$ to itself.
\dgi{What commutes:} Down-then-right equals right-then-down: $R_{a^{-1}}\circ(\cdot)^{-1}=(\cdot)^{-1}\circ L_a$. Explicitly, for every $x\in G$: $(ax)^{-1}=(x^{-1})a^{-1}$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic $x\in G$ along both paths. Right then down: first apply $L_a$ to get $ax$, then invert to get $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ by Proposition~ [REF:p:invlaws@c1] (b). Down then right: first invert $x$ to get $x^{-1}$, then apply $R_{a^{-1}}$ to get $x^{-1} a^{-1}$. Both paths yield $x^{-1} a^{-1}$, and they agree because $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1} a^{-1}$ holds in any group.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark uses this square to explain the rearrangement theorem in a conceptual way: $L_a$ is a bijection because the square writes it as $L_a=(\cdot)^{-1}\circ R_{a^{-1}}\circ(\cdot)^{-1}$, a composite of bijections (inversion is its own inverse and $R_{a^{-1}}$ has inverse $R_a$), so its inverse as a set-map is $(\cdot)^{-1}\circ R_a\circ(\cdot)^{-1}=L_{a^{-1}}$; i.e.\ the diagram displays how inversion converts left multiplication into right multiplication. It also shows that the cancellation-law content ($L_a$ injective) is captured by a simple conjugation via the inversion involution.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $G=S_3$, take $a=(1\,2)$. Then $L_a$ maps $(1\,3)$ to $(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)$. Inverting: $((1\,2)(1\,3))^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)^{-1}=(1\,2\,3)$. Other path: invert $(1\,3)$ to get $(1\,3)$ (a transposition is its own inverse), then right-multiply by $a^{-1}=(1\,2)$: $(1\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,2\,3)$. Both yield $(1\,2\,3)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes expect inversion to intertwine $L_a$ with $L_{a^{-1}}$ (left-multiply by $a^{-1}$), but the socks-shoes law reverses the side: $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ is right multiplication by $a^{-1}$, not left. The diagram makes this reversal of side unavoidable and visible.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that inversion in a group converts left multiplication by $a$ into right multiplication by $a^{-1}$, so the two translations are intertwined by the inversion involution rather than being related by a naive left-to-left substitution.
\end{dgx}
Commutativity of this square is the identity $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ from Proposition~ [REF:p:invlaws@c1] (b), now read as ``inverting turns left multiplication by $a$ into right multiplication by $a^{-1}$.''
\end{remark}

Type: remark
Title: Additive number groups
Label: r:addnumber-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark}[Additive number groups] 
Each of
\[
(Z,+),\quad(Q,+),\quad(R,+),\quad(C,+)
\]
is an abelian group: addition is associative and commutative, the identity is $0$, and the inverse of $x$ is $-x$. They sit inside one another, $Z\subsetQ\subsetR\subsetC$, each a subgroup of the next under the same $+$. Note $(Z,+)$ is the only one of the four in which a single element, namely $1$ (or $-1$), generates the whole group: $Z=\langle 1\rangle$.
\end{remark}
label: r:addnumber-mrg@c1

Type: remark
Title: Multiplicative number groups, and what gets deleted
Label: r:multnumber-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark}[Multiplicative number groups, and what gets deleted] 
Under multiplication the picture is more delicate because $0$ is never invertible. Writing $A^{\times}=A\setminus\{0\}$ for a field $A$:
\[
(Q^{\times},\cdot),\quad(R^{\times},\cdot),\quad(C^{\times},\cdot)
\]
are abelian groups (identity $1$, inverse $x^{-1}=1/x$), but $(Q,\cdot),(R,\cdot),(C,\cdot)$ are not, since $0$ has no inverse. By contrast $(Z\setminus\{0\},\cdot)$ is still not a group: e.g.\ $2$ has no integer inverse (axiom (G3) fails, not merely the deletion of $0$). The positive reals and positive rationals form groups under multiplication,
\[
(R^{+},\cdot),\qquad(Q^{+},\cdot),
\]
because a product of positives is positive (closure) and $1/x>0$ when $x>0$ (inverses); these are the multiplicative analogues of the additive groups above, and $x\mapsto\log x$ is a bijection $R^{+}\toR$ carrying $\cdot$ to $+$.
\end{remark}
label: r:multnumber-mrg@c1

Type: remark
Title: The trivial group and $(Z/(n)Z,+)$
Label: r:trivialandzn-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark}[The trivial group and $(Z/(n)Z,+)$] 
The smallest example is the trivial group $\{e\}$ with the only possible operation $e\ast e=e$; it is abelian and $e^{-1}=e$. At the other extreme of ``small but interesting'' is the additive group of residues
\[
(Z/(n)Z,+),\qquad Z/(n)Z=\{\bar0,\bar1,\dots,\overline{n-1}\},\quad \bar a+\bar b=\overline{a+b},
\]
which is an abelian group of order $n$ for every $n\ge1$: identity $\bar0$, inverse $-\bar a=\overline{n-a}$ (and $-\bar0=\bar0$). This is genuinely a group even though $(Z/(n)Z,\cdot)$ is not (the fragment's worked example); deleting non-units from $Z/(n)Z$ under multiplication leaves the multiplicative group $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ of order $\varphi(n)$, treated later.
\end{remark}
label: r:trivialandzn-mrg@c1

\]
which is an abelian group of order $n$ for every $n\ge1$: identity $\bar0$, inverse $-\bar a=\overline{n-a}$ (and $-\bar0=\bar0$). Type: definition
Title: Integer powers
Label: d:powers-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{definition}[Integer powers] 
Let $G$ be a group, $x\in G$. Define $x^0=1$ (the identity), and for $n\ge1$
\[
x^n=\underbrace{x\,x\cdots x}_{n factors},\qquad x^{-n}=(x^{-1})^n=(x^n)^{-1} .
\]
By generalized associativity (Remark~ [REF:r:genassoc@c1] ) the usual laws of exponents hold for all integers $m,n$:
\[
x^m x^n=x^{m+n},\qquad (x^m)^n=x^{mn}.
\]
In additive notation (e.g.\ in $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ or $(Z,+)$) one writes $nx$ in place of $x^n$, so ``$x^n=1$'' reads ``$nx=0$''.
\end{definition}
label: d:powers-mrg@c1

\]

Content:
\begin{remark}[$x^mx^n=x^{m+n}$ but NOT $(xy)^n=x^ny^n$] 
The single-element laws above need no commutativity. The two-element law $(xy)^n=x^ny^n$ does: it holds for all $n$ iff $xy=yx$. For example in $D_8$, $(rs)^2=rsrs=r(sr)s=r(r^{-1} s)s=s^2=1$, whereas $r^2s^2=r^2\ne1$. So never distribute a power over a product in a nonabelian group.
\end{remark}
label: r:powerlaws-mrg@c1

Type: definition
Title: Order of an element
Label: d:order-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{definition}[Order of an element] 
The order of $x\in G$, written $\ord{x}$, is the least positive integer $n$ with $x^n=1$, if such an $n$ exists; otherwise $x$ has infinite order, $\ord{x}=\infty$. Equivalently $\ord{x}=\bigl|\langle x\rangle\bigr|$, the size of the cyclic subgroup generated by $x$. The identity is the unique element of order $1$.
\end{definition}
label: d:order-mrg@c1

Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > Powers of an element and the order of an element
Type: proposition
Title: When $x^k=1$
Label: p:orderdivides-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{proposition}[When $x^k=1$] 
Let $x\in G$ have finite order $n=\ord{x}$. For an integer $k$,
\[
x^k=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\mid k.
\]
Consequently $x^a=x^b$ iff $a\equiv b\pmod n$, and the distinct powers of $x$ are exactly $1,x,x^2,\dots,x^{n-1}$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:orderdivides-mrg@c1

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-29402511a50bb6a87f57
Content:
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) If $k=qn$ then $x^k=(x^n)^q=1^q=1$. ($\Rightarrow$) Divide: $k=qn+r$ with $0\le r<n$. Then $1=x^k=(x^n)^q x^r=x^r$, and by minimality of $n$ this forces $r=0$, i.e.\ $n\mid k$. The last claims follow by applying this to $k=a-b$ and noting $1,x,\dots,x^{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct (a coincidence $x^i=x^j$, $0\le i<j<n$, would give $x^{j-i}=1$ with $0<j-i<n$).
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Orders in $Z$, $R^{\times}$, and $C^{\times}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in $Z$, $R^{\times}$, and $C^{\times}$}
Compute the order of each element in several of the book's standard groups, distinguishing finite from infinite order.
\wrec Apply Definition~ [REF:d:order-mrg@c1] directly: hunt for the least $n$ with $x^n=1$ (additively $nx=0$). The trigger is ``order of an element''; in the infinite groups below ($Z$, $R^{\times}$, $C^{\times}$) most elements have infinite order, and finite order signals a root of unity or a torsion phenomenon.
\wsol
\emph{In $(Z,+)$.} Here $x^n$ means $nx$. For $x=0$, $\ord{0}=1$. For any $x\ne0$, $nx=0$ forces $n=0$, so no positive $n$ works: $\ord{x}=\infty$. Every nonzero integer has infinite order.

\emph{In $(R^{\times},\cdot)$.} $\ord{1}=1$ and $\ord{-1}=2$ (since $(-1)^2=1$ and $(-1)^1=-1\ne1$). Any other $x$ ($x\ne\pm1$) has $|x^n|=|x|^n\ne1$ unless $|x|=1$, so $x=\pm1$ are the only elements of finite order; all others have infinite order, e.g.\ $\ord{2}=\infty$.

\emph{In $(C^{\times},\cdot)$.} The element $i$ has powers $i,i^2=-1,i^3=-i,i^4=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$. A primitive $n$th root of unity $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$ has $\ord{\zeta}=n$ exactly (its powers $1,\zeta,\dots,\zeta^{n-1}$ are distinct). A complex number of modulus $\ne1$, or of modulus $1$ but with irrational angle divided by $2\pi$, has infinite order.

Check. In $C^{\times}$, $\ord{i}=4$ matches Proposition~ [REF:p:orderdivides-mrg@c1] : $i^k=1\iff4\mid k$, and indeed $i^{8}=1$, $i^{6}=i^2=-1\ne1$. The four distinct powers are $1,i,-1,-i$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Orders in $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{R}^{\times}$, and $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$}
Compute the order of each element in several of the book's standard groups, distinguishing finite from infinite order.
\wrec Apply Definition~\ref{d:order-mrg@c1} directly: hunt for the least $n$ with $x^n=1$ (additively $nx=0$). The trigger is ``order of an element''; in the infinite groups below ($\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{R}^{\times}$, $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$) most elements have infinite order, and finite order signals a root of unity or a torsion phenomenon.
\wsol
\emph{In $(\mathbb{Z},+)$.} Here $x^n$ means $nx$. For $x=0$, $\ord{0}=1$. For any $x\ne0$, $nx=0$ forces $n=0$, so no \emph{positive} $n$ works: $\ord{x}=\infty$. Every nonzero integer has infinite order.

\emph{In $(\mathbb{R}^{\times},\cdot)$.} $\ord{1}=1$ and $\ord{-1}=2$ (since $(-1)^2=1$ and $(-1)^1=-1\ne1$). Any other $x$ ($x\ne\pm1$) has $|x^n|=|x|^n\ne1$ unless $|x|=1$, so $x=\pm1$ are the only elements of finite order; all others have infinite order, e.g.\ $\ord{2}=\infty$.

\emph{In $(\mathbb{C}^{\times},\cdot)$.} The element $i$ has powers $i,i^2=-1,i^3=-i,i^4=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$. A primitive $n$th root of unity $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$ has $\ord{\zeta}=n$ exactly (its powers $1,\zeta,\dots,\zeta^{n-1}$ are distinct). Type: example
Title: Orders in $(Z/(n)Z,+)$: the formula $\ord{\bar a}=n/\gcd(a,n)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in $(Z/(n)Z,+)$: the formula $\ord{\bar a}=n/\gcd(a,n)$}
In the additive group $Z/(12)Z$ find the order of $\bar a$ for several $a$, and state the general rule.
\wrec In $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ the relation $x^k=1$ is the additive $k\,\bar a=\bar 0$, i.e.\ $n\mid ka$; the least such $k>0$ is governed by $\gcd(a,n)$. Trigger: order of an element in a cyclic additive group -- reach for the gcd formula rather than listing multiples blindly.
\wsol
We seek the least $k\ge1$ with $k\,\bar a=\bar0$ in $Z/(12)Z$, i.e.\ $12\mid ka$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\bar1$: least $k$ with $12\mid k$ is $k=12$, so $\ord{\bar1}=12$.
\item $\bar3$: $12\mid 3k\iff 4\mid k$, least is $k=4$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$.
\item $\bar4$: $12\mid 4k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar4}=3$.
\item $\bar8$: $12\mid 8k\iff 3\mid 2k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar8}=3$.
\item $\bar0$: $\ord{\bar0}=1$.
\end{itemize}
In general $\ord{\bar a}=\dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ in $(Z/(n)Z,+)$: since $k\bar a=\bar0\iff n\mid ka\iff \dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}\mid k$ (dividing $n\mid ka$ through by $\gcd(a,n)$ and using that $\tfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ and $\tfrac{a}{\gcd(a,n)}$ are coprime).
Check. For $a=3,n=12$: $n/\gcd(a,n)=12/3=4$, matching $\ord{\bar3}=4$; and $4\bar3=\overline{12}=\bar0$ while $1\bar3,2\bar3,3\bar3=\bar3,\bar6,\bar9\ne\bar0$. The elements of order $12$ (the generators of $Z/(12)Z$) are exactly the $\bar a$ with $\gcd(a,12)=1$, namely $\bar1,\bar5,\bar7,\overline{11}$.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Orders in $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$: the formula $\ord{\bar a}=n/\gcd(a,n)$}
In the additive group $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ find the order of $\bar a$ for several $a$, and state the general rule.
\wrec In $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$ the relation $x^k=1$ is the additive $k\,\bar a=\bar 0$, i.e.\ $n\mid ka$; the least such $k>0$ is governed by $\gcd(a,n)$. Trigger: order of an element in a cyclic additive group -- reach for the gcd formula rather than listing multiples blindly.
\wsol
We seek the least $k\ge1$ with $k\,\bar a=\bar0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ $12\mid ka$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\bar1$: least $k$ with $12\mid k$ is $k=12$, so $\ord{\bar1}=12$.
\item $\bar3$: $12\mid 3k\iff 4\mid k$, least is $k=4$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$.
\item $\bar4$: $12\mid 4k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar4}=3$.
\item $\bar8$: $12\mid 8k\iff 3\mid 2k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar8}=3$.
\item $\bar0$: $\ord{\bar0}=1$.
\end{itemize}
In general $\ord{\bar a}=\dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$: since $k\bar a=\bar0\iff n\mid ka\iff \dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}\mid k$ (dividing $n\mid ka$ through by $\gcd(a,n)$ and using that $\tfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ and $\tfrac{a}{\gcd(a,n)}$ are coprime).
\textit{Check.} For $a=3,n=12$: $n/\gcd(a,n)=12/3=4$, matching $\ord{\bar3}=4$; and $4\bar3=\overline{12}=\bar0$ while $1\bar3,2\bar3,3\bar3=\bar3,\bar6,\bar9\ne\bar0$. The elements of order $12$ (the \emph{generators} of $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$) are exactly the $\bar a$ with $\gcd(a,12)=1$, namely $\bar1,\bar5,\bar7,\overline{11}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Orders in nonabelian $D_8$ and $S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in nonabelian $D_8$ and $S_3$}
Tabulate the orders of all elements of $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$ and of $S_3$.
\wrec Use $\ord{x}=$ least $n$ with $x^n=1$; for dihedral reflections and transpositions the order is forced to be $2$, while rotations and cycles inherit the order of the underlying cyclic shift. Trigger: orders in a small nonabelian group -- compute powers directly, exploiting $sr=r^{-1} s$ to reduce.
\wsol
In $D_8$ (order $8$). The rotations: $\ord{1}=1$; $\ord{r}=4$ (least $k$ with $r^k=1$ is $4$); $\ord{r^2}=2$ (since $(r^2)^2=r^4=1$, and $r^2\ne1$); $\ord{r^3}=4$. The reflections $s,rs,r^2s,r^3s$ each square to $1$: e.g.\ $(rs)^2=rsrs=r(sr)s=r(r^{-1} s)s=r r^{-1} s^2=1$, and similarly $(r^ks)^2=1$ for every $k$. None equals $1$, so each reflection has order $2$. Summary: one element of order $1$, five of order $2$ ($r^2,s,rs,r^2s,r^3s$), two of order $4$ ($r,r^3$).

In $S_3$ (order $6$). The identity has order $1$. The three transpositions $(1\,2),(1\,3),(2\,3)$ square to the identity, so each has order $2$. The two $3$-cycles $(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)$ satisfy $(1\,2\,3)^3=\id$ with $(1\,2\,3)$ and $(1\,2\,3)^2=(1\,3\,2)$ both $\ne\id$, so each has order $3$.
Check. The orders tally with the group sizes: in $D_8$, $1+5+2=8$ elements; in $S_3$, $1+3+2=6$. Every order divides the group order ($1,2,4\mid8$ and $1,2,3\mid6$), as Lagrange's theorem will later guarantee.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > Powers of an element and the order of an element
Type: remark
Title: Order of $x$ versus order of $x^{-1}$
Label: r:orderfacts-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark}[Order of $x$ versus order of $x^{-1}$] 
A fact used constantly: $\ord{x^{-1}}=\ord{x}$, because $x^n=1\iff(x^{-1})^n=(x^n)^{-1}=1$, so $x$ and $x^{-1}$ have exactly the same powers equal to $1$. More generally, for any $g\in G$ the element $gxg^{-1}$ has the same order as $x$, since $(gxg^{-1})^n=gx^ng^{-1}$, which equals $1$ exactly when $x^n=1$. Thus order is unchanged by inversion -- the first reason orders organize the structure of a group.
\end{remark}
label: r:orderfacts-mrg@c1

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > Order of an element; the additive group $Z/(n)Z$ and the unit group $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$
Type: definition
Label: d:zn@c1
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Fix $n\ge 1$. The set $Z/(n)Z=\{\bar 0,\bar 1,\dots,\overline{n-1}\}$ of residue classes mod $n$ is a group under addition $\bar a+\bar b=\overline{a+b}$, of order $n$, with identity $\bar 0$ and inverse $-\bar a=\overline{n-a}$. The unit group is
\[
(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}=\{\,\bar a\inZ/(n)Z\st \gcd(a,n)=1\,\},
\]
a group under multiplication $\bar a\cdot\bar b=\overline{ab}$, of order $\varphi(n)$ (Euler's totient).
\end{definition}
label: d:zn@c1

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > Order of an element; the additive group $Z/(n)Z$ and the unit group $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-de70f344ecdcacbd4b41
Content:
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) If $\gcd(a,n)=1$, Bezout gives integers $u,v$ with $au+nv=1$, so $\overline{a}\,\overline{u}=\overline{au}=\overline{1-nv}=\bar 1$; thus $\bar u=\bar a^{-1}$.
($\Rightarrow$) If $\bar a\,\bar b=\bar 1$ then $ab\equiv 1\pmod n$, i.e. $ab-1=nk$ for some $k\inZ$, so $ab-nk=1$ and any common divisor of $a$ and $n$ divides $1$; hence $\gcd(a,n)=1$.
Closure: $\gcd(a,n)=\gcd(b,n)=1\Longrightarrow \gcd(ab,n)=1$. Associativity and $\bar 1$ are inherited from $Z$, and inverses exist by the equivalence just proved. So $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ is a group of order $\varphi(n)=\#\{1\le a\le n\st \gcd(a,n)=1\}$.
\end{proof}

Title: How to compute $\ord{x}$ in any group
Content:
\begin{method}{How to compute $\ord{x}$ in any group}
Trigger: you are handed a specific element $x$ and asked ``what is $|x|$?'' or ``does $x$ have finite order?''
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute the powers $x^1,x^2,x^3,\dots$ (additively: $1x,2x,3x,\dots$) one at a time.
\item The order is the FIRST exponent $k>0$ that returns the identity ($1$ multiplicatively, $0$ additively). Stop there.
\item Shortcut in $(Z/(n)Z,+)$: $\ord{\bar a}=n/\gcd(a,n)$ (Prop.~ [REF:p:order-zn@c1] ); no power-listing needed.
\item Shortcut in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$: $\ord{\bar a}$ must divide $\varphi(n)$ (Lagrange), so only test exponents that divide $\varphi(n)$.
\item If no power ever returns the identity (e.g. a nonzero rational under $+$, or a real $\ne\pm1$ under $\times$), then $\ord{x}=\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: How to identify the units $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$
Content:
\begin{method}{How to identify the units $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$}
Trigger: you must list $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$, or decide whether a given $\bar a$ is invertible mod $n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item List $a=1,2,\dots,n-1$ (and include $a=1$ always; never include $\bar 0$ for $n>1$).
\item Keep exactly those $a$ with $\gcd(a,n)=1$ (Prop.~ [REF:p:unit-iff-coprime@c1] ). Discard any $a$ sharing a prime factor with $n$.
\item Count: $\#(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}=\varphi(n)$. Sanity-check via $\varphi(p^k)=p^k-p^{k-1}$ and $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$ for $\gcd(m,n)=1$.
\item To find an inverse of a unit $\bar a$, run the extended Euclidean algorithm on $a,n$ to get $au+nv=1$; then $\bar a^{-1}=\bar u$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Do not confuse the two groups. In $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ every class is present and the operation is $+$; in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ only the coprime classes are present and the operation is $\times$. ``$\ord{\bar 3}$ mod $12$'' is ambiguous until you say which group; additively $\ord{\bar 3}=4$, but $\bar 3$ is not even an element of $(Z/(12)Z)^{\times}$ since $\gcd(3,12)=3\ne 1$.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Orders of several elements of $(Z/(12)Z,+)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders of several elements of $(Z/(12)Z,+)$}
Compute $\ord{\bar a}$ in $(Z/(12)Z,+)$ for $a=0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9$.
\wrec This is an additive group $Z/(12)Z$, so the shortcut $\ord{\bar a}=12/\gcd(a,12)$ from Prop.~ [REF:p:order-zn@c1] applies directly; the only computation needed is a gcd for each $a$.
\wsol We tabulate $d=\gcd(a,12)$ and $\ord{\bar a}=12/d$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
a & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 9\\\hline
\gcd(a,12) & 12 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 & 4 & 3\\
\ord{\bar a}=12/\gcd & 1 & 12 & 6 & 4 & 3 & 2 & 3 & 4
\end{array}
\]
Spot-check $a=8$ by listing additive multiples: $\bar 8,\ \overline{16}=\bar 4,\ \overline{24}=\bar 0$; that is $1\cdot\bar8=\bar8$, $2\cdot\bar8=\bar4$, $3\cdot\bar8=\bar0$, so $\ord{\bar 8}=3$, matching $12/\gcd(8,12)=12/4=3$. Sanity check: every order divides $|Z/(12)Z|=12$, and indeed $\{1,12,6,4,3,2,3,4\}$ all divide $12$. Also $\ord{\bar 0}=1$ (the identity), as required.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{An element of order $7$ in $Z/(n)Z$}
In $(Z/(14)Z,+)$, find $\ord{\bar 4}$ and $\ord{\bar 2}$.
\wrec Additive group again, so use $\ord{\bar a}=14/\gcd(a,14)$. The trigger is simply ``order in $Z/(n)Z$ under $+$.''
\wsol $\gcd(4,14)=2$, so $\ord{\bar 4}=14/2=7$. Check: $1\cdot\bar4=\bar4,\ 2\cdot\bar4=\bar8,\ 3\cdot\bar4=\overline{12},\ 4\cdot\bar4=\overline{16}=\bar2,\ 5\cdot\bar4=\bar6,\ 6\cdot\bar4=\overline{10},\ 7\cdot\bar4=\overline{14}=\bar0$. \end{wex}

Title: Generators of $Z/(10)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Generators of $Z/(10)Z$}
Which classes $\bar a$ generate $(Z/(10)Z,+)$, i.e. have $\ord{\bar a}=10$?
\wrec By Prop.~ [REF:p:order-zn@c1] , $\ord{\bar a}=10 \Longleftrightarrow \gcd(a,10)=1$. So generators $=$ units mod $10$. Trigger: ``which elements have full order $n$.''
\wsol Test $a=1,\dots,9$: $\gcd$ with $10$ equals $1$ exactly for $a\in\{1,3,7,9\}$ (the others share factor $2$ or $5$). So the generators are $\bar1,\bar3,\bar7,\bar9$, and there are $\varphi(10)=\varphi(2)\varphi(5)=1\cdot4=4$ of them. Check $a=3$: $\bar3,\bar6,\bar9,\overline{12}=\bar2,\bar5,\bar8,\overline{11}=\bar1,\bar4,\bar7,\overline{10}=\bar0$ -- exactly $10$ distinct classes before returning to $\bar0$, so $\ord{\bar 3}=10$. Sanity check: number of generators of a cyclic group of order $n$ is $\varphi(n)$, and $\varphi(10)=4$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Reading off an order without the formula}
In $(Z/(9)Z,+)$ compute $\ord{\bar 6}$ both by listing and by the gcd formula, and confirm they agree.
\wrec Additive cyclic group; the point is to verify the shortcut against brute force.
\wsol Listing: $1\cdot\bar6=\bar6,\ 2\cdot\bar6=\overline{12}=\bar3,\ 3\cdot\bar6=\overline{18}=\bar0$. First return at $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar6}=3$. Formula: $\gcd(6,9)=3$, $\ord{\bar6}=9/3=3$. \end{wex}

Title: List $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ and the order of each unit
Content:
\begin{wex}{List $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ and the order of each unit}
Write out $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ and compute $\ord{\bar a}$ (under multiplication) for every $\bar a$ in it.
\wrec ``List $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$'' triggers the gcd filter (keep $a$ with $\gcd(a,15)=1$); ``order of each'' triggers power-listing, restricted to divisors of $\varphi(15)$ by Lagrange.
\wsol $15=3\cdot5$, so $\varphi(15)=\varphi(3)\varphi(5)=2\cdot4=8$. Discard multiples of $3$ ($3,6,9,12$) and of $5$ ($5,10$). The survivors among $1,\dots,14$ are
\[
(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar4,\bar7,\bar8,\overline{11},\overline{13},\overline{14}\},\qquad \#=8=\varphi(15).\ \checkmark
\]
Possible orders divide $8$: i.e. $1,2,4,8$. Compute each (all mod $15$):
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\bar a & powers until \bar1 & \ord{\bar a}\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & 1\\
\bar2 & \bar2,\ \bar4,\ \bar8,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 4\\
\bar4 & \bar4,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 2\\
\bar7 & \bar7,\ \overline{49}=\bar4,\ \overline{28}=\overline{13},\ \overline{91}=\bar1 & 4\\
\bar8 & \bar8,\ \overline{64}=\bar4,\ \overline{32}=\bar2,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 4\\
\overline{11} & \overline{11},\ \overline{121}=\bar1 & 2\\
\overline{13} & \overline{13},\ \overline{169}=\bar4,\ \overline{52}=\bar7,\ \overline{91}=\bar1 & 4\\
\overline{14} & \overline{14},\ \overline{196}=\bar1 & 2
\end{array}
\]
where e.g. $7^2=49=45+4\equiv\bar4$, $7^3=7\cdot4=28=15+13\equiv\overline{13}$, $7^4=7\cdot13=91=90+1\equiv\bar1$. Sanity check: every order is $1$, $2$, or $4$, each dividing $\varphi(15)=8$ (Lagrange).\ $\checkmark$ Note no element has order $8$, so $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ is NOT cyclic; in fact it is $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}\cong Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(4)Z$.
\end{wex}

\wrec ``List $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$'' triggers the gcd filter (keep $a$ with $\gcd(a,15)=1$); ``order of each'' triggers power-listing, restricted to divisors of $\varphi(15)$ by Lagrange.

\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\bar a & \text{powers until }\bar1 & \ord{\bar a}\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & 1\\
\bar2 & \bar2,\ \bar4,\ \bar8,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 4\\

Title: Why $\bar6$ is a unit mod $25$ but not mod $9$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why $\bar6$ is a unit mod $25$ but not mod $9$}
Decide whether $\bar 6\in(Z/(25)Z)^{\times}$ and whether $\bar 6\in(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}$, and (where it is a unit) find $\ord{\bar 6}$ and its inverse.
\wrec ``Is $\bar a$ a unit mod $n$?'' triggers the criterion $\gcd(a,n)=1$ (Prop.~ [REF:p:unit-iff-coprime@c1] ). The two moduli differ by their prime factors, which is exactly what the gcd sees.
\wsol Mod $25$: $\gcd(6,25)=1$ (since $25=5^2$ and $5\nmid 6$), so $\bar6\in(Z/(25)Z)^{\times}$. Mod $9$: $\gcd(6,9)=3\ne1$ (both divisible by $3$), so $\bar6\notin(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}$ -- it has no multiplicative inverse. Concretely mod $9$ the multiples $6\cdot1=6,\,6\cdot2=12\equiv3,\,6\cdot3=18\equiv0,\dots$ never hit $\bar1$, confirming non-invertibility. Inverse mod $25$ by Euclid: $25=4\cdot6+1$, so $1=25-4\cdot6$, giving $-4\cdot6\equiv1$, i.e. $\bar6^{-1}=\overline{-4}=\overline{21}$. Check $6\cdot21=126=125+1\equiv\bar1\pmod{25}$.\ $\checkmark$ Order of $\bar6$ mod $25$: $\varphi(25)=25-5=20$, so $\ord{\bar 6}\mid20$. Compute $6^2=36\equiv\overline{11}$, $6^4\equiv11^2=121\equiv\overline{21}$, $6^5=6^4\cdot6\equiv21\cdot6=126\equiv\bar1$. First return at $5$, so $\ord{\bar 6}=5$, and $5\mid20$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Title: $\ord{-1}=2$ in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ (and the same fact in $R^\times$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\ord{-1}=2$ in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ (and the same fact in $R^\times$)}
Show $\ord{\overline{-1}}=2$ in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ for every $n\ge3$, and verify it concretely for $n=8$. Compare with $\ord{-1}=2$ in $(R^\times,\cdot)$.
\wrec ``Order of $-1$'' triggers the smallest-power computation: $(-1)^1=-1\ne1$, $(-1)^2=1$. The only subtlety is that we need $\overline{-1}\ne\bar1$, which forces $n\ge3$.
\wsol For $n\ge3$, $\overline{-1}=\overline{n-1}\ne\bar1$ (since $n-1\ge2$), so $\ord{\overline{-1}}\ne1$. And $(\overline{-1})^2=\overline{1}$, so $\ord{\overline{-1}}=2$. Note $\gcd(n-1,n)=\gcd(-1,n)=1$, so $\overline{-1}$ really is a unit. Concretely $n=8$: $\overline{-1}=\bar7$, and $7^2=49=48+1\equiv\bar1\pmod 8$, while $\bar7\ne\bar1$; hence $\ord{\bar 7}=2$. In $R^\times$: $(-1)^1=-1\ne1$ but $(-1)^2=1$, so $\ord{-1}=2$ there too. Sanity check: in any group an element $x\ne1$ with $x^2=1$ (i.e. $x=x^{-1}$) has order exactly $2$; that is precisely the case here.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Title: Order of $\bar2$ in three different unit groups
Content:
\begin{wex}{Order of $\bar2$ in three different unit groups}
Compute $\ord{\bar 2}$ in $(Z/(7)Z)^{\times}$, $(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}$, and $(Z/(17)Z)^{\times}$.
\wrec Each is a unit group; $\bar2$ is a unit iff $n$ is odd, which holds for $7,9,17$. Use Lagrange to limit candidate orders to divisors of $\varphi(n)$, then list powers of $2$.
\wsol Mod $7$ ($\varphi(7)=6$, divisors $1,2,3,6$): $2,4,8\equiv1$. So $\ord{\bar2}=3\mid6$.\ $\checkmark$
Mod $9$ ($\varphi(9)=6$): $2,4,8,16\equiv7,14\equiv5,10\equiv1$. Powers $2^1,\dots,2^6$ give $2,4,8,7,5,1$; first return at $6$, so $\ord{\bar 2}=6$ -- $\bar2$ is a generator, $(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic.\ $\checkmark$
Mod $17$ ($\varphi(17)=16$, divisors $1,2,4,8,16$): $2^2=4,\ 2^4=16\equiv\overline{-1},\ 2^8\equiv(-1)^2=1$. First return at $8$ (not at $4$, since $2^4\equiv16\ne1$), so $\ord{\bar 2}=8\mid16$.\ $\checkmark$ Sanity check: in each case the order divides $\varphi(n)$, as Lagrange demands.
\end{wex}

Title: An element of infinite order in $(Q,+)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{An element of infinite order in $(Q,+)$}
Show $\tfrac12\in(Q,+)$ has infinite order. Contrast with $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ where every order is finite.
\wrec ``Infinite order'' triggers: prove NO positive multiple is the identity. Here the identity of $(Q,+)$ is $0$, and we examine $k\cdot\tfrac12$.
\wsol For any integer $k>0$, $k\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac{k}{2}$. This equals the additive identity $0$ only if $k=0$, which is not allowed ($k>0$). Hence $k\cdot\tfrac12\ne0$ for all $k>0$, so $\ord{\tfrac12}=\infty$. The same argument shows every nonzero $q\inQ$ has infinite additive order: $kq=0$ with $q\ne0$ forces $k=0$. Sanity check: $Q$ is torsion-free under $+$; the only finite-order element is $0$ itself, with $\ord{0}=1$. This is exactly why $(Q,+)$ cannot be isomorphic to any finite $Z/(n)Z$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Infinite order via a homomorphism to $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Infinite order via a homomorphism to $Z$}
In $(Q^{\times},\cdot)$ show $\ord{3}=\infty$ by mapping to $(Z,+)$.
\wrec When direct power-listing is awkward, look for a homomorphism $\varphi$ into a torsion-free group: if $\varphi(x)$ has infinite order, so does $x$. The $3$-adic valuation $v_3$ is such a map.
\wsol Let $v_3:Q^\times\toZ$ send a rational to the exponent of $3$ in its prime factorization; it is a homomorphism: $v_3(xy)=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$. The square below commutes (top: multiply two rationals; map down by $v_3$; bottom: add the valuations):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
 Q^\times\timesQ^\times \arrow[r, "m"] \arrow[d, "v_3\times v_3"'] & Q^\times \arrow[d, "v_3"] \\
 Z\timesZ \arrow[r, "+"'] & Z
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four groups: $Q^\times\timesQ^\times$ (the direct product of the multiplicative group of nonzero rationals with itself), $Q^\times$ (nonzero rationals under multiplication), $Z\timesZ$ (the direct product of the integers under addition), and $Z$ (integers under addition). The top row lives in the multiplicative world; the bottom row in the additive world.
\dgi{Arrows:} $m:Q^\times\timesQ^\times\toQ^\times$ is the group multiplication $(x,y)\mapsto xy$. The left vertical $v_3\times v_3:(x,y)\mapsto(v_3(x),v_3(y))$ applies the $3$-adic valuation componentwise. The right vertical $v_3:Q^\times\toZ$ sends a nonzero rational to the exponent of $3$ in its prime factorization (negative for denominator factors). The bottom $+:Z\timesZ\toZ$ is ordinary integer addition $(a,b)\mapsto a+b$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Going right-then-down equals going down-then-right: $v_3(xy)=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$ for all $x,y\inQ^\times$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} This is precisely the statement that $v_3$ is a group homomorphism from $(Q^\times,\cdot)$ to $(Z,+)$. For any nonzero rationals $x=3^a\frac{p}{q}$ and $y=3^b\frac{r}{s}$ (with $3\nmid p,q,r,s$), the product $xy=3^{a+b}\frac{pr}{qs}$ has $v_3(xy)=a+b=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is used to prove $\ord{3}=\infty$ in $(Q^\times,\cdot)$ without listing powers. Since $v_3$ is a homomorphism into the torsion-free group $(Z,+)$ and $v_3(3)=1$ has infinite additive order, $3$ itself must have infinite multiplicative order. The commutativity square makes the homomorphism property precise and visible.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $x=6=2\cdot3$ and $y=\frac{3}{5}$. Then $v_3(x)=1$, $v_3(y)=1$, and $xy=\frac{18}{5}=2\cdot3^2\cdot5^{-1}$, so $v_3(xy)=2=1+1$. The square commutes for this pair.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $v_3$ lands in $Z_{\ge0}$; in fact $v_3(\frac{1}{3})=-1\inZ$, so the codomain must be all of $Z$, not just the nonneg integers.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a homomorphism into a torsion-free group transfers the problem of infinite order from $Q^\times$ to $Z$, where it is obvious.
\end{dgx}
Now $v_3(3^k)=k$. If $3^k=1$ for some $k>0$ then $k=v_3(3^k)=v_3(1)=0$, contradicting $k>0$. Hence $\ord{3}=\infty$. Sanity check: directly, $3^k\ge3>1$ for $k>0$, confirming no positive power is $1$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Basic Axioms and Examples > Order of an element; the additive group $Z/(n)Z$ and the unit group $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ > One unifying commutative diagram
Type: prose
Part: 1/2
Content:
For a cyclic group the assignment $k\mapsto x^k$ is the universal way orders appear. If $\ord{x}=n<\infty$, the homomorphism $Z\to G$, $k\mapsto x^k$, has kernel exactly $nZ$ and factors uniquely through $Z/(n)Z$; if $\ord{x}=\infty$, the map is injective (kernel $\{0\}$), so $\langle x\rangle\congZ$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 1 \arrow[r] & nZ \arrow[r, hook] & Z \arrow[r, two heads, "k\,\mapsto\,x^k"] & \langle x\rangle \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five terms: the trivial group $1$, the subgroup $nZ\leZ$ of multiples of $n$ (a normal subgroup of $Z$), the group $Z$ of integers, the cyclic subgroup $\langle x\rangle\le G$ (a group generated by a single element $x$ of order $n$), and the trivial group $1$ again. This is a short exact sequence of groups.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost $1\to nZ$ is the unique map from the trivial group. The map $nZ\hookrightarrowZ$ is the inclusion (injective), indicated by the hook arrow. The map $Z\to\langle x\rangle$, $k\mapsto x^k$, is the evaluation homomorphism (surjective onto $\langle x\rangle$, indicated by the double-head). The rightmost $\langle x\rangle\to 1$ is the unique map to the trivial group.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at $nZ$: $\operatorname{im}(1\to nZ)=\{0\}=\operatorname{ker}(nZ\hookrightarrowZ)$ since the inclusion is injective. Exactness at $Z$: $\operatorname{im}(nZ\hookrightarrowZ)=nZ=\operatorname{ker}(k\mapsto x^k)$ because $x^k=1$ iff $n\mid k$. Exactness at $\langle x\rangle$: $\operatorname{im}(k\mapsto x^k)=\langle x\rangle=\operatorname{ker}(\langle x\rangle\to 1)$ since the map to the trivial group has full kernel.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The key exactness condition is at $Z$: the kernel of $k\mapsto x^k$ is $\{k\inZ : x^k=1\}$. Since $\ord{x}=n$, an integer $k$ satisfies $x^k=1$ if and only if $n\mid k$, i.e. $k\in nZ$. This is exactly the image of the inclusion, establishing exactness.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This exact sequence packages the fundamental relationship between $\ord{x}$ and the structure of $\langle x\rangle$: it says $\langle x\rangle\congZ/nZ$ (by the first isomorphism theorem) and makes the kernel $nZ$ explicit. The diagram appears here to set up the factoring triangle below.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=Z/(12)Z$, $x=\bar 4$. Then $\ord{\bar 4}=3$ and $\langle\bar4\rangle=\{\bar0,\bar4,\bar8\}$. The sequence is $1\to3Z\hookrightarrowZ\xrightarrow{k\mapsto k\bar4}\{\bar0,\bar4,\bar8\}\to1$; check $k\bar4=\bar0$ iff $12\mid4k$ iff $3\mid k$, so $\ker=3Z$. $\checkmark$
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse the subgroup $nZ\leZ$ with the quotient group $Z/(n)Z=Z/nZ$; these are different objects. The sequence records the kernel of the evaluation map as the subgroup $nZ$, not as a quotient.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the order of $x$ is the unique positive integer $n$ for which the kernel of the evaluation map $Z\to\langle x\rangle$ is exactly $nZ$, encoding $\langle x\rangle\congZ/nZ$.
\end{dgx}
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
 Z \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, two heads, "k\,\mapsto\,x^k"'] & Z/(n)Z \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\varphi"] \\ & \langle x\rangle
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three groups: $Z$ (integers under addition), $Z/(n)Z=Z/nZ$ (the quotient group of residue classes mod $n$, order $n$), and $\langle x\rangle$ (the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $x$, where $\ord{x}=n<\infty$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi:Z\toZ/(n)Z$, $k\mapsto\bar k$, is the canonical surjection (the quotient map killing $nZ$), shown with a double-head. The diagonal $k\mapsto x^k$ is the evaluation homomorphism, a surjection onto $\langle x\rangle$ with kernel $nZ$. The dashed vertical $\varphi:Z/(n)Z\to\langle x\rangle$ is the unique induced isomorphism given by the universal property of the quotient; it sends $\bar k\mapsto x^k$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\varphi\circ\pi = (k\mapsto x^k)$, i.e., $\varphi(\bar k)=x^k$ for all $k\inZ$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\varphi$: if $\bar k=\bar k'$ then $k\equiv k'\pmod n$, so $n\mid(k-k')$, so $x^{k-k'}=1$ (since $\ord{x}=n$), giving $x^k=x^{k'}$. Hence $\varphi(\bar k):=x^k$ does not depend on the coset representative, and the universal property of $Z/(n)Z$ produces a unique such $\varphi$ making the triangle commute. Injectivity: $\varphi(\bar k)=1$ means $x^k=1$ means $n\mid k$ means $\bar k=\bar 0$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the universal-property factoring that characterizes all finite cyclic groups: any surjection $Z\to\langle x\rangle$ with kernel $nZ$ factors uniquely through $Z/(n)Z$, giving an isomorphism $Z/(n)Z\cong\langle x\rangle$. The diagram unifies the earlier short exact sequence with the explicit structure of $\langle x\rangle$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$ and $x=(1\,2\,3)$. Then $\ord{x}=3$, $\langle x\rangle=\{e,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, and $n=3$. The induced $\varphi:Z/(3)Z\to\langle x\rangle$ sends $\bar0\mapsto e$, $\bar1\mapsto(1\,2\,3)$, $\bar2\mapsto(1\,3\,2)$, an isomorphism.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow exists and is unique ONLY because $\ker(k\mapsto x^k)=nZ=\ker\pi$.

\begin{pitfall}
Lagrange tells you $\ord{\bar a}$ divides $\varphi(n)$ in $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$, but NOT that it equals $\varphi(n)$. In $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ every element has order $1,2,$ or $4$, none equal to $\varphi(15)=8$, so $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ has no generator. Always test the candidate divisors; do not assume the group is cyclic.
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Label: r:notation-bar-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark} 
D\&F write the elements of $Z/(n)Z$ as the bars $\bar a$ (or $\overline{a}$), where $\bar a=\bar b$ exactly when $n\mid(a-b)$. The set $Z/(n)Z$ carries two natural operations, $+$ and $\times$, but only $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ is a group for every $n$; under $\times$ one passes to the units $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ to get a group. The phrase ``the integers mod $n$'' refers to the additive group, while ``$(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$'' or ``the units mod $n$'' refers to the multiplicative group.
\end{remark}
label: r:notation-bar-mrg@c1

Type: remark
Label: r:zn-cyclic-named-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark} 
For every $n\ge1$ the additive group $(Z/(n)Z,+)$ is generated by the single element $\bar 1$, since $\bar k=k\cdot\bar 1$ for all $k$. Thus $Z/(n)Z=\langle \bar 1\rangle$ is cyclic of order $n$. This is the model D\&F use whenever they say ``the cyclic group of order $n$.''
\end{remark}
label: r:zn-cyclic-named-mrg@c1

Type: example
Title: The complete addition table of $(Z/(6)Z,+)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The complete addition table of $(Z/(6)Z,+)$}
Write out the Cayley table for $(Z/(6)Z,+)$ and read off the inverse of each element.
\wrec This is the defining operation $\bar a+\bar b=\overline{a+b}$ of Definition~ [REF:d:zn@c1] applied to every pair; the table makes the group axioms (closure, identity row/column, a unique $\bar 0$ in each row giving inverses) visible at a glance.
\wsol Entries are $\overline{a+b}\bmod 6$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
+ & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\\hline
\bar0 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0\\
\bar2 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2\\
\bar4 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4
\end{array}
\]
The $\bar0$ entries locate inverses: $-\bar0=\bar0$, $-\bar1=\bar5$, $-\bar2=\bar4$, $-\bar3=\bar3$, $-\bar4=\bar2$, $-\bar5=\bar1$, matching $-\bar a=\overline{6-a}$. The table is symmetric across the main diagonal, recording that $(Z/(6)Z,+)$ is abelian. Sanity check: each row is a permutation of the six classes (the Latin-square property every group table has).\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The complete addition table of $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$}
Write out the Cayley table for $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$ and read off the inverse of each element.
\wrec This is the defining operation $\bar a+\bar b=\overline{a+b}$ of Definition~\ref{d:zn@c1} applied to every pair; the table makes the group axioms (closure, identity row/column, a unique $\bar 0$ in each row giving inverses) visible at a glance.
\wsol Entries are $\overline{a+b}\bmod 6$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
+ & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\\hline
\bar0 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0\\
\bar2 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2\\
\bar4 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4
\end{array}
\]
The $\bar0$ entries locate inverses: $-\bar0=\bar0$, $-\bar1=\bar5$, $-\bar2=\bar4$, $-\bar3=\bar3$, $-\bar4=\bar2$, $-\bar5=\bar1$, matching $-\bar a=\overline{6-a}$. The table is symmetric across the main diagonal, recording that $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$ is abelian. Sanity check: each row is a permutation of the six classes (the Latin-square property every group table has).\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The complete multiplication table of $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The complete multiplication table of $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}$}
List $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}$, write out its multiplication table, and find the order of each element.
\wrec ``List $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$'' invokes the gcd filter (Prop.~ [REF:p:unit-iff-coprime@c1] ); the table then exhibits the multiplicative group structure, and orders are read directly from the diagonal of squares.
\wsol $\gcd(a,8)=1$ for $a\in\{1,3,5,7\}$, so $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar5,\bar7\}$ and $\varphi(8)=4$. Entries $\overline{ab}\bmod 8$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\times & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar1 & \bar7 & \bar5\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar7 & \bar1 & \bar3\\
\bar7 & \bar7 & \bar5 & \bar3 & \bar1
\end{array}
\]
Every diagonal square is $\bar1$: $3^2=9\equiv\bar1$, $5^2=25\equiv\bar1$, $7^2=49\equiv\bar1$. Hence $\ord{\bar3}=\ord{\bar5}=\ord{\bar7}=2$ and $\ord{\bar1}=1$. So $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}$ has no element of order $4=\varphi(8)$; it is the Klein four-group, $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$, NOT cyclic. Sanity check: each element is its own inverse, consistent with $x^2=\bar1$ throughout; every order divides $\varphi(8)=4$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{The complete multiplication table of $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$}
List $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, write out its multiplication table, and find the order of each element.
\wrec ``List $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$'' invokes the gcd filter (Prop.~\ref{p:unit-iff-coprime@c1}); the table then exhibits the multiplicative group structure, and orders are read directly from the diagonal of squares.
\wsol $\gcd(a,8)=1$ for $a\in\{1,3,5,7\}$, so $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar5,\bar7\}$ and $\varphi(8)=4$. Entries $\overline{ab}\bmod 8$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\times & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar1 & \bar7 & \bar5\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar7 & \bar1 & \bar3\\
\bar7 & \bar7 & \bar5 & \bar3 & \bar1
\end{array}
\]
Every diagonal square is $\bar1$: $3^2=9\equiv\bar1$, $5^2=25\equiv\bar1$, $7^2=49\equiv\bar1$. Hence $\ord{\bar3}=\ord{\bar5}=\ord{\bar7}=2$ and $\ord{\bar1}=1$. So $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ has no element of order $4=\varphi(8)$; it is the Klein four-group, $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, NOT cyclic. Sanity check: each element is its own inverse, consistent with $x^2=\bar1$ throughout; every order divides $\varphi(8)=4$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ for $n=5,7,9,10$: which are cyclic
Content:
\begin{wex}{$(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ for $n=5,7,9,10$: which are cyclic}
Determine $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ and the order of a small candidate generator for $n=5,7,9,10$, and state which of these unit groups is cyclic.
\wrec D\&F use small moduli to illustrate that some $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$ have a generator (a single power runs through all units) and some do not. Lagrange limits the orders to divisors of $\varphi(n)$.
\wsol
$n=5$: $(Z/(5)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar3,\bar4\}$, $\varphi(5)=4$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,3,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=4$ and $\bar2$ is a generator; $(Z/(5)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic.
$n=7$: $(Z/(7)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\dots,\bar6\}$, $\varphi(7)=6$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=6$; $(Z/(7)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic.
$n=9$: $(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar4,\bar5,\bar7,\bar8\}$, $\varphi(9)=6$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,8,7,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=6$; $(Z/(9)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic.
$n=10$: $(Z/(10)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar7,\bar9\}$, $\varphi(10)=4$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,9,7,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$; $(Z/(10)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic.
Sanity check: in each case the listed generator's powers reproduce exactly the $\varphi(n)$ units, and every order divides $\varphi(n)$. (Contrast $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}$ above and $(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ earlier, which are not cyclic.)\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ for $n=5,7,9,10$: which are cyclic}
Determine $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and the order of a small candidate generator for $n=5,7,9,10$, and state which of these unit groups is cyclic.
\wrec D\&F use small moduli to illustrate that some $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ have a generator (a single power runs through all units) and some do not. Lagrange limits the orders to divisors of $\varphi(n)$.
\wsol
\textbf{$n=5$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar3,\bar4\}$, $\varphi(5)=4$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,3,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=4$ and $\bar2$ is a generator; $(\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=7$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\dots,\bar6\}$, $\varphi(7)=6$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=6$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=9$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar4,\bar5,\bar7,\bar8\}$, $\varphi(9)=6$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,8,7,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=6$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=10$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar7,\bar9\}$, $\varphi(10)=4$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,9,7,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
Sanity check: in each case the listed generator's powers reproduce exactly the $\varphi(n)$ units, and every order divides $\varphi(n)$. (Contrast $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ above and $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ earlier, which are not cyclic.)\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Orders in $S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in $S_3$}
In the symmetric group $S_3$ (permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$, composed right-to-left), compute the order of each element.
\wrec D\&F compute orders in $S_3$ soon after defining order, to show finite groups can have several different orders. Disjoint-cycle structure determines order: a single $k$-cycle has order $k$.
\wsol The six elements are the identity, three transpositions, and two $3$-cycles. As cycles:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\sigma & type & \ord{\sigma}\\\hline
\id & identity & 1\\
(1\,2),\ (1\,3),\ (2\,3) & transposition & 2\\
(1\,2\,3),\ (1\,3\,2) & 3-cycle & 3
\end{array}
\]
Check a transposition: $(1\,2)^2=\id$, and $(1\,2)\ne\id$, so order $2$. Check a $3$-cycle: $(1\,2\,3)^2=(1\,3\,2)\ne\id$, $(1\,2\,3)^3=\id$, so order $3$. Sanity check: $|S_3|=6$ and the orders $1,2,3$ all divide $6$; no element has order $6$, so $S_3$ is not cyclic.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Orders in the dihedral group $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in the dihedral group $D_8$}
In $D_8=\langle r,s\rangle$ with $r^4=s^2=1$ and $sr=r^{-1} s$, find the order of every element.
\wrec D\&F use the dihedral groups as a standard source of mixed orders: a rotation $r^k$ has order $4/\gcd(k,4)$, while every reflection $sr^k$ squares to the identity.
\wsol The eight elements are $1,r,r^2,r^3,s,sr,sr^2,sr^3$. Rotations: $\ord{1}=1$, $\ord{r}=\ord{r^3}=4$, $\ord{r^2}=2$. Reflections: each satisfies $(sr^k)^2=sr^k sr^k=s(r^k s)r^k=s(s r^{-k})r^k=s^2=1$, using $r^k s=s r^{-k}$; and $sr^k\ne1$, so $\ord{sr^k}=2$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. Collected:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc|cccc}
g & 1 & r & r^2 & r^3 & s & sr & sr^2 & sr^3\\\hline
\ord{g} & 1 & 4 & 2 & 4 & 2 & 2 & 2 & 2
\end{array}
\]
Sanity check: all orders divide $|D_8|=8$; there are exactly $\varphi(4)=2$ elements of order $4$ inside the rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle\congZ/(4)Z$, namely $r$ and $r^3$, as the cyclic theory predicts.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Title: Orders in the quaternion group $Q_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Orders in the quaternion group $Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $ij=k$, find the order of every element.
\wrec D\&F present $Q_8$ as a group where, unlike $D_8$, there is a unique element of order $2$ and every non-identity element except $-1$ has order $4$. Use $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $(-1)^2=1$.
\wsol $\ord{1}=1$. Since $(-1)^2=1$ and $-1\ne1$, $\ord{-1}=2$. For $i$: $i^2=-1$, $i^3=-i$, $i^4=(-1)^2=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$; the same computation gives $\ord{-i}=\ord{j}=\ord{-j}=\ord{k}=\ord{-k}=4$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
g & value & \ord{g}\\\hline
1 & 1 & 1\\
-1 & -1 & 2\\
\pm i,\ \pm j,\ \pm k & square to -1 & 4
\end{array}
\]
Sanity check: all orders divide $|Q_8|=8$; there is exactly one element of order $2$ (namely $-1$), in contrast with $D_8$, which has five (the half-turn $r^2$ and the four reflections). So $D_8$ and $Q_8$ are non-isomorphic groups of the same order.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Orders in the quaternion group $Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $ij=k$, find the order of every element.
\wrec D\&F present $Q_8$ as a group where, unlike $D_8$, there is a \emph{unique} element of order $2$ and every non-identity element except $-1$ has order $4$. Use $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $(-1)^2=1$.
\wsol $\ord{1}=1$. Since $(-1)^2=1$ and $-1\ne1$, $\ord{-1}=2$. For $i$: $i^2=-1$, $i^3=-i$, $i^4=(-1)^2=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$; the same computation gives $\ord{-i}=\ord{j}=\ord{-j}=\ord{k}=\ord{-k}=4$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
g & \text{value} & \ord{g}\\\hline
1 & 1 & 1\\
-1 & -1 & 2\\
\pm i,\ \pm j,\ \pm k & \text{square to } -1 & 4
\end{array}
\]
Sanity check: all orders divide $|Q_8|=8$; there is exactly one element of order $2$ (namely $-1$), in contrast with $D_8$, which has five (the half-turn $r^2$ and the four reflections). So $D_8$ and $Q_8$ are non-isomorphic groups of the same order.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Infinite order in $\GL_2(R)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Infinite order in $\GL_2(R)$}
Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\in\GL_2(R)$. Show $\ord{A}=\infty$, and contrast with $B=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which has finite order.
\wrec D\&F use $\GL_n$ as the standard infinite group in which individual elements may still have finite or infinite order. Compute the powers directly.
\wsol By induction $A^k=\begin{pmatrix}1 & k\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. For $k>0$ the top-right entry is $k\ne0$, so $A^k\ne I$ for every $k\ge1$; hence $\ord{A}=\infty$. For $B$: $B^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}=-I$, $B^3=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $B^4=I$, so $\ord{B}=4$ (this $B$ is rotation by $90^\circ$). Sanity check: $\det A=\det B=1\ne0$, so both lie in $\GL_2(R)$; a single group can contain elements of every order, finite and infinite.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Label: r:additive-vs-mult-orders-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{remark} 
The contrast across these examples is the recurring D\&F theme. The additive groups $(R,+)$, $(Q,+)$, $(Z,+)$ are torsion-free: the identity $0$ is the only element of finite order ($\ord{0}=1$), since $kx=0$ with $k>0$ forces $x=0$. The multiplicative group $(R^\times,\cdot)$ has just two elements of finite order, $\ord{1}=1$ and $\ord{-1}=2$, and $(Q^\times,\cdot)$ has the same two. By comparison the finite groups $Z/(n)Z$, $(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$, $S_3$, $D_8$, $Q_8$ realize a whole range of orders. Passing from $+$ to $\times$, or from $Z$ to $Z/(n)Z$, is exactly what creates nontrivial finite orders.
\end{remark}
label: r:additive-vs-mult-orders-mrg@c1
