 arrow $\ker\rho\hookrightarrow G$: the inclusion of the kernel as a subgroup. Horizontal $\rho\colon
 G\to\Sym(A)$: the permutation representation. Vertical two-headed arrow $G\twoheadrightarrow G/\ker\rho$:
 the canonical surjection $\pi\colon g\mapsto g\ker\rho$. Dashed hooked arrow $\overline{\rho}\colon
 G/\ker\rho\hookrightarrow\Sym(A)$: the induced injective homomorphism, $\overline{\rho}(g\ker\rho):=
 \rho(g)$.

 The top row is exact: $\operatorname{im}(1\to\ker\rho)=\{1\}=\ker(\ker\rho\hookrightarrow G)$,

 =\ker\rho$ is the identity coset.

\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow $\overline{\rho}$ is injective (not an isomorphism onto
  all of $\Sym(A)$), because $\rho$ need not be surjective. Students sometimes expect $G/\ker\rho
  \cong\Sym(A)$; the correct statement is $G/\ker\rho\cong\rho(G)$, a subgroup.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that every permutation representation factors canonically
  through its own quotient, giving an \emph{injective} representation of $G/\ker\rho$ and pinpointing
  exactly which part of $G$ the action ``sees.''
\end{dgx}

Type: method
Title: Verify an action, build $\rho$, find the kernel, decide faithfulness
Content:
\begin{method}{Verify an action, build $\rho$, find the kernel, decide faithfulness}
Given a candidate map $G\times A\to A$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (A1) Check $1\cdot a=a$ for every $a$ (just plug in the identity).
\item (A2) Check $(gh)\cdot a=g\cdot(h\cdot a)$ for all $g,h,a$; do the two sides
separately and compare. This is where a fake ``action'' usually dies.
\item Build $\rho$. For each $g$, write $\sigma_g=(a\mapsto g\cdot a)$ as an explicit
permutation of $A$ (in cycle notation if $A$ is finite and labeled $1,\dots,n$).
\item Kernel. Solve $g\cdot a=a$ simultaneously for all $a$; the set of such $g$
is $\ker\rho$ (a normal subgroup of $G$).
\item Faithful? The action is faithful iff that kernel is $\{1\}$ iff distinct $g$ give
distinct permutations $\sigma_g$.
\end{enumerate}
Trigger. Use this checklist whenever you are handed a rule ``$g\cdot a=\dots$'' and asked
``is it an action / what is its permutation representation / is it faithful?''
\end{method}

Section: Introduction to Groups > Group Actions > Example family 1: the left regular action and Cayley's theorem
Type: theorem
Title: Cayley
Label: t:cayley@c1
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Cayley] 
Every group $G$ acts on itself by left multiplication, $g\cdot x=gx$. This action is faithful,
so $\rho\colon G\hookrightarrow\Sym(G)$ embeds $G$ as a subgroup of $\Sym(G)$. If $|G|=n$ then
$G\cong$ a subgroup of $S_n$.
\end{theorem}
label: t:cayley@c1

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Group Actions > Example family 1: the left regular action and Cayley's theorem
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-eea96296f7c3ce13216c
Content:
\begin{proof}
(A1): $1\cdot x=1x=x$. (A2): $(gh)\cdot x=(gh)x=g(hx)=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ by associativity.
Kernel: $g\cdot x=x$ for all $x$ means $gx=x$ for all $x$; taking $x=1$ gives $g=1$, so
$\ker\rho=1$ and $\rho$ is injective. With $|G|=n$, choosing a labeling $G\leftrightarrow\{1,\dots,n\}$
gives $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$, so $G\cong\rho(G)\sgr S_n$.
\end{proof}

\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em]
G \arrow[r, hook, "\rho\,:\,g\,\mapsto\,(x\mapsto gx)"] & \Sym(G)
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two nodes. $G$ is the group viewed simultaneously as the group acting and as the set
 being acted on (the regular action uses the group as its own set). $\Sym(G)$ is the symmetric group
 of all bijections from the underlying set of $G$ to itself; its order is $|G|!$ if $G$ is finite.
\dgi{Arrows:} A single hooked arrow $\rho\colon G\hookrightarrow\Sym(G)$, labeled by its formula.
 The hook denotes injectivity. For each $g\in G$, $\rho(g)$ is the bijection $x\mapsto gx$
 (left multiplication by $g$). This is the permutation representation of the left regular action.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is only one arrow, so commutativity is not the key property; the essential
 statement is that $\rho$ is a homomorphism and is injective: $\rho(gh)(x)=(gh)x
 =g(hx)=\rho(g)(\rho(h)(x))$, so $\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)$; and $\rho(g)=\id$ iff $gx=x$ for all
 $x$ iff $g=1$ (take $x=1$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The homomorphism property comes directly from associativity in $G$:
 $\rho(gh)=\sigma_{gh}$ and $\sigma_{gh}(x)=(gh)x=g(hx)=\sigma_g(\sigma_h(x))=(\rho(g)\rho(h))(x)$.
 Injectivity follows because left-multiplying by any $g\ne1$ moves the identity element $1$ to $g
 \ne1$, so no nonidentity element is in the kernel.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is Cayley's theorem (Theorem~ [REF:t:cayley@c1] ) summarized in one
 arrow: every group embeds into a symmetric group. The diagram records the embedding without
 specifying $|G|$, making the result universal.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $G=Z/(4)Z$: $\rho(1)=(1\,2\,3\,4)$ as computed in the worked example below.
 The image $\rho(Z/(4)Z)=\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle\sgr S_4$ is a cyclic subgroup of order $4$. The hook
 reflects that $\rho$ is injective and $Z/(4)Z\cong\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The arrow is into $\Sym(G)$, which treats $G$ as a bare set of $|G|$ elements.
 Students confuse the two roles of $G$: as a group (source of $\rho$) and as a set (on which $\Sym(G)$
 acts). The bijection $\rho(g)$ is not a group homomorphism of $G$; it is just a permutation.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the left regular action is always faithful, which
 is why every group embeds as a concrete subgroup of a symmetric group.
\end{dgx}

Type: example
Title: Left regular action of $Z/(4)Z$, representation into $S_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Left regular action of $Z/(4)Z$, representation into $S_4$}
Take $G=Z/(4)Z=\{0,1,2,3\}$ acting on itself, $g\cdot x=g+x$. Label elements by
$0\leftrightarrow1,\ 1\leftrightarrow2,\ 2\leftrightarrow3,\ 3\leftrightarrow4$. Compute $\rho$ and $\ker\rho$.
\wrec ``$G$ on itself by the group operation'' is the left regular action; Cayley
(Thm.~ [REF:t:cayley@c1] ) says it is automatically an action and faithful. The work is to write each
$\sigma_g$ as an explicit element of $S_4$.
\wsol
Axioms come free from Cayley. Now $\sigma_g(x)=g+x\pmod 4$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=0$: $x\mapsto x$, so $\sigma_0=\id=()$.
\item $g=1$: $0\mapsto1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto0$, i.e.\ labels $1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto4\mapsto1$,
so $\sigma_1=(1\,2\,3\,4)$.
\item $g=2$: $0\mapsto2,1\mapsto3,2\mapsto0,3\mapsto1$, so $\sigma_2=(1\,3)(2\,4)$.
\item $g=3$: $0\mapsto3\mapsto2\mapsto1\mapsto0$, so $\sigma_3=(1\,4\,3\,2)$.
\end{itemize}
So $\rho(Z/(4)Z)=\{(),(1\,2\,3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4\,3\,2)\}=\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle$, a cyclic subgroup
of $S_4$ of order $4$. Kernel: $\sigma_g=\id$ forces $g+x=x$ for all $x$, i.e.\ $g=0$, so
$\ker\rho=\{0\}=1$ and the action is faithful.
Check. $\sigma_1^2=(1\,2\,3\,4)^2=(1\,3)(2\,4)=\sigma_2$ and
$\rho(1+1)=\rho(2)=\sigma_2$ -- the homomorphism property holds. $\rho$ has image of order $4=|Z/(4)Z|$,
confirming injectivity.
\end{wex}

Title: Left regular action of $V_4$, representation into $S_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Left regular action of $V_4$, representation into $S_4$}
Let $V_4=\{1,a,b,c\}$ with $a^2=b^2=c^2=1$, $ab=c$. Label $1\leftrightarrow1,a\leftrightarrow2,
b\leftrightarrow3,c\leftrightarrow4$. Find $\rho(V_4)\sgr S_4$.
\wrec Same regular action; faithful by Cayley. We just tabulate left-multiplication columns.
\wsol Since $V_4$ is abelian with $ab=c$, the products are $ac=a(ab)=a^2b=b$, $bc=b(ab)=ab^2=a$,
and similarly $ca=b$, $cb=a$. Left-multiply by $a$:
$a\cdot1=a,\ a\cdot a=1,\ a\cdot b=ab=c,\ a\cdot c=ac=b$. So
$\sigma_a$ sends $1\mapsto2,2\mapsto1,3\mapsto4,4\mapsto3$, i.e.\ $\sigma_a=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.
Left-multiply by $b$: $b\cdot1=b,\ b\cdot a=ba=ab=c,\ b\cdot b=1,\ b\cdot c=bc=a$, so
$\sigma_b:1\mapsto3,3\mapsto1,2\mapsto4,4\mapsto2$, i.e.\ $\sigma_b=(1\,3)(2\,4)$. And
$c\cdot1=c,\ c\cdot a=ca=b,\ c\cdot b=cb=a,\ c\cdot c=1$, so $\sigma_c=(1\,4)(2\,3)$. Hence
\[
\rho(V_4)=\{(),(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}\sgr S_4,
\]
the standard copy of $V_4$ in $S_4$. Kernel $=1$ (regular actions are faithful).
Check. $\sigma_a\sigma_b=(1\,2)(3\,4)\cdot(1\,3)(2\,4)$; apply right factor then left:
$1\mapsto3\mapsto4,2\mapsto4\mapsto3,3\mapsto1\mapsto2,4\mapsto2\mapsto1$ gives $(1\,4)(2\,3)=\sigma_c
=\rho(ab)$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: Left regular action of $S_3$, image inside $S_6$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Left regular action of $S_3$, image inside $S_6$}
Cayley embeds $S_3$ (order $6$) into $S_6$. Compute $\sigma_g$ for the transposition
$g=(1\,2)\in S_3$, where $S_3$ acts on its own $6$ elements.
\wrec Regular action of a nonabelian group; faithful. The subtlety is that the indices ``$1\dots6$''
label the group elements, not the points $S_3$ originally permuted.
\wsol List $S_3=\{e_1{=}1,\,e_2{=}(1\,2),\,e_3{=}(1\,3),\,e_4{=}(2\,3),\,e_5{=}(1\,2\,3),\,
e_6{=}(1\,3\,2)\}$. With $g=(1\,2)$ compute $g e_i$ (product in $S_3$, composing right to left):
$g e_1=(1\,2)=e_2$; $g e_2=(1\,2)(1\,2)=1=e_1$; $g e_3=(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)=e_6$;
$g e_4=(1\,2)(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3)=e_5$; $g e_5=(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)=(2\,3)=e_4$;
$g e_6=(1\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,3)=e_3$. So on the labels,
$\sigma_g=(1\,2)(3\,6)(4\,5)\in S_6$. This is a product of three transpositions, hence an odd
permutation moving all $6$ points (no fixed points) -- indeed every nonidentity element of a
regular action is fixed-point-free.
Check. $g^2=1$ in $S_3$, and $\sigma_g^2=\bigl((1\,2)(3\,6)(4\,5)\bigr)^2=()$, matching
$\rho(g^2)=\rho(1)=\id$. The kernel is trivial since $g e_1=e_2\ne e_1$ already for $g=e_2$, etc.
\end{wex}

Section: Introduction to Groups > Group Actions > Example family 1: the left regular action and Cayley's theorem
Type: example
Title: Why ``left mult'' is needed: $g\cdot x=xg$ is not a left action
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why ``left mult'' is needed: $g\cdot x=xg$ is not a left action}
Show that $g\cdot x:=xg$ on $G$ fails (A2) unless $G$ is abelian, and fix it.
\wrec Test (A2) literally; a swapped order is the classic trap that produces an anti-homomorphism.
\wsol $(gh)\cdot x=x(gh)=xgh$, but $g\cdot(h\cdot x)=g\cdot(xh)=(xh)g=xhg$. These agree for all
$x$ iff $gh=hg$ for all $g,h$, i.e.\ iff $G$ abelian. So for nonabelian $G$ it is not a left action.
Fix: $g\cdot x:=xg^{-1}$ is a left action: $(gh)\cdot x=x(gh)^{-1}=xh^{-1} g^{-1}
=(xh^{-1})g^{-1}=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$, and $1\cdot x=x1^{-1}=x$.
Check. Kernel of the fixed action: $xg^{-1}=x$ for all $x$ $\Rightarrow g^{-1}=1\Rightarrow
g=1$, so it is also faithful (this is the right regular action recast on the left).
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{proposition}[$D_8$ acts faithfully on the $4$ vertices] 
$D_8$ acts on $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ by its geometric action on the square's vertices. The representation
$\rho\colon D_8\to S_4$ is injective ($\ker\rho=1$), and $\rho(r)=(1\,2\,3\,4)$,
$\rho(s)=(2\,4)$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:d8@c1

Content:
\begin{proof}
Symmetries of the square permute its vertices, and composing symmetries composes the permutations,
so (A1),(A2) hold and $\rho$ is a homomorphism. Rotation by $90^\circ$ sends $1\to2\to3\to4\to1$, so
$\rho(r)=(1\,2\,3\,4)$. The reflection across the $1$--$3$ diagonal fixes $1,3$ and swaps $2,4$, so
$\rho(s)=(2\,4)$. A symmetry fixing all four vertices is the identity, so $\ker\rho=1$ and $\rho$
is injective; thus $D_8\cong\rho(D_8)\sgr S_4$, the image being a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $S_4$.
\end{proof}

Title: Build the full table $\rho\colon D_8\to S_4$ and check the relations
Content:
\begin{wex}{Build the full table $\rho\colon D_8\to S_4$ and check the relations}
Write $\rho(g)$ for all eight $g\in D_8=\{1,r,r^2,r^3,s,sr,sr^2,sr^3\}$ and verify $sr=r^{-1} s$ at
the level of permutations.
\wrec We have the generators' images (Prop.~ [REF:p:d8@c1] ); since $\rho$ is a homomorphism, every other
image is a product. Use $\rho(sr^k)=\rho(s)\rho(r)^k=S R^k$, composing right to left.
\wsol With $R:=\rho(r)=(1\,2\,3\,4)$ and $S:=\rho(s)=(2\,4)$ we first record the rotation powers
$R^2=(1\,3)(2\,4)$, $R^3=(1\,4\,3\,2)$. Now compute each $\rho(sr^k)=S R^k$ by applying $R^k$ first,
then $S$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $k=0$: $\rho(s)=S=(2\,4)$.
\item $k=1$: $S R$. Apply $R$ then $S$: $1\mapsto2\mapsto4$, $4\mapsto1\mapsto1$, so
$1\leftrightarrow4$; $2\mapsto3\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto4\mapsto2$, so $2\leftrightarrow3$. Hence
$\rho(sr)=(1\,4)(2\,3)$.
\item $k=2$: $S R^2$. Apply $R^2$ then $S$: $1\mapsto3\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto1\mapsto1$, so
$1\leftrightarrow3$; $2\mapsto4\mapsto2$ and $4\mapsto2\mapsto4$ are fixed. Hence
$\rho(sr^2)=(1\,3)$.
\item $k=3$: $S R^3$. Apply $R^3$ then $S$: $1\mapsto4\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto1\mapsto1$, so
$1\mapsto2\mapsto1$ gives $1\leftrightarrow2$; $3\mapsto2\mapsto4$, $4\mapsto3\mapsto3$, so
$3\leftrightarrow4$. Hence $\rho(sr^3)=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.
\end{itemize}
The complete table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
g & 1 & r & r^2 & r^3 & s & sr & sr^2 & sr^3\\\hline
\rho(g) & () & (1\,2\,3\,4) & (1\,3)(2\,4) & (1\,4\,3\,2) & (2\,4) & (1\,4)(2\,3) & (1\,3) & (1\,2)(3\,4)
\end{array}
\]
\textbf{Verify $sr=r^{-1} s$:} LHS $=\rho(sr)=(1\,4)(2\,3)$. RHS $=R^{-1} S$ with
$R^{-1}=(1\,4\,3\,2)$: apply $S=(2\,4)$ then $R^{-1}$: $1\mapsto1\mapsto4$, $4\mapsto2\mapsto1$, so
$1\leftrightarrow4$; $2\mapsto4\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto3\mapsto2$, so $2\leftrightarrow3$. Thus
$R^{-1} S=(1\,4)(2\,3)=$ LHS. Check. All $8$ images are distinct, reconfirming $\ker\rho=1$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $D_8$ acting on the $2$ diagonals: a non-faithful action
Content:
\begin{wex}{$D_8$ acting on the $2$ diagonals: a non-faithful action}
Let $D_8$ act on the set $A=\{d_{13},d_{24}\}$ of the square's two diagonals. Compute $\rho\colon
D_8\to S_2$ and its kernel.
\wrec Same group, smaller set, so the rep lands in $S_2$ (order $2$) while $|D_8|=8$; a
counting clash ($8>2$) forces a nontrivial kernel -- a textbook non-faithful action.
\wsol $r$ (rotate $90^\circ$) sends diagonal $1$--$3$ to $2$--$4$, so it swaps $d_{13}\leftrightarrow
d_{24}$: $\rho(r)=(d_{13}\,d_{24})$. The reflection $s$ across $1$--$3$ fixes that axis and maps the
other diagonal to itself, so $\rho(s)=\id$. Since $r,s$ generate $D_8$, the image is
$\langle (d_{13}\,d_{24})\rangle=S_2$. The homomorphism $\rho\colon D_8\to S_2$ is onto $S_2$, so by the
first isomorphism theorem $|\ker\rho|=8/2=4$. Explicitly $g\in\ker\rho$ iff $g$ fixes each
diagonal: these are $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$ (check: $r^2$ rotates $180^\circ$ fixing both diagonals; $s$
and $sr^2$ are the two reflections through the diagonals). So $\ker\rho=\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}\cong V_4$,
the action is not faithful.
Check. $|\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}|=4$ matches $8/|\im\rho|=8/2=4$, and one verifies this set is a
subgroup (indeed normal, as kernels must be).
\end{wex}

Title: $S_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is faithful
Content:
\begin{wex}{$S_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is faithful}
The natural action $\sigma\cdot i=\sigma(i)$ of $S_n$ on $A=\{1,\dots,n\}$. Show it is an action and
compute its kernel.
\wrec ``$\sigma\cdot i=\sigma(i)$'' is the defining/tautological action; $\rho$ is the identity map
$S_n\to\Sym(A)=S_n$, the cleanest possible representation.
\wsol (A1): $1\cdot i=\id(i)=i$. (A2): $(\sigma\tau)\cdot i=(\sigma\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))=
\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot i)$ -- this is literally how composition in $S_n$ is defined. So $\rho(\sigma)
=\sigma$ and $\rho=\id_{S_n}$. Kernel: $\sigma(i)=i$ for all $i$ means $\sigma=\id$, so
$\ker\rho=1$ and the action is faithful (trivially, $\rho$ is a bijection).
Check. For $n=3$, $\rho((1\,2))=(1\,2)$, and distinct group elements give distinct
permutations because they are those permutations.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A subgroup action: $A_4$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$, still faithful}
Restrict the natural $S_4$-action to $A_4$. Is it faithful? What is $\rho(A_4)$?
\wrec Restricting a faithful action to a subgroup stays faithful, because the kernel only shrinks:
$\ker(\rho|_H)=H\cap\ker\rho$.
\wsol The restriction sends $\sigma\in A_4$ to $\sigma\in S_4$, so $\rho|_{A_4}$ is the inclusion
$A_4\hookrightarrow S_4$. Kernel $=A_4\cap\ker(natural)=A_4\cap\{1\}=\{1\}$, so faithful;
$\rho(A_4)=A_4\sgr S_4$. Check. E.g.\ $(1\,2\,3)\in A_4$ maps to the nonidentity
$(1\,2\,3)$, so it is not in the kernel; only $\id$ fixes all four points.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: Conjugation action
Label: p:conj@c1
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Conjugation action] 
$G$ acts on itself by conjugation $g\cdot x:=gxg^{-1}$. The representation
$\rho\colon G\to\Sym(G)$ has image inside $\Aut(G)$ (each $\sigma_g$ is the inner automorphism
$x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$), and
\[
\ker\rho=Z(G)=\{g\in G: gx=xg\ \forall x\in G\}.
\]
Hence $\rho$ induces $G/Z(G)\cong\Inn(G)\sgr\Aut(G)$, and the action is faithful iff $Z(G)=1$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:conj@c1

\begin{proof}
(A1): $1\cdot x=1x1^{-1}=x$. (A2): $(gh)\cdot x=(gh)x(gh)^{-1}=g(hxh^{-1})g^{-1}=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$.
Each $\sigma_g$ respects multiplication: $\sigma_g(xy)=g(xy)g^{-1}=(gxg^{-1})(gyg^{-1})
=\sigma_g(x)\sigma_g(y)$, so $\sigma_g\in\Aut(G)$. Kernel: $gxg^{-1}=x$ for all $x$ $\Longleftrightarrow gx=xg$ for
all $x$ $\Longleftrightarrow g\in Z(G)$. The first isomorphism theorem gives $G/Z(G)\cong\rho(G)=\Inn(G)$.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\rho"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & \Aut(G) \\
G/Z(G) \arrow[ur, hook, dashed, "\cong\,\Inn(G)"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three nodes. $G$ is the group acting on itself by conjugation. $\Aut(G)$ is the
 automorphism group of $G$ (all group isomorphisms $G\to G$); it is the ambient target because each
 conjugation $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$ is an automorphism. $G/Z(G)$ is the quotient of $G$ by its center
 $Z(G)=\ker\rho$; elements are cosets $gZ(G)$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal $\rho\colon G\to\Aut(G)$: the conjugation representation sending $g$
 to the inner automorphism $\iota_g\colon x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$; its image is $\Inn(G)$. Left vertical
 two-headed arrow $\pi\colon G\twoheadrightarrow G/Z(G)$: the canonical quotient map, surjective.
 Dashed hooked arrow $G/Z(G)\hookrightarrow\Aut(G)$, labeled $\cong\Inn(G)$: the induced injection
 $\overline{\rho}(gZ(G)):=\iota_g$, which is an isomorphism onto $\Inn(G)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} $\rho = \overline{\rho}\circ\pi$: i.e.\ $\iota_g=\overline{\rho}(gZ(G))$ for
 all $g\in G$, so the two paths from $G$ to $\Aut(G)$ agree.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness: if $gZ(G)=g'Z(G)$ then $g^{-1}g'\in Z(G)$, so
 $g^{-1}g'$ commutes with every $x$; then $g'^{-1}xg'=g^{-1}xg$ for all $x$, i.e.\ $\iota_{g'}=
 \iota_g$. Hence $\overline{\rho}$ is independent of the coset representative. Commutativity then
 holds by construction. Injectivity: $\overline{\rho}(gZ(G))=\id$ iff $gxg^{-1}=x$ for all $x$
 iff $g\in Z(G)$ iff $gZ(G)$ is the identity coset.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the first isomorphism theorem for the conjugation action of
 Proposition~ [REF:p:conj@c1] : it identifies $\Inn(G)$ concretely as $G/Z(G)$, explaining why large
 centers produce small inner automorphism groups and why $Z(G)=1$ forces the action to be faithful.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $G=D_8$: $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}$, so $G/Z(G)\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z=V_4$ and
 $\Inn(D_8)\cong V_4$ (four inner automorphisms). The coset $rZ$ maps to $\iota_r\in\Aut(D_8)$,
 the automorphism conjugating by $r$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The hooked arrow lands in $\Aut(G)$, not in $\Sym(G)$; inner automorphisms
 are group automorphisms, not arbitrary bijections. Also, $G/Z(G)\cong\Inn(G)$ is an isomorphism
 of groups, but $G/Z(G)$ is not a subgroup of $G$ itself; it lives inside $\Aut(G)$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the inner automorphism group is always isomorphic
 to $G$ modulo its center, so the center measures exactly how much of $G$ is ``invisible'' to the
 conjugation action.
\end{dgx}

\begin{wex}{Conjugation on $Q_8$: kernel $Z(Q_8)=\{\pm1\}$}

commute; thus $i,j,k\notin Z$. The elements $\pm1$ are central ($1$ trivially, and
$(-1)x=x(-1)=-x$). So $Z(Q_8)=\{1,-1\}$ and $\ker\rho=\{\pm1\}$; the action is not faithful and

$i j i^{-1}=i j(-i)=(ij)(-i)=k(-i)=-(ki)=-j\ne j$, so $i\notin\ker\rho$ -- the kernel really is
just $\{\pm1\}$.
\end{wex}

Title: Conjugation on $S_3$ is faithful ($Z(S_3)=1$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugation on $S_3$ is faithful ($Z(S_3)=1$)}
Show conjugation makes $S_3$ act faithfully on itself, and identify $\Inn(S_3)$.
\wrec Faithful iff $Z(G)=1$; for $S_n$ with $n\ge3$ the center is trivial.
\wsol Suppose $g\in Z(S_3)$. Conjugation by $g$ preserves cycle type, and if $g$ commutes with the
transposition $(1\,2)$ then $g(1\,2)g^{-1}=(1\,2)$, i.e.\ $g$ fixes the pair $\{1,2\}$; commuting with
$(2\,3)$ likewise fixes $\{2,3\}$. The only $g$ fixing $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ setwise and lying in
$S_3$ is $g=1$. So $Z(S_3)=1$, $\ker\rho=1$, the action is faithful, and
$\Inn(S_3)\cong S_3/Z(S_3)=S_3$, of order $6$.
Check. $(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)^{-1}=(2\,1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\ne(1\,2\,3)$, so $(1\,2)$ acts
nontrivially -- consistent with a trivial kernel.
\end{wex}

Title: Conjugation on an abelian group is trivial (maximally non-faithful)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugation on an abelian group is trivial (maximally non-faithful)}
Describe the conjugation action of an abelian $G$ (say $G=Z/(6)Z$) and its kernel.
\wrec If $G$ is abelian, every $gxg^{-1}=x$, so the action is the trivial action and the kernel is
all of $G$ -- the extreme opposite of faithful.
\wsol For abelian $G$: $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}=gg^{-1} x=x$ for all $g,x$. Thus $\sigma_g=\id$ for every
$g$, $\rho$ is the constant map to $\id$, and $\ker\rho=Z(G)=G$ (consistent with $Z(G)=G$ for
abelian $G$). For $G=Z/(6)Z$, $\rho(Z/(6)Z)=\{\id\}$ and $\ker\rho=Z/(6)Z$.
Check. $\Inn(Z/(6)Z)\congZ/(6)Z/Z(Z/(6)Z)=Z/(6)Z/Z/(6)Z=1$, the trivial group, exactly as ``no
nontrivial inner automorphisms'' predicts.
\end{wex}

\wrec If $G$ is abelian, every $gxg^{-1}=x$, so the action is the trivial action and the kernel is

\wsol For abelian $G$: $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}=gg^{-1} x=x$ for all $g,x$. Thus $\sigma_g=\id$ for every
$g$, $\rho$ is the constant map to $\id$, and $\ker\rho=Z(G)=G$ (consistent with $Z(G)=G$ for
abelian $G$). For $G=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$, $\rho(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z})=\{\id\}$ and $\ker\rho=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$.
\textit{Check.} $\Inn(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}/Z(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}=1$, the trivial group, exactly as ``no

Title: A coset action and its core: $S_3$ on cosets of $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A coset action and its core: $S_3$ on cosets of $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$}
Let $G=S_3$ act by left multiplication on the left cosets of $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$, i.e.\ on
$A=\{H,(1\,3)H,(2\,3)H\}$ (three cosets). Find $\rho\colon S_3\to\Sym(A)$ and $\ker\rho$.
\wrec Action on cosets $g\cdot(xH)=(gx)H$ is a standard action; its kernel is the
normal core $\bigcap_{x\in S_3}xHx^{-1}$, the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$.
\wsol First name the three cosets. Composing right to left,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1&=H=\{1,(1\,2)\},\\
c_2&=(1\,3)H=\{(1\,3),\,(1\,3)(1\,2)\}=\{(1\,3),(1\,2\,3)\},\\
c_3&=(2\,3)H=\{(2\,3),\,(2\,3)(1\,2)\}=\{(2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now act by the generators, computing $g\cdot c=(g\cdotrep)H$ and reading off which coset
contains the result.
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=(1\,2\,3)$: $g\cdot1=(1\,2\,3)\in c_2$; $g\cdot(1\,3)=(1\,2\,3)(1\,3)=(2\,3)\in c_3$;
$g\cdot(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3)(2\,3)=(1\,2)\in c_1$. So $\rho((1\,2\,3))=(c_1\,c_2\,c_3)$.
\item $g=(1\,2)$: $g\cdot1=(1\,2)\in c_1$; $g\cdot(1\,3)=(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\in c_3$;
$g\cdot(2\,3)=(1\,2)(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3)\in c_2$. So $\rho((1\,2))=(c_2\,c_3)$.
\item $g=(1\,3)$: $g\cdot1=(1\,3)\in c_2$; $g\cdot(1\,3)=1\in c_1$;
$g\cdot(2\,3)=(1\,3)(2\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\in c_3$, so $c_3$ is fixed. Hence $\rho((1\,3))=(c_1\,c_2)$.
\end{itemize}
Thus $\rho$ sends $(1\,2\,3)\mapsto(c_1\,c_2\,c_3)$, $(1\,2)\mapsto(c_2\,c_3)$,
$(1\,3)\mapsto(c_1\,c_2)$, and these already generate all of $\Sym(A)\cong S_3$. Hence $\rho$ is
onto, and since $|S_3|=6=|\Sym(A)|$ it is an isomorphism, so $\ker\rho=1$: the action is faithful.
Equivalently $\ker\rho=\operatorname{core}(H)=\bigcap_{x}xHx^{-1}$, and as $|H|=2$ with $H$ not
normal this intersection is trivial.
Check. The core is the largest normal subgroup inside $H$; the only normal subgroups of
$S_3$ are $1$, $A_3$, $S_3$, and the only one contained in the $2$-element $H$ is $1$. For a
genuinely non-faithful coset action take $G=Q_8$ on the four cosets of $H=\langle -1\rangle$: there
$\langle -1\rangle\nor Q_8$, so $\operatorname{core}(H)=\langle -1\rangle=Z(Q_8)\ne1$ and $\ker\rho=\langle -1\rangle$.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
``Faithful'' is about the whole action: $\ker\rho=\{g:g\cdot a=a for all a\}$.
One element $g$ fixing one point $a$ (a stabilizer) is unrelated; do not confuse
$\ker\rho=\bigcap_a G_a$ (intersection of all stabilizers) with a single stabilizer $G_a$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Title: The three diagrams to keep in mind
Content:
\begin{remark}[The three diagrams to keep in mind]
(1) An action is a homomorphism $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(A)$ (Thm.~ [REF:t:equiv@c1] ); (2) the
regular action gives Cayley's embedding $G\hookrightarrow\Sym(G)$ (Thm.~ [REF:t:cayley@c1] ); (3) every
action factors as $G\twoheadrightarrow G/\ker\rho\hookrightarrow\Sym(A)$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\rho"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & \Sym(A) \\
G/\ker\rho \arrow[ur, hook, dashed, "\overline{\rho}"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three nodes. $G$ is the group performing any given action on a set $A$.
 $\Sym(A)$ is the symmetric group on the set $A$, the universal target for permutation
 representations of groups acting on $A$. $G/\ker\rho$ is the quotient of $G$ by the kernel
 of the permutation representation $\rho$; it is the ``effective'' part of $G$ that acts
 non-trivially.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(A)$: the permutation representation of the given
 action. Left vertical two-headed $\pi\colon G\twoheadrightarrow G/\ker\rho$: the canonical
 surjection $g\mapsto g\ker\rho$, which collapses elements that act identically. Dashed hooked
 $\overline{\rho}\colon G/\ker\rho\hookrightarrow\Sym(A)$: the induced injective map
 $\overline{\rho}(g\ker\rho):=\rho(g)$, guaranteed by the universal property of the quotient since
 $\ker\rho\subseteq\ker\rho$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle: $\rho=\overline{\rho}\circ\pi$, meaning $\rho(g)=\overline{\rho}
 (g\ker\rho)$ for every $g\in G$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\overline{\rho}$: if $g\ker\rho=g'\ker\rho$ then $g^{-1}
 g'\in\ker\rho$, so $\rho(g^{-1}g')=\id$, hence $\rho(g)=\rho(g')$; the output of $\overline{\rho}$
 does not depend on which representative of the coset is used. Commutativity then reads
 $\overline{\rho}(\pi(g))=\overline{\rho}(g\ker\rho)=\rho(g)$, which is immediate. Injectivity of
 $\overline{\rho}$: $\overline{\rho}(g\ker\rho)=\id$ iff $\rho(g)=\id$ iff $g\in\ker\rho$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the master diagram of the whole section: it says every group
 action factors universally as a surjection (onto the quotient by the kernel) followed by an
 injection (into $\Sym(A)$). The action is faithful iff $\ker\rho=1$ iff $\pi$ is an isomorphism
 iff the bottom-left vertex equals $G$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Conjugation action of $G=D_8$ on itself: $\ker\rho=Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}$, so
 $G/\ker\rho\cong V_4$ and $\overline{\rho}\colon V_4\hookrightarrow\Aut(D_8)$ is the injective map
 whose image is $\Inn(D_8)$. The quotient $\pi$ collapses each coset $\{g,gr^2\}$ to a single
 element of $V_4$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read $\overline{\rho}$ as an isomorphism onto $\Sym(A)$.
 It is only injective; $\rho(G)$ is typically a proper subgroup of $\Sym(A)$ (e.g., the
 image of $D_8$ acting on $4$ vertices is a subgroup of $S_4$ of order $8$, not all $24$ elements).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that every action, no matter how non-faithful, contains
 a faithful action of the quotient $G/\ker\rho$ inside it, and this quotient is the largest quotient
 of $G$ that acts faithfully on $A$.
\end{dgx}

The action is faithful exactly when $\pi$ is an isomorphism, i.e.\ when the left arrow has trivial
kernel.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: Trivial action
Label: d:trivial-mrg@c1
Content:
\begin{definition}[Trivial action] 
For any group $G$ and nonempty set $A$, the rule $g\cdot a=a$ for all $g\in G$, $a\in A$, is an
action, the trivial action of $G$ on $A$. Each $\sigma_g=\id_A$, so $\rho$ is the constant map
$g\mapsto\id_A$ and $\ker\rho=G$; it is faithful only when $G=1$.
\end{definition}
label: d:trivial-mrg@c1

Type: example
Title: D\&F Example: the trivial action and what it ``sees''
Content:
\begin{wex}{D\&F Example: the trivial action and what it ``sees''}
Verify that $g\cdot a=a$ is an action of any $G$ on any nonempty $A$, and identify its kernel.
\wrec This is Def.~ [REF:d:trivial-mrg@c1] ; the only work is to confirm the two axioms and read off
$\ker\rho$, which exhibits the extreme opposite of a faithful action.
\wsol Axiom (A1): $1\cdot a=a$ by definition. Axiom (A2):
$g\cdot(h\cdot a)=g\cdot a=a$ and $(gh)\cdot a=a$, so the two sides agree. Every $\sigma_g$ is
$\id_A$, hence $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(A)$ is the constant map onto $\{\id_A\}$ and
$\ker\rho=\{g:g\cdot a=a\ \forall a\}=G$.
Check. The action is faithful $\Longleftrightarrow\ker\rho=1\Longleftrightarrow G=1$; for $|G|>1$ the trivial action is
maximally non-faithful, which is why a nontrivial action is required to ``see'' anything about $G$.
This is the opposite extreme to the faithful regular and natural actions worked above.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: D\&F Example: $F^\times$ acting on a vector space by scalar multiplication
Content:
\begin{wex}{D\&F Example: $F^\times$ acting on a vector space by scalar multiplication}
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $G=F^\times=F\setminus\{0\}$ act on $A=V$ by
$a\cdot v=av$ (scalar multiplication). Check the axioms and find the kernel.
\wrec D\&F give this as the prototype where the ``set'' $V$ carries extra structure but the acting
group is just the multiplicative group of scalars; the vector-space axioms supply (A1),(A2)
directly.
\wsol Axiom (A1): $1\cdot v=1v=v$ for all $v$, by the unit axiom of a vector space. Axiom (A2): for
$a,b\in F^\times$, $a\cdot(b\cdot v)=a(bv)=(ab)v=(ab)\cdot v$, the associativity of scalar
multiplication. So this is an action of $F^\times$ on $V$. Kernel: $a\cdot v=v$ for all
$v\in V$ means $av=v$, i.e.\ $(a-1)v=0$ for all $v$; choosing any $v\ne0$ forces $a=1$. Hence
$\ker\rho=\{1\}$ and (for $V\ne0$) the action is faithful.
Check. Each nonzero scalar $a$ gives the bijection $v\mapsto av$ of $V$ with inverse
$v\mapsto a^{-1} v$, confirming $\sigma_a\in\Sym(V)$; distinct scalars scale some $v\ne0$
differently, so $\rho$ is injective.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: D\&F Example: $D_{2n}$ acting on the $n$ vertices of a regular $n$-gon
Content:
\begin{wex}{D\&F Example: $D_{2n}$ acting on the $n$ vertices of a regular $n$-gon}
Show $D_{2n}$ acts on the set $A=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ of vertices, written cyclically, and describe
$\sigma_r$ and $\sigma_s$ for the standard generators (D\&F's convention $r^n=s^2=1$,
$sr=r^{-1} s$, with $s$ fixing vertex $1$).
\wrec D\&F introduce $D_{2n}$ as the symmetries of the regular $n$-gon, so the action on vertices is
the defining one; it motivates writing each symmetry as a permutation. The $D_8$ table
(Prop.~ [REF:p:d8@c1] ) is the special case $n=4$, which we do not redo here.
\wsol Each symmetry of the $n$-gon carries vertices to vertices bijectively, and composing
symmetries composes their vertex permutations, so (A1),(A2) hold (the symmetry doing nothing is the
identity permutation). For the rotation $r$ by $2\pi/n$,
\[
\sigma_r=(1\,2\,3\,\cdots\,n),
\]
an $n$-cycle. For the reflection $s$ fixing vertex $1$,
\[
\sigma_s=(2\;n)(3\;n{-}1)(4\;n{-}2)\cdots,
\]
fixing vertex $1$ and pairing $k$ with $n{+}2{-}k$ (so for even $n$ the middle vertex $\tfrac{n}{2}+1$
is also fixed; for odd $n$ only vertex $1$ is fixed). Since the generators map to nonidentity
permutations and a symmetry fixing every vertex is the identity, $\ker\rho=1$ and
$\rho\colon D_{2n}\to S_n$ is injective, so $D_{2n}\cong\rho(D_{2n})\sgr S_n$.
Check. For $n=4$, $\sigma_r=(1\,2\,3\,4)$ and $\sigma_s=(2\,4)$ (the pair $k\leftrightarrow
n{+}2{-}k$ gives $2\leftrightarrow4$, with $1,3$ fixed), recovering the $D_8$ data of
Prop.~ [REF:p:d8@c1] ; for $n=5$, $\sigma_s=(2\,5)(3\,4)$; the relation $sr=r^{-1} s$ becomes
$\sigma_s\sigma_r=\sigma_r^{-1}\sigma_s$ in $S_n$, the permutation identity verified there.
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Title: Reading the example list
Content:
\begin{remark}[Reading the example list]
Across D\&F's list the single fact at work is the correspondence of Thm.~ [REF:t:equiv@c1] : an action of
$G$ on $A$ is the same data as a homomorphism $G\to\Sym(A)$, and the kernel of the action equals the
kernel of that homomorphism, so ``faithful'' means ``injective.'' The examples populate the full
range: the trivial action ($\rho$ constant, $\ker\rho=G$); scalar multiplication, the natural
$S_n$-action, the left regular action, and $D_{2n}$ on vertices ($\rho$ injective, $\ker\rho=1$); and
the coset and conjugation actions worked above (intermediate kernels, the normal core and $Z(G)$).
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item $F^\times$ acts on $F$ by $g\cdot a=ga$; state the axioms used.
\item Show $Z$ acts on itself by $z\cdot a=z+a$.
\item Show $R$ acts on $R^2$ by $r\cdot(x,y)=(x+ry,y)$.
\item Fix $a$: show the kernel and $G_a=\{g:g\cdot a=a\}$ are subgroups.
\item Kernel of an action $=$ kernel of its permutation representation.
\item $G$ acts faithfully iff the kernel is $\{1\}$.
\item Show the scalar action on a vector space is faithful.
\item How do $(1\,2)$ and $(1\,2\,3)$ act on the six $2$-subsets of
 $\{1,2,3,4\}$?
\item Repeat for ordered $k$-tuples.
\item For which $k$ is the action of $S_n$ on (a) $k$-subsets, (b) $k$-tuples
 faithful?
\item Cycle decompositions of the eight elements of $D_8$ on the square's
 vertices.
\item For $n$ even, find the kernel of $D_{2n}$ on opposite-vertex pairs.
\item Find the kernel of the left regular action.
\item $g\cdot a=ag$ is not a left action when $G$ is non-abelian.
\item $g\cdot a=ag^{-1}$ is a left action.
\item $g\cdot a=gag^{-1}$ is a left action (conjugation).
\item Conjugation by $g$ is an automorphism; deduce $|x|=|gxg^{-1}|$.
\item $a\sim b\iff a=hb$ is an equivalence relation.
\item $H\le G$ acts by left multiplication; deduce Lagrange's theorem.
\item Rigid motions of a tetrahedron embed in $S_4$.
\item Rigid motions of a cube $\cong S_4$.
\item Rigid motions of an octahedron $\cong S_4$; dual to the cube.
\item Why is the cube's action on $3$ pairs of opposite faces not faithful?
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Groups > Group Actions > D\&F's example list: trivial action, scalar multiplication, and $D_{2n}$ on $n$ vertices
Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $G=D_8=\langle r,s\rangle$ act on the four vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ of the square (labeled counterclockwise) in the natural way, with $r$ the rotation sending $1\mapsto 2\mapsto 3\mapsto 4\mapsto 1$ and $s$ the reflection fixing the diagonal through vertices $1$ and $3$. For each of $r$, $s$, $rs$, and $r^2$, write the resulting permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ in cycle notation. Then verify directly that $\sigma_r\sigma_s=\sigma_{rs}$ (composing permutations right-to-left), confirming the action is a homomorphism on these elements.

\item Let $G$ act on itself by left multiplication: $g\cdot x=gx$ for $g,x\in G$. Prove this is a (left) group action, and prove it is faithful for every group $G$. Then show that for $G$ nontrivial this action has no fixed points, i.e. there is no $x\in G$ with $g\cdot x=x$ for all $g\in G$.

\item Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation: $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}$. Verify the two axioms of a group action. Show that the kernel of this action (the set of $g$ acting trivially, i.e. $gxg^{-1}=x$ for all $x$) equals $Z(G)$. Compute this kernel explicitly when $G=Q_8$ and when $G=S_3$.

\item Let $G=(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar5,\bar7\}$ act on the set $A=Z/(8)Z$ by $\bar a\cdot \bar x=\overline{ax}$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Check this is a well-defined action.
 \item Compute the orbit and the stabilizer of $\bar2$, and of $\bar1$.
 \item Determine the kernel of the action, i.e. the set of $\bar a$ with $\overline{ax}=\bar x$ for all $\bar x\inZ/(8)Z$.
 \end{enumerate}

\item Let $G$ act on a set $A$, and fix $a\in A$. Recall the stabilizer $G_a=\{g\in G\st g\cdot a=a\}$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Prove $G_a\sgr G$.
 \item Prove that if $b=g\cdot a$ lies in the orbit of $a$, then $G_b=gG_a g^{-1}$. Conclude that points in the same orbit have conjugate stabilizers.
 \end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $G$ acts on a set $A$. Define a relation on $A$ by $a\sim b$ iff $b=g\cdot a$ for some $g\in G$. Prove $\sim$ is an equivalence relation (its classes are the orbits). Then, for the action of $G=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\sgr S_5$ on $A=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, list all orbits explicitly.

\item Let $G=S_4$ act on the set $A$ of the three unordered partitions of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ into two pairs, namely $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$, $\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}$, $\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\}$, by relabeling points. This gives a homomorphism $\varphi:S_4\to \Sym(A)\cong S_3$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Compute the images $\varphi((1\,2))$ and $\varphi((1\,2\,3))$ as permutations of the three partitions.
 \item Show $\varphi$ is surjective.
 \item Identify $\ker\varphi$ as an explicit subgroup of $S_4$ and give its order.
 \end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $G$ be a group and $A$ a set. Let $\varphi:G\to\Sym(A)$ be a homomorphism, and define $g\cdot a=\varphi(g)(a)$. Prove that this defines a group action by checking the two diagrams below commute for all $g,h\in G$ (here $\cdot_g:A\to A$ denotes $a\mapsto g\cdot a$, and $\id$ is the identity map of $A$):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, "\textstyle\cdot_h"] \arrow[dr, "\textstyle\cdot_{gh}"'] & A \arrow[d, "\textstyle\cdot_g"] \\
& A
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, "\textstyle\cdot_1"] \arrow[dr, "\id"'] & A \arrow[d, "\id"] \\
& A
\end{tikzcd}\]
Conversely, prove that any action $G\times A\to A$ arises this way from a unique homomorphism $G\to\Sym(A)$, and state precisely what ``the action is faithful'' means about that homomorphism.

\item (Cayley's theorem via the regular representation.) Let $G$ be a group and let $\lambda:G\to\Sym(G)$ be the permutation representation of the left-multiplication action $g\cdot x=gx$, so $\lambda(g)$ is the map $x\mapsto gx$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Show $\lambda$ is a homomorphism by verifying the triangle commutes for all $g,h$:
 \[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]

 \end{tikzcd}\]
 \item Show $\ker\lambda=1$ and conclude $\lambda$ is injective, so $G$ embeds as a subgroup of $\Sym(G)$:
 \[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]

 \end{tikzcd}\]
 \item When $|G|=n$, deduce that $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_n$.
 \end{enumerate}

\item (Kernel of an action.) Let $G$ act on $A$ with permutation representation $\varphi:G\to\Sym(A)$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Prove $\ker\varphi=\bigcap_{a\in A}G_a$, the intersection of all point stabilizers, and that $\ker\varphi\nor G$.
 \item Using the first isomorphism theorem, fill in the unique dashed map making the diagram commute, and state what it is:
 \[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
 G \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & G/\ker\varphi \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\overline{\varphi}"] \\
 & \Sym(A)
 \end{tikzcd}\]
 \item Conclude that $G/\ker\varphi$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Sym(A)$.
 \end{enumerate}

\item Let $G$ be a group and $H\sgr G$ with $[G:H]=n$. Let $G$ act on the set $A=\{gH\st g\in G\}$ of left cosets by $g\cdot(xH)=(gx)H$, with permutation representation $\pi_H:G\to\Sym(A)\cong S_n$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Verify this is a well-defined action.
 \item Show $\ker\pi_H=\bigcap_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}$, the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$.
 \item Specialize to $G=S_3$ and $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ (so $n=3$). Describe $\pi_H$ explicitly and identify $\ker\pi_H$.
 \end{enumerate}

\item Let $\varphi:G\to\Sym(A)$ and $\psi:G\to\Sym(B)$ be two permutation representations, and suppose $f:A\to B$ is a bijection that is $G$-equivariant, i.e. $f(g\cdot a)=g\cdot f(a)$ for all $g\in G,\,a\in A$. Show this is equivalent to the commutativity of the square
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, "f"] \arrow[d, "\varphi(g)"'] & B \arrow[d, "\psi(g)"] \\
A \arrow[r, "f"'] & B
\end{tikzcd}\]
for every $g\in G$. Deduce that if such an $f$ exists then $\ker\varphi=\ker\psi$, and that $\psi(g)=f\circ\varphi(g)\circ f^{-1}$ exhibits the two representations as conjugate inside $\Sym(A)$ once $B$ is identified with $A$ via $f$.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 1.1.1] Determine which operations are associative: (a) $a\ast b=a-b$ on $Z$;

 (d) $(a,b)\ast(c,d)=(ad+bc,bd)$ on $Z\timesZ$; (e) $a\ast b=\frac{a}{b}$ on $Q-\{0\}$.
\item [DF 1.1.2] Which operations in the preceding problem are commutative?
\item [DF 1.1.6] Which are groups under addition: lowest-terms rationals with (a) odd
 denominator, (b) even denominator; (c) $|x|<1$; (d) $|x|\ge1$ together with $0$;
 (e) denominators $1$ or $2$; (f) denominators $1,2,$ or $3$.
\item [DF 1.1.11] Find the orders of every element of the additive group $Z/(12)Z$.
\item [DF 1.1.12] Find the orders of $\bar1,\overline{-1},\bar5,\bar7,\overline{-7},\overline{13}$
 in $(Z/(12)Z)^{\times}$.
\item [DF 1.1.13] Find the orders of $\bar1,\bar2,\bar6,\bar9,\overline{10},\overline{12},

 \overline{17}$ in $(Z/(36)Z)^{\times}$.

\item [DF 1.1.20] Show that $x$ and $x^{-1}$ have the same order.

\item [DF 1.4.3] Show $\GL_2(\F_2)$ is non-abelian.
\item [DF 1.5.1] Compute the order of each element of $Q_8$.
\item [DF 1.6.15] For $\pi:R^2\toR$, $\pi(x,y)=x$, find $\ker\pi$.
\item [DF 1.6.16] Find the kernels of the projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $A\times B$.
\item [DF 1.7.1] $F^\times$ acts on $F$ by $g\cdot a=ga$; state the axioms used.
\item [DF 1.7.2] Show $Z$ acts on itself by $z\cdot a=z+a$.
\item [DF 1.7.3] Show $R$ acts on $R^2$ by $r\cdot(x,y)=(x+ry,y)$.
\item [Artin 1.1] Prove the law $ab=a$ on a set $S$ is associative; for which $S$ does it have an identity?

 a cyclic subgroup of $C^\times$ of order $n$; (b) determine the product of all of them.

\item [DF 1.7.5] Show the kernel of an action equals the kernel of its permutation representation.
\item [DF 1.7.6] Show $G$ acts faithfully iff the kernel is $\{1\}$.
\item [DF 1.7.7] Show the scalar action on a vector space is faithful.
\item [DF 1.7.8] How do $(1\,2)$ and $(1\,2\,3)$ act on the six $2$-subsets of $\{1,2,3,4\}$?
\item [DF 1.7.11] Find the cycle decompositions of the eight elements of $D_8$ on the square's vertices.
\item [DF 1.7.13] Find the kernel of the left regular action.
\item [DF 1.7.14] Show $g\cdot a=ag$ is not a left action when $G$ is non-abelian.
\item [DF 1.7.15] Show $g\cdot a=ag^{-1}$ is a left action.
\item [DF 1.7.16] Show $g\cdot a=gag^{-1}$ is a left action (conjugation).
\item [DF 1.7.17] Show conjugation by $g$ is an automorphism; deduce $\ord{x}=\ord{gxg^{-1}}$.
\item [DF 1.7.18] Show $a\sim b\iff a=hb$ is an equivalence relation.
\item [Artin 1.3] For the shift map $s(n)=n+1$ on $Z^+$, prove $s$ has no right inverse but infinitely many left inverses.
\item [Artin 2.2] If $S$ has an associative law with identity, prove the invertible elements form a group.
\item [Artin 2.3] For $x,y,z,w\in G$: (a) solve $xyzw=1$ for $y$; (b) does $xyz=1$ force $yzx=1$? force $yxz=1$?
\item [Artin 2.4] Decide which of the listed pairs $H\subseteq G$ make $H$ a subgroup of $G$.
\item [Artin 2.5] Show that if $H\subseteq G$ has any identity, it must be the identity of $G$; same for inverses.
\item [Artin 2.6] Define $G^{\circ}$ with $a\ast b=ba$ on the same set; prove $G^{\circ}$ is a group.
\item [Artin 3.2] If $a,b$ are positive integers with $a+b$ prime, prove $\gcd(a,b)=1$.
\item [Artin 4.1] If $a$ has order $7$ and $a^3b=ba^3$, prove $ab=ba$.
\item [Artin 4.3] Prove that $ab$ and $ba$ have the same order.
\item [Artin 4.5] Prove that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, working with exponents.
\item [Artin 4.6] (a) For cyclic groups of orders $6,5,8$, how many elements generate the group?
 (b) Describe the count for arbitrary order $n$.
\item [Artin 4.7] If $x,y,xy$ all have order $2$, prove $H=\{1,x,y,xy\}$ is a subgroup of order $4$.
\item [Artin 4.10] Show by example that a product of elements of finite order need not have finite order;
 what if the group is abelian?
\item [Artin 5.1] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is surjective, prove that $G$ cyclic implies $G'$ cyclic, and $G$ abelian implies $G'$ abelian.
\item [Artin 5.2] Prove $K\cap H$ is a subgroup of $H$, and is normal in $H$ when $K\nor G$.
\item [Artin 5.3] For $\varphi:U\to F^\times$ sending an upper triangular $A$ to $a^2$, prove $\varphi$ is a
 homomorphism and find its kernel and image.
\item [Artin 5.4] For $f:R\toC^\times$, $f(x)=e^{ix}$, prove $f$ is a homomorphism and find its kernel and image.
\item [Artin 6.1] For $G'$ the group of matrices $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, decide whether
 $x\mapsto$ this matrix is an isomorphism $R\to G'$.
\item [Artin 6.2] Describe all homomorphisms $Z\toZ$; determine which are injective, surjective, isomorphisms.
\item [Artin 6.4] Prove that in any group $ab$ and $ba$ are conjugate.
\item [Artin 6.7] For $H\le G$ and fixed $g$, prove $gHg^{-1}$ is a subgroup of $G$.
\item [Artin 6.9] Prove a group $G$ and its opposite group $G^{\circ}$ are isomorphic.
\item [Artin 6.11] If $\{1,a\}$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, prove $a$ is in the center.
\item [Artin 7.1] Prove $a\sim b$ iff $b=gag^{-1}$ for some $g$ is an equivalence relation on $G$.
\item [Fraleigh 1.42] For associative $\ast$, show $H=\{a\in S\mid a\ast x=x\ast a for all x\}$ is closed under $\ast$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.10] For $n\inZ^+$ and $nZ=\{nm\mid m\inZ\}$: (a) show $\langle nZ,+\rangle$ is a group; (b) show $nZ\congZ$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.19] On $S=R\setminus\{-1\}$ with $a\ast b=a+b+ab$: (a) show $\ast$ is a binary operation;
 (b) show $\langle S,\ast\rangle$ is a group; (c) solve $2\ast x\ast3=7$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.28] If $a\neq e$ has order $2$ in a group, prove $b^{-1} ab$ has order $2$ for any $b$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.29] If a finite group has even order, prove there is $a\neq e$ with $a\ast a=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.31] Prove a group has exactly one idempotent element.
\item [Fraleigh 2.32] Prove that if $x\ast x=e$ for all $x$, then $G$ is abelian.
\item [Fraleigh 2.33] By induction, prove $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$ in an abelian group.
\item [Fraleigh 2.36] In a finite group, prove that for any $a$ there is $n\inZ^+$ with $a^n=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.37] If $(ab)^2=a^2b^2$ in a group, prove $ab=ba$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.39] If $abc=e$ in a group, prove $bca=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.42] Prove $(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$.
\item [Fraleigh 3.35] Prove or disprove: for any $n$ and $a\inZ/(n)Z$, $x+_n x=a$ has at most two solutions.
\item [Fraleigh 3.44] Prove that $\langle Z/(n)Z,+_n\rangle$ is associative without using associativity of $U_n$.
\item [Fraleigh 4.14] Write the group table for $D_3$ and compare with $S_3$; are they isomorphic?
\item [Fraleigh 4.18] Verify that $H=\{\iota,\mu,\rho^2,\mu\rho^2\}\subseteq D_4$ is a group.
\item [Fraleigh 4.30] In $D_n$ prove $\rho^k\mu=\mu\rho^{n-k}$.
\item [Fraleigh 4.31] Show $S_n$ is nonabelian for $n\ge3$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.35] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is a homomorphism and $a\in\ker\varphi$, show $gag^{-1}\in\ker\varphi$ for all $g$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.36] Prove a homomorphism $\varphi$ is one-to-one iff $\ker\varphi$ is trivial.
\item [Fraleigh 8.37] For a homomorphism $\varphi$, show $\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)$ iff $a^{-1} b\in\ker\varphi$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.39] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ and $\gamma:G'\to G''$ are homomorphisms, show $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is a homomorphism.
\item [Fraleigh 8.48] Show that if $\sigma$ is a cycle of odd length, then $\sigma^2$ is a cycle.
\end{exers}

\item [Artin 4.3] Prove that $ab$ and $ba$ have the same order.
\item [Artin 4.5] Prove that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, working with exponents.
\item [Artin 4.6] (a) For cyclic groups of orders $6,5,8$, how many elements generate the group?
   (b) Describe the count for arbitrary order $n$.
\item [Artin 4.7] If $x,y,xy$ all have order $2$, prove $H=\{1,x,y,xy\}$ is a subgroup of order $4$.
\item [Artin 4.10] Show by example that a product of elements of finite order need not have finite order;
   what if the group is abelian?
\item [Artin 5.1] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is surjective, prove that $G$ cyclic implies $G'$ cyclic, and $G$ abelian implies $G'$ abelian.
\item [Artin 5.2] Prove $K\cap H$ is a subgroup of $H$, and is normal in $H$ when $K\nor G$.
\item [Artin 5.3] For $\varphi:U\to F^\times$ sending an upper triangular $A$ to $a^2$, prove $\varphi$ is a
   homomorphism and find its kernel and image.
\item [Artin 5.4] For $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}^\times$, $f(x)=e^{ix}$, prove $f$ is a homomorphism and find its kernel and image.
\item [Artin 6.1] For $G'$ the group of matrices $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, decide whether
   $x\mapsto$ this matrix is an isomorphism $\mathbb{R}\to G'$.
\item [Artin 6.2] Describe all homomorphisms $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$; determine which are injective, surjective, isomorphisms.
\item [Artin 6.4] Prove that in any group $ab$ and $ba$ are conjugate.
\item [Artin 6.7] For $H\le G$ and fixed $g$, prove $gHg^{-1}$ is a subgroup of $G$.
\item [Artin 6.9] Prove a group $G$ and its opposite group $G^{\circ}$ are isomorphic.
\item [Artin 6.11] If $\{1,a\}$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, prove $a$ is in the center.
\item [Artin 7.1] Prove $a\sim b$ iff $b=gag^{-1}$ for some $g$ is an equivalence relation on $G$.
\item [Fraleigh 1.42] For associative $\ast$, show $H=\{a\in S\mid a\ast x=x\ast a\text{ for all }x\}$ is closed under $\ast$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.10] For $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and $n\mathbb{Z}=\{nm\mid m\in\mathbb{Z}\}$: (a) show $\langle n\mathbb{Z},+\rangle$ is a group; (b) show $n\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.19] On $S=\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}$ with $a\ast b=a+b+ab$: (a) show $\ast$ is a binary operation;
   (b) show $\langle S,\ast\rangle$ is a group; (c) solve $2\ast x\ast3=7$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.28] If $a\neq e$ has order $2$ in a group, prove $b^{-1} ab$ has order $2$ for any $b$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.29] If a finite group has even order, prove there is $a\neq e$ with $a\ast a=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.31] Prove a group has exactly one idempotent element.
\item [Fraleigh 2.32] Prove that if $x\ast x=e$ for all $x$, then $G$ is abelian.
\item [Fraleigh 2.33] By induction, prove $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$ in an abelian group.
\item [Fraleigh 2.36] In a finite group, prove that for any $a$ there is $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ with $a^n=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.37] If $(ab)^2=a^2b^2$ in a group, prove $ab=ba$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.39] If $abc=e$ in a group, prove $bca=e$.
\item [Fraleigh 2.42] Prove $(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$.
\item [Fraleigh 3.35] Prove or disprove: for any $n$ and $a\in\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $x+_n x=a$ has at most two solutions.
\item [Fraleigh 3.44] Prove that $\langle \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+_n\rangle$ is associative without using associativity of $U_n$.
\item [Fraleigh 4.14] Write the group table for $D_3$ and compare with $S_3$; are they isomorphic?
\item [Fraleigh 4.18] Verify that $H=\{\iota,\mu,\rho^2,\mu\rho^2\}\subseteq D_4$ is a group.
\item [Fraleigh 4.30] In $D_n$ prove $\rho^k\mu=\mu\rho^{n-k}$.
\item [Fraleigh 4.31] Show $S_n$ is nonabelian for $n\ge3$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.35] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is a homomorphism and $a\in\ker\varphi$, show $gag^{-1}\in\ker\varphi$ for all $g$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.36] Prove a homomorphism $\varphi$ is one-to-one iff $\ker\varphi$ is trivial.
\item [Fraleigh 8.37] For a homomorphism $\varphi$, show $\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)$ iff $a^{-1} b\in\ker\varphi$.
\item [Fraleigh 8.39] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ and $\gamma:G'\to G''$ are homomorphisms, show $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is a homomorphism.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Subgroups: definition and recognition
Type: definition
Label: d:subgroup@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Let $G$ be a group under an operation $\cdot$. A subset $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup of $G$, written $H\sgr G$, if $H$ is itself a group under the operation $\cdot$ restricted to $H$. We write $H\psgr G$ when $H\sgr G$ and $H\neq G$ (a proper subgroup). Every group has the two trivial subgroups $\{1\}$ and $G$ itself.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
($\Longrightarrow$) If $H\sgr G$ then $H$ is a group, so it is nonempty, its operation lands inside $H$ (giving (1)), and each $a\in H$ has an inverse in $H$ (giving (2)).

($\Leftarrow$) Assume (0),(1),(2). By (1) the restricted operation is a genuine binary operation on $H$. Associativity holds in $H$ because it already holds for all elements of $G$, in particular for elements of $H$. Since $H\neq\varnothing$, pick $a\in H$; by (2) $a^{-1}\in H$, and by (1) $aa^{-1}=1\in H$, so $H$ contains an identity. For each $a\in H$, (2) gives $a^{-1}\in H$, which is a two-sided inverse. Hence $H$ is a group, i.e. $H\sgr G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Identity and inverses agree] 
If $H\sgr G$ then the identity $1_H$ of $H$ equals the identity $1_G$ of $G$, and for $h\in H$ the inverse of $h$ computed in $H$ equals the inverse $h^{-1}$ computed in $G$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In $H$ we have $1_H\,1_H=1_H$. Viewing this equation in $G$ and multiplying both sides on the right by $(1_H)^{-1}$ (the inverse in $G$, which exists since $1_H\in G$) gives $1_H=1_G$. For $h\in H$ let $h'$ be its inverse in $H$, so $hh'=1_H=1_G$. Multiplying on the left in $G$ by $h^{-1}$ gives $h'=h^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

Label: r:two-step@c2
Content:
\begin{remark} 
Conditions (1) and (2) of Proposition~ [REF:p:subgrp-long@c2] can be merged into one (the ``one-step'' test): a nonempty $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup iff $ab^{-1}\in H$ for all $a,b\in H$. Indeed, taking $a=b$ gives $1\in H$; taking $a=1$ gives $b^{-1}\in H$ for all $b\in H$; and then $a(b^{-1})^{-1}=ab\in H$ gives closure. For finite $H$ one may even drop (2): a nonempty finite subset closed under products is a subgroup, because powers $a,a^2,a^3,\dots$ must repeat, forcing some $a^k=1$ and $a^{-1}=a^{k-1}\in H$.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Subgroups: definition and recognition
Type: method
Title: The ``Is $H$ a subgroup?'' checklist
Content:
\begin{method}{The ``Is $H$ a subgroup?'' checklist}
Recognition trigger. Use this whenever you are handed a subset $H$ of a known group $G$ and asked whether $H\sgr G$, or asked to prove some described set is a subgroup. Do NOT re-verify associativity --- it is inherited from $G$ for free.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Nonempty / identity. Exhibit a concrete element of $H$; the cleanest is to show $1_G\in H$. If $1_G\notin H$, stop: $H$ is not a subgroup.
\item Closed under products. Take arbitrary $a,b\in H$ (write out what membership means), form $ab$, and verify $ab$ satisfies the defining condition of $H$.
\item Closed under inverses. Take arbitrary $a\in H$, form $a^{-1}$, and verify $a^{-1}\in H$.
\end{enumerate}
Shortcuts. If $H$ is finite and nonempty, step (3) is automatic once step (2) holds (Remark~ [REF:r:two-step@c2] ). To disprove, it suffices to break one clause with a single explicit counterexample.
\end{method}

Title: $nZ\sgrZ$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$nZ\sgrZ$}
Fix $n\inZ$ and let $nZ=\{nk\st k\inZ\}$. Show $nZ\sgr(Z,+)$.
\wrec A described subset of a known group $(Z,+)$: run the three-clause checklist. The operation is written additively, so ``product $ab$'' means the sum $a+b$, ``identity $1$'' means $0$, and ``inverse $a^{-1}$'' means $-a$.
\wsol Nonempty/identity: $0=n\cdot 0\in nZ$, so $0\in nZ$ and $nZ\neq\varnothing$. Closed under $+$: take $a,b\in nZ$, say $a=nk$ and $b=n\ell$ with $k,\ell\inZ$. Then $a+b=nk+n\ell=n(k+\ell)$, and $k+\ell\inZ$, so $a+b\in nZ$. Closed under inverses: for $a=nk\in nZ$ we have $-a=-nk=n(-k)$ with $-k\inZ$, so $-a\in nZ$. All three clauses hold, hence $nZ\sgrZ$. Check. For $n=3$, $6,9\in 3Z$ and $6+9=15=3\cdot 5\in 3Z$; also $-6=3\cdot(-2)\in 3Z$. Note $nZ=Z$ when $n=\pm1$ and $nZ=\{0\}$ when $n=0$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\SL_n(R)\sgr\GL_n(R)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\SL_n(R)\sgr\GL_n(R)$}
Let $\SL_n(R)=\{A\in\GL_n(R)\st\det A=1\}$. Show it is a subgroup of $\GL_n(R)$ (invertible real $n\times n$ matrices under multiplication).
\wrec A subset cut out by a condition ($\det=1$) inside a matrix group. Run the checklist, using the multiplicativity of $\det$: $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$ and $\det(A^{-1})=(\det A)^{-1}$.
\wsol Identity: $\det(I)=1$, so $I\in\SL_n(R)$ and the set is nonempty. Closed under products: if $A,B\in\SL_n(R)$ then $\det A=\det B=1$, so $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)=1\cdot 1=1$, hence $AB\in\SL_n(R)$ (and $AB$ is invertible, so it lies in $\GL_n(R)$). Closed under inverses: if $A\in\SL_n(R)$ then $\det A=1\neq 0$, so $A^{-1}$ exists, and $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det(A)=1/1=1$, hence $A^{-1}\in\SL_n(R)$. Therefore $\SL_n(R)\sgr\GL_n(R)$. Check. $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ has $\det A=2-1=1$, and $A^{-1}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{psmallmatrix}$ has $\det=2-1=1$; both lie in $\SL_2(R)$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Torsion subgroup of an abelian group
Content:
\begin{wex}{Torsion subgroup of an abelian group}
Let $G$ be abelian and set $T=\{g\in G\st \ord{g}<\infty\}$ (the elements of finite order). Show $T\sgr G$.
\wrec Described as ``all elements satisfying a finiteness condition.'' The condition is about orders, so the tool is: $\ord{g}<\infty$ means $g^m=1$ for some $m\geq 1$. We will need commutativity to combine two finite-order elements --- this is exactly where abelianness is used.
\wsol Identity: $\ord{1}=1<\infty$, so $1\in T$ and $T\neq\varnothing$. Closed under products: let $a,b\in T$, say $a^m=1$ and $b^n=1$ with $m,n\geq 1$. Since $G$ is abelian, $a$ and $b$ commute, so $(ab)^{mn}=a^{mn}b^{mn}=(a^m)^n(b^n)^m=1^n\cdot 1^m=1$. Thus $\ord{ab}$ divides $mn$, in particular $\ord{ab}<\infty$, so $ab\in T$. Closed under inverses: if $a\in T$ with $a^m=1$, then $(a^{-1})^m=(a^m)^{-1}=1^{-1}=1$, so $\ord{a^{-1}}<\infty$ and $a^{-1}\in T$. Hence $T\sgr G$. Check. In $G=(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ (abelian, order $8$), $2$ has order $4$ ($2,4,8,16\equiv1$) and $4$ has order $2$; their product $2\cdot4=8$ has order $4$ ($8,64\equiv4,512\equiv2,\dots$ returns to $1$ at the $4$th power), again of finite order, consistent with $T=G$ here.
\end{wex}

Title: NON-example: the odd integers
Content:
\begin{wex}{NON-example: the odd integers}
Let $O=\{odd integers\}=\{\dots,-3,\allowbreak-1,\allowbreak1,\allowbreak3,\dots\}\subseteqZ$. Decide whether $O\sgr(Z,+)$.
\wrec A described subset of $(Z,+)$: run the checklist, but as soon as one clause fails we may stop and declare ``not a subgroup.'' Quickest clause to test for $O$ is the identity, since $0$ is even.
\wsol Identity fails: the additive identity of $Z$ is $0$, which is even, so $0\notin O$. By Proposition~ [REF:p:agree@c2] a subgroup must contain $1_G=0$, so $O$ is not a subgroup. Closure also fails, independently: $1\in O$ and $3\in O$ but $1+3=4\notin O$ (sum of two odds is even). Conclusion. $O\not\sgrZ$: it lacks the identity $0$ (although $O\neq\varnothing$) and fails clause (1). Check. Two failures confirm each other; a single one already suffices.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: NON-example vs example inside $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{NON-example vs example inside $D_8$}
In $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$, compare the subsets $A=\{1,s\}$ and $B=\{1,s,sr\}$.
\wrec Two finite subsets of a finite group. By the finite shortcut (Remark~ [REF:r:two-step@c2] ), once a nonempty finite set is closed under products it is automatically a subgroup, so closure under products is the decisive test. Use the relation $srs=r^{-1}$, i.e. $sr=r^{-1} s$, to simplify products.
\wsol \emph{For $A=\{1,s\}$:} it is nonempty and finite. Products: $1\cdot1=1$, $1\cdot s=s$, $s\cdot1=s$, and $s\cdot s=s^2=1$. Every product lands in $A$, so $A$ is closed; being finite and nonempty, $A\sgr D_8$ (indeed $\ord{s}=2$ so $A=\langle s\rangle$).
\emph{For $B=\{1,s,sr\}$:} test closure. Compute $s\cdot(sr)=(ss)r=s^2r=r$. But $r\notin B$ (the elements of $B$ are $1$, $s$, and $sr$, none equal to $r$ since $r\neq 1$, $r\neq s$, and $r\neq sr$ as that would force $s=1$). Closure under products fails, so $B\not\sgr D_8$. Check. $|B|=3$ does not divide $|D_8|=8$, so by Lagrange's theorem (Chapter 3) $B$ could never have been a subgroup --- consistent with our direct computation.
\end{wex}

Title: The unit circle $S^1\sgrC^\times$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The unit circle $S^1\sgrC^\times$}
Let $S^1=\{z\inC^\times\st |z|=1\}$ where $C^\times=C\setminus\{0\}$ under multiplication. Show $S^1\sgrC^\times$.
\wrec A subset of the multiplicative group $C^\times$ cut out by the condition $|z|=1$. The relevant tool is multiplicativity of modulus: $|zw|=|z|\,|w|$ and $|z^{-1}|=|z|^{-1}$ for $z\neq0$.
\wsol Identity: $|1|=1$, so $1\in S^1$ and $S^1\neq\varnothing$. Closed under products: if $z,w\in S^1$ then $|z|=|w|=1$, so $|zw|=|z|\,|w|=1\cdot1=1$, hence $zw\in S^1$. Closed under inverses: if $z\in S^1$ then $z\neq0$ and $|z^{-1}|=1/|z|=1/1=1$, so $z^{-1}\in S^1$. Therefore $S^1\sgrC^\times$. Check. $z=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}i$ has $|z|^2=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$; its inverse is its conjugate $\bar z=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}i$, which also has modulus $1$ and lies in $S^1$.
\end{wex}

Title: A bare-definition / one-step variation: $\langle i\rangle\sgr Q_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A bare-definition / one-step variation: $\langle i\rangle\sgr Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$, show $H=\{1,i,-1,-i\}$ is a subgroup, using the one-step test $ab^{-1}\in H$.
\wrec We are told to use the one-step criterion (Remark~ [REF:r:two-step@c2] ): for nonempty $H$, $H\sgr G$ iff $ab^{-1}\in H$ for all $a,b\in H$. Trigger: a finite explicit subset and an instruction (or convenience) to do a single combined check. Recall in $Q_8$: $i^2=-1$, $i^{-1}=-i$, $(-1)^{-1}=-1$, $(-i)^{-1}=i$.
\wsol $H\neq\varnothing$ since $1\in H$. Note $H=\{i^0,i^1,i^2,i^3\}=\langle i\rangle$, the cyclic group generated by $i$ (as $i$ has order $4$: $i,i^2=-1,i^3=-i,i^4=1$). For any $a,b\in H$, both are powers of $i$, say $a=i^p,b=i^q$; then $ab^{-1}=i^p(i^q)^{-1}=i^{p-q}$, which is again a power of $i$ and hence in $H$. Thus the one-step condition holds and $H\sgr Q_8$. Check, a sample: $a=i$, $b=-1=i^2$ give $ab^{-1}=i\cdot(-1)^{-1}=i\cdot(-1)=-i\in H$; and $a=-i$, $b=i$ give $ab^{-1}=(-i)(i^{-1})=(-i)(-i)=i^2=-1\in H$. Both land in $H$, as predicted.
\end{wex}

Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Subgroups: definition and recognition > Closure-check table.
Type: prose
Content:
The decisive computation in the $D_8$ non-example is a closure table: list the candidate elements down the side and across the top, fill in each product, and a subset is closed exactly when every entry lies back in the subset. For $B=\{1,s,sr\}\subseteq D_8$ the table immediately exposes the escape $s\cdot sr=r\notin B$.

 
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc}
$\cdot$ & $1$ & $s$ & $sr$\\
\hline
$1$ & $1$ & $s$ & $sr$\\
$s$ & $s$ & $1$ & $r$\\
$sr$ & $sr$ & $\mathbf{r^{-1}}$ & $1$\\
\end{tabular}
 

The bold entries $r$ and $r^{-1}=r^3$ both lie outside $B$, so $B$ is not closed; even one such entry would disqualify it. The entries are computed from $sr=r^{-1} s$: namely $s\cdot sr=s^2r=r$, and $sr\cdot s=s(rs)=s(s r^{-1})=s^2r^{-1}=r^{-1}$. The remaining product $sr\cdot sr=s\,r\,s\,r=s(rs)r=s(sr^{-1})r=s^2r^{-1} r=r^{-1} r=1$ lands back in $B$, but the two off-list entries $r$ and $r^{-1}$ already break closure.

Type: proposition
Label: p:subcrit@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
Let $G$ be a group and $H\subseteq G$. Then $H\sgr G$ if and only if
\[
(a)\quad H\neq\varnothing,\qquadand\qquad(b)\quad \forall\,x,y\in H,\ \ xy^{-1}\in H.
\]
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > The subgroup criterion
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-b1ca30853b178a88b876
Content:
\begin{proof}
($\Longrightarrow$) If $H\sgr G$ then $H$ contains the identity, so $H\neq\varnothing$, giving (a). For $x,y\in H$, subgroup closure under inverses gives $y^{-1}\in H$, and closure under the product gives $xy^{-1}\in H$, giving (b).

($\Leftarrow$, that is the substantive direction) Assume (a) and (b). By (a) pick some $a\in H$. Apply (b) with $x=y=a$: then $aa^{-1}=1\in H$, so $H$ contains the identity. Next, for any $a\in H$, apply (b) with $x=1$ and $y=a$: $1\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\in H$, so $H$ is closed under inverses. Finally, for $a,b\in H$ we have just shown $b^{-1}\in H$; apply (b) with $x=a$, $y=b^{-1}$ to get $a(b^{-1})^{-1}=ab\in H$, so $H$ is closed under the product. Associativity holds in $H$ because it holds in $G$ and $H\subseteq G$. Thus $H$ is a group under the operation of $G$, i.e. $H\sgr G$.
\end{proof}

\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > The subgroup criterion
Type: method
Title: One-step criterion vs. the full definition
Content:
\begin{method}{One-step criterion vs. the full definition}
Recognition trigger. You are handed a subset $H$ of a known group $G$ and asked ``is $H$ a subgroup?'' Do NOT re-verify associativity --- it is inherited. Instead:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Nonempty. Exhibit one explicit element of $H$ (usually check $1\in H$; that already settles (a)).
\item One-step closure. Take arbitrary $x,y\in H$, write the defining property each satisfies, and compute $xy^{-1}$. Show $xy^{-1}$ satisfies the same defining property.
\item Conclude $H\sgr G$ by Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] .
\end{enumerate}
When to use which: use the one-step criterion whenever $H$ is described by a closed-form condition (a determinant value, a modulus, a divisibility, a matrix shape). Use the raw two-step version (check products and inverses separately) only when computing $xy^{-1}$ in one shot is awkward and splitting is clearer. Never bother re-proving associativity.
\end{method}

\begin{wex}{$nZ\sgrZ$}
Show that $nZ=\{nk\st k\inZ\}$ is a subgroup of $(Z,+)$ for every integer $n\ge 0$.
\wrec $nZ$ is a subset of the group $Z$ defined by a closed-form condition (``is a multiple of $n$''), so the one-step criterion applies. The operation is $+$, so ``$xy^{-1}$'' here means $x-y$.
\wsol (a) Nonempty: $0=n\cdot 0\in nZ$. (b) One-step: take $x,y\in nZ$, say $x=na$ and $y=nb$ with $a,b\inZ$. Then
\[
x-y=na-nb=n(a-b),
\]
and $a-b\inZ$, so $x-y\in nZ$. By Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] , $nZ\sgrZ$.\\
Check. With $n=3$, $x=6$, $y=15$: $x-y=-9=3\cdot(-3)\in 3Z$. Correct.
\end{wex}

x-y=na-nb=n(a-b),
\]
and $a-b\in\mathbb{Z}$, so $x-y\in n\mathbb{Z}$. By Proposition~\ref{p:subcrit@c2}, $n\mathbb{Z}\sgr\mathbb{Z}$.\\

Title: $\{A\in\GL_n(R)\st \det A=\pm1\}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\{A\in\GL_n(R)\st \det A=\pm1\}$}
Let $H=\{A\in\GL_n(R)\st \det A\in\{1,-1\}\}$. Show $H\sgr\GL_n(R)$.
\wrec $H$ is a subset of the group $\GL_n(R)$ cut out by the condition $\det A=\pm1$. The trigger is the closed-form determinant condition; use the one-step test with the multiplicativity $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ and $\det(A^{-1})=(\det A)^{-1}$.
\wsol (a) Nonempty: $\det I=1$, so $I\in H$. (b) One-step: take $A,B\in H$, so $\det A=\pm1$ and $\det B=\pm1$. Then $B$ is invertible (determinant nonzero) and
\[

\begin{wex}{The unit circle $\{z\inC^\times\st |z|=1\}$}

Title: Unipotent upper-triangular matrices
Content:
\begin{wex}{Unipotent upper-triangular matrices}
Let $U=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\st a\inR\right\}\subseteq\GL_2(R)$ (upper triangular, $1$'s on the diagonal). Show $U\sgr\GL_2(R)$.
\wrec Subset of $\GL_2(R)$ defined by a matrix shape condition. One-step test; the trick is to compute the inverse of such a matrix explicitly, then multiply.
\wsol Write $M(a)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Nonempty: $M(0)=I\in U$. (b) One-step: take $M(a),M(b)\in U$. First, $\det M(b)=1\neq 0$ so it is invertible, and
\[
M(b)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=M(-b).
\]
Then
\[
M(a)M(b)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&a-b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=M(a-b)\in U.
\]
By Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] , $U\sgr\GL_2(R)$.\\
Check. $a=5$, $b=2$: $M(5)M(2)^{-1}=M(3)$, which has $1$'s on the diagonal and lies in $U$. Indeed $a\mapsto M(a)$ is a bijection $R\to U$ with $M(a)M(b)=M(a+b)$, so $U$ is just $(R,+)$ in disguise. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: A non-example: $xy^{-1}\notin H$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-example: $xy^{-1}\notin H$}
In $G=(Z,+)$, let $H=\{n\inZ\st n\ge 0\}=Z_{\ge0}$ (the nonnegative integers). Decide whether $H\sgrZ$.
\wrec This is a disproof task. $H$ is nonempty and closed under the product ($+$), which tempts one into thinking it is a subgroup --- but the criterion demands $xy^{-1}\in H$, i.e.\ $x-y\in H$. To refute (b), exhibit a single pair $x,y\in H$ with $x-y\notin H$.
\wsol (a) $0\in H$, so nonempty: fine. (b) fails: take $x=1\in H$, $y=2\in H$. Then
\[
xy^{-1}=x-y=1-2=-1\notin H,
\]
since $-1<0$. So condition (b) of Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] fails for the explicit pair $(1,2)$. Therefore $H\not\sgrZ$.\\
Check. The underlying reason is that $H$ contains no inverses: $1\in H$ but $-1\notin H$. This is exactly the pitfall above --- closure under products is not enough for an infinite set.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Label: p:finsubcrit@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
Let $G$ be a group and let $H$ be a finite nonempty subset of $G$ that is closed under the operation of $G$ (i.e.\ $xy\in H$ for all $x,y\in H$). Then $H\sgr G$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:finsubcrit@c2

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-11e71ff07102a586aa71
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] it suffices to show that for each $x\in H$ we have $x^{-1}\in H$ (closure under products then gives $xy^{-1}\in H$). Fix $x\in H$. By closure, all positive powers $x,x^2,x^3,\dots$ lie in $H$. Since $H$ is finite, these cannot all be distinct, so there exist integers $i<j$ with $x^i=x^j$. Cancelling in $G$ gives $x^{\,j-i}=1$ with $n:=j-i\ge 1$, so $1=x^n\in H$. If $n=1$ then $x=1$ and $x^{-1}=1=x\in H$. If $n\ge 2$ then
\[
x\cdot x^{\,n-1}=x^n=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^{-1}=x^{\,n-1},
\]
and $x^{\,n-1}\in H$ because $n-1\ge1$ is a positive power. Either way $x^{-1}\in H$, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: When the finite criterion saves work
Content:
\begin{method}{When the finite criterion saves work}
Recognition trigger. $H$ is a finite subset of $G$ (e.g.\ an explicitly listed finite set, or any subset of a finite group) and you want to prove $H\sgr G$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Confirm $H$ is nonempty and finite.
\item Check closure under the product ONLY: verify $xy\in H$ for all $x,y\in H$ (for a small explicit set, fill in the multiplication table; for a structured set, give a closure argument).
\item Invoke Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] ; inverses and the identity come for free.
\end{enumerate}
Use this whenever checking $x^{-1}\in H$ separately would be extra labor --- the finite criterion lets you skip the inverse check entirely.
\end{method}

Title: $\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}=\langle r\rangle\sgr D_8$ via the finite criterion
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}=\langle r\rangle\sgr D_8$ via the finite criterion}
In $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$, let $H=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$. Show $H\sgr D_8$.
\wrec $H$ is a finite ($4$-element) subset of the finite group $D_8$. The finite criterion (Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] ) applies: just check closure under the product; do not bother with inverses.
\wsol Nonempty and finite: $|H|=4$. Closure: every element of $H$ is a power $r^i$ with $0\le i\le 3$, and $r^i r^j=r^{i+j}=r^{(i+j)\bmod 4}$ since $r^4=1$. The exponent $(i+j)\bmod4\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, so $r^i r^j\in H$ always. Concretely:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\cdot & 1 & r & r^2 & r^3\\\hline
1 & 1 & r & r^2 & r^3\\
r & r & r^2 & r^3 & 1\\
r^2 & r^2 & r^3 & 1 & r\\
r^3 & r^3 & 1 & r & r^2
\end{array}
\]
Every entry lies in $H$, so $H$ is closed under the product. By Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] , $H\sgr D_8$. (Indeed $H=\langle r\rangle$, the cyclic rotation subgroup of order $4$.)\\
Check. Inverses appear automatically, as promised: $r^{-1}=r^3$, $(r^2)^{-1}=r^2$, $(r^3)^{-1}=r$, all in $H$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $V_4=\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}\sgr D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$V_4=\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}\sgr D_8$}
In $D_8$ let $H=\{1,\,r^2,\,s,\,sr^2\}$. Show $H\sgr D_8$.
\wrec Finite $4$-element subset of finite $D_8$; check product-closure only. Here we must use the relation $sr=r^{-1} s=r^3 s$ to move $s$ past $r$, and $r^4=1$, $s^2=1$.
\wsol Nonempty, finite: $|H|=4$. Closure: note $r^2$ commutes with $s$, since $sr^2=(sr)r=r^3 s r=r^3 r^3 s=r^6 s=r^2 s$ (using $sr=r^3s$ twice and $r^6=r^2$). So $sr^2=r^2 s$, and each element squares as $1^2=1$, $(r^2)^2=r^4=1$, $s^2=1$, $(sr^2)^2=sr^2sr^2=s(r^2 s)r^2=s(sr^2)r^2=s^2 r^4=1$. The products:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\cdot & 1 & r^2 & s & sr^2\\\hline
1 & 1 & r^2 & s & sr^2\\
r^2 & r^2 & 1 & sr^2 & s\\
s & s & sr^2 & 1 & r^2\\
sr^2 & sr^2 & s & r^2 & 1
\end{array}
\]
For instance $r^2\cdot s=r^2 s=sr^2\in H$, and $s\cdot sr^2=s^2 r^2=r^2\in H$, and $sr^2\cdot s=s r^2 s=s\,s r^2=r^2$ (using $r^2 s=sr^2$). Every entry is in $H$, so $H$ is closed. By Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] , $H\sgr D_8$. (This is a Klein four-group $V_4$ inside $D_8$.)\\
Check. The table is symmetric with $1$ on the diagonal, so each element is its own inverse, all inside $H$. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Finite criterion needs finiteness: where the power argument stalls}
Take $G=(Q^\times,\cdot)$ and $H=\{2^k\st k\inZ_{\ge0}\}=\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}$. Is $H$ closed under multiplication? Does the finite criterion apply? Decide whether $H\sgrQ^\times$.
\wrec This probes the hypothesis of Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] : $H$ is closed under products but infinite, so the finite criterion does not apply --- and we expect inverses to be missing. Fall back to the one-step criterion to disprove.
\wsol Closure under product: $2^a\cdot 2^b=2^{a+b}\in H$ for $a,b\ge0$, so yes, $H$ is closed under multiplication. But $H$ is infinite, so Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] gives no conclusion. One-step test fails: take $x=1\in H$ and $y=2\in H$; then
\[
xy^{-1}=1\cdot 2^{-1}=\tfrac12\notin H,
\]
since $\tfrac12=2^{-1}$ has a negative exponent and $H$ contains only nonnegative powers. So condition (b) of Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] fails, and $H\not\sgrQ^\times$.\\
Check. Tracing the proof of Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] , the powers $2,2^2,2^3,\dots$ are all distinct (no repeat $x^i=x^j$), so the argument that forces $x^{-1}$ never triggers --- exactly because $H$ is infinite. Correct, and it shows the finiteness hypothesis cannot be dropped.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
Do not apply the finite criterion to a finite subset of an infinite group without first checking closure carefully, and never apply it to an infinite set. The set $\{1,2,4,\dots\}$ above is closed under products yet is not a subgroup --- its infiniteness is the whole reason.
\end{pitfall}

Title: The chains $Z\sgrQ\sgrR\sgrC$ and $Q^\times\sgrR^\times\sgrC^\times$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The chains $Z\sgrQ\sgrR\sgrC$ and $Q^\times\sgrR^\times\sgrC^\times$}
Show that under addition $Z\sgrQ\sgrR\sgrC$, and that under multiplication $Q^\times\sgrR^\times\sgrC^\times$ (nonzero elements).
\wrec Each link is a subset of a known group closed under the operation, so run the one-step criterion (Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] ) on each inclusion; transitivity then chains them. Additively ``$xy^{-1}$'' means $x-y$; multiplicatively it means $x/y$.
\wsol Additive chain. For $Z\sgrQ$: $0\inZ$, and for $x,y\inZ$, $x-y\inZ$. For $Q\sgrR$: $0\inQ$, and a difference of rationals is rational. For $R\sgrC$: $0\inR$, and a difference of reals is real. By Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] each is a subgroup, and by transitivity $Z\sgrC$ as well. Multiplicative chain. For $Q^\times\sgrR^\times$: $1\inQ^\times$, and for nonzero rationals $x,y$ the quotient $x/y$ is a nonzero rational. For $R^\times\sgrC^\times$: $1\inR^\times$, and a quotient of nonzero reals is a nonzero real. So $Q^\times\sgrR^\times\sgrC^\times$, hence $Q^\times\sgrC^\times$. Check. The additive and multiplicative chains are genuinely different containments --- e.g.\ $\tfrac12\inQ$ but $\tfrac12\notinZ$, while $\tfrac12\inQ^\times$; and $0\inC$ lies in every additive stage but in no multiplicative stage, since $C^\times=C\setminus\{0\}$.
\end{wex}

Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Further subgroup examples: chains, exponent sets, and unions
Type: example
Title: $H_n=\{x\st x^n=1\}$ in an abelian group
Content:
\begin{wex}{$H_n=\{x\st x^n=1\}$ in an abelian group}
Let $G$ be abelian and fix an integer $n\ge1$. Let $H_n=\{x\in G\st x^n=1\}$. Show $H_n\sgr G$.
\wrec A subset of $G$ cut out by the closed-form condition $x^n=1$; use the one-step criterion (Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] ), expanding $(xy^{-1})^n$ with commutativity.
\wsol (a) Nonempty: $1^n=1$, so $1\in H_n$. (b) One-step: take $x,y\in H_n$, so $x^n=1$ and $y^n=1$. Since $G$ is abelian, $x$ and $y^{-1}$ commute, so
\[
(xy^{-1})^n=x^n(y^{-1})^n=x^n(y^n)^{-1}=1\cdot1^{-1}=1,
\]
hence $xy^{-1}\in H_n$. By Proposition~ [REF:p:subcrit@c2] , $H_n\sgr G$. Check. In $G=(Z/(15)Z)^{\times}$ (abelian, order $8$) with $n=2$,
\[
H_2=\{x\st x^2\equiv1\ (mod\ 15)\}=\{1,4,11,14\},
\]
since $4^2=16\equiv1$, $11^2=121\equiv1$, $14^2=196\equiv1$, while $2,7,8,13$ all square to $4$. And it is closed: $4\cdot11=44\equiv14\in H_2$, $4\cdot4=16\equiv1\in H_2$, as predicted. (Commutativity is essential: in a nonabelian group $\{x\st x^n=1\}$ can fail to be a subgroup, exactly as the torsion set did.)
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Further subgroup examples: chains, exponent sets, and unions
Type: remark
Label: r:union-not-subgroup-mrg@c2
Content:
\begin{remark} 
If $H,K\sgr G$ then $H\cup K\sgr G$ if and only if $H\subseteq K$ or $K\subseteq H$. Indeed, if neither contains the other, pick $h\in H\setminus K$ and $k\in K\setminus H$; the product $hk$ cannot lie in $H$ (else $k=h^{-1}(hk)\in H$) nor in $K$ (else $h=(hk)k^{-1}\in K$), so $hk\notin H\cup K$ and closure fails. The intersection $H\cap K$ is, by contrast, always a subgroup, by a single one-step check valid in both $H$ and $K$ at once.
\end{remark}
label: r:union-not-subgroup-mrg@c2
