Type: example
Title: A union of two subgroups that fails closure
Content:
\begin{wex}{A union of two subgroups that fails closure}
In the Klein four-group $V_4=\{1,a,b,ab\}$ (every nonidentity element of order $2$, $ab=ba$), let $H=\{1,a\}$ and $K=\{1,b\}$. Show $H,K\sgr V_4$ but $H\cup K\not\sgr V_4$.
\wrec Each of $H,K$ is finite and closed under products, hence a subgroup (Proposition~ [REF:p:finsubcrit@c2] ); the union illustrates Remark~ [REF:r:union-not-subgroup-mrg@c2] since neither contains the other. To disprove, exhibit a product of an $H$-element and a $K$-element that escapes the union.
\wsol $H=\{1,a\}=\langle a\rangle$ and $K=\{1,b\}=\langle b\rangle$ are subgroups (each is $\{1,x\}$ with $x^2=1$, closed under products). Now $H\cup K=\{1,a,b\}$. Take $a\in H\cup K$ and $b\in H\cup K$: their product is $ab$, and $ab\notin\{1,a,b\}$ (it is the fourth, distinct element of $V_4$). So $H\cup K$ is not closed under products, hence $H\cup K\not\sgr V_4$. Check. Neither $H\subseteq K$ nor $K\subseteq H$ holds, exactly the situation Remark~ [REF:r:union-not-subgroup-mrg@c2] predicts will fail; and $|H\cup K|=3$ does not divide $|V_4|=4$, a second confirmation via Lagrange (Chapter~3).
\end{wex}

Title: the diagonal $\Delta\sgr G\times G$
Content:
\begin{wex}{the diagonal $\Delta\sgr G\times G$}
Show $\Delta=\{(g,g)\st g\in G\}$ is a subgroup of $G\times G$.
\wrec A described subset of the known group $G\times G$; apply the one-step criterion.
Membership means ``both coordinates equal.''
\wsol Nonempty: $(1,1)\in\Delta$. For $(g,g),(h,h)\in\Delta$,
\[ (g,g)(h,h)^{-1}=(g,g)(h^{-1},h^{-1})=(gh^{-1},\,gh^{-1})\in\Delta, \]
since the two coordinates agree. By the criterion $\Delta\sgr G\times G$. Check.
$g\mapsto(g,g)$ shows $\ord{\Delta}=\ord{G}$.
\end{wex}

Title: upper-triangular invertible matrices
Content:
\begin{wex}{upper-triangular invertible matrices}
Show $B=\left\{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\st ad\neq0\right\}
\sgr\GL_2(R)$.
\wrec A subset of $\GL_2(R)$ cut out by ``lower-left entry $=0$.'' One-step criterion,
using that triangular$\,\times\,$triangular is triangular and the inverse of a
triangular matrix is triangular.
\wsol Nonempty: $I\in B$. Product:
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)
\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a'&b'\\0&d'\end{smallmatrix}\right)
=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}aa'&ab'+bd'\\0&dd'\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in B$ (and
$aa',dd'\neq0$). Inverse:
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)^{-1}
=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1/a&-b/(ad)\\0&1/d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in B$. Hence
$B\sgr\GL_2(R)$.
\end{wex}

Section: Subgroups > Definition and Examples > Maps and commutative diagrams
Type: prose
Part: 1/3
Content:
Three structural facts of this section are cleanest when drawn as diagrams of
homomorphisms and inclusions.

\noindent(a) Transitivity of $\sgr$ is composition of inclusions.
If $K\sgr H$ and $H\sgr G$ then $K\sgr G$, because the inclusion $K\hookrightarrow G$ is
the composite of $K\hookrightarrow H$ and $H\hookrightarrow G$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
K \arrow[r, hook] & H \arrow[r, hook] & G
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three groups: $K$ (a subgroup of $H$), $H$ (a subgroup of $G$), and $G$ (the ambient group). Each is a group under the same operation.
\dgi{Arrows:} The left arrow $K\hookrightarrow H$ is the inclusion map $\iota_1: k\mapsto k$, viewing $k$ as an element of $H$. The right arrow $H\hookrightarrow G$ is the inclusion $\iota_2: h\mapsto h$, viewing $h$ as an element of $G$. Both are injective group homomorphisms (inclusions); the composite $\iota_2\circ\iota_1: K\hookrightarrow G$ sends $k\mapsto k$ directly, establishing $K\sgr G$.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is a single directed path from $K$ to $G$: the composite $\iota_2\circ\iota_1$. The diagram records that this composite is itself an inclusion, i.e.\ $\iota_2\circ\iota_1 = \iota_{K\hookrightarrow G}$, the direct inclusion of $K$ into $G$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $k\in K$. Along the unique path: first $k\mapsto k\in H$, then $k\mapsto k\in G$. The composite sends $k\mapsto k\in G$, which is exactly the direct inclusion. The agreement is trivial because all three maps are identity-on-elements inclusions; composing two identity-on-elements maps is still identity-on-elements.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram records the proof of transitivity of $\sgr$: to show $K\sgr G$ it suffices to exhibit the factoring $K\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow G$, because a composite of injective group homomorphisms is an injective group homomorphism. The author places it here to make the transitivity argument visual and to signal that inclusion is a genuine category-theoretic morphism, not just a set-containment symbol.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $K=4Z\sgr H=2Z\sgr G=Z$ (all under addition). The chain $4Z\hookrightarrow2Z\hookrightarrowZ$ gives $4Z\sgrZ$ by transitivity: $8-4=4\in4Z$, so $4Z$ passes the one-step test directly in $Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the two arrows as saying $K$ must be normal in $G$, or that some quotient exists. The arrows here are plain inclusions (hooked arrows $\hookrightarrow$), not quotient or surjection arrows; they record only that elements of $K$ sit inside $H$ sit inside $G$, with no normality claimed.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that transitivity of the subgroup relation is just composition of inclusion homomorphisms, turning a textual argument into a one-glance arrow-chase.
\end{dgx}

$H,K\sgr G$ the subgroup $H\cap K$ is the largest one mapping into both $H$ and $K$
compatibly with their inclusions into $G$. This ``universal corner'' is precisely why
$H\cap K\sgr G$ (Exercise: intersections of subgroups are subgroups).
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
H\cap K \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, hook] & H \arrow[d, hook] \\
K \arrow[r, hook] & G
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four groups: the intersection $H\cap K$ (upper-left), the subgroup $H\sgr G$ (upper-right), the subgroup $K\sgr G$ (lower-left), and the ambient group $G$ (lower-right). Each arrow goes by inclusion.

\noindent(c) A kernel is automatically a subgroup: $\SL_n=\ker\det$.
The determinant $\det:\GL_n(F)\to F^\times$ is a homomorphism, and $\SL_n(F)$ is exactly
its kernel. This gives a short exact sequence and is the slickest proof that
$\SL_n(F)\sgr\GL_n(F)$ --- no checklist needed, because kernels of homomorphisms are
always subgroups.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
1 \arrow[r] & \SL_n(F) \arrow[r, hook] & \GL_n(F) \arrow[r, two heads, "\det"] & F^\times \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five nodes: the trivial group $1$ (repeated at both ends), the special linear group $\SL_n(F)=\{A\in\GL_n(F)\st\det A=1\}$ (a normal subgroup), the general linear group $\GL_n(F)$ of invertible $n\times n$ matrices over a field $F$, and the multiplicative group $F^\times=F\setminus\{0\}$ of nonzero field elements.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost arrow $1\to\SL_n(F)$ is the unique map sending the trivial group's element to the identity matrix $I$. The arrow $\SL_n(F)\hookrightarrow\GL_n(F)$ is the inclusion $A\mapsto A$. The arrow $\GL_n(F)\xrightarrow{\det}F^\times$ is the determinant homomorphism $A\mapsto\det A$. The rightmost arrow $F^\times\to 1$ is the unique map to the trivial group.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is a short exact sequence, so exactness holds at each internal node. At $\SL_n(F)$: $\operatorname{im}(1\to\SL_n(F))=\{I\}=\operatorname{ker}(\SL_n(F)\hookrightarrow\GL_n(F))$, i.e.\ the inclusion is injective. At $\GL_n(F)$: $\operatorname{im}(\SL_n(F)\hookrightarrow\GL_n(F))=\SL_n(F)=\operatorname{ker}(\det)$, since $\det A=1\iff A\in\SL_n(F)$. At $F^\times$: $\operatorname{im}(\det)=F^\times$ (det is surjective: any $c\in F^\times$ is achieved by $\operatorname{diag}(c,1,\dots,1)$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For the kernel condition at $\GL_n(F)$: if $A\in\SL_n(F)$ then $\det A=1$, so $A\in\operatorname{ker}(\det)$; conversely if $\det A=1$ then $A\in\SL_n(F)$. This is the definition of $\SL_n(F)$. The exactness at $F^\times$ follows because $\operatorname{diag}(c,1,\dots,1)$ has determinant $c$ for any $c\neq0$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram gives the shortest proof that $\SL_n(F)\sgr\GL_n(F)$: kernels of homomorphisms are always subgroups (since $\phi(xy^{-1})=\phi(x)\phi(y)^{-1}=1\cdot1^{-1}=1$ when $\phi(x)=\phi(y)=1$), so no three-clause checklist is needed. The author places it here to show that the determinant constraint ``$\det=1$'' is not just an algebraic coincidence but an instance of a general structural principle about kernels.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $n=2$ and $F=R$. The matrix $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&0\\0&1/2\end{psmallmatrix}$ has $\det A=1$, so $A\in\SL_2(R)$; its image under $\det$ is $1\inR^\times$. The matrix $B=\begin{psmallmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ has $\det B=3\neq1$, so $B\notin\SL_2(R)$; $\det$ maps $B$ to $3$, which is a nonzero element of $R^\times$, demonstrating surjectivity.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think the short exact sequence says $\GL_n(F)\cong\SL_n(F)\times F^\times$ (a direct product splitting). \dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $\SL_n(F)$ is the kernel of the determinant homomorphism, so its subgroup status is an immediate instance of the general principle that kernels are always subgroups, bypassing any direct verification.
\end{dgx}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Prove each is a subgroup: (a) $\{a+ai\st a\inR\}\sgr(C,+)$;
 (b) the unit circle $\{z\inC\st|z|=1\}\sgrC^\times$;
 (c) $\{a/b\inQ\st b\mid n\}\sgr(Q,+)$ ($n$ fixed);
 (d) $\{a/b\inQ\st\gcd(b,n)=1\}\sgr(Q,+)$;
 (e) $\{x\inR^\times\st x^2\inQ\}\sgrR^\times$.
\item Prove each is not a subgroup: (a) the $2$-cycles in $S_n$ ($n\ge3$);
 (b) the reflections in $D_{2n}$; (c) $\{x\in G\st\ord{x}=n\}\cup\{1\}$, $n$ composite and $G$ a group containing an element of order $n$;
 (d) the odd integers together with $0$; (e) $\{x\inR\st x^2\inQ\}$ in $(R,+)$.
\item Show $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$ and $\{1,r^2,sr,sr^3\}$ are subgroups of $D_8$.
\item Exhibit a group $G$ and an infinite subset $H$ closed under the operation but not a
 subgroup.
\item Prove a group of order $n>2$ has no subgroup of order $n-1$.
\item $G$ abelian: prove the torsion set $\{g\st\ord{g}<\infty\}\sgr G$; give a
 non-abelian example where this set is not a subgroup.
\item Fix $n>1$. Find the torsion subgroup of $Z\timesZ/(n)Z$, and show the elements of infinite
 order together with $1$ do not form a subgroup.
\item For $H,K\sgr G$, prove $H\cup K\sgr G\iff H\subseteq K$ or $K\subseteq H$.
\item Prove $\SL_n(F)=\{A\in\GL_n(F)\st\det A=1\}\sgr\GL_n(F)$.
\item (a) Prove $H\cap K\sgr G$ for $H,K\sgr G$; (b) prove the intersection of any
 nonempty family of subgroups is a subgroup.
\item Prove $\{(a,1)\}$, $\{(1,b)\}$, and (when $B=A$) the diagonal $\{(a,a)\}$ are
 subgroups of $A\times B$.
\item $A$ abelian, $n\inZ$: prove $A^n=\{a^n\}$ and $A[n]=\{a\st a^n=1\}$ are subgroups.
\item $H\sgr(Q,+)$ with $1/x\in H$ for all $x\in H\setminus\{0\}$: prove $H=0$ or
 $H=Q$.
\item Show $\{x\in D_{2n}\st x^2=1\}$ is not a subgroup ($n\ge3$).
\item Prove the union of an ascending chain $H_1\sgr H_2\sgr\cdots$ of subgroups is a
 subgroup.
\item Prove the upper-triangular matrices in $\GL_n(F)$ form a subgroup.
\item Prove the upper-triangular matrices with $1$'s on the diagonal form a subgroup of
 $\GL_n(F)$.
\end{exers}

Type: definition
Label: d:cent@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Let $G$ be a group and $A\subseteq G$ a nonempty subset. The centralizer of $A$ in $G$ is
\[
C_G(A)=\{g\in G\st gag^{-1}=a\ for all a\in A\}
=\{g\in G\st ga=ag\ for all a\in A\}.
\]
When $A=\{a\}$ is a single element we write $C_G(a)=\{g\in G\st gag^{-1}=a\}=\{g\in G\st ga=ag\}$. Thus $C_G(a)$ is the set of all elements that commute with $a$, and $C_G(A)$ is the set of elements that commute with every element of $A$. The two displayed descriptions agree because $gag^{-1}=a\Longleftrightarrow ga=ag$ (multiply on the right by $g$).
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
We use the subgroup criterion. First $1\in C_G(A)$ since $1a1^{-1}=a$ for all $a\in A$, so $C_G(A)\neq\varnothing$.

Closure. Suppose $x,y\in C_G(A)$ and fix $a\in A$. Then $xa=ax$ and $ya=ay$, so
\[
(xy)a=x(ya)=x(ay)=(xa)y=(ax)y=a(xy).
\]
Hence $xy$ commutes with every $a\in A$, i.e.\ $xy\in C_G(A)$.

Inverses. Suppose $x\in C_G(A)$ and fix $a\in A$. From $xa=ax$, multiply on the left and right by $x^{-1}$:
\[
x^{-1}(xa)x^{-1}=x^{-1}(ax)x^{-1}\Longrightarrow ax^{-1}=x^{-1} a.
\]
So $x^{-1} a=ax^{-1}$ for all $a\in A$, i.e.\ $x^{-1}\in C_G(A)$. By the subgroup criterion $C_G(A)\sgr G$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Label: r:cent-facts@c2
Content:
\begin{remark} 
Two facts make computations fast.
(1) Intersection formula: since $g\in C_G(A)$ iff $g$ commutes with each $a\in A$,
\[
C_G(A)=\bigcap_{a\in A}C_G(a).
\]
(2) Generators suffice: if $A=\langle S\rangle$ then $C_G(A)=C_G(S)$, because an element commuting with each generator commutes with every product of generators and their inverses. In particular $C_G(\langle x\rangle)=C_G(x)$.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: How to compute a centralizer $C_G(a)$ (and $C_G(A)$)
Content:
\begin{method}{How to compute a centralizer $C_G(a)$ (and $C_G(A)$)}
Use this whenever you must find all elements commuting with a fixed element $a$ (or with a whole subset $A$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Single element $C_G(a)$. Test each $g\in G$ (or each coset/type of element) by checking $ga=ag$. In a group given by generators and relations (e.g.\ $D_{2n}$ with $sr=r^{-1} s$, or $Q_8$), push every product to a normal form and compare; do not test brute force if a relation settles it.
\item Powers are free. Every power of $a$ commutes with $a$, so $\langle a\rangle\subseteq C_G(a)$ automatically. You only need to test elements outside $\langle a\rangle$.
\item Use the relation to predict failures. In $D_{2n}$, $s r^k=r^{-k}s$, so a reflection $s r^j$ commutes with $r^k$ iff $r^k=r^{-k}$, i.e.\ iff $r^{2k}=1$. This tells you instantly which rotations are centralized by reflections.
\item Subset $A$: intersect. Compute $C_G(a)$ for each $a$ in a generating set $S$ of $A$, then take $\bigcap_{a\in S}C_G(a)$ (Remark~ [REF:r:cent-facts@c2] ).
\item Sanity checks. The answer must be a subgroup (closed, contains $1$, contains inverses), must contain $\langle a\rangle$, and (by Lagrange) its order must divide $|G|$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

\begin{pitfall}
$C_G(a)$ is the set of elements that commute with $a$, not the set of elements that commute with everything (that is the center $Z(G)=C_G(G)$). Also $C_G(a)$ need not be abelian, and need not equal $\langle a\rangle$.

Title: $C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle$
Label: wex:cent-d8-r@c2
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle$} 
Compute the centralizer of the rotation $r$ in $D_8$.
\wrec This is a single-element centralizer in a group with a relation $sr=r^{-1} s$. By the method, powers of $r$ are free ($\langle r\rangle\subseteq C_{D_8}(r)$); the relation predicts that a reflection commutes with $r^k$ iff $r^{2k}=1$, so we only need to test the reflections and apply that test with $k=1$.
\wsol The rotations $\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}=\langle r\rangle$ all commute with $r$ (powers of the same element commute). Now test a reflection $sr^j$:
\[
(sr^j)\,r=sr^{\,j+1},\qquad r\,(sr^j)=(rs)r^j=(s r^{-1})r^j=s r^{\,j-1},
\]
using $rs=sr^{-1}$. These are equal iff $r^{\,j+1}=r^{\,j-1}$, i.e.\ $r^2=1$. But $\ord{r}=4$, so $r^2\neq1$ and no reflection commutes with $r$. Hence
\[
C_{D_8}(r)=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}=\langle r\rangle.
\]
Check. $\langle r\rangle$ is a subgroup of order $4$, and $4\mid 8$. It contains $r$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: $C_{D_8}(s)=\{1,s,r^2,sr^2\}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{D_8}(s)=\{1,s,r^2,sr^2\}$}
Compute the centralizer of the reflection $s$ in $D_8$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer again. Now $a=s$ is a reflection; $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$ is free. We must test each rotation $r^k$ (does $r^k$ commute with $s$?) and each reflection $sr^j$. The relation $r^k s=s r^{-k}$ does the rotation tests in one line.
\wsol Rotations. $r^k$ commutes with $s$ iff $r^k s=s r^k$. But $r^k s=s r^{-k}$, so we need $s r^{-k}=s r^{k}$, i.e.\ $r^{2k}=1$. With $\ord{r}=4$ this holds iff $4\mid 2k$, i.e.\ $k$ even: $k=0,2$. So $1$ and $r^2$ commute with $s$, while $r,r^3$ do not.

Reflections. Test $sr^j$:
\[
(sr^j)s=s(r^j s)=s(s r^{-j})=s^2 r^{-j}=r^{-j},\qquad
s(sr^j)=s^2 r^j=r^j .
\]
Equal iff $r^{-j}=r^j$, i.e.\ $r^{2j}=1$, i.e.\ $j$ even: $j=0,2$. So $s$ (the $j=0$ case) and $sr^2$ commute with $s$, while $sr,sr^3$ do not. Collecting:
\[
C_{D_8}(s)=\{1,\,s,\,r^2,\,sr^2\}.
\]
Check. Order $4$, and $4\mid8$. It contains $s$. It is closed: e.g.\ $r^2\cdot s=sr^{-2}=sr^2$ (since $r^{-2}=r^2$) is in the set, and $(sr^2)^2=sr^2sr^2=s(r^2 s)r^2=s(sr^{-2})r^2=s^2r^{-2}r^2=1$. So it is the Klein four-group $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: $C_{D_8}(r^2)=D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{D_8}(r^2)=D_8$}
Compute the centralizer of $r^2$ in $D_8$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer. The key trigger: $r^2$ has order $2$, so $r^{-2}=r^2$. The relation $r^2$-with-reflection test reduces to $r^{2k}=1$ with $k=2$, which is automatically true since $r^4=1$. Expect everything to commute, i.e.\ $r^2\in Z(D_8)$.
\wsol Rotations commute with $r^2$ trivially (powers of $r$). Reflections: test $sr^j$ against $r^2$:
\[
(sr^j)r^2=sr^{\,j+2},\qquad r^2(sr^j)=(r^2 s)r^j=(s r^{-2})r^j=s r^{\,j-2}.
\]
Since $r^{-2}=r^2$ (as $r^4=1$), we have $sr^{\,j-2}=sr^{\,j+2}$, so the two are equal for every $j$. Thus every reflection commutes with $r^2$, and
\[
C_{D_8}(r^2)=D_8.
\]
Check. This says $r^2\in Z(D_8)$, which is the known center of $D_8$. Order $8=|D_8|$, divides $|D_8|$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{S_3}\big((1\,2)\big)=\{1,(1\,2)\}$}
Compute the centralizer of the transposition $(1\,2)$ in $S_3$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer in $S_3=\{1,(1\,2),(1\,3),(2\,3),(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$. No slick relation; scan all six elements and test $g\,(1\,2)=(1\,2)\,g$ by composing permutations (apply right factor first).
\wsol $\langle (1\,2)\rangle=\{1,(1\,2)\}$ is free (both commute with $(1\,2)$). Test the rest.
\[
(1\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,2\,3),\quad (1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\ \Rightarrow\ unequal, (1\,3)\notin C.
\]
\[
(2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3\,2),\quad (1\,2)(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3)\ \Rightarrow\ unequal, (2\,3)\notin C.
\]
\[
(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3),\quad (1\,2)(1\,2\,3)=(2\,3)\ \Rightarrow\ unequal, (1\,2\,3)\notin C.
\]
\[
(1\,3\,2)(1\,2)=(2\,3),\quad (1\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,3)\ \Rightarrow\ unequal, (1\,3\,2)\notin C.
\]
Hence $C_{S_3}\big((1\,2)\big)=\{1,(1\,2)\}=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$.
Check. Order $2$, and $2\mid 6$. As a sample composition verification: $(1\,3)(1\,2)$ computed right-to-left: $(1\,2)$ first sends $1\mapsto2$, then $(1\,3)$ fixes $2$, so $1\mapsto2$; $2\mapsto1\mapsto3$; $3\mapsto3\mapsto1$; that is $(1\,2\,3)$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: $C_{Q_8}(i)=\{\pm1,\pm i\}=\langle i\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{Q_8}(i)=\{\pm1,\pm i\}=\langle i\rangle$}
Compute the centralizer of $i$ in $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$, where $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$, and $ji=-k$, $kj=-i$, $ik=-j$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer. $\pm1$ are central, and powers of $i$ (namely $1,i,-1,-i$) are free. The quaternion relations $ij=-ji$, $ik=-ki$ are the trigger: distinct ``imaginary'' generators anticommute, so $j,k$ (and their negatives) cannot commute with $i$.
\wsol $\langle i\rangle=\{1,i,i^2,i^3\}=\{1,i,-1,-i\}$ all commute with $i$. Test $j$ and $k$:
\[
ij=k,\qquad ji=-k\ \Rightarrow\ ij\neq ji,\ so j\notin C_{Q_8}(i),
\]
\[
ik=-j,\qquad ki=j\ \Rightarrow\ ik\neq ki,\ so k\notin C_{Q_8}(i).
\]
Since $-j=(-1)j$ and $-1$ is central, $-j$ commutes with $i$ iff $j$ does; likewise $-k$. So $\pm j,\pm k$ are all excluded. Therefore
\[
C_{Q_8}(i)=\{1,-1,i,-i\}=\langle i\rangle.
\]
Check. $\langle i\rangle$ has order $4$, $4\mid8$, contains $i$, and is cyclic hence abelian (consistent with being a centralizer that contains $i$). Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: $C_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=\langle r\rangle$ via the subset rule
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=\langle r\rangle$ via the subset rule}
Compute the centralizer of the subgroup $A=\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$ in $D_8$.
\wrec This is a subset centralizer. By Remark~ [REF:r:cent-facts@c2] (2), $A$ is generated by $S=\{r\}$, so $C_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=C_{D_8}(r)$ -- no need to intersect over all four rotations. (If you prefer, $C_{D_8}(A)=\bigcap_{a\in A}C_{D_8}(a)$, and the smallest of these governs.)
\wsol Since $\langle r\rangle=\langle S\rangle$ with $S=\{r\}$, an element centralizes all of $\langle r\rangle$ iff it centralizes the single generator $r$. By the worked computation $C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle$ (first example above),
\[
C_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}.
\]
Cross-check by intersection. Using $C_{D_8}(A)=\bigcap_{a\in A}C_{D_8}(a)$:
\[
C_{D_8}(1)=D_8,\quad C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle,\quad C_{D_8}(r^2)=D_8,\quad C_{D_8}(r^3)=\langle r\rangle,
\]
(the last because $r^3=r^{-1}$ generates the same cyclic group, so its centralizer equals that of $r$). The intersection is $D_8\cap\langle r\rangle\cap D_8\cap\langle r\rangle=\langle r\rangle$. Both methods agree.
Check. Order $4$, $4\mid8$, contains $\langle r\rangle$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
When $A$ is a subgroup, do not assume $C_G(A)\supseteq A$; that holds only when $A$ is abelian (then every element of $A$ commutes with every other, so $A\subseteq C_G(A)$). Type: definition
Label: d:center@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Let $G$ be a group. The center of $G$ is
\[
Z(G)=\{g\in G\st gx=xg\ for all x\in G\}.
\]
Equivalently $Z(G)=C_G(G)$ (the centralizer of the whole group in itself), and since an element commutes with everything iff it commutes with every single element separately,
\[
Z(G)=\bigcap_{a\in G}C_G(a).
\]
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The center $Z(G)$ (D\&F 2.2)
Type: proposition
Label: p:center-subgroup@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
For any group $G$, $Z(G)\sgr G$, and $Z(G)$ is abelian. Moreover $Z(G)\nor G$ (it is a normal subgroup).
\end{proposition}
label: p:center-subgroup@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The center $Z(G)$ (D\&F 2.2)
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-2029a1c99dd5ccc6db6b
Content:
\begin{proof}
Nonempty: $1x=x=x1$ for all $x$, so $1\in Z(G)$. Closed: if $g,h\in Z(G)$ and $x\in G$ then $(gh)x=g(hx)=g(xh)=(gx)h=(xg)h=x(gh)$, so $gh\in Z(G)$. Inverses: if $g\in Z(G)$ then $gx=xg$ for all $x$; multiply on both sides by $g^{-1}$ to get $xg^{-1}=g^{-1} x$, so $g^{-1}\in Z(G)$. Hence $Z(G)\sgr G$ by the subgroup criterion. It is abelian because any two of its elements each commute with everything in $G$, in particular with each other. For normality: if $g\in Z(G)$ and $a\in G$ then $aga^{-1}=ag a^{-1} = g a a^{-1} = g\in Z(G)$ (using $ag=ga$), so $aZ(G)a^{-1}\subseteq Z(G)$ for every $a$; thus $Z(G)\nor G$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}
$Z(G)$ measures how far $G$ is from being abelian: $Z(G)=G$ exactly when $G$ is abelian, and a ``small'' center signals a highly noncommutative group. Note $Z(G)=\bigcap_a C_G(a)$ is an intersection of subgroups, hence automatically a subgroup --- this is the practical formula we exploit below.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: How to compute $Z(G)$ from a generating set
Content:
\begin{method}{How to compute $Z(G)$ from a generating set}
Recognition trigger. Use this whenever you are asked for $Z(G)$ and $G=\langle S\rangle$ for a small generating set $S$ (e.g.\ $D_{2n}=\langle r,s\rangle$, $Q_8=\langle i,j\rangle$, $S_3=\langle (1\,2),(1\,2\,3)\rangle$, $\GL_n(\F)$ generated by elementary/transvection-type matrices).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Reduce the test set. An element $g$ is central iff $gx=xg$ for all $x\in G$. But if $g$ commutes with each generator in $S$, it commutes with every product of generators and their inverses, hence with all of $G$. So
\[
Z(G)=\bigcap_{x\in S}C_G(x).
\]
You only need to test commutation against the generators.
\item Parametrize a general element $g$ of $G$ (e.g.\ $g=r^k$ or $g=r^k s$ in $D_{2n}$; $g=\sum$ of basis quaternions; $g=$ general matrix).
\item Impose $gx=xg$ for each generator $x\in S$ and solve the resulting equations for the parameters.
\item Collect the surviving $g$'s; that set is $Z(G)$. Always finish with $|Z(G)|$ and a sanity check (does $1$ lie in it? is the answer a subgroup?).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Center of the dihedral group
Label: t:center-dihedral@c2
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Center of the dihedral group] 
Let $D_{2n}=\langle r,s\st r^n=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$ with $n\ge3$. Then
\[
Z(D_{2n})=
\begin{cases}
\{1\}, & n\ odd,\\[2pt]
\{1,\,r^{n/2}\}, & n\ even.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}
label: t:center-dihedral@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The center $Z(G)$ (D\&F 2.2)
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-86eb534004f2e1edd175
Content:
\begin{proof}
By the method box, $Z=C(r)\cap C(s)$. Step 1 (rotations). For $r^k$: $r^k$ commutes with $r$ automatically; and $s r^k s^{-1} = (srs)^k = (r^{-1})^k = r^{-k}$, so $r^k$ commutes with $s$ iff $r^{-k}=r^{k}$, i.e.\ $r^{2k}=1$, i.e.\ $n\mid 2k$. For $0\le k<n$ this forces $k=0$, or $k=n/2$ when $n$ is even. Step 2 (reflections). For a reflection $r^k s$: it does not commute with $r$, since $r(r^k s)=r^{k+1}s$ while $(r^k s)r = r^k (sr) = r^k r^{-1} s = r^{k-1}s$, and $r^{k+1}s=r^{k-1}s$ would force $r^2=1$, impossible for $n\ge3$. So no reflection is central. Combining, $Z=\{1\}$ if $n$ is odd and $Z=\{1,r^{n/2}\}$ if $n$ is even.
\end{proof}

\begin{pitfall}
Do not confuse $Z(G)$ with $C_G(a)$ for a single element $a$. The centralizer $C_G(a)$ can be large (it always contains $\langle a\rangle$) even when $Z(G)=1$. \end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}$}
Compute the center of $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$ (the symmetries of the square, order $8$).
\wrec $D_8$ is generated by $S=\{r,s\}$, so by the method box $Z=C(r)\cap C(s)$: test each of the $8$ elements against just $r$ and $s$. This is the $n=4$ (even) case of Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] , predicting $\{1,r^{n/2}\}=\{1,r^2\}$.
\wsol The $8$ elements are $\{1,r,r^2,r^3,s,rs,r^2s,r^3s\}$.

Rotations $r^k$ vs $s$. Using $sr^k s = r^{-k}$, we have $r^k s = s r^{-k}$, so $r^k$ commutes with $s$ iff $r^{-k}=r^{k}$, i.e.\ $r^{2k}=1$, i.e.\ $4\mid 2k$, i.e.\ $k\in\{0,2\}$. Thus among rotations only $1$ and $r^2$ pass the $s$-test (and all rotations commute with $r$). So central rotations: $\{1,r^2\}$.

Reflections $r^k s$ vs $r$. Compute $r\cdot(r^k s)=r^{k+1}s$ and $(r^k s)\cdot r = r^k(sr)=r^k r^{-1}s = r^{k-1}s$. These differ ($r^{k+1}s\ne r^{k-1}s$ since $r^2\ne1$), so no reflection commutes with $r$. All four reflections are excluded.

Hence $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}$, of order $2$. Check. $r^2$ is central because $r^2 s = s r^{-2}=s r^{2}$ (as $r^4=1\Rightarrow r^{-2}=r^2$), and $r^2$ commutes with $r$; and $\{1,r^2\}=\langle r^2\rangle$ is indeed a subgroup. Matches Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] .
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Z(Q_8)=\{1,-1\}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(Q_8)=\{1,-1\}$}
Compute the center of $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$ (and $ji=-k$, etc.).
\wrec $Q_8=\langle i,j\rangle$, so $Z=C(i)\cap C(j)$. The defining relations are anticommutation rules ($ji=-ij$), which is exactly the signal that the noncentral generators fail to commute; only $\pm1$ are scalar.
\wsol Recall the products are anticommutative: $ij=k$, $ji=-k$, $jk=i$, $kj=-i$, $ki=j$, $ik=-j$.

Test $i$ against $j$: $ij=k$ but $ji=-k\ne k$. So $i\notin Z$. Likewise $\pm i$ fail.

Test $j$ against $i$: same computation, $ij\ne ji$, so $j\notin Z$; likewise $\pm j$ fail.

Test $k$ against $i$: $ki=j$ but $ik=-j\ne j$, so $k\notin Z$; likewise $\pm k$ fail.

Test $\pm1$: $1$ commutes with everything; $-1$ commutes with everything because $-1=(-1)\cdot1$ is a scalar: $(-1)x=-x=x(-1)$ for all $x$. So $\pm1\in Z$.

Hence $Z(Q_8)=\{1,-1\}$, order $2$. Check. Every element of $Q_8$ squares to $\pm1$, and $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, so $-1$ commutes with all squares and is genuinely central; the set $\{1,-1\}=\langle -1\rangle$ is a subgroup. (Aside: $Q_8/Z\cong V_4$, consistent with $|Z|=2$.)
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Z(S_3)=1$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(S_3)=1$}
Compute the center of the symmetric group $S_3$.
\wrec $S_3=\langle (1\,2),(1\,2\,3)\rangle$, so $Z=C((1\,2))\cap C((1\,2\,3))$. Symmetric groups $S_n$ for $n\ge3$ are nonabelian, and the quick test is: a single pair of generators that fail to commute already kills most elements.
\wsol The six elements: $1,(1\,2),(1\,3),(2\,3),(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)$. We compose permutations right-to-left (apply the rightmost factor first).

A central element must commute with the transposition $\tau=(1\,2)$ and the $3$-cycle $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)$. First note $\sigma$ and $\tau$ do not commute:
\[
\sigma\tau=(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3),\qquad \tau\sigma=(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)=(2\,3),
\]
and $(1\,3)\ne(2\,3)$. So neither $\sigma$ nor $\tau$ is central.

Transpositions. By symmetry each transposition fails: e.g.\ check $(1\,3)$ against $\sigma$: $\sigma(1\,3)=(1\,2\,3)(1\,3)=(2\,3)$ while $(1\,3)\sigma=(1\,3)(1\,2\,3)=(1\,2)$; unequal, so $(1\,3)\notin Z$. Similarly $(2\,3)\notin Z$.

$3$-cycles. $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)$ already fails against $\tau$ above. Its inverse $\sigma^2=(1\,3\,2)$: $\tau\sigma^2=(1\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,3)$ while $\sigma^2\tau=(1\,3\,2)(1\,2)=(2\,3)$; unequal, so $(1\,3\,2)\notin Z$.

Only $1$ survives. Hence $Z(S_3)=\{1\}$. Check. $|S_3|=6$ is nonabelian, and a nonabelian group cannot have $Z=G$, so $Z\ne S_3$; $S_3\cong D_6$ is the $n=3$ (odd) dihedral case, where Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] gives $Z=1$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z(\GL_n(\F))=\{\lambda I\st \lambda\in\F^\times\}$ (scalar matrices)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(\GL_n(\F))=\{\lambda I\st \lambda\in\F^\times\}$ (scalar matrices)}
Show the center of $\GL_n(\F)$ ($n\ge2$, $\F$ a field) consists exactly of the nonzero scalar matrices $\lambda I$, $\lambda\ne0$.
\wrec $\GL_n(\F)$ is generated by elementary matrices, but the cleanest test set is the transvections $E_{ij}=I+e_{ij}$ ($i\ne j$), where $e_{ij}$ has a single $1$ in position $(i,j)$. Commuting with all of these is what forces a matrix to be scalar; this is the ``intersect centralizers of a generating set'' method for a matrix group.
\wsol Let $A=(a_{pq})\in\GL_n(\F)$. It suffices that $A$ commute with each $E_{ij}=I+e_{ij}$, i.e.\ with each $e_{ij}$ (subtracting $I$). Use the rule $e_{ij}e_{kl}=\delta_{jk}e_{il}$.

Step 1: compute the commutator condition. $A e_{ij}=e_{ij}A$ as matrices. Now $(A e_{ij})_{pq}=\sum_t a_{pt}(e_{ij})_{tq}=a_{pi}\delta_{jq}$, which is nonzero only in column $j$, where its $p$-th entry is $a_{pi}$. And $(e_{ij}A)_{pq}=\sum_t (e_{ij})_{pt}a_{tq}=\delta_{ip}a_{jq}$, nonzero only in row $i$, where its $q$-th entry is $a_{jq}$. Setting $Ae_{ij}=e_{ij}A$:
\[
a_{pi}\,\delta_{jq}=\delta_{ip}\,a_{jq}\qquadfor all p,q.
\]

Step 2: read off the entries. Take $p\ne i$ and $q=j$: LHS $=a_{pi}$, RHS $=\delta_{ip}a_{jj}=0$, so $a_{pi}=0$ for all $p\ne i$ --- column $i$ is zero off the diagonal. Take $p=i$, $q\ne j$: LHS $=a_{ii}\delta_{jq}=0$, RHS $=a_{jq}$, so $a_{jq}=0$ for $q\ne j$ --- row $j$ is zero off the diagonal. Since this holds for all $i\ne j$, $A$ is diagonal. Take $p=i,q=j$: $a_{ii}=a_{jj}$. So all diagonal entries are equal: $A=\lambda I$.

Step 3: invertibility. $\lambda I\in\GL_n(\F)$ iff $\det(\lambda I)=\lambda^n\ne0$ iff $\lambda\ne0$. Conversely every $\lambda I$ ($\lambda\ne0$) commutes with all matrices, so lies in the center.

Hence $Z(\GL_n(\F))=\{\lambda I\st\lambda\in\F^\times\}\cong\F^\times$. Check. For $n=1$, $\GL_1(\F)=\F^\times$ is abelian and the statement degenerates to $Z=G$, consistent. For $n=2$, e.g.\ $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ and $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ do not commute, confirming non-scalar matrices are excluded.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z(G)=G$ iff $G$ abelian; e.g.\ $Z(Z/(n)Z)=Z/(n)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(G)=G$ iff $G$ abelian; e.g.\ $Z(Z/(n)Z)=Z/(n)Z$}
Show that $Z(G)=G$ if and only if $G$ is abelian, and illustrate with $G=Z/(n)Z$ and with a nonabelian contrast.
\wrec The trigger is the phrase ``$Z(G)=G$.'' By definition $g\in Z(G)$ means $g$ commutes with everything; $Z(G)=G$ says every element commutes with everything, which is precisely the definition of abelian. Whenever $G$ is given as abelian (e.g.\ $Z/(n)Z$, any cyclic or product of cyclic groups), you may immediately write $Z(G)=G$.
\wsol ($\Rightarrow$) If $Z(G)=G$ then every $g\in G$ satisfies $gx=xg$ for all $x\in G$; in particular for any $a,b\in G$, $ab=ba$, so $G$ is abelian. ($\Leftarrow$) If $G$ is abelian then $gx=xg$ holds for all $g,x$, so every $g\in Z(G)$, giving $Z(G)=G$ (and $Z(G)\subseteq G$ always). Hence the equivalence.

\emph{Example $Z/(n)Z$.} The group $Z/(n)Z=\{\,\overline0,\overline1,\dots,\overline{n-1}\,\}$ under addition has $\overline a+\overline b=\overline{a+b}=\overline b+\overline a$ for all $a,b$, so it is abelian; therefore $Z(Z/(n)Z)=Z/(n)Z$. Concretely for $n=6$: $\overline2+\overline5=\overline7=\overline1=\overline5+\overline2$, illustrating commutativity for a sample pair.

Contrast. For a nonabelian $G$, $Z(G)\psgr G$ strictly: e.g.\ $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}\ne D_8$ since $|Z|=2<8$. Check. The equivalence is logically airtight (it is just the definitions of ``central'' and ``abelian'' lined up), and $|Z(Z/(n)Z)|=n=|Z/(n)Z|$ confirms equality.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z(D_{12})=\{1,r^3\}$ (the $n=6$ even case)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(D_{12})=\{1,r^3\}$ (the $n=6$ even case)}
Compute $Z(D_{12})$, the center of the symmetries of a regular hexagon, $D_{12}=\langle r,s\st r^6=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$.
\wrec $D_{12}$ has $n=6$, which is even, so Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] predicts $Z=\{1,r^{n/2}\}=\{1,r^3\}$. We verify directly by intersecting $C(r)\cap C(s)$ over the generators $\{r,s\}$, exhibiting exactly why $r^3$ survives and the others do not.
\wsol The $12$ elements are $\{r^k,\,r^k s : 0\le k\le 5\}$.

Rotations $r^k$ vs $s$. As before $r^k s = s r^{-k}$, so $r^k$ commutes with $s$ iff $r^{2k}=1$, i.e.\ $6\mid 2k$, i.e.\ $3\mid k$. For $0\le k\le5$ this gives $k\in\{0,3\}$, i.e.\ $r^0=1$ and $r^3$. (Both automatically commute with $r$.) So central rotations are $\{1,r^3\}$.

Why $r^3$ works explicitly: $r^3 s = s r^{-3}=s r^{3}$ since $r^{-3}=r^{6-3}=r^3$. Good.

Why, say, $r^2$ fails: $r^2 s = s r^{-2}=s r^4\ne s r^2$ (since $r^4\ne r^2$), so $r^2\notin Z$. Likewise $r,r^4,r^5$ fail the $s$-test.

Reflections $r^k s$ vs $r$. $r(r^k s)=r^{k+1}s$ and $(r^k s)r=r^{k-1}s$; these are unequal because $r^2\ne1$. So no reflection commutes with $r$, and all six reflections are excluded.

Hence $Z(D_{12})=\{1,r^3\}$, order $2$. Check. $\{1,r^3\}=\langle r^3\rangle$ with $(r^3)^2=r^6=1$, a subgroup of order $2$; and $n=6$ even gives $r^{n/2}=r^3$, matching Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] exactly.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
A reflection $r^k s$ in $D_{2n}$ is never central for $n\ge3$, even when $n$ is even --- the lone central nontrivial element is the half-turn rotation $r^{n/2}$. Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Normalizers and the setwise stabilizer
Type: definition
Label: d:norm@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
The normalizer of $A$ in $G$ is
\[
N_G(A)=\{\,g\in G\st gAg^{-1}=A\,\}.
\]
Equivalently, $g\in N_G(A)$ iff conjugation by $g$ permutes $A$ among itself as a set: $gAg^{-1}=A$ (setwise), not necessarily $gag^{-1}=a$ for each $a$ (pointwise). Recall the centralizer $C_G(A)=\{g\st gag^{-1}=a for all a\in A\}=\{g\st ga=ag\ \forall a\in A\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
The single inclusion $gAg^{-1}\subseteq A$ already forces the reverse inclusion automatically: since $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$ is injective and $A$ is finite (in our examples), $gAg^{-1}\subseteq A$ with equal cardinality gives $gAg^{-1}=A$. \end{remark}

Type: proposition
Label: p:tower@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
For any nonempty $A\subseteq G$,
\[
C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)\sgr G,
\]
and moreover $A$ itself is contained in $N_G(A)$ whenever $A$ is a subgroup. If $A=H$ is a subgroup then $N_G(H)$ is the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $H$ is normal, and $H\nor N_G(H)$.
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Normalizers and the setwise stabilizer
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-a3a429b171a58382dea5
Content:
\begin{proof}
$N_G(A)\sgr G$. $1A1^{-1}=A$, so $1\in N_G(A)$. If $g,h\in N_G(A)$ then $(gh)A(gh)^{-1}=g(hAh^{-1})g^{-1}=gAg^{-1}=A$, so $gh\in N_G(A)$. If $gAg^{-1}=A$, conjugate by $g^{-1}$: $g^{-1} A g=g^{-1}(gAg^{-1})g=A$, so $g^{-1}\in N_G(A)$. Hence $N_G(A)\sgr G$.

$C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)$. $C_G(A)\sgr G$ by the same argument (identity is in it, and it is closed under products and inverses). If $g\in C_G(A)$ then $gag^{-1}=a\in A$ for every $a\in A$, so $gAg^{-1}=A$; thus $g\in N_G(A)$. Since $C_G(A)\subseteq N_G(A)$ and both are subgroups of $G$, $C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)$.

$H\nor N_G(H)$. For $H$ a subgroup, every $h\in H$ satisfies $hHh^{-1}=H$ (subgroups are conjugation-closed by themselves), so $H\subseteq N_G(H)$, hence $H\sgr N_G(H)$. The defining condition $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g\in N_G(H)$ is exactly normality of $H$ in $N_G(H)$. If $H\nor K\sgr G$ then $kHk^{-1}=H$ for all $k\in K$, so $K\subseteq N_G(H)$; thus $N_G(H)$ is the largest such $K$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: How to compute $N_G(H)$
Content:
\begin{method}{How to compute $N_G(H)$}
Use this whenever you must decide which $g$ conjugate a subgroup $H$ onto itself as a set (e.g. to find the largest subgroup in which $H$ is normal, or to detect normality).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Free wins first. $H\subseteq N_G(H)$ always, and $C_G(H)\subseteq N_G(H)$ always. List those elements; they are in for free.
\item Index-2 shortcut. If $[G:H]=2$ then $H\nor G$, so $N_G(H)=G$. Stop. (Two cosets $H$ and $gH$; the only options force $gH=Hg$.)
\item Generator test. Write $H=\langle a\rangle$ (or list generators). For finite $H$, $gHg^{-1}=H$ iff $gag^{-1}\in H$ for each generator $a$ (a homomorphic image of a generating set generates the image, so $gHg^{-1}\subseteq H$, and $|gHg^{-1}|=|H|$). So test ONLY the generators, not every element. (For infinite $H$ this gives only $gHg^{-1}\subseteq H$; also test $g^{-1} ag\in H$.)
\item Setwise, not pointwise. You only need $gag^{-1}$ to land somewhere in $H$, not back at $a$. (Pointwise would be the centralizer.)
\item Assemble a subgroup. $N_G(H)$ is a subgroup containing $H$; use Lagrange to limit its possible order, then confirm with coset reps.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)=\{1,s,r^2,sr^2\}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)=\{1,s,r^2,sr^2\}$}
In $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$, compute the normalizer of the reflection subgroup $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$.
\wrec Here $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$ has order $2$ but index $4$, so the index-2 shortcut does not apply; we must run the generator test. The single generator is $s$, so $g\in N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$ iff $gsg^{-1}\in\{1,s\}$. Since $gsg^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $s$ it has order $2$ and is $\ne1$, so the condition collapses to the setwise check $gsg^{-1}=s$, i.e. $g$ commutes with $s$. For this tiny subgroup the normalizer equals the centralizer $C_{D_8}(s)$.
\wsol Use the relation $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$, equivalently $s r=r^{-1} s$, and $sr^k s^{-1}=r^{-k}$. Conjugate $s$ by each of the $8$ elements $r^k$ and $sr^k$ ($k=0,1,2,3$). 

Rotations: $r^k s r^{-k}$. Since $r s=s r^{-1}$ we get $r^k s=s r^{-k}$, hence $r^k s r^{-k}=s r^{-k} r^{-k}=s r^{-2k}$. So:
\[
1\cdot s\cdot 1=s,\quad rsr^{-1}=sr^{-2},\quad r^2 s r^{-2}=s r^{-4}=s,\quad r^3 s r^{-3}=sr^{-6}=sr^2.
\]
Thus among rotations, $1$ and $r^2$ give $s$ (good); $r,r^3$ give $sr^{-2}=sr^2\notin\langle s\rangle$ (bad).

\begin{wex}{$N_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=D_8$ via index $2$}
In $D_8$ compute the normalizer of the rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$.
\wrec The trigger is the index-2 shortcut: $|\langle r\rangle|=4$ and $|D_8|=8$, so $[D_8:\langle r\rangle]=2$. Any subgroup of index $2$ is normal, hence its normalizer is the whole group. No element-by-element work is needed.
\wsol $[D_8:\langle r\rangle]=8/4=2$, so by the index-2 theorem $\langle r\rangle\nor D_8$, i.e. $g\langle r\rangle g^{-1}=\langle r\rangle$ for all $g$. Therefore $N_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)=D_8$.

For a direct confirmation of the setwise condition, the only nontrivial generator to test is $r$ against the reflection $s$: $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}=r^3\in\langle r\rangle$. Since $s$ and $r$ generate $D_8$ and both normalize $\langle r\rangle$ ($r r r^{-1}=r\in\langle r\rangle$ trivially), every element does.

Sanity check. $|N_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)|=8$ divides $8$, and $\langle r\rangle\subseteq N_{D_8}(\langle r\rangle)$ as it must. Contrast with the previous example: $\langle r\rangle$ is normal but $\langle s\rangle$ is not.
\end{wex}

Title: $N_{S_3}(\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle)=S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N_{S_3}(\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle)=S_3$}
Compute the normalizer in $S_3$ of the $3$-cycle subgroup $H=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle=\{e,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$.
\wrec Again the index-2 shortcut: $|H|=3$, $|S_3|=6$, so $[S_3:H]=2$. Index $2$ forces normality; $N_{S_3}(H)=S_3$. We can also confirm with the conjugation-of-cycles rule $\sigma(1\,2\,3)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(1)\,\sigma(2)\,\sigma(3))$.
\wsol Since $[S_3:H]=6/3=2$, $H\nor S_3$ and so $N_{S_3}(H)=S_3$.

Direct generator test: $H=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$, so check $\sigma(1\,2\,3)\sigma^{-1}$ for a transposition, say $\sigma=(1\,2)$:
\[
(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(\,(1\,2)(1)\ (1\,2)(2)\ (1\,2)(3)\,)=(2\,1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\in H.
\]
It landed on the other $3$-cycle (setwise inside $H$), not back on $(1\,2\,3)$, yet that is fine for the normalizer. Every transposition behaves the same way, and the powers of $(1\,2\,3)$ obviously normalize $H$, so all $6$ elements normalize $H$.

Sanity check. $|N_{S_3}(H)|=6$ divides $6$; $H\subseteq N_{S_3}(H)$. Note $C_{S_3}(H)=H$ here (a transposition does NOT commute with $(1\,2\,3)$, since it inverts it), so $C_{S_3}(H)=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\psgr N_{S_3}(H)=S_3$ strictly.
\end{wex}

Title: $N_{S_3}(\langle (1\,2)\rangle)=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N_{S_3}(\langle (1\,2)\rangle)=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$}
Compute the normalizer in $S_3$ of the transposition subgroup $K=\langle (1\,2)\rangle=\{e,(1\,2)\}$.
\wrec $|K|=2$, index $3$ (odd, $\ne2$), so no shortcut; run the generator test on $(1\,2)$ using $\sigma(1\,2)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(1)\,\sigma(2))$. A conjugate of $(1\,2)$ is again a transposition; it lies in $K=\{e,(1\,2)\}$ iff it equals $(1\,2)$. So here the setwise test again reduces to fixing $(1\,2)$.
\wsol Conjugate $(1\,2)$ by each $\sigma\in S_3$, using $\sigma(1\,2)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(1)\,\sigma(2))$:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
e:(1\,2)\in K & (1\,2):(1\,2)\in K\\
(1\,3):(3\,2)=(2\,3)\notin K & (2\,3):(1\,3)\notin K\\
(1\,2\,3):(2\,3)\notin K & (1\,3\,2):(3\,1)=(1\,3)\notin K
\end{array}
\]
(For $(1\,2\,3)$: it sends $1\mapsto2,2\mapsto3$, so $(1\,2)\mapsto(2\,3)$.) Only $e$ and $(1\,2)$ keep the conjugate inside $K$. Hence $N_{S_3}(K)=\{e,(1\,2)\}=K$.

Sanity check. $|N_{S_3}(K)|=2$ divides $6$; $K\subseteq N_{S_3}(K)$ as required, and equality says $K$ is its own normalizer (self-normalizing). This matches the fact that $\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ is NOT normal in $S_3$ (it has $3$ distinct conjugates).
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$, $ji=-k$, compute $N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)$ where $\langle i\rangle=\{1,i,-1,-i\}$.
\wrec $|\langle i\rangle|=4$, $|Q_8|=8$, so $[Q_8:\langle i\rangle]=2$: index-2 shortcut gives $N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$. In fact every subgroup of $Q_8$ is normal, so this is expected. We confirm with the generator test on $i$.
\wsol $[Q_8:\langle i\rangle]=8/4=2\Rightarrow \langle i\rangle\nor Q_8\Rightarrow N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$.

Confirm setwise by conjugating the generator $i$ by $j$ (the element outside $\langle i\rangle$): using $ji=-k$ and $j^{-1}=-j$,
\[
j\,i\,j^{-1}=(ji)(-j)=(-k)(-j)=kj.
\]
Now $kj=-i$ (since $jk=i\Rightarrow kj=-i$). So $j i j^{-1}=-i\in\langle i\rangle$. Conjugation by $j$ sends $i\mapsto -i$ (inverts it) but stays inside $\langle i\rangle$, exactly the setwise condition. Since $i,j$ generate $Q_8$ and both normalize $\langle i\rangle$, all of $Q_8$ does.

Sanity check. $|N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)|=8$ divides $8$; $\langle i\rangle\subseteq N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)$. Note $C_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=\langle i\rangle$ (since $j$ anticommutes with $i$: $ij=k$, $ji=-k$, so $ij\ne ji$), giving a strict inclusion $C_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=\langle i\rangle\psgr N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Strict inclusion $C_G(H)\psgr N_G(H)$ in $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Strict inclusion $C_G(H)\psgr N_G(H)$ in $D_8$}
Exhibit a subgroup $H$ of $G=D_8$ with $C_G(H)$ strictly smaller than $N_G(H)$, and show the setwise check that lets $N_G(H)$ grow.
\wrec We want a $g$ that is in $N_G(H)$ but not $C_G(H)$: it must move a generator of $H$ to a different element of $H$ (so setwise OK, pointwise fails). Take $H=\langle r^2\rangle=\{1,r^2\}$ in $D_8$. Since $r^2$ is central in $D_8$, actually $C_{D_8}(r^2)=D_8$; that is no good for a strict gap with this $H$. Instead take $H=\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$, whose generator $r$ is moved by $s$: $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\ne r$ but $r^{-1}\in H$.
\wsol Let $H=\langle r\rangle$. From Example with the index-2 shortcut, $N_{D_8}(H)=D_8$ (order $8$). Now compute $C_{D_8}(H)=C_{D_8}(r)$, the elements commuting with $r$:
\begin{itemize}
\item Rotations $r^k$ all commute with $r$: $r^k r=r r^k$. So $\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}\subseteq C_{D_8}(r)$.
\item A reflection $sr^k$: $(sr^k)r=sr^{k+1}$ while $r(sr^k)=(rs)r^k=(sr^{-1})r^k=sr^{k-1}$. These are equal iff $r^{k+1}=r^{k-1}$ iff $r^2=1$, false. So no reflection commutes with $r$.
\end{itemize}
Hence $C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle$, order $4$. Therefore
\[
C_{D_8}(H)=\langle r\rangle\ \psgr\ N_{D_8}(H)=D_8,\qquad 4<8.
\]
The setwise check that grows the normalizer: $s\in N_{D_8}(H)$ because $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}=r^3\in H$ (and $sr^2s^{-1}=r^{-2}=r^2\in H$, $sr^3s^{-1}=r\in H$), so $sHs^{-1}=\{1,r^3,r^2,r\}=H$ setwise; but $s\notin C_{D_8}(H)$ since $srs^{-1}=r^3\ne r$.

Sanity check. $C_{D_8}(H)=\langle r\rangle\psgr N_{D_8}(H)=D_8$ is consistent with Proposition~ [REF:p:tower@c2] ($C_G\sgr N_G$), the orders $4\mid8$ both divide $|D_8|$, and the inclusion is strict exactly because conjugation by $s$ inverts the generator while keeping $H$ invariant as a set.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Stabilizers and kernels of a group action
Type: prose
Content:
A group action turns abstract group elements into concrete symmetries of a set. Two subgroups fall out of any action for free: the stabilizer of a point (everything that fixes that point) and the kernel (everything that fixes every point). This section pins down exactly what these are, proves they are subgroups, and -- crucially -- shows that the normalizer $N_G(A)$ and centralizer $C_G(A)$ from D\&F 2.2 are nothing more than a stabilizer and a kernel for the conjugation action.

Type: definition
Label: d:action@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
A (left) action of a group $G$ on a set $A$ is a map $G\times A\to A$, written $g\cdot a$, such that
\[
g_1\cdot(g_2\cdot a)=(g_1g_2)\cdot a\quadand\quad 1\cdot a=a
\]
for all $g_1,g_2\in G$ and all $a\in A$. Equivalently (by D\&F 1.7), $g\mapsto\sigma_g$, where $\sigma_g(a)=g\cdot a$, is a homomorphism $G\to S_A$ (the symmetric group on $A$).
\end{definition}
label: d:action@c2

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Stabilizers and kernels of a group action
Type: definition
Label: d:stab@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Let $G$ act on $A$. For a point $a\in A$ the stabilizer of $a$ is
\[
G_a=\{\,g\in G\st g\cdot a=a\,\}.
\]
The kernel of the action is
\[
\ker=\{\,g\in G\st g\cdot a=a\ for all a\in A\,\}=\bigcap_{a\in A}G_a .
\]
The action is faithful if $\ker=1$. The kernel is exactly the kernel of the associated homomorphism $G\to S_A$, $g\mapsto\sigma_g$.
\end{definition}
label: d:stab@c2

Label: p:stab-subgroup@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
For each $a\in A$ the stabilizer $G_a\sgr G$. Consequently $\ker=\bigcap_{a\in A}G_a\sgr G$.
\end{proposition}

Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Stabilizers and kernels of a group action
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-3e104690018d68105235
Content:
\begin{proof}
Use the subgroup criterion. First $1\in G_a$ since $1\cdot a=a$, so $G_a\neq\varnothing$. Let $x,y\in G_a$, so $x\cdot a=a$ and $y\cdot a=a$. From $y\cdot a=a$ apply $y^{-1}$: $y^{-1}\cdot a=y^{-1}\cdot(y\cdot a)=(y^{-1} y)\cdot a=1\cdot a=a$, so $y^{-1}\in G_a$. Then $(xy^{-1})\cdot a=x\cdot(y^{-1}\cdot a)=x\cdot a=a$, so $xy^{-1}\in G_a$. Hence $G_a\sgr G$. An arbitrary intersection of subgroups is a subgroup, so $\ker=\bigcap_a G_a\sgr G$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Label: r:kernel-normal@c2
Content:
\begin{remark} 
The kernel is in fact normal: it is the kernel of the homomorphism $G\to S_A$, and kernels of homomorphisms are normal subgroups (D\&F 3.1). A single stabilizer $G_a$ need not be normal -- see the conjugation examples, where $G_a=C_G(a)$ can fail to be normal.
\end{remark}
label: r:kernel-normal@c2

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Conjugation actions recover $N_G(A)$ and $C_G(A)$
Type: theorem
Label: t:conj@c2
Content:
\begin{theorem} 
Let $G$ be a group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $G$ acts on the set $\mathcal P(G)$ of subsets of $G$ by $g\cdot S=gSg^{-1}$. For a fixed subset $A\subseteq G$ the stabilizer of $A$ under this action is the normalizer
\[
Stab(A)=\{\,g\in G\st gAg^{-1}=A\,\}=N_G(A).
\]
\item[(b)] $G$ acts on the set $G$ itself by $g\cdot a=gag^{-1}$. For a fixed subset $A\subseteq G$, the subgroup fixing every point of $A$ -- i.e.\ the kernel of the restricted action of $N_G(A)$ on the set $A$ -- is the centralizer
\[
\{\,g\st gag^{-1}=a\ \forall a\in A\,\}=\{\,g\st ga=ag\ \forall a\in A\,\}=C_G(A).
\]
In particular the stabilizer of a single point $a$ under conjugation is $Stab(a)=C_G(a)=C_G(\{a\})$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: t:conj@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Conjugation actions recover $N_G(A)$ and $C_G(A)$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f2bb7caf12f421b10afa
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) By Definition~ [REF:d:stab@c2] , $Stab(A)=\{g\st g\cdot A=A\}=\{g\st gAg^{-1}=A\}$, which is verbatim the definition of $N_G(A)$ in D\&F 2.2. By Proposition~ [REF:p:stab-subgroup@c2] it is a subgroup.

(b) For the conjugation action on points, $g$ fixes $a$ iff $gag^{-1}=a$ iff $ga=ag$. Intersecting over all $a\in A$,
\[
\bigcap_{a\in A}G_a=\{\,g\st ga=ag\ \forall a\in A\,\}=C_G(A),
\]
which is the definition of the centralizer. As an intersection of stabilizers (each a subgroup by Proposition~ [REF:p:stab-subgroup@c2] ) it is a subgroup; since $C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)$ (Proposition~ [REF:p:tower@c2] ), it is the kernel of the conjugation action of $N_G(A)$ on the set $A$ (in general $G$ itself does not act on $A$, since $gAg^{-1}$ need not equal $A$). Taking $A=\{a\}$ gives $Stab(a)=C_G(a)$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Stabilizer vs.\ kernel: which one is it, and how to compute it
Content:
\begin{method}{Stabilizer vs.\ kernel: which one is it, and how to compute it}
Recognition trigger. You have a group $G$ acting on a set $A$ (a literal action like ``$S_n$ permutes $\{1,\dots,n\}$,'' or a conjugation action). Ask which question is being posed:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Which $g$ fix ONE chosen point $a$? $\;\Rightarrow$ stabilizer $G_a$.
\item Which $g$ fix EVERY point at once? $\;\Rightarrow$ kernel $=\bigcap_a G_a$.
\end{enumerate}
Recipe to compute a stabilizer $G_a$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Write down the action rule $g\cdot a$ explicitly.
\item Set $g\cdot a=a$ and solve for the constraint on $g$.
\item Collect all such $g$; verify it is a subgroup (Prop.~ [REF:p:stab-subgroup@c2] guarantees it, but listing elements is a check).
\item Identify the abstract group (often $S_{n-1}$, a small cyclic/reflection group, or a matrix block group).
\end{enumerate}
Recipe to compute a kernel. Either (a) intersect the stabilizers $\bigcap_a G_a$, or (b) find $\ker$ of the homomorphism $G\to S_A$ -- i.e.\ which $g$ induce the identity permutation. The action is faithful exactly when this is $\{1\}$.
Conjugation dictionary. Conjugation on subsets: $Stab(A)=N_G(A)$. Conjugation on points of $A$: kernel $=C_G(A)$; single point: $Stab(a)=C_G(a)$.
\end{method}

Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Conjugation actions recover $N_G(A)$ and $C_G(A)$
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Stabilizer'' fixes a point setwise/as a point, not pointwise-inside-it. For conjugation on subsets, $g\in N_G(A)$ only requires $gAg^{-1}=A$ as a set -- elements may be permuted. Requiring each element to be fixed gives the smaller $C_G(A)$. Always $C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)$, and the inclusion is often strict.
\end{pitfall}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The $D_8$ action on the square
Type: example
Title: $S_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$: $Stab(n)\cong S_{n-1}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$S_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$: $Stab(n)\cong S_{n-1}$}
Let $S_n$ act on $A=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ in the natural way, $\sigma\cdot i=\sigma(i)$. Compute the stabilizer of the point $n$ and identify it up to isomorphism.
\wrec We are asked for the permutations fixing ONE chosen point $n$ -- trigger 1 of the method box, so this is a stabilizer $G_n$, not a kernel. The action rule is just ``apply the permutation,'' so set $\sigma(n)=n$.
\wsol Set the defining condition: $\sigma\in (S_n)_n$ iff $\sigma\cdot n=n$ iff $\sigma(n)=n$. Such a $\sigma$ permutes $\{1,\dots,n\}$ but pins $n$, hence it permutes the remaining $n-1$ symbols $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ arbitrarily and bijectively. The map
\[
\Phi:(S_n)_n\to S_{\{1,\dots,n-1\}}=S_{n-1},\qquad \Phi(\sigma)=\sigma|_{\{1,\dots,n-1\}}
\]
is well defined (restriction of a bijection fixing $n$ is a bijection of the rest), a homomorphism (restriction respects composition), injective (a $\sigma$ fixing $n$ is determined by its action on the other $n-1$ points), and surjective (any permutation of $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ extends by $n\mapsto n$). Hence $(S_n)_n\cong S_{n-1}$.

Check. Orders: $|(S_n)_n|=(n-1)!=|S_{n-1}|$, consistent. Also the orbit-stabilizer count $|S_n|=|orbit of n|\cdot|(S_n)_n|=n\cdot(n-1)!=n!$ is correct, since the orbit of $n$ is all of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (size $n$).
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The $D_8$ action on the square
Type: example
Title: $D_8$ on the $4$ vertices: a vertex stabilizer has order $2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$D_8$ on the $4$ vertices: a vertex stabilizer has order $2$}
With the labeling above, $D_8$ acts on $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$. Compute $Stab(1)$.
\wrec Single chosen point ($1$) under a geometric action $\Rightarrow$ stabilizer. To find it, list how each of the $8$ elements moves vertex $1$ and keep those returning $1\mapsto1$.
\wsol The reflection $s$ fixes vertex $1$, so $s\cdot1=1$. Hence for every $k$ we have $r^k s\cdot1=r^k\cdot(s\cdot1)=r^k\cdot1$, so the reflection block $\{s,rs,r^2s,r^3s\}$ moves vertex $1$ in exactly the same pattern as the rotation block $\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$. Using $r^k\cdot1$ with $r:1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto4\mapsto1$ gives the table
\[
\begin{array}{l|cccc|cccc}
g & 1 & r & r^2 & r^3 & s & rs & r^2s & r^3s\\\hline
g\cdot 1 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4
\end{array}
\]
The elements sending $1\mapsto1$ are exactly $\{1,\,s\}$. Therefore
\[
Stab(1)=\{1,s\}=\langle s\rangle,
\]
of order $2$.

Check. Orbit-stabilizer: the orbit of $1$ is all four vertices (rotations reach them), so $|D_8|=|orbit|\cdot|Stab(1)|=4\cdot2=8$. Correct. By symmetry every vertex stabilizer has order $2$; for instance $Stab(2)=\{1,\,r^2s\}$, the reflection fixing the diagonal through $2$ and $4$.
\end{wex}

Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > The $D_8$ action on the square
Type: example
Title: $\GL_n(\F)$ on $\F^n$: stabilizer of $e_1$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\GL_n(\F)$ on $\F^n$: stabilizer of $e_1$}
Let $G=\GL_n(\F)$ act on column vectors $\F^n$ by $M\cdot v=Mv$. Compute $Stab(e_1)$, where $e_1=(1,0,\dots,0)^{\mathsf T}$.
\wrec One fixed vector $e_1$ $\Rightarrow$ stabilizer. The action is matrix-times-vector, so set $Me_1=e_1$ and read off the constraint on the entries of $M$.
\wsol The product $Me_1$ is the first column of $M$. So $Me_1=e_1$ forces the first column of $M$ to be $(1,0,\dots,0)^{\mathsf T}$. Writing $M$ in block form with this first column,
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & * \\ 0 & B\end{pmatrix},\qquad B\in\GL_{n-1}(\F),\ *\in\F^{1\times(n-1)},
\]
where the $0$ is the column of $n-1$ zeros below the leading $1$. Invertibility of $M$: expanding, $\det M=1\cdot\det B=\det B$, so $M$ is invertible iff $B$ is invertible. The bottom-left block is forced to be $0$ by $Me_1=e_1$, while the top-right row $*$ is free. Hence
\[
Stab(e_1)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1 & v^{\mathsf T}\\ 0 & B\end{pmatrix}\;\middle|\;B\in\GL_{n-1}(\F),\ v\in\F^{n-1}\right\}.
\]
This is the affine group $AGL_{n-1}(\F)\cong \F^{n-1}\rtimes\GL_{n-1}(\F)$ (the row $v^{\mathsf T}$ records a translation acting on the last $n-1$ coordinates).

Check. Take $n=2$, $\F=\F_2$. Then $Stab(e_1)=\left\{\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix},\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}\right\}$ (here $B\in\GL_1(\F_2)=\{1\}$ and $v\in\{0,1\}$), order $2$. Orbit-stabilizer: $|\GL_2(\F_2)|=6$ and the orbit of $e_1$ is the set of nonzero vectors $\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}$ (size $3$), so $6=3\cdot2$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Kernel of the $D_8$ vertex action is $1$ (faithfulness)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Kernel of the $D_8$ vertex action is $1$ (faithfulness)}
Show that the action of $D_8$ on the four vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is faithful, i.e.\ its kernel is trivial.
\wrec ``Fix EVERY point'' / ``faithful'' $\Rightarrow$ kernel, computed as $\bigcap_a G_a$ or as $\ker(D_8\to S_4)$. We intersect the vertex stabilizers.
\wsol From the previous example, $Stab(1)=\{1,s\}$. Compute another: $Stab(2)$. Using $g\cdot2$ for each $g$: $r\cdot2=3$, $r^2\cdot2=4$, $r^3\cdot2=1$, and $s\cdot2=4$ (the reflection across the $1$--$3$ axis swaps $2,4$), $r^2s\cdot2=r^2\cdot(s\cdot2)=r^2\cdot4=2$. So $Stab(2)=\{1,\,r^2s\}$. Now intersect:
\[
\ker=\bigcap_{a}G_a\subseteq Stab(1)\capStab(2)=\{1,s\}\cap\{1,r^2s\}=\{1\},
\]
since $s\neq r^2s$ (else $r^2=1$, false). Thus the kernel is already trivial after two vertices, so $\ker=1$ and the action is faithful.

Equivalently, the homomorphism $D_8\to S_4$ is injective: $|D_8|=8$ maps injectively into $|S_4|=24$, realizing $D_8$ as the symmetry subgroup of the square inside $S_4$.

Check. A nonidentity symmetry of a square must move at least one vertex (rotations move all four; reflections move at least two). So no nonidentity element fixes all vertices -- consistent with $\ker=1$.
\end{wex}

Title: Conjugation: $Stab(a)=C_G(a)$ and $Stab(A)=N_G(A)$ in $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugation: $Stab(a)=C_G(a)$ and $Stab(A)=N_G(A)$ in $D_8$}
In $G=D_8$ let $a=s$ (a single reflection) and let $A=\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$ (the rotation subgroup). Using conjugation actions, compute $Stab(s)=C_G(s)$ and $Stab(A)=N_G(A)$.
\wrec Conjugation on a point $\Rightarrow$ stabilizer $=$ centralizer (Thm.~ [REF:t:conj@c2] (b)). Conjugation on a subset $\Rightarrow$ stabilizer $=$ normalizer (Thm.~ [REF:t:conj@c2] (a)). So compute $\{g\st gsg^{-1}=s\}$ and $\{g\st gAg^{-1}=A\}$.
\wsol Centralizer of $s$. We need $gs=sg$. The standard relations give $sr=r^{-1} s$ and more generally $r^k s=s r^{-k}$. Test each $g$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=r^k$: $r^k s=s r^{-k}$, which equals $s r^k$ iff $r^{-k}=r^k$ iff $r^{2k}=1$ iff $k\in\{0,2\}$. So $1,r^2$ commute with $s$.
\item $g=s$: $s\cdot s=s\cdot s$ trivially, so $s\in C_G(s)$.
\item $g=r^2 s$: $(r^2s)s=r^2$, and $s(r^2s)=sr^2 s=r^{-2}=r^2$. Equal, so $r^2s\in C_G(s)$.
\item $g=rs,\,r^3s$: e.g.\ $(rs)s=r$ while $s(rs)=sr s=r^{-1}=r^3\neq r$. Not in $C_G(s)$. Similarly $r^3s$ fails.
\end{itemize}
Hence $C_G(s)=Stab(s)=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$, order $4$ (a Klein four-group $\cong V_4$).

Normalizer of $A=\langle r\rangle$. We need $gAg^{-1}=A$ as a set. Since $A=\langle r\rangle$ is the unique cyclic subgroup of order $4$, every conjugate $gAg^{-1}$ is again a subgroup of order $4$; the only such cyclic subgroup is $A$ itself (the other order-$4$ subgroups of $D_8$ are the two Klein fours $\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$ and $\{1,r^2,rs,r^3s\}$, not equal to $\langle r\rangle$, and conjugation preserves the property ``cyclic''). Therefore $gAg^{-1}=A$ for all $g\in D_8$, giving $N_G(A)=Stab(A)=D_8$.

Check. Consistency with the dictionary $C_G(A)\sgr N_G(A)$ and $|G|=|orbit|\cdot|Stab|$: the conjugacy class (orbit) of $s$ is $\{s,r^2s\}$ (since $rsr^{-1}=r^2 s$), size $2$, and $|D_8|=8=2\cdot4=|class of s|\cdot|C_G(s)|$. Correct. For $A$: orbit under conjugation is $\{A\}$ (size $1$) and $8=1\cdot|N_G(A)|=1\cdot8$. Correct, confirming $A\nor D_8$ (index $2$).
\end{wex}

Title: Kernel as $C_G(A)$: centralizer of a subset in $Q_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Kernel as $C_G(A)$: centralizer of a subset in $Q_8$}
Let $G=Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ act on itself by conjugation, and let $A=\{i,j\}$. Compute the centralizer $C_G(A)$, exhibiting it as the intersection $\bigcap_{a\in A}G_a$ of the point stabilizers, i.e.\ the kernel of the conjugation action of $N_G(A)$ on $A$ ($G$ itself does not act on $A$: $jij^{-1}=-i\notin A$).
\wrec ``Fix every element of $A$ under conjugation'' $\Rightarrow$ kernel of the conjugation-on-points action $=C_G(A)$ (Thm.~ [REF:t:conj@c2] (b)). Compute $C_G(i)\cap C_G(j)$.
\wsol Recall in $Q_8$: $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $ji=-k$, and $-1$ is central. Compute $C_G(i)=\{g\st gi=ig\}$. Since $i$ commutes with $\pm1,\pm i$ and anticommutes with $\pm j,\pm k$ (e.g.\ $ji=-ij$), we get $C_G(i)=\{\pm1,\pm i\}=\langle i\rangle$, order $4$. Likewise $C_G(j)=\{\pm1,\pm j\}=\langle j\rangle$, order $4$. Intersect:
\[
C_G(A)=C_G(i)\cap C_G(j)=\{\pm1,\pm i\}\cap\{\pm1,\pm j\}=\{\pm1\}=Z(Q_8).
\]
So the only elements conjugation-fixing both $i$ and $j$ are $\pm1$.

Check. Since $i,j$ generate $Q_8$ (as $ij=k$), centralizing both means centralizing everything, so $C_G(\{i,j\})=C_G(Q_8)=Z(Q_8)=\{\pm1\}$. This matches. It is moreover normal in $Q_8$, indeed central; but being the kernel of the action of $N_G(A)$ on $A$ only guarantees $C_G(A)\nor N_G(A)$ --- e.g.\ $C_{S_3}((1\,2))=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ is not normal in $S_3$.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: The $N_G(A)\to S_A$ homomorphism
Label: p:df-conj-hom-mrg@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition}[The $N_G(A)\to S_A$ homomorphism] 
Let $A$ be a nonempty subset of $G$. There is a homomorphism
\[
\varphi:\;N_G(A)\longrightarrow S_A,\qquad \varphi(g)=\sigma_g,\quad \sigma_g(a)=gag^{-1},
\]
whose kernel is exactly $C_G(A)$. Consequently $C_G(A)\nor N_G(A)$, with $C_G(A)$ the
elements of $N_G(A)$ that fix $A$ pointwise under conjugation and $N_G(A)$ those
that fix $A$ setwise.
\end{proposition}
label: p:df-conj-hom-mrg@c2

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-1bbb56adbe2d549cbfe1
Content:
\begin{proof}
For $g\in N_G(A)$ the map $\sigma_g:A\to A$, $a\mapsto gag^{-1}$, is a well-defined
bijection of $A$: it lands in $A$ because $gAg^{-1}=A$, and its inverse is $\sigma_{g^{-1}}$,
which also maps $A$ to $A$ since $g^{-1}\in N_G(A)$. Thus $\sigma_g\in S_A$. It is a
homomorphism: for $g,h\in N_G(A)$ and $a\in A$,
\[
\sigma_{gh}(a)=(gh)a(gh)^{-1}=g(hah^{-1})g^{-1}=\sigma_g\big(\sigma_h(a)\big),
\]
so $\varphi(gh)=\sigma_g\sigma_h=\varphi(g)\varphi(h)$. Finally $g\in\ker\varphi$ iff
$\sigma_g=\operatorname{id}_A$ iff $gag^{-1}=a$ for all $a\in A$ iff $g\in C_G(A)$. A kernel
is a normal subgroup of its domain, so $C_G(A)\nor N_G(A)$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark} 
If $G$ is abelian then $ga=ag$ for all $g,a$, so $C_G(A)=N_G(A)=G$ for every subset $A$
and every subgroup is normal. Hence $\varphi$ is trivial and the homomorphism of
Proposition~ [REF:p:df-conj-hom-mrg@c2] carries information only in nonabelian groups:
there it measures, via $N_G(A)/C_G(A)\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi\sgr S_A$, exactly how
conjugation reshuffles $A$ as a set.
\end{remark}

Title: Reading off $\varphi$ for $A=\langle r\rangle$ in $D_8$: every reflection inverts $\langle r\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading off $\varphi$ for $A=\langle r\rangle$ in $D_8$: every reflection inverts $\langle r\rangle$}
With $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$ and $A=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}=\langle r\rangle$, the
centralizer and normalizer are already known: $C_{D_8}(A)=\langle r\rangle$ (Worked
Example~ [REF:wex:cent-d8-r@c2] , $C_{D_8}(r)=\langle r\rangle$) and $N_{D_8}(A)=D_8$ (index $2$).
Use Proposition~ [REF:p:df-conj-hom-mrg@c2] to identify the permutation $\varphi(g)\in S_A$.
\wrec The kernel of $\varphi$ is $C_{D_8}(A)=\langle r\rangle$, so $\varphi$ collapses the rotations
and is determined by what a single reflection does to $A$. The relation
$sr^k s^{-1}=r^{-k}$ gives that action in one line.
\wsol The rotations $\langle r\rangle=\ker\varphi$ act trivially: $r^j r^k r^{-j}=r^k$ for all
$j,k$. For a reflection $sr^j$,
\[
(sr^j)\,r^k\,(sr^j)^{-1}=s\,r^k\,s^{-1}=r^{-k},
\]
so every reflection induces the same permutation
$1\mapsto1,\ r\mapsto r^3,\ r^2\mapsto r^2,\ r^3\mapsto r$, i.e.\ the transposition of $r$
and $r^3$ fixing $1,r^2$. Thus
\[
\operatorname{im}\varphi=\{\operatorname{id}_A,\ (r\ \ r^3)\}\sgr S_A,\qquad
|\operatorname{im}\varphi|=2.
\]
Check. $|\operatorname{im}\varphi|=[N_{D_8}(A):C_{D_8}(A)]=8/4=2$, consistent with
$N_{D_8}(A)/C_{D_8}(A)\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi$. Conjugation by $s$ moves $r$ to the
different element $r^3\in A$ -- allowed setwise (so $s\in N_{D_8}(A)$) but not
pointwise (so $s\notin C_{D_8}(A)$), which is precisely the strict gap
$C_{D_8}(A)=\langle r\rangle\ \psgr\ N_{D_8}(A)=D_8$.
\end{wex}

Title: Centralizer table of $S_3$ and the center as their intersection
Content:
\begin{wex}{Centralizer table of $S_3$ and the center as their intersection}
For $S_3=\{1,(1\,2),(1\,3),(2\,3),(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, tabulate $C_{S_3}(a)$ by cycle
type and read off $Z(S_3)=\bigcap_{a}C_{S_3}(a)$ together with the orbit-stabilizer
identity $|S_3|=|class of a|\cdot|C_{S_3}(a)|$.
\wrec The center is the intersection of all centralizers ($Z(G)=C_G(G)$,
Definition~ [REF:d:center@c2] ). Since $(1\,2)$ and $(1\,2\,3)$ generate $S_3$ it suffices to
intersect their two centralizers, both already computed
($C_{S_3}((1\,2))=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ and a $3$-cycle centralizes only the cyclic group it
generates). The new content is the table and the class-size cross-check.
\wsol One representative per conjugacy class:
\[
\begin{array}{l|l|c|c}
a & C_{S_3}(a) & |C_{S_3}(a)| & |class of a|\\\hline
1 & S_3 & 6 & 1\\
(1\,2) & \{1,(1\,2)\} & 2 & 3\\
(1\,2\,3) & \{1,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\} & 3 & 2
\end{array}
\]
(the entries for $(1\,3),(2\,3)$ match $(1\,2)$, and $(1\,3\,2)$ matches $(1\,2\,3)$).
Intersecting over the two generators,
\[
Z(S_3)=C_{S_3}\big((1\,2)\big)\cap C_{S_3}\big((1\,2\,3)\big)
=\{1,(1\,2)\}\cap\{1,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}=\{1\}.
\]
Check. The orders $2$ and $3$ are coprime, so the two centralizers meet only in
$1$; and each row satisfies orbit-stabilizer
$|class|\cdot|C_{S_3}(a)|=|S_3|=6$ ($1\cdot6=3\cdot2=2\cdot3=6$). Consistent with
$Z(S_3)=1$.
\end{wex}

Title: Conjugation as a permutation representation $\varphi:G\to S_G$, with $\ker\varphi=Z(G)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugation as a permutation representation $\varphi:G\to S_G$, with $\ker\varphi=Z(G)$}
Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation, $g\cdot a=gag^{-1}$, with permutation
representation $\varphi:G\to S_G$, $\varphi(g)=\sigma_g$ (this is the $A=G$ case of the
conjugation action in Theorem~ [REF:t:conj@c2] ). Identify $\ker\varphi$ and confirm
faithfulness amounts to $Z(G)=1$.
\wrec ``Acts trivially on every point'' selects the kernel; ``fixes one chosen point''
selects a stabilizer. For conjugation on all of $G$, Theorem~ [REF:t:conj@c2] (b) already gives
$\operatorname{Stab}(a)=C_G(a)$; intersecting over every point gives the kernel, which is
the new identification with $Z(G)$.
\wsol $g\in\ker\varphi$ iff $\sigma_g=\operatorname{id}_G$ iff $gag^{-1}=a$ for all $a\in G$
iff $g$ commutes with every element of $G$, i.e.
\[
\ker\varphi=\bigcap_{a\in G}\operatorname{Stab}(a)=\bigcap_{a\in G}C_G(a)
=\{g\st ga=ag\ \forall a\in G\}=Z(G),
\]
matching $Z(G)=C_G(G)$ of Definition~ [REF:d:center@c2] . Hence the conjugation
representation $\varphi:G\to S_G$ is faithful (its kernel is $1$) iff $Z(G)=1$.
Check. For $G=S_3$ the table above gives $Z(S_3)=1$, so $S_3\hookrightarrow S_6$ by
conjugation; for $G=D_8$ one has $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}\ne1$ (Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] ),
so the conjugation representation of $D_8$ is not faithful, its kernel being $\langle r^2\rangle$.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``$g$ acts trivially'' ($\sigma_g=\operatorname{id}$, i.e.\ $g\in\ker$) is a statement about
one element; ``the action is faithful'' ($\ker=1$) is a statement about the whole action.
For conjugation on $G$ these read: a single $g$ acts trivially iff $g\in Z(G)$, while the
action is faithful iff $Z(G)=1$. So the kernel measures exactly the failure of
faithfulness, and for the conjugation representation that kernel is precisely $Z(G)$.
\end{pitfall}

Title: $C_{S_4}\big((1\,2)(3\,4)\big)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{S_4}\big((1\,2)(3\,4)\big)$}
Compute the centralizer of $\tau=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ in $S_4$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer in $S_n$: $\sigma$ commutes with $\tau$ iff
$\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\tau$. Since $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma1\,\sigma2)(\sigma3\,\sigma4)$,
this holds iff $\sigma$ preserves the partition $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$.
\wsol The permutations preserving $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$ may swap the two blocks and may
flip inside a block:
\[ \{e,\,(1\,2),\,(3\,4),\,(1\,2)(3\,4),\,(1\,3)(2\,4),\,(1\,4)(2\,3),\,(1\,3\,2\,4),\,
 (1\,4\,2\,3)\}, \]
of order $8$ (a copy of $D_8$). So $\ord{C_{S_4}(\tau)}=8$. Check. $8\mid24$, and
the number of conjugates of $\tau$ is $24/8=3$ --- exactly the three $(2,2)$-elements.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$C_{S_4}\big((1\,2)(3\,4)\big)$}

$\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\tau$. Since $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma1\,\sigma2)(\sigma3\,\sigma4)$,
this holds iff $\sigma$ \emph{preserves the partition} $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$.
\wsol The permutations preserving $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$ may swap the two blocks and may
flip inside a block:
\[ \{e,\,(1\,2),\,(3\,4),\,(1\,2)(3\,4),\,(1\,3)(2\,4),\,(1\,4)(2\,3),\,(1\,3\,2\,4),\,
   (1\,4\,2\,3)\}, \]
of order $8$ (a copy of $D_8$). So $\ord{C_{S_4}(\tau)}=8$. \textit{Check.} $8\mid24$, and
the number of conjugates of $\tau$ is $24/8=3$ --- exactly the three $(2,2)$-elements.
\end{wex}

Title: $C_{Q_8}(j)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_{Q_8}(j)$}
Find the centralizer of $j$ in $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$.
\wrec Single-element centralizer; use $ij=k$, $ji=-k$, so $i$ and $k$ anticommute
with $j$ while $\pm1,\pm j$ commute with it.
\wsol $j$ commutes with $1,-1,j,-j$, but $ij=k\neq-k=ji$, so $\pm i,\pm k\notin C$. Thus
$C_{Q_8}(j)=\{\pm1,\pm j\}=\langle j\rangle$, order $4$. Check. $\langle j\rangle\sgr C_{Q_8}(j)$
always; here they are equal.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z(D_{16})$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z(D_{16})$}
Find the center of $D_{16}$ (symmetries of the octagon; $r^8=s^2=1$, $sr=r^{-1} s$).
\wrec $D_{2n}$ with $n=8$ even, so Theorem~ [REF:t:center-dihedral@c2] predicts
$Z=\{1,r^{n/2}\}=\{1,r^4\}$. Verify by intersecting $C(r)\cap C(s)$.
\wsol No reflection is central ($sr^k$ commutes with $r$ only if $r^2=1$, false). A
rotation $r^a$ commutes with $s$ iff $r^a=r^{-a}$, i.e.\ $r^{2a}=1$, i.e.\ $a\in\{0,4\}$.
Hence $Z(D_{16})=\{1,r^4\}$. Check. $r^4=r^{-4}$ has order $2$, so $sr^4=r^4 s$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$N_{S_4}\big(\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle\big)$}
Compute the normalizer of $H=\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle=\{e,\allowbreak(1234),\allowbreak(13)(24),\allowbreak(1432)\}$ in $S_4$.
\wrec Setwise stabilizer of $H$ under conjugation. A conjugate of a $4$-cycle is a

(a rotation or a reflection). These are $\langle (1234),(13)\rangle$, of order $8$. So
$\ord{N_{S_4}(H)}=8$. Check. $H\sgr N$, index $24/8=3$ = number of conjugate
cyclic subgroups of order $4$.

Title: counting $S_5$ through a stabilizer
Content:
\begin{wex}{counting $S_5$ through a stabilizer}
$S_5$ acts on $\{1,\dots,5\}$. Find $\ord{Stab(5)}$ and recount $\ord{S_5}$.
\wrec The action is transitive (the orbit of $5$ is all of $\{1,\dots,5\}$), so
$\ord{G}=\ord{orbit}\cdot\ord{Stab}$ (orbit--stabilizer, previewed below).
\wsol $Stab(5)=\{\sigma\st\sigma(5)=5\}$ is the copy of $S_4$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$,
so $\ord{Stab(5)}=24$. The orbit has size $5$, so
$\ord{S_5}=5\cdot24=120=5!$.
\end{wex}

$S_5$ acts on $\{1,\dots,5\}$. Find $\ord{\mathrm{Stab}(5)}$ and recount $\ord{S_5}$.

\noindent The recount above is an instance of the orbit--stabilizer bijection: for
$G$ acting on $S$, cosets of $G_s$ correspond to points of the orbit of $s$. We will prove
this in Chapter~4; as a diagram it is
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G/G_s \arrow[r, "\sim", "gG_s\,\mapsto\,g\cdot s"'] & orbit(s),
\end{tikzcd}\]
so $\ord{orbit(s)}=[G:G_s]$ --- the principle behind every counting argument of
this kind.

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $G/G_s$ is the set of left cosets of the stabilizer $G_s$ in $G$ (not a
 group in general, just a set of cosets). $orbit(s)=\{g\cdot s\st g\in G\}$ is
 the orbit of $s$ under the action, a subset of the set $A$ on which $G$ acts.
\dgi{Arrows:} The single arrow labeled $\sim$ is the bijection $\Phi:G/G_s\to
 orbit(s)$, $gG_s\mapsto g\cdot s$. It is an induced map from the quotient: it
 takes a coset $gG_s$ and evaluates $g$ at $s$. The label $\sim$ signals that this arrow
 is a bijection (an isomorphism of sets).
\dgi{What commutes:} There is only one path from $G/G_s$ to $orbit(s)$, so the
 diagram records a single well-defined map rather than a path-equality. The content is
 the two-sided inverse: $\Phi$ is injective (if $g\cdot s=h\cdot s$ then $h^{-1} g\in G_s$
 so $gG_s=hG_s$) and surjective (every $g\cdot s$ in the orbit is hit by the coset $gG_s$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\Phi$ is the key step: if $gG_s=hG_s$ then
 $h^{-1} g\in G_s$, i.e.\ $(h^{-1} g)\cdot s=s$, so $g\cdot s=h\cdot(h^{-1} g\cdot s)=h\cdot s$.
 Thus the formula $gG_s\mapsto g\cdot s$ does not depend on which representative of the
 coset we pick -- this is the well-definedness check for a quotient-induced map.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is placed immediately after the $D_8$-on-vertices
 and $S_5$ examples to explain why those counting arguments work: the coset count $[G:G_s]$
 equals the orbit size because the bijection $\Phi$ matches them one-to-one. Every orbit-
 stabilizer equation $|G|=|orbit|\cdot|G_s|$ is a consequence of this bijection
 together with Lagrange's theorem ($|G|=[G:G_s]\cdot|G_s|$).
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$ acting on $\{1,2,3\}$ by evaluation, $s=1$. Then
 $G_1=\{e,(2\,3)\}\congZ/2$ (order $2$), and the orbit of $1$ is $\{1,2,3\}$ (size $3$).
 The bijection sends $eG_1\mapsto1$, $(1\,2)G_1\mapsto2$, $(1\,3)G_1\mapsto3$, confirming
 three cosets $\leftrightarrow$ three orbit elements.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse $G/G_s$ (a set of cosets, not a quotient
 group) with the orbit itself. The arrow $\Phi$ is a bijection of sets, not a group
 isomorphism; $G/G_s$ inherits a group structure only when $G_s\nor G$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the orbit of $s$ is in bijection with the
 set of cosets of the stabilizer, so computing the size of an orbit always reduces to counting cosets.
\end{dgx}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Centralizers, Normalizers, Stabilizers, and Kernels > Maps and commutative diagrams
Type: prose
Part: 1/3
Content:
The centralizer, normalizer, and kernel of this section are all instances of a single
idea: turn the situation into a homomorphism and look at its kernel.

\noindent(a) An action is a homomorphism to a symmetric group. An
action of $G$ on a set $S$ is the same thing as a homomorphism
$\rho:G\to\operatorname{Sym}(S)$, $g\mapsto(s\mapsto g\cdot s)$
(Definition~ [REF:d:action@c2] ). The stabilizer $G_s$ is the set of $g$ fixing $s$, and the
kernel of the action is $\ker\rho=\bigcap_{s\in S}G_s$ --- an intersection of subgroups,
hence a subgroup (Proposition~ [REF:p:stab-subgroup@c2] ).
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\rho"] & \operatorname{Sym}(S)
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $G$ is the group acting. $\operatorname{Sym}(S)$ is the symmetric group on
 the set $S$ (all bijections $S\to S$ under composition). This is the universal target for
 any action of $G$ on $S$.

 $\iota_g$ is an automorphism of $G$ (a bijective homomorphism), and $\phi$ is a
 homomorphism: $\iota_{gh}=\iota_g\circ\iota_h$.

 means $gxg^{-1}=x$ for all $x$, i.e.\ $gx=xg$ for all $x$, so $g\in Z(G)$. Well-
 definedness of $\phi$: $\iota_g$ is a bijection (with inverse $\iota_{g^{-1}}$) and a

Type: definition
Label: d:cyclic@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
A group $H$ is cyclic if there exists $x\in H$ with $H=\langle x\rangle=\{x^n \st n\inZ\}$; such an $x$ is a generator. We write the abstract cyclic group of order $n$ as $Z_n$, and use $Z$ for the infinite cyclic group.
\end{definition}
label: d:cyclic@c2

Type: prose
Content:
Two free facts fall out of the definition immediately. First, a cyclic group is abelian: any two elements of $\langle x\rangle$ are powers $x^a,x^b$, and $x^a x^b=x^{a+b}=x^{b+a}=x^b x^a$. Second, $\langle x\rangle=\langle x^{-1}\rangle$, because $x=(x^{-1})^{-1}$ lies in $\langle x^{-1}\rangle$ and conversely, so each generates the other's group.

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Cyclic'' is much stronger than ``abelian.'' $V_4$ is abelian but not cyclic: no single element has order $4$, so no element generates all of $V_4$. Cyclic $\Longrightarrow$ abelian, never the reverse.
\end{pitfall}
