Title: $\langle (1\,2),(2\,3)\rangle=S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle (1\,2),(2\,3)\rangle=S_3$}
Show the transpositions $(1\,2)$ and $(2\,3)$ generate $S_3$.
\wrec Ambient group is $S_3$, which is nonabelian, so we cannot use gcd or integer combinations --- we must do honest word closure (Method box, products in both orders). The trigger is two specific elements with ``$\langle \,\cdot\,\rangle$.''
\wsol Seed: $1,(1\,2),(2\,3)$ (each transposition is its own inverse). Multiply (D\&F convention: rightmost permutation acts first):
\[
(1\,2)(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3),\qquad (2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3\,2).
\]
Adjoin these two $3$-cycles. One more product gives the last missing element:
\[
(1\,2)\,(1\,2\,3)=(2\,3)\quad(already have);\qquad (1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3).
\]
Now the closure is $\{1,(1\,2),(1\,3),(2\,3),(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, which is all $6$ elements of $S_3$, and further products produce nothing new.
Check. $\lvert S_3\rvert=3!=6$ and our closure has $6$ elements, so $\langle (1\,2),(2\,3)\rangle=S_3$. (Indeed adjacent transpositions generate $S_n$ in general.)
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\langle s,r^2\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}\cong V_4$ in $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle s,r^2\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}\cong V_4$ in $D_8$}
In $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$, compute $\langle s,r^2\rangle$.
\wrec Nonabelian ambient $D_8$: do word closure. Key relations to apply during closure: $s^2=1$, $r^4=1$, and the conjugation rule $sr=r^{-1} s$, i.e.\ $r^2s=sr^{-2}=sr^2$ (since $r^{-2}=r^2$ in $D_8$).
\wsol Seed: $1,\ s\ (s^{-1}=s),\ r^2\ ((r^2)^{-1}=r^{-2}=r^2)$. Form products:
\[
s\cdot r^2=sr^2,\qquad r^2\cdot s=sr^{-2}=sr^2\quad(same element, so the set is commutative here).
\]
Check the new element squares to $1$: $(sr^2)^2=sr^2sr^2=s(r^2s)r^2=s(sr^{-2})r^2=s^2r^{-2}r^2=1$. Also $(r^2)^2=r^4=1$. No further products escape: $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$ is closed.
Check. The closure has $4$ elements, all of order dividing $2$, and it is abelian (we saw $s\,r^2=r^2\,s$). A group of order $4$ with every non-identity element of order $2$ is the Klein four-group, so $\langle s,r^2\rangle\cong V_4$. Sanity: $\lvert D_8\rvert=8$, and $4\mid 8$ as Lagrange demands.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\langle i,j\rangle=Q_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle i,j\rangle=Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$ (and $ji=-k$, etc.), compute $\langle i,j\rangle$.
\wrec Nonabelian ambient $Q_8$: word closure, products in both orders, using the quaternion multiplication relations. Trigger: ``$\langle i,j\rangle$.''
\wsol Seed: $1,\ i,\ i^{-1}=-i\ (since i^2=-1\Rightarrow i^{-1}=-i),\ j,\ j^{-1}=-j$. Generate:
\[
ij=k,\qquad ji=-k,\qquad i^2=-1,\qquad (-1)\cdot1=-1.
\]
Adjoining $k$ and $-1$, then $-k=(-1)k$, $-i=(-1)i$, $-j=(-1)j$, the set becomes $\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$. Every further product stays inside (e.g.\ $jk=i$, $kj=-i$, $ki=j$), so the closure is all $8$ units.
Check. $\lvert\langle i,j\rangle\rvert=8=\lvert Q_8\rvert$, so $\langle i,j\rangle=Q_8$. Note $j\notin\langle i\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm i\}$ (order $4$), so a single generator is genuinely insufficient --- both $i$ and $j$ are needed.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
In a nonabelian group you may not reorder letters: $\langle i,j\rangle$ in $Q_8$ needs both $ij=k$ and $ji=-k$. Skipping the reversed products (or trying to ``collect exponents'' as in the abelian case) will undercount the subgroup. Only after you prove the elements commute --- as with $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$ in $D_8$ --- may you treat the closure abelianly.
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Title: Generated-by language and ``finitely generated''
Content:
\begin{remark}[Generated-by language and ``finitely generated'']
Beyond the notation $\langle A\rangle$ and $\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle$ already fixed in Definition~ [REF:d:gen@c2] , D\&F uses two phrasings throughout:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G$ is generated by $A$ (equivalently $A$ generates $G$) means $\langle A\rangle=G$.
\item A group $G$ is called finitely generated if $G=\langle A\rangle$ for some finite set $A$.
\end{itemize}
The single-element case $\langle x\rangle$ is exactly the cyclic subgroup studied in the previous section; the present construction is its generalization to arbitrary $A$, and the next example checks that the two uses of the symbol $\langle x\rangle$ agree.
\end{remark}

Section: Subgroups > Subgroups Generated by Subsets > Further examples and the book's language
Type: example
Title: $\langle x\rangle$ recovers the cyclic subgroup
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle x\rangle$ recovers the cyclic subgroup}
For a single element $x\in G$ (with $G$ possibly nonabelian), verify that the word description of $\langle \{x\}\rangle$ collapses to $\{x^n\st n\inZ\}$.
\wrec Single generator, $A=\{x\}$. Theorem~ [REF:t:words@c2] (word description) applies: words use only the one letter $x$ and its inverse $x^{-1}$, so commutativity of the ambient group is irrelevant here.
\wsol A word $a_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots a_k^{\varepsilon_k}$ with every $a_i=x$ is $x^{\varepsilon_1}x^{\varepsilon_2}\cdots x^{\varepsilon_k}=x^{\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_k}$, an integer power of $x$. Conversely every $x^n$ ($n\inZ$) is such a word: take $n$ copies of $x$ if $n>0$, of $x^{-1}$ if $n<0$, and the empty word if $n=0$. Hence $\langle \{x\}\rangle=\{x^n\st n\inZ\}=\langle x\rangle$.
Check. This matches the cyclic-subgroup meaning of $\langle x\rangle$ from the prior section, so writing $\langle x\rangle$ for both is consistent. If $\ord{x}=m<\infty$ the distinct powers are $1,x,\dots,x^{m-1}$, recovering $\lvert\langle x\rangle\rvert=\ord{x}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Z=\langle 1\rangle$ and $Z/(n)Z=\langle \overline 1\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z=\langle 1\rangle$ and $Z/(n)Z=\langle \overline 1\rangle$}
Exhibit single generators for the basic cyclic groups $Z$ and $Z/(n)Z$.
\wrec One generator suffices for a cyclic group; here $G$ is cyclic with a named candidate generator, so $\langle x\rangle=G$ reduces to checking that $x$ reaches every element.
\wsol In $(Z,+)$, every integer is $m=m\cdot 1$, an integer multiple of $1$, so $\langle 1\rangle=\{m\cdot 1\st m\inZ\}=Z$. In $(Z/(n)Z,+)$, every class is $\overline m=m\cdot\overline 1$, so $\langle \overline 1\rangle=Z/(n)Z$.
Check. For $Z/(n)Z$ this agrees with $\lvert\langle \overline 1\rangle\rvert=n/\gcd(1,n)=n=\lvertZ/(n)Z\rvert$. More generally $\overline a$ generates $Z/(n)Z$ iff $\gcd(a,n)=1$; for $n=12$ the generators are $\overline 1,\overline 5,\overline 7,\overline{11}$, the four units mod $12$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > Subgroups Generated by Subsets > Further examples and the book's language
Type: example
Title: $D_{2n}=\langle r,s\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$D_{2n}=\langle r,s\rangle$}
In $D_{2n}=\langle r,s\st r^n=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$, show that the rotation $r$ and reflection $s$ generate the whole group.
\wrec Nonabelian ambient $D_{2n}$. The defining relations name $\{r,s\}$ as a generating set, so the task is to confirm the word closure already has all $2n$ elements. The tool is the master relation $r^k s=s\,r^{-k}$, used to put every word into normal form.
\wsol Take any word in $r,s,r^{-1},s^{-1}$. Since $s^{-1}=s$, every letter is a power of $r$ or a single $s$. Using $r^k s=s\,r^{-k}$ one moves each $s$ leftward past the $r$-powers; since $s^2=1$, at most one $s$ survives. Thus every element reduces to $r^i$ or $s\,r^i$ with $0\le i\le n-1$. These are the $n$ rotations $1,r,\dots,r^{n-1}$ and the $n$ reflections $s,sr,\dots,sr^{n-1}$, i.e.\ all $2n$ elements. Hence $\langle r,s\rangle=D_{2n}$.
Check. The count is $n+n=2n=\lvert D_{2n}\rvert$. Concretely in $D_8$ ($n=4$) the eight elements $\{1,r,r^2,r^3,s,sr,sr^2,sr^3\}$ are all reached, matching $\lvert D_8\rvert=8$ and the normal form used throughout these notes.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A single reflection generates only an order-$2$ subgroup
Content:
\begin{wex}{A single reflection generates only an order-$2$ subgroup}
In $D_{2n}$, compute $\langle s\rangle$ for a reflection $s$.
\wrec Single generator $s$ with $s^2=1$, so $\ord{s}=2$; by the single-generator description $\langle s\rangle=\{s^n\st n\inZ\}$ has order $\ord{s}$.
\wsol Since $s^2=1$, the powers of $s$ are $s^0=1$ and $s^1=s$, so $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$, a subgroup of order $2$.
Check. $2\mid 2n$, as Lagrange requires, and a single reflection cannot produce any rotation $r^i$ with $i\not\equiv 0$, confirming $\langle s\rangle\neq D_{2n}$ for $n\ge 2$. So two generators (such as $r,s$) are genuinely needed to reach all of $D_{2n}$.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: Pairwise-commuting generators
Label: p:comm-gen-mrg@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Pairwise-commuting generators] 
Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}\subseteq G$ and suppose the generators commute pairwise, $a_ia_j=a_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Then every element of $\langle A\rangle$ can be written in the collected form
\[
a_1^{m_1}a_2^{m_2}\cdots a_n^{m_n},\qquad m_1,\dots,m_n\inZ,
\]
and $\langle A\rangle$ is abelian.
\end{proposition}
label: p:comm-gen-mrg@c2

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-a0f77665207f3b74ab89
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~ [REF:t:words@c2] each element of $\langle A\rangle$ is a word in the $a_i^{\pm1}$. Because the generators commute pairwise, any two adjacent letters may be swapped; repeatedly swapping sorts every word so that all $a_1^{\pm1}$ come first, then all $a_2^{\pm1}$, and so on, and within the $a_i$-block the exponents add to a single integer $m_i$, giving $a_1^{m_1}\cdots a_n^{m_n}$. Two such collected expressions commute, since each $a_i$ commutes with every $a_j$, so $\langle A\rangle$ is abelian. (This refines Corollary~ [REF:c:abelian@c2] : there the whole group was abelian, here only the chosen generators need commute.)
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: Using ``smallest'' to identify $\langle A\rangle$ without listing words
Content:
\begin{remark}[Using ``smallest'' to identify $\langle A\rangle$ without listing words]
Definition~ [REF:d:gen@c2] packages $\langle A\rangle$ as an intersection so that, to prove a candidate set $K$ equals $\langle A\rangle$, one need not enumerate words: show $K\sgr G$ and $A\subseteq K$ (forcing $\langle A\rangle\subseteq K$ by the smallest property), then show every generator's contributions land in $\langle A\rangle$ (forcing $K\subseteq\langle A\rangle$). The $D_{2n}=\langle r,s\rangle$ and $Z=\langle 1\rangle$ computations above are both instances of this two-inclusion pattern.
\end{remark}

Type: prose

Content:
The phrase ``smallest subgroup containing $A$'' is a universal property, and universal
properties are diagrams.

\noindent(a) The universal property of $\langle A\rangle$. $\langle A\rangle$ is the
smallest subgroup containing $A$: for every subgroup $H$ with $A\subseteq H$, the

homomorphism from $\langle A\rangle$ to $H$ that restricts to the given inclusion of $A$.

\noindent(b) Generation is functorial. A homomorphism $f:G\to K$
carries $\langle A\rangle$ onto $\langle f(A)\rangle$, because $f$ of a word in $A$ is a word in $f(A)$
(Theorem~ [REF:t:words@c2] ). Every square below commutes; in particular generators map to
generators.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "f"'] & \langle A\rangle \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[r, hook] & G \arrow[d, "f"] \\
f(A) \arrow[r, hook] & \langle f(A)\rangle \arrow[r, hook] & K
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Six objects in a $2 \times 3$ grid. Top row: subset $A \subseteq G$, the subgroup
$\langle A\rangle \sgr G$, and the ambient group $G$. Bottom row: image set $f(A) \subseteq K$, the subgroup
$\langle f(A)\rangle \sgr K$, and the ambient group $K$. Here $f: G \to K$ is a group homomorphism.
\dgi{Arrows:} The two horizontal inclusions in the top row are $A \hookrightarrow \langle A\rangle
\hookrightarrow G$ (set inclusion then subgroup inclusion). Similarly $f(A) \hookrightarrow
\langle f(A)\rangle \hookrightarrow K$ in the bottom row. The three vertical arrows are all labeled $f$:
the leftmost sends $a \mapsto f(a)$, the middle restricts $f$ to $\langle A\rangle$ (which is again
denoted $f$ since it is the same map on a subset of $G$), and the rightmost is $f: G \to K$ itself.
\dgi{What commutes:} Each of the two squares commutes independently.
Left square: $f \circ \iota_{A,\langle A\rangle} = \iota_{f(A),\langle f(A)\rangle} \circ f$, i.e.\ including $A$
into $\langle A\rangle$ and then applying $f$ gives the same result as applying $f$ to $A$ and then
including $f(A)$ into $\langle f(A)\rangle$.
Right square: $f \circ \iota_{\langle A\rangle,G} = \iota_{\langle f(A)\rangle,K} \circ f|_{\langle A\rangle}$, i.e.\
including $\langle A\rangle$ into $G$ then applying $f$ equals restricting $f$ to $\langle A\rangle$ then
including into $K$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For the left square, take $a \in A$. Down-then-right: $a \mapsto f(a)
\in f(A) \hookrightarrow \langle f(A)\rangle$. Right-then-down: $a \in A \hookrightarrow \langle A\rangle$,
then $f(a) \in \langle f(A)\rangle$. Both paths give $f(a)$ sitting in $\langle f(A)\rangle$, so they agree.
The key fact: $f$ sends every generator $a \in A$ to $f(a) \in f(A)$, and since $f$ is a
homomorphism it sends every word $a_1^{\varepsilon_1} \cdots a_k^{\varepsilon_k}$ to
$f(a_1)^{\varepsilon_1} \cdots f(a_k)^{\varepsilon_k}$, which is a word in $f(A)$, hence in
$\langle f(A)\rangle$. This is exactly Theorem~ [REF:t:words@c2] applied to $f$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram encodes the sentence ``$f(\langle A\rangle) = \langle f(A)\rangle$''
in a way that also records where each inclusion sits. It confirms that generating sets behave
well under homomorphisms: the image of the generated subgroup is the subgroup generated by
the image of the generating set. This is used implicitly whenever one argues that a homomorphism
is surjective by checking it hits a generating set.

= \{\overline{0},\overline{2},\overline{4}\}$. The left square sends $2 \mapsto \overline{2}$
both ways; the right square confirms $f(2Z) = \{\overline{0},\overline{2},\overline{4}\}
= \langle \overline{2}\rangle$, as the diagram predicts.

correct statement is $f(\langle A\rangle) = \langle f(A)\rangle$, which equals $K$ only when $f(A)$ generates $K$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a group homomorphism is compatible with
generation, carrying the subgroup generated by $A$ to the subgroup generated by the image of $A$.
\end{dgx}

\noindent(c) The universal property of the free group. The ``most
general'' group generated by a set $S$ is the free group $F(S)$: any set map $S\to G$
extends to a unique homomorphism $F(S)\to G$. This is the precise meaning of ``the
generators satisfy no relations,'' and it is why $S_n=\langle (1\,2),(1\,2\cdots n)\rangle$ etc.\
are described by giving generators and relations.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
S \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & F(S) \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\bar f"] \\
& G
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects. The set $S$ (not yet a group -- just a generating alphabet, e.g.\
$S = \{a, b\}$ for a two-generator free group). The free group $F(S)$, the group of all reduced
words in $S \cup S^{-1}$ with no relations other than $ss^{-1} = 1$. The target group $G$,
an arbitrary group equipped with a set map $f: S \to G$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota: S \to F(S)$ is the canonical inclusion sending each letter $s \in S$ to
the length-one word $s \in F(S)$ (the set-theoretic embedding, not a group homomorphism since
$S$ is not a group). $f: S \to G$ is any set map (possibly $f(s_1) = f(s_2)$ for distinct
$s_1, s_2$; no homomorphism condition required on $f$ since $S$ has no group structure).
The dashed arrow $\bar{f}: F(S) \to G$ is the unique group homomorphism extending $f$:
it sends the word $s_1^{\varepsilon_1} \cdots s_k^{\varepsilon_k}$ to
$f(s_1)^{\varepsilon_1} \cdots f(s_k)^{\varepsilon_k} \in G$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\bar{f} \circ \iota = f$, i.e.\ restricting
$\bar{f}$ to the generating set $S \subset F(S)$ recovers the original set map $f$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For any $s \in S$, $\bar{f}(\iota(s)) = \bar{f}(s) = f(s)$ by the
definition of $\bar{f}$ (it is defined to send each generator $s$ of $F(S)$ to $f(s)$, and
then extended to all words by the homomorphism rule). Uniqueness: any homomorphism $h: F(S)
\to G$ satisfying $h \circ \iota = f$ must send $s \mapsto f(s)$ for each $s$; since $F(S)$
is generated by $S$, this determines $h$ on all of $F(S)$ (a homomorphism is determined by
its values on generators), so $h = \bar{f}$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram explains why generators and relations suffice to
define a group homomorphism out of any group $G = \langle a_1, \dots, a_n \mid relations\rangle$:
one first defines a set map on the generators, extends freely to $F(S)$ via $\bar{f}$, and then
checks the relations are preserved (which forces $\bar{f}$ to factor through the quotient $G$).
The author places it here to make precise the phrase ``no relations'' and to connect subgroup
generation to the broader framework of presentations.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Let $S = \{x\}$ (one letter), $G = Z/(6)Z$, $f(x) = \overline{2}$.
Then $F(S) = Z$ (the free group on one generator is $Z$), and $\bar{f}: Z \to Z/(6)Z$
sends $n \mapsto \overline{2n}$, a group homomorphism. The triangle: $\bar{f}(\iota(x)) =
\bar{f}(1) = \overline{2} = f(x)$. The image is $\langle \overline{2}\rangle = \{\overline{0},
\overline{2}, \overline{4}\}$, a proper subgroup of $Z/(6)Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The map $\iota: S \to F(S)$ is a set map, not a group homomorphism
(since $S$ has no group structure). Students sometimes write ``$\iota$ is a homomorphism,''
which is meaningless. Also, $\bar{f}$ need not be injective or surjective: the free group
is big (it surjects onto every group generated by $|S|$ elements), but $\bar{f}$ can collapse
much of $F(S)$ depending on what relations hold in $G$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that specifying a group homomorphism out of $F(S)$
is the same as specifying a set map out of $S$, making the free group the universal group
generated by the set $S$ with no constraints.
\end{dgx}

\dgi{Common pitfall:} The map $\iota: S \to F(S)$ is a set map, not a group homomorphism
(since $S$ has no group structure). Students sometimes write ``$\iota$ is a homomorphism,''
which is meaningless. Also, $\bar{f}$ need not be injective or surjective: the free group
is big (it surjects onto every group generated by $|S|$ elements), but $\bar{f}$ can collapse
much of $F(S)$ depending on what relations hold in $G$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that specifying a group homomorphism out of $F(S)$
is the same as specifying a set map out of $S$, making the free group the universal group
generated by the set $S$ with no constraints.
\end{dgx}

 $\langle A\rangle\vee\langle B\rangle$ in the subgroup lattice.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: prose
Content:
Every group $G$ has a collection $L(G)$ of all its subgroups. This collection is partially ordered by inclusion ($H\le K$ means $H$ is a subgroup of $K$), and it has enough structure to be drawn as a single picture --- the Hasse diagram --- from which every containment, every intersection, and every ``smallest subgroup containing two given ones'' can be read off by eye. This section sets up that picture and the two operations (meet and join) that make $L(G)$ a lattice.

This section sets up that picture and the two operations (meet and join) that make $\mathcal{L}(G)$ a lattice.

Type: definition
Label: d:poset@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
For a group $G$, write $H\sgr K$ to mean $H$ is a subgroup of $K$. The relation $\sgr$ on the set $L(G)$ of all subgroups of $G$ is a partial order: it is reflexive ($H\sgr H$), antisymmetric ($H\sgr K$ and $K\sgr H$ force $H=K$), and transitive ($H\sgr K\sgr L$ gives $H\sgr L$).
\end{definition}
label: d:poset@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: definition
Label: d:cover@c2
Content:
\begin{definition} 
Let $B\psgr A$ (so $B$ is a proper subgroup of $A$). We say $A$ covers $B$, written $B\lessdot A$, if there is no subgroup $C$ with $B\psgr C\psgr A$ --- that is, nothing strictly between them. The Hasse diagram of $G$ has one vertex per subgroup, drawn so that $B$ sits lower than $A$ whenever $B\psgr A$, and an edge (segment) joins $B$ to $A$ exactly when $A$ covers $B$. The trivial subgroup $1=\{e\}$ is the unique bottom vertex; $G$ is the unique top vertex.
\end{definition}
label: d:cover@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: remark
Label: r:transitive@c2
Content:
\begin{remark} 
We do not draw an edge for every containment, only for coverings. A containment $B\psgr A$ that is not a covering is recovered from the diagram as an upward path of two or more edges. For instance in $Z/(12)Z$ we have $\langle 6\rangle\psgr Z/(12)Z$ but the edge from $\langle 6\rangle$ does not go straight to the top; the containment is read off as a path through $\langle 2\rangle$ or through $\langle 3\rangle$. This is why Hasse diagrams stay readable: transitivity is encoded by paths, not by a tangle of extra segments.
\end{remark}
label: r:transitive@c2

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: proposition
Label: p:intersub@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
For any nonempty family $\{H_i\}_{i\in I}$ of subgroups of $G$, the intersection $\bigcap_{i\in I}H_i$ is a subgroup of $G$. Consequently $H\cap K$ and $\langle H,K\rangle$ both exist and are subgroups, so $L(G)$ is a lattice: every pair has a meet and a join.
\end{proposition}
label: p:intersub@c2

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-5dbd01ddfa708f1ddea7
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $D=\bigcap_i H_i$. Since $e\in H_i$ for every $i$, $e\in D$, so $D\ne\varnothing$. If $a,b\in D$ then $a,b\in H_i$ for each $i$; each $H_i$ is a subgroup, so $ab^{-1}\in H_i$ for each $i$, hence $ab^{-1}\in D$. By the subgroup criterion $D\sgr G$. For the join, let $S$ be the (nonempty, since $G\inS$) collection of all subgroups containing $H\cup K$; then $\langle H,K\rangle=\bigcap_{S\inS}S$ is a subgroup by the first part, and it is by construction the smallest subgroup above both $H$ and $K$. The meet $H\cap K$ is the case of two subgroups.
\end{proof}

Type: proposition
Label: p:cycliclattice@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
Let $G=Z/(n)Z=\langle x\rangle$ be cyclic of order $n$. For each divisor $d\mid n$ there is exactly one subgroup of order $d$, namely $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle$, and these are all the subgroups. Containment matches divisibility:
\[
\langle x^{n/d_1}\rangle\sgr \langle x^{n/d_2}\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_1\mid d_2 .
\]
Hence the Hasse diagram of $Z/(n)Z$ is exactly the divisor lattice of $n$: vertices are the divisors of $n$, with $d_1$ below $d_2$ when $d_1\mid d_2$, and a covering edge when $d_2/d_1$ is prime.
\end{proposition}
label: p:cycliclattice@c2

\[
\langle x^{n/d_1}\rangle\sgr \langle x^{n/d_2}\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_1\mid d_2 .
\]
Hence the Hasse diagram of $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ is exactly the \emph{divisor lattice} of $n$: vertices are the divisors of $n$, with $d_1$ below $d_2$ when $d_1\mid d_2$, and a covering edge when $d_2/d_1$ is prime.
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8efe1a3b089618dd519c
Content:
\begin{proof}
By the classification of subgroups of a cyclic group, every subgroup of $\langle x\rangle$ is cyclic of the form $\langle x^m\rangle$, and $\langle x^m\rangle=\langle x^{\gcd(m,n)}\rangle$ has order $n/\gcd(m,n)$. As $\gcd(m,n)$ ranges over the divisors of $n$, the order $n/\gcd(m,n)$ ranges over the divisors of $n$, each occurring for a unique subgroup; so there is exactly one subgroup of each order $d\mid n$, equal to $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle$. For containment, $\langle x^{n/d_1}\rangle\sgr\langle x^{n/d_2}\rangle$ holds iff the order $d_1$ divides the order $d_2$ (a subgroup of a cyclic group of order $d_2$ has order dividing $d_2$, and there is a unique one of each such order), i.e. iff $d_1\mid d_2$. A covering corresponds to a divisibility $d_1\mid d_2$ with no divisor strictly between, i.e. $d_2/d_1$ prime.
\end{proof}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: method
Title: How to build the subgroup lattice (Hasse diagram) of a finite group
Content:
\begin{method}{How to build the subgroup lattice (Hasse diagram) of a finite group}
Use this whenever you are asked to ``draw the lattice of subgroups'' or to read a join/meet off a picture.
\begin{enumerate}
\item List all subgroups, grouped by order. By Lagrange every subgroup order divides $|G|$, so you only need to search orders $d\mid |G|$. For cyclic $G=Z/(n)Z$ this is automatic: one subgroup $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle$ per divisor $d$ (Proposition~ [REF:p:cycliclattice@c2] ). For non-cyclic $G$, find all subgroups of each allowed order directly (e.g. all cyclic $\langle g\rangle$, then larger ones).
\item Place vertices vertically by order. Bottom row: the trivial group $1$ (order $1$). Top: $G$ (order $|G|$). Subgroups of equal order sit at the same height; larger order sits higher.
\item Draw covering edges only. Join $B$ up to $A$ iff $B\psgr A$ with nothing in between (Definition~ [REF:d:cover@c2] ). A quick test: if $B\psgr A$ and the index $[A:B]$ is prime, then $A$ covers $B$ (no room for an intermediate subgroup by Lagrange). Never draw an edge for a containment that already factors through a third subgroup.
\item Read joins and meets off the picture. $H\wedge K=H\cap K$ is the highest vertex lying below both $H$ and $K$ (their highest common lower bound). $H\vee K=\langle H,K\rangle$ is the lowest vertex lying above both. ``Below/above'' means reachable by a downward/upward path of edges.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > The subgroup lattice: Hasse diagrams, joins, and meets
Type: method
Title: How to read a join $H\vee K$ and meet $H\wedge K$ off a Hasse diagram
Content:
\begin{method}{How to read a join $H\vee K$ and meet $H\wedge K$ off a Hasse diagram}
Use this whenever a problem gives you two specific subgroups and asks for their intersection or the subgroup they generate.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Locate $H$ and $K$ as vertices.
\item Meet $H\wedge K=H\cap K$: trace downward from both. The meet is the highest vertex reachable by a downward path from $H$ and from $K$. If their only common lower vertex is $1$, then $H\cap K=1$.
\item Join $H\vee K=\langle H,K\rangle$: trace upward from both. The join is the lowest vertex reachable by an upward path from $H$ and from $K$. If their only common upper vertex is $G$, then $\langle H,K\rangle=G$.
\item Confirm by orders if unsure: $|H\cap K|$ divides $\gcd(|H|,|K|)$; and $|\langle H,K\rangle|$ is a multiple of $\lcm(|H|,|K|)$ dividing $|G|$. Often this pins the answer.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: A meet and join inside $Z/(12)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A meet and join inside $Z/(12)Z$}
In $Z/(12)Z=\langle x\rangle$ compute $\langle x^4\rangle\wedge\langle x^6\rangle$ and $\langle x^4\rangle\vee\langle x^6\rangle$, where $\langle x^4\rangle$ has order $3$ and $\langle x^6\rangle$ has order $2$.
\wrec
Two named subgroups of a cyclic group; use the reading-off Method on the $Z/(12)Z$ grid, and double-check with the cyclic shortcut $\langle x^a\rangle\cap\langle x^b\rangle=\langle x^{\lcm(a,b)}\rangle$ and $\langle x^a,x^b\rangle=\langle x^{\gcd(a,b)}\rangle$.
\wsol
Meet (down). On the grid, $\langle x^4\rangle$ (order $3$) and $\langle x^6\rangle$ (order $2$) have only $1$ below both. So $\langle x^4\rangle\wedge\langle x^6\rangle=1$. Shortcut check. $\langle x^4\rangle\cap\langle x^6\rangle=\langle x^{\lcm(4,6)}\rangle=\langle x^{12}\rangle=\langle e\rangle=1$. Agrees; also $\gcd(2,3)=1$ forces the trivial meet.

Join (up). Upward from order-$3$ and order-$2$ vertices, the lowest common upper vertex is $\langle x^2\rangle$ (order $6$). So $\langle x^4\rangle\vee\langle x^6\rangle=\langle x^2\rangle$. Shortcut check. $\langle x^4,x^6\rangle=\langle x^{\gcd(4,6)}\rangle=\langle x^2\rangle$, of order $12/\gcd(2,12)=6$. Agrees, and $6=\lcm(2,3)$ as the order test demands.

Check. Meet has order $1\mid\gcd(2,3)=1$; join has order $6$, a multiple of $\lcm(2,3)=6$ dividing $12$. Both consistent. Note $\langle x^2\rangle\neZ/(12)Z$ here: the join of two proper subgroups need not be the whole group --- contrast with the $S_3$ transpositions, whose join was everything.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
The subgroup lattice of a finite group $G$ is the Hasse diagram of all subgroups of $G$ ordered by inclusion: the trivial subgroup $1$ at the bottom, $G$ at the top, and an upward edge $H$---$K$ exactly when $H\psgr K$ with no subgroup strictly between them. Once drawn, the lattice is a single picture from which we can read inclusions and indices, and which (together with a few conjugation checks) locates normal subgroups and normalizers. This section builds the three canonical lattices and turns them into computational tools.

\begin{definition} 
In the subgroup lattice of $G$, we draw an edge $H$---$K$ (with $H$ below $K$) precisely when $H\psgr K$ and there is no subgroup $L$ with $H\psgr L\psgr K$. We say $K$ covers $H$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Label: p:d8subs@c2
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
$D_8$ has exactly ten subgroups: the trivial group $1$; the whole group $D_8$; one cyclic order-$4$ subgroup $\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$ and two Klein four-groups $\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$ and $\langle r^2,rs\rangle=\{1,r^2,rs,r^3s\}$; and five order-$2$ subgroups $\langle r^2\rangle,\langle s\rangle,\langle rs\rangle,\langle r^2s\rangle,\langle r^3s\rangle$.
\end{proposition}
label: p:d8subs@c2

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > Using subgroup lattices: $D_8$, $Q_8$, and $Z/(24)Z$ > The lattice of $D_8$ and its ten subgroups
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-b0214458e7684cf0c32b
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Lagrange every proper nontrivial subgroup has order $2$ or $4$. An order-$2$ subgroup is $\langle x\rangle$ for an element $x$ of order $2$; the five involutions are $r^2,s,rs,r^2s,r^3s$ (the elements $r,r^3$ have order $4$), giving five order-$2$ subgroups. An order-$4$ subgroup $H$ has index $2$, hence is normal, and is either cyclic or Klein four. The only elements of order $4$ are $r,r^3$, both generating $\langle r\rangle$, so there is exactly one cyclic order-$4$ subgroup. A Klein four subgroup consists of $1$ and three commuting involutions; since $r^2$ is central and $s\cdot r^2s=r^2$, $\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$ and $\{1,r^2,rs,r^3s\}$ are subgroups, and conversely a Klein four subgroup contains at most one rotation besides $1$ (namely $r^2$), hence two distinct commuting reflections $r^is,r^js$. Since $(r^is)(r^js)=r^{i-j}$ and $(r^js)(r^is)=r^{j-i}$, these commute iff $r^{2(i-j)}=1$, i.e.\ iff $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ (e.g.\ $s(rs)=srs=r^{-1}=r^3$ while $(rs)s=r$, so $s$ and $rs$ do not commute). So the pair is $\{s,r^2s\}$ or $\{rs,r^3s\}$, and the subgroup is one of the two above; hence no others exist. Total: $1+5+3+1=10$.
\end{proof}

Title: List the subgroups of $D_8$ by order
Content:
\begin{wex}{List the subgroups of $D_8$ by order}
Produce the full subgroup list of $D_8$ organized by order, and confirm the count is ten.
\wrec The trigger is ``small group, want all subgroups.'' Use Lagrange to bound the possible orders ($1,2,4,8$), then enumerate order-$2$ subgroups via involutions and order-$4$ subgroups via the cyclic-vs-Klein dichotomy. This is exactly Proposition~ [REF:p:d8subs@c2] 's method applied as a checklist.
\wsol Order $1$: $1$. Order $8$: $D_8$. Order $2$: find all $x$ with $x^2=1,\ x\neq1$. Check each non-identity element: $r,r^3$ have order $4$; $r^2$ has order $2$; $s^2=1$; $(rs)^2=rsrs=r(srs)=r\cdot r^{-1}=1$ and likewise $(r^2s)^2=(r^3s)^2=1$. So the involutions are $r^2,s,rs,r^2s,r^3s$, giving five subgroups. Order $4$: cyclic ones need order-$4$ elements $r,r^3$, both giving $\langle r\rangle$ (one subgroup); Klein ones are $\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$ and $\{1,r^2,rs,r^3s\}$ (two subgroups). Total $=1+1+5+1+2=10$.

Check. Every involution appears in at least one order-$4$ subgroup ($r^2$ in all three; $s,r^2s$ in $\langle r^2,s\rangle$; $rs,r^3s$ in $\langle r^2,rs\rangle$), consistent with the lattice edges. Count $10$ matches Proposition~ [REF:p:d8subs@c2] .
\end{wex}

Type: proposition

Content:
\begin{proposition} 
$Q_8$ has exactly six subgroups: $1$, $\langle -1\rangle=\{\pm1\}$, $\langle i\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm i\}$, $\langle j\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm j\}$, $\langle k\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm k\}$, and $Q_8$. Every subgroup is normal.
\end{proposition}
label: p:q8@c2

Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > Using subgroup lattices: $D_8$, $Q_8$, and $Z/(24)Z$ > The lattice of $Q_8$: every subgroup is normal
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-c03a7876c1b948035271
Content:
\begin{proof}
The only element of order $2$ is $-1$ (since $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1\neq1$), giving the unique order-$2$ subgroup $\langle -1\rangle$. The order-$4$ subgroups are cyclic generated by an order-$4$ element; the order-$4$ elements are $\pm i,\pm j,\pm k$, and $\langle i\rangle=\langle -i\rangle$, $\langle j\rangle=\langle -j\rangle$, $\langle k\rangle=\langle -k\rangle$, giving three. With $1$ and $Q_8$ that is six. Each order-$4$ subgroup has index $2$, hence is normal; $\langle -1\rangle=Z(Q_8)$ is normal as the center; and $1,Q_8$ are normal. So all six are normal.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: The lattice of $Q_8$ and universal normality
Content:
\begin{wex}{The lattice of $Q_8$ and universal normality}
Draw the subgroup lattice of $Q_8$ and explain why every subgroup is normal.
\wrec ``Every subgroup normal'' is triggered by two recognizable patterns combined: (a) index-$2$ subgroups are automatically normal, and (b) a subgroup contained in the center, or equal to it, is normal. In $Q_8$ all proper nontrivial subgroups are either index $2$ or the center, so both triggers cover everything.
\wsol By Proposition~ [REF:p:q8@c2] the subgroups are $1,\langle -1\rangle,\langle i\rangle,\langle j\rangle,\langle k\rangle,Q_8$. For normality: $1$ and $Q_8$ are always normal. The three order-$4$ subgroups have index $|Q_8|/4=2$, and any subgroup of index $2$ is normal (its two cosets are $H$ and $G\setminus H$, the same as left or right). Finally $\langle -1\rangle$ is the center, and $gZg^{-1}=Z$ for the center $Z$ of any group, so $\langle -1\rangle\nor Q_8$. Hence all six subgroups are normal.

Check. A direct conjugation, e.g.\ $j\,i\,j^{-1}$: since $ji=-k$ and $j^{-1}=-j$, we get $j i j^{-1}=(-k)(-j)=kj=-i\in\langle i\rangle$. Thus $j\langle i\ranglej^{-1}=\langle i\rangle$, confirming $\langle i\rangle\nor Q_8$ as predicted.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Label: t:cyclic@c2
Content:
\begin{theorem} 
Let $G=\langle x\rangle$ be cyclic of order $n$. For each divisor $d\mid n$ there is exactly one subgroup of order $d$, namely $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle$, and these are all the subgroups. Consequently $H\sgr K$ in the lattice iff $|H|\mid|K|$, so the subgroup lattice of $Z/(n)Z$ is isomorphic to the lattice of divisors of $n$ under divisibility.
\end{theorem}
label: t:cyclic@c2

Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > Using subgroup lattices: $D_8$, $Q_8$, and $Z/(24)Z$ > The lattice of $Z/(24)Z$: a divisor lattice
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f45614b953adc7cb6124
Content:
\begin{proof}
A subgroup of $\langle x\rangle$ is cyclic, of the form $\langle x^a\rangle$, and $|\langle x^a\rangle|=n/\gcd(a,n)$, which runs over all divisors of $n$ as $a$ varies. If $\langle x^a\rangle$ and $\langle x^b\rangle$ both have order $d$, then both equal $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle$ (the unique subgroup of order $d$), so each order occurs once. Containment $\langle x^{n/d}\rangle\sgr\langle x^{n/e}\rangle$ holds iff $d\mid e$, i.e.\ iff orders divide, which is exactly the divisor lattice.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
In $Z/(n)Z$ the subgroup ``$\langle m\rangle$'' means the cyclic subgroup generated by the residue $m$, and $|\langle m\rangle|=n/\gcd(m,n)$, not $n/m$. For $Z/(24)Z$, $\langle 6\rangle$ has order $24/\gcd(6,24)=24/6=4$, but $\langle 8\rangle$ has order $24/\gcd(8,24)=24/8=3$. Compute the gcd; do not just divide by the label.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{wex}{Subgroup of $Z/(24)Z$ of each order, and one containment}
List the eight subgroups of $Z/(24)Z$ with their orders, and decide whether $\langle 6\rangle\sgr\langle 2\rangle$.
\wrec Cyclic group of order $24$ $\Rightarrow$ Theorem~ [REF:t:cyclic@c2] : subgroups correspond to divisors of $24$, and containment is divisibility of orders. The containment question is answered purely by ``does $|\langle 6\rangle|$ divide $|\langle 2\rangle|$?''
\wsol Divisors of $24$: $1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24$. Order-$d$ subgroup is $\langle 24/d\rangle$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 12 & 24\\\hline
\langle 24/d\rangle & \langle 24\rangle=1 & \langle 12\rangle & \langle 8\rangle & \langle 6\rangle & \langle 4\rangle & \langle 3\rangle & \langle 2\rangle & \langle 1\rangle
\end{array}
\]
Now $|\langle 6\rangle|=24/\gcd(6,24)=4$ and $|\langle 2\rangle|=24/\gcd(2,24)=12$. Since $4\mid12$, Theorem~ [REF:t:cyclic@c2] gives $\langle 6\rangle\sgr\langle 2\rangle$.

Check directly: $\langle 6\rangle=\{0,6,12,18\}$ and $\langle 2\rangle=\{0,2,4,\dots,22\}$; indeed $6,12,18$ are even, so $\langle 6\rangle\subseteq\langle 2\rangle$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: method
Title: Using the lattice to (a) spot normal subgroups and (b) locate $N_G(H)$
Content:
\begin{method}{Using the lattice to (a) spot normal subgroups and (b) locate $N_G(H)$}
Recognition trigger. Use this whenever you have the lattice drawn and want normality or a normalizer without brute-force conjugating every element.

(a) Normal subgroups.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Any subgroup of index $2$ (one level below the top, with $|G:H|=2$) is normal --- mark it immediately.
\item The center $Z(G)$ and any subgroup contained in $Z(G)$ is normal; locate $Z(G)$ as the largest subgroup every node is ``compatible'' with (in $D_8$ and $Q_8$ this is the unique central involution's group).
\item A subgroup that is the unique subgroup of its order is characteristic, hence normal (conjugation permutes same-order subgroups, and a singleton orbit is fixed).
\item For the remaining small subgroups, conjugation permutes the subgroups of each fixed order; $H\nor G$ iff that orbit is $\{H\}$. Read off the same-order siblings from the lattice and test whether a single conjugation moves $H$ to a sibling.
\end{enumerate}

(b) The normalizer $N_G(H)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $N_G(H)$ is a subgroup with $H\sgr N_G(H)\sgr G$, so it lies on the chain above $H$ in the lattice --- only those finitely many candidates can occur.
\item $H\nor G$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $N_G(H)=G$ (top). If $H$ is not normal, $N_G(H)$ is a proper subgroup containing $H$.
\item Test candidates from largest down: $g\in N_G(H)$ iff $gHg^{-1}=H$. The first proper overgroup $K$ with every generator of $K$ normalizing $H$, and with no larger overgroup doing so, is $N_G(H)$.
\item Sanity: $|G:N_G(H)|$ equals the number of distinct conjugates $gHg^{-1}$ (the orbit size), which you can also count among the same-order siblings in the lattice.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: All normal subgroups of $D_8$ from the lattice
Content:
\begin{wex}{All normal subgroups of $D_8$ from the lattice}
Using the $D_8$ lattice, find every normal subgroup and justify each.
\wrec Apply Method (a) point-by-point: index-$2$ rule for the order-$4$ row, center rule for $\langle r^2\rangle$, uniqueness for $\langle r\rangle$, and the same-order-orbit test for the order-$2$ reflections.
\wsol Index $2$ (order $4$): $\langle r\rangle,\langle r^2,s\rangle,\langle r^2,rs\rangle$ each have index $8/4=2$, hence are normal. Center: $Z(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$ (since $r^2$ commutes with $r$ and with $s$ as $sr^2s=r^{-2}=r^2$), and the center is always normal, so $\langle r^2\rangle\nor D_8$. Trivial cases: $1$ and $D_8$. Reflection subgroups $\langle s\rangle,\langle rs\rangle,\langle r^2s\rangle,\langle r^3s\rangle$ (order $2$): these are not normal. Conjugate $\langle s\rangle$ by $r$: $rsr^{-1}=r(sr^{-1})$, and $sr^{-1}=sr^3=r^{-3}s=rs$; hence $rsr^{-1}=r\cdot rs=r^2 s\notin\langle s\rangle$. So $r\langle s\rangler^{-1}=\langle r^2s\rangle\neq\langle s\rangle$, and similarly conjugation by $r$ sends $\langle rs\rangle$ to $\langle r^3s\rangle$ (since $r(rs)r^{-1}=r^3s$), swapping that pair. Each reflection subgroup has a $2$-element conjugacy orbit, so none is normal.

Thus the normal subgroups are exactly $1,\ \langle r^2\rangle,\ \langle r\rangle,\ \langle r^2,s\rangle,\ \langle r^2,rs\rangle,\ D_8$ --- six of the ten.

Check. The quotient $D_8/\langle r^2\rangle$ has order $4$ and is abelian ($\cong V_4$), consistent with $\langle r^2\rangle=[D_8,D_8]$ being normal; and the three index-$2$ subgroups being normal matches the rule. The four reflection subgroups split into two orbits of size $2$ ($\{\langle s\rangle,\langle r^2s\rangle\}$ and $\{\langle rs\rangle,\langle r^3s\rangle\}$), accounting for the non-normal ones.
\end{wex}

Title: $N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$ via the lattice
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$ via the lattice}
Compute $N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$ by restricting to the overgroups of $\langle s\rangle$, then verify.
\wrec $\langle s\rangle$ is a non-normal order-$2$ subgroup (from the previous example), so by Method (b) its normalizer is a proper overgroup: read the chain above $\langle s\rangle$ in the lattice. The only overgroups of $\langle s\rangle$ are $\langle s\rangle$ itself, $\langle r^2,s\rangle$, and $D_8$.
\wsol Candidates from the lattice: $\langle s\rangle\sgr N\sgr D_8$ with $N\in\{\langle s\rangle,\langle r^2,s\rangle,D_8\}$. We know $N\neq D_8$ (not normal). Test $\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$: its generators are $r^2$ and $s$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $s\in N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$ trivially ($s\langle s\rangles^{-1}=\langle s\rangle$).
\item $r^2$: $r^2 s r^{-2}=r^2 s r^2$. Since $r^2$ is central, $r^2 s r^2=s r^2 r^2=s r^4=s\in\langle s\rangle$. So $r^2$ normalizes $\langle s\rangle$.
\end{itemize}
Every generator of $\langle r^2,s\rangle$ normalizes $\langle s\rangle$, so $\langle r^2,s\rangle\sgr N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)$. Since the only larger subgroup is $D_8$, which does not normalize $\langle s\rangle$ (because $r\langle s\rangler^{-1}=\langle r^2s\rangle\neq\langle s\rangle$ from the previous example), we get
\[
N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)=\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}.
\]

Check via orbit count: $|D_8:N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)|=8/4=2$, so $\langle s\rangle$ should have exactly $2$ conjugates. Indeed its conjugates are $\langle s\rangle$ and $\langle r^2s\rangle$, two subgroups --- matching. (Note $N_{D_8}(\langle s\rangle)\supsetneq\langle s\rangle$ strictly even though $\langle s\rangle$ is not normal, illustrating $H\sgr N_G(H)\sgr G$.)
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)$ and $N_{Z/(24)Z}(\langle 6\rangle)$}
Find both normalizers using the lattices.
\wrec In an abelian group every subgroup is normal, so $N_G(H)=G$ automatically --- that is the trigger for $Z/(24)Z$. In $Q_8$ every subgroup is normal (Proposition~ [REF:p:q8@c2] ), so again $N_G(H)=G$. Both reduce to Method (b) step 2: normal $\Rightarrow$ normalizer is the top.
\wsol $Q_8$: $\langle i\rangle$ has index $8/4=2$, hence normal, so $N_{Q_8}(\langle i\rangle)=Q_8$. \emph{$Z/(24)Z$:} $Z/(24)Z$ is abelian, so $g+\langle 6\rangle-g=\langle 6\rangle$ for all $g$ (equivalently $g\langle 6\rangleg^{-1}=\langle 6\rangle$), giving $N_{Z/(24)Z}(\langle 6\rangle)=Z/(24)Z$.

Check. Normalizer at the top of the lattice $\Leftrightarrow$ single conjugate $\Leftrightarrow$ $|G:N_G(H)|=1$. For $\langle i\rangle$: $j i j^{-1}=-i\in\langle i\rangle$ as computed earlier, so conjugation fixes $\langle i\rangle$, giving one conjugate. For $\langle 6\rangle$: abelian, one conjugate. Both consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: A non-normal normalizer in $S_3$ for contrast
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-normal normalizer in $S_3$ for contrast}
In $S_3=\{e,\allowbreak(12),\allowbreak(13),\allowbreak(23),\allowbreak(123),\allowbreak(132)\}$, draw the relevant overgroups and compute $N_{S_3}(\langle (12)\rangle)$.
\wrec $\langle (12)\rangle$ is an order-$2$ subgroup of a non-abelian group, and the order-$2$ subgroups (transpositions) form one conjugacy orbit, so we expect a proper normalizer. By Method (b) read the chain above $\langle (12)\rangle$: the only overgroups are $\langle (12)\rangle$ and $S_3$ (no order-$4$ subgroup exists since $4\nmid6$).
\wsol Overgroups of $\langle (12)\rangle$ in the lattice: $\langle (12)\rangle$ (order $2$) and $S_3$ (order $6$); there is no subgroup of order $4$ because $4\nmid 6$. Is $\langle (12)\rangle\nor S_3$? Conjugate by $(123)$: $(123)(12)(123)^{-1}=(123)(12)(132)$. Computing, $(123)(12)(132)=(23)\notin\langle (12)\rangle$. So $\langle (12)\rangle$ is not normal, hence $N_{S_3}(\langle (12)\rangle)\neq S_3$. The only smaller overgroup is $\langle (12)\rangle$ itself, so
\[
N_{S_3}(\langle (12)\rangle)=\langle (12)\rangle.
\]

Check. $|S_3:N|=6/2=3$, predicting $3$ conjugates; indeed the transpositions $(12),(13),(23)$ are all conjugate, giving exactly $3$ subgroups $\langle (12)\rangle,\langle (13)\rangle,\langle (23)\rangle$. Consistent, and this shows $N_G(H)=H$ is possible (the lattice chain above $H$ may have nothing strictly between $H$ and $G$).
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
A subgroup lattice does not determine a group up to isomorphism. The standard example: $Z_2\times Z_8$ and the modular group of order $16$,
\[
M=M_{16}=\langle u,v\st u^8=v^2=1,\ vuv^{-1}=u^5\rangle,
\]
have isomorphic subgroup lattices but are not isomorphic groups.

Section: Subgroups > The Lattice of Subgroups > Using subgroup lattices: $D_8$, $Q_8$, and $Z/(24)Z$ > The same-lattice, non-isomorphic remark
Type: example
Title: Why same lattice does not force isomorphism
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why same lattice does not force isomorphism}
Explain how $Z_2\times Z_8$ and $M_{16}$ can share a subgroup lattice yet fail to be isomorphic, and give a concrete invariant that distinguishes them.
\wrec The trigger is the phrase ``same lattice, not isomorphic.'' The lattice records only which subgroups contain which; it is blind to how elements multiply (commutativity, conjugation). So to separate the two groups we must exhibit a group-theoretic invariant that the lattice cannot see --- abelian vs.\ non-abelian is the cleanest.
\wsol Both groups have order $16$, and their subgroup lattices coincide combinatorially: each has $11$ subgroups, with exactly $1$ of order $1$, three of order $2$, three of order $4$, three of order $8$, and $1$ of order $16$, arranged with identical inclusions (this is the content of the D\&F remark). Crucially this is not because $M_{16}$ has all subgroups normal --- it does not: from $vuv^{-1}=u^5$ one gets $uvu^{-1}=u^4v$, so the order-$2$ subgroup $\langle v\rangle$ is non-normal, with conjugate $\langle u^4v\rangle$. The relation $vuv^{-1}=u^5$ does guarantee that $u^5$ generates the same cyclic subgroups as $u$ (since $\gcd(5,8)=1$, e.g.\ $\langle u^5\rangle=\langle u\rangle$), so conjugation by $v$ fixes every subgroup of $\langle u\rangle$; but that alone does not force equal lattices (in $D_{16}$, $srs^{-1}=r^7$ with $\gcd(7,8)=1$, yet $D_{16}$ has $19$ subgroups). The agreement is a direct check: writing $Z_2\times Z_8=\langle x\rangle\times\langle y\rangle$ with $\ord{x}=2$, $\ord{y}=8$, the bijection $u^iv^j\mapsto y^ix^j$ carries the $11$ subgroups of $M_{16}$ exactly onto the $11$ subgroups of $Z_2\times Z_8$ (e.g.\ $\langle uv\rangle=\{u^{2k},u^{2k+1}v\}\mapsto\{y^{2k},y^{2k+1}x\}=\langle xy\rangle$). Hence the lattices agree even though the multiplication does not.

But the groups differ on a lattice-invisible invariant:
\begin{itemize}
\item $Z_2\times Z_8$ is abelian: every pair of elements commutes, so its center is the whole group and $|Z|=16$.
\item $M_{16}$ is non-abelian: $vuv^{-1}=u^5\neq u$ (since $u^5\neq u$ as $u$ has order $8$), so $u$ and $v$ do not commute. Its center is $\langle u^2\rangle\cong Z_4$, of order $4$.
\end{itemize}
Since $|Z(Z_2\times Z_8)|=16\neq4=|Z(M_{16})|$, and the order of the center is an isomorphism invariant, the two groups are not isomorphic.

Check. An isomorphism must send center to center, so it would force $16=|Z(Z_2\times Z_8)|=|Z(M_{16})|=4$, a contradiction. Equivalently, one group is abelian and the other is not --- an invariant the bare inclusion lattice cannot record. This is precisely why we must verify isomorphism by group operations, never by lattice shape alone.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Never conclude ``$G\cong H$ because they have the same subgroup lattice.'' The lattice forgets multiplication. $Z_2\times Z_8$ vs.\ $M_{16}$ (both order $16$, identical lattices, one abelian and one not) is the canonical counterexample. Likewise, do not read commutativity or element orders off a Hasse diagram --- it only encodes containments.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{wex}{Reading joins and meets off the $D_8$ lattice}
Using the $D_8$ lattice already drawn, compute (a) $\langle s\rangle\vee\langle r^2s\rangle$, (b) $\langle s\rangle\vee\langle rs\rangle$, and
(c) $\langle r\rangle\cap\langle r^2,s\rangle$.
\wrec Each part names two specific subgroups of $D_8$ and asks for a join or an intersection, so this is the
reading-off Method applied to the flagship non-abelian example. We trace up for joins, down for meets, and
confirm with element computations using $sr=r^{-1} s$.
\wsol (a) $\langle s\rangle\vee\langle r^2s\rangle$. Both $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$ and $\langle r^2s\rangle=\{1,r^2s\}$ lie under the
single order-$4$ subgroup $\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$, and that is the lowest common upper vertex. So
$\langle s\rangle\vee\langle r^2s\rangle=\langle r^2,s\rangle$. Confirm: $s\cdot r^2s=r^{-2}=r^2$ (using $sr^2=r^{-2}s$), so the
join contains $r^2$, hence contains $\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$; its order is a multiple of $\lcm(2,2)=2$ exceeding $2$
and dividing $8$, and the Klein group of order $4$ is the smallest such, giving $\langle r^2,s\rangle$.

(b) $\langle s\rangle\vee\langle rs\rangle$. Here $\langle s\rangle$ sits under $\langle r^2,s\rangle$ only, while $\langle rs\rangle$ sits under
$\langle r^2,rs\rangle$ only; their only common upper vertex is the top. So $\langle s\rangle\vee\langle rs\rangle=D_8$. Confirm:
$s\cdot rs=(sr)s=r^{-1} s\,s=r^{-1}=r^3$, an element of order $4$, so the join contains $\langle r\rangle$ as well as the
involution $s\notin\langle r\rangle$; its order is a multiple of $4$ strictly exceeding $4$ and dividing $8$, hence
$8=|D_8|$.

(c) $\langle r\rangle\cap\langle r^2,s\rangle$. Tracing down from the cyclic order-$4$ subgroup
$\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,r^2,r^3\}$ and from the Klein order-$4$ subgroup $\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$, the highest
common lower vertex is $\langle r^2\rangle$. So $\langle r\rangle\cap\langle r^2,s\rangle=\langle r^2\rangle$. Confirm: the common elements
are exactly $\{1,r^2\}=\langle r^2\rangle$, since $r,r^3\notin\langle r^2,s\rangle$ and $s,r^2s\notin\langle r\rangle$.

$D_8$ --- contrast (b), where the two atoms lie under different order-$4$ groups and so are forced all
the way to the top. Part (c) shows the meet of the two ``different kinds'' of order-$4$ subgroup is the center
$\langle r^2\rangle=Z(D_8)$, the unique nontrivial subgroup lying below all three order-$4$ subgroups, exactly as the lattice
picture displays.
\end{wex}

The lattice itself is a diagram; two more diagrams capture how joins/meets and
isomorphisms interact with it.

\noindent(a) Join and meet form a diamond. For $H,K\sgr G$ the meet is
$H\cap K$ (the largest subgroup below both) and the join is $\langle H,K\rangle$ (the smallest
subgroup above both), giving a commuting diamond of inclusions
(Definition~ [REF:d:meetjoin@c2] ). ``Reading a join'' means tracing the two upward edges to
their first common vertex.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
& \langle H,K\rangle & \\
H \arrow[ur, hook] & & K \arrow[ul, hook'] \\
& H\cap K \arrow[ul, hook] \arrow[ur, hook'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four vertices, all subgroups of $G$. Bottom vertex: $H\cap K$, the meet (intersection), itself a subgroup by Proposition~ [REF:p:intersub@c2] . Left vertex: $H$. Right vertex: $K$. Top vertex: $\langle H,K\rangle$, the join (the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing both $H$ and $K$). All four are subgroups; $H\cap K\sgr H,K\sgr\langle H,K\rangle\sgr G$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Four hooked inclusion arrows. Bottom-left $\hookrightarrow$: $H\cap K\hookrightarrow H$ (inclusion, $H\cap K\sgr H$). Bottom-right $\hookrightarrow$: $H\cap K\hookrightarrow K$ (inclusion, $H\cap K\sgr K$). Top-left $\hookrightarrow$: $H\hookrightarrow\langle H,K\rangle$ (inclusion, $H\sgr\langle H,K\rangle$). Top-right $\hookrightarrow$: $K\hookrightarrow\langle H,K\rangle$ (inclusion, $K\sgr\langle H,K\rangle$). All four are canonical set inclusions; no quotient or induced map is present.
\dgi{What commutes:} Both paths from $H\cap K$ to $\langle H,K\rangle$ agree: going via $H$ gives $H\cap K\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow\langle H,K\rangle$, and going via $K$ gives $H\cap K\hookrightarrow K\hookrightarrow\langle H,K\rangle$. Since all arrows are inclusions, both composites are the same set-inclusion $H\cap K\subseteq\langle H,K\rangle$. Similarly the two ``upward'' inclusions of $H$ and $K$ into $\langle H,K\rangle$ commute trivially.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $x\in H\cap K$. Via the left path: $x\in H\cap K\subseteq H\subseteq\langle H,K\rangle$, so $x$ maps to itself in $\langle H,K\rangle$. Via the right path: $x\in H\cap K\subseteq K\subseteq\langle H,K\rangle$, same element $x$ in $\langle H,K\rangle$. The two paths agree because inclusions are identity-on-elements; there is nothing to check beyond $H\cap K\subseteq H$ and $H\cap K\subseteq K$, both obvious from the definition of intersection.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diamond is the visual definition of a lattice: it records that $L(G)$ has both a greatest lower bound ($H\cap K$) and a least upper bound ($\langle H,K\rangle$) for every pair $H,K$. The diagram places the four objects in their correct relative position so that ``reading a meet'' means going to the bottom vertex and ``reading a join'' means going to the top, exactly the reading-off Method described just before. Without this picture the abstract lattice axioms are hard to parse at a glance.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$, $H=\langle (12)\rangle$, $K=\langle (13)\rangle$. Then $H\cap K=\{e\}=1$ (bottom), $\langle H,K\rangle=S_3$ (top, since the join of two distinct transpositions is the whole group), and the diamond has atoms $\langle (12)\rangle$ and $\langle (13)\rangle$ in the middle. All four inclusion arrows are the set inclusions $\{e\}\subset\{e,(12)\}\subset S_3$ and $\{e\}\subset\{e,(13)\}\subset S_3$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the top vertex as the set-union $H\cup K$ or the product set $HK=\{hk:h\in H,k\in K\}$, neither of which need be a subgroup. The top vertex is $\langle H,K\rangle$, the subgroup generated by $H\cup K$; in the $S_3$ example $\langle (12)\rangle\cup\langle (13)\rangle=\{e,(12),(13)\}$ is not a subgroup, but $\langle \langle (12)\rangle,\langle (13)\rangle\rangle=S_3$ is.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the meet-join diamond makes visible, in a single picture, that every pair of subgroups has a greatest lower bound (intersection) and a least upper bound (generated subgroup), the two operations that make $L(G)$ a lattice.
\end{dgx}

\noindent(b) Isomorphic groups have identical lattices. An isomorphism
$\varphi:G\to G'$ sends each subgroup $H$ to $\varphi(H)$ and preserves all inclusions, so
it induces an isomorphism of subgroup lattices: the square below commutes for every
$H\sgr G$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
H \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi|_H"', "\sim"] & G \arrow[d, "\varphi"', "\sim"] \\
\varphi(H) \arrow[r, hook] & G'
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four vertices. Top-left: $H$, a subgroup of $G$. Top-right: $G$, a group. Bottom-left: $\varphi(H)$, the image of $H$ under $\varphi$, which is a subgroup of $G'$ (isomorphisms send subgroups to subgroups). Bottom-right: $G'$, a group isomorphic to $G$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal $\hookrightarrow$: the inclusion $H\hookrightarrow G$ (canonical, $H\sgr G$). Right vertical $\varphi:G\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}G'$: a group isomorphism, bijective and a homomorphism. Left vertical $\varphi|_H$: the restriction of $\varphi$ to $H$, $h\mapsto\varphi(h)$; it is an isomorphism of $H$ onto its image $\varphi(H)\sgr G'$ (marked $\sim$). Bottom horizontal $\hookrightarrow$: the inclusion $\varphi(H)\hookrightarrow G'$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The square commutes: the two paths from $H$ to $G'$ are equal. Top-then-right: $H\hookrightarrow G\xrightarrow{\varphi}G'$, sending $h\in H$ to $\varphi(h)\in G'$. Left-then-bottom: $H\xrightarrow{\varphi|_H}\varphi(H)\hookrightarrow G'$, sending any $h\in H$ to $\varphi(h)\in\varphi(H)\subseteq G'$. Both give $h\mapsto\varphi(h)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $h\in H$. Along the top-then-right path: $h$ is viewed in $G$ via inclusion, then $\varphi$ sends it to $\varphi(h)\in G'$. Along the left-then-bottom path: $H$ is mapped to its image $\varphi(H)\subseteq G'$, and $h\in H$ lands at $\varphi(h)\in\varphi(H)$, then the inclusion puts it in $G'$. Both agree because $\varphi$ is a function: the image of $h$ under $\varphi$ is the same regardless of which route we describe it.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram encodes the key fact that an isomorphism $\varphi$ not only identifies $G$ with $G'$ as groups but also identifies their entire subgroup lattices: every $H\sgr G$ corresponds to $\varphi(H)\sgr G'$, and inclusion is preserved. This is why the remark ``isomorphic groups have identical lattices'' is diagrammatically immediate --- $\varphi$ induces a lattice isomorphism $L(G)\toL(G')$. It also sets up the punch line: the converse fails because the lattice forgets multiplication.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=Z/(6)Z$, $G'=Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ (isomorphic by the Chinese remainder theorem), and $H=\langle \bar2\rangle\sgrZ/(6)Z$ of order $3$. The isomorphism $\varphi:Z/(6)Z\toZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ sends $\bar2\mapsto(\bar0,\bar2)$, so $\varphi(H)=\{(\bar0,\bar0),(\bar0,\bar1),(\bar0,\bar2)\}=\{0\}\timesZ/(3)Z\sgrZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$. The square commutes: $\varphi(\bar2)=(\bar0,\bar2)$ by either path.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The left arrow is the restriction $\varphi|_H$, not an inclusion. Students sometimes read it as an inclusion $H\hookrightarrow G'$, but $H$ need not be a subgroup of $G'$ --- only $\varphi(H)$ is. The lattice map $H\mapsto\varphi(H)$ acts on subgroups, not on elements, so it is not an arrow of this square: the square is drawn once for each $H\sgr G$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that an isomorphism $\varphi:G\xrightarrow{\sim}G'$ induces a bijection on subgroup lattices, making every inclusion $H\sgr G$ correspond to $\varphi(H)\sgr G'$, which is why isomorphic groups always have identical subgroup lattices.
\end{dgx}
The converse fails: $Z_2\times Z_8$ and the modular group $M$ of order $16$ have
identical lattices but are not isomorphic, so the lattice alone cannot recover the group.

\item For $H,K\sgr G$, exhibit all possible sublattices showing only $G,1,H,K$ and their
 joins/meets; describe what distinguishes the cases.
\item In $D_{16}$, list all subgroups (a) contained in $\langle sr^2,r^4\rangle$; (b) contained in
 $\langle sr^7,r^4\rangle$; (c) containing $\langle r^4\rangle$; (d) containing $\langle s\rangle$.
\item Show $\langle s,r^2\rangle\sgr D_8$ is isomorphic to $V_4$.
\item Use the lattice to find all $12$ pairs of elements that generate $D_8$.
\item Use the lattice to find all $8$ elements $x$ with $D_{16}=\langle x,s\rangle$.
\item Use lattices to find the centralizer of every element of (a) $D_8$; (b) $Q_8$;
 (c) $S_3$; (d) $D_{16}$.
\item Find $Z(D_{16})$.
\item Find the normalizer of every subgroup of (a) $S_3$; (b) $Q_8$.
\item Draw the lattices of subgroups of (a) $Z/(16)Z$; (b) $Z/(24)Z$; (c) $Z/(48)Z$.
\item Classify groups of order $4$: prove $\ord{G}=4\Longrightarrow G\cong Z_4$ or $G\cong V_4$.
\item For the quasidihedral group $QD_{16}=\langle a,\tau\st a^8=\tau^2=1,\ a\tau=\tau a^3\rangle$,
 fill in the missing subgroups of its (non-planar) lattice, each with $\le2$ generators.
\item Draw the lattice of $Z_2\times Z_4$, each subgroup with $\le2$ generators.
\item Draw the lattice of $Z_2\times Z_8$, each subgroup with $\le2$ generators.
\item For the modular group $M=M_{16}=\langle u,v\st u^8=v^2=1,\ vuv^{-1}=u^5\rangle$ of order $16$, show its
 lattice matches that of $Z_2\times Z_8$, yet $M\not\cong Z_2\times Z_8$.
\item Describe the isomorphism type of each of the three order-$8$ subgroups of $D_{16}$.
\item Show that in $QD_{16}$ every element of order $2$ lies in $\langle \tau,a^2\rangle$.
\item Show that in $M$, $\{x\in M\st x^2=1\}$ is a subgroup isomorphic to $V_4$.
\item Find the centralizer of every element of $QD_{16}$.
\item Find $N_{D_{16}}(\langle s,r^4\rangle)$.
\item Find $N_{QD_{16}}(\langle \tau a\rangle)$ and $N_{QD_{16}}(\langle \tau,a^4\rangle)$.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that the lattice of subgroups of $Z/(n)Z$ is the divisor lattice of $n$.
\item Show $Z/(p^2q)Z$ ($p,q$ distinct primes) has exactly $6$ subgroups, and draw the
 lattice.

\item Verify directly in $Q_8$ that the join of $\langle i\rangle$ and $\langle j\rangle$ is $Q_8$ and the
 meet is $\langle -1\rangle$.
\item Using Exercise~14, give two non-isomorphic groups with identical subgroup
 lattices, and explain why the lattice cannot detect the difference.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Draw the join/meet diamond for $H=\langle r\rangle$ and $K=\langle s\rangle$ in $D_8$; identify
 $H\cap K$ and $\langle H,K\rangle$, and read off $[D_8:H]$.
\item Let $\varphi:G\to G'$ be an isomorphism. Prove $H\mapsto\varphi(H)$ is a lattice
 isomorphism by checking that the square with rows $H\hookrightarrow G$ and
 $\varphi(H)\hookrightarrow G'$ (and down-arrows $\varphi$) commutes for every $H\sgr G$.
\item Draw the diamond for two distinct order-$2$ subgroups of $V_4$ and compute their
 join and meet.
\item Explain, using the lattice-isomorphism square, why the identical lattices of
 $Z_2\times Z_8$ and the modular group $M_{16}$ do not force the groups to be
 isomorphic --- i.e.\ why no group isomorphism completes the square.
\end{exers}

\item [DF 2.1.1] Prove each is a subgroup: (a) $\{a+ai\st a\inR\}\sgr(C,+)$;

 (c) $\{a/b\inQ\st b\mid n\}\sgr(Q,+)$ ($n$ fixed);
 (d) $\{a/b\inQ\st\gcd(b,n)=1\}\sgr(Q,+)$;
 (e) $\{x\inR^\times\st x^2\inQ\}\sgrR^\times$.
\item [DF 2.1.2] Prove each is not a subgroup: (a) the $2$-cycles in $S_n$ ($n\ge3$);
 (b) the reflections in $D_{2n}$; (c) $\{x\in G\st\ord{x}=n\}\cup\{1\}$, $n$ composite and $G$ containing an element of order $n$;
 (d) the odd integers together with $0$; (e) $\{x\inR\st x^2\inQ\}$ in $(R,+)$.
\item [DF 2.1.3] Show $\{1,r^2,s,sr^2\}$ and $\{1,r^2,sr,sr^3\}$ are subgroups of $D_8$.
\item [DF 2.1.9] Prove $\SL_n(F)=\{A\in\GL_n(F)\st\det A=1\}\sgr\GL_n(F)$.
\item [DF 2.1.11] Prove $\{(a,1)\}$, $\{(1,b)\}$, and (when $B=A$) the diagonal
 $\{(a,a)\}$ are subgroups of $A\times B$.
\item [DF 2.1.14] Show $\{x\in D_{2n}\st x^2=1\}$ is not a subgroup ($n\ge3$).
\item [DF 2.2.1] Prove $C_G(A)=\{g\st g^{-1} ag=a\ \forall a\in A\}$ is a subgroup.
\item [DF 2.2.2] Prove $C_G(Z(G))=G$, and deduce $N_G(Z(G))=G$.
\item [DF 2.2.4] For $S_3,D_8,Q_8$, compute the centralizer of each element and the
 center of each.
\item [DF 2.3.3] Find all generators of $Z/(48)Z$.
\item [DF 2.3.4] Find all generators of $Z/(202)Z$.
\item [DF 2.3.5] Find the number of generators of $Z/(49000)Z$.
\item [DF 2.3.10] Find $\ord{\overline{30}}$ in $Z/(54)Z$, and list the elements and
 orders of $\langle \overline{30}\rangle$.
\item [DF 2.3.11] Find all cyclic subgroups of $D_8$ and a non-cyclic proper subgroup.
\item [DF 2.3.14] For $\sigma=(1\,2\,\cdots\,12)$, compute $\sigma^a$ for
 $a=13,65,626,1195,-6,-81,-570,-1211$.
\item [DF 2.4.1] Prove $H\sgr G\Longrightarrow\langle H\rangle=H$.
\item [DF 2.4.5] Prove two distinct elements of order $2$ in $S_3$ generate $S_3$.
\item [DF 2.4.6] Prove $\langle (1\,2),(1\,2)(3\,4)\rangle$ is non-cyclic of order $4$.
\item [DF 2.5.3] Show $\langle s,r^2\rangle\sgr D_8$ is isomorphic to $V_4$.
\item [DF 2.5.7] Find $Z(D_{16})$.
\item [Artin 2.4] In which of these cases is $H$ a subgroup of $G$? (a) $G=\GL_n(C)$,
 $H=\GL_n(R)$; (b) $G=R^\times$, $H=\{1,-1\}$; (c) $G=(Z,+)$, $H$ the positive
 integers; (d) $G=R^\times$, $H$ the positive reals.
\item [Artin 3.1] Let $a=123$, $b=321$. Compute $d=\gcd(a,b)$ and write $d=ra+sb$.
\item [Artin 4.2] An $n$th root of unity is $z\inC$ with $z^n=1$. (a) Prove the $n$th
 roots of unity form a cyclic subgroup of $C^\times$ of order $n$; (b) determine their
 product.
\item [Artin 4.6] (a) For a cyclic group of order $6$, how many elements generate it?

 $\langle 6Z,+\rangle$, $\{6^n\}$, $\{a+b\sqrt2\st a,b\inZ\}$ are cyclic; list generators.
\item [Fraleigh 5.41] For $B\subseteq A$, $b\in B$: determine whether
 $\{\sigma\in S_A\st\sigma(b)=b\}$ is a subgroup of $S_A$.
\item [Fraleigh 5.44] For $B\subseteq A$: determine whether
 $\{\sigma\in S_A\st\sigma[B]=B\}$ is a subgroup of $S_A$.
\item [Fraleigh 5.45] If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is an isomorphism and $H\sgr G$, prove
 $\varphi[H]\sgr G'$.
\item [Fraleigh 5.47] If $H,K$ are subgroups of an abelian group $G$, prove
 $\{hk\st h\in H,k\in K\}$ is a subgroup.
\item [Fraleigh 5.48] Find a group $G$ and subgroups $H,K$ for which the set
 $\{hk\}$ of the previous exercise is not a subgroup.
\item [Fraleigh 5.53] In an abelian group $G$, prove the solutions of $x^2=e$ form a
 subgroup.
\item [Fraleigh 5.58] Let $a\in G$. Prove $H_a=\{x\in G\st xa=ax\}$ is a subgroup.
\item [Fraleigh 5.61] Prove that if $H\sgr G$ and $K\sgr G$, then $H\cap K\sgr G$.
\item [Fraleigh 5.62] Prove that every cyclic group is abelian.
\item [Fraleigh 6.13] Find the number of automorphisms of $Z/(6)Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.14] Find the number of automorphisms of $Z/(8)Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.16] Find the number of automorphisms of $Z/(84)Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.54] For integers $r,s$, show $\{nr+ms\st n,m\inZ\}$ is a subgroup
 of $Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.56] If $ab$ has finite order $n$, show $ba$ also has order $n$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.62] For distinct primes $p,q$, find the number of generators of
 $Z/(pq)Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.63] For a prime $p$ and integer $r\ge1$, find the number of generators
 of $Z/(p^r)Z$.
\item [Fraleigh 6.66] Show $Z/(p)Z$ has no proper nontrivial subgroups when $p$ is prime.
\item [Fraleigh 7.13] Explain how to tell from a Cayley digraph whether the group is
 commutative.
\item [Fraleigh 7.16] Does the small inside triangle in the Cayley digraph of $Z/(6)Z$
 (with $S=\{2,3\}$) exhibit a cyclic subgroup? Why or why not?
\item [Fraleigh 7.18] Draw a Cayley digraph for $Z/(8)Z$ with generating set
 $S=\{2,5\}$.
\item [Fraleigh 7.22] Prove there are at least three different abelian groups of order $8$.
\end{exers}

 actions and find $\ord{G_i}$.

 $N_G(H)=G\Longrightarrow H\sgr Z(G)$.

 $(F,+)$.

 this can fail without commuting, and give commuting $x,y$ with

\item [DF 2.3.23] Show $(Z/(2^n)Z)^{\times}$ is not cyclic for $n\ge3$.
\item [DF 2.3.24] $G$ finite, $x\in G$: prove $g\in N_G(\langle x\rangle)\iff gxg^{-1}=x^a$ for some
 $a\inZ$.
\item [DF 2.3.25] $G$ cyclic of order $n$, $\gcd(k,n)=1$: prove $x\mapsto x^k$ is
 surjective, and extend to any finite group of order $n$.
\item [DF 2.3.26] $\Aut(Z_n)$: prove $\sigma_a:x\mapsto x^a$ is an automorphism
 $\iff\gcd(a,n)=1$, and $\Aut(Z_n)\cong(Z/(n)Z)^{\times}$, abelian of order $\varphi(n)$.
\item [DF 2.4.3] Prove that if $H$ is abelian then $\langle H,Z(G)\rangle$ is abelian; give an
 abelian $H$ with $\langle H,C_G(H)\rangle$ not abelian.
\item [DF 2.4.9] Prove $\SL_2(\F_3)=\gen{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),

\item [DF 2.4.10] Prove the subgroup of $\SL_2(\F_3)$ generated by

\item [DF 2.4.11] Prove $\SL_2(\F_3)\not\cong S_4$ (both of order $24$).
\item [DF 2.4.12] Prove the upper-triangular subgroup of $\GL_3(\F_2)$ is $\cong D_8$.
\item [DF 2.4.14] Finitely generated groups: (a) finite groups are f.g.; (b) $Z$ is
 f.g.; (c) a f.g.\ subgroup of $Q$ is cyclic; (d) $Q$ is not f.g.
\item [DF 2.4.16] Maximal subgroups: (a) every proper subgroup of a finite group lies in
 a maximal one; (b) the rotation subgroup of $D_{2n}$ is maximal; (c) $H$ is maximal in
 $Z_n=\langle x\rangle\iff H=\langle x^p\rangle$ for a prime $p\mid n$.
\item [DF 2.4.17] (Zorn) Prove every nontrivial finitely generated group has a maximal
 subgroup.
\item [DF 2.4.18] Pr\"ufer group $Z_{p^\infty}=\{z\inC\st z^{p^n}=1 some n\}$,

 proper subgroup is some $H_k$; and $Z_{p^\infty}$ is not f.g.
\item [DF 2.4.19] A nontrivial abelian group is divisible if every element has a $k$th
 root for each $k\neq0$.

Type: definition
Title: Left and right cosets
Content:
\begin{definition}[Left and right cosets]
For $g \in G$ the left coset of $N$ containing $g$ is
\[
 gN = \{\, gn \st n \in N \,\},
\]
and the right coset is $Ng = \{\, ng \st n \in N \,\}$. The set of all left cosets is denoted $G/N$ (read ``$G$ mod $N$''), and the number of left cosets is the index $[G:N]$.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Two left cosets are equal or disjoint, and $aN = bN \iff a^{-1} b \in N$. The cosets partition $G$, each has the same cardinality $|N|$, and when $G$ is finite Lagrange's theorem gives $|G| = [G:N]\,|N|$. None of this requires $N$ to be normal; normality is needed only to multiply cosets.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: The proposed product on $G/N$
Content:
\begin{definition}[The proposed product on $G/N$]
We attempt to make $G/N$ a group by setting, for cosets $X = aN$ and $Y = bN$,
\[
 (aN)(bN) \;=\; (ab)N.
\]
The issue: a coset has many names ($aN = a'N$ whenever $a^{-1} a' \in N$), so we must check the answer $(ab)N$ does not depend on which representatives $a,b$ we chose. This is the well-definedness question.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Quotient Groups and Homomorphisms > Definitions and Examples > Cosets and the quotient group $G/N$
Type: theorem
Title: Well-definedness of the coset product $\iff$ normality
Label: thm:welldef@c3
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Well-definedness of the coset product $\iff$ normality] 
Let $N \le G$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[(1)] The product $(aN)(bN) = (ab)N$ is well defined on $G/N$ (independent of representatives).
 \item[(2)] $gN g^{-1} = N$ for all $g \in G$ (equivalently $gNg^{-1} \subseteq N$ for all $g$); i.e.\ $N \nor G$.
 \item[(3)] $gN = Ng$ for all $g \in G$ (every left coset is a right coset).
\end{enumerate}
When these hold, $G/N$ with this product is a group, the quotient group, with identity $N = 1N$ and inverse $(aN)^{-1} = a^{-1} N$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:welldef@c3

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Quotient Groups and Homomorphisms > Definitions and Examples > Cosets and the quotient group $G/N$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-cb277b9f6718a9023cb9
Content:
\begin{proof}
$(2)\iff(3)$: $gNg^{-1} = N \iff gN = Ng$ on multiplying by $g$ on the right. Moreover $gNg^{-1}\subseteq N$ for all $g$ forces equality: applying the inclusion to $g^{-1}$ gives $g^{-1} N g\subseteq N$, i.e.\ $N\subseteq gNg^{-1}$, so $gNg^{-1} = N$.

$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$: Suppose $aN = a'N$ and $bN = b'N$, so $a' = a n_1$ and $b' = b n_2$ with $n_1,n_2 \in N$. Then
\[
 a'b' = a n_1 b n_2 = a b\,(b^{-1} n_1 b)\,n_2 .
\]
By (2), $b^{-1} n_1 b \in b^{-1} N b = N$, so $b^{-1} n_1 b = n_3 \in N$ and $a'b' = ab\,n_3 n_2 \in (ab)N$. Hence $a'b'N = abN$: the product is well defined.

$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: Assume the product is well defined. Fix $g \in G$ and $n \in N$. Since $n \in N$ we have $nN = N = 1N$, so $gn$ and $g$ are two representatives of the same left coset: $(gn)N = gN$. Likewise $g^{-1} N = g^{-1} N$. Apply well-definedness to the two equal pairs $\bigl((gn)N,\ g^{-1} N\bigr)$ and $\bigl(gN,\ g^{-1} N\bigr)$:
\[
 \bigl((gn)N\bigr)\bigl(g^{-1} N\bigr) = \bigl(gN\bigr)\bigl(g^{-1} N\bigr)
 \;\Longrightarrow\;
 (gng^{-1})N = (gg^{-1})N = N .
\]
Thus $gng^{-1} \in N$. As $g \in G$ and $n \in N$ were arbitrary, $gNg^{-1} \subseteq N$ for all $g$, hence $N \nor G$.

Group axioms when (2) holds: associativity is inherited from $G$, since
\[
 (aN)\bigl((bN)(cN)\bigr) = a(bc)N = (ab)c\,N = \bigl((aN)(bN)\bigr)(cN);
\]
the identity is $N = 1N$ since $(aN)(1N) = aN$; and the inverse of $aN$ is $a^{-1} N$ since $(aN)(a^{-1} N) = aa^{-1} N = N$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: Quotient group via fibers, D\&F's viewpoint
Content:
\begin{remark}[Quotient group via fibers, D\&F's viewpoint]
Equivalently, when $N \nor G$, the cosets are exactly the fibers of any homomorphism with kernel $N$, and ``multiply the cosets'' means ``multiply the fibers as subsets'': the subset product $(aN)(bN) = \{\, xy \st x \in aN,\ y \in bN \,\}$ is itself a single coset, namely $(ab)N$. The subset product $XY=\{\,xy \st x\in X,\ y\in Y\,\}$ being a single coset for all cosets $X,Y$ is yet another equivalent of normality.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: The natural projection
Label: thm:proj@c3
Content:
\begin{theorem}[The natural projection] 
Let $N \nor G$. The map
\[
 \pi : G \longrightarrow G/N, \qquad \pi(g) = gN,
\]
is a surjective homomorphism with $\ker \pi = N$. Consequently $N$ is normal in $G$ iff it is the kernel of some homomorphism out of $G$, and $\ord{G/N} = [G:N]$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:proj@c3

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-042407b85ffc13506651
Content:
\begin{proof}
Homomorphism: $\pi(gh) = (gh)N = (gN)(hN) = \pi(g)\pi(h)$, using the quotient product. Surjective: every coset $gN$ equals $\pi(g)$. Kernel: $\pi(g) = N$ (the identity of $G/N$) $\iff gN = N \iff g \in N$, so $\ker\pi = N$. The number of cosets is $[G:N]$ by definition, hence $\ord{G/N} = [G:N]$. Finally, kernels are always normal, and $\pi$ exhibits any normal $N$ as a kernel, giving the ``iff.''
\end{proof}

Content:
The inclusion of $N$ and the projection $\pi$ fit into the triangle
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
 N \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "1"'] & G \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"] \\
 & G/N
\end{tikzcd}\]
in which $\pi \circ \iota$ collapses all of $N$ to the identity coset $N$.

Title: Computing inside $G/N$: reduce representatives
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing inside $G/N$: reduce representatives}
Trigger. You must add/multiply cosets, find the order of $gN$, or identify the isomorphism type of $G/N$.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Multiply by representatives. $(aN)(bN) = (ab)N$; just multiply $a,b$ in $G$, then re-coset.
 \item Reduce mod $N$. Replace the answer $abN$ by the simplest name: $abN = cN$ whenever $c^{-1}(ab)\in N$. In $Z$ this is ``reduce mod $n$.''
 \item Identity test. $gN = N \iff g \in N$. So in $G/N$ a relation $gN = 1$ means $g\in N$.
 \item Order of a coset. $\ord{gN}$ is the least $k\ge 1$ with $g^k \in N$ (it divides $\ord{g}$ when $g$ has finite order).
 \item Identify the type. Compute $|G/N| = [G:N]$, then match generators/orders to a known group of that order.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

\begin{pitfall}
The product $(aN)(bN)=(ab)N$ is not automatic. For a non-normal $N$ it depends on the chosen representatives, so it is no operation at all. Always confirm $N\nor G$ before computing in ``$G/N$.'' A clean witness of failure: pick $a'=an$ with $n\in N$ but $b^{-1} n b \notin N$; then $(a'b)N \ne (ab)N$ even though $a'N=aN$.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{pitfall}
$gN = Ng$ as sets does not mean $gn = ng$ for each $n$. Normality is a setwise condition: conjugation by $g$ permutes $N$ (i.e.\ $gNg^{-1} = N$), but it need not fix elements. Do not confuse normal with central.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: $Z/nZ$ as a quotient of $(Z,+)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/nZ$ as a quotient of $(Z,+)$}
Take $G = (Z,+)$ and $N = nZ = \{\dots,-2n,-n,0,n,2n,\dots\}$ for a fixed $n \ge 1$. Describe $G/N$, its operation, and its order.
\wrec Additive abelian group, so every subgroup is normal (Example below). The cosets are residue classes; this is the prototype of every quotient.
\wsol Since $Z$ is abelian, $nZ \nor Z$, so $Z/nZ$ is a group. A coset is
\[
 a + nZ = \{\, a + nk \st k\inZ \,\} = \overline{a},
\]
and $a + nZ = b + nZ \iff a - b \in nZ \iff a \equiv b \pmod n$. By the division algorithm every integer is congruent to exactly one of $0,1,\dots,n-1$, so the distinct cosets are $\overline{0},\overline{1},\dots,\overline{n-1}$ and $\ord{Z/nZ} = [Z:nZ] = n$. The (well-defined) operation is
\[
 (a + nZ) + (b + nZ) = (a+b) + nZ, \quadi.e.\quad \overline{a} + \overline{b} = \overline{a+b}.
\]
Concretely with $n = 6$: $\overline{4} + \overline{5} = \overline{9} = \overline{3}$, and $\overline{2} + \overline{4} = \overline{6} = \overline{0}$. The projection is $\pi(a) = \overline a$, with $\ker\pi = 6Z$.
Check. $\overline 0$ is the identity ($\overline a + \overline 0 = \overline a$); the inverse of $\overline 4$ in $Z/6Z$ is $\overline 2$ since $\overline 4 + \overline 2 = \overline 6 = \overline 0$. And indeed $|Z/6Z| = 6 = [Z:6Z]$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ as a quotient of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$}
Take $G = (\mathbb{Z},+)$ and $N = n\mathbb{Z} = \{\dots,-2n,-n,0,n,2n,\dots\}$ for a fixed $n \ge 1$. Describe $G/N$, its operation, and its order.
\wrec Additive abelian group, so every subgroup is normal (Example below). The cosets are residue classes; this is the prototype of every quotient.
\wsol Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian, $n\mathbb{Z} \nor \mathbb{Z}$, so $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a group. A coset is
\[
