Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $G$ act on the set $A$. Show that the relation $a \sim b$ iff $b = g\cdot a$ for some $g \in G$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, and that its classes are exactly the orbits $\orb(a)$.

\item Let $G = D_8 = \langle r,s\rangle$ act on the four vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ of a square (labeled cyclically), with $r$ the rotation $(1\,2\,3\,4)$ and $s$ the reflection $(2\,4)$. Write down the permutation representation $\rho : G \to S_4$ explicitly (give the image of $r$ and of $s$), and compute $\Stab_G(1)$ and the orbit $\orb(1)$. Verify $|\orb(1)|\cdot|\Stab_G(1)| = |G|$.

\item Let $G$ act on $A$ and fix $a \in A$. Prove that for all $g \in G$, $\Stab_G(g\cdot a) = g\,\Stab_G(a)\,g^{-1}$. Conclude that points in the same orbit have conjugate stabilizers.

\item Let $G$ act on itself by left multiplication, $g\cdot x = gx$. Show this action is faithful and transitive, and that the induced map $G \to \Sym(G)$ is the (left regular) representation. Deduce Cayley's theorem: every group of order $n$ embeds in $S_n$.

\item Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation, $g\cdot x = gxg^{-1}$. Identify the orbits, the stabilizer $\Stab_G(x)$, and the kernel of the corresponding permutation representation $G \to \Sym(G)$.

\item Let $G$ be a group of order $30$ act on a set $A$ with $|A| = 8$. Prove that every orbit has size dividing $30$, hence size in $\{1,2,3,5,6\}$ (the divisors of $30$ that are $\le 8$), and that the orbit sizes sum to $8$. List all possible multisets of orbit sizes, and conclude that at least one orbit has size $1$ (a fixed point) unless the orbit sizes can be chosen from $\{2,3,5,6\}$ summing to $8$ -- determine exactly which multisets force a fixed point.

\item For $G = Q_8$ acting on itself by conjugation, compute the class equation $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum [G : C_G(x_i)]$ explicitly, naming a representative $x_i$ for each noncentral class. (Here $Z(Q_8) = \{\pm 1\}$ and the noncentral classes are $\{i,-i\},\{j,-j\},\{k,-k\}$, giving $8 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2$.)

\item Let $G = S_4$. Using that conjugacy classes correspond to cycle types, write the class equation of $S_4$. Verify the class sizes sum to $24$ and each divides $24$. (The class sizes are $1, 6, 3, 8, 6$.)

\item Let $G$ act transitively on a finite set $A$ with $|A| > 1$. Prove there exists $g \in G$ that fixes no point of $A$ (Jordan). Suggestion: the number of fixed points averaged over $G$ equals the number of orbits, which is $1$; since the identity fixes all $|A| > 1$ points, some element must fix none.

\item Let $p$ be prime and let $G$ be a group of order $p^n$ act on a finite set $A$. Prove $|A| \equiv |A^G| \pmod p$, where $A^G = \{a \in A : g\cdot a = a \ \forall g\}$ is the fixed-point set. Deduce that if $p \mid |A|$ then $p \mid |A^G|$ (so $|A^G|\ge p$ as soon as $A^G\ne\varnothing$), that $A^G$ is nonempty whenever $p \nmid |A|$, and that a nontrivial $p$-group has nontrivial center.

\item Compute $\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$ for $p$ prime and show $|\Aut(Z/(p)Z)| = p-1$. More generally show $\Aut(Z/(n)Z) \cong (Z/(n)Z)^\times$ and compute its order via Euler's $\varphi$.

\item Let $G$ have order $p^2$ with $p$ prime. Using the class equation, prove $G$ is abelian, hence $G \cong Z/(p^2)Z$ or $G \cong Z/(p)Z\timesZ/(p)Z$.

\item Let $G = S_3$ act on the set $A$ of its three $2$-element subsets $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}$. Build the permutation representation $\rho : S_3 \to \Sym(A) \cong S_3$, determine $\ker\rho$, and decide whether $\rho$ is faithful.

\item Let $G$ act on $A$ and $B$. Define the diagonal action of $G$ on $A \times B$ by $g\cdot(a,b) = (g\cdot a,\, g\cdot b)$. Verify this is an action, and for $G = Z/(4)Z$ acting on $A = B = Z/(4)Z$ by addition (translation), find all orbits on $A \times B$ and their sizes.

\item Let $G$ act on the left cosets $A = G/H$ of a subgroup $H \le G$ by $g\cdot(xH) = (gx)H$. Show this action is transitive, compute $\Stab_G(H)$, and show $\ker$ of the representation $G \to \Sym(G/H)$ equals $\bigcap_{x \in G} xHx^{-1}$ (the core of $H$).

\item Let $G$ be a finite group and $H \le G$ with $[G:H] = p$ the smallest prime dividing $|G|$. Using the action of $G$ on $G/H$ and the resulting map $G \to S_p$, prove $H \nor G$.

\end{exers}

Deduce that if $p \mid |A|$ then $p \mid |A^G|$ (so $|A^G|\ge p$ as soon as $A^G\ne\varnothing$), that $A^G$ is nonempty whenever $p \nmid |A|$, and that a nontrivial $p$-group has nontrivial center.

\item Compute $\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})$ for $p$ prime and show $|\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})| = p-1$. More generally show $\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^\times$ and compute its order via Euler's $\varphi$.

\item Let $G$ have order $p^2$ with $p$ prime. Using the class equation, prove $G$ is abelian, hence $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/(p^2)\mathbb{Z}$ or $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}$.

\item Let $G = S_3$ act on the set $A$ of its three $2$-element subsets $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}$. Build the permutation representation $\rho : S_3 \to \Sym(A) \cong S_3$, determine $\ker\rho$, and decide whether $\rho$ is faithful.

\item Let $G$ act on $A$ and $B$. Define the diagonal action of $G$ on $A \times B$ by $g\cdot(a,b) = (g\cdot a,\, g\cdot b)$. Verify this is an action, and for $G = \mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ acting on $A = B = \mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ by addition (translation), find all orbits on $A \times B$ and their sizes.

\item Let $G$ act on the left cosets $A = G/H$ of a subgroup $H \le G$ by $g\cdot(xH) = (gx)H$. Show this action is transitive, compute $\Stab_G(H)$, and show $\ker$ of the representation $G \to \Sym(G/H)$ equals $\bigcap_{x \in G} xHx^{-1}$ (the core of $H$).

\item Let $G$ be a finite group and $H \le G$ with $[G:H] = p$ the smallest prime dividing $|G|$. Using the action of $G$ on $G/H$ and the resulting map $G \to S_p$, prove $H \nor G$.

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item (Cauchy via actions) Let $p$ divide $|G|$. Let $Z/(p)Z$ act on $X = \{(x_1,\dots,x_p) \in G^p : x_1 x_2 \cdots x_p = 1\}$ by cyclic rotation of coordinates. Show $|X| = |G|^{p-1}$, that $Z/(p)Z$ acts on $X$, and apply $|X| \equiv |X^{Z/(p)Z}| \pmod p$ to produce an element of order $p$.

\item Let $G$ act $2$-transitively on $A$ (for any two ordered pairs of distinct points there is $g$ carrying one to the other). Prove that for $a \in A$, the stabilizer $\Stab_G(a)$ acts transitively on $A \setminus \{a\}$, and that $|G| = |A|(|A|-1)\,|\Stab_G(a,b)|$ for distinct $a,b$, where $\Stab_G(a,b)$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $\{a,b\}$.

\item Let $G$ be a finite group acting transitively on $A$ with $|A| = n \ge 2$. Show that the number of orbits of $G$ on $A \times A$ (the rank of the action) equals the number of $\Stab_G(a)$-orbits on $A$, and is at least $2$.

\item Let $G$ act on $A$ and let $N = \ker(G \to \Sym(A))$ be the kernel. Prove $N = \bigcap_{a\in A}\Stab_G(a)$, that $N \nor G$, and that the induced action of $G/N$ on $A$ is faithful with the same orbits.

\item (Counting necklaces) Using Burnside's lemma, the number of orbits equals $|G|^{-1}\sum_{g}|\Fix(g)|$ where $\Fix(g) = \{a : g\cdot a = a\}$. Let $Z/(6)Z$ act by rotation on the $2^6$ colorings of $6$ beads with $2$ colors. Compute the number of distinct necklaces.

\item Let $G$ be a finite simple group acting nontrivially on a set $A$ with $|A| = n$. Prove $G$ embeds in $S_n$, and hence $A_5$ has no faithful action on a set with fewer than $5$ points. Conclude $|G| \mid n!$.

\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item An action of $G$ on $A$ is the same data as a homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(A)$. State the two action axioms and verify they are equivalent to $\rho$ being a homomorphism filling
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] G \arrow[r, "\rho"] & \Sym(A) \end{tikzcd}\]
i.e. $\rho(gh) = \rho(g)\rho(h)$ and $\rho(1) = \id_A$.

\item Let $G$ act transitively on $A$ and fix $a \in A$. Prove the orbit-stabilizer map is a well-defined $G$-set bijection making
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em] G/\Stab_G(a) \arrow[r, "\sim"', "{g\,\Stab_G(a)\,\mapsto\, g\cdot a}"] & A \end{tikzcd}\]
commute with the $G$-actions (left multiplication on cosets, the given action on $A$). Deduce $|A| = [G:\Stab_G(a)]$.

\item Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation. Show this is the homomorphism $\psi : G \to \Aut(G)$, $g \mapsto (x \mapsto gxg^{-1})$, with image $\Inn(G)$, and that $\ker\psi = Z(G)$, giving the exact sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] 1 \arrow[r] & Z(G) \arrow[r, hook] & G \arrow[r, "\psi"] & \Aut(G) \arrow[r, two heads] & \Aut(G)/\Inn(G) \arrow[r] & 1 \end{tikzcd}\]
Identify the cokernel-side quotient $\Aut(G)/\Inn(G)$ as $\operatorname{Out}(G)$.

\item Let $H \le G$ and consider the action of $G$ on $G/H$. Show the permutation representation factors as
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] G \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[rd, "\rho"'] & G/K \arrow[d, hook] \\ & \Sym(G/H) \end{tikzcd}\]
where $K = \ker\rho = \bigcap_{x\in G} xHx^{-1}$ is the core of $H$, $\pi$ is the quotient map, and the vertical arrow is the induced faithful action. Conclude $G/K$ embeds in $S_{[G:H]}$.

\item Let $G$ act on sets $A$ and $B$. A map $f : A \to B$ is $G$-equivariant if $f(g\cdot a) = g\cdot f(a)$ for all $g,a$, i.e. for each $g$ the square
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] A \arrow[r, "f"] \arrow[d, "g\cdot"'] & B \arrow[d, "g\cdot"] \\ A \arrow[r, "f"'] & B \end{tikzcd}\]
commutes. Prove that an equivariant $f$ sends orbits to orbits and that if $f$ is a bijection it carries $\Stab_G(a)$ isomorphically onto $\Stab_G(f(a))$.

\end{exers}

Content:
We isolate the simplest action a group has on itself --- left multiplication --- and extract from it Cayley's theorem and, more flexibly, the action on cosets of a subgroup. The coset action is the single most useful counting tool in this chapter: it manufactures a homomorphism $G\to S_m$ out of nothing but a subgroup of index $m$, and its kernel is canonically described.

Type: definition
Title: Left regular action
Content:
\begin{definition}[Left regular action]
Let $G$ be a group. The left regular action of $G$ on the set $A=G$ is
\[
g\cdot x = gx \qquad (g\in G,\ x\in G),
\]
the product taken in $G$. This is a (left) group action: $1\cdot x = 1x = x$, and $g\cdot(h\cdot x)=g(hx)=(gh)x=(gh)\cdot x$ by associativity.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Do not confuse the action with the group operation conceptually: $G$ acts on the set of its own elements. The permutation attached to $g$ is left-translation $\lambda_g\colon x\mapsto gx$, which is a bijection of the set $G$ (with inverse $\lambda_{g^{-1}}$), but $\lambda_g$ is essentially never a group homomorphism $G\to G$.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: Cayley
Label: thm:cayley@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Cayley] 
Let $G$ be a group. The left regular action affords an injective homomorphism
\[
\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow \Sym(G),\qquad \lambda(g)=\lambda_g,\ \ \lambda_g(x)=gx.
\]
Hence $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Sym(G)$. If $\ord{G}=n<\infty$, then $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$ and so $G$ embeds in $S_n$.
\end{theorem}

Type: prose
Content:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, hook, "\lambda"] & \Sym(G) \arrow[r, "\sim"] & S_n
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects in a horizontal chain.
$G$ is the abstract group being embedded.
$\Sym(G)$ is the symmetric group on the underlying set of $G$, i.e.\ the group of all bijections $G\to G$; it is a group under composition.
$S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ for $n=\ord{G}$; once a bijection $G\xrightarrow{\sim}\{1,\dots,n\}$ is fixed, $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$ concretely.
\dgi{Arrows:} The first arrow $\lambda\colon G\hookrightarrow\Sym(G)$ is the left regular representation: $\lambda(g)=\lambda_g$ where $\lambda_g(x)=gx$ for every $x\in G$.
The hook indicates it is injective (proved below via $\ker\lambda=\{1\}$).
The second arrow $\Sym(G)\xrightarrow{\sim} S_n$ is the isomorphism induced by any fixed labelling of the elements of $G$ as $x_1,\dots,x_n$; it sends a bijection $\sigma\colon G\to G$ to the permutation of indices $i\mapsto j$ where $\sigma(x_i)=x_j$.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no square here; the diagram is a straight chain of two maps.
The implicit equality is $G\cong\lambda(G)\le\Sym(G)\cong S_n$: following the two arrows in sequence gives an injective group homomorphism $G\hookrightarrow S_n$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Start with $g\in G$.
Along the left arrow, $g$ maps to the left-translation $\lambda_g\in\Sym(G)$.
Along the right isomorphism, $\lambda_g$ maps to the permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ it induces via the labelling.
The composite is a group homomorphism because $\lambda$ is a homomorphism (by the action axioms) and the labelling isomorphism is a homomorphism; injective because $\ker\lambda=\{1\}$ (if $\lambda_g=\id$ then $g\cdot 1=1$ forces $g=1$).
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the punchline of Cayley's theorem: every abstract group is concretely realized inside a symmetric group.
The diagram makes visible both the embedding $\lambda$ and the specific identification $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$ that lets one say ``$G$ embeds in $S_n$.''
Without the diagram, the two steps --- defining $\lambda$ and identifying $\Sym(G)$ with $S_n$ --- could blur together.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $G=Z/(4)Z$, label $x_i=i-1$.
$\lambda_1(x)=x+1\pmod{4}$ gives the permutation $1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto4\mapsto1$, i.e.\ the $4$-cycle $(1\,2\,3\,4)\in S_4$.
The chain $Z/(4)Z\hookrightarrow\Sym(Z/(4)Z)\cong S_4$ sends $1\mapsto\lambda_1\mapsto(1\,2\,3\,4)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\lambda(g)=\lambda_g$ is a map $G\to G$ (a group endomorphism).
It is not: $\lambda_g$ is a permutation of the set $G$, so $\lambda$ maps into $\Sym(G)$, not into $G$.
Also, the isomorphism $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$ depends on a choice of labelling; the embedding $G\hookrightarrow S_n$ changes by conjugation when the labelling changes, but injectivity does not.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the left regular action provides a canonical injective group homomorphism $G\to\Sym(G)$, hence (once the elements of $G$ are labelled $1,\dots,n$) an embedding $G\hookrightarrow S_n$, realizing any abstract group of order $n$ as a concrete subgroup of the symmetric group $S_n$.
\end{dgx}

Content:
\begin{proof}
By the general permutation-representation theorem (\S4.1), every action of $G$ on a set $A$ gives a homomorphism $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(A)$ with kernel
\[
\ker\rho=\{\,g\in G: g\cdot a=a for all a\in A\,\}.
\]
Apply this to $A=G$ with $g\cdot x=gx$. Then $g\in\ker\lambda$ iff $gx=x$ for all $x\in G$. Taking $x=1$ gives $g\cdot 1=g=1$. Thus $\ker\lambda=\{1\}$ and $\lambda$ is injective, so $G\cong\lambda(G)\le\Sym(G)$. If $\ord{G}=n$, a bijection $G\to\{1,\dots,n\}$ induces $\Sym(G)\cong S_n$, and composing gives an embedding $G\hookrightarrow S_n$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}[Image of Cayley's embedding]
Each nonidentity $\lambda_g$ is a fixed-point-free permutation of $G$: if $gx=x$ then $g=1$. Consequently every nonidentity $\lambda_g$ is a product of cycles all of the same length $\ord{g}$, and there are exactly $n/\ord{g}$ of them. (This is the cycle structure of the regular representation.)
\end{remark}

Title: Using Cayley's theorem / the regular representation
Content:
\begin{method}{Using Cayley's theorem / the regular representation}
Trigger. You want to realize an abstract group concretely inside a symmetric group, or you need a permutation whose cycle type encodes element orders.\\[2pt]
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Fix an ordering/labelling $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of the elements of $G$.
\item For each generator $g$, compute $\lambda_g(x_i)=g x_i$ and read off the permutation of indices.
\item Write $\lambda_g$ in cycle notation. Sanity check: $\lambda_g$ moves every point unless $g=1$ (fixed-point free), and its cycles all have length $\ord{g}$, giving $n/\ord{g}$ cycles.
\item The map $g\mapsto\lambda_g$ is the embedding $G\hookrightarrow S_n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

\begin{wex}{Cayley for $Z/(4)Z$}
Realize $Z/(4)Z=\{0,1,2,3\}$ (addition mod $4$) as a subgroup of $S_4$ via its left regular representation.
\wrec Cayley's theorem (Thm.~ [REF:thm:cayley@c4] ): the left regular action gives $\lambda\colon G\hookrightarrow S_n$. Here ``multiply'' means ``add mod $4$.''
\wsol Label the points $1\!:\!0,\ 2\!:\!1,\ 3\!:\!2,\ 4\!:\!3$ (point $i$ is the element $i-1$). For $g=1$, $\lambda_1(x)=x+1$:
\[
0\mapsto 1\mapsto 2\mapsto 3\mapsto 0,\quadi.e. labels 1\mapsto 2\mapsto 3\mapsto 4\mapsto 1,
\]
so $\lambda_1=(1\,2\,3\,4)$. Then
\[
\lambda_2=\lambda_1^2=(1\,3)(2\,4),\qquad \lambda_3=\lambda_1^3=(1\,4\,3\,2),\qquad \lambda_0=\id.
\]
Thus $Z/(4)Z\cong\langle (1\,2\,3\,4)\rangle\le S_4$.

Check. $\ord{1}=4$ so $\lambda_1$ should be a single $4$-cycle: it is. $\ord{2}=2$ so $\lambda_2$ should be $4/2=2$ transpositions: $(1\,3)(2\,4)$. Fixed-point-free for all nonidentity elements. Good.
\end{wex}

Title: Cayley for $V_4$ into $S_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cayley for $V_4$ into $S_4$}
Embed the Klein four-group $V_4=\{1,a,b,c\}$ with $a^2=b^2=c^2=1$, $ab=c$, into $S_4$.
\wrec Cayley's theorem: left regular representation of $V_4$, an order-$4$ group, lands in $S_4$.
\wsol Label $1\!:\!1,\ 2\!:\!a,\ 3\!:\!b,\ 4\!:\!c$. Compute $\lambda_a(x)=ax$:
\[
a\cdot 1=a,\quad a\cdot a=1,\quad a\cdot b=ab=c,\quad a\cdot c=ac=a(ab)=a^2b=b,
\]
so labels $1\mapsto 2,\ 2\mapsto1,\ 3\mapsto4,\ 4\mapsto3$, giving $\lambda_a=(1\,2)(3\,4)$. Similarly $\lambda_b(x)=bx$:
\[
b\cdot1=b,\qquad b\cdot a=ba=ab=c,\qquad b\cdot b=1,\qquad b\cdot c=bc=b(ab)=(ba)b=(ab)b=ab^2=a.
\]
So $1\mapsto3,\ 2\mapsto4,\ 3\mapsto1,\ 4\mapsto2$, giving $\lambda_b=(1\,3)(2\,4)$. And $\lambda_c=\lambda_a\lambda_b$ corresponds to $c=ab$:
\[
\lambda_c=(1\,4)(2\,3).
\]
Thus $V_4\cong\{\id,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}\le S_4$, the standard copy.

Check. Every nonidentity element has order $2$, so each $\lambda$ is $4/2=2$ transpositions: confirmed. The three images plus identity form exactly the normal Klein four-subgroup of $S_4$. Closure: $(1\,2)(3\,4)\cdot(1\,3)(2\,4)=(1\,4)(2\,3)$, matching $ab=c$. Good.
\end{wex}

Title: Cayley for $S_3$ into $S_6$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cayley for $S_3$ into $S_6$}
Describe the cycle type of $\lambda_g$ for the regular representation $S_3\hookrightarrow S_6$ as $g$ ranges over $S_3$.
\wrec Cayley plus the cycle-structure remark: nonidentity $\lambda_g$ is fixed-point free with all cycles of length $\ord{g}$.
\wsol Here $n=6$. By element orders in $S_3$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=1$: $\lambda_g=\id$.
\item $g$ a transposition ($\ord{g}=2$, three such $g$): $\lambda_g$ is $6/2=3$ transpositions, type $2^3$.
\item $g$ a $3$-cycle ($\ord{g}=3$, two such $g$): $\lambda_g$ is $6/3=2$ three-cycles, type $3^2$.
\end{itemize}
So the image consists of $\id$, three permutations of type $2^3$, and two of type $3^2$.

Check. The element count matches $|S_3|=6=1+3+2$. For a transposition $g$, $\lambda_g$ has type $2^3$ with sign $(-1)^3=-1$, so $\lambda_g$ is an odd permutation of $S_6$; for a $3$-cycle $g$, $\lambda_g$ has type $3^2$ with sign $(+1)^2=+1$, an even permutation. Consistent with $S_3$ having a sign map. Good.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Order $6$ with no $6$-cycle image? (cyclic vs. noncyclic)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Order $6$ with no $6$-cycle image? (cyclic vs. noncyclic)}
For which groups $G$ of order $6$ does the regular representation contain a $6$-cycle?
\wrec Cayley plus cycle structure: $\lambda_g$ is a single $n$-cycle iff $\ord{g}=n=\ord{G}$, i.e. iff $g$ generates $G$.
\wsol A nonidentity $\lambda_g$ is one $6$-cycle iff $\ord{g}=6$, i.e. $g$ generates $G$, i.e. $G$ is cyclic. For $G=Z/(6)Z$ the generator $1$ gives $\lambda_1=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6)$, a $6$-cycle. For $G=S_3$ there is no element of order $6$ (orders are $1,2,3$), so no $\lambda_g$ is a $6$-cycle: the regular representation of $S_3$ contains only types $2^3$ and $3^2$ (and $\id$).

Check. $Z/(6)Z$ has $\phi(6)=2$ generators, giving two $6$-cycles $(1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6)$ and its inverse; consistent with $Z/(6)Z$ cyclic. $S_3$ noncyclic, no $6$-cycle. Good.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Cayley says $G\le S_n$ for $n=\ord G$, but $n$ is usually far from optimal. E.g. $Z/(6)Z\hookrightarrow S_6$ via the regular action, yet $Z/(6)Z$ also embeds in $S_5$ (as $(1\,2)(3\,4\,5)$). Cayley gives an embedding, not the smallest one. Do not claim ``the least $n$ with $G\le S_n$ is $\ord G$.''
\end{pitfall}

Type: theorem
Title: Coset action; kernel is the core
Label: thm:coset@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Coset action; kernel is the core] 
Let $G$ be a group, $H\le G$, and let $A=\{\,gH : g\in G\,\}$ be the set of left cosets of $H$, so $|A|=[G:H]$. Then $G$ acts on $A$ by left multiplication,
\[
g\cdot(xH)=(gx)H,
\]
and this affords a homomorphism
\[
\rho_H\colon G\longrightarrow \Sym(A)\cong S_{[G:H]}.
\]
Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the action is transitive;
\item the stabilizer of the coset $1H=H$ is exactly $H$;
\item $\displaystyle \ker\rho_H=\bigcap_{x\in G} xHx^{-1}$, and this is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$. It is called the core of $H$ in $G$, written $\operatorname{core}_G(H)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: thm:coset@c4

Type: prose
Content:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\rho_H"] \arrow[rd, "onto"', two heads] & S_{[G:H]} \\
& G/\ker\rho_H \arrow[u, hook, "\bar\rho_H"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\ker\rho_H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)=\bigcap_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}.\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects arranged in a triangle.
$G$ is the ambient group (upper-left).
$S_{[G:H]}=S_m$ where $m=[G:H]$ is the symmetric group on $m$ letters, which receives the coset-action permutations (upper-right).
$G/\ker\rho_H$ is the quotient of $G$ by the core $K=\ker\rho_H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$, a normal subgroup; it is the group of cosets $gK$ (lower-right).
The displayed equation identifies $K$ explicitly as the intersection $\bigcap_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}$ of all conjugates of $H$.
\dgi{Arrows:}
$\rho_H\colon G\to S_m$ is the coset permutation representation: $\rho_H(g)$ is the permutation of left cosets $xH$ given by $\rho_H(g)(xH)=(gx)H$.
The diagonal surjection $G\twoheadrightarrow G/K$ is the canonical quotient map $g\mapsto gK$, which is surjective by construction (marked ``onto'').
$\bar\rho_H\colon G/K\hookrightarrow S_m$ is the induced (or factor) map $gK\mapsto\rho_H(g)$; the hook signals it is injective (its kernel is trivial because $K=\ker\rho_H$ by construction).
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\bar\rho_H\circ\pi=\rho_H$, where $\pi\colon G\twoheadrightarrow G/K$ is the quotient map.
Explicitly: following the top-right arrow gives $g\mapsto\rho_H(g)$; following the diagonal then the right arrow gives $g\mapsto gK\mapsto\bar\rho_H(gK)=\rho_H(g)$.
Both paths agree.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\bar\rho_H$: if $gK=g'K$ then $g'=gk$ for some $k\in K=\ker\rho_H$, so $\rho_H(g')=\rho_H(g)\rho_H(k)=\rho_H(g)\cdot\id=\rho_H(g)$.
Thus $\bar\rho_H(gK)$ is independent of the coset representative, and $\bar\rho_H\circ\pi=\rho_H$ holds by this very definition.
This is exactly the universal property of the quotient: a homomorphism out of $G$ whose kernel contains $K$ factors uniquely through $G/K$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram encodes the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to $\rho_H$, and makes the coset action's structure transparent: the quotient $G/K$ embeds faithfully in $S_m$, so $\ord{G/K}=[G:K]$ divides $m!=([G:H])!$.
This divisibility (Corollary~ [REF:cor:divis@c4] ) is the key tool for proving normality and non-simplicity conclusions from small-index subgroups.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$, $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$, $m=3$.
The kernel is $K=\ker\rho_H=\{1\}$ (computed in the worked example), so $G/K\cong S_3$ embeds injectively in $S_3$, actually as an isomorphism.
The triangle collapses to $S_3\xrightarrow{\sim}G/\{1\}\hookrightarrow S_3$.
For contrast, if $G=D_8$ and $H$ is the Klein four-subgroup of index $2$, then $K=H$ and the triangle yields $D_8/H\congZ/2Z\hookrightarrow S_2$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students forget to verify well-definedness of $\bar\rho_H$ before claiming the triangle commutes.
The induced map is only defined on cosets $gK$ (not on individual elements) because $K$ is specifically $\ker\rho_H$; if $K$ were merely a subgroup not contained in $\ker\rho_H$, the formula $\bar\rho_H(gK)=\rho_H(g)$ would depend on the representative and would fail to be a function.
Another common error: reading the hook on $\bar\rho_H$ as meaning $G/K\cong S_m$; it only means $G/K$ embeds in $S_m$, not that the embedding is surjective.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the coset action $\rho_H$ factors through the quotient $G/\operatorname{core}_G(H)$, which then embeds faithfully in $S_m$, giving the divisibility $[G:\operatorname{core}_G(H)]\mid([G:H])!$ and the mechanism behind every ``small-index subgroup'' normality or non-simplicity argument.
\end{dgx}

Type: proof
Content:
\begin{proof}
Well-defined action. If $xH=x'H$ then $x'=xh$ for some $h\in H$, so $(gx')H=(gxh)H=(gx)hH=(gx)H$; thus $g\cdot(xH)$ depends only on the coset. The action axioms hold by associativity exactly as for the regular action.

(1) Transitivity. Given cosets $xH,yH$, the element $g=yx^{-1}$ satisfies $g\cdot(xH)=(yx^{-1}x)H=yH$.

(2) Stabilizer of $H$. $g\cdot H=H$ iff $gH=H$ iff $g\in H$. So $\Stab(H)=H$.

(3) Kernel. By the general formula, $\ker\rho_H=\bigcap_{xH\in A}\Stab(xH)$. Now $g\cdot(xH)=xH$ iff $(gx)H=xH$ iff $x^{-1}gx\in H$ iff $g\in xHx^{-1}$. Hence $\Stab(xH)=xHx^{-1}$ and
\[
\ker\rho_H=\bigcap_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}=:K.
\]
$K$ is normal (it is a kernel). $K\le H$ (take $x=1$). Finally, if $N\nor G$ and $N\le H$, then for every $x$, $N=xNx^{-1}\le xHx^{-1}$, so $N\le\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}=K$. Thus $K$ is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$.
\end{proof}

Label: cor:divis@c4
Content:
\begin{corollary}[Index--order divisibility] 
With $K=\ker\rho_H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$, the induced map $\bar\rho_H\colon G/K\hookrightarrow S_{[G:H]}$ is injective, so
\[
[G:K]=\ord{G/K}\ \ divides\ \ [G:H]!\,.
\]
\end{corollary}
label: cor:divis@c4

Title: Smallest-prime index forces normality
Label: cor:smallprime@c4
Content:
\begin{corollary}[Smallest-prime index forces normality] 
Let $G$ be a finite group and $H\le G$ with $[G:H]=p$, where $p$ is the smallest prime dividing $\ord G$. Then $H\nor G$.
\end{corollary}
label: cor:smallprime@c4

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-1a292947c43fd24f3da4
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $K=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$ and put $k=[H:K]$. By Cor.~ [REF:cor:divis@c4] , $[G:K]\mid p!$. Also $[G:K]=[G:H]\cdot[H:K]=p\,k$, so $pk\mid p!$, giving $k\mid (p-1)!$. But $k=[H:K]$ divides $\ord G$ (since $K\le H\le G$), and every prime divisor of $\ord G$ is $\ge p$. A prime $q\mid k$ would satisfy $q\mid(p-1)!$, forcing $q\le p-1<p$, contradicting minimality of $p$ unless $k$ has no prime divisors, i.e. $k=1$. Hence $K=H$, so $H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)\nor G$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Coset (permutation) representation and the core
Content:
\begin{method}{Coset (permutation) representation and the core}
Trigger. A subgroup $H$ of small index $m=[G:H]$ appears; you want a homomorphism $G\to S_m$, a normal subgroup inside $H$, or a normality/non-simplicity conclusion.\\[2pt]
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item List the $m$ left cosets $g_1H,\dots,g_mH$ (with $g_1=1$). This is the set $A$.
\item For each generator $g$, compute $g\cdot(g_iH)=(gg_i)H$ and identify which coset it equals; record the permutation $\rho_H(g)\in S_m$.
\item $\ker\rho_H=\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$ is the largest normal subgroup inside $H$. In practice intersect the conjugates, or read it off as $\bigcap_i\Stab(g_iH)$.
\item Conclusions. $[G:\ker\rho_H]\mid m!$ (Cor.~ [REF:cor:divis@c4] ); if $m$ is the least prime dividing $\ord G$ then $H\nor G$ (Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] ); if $m>1$ and $\ord G\nmid m!$ then $\rho_H$ has nontrivial kernel, contained in $H\ne G$, so $G$ has a proper nontrivial normal subgroup (not simple).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Coset action of $S_3$ on $S_3/\langle (1\,2)\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Coset action of $S_3$ on $S_3/\langle (1\,2)\rangle$}
Let $G=S_3$ and $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle=\{1,(1\,2)\}$, so $[G:H]=3$. Compute $\rho_H\colon S_3\to S_3$ explicitly and find $\ker\rho_H$.
\wrec Coset action (Thm.~ [REF:thm:coset@c4] ): left multiplication on the $3$ cosets of $H$ gives $\rho_H\colon G\to S_3$ with kernel the core of $H$.
\wsol The three left cosets are
\[
c_1=H=\{1,(1\,2)\},\quad c_2=(1\,3)H=\{(1\,3),(1\,3)(1\,2)\}=\{(1\,3),(1\,2\,3)\},
\]
\[
c_3=(2\,3)H=\{(2\,3),(2\,3)(1\,2)\}=\{(2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}.
\]
(Recall right-to-left composition: for $(1\,3)(1\,2)$, apply $(1\,2)$ first: $1\mapsto2\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto1\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto3\mapsto1$, giving $(1\,2\,3)$.)

Now compute $\rho_H(g)$ on $\{c_1,c_2,c_3\}$.

$g=(1\,2\,3)$:
$g c_1=(1\,2\,3)H$. Since $(1\,2\,3)\in c_2$, $(1\,2\,3)H=c_2$.
$g c_2=(1\,2\,3)(1\,3)H$; here $(1\,2\,3)(1\,3)=(2\,3)$ (apply $(1\,3)$ first then $(1\,2\,3)$: $1\mapsto3\mapsto1$, $2\mapsto2\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto1\mapsto2$, that is $(2\,3)$), so $gc_2=(2\,3)H=c_3$.
$g c_3=(1\,2\,3)(2\,3)H$; here $(1\,2\,3)(2\,3)=(1\,2)$ (apply $(2\,3)$ then $(1\,2\,3)$: $1\mapsto1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto3\mapsto1$, $3\mapsto2\mapsto3$, that is $(1\,2)$), and $(1\,2)\in H$, so $gc_3=c_1$.
Thus $\rho_H((1\,2\,3))=(c_1\,c_2\,c_3)$, a $3$-cycle.

$g=(1\,2)$: $gc_1=(1\,2)H=c_1$ (fixes $c_1$). $gc_2=(1\,2)(1\,3)H$; here $(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)\in c_3$, so $gc_2=c_3$. $gc_3=(1\,2)(2\,3)H$; here $(1\,2)(2\,3)=(1\,2\,3)$ (apply $(2\,3)$ then $(1\,2)$: $1\mapsto1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto3\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto2\mapsto1$, that is $(1\,2\,3)$) $\in c_2$, so $gc_3=c_2$. Thus $\rho_H((1\,2))=(c_2\,c_3)$, a transposition.

Hence $\rho_H$ is an isomorphism $S_3\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Sym(\{c_1,c_2,c_3\})\cong S_3$. Therefore $\ker\rho_H=\{1\}=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$.

Check. Independently, $\operatorname{core}_G(H)=\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}$. The conjugates of $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ are $\langle (1\,2)\rangle,\langle (1\,3)\rangle,\langle (2\,3)\rangle$, whose intersection is $\{1\}$. Matches $\ker\rho_H=1$. Also $[G:\ker]=6\mid 3!=6$: tight. Good.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Kernel = core: $H=\langle s\rangle$ in $D_8$ acting on $G/\langle s\rangle$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Kernel = core: $H=\langle s\rangle$ in $D_8$ acting on $G/\langle s\rangle$}
Let $G=D_8=\langle r,s\mid r^4=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1}s\rangle$ and $H=\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$, $[G:H]=4$. Find $\operatorname{core}_G(H)=\ker\rho_H$.
\wrec Coset action: kernel is the largest normal subgroup inside $H$, computable as $\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}$.
\wsol Since $\ord{H}=2$, any normal subgroup inside $H$ is $\{1\}$ or $H$ itself. Is $H=\langle s\rangle\nor G$? Conjugate: $rsr^{-1}=r(sr^{-1})=r(rs)=r^2 s$ (using $sr^{-1}=rs$, from $sr=r^{-1}s\Rightarrow sr^{-1}=rs$). So $rsr^{-1}=r^2s\notin\{1,s\}=H$. Thus $H\not\nor G$, and the only normal subgroup contained in $H$ is $\{1\}$.

Therefore $\operatorname{core}_G(H)=\ker\rho_H=\{1\}$, i.e. the coset action $\rho_H\colon D_8\hookrightarrow S_4$ is faithful.

Check. Confirm via the conjugate intersection: $sHs^{-1}=H$ but $rHr^{-1}=\{1,r^2s\}$, and $H\cap rHr^{-1}=\{1\}$ already. So $\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}=\{1\}$. Consistent. Note $\ord{G}=8\mid 4!=24$, so a faithful map into $S_4$ is possible; indeed $D_8\le S_4$ as symmetries of the square. Good.
\end{wex}

Title: Nontrivial core
Content:
\begin{wex}{Nontrivial core}
Let $G=D_8$ and $H=\langle r^2,s\rangle=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}$ (a Klein four-subgroup), $[G:H]=2$. Find $\ker\rho_H$ and $\operatorname{core}_G(H)$.
\wrec Coset action; kernel = core. Index $2$ is the smallest prime dividing $8$, so Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] predicts $H\nor G$, forcing $\operatorname{core}_G(H)=H$.
\wsol $[G:H]=2$, so by Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] (or the index-$2$ remark) $H\nor G$. The largest normal subgroup of $G$ inside $H$ is then $H$ itself, so
\[
\ker\rho_H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)=H=\{1,r^2,s,r^2s\}.
\]
The map $\rho_H\colon G\to S_2$ has image of order $[G:H]=2$ and kernel $H$.

Check. $[G:\ker\rho_H]=[G:H]=2\mid 2!=2$. And $G/H\cong\rho_H(G)\le S_2$ has order $2$: matches. Verify normality directly: $rsr^{-1}=r^2s\in H$ and $r(r^2)r^{-1}=r^2\in H$, so indeed $H\nor G$. Good.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Index = smallest prime $\Rightarrow$ normal: subgroup of index $3$ in a group of order $33$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Index = smallest prime $\Rightarrow$ normal: subgroup of index $3$ in a group of order $33$}
Let $\ord G=33=3\cdot 11$ and suppose $H\le G$ with $[G:H]=3$. Show $H\nor G$.
\wrec Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] : the smallest prime dividing $\ord G=33$ is $3$, and $[G:H]=3$.
\wsol The primes dividing $33$ are $3$ and $11$; the smallest is $p=3=[G:H]$. By Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] , $H\nor G$.

We re-derive it concretely. Let $K=\operatorname{core}_G(H)\nor G$. Then $[G:K]\mid 3!=6$ and $\ord{G/K}=[G:K]$ divides $\ord G=33$. So $[G:K]\mid\gcd(6,33)=3$. Since $K\le H$ gives $[G:K]\ge[G:H]=3$, we get $[G:K]=3=[G:H]$, hence $K=H$. Therefore $H=K\nor G$.

Check. $\gcd(6,33)=3$; $[G:K]\in\{1,3\}$ but $\ge3$, so $=3$. $K\le H$ with equal index $\Rightarrow K=H$. The logic used only $3=[G:H]=$ least prime. Good.
\end{wex}

Title: Forcing non-simplicity from a small-index subgroup
Content:
\begin{wex}{Forcing non-simplicity from a small-index subgroup}
Suppose $\ord G=24$ and $G$ has a subgroup $H$ with $[G:H]=3$. Show $G$ is not simple.
\wrec Coset action $\rho_H\colon G\to S_3$ with $\ker\rho_H=\operatorname{core}_G(H)$; use the order obstruction $[G:\ker]\mid 3!$ (Cor.~ [REF:cor:divis@c4] ).
\wsol $\rho_H\colon G\to S_3$ has $\ord{G/\ker\rho_H}\mid 3!=6$. If $\ker\rho_H=\{1\}$ then $G\hookrightarrow S_3$, so $24=\ord G\mid 6$, false. Hence $\ker\rho_H\ne\{1\}$. Also $\ker\rho_H\le H\subsetneq G$, so $\ker\rho_H\ne G$. Thus $\ker\rho_H$ is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$: $G$ is not simple.

Check. The obstruction is $24\nmid 6$. More precisely $[G:\ker]\mid\gcd(6,24)=6$, but $[G:\ker]\ge3$ and divides $24$, so $[G:\ker]\in\{3,6\}$; either way $\ker$ has order $8$ or $4$, a genuine normal subgroup. Good.
\end{wex}

Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The core is built from conjugates $xHx^{-1}$, not from $H$ alone. A common error is to take $\ker\rho_H=H$ ``because the stabilizer of $H$ is $H$.'' The stabilizer of the basepoint $1H$ is $H$, but the kernel is the intersection of the stabilizers of all cosets, $\bigcap_x xHx^{-1}$, which can be much smaller. Equality $\ker\rho_H=H$ holds iff $H\nor G$.
\end{pitfall}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Cor.~ [REF:cor:smallprime@c4] needs $p$ to be the smallest prime dividing $\ord G$, not just any prime. In $A_4$ ($\ord{A_4}=12$) the subgroup of index $3$ (order $4$, the Klein four $V$) is normal --- here $3$ is not the least prime, yet it happens to work --- but a subgroup of index $3$ is not guaranteed normal in general when $3$ is not the smallest prime. The theorem only guarantees normality at the least prime; e.g. $A_4$ has subgroups of index $4$ (order $3$) that are not normal, and $4$ is not a prime dividing $12$.
\end{pitfall}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item[] Let $G$ be a group and let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.
\item Let $G = \{1, a, b, c\}$ be the Klein 4-group whose group table is written out in Section 2.5.
\item[] (a) Label $1, a, b, c$ with the integers $1, 2, 4, 3$, respectively, and prove that under the left regular representation of $G$ into $S_4$ the nonidentity elements are mapped as follows:
\[
a \mapsto (1\ 2)(3\ 4) \qquad b \mapsto (1\ 4)(2\ 3) \qquad c \mapsto (1\ 3)(2\ 4).
\]
\item[] (b) Relabel $1, a, b, c$ as $1, 2, 3, 4$, respectively, and compute the image of each element of $G$ under the left regular representation of $G$ into $S_4$. \end{exers}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $G$ be a group acting on itself by left multiplication, $g\cdot x=gx$. Verify directly that this is a group action and that the induced homomorphism $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(G)$ has $\ker\rho=1$.

\item For $G=Z_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ under addition, write down the permutation $\rho(1)\in\Sym(G)$ in cycle notation (label the points $0,1,2,3$). Confirm $\rho(1)$ is a $4$-cycle and that $\rho(2)=\rho(1)^2$ is a product of two transpositions.

\item Let $G=D_8=\langle r,s\rangle$ with $r^4=s^2=1$, $sr=r^{-1} s$. Using the left regular representation $\rho\colon D_8\hookrightarrow\Sym(D_8)\cong S_8$, determine the cycle type of $\rho(r)$ and of $\rho(s)$. (Each should be a product of cycles all of the same length equal to the order of the element.)

\item Prove that in the left regular representation, every nonidentity element $g\in G$ acts as a product of $|G|/\ord{g}$ disjoint cycles, each of length $\ord{g}$. Deduce that $\rho(g)$ has no fixed points for $g\neq 1$.

\item Use the previous problem to show: if $|G|=2m$ with $m$ odd, then $G$ has a subgroup of index $2$. (Hint: find an element of order $2$ whose image under the regular representation is an odd permutation, then consider $\ker(\sgn\circ\rho)$.)

\item Let $H\le G$ with $[G:H]=n$. Describe the action of $G$ on the left cosets $G/H$ by left multiplication and write the induced map $\pi_H\colon G\to\Sym(G/H)\cong S_n$. Show that $\ker\pi_H=\bigcap_{g\in G}gHg^{-1}$ and that this kernel is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$.

\item Prove that if $G$ is a finite group, $H\le G$, and $[G:H]=p$ is the smallest prime dividing $|G|$, then $H\nor G$. (Apply the action on $G/H$ and bound $[G:\ker\pi_H]$.)

\item Let $G$ be a group of order $n$ and let $p$ be the smallest prime dividing $n$. Using the previous result, show that any subgroup of index $p$ is normal. Then conclude that every subgroup of index $2$ is normal.

\item Let $G=Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$. Take $H=\langle i\rangle$. List the left cosets $G/H$, write the permutation $\pi_H(j)\in\Sym(G/H)\cong S_2$, and identify $\ker\pi_H$.

\item Let $G$ act on $G/H$ by left multiplication where $H\le G$ and $[G:H]=n$. Prove the action is transitive and that the stabilizer of the coset $1H$ is exactly $H$. Identify the resulting bijection $G/H\to\Orb(1H)$ explicitly.

\item Suppose $|G|=12$ and $G$ has a subgroup $H$ with $[G:H]=3$. Show $\ker\pi_H$ is a nontrivial normal subgroup of $G$, and conclude $G$ is not simple.

\item Let $G$ be a finite simple group containing a subgroup $H$ of index $n>1$. Prove that $|G|$ divides $n!$. (Use $\pi_H$ and that $G$ simple forces $\ker\pi_H=1$.)

\item Use the previous problem to show there is no simple group of order $112=2^4\cdot 7$ possessing a subgroup of index $4$. More generally, show a simple group of order $|G|$ has no proper subgroup of index $n$ with $|G|\nmid n!$.

\item Let $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(G)$ be the left regular representation. Show that the image $\rho(G)$ is a transitive subgroup of $\Sym(G)$ acting on the $|G|$ points, and that $\rho(G)$ acts on $G$ with trivial point stabilizers (a regular/sharply transitive action).

\item Let $G$ be a group of order $33=3\cdot 11$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of order $11$ (assume one exists). Show $[G:H]=3$ is the smallest prime dividing $|G|$, hence $H\nor G$, and use this to argue $G\congZ_{33}$ is cyclic.

\item Let $H,K\le G$ with $H\le K\le G$. Compare the actions of $G$ on $G/H$ and $G/K$ by exhibiting a $G$-equivariant surjection $\sigma\colon G/H\to G/K$, $gH\mapsto gK$. Verify $G$-equivariance: $\sigma(g'\cdot gH)=g'\cdot\sigma(gH)$ for all $g'\in G$.

\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $G$ be a finite group of order $n$. Prove that $G$ embeds in $S_n$, and that if $G$ has no subgroup of index $2$ then the regular representation embeds $G$ in $A_n$. Show that the converse fails: the regular representation of $V_4$ already lies in $A_4$, although $V_4$ has subgroups of index $2$. (Use the cycle-type description of the regular representation to compute $\sgn\circ\rho$, and show that whenever $\sgn\circ\rho\colon G\to\{\pm1\}$ is nontrivial its kernel is a subgroup of index $2$.)

\item Show that the left regular representation $\rho\colon G\to\Sym(G)$ and the right regular representation $\lambda\colon G\to\Sym(G)$, $\lambda(g)\colon x\mapsto xg^{-1}$, have images that centralize each other inside $\Sym(G)$; that is, $\rho(g)$ and $\lambda(h)$ commute for all $g,h\in G$. Identify $\rho(G)\cap\lambda(G)$ with $Z(G)$ via these embeddings.

\item Let $G$ be a finite group, $p$ the smallest prime dividing $|G|$, and $H\le G$ with $[G:H]=p$ (do not assume $H$ is normal). Consider the coset action $\pi_H\colon G\to\Sym(G/H)\cong S_p$. Prove that $[G:\ker\pi_H]$ divides $p$ and is greater than $1$, hence equals $p$; deduce $\ker\pi_H=H$ and conclude $H\nor G$.

\item Let $G$ be a group with a subgroup $H$ of finite index $n$. Prove (Poincare) that $H$ contains a normal subgroup $N\nor G$ with $[G:N]\le n!$. For $G=S_n$ acting on $G/H$ where $H$ is the point stabilizer $S_{n-1}$ of index $n$, determine the core of $H$ and decide for which $n$ that core is trivial and $[G:N]=n!$ holds exactly.

\item Let $G$ be a group in which every proper subgroup has finite index. Must $G$ be finite? Either prove it, or analyze what the coset actions $G\to\Sym(G/H)$ tell you when $[G:H]=n<\infty$ for every proper $H$.

\item Let $p$ be a prime and $G$ a group of order $p^2$. Using the action of $G$ on the left cosets of a subgroup of order $p$, prove that every subgroup of order $p$ is normal in $G$, and conclude $G$ is abelian.

\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Cayley's Theorem and Actions by Left Multiplication > The action on cosets and the core
Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item For the action of $G$ on $G/H$ by left multiplication ($[G:H]=n$), fill in and justify the factorization
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\pi_H"] \arrow[rd, two heads, "q"'] & \Sym(G/H) \\
& G/K \arrow[u, hook, "\bar\pi_H"']
\end{tikzcd}\]
where $K=\ker\pi_H$ and $q$ is the quotient map. Identify $K$ as $\bigcap_{g\in G}gHg^{-1}$ and explain why the injection $G/K\hookrightarrow\Sym(G/H)$ exists.

\item Let $H\le G$ with stabilizer of the base coset equal to $H$. Show the orbit-stabilizer map is a $G$-equivariant bijection by verifying the diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5.5em]
G/H \arrow[r, "\sim", "{gH\mapsto g\cdot(1H)}"'] & \Orb(1H)
\end{tikzcd}\]
commutes with the left-multiplication actions on both sides; i.e. that translating by $g'$ before and after the map agree.

\item Let $G$ be finite, $|G|=n$, and let $\rho$ be the left regular representation. Show the composite below is a homomorphism, compute its image, and state the condition for it to be surjective onto $\{\pm 1\}$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\rho"] & \Sym(G) \arrow[r, "\sgn"] & \{\pm 1\}
\end{tikzcd}\]
When $\sgn\circ\rho$ is surjective, identify its kernel and the resulting short exact sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]

Content:
We now study one of the most important actions a group has on itself: conjugation. The orbits of this action are the conjugacy classes, and counting them yields the class equation -- a single numerical identity that drives a remarkable amount of structure theory for finite groups (most famously for $p$-groups).

Type: definition
Title: Conjugation action
Content:
\begin{definition}[Conjugation action]
Let $G$ be a group. The map
\[
G \times G \longrightarrow G, \qquad g \cdot x = g x g^{-1}
\]
is a (left) group action of $G$ on itself, called the conjugation action. The element $g x g^{-1}$ is the conjugate of $x$ by $g$. Two elements $x,y \in G$ are conjugate if $y = g x g^{-1}$ for some $g \in G$. More generally, $G$ acts by conjugation on the set $S$ of all subsets of $G$ via $g \cdot S = gSg^{-1} = \{\, gsg^{-1} : s \in S\,\}$; two subsets are conjugate when they lie in the same orbit.
\end{definition}

\end{definition}

Type: prose
Content:
That this is an action is a direct check: $1 \cdot x = 1x1^{-1} = x$, and
\[
g_1 \cdot (g_2 \cdot x) = g_1(g_2 x g_2^{-1})g_1^{-1} = (g_1 g_2) x (g_1 g_2)^{-1} = (g_1 g_2)\cdot x .
\]
The associated permutation representation is the map sending $g$ to the inner automorphism $\psi_g(x) = gxg^{-1}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=tiny]
G \arrow[r, "\psi"] & \Sym(G) \\
g \arrow[r, mapsto] & \psi_g .
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two objects: the group $G$ (on the left) and the symmetric group $\Sym(G)$ (on the right), which is the group of all bijections $G \to G$ under composition. The secondary row records the element-level action: a generic group element $g \in G$ and the inner automorphism $\psi_g \in \Sym(G)$ defined by $\psi_g(x) = gxg^{-1}$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The single arrow $\psi\colon G \to \Sym(G)$ is the permutation representation of the conjugation action. It is a group homomorphism (not merely a set map) sending each $g$ to the function ``conjugate by $g$.'' The mapsto arrow $g \mapsto \psi_g$ spells out the formula.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is only one arrow, so no path-equality to check; instead the key property is that $\psi$ is a homomorphism: $\psi(g_1 g_2) = \psi_{g_1 g_2} = \psi_{g_1} \circ \psi_{g_2} = \psi(g_1) \circ \psi(g_2)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase: $\psi_{g_1 g_2}(x) = (g_1 g_2)x(g_1 g_2)^{-1} = g_1(g_2 x g_2^{-1})g_1^{-1} = \psi_{g_1}(\psi_{g_2}(x))$. The associativity of $G$ is the only ingredient needed.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} Every group action is equivalent to a homomorphism into a symmetric group; this diagram makes that correspondence explicit for conjugation. It also sets up the identification $\operatorname{im}\psi = \Inn(G) \le \Aut(G) \le \Sym(G)$ and $\ker\psi = Z(G)$, facts invoked throughout the section.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $G = S_3$ and $g = (1\,2\,3)$, the map $\psi_g$ sends each transposition $(a\,b)$ to the transposition $(\tau(a)\,\tau(b))$ where $\tau = g$; concretely $\psi_g((1\,2)) = (2\,3)$, a non-trivial element of $\Aut(S_3)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read $\psi$ as a map of sets and forget it is a group homomorphism. The content is precisely that conjugation respects the group operation, which is what lets the image land in $\Aut(G)$ rather than merely in $\Sym(G)$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the conjugation action of $G$ on itself is encoded by a single group homomorphism $\psi\colon G \to \Sym(G)$, whose kernel is $Z(G)$ and whose image is the group of inner automorphisms.
\end{dgx}
Each $\psi_g$ is not merely a permutation of the set $G$ but an automorphism of $G$ (it preserves the product: $\psi_g(xy) = gxy g^{-1} = (gxg^{-1})(gyg^{-1}) = \psi_g(x)\psi_g(y)$), so the image lands in $\Aut(G) \le \Sym(G)$ and we get $\psi\colon G \to \Aut(G)$ with image $\Inn(G)$. Its kernel is exactly the center $Z(G)$.

\begin{definition}[Conjugacy class]
The orbit of $x$ under the conjugation action,
\[
K_x \;=\; \{\, g x g^{-1} : g \in G \,\},
\]
is the conjugacy class of $x$. The conjugacy classes partition $G$ into disjoint pieces (they are the equivalence classes of the relation ``is conjugate to'').
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Class size $=$ index of the centralizer
Label: prop:classsize@c4
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Class size $=$ index of the centralizer] 
For $x \in G$, the stabilizer of $x$ under the conjugation action is the centralizer
\[
G_x \;=\; \{\, g \in G : gxg^{-1} = x \,\} \;=\; \{\, g \in G : gx = xg \,\} \;=\; C_G(x).
\]
Consequently, by the orbit--stabilizer theorem, the number of conjugates of $x$ equals
\[
\bigl|K_x\bigr| \;=\; [G:C_G(x)].
\]
In particular $|K_x|$ divides $|G|$ when $G$ is finite, and $|K_x| = 1$ iff $x \in Z(G)$.
\end{proposition}
label: prop:classsize@c4

\]

\]
In particular $|\mathcal{K}_x|$ divides $|G|$ when $G$ is finite, and $|\mathcal{K}_x| = 1$ iff $x \in Z(G)$.

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-6366df9201336268e2f6
Content:
\begin{proof}
$g$ fixes $x$ under conjugation $\Longleftrightarrow gxg^{-1} = x \Longleftrightarrow gx = xg \Longleftrightarrow g \in C_G(x)$; that is the definition of the centralizer. Orbit--stabilizer gives the bijection
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em]
G/C_G(x) \arrow[r, "\sim", "{\,gC_G(x)\,\mapsto\, gxg^{-1}\,}"'] & K_x ,
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two objects: the left coset space $G/C_G(x)$ (the set of left cosets of the centralizer of $x$ in $G$; this is a set, not a group in general) and the conjugacy class $K_x = \{gxg^{-1} : g \in G\} \subseteq G$ (also a set, one orbit of the conjugation action).
\dgi{Arrows:} The single arrow is the bijection $\varphi\colon G/C_G(x) \to K_x$ sending a coset $gC_G(x)$ to the conjugate $gxg^{-1}$. It is an instance of the orbit-stabilizer theorem, which produces a canonical bijection from coset space to orbit whenever a group acts on a set.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is one arrow, so well-definedness is the key claim: if $gC_G(x) = hC_G(x)$ then $gxg^{-1} = hxh^{-1}$. (No two-path commutativity to check.)
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness: $gC_G(x) = hC_G(x)$ means $h^{-1}g \in C_G(x)$, i.e., $h^{-1}g$ commutes with $x$, i.e., $(h^{-1}g)x(h^{-1}g)^{-1} = x$. Rearranging: $gxg^{-1} = hxh^{-1}$. So the coset representative chosen does not affect the output; $\varphi$ is well-defined and is a bijection because $\varphi$ is surjective by definition of $K_x$ and injective by reversing the argument.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This bijection converts the abstract orbit into a countable coset space, giving the formula $|K_x| = [G : C_G(x)]$, the central computational tool for finding conjugacy class sizes throughout the section and in the class equation.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $S_3$ with $x = (1\,2\,3)$: $C_{S_3}(x) = \langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$ has order $3$, so $G/C_G(x)$ has two cosets $\{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$ and $\{(1\,2), \ldots\}$, mapped to $(1\,2\,3)$ and $(1\,3\,2)$ respectively, matching $|K_x| = 2$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The map sends a coset to a conjugate, not a group element to a conjugate. Writing $g \mapsto gxg^{-1}$ (without the coset) gives a well-defined map $G \to K_x$, but in general not an injective one: two elements in the same coset give the same conjugate, while two elements in different cosets give different conjugates -- which is precisely the content of the bijection.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that orbit-stabilizer converts an orbit (hard to count directly) into a coset space (easy to count), yielding $|K_x| = [G : C_G(x)]$ as a clean index formula.
\end{dgx}
so $|K_x| = [G:C_G(x)]$. Since this is an index, it divides $|G|$ for finite $G$. Finally $|K_x| = 1$ means $gxg^{-1} = x$ for all $g$, i.e.\ $x$ commutes with everything, i.e.\ $x \in Z(G)$.
\end{proof}

Section: Group Actions > Conjugation and the Class Equation > The size of a conjugacy class
Type: method
Title: Computing one conjugacy class
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing one conjugacy class}
Trigger. You are asked for the conjugacy class of a specific $x$, or for $|K_x|$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Find $C_G(x) = \{g : gx = xg\}$ -- list which elements commute with $x$. It always contains $\langle x\rangle$ and $Z(G)$.
\item Compute $|C_G(x)|$ and then $|K_x| = [G:C_G(x)] = |G|/|C_G(x)|$.
\item Produce the conjugates by conjugating $x$ by a transversal of $C_G(x)$ (one $g$ per coset). Stop when you have collected $|K_x|$ distinct elements.
\item Check. Class size divides $|G|$; the class is a single element iff $x$ is central.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Class of a reflection in $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Class of a reflection in $D_8$}
In $D_8 = \langle r,s \mid r^4 = s^2 = 1,\ sr = r^{-1} s\rangle$, find the conjugacy class of the reflection $s$.
\wrec Conjugation action; the class of $s$ has size $[D_8:C_{D_8}(s)]$, so first pin down which elements commute with $s$.
\wsol $|D_8| = 8$. The centralizer of $s$ contains $\langle s\rangle = \{1,s\}$ and the center $Z(D_8) = \{1, r^2\}$, so $\{1,s,r^2,r^2 s\} \le C_{D_8}(s)$, giving $|C_{D_8}(s)| \ge 4$. Now $rs = s r^{-1} = s r^3 \ne sr$, so $r \notin C_{D_8}(s)$; thus $C_{D_8}(s) \ne D_8$ and $|C_{D_8}(s)| = 4$. Hence
\[
|K_s| = [D_8:C_{D_8}(s)] = 8/4 = 2.
\]
Conjugating by $r$: using $sr^{-1} = rs$ we get $r s r^{-1} = r(s r^{-1}) = r(rs) = r^2 s$. So $K_s = \{s,\, r^2 s\}$.
Check. $2 \mid 8$. The four reflections split into two classes $\{s, r^2 s\}$ and $\{rs, r^3 s\}$, each of size $2$ -- consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: Class of $i$ in $Q_8$

\begin{wex}{Class of $i$ in $Q_8$}
Find the conjugacy class of $i$ in $Q_8$.
\wrec $|K_i| = [Q_8:C_{Q_8}(i)]$; compute the centralizer first.
\wsol $C_{Q_8}(i) \supseteq \langle i\rangle = \{1,-1,i,-i\}$, of order $4$. Does $j$ commute with $i$? $ji = -k$ while $ij = k$, so $ji \ne ij$ and $j \notin C_{Q_8}(i)$. Thus $C_{Q_8}(i) = \{\pm 1, \pm i\}$, order $4$, and $|K_i| = 8/4 = 2$. Conjugate $i$ by $j$ (with $j^{-1} = -j$): $j i j^{-1} = (ji)(-j) = (-k)(-j) = kj$, and $kj = -i$, so $j i j^{-1} = -i$. Hence $K_i = \{i,-i\}$.
Check. $2 \mid 8$; and $i,-i$ are exactly the two noncentral powers of $i$ -- consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: The Class Equation
Label: thm:classeqn@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[The Class Equation] 
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $g_1,\dots,g_r$ be representatives of the distinct conjugacy classes of $G$ that are not contained in $Z(G)$. Then
\[
\boxed{\;\ord{G} \;=\; \ord{Z(G)} \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} [G:C_G(g_i)].\;}
\]
\end{theorem}
label: thm:classeqn@c4

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Conjugation and the Class Equation > The class equation
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-cc0901dd61de1cb4a89e
Content:
\begin{proof}
The conjugacy classes partition $G$, so $|G|$ is the sum of the sizes of the distinct classes. A class is a singleton exactly when its representative is central (Proposition~ [REF:prop:classsize@c4] ); the singleton classes are the $|Z(G)|$ one-element sets $\{z\}$ for $z \in Z(G)$, contributing $|Z(G)|$ in total. Every remaining class has size $> 1$, with representative $g_i \notin Z(G)$ and size $[G:C_G(g_i)]$. Summing,
\[
|G| = \underbrace{\sum_{z \in Z(G)} 1}_{=\,|Z(G)|} \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} [G:C_G(g_i)] = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^{r}[G:C_G(g_i)]. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Writing the class equation of a finite group
Content:
\begin{method}{Writing the class equation of a finite group}
Trigger. ``find the class equation of $G$'' or ``how many conjugacy classes does $G$ have.''
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute $|Z(G)|$; each central element is its own class (a $1$).
\item For each non-central element, find its class size $[G:C_G(g)]$; group elements into classes so you never double-count.
\item Write $|G| = |Z(G)| + (non-central class sizes)$; every summand divides $|G|$, and the central part is $|Z(G)|$ copies of $1$.
\item Check. The right side sums to $|G|$, and the count of summands equals the number of conjugacy classes.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Class equation of $A_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Class equation of $A_4$}
Write the class equation of $A_4$, $|A_4| = 12$.
\wrec In $S_n$ a class may split when restricted to $A_n$; check whether the cycle-type class stays whole by testing if some odd permutation centralizes a representative.
\wsol Elements of $A_4$: $e$ (1); three double-transpositions $(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)$; eight $3$-cycles. The double-transpositions form one class of size $3$ (they are all conjugate in $A_4$). The eight $3$-cycles split into two $A_4$-classes of size $4$: for $g = (1\,2\,3)$, $|C_{A_4}(g)| = 3$ (only powers of $g$ centralize it inside $A_4$), so $|K_g| = 12/3 = 4$; conjugating by even permutations cannot reach $(1\,3\,2)$, which heads the other class. Hence
\[
12 \;=\; 1 + 3 + 4 + 4.
\]
Check. $1+3+4+4 = 12$; $Z(A_4) = \{e\}$ so $|Z| = 1$; four classes. (Contrast: in $S_4$ all eight $3$-cycles are one class -- splitting is genuine.)
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: Conjugacy classes of $S_n$
Label: thm:Snconj@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Conjugacy classes of $S_n$] 
Two elements of $S_n$ are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type. Concretely, if $\sigma = (a_1\,a_2\,\cdots\,a_k)(b_1\,b_2\,\cdots)\cdots$ in disjoint-cycle form and $\tau \in S_n$, then
\[
\tau \sigma \tau^{-1} \;=\; (\tau(a_1)\,\tau(a_2)\,\cdots\,\tau(a_k))(\tau(b_1)\,\tau(b_2)\,\cdots)\cdots .
\]
Thus the conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are indexed by the partitions of $n$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:Snconj@c4

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-6dcae7accafd836b93d9
Content:
\begin{proof}
Formula. For a $k$-cycle $(a_1\cdots a_k)$ and any $\tau$, evaluate $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ at $\tau(a_j)$: $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}(\tau(a_j)) = \tau\sigma(a_j) = \tau(a_{j+1})$ (indices mod $k$), so $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = (\tau(a_1)\cdots\tau(a_k))$, a $k$-cycle. Applying this to each disjoint cycle of $\sigma$ (and noting $\tau$ keeps the cycles disjoint, being a bijection) shows $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ has the same cycle type as $\sigma$. Converse. If $\sigma,\sigma'$ have the same cycle type, align their cycles and let $\tau$ be the bijection sending the entries of $\sigma$ to the correspondingly-placed entries of $\sigma'$; then $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = \sigma'$ by the formula. Hence ``same cycle type'' is exactly conjugacy, and cycle types are partitions of $n$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Counting a cycle-type class
Label: thm:countclass@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Counting a cycle-type class] 
If a cycle type has $m_k$ cycles of length $k$ (so $\sum_k k\, m_k = n$, counting fixed points as $1$-cycles), the number of permutations of that type, equivalently the size of the conjugacy class, is
\[
\frac{n!}{\displaystyle \prod_{k\ge 1} k^{\,m_k}\, m_k!}.
\]
\end{theorem}
label: thm:countclass@c4

\begin{proof}
Fill the cycle skeleton with the $n$ symbols in one of $n!$ orders. Each cycle of length $k$ has $k$ cyclic rotations giving the same permutation, accounting for $\prod_k k^{m_k}$; and the $m_k$ cycles of equal length $k$ can be permuted among themselves without changing the permutation, accounting for $\prod_k m_k!$. Title: Conjugacy in $S_n$
Content:
\begin{method}{Conjugacy in $S_n$}
Trigger. ``are these two permutations conjugate in $S_n$?'' or ``how many elements / classes of a given type?''
\begin{enumerate}
\item Write each permutation in disjoint cycles (include fixed points to read the full type).
\item Conjugate by relabeling: $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ just applies $\tau$ to each entry -- so two are conjugate iff same multiset of cycle lengths.
\item Count a class by $n!/\prod_k k^{m_k} m_k!$. Sum over all partitions of $n$ to recover $n!$.
\item Check. Class sizes are integers dividing $n!$ and sum to $n!$; the number of classes equals $p(n)$, the number of partitions.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Conjugacy classes of $S_4$ by cycle type
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugacy classes of $S_4$ by cycle type}
List all conjugacy classes of $S_4$ with their sizes, and verify they sum to $24$.
\wrec In $S_n$ classes $=$ partitions of $n$; size given by $n!/\prod k^{m_k}m_k!$.
\wsol Partitions of $4$ and counts ($n = 4$, $n! = 24$):
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
type 1^4 \ (e): & \dfrac{24}{1^4\cdot 4!} = 1, & \\[4pt]
type 2\,1^2 \ (a\,b): & \dfrac{24}{2^1 1!\cdot 1^2 2!} = \dfrac{24}{2\cdot 2}=6, & transpositions\\[6pt]
type 2^2 \ (a\,b)(c\,d): & \dfrac{24}{2^2 2!} = \dfrac{24}{8}=3, & double transpositions\\[6pt]
type 3\,1 \ (a\,b\,c): & \dfrac{24}{3^1 1!\cdot 1\cdot 1!} = \dfrac{24}{3}=8, & 3-cycles\\[6pt]
type 4 \ (a\,b\,c\,d): & \dfrac{24}{4^1 1!} = 6, & 4-cycles.
\end{array}
\]
So the class equation of $S_4$ is
\[
24 \;=\; 1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6 .
\]
Check. $1+6+3+8+6 = 24$; five classes $=p(4)=5$; $Z(S_4)=\{e\}$, so the lone singleton is the identity -- consistent. (The even classes $1+3+8 = 12 = |A_4|$ also check out.)
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Are these conjugate in $S_5$?}
Decide whether $\sigma = (1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$ and $\tau = (1\,4)(2\,5\,3)$ are conjugate in $S_5$, and if so exhibit a conjugator.
\wrec Conjugate in $S_n$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ same cycle type; build the conjugator by aligning cycles.
\wsol Both have type $3+2$ (a $3$-cycle and a disjoint $2$-cycle): $\sigma$ acts as a $3$-cycle on $\{1,2,3\}$ and a $2$-cycle on $\{4,5\}$; $\tau = (2\,5\,3)(1\,4)$ acts as a $3$-cycle on $\{2,5,3\}$ and a $2$-cycle on $\{1,4\}$. Same type $\Longrightarrow$ conjugate. To build $\rho$ with $\rho\sigma\rho^{-1} = \tau$, map $\sigma$'s cycles onto $\tau$'s entry-by-entry: $1\mapsto 2,\,2\mapsto 5,\,3\mapsto 3,\,4\mapsto 1,\,5\mapsto 4$, i.e.\ $\rho = (1\,2\,5\,4)$. Check. $\rho\sigma\rho^{-1} = (\rho(1)\,\rho(2)\,\rho(3))(\rho(4)\,\rho(5)) = (2\,5\,3)(1\,4) = \tau$. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Counting $5$-cycles in $S_5$}
How many $5$-cycles are in $S_5$, and what is the centralizer of one?
\wrec Size of a cycle-type class $= n!/\prod k^{m_k}m_k!$; centralizer order $= |G|/|class|$.

Title: Counting double transpositions in $S_6$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Counting double transpositions in $S_6$}
Count the elements of type $2^2 1^2$ in $S_6$.
\wrec $n!/\prod k^{m_k}m_k!$ with $m_2 = 2$, $m_1 = 2$.
\wsol $n = 6$, $n! = 720$. Here $m_2 = 2,\ m_1 = 2$:
\[
\frac{720}{(2^2\cdot 2!)\,(1^2\cdot 2!)} = \frac{720}{(4\cdot 2)(1\cdot 2)} = \frac{720}{16} = 45.
\]
Check. $45 \mid 720$ ($720/45 = 16$), so the centralizer of such an element has order $16$ -- a $2$-group, plausible. Counting directly: choose the two moved pairs, $\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2}/2! = 15\cdot 6/2 = 45$. Matches.
\end{wex}

Title: $p$-groups have nontrivial center
Label: thm:pgroupcenter@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[$p$-groups have nontrivial center] 
If $p$ is a prime and $|G| = p^a$ with $a \ge 1$, then $Z(G) \ne 1$; that is, $p \mid |Z(G)|$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:pgroupcenter@c4

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Conjugation and the Class Equation > Applications of the class equation
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-79448574337ae2c0f889
Content:
\begin{proof}
Write the class equation $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^r [G:C_G(g_i)]$ over non-central representatives $g_i$. For each such $g_i$ we have $C_G(g_i) \ne G$ (else $g_i$ would be central), so $[G:C_G(g_i)] > 1$. As an index it divides $|G| = p^a$, hence $[G:C_G(g_i)] = p^{b_i}$ with $b_i \ge 1$, so $p \mid [G:C_G(g_i)]$. Therefore $p$ divides $|G|$ and the entire sum $\sum_i [G:C_G(g_i)]$, and rearranging the class equation gives
\[
|Z(G)| = |G| - \sum_{i=1}^r [G:C_G(g_i)] \equiv 0 \pmod p .
\]
Since $1 \in Z(G)$ gives $|Z(G)| \ge 1$ and $p \mid |Z(G)|$, we get $|Z(G)| \ge p > 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Groups of order $p^2$ are abelian] 
If $|G| = p^2$ for a prime $p$, then $G$ is abelian (so $G \cong Z/(p^2)Z$ or $G \cong Z/(p)Z\timesZ/(p)Z$).
\end{corollary}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Conjugation and the Class Equation > Applications of the class equation
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f430f1344cb4d9afa8ea
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~ [REF:thm:pgroupcenter@c4] , $Z(G) \ne 1$, so $|Z(G)| \in \{p, p^2\}$. If $|Z(G)| = p^2$ then $G = Z(G)$ is abelian and we are done. Suppose instead $|Z(G)| = p$. Then $|G/Z(G)| = p^2/p = p$, so $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic. But it is a standard lemma that if $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic then $G$ is abelian: write $G/Z(G) = \langle xZ(G)\rangle$; every $g \in G$ is $g = x^m z$ for some integer $m$ and $z \in Z(G)$, and two such elements $x^{m}z,\ x^{n}w$ commute because powers of $x$ commute with each other and $z,w$ are central. So $G$ is abelian, which forces $Z(G) = G$ and contradicts $|Z(G)| = p < p^2$. Hence the case $|Z(G)| = p$ is impossible, $|Z(G)| = p^2$, and $G$ is abelian. The classification into $Z/(p^2)Z$ and $Z/(p)Z\timesZ/(p)Z$ follows from the structure of finite abelian groups.
\end{proof}

Title: Using the class equation modulo $p$

\begin{method}{Using the class equation modulo $p$}
Trigger. $|G|$ is a prime power $p^a$ (or you need to show some central element exists).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Write $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum [G:C_G(g_i)]$ over non-central classes.
\item Each non-central index $[G:C_G(g_i)]$ is a power $p^{b_i}$, $b_i \ge 1$, hence $\equiv 0 \pmod p$.
\item Reduce mod $p$: $0 \equiv |Z(G)| + 0$, so $p \mid |Z(G)|$, forcing $Z(G) \ne 1$.
\item Check. Consistency -- the central summand $|Z(G)|$ plus a multiple of $p$ equals $p^a$, also a multiple of $p$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

\wsol Class equation: $27 = |Z(G)| + \sum_i [G:C_G(g_i)]$ with each non-central index a power $3^{b_i}$, $b_i \ge 1$, so each is divisible by $3$. Reducing mod $3$: $0 \equiv |Z(G)| + 0 \pmod 3$, so $3 \mid |Z(G)|$. As $|Z(G)| \ge 1$, we get $|Z(G)| \in \{3, 9, 27\}$, in particular $Z(G) \ne 1$.

\begin{wex}{Order $p^2$ is abelian: $|G| = 25$}

\wrec $25 = 5^2$; use $Z(G) \ne 1$ and the $G/Z(G)$-cyclic lemma.
\wsol By Theorem~ [REF:thm:pgroupcenter@c4] , $Z(G) \ne 1$, so $|Z(G)| \in \{5,25\}$. Type: proposition
Title: Number of conjugates of a subgroup
Label: prop:numconj@c4
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Number of conjugates of a subgroup] 
Let $H \le G$. Under the conjugation action of $G$ on its subsets, the stabilizer of $H$ is the normalizer $N_G(H) = \{g \in G : gHg^{-1} = H\}$. Hence the number of distinct conjugate subgroups $gHg^{-1}$ equals
\[
\bigl|\{\, gHg^{-1} : g \in G\,\}\bigr| \;=\; [G:N_G(H)] .
\]
In particular this number divides $|G|$, and it equals $1$ iff $H \nor G$.
\end{proposition}
label: prop:numconj@c4

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-81ebe8dc52624fd0c0fe
Content:
\begin{proof}
$g$ stabilizes $H$ under conjugation $\Longleftrightarrow gHg^{-1} = H \Longleftrightarrow g \in N_G(H)$, by definition of the normalizer. Orbit--stabilizer applied to this action on subsets gives the bijection
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em]
G/N_G(H) \arrow[r, "\sim", "{\,gN_G(H)\,\mapsto\, gHg^{-1}\,}"'] & \{\,gHg^{-1} : g\in G\,\},
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two objects: the coset space $G/N_G(H)$ (left cosets of the normalizer $N_G(H)$ in $G$; again a set, not a group in general) and the set $\{gHg^{-1} : g \in G\}$ of all distinct conjugates of the subgroup $H \le G$ (the orbit of $H$ under the conjugation action of $G$ on its power set).
\dgi{Arrows:} The bijection $\Phi\colon G/N_G(H) \to \{gHg^{-1} : g \in G\}$ sends a coset $gN_G(H)$ to the conjugate subgroup $gHg^{-1}$. This is the orbit-stabilizer bijection applied to the action of $G$ by conjugation on the set of subsets of $G$, with stabilizer of $H$ equal to $N_G(H)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Well-definedness is the key: if $gN_G(H) = g'N_G(H)$, then $gHg^{-1} = g'Hg'^{-1}$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness: $gN_G(H) = g'N_G(H)$ means $g^{-1}g' \in N_G(H)$, i.e., $(g^{-1}g')H(g^{-1}g')^{-1} = H$. Conjugating by $g$ on both sides: $g' H g'^{-1} = g H g^{-1}$. So the coset representative does not affect the conjugate subgroup produced. Injectivity and surjectivity follow as in the element case. If one mistakenly uses $C_G(H)$ instead of $N_G(H)$, the map $gC_G(H) \mapsto gHg^{-1}$ is still well defined (every element of $C_G(H) \le N_G(H)$ sends $H$ to itself, even fixing it pointwise), but it is no longer injective when $C_G(H) \ne N_G(H)$: the $[N_G(H) : C_G(H)]$ cosets of $C_G(H)$ lying in $N_G(H)$ all go to $H$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This bijection is the subgroup analogue of the element bijection from the class-size proposition. It shows the number of conjugate subgroups equals the index $[G : N_G(H)]$, giving a divisibility condition ($|G|$ finite) and a normality criterion ($H \nor G$ iff there is exactly one conjugate iff $N_G(H) = G$).
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $D_8$ with $H = \langle s\rangle$: $N_{D_8}(H) = \{1, s, r^2, r^2 s\}$ has order $4$, so $[D_8 : N_{D_8}(H)] = 2$, matching the count of two conjugate subgroups $\langle s\rangle$ and $\langle r^2 s\rangle$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse the normalizer $N_G(H)$ (which controls how many conjugate subgroups there are) with the centralizer $C_G(H)$ (which controls elements that fix $H$ pointwise). The number of conjugates is $[G : N_G(H)]$, not $[G : C_G(H)]$: since $[G : C_G(H)] = [G : N_G(H)]\,[N_G(H) : C_G(H)]$, for finite $G$ using the centralizer overcounts by the factor $[N_G(H) : C_G(H)]$ (the answers agree only when $C_G(H) = N_G(H)$).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the orbit-stabilizer theorem for the conjugation action on subsets converts the count of conjugate subgroups into the computable index $[G : N_G(H)]$, encoding normality as the condition that this index equals $1$.
\end{dgx}
so the number of conjugates is $[G:N_G(H)]$. It divides $|G|$, and it is $1$ exactly when $N_G(H) = G$, i.e.\ when $H$ is normal.
\end{proof}

\begin{method}{Counting conjugates of a subgroup}
Trigger. ``how many subgroups are conjugate to $H$'' or ``is $H$ normal.''

\begin{wex}{Conjugates of $\langle s\rangle$ in $D_8$}
Count the subgroups of $D_8$ conjugate to $H = \langle s\rangle = \{1,s\}$.
\wrec Number of conjugates $= [D_8:N_{D_8}(H)]$; find the normalizer.

\begin{wex}{Conjugates of $\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ in $S_3$}
Count the subgroups of $S_3$ conjugate to $H = \langle (1\,2)\rangle$.
\wrec $[S_3:N_{S_3}(H)]$; find which elements normalize $H$.
\wsol $N_{S_3}(H) \supseteq H = \{e,(1\,2)\}$, order $2$. A $3$-cycle conjugates $(1\,2)$ to a different transposition (e.g.\ $(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3\,2) = (2\,3)$), so no $3$-cycle normalizes $H$; thus $N_{S_3}(H) = H$, order $2$, and the number of conjugates is $6/2 = 3$: namely $\langle (1\,2)\rangle,\langle (1\,3)\rangle,\langle (2\,3)\rangle$.
Check. $3 \mid 6$; there are exactly three order-$2$ subgroups in $S_3$ and they are all conjugate -- matches.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A normal subgroup has one conjugate}
Count the conjugates of $A_3 = \langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$ in $S_3$.
\wrec Number of conjugates $=1 \Longleftrightarrow H \nor G \Longleftrightarrow N_G(H) = G$.
\wsol $A_3$ has index $2$ in $S_3$, hence is normal, so $N_{S_3}(A_3) = S_3$ and the number of conjugates is $6/6 = 1$. Directly: conjugating a $3$-cycle gives a $3$-cycle, so $gA_3 g^{-1} = A_3$ for all $g$.
Check. index-$2$ subgroups are always normal; count $1$ as expected.

Title: Conjugates of a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $S_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Conjugates of a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $S_4$}
Count the subgroups of $S_4$ conjugate to a Sylow $2$-subgroup $P$ ($|P| = 8$), and identify $N_{S_4}(P)$.
\wrec $[S_4:N_{S_4}(P)]$ gives the count; for a Sylow subgroup the count is also the Sylow number $n_2$.
\wsol $|S_4| = 24 = 2^3\cdot 3$, so $|P| = 8$ and $[S_4:P] = 3$. Since $P \le N_{S_4}(P) \le S_4$, the order $|N_{S_4}(P)|$ is a multiple of $8$ dividing $24$, so it is $8$ or $24$. $P$ is not normal in $S_4$ (e.g.\ $S_4$ has more than one Sylow $2$-subgroup), so $|N_{S_4}(P)| \ne 24$; thus $N_{S_4}(P) = P$, order $8$, and the number of conjugates is $24/8 = 3$.
Check. $3 \mid 24$; $n_2 = 3 \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ and $3 \mid 3$, consistent with Sylow's theorem. So $S_4$ has exactly three Sylow $2$-subgroups, all conjugate.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Conjugates of $\langle i\rangle$ in $Q_8$}
Count the conjugates of $H = \langle i\rangle = \{1,-1,i,-i\}$ in $Q_8$.
\wrec $[Q_8:N_{Q_8}(H)]$; index-$2$ subgroups are normal.
\wsol $|H| = 4$ and $[Q_8:H] = 8/4 = 2$, so $H$ has index $2$ and is therefore normal: $N_{Q_8}(H) = Q_8$. The number of conjugates is $8/8 = 1$.
Check. Every index-$2$ subgroup is normal, so a single conjugate -- and indeed $\langle i\rangle,\langle j\rangle,\langle k\rangle$ are three distinct normal subgroups, each its own sole conjugate. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{remark}
Proposition~ [REF:prop:numconj@c4] is the engine behind Sylow's theorems: applying it to a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ shows the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups is $[G:N_G(P)]$, which combined with a counting argument yields $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$ and $n_p \mid |G|$. Conjugation -- of elements and of subgroups -- is thus the common thread running from the class equation through the structure of $p$-groups to the Sylow theory of the next section.
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Suppose $G$ has a left action on a set $A$, denoted by $g \cdot a$ for all $g \in G$ and $a \in A$. Denote the corresponding right action on $A$ by $a \cdot g$. Prove that the (equivalence) relations $\sim$ and $\sim'$ defined by
\[
a \sim b \quad if and only if \quad a = g \cdot b \quad for some g \in G
\]
and
\[
a \sim' b \quad if and only if \quad a = b \cdot g \quad for some g \in G
\]
are the same relation (i.e., $a \sim b$ if and only if $a \sim' b$).
\item Find all the conjugacy classes and their sizes in the following groups: (a) $D_8$ \quad (b) $Q_8$ \quad (c) $A_4$.
\item Find all the conjugacy classes and their sizes in the following groups: (a) $Z_2 \times S_3$ \quad (b) $S_3 \times S_3$ \quad (c) $Z_3 \times A_4$.
\item Prove that if $S \subseteq G$ and $g \in G$ then $g N_G(S) g^{-1} = N_G(g S g^{-1})$ and $g C_G(S) g^{-1} = C_G(g S g^{-1})$.
\item If the center of $G$ is of index $n$, prove that every conjugacy class has at most $n$ elements.
\item Assume $G$ is a non-abelian group of order 15. Prove that $Z(G) = 1$. Use the fact that $\langle g\rangle \le C_G(g)$ for all $g \in G$ to show that there is at most one possible class equation for $G$. [Use Exercise 36, Section 3.1.]
\item For $n = 3, 4, 5$ and 7 make tables of the partitions of $n$ and give representatives for the corresponding conjugacy classes of $S_n$.
\item Prove that $Z(S_n) = 1$ for all $n \ge 3$.
\item Show that $|C_{S_n}((1\,2)(3\,4))| = 8 \cdot (n-4)!$ for all $n \ge 4$. Determine the elements in this centralizer.
\item Let $\sigma$ be the 5-cycle $(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ in $S_5$. In each of (a) to (c) find an explicit element $\tau \in S_5$ which accomplishes the specified conjugation:
(a) $\tau \sigma \tau^{-1} = \sigma^2$
(b) $\tau \sigma \tau^{-1} = \sigma^{-1}$
(c) $\tau \sigma \tau^{-1} = \sigma^{-2}$.
\item In each of (a)~--~(d) determine whether $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are conjugate. If they are, give an explicit permutation $\tau$ such that $\tau \sigma_1 \tau^{-1} = \sigma_2$.
(a) $\sigma_1 = (1\,2)(3\,4\,5)$ and $\sigma_2 = (1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$
(b) $\sigma_1 = (1\,5)(3\,7\,2)(10\,6\,8\,11)$ and $\sigma_2 = (3\,7\,5\,10)(4\,9)(13\,11\,2)$
(c) $\sigma_1 = (1\,5)(3\,7\,2)(10\,6\,8\,11)$ and $\sigma_2 = \sigma_1^3$
(d) $\sigma_1 = (1\,3)(2\,4\,6)$ and $\sigma_2 = (3\,5)(2\,4)(5\,6)$.
\item Find a representative for each conjugacy class of elements of order 4 in $S_8$ and in $S_{12}$.
\item Find all finite groups which have exactly two conjugacy classes.
\item In Exercise 1 of Section 2 two labellings of the elements $\{1, a, b, c\}$ of the Klein 4-group $V$ were chosen to give two versions of the left regular representation of $V$ into $S_4$. Let $\pi_1$ be the version of regular representation obtained in part (a) of that exercise and let $\pi_2$ be the version obtained via the labelling in part (b). Let $\tau = (2\,4)$. Show that $\tau \circ \pi_1(g) \circ \tau^{-1} = \pi_2(g)$ for each $g \in V$ (i.e., conjugation by $\tau$ sends the image of $\pi_1$ to the image of $\pi_2$ elementwise).
\item Find an element of $S_8$ which conjugates the subgroup of $S_8$ obtained in part (a) of Exercise 3, Section 2 to the subgroup of $S_8$ obtained in part (b) of that same exercise (both of these subgroups are isomorphic to $D_8$).
\item Find an element of $S_4$ which conjugates the subgroup of $S_4$ obtained in part (a) of Exercise 5, Section 2 to the subgroup of $S_4$ obtained in part (b) of that same exercise (both of these subgroups are isomorphic to $D_8$).
\item Let $A$ be a nonempty set and let $X$ be any subset of $S_A$. Let
\[
F(X) = \{a \in A \mid \sigma(a) = a for all \sigma \in X\} \qquad --- the fixed set of X.
\]
Let $M(X) = A - F(X)$ be the elements which are moved by some element of $X$. Let $D = \{\sigma \in S_A \mid |M(\sigma)| < \infty\}$. Prove that $D$ is a normal subgroup of $S_A$.
\item Let $A$ be a set, let $H$ be a subgroup of $S_A$ and let $F(H)$ be the fixed points of $H$ on $A$ as defined in the preceding exercise. Prove that if $\tau \in N_{S_A}(H)$ then $\tau$ stabilizes the set $F(H)$ and its complement $A - F(H)$.
\item Assume $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, $K$ is a conjugacy class of $G$ contained in $H$ and $x \in K$. Prove that $K$ is a union of $k$ conjugacy classes of equal size in $H$, where $k = [G:H C_G(x)]$. Deduce that a conjugacy class in $S_n$ which consists of even permutations is either a single conjugacy class under the action of $A_n$ or is a union of two classes of the same size in $A_n$. [Let $A = C_G(x)$ and $B = H$ so $A \cap B = C_H(x)$. Draw the lattice diagram associated to the Second Isomorphism Theorem and interpret the appropriate indices. See also Exercise 9, Section 1.]
\item Let $\sigma \in A_n$. Show that all elements in the conjugacy class of $\sigma$ in $S_n$ (i.e., all elements of the same cycle type as $\sigma$) are conjugate in $A_n$ if and only if $\sigma$ commutes with an odd permutation. [Use the preceding exercise.]
\item Let $K$ be a conjugacy class in $S_n$ and assume that $K \subseteq A_n$. Show $\sigma \in S_n$ does not commute with any odd permutation if and only if the cycle type of $\sigma$ consists of distinct odd integers. Deduce that $K$ consists of two conjugacy classes in $A_n$ if and only if the cycle type of an element of $K$ consists of distinct odd integers. [Assume first that $\sigma \in K$ does not commute with any odd permutation. Observe that $\sigma$ commutes with each individual cycle in its cycle decomposition --- use this to show that all its cycles must be of odd length. If two cycles have the same odd length, $k$, find a product of $k$ transpositions which interchanges them and commutes with $\sigma$.
