embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Discrete Groups, Lattices, and the Crystallographic Restriction > The point group is finite
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8562d9410733356c77b1
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $\Gamma=\{\,\theta\inR \st \rho_\theta\in\overline G\,\}$ be the set of rotation angles in $\overline G$. It is a subgroup of $R$ (composing rotations adds angles) containing $2\pi$, and it is discrete because $\overline G$ contains no arbitrarily small rotations. A discrete subgroup of $R$ is infinite cyclic (the line case of Theorem~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:classify@c4] ): take the smallest positive angle $\theta_0$, so $\Gamma=Z\theta_0$; since $2\pi\in\Gamma$ we get $2\pi=n\theta_0$, i.e. $\theta_0=2\pi/n$ for some positive integer $n$. So the rotations in $\overline G$ form a cyclic group of order $n$. If $\overline G$ contains a reflection, it is dihedral $D_n$; otherwise it is cyclic $C_n$. Either way $\lvert\overline G\rvert<\infty$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Why ``discrete'' is essential
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why ``discrete'' is essential}
Problem. Show the full group $SO(2)$ of all rotations about the origin is a subgroup of $O(2)$ that is not discrete, and exhibit arbitrarily small rotations in it.
\wrec Proposition~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:Ofinite@c4] concludes finiteness only under discreteness; to see the hypothesis is needed, produce a non-discrete subgroup violating the conclusion.
\wsol
$SO(2)=\{\,\rho_\theta \st \theta\inR\,\}$ is closed under composition and inverses, so it is a subgroup. For any $\varepsilon>0$ the rotation $\rho_{\varepsilon/2}$ is a nonzero rotation with angle $\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$, so no single $\varepsilon$ bounds all nonzero angles from below: $SO(2)$ is not discrete. And it is infinite, so the finiteness conclusion genuinely fails.
Check. The rotations $\rho_{2\pi/n}$ generate the finite cyclic group $C_n\sgrSO(2)$ for each $n$, and these $C_n$ are discrete --- discreteness, not membership in $O(2)$, is exactly what forces finiteness.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Why ``discrete'' is essential}
Problem. Show the full group $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ of all rotations about the origin is a subgroup of $\mathrm{O}(2)$ that is \emph{not} discrete, and exhibit arbitrarily small rotations in it.
\wrec Proposition~\ref{art:discrete_groups:Ofinite@c4} concludes finiteness only \emph{under} discreteness; to see the hypothesis is needed, produce a non-discrete subgroup violating the conclusion.
\wsol
$\mathrm{SO}(2)=\{\,\rho_\theta \st \theta\in\mathbb{R}\,\}$ is closed under composition and inverses, so it is a subgroup. For any $\varepsilon>0$ the rotation $\rho_{\varepsilon/2}$ is a nonzero rotation with angle $\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$, so no single $\varepsilon$ bounds all nonzero angles from below: $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ is not discrete. And it is infinite, so the finiteness conclusion genuinely fails.
\textit{Check.} The rotations $\rho_{2\pi/n}$ generate the finite cyclic group $C_n\sgr\mathrm{SO}(2)$ for each $n$, and these $C_n$ \emph{are} discrete --- discreteness, not membership in $\mathrm{O}(2)$, is exactly what forces finiteness.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: $\overline G$ preserves $L$
Label: art:discrete_groups:preserveL@c4
Content:
\begin{proposition}[$\overline G$ preserves $L$] 
Let $G\sgr M$, with translation group $L$ and point group $\overline G$. For every $a\in L$ and every $\overline g\in\overline G$, we have $\overline g(a)\in L$. Equivalently, $\overline G$ lies in the group of symmetries of $L$ regarded as a figure in $V$.
\end{proposition}
label: art:discrete_groups:preserveL@c4

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-b511b0705a6f9e5b1176
Content:
\begin{proof}
Take $g\in G$ with image $\overline g$, and set $a'=\overline g(a)$. Write $g=t_b\varphi$ with $\varphi\inO(2)$, so $\overline g=\varphi$ and $a'=\varphi(a)$. Conjugating the translation $t_a$ (which is in $G$ since $a\in L$) by $g$, and using $\varphi\,t_a\,\varphi^{-1}=t_{\varphi(a)}$,
\[
g\,t_a\,g^{-1}=(t_b\varphi)\,t_a\,(\varphi^{-1} t_{-b})=t_b\,t_{\varphi(a)}\,t_{-b}=t_{\varphi(a)}=t_{a'}.
\]
Both $g$ and $t_a$ lie in $G$, so the conjugate $t_{a'}\in G$; therefore $a'\in L$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
It is genuinely important that $\overline G$ acts on $L\subseteq V$, not that $G$ acts on $L$: the elements of $G$ are isometries of $P$, while $L$ lives in $V$, and $P$ is identified with $V$ only after an origin is chosen. The clean statement is the one above --- the orthogonal point group permutes the lattice.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: Crystallographic restriction
Label: art:discrete_groups:crystal@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Crystallographic restriction] 
Let $L\sgr V$ be a nontrivial discrete subgroup and let $H\sgrO(2)$ be a subgroup carrying $L$ to itself. Then every rotation in $H$ has order $1,2,3,4,$ or $6$; consequently $H$ is one of $C_n$ or $D_n$ with $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$. In particular five-fold rotational symmetry is impossible.
\end{theorem}
label: art:discrete_groups:crystal@c4

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Discrete Groups, Lattices, and the Crystallographic Restriction > The point group operates on the lattice
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-9c2ff572f84b630d114b
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $\rho\in H$ be a nontrivial rotation, through an angle $\theta$ with $0<\theta\le\pi$ (replace $\rho$ by $\rho^{-1}$ if necessary), and let $a\in L$ be a nonzero vector of minimal length (Lemma~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:minvec@c4] ). Since $H$ preserves $L$, $\rho(a)\in L$, hence $b=\rho(a)-a\in L$. By minimality $\lvert b\rvert\ge\lvert a\rvert$. But $\lvert b\rvert=\lvert\rho(a)-a\rvert=2\lvert a\rvert\sin(\theta/2)$, and $2\sin(\theta/2)<1$ exactly when $0<\theta<\pi/3=2\pi/6$. So $\lvert b\rvert<\lvert a\rvert$ for $0<\theta<2\pi/6$, which is forbidden; hence $\theta\ge2\pi/6$ for every nontrivial rotation in $H$. Thus $H$ is discrete, hence finite by Proposition~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:Ofinite@c4] ; its rotations form a cyclic group generated by $\rho_{2\pi/n}$, and $2\pi/n\ge2\pi/6$ gives $n\le6$, so $\rho$ has order at most $6$. Order $5$ ($\theta=2\pi/5$) is also excluded: there $b'=\rho^2(a)+a$ satisfies $\lvert b'\rvert<\lvert a\rvert$ (a short computation with $\cos(4\pi/5)=-(1+\sqrt5)/4<-1/2$ gives $\lvert b'\rvert^2=\lvert a\rvert^2(2+2\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5})<\lvert a\rvert^2$), again contradicting minimality. So only orders $1,2,3,4,6$ survive, and by Proposition~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:Ofinite@c4] $H$ is the corresponding $C_n$ or $D_n$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: The point group operating on a lattice
Content:
\begin{wex}{The point group operating on a lattice}
Problem. Let $L=Z^2$ be the square lattice and let $\overline g=\rho_{\pi/2}$ be the quarter-turn. Verify $\overline g$ permutes $L$, find the order of $\overline g$ as a symmetry of $L$, and locate it on the crystallographic list.
\wrec This is Proposition~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:preserveL@c4] made concrete (check $\overline g(a)\in L$ on a basis) followed by the order test of Theorem~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:crystal@c4] .
\wsol
On the standard basis, $\rho_{\pi/2}(1,0)=(0,1)$ and $\rho_{\pi/2}(0,1)=(-1,0)$, both in $Z^2$; since $\rho_{\pi/2}$ is linear it sends every integer combination to an integer combination, so $\overline g(L)=L$. As a symmetry $\overline g$ has order $4$ (four quarter-turns return to the identity), and $4\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, consistent with the restriction. The full symmetry group of $Z^2$ in $O(2)$ is $D_4$ (the quarter-turn together with a reflection).
Check. Test the theorem's inequality with $a=(1,0)$: $b=\rho_{\pi/2}(a)-a=(-1,1)$ has $\lvert b\rvert=\sqrt2\ge1=\lvert a\rvert$, no contradiction, so order $4$ is allowed. For $\theta=2\pi/5$ this first test still passes ($2\sin36^\circ\approx1.18\ge1$); the lattice vector that is forced to be shorter than $a$ is $\rho^2(a)+a$, of length $2\cos72^\circ\,\lvert a\rvert\approx0.618\,\lvert a\rvert$ (next example) --- which is why no lattice has five-fold symmetry.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Discrete Groups, Lattices, and the Crystallographic Restriction > The point group operates on the lattice
Type: example
Title: No five-fold lattice symmetry, directly
Content:
\begin{wex}{No five-fold lattice symmetry, directly}
Problem. Suppose a nonzero discrete $L\sgr V$ admits a rotation $\rho$ of order $5$ as a symmetry. Derive a contradiction using a minimal vector.
\wrec The crystallographic restriction in action: assume the forbidden order and manufacture a shorter lattice vector (Theorem~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:crystal@c4] ).
\wsol
Let $a\in L$ be a shortest nonzero vector and $\theta=2\pi/5$. Then $\rho(a),\rho^2(a)\in L$, so $b'=\rho^2(a)+a\in L$. Compute
\[
\lvert b'\rvert^2=\lvert a\rvert^2+\lvert a\rvert^2+2\lvert a\rvert^2\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}=2\lvert a\rvert^2\bigl(1+\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}\bigr).
\]
Since $\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}=-\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\approx-0.809$, we get $\lvert b'\rvert^2\approx2\lvert a\rvert^2(0.191)\approx0.382\,\lvert a\rvert^2<\lvert a\rvert^2$. So $b'$ is a nonzero lattice vector shorter than $a$ --- contradicting minimality. (It is nonzero: $\rho^2(a)=-a$ would force $\rho^2$ to be the half-turn, of order $2$, incompatible with $\rho$ of order $5$.)
Check. The same computation with $\theta=2\pi/6$ gives $\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\tfrac12$, so $\lvert b'\rvert^2=2\lvert a\rvert^2(1-\tfrac12)=\lvert a\rvert^2$, exactly the borderline --- order $6$ is allowed, order $5$ is not, precisely as the theorem predicts.
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Title: Where this goes
Content:
\begin{remark}[Where this goes]
When $L$ is trivial, $\pi$ is injective on $G$, so $G\cong\overline G$ is finite cyclic or dihedral --- the symmetry groups of bounded figures. When $L$ is infinite cyclic ($Z a$), $G$ is the symmetry group of a frieze pattern. When $L$ is a full lattice, $G$ is a plane crystallographic group; the crystallographic restriction cuts the possible point groups down to $C_n,D_n$ with $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, and a finer analysis sorts these into the $17$ wallpaper groups.
\end{remark}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
$G$ does not act on its own translation lattice $L$. The elements of $G$ are isometries of the plane $P$; $L$ is a set of vectors in $V$. Only after fixing an origin (identifying $P$ with $V$) does the question even make sense, and whether such an origin can be chosen so that $G$ stabilizes $L$ depends on the group. The clean, always-valid statement is Proposition~ [REF:art:discrete_groups:preserveL@c4] : the point group $\overline G\sgrO(2)$ permutes $L$.
\end{pitfall}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Discrete Groups, Lattices, and the Crystallographic Restriction > The crystallographic restriction
Type: prose
Content:
A two-dimensional lattice is the set of integer combinations of two independent vectors,
\[
L=Z a+Z b=\{ma+nb\st m,n\inZ\},
\]
the translation group of a planar crystal or wallpaper pattern. A rotation that maps the
pattern to itself must in particular map $L$ to itself. The remarkable fact, due to the rigidity
of $L$, is that only a handful of rotation orders are compatible with a lattice: the orders
$1,2,3,4,6$ and no others. In particular there is no lattice with $5$-fold or $7$-fold symmetry.

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: definition
Title: Discrete subgroup and lattice
Content:
\begin{definition}[Discrete subgroup and lattice]
A subgroup $L$ of the additive group $R^2$ of translation vectors is discrete if there is
$\varepsilon>0$ with $\lvert v\rvert\ge\varepsilon$ for every nonzero $v\in L$; equivalently, distinct
points of $L$ are separated by distance at least $\varepsilon$. A discrete subgroup spanned over
$Z$ by two independent vectors is a lattice. A nonzero $v\in L$ is a minimal vector
if $L$ contains no shorter nonzero vector.
\end{definition}
latex:
\begin{definition}[Discrete subgroup and lattice]
A subgroup $L$ of the additive group $\mathbb{R}^2$ of translation vectors is \emph{discrete} if there is
$\varepsilon>0$ with $\lvert v\rvert\ge\varepsilon$ for every nonzero $v\in L$; equivalently, distinct
points of $L$ are separated by distance at least $\varepsilon$. A discrete subgroup spanned over
$\mathbb{Z}$ by two independent vectors is a \emph{lattice}. A nonzero $v\in L$ is a \emph{minimal vector}
if $L$ contains no shorter nonzero vector.

\begin{remark}
Discreteness guarantees a minimal vector exists: a bounded disk meets $L$ in only finitely many
points (the $\varepsilon$-separation packs at most one lattice point per small square), so the
finitely many nonzero points of $L$ inside the disk of radius $\lvert a\rvert$ about the origin include
one of least length. This is the only existence fact the main proof needs.
\end{remark}

Type: proposition
Title: The point group preserves the lattice
Label: art:crystallographic:preserve@c4
Content:
\begin{proposition}[The point group preserves the lattice]
 
Let $G\sgr M$ be a discrete group of isometries of the plane with translation lattice $L$ and
point group $\overline G\sgr O(2)$. If $g\in G$ has image $\overline g\in\overline G$ and
$a\in L$, then $\overline g(a)\in L$. Equivalently, every element of $\overline G$ maps $L$ to
itself, so $\overline G$ is a subgroup of the symmetry group of $L$.
\end{proposition}
label: art:crystallographic:preserve@c4

\begin{proof}
Write $g=t_b\varphi$ with $\varphi\inO(2)$ the linear part, so $\overline g=\varphi$. Let
$t_a\in G$ be the translation by $a$ and put $a'=\varphi(a)$. A direct computation with the
composition rule $t_c\psi=\psi\,t_{\psi^{-1}(c)}$ for isometries gives
\[
g\,t_a\,g^{-1}=(t_b\varphi)\,t_a\,(\varphi^{-1} t_{-b})
=t_b\,t_{\varphi(a)}\,\varphi\varphi^{-1}\,t_{-b}
=t_{a'},
\]
the conjugate of a translation being the translation by the rotated vector. Since $G$ is a group,
$t_{a'}=g\,t_a\,g^{-1}\in G$, hence $a'=\varphi(a)\in L$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Crystallographic restriction
Label: art:crystallographic:main@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Crystallographic restriction]
 
Let $L\subsetR^2$ be a lattice and let $H\sgrO(2)$ be a subgroup of the symmetry group
of $L$. Then every rotation in $H$ has order $1,2,3,4$, or $6$; consequently $H$ is one of the
cyclic groups $C_n$ or dihedral groups $D_n$ with $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$. In particular a rotation of
order $5$ (or of order $7$, or any order outside this list) cannot be a symmetry of a lattice.
\end{theorem}
label: art:crystallographic:main@c4

Let $L\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a lattice and let $H\sgr\mathrm{O}(2)$ be a subgroup of the symmetry group
of $L$. Then every rotation in $H$ has order $1,2,3,4$, or $6$; consequently $H$ is one of the
cyclic groups $C_n$ or dihedral groups $D_n$ with $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$. In particular a rotation of
order $5$ (or of order $7$, or any order outside this list) cannot be a symmetry of a lattice.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Group Actions > Discrete Groups, Lattices, and the Crystallographic Restriction > The crystallographic restriction
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-5ab92a0f659a45d9fe12
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $\rho\in H$ be a rotation through an angle $\theta$ with $0<\theta\le\pi$ (replacing $\rho$ by
$\rho^{-1}$ if needed does not change its order). Let $a$ be a minimal vector of $L$, of length
$r=\lvert a\rvert>0$. Since $H$ preserves $L$, the vector $\rho(a)$ lies in $L$, and therefore so does
\[
b=\rho(a)-a\in L.
\]
Both $a$ and $\rho(a)$ have length $r$, and the angle between them is $\theta$, so $a,\rho(a),b$
form an isosceles triangle and
\[
\lvert b\rvert=2r\sin\!\Big(\tfrac{\theta}{2}\Big).
\]
Because $a$ is a minimal vector and $b\in L$ is nonzero (as $\theta\ne0$), we need
$\lvert b\rvert\ge r$, i.e.
\[
2\sin\!\Big(\tfrac{\theta}{2}\Big)\ge1,\qquadso\qquad
\sin\!\Big(\tfrac{\theta}{2}\Big)\ge\tfrac12,\qquad
\tfrac{\theta}{2}\ge\tfrac{\pi}{6},\qquad \theta\ge\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{2\pi}{6}.
\]
A rotation of order $n$ has $\theta=2\pi/n$ as its smallest positive angle, so $2\pi/n\ge 2\pi/6$
forces $n\le 6$. Discreteness makes $H$ finite, hence (being a finite subgroup of $O(2)$)
cyclic $C_n$ or dihedral $D_n$.

It remains to exclude $n=5$, the one survivor of $n\le6$ not already in the list. Suppose
$\theta=2\pi/5$. Apply the symmetry again: $\rho^2(a)\in L$, so
\[
b'=\rho^2(a)+a\in L .
\]
Now $\rho^2(a)$ has length $r$ and makes angle $2\theta=4\pi/5$ with $a$, so the parallelogram
diagonal $b'=\rho^2(a)+a$ has length
\[
\lvert b'\rvert=2r\cos\!\Big(\tfrac{2\theta}{2}\Big)=2r\cos\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi}{5}\Big)
=2r\cos 72^\circ\approx 0.618\,r<r .
\]
Thus $b'$ is a nonzero lattice vector strictly shorter than the minimal vector $a$, a
contradiction. Hence $\theta=2\pi/5$ is impossible and $n=5$ is ruled out, leaving exactly
$n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Deciding whether a rotation order is lattice-compatible
Content:
\begin{method}{Deciding whether a rotation order is lattice-compatible}
Trigger. ``can an $n$-fold rotation be a symmetry of a $2$D lattice / wallpaper pattern?''
\begin{enumerate}
\item Take a minimal lattice vector $a$ of length $r$ and rotate it: $\rho(a)-a$ is a lattice
 vector of length $2r\sin(\pi/n)$.
\item Demand $2r\sin(\pi/n)\ge r$, i.e.\ $\sin(\pi/n)\ge\tfrac12$. This passes only for
 $n\le 6$.
\item Among the survivors, test $n=5$ separately: $\rho^2(a)+a$ has length $2r\cos(2\pi/5)<r$,
 a contradiction. So the admissible orders are exactly $1,2,3,4,6$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: $5$-fold symmetry is impossible
Content:
\begin{wex}{$5$-fold symmetry is impossible}
Show that no planar lattice has a rotational symmetry of order $5$.
\wrec Use the crystallographic restriction: build a lattice vector shorter than the minimal one.
\wsol Let $\rho$ be rotation by $\theta=2\pi/5=72^\circ$ and let $a$ be a minimal vector,
$\lvert a\rvert=r$. Then $\rho^2(a)\in L$ makes angle $4\pi/5=144^\circ$ with $a$, so
\[
b'=\rho^2(a)+a\in L,\qquad
\lvert b'\rvert=2r\cos\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi}{5}\Big)=2r\cos 72^\circ\approx0.618\,r<r .
\]
This nonzero lattice vector is shorter than the minimal vector, a contradiction. Hence no
$5$-fold lattice symmetry exists.
Check. The first test $2\sin(\pi/5)=2\sin36^\circ\approx1.176\ge1$ does not exclude
$n=5$, which is exactly why the auxiliary vector $\rho^2(a)+a$ is needed. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Title: $6$-fold symmetry is allowed --- the hexagonal lattice
Content:
\begin{wex}{$6$-fold symmetry is allowed --- the hexagonal lattice}
Verify that the order $n=6$ is compatible, and exhibit the lattice.
\wrec Order $6$ is on the admissible list; check the inequality is met with equality and name a
realizing lattice.
\wsol For $n=6$, $\theta=\pi/3=60^\circ$, and $\lvert\rho(a)-a\rvert=2r\sin30^\circ=2r\cdot\tfrac12=r$.
The bound $\lvert\rho(a)-a\rvert\ge r$ holds with equality: $\rho(a)-a$ is itself a minimal
vector, so no contradiction arises. The realizing lattice is the hexagonal (triangular) lattice
$L=Z a+Z b$ with $\lvert a\rvert=\lvert b\rvert=r$ and angle $60^\circ$ between $a$ and $b$; its symmetry
group is $D_6$, with a $6$-fold rotation about each lattice point.
Check. The six vectors $\rho^k(a)$, $k=0,\dots,5$, are the six minimal vectors of the
hexagonal lattice, all of length $r$, consistent with equality in the bound. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Title: Which $n\le6$ are realized, and by which lattice
Content:
\begin{wex}{Which $n\le6$ are realized, and by which lattice}
List, for each admissible order, a lattice realizing it.
\wrec Match each $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$ to a standard plane lattice.
\wsol
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
n & a lattice with an $n$-fold rotation\\\hline
1 & any lattice (trivial rotation only), generic oblique lattice\\
2 & every lattice has $-\,id$, the $180^\circ$ rotation; oblique lattice\\
3 & hexagonal lattice (also carries $C_3\sgr C_6$)\\
4 & square lattice Z e_1+Z e_2,\ symmetry D_4\\
6 & hexagonal lattice, symmetry D_6
\end{array}
\]
Order $5$ is absent, as is every $n\ge7$.
Check. The orders present, $\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, are exactly the lattice-compatible set from
the theorem; every plane lattice automatically has the order-$2$ symmetry $v\mapsto-v$, so $C_2$ always lies in the full symmetry group of the lattice
(a subgroup $H$, such as $C_1$ or $C_3$, need not contain it). \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Title: Quasicrystals
Content:
\begin{remark}[Quasicrystals]
The restriction forbids periodic $5$-fold symmetry, not $5$-fold symmetry as such. Dropping
the requirement that the pattern repeat by a lattice, one can build aperiodic tilings --- the
Penrose tiling is the famous example --- whose diffraction patterns show sharp $10$-fold
(hence $5$-fold) spots. Physical solids with exactly this aperiodic long-range order,
quasicrystals, were discovered by Shechtman in $1982$ and earned the $2011$ Nobel Prize in
Chemistry. They evade the theorem precisely because their translation group is not a
lattice, so the minimal-vector argument has no minimal vector to exploit.
\end{remark}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The bound $\lvert\rho(a)-a\rvert\ge\lvert a\rvert$ alone rules out only $n\ge7$; it does not exclude
$n=5$, since $2\sin(\pi/5)\approx1.18\ge1$. The order $5$ must be killed by the second
vector $\rho^2(a)+a$. Skipping that step is the common error in stating the proof. Note too that
the theorem is special to dimension $2$ (and $3$): in higher dimensions lattices with $5$-fold
symmetry do exist, e.g.\ the root lattice underlying the $4$-dimensional analogue.
\end{pitfall}

Content:
We continue the analysis of discrete groups of isometries $G\leM$ of the Euclidean plane, where $M$ is the group of all isometries. Such a $G$ comes with two pieces of data: its translation group
\[
L=\{\,v\in V:\ t_v\in G\,\},
\]
the set of translation vectors $v$ for which the translation $t_v$ lies in $G$, and its point group $\overline G\leO(2)$, the image of $G$ under the homomorphism $\pi:M\toO(2)$ that forgets the translation part of an isometry. When $L$ is the trivial group, $G$ is cyclic or dihedral; when $L$ is infinite cyclic, $G$ is the symmetry group of a frieze pattern. The remaining case --- when $L$ is a full lattice --- is the subject here.

Type: definition
Title: Plane crystallographic group
Content:
\begin{definition}[Plane crystallographic group]
A subgroup $G\leM$ is a (two-dimensional) plane crystallographic group, or wallpaper group, if it is discrete and its translation group $L$ is a lattice: there are two linearly independent vectors $a,b\in V$ with
\[
L=Z a+Z b=\{\,m a+n b:\ m,n\inZ\,\}.
\]
Equivalently, $G$ has two independent translational symmetries and no points of accumulation. These are exactly the symmetry groups of doubly periodic plane figures --- wallpaper patterns, and cross-sections of two-dimensional crystals such as graphite.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
The point group $\overline G$ acts on the translation space $V$ but not on the plane $P$ itself (without a chosen origin, $P$ and $V$ are different objects). The key compatibility, due to the conjugation identity $g\,t_a\,g^{-1}=t_{\overline g(a)}$, is that $\overline G$ carries the lattice $L$ to itself: if $a\in L$ and $\overline g\in\overline G$, then $\overline g(a)\in L$. Thus $\overline G$ is a subgroup of the symmetry group of the lattice $L$, regarded as a figure in $V$. This single fact forces a severe restriction.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: Crystallographic restriction
Label: art:plane_groups:restriction@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Crystallographic restriction] 
Let $L$ be a lattice in $V$, and let $H\leO(2)$ be a subgroup of the group of symmetries of $L$ (so $H$ carries $L$ to itself). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] every rotation in $H$ has order $1,2,3,4$, or $6$; and
\item[(b)] $H$ is one of the groups $C_n$ or $D_n$ with $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular a rotation of order $5$ is impossible: there is no wallpaper pattern with five-fold rotational symmetry.
\end{theorem}
label: art:plane_groups:restriction@c4

Content:
\begin{proof}
We prove (a); part (b) follows from (a) together with the classification of finite subgroups of $O(2)$ as $C_n$ or $D_n$. Let $\rho_\theta\in H$ be a rotation through angle $\theta>0$, and choose a nonzero $a\in L$ of minimal length. Since $H$ carries $L$ to itself, $\rho_\theta(a)\in L$, and hence
\[
b=\rho_\theta(a)-a\in L .
\]
By minimality $|a|\le|b|$. A short computation gives $|b|^2=|a|^2(2-2\cos\theta)$, so $|b|\ge|a|$ forces $2-2\cos\theta\ge1$, i.e. $\cos\theta\le\tfrac12$, i.e. $\theta\ge 2\pi/6$. Thus the smallest rotation angle in $H$ is at least $2\pi/6$, so a rotation has order at most $6$.

It remains to exclude order $5$, i.e. $\theta=2\pi/5$. For that angle consider instead
\[
b'=\rho_\theta^2(a)+a\in L .
\]
One computes $|b'|^2=|a|^2\bigl(2+2\cos 2\theta\bigr)=|a|^2(2+2\cos(4\pi/5))$, and since $\cos(4\pi/5)=-\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}<-\tfrac12$ we get $|b'|<|a|$, contradicting minimality. So order $5$ cannot occur, and every rotation in $H$ has order $1,2,3,4$, or $6$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The point group records only the angles of rotation and the lines of reflection or glide; it does not determine $G$. Two complications arise. First, the lattice $L$ and the point group $\overline G$ together still leave room for genuinely different groups $G$. Second, and more subtly, a reflection in the point group $\overline G$ need not be realized in $G$ by an honest reflection: it may be present in $G$ only through glide reflections. Recall a glide reflection is the composite $t_w\,r$ of a reflection $r$ across a line $\ell$ with a translation $t_w$ along $\ell$; it has no fixed point, whereas an ordinary reflection fixes its whole axis.
\end{remark}

Title: Classification of plane crystallographic groups
Label: art:plane_groups:seventeen@c4
Local macros: \arraystretch := 1.25
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Classification of plane crystallographic groups] 
Up to isomorphism (equivalently, up to an affine change of coordinates), there are exactly $17$ plane crystallographic groups. They are distributed over the allowed point groups $C_n,D_n$ ($n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$) as follows.
\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
point group & order & \# wallpaper types & which \\
\hline
C_1 & 1 & 1 & p1 \\
C_2 & 2 & 1 & p2 \\
C_3 & 3 & 1 & p3 \\
C_4 & 4 & 1 & p4 \\
C_6 & 6 & 1 & p6 \\
\hline
D_1 & 2 & 3 & pm, pg, cm \\
D_2 & 4 & 4 & pmm, pmg, pgg, cmm \\
D_3 & 6 & 2 & p3m1, p31m \\
D_4 & 8 & 2 & p4m, p4g \\
D_6 & 12 & 1 & p6m \\
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{|c|}{total} & 17 & \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
The five cyclic point groups give one type each ($5$ in all); the dihedral point groups split into $12$ types, the extra ones distinguished by whether a reflection in $\overline G$ is realized by a true reflection or only by a glide, by the shape (square, rectangular, rhombic, hexagonal) of the underlying lattice, and, for the pair p3m1, p31m (both on the hexagonal lattice, both with true reflections in three directions), by how the mirror lines sit relative to the lattice: in p3m1 every $3$-fold rotation center lies on a mirror line, in p31m some do not.
\end{theorem}
label: art:plane_groups:seventeen@c4

Type: example
Title: The point group of the brick pattern is $D_2$, not $C_2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The point group of the brick pattern is $D_2$, not $C_2$}
Problem. Determine the point group of the brick pattern above, and explain why it is $D_2$ even though the group contains no reflection.
\wrec Apply the recipe: first the rotations fix $n$, then the presence of glide/reflection symmetry decides $C_n$ vs.\ $D_n$.
\wsol
Rotations: the only nontrivial rotational symmetry is the half-turn $\rho_\pi$ about a brick center (or the midpoint of a short edge). No $90^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ rotation preserves the staggered rows, so $n=2$.
Reflection or glide: a horizontal reflection alone fails (it reverses the slant of the strokes or puts the offset rows out of register), but the glide across the dashed line --- the reflection across the middle line of the row just below it, followed by the translation by $c=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ --- does preserve the pattern. The point group is the image in $O(2)$, and the linear part of a glide reflection is an honest reflection $r$. So $r\in\overline G$.
Check. $\overline G$ contains $1,\rho_\pi,r$, hence also $\rho_\pi r$, giving $\overline G=D_2$ of order $4$. Yet $G$ itself has no element with reflection-type fixed line, so $G\ne D_2$ as an isometry group: the point group sees the mirror, the isometry group realizes it only as a glide. This is precisely why $\overline G$ and $L$ do not determine $G$.
\end{wex}

Title: Five-fold symmetry is impossible
Content:
\begin{wex}{Five-fold symmetry is impossible}
Problem. Show directly that no wallpaper pattern can have a rotation of order $5$.
\wrec This is exactly the content of part (a) of the crystallographic restriction (Theorem~ [REF:art:plane_groups:restriction@c4] ); reproduce the minimal-vector argument for $\theta=2\pi/5$.
\wsol
Suppose $\rho_\theta$ with $\theta=2\pi/5$ were a symmetry, so $\rho_\theta\in\overline G$ carries $L$ to itself. Pick $a\in L$ nonzero of minimal length and set $b'=\rho_\theta^2(a)+a$, which lies in $L$. Then
\[
|b'|^2=|a|^2\bigl(2+2\cos2\theta\bigr)=|a|^2\bigl(2+2\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}\bigr).
\]
Numerically $\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}\approx-0.809$, so $2+2\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{5}\approx0.382$ and $|b'|\approx0.618\,|a|<|a|$.
Check. $b'\in L$ is a nonzero vector shorter than $a$, contradicting the minimality of $a$. Hence $\theta=2\pi/5$ is impossible, and order $5$ is excluded --- consistent with the table allowing only $n\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$.
\end{wex}

\begin{remark}
Artin works out the cases $C_4$ and $D_4$ explicitly to model the method. After choosing the minimal vector $a$ and setting $b=\rho_{\pi/2}(a)$, one shows the lattice $L$ is square with basis $(a,b)$ (Lemma $6.6.2$); rescaling makes $L=Z^2$. For $\overline G=C_4$ one finds $G=\{\,t_v\rho^i:\ v\in L,\ 0\le i<4\,\}$ (Proposition $6.6.3$), the single type p4. For $\overline G=D_4$ a short computation shows the reflection generator $g$ with $\overline g=r$ must satisfy $u\in\{(0,0),\,c\}$ with $c=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$: the case $u=(0,0)$ gives a true reflection (type p4m), and the case $u=c$ realizes the reflection only as a glide (type p4g), exactly the two $D_4$ types of the table (Proposition $6.6.4$).
\end{remark}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Same point group does not mean same group. The brick pattern and a mirror-symmetric rectangular pattern both have point group $D_2$, but they are different wallpaper types (pgg vs.\ pmm) because one realizes the reflection only as a glide. Never read off the wallpaper type from $\overline G$ alone --- you must also examine how each mirror sits relative to the lattice, and the lattice's shape.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{pitfall}
\textbf{The point group lives in $O(2)$, the group $G$ lives in $M$.} A glide reflection $t_w r\in G$ has linear part the reflection $r$, so it contributes $r$ to $\overline G$ even though $t_w r$ itself fixes no line. Confusing an element of $G$ with its image in $\overline G$ is the source of most errors in classifying these groups.
\end{pitfall}

Section: Group Actions > Finite Subgroups of the Rotation Group $SO(3)$ > Finite subgroups of $SO(3)$: the Platonic symmetries
Type: prose
Content:
We classify the finite groups of rotations of $R^3$. The answer is short and famous: besides
the cyclic and dihedral families there are exactly three exceptional groups, the rotation
groups of the regular polyhedra. The proof is a counting argument run on the poles of
the group --- the points where rotation axes pierce the unit sphere --- and it leans on the
orbit--stabilizer (counting) formula $|\Orb(p)|\cdot|\Stab(p)|=|G|$.

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The dihedral groups appear here as honest rotation groups. A reflection of a plane is
realized in $R^3$ by a rotation through angle $\pi$ about an axis lying in that plane. So
$D_k$ is generated by a rotation $x$ of angle $2\pi/k$ about the vertical axis together with a
rotation $y$ of angle $\pi$ about a horizontal axis; with $c=\cos(2\pi/k)$ and $s=\sin(2\pi/k)$,
\[
x=\begin{pmatrix} c & -s & 0\\ s & c & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
y=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{remark}

Title: Pole
Content:
\begin{definition}[Pole]
Let $G\sgrSO(3)$ be finite of order $N>1$. Every $g\ne 1$ in $SO(3)$ is a
rotation about a unique axis; that axis meets the unit sphere $S^2$ in two points. A
pole of $G$ is a point $p\in S^2$ fixed by some $g\in G$ with $g\ne 1$. Write $P$ for
the set of all poles of $G$.
\end{definition}

For a pole $p$ the stabilizer $\Stab(p)=G_p$ is the set of elements of $G$ rotating about the
axis through $p$. It is cyclic, generated by the rotation of smallest positive angle; write
$r_p=|G_p|$. Since $p$ is a pole, $r_p>1$. The nonidentity elements of $G$ fixing $p$ are exactly the
$r_p-1$ nonidentity elements of $G_p$.

Type: theorem
Title: The pole-counting formula
Label: art:so3:formula@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[The pole-counting formula] 
Let $G\sgrSO(3)$ be finite of order $N>1$, with pole-orbits $O_1,\dots,O_k$. Write
$r_i=r_p$ and $n_i=|O_i|$ for $p\in O_i$ (these depend only on the orbit), so that
$r_i n_i=N$. Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{r_i}\Bigr)=2-\tfrac{2}{N}.
\]
\end{theorem}
label: art:so3:formula@c4

Type: proof

Content:
\begin{proof}
Count spins: pairs $(g,p)$ with $g\ne 1$ and $gp=p$. Counting by group elements, each
$g\ne 1$ is a nontrivial rotation, hence has exactly two poles, so there are $2(N-1)$ spins.
Counting by poles, the pole $p$ occurs in $r_p-1$ spins. Equating,
\[
\sum_{p\in P}(r_p-1)=2(N-1).
\]
Now collect by orbits. By orbit--stabilizer $r_p\,n_p=N$ (where $n_p=|\Orb(p)|$); poles in the
same orbit share the same $r_p$ and $n_p$. Each orbit $O_i$ contributes $n_i$ equal terms
$r_i-1$, so the left side is $\sum_i n_i(r_i-1)=2N-2$. Divide by $N$ and use $n_i/N=1/r_i$:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{n_i(r_i-1)}{N}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{r_i}\Bigr)=2-\frac{2}{N}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Reading the constraint $\sum_i\bigl(1-\tfrac1{r_i}\bigr)=2-\tfrac2N$
Content:
\begin{method}{Reading the constraint $\sum_i\bigl(1-\tfrac1{r_i}\bigr)=2-\tfrac2N$}
Trigger. You must enumerate the finite subgroups of $SO(3)$, or bound the
number of pole-orbits.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The right side $2-\tfrac2N$ lies in $[1,2)$ for $N\ge2$.
\item Each $r_i\ge2$, so each term $1-\tfrac1{r_i}\ge\tfrac12$. Hence $k\le 3$: four or more
 terms already sum to at least $2>2-\tfrac2N$.
\item Tabulate by number of orbits ($k=1,2,3$). The case $k=3$ forces $\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{r_3}>1$
 with $2\le r_1\le r_2\le r_3$; its solutions are the infinite family $(2,2,r)$, $r\ge2$, and the
 three triples $(2,3,3),(2,3,4),(2,3,5)$.
\item Each surviving triple $(r_1,r_2,r_3)$ pins down $N$ and the orbit sizes $n_i=N/r_i$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Section: Group Actions > Finite Subgroups of the Rotation Group $SO(3)$ > The case analysis
Type: prose
Content:
There can be at most three orbits. We run through $k=1,2,3$.

One orbit. The formula reads $1-\tfrac1{r_1}=2-\tfrac2N$. The left side is $<1$ while
the right is $\ge1$ (as $N\ge2$): impossible.

Two orbits. Here $\bigl(1-\tfrac1{r_1}\bigr)+\bigl(1-\tfrac1{r_2}\bigr)=2-\tfrac2N$,
i.e.\ $\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{r_2}=\tfrac2N$. Since $r_i\mid N$ and $r_i\le N$, each
$\tfrac1{r_i}\ge\tfrac1N$, with equality forced: $r_1=r_2=N$ and $n_1=n_2=1$. Two poles, each
fixed by all of $G$, so $G$ rotates about the single line $\ell$ through them: $G=C_N$.

Three orbits. Now $\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{r_3}=1+\tfrac2N>1$ with
$2\le r_1\le r_2\le r_3$. If $r_1\ge3$ the left side is $\le 3\cdot\tfrac13=1$, contradiction;
so $r_1=2$. Then $\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{r_3}=\tfrac12+\tfrac2N>\tfrac12$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $r_2=2$ as well, $r_3=k$ is arbitrary and $N=2k$: the orbit data $(r_i)=(2,2,k)$,
 $(n_i)=(k,k,2)$. Half of $G$ fixes the polar pair, the other half swaps it by a $\pi$-rotation
 about a perpendicular axis. This is the dihedral group $D_k$ of a regular $k$-gon in the plane
 perpendicular to $\ell$.
\item If $r_2=3$: from $\tfrac13+\tfrac1{r_3}>\tfrac12$ we get $r_3<6$, and $r_3\ge r_2=3$, so
 $r_3\in\{3,4,5\}$. ($r_2\ge4$ already fails: $\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12$ leaves no room.)
\end{itemize}
The three triples with $r_1=2,r_2=3$ are
\[
(2,3,3)\!:\,N=12;\qquad (2,3,4)\!:\,N=24;\qquad (2,3,5)\!:\,N=60,
\]
the tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral groups $T,O,I$. This proves
Theorem~ [REF:art:so3:main@c4] .

\begin{remark}
In each polyhedral case the three orbit sizes $n_i=N/r_i$ count, in order, the edge-centers,
face-centers, and vertices of the associated regular solid (the larger $r_i$, the more
rotations fix that pole, hence the fewer such poles). The poles with $r_i=2$ sit above
edge-midpoints; the vertex-poles carry the highest-order rotations.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: The tetrahedral group $T$: counting its $14$ poles and $22$ spins
Content:
\begin{wex}{The tetrahedral group $T$: counting its $14$ poles and $22$ spins}
The rotation group $T$ of a regular tetrahedron $\Delta$ has order $12$. Verify the spin count
directly, without the abstract formula.
\wrec Poles sit above the centers of faces, the vertices, and the centers of edges; count
spins two ways and check they agree with $2(N-1)$.
\wsol $\Delta$ has $4$ faces, $4$ vertices, $6$ edges, so
\[
|P|=4+4+6=14.
\]
Each $g\ne 1$ (there are $11$) has two poles, giving $2\cdot 11=22$ spins. By pole-type: a
face axis has stabilizer of order $3$, contributing $r-1=2$ spins per pole, over $4$ faces; a
vertex axis likewise $r=3$, contributing $2$ spins over $4$ vertices; an edge axis has $r=2$,
contributing $1$ spin over $6$ edges. Total
\[
2\cdot 4+2\cdot 4+1\cdot 6=8+8+6=22.
\]
Check. $22=2(N-1)=2(12-1)$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The icosahedral triple $(2,3,5)$ gives $N=60$}

\wsol $\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\tfrac15=\tfrac{15+10+6}{30}=\tfrac{31}{30}=1+\tfrac1{30}$, so

=\tfrac12+\tfrac23+\tfrac45=\tfrac{15+20+24}{30}=\tfrac{59}{30}=2-\tfrac{2}{60}$. \checkmark

\begin{pitfall}
The poles in an orbit need not be the vertices of a regular polyhedron. For the cube,
the $12$ edge-centers form a single orbit but span a truncated figure (a cuboctahedron),
not a Platonic solid. In the polyhedral cases the two orbits with $r_i\ge3$ are the vertex sets of a regular
polyhedron and of its dual; only the $r_1=2$ orbit of edge-centers can fail to be one. Likewise, ``at most three orbits'' counts pole-orbits, not
group elements; a single orbit can be large ($n_i=N/r_i$).
\end{pitfall}

\begin{remark}
With $r_1=2$ the integer constraint $\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{r_3}>1$ reads

regular polyhedra'' and ``only three exceptional rotation groups'' come from the same
combinatorial fact. The five solids have Schl\"afli symbols $\{3,3\},\{4,3\},\{3,4\},\{5,3\},\{3,5\}$
($p$-gonal faces, $q$ at each vertex); here they appear as the triples $(2,3,q)$ for $q=3,4,5$,
a solid and its dual giving the same triple, while the remaining solutions $(2,2,k)$ are the
dihedral family.
\end{remark}

Type: prose
Content:
A group action partitions the set it acts on into orbits, and the first quantitative question
is: how many orbits are there? For symmetry-counting problems --- how many genuinely
different bead necklaces, or face-colorings of a cube, exist once we identify configurations
that differ by a rotation --- the orbits are the answer. Artin's Counting Formula
(Proposition 6.9.2) relates the size of one orbit to a stabilizer; averaging that relation over
the whole group turns the geometric question into a clean arithmetic one. Throughout, $G$ is a
finite group acting on a finite set $S$.

Section: Group Actions > Counting Orbits: the Cauchy--Frobenius Formula > Counting orbits: the Cauchy--Frobenius (Burnside) formula
Type: theorem
Title: Counting Formula, Artin 6.9.2
Label: art:burnside:os@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Counting Formula, Artin 6.9.2] 
Let $G$ act on a finite set $S$ and let $s \in S$. Writing $\Orb(s)$ for the orbit and
$\Stab(s) = \{\,g \in G : g\cdot s = s\,\}$ for the stabilizer,
\[
\ord G = \lvert\Stab(s)\rvert \cdot \lvert\Orb(s)\rvert,
\qquadequivalently\qquad
\lvert\Orb(s)\rvert = [G:\Stab(s)] .
\]
In particular the size of every orbit divides $\ord G$.
\end{theorem}
label: art:burnside:os@c4

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8f00d312e1596442a7c7
Content:
\begin{proof}
The stabilizer $H = \Stab(s)$ is a subgroup of $G$. Define $\varphi\colon G/H \to \Orb(s)$ on
left cosets by $\varphi(gH) = g\cdot s$. This is well defined and injective: $g_1 H = g_2 H$
iff $g_2^{-1} g_1 \in H$ iff $g_2^{-1} g_1 \cdot s = s$ iff $g_1\cdot s = g_2\cdot s$. It is
surjective by definition of the orbit. Hence $\lvert\Orb(s)\rvert = [G:H]$, and Lagrange's
theorem $\ord G = \lvert H\rvert \cdot [G:H]$ gives the product form.
\end{proof}

We record the partition consequence Artin uses repeatedly: if $S$ splits into orbits
$O_1, \dots, O_k$, then $\lvert S\rvert = \lvert O_1\rvert + \cdots + \lvert O_k\rvert$, each
summand an index $[G:\Stab(s_i)]$. The Cauchy--Frobenius formula is the dual count: instead
of summing orbit sizes over orbits, sum fixed-point counts over group elements.

Content:
\begin{definition}[Fixed-point set]
For $g \in G$ acting on $S$, the fixed-point set is
\[
\Fix(g) = \{\, s \in S : g \cdot s = s \,\} \subseteq S .
\]
Its size $\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert$ counts the elements left in place by $g$.
\end{definition}

Type: theorem
Title: Cauchy--Frobenius / Burnside Counting Formula
Label: art:burnside:cf@c4
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Cauchy--Frobenius / Burnside Counting Formula] 
Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $S$, and let $N$ be the number of orbits. Then
\[
N = \frac{1}{\ord G} \sum_{g \in G} \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert ,
\]
i.e.\ the number of orbits equals the average number of fixed points of the elements of
$G$.
\end{theorem}
label: art:burnside:cf@c4

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-0492df44fb1c92fb25bc
Content:
\begin{proof}
Count the set of incident pairs
$P = \{\,(g,s) \in G \times S : g\cdot s = s\,\}$ in two ways. Summing over group elements,
\[
\lvert P\rvert = \sum_{g \in G} \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert .
\]
Summing over points, $\lvert P\rvert = \sum_{s \in S} \lvert\Stab(s)\rvert$. Group the second sum
by orbits. For $s$ in a fixed orbit $O$, Theorem~ [REF:art:burnside:os@c4] gives
$\lvert\Stab(s)\rvert = \ord G / \lvert\Orb(s)\rvert = \ord G / \lvert O\rvert$, and there are
$\lvert O\rvert$ such points, so each orbit contributes
$\lvert O\rvert \cdot (\ord G / \lvert O\rvert) = \ord G$. With $N$ orbits,
\[
\sum_{s \in S} \lvert\Stab(s)\rvert = \sum_{orbits O} \ord G = N \cdot \ord G .
\]
Equating the two counts of $\lvert P\rvert$ gives
$\sum_{g} \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = N \cdot \ord G$, and dividing by $\ord G$ yields the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proof is exactly Artin's orbit-stabilizer relation applied to the ``elements'' inside one
orbit: every point of an orbit has a stabilizer of the same order $\ord G / \lvert O\rvert$, and
the $\lvert O\rvert$ stabilizers of an orbit pool to $\ord G$ pairs. The double count is the whole
idea --- no characters, no representation theory. Despite the traditional name, the formula
predates Burnside; it is due to Cauchy and Frobenius, which is why the neutral name is now
preferred.

Type: method
Title: Burnside enumeration recipe
Content:
\begin{method}{Burnside enumeration recipe}
Trigger. You must count configurations up to a symmetry group $G$ (rotations of
a polygon/polyhedron, reflections, etc.): necklaces, colorings, labelings.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Identify $S$ (all raw configurations, ignoring symmetry) and the acting group $G$.
\item For each $g \in G$ compute $\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert$: a coloring is fixed by $g$ iff it is
constant on every cycle of the permutation $g$ induces on the slots. If there are $c$ colors and
$g$ has $\operatorname{cyc}(g)$ cycles on the slots, then
$\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = c^{\operatorname{cyc}(g)}$.
\item Average: $N = \dfrac{1}{\ord G}\sum_{g} \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert$. Group $g$'s by conjugacy class
to avoid repeating identical counts.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Two-color bead necklaces on a square (rotations)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Two-color bead necklaces on a square (rotations)}
How many distinct ways are there to color the $4$ corner beads of a square with $2$ colors
(black/white), where two colorings are the same if a rotation carries one to the other? Here
$G = Z/4Z = \{\,e, r, r^2, r^3\,\}$ is the cyclic group of rotations by $0,90,180,270$ degrees,
acting on the $S = 2^4 = 16$ raw colorings.
\wrec Counting colorings up to rotation is the signature Burnside situation
(Theorem~ [REF:art:burnside:cf@c4] ): average $\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert$, computing each fixed count from
the cycle structure of $g$ on the four bead positions.
\wsol
Label positions $1,2,3,4$ around the square. The rotation $r$ acts as the $4$-cycle
$(1\,2\,3\,4)$; a coloring is $r$-fixed iff all four beads share a color.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
g & cycles on positions & \operatorname{cyc}(g) & \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = 2^{\operatorname{cyc}(g)} \\\hline
e & (1)(2)(3)(4) & 4 & 2^4 = 16 \\
r & (1\,2\,3\,4) & 1 & 2^1 = 2 \\
r^2 & (1\,3)(2\,4) & 2 & 2^2 = 4 \\
r^3 & (1\,4\,3\,2) & 1 & 2^1 = 2
\end{array}
\]
Average over $\ord G = 4$:
\[
N = \frac{1}{4}\bigl(16 + 2 + 4 + 2\bigr) = \frac{24}{4} = 6 .
\]
Check. The six classes are easy to list by number of black beads up to rotation:
$0$ black (1 way), $1$ black (1), $2$ black adjacent (1), $2$ black opposite (1), $3$ black (1),
$4$ black (1) --- total $6$, matching.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Necklaces with the full dihedral symmetry
Content:
\begin{wex}{Necklaces with the full dihedral symmetry}
Same square of $4$ beads and $2$ colors, but now allow reflections too, so
$G = D_8$ (the dihedral group of order $8$: four rotations and four reflections). Count colorings
up to this larger symmetry.
\wrec Same formula; the new group elements (reflections) contribute their own fixed counts. We
reuse the rotation data from the previous example and add the four reflections.
\wsol
The four rotations contribute $16 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 24$ as before. The reflections of a square come in
two geometric types acting on positions $1,2,3,4$ (corners in order):
vertex axes (through two opposite corners) fix those two corners and swap the other two,
e.g.\ $(1)(3)(2\,4)$, so $\operatorname{cyc} = 3$, $\lvert\Fix\rvert = 2^3 = 8$; there are $2$ of
these. Edge axes (through midpoints of opposite sides) swap corners in two pairs,
e.g.\ $(1\,2)(3\,4)$, so $\operatorname{cyc} = 2$, $\lvert\Fix\rvert = 2^2 = 4$; there are $2$ of
these.
\[
N = \frac{1}{8}\Bigl(\underbrace{16+2+4+2}_{rotations} \;+\; \underbrace{8 + 8}_{vertex axes} \;+\; \underbrace{4 + 4}_{edge axes}\Bigr)
= \frac{1}{8}(24 + 16 + 8) = \frac{48}{8} = 6 .
\]
Check. Adding reflections cannot increase the orbit count (it can only merge
orbits), and indeed $6 \le 6$ here: of the rotation-classes, $1$ black, $3$ black, and the two
$2$-black types each already coincide with their mirror images, so no further merging occurs and
the count stays $6$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Face colorings of a cube (Artin's octahedral group)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Face colorings of a cube (Artin's octahedral group)}
Artin's octahedral group $O$ is the group of $24$ rotations of a cube (Section 6.10). In how many
ways can the $6$ faces be painted with $c$ colors, identifying colorings related by a rotation?
Here $S = c^6$ and $G = O$, $\ord O = 24$.
\wrec Burnside over the rotation group of the cube. We need the cycle structure of each rotation
on the six faces, organized by conjugacy class --- the standard inventory of $O$.
\wsol
The $24$ rotations of the cube fall into five conjugacy classes; for each we read off the cycle
type on the $6$ faces and apply $\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = c^{\operatorname{cyc}(g)}$:
\[
\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}
class of g & \#\,g & face cycle type & \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert \\\hline
identity & 1 & 1+1+1+1+1+1 & c^6 \\
face axis, \pm 90^\circ & 6 & 1+1+4 & c^3 \\
face axis, 180^\circ & 3 & 1+1+2+2 & c^4 \\
vertex axis, \pm 120^\circ & 8 & 3+3 & c^2 \\
edge axis, 180^\circ & 6 & 2+2+2 & c^3
\end{array}
\]
Averaging,
\[
N(c) = \frac{1}{24}\Bigl(c^6 + 6c^3 + 3c^4 + 8c^2 + 6c^3\Bigr)
= \frac{c^6 + 3c^4 + 12c^3 + 8c^2}{24} .
\]
For $c = 2$: $N(2) = (64 + 48 + 96 + 32)/24 = 240/24 = 10$. For $c = 3$:
$N(3) = (729 + 243 + 324 + 72)/24 = 1368/24 = 57$.
Check. The face axes give $6/2 = 3$ axes with $\pm 90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ each:
$6 + 3 = 9$ rotations, plus $8$ vertex-axis and $6$ edge-axis, plus the identity, totals
$1 + 9 + 8 + 6 = 24 = \ord O$, accounting for every rotation. The value $N(2)=10$ is the classic
``ten distinct two-color cubes'' count.
\end{wex}

Artin's octahedral group $O$ is the group of $24$ rotations of a cube (Section 6.10). In how many
ways can the $6$ faces be painted with $c$ colors, identifying colorings related by a rotation?
Here $S = c^6$ and $G = O$, $\ord O = 24$.
\wrec Burnside over the rotation group of the cube. We need the cycle structure of each rotation
\emph{on the six faces}, organized by conjugacy class --- the standard inventory of $O$.
\wsol
The $24$ rotations of the cube fall into five conjugacy classes; for each we read off the cycle
type on the $6$ faces and apply $\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = c^{\operatorname{cyc}(g)}$:
\[
\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}
\text{class of } g & \#\,g & \text{face cycle type} & \lvert\Fix(g)\rvert \\\hline
\text{identity} & 1 & 1+1+1+1+1+1 & c^6 \\
\text{face axis, } \pm 90^\circ & 6 & 1+1+4 & c^3 \\
\text{face axis, } 180^\circ & 3 & 1+1+2+2 & c^4 \\
\text{vertex axis, } \pm 120^\circ & 8 & 3+3 & c^2 \\
\text{edge axis, } 180^\circ & 6 & 2+2+2 & c^3
\end{array}
\]
Averaging,
\[
N(c) = \frac{1}{24}\Bigl(c^6 + 6c^3 + 3c^4 + 8c^2 + 6c^3\Bigr)
= \frac{c^6 + 3c^4 + 12c^3 + 8c^2}{24} .
\]
For $c = 2$: $N(2) = (64 + 48 + 96 + 32)/24 = 240/24 = 10$. For $c = 3$:
$N(3) = (729 + 243 + 324 + 72)/24 = 1368/24 = 57$.
\textit{Check.} The face axes give $6/2 = 3$ axes with $\pm 90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ each:
$6 + 3 = 9$ rotations, plus $8$ vertex-axis and $6$ edge-axis, plus the identity, totals
$1 + 9 + 8 + 6 = 24 = \ord O$, accounting for every rotation. The value $N(2)=10$ is the classic
``ten distinct two-color cubes'' count.
\end{wex}

Title: Pairs of faces of the cube: recovering Artin's 3 and 12
Content:
\begin{wex}{Pairs of faces of the cube: recovering Artin's 3 and 12}
Artin notes (Section 6.10) that $O$ acts on the $15$ unordered pairs of faces of a cube, splitting
them into the $3$ pairs of opposite faces and the $12$ pairs of adjacent faces.
Recover these orbit sizes with the Counting Formula, and verify the orbit count via Burnside.
\wrec Two checks: (i) orbit sizes by Theorem~ [REF:art:burnside:os@c4] ; (ii) the number of orbits by
Theorem~ [REF:art:burnside:cf@c4] . The action is on $S = $ the $15$ unordered face-pairs.
\wsol
(i) Orbit sizes. Fix a pair of opposite faces $U$. Its stabilizer is the set of rotations
sending $\{$top$,$bottom$\}$ to itself; Artin records $\lvert\Stab(U)\rvert = 8$ (rotations about
the vertical axis together with the $180^\circ$ flips). Then
$\lvert\Orb(U)\rvert = \ord O / \lvert\Stab(U)\rvert = 24/8 = 3$ --- the three axis-directions.
For a pair of adjacent faces $U'$, the stabilizer consists of the identity and the half-turn
about the axis through the midpoint of their common edge, so it has order $2$, giving orbit
size $24/2 = 12$.
$3 + 12 = 15$ exhausts $S$.
(ii) Orbit count by Burnside. We expect $N = 2$. Class by class on the $15$ pairs: the
identity fixes all $15$; each of the $6$ quarter-turns about a face axis fixes only the pair of
faces on its axis; each of the $3$ face half-turns fixes $3$ pairs (the three pairs of opposite
faces); the $8$ vertex rotations fix none (they permute the faces in two $3$-cycles); each of
the $6$ edge half-turns fixes the $3$ pairs of faces it swaps. So
\[
N = \frac{1}{24}\sum_{g\in O}\lvert\Fix(g)\rvert = \frac{1}{24}\bigl(15 + 6\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 3 + 8\cdot 0 + 6\cdot 3\bigr) = \frac{48}{24} = 2 .
\]
Check. Both methods agree with Artin: orbit sizes $3$ and $12$ (summing to $15$), and
$N = 2$ orbits. The stabilizer order $8$ for an opposite-face pair is exactly the value Artin
states in Section 6.10.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Burnside counts orbits of the exact group you average over. Including reflections
(dihedral) versus rotations only (cyclic) generally gives different answers; the necklace
examples above happened to agree, but for larger bead counts they diverge. Decide first whether
mirror images count as ``the same.''
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The two summation directions are worth keeping side by side. Partitioning $S$ into orbits sums
orbit sizes: $\lvert S\rvert = \sum_O [G:\Stab(s_O)]$, the count Artin uses for the
dodecahedron's $12 = 1 + 1 + 5 + 5$ face partition under a cyclic stabilizer of order $5$.
Cauchy--Frobenius instead sums fixed-point counts over $G$ to extract the number of
orbits. Both rest on the single identity
$\lvert\Orb(s)\rvert\cdot\lvert\Stab(s)\rvert = \ord G$ of Theorem~ [REF:art:burnside:os@c4] .
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 4.1.7] Define a block for a transitive $G\le\Sym(A)$ and prove: (a) if $a\in B$ then $G_B=\{\sigma\st\sigma(B)=B\}$ is a subgroup containing $G_a$; (b) the distinct images of a block partition $A$; (c) $S_4$ is primitive on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ while $D_8$ is not primitive on the square's vertices; (d) $G$ is primitive iff each $G_a$ is maximal.
\item [DF 4.1.8] Define doubly transitive and prove: (a) $S_n$ is doubly transitive on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ for $n\ge 2$; (b) a doubly transitive group is primitive, so $D_8$ is not doubly transitive on the square.
\item [DF 4.1.9] For $G$ transitive on finite $A$ and $H\nor G$ with $H$-orbits $\mathcal O_1,\dots,\mathcal O_r$: (a) prove $G$ permutes the $\mathcal O_i$ transitively, so all have equal size; (b) prove $|\mathcal O_1|=|H:H\cap G_a|$ and $r=|G:HG_a|$.
\item [DF 4.1.10] For subgroups $H,K\le G$ define the double coset $HxK$ and prove: (a) it is a union of left cosets of $K$ forming an $H$-orbit; (b) it is a union of right cosets of $H$; (c) double cosets partition $G$; (d) $|HxK|=|K|\cdot|H:H\cap xKx^{-1}|$; (e) $|HxK|=|H|\cdot|K:K\cap x^{-1} Hx|$.
\item [DF 4.2.13] Prove that a finite group $G$ of composite order $n$ having a subgroup of order $k$ for every $k\mid n$ is not simple.
\item [DF 4.2.--Q8] Prove $Q_8$ embeds in $S_8$ but in no $S_n$ with $n\le 7$.
\item [DF 4.3.6] If $G$ is non-abelian of order $15$, prove $Z(G)=1$ and that there is at most one possible class equation for $G$.
\item [DF 4.3.17] For $X\subseteq S_A$ with moved set $M(\sigma)$, prove $D=\{\sigma\in S_A\st|M(\sigma)|<\infty\}$ is a normal subgroup of $S_A$.
\item [DF 4.3.19] For $H\nor G$ and a conjugacy class $\mathcal K\subseteq H$ with $x\in\mathcal K$, prove $\mathcal K$ splits into $k=[G:HC_G(x)]$ classes of equal size in $H$; deduce the $S_n$-versus-$A_n$ splitting of even classes.
\item [DF 4.3.20] Prove $\sigma\in A_n$ has its $S_n$-class remain a single $A_n$-class iff $\sigma$ commutes with an odd permutation.
\item [DF 4.3.21] Prove $\sigma$ commutes with no odd permutation iff its cycle type consists of distinct odd integers; deduce the criterion for an $S_n$-class to split in $A_n$.
\item [DF 4.3.23] Prove that if $M$ is a maximal subgroup of $G$ then $N_G(M)=M$ or $G$; deduce the bound $(|M|-1)[G:M]$ on nonidentity elements in conjugates of a nonnormal maximal $M$.
\item [DF 4.3.24] Prove a finite group $G$ is not the union of the conjugates of any proper subgroup.
\item [DF 4.3.25] For $G=\GL_2(C)$ and $H$ the upper-triangular subgroup, prove every element of $G$ is conjugate into $H$, so $G$ is a union of conjugates of $H$.
\item [DF 4.3.27] If $G$ is transitive on finite $A$ with $|A|>1$, show some $\sigma\in G$ is fixed-point free.
\item [DF 4.3.30] For primes $p<q$, prove a non-abelian group of order $pq$ has a nonnormal subgroup of index $q$, hence embeds in $S_q$ as a subgroup of $N_{S_q}(\langle (1\,2\cdots q)\rangle)$.
\item [DF 4.3.33] For $n=2k$ even, determine the conjugacy classes of $D_{2n}$ and give the class equation.
\item [DF 4.3.34] Prove that for a prime $p$ and $P\le S_p$ of order $p$, $|N_{S_p}(P)|=p(p-1)$.
\item [DF 4.3.35] Find a formula (using the floor function) for the number of conjugacy classes of elements of order $p$ in $S_n$.
\item [DF 4.3.36] For the left and right regular representations $\pi,\lambda$ with $\sigma_g=\pi(g)$, $\tau_h=\lambda(h)$ (so $\tau_h(x)=xh^{-1}$): (a) prove $\sigma_g,\tau_h$ commute; (b) $\sigma_g=\tau_g$ iff $g$ has order $1$ or $2$ in $Z(G)$; (c) $\sigma_g=\tau_h$ iff $g,h\in Z(G)$ and $g=h^{-1}$, so $\lambda(G)\cap\pi(G)=Z(\lambda(G))=Z(\pi(G))$.
\item [DF 4.4.3] Prove that under any automorphism of $D_8$, $r$ has at most $2$ images and $s$ at most $4$; deduce $|\Aut(D_8)|\le 8$.

Type: definition
Title: External direct product
Content:
\begin{definition}[External direct product]
Let $G_1,G_2,\dots,G_n$ be groups (written multiplicatively, with identities $1_i$). The
(external) direct product $G_1\times G_2\times\cdots\times G_n$ is the set of all
$n$-tuples
\[
G_1\times\cdots\times G_n=\{\,(g_1,\dots,g_n)\st g_i\in G_i\ for all i\,\}
\]
with componentwise multiplication
\[
(g_1,\dots,g_n)\cdot(h_1,\dots,h_n)=(g_1h_1,\,g_2h_2,\,\dots,\,g_nh_n).
\]
The identity is $(1_1,\dots,1_n)$ and $(g_1,\dots,g_n)^{-1}=(g_1^{-1},\dots,g_n^{-1})$. When
every $G_i$ is abelian and written additively, the same construction is called the
direct sum and written $G_1\oplus\cdots\oplus G_n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[It is a group; its order] 
$G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_n$ is a group, and if every $G_i$ is finite then
\[
\ord{G}=\ord{G_1}\cdot\ord{G_2}\cdots\ord{G_n}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\ord{G_i}.
\]
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}
The operation is well defined since each $g_ih_i\in G_i$. Associativity holds coordinatewise:
the $i$-th coordinate of either bracketing of $(g_i)(h_i)(k_i)$ is $g_i(h_ik_i)=(g_ih_i)k_i$
by associativity in $G_i$. The element $e=(1_1,\dots,1_n)$ satisfies $e\cdot(g_i)=(1_ig_i)=(g_i)$
and similarly on the right, so $e$ is the identity. Finally $(g_i^{-1})$ inverts $(g_i)$
coordinatewise, so every element has an inverse; hence $G$ is a group. For the order: choosing
$(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ amounts to choosing each $g_i\in G_i$ independently, so by the multiplication
principle there are $\prod_i\ord{G_i}$ tuples.
\end{proof}

Title: Computing in a direct product
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing in a direct product}
Trigger. The group is presented as a product $G_1\times\cdots\times G_n$, or you
must count its elements.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Work slot by slot: multiply, invert, and reduce each coordinate inside its own
$G_i$. Coordinates never interact.
\item For the order of the group, multiply the orders: $\prod_i\ord{G_i}$.
\item Identity is the tuple of identities; inverse is the tuple of inverses.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Multiplying in $Z/(4)Z\times S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Multiplying in $Z/(4)Z\times S_3$}
Problem. In $Z/(4)Z\times S_3$ compute $(3,(1\,2))\cdot(2,(1\,2\,3))$ and the order of the
whole group.
\wrec Componentwise operation: add mod $4$ in the first slot, compose permutations in the
second; the order of the group is the product of the orders.
\wsol First slot: $3+2=5\equiv 1\pmod 4$. Second slot: apply $(1\,2\,3)$ then $(1\,2)$
(D\&F composes right-to-left). Track each point: $1\xmapsto{(1\,2\,3)}2\xmapsto{(1\,2)}1$,
$2\mapsto 3\mapsto 3$, $3\mapsto 1\mapsto 2$, giving $(2\,3)$. So the product is
$(1,(2\,3))$. Order of the group: $\ord{Z/(4)Z}\cdot\ord{S_3}=4\cdot 6=24$.
Check. The first slot reduces correctly, $5\bmod 4=1$; in the second slot $1\mapsto1$
is fixed while $2\leftrightarrow3$ are swapped, so the result is the transposition $(2\,3)$.
Both coordinates land in their groups, and $24=4\cdot 6$.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{proof}
Since multiplication is componentwise, induction on $m$ gives
$(g_1,\dots,g_n)^m=(g_1^{\,m},\dots,g_n^{\,m})$. Thus $(g_1,\dots,g_n)^m=(1_1,\dots,1_n)$
\Longleftrightarrow\ $g_i^{\,m}=1_i$ for every $i$ \Longleftrightarrow\ $\ord{g_i}\mid m$ for every $i$. The set of integers
$m$ divisible by every $\ord{g_i}$ is exactly the set of multiples of
$L:=\lcm(\ord{g_1},\dots,\ord{g_n})$ (a common multiple is divisible by the least common
multiple). The order of the tuple is the smallest positive such $m$, namely $L$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Order of $(g_1,\dots,g_n)$
Content:
\begin{method}{Order of $(g_1,\dots,g_n)$}
Trigger. You are asked for the order of a specific tuple, or the largest possible
order of an element.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Find each coordinate order $\ord{g_i}$ separately (in $Z/(m)Z$, $\ord{a}=m/\gcd(a,m)$).
\item Take the lcm of those numbers --- not the product, and not the
sum.
\item For the largest element order in $Z/(m_1)Z\times\cdots\timesZ/(m_n)Z$, the
exponent of the group is $\lcm(m_1,\dots,m_n)$; an element of that order exists (take a
generator in each slot), so the maximum equals $\lcm(m_1,\dots,m_n)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The order of a tuple is the lcm, never the product, of the coordinate orders. In
$Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ the element $(1,1)$ has order $\lcm(4,6)=12$, not $4\cdot6=24$ and not
$4+6=10$. Using the product $24$ is wrong on two counts: it equals the full group order
$\ord{Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z}=24$, which no element can match here, and it exceeds the exponent
$\lcm(4,6)=12$, which already bounds every element order.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Order of an element of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ (D\&F)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Order of an element of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ (D\&F)}
Problem. Find the order of $(2,3)$ and of $(1,1)$ in $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$.
\wrec Proposition~ [REF:prop:order-tuple@c5] : order $=\lcm$ of coordinate orders; in $Z/(m)Z$,
$\ord{a}=m/\gcd(a,m)$.
\wsol For $(2,3)$: in $Z/(4)Z$, $\ord{2}=4/\gcd(2,4)=4/2=2$; in $Z/(6)Z$,
$\ord{3}=6/\gcd(3,6)=6/3=2$. So $\ord{(2,3)}=\lcm(2,2)=2$. Check.
$(2,3)+(2,3)=(4,6)=(0,0)$, and $(2,3)\ne(0,0)$, confirming order $2$.\\
For $(1,1)$: $\ord{1}=4$ in $Z/(4)Z$ and $\ord{1}=6$ in $Z/(6)Z$, so
$\ord{(1,1)}=\lcm(4,6)=12$. Check. $12\cdot(1,1)=(12,12)=(0,0)$ since $4\mid12$ and
$6\mid12$; and $6\cdot(1,1)=(6,6)=(2,0)\ne(0,0)$, so the order is not $6$. Indeed $12$ is the
exponent of the group.
\end{wex}

\wrec Proposition~\ref{prop:order-tuple@c5}: order $=\lcm$ of coordinate orders; in $\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}$,
$\ord{a}=m/\gcd(a,m)$.

\begin{wex}{Order in $Z/(12)Z\timesZ/(18)Z$}
Problem. Find $\ord{(8,15)}$ in $Z/(12)Z\timesZ/(18)Z$.
\wrec Coordinatewise orders via $m/\gcd(a,m)$, then $\lcm$.
\wsol In $Z/(12)Z$: $\gcd(8,12)=4$, so $\ord{8}=12/4=3$. In $Z/(18)Z$: $\gcd(15,18)=3$, so

$6\cdot(8,15)=(48,90)=(0,0)$ since $48=4\cdot12$ and $90=5\cdot18$; and
$3\cdot(8,15)=(24,45)=(0,9)\ne(0,0)$, so the order exceeds $3$, consistent with $6$.
\end{wex}

Title: Order of a permutation/quaternion pair
Content:
\begin{wex}{Order of a permutation/quaternion pair}
Problem. In $D_8\times Q_8$ find the order of $(r,i)$, where $r$ is the rotation of order $4$
in $D_8$ ($n=4$) and $i\in Q_8$.
\wrec Order of a tuple is the lcm of coordinate orders; read off $\ord{r}=4$ and $\ord{i}=4$.
\wsol In $D_8$ we have $r^4=1$ and $r,r^2,r^3\ne1$, so $\ord{r}=4$. In $Q_8$, $i^2=-1$ and
$i^4=1$ with $i,i^2,i^3\ne1$, so $\ord{i}=4$. Thus $\ord{(r,i)}=\lcm(4,4)=4$. Check.
$(r,i)^4=(r^4,i^4)=(1,1)$ and $(r,i)^2=(r^2,i^2)=(r^2,-1)\ne(1,1)$, so the order is exactly
$4$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Largest order of an element of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\timesZ/(9)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Largest order of an element of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\timesZ/(9)Z$}
Problem. What is the largest order of any element of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\timesZ/(9)Z$?
\wrec The maximum element order equals the exponent $\lcm(m_1,\dots,m_n)$, attained by a
tuple of generators.
\wsol Compute $\lcm(4,6,9)$. Prime factorizations: $4=2^2$, $6=2\cdot3$, $9=3^2$. Take the
highest power of each prime: $2^2$ from $4$ and $3^2$ from $9$, giving $4\cdot9=36$. So the
maximum order is $36$, attained by $(1,1,1)$: indeed $\ord{(1,1,1)}=\lcm(4,6,9)=36$.
Check. No element can have larger order, since $g^{36}=(g_1^{36},g_2^{36},g_3^{36})=
(0,0,0)$ for every $g$ (as $4,6,9\mid36$), so $36$ is the exponent and bounds all orders;
and $(1,1,1)$ achieves it. Note $\ord{Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\timesZ/(9)Z}=4\cdot6\cdot9=216$, so the
group is far from cyclic.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: $Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z\congZ/(mn)Z$ iff coprime
Label: thm:crt@c5
Content:
\begin{theorem}[$Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z\congZ/(mn)Z$ iff coprime] 
For $m,n\in\Zpos$,
\[
Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z\congZ/(mn)Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gcd(m,n)=1.
\]
More generally, $Z/(m_1)Z\times\cdots\timesZ/(m_k)Z\congZ/(m_1\cdots m_k)Z$ iff the $m_i$ are
pairwise coprime. Equivalently, $Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z$ is cyclic \Longleftrightarrow\ $\gcd(m,n)=1$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:crt@c5
latex:
\begin{theorem}[$\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(mn)\mathbb{Z}$ iff coprime]\label{thm:crt@c5}
For $m,n\in\Zpos$,
\[
\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(mn)\mathbb{Z}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gcd(m,n)=1.
\]
More generally, $\mathbb{Z}/(m_1)\mathbb{Z}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{Z}/(m_k)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(m_1\cdots m_k)\mathbb{Z}$ iff the $m_i$ are
pairwise coprime. Equivalently, $\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic \Longleftrightarrow\ $\gcd(m,n)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both groups have order $mn$, so it suffices to decide when $Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z$ is cyclic,
i.e.\ has an element of order $mn$. By Proposition~ [REF:prop:order-tuple@c5] the maximum element
order is the exponent $\lcm(m,n)$. Using $\lcm(m,n)\cdot\gcd(m,n)=mn$, we get
$\lcm(m,n)=mn\Longleftrightarrow\gcd(m,n)=1$.

($\Leftarrow$) If $\gcd(m,n)=1$ then $(1,1)$ has order $\lcm(m,n)=mn$, so
$Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z=\langle (1,1)\rangle$ is cyclic of order $mn$, hence $\congZ/(mn)Z$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z\congZ/(mn)Z$ it is cyclic of order $mn$, so it has
an element of order $mn$; but every element has order dividing $\lcm(m,n)$, forcing
$\lcm(m,n)=mn$, i.e.\ $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The general statement follows by induction on $k$, since
$Z/(m_1)Z\times\cdots\timesZ/(m_k)Z$ is cyclic iff the orders of the standard generators
combine to an element of order $m_1\cdots m_k$, which happens iff the $m_i$ are pairwise
coprime.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Is $Z/(m_1)Z\times\cdots\timesZ/(m_k)Z$ cyclic?
Content:
\begin{method}{Is $Z/(m_1)Z\times\cdots\timesZ/(m_k)Z$ cyclic?}
Trigger. A product of cyclic groups; you must decide if it is cyclic, or identify it
as some $Z/(N)Z$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute $E=\lcm(m_1,\dots,m_k)$ and $N=m_1\cdots m_k$ (the group order).
\item Cyclic \Longleftrightarrow\ $E=N$ \Longleftrightarrow\ the $m_i$ are pairwise coprime. If so, the group
$\congZ/(N)Z$ and $(1,\dots,1)$ is a generator.
\item If $E<N$ the group is not cyclic; the maximum element order is $E$.
\end{enumerate}
Pairwise coprime is essential: $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ has $\lcm=6<18$, not
cyclic, even though $\gcd(2,3)=1$.
\end{method}

Title: $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$ but $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\not\congZ/(4)Z$ (D\&F)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$ but $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\not\congZ/(4)Z$ (D\&F)}
Problem. Show $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$ while $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\not\congZ/(4)Z$.
\wrec Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c5] : cyclic \Longleftrightarrow\ coordinate moduli coprime; compare $\lcm$ with the
group order.
\wsol For $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$: $\gcd(2,3)=1$, so $(1,1)$ has order $\lcm(2,3)=6=\ord{Z/(2)Z\times
Z/(3)Z}$, making the group cyclic, hence $\congZ/(6)Z$. Check. List multiples of $(1,1)$:
$(1,1),(0,2),(1,0),(0,1),(1,2),(0,0)$ --- six distinct elements, so $(1,1)$ generates.\\
For $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$: $\gcd(2,2)=2\ne1$, so $\lcm(2,2)=2<4$. Every nonidentity element
$(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ has order $2$, so there is no element of order $4$ and the group cannot be
cyclic; thus $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\not\congZ/(4)Z$ (this is the Klein four-group $V_4$). Check.
$Z/(4)Z$ has the element $1$ of order $4$, which $V_4$ lacks, so they are not isomorphic.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Is $Z/(6)Z\timesZ/(10)Z$ cyclic?
Content:
\begin{wex}{Is $Z/(6)Z\timesZ/(10)Z$ cyclic?}
Problem. Decide whether $Z/(6)Z\timesZ/(10)Z$ is cyclic, and find its maximum element order.
\wrec Cyclic \Longleftrightarrow\ moduli coprime; otherwise the max order is $\lcm$, strictly below the group
order.
\wsol $\gcd(6,10)=2\ne1$, so by Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c5] the group is not cyclic. The
group order is $6\cdot10=60$, but the maximum element order is
$E=\lcm(6,10)=\dfrac{6\cdot10}{\gcd(6,10)}=\dfrac{60}{2}=30$. Check. $(1,1)$ has order
$\lcm(6,10)=30\ne60$, so it is not a generator; since the exponent $30<60$, no element
generates. (As a sanity decomposition, $Z/(6)Z\timesZ/(10)Z\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\times
Z/(5)Z\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(30)Z$, which visibly is not cyclic because of the repeated factor $2$.)
\end{wex}

group order is $6\cdot10=60$, but the maximum element order is

Title: Three-factor CRT: $Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(5)Z\congZ/(60)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Three-factor CRT: $Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(5)Z\congZ/(60)Z$}
Problem. Show $Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(5)Z$ is cyclic and identify it.
\wrec Pairwise-coprime moduli $\Longrightarrow$ cyclic of order their product.
\wsol Check pairwise: $\gcd(3,4)=\gcd(3,5)=\gcd(4,5)=1$. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c5] the product
is cyclic of order $3\cdot4\cdot5=60$, so $\congZ/(60)Z$, with generator $(1,1,1)$.
Check. $\ord{(1,1,1)}=\lcm(3,4,5)=60=\ord{group}$, confirming $(1,1,1)$
generates and the group is $Z/(60)Z$.
\end{wex}

Problem. Show $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic and identify it.
\wrec Pairwise-coprime moduli $\Longrightarrow$ cyclic of order their product.
\wsol Check pairwise: $\gcd(3,4)=\gcd(3,5)=\gcd(4,5)=1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:crt@c5} the product

Title: A non-pairwise-coprime trap
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-pairwise-coprime trap}
Problem. Is $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ isomorphic to $Z/(24)Z$?
\wrec Apply CRT: $\congZ/(24)Z$ would require an element of order $24$.
\wsol $\gcd(4,6)=2\ne1$, so $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ is not cyclic; its maximum element order
is $\lcm(4,6)=12<24$. Hence $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\not\congZ/(24)Z$. Check. We already saw
$(1,1)$ has order $12$; since $12$ is the exponent, no element reaches $24$. (Refining:
$Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z\congZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\congZ/(12)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$, invariant factors
$2\mid12$.)
\end{wex}

\wsol $\gcd(4,6)=2\ne1$, so $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} cyclic; its maximum element order

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Direct Products > The Chinese remainder theorem for cyclic groups
Type: example
Title: $Z\timesZ$ is not cyclic
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z\timesZ$ is not cyclic}
Problem. Prove the infinite group $Z\timesZ$ (under coordinatewise addition) is not cyclic.
\wrec A cyclic group is generated by one element; show a single element cannot reach both
$(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
\wsol Suppose $Z\timesZ=\langle (a,b)\rangle$ for some $(a,b)$. Then every element is an integer
multiple $k\,(a,b)=(ka,kb)$. To get $(1,0)$ we need $kb=0$ with $ka=1$; from $ka=1$ we have
$k\ne0$, so $b=0$. With $b=0$ every element is $(ka,0)$, whose second coordinate is always
$0$, so $(0,1)$ can never be reached. So no single element generates: $Z\timesZ$ is not
cyclic. Check. Equivalently, a cyclic group is generated by one element and (if
infinite) is $\congZ$, which has rank $1$; but $Z\timesZ$ needs the two independent
generators $(1,0),(0,1)$ (rank $2$), so it cannot be $\congZ$. Concretely $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$
cannot both be expressed as multiples of a common $(a,b)$.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ is not cyclic}
Problem. Prove the infinite group $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ (under coordinatewise addition) is not cyclic.
\wrec A cyclic group is generated by one element; show a single element cannot reach both
$(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
\wsol Suppose $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}=\langle (a,b)\rangle$ for some $(a,b)$. Then every element is an integer
multiple $k\,(a,b)=(ka,kb)$. To get $(1,0)$ we need $kb=0$ with $ka=1$; from $ka=1$ we have
$k\ne0$, so $b=0$. With $b=0$ every element is $(ka,0)$, whose second coordinate is always
$0$, so $(0,1)$ can never be reached. So no single element generates: $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ is not
cyclic. \textit{Check.} Equivalently, a cyclic group is generated by one element and (if
infinite) is $\cong\mathbb{Z}$, which has rank $1$; but $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ needs the two independent
generators $(1,0),(0,1)$ (rank $2$), so it cannot be $\cong\mathbb{Z}$. Concretely $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$
cannot both be expressed as multiples of a common $(a,b)$.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: Canonical projections and injections
Label: def:proj-inj@c5
Content:
\begin{definition}[Canonical projections and injections] 
For $G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_n$ define, for each $i$, the $i$-th projection
$\pi_i:G\to G_i$ and the $i$-th injection $\iota_i:G_i\to G$ by
\[
\pi_i(g_1,\dots,g_n)=g_i,\qquad
\iota_i(g)=(1_1,\dots,1_{i-1},\,g,\,1_{i+1},\dots,1_n).
\]
Each $\pi_i$ is a surjective homomorphism with
$\ker\pi_i=\{(g_1,\dots,g_n)\st g_i=1_i\}\cong\prod_{j\ne i}G_j$, and each $\iota_i$ is an
injective homomorphism. The images $\widehat G_i:=\iota_i(G_i)\nor G$ are normal, pairwise
commuting, and generate $G$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[$\pi_i,\iota_i$ are homomorphisms]
With notation as above, $\pi_i$ and $\iota_i$ are group homomorphisms; $\pi_i$ is onto and
$\iota_i$ is one-to-one; and $\pi_i\circ\iota_i=\id_{G_i}$ while $\pi_j\circ\iota_i$ is the

Title: Universal property of the direct product
Label: thm:up@c5
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Universal property of the direct product] 
Let $G_1,\dots,G_n$ be groups and $G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_n$ with projections $\pi_i$.
For every group $T$ and every family of homomorphisms $f_i:T\to G_i$ ($1\le i\le n$), there
is a unique homomorphism $\varphi:T\to G$ with $\pi_i\circ\varphi=f_i$ for all $i$,
namely
\[
\varphi(t)=\bigl(f_1(t),\,f_2(t),\,\dots,\,f_n(t)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Direct Products > Projections, injections, and the universal property
Type: prose
Content:
For two factors the universal property is the commuting triangle: a map into $A\times B$ is
the same data as a pair of maps, one into each factor.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & T \arrow[dl, "f"'] \arrow[dr, "g"] \arrow[d, dashed, "{(f,g)}"] & \\
A & A\times B \arrow[l, two heads, "\pi_1"] \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi_2"'] & B
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The dashed arrow $(f,g)$ is the unique homomorphism making both triangles commute:
$\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$ and $\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$.

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes. $T$ is any group (the ``test'' source). $A$ and $B$ are the two
 factor groups. $A\times B$ is their external direct product, which sits in the middle of the
 bottom row.
\dgi{Arrows:} $f:T\to A$ and $g:T\to B$ are any two group homomorphisms (solid diagonal
 arrows). $\pi_1:A\times B\to A$ and $\pi_2:A\times B\to B$ are the canonical projections
 (solid horizontal arrows), defined by $\pi_1(a,b)=a$ and $\pi_2(a,b)=b$. The dashed
 vertical arrow $(f,g):T\to A\times B$ is the induced homomorphism, defined by
 $(f,g)(t)=(f(t),g(t))$; it is dashed to signal that it is the map whose existence and
 uniqueness the universal property asserts.
\dgi{What commutes:} Two triangles must commute simultaneously:
 $\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$ (left triangle: $T\to A\times B\to A$ equals $T\to A$) and
 $\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$ (right triangle: $T\to A\times B\to B$ equals $T\to B$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic $t\in T$. Along the left path:
 $(f,g)(t)=(f(t),g(t))$, then $\pi_1$ extracts the first coordinate, giving $f(t)$. Along
 the direct path $f(t)$ arrives at the same value. Right triangle: $\pi_2(f(t),g(t))=g(t)$,
 matching $g(t)$ directly. Both equalities hold by definition of $(f,g)$; no coset
 representative ambiguity arises because $(f,g)$ maps group elements, not cosets.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the pay-off of the universal property theorem
 proved just above. It encodes the slogan ``a map into $A\times B$ is exactly the
 same data as a pair of maps, one into each factor''. The theorem proves existence and
 uniqueness of the dashed arrow; the diagram organizes all four maps and their two
 commutativity conditions at a glance, replacing two equations with one picture.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $T=Z$, $f:Z\toZ/(4)Z$ the reduction mod $4$, and
 $g:Z\toZ/(6)Z$ the reduction mod $6$. Then $(f,g):Z\toZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ sends
 $k\mapsto(k\bmod 4,\,k\bmod 6)$. Check: $\pi_1((f,g)(5))=\pi_1(1,5)=1=5\bmod 4=f(5)$,
 and $\pi_2((f,g)(5))=5=5\bmod 6=g(5)$. Both triangles commute for every $k$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think the dashed arrow $(f,g)$ is determined only
 up to choice, or that it might not exist. The universal property guarantees both
 existence and uniqueness: there is exactly one homomorphism $T\to A\times B$ whose
 projections are $f$ and $g$. Also, do not confuse this ``into-product'' property with a
 dual ``out-of-product'' property: a homomorphism $A\times B\to T$ is determined by its
 restrictions to $A$ and $B$, but a given pair of homomorphisms $A\to T$, $B\to T$ extends to
 such a homomorphism only when their images commute elementwise in $T$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that giving a single homomorphism into a direct
 product is equivalent to independently giving one homomorphism into each factor, with the
 projections recovering the factors automatically.
\end{dgx}

Type: method
Title: Mapping into a product
Content:
\begin{method}{Mapping into a product}
Trigger. You must build (or recognize the unique) homomorphism $T\to G_1\times\cdots
\times G_n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Specify the coordinate maps $f_i=\pi_i\circ\varphi:T\to G_i$ separately; each may be any
homomorphism.
\item Assemble $\varphi=(f_1,\dots,f_n)$. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:up@c5] this is the only map with
those projections.
\item Kernel: $\ker\varphi=\bigcap_i\ker f_i$, since $\varphi(t)=1\Longleftrightarrow f_i(t)=1$ for all $i$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Direct Products > Projections, injections, and the universal property
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The universal property characterizes maps into a product via projections, not maps
out of it. A homomorphism $A\times B\to T$ is determined by its restrictions to $A$
and $B$, but a pair of homomorphisms $A\to T$, $B\to T$ need not come from any homomorphism
$A\times B\to T$: it does exactly when the two images commute elementwise in $T$. (The ``co-universal'' picture
with injections and coproducts works cleanly only for abelian groups.)
\end{pitfall}
