Title: $D_{12}\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$D_{12}\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z$}
Show the order-$12$ dihedral group factors as $D_{12}\cong D_6\timesZ/(2)Z\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z$, and count its involutions.
\wrec $D_{12}$ has central element $r^3$ of order $2$; quotient out to get $D_6$.
\wsol $D_{12}=\langle r,s\st r^6=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$. The element $z=r^3$ is central ($r^3 s=s r^{-3}=sr^3$ since $r^6=1$) of order $2$, with $\langle z\rangle\cap\langle r^2,s\rangle=1$ and $\langle r^2,s\rangle\cong D_6=S_3$. So $D_{12}\cong\langle r^2,s\rangle\times\langle r^3\rangle\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z$. \\
Involutions: the six reflections $r^k s$ ($k=0,\dots,5$) plus $r^3$: seven elements of order $2$. \\
Check. $(r^k s)^2=r^k s r^k s=r^k r^{-k}s^2=1$ for all $k$ (six involutions); $(r^3)^2=r^6=1$ (one more). Total $7$, matching the table. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Triage drill: a nonabelian order-$12$ group}
A nonabelian group $G$ of order $12$ has a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup, exactly one element of order $2$, and an element of order $4$. Identify $G$.
\wrec Run the order-$12$ method box: unique involution $+$ order-$4$ element pins it down.
\wsol Normal Sylow $3$-subgroup rules out $A_4$ ($n_3=4$). A unique involution rules out $D_{12}$ (seven) and $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$ (three); $Z/(12)Z$, which also has a unique involution, is excluded because $G$ is nonabelian. The only candidate with $\#\,\ord2=1$ and an order-$4$ element is $Dic_3=Z/(3)Z\sdpZ/(4)Z$. So $G\congDic_3$. \\
Check. Consistency -- $Dic_3$ has element orders $\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, a unique involution $b^2$, and $n_3=1$. All three given properties hold. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Groups of Small Order > Diagrams: the split exact sequence and the order-$12$ trichotomy
Type: prose
Part: 1/3
Content:
Every group of order $2p$, $pq$ (nonabelian case), or $12$ (nonabelian) arises as a (semi)direct product, hence sits in a split short exact sequence with a normal Sylow subgroup as kernel; so does $D_8=\langle r\rangle\sdp\langle s\rangle$, with kernel $\langle r\rangle$. The exception is $Q_8$: every nontrivial subgroup of $Q_8$ contains $-1$, so $Q_8$ is not a semidirect product of proper subgroups (it is a non-split extension). The split sequence is:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook] & H\sdp K \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[l, bend right=40, "s"'] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five nodes from left to right: the trivial group $1$; the normal subgroup $H$ (the normal Sylow $p$-subgroup, e.g.\ $Z/(q)Z$ when $|G|=pq$); the semidirect product $H\sdp K$ (the full group $G$); the complement $K$ (a Sylow subgroup of complementary order); and the trivial group $1$ again on the far right. Together they form a short exact sequence.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost arrow $1\to H$ is the zero map (inclusion of the identity). The hooked arrow $H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K$ is the canonical inclusion $h\mapsto(h,1_K)$, injective by definition. The two-headed arrow $H\sdp K\xrightarrow{\pi} K$ is the projection $\pi(h,k)=k$, surjective with kernel exactly $H$. The rightmost arrow $K\to 1$ sends everything to the identity. The bent arrow $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$ is the splitting: $s(k)=(1_H,k)$, a group homomorphism satisfying $\pi\circ s=\id_K$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The sequence is exact: $\im(1\to H)=1=\ker(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)$ (trivially); $\im(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)=H=\ker(\pi)$ (this is the key exactness); $\im(\pi)=K=\ker(K\to 1)$. The splitting condition: $\pi\circ s=\id_K$, i.e.\ $\pi(1_H,k)=k$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a coset representative: $\ker\pi=\{(h,k)\in H\sdp K : k=1_K\}=H\times\{1_K\}$, which is exactly the image of the inclusion $h\mapsto(h,1_K)$. The splitting $s(k)=(1_H,k)$ is a homomorphism because the multiplication in $H\sdp K$ restricts on $\{1_H\}\times K$ to the group law of $K$. The condition $\pi(s(k))=\pi(1_H,k)=k$ holds by definition of $\pi$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} Every semidirect product $H\sdp K$ that appears in the classification of groups of small order -- $D_{2p}$, $Z/(q)Z\sdpZ/(p)Z$, $D_8$, $A_4$, $D_{12}$, $Dic_3$ (but not $Q_8$, which is not a semidirect product of proper subgroups) -- sits in exactly such a sequence. The diagram encodes in one picture why $H\sdp K$ is determined up to isomorphism by the conjugation action $\varphi\colon K\to\Aut(H)$: the splitting $s$ records the embedding of $K$ back into $G$, and the only freedom is how $K$ acts on $H$ by conjugation via $s$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $G=S_3\congZ/(3)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$: $H=Z/(3)Z=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$, $K=Z/(2)Z=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$, $\pi$ sends each permutation to its coset mod $H$, and $s$ embeds $(1\,2)$ back as $(1\,2)\in S_3$. Exactness: $\ker\pi=\{1,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}=H$. The splitting: $\pi(s((1\,2)))=\pi((1\,2))=(1\,2)\in K$. \checkmark
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The bent arrow $s$ is a section of $\pi$ (a right inverse), not a section of the inclusion. Students sometimes think $s$ splits the sequence ``on the left'' and write $s\circ\iota=\id_H$; that is false -- $s$ goes $K\to H\sdp K$, not back to $H$. The correct condition is only $\pi\circ s=\id_K$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that every (semi)direct product is precisely a short exact sequence equipped with a group-homomorphism section, and the isomorphism type of the whole group is determined by how the section's image acts on the normal subgroup.
\end{dgx}
Here $H$ is the normal Sylow subgroup, $K$ a complement (Sylow subgroup of complementary order), $s$ the splitting, and the isomorphism type is fixed by $\varphi=\,$``conjugation'' $\colon K\to\Aut(H)$. A direct product is the special case $\varphi$ trivial, where the second projection also splits and both factors are normal:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & G \arrow[dl, two heads, "\pi_1"'] \arrow[dr, two heads, "\pi_2"] \arrow[d, "{=}", dashed] & \\
H & H\times K \arrow[l, two heads, "p_1"] \arrow[r, two heads, "p_2"'] & K
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes: $G$ at the top (a group abstractly given or arrived at via the classification argument); $H$ at the lower-left (a normal subgroup of $G$, the normal Sylow subgroup in the classification); $K$ at the lower-right (the complementary subgroup, also normal in the direct-product case); and $H\times K$ at the center bottom (the direct product, serving as the ``canonical model'' the diagram identifies $G$ with).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi_1\colon G\to H$ and $\pi_2\colon G\to K$ are the two group homomorphisms from $G$ to each factor. $p_1\colon H\times K\to H$ and $p_2\colon H\times K\to K$ are the standard coordinate projections, $p_1(h,k)=h$, $p_2(h,k)=k$. The dashed arrow $G\to H\times K$ (labelled $=$) is the canonical isomorphism $g\mapsto(\pi_1(g),\pi_2(g))$; it exists because both $H$ and $K$ are normal in $G$ with $H\cap K=1$ and $HK=G$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The left triangle: $p_1\circ(=)=\pi_1$. The right triangle: $p_2\circ(=)=\pi_2$. Concretely, for any $g\in G$ written uniquely as $g=hk$ with $h\in H,k\in K$: $p_1(h,k)=h=\pi_1(g)$ and $p_2(h,k)=k=\pi_2(g)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of the isomorphism $g\mapsto(\pi_1(g),\pi_2(g))$ rests on $H\cap K=1$ (so the decomposition $g=hk$ is unique) and $HK=G$ (so every $g$ decomposes). Commutativity of the triangles is then definitional: $\pi_1(g)$ is the $H$-component of $g$, and $p_1$ reads that component from the pair.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram distinguishes the direct product case ($\varphi$ trivial, both factors normal) from the strict semidirect product.

Every group of order $2p$, $pq$ (nonabelian case), or $12$ (nonabelian) arises as a (semi)direct product, hence sits in a \emph{split} short exact sequence with a normal Sylow subgroup as kernel; so does $D_8=\langle r\rangle\sdp\langle s\rangle$, with kernel $\langle r\rangle$. The exception is $Q_8$: every nontrivial subgroup of $Q_8$ contains $-1$, so $Q_8$ is not a semidirect product of proper subgroups (it is a non-split extension). The split sequence is:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook] & H\sdp K \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[l, bend right=40, "s"'] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five nodes from left to right: the trivial group $1$; the normal subgroup $H$ (the normal Sylow $p$-subgroup, e.g.\ $\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}$ when $|G|=pq$); the semidirect product $H\sdp K$ (the full group $G$); the complement $K$ (a Sylow subgroup of complementary order); and the trivial group $1$ again on the far right. Together they form a short exact sequence.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost arrow $1\to H$ is the zero map (inclusion of the identity). The hooked arrow $H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K$ is the canonical inclusion $h\mapsto(h,1_K)$, injective by definition. The two-headed arrow $H\sdp K\xrightarrow{\pi} K$ is the projection $\pi(h,k)=k$, surjective with kernel exactly $H$. The rightmost arrow $K\to 1$ sends everything to the identity. The bent arrow $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$ is the splitting: $s(k)=(1_H,k)$, a group homomorphism satisfying $\pi\circ s=\id_K$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The sequence is exact: $\im(1\to H)=1=\ker(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)$ (trivially); $\im(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)=H=\ker(\pi)$ (this is the key exactness); $\im(\pi)=K=\ker(K\to 1)$. The splitting condition: $\pi\circ s=\id_K$, i.e.\ $\pi(1_H,k)=k$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a coset representative: $\ker\pi=\{(h,k)\in H\sdp K : k=1_K\}=H\times\{1_K\}$, which is exactly the image of the inclusion $h\mapsto(h,1_K)$. The splitting $s(k)=(1_H,k)$ is a homomorphism because the multiplication in $H\sdp K$ restricts on $\{1_H\}\times K$ to the group law of $K$. The condition $\pi(s(k))=\pi(1_H,k)=k$ holds by definition of $\pi$.

Exactness: $\ker\pi=\{1,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}=H$. The splitting: $\pi(s((1\,2)))=\pi((1\,2))=(1\,2)\in K$. \checkmark
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The bent arrow $s$ is a section of $\pi$ (a right inverse), not a section of the inclusion. Students sometimes think $s$ splits the sequence ``on the left'' and write $s\circ\iota=\id_H$; that is false -- $s$ goes $K\to H\sdp K$, not back to $H$. The correct condition is only $\pi\circ s=\id_K$.

\end{dgx}
Here $H$ is the normal Sylow subgroup, $K$ a complement (Sylow subgroup of complementary order), $s$ the splitting, and the isomorphism type is fixed by $\varphi=\,$``conjugation'' $\colon K\to\Aut(H)$. A \emph{direct} product is the special case $\varphi$ trivial, where the second projection also splits and both factors are normal:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]

H & H\times K \arrow[l, two heads, "p_1"] \arrow[r, two heads, "p_2"'] & K
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes: $G$ at the top (a group abstractly given or arrived at via the classification argument); $H$ at the lower-left (a normal subgroup of $G$, the normal Sylow subgroup in the classification); $K$ at the lower-right (the complementary subgroup, also normal in the direct-product case); and $H\times K$ at the center bottom (the direct product, serving as the ``canonical model'' the diagram identifies $G$ with).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi_1\colon G\to H$ and $\pi_2\colon G\to K$ are the two group homomorphisms from $G$ to each factor. $p_1\colon H\times K\to H$ and $p_2\colon H\times K\to K$ are the standard coordinate projections, $p_1(h,k)=h$, $p_2(h,k)=k$. \dgi{What commutes:} The left triangle: $p_1\circ(=)=\pi_1$. The right triangle: $p_2\circ(=)=\pi_2$. Concretely, for any $g\in G$ written uniquely as $g=hk$ with $h\in H,k\in K$: $p_1(h,k)=h=\pi_1(g)$ and $p_2(h,k)=k=\pi_2(g)$.

Commutativity of the triangles is then definitional: $\pi_1(g)$ \emph{is} the $H$-component of $g$, and $p_1$ reads that component from the pair.

The nonabelian groups of order $12$ are exactly the three nontrivial $(H,K,\varphi)$ data:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=huge]
& Z/(3)Z\sdp_{\varphi}Z/(4)Z = Dic_3 \\
(normal P_3) \arrow[ur, "{K=Z/(4)Z}"] \arrow[r, "{K=Z/(2)Z^2}"'] & Z/(3)Z\sdp_{\varphi}Z/(2)Z^2 \cong D_{12} \\
(normal P_2=Z/(2)Z^2) \arrow[r, "{K=Z/(3)Z}"'] & Z/(2)Z^2\sdp_{\varphi}Z/(3)Z \cong A_4
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two source nodes on the left (classification data): ``(normal $P_3$)'' stands for the datum that the Sylow $3$-subgroup $P_3\congZ/(3)Z$ is normal in $G$, giving $H=Z/(3)Z$ in $H\sdp K$; this single node sends two arrows (to the upper and middle targets), one for each choice of complement $K$. The bottom-left source ``(normal $P_2=Z/(2)Z^2$)'' is the datum that instead the Sylow $2$-subgroup $P_2\congZ/(2)Z^2$ is normal ($n_3=4$ forces this). Three target nodes on the right: $Dic_3=Z/(3)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z$, $D_{12}\congZ/(3)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z^2$, and $A_4\congZ/(2)Z^2\sdp_\varphiZ/(3)Z$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each arrow is labelled by the complement $K$ chosen; the arrow records the assignment $(H,K,\varphi)\mapsto H\sdp_\varphi K$. Upper arrow from ``(normal $P_3$)'': complement $K=Z/(4)Z$, unique nontrivial action $Z/(4)Z\to\Aut(Z/(3)Z)\congZ/(2)Z$ (via the order-$2$ quotient), yields $Dic_3$. Middle arrow: complement $K=Z/(2)Z^2$, a nontrivial action (there are three, one for each kernel of order $2$ in $Z/(2)Z^2$, and all three give isomorphic groups), yields $D_{12}$. Bottom arrow: $H=Z/(2)Z^2$ normal, complement $K=Z/(3)Z$ acting by an order-$3$ automorphism permuting the three involutions cyclically, yields $A_4$.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is not a commutative diagram in the path-equality sense; it is a classification map. Each arrow is injective on isomorphism classes: distinct $(H,K,\varphi)$ triples in the diagram produce non-isomorphic groups (verified by the invariants in the method box: involution count $1, 7, 3$ and $n_3=1,1,4$ respectively). No two arrows point to the same group.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of each arrow -- i.e.\ that the semidirect product $H\sdp_\varphi K$ is a group of order $12$ -- follows from $|H||K|=3\cdot4=12$ or $4\cdot3=12$, and that the action $\varphi$ is a genuine group homomorphism. For $Dic_3$: $\varphi\colonZ/(4)Z\to\Aut(Z/(3)Z)$ factors through $Z/(4)Z\toZ/(4)Z/\langle b^2\rangle\congZ/(2)Z\cong\Aut(Z/(3)Z)$, well-defined since $\langle b^2\rangle$ is the kernel. For $A_4$: $\varphi\colonZ/(3)Z\to\Aut(Z/(2)Z^2)$ sends the generator to the $3$-cycle $(a\,b\,ab)$ on the three involutions; this is a homomorphism since that $3$-cycle has order $3$ in $\Aut(Z/(2)Z^2)\cong S_3$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The proof that $g(12)=5$ (three nonabelian classes) reduces to showing that the three arrows in this diagram hit distinct and exhaustive targets. Exhaustiveness comes from the Sylow argument: either $P_3\nor G$ ($n_3=1$, two choices of $K$) or $P_2\nor G$ ($n_3=4$, one choice). Distinctness comes from the invariants. The diagram makes both halves of the argument visible simultaneously.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Follow the middle arrow: $H=Z/(3)Z=\langle a\rangle$, $K=Z/(2)Z^2=\langle s,t\rangle$ with $s$ acting by inversion ($sas^{-1}=a^{-1}$) and $t$ acting trivially. Then $G\cong D_6\timesZ/(2)Z\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z\cong D_{12}$, the dihedral group of order $12$ (symmetries of the regular hexagon). The seven involutions are $r^k s$ ($k=0,\dots,5$) and $r^3$, confirming the middle target.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The two left-hand sources ``(normal $P_3$)'' and ``(normal $P_2$)'' are mutually exclusive outcomes of Sylow theory, not two choices available simultaneously. Students sometimes think they can mix the data (e.g.\ take $H=Z/(3)Z$ normal and $P_2$ normal with a nontrivial action), but if $P_3$ is not normal ($n_3=4$) then the counting argument forces $P_2\nor G$ uniquely; there is no fourth nonabelian case.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the three nonabelian groups of order $12$ are in bijection with the three nontrivial choices of normal Sylow subgroup and nontrivial complement-action, making the exhaustiveness and distinctness of the classification visible in a single picture.
\end{dgx}

\begin{pitfall}
A semidirect product $H\sdp K$ collapsing to a direct product (or to a smaller-looking group) is common: $Z/(3)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z=S_3$, and $Z/(3)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z^2\cong D_{12}\cong S_3\timesZ/(2)Z$ -- but $D_{12}\not\congZ/(3)Z\sdpZ/(4)Z=Dic_3$ even though both are ``$Z/(3)Z\sdp$ (order-$4$ group)''. The group $K$ and the action $\varphi$ both matter: $Z/(4)Z$ vs.\ $Z/(2)Z^2$ as the complement gives genuinely different groups. Always record the full datum $(H,K,\varphi)$, never just $|H|$ and $|K|$.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Classify all groups of order $51$ and all groups of order $55$, and state $g(51)$ and $g(55)$. (Each is a product of two distinct primes; apply the $p\mid q-1$ test, and note one case yields a nonabelian group while the other does not.)
\item Classify all groups of order $26$ directly: produce $r$ of order $13$ and $s$ of order $2$, show $\langle r\rangle\nor G$ via Sylow ($n_{13}\mid 2$, $n_{13}\equiv 1\,(13)$), and use $srs^{-1}\in\{r,r^{-1}\}$ to recover the two classes $Z/(26)Z$ and $D_{26}$.
\item Show the two abelian groups of order $12$ are $Z/(12)Z$ and $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(6)Z$, and separate them by their element-order spectra. Which has an element of order $12$? What is the exponent of the other, and how many generators does $Z/(12)Z$ have?
\item Distinguish the three abelian groups of order $8$ by counting involutions: verify $Z/(8)Z$, $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$, $Z/(2)Z^3$ have $1,3,7$ elements of order $2$ respectively. (For contrast, record the involution counts of the nonabelian $D_8$ and $Q_8$ as well.)
\item Let $|G|=12$ with $G$ nonabelian and $n_3=4$. Show $G\cong A_4$: count the elements of order $3$ forced by $n_3=4$, deduce that the remaining elements form the unique (normal) Sylow $2$-subgroup $V_4$, and identify $G\cong V_4\sdpZ/(3)Z$.
\item Let $|G|=2p$ with $p$ an odd prime. Prove that exactly two isomorphism classes exist by counting involutions in $\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$: the Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal, $\Aut(Z/(p)Z)\congZ/((p-1))Z$ has a unique element of order $2$, so the order-$2$ action is either trivial ($\LongrightarrowZ/(2p)Z$) or inversion ($\Longrightarrow D_{2p}$), with no third possibility.
\item Determine $g(13)$, $g(14)$, and $g(15)$, justifying each with one line (prime; $2p$; $pq$ with $p\nmid q-1$). Confirm your answers against the census table.
\item The dicyclic group $Dic_3$ has order $12$. Give a presentation, list its element-order spectrum, and locate the unique involution inside the presentation. Explain why, like $Q_8$, it has exactly one element of order $2$. (Compare: $Q_8$ is the order-$8$ dicyclic group.)
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Classify all groups of order $18$ up to isomorphism and compute $g(18)$. (Show the Sylow $3$-subgroup of order $9$ is normal, then analyze the action of $Z/(2)Z$ on each of $Z/(9)Z$ and $Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$; account for both abelian types and the three nonabelian ones, including $Z/(3)Z\times\Sym_3$ and the generalized dihedral $(Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(3)Z)\sdpZ/(2)Z$.)
\item Prove that every group of order $45$ is abelian and identify the two isomorphism classes. (Use Sylow to show both Sylow subgroups are normal and coprime, so $G\cong P_3\times P_5$; then classify $P_3$ of order $9$.)
\item Determine which orders $d\mid 12$ are realized as $|H|$ for some subgroup $H\sgr A_4$, and show $d=6$ is the unique missing divisor (a subgroup of index $2$ would be normal and contain every square, but the eight $3$-cycles are squares, $\sigma=(\sigma^2)^2$, giving more than $6$ elements). Specialize to list the abelian groups of orders $8$ and $27$.
\item Separate $D_8$ from $Q_8$ by counting Klein four-subgroups: show $D_8$ has exactly two subgroups isomorphic to $V_4$ while $Q_8$ has none (all three of $Q_8$'s order-$4$ subgroups, $\langle i\rangle,\langle j\rangle,\langle k\rangle$, are cyclic). Note that this distinguishes them even though both have $|Z|=2$ and $G/Z\cong V_4$; relate it to the involution counts ($5$ in $D_8$, $1$ in $Q_8$).
\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
This section develops two tightly linked ideas from Dummit \& Foote, Section 5.4. First, the
commutator $[x,y]=x^{-1} y^{-1} xy$ measures the failure of $x$ and $y$ to commute, and
the subgroup $G'=\langle [x,y]\st x,y\in G\rangle$ it generates is the smallest normal subgroup with
abelian quotient. Second, the recognition theorem for internal direct products gives a
clean checklist for asserting $G\cong H\times K$ from inside $G$.

Type: definition
Title: Commutator and commutator subgroup
Content:
\begin{definition}[Commutator and commutator subgroup]
For $x,y\in G$ define the commutator
\[
[x,y] \;=\; x^{-1} y^{-1} xy.
\]
For subgroups (or subsets) $A,B\le G$ define
\[
[A,B] \;=\; \langle \,[a,b]\st a\in A,\ b\in B\,\rangle.
\]
The commutator subgroup of $G$ is $G'=[G,G]=\langle \,[x,y]\st x,y\in G\,\rangle$.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Two algebraic identities are used constantly and follow by direct computation:
\[
xy \;=\; yx\,[x,y], \qquad\quad [x,y]^{-1} \;=\; [y,x].
\]
For the first, $yx\,[x,y]=yx\,x^{-1} y^{-1} xy = y\,y^{-1} xy = xy$. For the second,
$[x,y]^{-1}=(x^{-1} y^{-1} xy)^{-1} = y^{-1} x^{-1} y x = [y,x]$. Thus $[x,y]=1\Longleftrightarrow xy=yx$:
a commutator is trivial exactly when its two arguments commute.
\end{remark}

Type: proposition
Title: Basic properties of $G'$; D\&F 5.4, Prop.\ 7
Label: prop:commutator@c5
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Basic properties of $G'$; D\&F 5.4, Prop.\ 7] 
Let $G$ be a group, $G'=[G,G]$, and let $H\nor G$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $G'\pnor G$, and in fact $G'$ is characteristic in $G$; the quotient
$G/G'$ is abelian.
\item[(2)] $G/H$ is abelian $\Longleftrightarrow G'\le H$. ($G'$ is the smallest normal subgroup with
abelian quotient.)
\item[(3)] If $\varphi\colon G\to A$ is a homomorphism with $A$ abelian, then $G'\le\ker\varphi$,
so $\varphi$ factors through $G/G'$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
label: prop:commutator@c5

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-3fbf71f249b07a7f724f
Content:
\begin{proof}
(1) For any automorphism $\sigma\in\Aut(G)$ and any commutator,
$\sigma([x,y])=\sigma(x^{-1} y^{-1} xy)=\sigma(x)^{-1}\sigma(y)^{-1}\sigma(x)\sigma(y)=[\sigma(x),\sigma(y)]\in G'$.
Since $\sigma$ carries the generating set $\{[x,y]\}$ into itself, $\sigma(G')\le G'$; applying the
same to $\sigma^{-1}$ gives $\sigma(G')=G'$. Hence $G'$ is
characteristic, and in particular invariant under every inner automorphism, so $G'\pnor G$.
For the quotient, in $G/G'$ we have $\overline{x}\,\overline{y}=\overline{xy}=\overline{yx\,[x,y]}
=\overline{yx}\;\overline{[x,y]}=\overline{yx}$ because $[x,y]\in G'$ maps to $\overline{1}$. Thus
$G/G'$ is abelian.

(2) ($\Leftarrow$) If $G'\le H$ then $G/H$ is a quotient of the abelian group $G/G'$
(by the third isomorphism theorem $G/H\cong (G/G')/(H/G')$), hence abelian.
($\Rightarrow$) If $G/H$ is abelian then for all $x,y$, $\overline{x}\,\overline{y}=\overline{y}\,\overline{x}$
in $G/H$, i.e.\ $\overline{[x,y]}=\overline{x^{-1} y^{-1} xy}=\overline{1}$, so $[x,y]\in H$. As the
$[x,y]$ generate $G'$, we get $G'\le H$.

(3) Apply (2) with $H=\ker\varphi$: since $G/\ker\varphi\cong\im\varphi\le A$ is abelian,
$G'\le\ker\varphi$. The factoring through $G/G'$ is the universal property of the quotient.
\end{proof}

Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Recognizing Direct Products > Commutators, the commutator subgroup, and internal direct products
Type: method
Title: Computing $G'=[G,G]$
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $G'=[G,G]$}
Trigger. You are asked for the commutator subgroup, the abelianization $G/G'$, or to
test whether $G$ is abelian / find the smallest normal subgroup with abelian quotient.

Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Pick generators $g_1,\dots,g_m$ of $G$. It suffices to compute the commutators
$[g_i,g_j]$ of generators (every commutator is a product of conjugates of these and their inverses).
\item Let $N=\langle [g_i,g_j]\rangle^{G}$ be the normal closure. Since $G'\nor G$ contains every $[g_i,g_j]$,
$N\le G'$; since the images of the $g_i$ commute in $G/N$, the quotient $G/N$ is abelian and
$G'\le N$. Hence $G'=N$.
\item Lower bound: produce explicit nontrivial $[x,y]$ to show $G'\ge\langle those\rangle$.
\item Upper bound: exhibit $H\nor G$ with $G/H$ abelian; then $G'\le H$ by
Prop.~ [REF:prop:commutator@c5] (2). When the two bounds meet, you have $G'$.
\item Read off $G/G'$ (the abelianization) and check $|G'|\cdot|G/G'|=|G|$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $G'=1$ characterizes abelian groups
Content:
\begin{wex}{$G'=1$ characterizes abelian groups}
Show $G'=1\iff G$ abelian, and verify on $G=Z/(12)Z$ and on $G=\Sym_3$.
\wrec This is Corollary~ [REF:cor:abelian@c5] : a commutator is trivial iff its arguments commute, and
$G'$ is generated by all commutators.
\wsol By the corollary $G'=1\Longleftrightarrow G$ abelian. For $Z/(12)Z$ (abelian, additive), every commutator
$[x,y]=-x-y+x+y=0$, so $G'=\{0\}=1$; consistent with abelian. For $\Sym_3=\langle (1\,2\,3),(1\,2)\rangle$,
take $x=(1\,2\,3),\,y=(1\,2)$. Then $[x,y]=x^{-1} y^{-1} xy=(1\,3\,2)(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)$. Compose
right to left: $(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3)$; then $(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)$; then $(1\,3\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,2\,3)$.
So $[x,y]=(1\,2\,3)\ne e$, hence $G'\ne1$ and $\Sym_3$ is nonabelian.
Check. $A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\nor\Sym_3$ has abelian quotient $\Sym_3/A_3\congZ/(2)Z$, so
$G'\le A_3$; and we found $(1\,2\,3)\in G'$, so $A_3\le G'$. Thus $\Sym_3{}'=A_3$, of order $3$,
and $|G'|\cdot|G/G'|=3\cdot2=6=|\Sym_3|$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$G'$ for $A_4$}
Compute the commutator subgroup of the alternating group $A_4$ (order $12$).
\wrec Method box again: a nontrivial commutator forces $G'$ to contain a double transposition,
and the quotient by the Klein four-group is abelian, capping $G'$ from above.
\wsol Lower bound. Take $x=(1\,2\,3)$ and $y=(1\,2\,4)$ in $A_4$. Then
$[x,y]=x^{-1} y^{-1} xy=(1\,3\,2)(1\,4\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2\,4)$. Composing right to left gives
$[x,y]=(1\,2)(3\,4)$, a double transposition. Hence the Klein four-group
$V=\{e,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}\le A_4$ (a single double transposition generates $V$
together with its conjugates, and $V\le G'$ since $G'\nor A_4$) satisfies $V\le G'$, so $|G'|\ge4$.

abelian; therefore $G'\le V$ by Prop.~ [REF:prop:commutator@c5] (2).
Conclusion. $A_4{}'=V\cong V_4$, of order $4$, with abelianization $A_4/A_4{}'\congZ/(3)Z$.
Check. $|G'|\cdot|G/G'|=4\cdot3=12=|A_4|$.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
$G'$ is generated by commutators, but a single commutator need not be a typical element of $G'$,
and the set of commutators need not be a subgroup. Always pass through the subgroup they
generate (and use the upper-bound trick) rather than asserting $\{[x,y]\}$ is closed. Also: $G'$ is
characteristic, so $G'\nor G$ automatically; do not ``check normality'' of $G'$ by hand.
\end{pitfall}

Type: prose
Content:
We now isolate exactly when a group is, internally, a direct product of two of its subgroups.
First recall the universal property of the external direct product, which the internal version
must reproduce.

\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & T \arrow[dl, "f"'] \arrow[dr, "g"] \arrow[d, dashed, "{(f,g)}"] & \\
H & H\times K \arrow[l, two heads, "\pi_1"] \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi_2"'] & K
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes: $T$ is an arbitrary group (the ``test object'' or source); $H\times K$
is the external direct product of two groups $H$ and $K$; and $H$, $K$ are the factor groups
(targets of the projections). $H\times K$ is the central object encoding the universal property.
\dgi{Arrows:} $f\colon T\to H$ and $g\colon T\to K$ are arbitrary group homomorphisms. $\pi_1\colon
H\times K\to H$, $(h,k)\mapsto h$, is the canonical first projection; $\pi_2\colon H\times K\to K$,
$(h,k)\mapsto k$, is the canonical second projection. The dashed arrow $(f,g)\colon T\to H\times K$,
$t\mapsto (f(t),g(t))$, is the unique induced map guaranteed by the universal property.
\dgi{What commutes:} Two triangles: $\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$ (left triangle) and $\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$
(right triangle). That is, $(f,g)$ is the unique map making both diagrams commute simultaneously.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $t\in T$. The induced map sends $t\mapsto(f(t),g(t))$; applying
$\pi_1$ then gives $f(t)$, which equals $f(t)$ --- so $\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$. Applying $\pi_2$ gives
$g(t)=g(t)$ --- so $\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$. Uniqueness: if $\phi\colon T\to H\times K$ also satisfies
$\pi_1\circ\phi=f$ and $\pi_2\circ\phi=g$, then $\phi(t)=(\pi_1(\phi(t)),\pi_2(\phi(t)))=(f(t),g(t))$,
so $\phi=(f,g)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is placed here to anchor the meaning of the internal direct
product recognition theorem that follows. The theorem asserts $G\cong H\times K$ by constructing
$\psi\colon H\times K\to G$, $\psi(h,k)=hk$; the universal property here explains why having
projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ and the unique fill-in $(f,g)$ is the defining feature of the product ---
and the internal version must reproduce exactly this structure from inside $G$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $H=Z/(2)Z$, $K=Z/(3)Z$, $T=Z/(6)Z$. The map $f\colonZ/(6)Z\toZ/(2)Z$,
$n\mapsto n\bmod2$, and $g\colonZ/(6)Z\toZ/(3)Z$, $n\mapsto n\bmod3$, induce $(f,g)\colonZ/(6)Z\to
Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$, $n\mapsto(n\bmod2,n\bmod3)$, which is an isomorphism (CRT). Projecting back
via $\pi_1$ recovers $f$, and via $\pi_2$ recovers $g$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think the dashed arrow $(f,g)$ merely ``exists''; the
diagram records both existence and uniqueness. Also, do not confuse the induced map
$(f,g)\colon T\to H\times K$ with the pair of maps $(f,g)$ as abstract data --- the diagram says
there is exactly one group homomorphism into $H\times K$ whose projections are $f$ and $g$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the external direct product $H\times K$ is
characterized by the property that maps into it are in bijection with pairs of maps into the factors,
via the unique fill-in $(f,g)$, and the internal recognition theorem succeeds precisely by constructing
the isomorphism $G\cong H\times K$ that makes this same property hold inside $G$.
\end{dgx}

Type: theorem
Title: Recognition of internal direct products; D\&F 5.4, Thm.\ 9
Label: thm:recognition@c5
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Recognition of internal direct products; D\&F 5.4, Thm.\ 9] 
Let $G$ be a group with subgroups $H,K\le G$ satisfying
\[
\textnormal{(i) } H\nor G,\qquad \textnormal{(ii) } K\nor G,\qquad
\textnormal{(iii) } H\cap K=1,\qquad \textnormal{(iv) } HK=G.
\]
Then the map $\psi\colon H\times K\to G$, $\psi(h,k)=hk$, is an isomorphism; thus
$G\cong H\times K$. Conditions (i)--(iv) are equivalent to: $[H,K]=1$, $H\cap K=1$, and $HK=G$.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Recognizing Direct Products > Internal direct products: the recognition theorem
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-182eabc2a5f980c54803
Content:
\begin{proof}
Step 1: elements of $H$ and $K$ commute. Let $h\in H,\ k\in K$ and consider the
commutator $[h,k]=h^{-1} k^{-1} h k$. Group it two ways. First,
\[
[h,k]=h^{-1}\,(k^{-1} h k),
\]
where $k^{-1} h k\in H$ because $H\nor G$, so $[h,k]\in H$. Second,
\[
[h,k]=(h^{-1} k^{-1} h)\,k,
\]
where $h^{-1} k^{-1} h\in K$ because $K\nor G$, so $[h,k]\in K$. Hence $[h,k]\in H\cap K=1$,
i.e.\ $[h,k]=1$ and $hk=kh$ for all $h,k$. This
gives the equivalent reformulation with $[H,K]=1$.

Step 2: $\psi$ is a homomorphism. For $(h_1,k_1),(h_2,k_2)\in H\times K$,
\[
\psi(h_1,k_1)\psi(h_2,k_2)=h_1k_1h_2k_2 = h_1h_2k_1k_2 = \psi\big((h_1h_2),(k_1k_2)\big)
=\psi\big((h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)\big),
\]
where we used $k_1h_2=h_2k_1$ from Step~1. So $\psi$ is a homomorphism.

Step 3: $\psi$ is surjective. $\im\psi=HK=G$ by (iv).

Step 4: $\psi$ is injective. Suppose $\psi(h,k)=hk=1$. Then $h=k^{-1}\in H\cap K=1$,
so $h=k=1$ and $(h,k)$ is the identity of $H\times K$; thus $\ker\psi=1$. (Equivalently each
$g\in G$ has a unique expression $g=hk$: if $h_1k_1=h_2k_2$ then $h_2^{-1} h_1=k_2k_1^{-1}\in
H\cap K=1$.)

Hence $\psi$ is a bijective homomorphism, an isomorphism, and $G\cong H\times K$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The reformulation is genuinely useful: in the presence of $H\cap K=1$ and $HK=G$, the four-condition
version (both subgroups normal) and the commuting version ($[H,K]=1$ plus, say, just $H\nor G$) are
interchangeable. Indeed if $[H,K]=1$ and $HK=G$ then $K$ centralizes $H$ and $H$ centralizes $K$,
and every $g=hk$ conjugates $H$ to $H$ (because $k$ centralizes $H$ and $h$ normalizes $H$), so
$H\nor G$; symmetrically $K\nor G$.
\end{remark}

Title: The $H,K\nor G$, $H\cap K=1$, $HK=G$ checklist
Content:
\begin{method}{The $H,K\nor G$, $H\cap K=1$, $HK=G$ checklist}
Trigger. You suspect $G\cong H\times K$ and want to prove it from inside $G$ (no need to
build the external product by hand), or you must disprove a direct-product decomposition.

Recipe (to establish $G\cong H\times K$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Normality: verify $H\nor G$ and $K\nor G$ (e.g.\ both contain a generating set fixed
under conjugation, or have index giving the smallest prime, or are kernels of homomorphisms). For
the commuting form instead check $[H,K]=1$.
\item Trivial intersection: show $H\cap K=1$ (often by orders: a common element has order
dividing $\gcd(|H|,|K|)$; if that gcd is $1$ you are done).
\item Generation: show $HK=G$. Counting suffices when $H\cap K=1$, since
$|HK|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=|H||K|$; if this equals $|G|$ then $HK=G$.
\item Conclude $G\cong H\times K$ via Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] ; the iso is $(h,k)\mapsto hk$.
\end{enumerate}

To DISprove: show that every candidate pair $H,K$ of proper normal subgroups fails
one of (iii),(iv) --- typically the intersection is nontrivial (the subgroups all share the center),
or no two proper normal subgroups generate $G$.
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ internally
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ internally}
Realize $Z/(6)Z=Z/6Z$ as an internal direct product of two of its subgroups.
\wrec Recognition theorem in an abelian group: all subgroups are normal, so only $H\cap K=1$ and
$H+K=G$ remain.
\wsol Work additively. Let $H=\langle 3\rangle=\{0,3\}\congZ/(2)Z$ and $K=\langle 2\rangle=\{0,2,4\}\congZ/(3)Z$.
(i)--(ii) Normal: $Z/(6)Z$ is abelian, so $H,K\norZ/(6)Z$ automatically.
(iii) Intersection: $|H\cap K|$ divides $\gcd(2,3)=1$, so $H\cap K=\{0\}$. (Directly,
$\{0,3\}\cap\{0,2,4\}=\{0\}$.)
(iv) Generation: $|H+K|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=\dfrac{2\cdot3}{1}=6=|Z/(6)Z|$, so
$H+K=Z/(6)Z$.
By Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] , $Z/(6)Z\cong H\times K\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$. The iso sends
$(a,b)\inZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ (with $a\in\{0,3\},\,b\in\{0,2,4\}$) to $a+b$. Check the table:
$(0,0)\mapsto0$, $(3,0)\mapsto3$, $(0,2)\mapsto2$, $(0,4)\mapsto4$, $(3,2)\mapsto5$,
$(3,4)\mapsto7=1$. The six images $\{0,3,2,4,5,1\}$ are all of $Z/(6)Z$, confirming bijectivity.
This is the Chinese Remainder Theorem for groups, internally realized.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ internally}
Realize $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ as an internal direct product of two of its subgroups.
\wrec Recognition theorem in an abelian group: all subgroups are normal, so only $H\cap K=1$ and

\wsol Work additively. Let $H=\langle 3\rangle=\{0,3\}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ and $K=\langle 2\rangle=\{0,2,4\}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$.
\textbf{(i)--(ii) Normal:} $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian, so $H,K\nor\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ automatically.
\textbf{(iii) Intersection:} $|H\cap K|$ divides $\gcd(2,3)=1$, so $H\cap K=\{0\}$. (Directly,
$\{0,3\}\cap\{0,2,4\}=\{0\}$.)
\textbf{(iv) Generation:} $|H+K|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=\dfrac{2\cdot3}{1}=6=|\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}|$, so
$H+K=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:recognition@c5}, $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\cong H\times K\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. The iso sends
$(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ (with $a\in\{0,3\},\,b\in\{0,2,4\}$) to $a+b$. \textbf{Check the table:}
$(0,0)\mapsto0$, $(3,0)\mapsto3$, $(0,2)\mapsto2$, $(0,4)\mapsto4$, $(3,2)\mapsto5$,
$(3,4)\mapsto7=1$. The six images $\{0,3,2,4,5,1\}$ are all of $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$, confirming bijectivity.
This is the Chinese Remainder Theorem for groups, internally realized.
\end{wex}

Title: Recovering the factors of $\Sym_3\timesZ/(2)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Recovering the factors of $\Sym_3\timesZ/(2)Z$}
In $G=\Sym_3\timesZ/(2)Z$ (order $12$) recognize an internal direct product decomposition.
\wrec Apply the checklist to two coordinate subgroups of an externally given product, confirming the
internal recognition theorem reproduces the original factors.
\wsol Let $H=\Sym_3\times\{0\}$ and $K=\{e\}\timesZ/(2)Z$, viewed inside $G$.
Normal: $H=\ker(\pi_2)$ where $\pi_2\colon G\toZ/(2)Z$ is projection, and $K=\ker(\pi_1)$
where $\pi_1\colon G\to\Sym_3$; kernels are normal, so $H,K\nor G$.
Intersection: $H\cap K=\{(e,0)\}=1$ since a common element has trivial second coordinate
(from $H$) and trivial first coordinate (from $K$).
Generation: $|HK|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=\dfrac{6\cdot2}{1}=12=|G|$, so $HK=G$.
Hence $G\cong H\times K\cong\Sym_3\timesZ/(2)Z$, recovering the original factors.
Check. A typical element $\big((1\,2),1\big)=\big((1\,2),0\big)\cdot\big(e,1\big)$ with the
first factor in $H$ and second in $K$ --- a valid unique factorization, as the theorem guarantees.
\end{wex}

\wrec Apply the checklist to two coordinate subgroups of an externally given product, confirming the
internal recognition theorem reproduces the original factors.
\wsol Let $H=\Sym_3\times\{0\}$ and $K=\{e\}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, viewed inside $G$.

Type: example
Title: $Z/(15)Z^\times$ as an internal direct product
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(15)Z^\times$ as an internal direct product}
Show the unit group $G=(Z/15Z)^\times$ (order $\varphi(15)=8$) is internally a direct product of
two proper subgroups, and identify them.
\wrec Recognition theorem in an abelian group via the CRT splitting over the prime factors of
$15=3\cdot5$.
\wsol $G=\{1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14\}$ under multiplication mod $15$, abelian of order $8$. Use the CRT
factors
\[
H=\{x\in G\st x\equiv1\!\!\pmod5\},\qquad
K=\{x\in G\st x\equiv1\!\!\pmod3\}.
\]
Identify $H$. An element is $\equiv1\pmod5$ iff $5\mid(x-1)$; among the units only
$1$ and $11$ qualify (since $11-1=10$), so $H=\{1,11\}$. As $11^2=121=8\cdot15+1\equiv1\pmod{15}$,
$H\congZ/(2)Z$, the internal copy of the factor $(Z/3)^\times$ (the residue mod $5$ is fixed at $1$,
while $1,11$ have residues $1,2$ mod $3$).
Identify $K$. An element is $\equiv1\pmod3$ iff $3\mid(x-1)$; among the units $1,4,7,13$
qualify (the differences $0,3,6,12$ are divisible by $3$), so $K=\{1,4,7,13\}$. Take $7$:
$7^2=49\equiv4,\ 7^3\equiv28\equiv13,\ 7^4\equiv91\equiv1\pmod{15}$, so $K=\langle 7\rangle\congZ/(4)Z$.
Checklist. Abelian $\Rightarrow$ both normal. For the intersection, an element of
$H\cap K$ is $\equiv1\pmod5$ and $\equiv1\pmod3$, hence $\equiv1\pmod{15}$, i.e.\ equals $1$; so
$H\cap K=1$. Then $|HK|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=\dfrac{2\cdot4}{1}=8=|G|$, so $HK=G$.
Conclusion. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] ,
$(Z/15Z)^\times\cong H\times K\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(4)Z$.
Sanity check. This matches the CRT statement
$(Z/15)^\times\cong(Z/3)^\times\times(Z/5)^\times\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(4)Z$, since
$(Z/3)^\times\congZ/(2)Z$ and $(Z/5)^\times\congZ/(4)Z$.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z}^\times$ as an internal direct product}
Show the unit group $G=(\mathbb{Z}/15\mathbb{Z})^\times$ (order $\varphi(15)=8$) is internally a direct product of
two proper subgroups, and identify them.
\wrec Recognition theorem in an abelian group via the CRT splitting over the prime factors of
$15=3\cdot5$.
\wsol $G=\{1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14\}$ under multiplication mod $15$, abelian of order $8$. Use the CRT
factors
\[
H=\{x\in G\st x\equiv1\!\!\pmod5\},\qquad
K=\{x\in G\st x\equiv1\!\!\pmod3\}.
\]
\textbf{Identify $H$.} An element is $\equiv1\pmod5$ iff $5\mid(x-1)$; among the units only
$1$ and $11$ qualify (since $11-1=10$), so $H=\{1,11\}$. As $11^2=121=8\cdot15+1\equiv1\pmod{15}$,
$H\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, the internal copy of the factor $(\mathbb{Z}/3)^\times$ (the residue mod $5$ is fixed at $1$,
while $1,11$ have residues $1,2$ mod $3$).
\textbf{Identify $K$.} An element is $\equiv1\pmod3$ iff $3\mid(x-1)$; among the units $1,4,7,13$
qualify (the differences $0,3,6,12$ are divisible by $3$), so $K=\{1,4,7,13\}$. Take $7$:
$7^2=49\equiv4,\ 7^3\equiv28\equiv13,\ 7^4\equiv91\equiv1\pmod{15}$, so $K=\langle 7\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$.
\textit{Checklist.} Abelian $\Rightarrow$ both normal. For the intersection, an element of
$H\cap K$ is $\equiv1\pmod5$ and $\equiv1\pmod3$, hence $\equiv1\pmod{15}$, i.e.\ equals $1$; so
$H\cap K=1$. Then $|HK|=\dfrac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}=\dfrac{2\cdot4}{1}=8=|G|$, so $HK=G$.
\textit{Conclusion.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:recognition@c5},
$(\mathbb{Z}/15\mathbb{Z})^\times\cong H\times K\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$.
\textit{Sanity check.} This matches the CRT statement
$(\mathbb{Z}/15)^\times\cong(\mathbb{Z}/3)^\times\times(\mathbb{Z}/5)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$, since
$(\mathbb{Z}/3)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/5)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $(Z/nZ)^\times$ splits over prime powers
Content:
\begin{wex}{$(Z/nZ)^\times$ splits over prime powers}
Show that for $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_t^{a_t}$ the unit group splits as an internal direct product
\[
(Z/nZ)^\times \;\cong\; (Z/p_1^{a_1}Z)^\times\times\cdots\times(Z/p_t^{a_t}Z)^\times,
\]
and illustrate with $n=12$.
\wrec Iterated recognition theorem driven by the Chinese Remainder Theorem ring isomorphism, whose
unit groups multiply.
\wsol General statement. The CRT ring isomorphism $Z/nZ\cong\prod_iZ/p_i^{a_i}Z$
restricts to a group isomorphism on units, since a tuple is a unit iff each coordinate is. Inside
$(Z/nZ)^\times$ define $H_i=\{x\st x\equiv1\pmod{p_j^{a_j}}\ for all j\ne i\}$; then $H_i$
is the internal copy of $(Z/p_i^{a_i}Z)^\times$. Each $H_i\nor G$ (abelian), each $H_i$ meets
the product $\prod_{j\ne i}H_j$ in $1$ (an element of that product is $\equiv1\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}$, and an
element of $H_i$ is $\equiv1$ modulo every other prime power, so an element of both is $\equiv1\pmod n$), and $\prod_i|H_i|=\prod_i\varphi(p_i^{a_i})=\varphi(n)=|G|$ forces $H_1\cdots H_t=G$.
The recognition theorem (applied repeatedly) gives the internal direct product.
Illustration $n=12=2^2\cdot3$. $(Z/12)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$, order $\varphi(12)=4$. Set
$H=\{x\equiv1\pmod3\}=\{1,7\}\cong(Z/4)^\times\congZ/(2)Z$ (indeed $7\equiv1\pmod3$, $7\equiv3\pmod4$,
$7^2=49\equiv1$), and $K=\{x\equiv1\pmod4\}=\{1,5\}\cong(Z/3)^\times\congZ/(2)Z$ ($5\equiv1\pmod4$,
$5\equiv2\pmod3$, $5^2=25\equiv1$).
Checklist. Both normal (abelian); $H\cap K$: an element is $\equiv1\pmod4$ and
$\equiv1\pmod3$, so $\equiv1\pmod{12}$, hence $H\cap K=\{1\}$; $|HK|=\frac{2\cdot2}{1}=4=|G|$, so
$HK=G$.
Conclusion. $(Z/12)^\times\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z=V_4$. Check. Every nonidentity
element $5,7,11$ squares to $1$ ($5^2=25\equiv1,\ 7^2=49\equiv1,\ 11^2=121\equiv1$), so the group is
elementary abelian of order $4$, consistent with $V_4$.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ splits over prime powers}
Show that for $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_t^{a_t}$ the unit group splits as an internal direct product
\[
(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \;\cong\; (\mathbb{Z}/p_1^{a_1}\mathbb{Z})^\times\times\cdots\times(\mathbb{Z}/p_t^{a_t}\mathbb{Z})^\times,
\]
and illustrate with $n=12$.
\wrec Iterated recognition theorem driven by the Chinese Remainder Theorem ring isomorphism, whose
unit groups multiply.
\wsol \textbf{General statement.} The CRT ring isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\cong\prod_i\mathbb{Z}/p_i^{a_i}\mathbb{Z}$
restricts to a group isomorphism on units, since a tuple is a unit iff each coordinate is. Inside
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ define $H_i=\{x\st x\equiv1\pmod{p_j^{a_j}}\ \text{for all }j\ne i\}$; then $H_i$
is the internal copy of $(\mathbb{Z}/p_i^{a_i}\mathbb{Z})^\times$. Each $H_i\nor G$ (abelian), each $H_i$ meets
the product $\prod_{j\ne i}H_j$ in $1$ (an element of that product is $\equiv1\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}$, and an
element of $H_i$ is $\equiv1$ modulo every other prime power, so an element of both is $\equiv1\pmod n$), and $\prod_i|H_i|=\prod_i\varphi(p_i^{a_i})=\varphi(n)=|G|$ forces $H_1\cdots H_t=G$.
The recognition theorem (applied repeatedly) gives the internal direct product.
\textbf{Illustration $n=12=2^2\cdot3$.} $(\mathbb{Z}/12)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$, order $\varphi(12)=4$. Set
$H=\{x\equiv1\pmod3\}=\{1,7\}\cong(\mathbb{Z}/4)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ (indeed $7\equiv1\pmod3$, $7\equiv3\pmod4$,
$7^2=49\equiv1$), and $K=\{x\equiv1\pmod4\}=\{1,5\}\cong(\mathbb{Z}/3)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ ($5\equiv1\pmod4$,
$5\equiv2\pmod3$, $5^2=25\equiv1$).
\textit{Checklist.} Both normal (abelian); $H\cap K$: an element is $\equiv1\pmod4$ and
$\equiv1\pmod3$, so $\equiv1\pmod{12}$, hence $H\cap K=\{1\}$; $|HK|=\frac{2\cdot2}{1}=4=|G|$, so
$HK=G$.
\textit{Conclusion.} $(\mathbb{Z}/12)^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=V_4$. \textit{Check.} Every nonidentity
element $5,7,11$ squares to $1$ ($5^2=25\equiv1,\ 7^2=49\equiv1,\ 11^2=121\equiv1$), so the group is
elementary abelian of order $4$, consistent with $V_4$.
\end{wex}

Title: Why $D_8$ is NOT a direct product of proper subgroups
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why $D_8$ is NOT a direct product of proper subgroups}
Show $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\,sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$ cannot be written as an internal direct product
$H\times K$ of two proper nontrivial subgroups.
\wrec Recognition theorem run in reverse: a direct product of two proper factors would force a
specific center structure that $D_8$ lacks. The key obstruction is the center.
\wsol Suppose $D_8\cong H\times K$ with $H,K$ proper nontrivial. Then $|H||K|=8$ with each factor
$>1$; the only split into two factors each $>1$ is $\{|H|,|K|\}=\{2,4\}$. In a direct
product, the center is $Z(H\times K)=Z(H)\times Z(K)$. The order-$2$
factor is its own center, and the order-$4$ factor (either $Z/(4)Z$ or $V_4$) is abelian, so equals its
center; hence $Z(D_8)$ would have order $|Z(H)|\cdot|Z(K)|=2\cdot4=8$, i.e.\ $D_8$ would be abelian.
But $Z(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$ has order $2$, and $D_8$ is nonabelian (e.g.\ $rs\ne sr$). Contradiction.
Alternative direct argument via the recognition checklist. Any normal subgroup of $D_8$
of order $2$ must be central, hence equals $Z(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$ (the unique central involution). So if
$|H|=2$ then $H=\langle r^2\rangle$, and likewise the order-$4$ normal subgroup $K$ contains $r^2$ (every
subgroup of order $4$ in $D_8$ contains $\langle r^2\rangle$). Then $r^2\in H\cap K\ne1$, violating condition
(iii). Hence no valid decomposition exists.
Check. $D_8$ does have $\langle r\rangle\congZ/(4)Z$ normal and $\langle s\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$ with
$\langle r\rangle\cap\langle s\rangle=1$ and $\langle r\rangle\langle s\rangle=D_8$ --- but $\langle s\rangle$ is not normal
($r s r^{-1}=r^2 s\notin\langle s\rangle$), so condition (ii) fails; this realizes $D_8$ as a
semidirect (not direct) product $Z/(4)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$, the subject of the next section.
\end{wex}

$\langle r\rangle\cap\langle s\rangle=1$ and $\langle r\rangle\langle s\rangle=D_8$ --- but $\langle s\rangle$ is \emph{not normal}
($r s r^{-1}=r^2 s\notin\langle s\rangle$), so condition (ii) fails; this realizes $D_8$ as a
\emph{semidirect} (not direct) product $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\sdp\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, the subject of the next section.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Recognizing Direct Products > Internal direct products: the recognition theorem
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Having $H\nor G$, $H\cap K=1$, and $HK=G$ with $K$ not normal does not give a direct
product --- it gives a semidirect product $H\sdp K$. The split exact sequence below has a section $s$
but the extension need not be central/trivial:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook] & H\sdp K \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[l, bend right=40, "s"'] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five nodes in a sequence: the trivial group $1$ at each end; $H$ a normal subgroup;
$H\sdp K$ the semidirect product (the extension group); and $K$ the quotient group. This is a short
exact sequence of groups, encoding the extension of $K$ by $H$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost $1\to H$ is the unique map from the trivial group. $H\hookrightarrow
H\sdp K$ is the canonical inclusion $h\mapsto(h,1)$, indicated by the hooked arrow. $H\sdp K
\twoheadrightarrow K$ is the canonical surjection $(h,k)\mapsto k$, the projection onto the quotient
factor; it is surjective (two-headed). The rightward $K\to 1$ is the unique map to the trivial group.
The curved arrow $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$, $k\mapsto(1,k)$, is a section (splitting): it satisfies
$\pi\circ s=\id_K$, meaning the sequence splits. Its image $s(K)$ need not centralize $H$;
it does exactly when $K$ acts on $H$ trivially (i.e.\ $[H,K]=1$).
\dgi{What commutes:} The exactness conditions: $\im(1\to H)=1=\ker(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)$;
$\im(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)=H=\ker(H\sdp K\twoheadrightarrow K)$; $\im(H\sdp K
\twoheadrightarrow K)=K=\ker(K\to 1)$. Additionally the section satisfies $\pi\circ s=\id_K$:
the composite $K\xrightarrow{s} H\sdp K\xrightarrow{\pi} K$ is the identity.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For exactness at $H\sdp K$: every $(h,1)$ in the image of the inclusion maps
to $1\in K$ under the projection, so image $\subseteq$ kernel; conversely $(h,k)\mapsto1$ forces
$k=1$, giving $(h,1)\in\im(H\hookrightarrow H\sdp K)$, so kernel $\subseteq$ image. For the section:
$\pi(s(k))=\pi(1,k)=k=\id_K(k)$, confirmed by the formula. The section exists because the sequence
splits, which means $H\sdp K\cong H\rtimes K$ for some action of $K$ on $H$ --- the choice
of action (conjugation in $H\sdp K$) is exactly what makes it semidirect rather than direct.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram appears in the pitfall block immediately after the
recognition theorem to mark the boundary between direct and semidirect products. The sequence splits
(the section $s$ exists) in both cases; the difference is whether $s(K)$ centralizes $H$,
i.e.\ whether $[H,K]=1$. Displaying the split exact sequence makes that distinction concrete: the
four conditions of the theorem hold for a direct product, but removing the normality of $K$ while
keeping $H\nor G$, $H\cap K=1$, $HK=G$ yields exactly this more general split sequence.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $H=Z/(3)Z$, $K=Z/(2)Z$, $H\sdp K=\Sym_3$ (where $K$ acts by inversion on
$H$). The inclusion $Z/(3)Z\hookrightarrow\Sym_3$ sends $1\mapsto(1\,2\,3)$; the projection
$\Sym_3\twoheadrightarrowZ/(2)Z$ is the sign map; and the section $s\colonZ/(2)Z\to\Sym_3$ sends
$1\mapsto(1\,2)$ (a transposition). The section does not centralize $H=A_3$, confirming a
semidirect (not direct) product.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Seeing a split exact sequence, students sometimes assume the product must be
direct. Splitting means the section $s$ exists, but the extension is direct only when $s(K)$
centralizes $H$ --- equivalently $K\nor H\sdp K$. In the semidirect case $K$ is not normal, and
conjugation by $s(k)$ acts nontrivially on $H$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that splitting of the short exact sequence
$1\to H\to H\sdp K\to K\to 1$ captures the existence of $s$ but not centrality, so direct products
are the special split extensions where $s(K)$ also normalizes --- in fact centralizes --- $H$.
\end{dgx}

The product is direct precisely when, in addition, $K\nor G$ (equivalently $[H,K]=1$), which
makes $s(K)$ centralize $H$. The $D_8$ example above is exactly the non-direct case.
\end{pitfall}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $G$ be a group. Prove that if $x, y \in G$ then $[y, x] = [x, y]^{-1}$. Deduce that for any subsets $A$ and $B$ of $G$, $[A, B] = [B, A]$ (recall that $[A, B]$ is the subgroup of $G$ generated by the commutators $[a, b]$).

\item Prove that a subgroup $H$ of $G$ is normal if and only if $[G, H] \le H$.

\item Let $a, b, c \in G$. Prove that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $[a, bc] = [a, c](c^{-1}[a, b]c)$
\item[(b)] $[ab, c] = (b^{-1}[a, c]b)[b, c]$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Find the commutator subgroups of $S_4$ and $A_4$.

\item Prove that $A_n$ is the commutator subgroup of $S_n$ for all $n \ge 5$.

\item Exhibit a representative of each cycle type of $A_5$ as a commutator in $S_5$.

\item Prove that if $p$ is a prime and $P$ is a non-abelian group of order $p^3$ then $P' = Z(P)$.

\item Assume $x, y \in G$ and both $x$ and $y$ commute with $[x, y]$. Prove that for all $n \in Z^+$, $(xy)^n = x^n y^n [y, x]^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}$.

\item Prove that if $p$ is an odd prime and $P$ is a group of order $p^3$ then the $p$th power map $x \mapsto x^p$ is a homomorphism of $P$ into $Z(P)$. If $P$ is not cyclic, show that the kernel of the $p$th power map has order $p^2$ or $p^3$. Is the squaring map a homomorphism in non-abelian groups of order 8? Where is the oddness of $p$ needed in the above proof? [Use Exercise 8.]

\item Prove that a finite abelian group is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups.

\item Prove that if $G = HK$ where $H$ and $K$ are characteristic subgroups of $G$ with $H \cap K = 1$ then $\Aut(G) \cong \Aut(H) \times \Aut(K)$. Deduce that if $G$ is an abelian group of finite order then $\Aut(G)$ is isomorphic to the direct product of the automorphism groups of its Sylow subgroups.

\item Use Theorem 4.17 to describe the automorphism group of a finite cyclic group.

\item Prove that $D_{8n}$ is not isomorphic to $D_{4n} \times Z_2$.

\item Let $G = \{(a_{ij}) \in GL_n(F) \mid a_{ij} = 0 if i > j, and a_{11} = a_{22} = \cdots = a_{nn}\}$, where $F$ is a field, be the group of upper triangular matrices all of whose diagonal entries are equal. Prove that $G \cong D \times U$, where $D$ is the group of all nonzero multiples of the identity matrix and $U$ is the group of upper triangular matrices with 1's down the diagonal.

\item If $A$ and $B$ are normal subgroups of $G$ such that $G/A$ and $G/B$ are both abelian, prove that $G/(A \cap B)$ is abelian.

\item Prove that if $K$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ then $K' \trianglelefteq G$.

\item If $K$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ and $K$ is cyclic, prove that $G' \le C_G(K)$. [Recall that the automorphism group of a cyclic group is abelian.]

\item Let $K_1, K_2, \ldots, K_n$ be non-abelian simple groups and let $G = K_1 \times K_2 \times \cdots \times K_n$. Prove that every normal subgroup of $G$ is of the form $G_I = \prod_{i \in I} K_i$ for some subset $I$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ (where $G_I$ is defined in Exercise 2 of Section 1). [If $N \trianglelefteq G$ and $x = (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in N$ with some $a_i \ne 1$, then show that there is some $g_i \in G_i$ not commuting with $a_i$. Show $[(1, \ldots, g_i, \ldots, 1), x] \in K_i \cap N$ and deduce $K_i \le N$.]

\item A group $H$ is called perfect if $H' = H$ (i.e., $H$ equals its own commutator subgroup).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that every non-abelian simple group is perfect.
\item[(b)] Prove that if $H$ and $K$ are perfect subgroups of a group $G$ then $\langle H, K\rangle$ is also perfect. Extend this to show that the subgroup of $G$ generated by any collection of perfect subgroups is perfect.
\item[(c)] Prove that any conjugate of a perfect subgroup is perfect.
\item[(d)] Prove that any group $G$ has a unique maximal perfect subgroup and that this subgroup is normal.
\end{enumerate}

\item If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are groups, prove that $\Aut(G_1 \times G_2)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Aut(G_1) \times \Aut(G_2)$.

\item Let $H(F)$ be the Heisenberg group over the field $F$, cf. Exercise 11 of Section 1.4. Find an explicit formula for the commutator $[X, Y]$, where $X, Y \in H(F)$, and show that the commutator subgroup of $H(F)$ equals the center of $H(F)$ (cf. Section 2.2, Exercise 14).
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Recognizing Direct Products > Internal direct products: the recognition theorem
Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item In $D_{10}=\langle r,s\st r^5=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$, compute the commutator $[r,s]$ explicitly and use it to determine the commutator subgroup $D_{10}{}'$ and the abelianization $D_{10}/D_{10}{}'$. \\
Answer. $[r,s]=r^{-1} s^{-1} rs=r^{-1}(s^{-1} rs)=r^{-1} r^{-1}=r^{-2}=r^3$. Since $5$ is prime, $\langle r^3\rangle=\langle r\rangle$, so $D_{10}{}'=\langle r\rangle\congZ/(5)Z$ (a normal subgroup with abelian quotient capping it from above), and $D_{10}/D_{10}{}'\congZ/(2)Z$. Check: $5\cdot2=10$.

\item In an arbitrary group $G$, assume the single commutator $c=[x,y]$ is central in $G$ and expand $(xy)^2$ in the form $x^2y^2c^{\pm1}$, identifying the sign. \\
Answer. From $xy=yx\,[x,y]$ we get $yx=xy\,[x,y]^{-1}=xy\,[y,x]=xy\,c^{-1}$. Hence
$(xy)^2=x(yx)y=x(xy\,c^{-1})y=x^2y^2c^{-1}$, where the central $c^{-1}$ slides freely past $y$. Thus
$(xy)^2=x^2y^2[y,x]$, the $n=2$ instance of the centered power formula $(xy)^n=x^ny^n[y,x]^{n(n-1)/2}$.

\item Compute $G'$ and the abelianization $G/G'$ for (a) $G=Z/(8)Z$ (additive) and (b) $G=\Sym_4$. \\
Answer. (a) $Z/(8)Z$ is abelian, so by Corollary~ [REF:cor:abelian@c5] $G'=0$ and $G/G'\congZ/(8)Z$. (b) Every commutator lies in $A_4$ (it is even, as $\sgn$ is a homomorphism to the abelian $\{\pm1\}$), so $\Sym_4{}'\le A_4$; conversely $A_4$ is generated by the $3$-cycles, each of which is a commutator (e.g.\ $[(1\,2),(1\,3)]=(1\,2)(1\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,2\,3)$; every $3$-cycle is conjugate to this one, and conjugates of commutators are commutators), so $A_4\le\Sym_4{}'$. Since $\Sym_4/A_4\congZ/(2)Z$ is abelian, $G'\le A_4$ too; hence $\Sym_4{}'=A_4$ and $\Sym_4/\Sym_4{}'\congZ/(2)Z$. Check: $12\cdot2=24$.

\item Realize $Z/(10)Z=Z/10Z$ as an internal direct product of two proper subgroups via the recognition theorem. \\
Answer. (Additive.) Let $H=\langle 5\rangle=\{0,5\}\congZ/(2)Z$ and $K=\langle 2\rangle=\{0,2,4,6,8\}\congZ/(5)Z$. Abelian $\Rightarrow$ both normal. $|H\cap K|\mid\gcd(2,5)=1$, so $H\cap K=\{0\}$; then $|H+K|=\frac{2\cdot5}{1}=10=|Z/(10)Z|$, so $H+K=Z/(10)Z$. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] , $Z/(10)Z\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(5)Z$.

\item Test the four recognition conditions for $H=\langle r\rangle$ and $K=\langle s\rangle$ in $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$. Exactly one condition fails --- identify it and state the correct conclusion. \\
Answer. $H=\langle r\rangle\congZ/(4)Z$ is normal (index $2$); $K=\langle s\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$; $H\cap K=1$ (the reflection $s$ is not a rotation, so $s\notin\langle r\rangle$, and the only common element is $1$); and $HK=D_8$ (counting $|HK|=\frac{4\cdot2}{1}=8$). But $K\nor G$ fails: $rsr^{-1}=r^2s\notin\langle s\rangle$. So condition (ii) breaks, and $D_8$ is the semidirect product $Z/(4)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$, not a direct product.

\item Show that $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}=(Z/8Z)^\times$ is an internal direct product of two subgroups of order $2$, and identify the resulting group up to isomorphism. \\
Answer. $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}=\{1,3,5,7\}$, order $4$, abelian. Take $H=\langle 3\rangle=\{1,3\}$ (since $3^2=9\equiv1$) and $K=\langle 5\rangle=\{1,5\}$ (since $5^2=25\equiv1$), each of order $2$. $H\cap K=\{1\}$, and $|HK|=\frac{2\cdot2}{1}=4=|G|$, so $HK=G$; abelian gives both normal. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] , $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}\congZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z=V_4$ --- consistent with every nonidentity element squaring to $1$ ($3^2,5^2,7^2\equiv1\pmod8$).

\item Compute the commutator subgroup and abelianization of $D_{12}=\langle r,s\st r^6=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$. \\
Answer. Lower bound. $[r,s]=r^{-1}(s^{-1} rs)=r^{-1} r^{-1}=r^{-2}$, so $\langle r^2\rangle=\{1,r^2,r^4\}\le D_{12}{}'$, of order $3$. Upper bound. $\langle r^2\rangle\nor D_{12}$ and the quotient $D_{12}/\langle r^2\rangle$ has order $4$, generated by commuting involutions $\bar r,\bar s$ (since $\bar r^2=1$ and $\bar s\bar r=\bar r^{-1}\bar s=\bar r\bar s$), hence abelian; so $D_{12}{}'\le\langle r^2\rangle$ by Proposition~ [REF:prop:commutator@c5] (2). The bounds meet: $D_{12}{}'=\langle r^2\rangle\congZ/(3)Z$, abelianization $D_{12}/D_{12}{}'\cong V_4$. Check: $3\cdot4=12$.

\item Suppose $H\nor G$ and $K\nor G$ with $H\cap K=1$ and $HK=G$. Using the commutator trick, prove that every element of $H$ commutes with every element of $K$. \\
Answer. Fix $h\in H,\ k\in K$ and form $[h,k]=h^{-1} k^{-1} hk$. Grouping as $h^{-1}(k^{-1} hk)$ shows $[h,k]\in H$ (since $k^{-1} hk\in H$ by $H\nor G$); grouping as $(h^{-1} k^{-1} h)k$ shows $[h,k]\in K$ (since $h^{-1} k^{-1} h\in K$ by $K\nor G$). Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that $G/G'$ is the largest abelian quotient: for every homomorphism $\varphi\colon G\to A$ with $A$ abelian there is a unique homomorphism $\overline{\varphi}\colon G/G'\to A$ with $\varphi=\overline{\varphi}\circ\pi$, where $\pi\colon G\to G/G'$ is the quotient map. \\
Answer. For any $x,y$, $\varphi([x,y])=[\varphi(x),\varphi(y)]=1$ since $A$ is abelian, so $G'\le\ker\varphi$. With $G'\le\ker\varphi$ in hand, the universal property of quotients yields a unique $\overline{\varphi}\colon G/G'\to A$ with $\overline{\varphi}\circ\pi=\varphi$ (well-defined because $G'\le\ker\varphi$; unique because $\pi$ is surjective). Equivalently, abelianization is left adjoint to the inclusion of abelian groups into all groups.

\item Let $P$ be a nonabelian group of order $p^3$ ($p$ prime). Prove $P'=Z(P)$ and that both have order $p$. \\
Answer. $Z(P)\ne1$ ($p$-group), and $|Z(P)|\ne p^2$: otherwise $P/Z(P)$ would have order $p$, hence cyclic, forcing $P$ abelian. Also $|Z(P)|\ne p^3$ (nonabelian). So $|Z(P)|=p$ and $P/Z(P)$ has order $p^2$, hence is abelian; by Proposition~ [REF:prop:commutator@c5] (2), $P'\le Z(P)$, so $|P'|\le p$. But $P$ nonabelian gives $P'\ne1$, so $|P'|=p=|Z(P)|$ and the inclusion $P'\le Z(P)$ is an equality: $P'=Z(P)$.

\item Let $H,K\nor G$ with $H\cap K=1$, both $H$ and $K$ abelian, and $G=HK$. Prove $G$ is abelian and $G\cong H\times K$. Then use the center to disprove any direct decomposition of $D_8$ into two proper factors. \\
Answer. By the recognition Step~1, $[H,K]=1$; together with $H,K$ abelian this makes any two elements $h_1k_1,h_2k_2$ commute, so $G$ is abelian, and Theorem~ [REF:thm:recognition@c5] gives $G\cong H\times K$. For $D_8$: a split $D_8\cong H\times K$ with proper factors forces $\{|H|,|K|\}=\{2,4\}$; then $Z(D_8)=Z(H)\times Z(K)=H\times K$ has order $2\cdot4=8$, making $D_8$ abelian --- contradicting $|Z(D_8)|=2$. So $D_8$ is not a direct product of proper subgroups.

\item Determine $A_4{}'$ by the lower-/upper-bound method and confirm the order identity $|G'|\cdot|G/G'|=|G|$. \\
Answer. Lower bound: $[(1\,2\,3),(1\,2\,4)]=(1\,2)(3\,4)$, a double transposition, and its $A_4$-conjugates give the Klein four-group $V=\{e,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}\le A_4{}'$ (as $A_4{}'\nor A_4$). Upper bound: $V\nor A_4$ with $A_4/V\congZ/(3)Z$ abelian, so $A_4{}'\le V$ by Proposition~ [REF:prop:commutator@c5] (2). The bounds meet: $A_4{}'=V\cong V_4$, abelianization $A_4/A_4{}'\congZ/(3)Z$, and $|G'|\cdot|G/G'|=4\cdot3=12=|A_4|$.

\end{exers}

Content:
The direct product $H\times K$ is the case in which $H$ and $K$ commute past one another:
$(h,1)(1,k)=(h,k)=(1,k)(h,1)$. The semidirect product relaxes this. We keep $H$ normal, but
allow conjugation by elements of $K$ to act on $H$ as a nontrivial automorphism. The bookkeeping
for that action is a homomorphism $\varphi\colon K\to\Aut(H)$.

Title: External semidirect product
Content:
\begin{definition}[External semidirect product]
Let $H$ and $K$ be groups and let $\varphi\colon K\to\Aut(H)$ be a homomorphism. Write
$\varphi(k)=\varphi_k\in\Aut(H)$, and write the action multiplicatively: $k\cdot h:=\varphi_k(h)$.
The semidirect product $H\sdp_\varphi K$ is the set $H\times K$ with multiplication
\[
(h_1,k_1)\,(h_2,k_2)\;=\;\bigl(h_1\,\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),\;k_1k_2\bigr).
\]
When $\varphi$ is understood we write $H\sdp K$.
\end{definition}

Content:
\begin{proposition}[$H\sdp_\varphi K$ is a group; D\&F Thm.~5.5.10] 
With $H,K,\varphi$ as above, $H\sdp_\varphi K$ is a group of order $\ord H\ord K$. Identifying
$h\leftrightarrow(h,1)$ and $k\leftrightarrow(1,k)$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the maps $h\mapsto(h,1)$ and $k\mapsto(1,k)$ are injective homomorphisms, so $H$ and $K$
are (isomorphic to) subgroups; with these identifications every element factors uniquely as
$(h,k)=hk$;
\item $H\nor H\sdp K$ and $K\sgr H\sdp K$, with $H\cap K=1$ and $HK=H\sdp K$;
\item for $h\in H,\ k\in K$ one has $khk^{-1}=\varphi_k(h)$, i.e. conjugation by $k$ realizes
$\varphi_k$;
\item $H\sdp_\varphi K$ is abelian $\Longleftrightarrow$ $\varphi$ is trivial and both $H,K$ are abelian; in
particular $H\sdp_\varphi K=H\times K$ (direct product) $\Longleftrightarrow$ $\varphi$ is the trivial
homomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
label: prop:sdp@c5

Content:
\begin{proof}
Associativity. Compute both bracketings of $(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)(h_3,k_3)$. Left first:
\[
\bigl[(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)\bigr](h_3,k_3)
=\bigl(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),\,k_1k_2\bigr)(h_3,k_3)
=\bigl(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2)\,\varphi_{k_1k_2}(h_3),\;k_1k_2k_3\bigr).
\]
Right first, using that $\varphi$ is a homomorphism ($\varphi_{k_1k_2}=\varphi_{k_1}\varphi_{k_2}$)
and that $\varphi_{k_1}$ is an automorphism:
\[
(h_1,k_1)\bigl[(h_2,k_2)(h_3,k_3)\bigr]
=(h_1,k_1)\bigl(h_2\varphi_{k_2}(h_3),\,k_2k_3\bigr)
=\bigl(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2)\,\varphi_{k_1}(\varphi_{k_2}(h_3)),\;k_1k_2k_3\bigr).
\]
Since $\varphi_{k_1}(\varphi_{k_2}(h_3))=\varphi_{k_1k_2}(h_3)$, the two agree.

Identity and inverses. $(1,1)$ is the identity: $(1,1)(h,k)=(\varphi_1(h),k)=(h,k)$ because
$\varphi_1=\id_H$, and $(h,k)(1,1)=(h\varphi_k(1),k)=(h,k)$. The inverse of $(h,k)$ is
$(\varphi_{k^{-1}}(h^{-1}),\,k^{-1})$: indeed
\[
(h,k)\bigl(\varphi_{k^{-1}}(h^{-1}),k^{-1}\bigr)
=\bigl(h\,\varphi_k(\varphi_{k^{-1}}(h^{-1})),\,kk^{-1}\bigr)
=\bigl(h\,\varphi_{kk^{-1}}(h^{-1}),\,1\bigr)=(h\,h^{-1},1)=(1,1).
\]
So $H\sdp K$ is a group, and as a set it is $H\times K$, so $\ord{H\sdp K}=\ord H\ord K$.

(1) On the slice $\{(h,1)\}$ the rule reads $(h_1,1)(h_2,1)=(h_1\varphi_1(h_2),1)=(h_1h_2,1)$,
so $h\mapsto(h,1)$ is an injective homomorphism. On $\{(1,k)\}$ the rule reads
$(1,k_1)(1,k_2)=(\varphi_{k_1}(1),k_1k_2)=(1,k_1k_2)$, so $k\mapsto(1,k)$ is too. Finally
$(h,1)(1,k)=(h,k)$, and uniqueness of $h,k$ is uniqueness of coordinates.

(2),(3) Compute the conjugate of $(h,1)$ by $(1,k)$:
\[
(1,k)(h,1)(1,k)^{-1}=(\varphi_k(h),k)(1,k^{-1})=(\varphi_k(h),1).
\]
With the identification $khk^{-1}=\varphi_k(h)\in H$; this proves (3) and shows $H$ is normalized by
$K$. Since $H$ is also normalized by itself and $H\sdp K=HK$ (as $(h,k)=(h,1)(1,k)$), we get
$H\nor H\sdp K$. Coordinatewise $(h,k)=(1,1)$ forces $h=1,k=1$, so $H\cap K=1$, and $\ord{HK}=\ord
H\ord K=\ord{H\sdp K}$ gives $HK=H\sdp K$.

(4) If $\varphi$ is trivial then $\varphi_k=\id_H$ for all $k$ and the rule becomes
$(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)=(h_1h_2,k_1k_2)$, the direct product. Conversely, if the group is abelian then in
particular $(1,k)(h,1)=(h,1)(1,k)$, i.e. $(\varphi_k(h),k)=(h,k)$, so $\varphi_k=\id_H$ for all $k$;
abelianness of the product also forces $H,K$ abelian.
\end{proof}

$(h,1)(1,k)=(h,k)$, and uniqueness of $h,k$ is uniqueness of coordinates.

\emph{(2),(3)} Compute the conjugate of $(h,1)$ by $(1,k)$:
\[
(1,k)(h,1)(1,k)^{-1}=(\varphi_k(h),k)(1,k^{-1})=(\varphi_k(h),1).
\]
With the identification $khk^{-1}=\varphi_k(h)\in H$; this proves (3) and shows $H$ is normalized by
$K$. Since $H$ is also normalized by itself and $H\sdp K=HK$ (as $(h,k)=(h,1)(1,k)$), we get
$H\nor H\sdp K$. Coordinatewise $(h,k)=(1,1)$ forces $h=1,k=1$, so $H\cap K=1$, and $\ord{HK}=\ord
H\ord K=\ord{H\sdp K}$ gives $HK=H\sdp K$.

\emph{(4)} If $\varphi$ is trivial then $\varphi_k=\id_H$ for all $k$ and the rule becomes
$(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)=(h_1h_2,k_1k_2)$, the direct product. Conversely, if the group is abelian then in
particular $(1,k)(h,1)=(h,1)(1,k)$, i.e. $(\varphi_k(h),k)=(h,k)$, so $\varphi_k=\id_H$ for all $k$;
abelianness of the product also forces $H,K$ abelian.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Building an external semidirect product
Content:
\begin{method}{Building an external semidirect product}
Trigger. You want a group containing a normal copy of $H$ and a complementary copy of $K$ in
which $K$ acts on $H$ in a prescribed way (e.g. inversion, a cyclic permutation of generators, a
field automorphism).

Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Pick $H,K$ and decide the desired action of each $k\in K$ as an automorphism of $H$.
\item Package it as a homomorphism $\varphi\colon K\to\Aut(H)$, $k\mapsto\varphi_k$. Check it is
a homomorphism: $\varphi_{k_1k_2}=\varphi_{k_1}\circ\varphi_{k_2}$ and $\varphi_1=\id$. (Often you
only need to send a generator of $K$ to a chosen automorphism whose order divides the order of that
generator.)
\item Form $H\sdp_\varphi K$ with $(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)=(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),k_1k_2)$.
\item Identify a presentation/known group via the relation $khk^{-1}=\varphi_k(h)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
A function $K\to\Aut(H)$ must be a homomorphism. ``Send the generator $x$ of $K=Z/(n)Z$ to an
automorphism $\alpha$'' is well defined as a homomorphism iff $\alpha^{\,n}=\id$, i.e.
$\ord\alpha\mid n$ inside $\Aut(H)$. Choosing $\alpha$ of the wrong order does not give a semidirect
product at all.
\end{pitfall}

Type: theorem
Title: Recognition / internal semidirect product; D\&F Thm.~5.5.12
Label: thm:internal@c5
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Recognition / internal semidirect product; D\&F Thm.~5.5.12] 
Let $G$ be a group with subgroups $H,K$ such that
\[
H\nor G,\qquad K\sgr G,\qquad H\cap K=1,\qquad HK=G.
\]
Let $\varphi\colon K\to\Aut(H)$ be the conjugation action $\varphi_k(h)=khk^{-1}$. Then the map
\[
\Phi\colon H\sdp_\varphi K\longrightarrow G,\qquad (h,k)\longmapsto hk,
\]
is an isomorphism. In this situation we say $G$ is the internal semidirect product of $H$ by
$K$ and write $G=H\sdp K$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:internal@c5

\]

\begin{proof}
$\varphi$ lands in $\Aut(H)$ because $H\nor G$ makes $h\mapsto khk^{-1}$ an automorphism of $H$, and
$k\mapsto(h\mapsto khk^{-1})$ is a homomorphism since $(k_1k_2)h(k_1k_2)^{-1}=k_1(k_2hk_2^{-1})k_1^{-1}$.

$\Phi$ is a bijection. Since $HK=G$, $\Phi$ is onto. If $h_1k_1=h_2k_2$ then
$h_2^{-1} h_1=k_2k_1^{-1}\in H\cap K=1$, so $h_1=h_2$, $k_1=k_2$; thus $\Phi$ is one-to-one. (As a
count, $\Phi$ is an injection between finite sets of equal size, since
$\ord{H\sdp K}=\ord H\ord K=\ord{HK}=\ord G$, the middle equality holding because $H\cap K=1$.)

$\Phi$ is a homomorphism. Using $k_1h_2k_1^{-1}=\varphi_{k_1}(h_2)$,
\[
\Phi\bigl((h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),\,k_1k_2\bigr)
=h_1\,(k_1h_2k_1^{-1})\,k_1k_2=h_1k_1\,h_2k_2=\Phi(h_1,k_1)\Phi(h_2,k_2).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: Splitting / split exact sequences
Content:
\begin{remark}[Splitting / split exact sequences]
A semidirect product is exactly a split extension. The data $1\to H\to G\to K\to1$ together with a
homomorphic section $s\colon K\to G$ (a splitting, $\pi\circ s=\id_K$) gives $G=H\sdp s(K)$.
The diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] & H\sdp K \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[l, bend right=40, "s"'] & 1
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The five nodes are: the trivial group $1$ (appearing at both ends), the normal
subgroup $H$ (a group), the semidirect product $H\sdp_\varphi K$ (the middle group, containing
copies of both $H$ and $K$), and the complement $K$ (a group). This is a short exact sequence
of groups with an extra section arrow (a right inverse of $\pi$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon H\to H\sdp K$, $\iota(h)=(h,1)$, is the inclusion of $H$ as the
first factor (a normal subgroup embedding). $\pi\colon H\sdp K\to K$, $\pi(h,k)=k$, is the
projection onto the second factor (a surjective homomorphism, drawn with two heads). $s\colon
K\to H\sdp K$, $s(k)=(1,k)$, is the canonical section or splitting (bent arrow, going right to
left in the display), a homomorphism satisfying $\pi\circ s=\id_K$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at $H$: $\ker\iota=1=\im(trivial map)$, so $\iota$ is
injective. Exactness at $H\sdp K$: $\im\iota=H\times\{1\}=\ker\pi$. Exactness at $K$: $\pi$ is
surjective ($\im\pi=K$). The splitting condition: $\pi\circ s=\id_K$, i.e. $\pi(s(k))=\pi(1,k)=k$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For exactness, $\pi(\iota(h))=\pi(h,1)=1$, so $\im\iota\subseteq\ker\pi$;
and if $\pi(h,k)=k=1$ then $(h,k)=(h,1)=\iota(h)$, so $\ker\pi\subseteq\im\iota$. For the
splitting: $(\pi\circ s)(k)=\pi(1,k)=k$ directly from the definitions of $s$ and $\pi$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram encodes exactly why a semidirect product is called a
split extension: the sequence $1\to H\to H\sdp K\to K\to1$ is exact (so $H\sdp K$ is an
extension of $K$ by $H$), and $s$ is a homomorphic right inverse to $\pi$ (the splitting). This
is the diagrammatic equivalent of Proposition~ [REF:prop:sdp@c5] : the section $s$ makes $K$ into a
complement of $H$, and the action $\varphi_k(h)=khk^{-1}$ is read off from conjugation by $s(k)$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $H=Z/(n)Z$, $K=Z/(2)Z$, $\varphi_s=$ inversion, giving $D_{2n}$.
Then $\iota(r)=(r,1)$, $\pi(r,1)=1$, $\pi(0,s)=s$, $s(s)=(0,s)$. Check: $\pi(s(s))=\pi(0,s)=s$
and $\im\iota=\{(r^i,1)\}=\ker\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse the section $s$ with the inclusion $\iota$. They are
different maps with different domains: $\iota\colon H\to H\sdp K$ and $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$.
Also, $s$ need not make $s(K)$ normal in $H\sdp K$ (it is normal only in the trivial-action /
direct-product case), so do not read ``splits'' as ``both inclusions are normal.''
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a semidirect product $H\sdp_\varphi K$ is
precisely a short exact sequence $1\to H\to H\sdp K\to K\to1$ equipped with a homomorphic
splitting $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$, and this splitting encodes the entire conjugation action $\varphi$.
\end{dgx}
commutes, where $\iota(h)=(h,1)$, $\pi(h,k)=k$, $s(k)=(1,k)$. Exactness is
$\im\iota=\ker\pi=H\times\{1\}$, and $\pi s=\id_K$ is the splitting. Conversely a direct product is the
case where $s(K)\nor G$ as well, i.e. both inclusions are normal. (D\&F: the extension splits $\Longleftrightarrow$
$H$ has a complement in $G$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $G$ is a semidirect product.)
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Trivial action $=$ direct product]
If $\varphi$ is trivial, the section's image $s(K)=\{1\}\times K$ is also normal, the two projections
both split, and $H\sdp_\varphi K=H\times K$. Thus the direct product is the degenerate semidirect
product.
\end{corollary}

Title: Recognizing $G$ as an internal semidirect product
Content:
\begin{method}{Recognizing $G$ as an internal semidirect product}
Trigger. You suspect a given $G$ is $H\sdp K$ for visible subgroups $H,K$ (e.g. a normal
Sylow subgroup and a complement).

Checklist (all four).
\begin{enumerate}
\item $H\nor G$ (often: $H$ is a unique Sylow subgroup, hence normal).
\item $K\sgr G$ (any complementary subgroup).
\item $H\cap K=1$ (e.g. coprime orders force this).
\item $HK=G$, equivalently $\ord H\ord K=\ord G$ with $H\cap K=1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then read off the action $\varphi_k(h)=khk^{-1}$ to name the group. If $\varphi$ is trivial you have a
direct product; otherwise a genuine (nonabelian, when $H$ or $K$ is nontrivially acted on) semidirect
product.
\end{method}

\begin{pitfall}
You need both $H\nor G$ and $HK=G$ and $H\cap K=1$. Dropping ``$HK=G$'' (equivalently the order
count) is fatal: in $Z/(4)Z=\{0,1,2,3\}$ take $H=\{0,2\}\norZ/(4)Z$ and $K=\{0,2\}$; then $H\nor G$,
$K\sgr G$, but $H\cap K=H\neq1$ and $HK=H\neq G$ -- no decomposition. Also: $K$ need not be
normal; if it is, you actually have a direct product.
\end{pitfall}

Title: $D_{2n}\congZ/(n)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$ via inversion
Content:
\begin{wex}{$D_{2n}\congZ/(n)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$ via inversion}
Build the dihedral group $D_{2n}$ as a semidirect product $Z/(n)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z$, exhibiting the
homomorphism $\varphi$ explicitly, and match the standard presentation $r^n=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$.
\wrec We want a normal cyclic group of rotations $H=\langle r\rangle\congZ/(n)Z$ and an order-2 complement
$K=\langle s\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$ with $s$ acting on $H$ by inversion. Inversion $\iota\colon a\mapsto-a$ is an
automorphism of $Z/(n)Z$ of order $\le2$, so it defines a homomorphism $Z/(2)Z\to\Aut(Z/(n)Z)$; the
internal-recognition theorem then identifies $Z/(n)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$ with $D_{2n}$.
\wsol Let $H=Z/(n)Z$ (written additively, generator $r$ of order $n$) and $K=Z/(2)Z=\{1,s\}$. Inversion
$\iota\in\Aut(Z/(n)Z)$ satisfies $\iota(a)=-a$ and $\iota^2(a)=-(-a)=a$, so $\ord\iota\mid2$. Define
\[
\varphi\colonZ/(2)Z\to\Aut(Z/(n)Z),\qquad \varphi_1=\id,\ \ \varphi_s=\iota.
\]
This is a homomorphism because $\varphi_{s^2}=\varphi_1=\id=\iota^2=\varphi_s\varphi_s$. Form
$G=Z/(n)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z$. By Prop.~ [REF:prop:sdp@c5] it has order $n\cdot2=2n$, $H\nor G$, $K\sgr G$,
$H\cap K=1$, and
\[
s\,r\,s^{-1}=\varphi_s(r)=\iota(r)=r^{-1} .
\]
Thus $G=\langle r,s\rangle$ with $r^n=1$, $s^2=1$, $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$ -- precisely the presentation of $D_{2n}$.
The map $r\mapsto r,\ s\mapsto s$ extends to an isomorphism $G\cong D_{2n}$.
Check. $\ord G=2n=\ord{D_{2n}}$. Compute a product in the model:
$(r,1)(0,s)(r,1)=(r,s)(r,1)=(r\,\varphi_s(r),s)=(r\,r^{-1},s)=(0,s)$, i.e. $r\,s\,r=s$, equivalently
$srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$. Consistent. For $n\ge3$ the action is nontrivial, so $G$ is nonabelian, as expected.
\end{wex}

The map $r\mapsto r,\ s\mapsto s$ extends to an isomorphism $G\cong D_{2n}$.
\textit{Check.} $\ord G=2n=\ord{D_{2n}}$. Compute a product in the model:
$(r,1)(0,s)(r,1)=(r,s)(r,1)=(r\,\varphi_s(r),s)=(r\,r^{-1},s)=(0,s)$, i.e. $r\,s\,r=s$, equivalently
$srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$. Consistent. For $n\ge3$ the action is nontrivial, so $G$ is nonabelian, as expected.
\end{wex}
