Title: A nonabelian group of order $21=3\cdot7$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A nonabelian group of order $21=3\cdot7$}
Construct a nonabelian group of order $21$ as $Z/(7)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(3)Z$, and find the order of the
generators. Why does $3\mid7-1$ matter?
\wrec $\Aut(Z/(7)Z)\cong(Z/(7)Z)^\times\congZ/(6)Z$ is cyclic of order $6$, which has a (unique) subgroup of
order $3$ because $3\mid6$ (equivalently $3\mid7-1$). A nontrivial $\varphi\colonZ/(3)Z\to\Aut(Z/(7)Z)$
exists exactly when $3\mid\ord{\Aut(Z/(7)Z)}=6$. That nontrivial action yields a nonabelian semidirect
product.
\wsol $\Aut(Z/(7)Z)=(Z/(7)Z)^\times=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ under multiplication mod $7$, cyclic of order $6$
generated by $3$ (powers: $3,2,6,4,5,1$). An element of order $3$ is $2$, since $2^1=2,\,2^2=4,\,
2^3=8\equiv1\pmod7$. Let $\alpha\in\Aut(Z/(7)Z)$ be multiplication by $2$: $\alpha(a)=2a\bmod7$, with
$\ord\alpha=3$. Define
\[
\varphi\colonZ/(3)Z\to\Aut(Z/(7)Z),\qquad \varphi(\overline1)=\alpha,
\]
well defined because $\ord\alpha=3\mid3$. Set $G=Z/(7)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(3)Z$, of order $7\cdot3=21$. Writing
$x$ for the generator $(\overline1,0)$ of $Z/(7)Z$ (order $7$) and $y$ for $(0,\overline1)$ of $Z/(3)Z$
(order $3$), the defining relation is
\[
y\,x\,y^{-1}=\varphi(\overline1)(x)=2x=x^2\quad(additively 2\cdot\overline1),
\]
so $G=\langle x,y\mid x^7=1,\ y^3=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^2\rangle$.
Check. Apply the relation three times: $y^3 x y^{-3}=x^{2^3}=x^{8}=x$ (since $8\equiv1\bmod7$),
consistent with $y^3=1$. The action is nontrivial ($2\not\equiv1$), so $G$ is nonabelian; its order
$21$ is correct. This is the unique nonabelian group of order $21$.
\end{wex}

Title: The nonabelian group of order $pq$ ($q\mid p-1$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{The nonabelian group of order $pq$ ($q\mid p-1$)}
For primes $q<p$ with $q\mid p-1$, build a nonabelian group of order $pq$ as $Z/(p)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(q)Z$.
\wrec $\Aut(Z/(p)Z)\cong(Z/(p)Z)^\times\congZ/((p-1))Z$ is cyclic of order $p-1$. Since $q\mid p-1$, this
cyclic group has a unique subgroup of order $q$, giving a nontrivial homomorphism
$\varphi\colonZ/(q)Z\to\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$. (If $q\nmid p-1$ the only homomorphism is trivial and every group
of order $pq$ is cyclic.)
\wsol Let $H=Z/(p)Z$, $K=Z/(q)Z$. Choose a generator $g$ of the cyclic group $(Z/(p)Z)^\times$ and set
$t=g^{(p-1)/q}\bmod p$, so that $t$ has multiplicative order exactly $q$ mod $p$ (since
$t^q=g^{p-1}\equiv1$ and no smaller power is $1$). Let $\alpha\in\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$ be multiplication by
$t$; then $\ord\alpha=q$. Define $\varphi\colonZ/(q)Z\to\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$ by $\varphi(\overline1)=\alpha$
(legitimate since $\ord\alpha=q\mid q$), and put $G=Z/(p)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(q)Z$, $\ord G=pq$. With
generators $x$ (order $p$), $y$ (order $q$):
\[
G=\langle x,y\mid x^p=1,\ y^q=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^{t}\rangle,\qquad t^q\equiv1\ (\bmod p),\ t\not\equiv1.
\]
Check. Iterating the relation $q$ times gives $y^q x y^{-q}=x^{t^q}=x^{1}=x$, consistent with
$y^q=1$. Nontriviality $t\not\equiv1$ makes $G$ nonabelian. Different choices of $t$ (i.e. different
generators of the order-$q$ subgroup of $(Z/(p)Z)^\times$) give isomorphic groups, because composing
$\varphi$ with an automorphism of $Z/(q)Z$ relabels the generator $y$; so there is a unique nonabelian
group of order $pq$.
\end{wex}

Title: When is $H\sdp K$ abelian? Recognize the direct product
Content:
\begin{wex}{When is $H\sdp K$ abelian? Recognize the direct product}
Decide, for $H=Z/(5)Z$ and $K=Z/(4)Z$, which homomorphisms $\varphi\colonZ/(4)Z\to\Aut(Z/(5)Z)$ make
$Z/(5)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z$ abelian, and identify the abelian case.
\wrec By Prop.~ [REF:prop:sdp@c5] (4) a semidirect product is abelian iff $\varphi$ is trivial (and the
factors abelian). So we just need to know which $\varphi$ are trivial; the trivial one gives the
direct product $Z/(5)Z\timesZ/(4)Z\congZ/(20)Z$.
\wsol $\Aut(Z/(5)Z)\cong(Z/(5)Z)^\times\congZ/(4)Z$, cyclic of order $4$ generated by $2$ ($2,4,3,1$).
A homomorphism $\varphi\colonZ/(4)Z\to\Aut(Z/(5)Z)\congZ/(4)Z$ is determined by the image of a generator,
and there are $\gcd(4,4)=4$ choices; the possible orders of $\varphi(\overline1)$ are divisors of $4$.
Exactly one homomorphism is trivial: $\varphi(\overline1)=\id$. For that one,
\[
Z/(5)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z=Z/(5)Z\timesZ/(4)Z\congZ/(20)Z\quad(abelian, cyclic since \gcd(5,4)=1).
\]
Every nontrivial $\varphi$ (e.g. $\varphi(\overline1)=$ mult.\ by $2$, order $4$; or mult.\ by $4$,
order $2$) gives a nonabelian group of order $20$, because then some $\varphi_k\neq\id$ and
$(1,k)(h,1)=(\varphi_k(h),k)\neq(h,k)=(h,1)(1,k)$.
Check. Take $\varphi(\overline1)=$ mult.\ by $4=-1$ (inversion, order $2$); then
$y x y^{-1}=x^{-1}\neq x$, so noncommutative, and $\ord G=20$. The unique abelian outcome is
$Z/(20)Z$, matching the classification of abelian groups of order $20$: of $Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(5)Z\congZ/(20)Z$ and
$Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(5)Z$, only the first contains a copy of $K=Z/(4)Z$.
\end{wex}
latex:

\]

Title: The affine group $Z/(n)Z\sdp(Z/(n)Z)^\times=\operatorname{Aff}(Z/(n)Z)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The affine group $Z/(n)Z\sdp(Z/(n)Z)^\times=\operatorname{Aff}(Z/(n)Z)$}
Realize the group of invertible affine maps $x\mapsto ax+b$ on $Z/(n)Z$ (with $a\in(Z/(n)Z)^\times$,
$b\inZ/(n)Z$) as a semidirect product, and identify its order.
\wrec Translations $T_b\colon x\mapsto x+b$ form a normal copy of $H=Z/(n)Z$ (they are the kernel of
``read off the linear part $a$''); multiplications $M_a\colon x\mapsto ax$ form a complement
$K=(Z/(n)Z)^\times$ acting on translations by $M_a T_b M_a^{-1}=T_{ab}$. That conjugation is the
action $\varphi_a(b)=ab$, so $\operatorname{Aff}(Z/(n)Z)=Z/(n)Z\sdp_\varphi(Z/(n)Z)^\times$.
\wsol Let $H=Z/(n)Z$ (additive, the $b$'s) and $K=(Z/(n)Z)^\times=\{a\inZ/(n)Z:\gcd(a,n)=1\}$
(multiplicative, the $a$'s). Define
\[
\varphi\colon(Z/(n)Z)^\times\to\Aut(Z/(n)Z),\qquad \varphi_a(b)=a\,b\ (\bmod n).
\]
This is a homomorphism: $\varphi_{a_1a_2}(b)=a_1a_2b=\varphi_{a_1}(\varphi_{a_2}(b))$, and each
$\varphi_a$ is invertible (inverse $\varphi_{a^{-1}}$), hence in $\Aut(Z/(n)Z)$ -- in fact
$\varphi\colon(Z/(n)Z)^\times\to\Aut(Z/(n)Z)$ is the standard isomorphism. The semidirect product law
\[
(b_1,a_1)(b_2,a_2)=(b_1+a_1b_2,\ a_1a_2)
\]
matches composition of affine maps: $(x\mapsto a_1x+b_1)\circ(x\mapsto a_2x+b_2)=
x\mapsto a_1a_2x+(a_1b_2+b_1)$. So $\operatorname{Aff}(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z\sdp_\varphi(Z/(n)Z)^\times$.
Order. $\ord{\operatorname{Aff}(Z/(n)Z)}=\ord{Z/(n)Z}\cdot\ord{(Z/(n)Z)^\times}=n\,\phi(n)$. For
$n=5$: $5\cdot4=20$ (this is the nonabelian group of order $20$ above with the full action). The
conjugation relation $M_aT_bM_a^{-1}=T_{ab}$ is exactly $\varphi_a(b)=ab$, confirming the internal
recognition with $H=\{T_b\}\nor G$, $K=\{M_a\}$, $H\cap K=\{T_0\}=1$, $HK=G$.
\end{wex}
latex:

Title: Classify all groups of order $pq$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Classify all groups of order $pq$}
Let $p>q$ be primes. Classify all groups $G$ of order $pq$ up to isomorphism, distinguishing the cases
$q\nmid p-1$ and $q\mid p-1$.
\wrec Sylow theory forces a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup $P\congZ/(p)Z$ and a Sylow $q$-subgroup
$Q\congZ/(q)Z$ with $P\cap Q=1$, $PQ=G$. So $G=P\sdp_\varphi Q$ for some
$\varphi\colonZ/(q)Z\to\Aut(Z/(p)Z)\congZ/((p-1))Z$, and we enumerate such $\varphi$.
\wsol Normality of $P$. The number $n_p$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups satisfies $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$
and $n_p\mid q$; since $q<p$ the only possibility is $n_p=1$, so $P\nor G$. Take any
$Q\in\operatorname{Syl}_q(G)$. Then $P\nor G$, $Q\sgr G$, $P\cap Q=1$ (coprime orders),
$\ord{PQ}=pq=\ord G$ so $PQ=G$. By Thm.~ [REF:thm:internal@c5] , $G=Z/(p)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(q)Z$ with
$\varphi\colonZ/(q)Z\to\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$. Now $\Aut(Z/(p)Z)\congZ/((p-1))Z$ is cyclic.
\begin{itemize}
\item Case $q\nmid p-1$. A homomorphism $Z/(q)Z\toZ/((p-1))Z$ has image of order dividing
$\gcd(q,p-1)=1$, so $\varphi$ is trivial. Then $G=Z/(p)Z\timesZ/(q)Z\congZ/(pq)Z$. Up to isomorphism
there is one group: the cyclic group $Z/(pq)Z$.
\item Case $q\mid p-1$. Now $\gcd(q,p-1)=q$, so there are exactly $q$ homomorphisms
$Z/(q)Z\to\Aut(Z/(p)Z)$ ($\varphi(\overline1)$ any element of the order-$q$ subgroup), one trivial and
$q-1$ nontrivial. The trivial one gives $Z/(pq)Z$. All $q-1$ nontrivial ones give isomorphic
nonabelian groups: if $\varphi,\varphi'$ are nontrivial then $\varphi'=\varphi\circ\beta$ for some
$\beta\in\Aut(Z/(q)Z)$, and $(h,k)\mapsto(h,\beta^{-1}(k))$ is an isomorphism
$Z/(p)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(q)Z\toZ/(p)Z\sdp_{\varphi'}Z/(q)Z$. So there are exactly two groups: the
cyclic $Z/(pq)Z$ and one nonabelian $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^t\rangle$ ($t$ of order $q$ mod $p$).
\end{itemize}
Check. $pq=21$: $p=7,q=3$, $3\mid6$, so two groups ($Z/(21)Z$ and the order-$21$ nonabelian
group of the earlier example). $pq=15$: $p=5,q=3$, $3\nmid4$, so one group, $Z/(15)Z$ -- matching the
known fact that every group of order $15$ is cyclic.
\end{wex}

and $n_p\mid q$; since $q<p$ the only possibility is $n_p=1$, so $P\nor G$. Take any
$Q\in\operatorname{Syl}_q(G)$. Then $P\nor G$, $Q\sgr G$, $P\cap Q=1$ (coprime orders),
$\ord{PQ}=pq=\ord G$ so $PQ=G$. By Thm.~\ref{thm:internal@c5}, $G=\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}$ with
$\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})$. Now $\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/((p-1))\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Case $q\nmid p-1$.} A homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/((p-1))\mathbb{Z}$ has image of order dividing
$\gcd(q,p-1)=1$, so $\varphi$ is trivial. Then $G=\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(pq)\mathbb{Z}$. Up to isomorphism
there is \emph{one} group: the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/(pq)\mathbb{Z}$.
\item \textbf{Case $q\mid p-1$.} Now $\gcd(q,p-1)=q$, so there are exactly $q$ homomorphisms
$\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})$ ($\varphi(\overline1)$ any element of the order-$q$ subgroup), one trivial and
$q-1$ nontrivial. The trivial one gives $\mathbb{Z}/(pq)\mathbb{Z}$. All $q-1$ nontrivial ones give \emph{isomorphic}
nonabelian groups: if $\varphi,\varphi'$ are nontrivial then $\varphi'=\varphi\circ\beta$ for some
$\beta\in\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z})$, and $(h,k)\mapsto(h,\beta^{-1}(k))$ is an isomorphism
$\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_{\varphi'}\mathbb{Z}/(q)\mathbb{Z}$. So there are exactly \emph{two} groups: the
cyclic $\mathbb{Z}/(pq)\mathbb{Z}$ and one nonabelian $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^t\rangle$ ($t$ of order $q$ mod $p$).
\end{itemize}
\textit{Check.} $pq=21$: $p=7,q=3$, $3\mid6$, so two groups ($\mathbb{Z}/(21)\mathbb{Z}$ and the order-$21$ nonabelian
group of the earlier example). $pq=15$: $p=5,q=3$, $3\nmid4$, so one group, $\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z}$ -- matching the
known fact that every group of order $15$ is cyclic.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Internal recognition inside $S_4$: $S_4\cong V_4\sdp S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Internal recognition inside $S_4$: $S_4\cong V_4\sdp S_3$}
Show $S_4$ is an internal semidirect product $V_4\sdp K$ with $K\cong S_3$, and identify the action.
\wrec $V_4=\{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is normal in $S_4$ (it is the kernel of the action on the
three ``partitions,'' or: it is a union of conjugacy classes plus identity). Take
$K=\operatorname{Sym}\{1,2,3\}$, the stabilizer of the point $4$, of order $6$. The orders are not
coprime ($\gcd(4,6)=2$), but recognition does not need coprimality: we still have
$\ord{V_4}\ord K=4\cdot6=24=\ord{S_4}$ and $V_4\cap K=1$, so the four-point checklist applies directly.
\wsol Normality. $V_4\nor S_4$: conjugating a product of two disjoint transpositions gives
another such, so $V_4$ is closed under conjugation; with the identity it is a normal subgroup of order
$4$. Complement. Let $K=\{\sigma\in S_4:\sigma(4)=4\}\cong S_3$, $\ord K=6$.
Intersection. Every non-identity element of $V_4$ is a product of two disjoint transpositions,
hence moves all four points; in particular it moves $4$. So no non-identity element of $V_4$ lies in
the point-stabilizer $K$, giving $V_4\cap K=\{e\}$. Product.
$\ord{V_4K}=\frac{\ord{V_4}\ord K}{\ord{V_4\cap K}}=\frac{4\cdot6}{1}=24=\ord{S_4}$, so $V_4K=S_4$. By
Thm.~ [REF:thm:internal@c5] , $S_4=V_4\sdp_\varphi K$ where $\varphi_k(v)=kvk^{-1}$. Action.
$K\cong S_3$ permutes the three nonidentity elements of $V_4$ faithfully, giving
$\varphi\colon S_3\to\Aut(V_4)\cong S_3$ an isomorphism. So the action is the full permutation of the
three involutions.
Check. $\ord{S_4}=24=4\cdot6$. Since $\varphi$ is nontrivial, the product is nonabelian, and
indeed $S_4$ is nonabelian. The map $\Phi(v,k)=vk$ is the claimed isomorphism $V_4\sdp S_3\to S_4$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: remark
Title: Universal-property contrast
Content:
\begin{remark}[Universal-property contrast]
The direct product $A\times B$ is characterized by its projections: any pair $f\colon T\to A$,
$g\colon T\to B$ factors uniquely through $A\times B$,
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
& T \arrow[dl, "f"'] \arrow[dr, "g"] \arrow[d, dashed, "{(f,g)}"] & \\
A & A\times B \arrow[l, two heads, "\pi_1"] \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi_2"'] & B
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $T$ is any group (a ``test object'' equipped with maps to both factors). $A$ and
$B$ are two groups. $A\times B$ is their direct product, the universal object. Four nodes in a
triangular arrangement.
\dgi{Arrows:} $f\colon T\to A$ and $g\colon T\to B$ are arbitrary homomorphisms (the given data).
$(f,g)\colon T\to A\times B$, $t\mapsto(f(t),g(t))$, is the unique induced homomorphism (dashed,
signifying existence and uniqueness). $\pi_1\colon A\times B\to A$, $(a,b)\mapsto a$, is the
first projection (surjective). $\pi_2\colon A\times B\to B$, $(a,b)\mapsto b$, is the second
projection (surjective).
\dgi{What commutes:} Two triangles commute: $\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$ (left triangle) and
$\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$ (right triangle). Together: the unique dashed map satisfies both
$\pi_1\circ(f,g)=f$ and $\pi_2\circ(f,g)=g$ simultaneously.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic $t\in T$ along the left triangle: $(f,g)(t)=(f(t),g(t))$,
then $\pi_1(f(t),g(t))=f(t)$. Along the right: $\pi_2(f(t),g(t))=g(t)$. Both equalities hold by
definition of the direct-product map. Uniqueness: if $(h_1,h_2)\colon T\to A\times B$ also
satisfies $\pi_i\circ h=$ the given maps, then $h(t)=(h_1(t),h_2(t))=(f(t),g(t))$, so $h=(f,g)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark uses this diagram to contrast with the semidirect product.
The direct product is a categorical product: it comes with two projections and the unique factoring
property above. The semidirect product $H\sdp K$ does not have this property because the
second inclusion $s\colon K\to H\sdp K$ is not a normal complement, so there is no symmetric pair
of projections satisfying such a universal property.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $A=Z/(2)Z$, $B=Z/(3)Z$, $T=Z/(6)Z$. Map $f\colonZ/(6)Z\toZ/(2)Z$ by reduction
mod $2$ and $g\colonZ/(6)Z\toZ/(3)Z$ by reduction mod $3$. The unique $(f,g)\colonZ/(6)Z\toZ/(2)Z\times
Z/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$ sends $\overline1\mapsto(\overline1,\overline1)$; both projections recover $f$ and
$g$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow goes into $A\times B$, not out of it. Students
sometimes read the projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ as the given data and $(f,g)$ as a projection; it is
the reverse. Also, the universality only produces a homomorphism $(f,g)$; it does not say $T\cong
A\times B$; $(f,g)$ is an isomorphism exactly when it is bijective (for finite groups, exactly when
$\ker f\cap\ker g=1$ and $\ord T=\ord A\,\ord B$, as for $Z/(6)Z\toZ/(2)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ above, although neither
$f$ nor $g$ is an isomorphism).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the direct product $A\times B$ is the unique
(up to isomorphism) group equipped with projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ such that any two homomorphisms
out of a test group $T$ factor through it, a property the semidirect product lacks because its two
inclusions are not symmetric.
\end{dgx}
The semidirect product has no such symmetric universal property -- it is not a product in the
categorical sense, because $K$ does not map out as a normal complement. What it does have is the split
exact sequence above: the section $s$ is the extra datum that the direct product upgrades to a normal
section.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Semidirect Products > Worked examples
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``$H\nor G$, $K\nor G$, $H\cap K=1$, $HK=G$'' (both normal) is the criterion for the direct
product $G\cong H\times K$, not the semidirect one. For a genuine semidirect product you only get
$H\nor G$; the complement $K$ need not be normal, and is not when the action is nontrivial. Conversely,
do not assume $K\nor G$ ``for symmetry'' -- in $D_{2n}$ ($n\ge3$) the reflection subgroup $\langle s\rangle$ is
not normal.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 1/3
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Prove that $C_K(H) = \ker\varphi$ (recall that $C_K(H) = C_G(H) \cap K$).
\item Prove that $C_H(K) = N_H(K)$.
\item In Example 1 following the proof of Proposition 11 prove that every element of $G - H$ has order 2. Prove that $G$ is abelian if and only if $h^2 = 1$ for all $h \in H$.
\item Let $p = 2$ and check that the construction of the two non-abelian groups of order $p^3$ is valid in this case. Prove that both resulting groups are isomorphic to $D_8$.
\item Let $G = \operatorname{Hol}(Z_2 \times Z_2)$. (a) Prove that $G = H \sdp K$ where $H \cong Z_2 \times Z_2$ and $K \cong S_3$. Deduce that $|G| = 24$. (b) Prove that $G$ is isomorphic to $S_4$. [Obtain a homomorphism from $G$ into $S_4$ by letting $G$ act on the left cosets of $K$. Use Exercise 1 to show this representation is faithful.]
\item Assume that $K$ is a cyclic group, $H$ is an arbitrary group and $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are homomorphisms from $K$ into $\Aut(H)$ such that $\varphi_1(K)$ and $\varphi_2(K)$ are conjugate subgroups of $\Aut(H)$. If $K$ is infinite assume $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are injective. Prove by constructing an explicit isomorphism that $H \sdp_{\varphi_1} K \cong H \sdp_{\varphi_2} K$ (in particular, if the subgroups $\varphi_1(K)$ and $\varphi_2(K)$ are equal in $\Aut(H)$, then the resulting semidirect products are isomorphic). [Suppose $\sigma\varphi_1(K)\sigma^{-1} = \varphi_2(K)$ so that for some $a \in Z$ we have $\sigma\varphi_1(k)\sigma^{-1} = \varphi_2(k)^a$ for all $k \in K$. Show the map $\psi: H \sdp_{\varphi_1} K \to H \sdp_{\varphi_2} K$ defined by $\psi(h,k) = (\sigma(h),k^a)$ is a homomorphism. Show $\psi$ is bijective by constructing a 2-sided inverse.]
\item This exercise describes thirteen isomorphism types of groups of order 56. (It is not too difficult to show that every group of order 56 is isomorphic to one of these.) (a) Prove that there are three abelian groups of order 56. (b) Prove that every group of order 56 has either a normal Sylow 2-subgroup or a normal Sylow 7-subgroup. (c) Construct the following non-abelian groups of order 56 which have a normal Sylow 7-subgroup and whose Sylow 2-subgroup $S$ is as specified: one group when $S \cong Z_2 \times Z_2 \times Z_2$; two nonisomorphic groups when $S \cong Z_4 \times Z_2$; one group when $S \cong Z_8$; two nonisomorphic groups when $S \cong Q_8$; three nonisomorphic groups when $S \cong D_8$. [For a particular $S$, two groups are not isomorphic if the kernels of the maps from $S$ into $\Aut(Z_7)$ are not isomorphic.] (d) Let $G$ be a group of order 56 with a nonnormal Sylow 7-subgroup. Prove that if $S$ is the Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$ then $S \cong Z_2 \times Z_2 \times Z_2$. [Let an element of order 7 act by conjugation on the seven nonidentity elements of $S$ and deduce that they all have the same order.] (e) Prove that there is a unique group of order 56 with a nonnormal Sylow 7-subgroup. [For existence use the fact that $|\GL_3(\F_2)| = 168$; for uniqueness use Exercise 6.]
\item Construct a non-abelian group of order 75. Classify all groups of order 75 (there are three of them). [Use Exercise 6 to show that the non-abelian group is unique.] (The classification of groups of order $pq^2$, where $p$ and $q$ are primes with $p < q$ and $p$ not dividing $q - 1$, is quite similar.)
\item Show that the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ is an element of order 5 in $\GL_2(\F_{19})$. Use this matrix to construct a non-abelian group of order 1805 and give a presentation of this group. Classify groups of order 1805 (there are three isomorphism types). [Use Exercise 6 to prove uniqueness of the non-abelian group.] (A general method for finding elements of prime order in $\GL_n(\F_p)$ is described in the exercises in Section 12.2; this particular matrix of order 5 in $\GL_2(\F_{19})$ appears in Exercise 16 of that section as an illustration of the method.)
\item This exercise classifies the groups of order 147 (there are six isomorphism types). (a) Prove that there are two abelian groups of order 147. (b) Prove that every group of order 147 has a normal Sylow 7-subgroup. (c) Prove that there is a unique non-abelian group whose Sylow 7-subgroup is cyclic. (d) Let $t_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $t_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ be elements of $\GL_2(\F_7)$. Prove $P = \langle t_1, t_2\rangle$ is a Sylow 3-subgroup of $\GL_2(\F_7)$ and that $P \cong Z_3 \times Z_3$. Deduce that every subgroup of $\GL_2(\F_7)$ of order 3 is conjugate in $\GL_2(\F_7)$ to a subgroup of $P$. (e) By Example 3 in Section 1 the group $P$ has four subgroups of order 3 and these are: $P_1 = \langle t_1\rangle$, $P_2 = \langle t_2\rangle$, $P_3 = \langle t_1 t_2\rangle$, and $P_4 = \langle t_1 t_2^2\rangle$. For $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$ let $G_i = (Z_7 \times Z_7) \sdp_{\varphi_i} Z_3$, where $\varphi_i$ is an isomorphism of $Z_3$ with the subgroup $P_i$ of $\Aut(Z_7 \times Z_7)$. For each $i$ describe $G_i$ in terms of generators and relations.

[Use Exercise 6 to show that the non-abelian group is unique.] (The classification of groups of order $pq^2$, where $p$ and $q$ are primes with $p < q$ and $p$ not dividing $q - 1$, is quite similar.)
\item Show that the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ is an element of order 5 in $\GL_2(\F_{19})$. Use this matrix to construct a non-abelian group of order 1805 and give a presentation of this group. Classify groups of order 1805 (there are three isomorphism types). [Use Exercise 6 to prove uniqueness of the non-abelian group.] (A general method for finding elements of prime order in $\GL_n(\F_p)$ is described in the exercises in Section 12.2; this particular matrix of order 5 in $\GL_2(\F_{19})$ appears in Exercise 16 of that section as an illustration of the method.)
\item This exercise classifies the groups of order 147 (there are six isomorphism types). (a) Prove that there are two abelian groups of order 147. (b) Prove that every group of order 147 has a normal Sylow 7-subgroup. (c) Prove that there is a unique non-abelian group whose Sylow 7-subgroup is cyclic. (d) Let $t_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $t_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ be elements of $\GL_2(\F_7)$. Prove $P = \langle t_1, t_2\rangle$ is a Sylow 3-subgroup of $\GL_2(\F_7)$ and that $P \cong \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3$. Deduce that every subgroup of $\GL_2(\F_7)$ of order 3 is conjugate in $\GL_2(\F_7)$ to a subgroup of $P$. (e) By Example 3 in Section 1 the group $P$ has four subgroups of order 3 and these are: $P_1 = \langle t_1\rangle$, $P_2 = \langle t_2\rangle$, $P_3 = \langle t_1 t_2\rangle$, and $P_4 = \langle t_1 t_2^2\rangle$. For $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$ let $G_i = (\mathbb{Z}_7 \times \mathbb{Z}_7) \sdp_{\varphi_i} \mathbb{Z}_3$, where $\varphi_i$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}_3$ with the subgroup $P_i$ of $\Aut(\mathbb{Z}_7 \times \mathbb{Z}_7)$. For each $i$ describe $G_i$ in terms of generators and relations.

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 3/3
Content:
Exercise 16, Section 2.1). (a) Prove that $G$ is the semidirect product $U \sdp D$ where $U$ is the set of upper triangular matrices with 1's down the diagonal (cf. Exercise 17, Section 2.1) and $D$ is the set of diagonal matrices in $\GL_n(F)$. (b) Let $n = 2$. Recall that $U \cong F$ and $D \cong F^\times \times F^\times$ (cf. Exercise 11 in Section 3.1). Describe the homomorphism from $D$ into $\Aut(U)$ explicitly in terms of these isomorphisms (i.e., show how each element of $F^\times \times F^\times$ acts as an automorphism on $F$).
\item Let $K$ and $L$ be groups, let $n$ be a positive integer, let $\rho: K \to S_n$ be a homomorphism and let $H$ be the direct product of $n$ copies of $L$. In Exercise 8 of Section 1 an injective homomorphism $\psi$ from $S_n$ into $\Aut(H)$ was constructed by letting the elements of $S_n$ permute the $n$ factors of $H$. The composition $\psi \circ \rho$ is a homomorphism from $K$ into $\Aut(H)$. The wreath product of $L$ by $K$ is the semidirect product $H \sdp K$ with respect to this homomorphism and is denoted by $L \wr K$ (this wreath product depends on the choice of permutation representation $\rho$ of $K$ --- if none is given explicitly, $\rho$ is assumed to be the left regular representation of $K$). (a) Assume $K$ and $L$ are finite groups and $\rho$ is the left regular representation of $K$. Find $|L \wr K|$ in terms of $|K|$ and $|L|$. (b) Let $p$ be a prime, let $K = L = Z_p$ and let $\rho$ be the left regular representation of $K$. Prove that $Z_p \wr Z_p$ is a non-abelian group of order $p^{p+1}$ and is isomorphic to a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S_{p^2}$. [The $p$ copies of $Z_p$ whose direct product makes up $H$ may be represented by $p$ disjoint $p$-cycles; these are cyclically permuted by $K$.]
\item Let $n$ be an integer $> 1$. Prove the following classification: every group of order $n$ is abelian if and only if $n = p_1^{\alpha_1} p_2^{\alpha_2} \cdots p_r^{\alpha_r}$, where $p_1, \ldots, p_r$ are distinct primes, $\alpha_i = 1$ or 2 for all $i \in \{1, \ldots, r\}$ and $p_i$ does not divide $p_j^{\alpha_j} - 1$ for all $i$ and $j$. [See Exercise 56 in Section 4.5.]
\item Let $H(\F_p)$ be the Heisenberg group over the finite field $\F_p = Z/pZ$ (cf. Exercise 20 in Section 4). Prove that $H(\F_2) \cong D_8$ and that for odd $p$, $H(\F_p)$ has exponent $p$ and is isomorphic to the first non-abelian group in Example 7.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
 \item Let $H=Z/(3)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$ and let $\tau\in\Aut(H)$ be the coordinate swap $\tau(a,b)=(b,a)$. Check that $\tau^2=\id$, so that $\varphi\colonZ/(2)Z\to\Aut(H)$ with $\varphi(\overline1)=\tau$ is a well-defined homomorphism. Form the order-$18$ group $H\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z$, and using the multiplication rule $(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)=(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),k_1k_2)$ compute the product $\bigl((1,0),\overline1\bigr)\bigl((0,1),\overline1\bigr)$ and the inverse of $\bigl((1,0),\overline1\bigr)$. Confirm by the conjugation rule of Proposition~ [REF:prop:sdp@c5] (3) that the order-$2$ element $\bigl((0,0),\overline1\bigr)$ swaps the two $Z/(3)Z$ factors.
 \item Build a nonabelian group of order $20$ as $Z/(5)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z$ by sending the generator $\overline 1\inZ/(4)Z$ to the automorphism ``multiplication by $2$'' of $Z/(5)Z$. Verify this automorphism has order $4$ and that $\varphi$ is therefore a legitimate homomorphism, give the presentation $\langle x,y\st x^5=y^4=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^2\rangle$, and explain precisely where the divisibility $4\mid 5-1$ is used.
 \item Exhibit $A_4$ as an internal semidirect product $V_4\sdp\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$, where $V_4=\{e,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}$. Verify the four conditions of Theorem~ [REF:thm:internal@c5] : $V_4\nor A_4$, $\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\sgr A_4$, $V_4\cap\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle=1$, and $V_4\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle=A_4$. Then compute the conjugation action of $(1\,2\,3)$ on the three involutions of $V_4$ and identify $\varphi\colonZ/(3)Z\to\Aut(V_4)$ as a cyclic permutation of order $3$.
 \item For a general external product $G=H\sdp_\varphi K$, prove that an element $(h_0,k_0)$ is central if and only if $h_0\in H^K$ (the set of $\varphi$-fixed points), $k_0\in Z(K)$, and $h_0\,\varphi_{k_0}(h)=h\,h_0$ for all $h\in H$ (i.e.\ $\varphi_{k_0}$ is conjugation by $h_0^{-1}$; for abelian $H$ this says $\varphi_{k_0}=\id$). Deduce that $Z(G)\cap H=H^K\cap Z(H)$ (which is $H^K$ when $H$ is abelian), and conclude that if $H$ is abelian and $\varphi$ is faithful with no nonzero fixed points then $Z(G)=1$. Verify the latter on the group $Z/(5)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z$ of the previous problem.
 \item In $D_{2n}$ with $n\ge3$, written $\langle r,s\st r^n=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$, show that the rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle$ is normal but the reflection subgroup $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$ is not (compute $r\,s\,r^{-1}$ and check it does not lie in $\langle s\rangle$). Explain how this exhibits $D_{2n}$ as a genuine semidirect product rather than a direct product.
 \item Determine how many semidirect products $Z/(11)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(5)Z$ arise up to isomorphism. Use that $\Aut(Z/(11)Z)\congZ/(10)Z$ has a unique subgroup of order $5$ to count the homomorphisms $Z/(5)Z\to\Aut(Z/(11)Z)$, identify the trivial one with $Z/(55)Z$, and explain why the nontrivial ones all give isomorphic nonabelian groups of order $55$.
 \item Verify the internal-recognition checklist of Theorem~ [REF:thm:internal@c5] for $S_3$ with $H=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$ and $K=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$: check $H\nor S_3$, $K\sgr S_3$, $H\cap K=1$, and $HK=S_3$. Then compute $\varphi_{(1\,2)}\bigl((1\,2\,3)\bigr)$ by conjugation and conclude $S_3\congZ/(3)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z$ with the inversion action.
 \item Show that sending the generator of $Z/(2)Z$ to an automorphism of $Z/(7)Z$ of order $3$ does not define a semidirect product. Explain, in terms of the requirement $\varphi(1)^2=\id$, exactly which automorphisms of $Z/(7)Z$ do give a homomorphism $Z/(2)Z\to\Aut(Z/(7)Z)$, and name the two groups $Z/(7)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(2)Z$ that result.

\end{exers}

Check that $\tau^2=\id$, so that $\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(H)$ with $\varphi(\overline1)=\tau$ is a well-defined homomorphism. Form the order-$18$ group $H\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, and using the multiplication rule $(h_1,k_1)(h_2,k_2)=(h_1\varphi_{k_1}(h_2),k_1k_2)$ compute the product $\bigl((1,0),\overline1\bigr)\bigl((0,1),\overline1\bigr)$ and the inverse of $\bigl((1,0),\overline1\bigr)$. Confirm by the conjugation rule of Proposition~\ref{prop:sdp@c5}(3) that the order-$2$ element $\bigl((0,0),\overline1\bigr)$ swaps the two $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ factors.
  \item Build a nonabelian group of order $20$ as $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ by sending the generator $\overline 1\in\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ to the automorphism ``multiplication by $2$'' of $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$. Verify this automorphism has order $4$ and that $\varphi$ is therefore a legitimate homomorphism, give the presentation $\langle x,y\st x^5=y^4=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^2\rangle$, and explain precisely where the divisibility $4\mid 5-1$ is used.
  \item Exhibit $A_4$ as an internal semidirect product $V_4\sdp\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$, where $V_4=\{e,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}$. Verify the four conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:internal@c5}: $V_4\nor A_4$, $\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\sgr A_4$, $V_4\cap\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle=1$, and $V_4\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle=A_4$. Then compute the conjugation action of $(1\,2\,3)$ on the three involutions of $V_4$ and identify $\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(V_4)$ as a cyclic permutation of order $3$.
  \item For a general external product $G=H\sdp_\varphi K$, prove that an element $(h_0,k_0)$ is central if and only if $h_0\in H^K$ (the set of $\varphi$-fixed points), $k_0\in Z(K)$, and $h_0\,\varphi_{k_0}(h)=h\,h_0$ for all $h\in H$ (i.e.\ $\varphi_{k_0}$ is conjugation by $h_0^{-1}$; for abelian $H$ this says $\varphi_{k_0}=\id$). Deduce that $Z(G)\cap H=H^K\cap Z(H)$ (which is $H^K$ when $H$ is abelian), and conclude that if $H$ is abelian and $\varphi$ is faithful with no nonzero fixed points then $Z(G)=1$. Verify the latter on the group $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ of the previous problem.
  \item In $D_{2n}$ with $n\ge3$, written $\langle r,s\st r^n=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$, show that the rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle$ is normal but the reflection subgroup $\langle s\rangle=\{1,s\}$ is not (compute $r\,s\,r^{-1}$ and check it does not lie in $\langle s\rangle$). Explain how this exhibits $D_{2n}$ as a genuine semidirect product rather than a direct product.
  \item Determine how many semidirect products $\mathbb{Z}/(11)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ arise up to isomorphism. Use that $\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(11)\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z}$ has a unique subgroup of order $5$ to count the homomorphisms $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(11)\mathbb{Z})$, identify the trivial one with $\mathbb{Z}/(55)\mathbb{Z}$, and explain why the nontrivial ones all give isomorphic nonabelian groups of order $55$.
  \item Verify the internal-recognition checklist of Theorem~\ref{thm:internal@c5} for $S_3$ with $H=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$ and $K=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$: check $H\nor S_3$, $K\sgr S_3$, $H\cap K=1$, and $HK=S_3$. Then compute $\varphi_{(1\,2)}\bigl((1\,2\,3)\bigr)$ by conjugation and conclude $S_3\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ with the inversion action.
  \item Show that sending the generator of $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ to an automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z}$ of order $3$ does \emph{not} define a semidirect product. Explain, in terms of the requirement $\varphi(1)^2=\id$, exactly which automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z}$ \emph{do} give a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})$, and name the two groups $\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z}\sdp_\varphi\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ that result.

\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
 \item Let $1\to H\xrightarrow{\iota}G\xrightarrow{\pi}K\to1$ be a short exact sequence with $K$ cyclic of order $n$. Prove that the sequence splits if and only if $G$ contains an element $t$ of order $n$ with $\pi(t)$ a generator of $K$. (Hint: given such $t$, show $\langle t\rangle$ is a complement to $\iota(H)$ and define the splitting by $s\bigl(\pi(t)^j\bigr)=t^j$; conversely, $t=s(generator)$ satisfies $t^n=s(1)=1$ and $\pi(t)$ generates $K$.) Use this to show the sequence $1\toZ/(3)Z\toZ/(9)Z\toZ/(3)Z\to1$ does not split, so $Z/(9)Z$ is a non-split extension of $Z/(3)Z$ by $Z/(3)Z$.
 \item For $n\ge3$ exhibit $S_n$ as an internal semidirect product $A_n\sdp\langle (1\,2)\rangle$. Verify $A_n\nor S_n$, $\langle (1\,2)\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$, $A_n\cap\langle (1\,2)\rangle=1$, and $A_n\langle (1\,2)\rangle=S_n$ (note coprimality is not needed), and identify the action $\varphi\colonZ/(2)Z\to\Aut(A_n)$ as conjugation by the transposition $(1\,2)$. Explain why $\varphi$ is nontrivial, so the product is not direct.
 \item Prove that $Q_8$ is not isomorphic to any nontrivial semidirect product $H\sdp K$ of proper subgroups. (Hint: such a decomposition would need $H\cap K=1$ with $\{\ord H,\ord K\}=\{2,4\}$; analyze the order-$2$ subgroups of $Q_8$ and show every subgroup of order $4$ contains the unique element $-1$ of order $2$.) Conclude that $Q_8$ is a non-split extension.
 \item Determine all isomorphism types of $Z/(3)Z\sdp_\varphiZ/(4)Z$, i.e.\ all groups of order $12$ with normal Sylow $3$-subgroup and cyclic complement $Z/(4)Z$. Using $\Aut(Z/(3)Z)\congZ/(2)Z$, count the homomorphisms $Z/(4)Z\to\Aut(Z/(3)Z)$, show there are exactly two resulting groups, identify the trivial case as $Z/(12)Z$, and give the presentation $\langle x,y\st x^3=y^4=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^{-1}\rangle$ of the nonabelian one (the dicyclic group of order $12$).

\end{exers}

Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Semidirect Products > Worked examples
Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
 \item Consider the semidirect product $H\sdp_\varphi K$ with $\iota(h)=(h,1)$, $\pi(h,k)=k$, and $s(k)=(1,k)$. Verify that
 \[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] & H\sdp_\varphi K \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[l, bend right=40, "s"'] & 1
 \end{tikzcd}\]
 is a short exact sequence with $\im\iota=\ker\pi=H\times\{1\}$ and $\pi\circ s=\id_K$ (so the extension splits). Then compute $s(k)\,\iota(h)\,s(k)^{-1}$ in $H\sdp_\varphi K$ and confirm it equals $(\varphi_k(h),1)$, so that the conjugation action induced by the splitting recovers $\varphi$.
 \item Exhibit the sign sequence $1\to A_n\xrightarrow{\iota}S_n\xrightarrow{\sgn}Z/(2)Z\to1$ for $n\ge3$, where $\iota$ is inclusion and $\sgn$ is the sign homomorphism (with $-1$ identified with the nontrivial element of $Z/(2)Z$). Define a splitting $s\colonZ/(2)Z\to S_n$ by sending the nontrivial element to the transposition $(1\,2)$, check that $s^2=1$ makes it a homomorphism with $\sgn\circ s=\id$, draw the resulting split exact sequence, and conclude $S_n\cong A_n\sdp\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ with the conjugation action.
 \item Compare a semidirect product with the trivial (direct-product) extension by drawing the morphism of short exact sequences
 \[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, equal] & H\sdp_\varphi K \arrow[r, two heads] \arrow[d, dashed, "u"] & K \arrow[r] \arrow[d, equal] & 1 \\
 1 \arrow[r] & H \arrow[r, hook] & H\times K \arrow[r, two heads] & K \arrow[r] & 1
 \end{tikzcd}\]
 with $u(h,k)=(h,k)$. Show that $u$ is a homomorphism making both squares commute if and only if $\varphi$ is trivial, so $u$ is an equivalence of the two extensions exactly when $H\sdp_\varphi K=H\times K$. Explain why this is the diagrammatic content of ``the direct product is the degenerate semidirect product.''
 \item Draw the sequence $1\toZ/(2)Z\xrightarrow{\iota}Z/(4)Z\xrightarrow{\pi}Z/(2)Z\to1$, where $\iota$ identifies $Z/(2)Z$ with $\langle x^2\rangle\sgrZ/(4)Z=\langle x\rangle$ and $\pi$ is reduction modulo $\langle x^2\rangle$. Prove this sequence does not split: any section $s\colonZ/(2)Z\toZ/(4)Z$ would require an order-$2$ element mapping onto the generator of the quotient, but the only order-$2$ element $x^2$ lies in $\ker\pi$. Conclude that $Z/(4)Z$ is a non-split extension and in particular $Z/(4)Z\not\congZ/(2)Z\sdpZ/(2)Z$ (which would be $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$).

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 5.1.2] For $G = G_1 \times \cdots \times G_n$, proper nonempty $I \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $J$ its complement, prove $G_I \cong \prod_{i\in I} G_i$, that $G_I \nor G$ with $G/G_I \cong G_J$, and $G \cong G_I \times G_J$.
\item [DF 5.1.3] With the preceding notation and disjoint nonempty $I,K$, prove $xy = yx$ for all $x \in G_I$, $y \in G_K$.
\item [DF 5.1.7] For groups $G_i$ and fixed $\pi \in S_n$, prove the reindexing map $\varphi_\pi : \prod G_i \to \prod G_{\pi^{-1}(i)}$, $(g_i) \mapsto (g_{\pi^{-1}(i)})$, is an isomorphism.
\item [DF 5.1.9] For a field $F$, use the preceding to show the $n \times n$ permutation matrices form a subgroup of $\GL_n(F)$ isomorphic to $S_n$.
\item [DF 5.1.14] For $G = A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n$ with $B_i \nor A_i$, prove $\prod B_i \nor G$ and $(\prod A_i)/(\prod B_i) \cong \prod (A_i/B_i)$.
\item [DF 5.1.15] For an arbitrary index set $I$ and groups $(G_i,\star_i)$, verify that componentwise multiplication on $\prod_{i\in I} G_i$ is well defined and associative, with identity $\prod 1_i$ and inverses $\prod a_i^{-1}$.
\item [DF 5.1.16] State and prove the generalization of Proposition 2 to arbitrary direct products.
\item [DF 5.2.5] For a finite abelian group $G$ of type $(n_1,\ldots,n_t)$, prove $G$ has an element of order $m$ iff $m \mid n_1$, and deduce $G$ has exponent $n_1$.
\item [DF 5.2.6] Prove every finite group has finite exponent; give an infinite group of finite exponent; ask whether a finite group of exponent $m$ must have an element of order $m$.
\item [DF 5.2.7] For an abelian $p$-group $A = \langle x_1\rangle\times\cdots\times\langle x_n\rangle$ with $|x_i|=p^{\alpha_i}>1$, study the $p$th-power map $\varphi: x \mapsto x^p$: prove it is a homomorphism, describe its image and kernel by generators, and show $\ker\varphi$ and $A/\im\varphi$ each have rank $n$ and are $\cong E_{p^n}$.
\item [DF 5.2.8] For a finite abelian group $A$ and prime $p$, with $A^p = \{a^p\}$ and $A_p = \{x : x^p=1\}$, prove $A/A^p \cong A_p$, and that the number of subgroups of order $p$ equals the number of index $p$.
\item [DF 5.2.10] For the free abelian group $A$ of rank $n$ and $k \in Z^+$, prove $A/kA \cong (Z/kZ)^n$.
\item [DF 5.2.13] For $A = \langle x_1\rangle\times\cdots\times\langle x_r\rangle$ with $|x_i|=n_i$, find a presentation of $A$ and prove the universal property: commuting $g_i$ with $g_i^{n_i}=1$ yield a unique homomorphism $x_i \mapsto g_i$.
\item [DF 5.4.2] Prove a subgroup $H \le G$ is normal iff $[G,H] \le H$.
\item [DF 5.4.3] Prove $[a,bc] = [a,c](c^{-1} [a,b]c)$ and $[ab,c] = (b^{-1} [a,c]b)[b,c]$.
\item [DF 5.4.8] If $x,y \in G$ both commute with $[x,y]$, prove $(xy)^n = x^n y^n [y,x]^{n(n-1)/2}$ for all $n \in Z^+$.
\item [DF 5.4.10] Prove a finite abelian group is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups.
\item [DF 5.4.15] If $A,B \nor G$ with $G/A$ and $G/B$ abelian, prove $G/(A\cap B)$ is abelian.
\item [DF 5.4.16] If $K \nor G$, prove $K' \nor G$.
\item [DF 5.4.17] If $K \nor G$ is cyclic, prove $G' \le C_G(K)$.
\item [DF 5.4.21] If $G_1,G_2$ are groups, prove $\Aut(G_1 \times G_2)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Aut(G_1) \times \Aut(G_2)$.
\item [DF 5.5.3] In Example 1 after Proposition 11, prove every element of $G - H$ has order $2$, and $G$ is abelian iff $h^2=1$ for all $h\in H$.
\item [DF 5.5.11] Classify the groups of order $28$ (there are four isomorphism types).
\item [DF 5.5.12] Classify the groups of order $20$ (there are five isomorphism types).
\item [DF 5.5.16] Show there are exactly $4$ homomorphisms $Z_2 \to \Aut(Z_8)$, giving the semidirect products $Z_8 \times Z_2$, $D_{16}$, $QD_{16}$, and the modular group $M$.
\item [Artin 11.3] Prove that the product of two infinite cyclic groups is not infinite cyclic.
\item [Artin 11.4] In each case decide whether $G \cong H \times K$: (a) $G=R^\times$, $H=\{\pm 1\}$, $K=R_{>0}$; (b) $G$ invertible upper-triangular $2\times2$, $H$ diagonal, $K$ unipotent; (c) $G=C^\times$, $H$ the unit circle, $K=R_{>0}$.
\item [Artin 11.6] If $G$ has normal subgroups of orders $3$ and $5$, prove $G$ contains an element of order $15$.
\item [Artin 11.7] For $H \le G$ and a homomorphism $\varphi: G \to H$ restricting to the identity on $H$, with $N = \ker\varphi$, describe the product map $H \times N \to G$.
\item [Artin 11.8] For groups $G,G',H$, establish a bijection between homomorphisms $H \to G \times G'$ and pairs $(\varphi,\varphi')$ with $\varphi: H \to G$, $\varphi': H \to G'$.
\item [Artin 11.9] For subgroups $H,K \le G$, prove $HK$ is a subgroup iff $HK = KH$.
\item [Artin M.2] (a) Prove every group of even order has an element of order $2$; (b) prove every group of order $21$ has an element of order $3$.
\item [Fraleigh 9.27] If there are $r$ abelian groups of order $m$ and $s$ of order $n$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$, show there are $rs$ abelian groups of order $mn$.

\item [Fraleigh 9.37] For distinct primes $p,q$, compare the number of abelian groups of order $p^r$ with the number of order $q^r$.
\item [Fraleigh 9.38] For an abelian $G$ of order $72$, decide whether the number of subgroups of order $8$, and of order $4$, is determined.
\item [Fraleigh 9.39] For an abelian group $G$, show the elements of finite order form a subgroup (the torsion subgroup).

Section: Direct and Semidirect Products and Abelian Groups > Graded Problem Bank > Hard
Type: exercise_set
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 5.1.4] For finite groups $A,B$ and prime $p$, prove every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $A \times B$ is $P \times Q$ with $P \in \Syl_p(A)$, $Q \in \Syl_p(B)$, so $n_p(A\times B) = n_p(A)n_p(B)$; generalize to finitely many factors.
\item [DF 5.1.8] For $G_1 = \cdots = G_n$, show each $\varphi_\pi \in \Aut(G)$ and that $\pi \mapsto \varphi_\pi$ is an injective homomorphism $S_n \hookrightarrow \Aut(G)$.
\item [DF 5.1.12] Define the central product $A * B = (A\times B)/Z$; prove the images of $A,B$ in $A*B$ are isomorphic to $A,B$ and meet in a central $\cong Z_1$, find $|A*B|$, and show $Z_4 D_8 \cong Z_4 Q_8$.
\item [DF 5.1.13] Give presentations for the central products $Z_4 D_8$ and $Z_4 Q_8$ of the preceding exercise.
\item [DF 5.1.17] For an index set $I$ and groups $G_i$, prove the restricted direct product is a normal subgroup of the direct product, and for $I=Z^+$ and $G_i = Z/p_iZ$ ($p_i$ the $i$th prime) show every element has finite order while the full product has infinite-order elements (it is the torsion subgroup).
\item [DF 5.1.18] In (a)--(e) give an example of a group with the stated property (e.g. infinite with every element of order $1$ or $2$; $G \cong G \times G$ nontrivial).
\item [DF 5.2.11] For a nontrivial finite abelian $G$ of rank $t$, prove the rank equals the max of the ranks of its Sylow subgroups, and $G$ needs exactly $t$ generators.
\item [DF 5.2.12] For $n,m$ with $d=(n,m)$ and the central product $A$ of $\langle x\rangle,\langle y\rangle$ with order-$d$ identified, describe $A$ as a direct product of two cyclic groups.
\item [DF 5.3.1] Prove $D_{16}$, $Z_2 \times D_8$, $Z_2 \times Q_8$, $Z_4 * D_8$, $QD_{16}$, and $M$ are pairwise nonisomorphic non-abelian groups of order $16$.
\item [DF 5.4.5] Prove $A_n$ is the commutator subgroup of $S_n$ for all $n \ge 5$.
\item [DF 5.4.7] Prove that if $p$ is prime and $P$ is a non-abelian group of order $p^3$, then $P' = Z(P)$.
\item [DF 5.4.9] For an odd prime $p$ and $|P|=p^3$, prove $x \mapsto x^p$ is a homomorphism $P \to Z(P)$; if $P$ is not cyclic the kernel has order $p^2$ or $p^3$; discuss the squaring map for order $8$ and where oddness is used.

Type: definition
Title: Upper central series
Content:
\begin{definition}[Upper central series]
The upper central series of $G$ is the chain of subgroups
\[
1=Z_0\sgr Z_1\sgr Z_2\sgr\cdots
\]
defined inductively by $Z_0=1$ and, for $i\ge 0$,
\[
Z_{i+1}/Z_i \;=\; Z\!\left(G/Z_i\right).
\]
Equivalently, $Z_{i+1}=\{\,g\in G:[g,x]\in Z_i for all x\in G\,\}$ is the full preimage in $G$ of the center of $G/Z_i$. In particular $Z_1=Z(G)$.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: Lower central series
Content:
\begin{definition}[Lower central series]
The lower central series of $G$ is the chain
\[
G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\gamma_3\ge\cdots,\qquad
\gamma_1=G,\quad \gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G].
\]
So $\gamma_2=[G,G]=G'$ is the commutator subgroup, $\gamma_3=[G',G]$, and so on. Each $\gamma_i$ is characteristic in $G$ (hence normal), and $\gamma_i/\gamma_{i+1}$ is contained in the center of $G/\gamma_{i+1}$, so the successive quotients are abelian and central.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: Nilpotent group; nilpotency class
Content:
\begin{definition}[Nilpotent group; nilpotency class]
A group $G$ is nilpotent if $Z_c=G$ for some $c\ge 0$, i.e.\ the upper central series reaches $G$ in finitely many steps. The least such $c$ is the nilpotency class of $G$. A nontrivial group has class $\ge 1$; class $1$ means $G=Z(G)$, i.e.\ $G$ is abelian (and nontrivial).
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Upper and lower series have equal length
Label: prop:equal-length@c6
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Upper and lower series have equal length] 
For a group $G$ and an integer $c\ge 0$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $Z_c=G$ (upper central series reaches $G$ at step $c$);
\item[(b)] $\gamma_{c+1}=1$ (lower central series reaches $1$ at step $c+1$).
\end{enumerate}
Hence $G$ is nilpotent iff the lower central series terminates at $1$, and the two series have the same length: the class $c$ is the least $c$ with $Z_c=G$ and also the least $c$ with $\gamma_{c+1}=1$.
\end{proposition}
label: prop:equal-length@c6

Type: proof

Content:
\begin{proof}
The two series interleave: we prove the dovetailing bound $\gamma_{i+1}\le Z_{c-i}$ for $0\le i\le c$ whenever $Z_c=G$, and the dual bound $\gamma_{c+1-i}\le Z_i$ for $0\le i\le c$ whenever $\gamma_{c+1}=1$. The single ingredient is that elements of $Z_j$ are central modulo $Z_{j-1}$, which gives
\[
[Z_j,G]\le Z_{j-1}\qquad(j\ge 1).
\]

$(a)\Longrightarrow(b)$: Assume $Z_c=G$. We show $\gamma_{i+1}\le Z_{c-i}$ by induction on $i$. For $i=0$: $\gamma_1=G=Z_c=Z_{c-0}$. Assume $\gamma_i\le Z_{c-i+1}$. Then
\[
\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]\le[Z_{c-i+1},G]\le Z_{c-i},
\]
where the last step is the displayed inclusion with $j=c-i+1$. Taking $i=c$ gives $\gamma_{c+1}\le Z_0=1$, so $\gamma_{c+1}=1$.

$(b)\Longrightarrow(a)$: Assume $\gamma_{c+1}=1$. We show $\gamma_{c+1-i}\le Z_i$ by induction on $i$. The base $i=0$ is $\gamma_{c+1}=1\le Z_0$. For the inductive step, suppose $\gamma_{c+1-(i-1)}=\gamma_{c-i+2}\le Z_{i-1}$. Then for $g\in\gamma_{c-i+1}$ we have
\[
[g,G]\le[\gamma_{c-i+1},G]=\gamma_{c-i+2}\le Z_{i-1},
\]
so $g$ is central modulo $Z_{i-1}$, i.e.\ $g\in Z_i$; thus $\gamma_{c-i+1}\le Z_i$. Taking $i=c$ gives $G=\gamma_1\le Z_c$, so $Z_c=G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The two series ``zip'' past each other: in a class-$c$ group, $\gamma_{i+1}\le Z_{c-i}$ for $0\le i\le c$. Drawn as facing chains, the lower series descending on the left meets the upper series ascending on the right exactly at length $c$.
\end{remark}

\vdots \arrow[d, no head] & & \vdots \arrow[d, no head] \\
\gamma_c \arrow[d, no head] & & Z_1=Z(G) \arrow[d, no head] \\
\gamma_{c+1}=1 & & Z_0=1
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\dgi{Objects:} Two descending chains of normal subgroups of a nilpotent group $G$ of class $c$. Left column: the lower central series $G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_{c+1}=1$, where each $\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]$ is generated by commutators. Right column: the upper central series $1=Z_0\sgr Z_1\sgr\cdots\sgr Z_c=G$, where each $Z_{i+1}$ is the full preimage of $Z(G/Z_i)$. Both chains consist of characteristic (hence normal) subgroups of $G$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Every arrow is drawn with no head, indicating a strict inclusion of subgroups (not a homomorphism). Downward arrows on the left record $\gamma_{i+1}\le\gamma_i$; downward arrows on the right record $Z_{i-1}\le Z_i$ (written top-to-bottom, so the upper series appears reversed). There are no horizontal arrows; the diagram juxtaposes the two chains but does not draw any explicit inter-column map.
\dgi{What commutes:} The diagram has no composable arrows and hence no path equality to state. Its content is the dovetailing bound: for all $0\le i\le c$, $\gamma_{i+1}\le Z_{c-i}$. Reading across any horizontal level, the lower-series term $\gamma_{i+1}$ sits inside the upper-series term $Z_{c-i}$ beside it.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase the bound by induction. Base: $\gamma_1=G=Z_c=Z_{c-0}$. Inductive step: suppose $\gamma_i\le Z_{c-i+1}$. Then $\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]\le[Z_{c-i+1},G]\le Z_{c-i}$, using the key inclusion $[Z_j,G]\le Z_{j-1}$ (elements of $Z_j$ are central modulo $Z_{j-1}$). Taking $i=c$ gives $\gamma_{c+1}\le Z_0=1$, so the lower series terminates.

It makes the abstract induction visible --- the series descend and ascend in lockstep, meeting exactly at length $c$ on both sides.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the lower and upper central series of a nilpotent group interleave symmetrically, each dovetailing inside the other, so they must terminate in exactly the same number of steps.

Type: method
Title: Building the upper central series of a finite group
Content:
\begin{method}{Building the upper central series of a finite group}
Trigger. You are asked for $Z_i(G)$, the class of $G$, or to test nilpotency of a specific finite group.\\
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute $Z_1=Z(G)$ directly.
\item Form $\bar G=G/Z_1$ and compute $Z(\bar G)$; pull back to $G$ to get $Z_2$ (the preimage of $Z(\bar G)$).
\item Repeat: $Z_{i+1}=$ preimage in $G$ of $Z(G/Z_i)$. Stop when $Z_i=Z_{i-1}$ (stabilized) or $Z_i=G$ (reached the top).
\item If the series reaches $G$, the class is the index where it first equals $G$. If it stalls below $G$, $G$ is not nilpotent.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Center of $D_8$ and the start of its upper series
Content:
\begin{wex}{Center of $D_8$ and the start of its upper series}
Let $D_8=\langle r,s\mid r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$. Find $Z(D_8)$.
\wrec Center first: $Z_1=Z(G)$ is step 1 of the upper central series, and for a $2$-group we expect it to be nontrivial.
\wsol We test each noncentral generator. Since $srs=r^{-1}\ne r$, $r\notin Z$; since $rs\ne sr$, $s\notin Z$. The element $r^2$ satisfies $s r^2 s=(srs)^2=r^{-2}=r^2$ (as $r^4=1$), and $r^2$ commutes with $r$, so $r^2\in Z$. The eight elements are $1,r,r^2,r^3,s,rs,r^2s,r^3s$; checking conjugation by $s$ sends $r^k\mapsto r^{-k}$ and conjugation by $r$ sends $r^k s\mapsto r^{k+2}s$, so only $1$ and $r^2$ are fixed by all conjugations. Thus $Z(D_8)=\{1,r^2\}\congZ/2Z$.
Check. $|Z|=2$ divides $|G|=8$, and $G/Z(G)$ has order $4$; if it were cyclic $G$ would be abelian, so $G/Z\cong V_4$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: Full upper central series of $D_8$ (class $2$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Full upper central series of $D_8$ (class $2$)}
Compute $1=Z_0\sgr Z_1\sgr Z_2\sgr\cdots$ for $D_8$ and state its nilpotency class.
\wrec Iterate the center-of-quotient construction; $D_8$ is a $2$-group so the series must reach $G$.
\wsol From the previous example $Z_1=\{1,r^2\}$. Now $\bar G=D_8/Z_1$ has order $4$. The images $\bar r,\bar s$ satisfy $\bar r^2=\overline{r^2}=\bar 1$ and $\bar s^2=\bar 1$ and $\bar s\bar r\bar s=\overline{r^{-1}}=\bar r$ (since $r$ and $r^{-1}$ differ by $r^2\in Z_1$), so $\bar G\cong V_4$, which is abelian. Hence $Z(\bar G)=\bar G$, and pulling back, $Z_2=G$. The series is
\[
1\sgr \{1,r^2\}\sgr D_8,
\]
so $D_8$ is nilpotent of class $2$.
Check. Cross-check with the lower series: $\gamma_2=[D_8,D_8]=\langle r^2\rangle$ (the only nontrivial commutators are powers of $r^2$, e.g.\ $[r,s]=r^{-1} s^{-1} r s=r^{-1}\cdot r^{-1}=r^{-2}=r^2$), and $\gamma_3=[\gamma_2,G]=[\langle r^2\rangle,G]=1$ since $r^2$ is central. So $\gamma_3=1$ at index $3=c+1$, confirming class $c=2$.
\end{wex}

Title: $Q_8$ is nilpotent of class $2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q_8$ is nilpotent of class $2$}
For the quaternion group $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$, find the upper central series and the class.
\wrec $2$-group, so nilpotent; compute $Z_1$ then the quotient.
\wsol Each of $i,j,k$ has $-1$ as its square and they anticommute ($ij=k=-ji$), so $i,j,k\notin Z$. But $-1$ commutes with everything: $(-1)x=x(-1)$ for all $x$. Thus $Z_1=Z(Q_8)=\{\pm1\}\congZ/2Z$. Then $Q_8/\{\pm1\}$ has order $4$ with every nonidentity element of order $2$ (the image of $i$ squares to the image of $-1$, which is the identity), so it is $V_4$, abelian. Hence $Z_2=Q_8$ and the class is $2$:
\[
1\sgr\{\pm1\}\sgr Q_8.
\]
Check. $\gamma_2=[Q_8,Q_8]=\{\pm1\}$ (e.g.\ $[i,j]=i^{-1} j^{-1} ij=(-i)(-j)(i)(j)=(ij)(ij)=k^2=-1$), and $\gamma_3=[\{\pm1\},Q_8]=1$. Class $2$ again.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $S_3$ is NOT nilpotent
Content:
\begin{wex}{$S_3$ is NOT nilpotent}
Show $S_3$ is not nilpotent by computing both series.
\wrec If $Z(G)=1$ the upper series never leaves $1$; if $G'=G$ the lower series never leaves $G$. Either stalls $\Longrightarrow$ not nilpotent.
\wsol Center: $S_3$ is nonabelian with trivial center, $Z(S_3)=1$. Hence $Z_0=Z_1=1$, and since $G/Z_0=S_3$ has trivial center, every $Z_i=1$. The upper series stalls at $1\ne S_3$, so $S_3$ is not nilpotent. Lower series: $\gamma_2=[S_3,S_3]=A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\congZ/3Z$, and $\gamma_3=[A_3,S_3]$. A transposition conjugates the $3$-cycle to its inverse, so $[(1\,2\,3),(1\,2)]=(1\,3\,2)(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,3\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,2\,3)\in A_3$; in fact $[A_3,S_3]=A_3$, so $\gamma_2=\gamma_3=A_3\ne 1$. The lower series stalls at $A_3$.
Check. Both diagnostics agree: $Z_1=1$ and $\gamma_2$ does not descend to $1$. $S_3$ is solvable (its derived series is $S_3\ge A_3\ge 1$) but not nilpotent --- a clean separation of the two notions.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: $p$-groups are nilpotent
Label: thm:pgrp-nilpotent@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[$p$-groups are nilpotent] 
Every finite $p$-group is nilpotent. More precisely, if $|G|=p^n$ then the upper central series of $G$ reaches $G$, and the class is at most $n-1$ when $n\ge 2$ (and class $\le n$ in general).
\end{theorem}
label: thm:pgrp-nilpotent@c6

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Further Topics in Group Theory > $p$-Groups, Nilpotent Groups, and Solvable Groups > Finite $p$-groups are nilpotent
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f2d11d35ec5fc5bae096
Content:
\begin{proof}
The key fact is that a nontrivial finite $p$-group has nontrivial center: $G$ acts on itself by conjugation, the class equation gives $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum[G:C_G(x_i)]$ over noncentral class representatives, every index $[G:C_G(x_i)]$ is a positive power of $p$, and $p\mid|G|$, so $p\mid|Z(G)|$, forcing $|Z(G)|>1$.

Now run the upper central series. If $Z_i\ne G$, then $G/Z_i$ is a nontrivial finite $p$-group, so $Z(G/Z_i)\ne 1$, i.e.\ $Z_{i+1}/Z_i\ne 1$ and $Z_{i+1}\gneq Z_i$. Thus the series strictly increases at every step below $G$. Since $|G|=p^n$ is finite, the chain $1=Z_0\lneq Z_1\lneq\cdots$ cannot grow forever; it must reach $G$. Hence $G$ is nilpotent.

For the class bound, let $c$ be the class. Each strict step multiplies the order by at least $p$, so $|Z_i|\ge p^i$ for $i\le c$, whence $c\le n$. If $n\ge2$ and $c=n$, then $|Z_i|=p^i$ for every $i\le n$, so $G/Z_{n-2}$ has order $p^2$ and is therefore abelian; then $Z(G/Z_{n-2})=G/Z_{n-2}$, i.e.\ $Z_{n-1}=G$, contradicting $c=n$. Hence $c\le n-1$ when $n\ge2$.
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``$p$-group'' here means a finite group of prime-power order. Infinite $p$-groups (e.g.\ the semidirect product $Z_{2^\infty}\sdpZ/2Z$ in which $Z/2Z$ acts on the Pr\"ufer $2$-group $Z_{2^\infty}$ by inversion, or an infinite restricted wreath product) need not be nilpotent; the Pr\"ufer group $Z_{p^\infty}$ itself is abelian, hence nilpotent of class $1$. The proof above uses finiteness twice: for the class equation and to guarantee the strictly increasing chain terminates.
\end{pitfall}

\wrec Abelian nontrivial $\Longrightarrow$ class $1$; it is also a $p$-group, so Theorem [REF:thm:pgrp-nilpotent@c6] applies trivially.

Type: theorem
Title: Characterization of finite nilpotent groups
Label: thm:nilpotent-char@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Characterization of finite nilpotent groups] 
Let $G$ be a finite group. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $G$ is nilpotent.
\item[(2)] Every Sylow subgroup of $G$ is normal in $G$.
\item[(3)] $G$ is the (internal) direct product of its Sylow subgroups: if $|G|=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$ with Sylow $p_i$-subgroup $P_i$, then $G\cong P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$.
\item[(4)] Every maximal subgroup of $G$ is normal in $G$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: thm:nilpotent-char@c6

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Further Topics in Group Theory > $p$-Groups, Nilpotent Groups, and Solvable Groups > Characterizations of finite nilpotent groups
Type: proof
Title: Proof (sketch with the key implications)
Relation: proof_of=unit-11813d67ad2dc58011e2
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof (sketch with the key implications)]
$(1)\Longrightarrow(4)$: Let $M$ be maximal. A standard fact for nilpotent groups is that proper subgroups are properly contained in their normalizers (``normalizers grow''), proved by induction on the class using the central series: if $H\lneq G$ then $H\lneq N_G(H)$. Hence $M\lneq N_G(M)\le G$ forces $N_G(M)=G$, i.e.\ $M\nor G$.

$(4)\Longrightarrow(2)$: Let $P\in\Syl_p(G)$. If $P$ is not normal, then $N_G(P)\lneq G$, so $N_G(P)\le M$ for some maximal $M$. By (4), $M\nor G$. By the Frattini argument (Theorem [REF:thm:frattini-arg@c6] below) applied with $M\nor G$ and $P\in\Syl_p(M)$ (indeed $P\le N_G(P)\le M$, so $P$ is Sylow in $M$), $G=M\,N_G(P)$. But $N_G(P)\le M$, so $G=M$, contradicting $M\lneq G$. Hence every Sylow subgroup is normal.

Building up, $P_1\cdots P_r$ is an internal direct product of order $\prod p_i^{a_i}=|G|$, so $G=P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$.

$(3)\Longrightarrow(1)$: A finite direct product of nilpotent groups is nilpotent (the upper central series of a product is the product of the upper central series, so its length is the max of the factors' classes). Each $P_i$ is a $p$-group, hence nilpotent by Theorem [REF:thm:pgrp-nilpotent@c6] ; therefore $G$ is nilpotent. This closes the cycle $(1)\Longrightarrow(4)\Longrightarrow(2)\Longrightarrow(3)\Longrightarrow(1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The class of a finite nilpotent group $G=P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$ equals $\max_i\,\operatorname{class}(P_i)$. So nilpotency of a finite group is ``Sylow-local'': it holds iff it holds prime-by-prime, after detaching the Sylow subgroups into a direct product.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Sylow-normal nilpotency test (finite groups)
Content:
\begin{method}{Sylow-normal nilpotency test (finite groups)}
Trigger. ``Is this finite group nilpotent?'' --- when you know $|G|$ and can count Sylow subgroups.\\
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Factor $|G|=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$.
\item For each prime $p_i$, use Sylow's theorem: count $n_{p_i}$ (the number of Sylow $p_i$-subgroups), with $n_{p_i}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$ and $n_{p_i}\mid m_i$ where $m_i=|G|/p_i^{a_i}$.
\item $G$ is nilpotent $\iff n_{p_i}=1$ for every $i$ (all Sylow subgroups normal).
\item If so, $G\cong P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$; the class is the max of the Sylow classes.
\end{enumerate}
Shortcut. If even one prime forces $n_p>1$, $G$ is not nilpotent.
\end{method}

Title: Nilpotent groups of order $12$: resolve carefully
Content:
\begin{wex}{Nilpotent groups of order $12$: resolve carefully}
Decide which groups of order $12$ are nilpotent.
\wrec Sylow-normal test: $12=2^2\cdot 3$; nilpotent $\iff$ both the Sylow $2$- and Sylow $3$-subgroups are normal $\iff G\cong P_2\times P_3$.
\wsol The five groups of order $12$ are $Z/12Z$, $Z/2Z\timesZ/6Z$, $A_4$, $D_{12}$, and $\operatorname{Dic}_3=Q_{12}$ (the dicyclic group). A nilpotent group of order $12$ would be $P_2\times P_3$ with $|P_2|=4$, $|P_3|=3$: that is $(Z/4Z or V_4)\timesZ/3Z$, giving exactly $Z/4Z\timesZ/3Z\congZ/12Z$ and $V_4\timesZ/3Z\congZ/2Z\timesZ/6Z$. These two abelian groups are nilpotent (class $1$). The three nonabelian groups are not: in $A_4$, $n_3=4\ne1$ (the four Sylow $3$-subgroups), so its Sylow $3$-subgroup is not normal; in $D_{12}$ and $Q_{12}$, the Sylow $2$-subgroup is not normal (equivalently their center is too small to climb to $G$).
Check. So among order-$12$ groups, exactly the two abelian ones are nilpotent. In particular there is no nonabelian nilpotent group of order $12$: that would need a nonabelian Sylow factor, impossible for $|P_2|=4,|P_3|=3$. Both $Z/12Z$ and $Z/2Z\timesZ/6Z$ have class $1$.
\end{wex}

Title: $A_4$ is not nilpotent
Content:
\begin{wex}{$A_4$ is not nilpotent}
Confirm $A_4$ (order $12$) fails the Sylow-normal test.
\wrec Count $n_3$ in $A_4$.
\wsol $|A_4|=12=2^2\cdot3$. The Sylow $3$-subgroups are generated by $3$-cycles; $A_4$ has eight $3$-cycles, grouped into four subgroups of order $3$ (each containing $2$ nonidentity elements). So $n_3=4$, which satisfies $4\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $4\mid 4$. Since $n_3=4\ne1$, the Sylow $3$-subgroup is not normal, so $A_4$ is not nilpotent.
Check. Directly: $Z(A_4)=1$ (no nonidentity element is fixed by all conjugations in $A_4$), so the upper series stalls at $1$. $A_4$ is solvable but not nilpotent.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A nilpotent group of order $24$: $Q_8\timesZ/3Z$}
Exhibit a nonabelian nilpotent group of order $24$ and give its class.
\wrec $G\cong P_2\times P_3$ with both Sylow normal; pick a nonabelian Sylow $2$-subgroup.
\wsol Take $G=Q_8\timesZ/3Z$, order $8\cdot3=24$. Both factors are the (unique, hence normal) Sylow subgroups: $Q_8\in\Syl_2(G)$, $Z/3Z\in\Syl_3(G)$, and a direct factor is normal. \end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Every Sylow subgroup normal'' is much stronger than ``some Sylow subgroup normal''. A group can have a normal Sylow subgroup (even be solvable) without being nilpotent: $S_3$ has a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup but its Sylow $2$-subgroups (the three order-$2$ subgroups) are not normal, so $S_3$ is not nilpotent. You need all primes to cooperate.
\end{pitfall}

Type: definition
Title: Frattini subgroup
Content:
\begin{definition}[Frattini subgroup]
The Frattini subgroup $\Frat(G)$ of a finite group $G$ is the intersection of all maximal subgroups of $G$:
\[
\Frat(G)=\bigcap\{\,M:M\ is a maximal subgroup of G\,\}.
\]
If $G$ has no maximal subgroups (the case $G=1$), set $\Frat(G)=G=1$. The Frattini subgroup is characteristic in $G$ (any automorphism permutes the maximal subgroups), hence $\Frat(G)\nor G$.
\end{definition}

Title: Nongenerators
Label: prop:nongen@c6
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Nongenerators] 
$\Frat(G)$ is exactly the set of nongenerators of $G$: an element $x$ such that whenever $G=\langle x,Y\rangle$ for a subset $Y$, already $G=\langle Y\rangle$. Consequently, if $\langle Y,\Frat(G)\rangle=G$ then $\langle Y\rangle=G$ (Frattini elements are dispensable in any generating set).
\end{proposition}
label: prop:nongen@c6

\begin{proof}
If $x\notin\Frat(G)$, then $x\notin M$ for some maximal $M$; then $G=\langle x,M\rangle$ but $\langle M\rangle=M\ne G$, so $x$ is a generator-contributor, not a nongenerator. Conversely, if $x\in\Frat(G)$ and $G=\langle x,Y\rangle$ with $\langle Y\rangle\ne G$, then $\langle Y\rangle$ lies in some maximal $M$; since $x\in\Frat(G)\le M$, we get $\langle x,Y\rangle\le M\ne G$, a contradiction. So $\langle Y\rangle=G$, i.e.\ $x$ is a nongenerator.
\end{proof}

Title: Frattini's argument
Label: thm:frattini-arg@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Frattini's argument] 
Let $G$ be a finite group, $N\nor G$, and $P\in\Syl_p(N)$ a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N$. Then
\[
G=N\,N_G(P),
\]
where $N_G(P)$ is the normalizer of $P$ in $G$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:frattini-arg@c6

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-d5fabc3243d6fc0a4eed
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $g\in G$. Since $N\nor G$, conjugation by $g$ maps $N$ to itself, so $gPg^{-1}\le N$ and $gPg^{-1}\in\Syl_p(N)$ (conjugation preserves order and $p$-subgroup-ness). By Sylow's theorem applied inside $N$, all Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N$ are $N$-conjugate, so there is $n\in N$ with $n(gPg^{-1})n^{-1}=P$, i.e.\ $(ng)P(ng)^{-1}=P$. Thus $ng\in N_G(P)$. Writing $g=n^{-1}(ng)$ with $n^{-1}\in N$ and $ng\in N_G(P)$ shows $g\in N\,N_G(P)$. As $g$ was arbitrary, $G=N\,N_G(P)$.
\end{proof}

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
P \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, hook'] & N \arrow[d, hook, "{\nor}"] \\
N_G(P) \arrow[r, hook] & G
\end{tikzcd}
\qquadwith\qquad G=N\cdot N_G(P).
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four subgroups of the finite group $G$ arranged in a commutative square. Top-left: the Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of $N$. Top-right: the normal subgroup $N\nor G$. Bottom-left: the normalizer $N_G(P)$, the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $P$ is normal. Bottom-right: the ambient group $G$.
\dgi{Arrows:} All four arrows are inclusions (hook arrows). Top horizontal: $P\hookrightarrow N$ (given: $P\in\Syl_p(N)$, so $P\le N$). Left vertical: $P\hookrightarrow N_G(P)$ (by definition $P$ normalizes itself, so $P\le N_G(P)$). Right vertical: $N\hookrightarrow G$ labelled $\nor$ (the hypothesis $N\nor G$). Bottom horizontal: $N_G(P)\hookrightarrow G$ (a normalizer is always a subgroup).
\dgi{What commutes:} The square commutes because both composite inclusions $P\to G$ agree: going right-then-down gives $P\le N\le G$, and going down-then-right gives $P\le N_G(P)\le G$. Both paths simply assert $P\le G$, the same subgroup. The key output is not in the square itself but is stated alongside: $G=N\cdot N_G(P)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} An inclusion square of subgroups always commutes: both paths from $P$ to $G$ send every element $x\in P$ to the same element $x\in G$. No well-definedness issue arises because all maps are literal set-inclusions. The proof of $G=N\cdot N_G(P)$ is external: for any $g\in G$, use $N\nor G$ to see $gPg^{-1}\le N$ is Sylow in $N$, then Sylow-conjugacy inside $N$ gives $n\in N$ with $ngPg^{-1}n^{-1}=P$, so $ng\in N_G(P)$ and $g=n^{-1}(ng)\in N\cdot N_G(P)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram encodes the hypothesis and conclusion of the Frattini argument in one picture, making it easy to apply in the proof that $\Frat(G)$ is nilpotent: taking $N=\Frat(G)$ and a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of $\Frat(G)$, the square shows $P\le N_G(P)$ and $N_G(P)\le G$, while Frattini's argument gives $G=\Frat(G)\cdot N_G(P)$; the nongenerator property then forces $N_G(P)=G$, so $P\nor G$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$, $N=A_3\nor S_3$, and $P=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\in\Syl_3(A_3)$. Then $N_G(P)=S_3$ (since $P$ is the unique Sylow $3$-subgroup of $A_3$ and all of $S_3$ normalizes it), and indeed $S_3=A_3\cdot S_3=G$. The diagram shows $P\le A_3\le S_3$ and $P\le S_3\le S_3$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse the square with asserting $N\cap N_G(P)=P$; the diagram says only that both containments hold, not that $P$ is the intersection. Also, the label $\nor$ on the right vertical arrow is a property of $N$ in $G$, not of the arrow itself --- the inclusion $N\hookrightarrow G$ is a map, while $\nor$ is extra data (the normality hypothesis) used in the proof outside the square.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the four subgroups $P\le N\le G$ and $P\le N_G(P)\le G$ fit into a single inclusion square whose existence, combined with normality of $N$, forces the product decomposition $G=N\cdot N_G(P)$.
\end{dgx}

\begin{proof}
Let $P\in\Syl_p(\Frat(G))$. Since $\Frat(G)\nor G$, the Frattini argument (Theorem [REF:thm:frattini-arg@c6] ) gives $G=\Frat(G)\,N_G(P)$. By Proposition [REF:prop:nongen@c6] , the elements of $\Frat(G)$ are nongenerators, so $G=\langle N_G(P)\rangle=N_G(P)$, i.e.\ $P\nor G$ and in particular $P\nor\Frat(G)$. Thus every Sylow subgroup of $\Frat(G)$ is normal in $\Frat(G)$, so by Theorem [REF:thm:nilpotent-char@c6] $\Frat(G)$ is nilpotent.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Computing $\Frat(G)$
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $\Frat(G)$}
Trigger. You need $\Frat(G)$ for a specific $G$ (often a $p$-group or abelian group).\\
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item List the maximal subgroups (in a $p$-group, maximal subgroups are exactly the index-$p$ subgroups, all normal).
\item Intersect them.
\item Shortcut for $p$-groups: $\Frat(G)=G'\,G^p$, where $G^p=\langle g^p:g\in G\rangle$. The quotient $G/\Frat(G)$ is the largest elementary abelian $p$-quotient.
\item Shortcut for finite abelian $G$: $\Frat(G)=\bigcap_{p\,\mid\,|G|}\,pG$; equivalently $G/\Frat(G)\cong\prod_p(Z/pZ)^{r_p}$ where $r_p$ is the $p$-rank.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: $\Frat(Z/p^nZ)$

\begin{wex}{$\Frat(Z/p^nZ)$}
Compute the Frattini subgroup of the cyclic group $Z/p^nZ$.
\wrec Cyclic $p$-group: a unique maximal subgroup, of index $p$.
\wsol $Z/p^nZ$ is cyclic, so its subgroups are totally ordered: $0\le p^{n-1}Z/p^nZ\le\cdots\leZ/p^nZ$. The unique maximal subgroup is the index-$p$ subgroup $pZ/p^nZ\congZ/p^{n-1}Z$. The intersection over the (single) maximal subgroup is itself, so $\Frat(Z/p^nZ)=pZ/p^nZ\congZ/p^{n-1}Z$.
Check. The shortcut $\Frat=G'G^p=1\cdot G^p=pG$ gives the same answer, and $G/\Frat\congZ/pZ$ is elementary abelian of rank $1$. For $n=1$, $\Frat(Z/pZ)=0$.
\end{wex}

Title: $\Frat$ of an elementary abelian $p$-group is trivial
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Frat$ of an elementary abelian $p$-group is trivial}
Compute $\Frat(E)$ for $E=(Z/pZ)^k$.
\wrec Vector space over $\F_p$: maximal subgroups are the hyperplanes.
\wsol View $E$ as a $k$-dimensional $\F_p$-vector space. Its maximal subgroups are exactly the codimension-$1$ subspaces (hyperplanes). For any nonzero $v\in E$ there is a hyperplane avoiding $v$ (extend $v$ to a basis and drop it). Hence the intersection of all hyperplanes is $\{0\}$: $\Frat(E)=0$.
Check. Shortcut: $E'=0$ (abelian) and $E^p=\langle x^p\rangle=0$ (every element has order dividing $p$), so $\Frat(E)=E'E^p=0$. Then $E/\Frat(E)=E$ is itself elementary abelian of rank $k$, matching ``$G/\Frat(G)$ is the largest elementary abelian quotient''.
\end{wex}

Title: $\Frat(D_8)$ and the rank of $D_8/\Frat(D_8)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Frat(D_8)$ and the rank of $D_8/\Frat(D_8)$}
Compute $\Frat(D_8)$.
\wrec $2$-group: $\Frat=G'\,G^2$; maximal subgroups have index $2$.
\wsol The maximal (index-$2$) subgroups of $D_8$ are $\langle r\rangle\congZ/4Z$, $\langle r^2,s\rangle\cong V_4$, and $\langle r^2,rs\rangle\cong V_4$. Their intersection: $\langle r\rangle\cap\langle r^2,s\rangle=\langle r^2\rangle$, and $\langle r^2\rangle\le\langle r^2,rs\rangle$, so $\Frat(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle\congZ/2Z$.

Then $D_8/\Frat(D_8)$ has order $4$ and exponent $2$, so it is $(Z/2Z)^2$, elementary abelian of rank $2$ --- consistent with $D_8$ needing $2$ generators.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\Frat(S_3)$}

\wrec List maximal subgroups and intersect; $S_3$ is not a $p$-group, so no $p$-group shortcut.
\wsol The proper nontrivial subgroups of $S_3$ are $A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$ (order $3$, index $2$) and the three order-$2$ subgroups $\langle (1\,2)\rangle,\langle (1\,3)\rangle,\langle (2\,3)\rangle$ (index $3$). \end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The clean formula $\Frat(G)=G'G^p$ holds only for finite $p$-groups. For a general finite group you must either intersect all maximal subgroups directly or, in the abelian case, intersect $pG$ over the primes $p$ dividing $|G|$. Applying ``$G'G^p$'' to a non-$p$-group (e.g.\ choosing a single $p$) gives the wrong subgroup.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Why this matters
Content:
\begin{remark}[Why this matters]
For a finite $p$-group $G$, the quotient $G/\Frat(G)$ is a vector space over $\F_p$, and the Burnside Basis Theorem says a subset of $G$ generates $G$ iff its image spans $G/\Frat(G)$, and a minimal generating set of $G$ maps onto a basis of $G/\Frat(G)$. Thus the minimal number of generators of a $p$-group equals $\dim_{\F_p}\!\big(G/\Frat(G)\big)$ --- the rank we computed above ($1$ for $Z/p^nZ$, $k$ for $(Z/pZ)^k$, $2$ for $D_8$ and $Q_8$).
\end{remark}

Type: prose
Content:
This installment turns the commutator bracket into a machine. From $[x,y]=x^{-1} y^{-1} xy$ we build a canonical subgroup $G'=[G,G]$, the smallest normal subgroup with abelian quotient. Iterating $G\mapsto G'$ produces the derived series, and the groups it kills off in finitely many steps are exactly the solvable groups -- the class that sits between abelian/nilpotent on one side and the genuinely complicated (simple, perfect) groups on the other. We close with the two deep landmarks D\&F states without full proof: Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem and Philip Hall's theorem on Hall subgroups.

Type: definition
Title: Commutators and the commutator subgroup
Content:
\begin{definition}[Commutators and the commutator subgroup]
For $x,y\in G$ the commutator of $x$ and $y$ is
\[
[x,y]\;=\;x^{-1} y^{-1} xy.
\]
For subgroups $H,K\le G$, the subgroup $[H,K]=\langle \,[h,k]\st h\in H,\ k\in K\,\rangle$ is generated by all such commutators (the SET of commutators need not be a subgroup, so the generated subgroup is the right object). The commutator subgroup (or derived subgroup) of $G$ is
\[
G'\;=\;[G,G]\;=\;\langle \,[x,y]\st x,y\in G\,\rangle.
\]
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Universal property of $G'$
Label: prop:gprime@c6
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Universal property of $G'$] 
Let $G$ be a group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $G'\nor G$ (in fact $G'$ is characteristic in $G$).
\item[(b)] $G/G'$ is abelian.
\item[(c)] If $N\nor G$ then $G/N$ is abelian $\Longleftrightarrow G'\le N$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus $G'$ is the unique smallest normal subgroup with abelian quotient: $G/G'$ is the largest abelian quotient of $G$ (the abelianization $G^{ab}$).
\end{proposition}
label: prop:gprime@c6

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f97b0969a01ad4cee884
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) For $g\in G$ and any generator $[x,y]$ we have $g^{-1}[x,y]g=[g^{-1} xg,g^{-1} yg]\in G'$; as conjugation by $g$ is an automorphism sending generators of $G'$ into $G'$, it maps $G'$ into $G'$, so $G'\nor G$. Replacing conjugation by an arbitrary $\varphi\in\Aut(G)$ gives $\varphi(G')\le G'$, hence characteristic.

(b) In $G/G'$ we have $\overline{x}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{x}^{-1}\overline{y}^{-1}=\overline{xyx^{-1} y^{-1}}=\overline{[x^{-1},y^{-1}]}=\overline{1}$ since $[x^{-1},y^{-1}]\in G'$. So any two cosets commute.

(c) Suppose $G/N$ abelian. For $x,y\in G$, $\overline{x}\,\overline{y}=\overline{y}\,\overline{x}$ gives $\overline{[x,y]}=\overline{1}$, i.e. $[x,y]\in N$; as $N$ contains all generators of $G'$, $G'\le N$. Conversely if $G'\le N$ then by the correspondence theorem $G/N$ is a quotient of the abelian group $G/G'$, hence abelian.
\end{proof}
