Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The universal property is a factorization statement: every homomorphism $\varphi\colon G\to A$ into an abelian group $A$ kills $G'$ (because $\im\varphi$ abelian $\Longrightarrow G'\le\ker\varphi$), so it factors uniquely through the abelianization.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & G/G' \arrow[d, dashed, "{\exists!\,\overline{\varphi}}"] \\
& A
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three groups: $G$ (the source group), $G/G'$ (the abelianization, a quotient group), and $A$ (an arbitrary abelian group serving as the target.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi\colon G\twoheadrightarrow G/G'$ is the canonical surjective quotient map, $x\mapsto xG'$. $\varphi\colon G\to A$ is any group homomorphism into an abelian group. $\overline{\varphi}\colon G/G'\to A$ is the unique induced (dashed) map, defined by $\overline{\varphi}(xG')=\varphi(x)$; it is the only map making the triangle commute. Well-definedness: if $xG'=yG'$ then $y^{-1}x\in G'$, so $\varphi(y^{-1}x)\in\varphi(G')\le[A,A]=1$ (since $A$ is abelian, every commutator in $A$ is trivial, and $\varphi$ maps $G'=\langle[a,b]\rangle$ into $[\operatorname{im}\varphi,\operatorname{im}\varphi]=1$), giving $\varphi(x)=\varphi(y)$. So $\overline{\varphi}$ is independent of the coset representative.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\overline{\varphi}\circ\pi=\varphi$. That is, for all $x\in G$: $\overline{\varphi}(\pi(x))=\overline{\varphi}(xG')=\varphi(x)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Start with $x\in G$. Along $\pi$ then $\overline{\varphi}$: $x\xrightarrow{\pi}xG'\xrightarrow{\overline{\varphi}}\varphi(x)$. Along $\varphi$ directly: $x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\varphi(x)$. Both give $\varphi(x)$, by the definition of $\overline{\varphi}$ on cosets.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the universal property of the abelianization $G^{ab}=G/G'$: it is the initial abelian group receiving a map from $G$. Every abelian-target homomorphism out of $G$ factors uniquely through a single object. This turns the abstract characterization of $G'$ in Proposition~ [REF:prop:gprime@c6] (c) into a concrete factorization principle used whenever one wants to compare maps $G\to A$ to maps $G/G'\to A$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$, $G'=A_3$, $G/G'\congZ_2$, and $A=Z_2$ with $\varphi=\operatorname{sgn}$ (the sign map). Then $\overline{\varphi}\colonZ_2\toZ_2$ is the identity, and indeed $\operatorname{sgn}=\overline{\operatorname{sgn}}\circ\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often assume $\overline{\varphi}$ is defined on elements of $G$ rather than on cosets. The map lives on $G/G'$, and its well-definedness relies entirely on $G'\le\ker\varphi$ (i.e. $A$ abelian), which is exactly what the arrow $\varphi$ killing $G'$ encodes. Forgetting to check $G'\le\ker\varphi$ is the most common error.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the abelianization $G/G'$ is the universal abelian quotient of $G$: any homomorphism to an abelian group factors through it uniquely, so studying maps out of $G$ into abelian groups reduces to studying maps out of $G/G'$.
\end{dgx}
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Computing $G'$ in practice
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $G'$ in practice}
To find $G'=[G,G]$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Use a known abelianization. If you can spot the largest abelian quotient $G/N$ (e.g. via the sign map, a determinant, or a coordinate that becomes additive), then $G'\le N$; check generators of $N$ are commutators to get equality.
\item Generate from a few commutators. Compute $[g_i,g_j]$ for generators $g_i$ of $G$. Then $G'$ is the normal closure of these commutators (the subgroup generated by them and all their conjugates): if $N$ is that normal closure, the images of the $g_i$ commute in $G/N$, so $G/N$ is abelian and $G'\le N\le G'$. The subgroup generated by the $[g_i,g_j]$ alone can be too small: for $A_4=\langle (1\,2\,3),(1\,2)(3\,4)\rangle$ it is $\langle (1\,4)(2\,3)\rangle$, of order $2$, whereas $A_4'$ is the Klein four-group of double transpositions, of order $4$.
\item \textbf{Read off $|G^{ab}|$.} $|G/G'|=$ size of the abelianization; for a known presentation, abelianize the relations (make all generators commute) to compute $G^{ab}$.
\item Perfect check. $G'=G$ ($G$ perfect) iff $G$ has no nontrivial abelian quotient; true for nonabelian simple groups.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Commutator subgroup of $S_n$}
Show $(S_n)'=A_n$ for all $n\ge2$ (with $(S_2)'=1=A_2$).
\wrec The sign homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}\colon S_n\to\{\pm1\}$ is the canonical map to an abelian group, so $(S_n)'\le\ker(\operatorname{sgn})=A_n$ (Method, step 1). Then show $A_n$ is generated by commutators.
\wsol Since $\{\pm1\}$ is abelian, Proposition~ [REF:prop:gprime@c6] (c) gives $(S_n)'\le A_n$. For the reverse inclusion ($n\ge3$): $A_n$ is generated by $3$-cycles, and every $3$-cycle is a commutator. Indeed
\[
[(1\,2),(1\,3)]=(1\,2)^{-1}(1\,3)^{-1}(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,2)(1\,3)(1\,2)(1\,3).
\]
Compute right-to-left on $\{1,2,3\}$: apply $(1\,3)$ then $(1\,2)$ then $(1\,3)$ then $(1\,2)$. Track $1$: $(1\,3)$ sends $1\to3$, $(1\,2)$ fixes $3$, $(1\,3)$ sends $3\to1$, $(1\,2)$ sends $1\to2$; so $1\to2$. Track $2$: $(1\,3):2\to2$, $(1\,2):2\to1$, $(1\,3):1\to3$, $(1\,2):3\to3$; so $2\to3$. Track $3$: $(1\,3):3\to1$, $(1\,2):1\to2$, $(1\,3):2\to2$, $(1\,2):2\to1$; so $3\to1$. Hence the product is $(1\,2\,3)$, a $3$-cycle. By relabeling, every $3$-cycle is such a commutator, so $A_n\le(S_n)'$. Therefore $(S_n)'=A_n$.
Check. $|S_n/A_n|=2$ is the largest abelian quotient; consistent with $|(S_n)^{ab}|=2$ for $n\ge2$.
\end{wex}

Title: Commutator subgroup of $D_8$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Commutator subgroup of $D_8$}
Let $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$, the dihedral group of order $8$. Compute $D_8'$.
\wrec Use generator commutators (Method, step 2): there are few generators, so compute $[r,s]$ and friends directly.
\wsol Compute $[s,r]=s^{-1} r^{-1} s r=s r^{-1} s\, r$. Now $s r^{-1} s=r$ (from $srs=r^{-1}$, conjugating $r^{-1}$ gives $sr^{-1} s=r$), so $[s,r]=r\cdot r=r^2$. Thus $r^2\in D_8'$, giving $\langle r^2\rangle\le D_8'$. Conversely $D_8/\langle r^2\rangle$ has order $4$; its generators $\overline r,\overline s$ satisfy $\overline r^2=1,\ \overline s^2=1,\ \overline s\,\overline r\,\overline s=\overline r^{-1}=\overline r$, so it is abelian ($\congZ_2\timesZ_2$). By Proposition~ [REF:prop:gprime@c6] (c), $D_8'\le\langle r^2\rangle$. Hence
\[
D_8'=\langle r^2\rangle=\{1,r^2\}=Z(D_8)\congZ_2.
\]
Check. $|D_8/D_8'|=8/2=4$ and $(D_8)^{ab}\congZ_2\timesZ_2$, the abelianization of the presentation (set $r^2=s^2=1$, $r,s$ commuting). Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Commutator subgroup of $A_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Commutator subgroup of $A_4$}
Compute $A_4'$, where $A_4$ has order $12$.
\wrec $A_4$ has a normal Klein four-subgroup $V=\{e,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}$ with $A_4/V\congZ_3$ abelian, so $A_4'\le V$ (Method, step 1). Then produce a commutator inside $V$ to force equality.
\wsol Since $A_4/V\congZ_3$ is abelian, $A_4'\le V$. Now compute a single commutator landing in $V\setminus\{e\}$. Take $x=(1\,2\,3)$, $y=(1\,2\,4)$:
\[
[x,y]=x^{-1} y^{-1} x y=(1\,3\,2)(1\,4\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2\,4).
\]
Evaluate right-to-left. $1$: $(1\,2\,4):1\to2$, $(1\,2\,3):2\to3$, $(1\,4\,2):3\to3$, $(1\,3\,2):3\to2$; so $1\to2$. $2$: $(1\,2\,4):2\to4$, $(1\,2\,3):4\to4$, $(1\,4\,2):4\to2$, $(1\,3\,2):2\to1$; so $2\to1$. $3$: $(1\,2\,4):3\to3$, $(1\,2\,3):3\to1$, $(1\,4\,2):1\to4$, $(1\,3\,2):4\to4$; so $3\to4$. $4$: $(1\,2\,4):4\to1$, $(1\,2\,3):1\to2$, $(1\,4\,2):2\to1$, $(1\,3\,2):1\to3$; so $4\to3$. Thus $[x,y]=(1\,2)(3\,4)\in V$, a nontrivial element. Since $A_4'\nor A_4$ and $V$ is the unique minimal normal subgroup of $A_4$ containing a double transposition, $A_4'$ contains the full conjugacy class of $(1\,2)(3\,4)$, which generates $V$. Hence
\[
A_4'=V\congZ_2\timesZ_2.
\]
Check. $|A_4/A_4'|=12/4=3$, so $(A_4)^{ab}\congZ_3$, matching $A_4/V\congZ_3$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $\GL_n$ is (almost) perfect: $\SL_2(\F_5)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\GL_n$ is (almost) perfect: $\SL_2(\F_5)$}
Show $\SL_2(\F_5)$ is perfect, i.e. equals its own commutator subgroup.
\wrec Perfect check (Method, step 4): a nonabelian group with no nontrivial abelian quotient. $\SL_2(\F_5)$ has order $120$ and $\SL_2(\F_5)/\{\pm I\}\cong A_5$ is simple nonabelian; we use that $A_5$ is perfect plus the structure of the extension.
\wsol Let $G=\SL_2(\F_5)$, $|G|=120$, $Z=\{\pm I\}$, $G/Z\cong A_5$. The group $A_5$ is simple nonabelian, hence perfect: $(A_5)'=A_5$ (its only normal subgroups are $1$ and $A_5$, and $A_5$ is nonabelian so $(A_5)'\ne1$, forcing $(A_5)'=A_5$). Now $G'$ maps onto $(G/Z)'=(A_5)'=A_5$ under $G\to G/Z$, so $G'Z=G$ and $[G:G']\mid|Z|=2$. If $[G:G']=2$ then $G$ would have an index-$2$ (hence normal) subgroup $G'$ with $G/G'\congZ_2$; but in fact the transvections (elementary unipotent matrices) are products of commutators and generate all of $G$. Concretely $\SL_2(\F_q)$ is perfect for $q\ge4$, and $5\ge4$. Hence $G'=G$.
Check. A perfect group has trivial abelianization $G^{ab}=1$, consistent with $|G/G'|=1$. Its derived series is constant $G,G,G,\dots$, so $G$ is not solvable.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: Derived series and solvable groups
Content:
\begin{definition}[Derived series and solvable groups]
Define the derived series of $G$ by
\[
G^{(0)}=G,\qquad G^{(i+1)}=\big(G^{(i)}\big)'=\big[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}\big].
\]
So $G^{(1)}=G'$, $G^{(2)}=G''=[G',G']$, and so on. Each $G^{(i+1)}\nor G^{(i)}$ with abelian quotient, and in fact every $G^{(i)}$ is characteristic in $G$. The group $G$ is solvable if $G^{(n)}=1$ for some $n\ge0$; the least such $n$ is the derived length.
\end{definition}

We picture the chain descending to the trivial group:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=tiny]
G=G^{(0)} \arrow[d, dash, "{ab. quotient}"] \\
G^{(1)}=G' \arrow[d, dash] \\
G^{(2)}=G'' \arrow[d, dash, dashed] \\
G^{(n)}=1
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} A finite descending chain of groups: $G=G^{(0)}\supset G^{(1)}\supset G^{(2)}\supset\cdots\supset G^{(n)}=1$. Each $G^{(i)}$ is the $i$-th term of the derived series, a characteristic (hence normal) subgroup of $G$. The terminal object is the trivial group $1$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each vertical dash-arrow from $G^{(i)}$ to $G^{(i+1)}$ represents the inclusion $G^{(i+1)}\hookrightarrow G^{(i)}$ together with the associated normal quotient $G^{(i)}\twoheadrightarrow G^{(i)}/G^{(i+1)}$. The label ``ab. quotient'' on the first arrow records that $G^{(i)}/G^{(i+1)}$ is abelian at every step (it is the abelianization of $G^{(i)}$). The dashed segment from $G^{(2)}$ downward indicates a gap of unspecified length before reaching $1$.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no two-path commutativity here; instead, the key condition is the abelian-quotient constraint $G^{(i+1)}=(G^{(i)})'$, which means $G^{(i+1)}$ is the smallest normal subgroup of $G^{(i)}$ making the quotient $G^{(i)}/G^{(i+1)}$ abelian. Solvability is exactly the statement that this chain terminates: $G^{(n)}=1$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The chain is not a commutative square but a sequential filtration. Each step is canonical: $G^{(i+1)}$ is defined as $[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]$, the commutator subgroup of the previous term. The abelian-quotient property $G^{(i)}/G^{(i+1)} abelian$ holds by Proposition~ [REF:prop:gprime@c6] (b) applied to $G^{(i)}$, and there is no choice in the construction.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This chain is the definition of the derived series in pictorial form, placed immediately before the characterization theorem (Theorem~ [REF:thm:solv-char@c6] ). It makes visible exactly what solvability demands: a finite number of steps from $G$ to $1$, each with an abelian quotient. The picture motivates conditions (a) and (b) of that theorem simultaneously.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $S_4$: $S_4\supset A_4\supset V\supset 1$ with quotients of orders $2$, $3$, $4$ (the last is $V/1\congZ_2\timesZ_2$). This is the derived series with $n=3$, each quotient abelian.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse this chain with the lower central series $\gamma_i$. The derived series replaces each group by its own commutator subgroup $[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]$, while the lower central series uses $[\gamma_i,G]$ (commutators with the whole group). They agree at the first step ($G'=\gamma_2$) but can diverge thereafter; $G$ can be solvable without being nilpotent, meaning the derived series reaches $1$ while the lower central series does not.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that solvability is a finiteness condition on iteration of the commutator-subgroup operator: the derived series must reach $1$ in finitely many steps, with each step producing an abelian remainder.
\end{dgx}

Type: theorem
Title: Characterization of solvability
Label: thm:solv-char@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Characterization of solvability] 
For a group $G$ the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $G$ is solvable: $G^{(n)}=1$ for some $n$.
\item[(b)] $G$ has a chain $1=G_0\nor G_1\nor\cdots\nor G_k=G$ in which each quotient $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is abelian (an abelian series).
\item[(c)] (If $G$ is finite) $G$ has a chain as in (b) with each $G_{i+1}/G_i$ cyclic of prime order.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: thm:solv-char@c6

Relation: proof_of=unit-1b0ddeaa4b860e6a872c
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a)$\Longrightarrow$(b): Take $G_i=G^{(n-i)}$. Then $1=G^{(n)}=G_0\nor\cdots\nor G_n=G$ and $G_{i+1}/G_i=G^{(n-i-1)}/G^{(n-i)}$ is abelian by Proposition~ [REF:prop:gprime@c6] (b) applied to $G^{(n-i-1)}$.

(b)$\Longrightarrow$(a): We show $G^{(i)}\le G_{k-i}$ by induction. Base $G^{(0)}=G=G_k$. If $G^{(i)}\le G_{k-i}$, then since $G_{k-i}/G_{k-i-1}$ is abelian we have $(G_{k-i})'\le G_{k-i-1}$, so $G^{(i+1)}=(G^{(i)})'\le(G_{k-i})'\le G_{k-i-1}=G_{k-(i+1)}$. At $i=k$: $G^{(k)}\le G_0=1$, so $G$ is solvable.

(c)$\Longrightarrow$(b) is immediate (cyclic of prime order is abelian). (b)$\Longrightarrow$(c) for finite $G$: refine each abelian quotient. A finite abelian group $G_{i+1}/G_i$ has a composition series with quotients $Z_p$ (e.g. via the structure theorem); pulling back gives intermediate normal subgroups whose successive quotients are cyclic of prime order. Inserting these refines the chain to the form (c).
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Testing solvability via the derived series
Content:
\begin{method}{Testing solvability via the derived series}
Trigger. ``Is $G$ solvable?'' or ``find the derived length.''
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute $G^{(1)}=G'$ (use the $G'$ method above).
\item Compute $G^{(2)}=(G')'$, then $G^{(3)}$, \dots, halting when you reach $1$ or detect a repeat.
\item If the series reaches $1$: $G$ is solvable; the derived length is the step count.
\item If the series stabilizes at a nontrivial $H$ (i.e. $H'=H\ne1$, a perfect subgroup): $G$ is not solvable. In particular any nonabelian simple subquotient is a fatal obstruction.
\item Shortcuts. (i) $|G|=p^a$ ($p$-group) $\Longrightarrow$ nilpotent $\Longrightarrow$ solvable. (ii) $|G|=p^aq^b$ $\Longrightarrow$ solvable (Burnside). (iii) $|G|<60$ $\Longrightarrow$ solvable (smallest nonabelian simple group is $A_5$, order $60$). (iv) If $G$ has a nonabelian simple composition factor, $G$ is not solvable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Every group of order $pq$ is solvable
Content:
\begin{wex}{Every group of order $pq$ is solvable}
Let $|G|=pq$ with primes $p<q$. Show $G$ is solvable.
\wrec Build an explicit abelian (in fact cyclic-prime) series (Theorem~ [REF:thm:solv-char@c6] (c)) using Sylow theory: find a normal Sylow subgroup.
\wsol By Sylow's theorem the number $n_q$ of Sylow $q$-subgroups satisfies $n_q\equiv1\pmod q$ and $n_q\mid p$. Since $p<q$, the only divisor of $p$ that is $\equiv1\pmod q$ is $1$ (the other divisor $p$ satisfies $1<p<q$, so $p\not\equiv1\pmod q$), so $n_q=1$: the Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$ is normal, $Q\nor G$, $|Q|=q$, $Q\congZ_q$. Then
\[
1\;\nor\;Q\;\nor\;G,\qquad Q/1\congZ_q,\quad G/Q\congZ_p,
\]
both cyclic of prime order. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:solv-char@c6] (c) (or (b)), $G$ is solvable, derived length $\le2$.
Check. If $G$ is abelian, derived length $1$; if nonabelian (only possible when $q\equiv1\pmod p$, e.g. $|G|=6,S_3$ or $|G|=21$), $G'=Q$ and $G''=1$, derived length $2$. Either way solvable. Matches the general fact that $|G|=p^aq^b$ is solvable (Burnside).
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: Closure properties of solvable groups
Label: thm:closure@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Closure properties of solvable groups] 
Let $G$ be a group, $H\le G$ a subgroup, and $N\nor G$ a normal subgroup.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $G$ is solvable, then $H$ is solvable.
\item[(b)] If $G$ is solvable, then $G/N$ is solvable.
\item[(c)] (Extensions) If $N$ and $G/N$ are both solvable, then $G$ is solvable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: thm:closure@c6

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-1cbd388a8286a9825c69
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) By induction, $H^{(i)}\le G^{(i)}$: clearly $H^{(0)}=H\le G=G^{(0)}$, and if $H^{(i)}\le G^{(i)}$ then $H^{(i+1)}=[H^{(i)},H^{(i)}]\le[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]=G^{(i+1)}$. If $G^{(n)}=1$ then $H^{(n)}\le G^{(n)}=1$, so $H$ is solvable (derived length $\le$ that of $G$).

(b) Let $\pi\colon G\to G/N$. A commutator maps to a commutator: $\pi([x,y])=[\pi x,\pi y]$, so $\pi(G^{(i)})=(G/N)^{(i)}$ by induction. If $G^{(n)}=1$ then $(G/N)^{(n)}=\pi(G^{(n)})=1$, so $G/N$ is solvable.

(c) Suppose $(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ and $N^{(k)}=1$. From part (b)'s identity, $\pi(G^{(m)})=(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ means $G^{(m)}\le\ker\pi=N$. Then $G^{(m+k)}=(G^{(m)})^{(k)}\le N^{(k)}=1$. Hence $G$ is solvable with derived length $\le m+k$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The short exact sequence $1\to N\to G\to G/N\to1$ packages (a), (b) and (c): solvability of the two outer terms is equivalent to solvability of the middle term ((a) and (b) give ``middle $\Longrightarrow$ outer terms'', since $N\le G$ and $G/N$ is a quotient of $G$; (c) gives the converse).
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
1 \arrow[r] & N \arrow[r, hook] & G \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & G/N \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five objects in a row: the trivial groups $1$ at each end (initial and terminal), the normal subgroup $N\nor G$ (a group), the ambient group $G$, and the quotient group $G/N$. This is a short exact sequence of groups.
\dgi{Arrows:} $1\to N$ is the unique map from the trivial group (sends the identity to $e\in N$). $N\hookrightarrow G$ is the inclusion (injective, the hook arrowhead records this): $n\mapsto n$. $\pi\colon G\twoheadrightarrow G/N$ is the canonical surjective quotient map (two-head arrowhead): $g\mapsto gN$. $G/N\to 1$ is the unique map to the trivial group. Well-definedness of $\pi$ on cosets is automatic from the definition $gN=$ the coset of $g$; $N$ normal in $G$ makes $G/N$ a group.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at each node: (i) $\operatorname{im}(1\to N)=\{e\}=\operatorname{ker}(N\hookrightarrow G)$, i.e. the inclusion is injective; (ii) $\operatorname{im}(N\hookrightarrow G)=N=\operatorname{ker}\pi$, i.e. exactly $N$ collapses to $eN$ under $\pi$; (iii) $\operatorname{im}\pi=G/N=\operatorname{ker}(G/N\to 1)$, i.e. $\pi$ is surjective.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For exactness at $G$: $\ker\pi=\{g\in G:gN=N\}=N=\operatorname{im}(N\hookrightarrow G)$. Starting with $n\in N$, the inclusion sends it to $n\in G$, and then $\pi(n)=nN=N=eN$ since $n\in N$. Conversely if $\pi(g)=eN$ then $g\in N$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram packages Theorem~ [REF:thm:closure@c6] (b) and (c) in a single picture. Parts (b) says solvability passes from $G$ to $G/N$ (the right half of the sequence), part (c) says solvability of $N$ and $G/N$ forces solvability of $G$ (the two outer terms control the middle). The remark uses the exact sequence to state: ``solvability of the two ends is equivalent to solvability of the middle.'' It is placed here to turn the algebraic proof into a structural picture of an extension.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $G=S_3$, $N=A_3\congZ_3$: the sequence is $1\toZ_3\to S_3\toZ_2\to 1$. Both $Z_3$ (abelian) and $Z_2$ (abelian) are solvable, so by part (c) $S_3$ is solvable; and indeed $S_3$ is solvable of derived length $2$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Part (c) requires $N$ normal, not merely a subgroup. Students sometimes write the sequence with a non-normal $H$ and claim solvability of $G$ from solvability of $H$ and $G/H$. But $G/H$ is not a group unless $H\nor G$, so the sequence does not exist. Also, do not read the surjection $G\to G/N$ as a splitting: the sequence need not split, and $G$ need not be a semidirect product $N\rtimes(G/N)$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the solvability of a group extension is completely determined by the solvability of its kernel and quotient, making short exact sequences the natural language for building up solvable groups from simpler abelian pieces.
\end{dgx}
\end{remark}

\begin{wex}{Closure in action: $Z_2\times A_5$ and a solvable extension}
(i) Show $G=Z_2\times A_5$ is not solvable. (ii) Show that any group $G$ with a normal series $1\nor N\nor G$ where $N\congZ_3$ and $G/N\cong S_3$ is solvable.
\wrec Use Theorem~ [REF:thm:closure@c6] : (a) for the obstruction, (c) for building solvability from solvable pieces.
\wsol (i) $A_5\le G$ as a subgroup (the second factor). If $G$ were solvable, then by~ [REF:thm:closure@c6] (a) $A_5$ would be solvable; but $(A_5)'=A_5\ne1$, contradiction. So $G$ is not solvable.

Check. Such a $G$ has order $|N|\cdot|G/N|=3\cdot6=18$; indeed all groups of order $18=2\cdot3^2$ are solvable by Burnside, consistent with our conclusion.
\end{wex}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-398e5b5401b1cb612489
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $G$ be nilpotent with lower central series $G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_{c+1}=1$, where $\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]$. We claim $G^{(i)}\le\gamma_{i+1}$ by induction. Base: $G^{(0)}=G=\gamma_1$. Inductive step: if $G^{(i)}\le\gamma_{i+1}$ then
\[
G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]\le[\gamma_{i+1},\gamma_{i+1}]\le[\gamma_{i+1},G]=\gamma_{i+2},
\]
using $\gamma_{i+1}\le G$. Hence $G^{(c)}\le\gamma_{c+1}=1$, so $G$ is solvable (derived length $\le c$).

Converse counterexample: $S_3$ is solvable (derived series $S_3\ge A_3\ge1$) but not nilpotent. Its lower central series is $\gamma_1=S_3$, $\gamma_2=[S_3,S_3]=A_3$, and $\gamma_3=[A_3,S_3]$. Since $A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\nor S_3$ and a transposition inverts the $3$-cycle, $[(1\,2\,3),(1\,2)]=(1\,2\,3)^{-1}\big((1\,2)^{-1}(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)\big)=(1\,3\,2)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,2\,3)\ne1$ lies in $A_3$, in fact $\gamma_3=[A_3,S_3]=A_3$. So the lower central series stabilizes at $A_3\ne1$ and never reaches $1$: $S_3$ is not nilpotent.
\end{proof}

\begin{wex}{Nilpotent $\Longrightarrow$ solvable, with $S_3$ as the converse counterexample}
(i) Verify $D_8$ is nilpotent and solvable. (ii) Verify $S_3$ is solvable but not nilpotent, exhibiting both series.

\wsol (i) $D_8$. Lower central: $\gamma_1=D_8$, $\gamma_2=[D_8,D_8]=D_8'=\langle r^2\rangle$ (computed earlier), $\gamma_3=[\langle r^2\rangle,D_8]$. Since $r^2\in Z(D_8)$, every commutator $[r^2,g]=1$, so $\gamma_3=1$. Thus $D_8=\gamma_1\ge\langle r^2\rangle\ge1$ is nilpotent of class $2$. Derived: $D_8\ge\langle r^2\rangle\ge1$ (since $\langle r^2\rangle\congZ_2$ abelian), solvable of derived length $2$. Both terminate. Nilpotent and solvable.

(ii) $S_3$. Derived series $S_3\ge A_3\ge1$ (quotients $Z_2,Z_3$): solvable, length $2$. Lower central series $S_3\ge A_3\ge A_3\ge\cdots$ stabilizes at $A_3$ (since $[A_3,S_3]=A_3\ne1$): not nilpotent.
Check. A finite group is nilpotent iff it is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups iff every Sylow subgroup is normal. In $S_3$ the three Sylow $2$-subgroups (order $2$) are not normal ($n_2=3$), confirming non-nilpotence; in $D_8$ ($2$-group) every $p$-group is nilpotent, confirming nilpotence. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem
Label: thm:burnside@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem] 
Let $p,q$ be primes and $a,b\ge0$. Every group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable. Equivalently, a group whose order is divisible by at most two distinct primes is solvable.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:burnside@c6

Type: proof
Title: Sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-77972e4f069d103fdc56
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
The classical proof uses character theory of finite groups. One shows: if $G$ is a finite nonabelian simple group, then no nontrivial conjugacy class has size a prime power $p^k$ ($k\ge1$). The key lemma (via the column-orthogonality relations and algebraic-integer arguments on character values $\chi(g)$) is that a conjugacy class of size $p^k$ forces an irreducible character with $|\chi(g)|=|\chi(1)|$ at some $g\ne1$, producing a proper nontrivial normal subgroup -- contradicting simplicity. Now if $|G|=p^aq^b$ with $G$ a minimal counterexample (nonabelian simple), a Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q\ne1$ has nontrivial center; an element $g\in Z(Q)\setminus\{1\}$ has centralizer containing $Q$, so its class size divides $p^a$, i.e. is a power of $p$ -- contradiction. Hence no nonabelian simple group of order $p^aq^b$ exists, and by induction on $|G|$ (using Theorem~ [REF:thm:closure@c6] (c) on a minimal normal subgroup) every such group is solvable. A purely group-theoretic proof exists (Goldschmidt--Matsuyama--Bender) but is far longer.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Three distinct primes can fail: $|A_5|=60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5$ has three prime divisors and is not solvable. So ``two primes'' in Burnside is sharp. The smallest non-solvable group is $A_5$.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Using Burnside: orders forcing solvability
Content:
\begin{wex}{Using Burnside: orders forcing solvability}
Which of the following orders force every group of that order to be solvable: $200$, $108$, $105$, $60$?
\wrec Apply Burnside (Method shortcut (ii)): solvable is guaranteed if the order has at most two distinct prime factors; also recall $|G|<60\Longrightarrow$ solvable.
\wsol Factor each:
\begin{itemize}
\item $200=2^3\cdot5^2$: two primes $\Longrightarrow$ solvable (Burnside).
\item $108=2^2\cdot3^3$: two primes $\Longrightarrow$ solvable (Burnside).
\item $105=3\cdot5\cdot7$: three primes, so Burnside does not apply directly. We argue by Sylow counting. For the Sylow $7$-subgroups, $n_7\equiv1\pmod7$ and $n_7\mid15$, so $n_7\in\{1,15\}$ (note $15\equiv1\pmod7$, so $15$ is NOT excluded by the congruence). For the Sylow $5$-subgroups, $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$ and $n_5\mid21$, so $n_5\in\{1,21\}$. If both $n_7=15$ and $n_5=21$, the distinct Sylow $7$-subgroups contribute $15\cdot(7-1)=90$ elements of order $7$ and the distinct Sylow $5$-subgroups contribute $21\cdot(5-1)=84$ elements of order $5$; but $90+84=174>105$, impossible. So $n_5=1$ or $n_7=1$: some Sylow subgroup $P$ of prime order ($5$ or $7$) is normal. Then $G/P$ has order $21=3\cdot7$ or $15=3\cdot5$, solvable by Burnside, and $P$ is abelian; by~ [REF:thm:closure@c6] (c), $G$ is solvable. Every group of order $105$ is solvable (by Sylow counting $+$ [REF:thm:closure@c6] (c), not Burnside alone).
\item $60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5$: three primes; NOT forced. Indeed $A_5$ has order $60$ and is not solvable.
\end{itemize}
Check. Burnside gives ``solvable'' for $200,108$ instantly; the congruence alone does NOT pin $n_7=1$ for order $105$ (since $15\equiv1\pmod7$), but the element count does; $60$ is the cautionary case (three primes, and a genuine non-solvable example exists). Consistent with $A_5$ being minimal non-solvable.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: Philip Hall's theorem on Hall subgroups
Label: thm:hall@c6
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Philip Hall's theorem on Hall subgroups] 
Let $G$ be a finite solvable group of order $n$, and let $\pi$ be a set of primes. Write $n=mk$ where $m$ is the $\pi$-part of $n$ (product of the prime powers $p^{a}\,\|\,n$ with $p\in\pi$) and $\gcd(m,k)=1$. A Hall $\pi$-subgroup of $G$ is a subgroup of order $m$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Existence) $G$ has a Hall $\pi$-subgroup.
\item[(b)] (Conjugacy) Any two Hall $\pi$-subgroups of $G$ are conjugate in $G$.
\item[(c)] (Containment) Every $\pi$-subgroup of $G$ is contained in some Hall $\pi$-subgroup.
\end{enumerate}
Conversely (Hall's converse), if $G$ has a Hall $p'$-subgroup for every prime $p\mid|G|$, then $G$ is solvable.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:hall@c6

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Further Topics in Group Theory > $p$-Groups, Nilpotent Groups, and Solvable Groups > Two landmark theorems (stated)
Type: proof
Title: Sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-87857d34c1dd5242e90d
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
Existence is by induction on $|G|$. Take a minimal normal subgroup $N$ of the solvable group $G$; minimality plus solvability force $N$ to be an elementary abelian $p$-group for some prime $p$. Case $p\in\pi$: by induction $G/N$ has a Hall $\pi$-subgroup $\overline H=H/N$, and $H$ has order $|N|\cdot|\overline H|$, which is the $\pi$-part of $|G|$; so $H$ works. Case $p\notin\pi$: by induction $G/N$ has a Hall $\pi$-subgroup $H/N$ of order the $\pi$-part $m$ of $|G/N|=|G|/|N|$, hence of $|G|$; now $H$ is a group of order $m|N|$ with $N\nor H$ a normal Hall $p$-subgroup ($p\notin\pi$), and the Schur--Zassenhaus theorem gives a complement of order $m$ in $H$, which is the desired Hall $\pi$-subgroup of $G$. Conjugacy and containment are proved together by a similar induction using Schur--Zassenhaus and the conjugacy of complements. Hall generalizes Sylow ($\pi=\{p\}$) precisely to the solvable setting; for non-solvable $G$ Hall subgroups can fail to exist (see the pitfall).
\end{proof}

Section: Further Topics in Group Theory > $p$-Groups, Nilpotent Groups, and Solvable Groups > Two landmark theorems (stated)
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Hall's theorem is special to solvable groups. In $G=A_5$ ($|G|=60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5$), Hall $\pi$-subgroups can fail to exist. A Hall $\{2,5\}$-subgroup would have order $2^2\cdot5=20$ and a Hall $\{3,5\}$-subgroup would have order $3\cdot5=15$, but $A_5$ has no subgroup of order $15$ or $20$. For order $15$: a group of order $15$ is cyclic, so it would contain an element of order $15$; but $A_5$ has no element of order $15$ (element orders in $A_5$ are $1,2,3,5$), so no such subgroup exists. (Note: $A_4\le A_5$ is a genuine Hall $\{2,3\}$-subgroup of order $12$, so SOME Hall subgroups happen to exist; the point is that existence for every $\pi$ is exactly what fails outside the solvable case.)
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: A Hall subgroup of $S_4$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A Hall subgroup of $S_4$}
$S_4$ is solvable of order $24=2^3\cdot3$. For $\pi=\{2\}$ exhibit a Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup (order $8$); for $\pi=\{3\}$ a Hall $\{3\}$-subgroup (order $3$); verify the conjugacy clause.
\wrec Apply Hall's theorem (Theorem~ [REF:thm:hall@c6] ) in a known solvable group; a Hall $\{p\}$-subgroup is just a Sylow $p$-subgroup, so cross-check against Sylow.
\wsol $|S_4|=24=2^3\cdot3^1$.

\emph{Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup} ($m=2^3=8$): a Sylow $2$-subgroup. Take $P=\langle (1\,2\,3\,4),\,(1\,3)\rangle\cong D_8$, $|P|=8$. This is a Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup. By Sylow (or Hall conjugacy) all such are conjugate; $n_2\mid3$ and $n_2\equiv1\pmod2$ give $n_2\in\{1,3\}$, and in fact $n_2=3$ -- three conjugate Sylow $2$-subgroups, matching Hall's conjugacy clause.

\emph{Hall $\{3\}$-subgroup} ($m=3$): a Sylow $3$-subgroup, e.g. $\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\congZ_3$, order $3$. Here $n_3\equiv1\pmod3$, $n_3\mid8\Longrightarrow n_3\in\{1,4\}$, and in fact $n_3=4$ (the eight $3$-cycles lie in four subgroups of order $3$), four conjugates -- again Hall conjugacy.

The complement viewpoint: inside the chain $S_4\ge A_4\ge V$, the Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup $D_8$ meets $A_4$ in $V$ (order $4$) and projects onto $S_4/A_4\congZ_2$, illustrating that the order-$8$ Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup is a complement to the $\{3\}$-part: its order $8$ and that of any Hall $\{3\}$-subgroup ($3$) are coprime with product $24$.
Check. Orders multiply correctly: a Hall $\{2\}$-subgroup ($8$) and a Hall $\{3\}$-subgroup ($3$) have coprime orders $8,3$ with $8\cdot3=24=|S_4|$. All Hall $\pi$-subgroups for each fixed $\pi$ are conjugate ($n_2=3$, $n_3=4$ conjugates respectively), as Theorem~ [REF:thm:hall@c6] (b) predicts. Consistent.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
Do not confuse derived length with nilpotency class, and do not assume the derived series and lower central series coincide. For $S_3$: derived series reaches $1$ (length $2$) but lower central series stalls at $A_3$. They agree only in special cases; in general $G^{(i)}\le\gamma_{i+1}$ (the inclusion proved in Proposition~ [REF:prop:nilp-solv@c6] ), and this inclusion can be strict even in a nilpotent group: in $D_{16}$ (with $r$ of order $8$) the derived series is $D_{16}\ge\langle r^2\rangle\ge1$, so $D_{16}^{(2)}=1$, while $\gamma_3(D_{16})=\langle r^4\rangle\ne1$.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}

\item Prove Parts 2 and 4 of Theorem 1 for $G$ an infinite nilpotent group.

\item Prove that subgroups and quotient groups of nilpotent groups are nilpotent (your proof should work for infinite groups). Give an explicit example of a group $G$ which possesses a normal subgroup $H$ such that both $H$ and $G/H$ are nilpotent but $G$ is not nilpotent.

\item Find the upper and lower central series for $A_4$ and $S_4$.
\item Find the upper and lower central series for $A_5$ and $S_5$.

\item Prove that $G^{(i)}$ is a characteristic subgroup of $G$ for all $i$.
\item Show that if $G'/G''$ and $G''/G'''$ are both cyclic then $G'' = G'''$. [You may assume $G''' = 1$. Then $G/G''$ acts by conjugation on the cyclic group $G''$.]
\item Show that there is no group whose commutator subgroup is isomorphic to $S_4$. [Use the preceding exercise.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a $p$-subgroup of the finite group $G$, let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$ whose order is relatively prime to $p$ and let $\bar G = G/N$. Prove the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $N_{\bar G}(\bar P) = \overline{N_G(P)}$ [Use Frattini's Argument.]
\item[(b)] $C_{\bar G}(\bar P) = \overline{C_G(P)}$. [Use part (a).]
\end{enumerate}
\item Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is a characteristic subgroup of $G$.
\item When $G$ is a finite group prove that if $N \nor G$ then $\Phi(N) \leq \Phi(G)$. Give an explicit example where this containment does not hold if $N$ is not normal in $G$.
\item Compute $\Phi(S_3)$, $\Phi(A_4)$, $\Phi(S_4)$, $\Phi(A_5)$ and $\Phi(S_5)$.
\item Say an element $x$ of $G$ is a {\it nongenerator} if for every proper subgroup $H$ of $G$, $\langle x, H\rangle$ is also a proper subgroup of $G$. Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is the set of nongenerators of $G$ (here $|G| > 1$).
\item Let $G$ be a finite group. Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is nilpotent. [Use Frattini's Argument to prove that every Sylow subgroup of $\Phi(G)$ is normal in $G$.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a finite $p$-group and let $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\bar P$ is an elementary abelian $p$-group. [Show that $P' \leq \Phi(P)$ and that $x^p \in \Phi(P)$ for all $x \in P$.]
\item[(b)] Prove that if $N$ is any normal subgroup of $P$ such that $P/N$ is elementary abelian then $\Phi(P) \leq N$. State this (universal) property in terms of homomorphisms and commutative diagrams.
\item[(c)] Let $\bar P$ be elementary abelian of order $p^r$ (by (a)). Deduce from Exercise 24 that if $\bar x_1, \bar x_2, \dots, \bar x_r$ are any basis for the $r$-dimensional vector space $\bar P$ over $\F_p$ and if $x_i$ is any element of the coset $\bar x_i$, then $P = \langle x_1, x_2, \dots, x_r\rangle$. Show conversely that if $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_s$ is any set of generators for $P$, then $s \geq r$ (you may assume that every minimal generating set for an $r$-dimensional vector space has $r$ elements, i.e., every basis has $r$ elements). Deduce {\it Burnside's Basis Theorem}: a set $y_1, \dots, y_r$ is a minimal generating set for $P$ if and only if $\bar y_1, \dots, \bar y_r$ is a basis of $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$. Deduce that any minimal generating set for $P$ has $r$ elements.
\item[(d)] Prove that if $P/\Phi(P)$ is cyclic then $P$ is cyclic. Deduce that if $P/P'$ is cyclic then so is $P$.
\item[(e)] Let $\sigma$ be any automorphism of $P$ of prime order $q$ with $q \neq p$. Show that if $\sigma$ fixes the coset $x\Phi(P)$ then $\sigma$ fixes some element of this coset (note that since $\Phi(P)$ is characteristic in $P$ every automorphism of $P$ induces an automorphism of $P/\Phi(P)$). [Use the observation that $\sigma$ acts as a permutation of order $1$ or $q$ on the $p^a$ points in the coset $x\Phi(P)$.]
\item[(f)] Use parts (e) and (c) to deduce that every nontrivial automorphism of $P$ of order prime to $p$ induces a nontrivial automorphism on $P/\Phi(P)$. Deduce that any group of automorphisms of $P$ which has order prime to $p$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Aut(\bar P) = \GL_r(\F_p)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Generalize part (d) of the preceding exercise as follows: let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a $p$-group and let $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$ be elementary abelian of order $p^r$. Prove that $P$ has exactly $\frac{p^r - 1}{p - 1}$ maximal subgroups. [Since every maximal subgroup of $P$ contains $\Phi(P)$, the maximal subgroups of $P$ are, by the Lattice Isomorphism Theorem, in bijective correspondence with the maximal subgroups of the elementary abelian group $\bar P$.

\item Prove that $\mathbb{Q}$ has no maximal subgroups. [Recall Exercise 21, Section 3.2.]
\item Prove that $G^{(i)}$ is a characteristic subgroup of $G$ for all $i$.
\item Show that if $G'/G''$ and $G''/G'''$ are both cyclic then $G'' = G'''$. [You may assume $G''' = 1$. Then $G/G''$ acts by conjugation on the cyclic group $G''$.]
\item Show that there is no group whose commutator subgroup is isomorphic to $S_4$. [Use the preceding exercise.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a $p$-subgroup of the finite group $G$, let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$ whose order is relatively prime to $p$ and let $\bar G = G/N$. Prove the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $N_{\bar G}(\bar P) = \overline{N_G(P)}$ [Use Frattini's Argument.]
\item[(b)] $C_{\bar G}(\bar P) = \overline{C_G(P)}$. [Use part (a).]
\end{enumerate}
\item Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is a characteristic subgroup of $G$.
\item When $G$ is a finite group prove that if $N \nor G$ then $\Phi(N) \leq \Phi(G)$. Give an explicit example where this containment does not hold if $N$ is not normal in $G$.
\item Compute $\Phi(S_3)$, $\Phi(A_4)$, $\Phi(S_4)$, $\Phi(A_5)$ and $\Phi(S_5)$.
\item Say an element $x$ of $G$ is a {\it nongenerator} if for every proper subgroup $H$ of $G$, $\langle x, H\rangle$ is also a proper subgroup of $G$. Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is the set of nongenerators of $G$ (here $|G| > 1$).
\item Let $G$ be a finite group. Prove that $\Phi(G)$ is nilpotent. [Use Frattini's Argument to prove that every Sylow subgroup of $\Phi(G)$ is normal in $G$.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a finite $p$-group and let $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\bar P$ is an elementary abelian $p$-group. [Show that $P' \leq \Phi(P)$ and that $x^p \in \Phi(P)$ for all $x \in P$.]
\item[(b)] Prove that if $N$ is any normal subgroup of $P$ such that $P/N$ is elementary abelian then $\Phi(P) \leq N$. State this (universal) property in terms of homomorphisms and commutative diagrams.
\item[(c)] Let $\bar P$ be elementary abelian of order $p^r$ (by (a)). Deduce from Exercise 24 that if $\bar x_1, \bar x_2, \dots, \bar x_r$ are any basis for the $r$-dimensional vector space $\bar P$ over $\F_p$ and if $x_i$ is any element of the coset $\bar x_i$, then $P = \langle x_1, x_2, \dots, x_r\rangle$. Show conversely that if $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_s$ is any set of generators for $P$, then $s \geq r$ (you may assume that every minimal generating set for an $r$-dimensional vector space has $r$ elements, i.e., every basis has $r$ elements). Deduce {\it Burnside's Basis Theorem}: a set $y_1, \dots, y_r$ is a minimal generating set for $P$ if and only if $\bar y_1, \dots, \bar y_r$ is a basis of $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$. Deduce that any minimal generating set for $P$ has $r$ elements.
\item[(d)] Prove that if $P/\Phi(P)$ is cyclic then $P$ is cyclic. Deduce that if $P/P'$ is cyclic then so is $P$.
\item[(e)] Let $\sigma$ be any automorphism of $P$ of prime order $q$ with $q \neq p$. Show that if $\sigma$ fixes the coset $x\Phi(P)$ then $\sigma$ fixes some element of this coset (note that since $\Phi(P)$ is characteristic in $P$ every automorphism of $P$ induces an automorphism of $P/\Phi(P)$). [Use the observation that $\sigma$ acts as a permutation of order $1$ or $q$ on the $p^a$ points in the coset $x\Phi(P)$.]
\item[(f)] Use parts (e) and (c) to deduce that every nontrivial automorphism of $P$ of order prime to $p$ induces a nontrivial automorphism on $P/\Phi(P)$. Deduce that any group of automorphisms of $P$ which has order prime to $p$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Aut(\bar P) = \GL_r(\F_p)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Generalize part (d) of the preceding exercise as follows: let $p$ be a prime, let $P$ be a $p$-group and let $\bar P = P/\Phi(P)$ be elementary abelian of order $p^r$. Prove that $P$ has exactly $\frac{p^r - 1}{p - 1}$ maximal subgroups. [Since every maximal subgroup of $P$ contains $\Phi(P)$, the maximal subgroups of $P$ are, by the Lattice Isomorphism Theorem, in bijective correspondence with the maximal subgroups of the elementary abelian group $\bar P$.

One way of doing this is to use the result that an abelian group is isomorphic to its dual group (cf. Exercise 14 in Section 5.2) so the number of subgroups of index $p$ equals the number of subgroups of order $p$.]
\item Prove that if $p$ is a prime and $P = Z_p \times Z_{p^2}$ then $|\Phi(P)| = p$ and $P/\Phi(P) \cong Z_p \times Z_p$. Deduce that $P$ has $p+1$ maximal subgroups.
\item Prove that if $p$ is a prime and $P$ is a non-abelian group of order $p^3$ then $\Phi(P) = Z(P)$ and $P/\Phi(P) \cong Z_p \times Z_p$. Deduce that $P$ has $p+1$ maximal subgroups.
\item Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $P_1 = Z_p \times Z_{p^2}$ and let $P_2$ be the non-abelian group of order $p^3$ which has an element of order $p^2$. Prove that $P_1$ and $P_2$ have the same lattice of subgroups.
\item For any group $G$ a {\it minimal normal subgroup} is a normal subgroup $M$ of $G$ such that the only normal subgroups of $G$ which are contained in $M$ are $1$ and $M$. Prove that every minimal normal subgroup of a finite solvable group is an elementary abelian $p$-group for some prime $p$. [If $M$ is a minimal normal subgroup of $G$, consider its characteristic subgroups: $M'$ and $\{x^p \mid x \in M\}$.]
\item Prove that every maximal subgroup of a finite solvable group has prime power index. [Let $H$ be a maximal subgroup of $G$ and let $M$ be a minimal normal subgroup of $G$ --- cf. the preceding exercise. Apply induction to $G/M$ and consider separately the two cases: $M \leq H$ and $M \not\leq H$.]
\item Let $\pi$ be any set of primes. A subgroup $H$ of a finite group is called a {\it Hall $\pi$-subgroup} of $G$ if the only primes dividing $|H|$ are in the set $\pi$ and $|H|$ is relatively prime to $[G : H]$. (Note that if $\pi = \{p\}$, Hall $\pi$-subgroups are the same as Sylow $p$-subgroups. Hall subgroups were introduced in Exercise 10 of Section 3.3.) Prove the following generalization of Sylow's Theorem for solvable groups: if $G$ is a finite solvable group then for every set $\pi$ of primes, $G$ has a Hall $\pi$-subgroup and any two Hall $\pi$-subgroups (for the same set $\pi$) are conjugate in $G$. [Fix $\pi$ and proceed by induction on $|G|$, proving both existence and conjugacy at once. Let $M$ be a minimal normal subgroup of $G$, so $M$ is a $p$-group for some prime $p$. If $p \in \pi$, apply induction to $G/M$. If $p \notin \pi$, reduce to the case $|G| = p^a n$, where $p^a = |M|$ and $n$ is the order of a Hall $\pi$-subgroup of $G$. In this case let $N/M$ be a minimal normal subgroup of $G/M$, so $N/M$ is a $q$-group for some prime $q \neq p$. Let $Q \in \Syl_q(N)$. If $Q \nor G$ argue as before with $Q$ in place of $M$. If $Q$ is not normal in $G$, use Frattini's Argument to show $N_G(Q)$ is a Hall $\pi$-subgroup of $G$ and establish conjugacy in this case too.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime dividing the order of the finite solvable group $G$. Assume $G$ has no nontrivial normal subgroups of order prime to $p$. Let $P$ be the largest normal $p$-subgroup of $G$ (cf. Exercise 37, Section 4.5). Note that Exercise 31 above shows that $P \neq 1$. Prove that $C_G(P) \leq P$, i.e., $C_G(P) = Z(P)$. [Let $N = C_G(P)$ and use the preceding exercise to show $N = Z(P) \times H$ for some Hall $\pi$-subgroup $H$ of $N$ --- here $\pi$ is the set of all prime divisors of $|N|$ except for $p$. Show $H \nor G$ to obtain the desired conclusion: $H = 1$.]
\item Prove that if $G$ is a finite group in which every proper subgroup is nilpotent, then $G$ is solvable. [Show that a minimal counterexample is simple. Let $M$ and $N$ be distinct maximal subgroups chosen with $|M \cap N|$ as large as possible and apply Part 2 of Theorem 3 to show that $M \cap N = 1$. Now apply the methods of Exercise 53 in Section 4.5.]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $V$ be a nonzero finite dimensional vector space over the field of $p$ elements and let $\varphi$ be an element of $\GL(V)$ of order a power of $p$ (i.e., $V$ is a nontrivial elementary abelian $p$-group and $\varphi$ is an automorphism of $V$ of $p$-power order). Prove that there is some nonzero element $v \in V$ such that $\varphi(v) = v$, i.e., $\varphi$ has a nonzero fixed point on $V$.
\item Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over the field of $2$ elements and let $\varphi$ be an element of $\GL(V)$ of order $2$ (i.e., $V$ is a nontrivial elementary abelian $2$-group and $\varphi$ is an automorphism of $V$ of order $2$). Prove that the map $v \mapsto v + \varphi(v)$ is a homomorphism from $V$ to itself. Show that every element in the image of this map is fixed by $\varphi$. Deduce that the subspace of elements of $V$ which are fixed by $\varphi$ has dimension $\geq \frac{1}{2}(\dim V)$. (Note that if $G$ is the semidirect product of $V$ with $\langle \varphi\rangle$, where $V \nor G$ and $\varphi$ acts by conjugation on $V$ by sending each $v \in V$ to $\varphi(v)$, then the fixed points of $\varphi$ on $V$ are $C_V(\varphi)$ and the above map is simply the commutator map: $v \mapsto [v, \varphi]$. In this terminology the problem is to show that $|C_V(\varphi)|^2 \geq |V|$.)
\item Use the preceding exercise to prove that if $P$ is a $2$-group which has a cyclic center and $M$ is a subgroup of index $2$ in $P$, then the center of $M$ has rank $\leq 2$. [The group $P/M$ of order $2$ acts by conjugation on the $\F_2$ vector space $\{z \in Z(M) \mid z^2 = 1\}$ and the fixed points of this action are in the center of $P$.]
\end{exers}

Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}

\item For the dihedral group $D_{16}=\langle r,s\st r^8=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$ of order $16$, compute the lower central series $G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\gamma_3\ge\cdots$ and state the nilpotence class. (Do $D_{16}$, not the body's $D_8$ or $Q_8$.)
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
$\gamma_1=D_{16}$, $\gamma_2=[G,G]=\langle r^2\rangle$ (order $4$), $\gamma_3=[\gamma_2,G]=\langle r^4\rangle$ (order $2$), $\gamma_4=[\gamma_3,G]=1$. Since $\gamma_4=1$ but $\gamma_3\ne1$, the class is $3$. In general for $D_{2^n}=\langle r,s\st r^{2^{n-1}}=s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle$ one has $\gamma_{i+1}=\langle r^{2^i}\rangle$ for $i\ge1$, giving class $n-1$ (here $n=4$).

\item For $D_{16}$ compute the upper central series $1=Z_0\sgr Z_1\sgr Z_2\sgr\cdots$, identify each term, and confirm the general pattern $Z_i(D_{2^n})=\langle r^{2^{\,n-1-i}}\rangle$ for $0\le i\le n-2$ (a cyclic group), with the final term $Z_{n-1}=D_{2^n}$ jumping to the whole group; equivalently the quotients satisfy $D_{2^n}/Z_i\cong D_{2^{\,n-i}}$ for $0\le i\le n-2$. State the class.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
$Z_1=Z(D_{16})=\langle r^4\rangle$ (cyclic of order $2$): only $1$ and $r^4$ are fixed by all conjugations, since $s r^k s=r^{-k}$ forces $k\equiv-k\pmod 8$, i.e.\ $k\in\{0,4\}$. Passing to $\bar G=D_{16}/\langle r^4\rangle\cong D_8$, its center is $\langle r^2\rangle/\langle r^4\rangle$, so $Z_2=\langle r^2\rangle$ (cyclic of order $4$). Then $D_{16}/\langle r^2\rangle\cong V_4$ is abelian, so $Z_3=D_{16}$. Thus
\[
1\sgr\langle r^4\rangle\sgr\langle r^2\rangle\sgr D_{16},
\]
class $3$. This matches $Z_i=\langle r^{2^{\,3-i}}\rangle$ for $i=0,1,2$ (orders $1,2,4$) and the jump $Z_3=G$, and the quotient pattern $D_{16}/Z_1\cong D_8=D_{2^3}$, $D_{16}/Z_2\cong V_4=D_{2^2}$. The upper and lower series have equal length $3$ (Proposition: equal length).

\item Show that $G'=[G,G]$ is the unique smallest normal subgroup $N\nor G$ with $G/N$ abelian. Then compute $G'$ for the dihedral group $D_{10}$ (order $10$) and for the dicyclic group $\operatorname{Dic}_3=Q_{12}=\langle a,b\st a^6=1,\ b^2=a^3,\ bab^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$ (order $12$).
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Universal property. For $N\nor G$: $G/N$ is abelian $\Longleftrightarrow$ $[x,y]\in N$ for all $x,y\in G$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $G'\sgr N$. So $G'$ is contained in every such $N$, and $G/G'$ is itself abelian, making $G'$ the unique smallest one.
\emph{$D_{10}$:} $[r,s]=r^{-2}$ generates the rotation subgroup, so $G'=\langle r\rangle\congZ/(5)Z$ and $D_{10}/\langle r\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$.
\emph{$Q_{12}$:} $[a,b]=a^{-2}$, so $G'=\langle a^2\rangle$ has order $3$; the abelianization is $Q_{12}/\langle a^2\rangle\congZ/(4)Z$ (generated by the image of $b$, with $b^2=a^3$ of order $2$ mod $\langle a^2\rangle$).

\item Prove that a finite $p$-group has nontrivial center via the class equation, and deduce that every group of order $p^2$ is abelian (hence of class $1$).
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
The class equation $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i[G:C_G(x_i)]$ runs over noncentral conjugacy-class representatives $x_i$; each index $[G:C_G(x_i)]>1$ is a positive power of $p$, so $p$ divides the whole sum. Since $p\mid|G|$, it follows that $p\mid|Z(G)|$, so $Z(G)\ne1$. If $|G|=p^2$, then $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^2\}$. If $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$, hence is cyclic, which forces $G$ abelian (a generator coset and $Z(G)$ together commute) --- contradicting $|Z(G)|=p$. So $|Z(G)|=p^2$, i.e.\ $G=Z(G)$ is abelian, of class $1$.

\item Prove the normalizer condition for finite nilpotent groups: every proper subgroup $H\psgr G$ satisfies $H\psgr N_G(H)$. Then exhibit its failure in $S_3$.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Induct on the nilpotence class using $Z=Z(G)\ne1$. If $Z\not\sgr H$, pick $z\in Z\setminus H$; since $z$ is central it normalizes $H$, so $z\in N_G(H)\setminus H$ and $H\psgr N_G(H)$. If $Z\sgr H$, pass to $\bar G=G/Z$ (nilpotent of smaller class) and $\bar H=H/Z\psgr\bar G$; by induction $\bar H\psgr N_{\bar G}(\bar H)=N_G(H)/Z$, so $H\psgr N_G(H)$.
Failure in $S_3$: take the Sylow $2$-subgroup $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$. Its normalizer is $H$ itself (each of the four elements outside $H$ --- the two $3$-cycles and the transpositions $(1\,3)$, $(2\,3)$ --- conjugates $(1\,2)$ to $(1\,3)$ or $(2\,3)$, which is not in $H$), so $N_G(H)=H$. The condition fails, which reproves $S_3$ is not nilpotent.

\item Prove the closure properties of solvable groups: subgroups, quotients, and extensions ($N$ and $G/N$ solvable $\Longrightarrow$ $G$ solvable). State the derived-length bounds.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Subgroups: if $H\sgr G$ then $H^{(i)}\sgr G^{(i)}$ by induction (commutators of $H$ are commutators of $G$), so $G$ solvable $\Longrightarrow$ $H$ solvable with $\operatorname{dl}(H)\le\operatorname{dl}(G)$.
Quotients: if $\pi:G\to G/N$ is the projection then $\pi(G^{(i)})=(G/N)^{(i)}$, so $\operatorname{dl}(G/N)\le\operatorname{dl}(G)$.
Extensions: suppose $(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ and $N^{(k)}=1$. From $\pi(G^{(m)})=(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ we get $G^{(m)}\sgr N$, hence $G^{(m+k)}=(G^{(m)})^{(k)}\sgr N^{(k)}=1$. Thus $G$ is solvable with $\operatorname{dl}(G)\le m+k=\operatorname{dl}(G/N)+\operatorname{dl}(N)$.

\item For a finite $p$-group $G$ prove $\Frat(G)=G'\,G^p$ where $G^p=\langle g^p:g\in G\rangle$, and use it to compute $\Frat(G)$ and the generator rank $\dim_{\F_p}\!\big(G/\Frat(G)\big)$ for $G=Z/(8)Z$ and $G=Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(4)Z$.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Every maximal subgroup $M$ of the $p$-group $G$ is normal of index $p$, so $G/M\congZ/(p)Z$ is abelian of exponent $p$; hence $G'\sgr M$ and $g^p\in M$ for all $g\in G$.

$Z_1=Z(D_{16})=\langle r^4\rangle$ (cyclic of order $2$): only $1$ and $r^4$ are fixed by all conjugations, since $s r^k s=r^{-k}$ forces $k\equiv-k\pmod 8$, i.e.\ $k\in\{0,4\}$. Passing to $\bar G=D_{16}/\langle r^4\rangle\cong D_8$, its center is $\langle r^2\rangle/\langle r^4\rangle$, so $Z_2=\langle r^2\rangle$ (cyclic of order $4$). Then $D_{16}/\langle r^2\rangle\cong V_4$ is abelian, so $Z_3=D_{16}$. Thus
\[
1\sgr\langle r^4\rangle\sgr\langle r^2\rangle\sgr D_{16},
\]
class $3$. This matches $Z_i=\langle r^{2^{\,3-i}}\rangle$ for $i=0,1,2$ (orders $1,2,4$) and the jump $Z_3=G$, and the quotient pattern $D_{16}/Z_1\cong D_8=D_{2^3}$, $D_{16}/Z_2\cong V_4=D_{2^2}$. The upper and lower series have equal length $3$ (Proposition: equal length).

\item Show that $G'=[G,G]$ is the unique smallest normal subgroup $N\nor G$ with $G/N$ abelian. Then compute $G'$ for the dihedral group $D_{10}$ (order $10$) and for the dicyclic group $\operatorname{Dic}_3=Q_{12}=\langle a,b\st a^6=1,\ b^2=a^3,\ bab^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$ (order $12$).
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
\emph{Universal property.} For $N\nor G$: $G/N$ is abelian $\Longleftrightarrow$ $[x,y]\in N$ for all $x,y\in G$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $G'\sgr N$. So $G'$ is contained in every such $N$, and $G/G'$ is itself abelian, making $G'$ the unique smallest one.
\emph{$D_{10}$:} $[r,s]=r^{-2}$ generates the rotation subgroup, so $G'=\langle r\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ and $D_{10}/\langle r\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$.
\emph{$Q_{12}$:} $[a,b]=a^{-2}$, so $G'=\langle a^2\rangle$ has order $3$; the abelianization is $Q_{12}/\langle a^2\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ (generated by the image of $b$, with $b^2=a^3$ of order $2$ mod $\langle a^2\rangle$).

\item Prove that a finite $p$-group has nontrivial center via the class equation, and deduce that every group of order $p^2$ is abelian (hence of class $1$).
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
The class equation $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i[G:C_G(x_i)]$ runs over noncentral conjugacy-class representatives $x_i$; each index $[G:C_G(x_i)]>1$ is a positive power of $p$, so $p$ divides the whole sum. Since $p\mid|G|$, it follows that $p\mid|Z(G)|$, so $Z(G)\ne1$. If $|G|=p^2$, then $|Z(G)|\in\{p,p^2\}$. If $|Z(G)|=p$, then $G/Z(G)$ has order $p$, hence is cyclic, which forces $G$ abelian (a generator coset and $Z(G)$ together commute) --- contradicting $|Z(G)|=p$. So $|Z(G)|=p^2$, i.e.\ $G=Z(G)$ is abelian, of class $1$.

\item Prove the \emph{normalizer condition} for finite nilpotent groups: every proper subgroup $H\psgr G$ satisfies $H\psgr N_G(H)$. Then exhibit its failure in $S_3$.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
Induct on the nilpotence class using $Z=Z(G)\ne1$. If $Z\not\sgr H$, pick $z\in Z\setminus H$; since $z$ is central it normalizes $H$, so $z\in N_G(H)\setminus H$ and $H\psgr N_G(H)$. If $Z\sgr H$, pass to $\bar G=G/Z$ (nilpotent of smaller class) and $\bar H=H/Z\psgr\bar G$; by induction $\bar H\psgr N_{\bar G}(\bar H)=N_G(H)/Z$, so $H\psgr N_G(H)$.
\emph{Failure in $S_3$:} take the Sylow $2$-subgroup $H=\langle (1\,2)\rangle$. Its normalizer is $H$ itself (each of the four elements outside $H$ --- the two $3$-cycles and the transpositions $(1\,3)$, $(2\,3)$ --- conjugates $(1\,2)$ to $(1\,3)$ or $(2\,3)$, which is not in $H$), so $N_G(H)=H$. The condition fails, which reproves $S_3$ is not nilpotent.

\item Prove the closure properties of solvable groups: subgroups, quotients, and extensions ($N$ and $G/N$ solvable $\Longrightarrow$ $G$ solvable). State the derived-length bounds.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
\emph{Subgroups:} if $H\sgr G$ then $H^{(i)}\sgr G^{(i)}$ by induction (commutators of $H$ are commutators of $G$), so $G$ solvable $\Longrightarrow$ $H$ solvable with $\operatorname{dl}(H)\le\operatorname{dl}(G)$.
\emph{Quotients:} if $\pi:G\to G/N$ is the projection then $\pi(G^{(i)})=(G/N)^{(i)}$, so $\operatorname{dl}(G/N)\le\operatorname{dl}(G)$.
\emph{Extensions:} suppose $(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ and $N^{(k)}=1$. From $\pi(G^{(m)})=(G/N)^{(m)}=1$ we get $G^{(m)}\sgr N$, hence $G^{(m+k)}=(G^{(m)})^{(k)}\sgr N^{(k)}=1$. Thus $G$ is solvable with $\operatorname{dl}(G)\le m+k=\operatorname{dl}(G/N)+\operatorname{dl}(N)$.

\item For a finite $p$-group $G$ prove $\Frat(G)=G'\,G^p$ where $G^p=\langle g^p:g\in G\rangle$, and use it to compute $\Frat(G)$ and the generator rank $\dim_{\F_p}\!\big(G/\Frat(G)\big)$ for $G=\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z}$ and $G=\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
Every maximal subgroup $M$ of the $p$-group $G$ is normal of index $p$, so $G/M\cong\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian of exponent $p$; hence $G'\sgr M$ and $g^p\in M$ for all $g\in G$.

\emph{$Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(4)Z$:} $G'=0$ and $G^2=\{(0,0),(0,2)\}=\langle (0,2)\rangle$ of order $2$, so $\Frat$ has order $2$ and $G/\Frat\cong(Z/(2)Z)^2$ has rank $2$.

\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace

Base $i=1$: $[\gamma_1,\gamma_j]=[G,\gamma_j]=[\gamma_j,G]=\gamma_{j+1}=\gamma_{1+j}$. For $i=1,\ j=2$ the relation reads $[\gamma_1,\gamma_2]\sgr\gamma_3$; but $[\gamma_1,\gamma_2]=[G,\gamma_2]=\gamma_3$ by definition, so equality holds and in particular $\gamma_3\sgr[\gamma_1,\gamma_2]$.

\item Let $G$ be a finite group with $G/Z(G)$ cyclic. Prove that $G$ is already abelian, and deduce that the index $[G:Z(G)]$ is never a prime (more generally, never a number $n>1$ for which every group of order $n$ is cyclic).
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace

\[
(g^k z)(g^m z')=g^{k+m}zz'=g^{m}g^{k}z'z=(g^m z')(g^k z),
\]
using that $z,z'$ are central. Hence $G$ is abelian, i.e.\ $G=Z$, so $G/Z$ is the trivial group. The same argument rules out $[G:Z]$ being any order forcing cyclicity (e.g.\ $1$ excepted, any $n$ with a unique group, all of which would make $G/Z$ cyclic).

\item Let $G$ be a nilpotent group and let $N\nor G$ with $N\ne1$. Prove that $N$ meets the center nontrivially: $N\cap Z(G)\ne1$.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Use the upper central series $1=Z_0\sgr Z_1\sgr\cdots\sgr Z_c=G$ (with $Z_c=G$ since $G$ is nilpotent of class $c$). Because $N\cap Z_c=N\cap G=N\ne1$, there is a least index $i\ge1$ with $N\cap Z_i\ne1$; by minimality $N\cap Z_{i-1}=1$. Pick $1\ne x\in N\cap Z_i$. Hence $[x,g]\in N\cap Z_{i-1}=1$ for all $g$, so $x$ is central: $x\in N\cap Z(G)$. Thus $N\cap Z(G)\ne1$ (and in fact $i=1$).

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}

\item Prove that in a finite nilpotent group every maximal subgroup is normal of prime index, and that $G/\Frat(G)$ is abelian (indeed a direct product of elementary abelian pieces).
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Let $M$ be maximal. By the normalizer condition $M\psgr N_G(M)$, and maximality forces $N_G(M)=G$, so $M\nor G$. Then $G/M$ is a nontrivial group with no proper nontrivial subgroups, hence of prime order $p$; so $[G:M]=p$.
For the Frattini quotient, use $G\cong P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$ (Sylow factorization of a finite nilpotent group). The maximal subgroups of $G$ are exactly those omitting one index-$p_i$ line in a single factor, so
\[
G/\Frat(G)\cong\prod_i P_i/\Frat(P_i),
\]
and each $P_i/\Frat(P_i)$ is elementary abelian (Burnside). A product of elementary abelian groups is abelian, so $G/\Frat(G)$ is abelian.

\item Prove that the Frattini subgroup is multiplicative on finite direct products: $\Frat(G\times H)=\Frat(G)\times\Frat(H)$ for finite groups $G,H$. Use it to compute $\Frat(D_8\timesZ/(3)Z)$.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
For $M$ maximal in $G$ and $M'$ maximal in $H$, the subgroups $M\times H$ and $G\times M'$ are maximal in $G\times H$, so
\[
\Frat(G\times H)\sgr\Big(\bigcap_{M}M\Big)\times H\;\cap\;G\times\Big(\bigcap_{M'}M'\Big)=\Frat(G)\times\Frat(H).
\]
These need not be all the maximal subgroups (in $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$ the diagonal $\{(0,0),(1,1)\}$ is maximal too), so the reverse inclusion needs an argument. Let $L$ be any maximal subgroup of $G\times H$ and put $F=\Frat(G)\times1$, a normal subgroup of $G\times H$. If $F\not\sgr L$, then $LF=G\times H$ by maximality; writing $(g,1)=\ell f$ with $\ell\in L$, $f\in F\sgr G\times1$ forces $\ell\in L\cap(G\times1)$, so $G\times1=\big(L\cap(G\times1)\big)F$. Since $F=\Frat(G\times1)$ consists of nongenerators of $G\times1$ (Proposition~ [REF:prop:nongen@c6] ), $G\times1=L\cap(G\times1)\sgr L$, contradicting $F\not\sgr L$. Thus $\Frat(G)\times1\sgr L$, and likewise $1\times\Frat(H)\sgr L$, for every maximal $L$; hence $\Frat(G)\times\Frat(H)\sgr\Frat(G\times H)$, and equality holds.
Application. From the body, $\Frat(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$ (order $2$), and $\Frat(Z/(3)Z)=0$ (a group of prime order has no nontrivial proper subgroups). Hence
\[
\Frat(D_8\timesZ/(3)Z)=\langle r^2\rangle\times 0\congZ/(2)Z,
\]
of order $2$.

\item Prove the equal-length theorem: for $c\ge1$, $\gamma_{c+1}=1\ne\gamma_c$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $Z_c=G\ne Z_{c-1}$ (so both series give the same class $c$), using the dovetailing inclusions $\gamma_{i+1}\sgr Z_{c-i}$.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
The single ingredient is $[Z_j,G]\sgr Z_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$ (elements of $Z_j$ are central mod $Z_{j-1}$).
\emph{$Z_c=G\Longrightarrow\gamma_{c+1}=1$:} show $\gamma_{i+1}\sgr Z_{c-i}$ by induction. Base $i=0$: $\gamma_1=G=Z_c$. Step: $\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]\sgr[Z_{c-i+1},G]\sgr Z_{c-i}$. Taking $i=c$ gives $\gamma_{c+1}\sgr Z_0=1$.
\emph{$\gamma_{c+1}=1\Longrightarrow Z_c=G$:} dually show $\gamma_{c+1-i}\sgr Z_i$ by induction. Base $i=0$: $\gamma_{c+1}=1\sgr Z_0$. Step: if $g\in\gamma_{c-i+1}$ then $[g,G]\sgr\gamma_{c-i+2}\sgr Z_{i-1}$, so $g\in Z_i$. Taking $i=c$ gives $G=\gamma_1\sgr Z_c$.
Both directions give least index $c$, so the two series have equal length.

\item Prove that a nontrivial nilpotent group $G$ is never perfect: $G'\psgr G$. Deduce that a nontrivial finite $p$-group has a nontrivial abelian quotient and is therefore not its own commutator subgroup.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Let $G\ne1$ be nilpotent with lower central series $G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_{c+1}=1$, where $\gamma_2=G'$. If we had $G'=G$, i.e.\ $\gamma_2=\gamma_1$, then $\gamma_3=[\gamma_2,G]=[\gamma_1,G]=\gamma_2=G$, and by induction $\gamma_i=G$ for all $i$; the series would never reach $1$, contradicting nilpotence (which requires $\gamma_{c+1}=1$ with $G\ne1$). Hence $G'\psgr G$, so $G^{ab}=G/G'$ is a nontrivial abelian group.
In particular a nontrivial finite $p$-group $P$ is nilpotent, so $P'\psgr P$ and $P/P'\ne1$ is a nontrivial abelian quotient; thus $P$ is not perfect. (This is the reason every $p$-group of order $>1$ has at least one index-$p$, hence maximal, subgroup.)

\item Let $G$ be a finite group, $N\nor G$ with $N$ and $G/N$ nilpotent. Show by example that $G$ need not be nilpotent, and contrast this with solvability. Then compute the derived series and the lower central series of $\operatorname{Dic}_3=Q_{12}$, confirming it is solvable but not nilpotent.
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Nilpotence is not extension-closed. Take $G=S_3$, $N=A_3\congZ/(3)Z$. Both $N$ (abelian) and $G/N\congZ/(2)Z$ are nilpotent, yet $S_3$ is not nilpotent. So, unlike solvability (which is closed under extensions, Practice problem on closure), nilpotence can be destroyed by an extension of nilpotent groups.
\emph{$Q_{12}=\langle a,b\st a^6=1,\ b^2=a^3,\ bab^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$.} Derived series: $G'=\langle a^2\rangle\congZ/(3)Z$ (since $[a,b]=a^{-2}$), and $\langle a^2\rangle$ is cyclic hence abelian, so $G''=1$. Thus $G\ge\langle a^2\rangle\ge1$ is solvable of derived length $2$. Lower central series: $\gamma_2=[G,G]=\langle a^2\rangle$, and $\gamma_3=[\langle a^2\rangle,G]$. Now $[a^2,b]=a^{-2}(b^{-1} a^2 b)=a^{-2}a^{-2}=a^{-4}=a^2$ (as $a^6=1$), so $\gamma_3=\langle a^2\rangle=\gamma_2$; the lower central series stalls at $\langle a^2\rangle\ne1$. Hence $Q_{12}$ is solvable but not nilpotent, consistent with its Sylow $2$-subgroup ($\congZ/(4)Z$, of order $4$) not being normal.

\end{exers}

\emph{Application.} From the body, $\Frat(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$ (order $2$), and $\Frat(\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z})=0$ (a group of prime order has no nontrivial proper subgroups). Hence
\[
\Frat(D_8\times\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z})=\langle r^2\rangle\times 0\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},
\]
of order $2$.

\item Prove the equal-length theorem: for $c\ge1$, $\gamma_{c+1}=1\ne\gamma_c$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $Z_c=G\ne Z_{c-1}$ (so both series give the same class $c$), using the dovetailing inclusions $\gamma_{i+1}\sgr Z_{c-i}$.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
The single ingredient is $[Z_j,G]\sgr Z_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$ (elements of $Z_j$ are central mod $Z_{j-1}$).
\emph{$Z_c=G\Longrightarrow\gamma_{c+1}=1$:} show $\gamma_{i+1}\sgr Z_{c-i}$ by induction. Base $i=0$: $\gamma_1=G=Z_c$. Step: $\gamma_{i+1}=[\gamma_i,G]\sgr[Z_{c-i+1},G]\sgr Z_{c-i}$. Taking $i=c$ gives $\gamma_{c+1}\sgr Z_0=1$.
\emph{$\gamma_{c+1}=1\Longrightarrow Z_c=G$:} dually show $\gamma_{c+1-i}\sgr Z_i$ by induction. Base $i=0$: $\gamma_{c+1}=1\sgr Z_0$. Step: if $g\in\gamma_{c-i+1}$ then $[g,G]\sgr\gamma_{c-i+2}\sgr Z_{i-1}$, so $g\in Z_i$. Taking $i=c$ gives $G=\gamma_1\sgr Z_c$.
Both directions give least index $c$, so the two series have equal length.

\item Prove that a nontrivial nilpotent group $G$ is never perfect: $G'\psgr G$. Deduce that a nontrivial finite $p$-group has a nontrivial abelian quotient and is therefore not its own commutator subgroup.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
Let $G\ne1$ be nilpotent with lower central series $G=\gamma_1\ge\gamma_2\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_{c+1}=1$, where $\gamma_2=G'$. If we had $G'=G$, i.e.\ $\gamma_2=\gamma_1$, then $\gamma_3=[\gamma_2,G]=[\gamma_1,G]=\gamma_2=G$, and by induction $\gamma_i=G$ for all $i$; the series would never reach $1$, contradicting nilpotence (which requires $\gamma_{c+1}=1$ with $G\ne1$). Hence $G'\psgr G$, so $G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/G'$ is a nontrivial abelian group.
In particular a nontrivial finite $p$-group $P$ is nilpotent, so $P'\psgr P$ and $P/P'\ne1$ is a nontrivial abelian quotient; thus $P$ is not perfect. (This is the reason every $p$-group of order $>1$ has at least one index-$p$, hence maximal, subgroup.)

\item Let $G$ be a finite group, $N\nor G$ with $N$ and $G/N$ nilpotent. Show by example that $G$ need not be nilpotent, and contrast this with solvability. Then compute the derived series and the lower central series of $\operatorname{Dic}_3=Q_{12}$, confirming it is solvable but not nilpotent.
\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Answer.}\enspace
\emph{Nilpotence is not extension-closed.} Take $G=S_3$, $N=A_3\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. Both $N$ (abelian) and $G/N\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ are nilpotent, yet $S_3$ is not nilpotent. So, unlike solvability (which \emph{is} closed under extensions, Practice problem on closure), nilpotence can be destroyed by an extension of nilpotent groups.
\emph{$Q_{12}=\langle a,b\st a^6=1,\ b^2=a^3,\ bab^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$.} Derived series: $G'=\langle a^2\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ (since $[a,b]=a^{-2}$), and $\langle a^2\rangle$ is cyclic hence abelian, so $G''=1$. Thus $G\ge\langle a^2\rangle\ge1$ is solvable of derived length $2$. Lower central series: $\gamma_2=[G,G]=\langle a^2\rangle$, and $\gamma_3=[\langle a^2\rangle,G]$. Now $[a^2,b]=a^{-2}(b^{-1} a^2 b)=a^{-2}a^{-2}=a^{-4}=a^2$ (as $a^6=1$), so $\gamma_3=\langle a^2\rangle=\gamma_2$; the lower central series stalls at $\langle a^2\rangle\ne1$. Hence $Q_{12}$ is \textbf{solvable but not nilpotent}, consistent with its Sylow $2$-subgroup ($\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$, of order $4$) not being normal.

\end{exers}

Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}

\item (Factoring through the abelianization.) Prove that any homomorphism $\varphi:G\to A$ into an abelian group $A$ factors uniquely through the projection $\pi:G\to G/G'$, and verify the universal triangle for $G=Q_8$, $A=Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & A \\
G/G' \arrow[ur, dashed, "{\exists!\,\bar\varphi}"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
Since $\im\varphi\sgr A$ is abelian, $G'\sgr\ker\varphi$, so $\varphi$ is constant on cosets of $G'$ and descends to $\bar\varphi:G/G'\to A$ with $\bar\varphi\circ\pi=\varphi$; uniqueness holds because $\pi$ is surjective.
$Q_8$: $Q_8'=\langle -1\rangle$ and $Q_8^{ab}=Q_8/\langle -1\rangle\cong V_4$. Define $\varphi$ by $i\mapsto(1,0)$, $j\mapsto(0,1)$ (so $k=ij\mapsto(1,1)$ and $-1\mapsto(0,0)$); this kills $\langle -1\rangle$, so it factors as the isomorphism $\bar\varphi:Q_8^{ab}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$.

\item (Derived series of $S_4$ as inclusions.) Display $S_4\hookleftarrow A_4\hookleftarrow V_4\hookleftarrow 1$, naming each term and annotating each hook arrow with the index $[G^{(i)}:G^{(i+1)}]$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
S_4 & A_4 \arrow[l, hook'] & V_4 \arrow[l, hook'] & 1 \arrow[l, hook']
\end{tikzcd}\]
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
$G^{(0)}=S_4$, $G^{(1)}=[S_4,S_4]=A_4$ (index $2$), $G^{(2)}=[A_4,A_4]=V_4$ (index $3$), $G^{(3)}=[V_4,V_4]=1$ (index $4$). The successive quotients $Z/(2)Z,\ Z/(3)Z,\ V_4\cong(Z/(2)Z)^2$ are all abelian, so $S_4$ is solvable of derived length $3$. (This inclusion chain renders, as a diagram, the derived computation behind solvability; it is distinct from the quotient-map presentation used in 6.3.)

\item (Functoriality of the center quotient.) For nilpotent $G$ of class $\ge2$ and $q:G\to G/Z(G)$, show $q(\gamma_2(G))=\gamma_2(G/Z(G))$ and assemble the commuting square; verify for $G=D_{16}$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
\gamma_2(G) \arrow[r, "q|"] \arrow[d, hook] & \gamma_2\!\big(G/Z(G)\big) \arrow[d, hook] \\
G \arrow[r, "q"'] & G/Z(G)
\end{tikzcd}\]
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
A homomorphism sends commutators to commutators: $q[x,y]=[q(x),q(y)]$, so $q(\gamma_2(G))=q([G,G])=[q(G),q(G)]=\gamma_2(q(G))=\gamma_2(G/Z(G))$. The square commutes since the vertical maps are inclusions and the top is the restriction of $q$.
\emph{$D_{16}$:} $Z(D_{16})=\langle r^4\rangle$ and $\gamma_2(D_{16})=\langle r^2\rangle$. The quotient $D_{16}/\langle r^4\rangle\cong D_8$, and the image of $\langle r^2\rangle$ is $\langle \bar r^2\rangle=\gamma_2(D_8)$. Square verified.

\item (Extensions: solvability versus nilpotence.) Draw the short exact sequence $1\to A_3\to S_3\toZ/(2)Z\to1$ and use it to show that nilpotence is not closed under extensions, in contrast with the closure of solvability proved in the Practice problems. Label the derived-length and class data.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
1 \arrow[r] & A_3 \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] & S_3 \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & Z/(2)Z \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
The sequence is exact: $A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle\congZ/(3)Z\nor S_3$ with $\iota$ the inclusion, and $\pi$ the sign map with $\ker\pi=A_3$ and image $Z/(2)Z$.
Both ends are nilpotent (indeed abelian: $A_3$ of class $1$ and $Z/(2)Z$ of class $1$), yet the middle is not: $S_3$ has trivial center, so its upper central series stalls at $1$, and it is not nilpotent (shown earlier). Hence nilpotence does not pass through extensions of nilpotent kernel and quotient.
Contrast. Solvability does pass: here $A_3,Z/(2)Z$ solvable $\Longrightarrow S_3$ solvable, with $\operatorname{dl}(S_3)\le\operatorname{dl}(Z/(2)Z)+\operatorname{dl}(A_3)=1+1=2$, matching the derived series $S_3\ge A_3\ge1$. The obstruction to nilpotence is exactly that the extension is non-central: the conjugation action of $Z/(2)Z$ on $A_3$ is nontrivial (a transposition inverts the $3$-cycle), so no term of the upper central series climbs past $1$.

\item (Upper-central tower of quotients.) For nilpotent $G$ with $1=Z_0\psgr\cdots\psgr Z_c=G$ draw the tower $G\twoheadrightarrow G/Z_1\twoheadrightarrow\cdots\twoheadrightarrow 1$ and prove each kernel $Z_{i+1}/Z_i$ is central in $G/Z_i$; carry out $G=Q_8$ explicitly.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
G \arrow[r, two heads] & G/Z_1 \arrow[r, two heads] & \cdots \arrow[r, two heads] & G/Z_{c-1} \arrow[r, two heads] & G/Z_c=1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\par\smallskip\noindentAnswer.\enspace
By definition $Z_{i+1}/Z_i=Z(G/Z_i)$, which is the center, hence central in $G/Z_i$; the maps $G/Z_i\twoheadrightarrow G/Z_{i+1}$ are the canonical projections, each with central kernel $Z_{i+1}/Z_i$.
$Q_8$: from the body, $Z_1=\langle -1\rangle$ and $G/Z_1\cong V_4$ is abelian, so $Z_2/Z_1=Z(V_4)=V_4$, giving $Z_2=Q_8$. The tower is $Q_8\twoheadrightarrow V_4\twoheadrightarrow 1$ with central kernels $\langle -1\rangle$ then $V_4$; nilpotence class $2$.

\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
The Sylow theorems give us numerical control over a finite group $G$: for each prime $p$ dividing $|G|=p^a m$ (with $p\nmid m$), the number $n_p$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups satisfies
\[
n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}, \qquad n_p \mid m, \qquad n_p = [G:N_G(P)]
\]
for any $P\in\Syl_p(G)$. The art of D\&F 6.2 is to turn these arithmetic constraints into structural conclusions: that some Sylow subgroup is normal, that $G$ embeds in a small symmetric group, or that $G$ cannot be simple. We collect the standard moves, prove them, and then apply them to a battery of medium orders, culminating in the statement and proof-sketch that $A_5$ is the unique simple group of order $60$.

Throughout, recall the three engines that convert $n_p$ into structure.

Title: The three structural levers
Content:
\begin{theorem}[The three structural levers]
Let $G$ be a finite group, $p$ a prime dividing $|G|$, and $P\in\Syl_p(G)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textnormal{(L1)}] $n_p=1 \Longleftrightarrow P\nor G$. (A unique Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal.)
\item[\textnormal{(L2)}] (Sylow counting.) If $P$ has prime order $p$, then distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups intersect trivially, so the Sylow $p$-subgroups contribute exactly $n_p(p-1)$ elements of order $p$.
\item[\textnormal{(L3)}] (Action on $\Syl_p(G)$.) Conjugation gives a transitive action of $G$ on $\Syl_p(G)$, hence a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G\to \Sym(\Syl_p(G))\cong S_{n_p}$ whose kernel $\ker\varphi=\bigcap_{g\in G}gN_G(P)g^{-1}$ is the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $N_G(P)$ (the normal core of $N_G(P)$). If $1<n_p$ and $|G|\nmid n_p!$, then $\ker\varphi$ is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup, so $G$ is not simple.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(L1) By Sylow's theorem $G$ acts transitively on $\Syl_p(G)$ by conjugation, so the single Sylow $p$-subgroup (when $n_p=1$) is fixed by every conjugation, i.e.\ $gPg^{-1}=P$ for all $g$, which is exactly $P\nor G$. Conversely if $P\nor G$ then its conjugates are all $P$, so $n_p=1$.

(L2) If $|P|=p$ then $P$ is cyclic of prime order, so any two distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups $P_1\neq P_2$ have $P_1\cap P_2$ a proper subgroup of each, forcing $P_1\cap P_2=1$. Each $P_i$ contains $p-1$ elements of order $p$ and these sets are pairwise disjoint, giving $n_p(p-1)$ elements of order $p$ in total.

(L3) Transitivity of the conjugation action is again Sylow's theorem, and the stabilizer of $P$ is $N_G(P)$ by definition, so $n_p=[G:N_G(P)]$. The kernel of the induced map $\varphi\colon G\to\Sym(\Syl_p(G))$ is $\bigcap_g gN_G(P)g^{-1}$, the core of $N_G(P)$; this is normal in $G$ and is the largest normal subgroup contained in $N_G(P)$. The image $G/\ker\varphi$ embeds in $S_{n_p}$, so $|G/\ker\varphi|\mid n_p!$. If $n_p>1$ then $N_G(P)\neq G$, so $\ker\varphi\subseteq N_G(P)\subsetneq G$ shows $\ker\varphi$ is proper; and if additionally $|G|\nmid n_p!$ then $\ker\varphi\neq 1$ (else $G$ would embed in $S_{n_p}$). Hence $1\neq\ker\varphi\neq G$ and $G$ is not simple.
\end{proof}

The conjugation action of (L3) is the workhorse. We picture it as:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
G \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[dr, two heads, "{quotient}"'] & \Sym(\Syl_p(G))\cong S_{n_p} \\
 & G/\ker\varphi \arrow[u, dashed, hook, "{\bar\varphi}"']
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Here $\ker\varphi=\operatorname{core}_G(N_G(P))$ and the factorization $\varphi=\bar\varphi\circ(quotient)$ is the first isomorphism theorem; $\bar\varphi$ is injective.

Type: method
Title: The medium-order recipe
Content:
\begin{method}{The medium-order recipe}
To analyze a group $G$ of order $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$ (small $k$, modest exponents):
\begin{enumerate}
\item List $n_p$ candidates. For each prime $p\mid n$ write $|G|=p^a m$ and list the divisors of $m$ that are $\equiv 1\pmod p$. These are the only allowed values of $n_p$.
\item Hunt for a forced $n_p=1$. If for some $p$ the only admissible value is $n_p=1$, then $P\nor G$ (lever L1). You have found a normal subgroup.
\item Count elements (lever L2). If several primes force $n_p>1$ and the corresponding Sylow subgroups have prime order, add up the elements of prime order $n_p(p-1)$. If the totals overflow $|G|$, some $n_p$ must collapse to $1$. (This is the ``counting elements'' technique.)
\item Embed via the action (lever L3). If $n_p>1$ is unavoidable but small, map $G\to S_{n_p}$. Either $G$ embeds in $S_{n_p}$ (often a contradiction on order, or it pins $G$ down exactly), or the kernel is a proper normal subgroup.
\item Conclude. Normality of a Sylow subgroup $\Longrightarrow$ not simple; often a chain of such facts builds the whole structure (semidirect product decomposition).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

\begin{pitfall}
$n_p\equiv 1\pmod p$ is a constraint on $n_p$, not on $|G|$ directly. A common error is to use the congruence alone and forget that $n_p$ must also divide $m=|G|/p^a$. For $|G|=24=2^3\cdot 3$ and $p=2$: $m=3$, so $n_2\in\{1,3\}$ (divisors of $3$ that are odd), NOT $\{1,3,5,\dots\}$ (all odd numbers). (Testing divisors of $|G|$ instead of $m$ gives the same list: a divisor of $p^a m$ that is $\equiv1\pmod p$ is prime to $p$, hence divides $m$.)
\end{pitfall}

\begin{pitfall}
Lever L2 (disjointness of Sylows) needs $|P|=p$ prime. If $|P|=p^2$ two Sylow $p$-subgroups can intersect in a subgroup of order $p$, and the count $n_p(p^2-1)$ overcounts. Do not apply the counting bound blindly when $a\ge 2$.
\end{pitfall}
