Title: $R[x]/(x^2+1) \cong C$ is a field, so $(x^2+1)$ is maximal
Content:
\begin{wex}{$R[x]/(x^2+1) \cong C$ is a field, so $(x^2+1)$ is maximal}
Show $M = \langle x^2+1\rangle$ is a maximal ideal of $R[x]$.
\wrec Test maximality by the quotient: compute $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ and check it is a field.
\wsol Define $\varphi : R[x] \to C$ by $\varphi(f) = f(i)$ (evaluation at $i$). It is a surjective ring homomorphism (it hits $a + bi$ via $a + bx$). Its kernel is $\{f : f(i) = 0\}$; since $x^2 + 1 = (x-i)(x+i)$ is the minimal polynomial of $i$ over $R$, $\ker\varphi = \langle x^2+1\rangle$. By the First Isomorphism Theorem,
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & C \\
R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle \arrow[ur, dashed, "\overline\varphi"', "\cong"] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R[x]$ is the polynomial ring over the reals; $C$ is the field of complex numbers; $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is the quotient ring obtained by forcing $x^2 = -1$, whose elements are cosets $f + \langle x^2+1\rangle$, i.e.\ cosets of the form $(a + bx) + \langle x^2+1\rangle$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\varphi: R[x] \to C$ is evaluation at $i$, the surjective ring homomorphism $f \mapsto f(i)$, with $\ker\varphi = \langle x^2+1\rangle$. $\pi: R[x] \to R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is the canonical surjective quotient map, $f \mapsto f + \langle x^2+1\rangle$. $\overline\varphi: R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle \to C$ is the induced (dashed) isomorphism, defined by $\overline\varphi(f + \langle x^2+1\rangle) = f(i)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\overline\varphi \circ \pi = \varphi$, i.e.\ for every $f \in R[x]$, evaluating $f$ at $i$ equals first quotienting and then applying $\overline\varphi$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\overline\varphi$: if $f + \langle x^2+1\rangle = g + \langle x^2+1\rangle$, then $f - g = (x^2+1)h$ for some $h \in R[x]$, so $f(i) - g(i) = (i^2+1)h(i) = 0 \cdot h(i) = 0$, hence $f(i) = g(i)$. Element-chase: take $f \in R[x]$; the upper path gives $\varphi(f) = f(i)$; the lower path gives $\overline\varphi(\pi(f)) = \overline\varphi(f + \langle x^2+1\rangle) = f(i)$. They agree.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The First Isomorphism Theorem converts the abstract quotient $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ into the concrete field $C$, proving $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is maximal without any direct lattice argument. This is the template for all quotient-identifies-as-field arguments.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $f = x^3$. Upper path: $\varphi(x^3) = i^3 = -i$. Lower path: $x^3 + \langle x^2+1\rangle$; since $x^3 = x(x^2+1) - x$, the coset equals $-x + \langle x^2+1\rangle$, and $\overline\varphi(-x + \langle x^2+1\rangle) = -i$. Both paths give $-i$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow $\overline\varphi$ is induced by $\varphi$; it does not exist by magic --- it exists precisely because $\langle x^2+1\rangle = \ker\varphi$. If the kernel were larger or smaller, the induced map would not be well-defined or would fail to be injective. Do not assume an induced map exists before checking the kernel-containment condition.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the First Isomorphism Theorem converts the abstract quotient ring $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ into the familiar field $C$, making maximality of $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ an immediate consequence.
\end{dgx}
so $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle \cong C$, which is a field. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] , $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is maximal. Check. $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible over $R$ (no real roots), matching the $\F[x]$ shortcut.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\langle 2,x\rangle$ is maximal in $Z[x]$ because $Z[x]/\langle 2,x\rangle \cong \F_2$}
Show $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is maximal in $Z[x]$.
\wrec Quotient test: identify $Z[x]/\langle 2,x\rangle$ and check it is a field.
\wsol Define $\varphi : Z[x] \to Z/2Z = \F_2$ by reducing coefficients mod $2$ and setting $x \mapsto 0$, i.e.\ $\varphi(f) = f(0) \bmod 2 = (constant term of f) \bmod 2$. This is a surjective homomorphism. Its kernel is exactly the polynomials with even constant term, which we computed in the first worked example to be $\langle 2,x\rangle$. Hence
\[
Z[x]/\langle 2,x\rangle \;\cong\; \F_2,
\]
a field with two elements. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] , $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is maximal. Check. $|\F_2| = 2$ and every nonzero element ($1$) is a unit, so it is a field.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\langle x\rangle$ is maximal in $\F[x]$ for a field $\F$}

which is a field. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] , $\langle x\rangle$ is maximal. Check. $x$ is irreducible (degree $1$) in $\F[x]$, matching the irreducibility shortcut.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A maximal ideal of $Z$ that is determined by primality}
Which principal ideals $\langle n\rangle$ of $Z$ are maximal?
\wrec In $Z$, $\langle n\rangle$ maximal $\Longleftrightarrow Z/nZ$ a field $\Longleftrightarrow n$ prime.
\wsol $Z/nZ$ is a field iff $n$ is prime (for $n$ prime every nonzero residue is a unit by B\'ezout; for $n = ab$ composite, $\bar a$ is a zero divisor, not a unit). So $\langle n\rangle$ is maximal exactly when $n = p$ is prime. Check. $\langle 0\rangle = 0$ is not maximal since $0 \subsetneq \langle 2\rangle \subsetneq Z$; $\langle 1\rangle = Z$ is not proper; $\langle 6\rangle$ is not maximal since $\langle 6\rangle \subsetneq \langle 2\rangle \subsetneq Z$.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: Prime ideal
Content:
\begin{definition}[Prime ideal]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A proper ideal $P \subsetneq R$ is a prime ideal if for all $a, b \in R$,
\[
ab \in P \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a \in P \ or \ b \in P.
\]
(This generalizes Euclid's lemma: $p \mid ab \Longrightarrow p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$.)
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[$P$ prime $\Longleftrightarrow$ $R/P$ an integral domain] 
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ and $P$ a proper ideal. Then
\[
P is prime \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R/P is an integral domain.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\bar r = r + P$ for the image in $R/P$, so $\bar r = \bar 0 \Longleftrightarrow r \in P$. Then:
\[
P prime
\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \big(ab \in P \Longrightarrow a \in P or b \in P\big)
\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \big(\bar a \bar b = \bar 0 \Longrightarrow \bar a = \bar 0 or \bar b = \bar 0\big),
\]
which is precisely the statement that $R/P$ has no zero divisors. Since $P \neq R$, the quotient $R/P$ has $1 \neq 0$ and is commutative, so this says $R/P$ is an integral domain.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
The implications, and the quotient ladder, are summarized by:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi_M"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi_P"'] & R/M \ \ (field) \\
R/P \mathrlap{\ \ (domain)} &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\boxed{\ maximal \ \Longrightarrow\ prime\ }
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R$ is a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ (upper-left); $R/M$ is the quotient by a maximal ideal $M$ (upper-right, labelled ``field''); $R/P$ is the quotient by a prime ideal $P$ (lower-left, labelled ``domain''). There is no lower-right object --- the diagram is an L-shape, not a square.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi_M: R \twoheadrightarrow R/M$ is the canonical surjective quotient map modulo $M$. $\pi_P: R \twoheadrightarrow R/P$ is the canonical surjective quotient map modulo $P$. Both are ring homomorphisms with $\ker\pi_M = M$ and $\ker\pi_P = P$. There is no arrow between $R/M$ and $R/P$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The two paths do not share a target, so commutativity is not the point. The diagram instead records that from the single ring $R$, two different quotients are available: one by $M$ (yielding a field) and one by $P$ (yielding a domain). The implication maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime corresponds to the fact that every field is an integral domain.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} When $M$ is maximal, $R/M$ is a field; every field is an integral domain (if $ab = 0$ with $a \neq 0$, multiply by $a^{-1}$ to get $b = 0$); so $R/M$ is also a domain. The two quotients live independently, but the algebraic hierarchy field $\implies$ domain mirrors the ideal hierarchy maximal $\implies$ prime.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the organizing summary of Corollary~ [REF:cor:maxprime@c7] : the L-shape reminds you that maximality is strictly stronger than primality, both notions are tested via the corresponding quotient, and the one-way implication has a concrete reason (fields are domains) rather than being a coincidence.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $Z$: $M = \langle 5\rangle$ gives $\pi_M: Z \to \F_5$ (a field, so $\langle 5\rangle$ is maximal); $P = \langle 3\rangle$ gives $\pi_P: Z \to \F_3$ (also a field, so also prime). For a domain-only example: take $R = Z[x]$, $P = \langle x\rangle$, giving $\pi_P: Z[x] \to Z$ (a domain, so $\langle x\rangle$ prime but not maximal since $Z$ is not a field).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the L-shape as if $R/M$ and $R/P$ are related by a map (a projection or inclusion). They are not: no arrow connects $R/M$ to $R/P$ in general. If $M \supseteq P$ one can factor the quotient maps, but the diagram here does not assert that.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two canonical quotient maps of $R$ organize the ideal hierarchy --- maximal gives a field, prime gives a domain --- making the implication maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime a structural consequence of field $\Longrightarrow$ domain.
\end{dgx}
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M maximal \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & P prime \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & I proper ideal
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The three nodes are not rings or groups but properties that an ideal $I \subsetneq R$ can satisfy: being maximal (strongest), being prime (intermediate), and being a proper ideal (weakest).
\dgi{Arrows:} Two double-line implication arrows ($\Rightarrow$). The left arrow, ``$M$ maximal $\Rightarrow$ $P$ prime,'' is Corollary~ [REF:cor:maxprime@c7] : $R/M$ a field implies $R/M$ a domain. The right arrow, ``$P$ prime $\Rightarrow$ $I$ proper,'' is definitional: the prime ideal condition explicitly requires $P \subsetneq R$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Transitivity of implication: maximal $\Rightarrow$ prime $\Rightarrow$ proper. So maximal $\Rightarrow$ proper directly, which is also clear from the definition of maximal.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Left arrow: $R/M$ is a field (Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] ), every field is an integral domain (nonzero elements are units, hence not zero-divisors), so $R/M$ is a domain and $M$ is prime (Theorem~ [REF:thm:primedomain@c7] ). Right arrow: prime ideals are defined to be proper by assumption.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is a roadmap for the section: it tells you the logical hierarchy and reminds you that neither arrow reverses --- the counterexamples (prime-not-maximal: $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq Z[x]$; proper-not-prime: $\langle 4\rangle \subsetneq Z$) are essential knowledge, not edge cases.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $Z$: $\langle 7\rangle$ is maximal (hence prime, hence proper). $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime (since $Z$ is a domain) but not maximal. $\langle 4\rangle$ is proper but not prime ($2 \cdot 2 = 4 \in \langle 4\rangle$ yet $2 \notin \langle 4\rangle$). All three levels are populated.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The arrows are one-way implications about ideal properties, not maps between objects. A student may try to ``go backwards'' and conclude a prime is maximal --- this fails exactly when $R/P$ is a domain but not a field, e.g.\ $R/\langle x\rangle \cong Z$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the three tiers of ideals (maximal, prime, proper) are strictly ordered by implication, and tracking which quotient ring each tier corresponds to (field, domain, nonzero ring) gives the proof of every arrow.
\end{dgx}
(neither arrow reverses: $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq Z[x]$ is prime but not maximal; $\langle 4\rangle \subsetneq Z$ is proper but not prime).

\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R$ is a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ (upper-left); $R/M$ is the quotient by a maximal ideal $M$ (upper-right, labelled ``field''); $R/P$ is the quotient by a prime ideal $P$ (lower-left, labelled ``domain'').  There is no lower-right object --- the diagram is an L-shape, not a square.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi_M: R \twoheadrightarrow R/M$ is the canonical surjective quotient map modulo $M$.  $\pi_P: R \twoheadrightarrow R/P$ is the canonical surjective quotient map modulo $P$.  Both are ring homomorphisms with $\ker\pi_M = M$ and $\ker\pi_P = P$.  There is no arrow between $R/M$ and $R/P$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The two paths do not share a target, so commutativity is not the point.  The diagram instead records that from the single ring $R$, two different quotients are available: one by $M$ (yielding a field) and one by $P$ (yielding a domain).  The implication maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime corresponds to the fact that every field is an integral domain.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} When $M$ is maximal, $R/M$ is a field; every field is an integral domain (if $ab = 0$ with $a \neq 0$, multiply by $a^{-1}$ to get $b = 0$); so $R/M$ is also a domain.  The two quotients live independently, but the algebraic hierarchy field $\implies$ domain mirrors the ideal hierarchy maximal $\implies$ prime.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the organizing summary of Corollary~\ref{cor:maxprime@c7}: the L-shape reminds you that maximality is strictly stronger than primality, both notions are tested via the corresponding quotient, and the one-way implication has a concrete reason (fields are domains) rather than being a coincidence.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $\mathbb{Z}$: $M = \langle 5\rangle$ gives $\pi_M: \mathbb{Z} \to \F_5$ (a field, so $\langle 5\rangle$ is maximal); $P = \langle 3\rangle$ gives $\pi_P: \mathbb{Z} \to \F_3$ (also a field, so also prime).  For a domain-only example: take $R = \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $P = \langle x\rangle$, giving $\pi_P: \mathbb{Z}[x] \to \mathbb{Z}$ (a domain, so $\langle x\rangle$ prime but not maximal since $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a field).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the L-shape as if $R/M$ and $R/P$ are related by a map (a projection or inclusion).  They are not: no arrow connects $R/M$ to $R/P$ in general.  If $M \supseteq P$ one can factor the quotient maps, but the diagram here does not assert that.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two canonical quotient maps of $R$ organize the ideal hierarchy --- maximal gives a field, prime gives a domain --- making the implication maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime a structural consequence of field $\Longrightarrow$ domain.
\end{dgx}
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M \text{ maximal} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & P \text{ prime} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & I \text{ proper ideal}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The three nodes are not rings or groups but \emph{properties} that an ideal $I \subsetneq R$ can satisfy: being maximal (strongest), being prime (intermediate), and being a proper ideal (weakest).
\dgi{Arrows:} Two double-line implication arrows ($\Rightarrow$).  The left arrow, ``$M$ maximal $\Rightarrow$ $P$ prime,'' is Corollary~\ref{cor:maxprime@c7}: $R/M$ a field implies $R/M$ a domain.  The right arrow, ``$P$ prime $\Rightarrow$ $I$ proper,'' is definitional: the prime ideal condition explicitly requires $P \subsetneq R$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Transitivity of implication: maximal $\Rightarrow$ prime $\Rightarrow$ proper.  So maximal $\Rightarrow$ proper directly, which is also clear from the definition of maximal.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Left arrow: $R/M$ is a field (Theorem~\ref{thm:maxfield@c7}), every field is an integral domain (nonzero elements are units, hence not zero-divisors), so $R/M$ is a domain and $M$ is prime (Theorem~\ref{thm:primedomain@c7}).  Right arrow: prime ideals are defined to be proper by assumption.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is a roadmap for the section: it tells you the logical hierarchy and reminds you that \emph{neither arrow reverses} --- the counterexamples (prime-not-maximal: $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}[x]$; proper-not-prime: $\langle 4\rangle \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}$) are essential knowledge, not edge cases.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $\mathbb{Z}$: $\langle 7\rangle$ is maximal (hence prime, hence proper).  $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime (since $\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain) but not maximal.  $\langle 4\rangle$ is proper but not prime ($2 \cdot 2 = 4 \in \langle 4\rangle$ yet $2 \notin \langle 4\rangle$).  All three levels are populated.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The arrows are one-way implications about \emph{ideal properties}, not maps between objects.  A student may try to ``go backwards'' and conclude a prime is maximal --- this fails exactly when $R/P$ is a domain but not a field, e.g.\ $R/\langle x\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the three tiers of ideals (maximal, prime, proper) are strictly ordered by implication, and tracking which quotient ring each tier corresponds to (field, domain, nonzero ring) gives the proof of every arrow.
\end{dgx}
(neither arrow reverses: $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is prime but not maximal; $\langle 4\rangle \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}$ is proper but not prime).

\begin{method}{Testing primality via the quotient}
Trigger. Asked whether $P$ is prime in a commutative ring $R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Form $R/P$ and identify it. $P$ prime $\Longleftrightarrow R/P$ a domain (no zero divisors); $P$ maximal $\Longleftrightarrow R/P$ a field. Since field $\Longrightarrow$ domain, maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime.
\item Direct test: assume $ab \in P$ and deduce $a \in P$ or $b \in P$.
\item In $Z$: $\langle n\rangle$ prime $\Longleftrightarrow n = 0$ or $n = p$ prime (because $Z/nZ$ a domain $\Longleftrightarrow n = 0$ or $n$ prime).
\item To show not maximal but prime: exhibit a domain quotient that is not a field (e.g.\ $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \cong Z$).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: The ideals of $Z$: which are prime, which maximal
Content:
\begin{wex}{The ideals of $Z$: which are prime, which maximal}
Classify all ideals of $Z$ and determine which are prime and which maximal.
\wrec $Z$ is a PID, so every ideal is $\langle n\rangle$; test each via $Z/nZ$.
\wsol Every ideal of $Z$ is principal: $I = \langle n\rangle = nZ$ for a unique $n \geq 0$ (take $n$ the least positive element, or $n = 0$). Now use the quotients:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\langle 0\rangle = 0$: $Z/0Z \cong Z$ is a domain but not a field, so $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime, not maximal.
\item $\langle 1\rangle = Z$: not a proper ideal, so neither prime nor maximal.
\item $\langle p\rangle$, $p$ prime: $Z/pZ = \F_p$ is a field, so prime and maximal.
\item $\langle n\rangle$, $n = ab$ composite ($1 < a,b < n$): $\bar a \bar b = \bar n = \bar 0$ with $\bar a, \bar b \neq \bar 0$, so $Z/nZ$ has zero divisors --- neither prime nor maximal.
\end{itemize}
Check. Prime ideals of $Z$ are exactly $\langle 0\rangle$ and $\langle p\rangle$; the maximal ones are exactly the $\langle p\rangle$. Consistent with maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime, and $\langle 0\rangle$ shows the converse fails.
\end{wex}

Title: $\langle x\rangle$ is prime but not maximal in $Z[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle x\rangle$ is prime but not maximal in $Z[x]$}
Show $P = \langle x\rangle$ is prime but not maximal in $Z[x]$.
\wrec Use $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle$: prime $\Longleftrightarrow$ domain, maximal $\Longleftrightarrow$ field.
\wsol Evaluation at $0$, $ev_0 : Z[x] \to Z$, $f \mapsto f(0)$, is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $\{f : f(0) = 0\} = \langle x\rangle$. So
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
Z[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \arrow[r, "\cong"] & Z .
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $Z[x]$ is the polynomial ring with integer coefficients; $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle$ is the quotient ring forcing $x = 0$, whose elements are cosets $f + \langle x\rangle$ (canonically represented by the constant terms); $Z$ is the ring of integers.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi: Z[x] \twoheadrightarrow Z[x]/\langle x\rangle$ is the canonical surjective quotient map $f \mapsto f + \langle x\rangle$, whose kernel is $\langle x\rangle = \{f : f(0) = 0\}$. The second arrow $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \xrightarrow{\cong} Z$ is the natural isomorphism sending $f + \langle x\rangle$ to $f(0)$, the constant term of (any representative of) the coset.
\dgi{What commutes:} The composite $Z[x] \to Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \xrightarrow{\cong} Z$ equals the evaluation-at-zero map $ev_0: f \mapsto f(0)$ directly. That is, reducing mod $\langle x\rangle$ and then reading the constant term is the same as plugging in $x = 0$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of the isomorphism: if $f + \langle x\rangle = g + \langle x\rangle$, then $f - g \in \langle x\rangle$, so $x \mid (f-g)$, so $f(0) - g(0) = 0$. Hence $f(0) = g(0)$, and the map is well-defined. It is a ring homomorphism because evaluation at any point is a homomorphism; it is surjective because every integer $n$ is the constant term of the constant polynomial $n$, and injective because $f(0) = 0$ means $x \mid f$, i.e.\ $f + \langle x\rangle = \langle x\rangle$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The composite identifies $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle$ concretely as $Z$. Since $Z$ is an integral domain (no zero divisors) but not a field ($2$ has no inverse), the diagram simultaneously proves $\langle x\rangle$ is prime (Theorem~ [REF:thm:primedomain@c7] ) and not maximal (Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] ), giving the key counterexample to ``prime $\Longrightarrow$ maximal.''
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $f = 3x^2 + 5x + 7$. Directly: $ev_0(f) = 7$. Along the diagram: $f \mapsto f + \langle x\rangle \mapsto$ constant term $= 7$. For the zero-divisor test in $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle$: $(2 + \langle x\rangle)(3 + \langle x\rangle) = 6 + \langle x\rangle \neq \langle x\rangle$ in $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \cong Z$, confirming no zero divisors.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle \cong Z$ with the statement that $\langle x\rangle$ is prime in $Z$ (which makes no sense, as $\langle x\rangle \not\subseteq Z$). The prime in question is $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq Z[x]$, and the domain produced is $Z$, not $Z/xZ$ (a meaningless expression).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that quotienting $Z[x]$ by $\langle x\rangle$ is the same as setting $x = 0$, yielding $Z$, which is an integral domain but not a field, so $\langle x\rangle$ is prime but not maximal in $Z[x]$.
\end{dgx}
Now $Z$ is an integral domain, so $\langle x\rangle$ is prime (Theorem~ [REF:thm:primedomain@c7] ). But $Z$ is not a field ($2$ has no inverse in $Z$), so $\langle x\rangle$ is not maximal (Theorem~ [REF:thm:maxfield@c7] ). Check. Indeed $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq \langle 2,x\rangle \subsetneq Z[x]$, a strict chain of ideals above $\langle x\rangle$, confirming non-maximality; the strictly larger $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is a maximal ideal sitting over it (so is $\langle p,x\rangle$ for every prime $p$).
\end{wex}

Now $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain, so $\langle x\rangle$ is \emph{prime} (Theorem~\ref{thm:primedomain@c7}). Title: Prime vs.\ maximal in $Z/(n)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Prime vs.\ maximal in $Z/(n)Z$}
Find the prime and maximal ideals of $R = Z/(n)Z$ for $n = 12$.
\wrec Ideals of $Z/nZ$ correspond to divisors of $n$; test each quotient.
\wsol By the lattice theorem, ideals of $Z/12Z$ correspond to ideals of $Z$ containing $\langle 12\rangle$, i.e.\ to $\langle d\rangle$ with $d \mid 12$. The ideal $\langle \bar d\rangle = dZ/12Z$ has quotient
\[
(Z/12Z)\big/(dZ/12Z) \cong Z/dZ .
\]
So $\langle \bar d\rangle$ is prime/maximal $\Longleftrightarrow Z/dZ$ is a domain/field $\Longleftrightarrow d$ is prime (for a proper ideal we need $d > 1$). Divisors $d \mid 12$ with $d$ prime: $d = 2, 3$. Hence the prime ideals are $\langle \bar 2\rangle$ and $\langle \bar 3\rangle$, and they are also maximal. Check. In a finite commutative ring every prime ideal is maximal (a finite integral domain is a field), so ``prime'' and ``maximal'' coincide here --- consistent with $\{\langle \bar 2\rangle, \langle \bar 3\rangle\}$ being both lists. Note $\langle \bar 0\rangle$ is not prime since $Z/(12)Z$ itself has zero divisors ($\bar 3 \cdot \bar 4 = \bar 0$).
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Prime vs.\ maximal in $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$}
Find the prime and maximal ideals of $R = \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ for $n = 12$.
\wrec Ideals of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ correspond to divisors of $n$; test each quotient.
\wsol By the lattice theorem, ideals of $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$ correspond to ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$ containing $\langle 12\rangle$, i.e.\ to $\langle d\rangle$ with $d \mid 12$. The ideal $\langle \bar d\rangle = d\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$ has quotient
\[
(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z})\big/(d\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z} .
\]
So $\langle \bar d\rangle$ is prime/maximal $\Longleftrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain/field $\Longleftrightarrow d$ is prime (for a proper ideal we need $d > 1$). Divisors $d \mid 12$ with $d$ prime: $d = 2, 3$. Hence the prime ideals are $\langle \bar 2\rangle$ and $\langle \bar 3\rangle$, and they are \emph{also maximal}. \textit{Check.} In a finite commutative ring \emph{every} prime ideal is maximal (a finite integral domain is a field), so ``prime'' and ``maximal'' coincide here --- consistent with $\{\langle \bar 2\rangle, \langle \bar 3\rangle\}$ being both lists. Note $\langle \bar 0\rangle$ is not prime since $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ itself has zero divisors ($\bar 3 \cdot \bar 4 = \bar 0$).
\end{wex}

Title: $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is prime in $Z[x]$ but not maximal
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is prime in $Z[x]$ but not maximal}
Determine whether $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is prime/maximal in $Z[x]$.
\wrec Identify $Z[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$ and check domain vs.\ field.
\wsol Map $Z[x] \to Z[i]$ (the Gaussian integers) by $x \mapsto i$, i.e.\ $f \mapsto f(i)$. This is surjective ($a + bx \mapsto a + bi$) with kernel $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ (as $x^2 + 1$ is the minimal polynomial of $i$ over $Z$, and $Z[x]$ reductions confirm it). So
\[
Z[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle \;\cong\; Z[i].
\]
$Z[i]$ is an integral domain (a subring of $C$), so $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is prime. But $Z[i]$ is not a field ($2 = (1+i)(1-i)$ is not invertible; $\frac12 \notin Z[i]$), so $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is not maximal. Check. Contrast with $R[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle\congC$ (a field, so maximal) --- the base ring matters: over the field $R$ we get a field, over $Z$ only a domain.
\end{wex}

\wsol Map $\mathbb{Z}[x] \to \mathbb{Z}[i]$ (the Gaussian integers) by $x \mapsto i$, i.e.\ $f \mapsto f(i)$. This is surjective ($a + bx \mapsto a + bi$) with kernel $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ (as $x^2 + 1$ is the minimal polynomial of $i$ over $\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ reductions confirm it). So
\[

\]
$\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is an integral domain (a subring of $\mathbb{C}$), so $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is \emph{prime}. But $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is not a field ($2 = (1+i)(1-i)$ is not invertible; $\frac12 \notin \mathbb{Z}[i]$), so $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is \emph{not maximal}. \textit{Check.} Contrast with $\mathbb{R}[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle\cong\mathbb{C}$ (a field, so maximal) --- the base ring matters: over the field $\mathbb{R}$ we get a field, over $\mathbb{Z}$ only a domain.

\begin{wex}{A prime that is not maximal in two variables: $\langle y\rangle$ in $\F[x,y]$}
Let $\F$ be a field. Show $\langle y\rangle$ is prime but not maximal in $\F[x,y]$.
\wrec Quotient out $y$ and identify the ring.
\wsol Send $\F[x,y] \to \F[x]$ by $y \mapsto 0$ (reduce mod $y$). This is surjective with kernel $\langle y\rangle$, so
\[
\F[x,y]/\langle y\rangle \;\cong\; \F[x].
\]
$\F[x]$ is an integral domain (no zero divisors among polynomials), so $\langle y\rangle$ is prime. It is not a field ($x$ has no inverse), so $\langle y\rangle$ is not maximal. Check. $\langle y\rangle \subsetneq \langle x,y\rangle \subsetneq \F[x,y]$, and $\F[x,y]/\langle x,y\rangle \cong \F$ is a field, so $\langle x,y\rangle$ is a maximal ideal above $\langle y\rangle$ (so is $\langle x-a,y\rangle$ for every $a\in\F$).
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
``Prime'' does not imply ``maximal.'' The gap is exactly: $R/P$ a domain vs.\ $R/P$ a field. The standard counterexamples: $\langle 0\rangle$ in any domain that is not a field (e.g.\ $Z$, $\F[x]$), and $\langle x\rangle \subsetneq Z[x]$. The reverse implication maximal $\Longrightarrow$ prime always holds (Corollary~ [REF:cor:maxprime@c7] ) because every field is a domain. Also: the prime-ideal definition is only stated for commutative rings in this section; do not apply $ab \in P \Longrightarrow a\in P$ or $b\in P$ as the definition in a noncommutative ring.
\end{pitfall}

\item Let $L_j$ be the left ideal of $\Mat_n(R)$ consisting of arbitrary entries in the $j^{th}$ column and zero in all other entries and let $E_{ij}$ be the element of $\Mat_n(R)$ whose $i,j$ entry is $1$ and whose other entries are all $0$. Prove that $L_j = \Mat_n(R)E_{ij}$ for any $i$. [See Exercise 6, Section 2.]
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Prove that the augmentation ideal in the group ring $RG$ is generated by $\{g - 1 \mid g \in G\}$. Prove that if $G = \langle \sigma\rangle$ is cyclic then the augmentation ideal is generated by $\sigma - 1$.
\item (a) Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be an abelian group of order $p^n$. Prove that the nilradical of the group ring $\F_p G$ is the augmentation ideal (cf. Exercise 29, Section 3). [Use the preceding exercise.]\\
(b) Let $G = \{g_1, \ldots, g_n\}$ be a finite group and assume $R$ is commutative. Prove that if $r$ is any element of the augmentation ideal of $RG$ then $r(g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_n) = 0$. [Use the preceding exercise.]
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Prove that $R$ is a field if and only if $0$ is a maximal ideal.
\item Prove that if $M$ is an ideal such that $R/M$ is a field then $M$ is a maximal ideal (do not assume $R$ is commutative).
\item Prove that $R$ is a division ring if and only if its only left ideals are $(0)$ and $R$. (The analogous result holds when ``left'' is replaced by ``right.'')
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. Prove that the principal ideal generated by $x$ in the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is a prime ideal if and only if $R$ is an integral domain. Prove that $(x)$ is a maximal ideal if and only if $R$ is a field.
\item Let $R$ be an integral domain. Prove that $(a) = (b)$ for some elements $a, b \in R$ if and only if $a = ub$ for some unit $u$ of $R$.
\item Let $R$ be the ring of all continuous functions on $[0,1]$ and let $I$ be the collection of functions $f(x)$ in $R$ with $f(1/3) = f(1/2) = 0$. Prove that $I$ is an ideal of $R$ but is not a prime ideal.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Prove that if $P$ is a prime ideal of $R$ and $P$ contains no zero divisors then $R$ is an integral domain.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Let $I$ and $J$ be ideals of $R$ and assume $P$ is a prime ideal of $R$ that contains $IJ$ (for example, if $P$ contains $I \cap J$). Prove either $I$ or $J$ is contained in $P$.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative and suppose $I = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ and $J = (b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m)$ are two finitely generated ideals in $R$. Prove that the product ideal $IJ$ is finitely generated by the elements $a_i b_j$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, and $j = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
\item Let $\varphi : R \to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings.\\
(a) Prove that if $P$ is a prime ideal of $S$ then either $\varphi^{-1}(P) = R$ or $\varphi^{-1}(P)$ is a prime ideal of $R$. Apply this to the special case when $R$ is a subring of $S$ and $\varphi$ is the inclusion homomorphism to deduce that if $P$ is a prime ideal of $S$ then $P \cap R$ is either $R$ or a prime ideal of $R$.\\
(b) Prove that if $M$ is a maximal ideal of $S$ and $\varphi$ is surjective then $\varphi^{-1}(M)$ is a maximal ideal of $R$. Give an example to show that this need not be the case if $\varphi$ is not surjective.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Let $x$ be an indeterminate, let $f(x)$ be a monic polynomial in $R[x]$ of degree $n \geq 1$ and use the bar notation to denote passage to the quotient ring $R[x]/(f(x))$.\\
(a) Show that every element of $R[x]/(f(x))$ is of the form $\overline{p(x)}$ for some polynomial $p(x) \in R[x]$ of degree less than $n$, i.e.,
\[
R[x]/(f(x)) = \{\overline{a_0} + \overline{a_1}\overline{x} + \cdots + \overline{a_{n-1}}\overline{x}^{n-1} \mid a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1} \in R\}.
\]
[If $f(x) = x^n + b_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + b_0$ then $\overline{x}^n = -(\overline{b_{n-1}}\overline{x}^{n-1} + \cdots + \overline{b_0})$. Use this to reduce powers of $\overline{x}$ in the quotient ring.]\\
(b) Prove that if $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ are distinct polynomials in $R[x]$ which are both of degree less than $n$, then $\overline{p(x)} \neq \overline{q(x)}$. [Otherwise $p(x) - q(x)$ is an $R[x]$-multiple of the monic polynomial $f(x)$.]\\
(c) If $f(x) = a(x)b(x)$ where both $a(x)$ and $b(x)$ have degree less than $n$, prove that $\overline{a(x)}$ is a zero divisor in $R[x]/(f(x))$.\\
(d) If $f(x) = x^n - a$ for some nilpotent element $a \in R$, prove that $\overline{x}$ is nilpotent in $R[x]/(f(x))$.\\
(e) Let $p$ be a prime, assume $R = \F_p$ and $f(x) = x^p - a$ for some $a \in \F_p$. Prove that $\overline{x - a}$ is nilpotent in $R[x]/(f(x))$. [Use Exercise 26(c) of Section 3.]
\item Let $x^2 + x + 1$ be an element of the polynomial ring $E = \F_2[x]$ and use the bar notation to denote passage to the quotient ring $\F_2[x]/(x^2 + x + 1)$.\\
(a) Prove that $\overline{E}$ has 4 elements: $\overline{0}, \overline{1}, \overline{x}$ and $\overline{x+1}$.\\
(b) Write out the $4 \times 4$ addition table for $\overline{E}$ and deduce that the additive group $\overline{E}$ is isomorphic to the Klein 4-group.\\
(c) Write out the $4 \times 4$ multiplication table for $\overline{E}$ and prove that $\units{\overline{E}}$ is isomorphic to the cyclic group of order 3. Deduce that $\overline{E}$ is a field.
\item Let $x^4 - 16$ be an element of the polynomial ring $E = Z[x]$ and use the bar notation to denote passage to the quotient ring $Z[x]/(x^4 - 16)$.\\
(a) Find a polynomial of degree $\leq 3$ that is congruent to $7x^{13} - 11x^9 + 5x^5 - 2x^3 + 3$ modulo $(x^4 - 16)$.\\
(b) Prove that $\overline{x - 2}$ and $\overline{x + 2}$ are zero divisors in $\overline{E}$.
\item Let $x^3 - 2x + 1$ be an element of the polynomial ring $E = Z[x]$ and use the bar notation to denote passage to the quotient ring $Z[x]/(x^3 - 2x + 1)$.

Content:
Let $p(x) = 2x^7 - 7x^5 + 4x^3 - 9x + 1$ and let $q(x) = (x - 1)^4$.\\
(a) Express each of the following elements of $\overline{E}$ in the form $\overline{f(x)}$ for some polynomial $f(x)$ of degree $\leq 2$: $\overline{p(x)}, \overline{q(x)}, \overline{p(x) + q(x)}$ and $\overline{p(x)q(x)}$.\\
(b) Prove that $\overline{E}$ is not an integral domain.\\
(c) Prove that $\overline{x}$ is a unit in $\overline{E}$.
\item Prove that if $R$ is an integral domain and $R[[x]]$ is the ring of formal power series in the indeterminate $x$ then the principal ideal generated by $x$ is a prime ideal (cf. Exercise 3, Section 2). Prove that the principal ideal generated by $x$ is a maximal ideal if and only if $R$ is a field.
\item Let $R$ be a finite commutative ring with identity. Prove that every prime ideal of $R$ is a maximal ideal.
\item Prove that a nonzero finite commutative ring that has no zero divisors is a field (if the ring has an identity, this is Theorem~ [REF:thm:finite@c7] , so do not assume the ring has a $1$).
\item Prove that a finite ring with identity $1 \neq 0$ that has no zero divisors is a field (you may quote Wedderburn's Theorem).
\item Let $p \in \Zpos$ be a prime and let the $\F_p$-Quaternions be defined by
\[
a + bi + cj + dk, \quad a, b, c, d \in Z/pZ,
\]
where addition is componentwise and multiplication is defined using the same relations on $i, j, k$ as for the real Quaternions.\\
(a) Prove that the $\F_p$-Quaternions are a homomorphic image of the integral Quaternions (cf. Section 1).\\
(b) Prove that the $\F_p$-Quaternions contain zero divisors (and so they cannot be a division ring). [Use the preceding exercise.]
\item Prove that in a Boolean ring (cf. Exercise 15, Section 1) every prime ideal is a maximal ideal.
\item Prove that in a Boolean ring every finitely generated ideal is principal.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative and for each $a \in R$ there is an integer $n > 1$ (depending on $a$) such that $a^n = a$. Prove that every prime ideal of $R$ is a maximal ideal.
\item Prove that a prime ideal in a commutative ring $R$ contains every nilpotent element (cf. Exercise 13, Section 1). Deduce that the nilradical of $R$ (cf. Exercise 29, Section 3) is contained in the intersection of all the prime ideals of $R$. (It is shown in Section 15.1 that the nilradical of $R$ is equal to the intersection of all prime ideals of $R$.)
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$. Prove that if $a$ is a nilpotent element of $R$ then $1 - ab$ is a unit for all $b \in R$.
\item Prove that if $R$ is a commutative ring and $N = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m)$ where each $a_i$ is a nilpotent element, then $N$ is a nilpotent ideal (cf. Exercise 37, Section 3). Deduce that if the nilradical of $R$ is finitely generated then it is a nilpotent ideal.
\item Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite group of order a power of $p$ (i.e., a $p$-group). Prove that the augmentation ideal in the group ring $Z/(p)ZG$ is a nilpotent ideal. (Note that this ring may be noncommutative.) [Use Exercise 2.]
\item Let $I$ be an ideal of the commutative ring $R$ and define
\[
\rad I = \{r \in R \mid r^n \in I for some n \in \Zpos\}
\]
called the radical of $I$. Prove that $\rad I$ is an ideal containing $I$ and that the ideal $(\rad I)/I$ is the nilradical of the quotient ring $R/I$, i.e., $(\rad I)/I = N(R/I)$ (cf. Exercise 29, Section 3).
\item An ideal $I$ of the commutative ring $R$ is called a radical ideal if $\rad I = I$.\\
(a) Prove that every prime ideal of $R$ is a radical ideal.\\
(b) Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Prove that $0$ is a radical ideal in $Z/(n)Z$ if and only if $n$ is a product of distinct primes to the first power (i.e., $n$ is square free). Deduce that $(n)$ is a radical ideal of $Z$ if and only if $n$ is a product of distinct primes in $Z$.
\item Let $I$ be an ideal of the commutative ring $R$ and define
\[
\operatorname{Jac} I to be the intersection of all maximal ideals of R that contain I
\]
where the convention is that $\operatorname{Jac} R = R$. (If $I$ is the zero ideal, $\operatorname{Jac} 0$ is called the Jacobson radical of the ring $R$, so $\operatorname{Jac} I$ is the preimage in $R$ of the Jacobson radical of $R/I$.)\\
(a) Prove that $\operatorname{Jac} I$ is an ideal of $R$ containing $I$.\\
(b) Prove that $\rad I \subseteq \operatorname{Jac} I$, where $\rad I$ is the radical of $I$ defined in Exercise 30.\\
(c) Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Describe $\operatorname{Jac} nZ$ in terms of the prime factorization of $n$.
\item Let $R$ be the ring of all continuous functions from the closed interval $[0,1]$ to $R$ and for each $c \in [0,1]$ let $M_c = \{f \in R \mid f(c) = 0\}$ (recall that $M_c$ was shown to be a maximal ideal of $R$).\\
(a) Prove that if $M$ is any maximal ideal of $R$ then there is a real number $c \in [0,1]$ such that $M = M_c$.\\
(b) Prove that if $b$ and $c$ are distinct points in $[0,1]$ then $M_b \neq M_c$.\\
(c) Prove that $M_c$ is not equal to the principal ideal generated by $x - c$.\\
(d) Prove that $M_c$ is not a finitely generated ideal.
\item Let $R$ be the ring of all continuous functions from $R$ to $R$ and for each $c \in R$ let $M_c$ be the maximal ideal $\{f \in R \mid f(c) = 0\}$.\\
(a) Let $I$ be the collection of functions $f(x)$ in $R$ with compact support (i.e., $f(x) = 0$ for $|x|$ sufficiently large). Prove that $I$ is an ideal of $R$ that is not a prime ideal.\\
(b) Let $M$ be a maximal ideal of $R$ containing $I$ (properly, by (a)). Prove that $M \neq M_c$ for any $c \in R$ (cf. the preceding exercise).
\item Let $A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ be a nonzero finitely generated ideal of $R$. Prove that there is an ideal $B$ which is maximal with respect to the property that it does not contain $A$. [Use Zorn's Lemma.]
\item Assume $R$ is commutative.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Rings > Properties of Ideals > Prime ideals
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 3/3
Content:
Prove that the set of prime ideals in $R$ has a minimal element with respect to inclusion (possibly the zero ideal). [Use Zorn's Lemma.]
\item A commutative ring $R$ is called a local ring if it has a unique maximal ideal. Prove that if $R$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $M$ then every element of $R - M$ is a unit. Prove conversely that if $R$ is a commutative ring with $1$ in which the set of nonunits forms an ideal $M$, then $R$ is a local ring with unique maximal ideal $M$.
\item Prove that the ring of all rational numbers whose denominators is odd is a local ring whose unique maximal ideal is the principal ideal generated by $2$.
\item Following the notation of Exercise 26 in Section 1, let $K$ be a field, let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$ and let $R$ be the valuation ring of $v$. For each integer $k \geq 0$ define $A_k = \{r \in R \mid v(r) \geq k\} \cup \{0\}$.\\
(a) Prove that $A_k$ is a principal ideal and that $A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$.\\
(b) Prove that if $I$ is any nonzero ideal of $R$, then $I = A_k$ for some $k \geq 0$. Deduce that $R$ is a local ring with unique maximal ideal $A_1$.
\item Assume $R$ is commutative. Prove that the following are equivalent: (see also Exercises 13 and 14 in Section 1)\\
(i) $R$ has exactly one prime ideal\\
(ii) every element of $R$ is either nilpotent or a unit\\
(iii) $R/N(R)$ is a field (cf. Exercise 29, Section 3).
\item A proper ideal $Q$ of the commutative ring $R$ is called primary if whenever $ab \in Q$ and $a \notin Q$ then $b^n \in Q$ for some positive integer $n$. (Note that the symmetry between $a$ and $b$ in this definition implies that if $Q$ is a primary ideal and $ab \in Q$ with neither $a$ nor $b$ in $Q$, then a positive power of $a$ and a positive power of $b$ both lie in $Q$.) Establish the following facts about primary ideals.\\
(a) The primary ideals of $Z$ are $0$ and $(p^n)$, where $p$ is a prime and $n$ is a positive integer.\\
(b) Every prime ideal of $R$ is a primary ideal.\\
(c) An ideal $Q$ of $R$ is primary if and only if every zero divisor in $R/Q$ is a nilpotent element of $R/Q$.\\
(d) If $Q$ is a primary ideal then $\rad(Q)$ is a prime ideal (cf. Exercise 30).
\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. Prove that an ideal $I$ is the unit ideal (i.e.\ $I=R$) if and only if $I$ contains a unit. Deduce that the only ideals of a field $F$ are $\langle 0\rangle$ and $F$.

\item In $Z$, describe the ideal $\langle 6,15\rangle$ explicitly as a principal ideal $\langle d\rangle$, and find $d$. More generally show $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$ for $a,b\inZ$.

\item Determine whether each ideal of $Z$ is prime, maximal, both, or neither: $\langle 0\rangle$, $\langle 7\rangle$, $\langle 12\rangle$, $\langle 1\rangle$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $P$ an ideal. Prove $P$ is prime $\Longleftrightarrow R/P$ is an integral domain, and $M$ is maximal $\Longleftrightarrow R/M$ is a field. Use this to re-derive the previous problem's answers.

\item Show that every nonzero prime ideal of $Z$ is maximal. Give an example of a commutative ring in which some nonzero prime ideal is not maximal.

\item In $R=Z$, compute the ideal $\langle 4\rangle\cap\langle 6\rangle$, the product $\langle 4\rangle\langle 6\rangle$, and the sum $\langle 4\rangle+\langle 6\rangle$. Express each as a principal ideal $\langle n\rangle$.

\item Let $R=Q[x]$. Show that $\langle x^2-1\rangle$ is neither prime nor maximal, that $\langle x-1\rangle$ is maximal, and identify the field $R/\langle x-1\rangle$.

\item Let $R=Z[x]$. Show that $\langle x\rangle$ is prime but not maximal, and that $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is maximal. Identify $R/\langle 2,x\rangle$.

\item Let $\varphi\colonZ\toZ/(12)Z$ be the natural projection. List all ideals of $Z/(12)Z$, and for each determine whether it is prime or maximal. (Recall ideals of $Z/(n)Z$ correspond to divisors of $n$.)

\item Let $R$ be a finite commutative ring with $1$. Prove that every prime ideal of $R$ is maximal. (Hint: a finite integral domain is a field.)

\item Let $I,J$ be ideals of a commutative ring $R$ with $I+J=R$ (comaximal). Prove $IJ=I\cap J$.

\item Use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to write down an explicit ring isomorphism $Z/(15)Z\toZ/(3)Z\timesZ/(5)Z$, and find the element of $Z/(15)Z$ corresponding to $(2,3)$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. An element $x$ is nilpotent if $x^n=0$ for some $n\ge1$. Prove the set $\nil(R)$ of nilpotent elements (the nilradical) is an ideal, and compute $\nil(Z/(12)Z)$.

\item Prove that in a commutative ring with $1$, the nilradical is contained in every prime ideal. Conclude $\nil(Z/(12)Z)$ lies in $\langle 2\rangle$ and $\langle 3\rangle$.

\item Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $R$ with $1$. Define $\rad(I)=\{x\in R:x^n\in I for some n\ge1\}$. Show $\rad(I)$ is an ideal containing $I$, and compute $\rad(\langle 12\rangle)$ in $Z$.

\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. Prove that $R$ is a field if and only if its only ideals are $\langle 0\rangle$ and $R$. Show this fails for noncommutative rings by exhibiting the only two-sided ideals of $\Mat_2(\F)$ for a field $\F$ (and noting it is not a field).

\item (Prime avoidance, two-prime case.) Let $P_1,P_2$ be prime ideals of a commutative ring $R$ and let $I$ be an ideal with $I\subseteq P_1\cup P_2$. Prove $I\subseteq P_1$ or $I\subseteq P_2$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1\neq0$. Prove that $R$ contains a maximal ideal, and that every proper ideal is contained in some maximal ideal. (You may invoke Zorn's Lemma.)

\item Let $R=R[x]$. Classify all maximal ideals of $R$, showing each has the form $\langle x-a\rangle$ (with $R/\langle x-a\rangle\congR$) or $\langle x^2+bx+c\rangle$ with $b^2-4c<0$ (with quotient $\congC$). Conclude $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is maximal.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ in which every element $x$ satisfies $x^2=x$ (a Boolean ring). Prove every prime ideal of $R$ is maximal, and that $R/P\congZ/(2)Z$ for each prime $P$.

\item Let $I$ and $J$ be comaximal ideals of a commutative ring $R$ with $1$. Prove $I^m$ and $J^n$ are comaximal for all $m,n\ge1$.

\end{exers}

Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring homomorphism with $I\subseteq\ker\varphi$ an ideal of $R$, and let $\pi\colon R\to R/I$ be the projection. State and prove the universal property: there is a unique ring homomorphism $\overline{\varphi}\colon R/I\to S$ making the diagram commute, and $\overline{\varphi}$ is injective iff $I=\ker\varphi$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & S \\
R/I \arrow[ur, dashed, "\overline{\varphi}"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and let $I_1,I_2$ be comaximal ideals. Prove the map $r\mapsto(r+I_1,\,r+I_2)$ induces a ring isomorphism, so that the dashed arrow below is well defined and an isomorphism. Identify its kernel before passing to the quotient.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r, "{r\mapsto(r+I_1,\,r+I_2)}"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & R/I_1\times R/I_2 \\
R/(I_1\cap I_2) \arrow[ur, dashed, "\sim"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $\Frac(R)$, $\iota\colon R\to\Frac(R)$ the inclusion. Suppose $f\colon R\to F$ is an injective ring homomorphism into a field $F$. State and prove the universal property of the field of fractions exhibited by the diagram, identifying the formula for $\bar f$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(R) \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\bar f"] \\
& F
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R=Z$, $I_1=\langle 4\rangle$, $I_2=\langle 9\rangle$. Verify $I_1+I_2=Z$ and use the previous CRT diagram to produce an explicit isomorphism $Z/(36)Z\xrightarrow{\sim}Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(9)Z$. Draw the diagram with all arrows labeled, and compute the image of $\overline{17}$.

\item Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $K$. Show that the assignment $I\mapsto\varphi(I)$ gives an inclusion-preserving bijection between ideals of $R$ containing $K$ and ideals of $S$, and that this bijection sends prime (resp.\ maximal) ideals to prime (resp.\ maximal) ideals. Illustrate with $\varphi\colonZ\toZ/(12)Z$ in a diagram of the relevant quotients.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads] & S \arrow[d, two heads] \\
R/I \arrow[r, dashed, "\sim"] & S/\varphi(I)
\end{tikzcd}\]

\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
Throughout this section $R$ is a commutative ring with $1$. The motivating
question of D\&F 7.5 is: given a ring, how do we adjoin inverses to certain elements
so that they become units? For $R=Z$ we want to invert all nonzero integers and arrive
at $Q$; more generally we invert the elements of a chosen ``denominator set.'' The whole
construction is a vast generalization of building $Q$ out of $Z$, with the equality
$a/b=c/d \Longleftrightarrow ad=bc$ replaced by a careful equivalence relation.

Title: Multiplicatively closed set
Content:
\begin{definition}[Multiplicatively closed set]
A subset $D\subseteq R$ is multiplicatively closed if $1\in D$ and $D$ is closed
under multiplication: $a,b\in D\Longrightarrow ab\in D$. In this section we additionally require that
$D$ consist of nonzero elements that are not zero divisors, i.e.\ $0\notin D$ and no
$d\in D$ satisfies $dr=0$ for some $r\neq 0$. (Such a $D$ is the admissible denominator set
of D\&F's Theorem 15.)
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
The condition ``no zero divisors in $D$'' is exactly what makes the cancellation
$ad=bd\Longrightarrow a=b$ legal for $d\in D$, which is what is needed for the fraction relation below
to be an equivalence relation and for $R$ to embed (rather than collapse). If one drops it
one gets a more general localization $D^{-1} R$ in which $R$ need not embed -- that is the
subject of the more general theory; here we stay in the zero-divisor-free case of D\&F.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: D\&F 7.5, Theorem 15: existence of the ring of fractions
Label: thm:frac@c7
Content:
\begin{theorem}[D\&F 7.5, Theorem 15: existence of the ring of fractions] 
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $D$ be a nonempty multiplicatively closed subset of
$R$ containing no zero divisors (and $0\notin D$). On the set $R\times D$ define
\[
(a,d)\sim(b,e) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ae=bd .
\]
Then $\sim$ is an equivalence relation. Write $\dfrac{a}{d}$ for the class of $(a,d)$ and
let $D^{-1} R$ be the set of classes. The operations
\[
\frac{a}{d}+\frac{b}{e}=\frac{ae+bd}{de},
\qquad
\frac{a}{d}\cdot\frac{b}{e}=\frac{ab}{de}
\]
are well defined and make $D^{-1} R$ into a commutative ring with $1=\frac{d}{d}$ (any
$d\in D$) and $0=\frac{0}{1}$. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] The map $\iota\colon R\to D^{-1} R$, $\iota(r)=\dfrac{rd}{d}$ (any $d\in D$;
equivalently $\dfrac{r}{1}$) is an injective ring homomorphism, so $R$ is identified
with the subring $\iota(R)$.
\item[(2)] Every $d\in D$ becomes a unit in $D^{-1} R$: $\iota(d)^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{d}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Equivalence relation. Reflexivity and symmetry are clear from $ad=ad$ and
symmetry of $ae=bd$. For transitivity suppose $(a,d)\sim(b,e)$ and $(b,e)\sim(c,f)$, so
$ae=bd$ and $bf=ce$. Then
\[
(af)e=(ae)f=(bd)f=(bf)d=(ce)d=(cd)e .
\]
Thus $afe=cde$, and since $e\in D$ is not a zero divisor we cancel $e$ to get $af=cd$,
i.e.\ $(a,d)\sim(c,f)$.

Well-defined operations. Suppose $\frac{a}{d}=\frac{a'}{d'}$, i.e.\ $ad'=a'd$. For
multiplication, $\frac{a}{d}\frac{b}{e}=\frac{ab}{de}$ and
$\frac{a'}{d'}\frac{b}{e}=\frac{a'b}{d'e}$; we must check $(ab)(d'e)=(a'b)(de)$. Indeed
$(ab)(d'e)=(ad')(be)=(a'd)(be)=(a'b)(de)$. Addition is similar (and one also varies the
second fraction); the not-a-zero-divisor hypothesis is not even needed for
well-definedness once $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, but it is needed for
transitivity above.

Ring axioms. These are routine verifications mirroring the familiar arithmetic of
$Q$; associativity, distributivity and commutativity follow from those of $R$ after
clearing denominators. The additive identity is $\frac{0}{1}$ (note $\frac{0}{d}=\frac01$
since $0\cdot 1=0\cdot d$) and $1_{D^{-1} R}=\frac{d}{d}$, which equals $\frac{1}{1}$.

(1) $\iota$ is a homomorphism. $\iota(r)=\frac{r}{1}$. Then
$\iota(r)+\iota(s)=\frac{r}{1}+\frac{s}{1}=\frac{r+s}{1}=\iota(r+s)$ and
$\iota(r)\iota(s)=\frac{rs}{1}=\iota(rs)$, and $\iota(1)=\frac11=1$.
Injectivity: $\iota(r)=0$ means $\frac{r}{1}=\frac{0}{1}$, i.e.\ $r\cdot 1=0\cdot 1$
so $r=0$. (Here is where ``no zero divisors in $D$'' matters: $\frac{r}{1}=\frac01\Longleftrightarrow
rd=0$ for the chosen $d$; cancel $d$ to get $r=0$.)

(2) $D$ becomes units. For $d\in D$, $\frac{d}{1}\cdot\frac{1}{d}=\frac{d}{d}=1$, so
$\iota(d)$ is a unit with inverse $\frac1d$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Building / recognizing a ring of fractions $D^{-1} R$
Content:
\begin{method}{Building / recognizing a ring of fractions $D^{-1} R$}
Trigger. You want to make a chosen multiplicatively closed set $D$ of non-zero-
divisors invertible, or you meet a ring described as ``$R$ with the elements of $D$
inverted,'' ``fractions $a/d$ with $d\in D$,'' or ``smallest ring containing $R$ in which
the $d\in D$ are units.''
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Identify $R$ (commutative) and the denominator set $D$. Check $1\in D$, $D$ closed
under products, $0\notin D$, and $D$ has no zero divisors.
\item Form symbols $a/d$ with $a\in R,\ d\in D$, modulo $a/d=b/e\Longleftrightarrow ae=bd$.
\item Add/multiply by the schoolbook rules $\frac{a}{d}+\frac{b}{e}=\frac{ae+bd}{de}$,
$\frac{a}{d}\cdot\frac{b}{e}=\frac{ab}{de}$.
\item Identify $r\in R$ with $r/1$; each $d\in D$ is a unit with inverse $1/d$.
\item Special case (the most common): if $R$ is an integral domain and
$D=R\setminus\{0\}$, then $D^{-1} R=\Frac(R)$ is a field.
\end{enumerate}
Check. Verify $1/d$ really inverts $d$, and confirm $\iota$ is injective by
checking $r/1=0/1\Longrightarrow r=0$.
\end{method}

Title: The relation really needs ``no zero divisors''
Content:
\begin{wex}{The relation really needs ``no zero divisors''}
Show that if $D$ contains a zero divisor the relation $\sim$ can fail to be transitive (or
$\iota$ fails to be injective), using $R=Z/(6)Z$ and the multiplicatively closed set
$D=\{1,2,4\}$.
\wrec Transitivity of $\sim$ used cancellation by $e\in D$; the example tests what happens
when an element of $D$ kills something nonzero. \wsol In $Z/(6)Z$, $2\cdot 3=0$ and $3\neq 0$, so $2$ is a zero divisor; $D=\{1,2,4\}$ is
multiplicatively closed ($2\cdot2=4,\ 2\cdot4=8=2,\ 4\cdot4=16=4$) but contains the zero
divisor $2$. For the relation of Theorem~ [REF:thm:frac@c7] , $(3,1)\sim(0,2)$ since $3\cdot 2=0=0\cdot 1$,
and $(0,2)\sim(0,1)$ since $0\cdot 1=0\cdot 2$, but $(3,1)\not\sim(0,1)$ since
$3\cdot 1\neq 0\cdot 1$; so $\sim$ is not transitive. Repairing this with the localization
relation $\frac ad=\frac be\Longleftrightarrow(\exists u\in D)\ u(ae-bd)=0$, whose zero test is
$\frac r1=\frac01\Longleftrightarrow (\exists d\in D)\ rd=0$, we get $\frac31=\frac01$ because
$3\cdot 2=0$. So $\iota(3)=0$: the element $3\neq 0$ would die. This is exactly the
pathology the hypothesis ``$D$ has no zero divisors'' rules out, guaranteeing $\iota$
injective (Theorem~ [REF:thm:frac@c7] (1)). Check. Indeed $3\neq 0$ in $Z/(6)Z$ yet maps
to $0$, confirming injectivity fails when the hypothesis is dropped. \wsol
\end{wex}

Title: Field of fractions
Content:
\begin{definition}[Field of fractions]
Let $R$ be an integral domain. Take $D=R\setminus\{0\}$, which is multiplicatively closed
(product of nonzeros is nonzero in a domain) and contains no zero divisors (a domain has
none). The ring $D^{-1} R$ is then a field, called the field of fractions (or
quotient field) of $R$, written $\Frac(R)$ or $Q(R)$.
\end{definition}

Title: D\&F 7.5, Corollary 16: $\Frac(R)$ is a field
Label: cor:fracfield@c7
Content:
\begin{corollary}[D\&F 7.5, Corollary 16: $\Frac(R)$ is a field] 
If $R$ is an integral domain then $\Frac(R)$ is a field, and it is the smallest
field containing (an isomorphic copy of) $R$ in the following sense: if $K$ is any field
containing $R$ as a subring, then the subfield of $K$ generated by $R$ is isomorphic to
$\Frac(R)$. Concretely $\Frac(R)=\{\,a/b : a\in R,\ b\in R,\ b\neq 0\,\}$.
\end{corollary}
label: cor:fracfield@c7

\begin{proof}
$\Frac(R)$ is commutative with $1=\frac11\neq\frac01=0$ (since $1\neq0$ in $R$). Take any
nonzero $\frac{a}{b}\in\Frac(R)$. Nonzero means $\frac ab\neq\frac01$, i.e.\ $a\cdot1\neq
0\cdot b$, i.e.\ $a\neq 0$; hence $a\in D=R\setminus\{0\}$ and $\frac{b}{a}\in\Frac(R)$.
Then $\frac ab\cdot\frac ba=\frac{ab}{ab}=1$, so $\frac ab$ is a unit. Thus every nonzero
element is invertible and $\Frac(R)$ is a field. Minimality is the universal property,
Theorem~ [REF:thm:UP@c7] below: any field $K\supseteq R$ induces an injection
$\Frac(R)\hookrightarrow K$ whose image is the subfield $R$ generates.
\end{proof}

Label: thm:UP@c7
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Universal property of $\Frac(R)$, D\&F 7.5 Theorem 15(2)/Cor.~16]
 
Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $\Frac(R)$ and embedding
$\iota\colon R\hookrightarrow\Frac(R)$, $\iota(r)=r/1$. If $F$ is a field and
$f\colon R\to F$ is an injective ring homomorphism (more generally any ring hom
sending every nonzero element of $R$ to a unit of $F$), then there is a unique ring
homomorphism $\bar f\colon\Frac(R)\to F$ with $\bar f\circ\iota=f$, namely
\[
\bar f\!\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=f(a)\,f(b)^{-1} .
\]
Moreover $\bar f$ is itself injective. In a diagram:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(R) \arrow[d, dashed, hook, "\exists!\,\bar f"] \\
& F
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R$ is an integral domain (upper left). $\Frac(R)$ is the field of fractions
 of $R$ (upper right), a field in which every nonzero element of $R$ is a unit. $F$ is any
 field (lower right) together with an injective ring homomorphism from $R$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon R\hookrightarrow\Frac(R)$ is the canonical embedding $r\mapsto r/1$,
 a ring homomorphism that is injective because $R$ has no zero divisors. $f\colon R\to F$ is
 an injective ring homomorphism (the given data). $\bar f\colon\Frac(R)\to F$ is the induced
 (dashed) map defined by $\bar f(a/b)=f(a)f(b)^{-1}$; it is asserted to exist and be unique.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\bar f\circ\iota = f$. That is, for every $r\in R$,
 $\bar f(\iota(r))=f(r)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take $r\in R$. Along the top-then-down path: $\iota(r)=r/1$, then
 $\bar f(r/1)=f(r)f(1)^{-1}=f(r)\cdot 1=f(r)$. Along the direct path (the diagonal $f$):
 $f(r)$. Both give $f(r)$. Well-definedness of $\bar f$ on cosets: if $a/b=a'/b'$ then
 $ab'=a'b$, so $f(a)f(b')=f(a')f(b)$; multiplying both sides by $f(b)^{-1}f(b')^{-1}$ (units
 in $F$ since $b,b'\ne0$ and $f$ is injective into a field) gives $f(a)f(b)^{-1}=f(a')f(b')^{-1}$,
 confirming $\bar f$ is independent of the representative chosen.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the universal property of $\Frac(R)$: it encodes in one
 picture that $\Frac(R)$ is the smallest field containing $R$, in the categorical sense
 that any field $F$ receiving an injection from $R$ already receives one from $\Frac(R)$ via
 the unique $\bar f$. The dashed arrow and the uniqueness are the entire content of Theorem 15(2)/Corollary 16.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=Z$, $\Frac(R)=Q$, $F=R$, $f(n)=n$. Then $\bar f(a/b)=a/b\inR$
 is the standard embedding $Q\hookrightarrowR$, the unique ring hom extending $f$. There is
 no other way to embed $Q$ in $R$ that fixes $Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\bar f$ exists for any ring hom $f\colon R\to F$,
 not just injective ones. If $f$ kills a nonzero $r$, then $f(r)=0$ would need to be a unit
 (since $r/1\in\Frac(R)$ has an inverse $1/r$), but $0$ is not a unit in $F$. The injectivity
 hypothesis is essential; without it the formula $\bar f(a/b)=f(a)f(b)^{-1}$ breaks down: if
 $f(r)=0$ for some $r\neq 0$, it would require $\bar f(1/r)=f(1)f(r)^{-1}$, and $f(r)^{-1}=0^{-1}$
 is undefined.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $\Frac(R)$ is the universal initial step in
 embedding $R$ into a field: every injection of $R$ into a field factors uniquely and injectively
 through $\iota\colon R\hookrightarrow\Frac(R)$.
\end{dgx}
\end{theorem}

uniqueness.

$\frac ab=\frac cd$ then $ad=bc$, so $f(a)f(d)=f(b)f(c)$ in $F$; since $f(b),f(d)$ are units
(as $b,d\neq0$) multiply by $f(b)^{-1} f(d)^{-1}$ to get $f(a)f(b)^{-1}=f(c)f(d)^{-1}$.
Well-defined. It is a homomorphism:
\[
\bar f\!\left(\tfrac ab+\tfrac cd\right)=\bar f\!\left(\tfrac{ad+bc}{bd}\right)
=f(ad+bc)f(bd)^{-1}=\big(f(a)f(d)+f(b)f(c)\big)f(b)^{-1} f(d)^{-1}
=f(a)f(b)^{-1}+f(c)f(d)^{-1},
\]
and multiplicativity is immediate; $\bar f(\frac11)=1$.

$\bar f$ injective. If $\bar f(\frac ab)=0$ then $f(a)f(b)^{-1}=0$, so $f(a)=0$, so
$a=0$ (as $f$ injective), so $\frac ab=0$. A nonzero ring hom of a field is automatically
injective, recovering this.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Using the universal property to embed a domain in a field
Content:
\begin{method}{Using the universal property to embed a domain in a field}
Trigger. You must show a domain $R$ sits inside a field, or you have a map
$f\colon R\to F$ into a field and want to extend it to fractions, or you need to prove two
fields-of-fractions are isomorphic.
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Confirm $R$ is an integral domain (so $\Frac(R)$ exists and is a field).
\item Produce an injective ring hom $f\colon R\to F$ into your target field $F$.
\item Invoke Theorem~ [REF:thm:UP@c7] : get the unique $\bar f(\frac ab)=f(a)f(b)^{-1}$,
automatically injective, so $\Frac(R)\hookrightarrow F$.
\item For an isomorphism $\Frac(R)\cong K$: show $K$ is a field containing $R$ in which
every element is $a b^{-1}$ with $a,b\in R,\ b\neq0$; then $\bar f$ is onto, hence iso.
\end{enumerate}
Check. Verify $\bar f\circ\iota=f$ on generators of $R$ and that $\bar f$ hits
every element of $K$ for surjectivity.
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $\Frac(Z)=Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Frac(Z)=Q$}
Identify the field of fractions of $Z$ and verify the universal property by recovering the
standard embedding $Z\hookrightarrowQ$.
\wrec $Z$ is an integral domain and $D=Z\setminus\{0\}$, so $\Frac(Z)$ is the field of
all $a/b$ -- this is the definition of $Q$. \wsol $Z$ is a domain, so $\Frac(Z)=\{a/b:a\inZ,b\inZ\setminus\{0\}\}$ with
$\frac ab=\frac cd\Longleftrightarrow ad=bc$. That is precisely the usual construction of $Q$, so
$\Frac(Z)\congQ$ via $\frac ab\mapsto a/b$. Universal property: let $F$ be any field of
characteristic $0$ and $f\colonZ\to F$ the unique ring hom $f(n)=n\cdot 1_F$, which is
injective (char $0$). Then $\bar f(\frac ab)=f(a)f(b)^{-1}=(a\cdot1_F)(b\cdot1_F)^{-1}$
embeds $Q\hookrightarrow F$; this is the familiar fact that every characteristic-$0$ field
contains a copy of $Q$ (its prime subfield). Check. $\bar f(\frac11)=1_F$ and
$\bar f(\frac 21)=2\cdot1_F$, agreeing with $f$ on $Z$. \wsol
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\Frac(\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Q}$}
Identify the field of fractions of $\mathbb{Z}$ and verify the universal property by recovering the
standard embedding $\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain and $D=\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$, so $\Frac(\mathbb{Z})$ is the field of
all $a/b$ -- this is the definition of $\mathbb{Q}$. \wsol $\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain, so $\Frac(\mathbb{Z})=\{a/b:a\in\mathbb{Z},b\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\}$ with
$\frac ab=\frac cd\Longleftrightarrow ad=bc$. That is precisely the usual construction of $\mathbb{Q}$, so
$\Frac(\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Q}$ via $\frac ab\mapsto a/b$. Universal property: let $F$ be any field of
characteristic $0$ and $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to F$ the unique ring hom $f(n)=n\cdot 1_F$, which is
injective (char $0$). Then $\bar f(\frac ab)=f(a)f(b)^{-1}=(a\cdot1_F)(b\cdot1_F)^{-1}$
embeds $\mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow F$; this is the familiar fact that every characteristic-$0$ field
contains a copy of $\mathbb{Q}$ (its prime subfield). \textit{Check.} $\bar f(\frac11)=1_F$ and
$\bar f(\frac 21)=2\cdot1_F$, agreeing with $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}$. \wsol
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\Frac(\F[x])=\F(x)$, the field of rational functions
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Frac(\F[x])=\F(x)$, the field of rational functions}
For a field $\F$, identify $\Frac(\F[x])$.
\wrec $\F[x]$ is an integral domain (a polynomial ring over a field has no zero divisors,
by additivity of degrees), so its field of fractions is the quotients of polynomials. \wsol Since $\F$ is a field, $\F[x]$ is an integral domain: if $p,q\neq0$ then
$\deg(pq)=\deg p+\deg q$, so $pq\neq0$. Hence
\[
\Frac(\F[x])=\Big\{\tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} : p,q\in\F[x],\ q\neq0\Big\}=:\F(x),
\]
the field of rational functions in $x$ over $\F$, with $\frac pq=\frac rs\Longleftrightarrow ps=qr$.
It is a field by Corollary~ [REF:cor:fracfield@c7] : the inverse of nonzero $\frac pq$ is
$\frac qp$. Check. $\frac{x}{x^2+1}\cdot\frac{x^2+1}{x}=\frac{x(x^2+1)}{x(x^2+1)}=1$,
so $\frac{x}{x^2+1}$ is indeed a unit in $\F(x)$, as every nonzero element must be. \wsol
\end{wex}

\]

Title: $\Frac(Z[i])=Q(i)$, the Gaussian rationals
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Frac(Z[i])=Q(i)$, the Gaussian rationals}
Let $Z[i]=\{a+bi:a,b\inZ\}$ be the Gaussian integers. Show $\Frac(Z[i])=Q(i)$.
\wrec $Z[i]$ is an integral domain (subring of $C$), so $\Frac(Z[i])$ is the smallest
subfield of $C$ containing $Z[i]$; compute it. \wsol $Z[i]\subseteqC$ is a subring of a field, hence an integral domain, so
$\Frac(Z[i])$ exists and by Corollary~ [REF:cor:fracfield@c7] embeds as the subfield of $C$
generated by $Z[i]$. That subfield is $Q(i)=\{p+qi:p,q\inQ\}$. To see this, every
quotient $\frac{a+bi}{c+di}$ (with $c+di\neq0$) is computed by rationalizing:
\[
\frac{a+bi}{c+di}=\frac{(a+bi)(c-di)}{(c+di)(c-di)}
=\frac{(ac+bd)+(bc-ad)i}{c^2+d^2}
=\frac{ac+bd}{c^2+d^2}+\frac{bc-ad}{c^2+d^2}\,i\ \in\ Q(i),
\]
where $c^2+d^2\neq0$ since $c+di\neq0$. Conversely each $p+qi\inQ(i)$ with
$p=\frac{a}{m},q=\frac{b}{m}$ ($m\neq0$) equals $\frac{a+bi}{m}\in\Frac(Z[i])$. Hence
$\Frac(Z[i])=Q(i)$. Check. The inverse of $1+i$ is
$\frac{1}{1+i}=\frac{1-i}{(1+i)(1-i)}=\frac{1-i}{2}=\frac12-\frac12 i\inQ(i)$, and
$(1+i)(\frac12-\frac12 i)=\frac12-\frac12 i+\frac12 i-\frac12 i^2=\frac12+\frac12=1$. \wsol
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])=\mathbb{Q}(i)$, the Gaussian rationals}
Let $\mathbb{Z}[i]=\{a+bi:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ be the Gaussian integers. Show $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])=\mathbb{Q}(i)$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is an integral domain (subring of $\mathbb{C}$), so $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])$ is the smallest
subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ containing $\mathbb{Z}[i]$; compute it. \wsol $\mathbb{Z}[i]\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is a subring of a field, hence an integral domain, so
$\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])$ exists and by Corollary~\ref{cor:fracfield@c7} embeds as the subfield of $\mathbb{C}$
generated by $\mathbb{Z}[i]$. That subfield is $\mathbb{Q}(i)=\{p+qi:p,q\in\mathbb{Q}\}$. To see this, every
quotient $\frac{a+bi}{c+di}$ (with $c+di\neq0$) is computed by rationalizing:
\[
\frac{a+bi}{c+di}=\frac{(a+bi)(c-di)}{(c+di)(c-di)}
=\frac{(ac+bd)+(bc-ad)i}{c^2+d^2}
=\frac{ac+bd}{c^2+d^2}+\frac{bc-ad}{c^2+d^2}\,i\ \in\ \mathbb{Q}(i),
\]
where $c^2+d^2\neq0$ since $c+di\neq0$. Conversely each $p+qi\in\mathbb{Q}(i)$ with
$p=\frac{a}{m},q=\frac{b}{m}$ ($m\neq0$) equals $\frac{a+bi}{m}\in\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])$. Hence
$\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[i])=\mathbb{Q}(i)$. \textit{Check.} The inverse of $1+i$ is
$\frac{1}{1+i}=\frac{1-i}{(1+i)(1-i)}=\frac{1-i}{2}=\frac12-\frac12 i\in\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and
$(1+i)(\frac12-\frac12 i)=\frac12-\frac12 i+\frac12 i-\frac12 i^2=\frac12+\frac12=1$. \wsol
\end{wex}

Title: Localizing $Z$ at powers of $2$: $D^{-1}Z=Z[1/2]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing $Z$ at powers of $2$: $D^{-1}Z=Z[1/2]$}
Let $R=Z$ and $D=\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}=\{2^k:k\ge0\}$. Describe $D^{-1}Z$ and show it is
not a field.
\wrec $D$ is multiplicatively closed and contains no zero divisors (subset of the domain
$Z$), so Theorem~ [REF:thm:frac@c7] applies; we are inverting only the powers of $2$, not all
nonzero integers. \wsol $D=\{2^k\}$ is multiplicatively closed ($2^j2^k=2^{j+k}$, $1=2^0\in D$) and
zero-divisor-free. So
\[
D^{-1}Z=\Big\{\tfrac{a}{2^k} : a\inZ,\ k\ge0\Big\}=Z[1/2]\subseteqQ,
\]
the ring of dyadic rationals, with $\frac{a}{2^j}=\frac{b}{2^k}\Longleftrightarrow a2^k=b2^j$. The only
new units we created are the $\pm2^k$; for instance $3$ is not a unit in $Z[1/2]$
because $\frac13\notinZ[1/2]$ (it would require $3\mid 2^k$). Therefore $D^{-1}Z$ is a
proper subring of $Q$ and is not a field. Check. The units of $Z[1/2]$ are
exactly $\pm2^k$; e.g.\ $\frac12$ inverts $2$ since $\frac12\cdot 2=1$, but $\frac15$ is not
in the ring, so $5^{-1}$ does not exist. Note $\Frac(Z[1/2])=Q$ still, since $Z[1/2]$ is a
domain whose fractions recover all of $Q$. \wsol
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Localizing $\mathbb{Z}$ at powers of $2$: $D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$}
Let $R=\mathbb{Z}$ and $D=\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}=\{2^k:k\ge0\}$. Describe $D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ and show it is
\emph{not} a field.
\wrec $D$ is multiplicatively closed and contains no zero divisors (subset of the domain
$\mathbb{Z}$), so Theorem~\ref{thm:frac@c7} applies; we are inverting only the powers of $2$, not all
nonzero integers. \wsol $D=\{2^k\}$ is multiplicatively closed ($2^j2^k=2^{j+k}$, $1=2^0\in D$) and
zero-divisor-free. So
\[
D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}=\Big\{\tfrac{a}{2^k} : a\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\ge0\Big\}=\mathbb{Z}[1/2]\subseteq\mathbb{Q},
\]
the ring of dyadic rationals, with $\frac{a}{2^j}=\frac{b}{2^k}\Longleftrightarrow a2^k=b2^j$. The only
new units we created are the $\pm2^k$; for instance $3$ is \emph{not} a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$
because $\frac13\notin\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ (it would require $3\mid 2^k$). Therefore $D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ is a
proper subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ and is \emph{not} a field. \textit{Check.} The units of $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ are
exactly $\pm2^k$; e.g.\ $\frac12$ inverts $2$ since $\frac12\cdot 2=1$, but $\frac15$ is not
in the ring, so $5^{-1}$ does not exist. Note $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[1/2])=\mathbb{Q}$ still, since $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ is a
domain whose fractions recover all of $\mathbb{Q}$. \wsol
\end{wex}
