Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Rings > Rings of Fractions > The field of fractions of an integral domain
Type: example
Title: Universal property to embed a domain in a field
Content:
\begin{wex}{Universal property to embed a domain in a field}
Let $R$ be the domain $Z[\sqrt{-5}]=\{a+b\sqrt{-5}:a,b\inZ\}$. Show $R$ embeds in a field
and identify $\Frac(R)$, using the universal property.
\wrec $R\subseteqC$ is a domain; the inclusion $f\colon R\hookrightarrowC$ is an injective
ring hom into a field, so Theorem~ [REF:thm:UP@c7] extends it uniquely to $\Frac(R)$. \wsol $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a subring of $C$, hence an integral domain, so $\Frac(R)$ is a
field. Let $f\colon R\hookrightarrowC$ be inclusion, an injective ring hom into the field
$C$. By the universal property there is a unique injective ring hom
$\bar f\colon\Frac(R)\toC$, $\bar f(\frac{a+b\sqrt{-5}}{c+d\sqrt{-5}})=
(a+b\sqrt{-5})(c+d\sqrt{-5})^{-1}$. Its image is the subfield of $C$ generated by $R$, which
is $Q(\sqrt{-5})=\{p+q\sqrt{-5}:p,q\inQ\}$ (rationalize denominators using
$(c+d\sqrt{-5})(c-d\sqrt{-5})=c^2+5d^2\inQ$). Hence $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])\cong
Q(\sqrt{-5})$. Check. $(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}=\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{(2)^2+5}=
\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{9}=\frac29-\frac19\sqrt{-5}\inQ(\sqrt{-5})$, and
$(2+\sqrt{-5})(\frac29-\frac19\sqrt{-5})=\frac49-\frac29\sqrt{-5}+\frac29\sqrt{-5}
-\frac19(-5)=\frac49+\frac59=1$. The diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
Z[\sqrt{-5}] \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])
\arrow[d, dashed, "\cong\ \bar f"] \\
& Q(\sqrt{-5})\subseteqC
\end{tikzcd}\]
commutes, with $\bar f$ the asserted isomorphism. \wsol
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $Z[\sqrt{-5}]=\{a+b\sqrt{-5}:a,b\inZ\}$ is an integral domain (upper left),
 a subring of $C$. $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ is its abstract field of fractions (upper right).
 $Q(\sqrt{-5})=\{p+q\sqrt{-5}:p,q\inQ\}\subseteqC$ is the concrete subfield of $C$
 generated by $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ (lower right).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colonZ[\sqrt{-5}]\hookrightarrow\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ is the canonical
 embedding $z\mapsto z/1$, injective since $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain. $f\colonZ[\sqrt{-5}]
 \hookrightarrowQ(\sqrt{-5})\subseteqC$ is the natural ring inclusion, injective as a subring
 map. $\bar f\colon\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])\xrightarrow{\sim}Q(\sqrt{-5})$ is the induced map
 $\bar f(\frac{z}{w})=zw^{-1}$ (computed in $C$), asserted to be an isomorphism.
\dgi{What commutes:} $\bar f\circ\iota = f$: for every $z\inZ[\sqrt{-5}]$,
 $\bar f(z/1)=z\cdot 1^{-1}=z=f(z)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take $z\inZ[\sqrt{-5}]$. Via $\iota$ then $\bar f$: $z\mapsto z/1
 \mapsto f(z)f(1)^{-1}=f(z)$. Via $f$ directly: $z\mapsto f(z)$. Equal. Well-definedness of
 $\bar f$: if $z/w=z'/w'$ in $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ then $zw'=z'w$; applying $f$ (a ring hom)
 gives $f(z)f(w')=f(z')f(w)$ in $C$; since $w,w'\ne0$ and $f$ injective (into a field),
 $f(w),f(w')$ are nonzero hence units in $C$, so $f(z)f(w)^{-1}=f(z')f(w')^{-1}$ and $\bar f$
 is well defined on equivalence classes.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram makes concrete the abstract universal property from
 the theorem: instead of an unknown field $F$, here $F=C$ and the image of $\bar f$ is
 computed explicitly as $Q(\sqrt{-5})$. Surjectivity of $\bar f$ (rationalization of denominators
 shows every $p+q\sqrt{-5}\inQ(\sqrt{-5})$ is a quotient of elements of $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$) upgrades
 the injection to an isomorphism, identifying the abstract $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ with the
 concrete $Q(\sqrt{-5})$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}=\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{9}=\frac{2}{9}-\frac{1}{9}\sqrt{-5}
 \inQ(\sqrt{-5})$. In $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ this is the element $1/(2+\sqrt{-5})$, and $\bar f$
 sends it to $1\cdot(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}$ in $C$, landing in $Q(\sqrt{-5})$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The isomorphism label $\cong$ on the dashed arrow is the conclusion of a
 proof, not the starting assumption. Students sometimes read the diagram as defining $\bar f$ to
 be an isomorphism; in fact one must first show it is well defined (coset check above), then a
 homomorphism, then injective (automatic for a nonzero map of fields), then surjective (by the
 rationalization calculation). The dashed arrow starts as a candidate map.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the universal property of $\Frac(Z[\sqrt{-5}])$
 identifies it concretely with $Q(\sqrt{-5})$ by providing a computable isomorphism via
 rationalization of denominators.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Universal property to embed a domain in a field}
Let $R$ be the domain $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]=\{a+b\sqrt{-5}:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. Show $R$ embeds in a field
and identify $\Frac(R)$, using the universal property.
\wrec $R\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is a domain; the inclusion $f\colon R\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is an injective
ring hom into a field, so Theorem~\ref{thm:UP@c7} extends it uniquely to $\Frac(R)$. \wsol $R=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a subring of $\mathbb{C}$, hence an integral domain, so $\Frac(R)$ is a
field. Let $f\colon R\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be inclusion, an injective ring hom into the field
$\mathbb{C}$. By the universal property there is a unique injective ring hom
$\bar f\colon\Frac(R)\to\mathbb{C}$, $\bar f(\frac{a+b\sqrt{-5}}{c+d\sqrt{-5}})=
(a+b\sqrt{-5})(c+d\sqrt{-5})^{-1}$. Its image is the subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ generated by $R$, which
is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})=\{p+q\sqrt{-5}:p,q\in\mathbb{Q}\}$ (rationalize denominators using
$(c+d\sqrt{-5})(c-d\sqrt{-5})=c^2+5d^2\in\mathbb{Q}$). Hence $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])\cong
\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$. \textit{Check.} $(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}=\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{(2)^2+5}=
\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{9}=\frac29-\frac19\sqrt{-5}\in\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$, and
$(2+\sqrt{-5})(\frac29-\frac19\sqrt{-5})=\frac49-\frac29\sqrt{-5}+\frac29\sqrt{-5}
-\frac19(-5)=\frac49+\frac59=1$. The diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])
\arrow[d, dashed, "\cong\ \bar f"] \\
& \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})\subseteq\mathbb{C}
\end{tikzcd}\]
commutes, with $\bar f$ the asserted isomorphism. \wsol
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]=\{a+b\sqrt{-5}:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is an integral domain (upper left),
  a subring of $\mathbb{C}$. $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$ is its abstract field of fractions (upper right).
  $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})=\{p+q\sqrt{-5}:p,q\in\mathbb{Q}\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is the concrete subfield of $\mathbb{C}$
  generated by $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ (lower right).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]\hookrightarrow\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$ is the canonical
  embedding $z\mapsto z/1$, injective since $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain. $f\colon\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]
  \hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is the natural ring inclusion, injective as a subring
  map. $\bar f\colon\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ is the induced map
  $\bar f(\frac{z}{w})=zw^{-1}$ (computed in $\mathbb{C}$), asserted to be an isomorphism.
\dgi{What commutes:} $\bar f\circ\iota = f$: for every $z\in\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$,
  $\bar f(z/1)=z\cdot 1^{-1}=z=f(z)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take $z\in\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$. Via $\iota$ then $\bar f$: $z\mapsto z/1
  \mapsto f(z)f(1)^{-1}=f(z)$. Via $f$ directly: $z\mapsto f(z)$. Equal. Well-definedness of
  $\bar f$: if $z/w=z'/w'$ in $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$ then $zw'=z'w$; applying $f$ (a ring hom)
  gives $f(z)f(w')=f(z')f(w)$ in $\mathbb{C}$; since $w,w'\ne0$ and $f$ injective (into a field),
  $f(w),f(w')$ are nonzero hence units in $\mathbb{C}$, so $f(z)f(w)^{-1}=f(z')f(w')^{-1}$ and $\bar f$
  is well defined on equivalence classes.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram makes concrete the abstract universal property from
  the theorem: instead of an unknown field $F$, here $F=\mathbb{C}$ and the image of $\bar f$ is
  computed explicitly as $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$. Surjectivity of $\bar f$ (rationalization of denominators
  shows every $p+q\sqrt{-5}\in\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ is a quotient of elements of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$) upgrades
  the injection to an isomorphism, identifying the abstract $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$ with the
  concrete $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}=\frac{2-\sqrt{-5}}{9}=\frac{2}{9}-\frac{1}{9}\sqrt{-5}
  \in\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$. In $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$ this is the element $1/(2+\sqrt{-5})$, and $\bar f$
  sends it to $1\cdot(2+\sqrt{-5})^{-1}$ in $\mathbb{C}$, landing in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The isomorphism label $\cong$ on the dashed arrow is the conclusion of a
  proof, not the starting assumption. Students sometimes read the diagram as defining $\bar f$ to
  be an isomorphism; in fact one must first show it is well defined (coset check above), then a
  homomorphism, then injective (automatic for a nonzero map of fields), then surjective (by the
  rationalization calculation). The dashed arrow starts as a candidate map.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the universal property of $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}])$
  identifies it concretely with $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ by providing a computable isomorphism via
  rationalization of denominators.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Two presentations of the same field of fractions
Content:
\begin{wex}{Two presentations of the same field of fractions}
Show that $\Frac\big(Z[x]\big)$ and $\Frac\big(Q[x]\big)$ are isomorphic (both equal
$Q(x)$), illustrating that enlarging the domain inside its own fraction field changes
nothing.
\wrec Both $Z[x]$ and $Q[x]$ are integral domains lying in the field $Q(x)$; the
universal property forces both fraction fields to be the subfield they generate. \wsol $Z[x]\subseteqQ[x]\subseteqQ(x)$ are domains; $Q(x)=\Frac(Q[x])$ by the rational
functions example. The inclusion $f\colonZ[x]\hookrightarrowQ(x)$ is injective into a
field, so $\bar f\colon\Frac(Z[x])\hookrightarrowQ(x)$ is an injective ring hom onto the
subfield generated by $Z[x]$. That subfield already contains $\frac1n$ for every nonzero
integer $n$ (as $\frac{1}{n\cdot 1}$) and contains $x$, hence contains $Q[x]$ and all its
quotients, i.e.\ all of $Q(x)$. So $\bar f$ is onto: $\Frac(Z[x])\congQ(x)\cong
\Frac(Q[x])$. Check. $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{x}{2}\in\Frac(Z[x])$ maps to the same
element of $Q(x)$ as the obvious element of $\Frac(Q[x])$, and $\frac{1}{2}\inQ\subseteq
Q(x)$ is hit by $\frac{1}{2}\in\Frac(Z[x])$, confirming surjectivity. \wsol
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Two presentations of the same field of fractions}
Show that $\Frac\big(\mathbb{Z}[x]\big)$ and $\Frac\big(\mathbb{Q}[x]\big)$ are isomorphic (both equal
$\mathbb{Q}(x)$), illustrating that enlarging the domain inside its own fraction field changes
nothing.
\wrec Both $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ are integral domains lying in the field $\mathbb{Q}(x)$; the
universal property forces both fraction fields to be the subfield they generate. \wsol $\mathbb{Z}[x]\subseteq\mathbb{Q}[x]\subseteq\mathbb{Q}(x)$ are domains; $\mathbb{Q}(x)=\Frac(\mathbb{Q}[x])$ by the rational
functions example. The inclusion $f\colon\mathbb{Z}[x]\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}(x)$ is injective into a
field, so $\bar f\colon\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[x])\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}(x)$ is an injective ring hom onto the
subfield generated by $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. That subfield already contains $\frac1n$ for every nonzero
integer $n$ (as $\frac{1}{n\cdot 1}$) and contains $x$, hence contains $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and all its
quotients, i.e.\ all of $\mathbb{Q}(x)$. So $\bar f$ is onto: $\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[x])\cong\mathbb{Q}(x)\cong
\Frac(\mathbb{Q}[x])$. \textit{Check.} $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{x}{2}\in\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[x])$ maps to the same
element of $\mathbb{Q}(x)$ as the obvious element of $\Frac(\mathbb{Q}[x])$, and $\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{Q}\subseteq
\mathbb{Q}(x)$ is hit by $\frac{1}{2}\in\Frac(\mathbb{Z}[x])$, confirming surjectivity. \wsol
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Recognizing a fraction ring: a subring of $Q$ from integers coprime to $6$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Recognizing a fraction ring: a subring of $Q$ from integers coprime to $6$}
Let $D=\{n\inZ:\gcd(n,6)=1\}=\{\pm1,\pm5,\pm7,\pm11,\dots\}$ (integers coprime to $6$).
Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed and describe $D^{-1}Z$.
\wrec $D$ is closed under multiplication (coprimality to $6$ is multiplicative) and is
zero-divisor-free in the domain $Z$, so $D^{-1}Z$ is the subring of $Q$ where we invert
exactly the integers coprime to $6$. \wsol If $\gcd(m,6)=\gcd(n,6)=1$ then $\gcd(mn,6)=1$, and $1\in D$, $0\notin D$; so $D$ is
multiplicatively closed with no zero divisors. Then
\[
D^{-1}Z=\Big\{\tfrac{a}{b}\inQ : a\inZ,\ \gcd(b,6)=1\Big\},
\]
the subring of $Q$ of fractions whose reduced denominator is coprime to $6$, equivalently
divisible only by primes $\neq 2,3$. The units we created are all $\pm$ integers coprime to
$6$; $2$ and $3$ are not inverted, so this is not a field. Check. $\frac15\in
D^{-1}Z$ and $5\cdot\frac15=1$, but $\frac12\notin D^{-1}Z$ since $2$ is not coprime to $6$;
thus $2$ stays a non-unit, consistent with $D$ excluding multiples of $2$. \wsol
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Recognizing a fraction ring: a subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ from integers coprime to $6$}
Let $D=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:\gcd(n,6)=1\}=\{\pm1,\pm5,\pm7,\pm11,\dots\}$ (integers coprime to $6$).
Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed and describe $D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$.
\wrec $D$ is closed under multiplication (coprimality to $6$ is multiplicative) and is
zero-divisor-free in the domain $\mathbb{Z}$, so $D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ is the subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ where we invert
exactly the integers coprime to $6$. \wsol If $\gcd(m,6)=\gcd(n,6)=1$ then $\gcd(mn,6)=1$, and $1\in D$, $0\notin D$; so $D$ is
multiplicatively closed with no zero divisors. Then
\[
D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}=\Big\{\tfrac{a}{b}\in\mathbb{Q} : a\in\mathbb{Z},\ \gcd(b,6)=1\Big\},
\]
the subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ of fractions whose reduced denominator is coprime to $6$, equivalently
divisible only by primes $\neq 2,3$. The units we created are all $\pm$ integers coprime to
$6$; $2$ and $3$ are \emph{not} inverted, so this is not a field. \textit{Check.} $\frac15\in
D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ and $5\cdot\frac15=1$, but $\frac12\notin D^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ since $2$ is not coprime to $6$;
thus $2$ stays a non-unit, consistent with $D$ excluding multiples of $2$. \wsol
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Title: The construction as a universal arrow
Content:
\begin{remark}[The construction as a universal arrow]
Theorem~ [REF:thm:UP@c7] says $\iota\colon R\to\Frac(R)$ is the initial object among
ring homomorphisms from $R$ to fields that are injective: every such $f$ factors uniquely
through $\iota$. This is the same shape of statement as the First Isomorphism Theorem
triangle and the universal property of $R[x]$; recognizing the pattern
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(R) \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!"] \\
& F
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R$ is an integral domain (upper left). $\Frac(R)$ is the field of fractions of
 $R$ (upper right). $F$ is any field that receives an injective ring hom from $R$ (lower right).
 This remark strips the theorem down to its categorical skeleton.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon R\to\Frac(R)$ is the embedding $r\mapsto r/1$. $f\colon R\to F$ is
 the given injective ring hom (or more generally any ring hom sending nonzero elements to units).
 The dashed arrow $\exists!\colon\Frac(R)\to F$ is the unique extension, given by $a/b\mapsto
 f(a)f(b)^{-1}$; its uniqueness is signaled by the exclamation mark.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $(\exists!)\circ\iota = f$. Spelling it out: for
 every $r\in R$, the unique extension evaluated at $r/1$ returns $f(r)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The formula $a/b\mapsto f(a)f(b)^{-1}$ is forced: $\iota(r)=r/1$ must
 map to $f(r)$ to agree with $f$; writing $a/b=(a/1)(1/b)$ and $1/b=\iota(b)^{-1}$ in $\Frac(R)$,
 any ring hom must send $1/b$ to $f(b)^{-1}$. So the formula is the only candidate, and
 one checks (as in the proof) that it is indeed well defined and a homomorphism.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark reframes the theorem as a universal property of the same
 categorical shape as the First Isomorphism Theorem triangle and the universal property of
 polynomial rings. Recognizing this shape immediately tells you: (a) the extension exists, (b)
 it is unique, and (c) it is given by the explicit formula. No computation is needed once you
 see the triangle.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=Q[x]$, $\Frac(R)=Q(x)$, $F=R(t)$ (rational functions in $t$
 with real coefficients), $f$ the injective map $p(x)\mapsto p(t)$. The unique extension sends
 $p(x)/q(x)$ to the rational function $p(t)/q(t)\inR(t)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The ``$\exists!$'' on the dashed arrow refers to uniqueness among
 ring homs extending $f$, not uniqueness of ring homs from $\Frac(R)$ to $F$ in general.
 There can be many ring homs $\Frac(R)\to F$; the universal property pins down the one that
 makes the triangle commute.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that knowing only the triangle shape and the
 uniqueness label is enough to reconstruct the extension formula $a/b\mapsto f(a)f(b)^{-1}$
 and to recognize $\Frac(R)$ as an initial object in the category of fields receiving $R$.
\end{dgx}
is the fastest way to remember that the extension exists, is unique, and is given by
$a/b\mapsto f(a)f(b)^{-1}$.
\end{remark}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Fill in all the details in the proof of Theorem 15.
\item Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $D$ be a nonempty subset of $R$ that does not contain $0$ and is closed under multiplication. Prove that the ring of fractions $D^{-1}R$ is isomorphic to a subring of the quotient field of $R$ (hence is also an integral domain).
\item Let $F$ be a field. Prove that $F$ contains a unique smallest subfield $F_0$ and that $F_0$ is isomorphic to either $Q$ or $Z/(p)Z$ for some prime $p$ ($F_0$ is called the prime subfield of $F$). [See Exercise 26, Section 3.]
\item Prove that any subfield of $R$ must contain $Q$.
\item If $F$ is a field, prove that the field of fractions of $F[[x]]$ (the ring of formal power series in the indeterminate $x$ with coefficients in $F$) is the ring $F((x))$ of formal Laurent series (cf. Exercises 3 and 5 of Section 2). Show the field of fractions of the power series ring $Z[[x]]$ is properly contained in the field of Laurent series $Q((x))$. [Consider the series for $e^x$.]
\item Prove that the real numbers, $R$, contain a subring $A$ with $1 \in A$ and $A$ maximal (under inclusion) with respect to the property that $\tfrac{1}{2} \notin A$. [Use Zorn's Lemma.] (Exercise 13 in Section 15.3 shows $R$ is the quotient field of $A$, so $R$ is the quotient field of a proper subring.)
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Rings > Rings of Fractions > The field of fractions of an integral domain
Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1\neq 0$ and let $D$ be a nonempty multiplicatively closed subset of $R$ with $0\notin D$ and $1\in D$. Recall $D^{-1}R$ consists of equivalence classes $\frac{r}{d}$ under $\frac{r}{d}\sim\frac{r'}{d'}\Longleftrightarrow s(rd'-r'd)=0$ for some $s\in D$. Verify directly that addition $\frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad+bc}{bd}$ is well defined (independent of representatives).

\item In $D^{-1}R$ above, verify that multiplication $\frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ac}{bd}$ is well defined and that $\frac{0}{1}$ and $\frac{1}{1}$ are the additive and multiplicative identities.

\item Let $R=Z$ and $D=\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}=\{2^k:k\geq 0\}$. Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed, describe the elements of $D^{-1}Z$ explicitly as a subring of $Q$, and find $\units{(D^{-1}Z)}$.

\item Let $R=Z$ and let $P=(5)$, so $D=Z\setminus P=\{n\inZ:5\nmid n\}$. Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed and that $D^{-1}Z=Z_{(5)}=\{\frac{a}{b}\inQ:5\nmid b\}$. Identify the units and the unique maximal ideal of $Z_{(5)}$.

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain. Prove that the map $\iota:R\to\Frac(R)$, $r\mapsto\frac{r}{1}$, is an injective ring homomorphism, and that every nonzero element of $\Frac(R)$ has the form $\frac{a}{b}$ with $a,b\in R$, $b\neq 0$.

\item Compute $\Frac(R)$ for each: (a) $R=Z$; (b) $R=\F[x]$ with $\F$ a field; (c) $R=Z[i]$ (the Gaussian integers); (d) $R=Z[x]$.

\item Let $D=\{1,3,9,27,\dots\}\subseteqZ$. In $D^{-1}Z$, write $\frac{2}{9}+\frac{5}{3}$ and $\frac{2}{9}\cdot\frac{5}{3}$ as single fractions in lowest terms.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $D$ multiplicatively closed with $0\notin D$. Prove that the kernel of the canonical map $\iota:R\to D^{-1}R$, $r\mapsto\frac{r}{1}$, equals $\{r\in R: dr=0 for some d\in D\}$. Deduce $\iota$ is injective iff $D$ contains no zero divisor of $R$.

\item Let $D$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of the commutative ring $R$ with $0\in D$. Prove that $D^{-1}R$ is the zero ring (i.e.\ $\frac{1}{1}=\frac{0}{1}$).

\item Let $R=Z/6Z$ and $D=\{1,2,4\}$ (the powers of $2$ mod $6$, where $2^k$ cycles through $\{2,4,2,4,\dots\}$ and $2^0=1$). Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed, determine $\ker\iota$, and identify the ring $D^{-1}R$ (it is isomorphic to a familiar ring).

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $F=\Frac(R)$. Show that any field $K$ containing (an isomorphic copy of) $R$ contains an isomorphic copy of $F$. In particular $\Frac(R)$ is the smallest field containing $R$.

\item Let $D$ be multiplicatively closed in the commutative ring $R$, with $0\notin D$. Show that for $\frac{a}{b}\in D^{-1}R$, we have $\frac{a}{b}=0$ iff $sa=0$ for some $s\in D$.

\item Suppose $R$ is a commutative ring and $f\in R$ is not nilpotent. Let $D=\{1,f,f^2,f^3,\dots\}$. Show $0\notin D$, so $D^{-1}R$ (often written $R_f$) is a nonzero ring, and prove $\frac{f}{1}$ is a unit in $R_f$.

\item Let $F$ be a field. Show that for any multiplicatively closed $D\subseteq F$ with $0\notin D$, the natural map $F\to D^{-1}F$ is an isomorphism. (A field is already its own ring of fractions for every legal $D$.)

\item Let $R=Z[i]$ and $D=\{1,(1+i),(1+i)^2,\dots\}$. Show $1+i$ is not a zero divisor, so $\iota$ is injective, and exhibit the inverse of $\frac{1+i}{1}$ in $D^{-1}R$ as a fraction.

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item (Universal property.) Let $R$ be commutative with $D$ multiplicatively closed, $0\notin D$. Let $S$ be any commutative ring and $\varphi:R\to S$ a ring homomorphism with $\varphi(d)\in\units{S}$ for all $d\in D$. Prove there is a unique ring homomorphism $\Phi:D^{-1}R\to S$ with $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$, given by $\Phi(\frac{r}{d})=\varphi(r)\varphi(d)^{-1}$. Verify $\Phi$ is well defined.

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain and $D$ a multiplicatively closed subset with $0\notin D$. Prove that $D^{-1}R$ is also an integral domain, and that $\Frac(D^{-1}R)\cong\Frac(R)$.

\item (Localization commutes with quotients.) Let $R$ be commutative, $D$ multiplicatively closed with $0\notin D$, and $I$ an ideal of $R$ with $I\cap D=\varnothing$. Let $\bar D$ be the image of $D$ in $R/I$. Prove $D^{-1}R/(D^{-1}I)\cong \bar D^{-1}(R/I)$, where $D^{-1}I=\{\frac{a}{d}:a\in I,\,d\in D\}$ is an ideal of $D^{-1}R$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $P$ a prime ideal. Set $D=R\setminus P$. Show $D$ is multiplicatively closed and $0\notin D$, so the localization $R_P:=D^{-1}R$ exists. Prove $R_P$ is a local ring whose unique maximal ideal is $P_P=\{\frac{a}{d}:a\in P,\,d\notin P\}$, and that $R_P/P_P\cong\Frac(R/P)$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Prove that the set of zero divisors together with $0$ is a union of prime ideals, and using the multiplicative set $D$ of non--zero-divisors, describe the ``total ring of fractions'' $D^{-1}R$. Show that when $R$ is an integral domain this recovers $\Frac(R)$.

\item Let $R$ be a PID and $0\neq p\in R$ a prime element. Describe $\units{R_{(p)}}$ and show $R_{(p)}$ is a discrete valuation ring: every nonzero element has the form $u p^n$ with $u\in\units{R_{(p)}}$ and $n\geq 0$, and the ideals of $R_{(p)}$ are exactly $(p^n)$ for $n\geq 0$ together with $(0)$.

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item (Universal property of fractions.) Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $F=\Frac(R)$ and embedding $\iota:R\to F$. Let $f:R\to K$ be an injective ring homomorphism into a field $K$. Prove there is a unique ring homomorphism $\bar f$ making the diagram commute, and show $\bar f$ is injective.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(R) \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\bar f"] \\ & K \end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R$ be commutative, $D$ multiplicatively closed with $0\notin D$, and $\iota:R\to D^{-1}R$ the canonical map with $J=\ker\iota=\{r:dr=0 for some d\in D\}$. Show $\iota$ factors through $R/J$ and that the induced map is injective, giving the diagram below (a fractions version of the First Isomorphism Theorem). Identify the dashed arrow explicitly.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large] R \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & D^{-1}R \\ R/J \arrow[ur, dashed, hook, "\overline{\iota}"'] & \end{tikzcd}\]

\item (CRT as an isomorphism.) Let $R$ be a commutative ring with ideals $I_1,I_2$ satisfying $I_1+I_2=R$. Prove that the dashed map below, induced by $\varphi\colon r\mapsto(r+I_1,\,r+I_2)$, is a ring isomorphism, and identify $\ker\varphi$ as $I_1\cap I_2=I_1 I_2$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=huge] R \arrow[r, "{r\mapsto(r+I_1,\,r+I_2)}"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & R/I_1 \times R/I_2 \\ R/(I_1\cap I_2) \arrow[ur, dashed, "\cong"'] & \end{tikzcd}\]

\item (Universal property of fractions for $R$-algebras.) Let $R$ be an integral domain with $F=\Frac(R)$ and let $S$ be a commutative $R$-algebra via $\varphi:R\to S$ in which every nonzero element of $R$ maps to a unit. Using the universal property of fractions, complete the diagram with a unique $R$-algebra map $\Phi$, and state precisely the condition on $\varphi$ that makes $\Phi$ exist.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & F \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\ & S \end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $D\subseteq D'$ two multiplicatively closed subsets with $0\notin D'$. Show the canonical maps fit into a commutative triangle and that there is a unique ring homomorphism $\theta:D^{-1}R\to D'^{-1}R$ filling it in. Give $\theta$ on a fraction $\frac{r}{d}$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large] R \arrow[r, "\iota_D"] \arrow[dr, "\iota_{D'}"'] & D^{-1}R \arrow[d, dashed, "\theta"] \\ & D'^{-1}R \end{tikzcd}\]

\end{exers}

Type: definition
Title: Product of ideals; comaximal ideals
Content:
\begin{definition}[Product of ideals; comaximal ideals]
Let $I,J\subseteq R$ be ideals. Their product $IJ$ is the ideal generated by all products $ab$ with $a\in I$, $b\in J$:
\[
IJ \;=\; \langle \,ab \st a\in I,\ b\in J\,\rangle
\;=\;\Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k b_k \st n\ge 0,\ a_k\in I,\ b_k\in J\Bigr\}.
\]
The ideals $I$ and $J$ are comaximal (D\&F's term) if
\[
I+J \;=\; R.
\]
A finite family $I_1,\dots,I_k$ is pairwise comaximal if $I_i+I_j=R$ whenever $i\neq j$.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Comaximal means: no proper ideal (in particular no maximal ideal) contains both $I$ and $J$. Equivalently, $I+J=R$ iff $1\in I+J$ iff there exist $a\in I$, $b\in J$ with $a+b=1$. In $Z$, where every ideal is $\langle n\rangle=nZ$, we have $mZ+nZ=\gcd(m,n)Z$, so $mZ$ and $nZ$ are comaximal exactly when $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Always $IJ\subseteq I\cap J$ (each generator $ab\in I$ and $ab\in J$); comaximality forces equality (Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] ), but it is not necessary for it: $(x)\cap(y)=(xy)=(x)(y)$ in $Q[x,y]$, although $(x)+(y)=(x,y)\neqQ[x,y]$.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: Chinese Remainder Theorem, D\&F 7.6 Thm.~17
Label: thm:crt@c7
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Chinese Remainder Theorem, D\&F 7.6 Thm.~17] 
Let $I_1,\dots,I_k$ be ideals of $R$. The map
\[
\varphi\colon R \longrightarrow R/I_1\times R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k,
\qquad
\varphi(r)=\bigl(r+I_1,\;r+I_2,\;\dots,\;r+I_k\bigr),
\]
is a ring homomorphism with kernel $I_1\cap I_2\cap\cdots\cap I_k$. If for each $i\neq j$ the ideals $I_i$ and $I_j$ are comaximal, then $\varphi$ is surjective, and
\[
I_1\cap I_2\cap\cdots\cap I_k \;=\; I_1 I_2\cdots I_k,
\]
so that $\varphi$ induces a ring isomorphism
\[
R/(I_1 I_2\cdots I_k)\;=\;R/(I_1\cap\cdots\cap I_k)\;\cong\;R/I_1\times R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k.
\]
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}
Homomorphism and kernel. Each coordinate $r\mapsto r+I_j$ is the canonical projection $R\to R/I_j$, a ring homomorphism; a map into a product is a homomorphism iff each coordinate is, so $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism. Now $\varphi(r)=0$ means $r+I_j=I_j$, i.e. $r\in I_j$, for every $j$; hence $\ker\varphi=I_1\cap\cdots\cap I_k$.

Surjectivity (case $k=2$). Suppose $I_1+I_2=R$. Choose $x\in I_1$, $y\in I_2$ with $x+y=1$. Then
\[
\varphi(y)=(y+I_1,\;y+I_2)=(1+I_1,\;0+I_2)=(\overline 1,\overline 0),
\]
since $y=1-x\equiv 1\pmod{I_1}$ and $y\in I_2$. Symmetrically $\varphi(x)=(\overline 0,\overline 1)$. For an arbitrary target $(a+I_1,\;b+I_2)$ set $r=bx+ay$; then $r\equiv b\cdot 0+a\cdot 1=a\pmod{I_1}$ and $r\equiv b\cdot 1+a\cdot 0=b\pmod{I_2}$, so $\varphi(r)=(a+I_1,b+I_2)$. Thus $\varphi$ is onto.

Intersection equals product (case $k=2$). Always $I_1 I_2\subseteq I_1\cap I_2$. Conversely take $c\in I_1\cap I_2$. With $x+y=1$ as above,
\[
c=c\cdot 1=c(x+y)=\underbrace{cx}_{\in I_1 I_2}+\underbrace{cy}_{\in I_1 I_2},
\]
because $c\in I_2,\ x\in I_1\Rightarrow cx\in I_2 I_1=I_1 I_2$ and $c\in I_1,\ y\in I_2\Rightarrow cy\in I_1 I_2$. Hence $I_1\cap I_2\subseteq I_1 I_2$, giving equality. Combined with the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to the surjection $\varphi$, we get $R/(I_1\cap I_2)=R/(I_1 I_2)\cong R/I_1\times R/I_2$.

Induction to general $k$. Suppose $I_1,\dots,I_k$ are pairwise comaximal. We first show $I_1$ is comaximal with $J:=I_2\cdots I_k$. For each $j\ge 2$ pick $a_j\in I_1$, $b_j\in I_j$ with $a_j+b_j=1$. Then
\[
1=\prod_{j=2}^{k}(a_j+b_j)=\underbrace{(terms with some a_j)}_{\in I_1}+\;b_2 b_3\cdots b_k,
\]
and $b_2\cdots b_k\in I_2\cdots I_k=J$. Thus $1\in I_1+J$, so $I_1+J=R$. By the $k=2$ case, $I_1\cap J=I_1 J$ and $R/(I_1\cap J)\cong R/I_1\times R/J$. By induction $J=I_2\cdots I_k=I_2\cap\cdots\cap I_k$ and $R/J\cong R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k$. Composing,
\[
I_1\cap\cdots\cap I_k=I_1\cap J=I_1 J=I_1 I_2\cdots I_k,
\]
and $R/(I_1\cdots I_k)\cong R/I_1\times(R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k)$, as claimed.
\end{proof}

because $c\in I_2,\ x\in I_1\Rightarrow cx\in I_2 I_1=I_1 I_2$ and $c\in I_1,\ y\in I_2\Rightarrow cy\in I_1 I_2$. Hence $I_1\cap I_2\subseteq I_1 I_2$, giving equality. Combined with the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to the surjection $\varphi$, we get $R/(I_1\cap I_2)=R/(I_1 I_2)\cong R/I_1\times R/I_2$.

\emph{Induction to general $k$.} Suppose $I_1,\dots,I_k$ are pairwise comaximal. We first show $I_1$ is comaximal with $J:=I_2\cdots I_k$. For each $j\ge 2$ pick $a_j\in I_1$, $b_j\in I_j$ with $a_j+b_j=1$. Then
\[
1=\prod_{j=2}^{k}(a_j+b_j)=\underbrace{(\text{terms with some }a_j)}_{\in I_1}+\;b_2 b_3\cdots b_k,
\]
and $b_2\cdots b_k\in I_2\cdots I_k=J$. Thus $1\in I_1+J$, so $I_1+J=R$. By the $k=2$ case, $I_1\cap J=I_1 J$ and $R/(I_1\cap J)\cong R/I_1\times R/J$. By induction $J=I_2\cdots I_k=I_2\cap\cdots\cap I_k$ and $R/J\cong R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k$. Composing,
\[
I_1\cap\cdots\cap I_k=I_1\cap J=I_1 J=I_1 I_2\cdots I_k,
\]
and $R/(I_1\cdots I_k)\cong R/I_1\times(R/I_2\times\cdots\times R/I_k)$, as claimed.
\end{proof}

The structural picture is the factorization of $\varphi$ through the quotient by the kernel (First Isomorphism Theorem): writing $\pi$ for the quotient map $R\to R/(I_1\cap I_2)$, there is a unique $\overline{\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\overline{\varphi}\circ\pi$, and under comaximality $\overline{\varphi}$ is an isomorphism.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & R/I_1\times R/I_2 \\
R/(I_1\cap I_2) \arrow[ur, dashed, "{\overline{\varphi}}"', "{\cong}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three rings arranged in a triangle. The top-left vertex is $R$ itself (the ambient commutative ring with $1$). The top-right vertex is the product ring $R/I_1\times R/I_2$ (pairs of cosets, with coordinate-wise addition and multiplication). The bottom vertex is the quotient ring $R/(I_1\cap I_2)$, which equals $R/(I_1 I_2)$ under comaximality.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\varphi\colon R\to R/I_1\times R/I_2$, $r\mapsto(r+I_1,r+I_2)$, is the simultaneous-reduction map (a ring homomorphism whose kernel is $I_1\cap I_2$; it is onto when $I_1+I_2=R$, the case drawn here). $\pi\colon R\twoheadrightarrow R/(I_1\cap I_2)$ (double-headed arrow) is the canonical surjective quotient map, $r\mapsto r+(I_1\cap I_2)$. $\overline{\varphi}\colon R/(I_1\cap I_2)\to R/I_1\times R/I_2$ (dashed arrow) is the induced map guaranteed by the First Isomorphism Theorem; it satisfies $\overline{\varphi}(r+(I_1\cap I_2))=(r+I_1,r+I_2)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\varphi = \overline{\varphi}\circ\pi$. That is, going directly across the top (apply $\varphi$) gives the same result as going down then diagonally up (apply $\pi$ then $\overline{\varphi}$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $r\in R$. Along the top: $r\mapsto(r+I_1,r+I_2)$. Along the bottom path: $r\xmapsto{\pi} r+(I_1\cap I_2)\xmapsto{\overline{\varphi}}(r+I_1,r+I_2)$. These agree by definition of $\overline{\varphi}$. Well-definedness of $\overline{\varphi}$: if $r+(I_1\cap I_2)=r'+(I_1\cap I_2)$ then $r-r'\in I_1\cap I_2$, so $r-r'\in I_1$ and $r-r'\in I_2$, giving $(r+I_1,r+I_2)=(r'+I_1,r'+I_2)$; hence $\overline{\varphi}$ does not depend on the choice of coset representative.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram records the First Isomorphism Theorem step in the proof of CRT. The text has just established that $\ker\varphi=I_1\cap I_2$; the diagram makes visible that $\varphi$ factors through the quotient by its own kernel, and that under comaximality the dashed arrow $\overline{\varphi}$ upgrades to an isomorphism (marked $\cong$). Without seeing this factorization, the isomorphism $R/(I_1\cap I_2)\cong R/I_1\times R/I_2$ can look unmotivated.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R=Z$, $I_1=3Z$, $I_2=4Z$. Then $\varphi(r)=(r\bmod 3,r\bmod 4)$, $\pi(r)=r\bmod 12$, and $\overline{\varphi}(\bar r)=(r\bmod 3,r\bmod 4)$. For $r=5$: top path gives $(2,1)$; bottom path gives $5\bmod 12=5$, then $\overline{\varphi}(5)=(2,1)$. Both agree.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the dashed $\overline{\varphi}$ as automatically existing and being an isomorphism for any ideals. In fact the FIT gives the injection $\overline{\varphi}$ for free (since $\ker\pi=I_1\cap I_2=\ker\varphi$); surjectivity -- and hence the $\cong$ label -- requires the separate comaximality argument. The dashed arrow signals ``existence guaranteed by a universal property,'' not that it is automatically onto.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the CRT isomorphism is simply the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to $\varphi$, with comaximality supplying the surjectivity that turns the canonical injection $\overline{\varphi}$ into a full ring isomorphism.
\end{dgx}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Rings > The Chinese Remainder Theorem > Comaximal ideals and the Chinese remainder theorem
Type: method
Title: Applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem
Content:
\begin{method}{Applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem}
Recognition trigger. You see a quotient $R/N$ where the modulus $N$ factors as a product (or intersection) of ideals --- e.g. $Z/nZ$ with $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$, $\F[x]/(f)$ with $f=f_1\cdots f_r$ coprime --- or you must solve simultaneous congruences $r\equiv a_j\pmod{I_j}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Check comaximality pairwise. Show $I_i+I_j=R$ for all $i\neq j$, i.e. exhibit $a_{ij}\in I_i,\ b_{ij}\in I_j$ with $a_{ij}+b_{ij}=1$. In $Z$: $\gcd$ of the moduli is $1$. In $\F[x]$: the polynomials are pairwise coprime (run the Euclidean algorithm / B\'ezout).
\item Conclude the splitting. Comaximality $\Rightarrow$ $I_1\cap\cdots\cap I_k=I_1\cdots I_k$ and $R/(I_1\cdots I_k)\cong\prod_j R/I_j$.
\item Build the inverse (to solve systems). For each $j$ form an ``idempotent'' $e_j$ with $e_j\equiv 1\pmod{I_j}$ and $e_j\equiv 0\pmod{I_i}$ for $i\neq j$, using the B\'ezout coefficients. Then $r=\sum_j a_j e_j$ realizes the target $(a_1,\dots,a_k)$.
\end{enumerate}
Sanity check. Reduce your candidate $r$ modulo each $I_j$ and confirm you recover $a_j$; check the cardinalities multiply ($|R/N|=\prod|R/I_j|$) in the finite case.
\end{method}

Title: $Z/12Z\congZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ explicitly
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/12Z\congZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ explicitly}
Exhibit the isomorphism $Z/12Z\xrightarrow{\sim}Z/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ and its inverse.
\wrec Take $R=Z$, $I_1=4Z$, $I_2=3Z$; since $\gcd(4,3)=1$ these are comaximal, and $4Z\cap 3Z=4Z\cdot 3Z=12Z$, so Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] gives the iso $Z/12Z\congZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$.
\wsol
Comaximality / B\'ezout: $1=\underbrace{(-2)\cdot 4}_{=-8}+\underbrace{3\cdot 3}_{=9}$, with $-8\in 4Z$ and $9\in 3Z$. So $x=-8\equiv 4\pmod{12}$ lies in $4Z$ and $y=9$ lies in $3Z$, with $x+y=1$.

Forward map $\varphi(a)=(a\bmod 4,\;a\bmod 3)$. The full table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c||c|c}
a & (a\bmod 4,\,a\bmod 3) & a & (a\bmod 4,\,a\bmod 3)\\\hline
0 & (0,0) & 6 & (2,0)\\
1 & (1,1) & 7 & (3,1)\\
2 & (2,2) & 8 & (0,2)\\
3 & (3,0) & 9 & (1,0)\\
4 & (0,1) & 10& (2,1)\\
5 & (1,2) & 11& (3,2)
\end{array}
\]
All $12$ pairs in $Z/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ appear exactly once, confirming the bijection.

Inverse via idempotents. We need $e_1\equiv(1,0)$ and $e_2\equiv(0,1)$. From $x+y=1$ with $y=9\in 3Z$, $y\equiv 1\pmod 4$, so $e_1=9$ gives $\varphi(9)=(9\bmod 4,9\bmod 3)=(1,0)$. And $x=4$ (the residue of $-8$ mod $12$) gives $\varphi(4)=(0,1)$, so $e_2=4$. Hence the inverse of $(u,v)\inZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ is
\[
\psi(u,v)=9u+4v\ \ (\bmod\ 12).
\]
Check. $\psi(3,2)=27+8=35\equiv 11\pmod{12}$, and indeed $\varphi(11)=(3,2)$. Cardinalities: $|Z/12Z|=12=4\cdot 3$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\wrec Take $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $I_1=4\mathbb{Z}$, $I_2=3\mathbb{Z}$; since $\gcd(4,3)=1$ these are comaximal, and $4\mathbb{Z}\cap 3\mathbb{Z}=4\mathbb{Z}\cdot 3\mathbb{Z}=12\mathbb{Z}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:crt@c7} gives the iso $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol
\emph{Comaximality / B\'ezout:} $1=\underbrace{(-2)\cdot 4}_{=-8}+\underbrace{3\cdot 3}_{=9}$, with $-8\in 4\mathbb{Z}$ and $9\in 3\mathbb{Z}$. So $x=-8\equiv 4\pmod{12}$ lies in $4\mathbb{Z}$ and $y=9$ lies in $3\mathbb{Z}$, with $x+y=1$.

\emph{Forward map} $\varphi(a)=(a\bmod 4,\;a\bmod 3)$. The full table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c||c|c}
a & (a\bmod 4,\,a\bmod 3) & a & (a\bmod 4,\,a\bmod 3)\\\hline
0 & (0,0) & 6 & (2,0)\\
1 & (1,1) & 7 & (3,1)\\
2 & (2,2) & 8 & (0,2)\\
3 & (3,0) & 9 & (1,0)\\
4 & (0,1) & 10& (2,1)\\
5 & (1,2) & 11& (3,2)
\end{array}
\]
All $12$ pairs in $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ appear exactly once, confirming the bijection.

\emph{Inverse via idempotents.} We need $e_1\equiv(1,0)$ and $e_2\equiv(0,1)$. From $x+y=1$ with $y=9\in 3\mathbb{Z}$, $y\equiv 1\pmod 4$, so $e_1=9$ gives $\varphi(9)=(9\bmod 4,9\bmod 3)=(1,0)$. And $x=4$ (the residue of $-8$ mod $12$) gives $\varphi(4)=(0,1)$, so $e_2=4$. Hence the inverse of $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is
\[
\psi(u,v)=9u+4v\ \ (\bmod\ 12).
\]
\textit{Check.} $\psi(3,2)=27+8=35\equiv 11\pmod{12}$, and indeed $\varphi(11)=(3,2)$. Cardinalities: $|\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}|=12=4\cdot 3$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Title: Solving a system of congruences
Content:
\begin{wex}{Solving a system of congruences}
Find all integers $x$ with $x\equiv 2\pmod 3$, $x\equiv 3\pmod 5$, $x\equiv 2\pmod 7$.
\wrec This is the surjectivity half of Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] in $R=Z$ with $I_1=3Z,I_2=5Z,I_3=7Z$. Pairwise $\gcd$'s are $1$, so $\varphi\colonZ\toZ/3Z\timesZ/5Z\timesZ/7Z$ is onto with kernel $3\cdot5\cdot7\,Z=105Z$; the solution set is a single residue class mod $105$.
\wsol
Let $N=105$, $N_1=N/3=35,\ N_2=N/5=21,\ N_3=N/7=15$.

Invert each $N_j$ modulo its prime.
$35\equiv 2\pmod 3$, and $2\cdot 2=4\equiv 1$, so $N_1^{-1}\equiv 2\pmod 3$.
$21\equiv 1\pmod 5$, so $N_2^{-1}\equiv 1\pmod 5$.
$15\equiv 1\pmod 7$, so $N_3^{-1}\equiv 1\pmod 7$.

Assemble.
\[
x\equiv a_1 N_1 (N_1^{-1})+a_2 N_2(N_2^{-1})+a_3 N_3(N_3^{-1})
=2\cdot 35\cdot 2+3\cdot 21\cdot 1+2\cdot 15\cdot 1.
\]
Compute: $2\cdot 35\cdot 2=140$, $3\cdot 21=63$, $2\cdot 15=30$; sum $=140+63+30=233$. Reduce: $233-105=128,\ 128-105=23$, so $x\equiv 23\pmod{105}$.

Check. $23=3\cdot 7+2\Rightarrow 23\equiv 2\pmod 3$; $23=5\cdot 4+3\Rightarrow 23\equiv 3\pmod 5$; $23=7\cdot 3+2\Rightarrow 23\equiv 2\pmod 7$. All three hold. \checkmark The full solution set is $\{23+105k\st k\inZ\}$.
\end{wex}

Title: Decomposing $(Z/nZ)^{\times}$ and recomputing $\varphi(n)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Decomposing $(Z/nZ)^{\times}$ and recomputing $\varphi(n)$}
For $n=360$, use CRT to decompose $\units{(Z/360Z)}$ and recover Euler's totient $\varphi(360)$.
\wrec The ring iso $Z/nZ\cong\prod_i Z/p_i^{a_i}Z$ restricts to its units, giving $\units{(Z/nZ)}\cong\prod_i\units{(Z/p_i^{a_i}Z)}$, because a unit in a product is a tuple of units. Then $\varphi(n)=\prod_i\varphi(p_i^{a_i})$.
\wsol
Factor $360=2^3\cdot 3^2\cdot 5=8\cdot 9\cdot 5$. The three prime-power factors $8,9,5$ are pairwise coprime, so $8Z,9Z,5Z$ are pairwise comaximal in $Z$ and
\[
Z/360Z\;\cong\;Z/8Z\timesZ/9Z\timesZ/5Z.
\]
Passing to units (a ring iso carries units to units, multiplicatively),
\[
\units{(Z/360Z)}\;\cong\;\units{(Z/8Z)}\times\units{(Z/9Z)}\times\units{(Z/5Z)}.
\]
Counting orders: $\varphi(8)=8(1-\tfrac12)=4$, $\varphi(9)=9(1-\tfrac13)=6$, $\varphi(5)=5-1=4$. Hence
\[
\varphi(360)=\varphi(8)\,\varphi(9)\,\varphi(5)=4\cdot 6\cdot 4=96.
\]
Check (direct totient formula). $\varphi(360)=360\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)\bigl(1-\tfrac13\bigr)\bigl(1-\tfrac15\bigr)=360\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac45=360\cdot\tfrac{8}{30}=96$. \checkmark The decomposition also shows $\units{(Z/360Z)}\cong(Z/2Z\timesZ/2Z)\times(Z/6Z)\times(Z/4Z)$ as abelian groups (since $\units{(Z/8Z)}\congZ/2Z\timesZ/2Z$), confirming order $4\cdot 6\cdot 4=96$.
\end{wex}

\[
\mathbb{Z}/360\mathbb{Z}\;\cong\;\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Passing to units (a ring iso carries units to units, multiplicatively),
\[
\units{(\mathbb{Z}/360\mathbb{Z})}\;\cong\;\units{(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z})}\times\units{(\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z})}\times\units{(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})}.
\]
Counting orders: $\varphi(8)=8(1-\tfrac12)=4$, $\varphi(9)=9(1-\tfrac13)=6$, $\varphi(5)=5-1=4$. Hence
\[
\varphi(360)=\varphi(8)\,\varphi(9)\,\varphi(5)=4\cdot 6\cdot 4=96.
\]

Title: A non-comaximal example: surjectivity fails
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-comaximal example: surjectivity fails}
Let $R=Z$, $I_1=2Z$, $I_2=4Z$. Show the CRT map $\varphi\colonZ\toZ/2Z\timesZ/4Z$ is not surjective, and that $I_1\cap I_2\neq I_1 I_2$.
\wrec Here $I_1+I_2=2Z+4Z=\gcd(2,4)Z=2Z\neqZ$, so $I_1,I_2$ are not comaximal. The hypothesis of Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] fails, and we expect both conclusions (surjectivity and $\cap=product$) to break.
\wsol
Kernel and image. $\ker\varphi=2Z\cap 4Z=4Z$, so $\varphi$ factors as an injection $Z/4Z\hookrightarrowZ/2Z\timesZ/4Z$. But $|Z/4Z|=4$ while $|Z/2Z\timesZ/4Z|=8$, so $\varphi$ cannot be onto.

A missed target. Consider $(1+2Z,\;0+4Z)$. If $\varphi(r)$ equaled this, then $r\equiv 0\pmod 4$, forcing $r\equiv 0\pmod 2$ (as $4\mid r\Rightarrow 2\mid r$); but the first coordinate demands $r\equiv 1\pmod 2$ --- contradiction. So $(\overline 1,\overline 0)$ is not in the image.

Intersection vs.\ product. $I_1\cap I_2=2Z\cap 4Z=4Z$, whereas $I_1 I_2=(2Z)(4Z)=8Z$. Since $4Z\neq 8Z$, indeed $I_1\cap I_2\supsetneq I_1 I_2$. Check. $4\in 4Z=I_1\cap I_2$ but $4\notin 8Z=I_1 I_2$. \checkmark The two coordinates carry overlapping ($2$-adic) information, which is exactly the obstruction comaximality removes.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A non-comaximal example: surjectivity fails}
Let $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $I_1=2\mathbb{Z}$, $I_2=4\mathbb{Z}$. Show the CRT map $\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} surjective, and that $I_1\cap I_2\neq I_1 I_2$.
\wrec Here $I_1+I_2=2\mathbb{Z}+4\mathbb{Z}=\gcd(2,4)\mathbb{Z}=2\mathbb{Z}\neq\mathbb{Z}$, so $I_1,I_2$ are \emph{not} comaximal. The hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:crt@c7} fails, and we expect both conclusions (surjectivity and $\cap=\text{product}$) to break.
\wsol
\emph{Kernel and image.} $\ker\varphi=2\mathbb{Z}\cap 4\mathbb{Z}=4\mathbb{Z}$, so $\varphi$ factors as an \emph{injection} $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$. But $|\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}|=4$ while $|\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}|=8$, so $\varphi$ cannot be onto.

\emph{A missed target.} Consider $(1+2\mathbb{Z},\;0+4\mathbb{Z})$. If $\varphi(r)$ equaled this, then $r\equiv 0\pmod 4$, forcing $r\equiv 0\pmod 2$ (as $4\mid r\Rightarrow 2\mid r$); but the first coordinate demands $r\equiv 1\pmod 2$ --- contradiction. So $(\overline 1,\overline 0)$ is not in the image.

\emph{Intersection vs.\ product.} $I_1\cap I_2=2\mathbb{Z}\cap 4\mathbb{Z}=4\mathbb{Z}$, whereas $I_1 I_2=(2\mathbb{Z})(4\mathbb{Z})=8\mathbb{Z}$. Since $4\mathbb{Z}\neq 8\mathbb{Z}$, indeed $I_1\cap I_2\supsetneq I_1 I_2$. \textit{Check.} $4\in 4\mathbb{Z}=I_1\cap I_2$ but $4\notin 8\mathbb{Z}=I_1 I_2$. \checkmark The two coordinates carry overlapping ($2$-adic) information, which is exactly the obstruction comaximality removes.
\end{wex}

Title: CRT in $\F[x]$ for coprime polynomials
Content:
\begin{wex}{CRT in $\F[x]$ for coprime polynomials}
In $R=Q[x]$ let $f=x-1$, $g=x-2$. Realize the isomorphism $Q[x]/\bigl((x-1)(x-2)\bigr)\congQ[x]/(x-1)\timesQ[x]/(x-2)\congQ\timesQ$, and find the polynomial $p$ of degree $<2$ with $p\equiv 5\pmod{(x-1)}$ and $p\equiv 9\pmod{(x-2)}$.
\wrec $Q[x]$ is a PID; $(f)+(g)=(\gcd(f,g))$ and $\gcd(x-1,x-2)=1$, so the ideals are comaximal. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] , $Q[x]/(fg)\congQ[x]/(f)\timesQ[x]/(g)$. Evaluation $p\mapsto p(1)$ identifies $Q[x]/(x-1)\congQ$ (and similarly at $2$), turning ``$p\bmod(x-c)$'' into ``$p(c)$''.
\wsol
B\'ezout. $(x-1)-(x-2)=1$, so with $u=x-1\in(f)$ and $v=-(x-2)=2-x\in(g)$ we have $u+v=1$. Then $v=2-x\equiv 1\pmod{(x-1)}$ (value $1$ at $x=1$) and $v\equiv 0\pmod{(x-2)}$; symmetrically $u=x-1\equiv 0\pmod{(x-1)}$ and $\equiv 1\pmod{(x-2)}$ (value $1$ at $x=2$). So the idempotents are
\[
e_1=2-x\ \ (the (x-1)-component),\qquad e_2=x-1\ \ (the (x-2)-component).
\]
Assemble. $p=5\,e_1+9\,e_2=5(2-x)+9(x-1)=10-5x+9x-9=4x+1.$

Check by evaluation: $p(1)=4+1=5$ and $p(2)=8+1=9$. \checkmark Also $\deg p=1<2=\deg(fg)$, the canonical representative in $Q[x]/(fg)$. The whole isomorphism reads $\overline p\mapsto(p(1),p(2))$, i.e. $Q[x]/\bigl((x-1)(x-2)\bigr)\xrightarrow{\sim}Q\timesQ$ by simultaneous evaluation.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: CRT over a finite field: $\F_2[x]/(x^2+x)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{CRT over a finite field: $\F_2[x]/(x^2+x)$}
Show $\F_2[x]/(x^2+x)\cong\F_2\times\F_2$ and identify the four elements concretely.
\wrec Over $\F_2$, $x^2+x=x(x+1)$ with $\gcd(x,x+1)=1$ (B\'ezout: $(x+1)-x=1$). So $(x)$ and $(x+1)$ are comaximal in $\F_2[x]$, and CRT gives $\F_2[x]/(x(x+1))\cong\F_2[x]/(x)\times\F_2[x]/(x+1)\cong\F_2\times\F_2$.
\wsol
Identify each factor. Evaluation at $0$ gives $\F_2[x]/(x)\cong\F_2$, $p\mapsto p(0)$; evaluation at $1$ gives $\F_2[x]/(x+1)\cong\F_2$, $p\mapsto p(1)$. So the iso is $\overline p\mapsto(p(0),p(1))$.

Tabulate the $4$ classes (representatives of degree $<2$: $0,1,x,x+1$):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\overline p & (p(0),\,p(1))\\\hline
0 & (0,0)\\
1 & (1,1)\\
x & (0,1)\\
x+1 & (1,0)
\end{array}
\]
All four pairs of $\F_2\times\F_2$ occur once --- the map is a bijection, hence a ring iso. Check (idempotents). $e_1=x+1$ has $(p(0),p(1))=(1,0)$ and $e_2=x$ has $(0,1)$; indeed $e_1+e_2=2x+1=1$ in $\F_2[x]$ and $e_1 e_2=x(x+1)=x^2+x\equiv 0$, the defining relation. \checkmark So $\overline{x+1}$ and $\overline x$ are complementary idempotents, the algebraic shadow of the product decomposition.
\end{wex}

Title: Comaximality of distinct maximal ideals
Content:
\begin{wex}{Comaximality of distinct maximal ideals}
Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and let $M_1\neq M_2$ be maximal ideals. Show $M_1+M_2=R$, and deduce $R/(M_1 M_2)\cong R/M_1\times R/M_2$ (a product of two fields).
\wrec ``Distinct maximal ideals'' is the recognition cue for automatic comaximality: $M_1+M_2$ is an ideal containing $M_1$ properly, and maximality of $M_1$ leaves only $R$.
\wsol
Since $M_1\neq M_2$ and both are maximal, neither contains the other; pick $m\in M_2\setminus M_1$. Then $M_1+\langle m\rangle\supsetneq M_1$, and as $M_1$ is maximal, $M_1+\langle m\rangle=R$. But $M_1+\langle m\rangle\subseteq M_1+M_2$, so $M_1+M_2=R$: the ideals are comaximal. By Theorem~ [REF:thm:crt@c7] ,
\[
M_1\cap M_2=M_1 M_2,\qquad R/(M_1 M_2)\cong R/M_1\times R/M_2.
\]
Each $R/M_i$ is a field (quotient by a maximal ideal), so $R/(M_1 M_2)$ is a product of two fields.

Check (instance). $R=Z$, $M_1=5Z$, $M_2=7Z$: $5Z\cap 7Z=35Z=5Z\cdot 7Z$, and $Z/35Z\congZ/5Z\timesZ/7Z\cong\F_5\times\F_7$, a product of two fields of sizes $5,7$, total $35$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Comaximality of distinct maximal ideals}
Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and let $M_1\neq M_2$ be maximal ideals. Show $M_1+M_2=R$, and deduce $R/(M_1 M_2)\cong R/M_1\times R/M_2$ (a product of two fields).
\wrec ``Distinct maximal ideals'' is the recognition cue for automatic comaximality: $M_1+M_2$ is an ideal containing $M_1$ properly, and maximality of $M_1$ leaves only $R$.
\wsol
Since $M_1\neq M_2$ and both are maximal, neither contains the other; pick $m\in M_2\setminus M_1$. Then $M_1+\langle m\rangle\supsetneq M_1$, and as $M_1$ is maximal, $M_1+\langle m\rangle=R$. But $M_1+\langle m\rangle\subseteq M_1+M_2$, so $M_1+M_2=R$: the ideals are comaximal. By Theorem~\ref{thm:crt@c7},
\[
M_1\cap M_2=M_1 M_2,\qquad R/(M_1 M_2)\cong R/M_1\times R/M_2.
\]
Each $R/M_i$ is a field (quotient by a maximal ideal), so $R/(M_1 M_2)$ is a product of two fields.

\textit{Check (instance).} $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M_1=5\mathbb{Z}$, $M_2=7\mathbb{Z}$: $5\mathbb{Z}\cap 7\mathbb{Z}=35\mathbb{Z}=5\mathbb{Z}\cdot 7\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Z}/35\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}\cong\F_5\times\F_7$, a product of two fields of sizes $5,7$, total $35$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Comaximality is required for surjectivity, and it is what guarantees $\cap=\,$product --- not merely a convenience. Without it the kernel of $\varphi$ is $\bigcap I_j$, which can strictly contain $\prod I_j$ (see the $2Z,4Z$ example), and $\varphi$ need not be onto. The First Isomorphism Theorem always gives the injection $R/\bigcap I_j\hookrightarrow\prod R/I_j$; surjectivity is the extra content of the CRT.
\end{pitfall}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Pairwise comaximal is genuinely needed for $k\ge 3$; ``jointly $I_1+\cdots+I_k=R$'' is not enough. For example in $Z$ take $I_1=2Z,\ I_2=2Z,\ I_3=3Z$: then $I_1+I_2+I_3=Z$, yet $I_1,I_2$ are not comaximal ($2Z+2Z=2Z$), and $Z/(I_1\cap I_2\cap I_3)=Z/(2Z\cap 3Z)=Z/6Z$ has $6$ elements while $\prod R/I_j$ has $2\cdot 2\cdot 3=12$ --- no isomorphism. Always verify $I_i+I_j=R$ for every pair.
\end{pitfall}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
$IJ$ is the ideal generated by products, not the set of single products. Elements of $IJ$ are finite sums $\sum a_kb_k$. Writing ``$IJ=\{ab\st a\in I,b\in J\}$'' is wrong in general (that set need not be closed under addition). For principal ideals in a commutative ring it does collapse: $\langle a\rangle\langle b\rangle=\langle ab\rangle$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Title: Idempotents and the product structure
Content:
\begin{remark}[Idempotents and the product structure]
When $R\cong R_1\times R_2$ the elements $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$ are orthogonal idempotents: $e_i^2=e_i$, $e_1 e_2=0$, $e_1+e_2=1$. Conversely such a pair in any commutative ring $R$ splits it as $R\cong Re_1\times Re_2$. In the CRT setting the idempotents are exactly the B\'ezout-built elements $e_j$ of the Method box (e.g. $9$ and $4$ in $Z/12Z$; $x+1$ and $x$ in $\F_2[x]/(x^2+x)$). Thus ``solve a congruence system'' and ``find the complementary idempotents'' are the same computation.
\end{remark}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $R$ be a ring with identity $1 \neq 0$. An element $e \in R$ is called an idempotent if $e^2 = e$. Assume $e$ is an idempotent in $R$ and $er = re$ for all $r \in R$. Prove that $Re$ and $R(1-e)$ are two-sided ideals of $R$ and that $R \cong Re \times R(1-e)$. Show that $e$ and $1-e$ are identities for the subrings $Re$ and $R(1-e)$ respectively.

\item Let $R$ be a finite Boolean ring with identity $1 \neq 0$ (cf. Exercise 15 of Section 1). Prove that $R \cong Z/2Z \times \cdots \times Z/2Z$. [Use the preceding exercise.]

\item Let $R$ and $S$ be rings with identities. Prove that every ideal of $R \times S$ is of the form $I \times J$ where $I$ is an ideal of $R$ and $J$ is an ideal of $S$.

\item Prove that if $R$ and $S$ are nonzero rings then $R \times S$ is never a field.

\item Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ be integers which are relatively prime in pairs: $(n_i, n_j) = 1$ for all $i \neq j$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that the Chinese Remainder Theorem implies that for any $a_1, \ldots, a_k \in Z$ there is a solution $x \in Z$ to the simultaneous congruences
\[
x \equiv a_1 \bmod n_1, \quad x \equiv a_2 \bmod n_2, \quad \ldots, \quad x \equiv a_k \bmod n_k
\]
and that the solution $x$ is unique mod $n = n_1 n_2 \cdots n_k$.
\item[(b)] Let $n_i' = n / n_i$ be the quotient of $n$ by $n_i$, which is relatively prime to $n_i$ by assumption. Let $t_i$ be the inverse of $n_i'$ mod $n_i$. Prove that the solution $x$ in (a) is given by
\[
x = a_1 t_1 n_1' + a_2 t_2 n_2' + \cdots + a_k t_k n_k' \bmod n.
\]
Note that the elements $t_i$ can be quickly found by the Euclidean Algorithm as described in Section~8.1 (writing $a n_i + b n_i' = (n_i, n_i') = 1$ gives $t_i = b$) and that these then quickly give the solutions to the system of congruences above for any choice of $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$.
\item[(c)] Solve the simultaneous system of congruences
\[
x \equiv 1 \bmod 8, \quad x \equiv 2 \bmod 25, \quad and \quad x \equiv 3 \bmod 81
\]
and the simultaneous system
\[
y \equiv 5 \bmod 8, \quad y \equiv 12 \bmod 25, \quad and \quad y \equiv 47 \bmod 81.
\]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_k(x)$ be polynomials with integer coefficients of the same degree $d$. Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ be integers which are relatively prime in pairs (i.e., $(n_i, n_j) = 1$ for all $i \neq j$). Use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to prove there exists a polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients and of degree $d$ with
\[
f(x) \equiv f_1(x) \bmod n_1, \quad f(x) \equiv f_2(x) \bmod n_2, \quad \ldots, \quad f(x) \equiv f_k(x) \bmod n_k,
\]
i.e., the coefficients of $f(x)$ agree with the coefficients of $f_i(x)$ mod $n_i$. Show that if all the $f_i(x)$ are monic, then $f(x)$ may also be chosen monic. [Apply the Chinese Remainder Theorem in $Z$ to each of the coefficients separately.]

\item Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $n$ dividing $m$. Prove that the natural surjective ring projection $Z/mZ \to Z/nZ$ is also surjective on the units: $(Z/mZ)^{\times} \to (Z/nZ)^{\times}$.

\item In the next four exercises $I$ is a nonempty index set with a partial order $\leq$, and for each $i \in I$ let $A_i$ be an additive abelian group; assume also that $I$ is a directed set: for every $i, j \in I$ there is some $k \in I$ with $i \leq k$ and $j \leq k$. Suppose for every pair of indices $i, j$ with $i \leq j$ there is a map $\rho_{ij} : A_i \to A_j$ such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i.] $\rho_{jk} \circ \rho_{ij} = \rho_{ik}$ whenever $i \leq j \leq k$, and
\item[ii.] $\rho_{ii} = 1$ for all $i \in I$.
\end{enumerate}
Let $B$ be the disjoint union of all the $A_i$. Define a relation $\sim$ on $B$ by
\[
a \sim b if and only if there exists k with i \leq k, \ j \leq k and \rho_{ik}(a) = \rho_{jk}(b),
\]
for $a \in A_i$ and $b \in A_j$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $B$. (The set of equivalence classes is called the direct or inductive limit of the directed system $\{A_i\}$, and is denoted $\varinjlim A_i$. In the remaining parts of this exercise let $A = \varinjlim A_i$.)
\item[(b)] Let $\overline{x}$ denote the class of $x$ in $A$ and define $\rho_i : A_i \to A$ by $\rho_i(a) = \overline{a}$. Show that if each $\rho_{ij}$ is injective, then so is $\rho_i$ for all $i$ (so we may then identify each $A_i$ as a subset of $A$).
\item[(c)] Assume all $\rho_{ij}$ are group homomorphisms. For $a \in A_i$, $b \in A_j$ show that the operation
\[
\overline{a} + \overline{b} = \overline{\rho_{ik}(a) + \rho_{jk}(b)}
\]
where $k$ is any index with $i, j \leq k$, is well defined and makes $A$ into an abelian group. Deduce that the maps $\rho_i$ in (b) are group homomorphisms from $A_i$ to $A$.
\item[(d)] Show that if all $A_i$ are commutative rings with 1 and all $\rho_{ij}$ are ring homomorphisms that send 1 to 1, then $A$ may likewise be given the structure of a commutative ring with 1 such that all $\rho_i$ are ring homomorphisms.
\item[(e)] Under the hypotheses in (c) prove that the direct limit has the following universal property: if $C$ is any abelian group and $\varphi_i : A_i \to C$ are group homomorphisms such that $\varphi_i = \varphi_j \circ \rho_{ij}$ whenever $i \leq j$, then there is a unique group homomorphism $\varphi : A \to C$ such that $\varphi \circ \rho_i = \varphi_i$ for all $i$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I$ be the collection of open intervals $U = (a, b)$ on the real line containing a fixed real number $p$. Order these by reverse inclusion: $U \leq V$ if $V \subseteq U$ (note that $I$ is a directed set). For each $U$ let $A_U$ be the ring of continuous real valued functions on $U$.

For $V \subseteq U$ define the restriction maps $\rho_{UV} : A_U \to A_V$ by $f \mapsto f|_V$, the usual restriction of a function on $U$ to the smaller set $V$ (which is easily seen to be a ring homomorphism). Let $A = \varinjlim A_U$ be the direct limit. In the notation of the preceding exercise, show that the maps $\rho_U : A_U \to A$ are not injective but are all surjective ($A$ is called the ring of germs of continuous functions at $p$).

\item We now develop the notion of inverse limits; continue to assume $I$ is a partially ordered set (but not necessarily directed), and $A_i$ is a group for all $i \in I$. Suppose for every pair of indices $i, j$ with $i \leq j$ there is a map $\mu_{ji} : A_j \to A_i$ such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i.] $\mu_{ji} \circ \mu_{kj} = \mu_{ki}$ whenever $i \leq j \leq k$, and
\item[ii.] $\mu_{ii} = 1$ for all $i \in I$.
\end{enumerate}
Let $P$ be the subset of elements $(a_i)_{i \in I}$ in the direct product $\prod_{i \in I} A_i$ such that $\mu_{ji}(a_j) = a_i$ whenever $i \leq j$ (here again $i, j \in I$). The set $P$ is called the inverse or projective limit of the system $\{A_i\}$, and is denoted $\varprojlim A_i$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Assume all $\mu_{ji}$ are group homomorphisms. Show that $P$ is a subgroup of the direct product group (cf. Exercise 15, Section 5.1).
\item[(b)] Assume the hypotheses in (a), and let $I = Z^+$ (usual ordering). For each $i \in I$ let $\mu_i : P \to A_i$ be the projection of $P$ onto its $i$th component. Show that if each $\mu_{ji}$ is surjective, then so is $\mu_i$ for all $i$ (so each $A_i$ is a quotient group of $P$).
\item[(c)] Show that if all $A_i$ are commutative rings with 1 and all $\mu_{ji}$ are ring homomorphisms that send 1 to 1, then $P$ may likewise be given the structure of a commutative ring with 1 such that all $\mu_i$ are ring homomorphisms.
\item[(d)] Under the hypotheses in (a) prove that the inverse limit has the following universal property: if $D$ is any group and $\pi_i : D \to A_i$ are group homomorphisms such that $\pi_i = \mu_{ji} \circ \pi_j$ whenever $i \leq j$, then there is a unique homomorphism $\pi : D \to P$ such that $\mu_i \circ \pi = \pi_i$ for all $i$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $I = Z^+$, let $A_i = Z/p^iZ$ and let $\mu_{ji}$ be the natural projection maps $\mu_{ji} : a \pmod{p^j} \mapsto a \pmod{p^i}$. The inverse limit $\varprojlim Z/p^iZ$ is called the ring of $p$-adic integers, and is denoted by $Z_p$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that every element of $Z_p$ may be written uniquely as an infinite formal sum $b_0 + b_1 p + b_2 p^2 + b_3 p^3 + \cdots$ with each $b_i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$. Describe the rules for adding and multiplying such formal sums corresponding to addition and multiplication in the ring $Z_p$. [Write a least residue in each $Z/p^iZ$ in its base $p$ expansion and then describe the maps $\mu_{ji}$.] (Note in particular that $Z_p$ is uncountable.)
\item[(b)] Prove that $Z_p$ is an integral domain that contains a copy of the integers.
\item[(c)] Prove that $b_0 + b_1 p + b_2 p^2 + b_3 p^3 + \cdots$ as in (a) is a unit in $Z_p$ if and only if $b_0 \neq 0$.
\item[(d)] Prove that $p Z_p$ is the unique maximal ideal of $Z_p$ and $Z_p / p Z_p \cong Z/pZ$ (where $p = 0 + 1p + 0p^2 + 0p^3 + \cdots$). Prove that every nonzero ideal of $Z_p$ is of the form $p^n Z_p$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
\item[(e)] Show that if $a_1 \neq 0 \pmod{p}$ then there is an element $a = (a_i)$ in the inverse limit $Z_p$ satisfying $a_i^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^i}$ and $\mu_{j1}(a_j) = a_1$ for all $j$. Deduce that $Z_p$ contains $p-1$ distinct $(p-1)^{st}$ roots of 1.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. State precisely what it means for two ideals $I,J\subseteq R$ to be comaximal (coprime), and show that $I+J=R$ holds iff there exist $x\in I$, $y\in J$ with $x+y=1$.

\item In $Z$, decide which of the following pairs of ideals are comaximal: $(\langle 6\rangle,\langle 35\rangle)$, $(\langle 12\rangle,\langle 18\rangle)$, $(\langle 8\rangle,\langle 15\rangle)$, $(\langle 10\rangle,\langle 25\rangle)$. Justify each answer.

\item Use the CRT to exhibit the ring isomorphism $Z/(60)Z\cong Z/(4)Z\timesZ/(3)Z\timesZ/(5)Z$ explicitly: give the image of the generator $\overline{1}$ and find the element of $Z/(60)Z$ corresponding to the triple $(\overline{3},\overline{2},\overline{4})$.

\item Solve the simultaneous congruences
\[ x\equiv 2 \pmod{5},\qquad x\equiv 3\pmod{7},\qquad x\equiv 1\pmod{8} \]
and write the complete solution set as a residue class mod $280$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and let $I_1,\dots,I_k$ be pairwise comaximal ideals. Prove that $I_1\cap\dots\cap I_k=I_1 I_2\cdots I_k$.

\item Determine the number of units in $Z/(72)Z$ by first writing $Z/(72)Z$ as a product of rings via the CRT, then computing the unit group of each factor.

\item In the polynomial ring $\F_2[x]$, the polynomials $x^2+x+1$ and $x^3+x+1$ are irreducible and distinct. State the ring isomorphism the CRT gives for $\F_2[x]/\langle (x^2+x+1)(x^3+x+1)\rangle$ and identify each factor as a field of how many elements.

\item Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Prove directly from the CRT isomorphism $Z/(mn)Z\congZ/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z$ that the Euler $\varphi$-function is multiplicative: $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$.

\item Give an example of a commutative ring $R$ with $1$ and two ideals $I,J$ such that the natural map $R/(I\cap J)\to R/I\times R/J$ is injective but not surjective. (Take $R=Z$ and a non-comaximal pair.)

\item Let $R=Z[x]$. Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and let $I,J$ be comaximal ideals. Prove that $I^a$ and $J^b$ are comaximal for all positive integers $a,b$.

\item (Idempotents from the CRT.) Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and suppose $R\cong R_1\times R_2$ with $R_1$ and $R_2$ nonzero. Show that $R$ contains a nontrivial idempotent $e$ (i.e. $e^2=e$, $e\neq 0,1$), and conversely that a nontrivial idempotent $e\in R$ yields a decomposition $R\cong Re\times R(1-e)$ as rings, where $Re$ and $R(1-e)$ are rings with identities $e$ and $1-e$ respectively.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ in which $I_1,\dots,I_k$ are pairwise comaximal. Prove the surjectivity half of the CRT directly: construct, for each $i$, an element $e_i\in R$ with $e_i\equiv 1\pmod{I_i}$ and $e_i\equiv 0\pmod{I_j}$ for $j\neq i$, and use the $e_i$ to solve any prescribed system of congruences.

\item Show that $Z[i]/\langle 1+3i\rangle$ is isomorphic to $Z/(10)Z$. (Hint: $\langle 1+3i\rangle$ has norm $10$; relate $Z[i]/\langle 1+3i\rangle$ to $Z[i]/\langle 2\rangle$ and $Z[i]/\langle 5\rangle$ via comaximality of the relevant ideals, or reduce the relation $1+3i=0$.)

\item Let $f(x)\in\F_p[x]$ factor as $f=g_1^{a_1}\cdots g_r^{a_r}$ into distinct monic irreducibles. Prove $\F_p[x]/\langle f\rangle\cong\prod_{i=1}^r \F_p[x]/\langle g_i^{a_i}\rangle$, and conclude that $\F_p[x]/\langle f\rangle$ is a product of fields iff $f$ is squarefree (all $a_i=1$).

\item (Failure without comaximality.) Give ideals $I,J$ in a commutative ring $R$ with $1$ for which $IJ\subsetneq I\cap J$ strictly, and verify that the natural surjection $R/IJ\to R/(I\cap J)$ has nonzero kernel. Use $R=Z$, $I=J=\langle 2\rangle$.

\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $I,J$ comaximal ideals. Consider the map $\varphi\colon R\to R/I\times R/J$, $r\mapsto(r+I,\,r+J)$. Fill in the dashed arrow making the diagram commute, and state which theorem identifies it as an isomorphism:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & R/I\times R/J \\
R/(I\cap J) \arrow[ur, dashed, "\overline{\varphi}"', "\cong"] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
Prove the dashed map is well defined, injective (using $\ker\varphi=I\cap J$), and surjective (using $I+J=R$).

\item For $n=mk$ with $\gcd(m,k)=1$, draw and justify the commutative triangle exhibiting the CRT isomorphism for $Z/(n)Z$. Label the top arrow $1\mapsto(\overline{1},\overline{1})$ and explain why the top map and the vertical reduction map are ring homomorphisms:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
Z \arrow[r] \arrow[d, two heads] & Z/(m)Z\timesZ/(k)Z \\
Z/(n)Z \arrow[ur, dashed, "\cong"'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item (Universal property of $R[x]$.) Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $S$ be a commutative $R$-algebra via $\psi\colon R\to S$, and fix $s\in S$. Show there is a unique ring homomorphism $\Phi\colon R[x]\to S$ extending $\psi$ with $\Phi(x)=s$, by completing the diagram and proving uniqueness:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\psi"'] & R[x] \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& S
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then describe $\ker\Phi$ when $R=S=Z$ and $s=2$.

\item (Universal property of fractions.) Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $\Frac(R)$, and let $f\colon R\to F$ be an injective ring homomorphism into a field $F$. Prove there is a unique $\bar f$ making the triangle commute, and explain why injectivity of $f$ is needed:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "f"'] & \Frac(R) \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\bar f"] \\
& F
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a surjective ring homomorphism of commutative rings with $1$. Using the First Isomorphism Theorem for rings, complete the factorization and identify $\overline{\varphi}$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, two heads, "\pi"'] & S \\
R/\ker\varphi \arrow[ur, dashed, "\overline{\varphi}"', "\cong"] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
Apply this with $R=Z[x]$, $\varphi$ evaluation at $i\inC$ landing in $Z[i]$, to identify $\ker\varphi$ and the resulting isomorphism.

\end{exers}

\item [DF 7.1.12] Prove that any subring of a field which contains the identity is an integral domain.
\item [DF 7.1.15] Prove that every Boolean ring (with $a^2 = a$ for all $a$) is commutative.
\item [DF 7.1.18] Prove that $\{(r,r) \mid r\in R\}$ is a subring of $R\times R$.

\item [DF 7.2.9] For $\alpha = r + r^2 - 2s$, $\beta = -3r^2 + rs$ in $Z D_8$, compute $\beta\alpha$, $\alpha^2$, $\alpha\beta - \beta\alpha$, $\beta\alpha\beta$.
\item [DF 7.2.10] For $\alpha,\beta\inZ S_3$ given explicitly, compute $\alpha+\beta$, $2\alpha-3\beta$, $\alpha\beta$, $\beta\alpha$, $\alpha^2$.
\item [DF 7.2.11] Repeat the preceding $Z S_3$ computation with coefficients in $Z/(3)Z$.
\item [DF 7.3.1] Prove that the rings $2Z$ and $3Z$ are not isomorphic.
\item [DF 7.3.2] Prove that the rings $Z[x]$ and $Q[x]$ are not isomorphic.
\item [DF 7.3.3] Find all homomorphic images of $Z$.
\item [DF 7.3.4] Find all ring homomorphisms from $Z$ to $Z/30Z$, describing each kernel and image.
\item [DF 7.3.6] Decide which of the maps $\Mat_2(Z)\toZ$ (the $1,1$ entry, the trace, the determinant) are ring homomorphisms.
\item [DF 7.3.8] Decide which of $\{(a,a)\}$, $\{(2a,2b)\}$, $\{(2a,0)\}$, $\{(a,-a)\}$ are ideals of $Z\timesZ$.
\item [DF 7.3.13] Prove that $\Mat_2(R)$ contains a subring isomorphic to $C$.
\item [DF 7.4.4] Prove that a commutative ring $R$ is a field if and only if $0$ is a maximal ideal.
\item [DF 7.4.8] In an integral domain $R$, prove $(a) = (b)$ if and only if $a = ub$ for some unit $u$.
\item [DF 7.4.15] For $E=\F_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$, show $\overline E$ has four elements and write its addition and multiplication tables, deducing it is a field.
\item [DF 7.4.16] In $Z[x]/(x^4-16)$, reduce $7x^{13}-11x^9+5x^5-2x^3+3$ to degree $\le 3$, and show $\overline{x-2},\overline{x+2}$ are zero divisors.
\item [DF 7.5.4] Prove that any subfield of $R$ must contain $Q$.

\item [Artin 1.1] Prove that $7+\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2}$ are algebraic numbers.
\item [Artin 1.2] Prove that for $n\neq 0$, $\cos(2\pi/n)$ is an algebraic number.
\item [Artin 1.6] Decide whether $S$ is a subring of $R$: (a) $S$ the rationals $a/b$ with $3\nmid b$, $R=Q$; (b) $S$ integer combinations of $\{1,\cos nt,\sin nt\}$, $R$ the real functions of $t$.
\item [Artin 1.8] Determine the units in $Z/12Z$, $Z/8Z$, and $Z/nZ$.
\item [Artin 4.3] Identify the rings $Z[x]/(x^2-3,\,2x+4)$, $Z[i]/(2+i)$, $Z[x]/(6,\,2x-1)$, $Z[x]/(2x^2-4,\,4x-5)$, $Z[x]/(x^2+3,\,5)$.
\item [Artin 5.1] Let $\alpha$ be the residue of $x$ in $R=Z[x]/(x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1)$; express $(\alpha^3+\alpha^2+\alpha)(\alpha^5+1)$ in the basis $(1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\alpha^3)$.
\item [Artin 5.3] Describe the ring obtained from $Z/12Z$ by adjoining an inverse of $2$.
\item [Artin 6.2] Is $Z/(6)\cong Z/(2)\timesZ/(3)$?

aximal.
\item [DF 7.4.24] Prove every finitely generated ideal in a Boolean ring is principal.
\item [DF 7.4.26] Prove a prime ideal of a commutative ring contains every nilpotent, so the nilradical lies in the intersection of all primes.
\item [DF 7.4.27] Prove that if $a$ is nilpotent then $1-ab$ is a unit for all $b$ (commutative $R$).
\item [DF 7.4.30] For an ideal $I$ of commutative $R$, prove $\operatorname{rad} I$ is an ideal containing $I$ and $(\operatorname{rad} I)/I = N(R/I)$.
\item [DF 7.4.31] Prove every prime ideal is a radical ideal, and, for $n>1$, $(n)$ is radical in $Z$ iff $n$ is squarefree.
\item [DF 7.4.1] In $\Mat_n(R)$, prove $L_j = \Mat_n(R)E_{ij}$ for the column left ideal $L_j$ (any $i$).
\item [DF 7.4.2] Prove the augmentation ideal of $RG$ ($R$ commutative) is generated by $\{g-1\}$, and by $\sigma-1$ when $G=\langle \sigma\rangle$ is cyclic.
\item [DF 7.4.3] For a $p$-group $G$ over $\F_p$, prove the nilradical of $\F_p G$ is the augmentation ideal; and for finite $G$ with $R$ commutative, prove $r(g_1+\cdots+g_n)=0$ for every $r$ in the augmentation ideal.
\item [DF 7.6.1] For a central idempotent $e$, prove $Re$ and $R(1-e)$ are ideals with $R\cong Re\times R(1-e)$, and identify their unities.
\item [DF 7.6.3] Prove every ideal of $R\times S$ ($R,S$ with identity) has the form $I\times J$.
\item [DF 7.6.4] Prove that if $R,S$ are nonzero rings then $R\times S$ is never a field.
\item [DF 7.6.5] Solve the simultaneous congruences $x\equiv 1\ (8)$, $x\equiv 2\ (25)$, $x\equiv 3\ (81)$ (and a second system) via CRT, including the explicit $t_i n_i'$ formula.
\item [DF 7.6.7] For $n\mid m$, prove the projection $Z/mZ\toZ/nZ$ is surjective on units.

\item [Artin 1.3] For $\alpha=\sqrt{2}$, $\beta=\sqrt[3]{2}$, $\gamma=\alpha+\beta$, decide whether $Q[\alpha,\beta]=Q[\gamma]$ and whether $Z[\alpha,\beta]=Z[\gamma]$.
\item [Artin 1.7] Decide whether each structure is a ring; if not, say which axioms hold and fail: (a) subsets of $U$ under symmetric difference and intersection, (b) continuous $f:R\toR$ under $+$ and composition.
\item [Artin 2.1] For which positive integers $n$ does $x^2+x+1$ divide $x^4+3x^3+x^2+7x+5$ in $(Z/nZ)[x]$?
\item [Artin 3.1] Prove that an ideal of a ring $R$ is a subgroup of the additive group $R^{+}$.
\item [Artin 3.2] Prove that every nonzero ideal of the Gaussian integers contains a nonzero integer.
\item [Artin 3.3] Find generators for the kernels of the evaluation maps $R[x,y]\toR$ at $(0,0)$, $R[x]\toC$ at $2+i$, and $Z[x]\toR$ at $1+\sqrt{2}$.
\item [Artin 3.7] Determine the automorphisms of the polynomial ring $Z[x]$.
\item [Artin 3.8] Let $R$ have prime characteristic $p$; prove $x\mapsto x^p$ is a ring homomorphism (the Frobenius map).
\item [Artin 3.9] Prove that if $x$ is nilpotent then $1+x$ is a unit; and if $\operatorname{char} R=p>0$ and $a$ is nilpotent, then $1+a$ is unipotent.
\item [Artin 3.10] Determine all ideals of the formal power series ring $F[[t]]$ over a field $F$.
\item [Artin 3.12] For ideals $I,J$, prove $I+J=\{x+y\mid x\in I,\ y\in J\}$ is an ideal.
\item [Artin 3.13] Prove $I\cap J$ is an ideal; show $\{xy\}$ need not be, but finite sums $\sum x_\nu y_\nu$ form the product ideal $IJ$; relate $IJ$ and $I\cap J$.
\item [Artin 4.1] Apply the Correspondence Theorem to $Z[x]\toZ$, $x\mapsto 1$, describing the ideals of $Z[x]$ it identifies.
\item [Artin 4.2] What does the Correspondence Theorem say about ideals of $Z[x]$ containing $x^2+1$?
\item [Artin 4.4] Are the rings $Z[x]/(x^2+7)$ and $Z[x]/(2x^2+7)$ isomorphic?
\item [Artin 5.2] Adjoining $\alpha$ to $R$ with the relation $\alpha=a$ for $a\in R$; prove the result is isomorphic to $R$.
\item [Artin 5.5] Are there fields $F$ with $F[x]/(x^2)\cong F[x]/(x^2-1)$?
\item [Artin 6.1] For $\varphi:R[x]\toC\timesC$, $\varphi(x)=(1,i)$, $\varphi(r)=(r,r)$, determine the kernel and image.
\item [Artin 6.3] Classify rings of order $10$.
\item [Artin 7.2] Prove the polynomial ring $R[x]$ over a domain $R$ is a domain, and identify its units.
\item [Artin 7.3] Is there a domain containing exactly $15$ elements?
\item [Artin 7.5] Given a multiplicative set $S$ in a domain $R$, show the equivalence classes of $S$-fractions form a ring.
\item [Artin 8.3] Prove $\F_2[x]/(x^3+x+1)$ is a field but $\F_3[x]/(x^3+x+1)$ is not.
\item [Artin M.1] Prove or disprove: if $a^2=a$ for every $a$ in a nonzero ring $R$, then $R$ has characteristic $2$.

\item [Fraleigh 22.21] Give a homomorphism $\varphi:R\to R'$ of rings with unity with $\varphi(1)\neq 0'$ and $\varphi(1)\neq 1'$, or explain.
\item [Fraleigh 22.22] Is $\det:\Mat_n(R)\toR$ a ring homomorphism?

\item [DF 7.1.26] For a discrete valuation $\nu$ on $K$, prove the valuation ring $R$ is a subring with $1$, that $x$ or $x^{-1}$ lies in $R$ for $x\neq 0$, and that $x$ is a unit iff $\nu(x)=0$.

\item [DF 7.1.29] For $R=\operatorname{End}(A^{+})$ of a commutative ring with $1$, prove these operations make $R$ a ring with identity whose units are the group automorphisms of $A$.

\item [DF 7.2.13] For a conjugacy class $\mathcal K$ in finite $G$, prove $K=\sum_i k_i$ is central in $RG$, and that the class sums form a basis of the center of $RG$.

\item [DF 7.3.21] Prove every two-sided ideal of $\Mat_n(R)$ equals $\Mat_n(J)$ for some two-sided ideal $J$ of $R$.
\item [DF 7.3.23] For $S\sgr R$ and ideal $I$ with $S\cap I=0$, prove $\overline S\cong S$ in $R/I$.
\item [DF 7.3.26] Prove the $Z\to R$ characteristic map is a homomorphism with kernel $nZ$; find $\operatorname{char}$ of $Q,Z[x],(Z/nZ)[x]$; prove $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p$ when $R$ is commutative of prime characteristic $p$.
\item [DF 7.3.28] Prove an integral domain has characteristic $0$ or a prime.
\item [DF 7.3.30] Prove that in a commutative ring $N(R/N(R))=0$.
\item [DF 7.3.33] For $p(x)\in R[x]$ ($R$ commutative): prove $p$ is a unit iff $a_0$ is a unit and $a_1,\dots,a_n$ are nilpotent, and $p$ is nilpotent iff all $a_i$ are nilpotent.
\item [DF 7.4.13] For $\varphi:R\to S$ of commutative rings: prove $\varphi^{-1}(P)$ is prime or all of $R$, and $\varphi^{-1}(M)$ is maximal when $\varphi$ is surjective, with a counterexample otherwise.
\item [DF 7.4.14] For commutative $R$ and monic $f\in R[x]$ of degree $n$: prove every class in $R[x]/(f)$ has a unique degree-$<n$ representative; if $f=ab$ with $\deg a,\deg b<n$ then $\overline a$ is a zero divisor; handle the nilpotent cases $f=x^n-a$ and $f=x^p-a$ over $\F_p$.
\item [DF 7.4.15] For $E=\F_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$: prove $\overline E$ has $4$ elements, its additive group is the Klein four-group, and $\units{\overline E}$ is cyclic of order $3$, so $\overline E$ is a field.
\item [DF 7.4.18] For a domain $R$, prove $(x)$ is prime in $R[[x]]$, and maximal iff $R$ is a field.
