Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Euclidean domains
Type: prose
Content:
We are at the bottom of the refinement ladder of integral domains. The next three
sections strengthen ``integral domain'' in stages. Section 8.1 isolates the strongest
useful hypothesis: a domain equipped with a division algorithm. Everything good
about $Z$ and $\F[x]$ -- a working Euclidean algorithm, gcds as linear combinations,
every ideal principal -- flows from this one axiom.

\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
ED \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & PID \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & UFD \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & domain
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is a class of integral domains. From left to right:
 $ED$ = Euclidean domains (equipped with a norm admitting a Division Algorithm);
 $PID$ = principal ideal domains (every ideal is principal);
 $UFD$ = unique factorization domains (every nonzero nonunit factors uniquely into
 irreducibles up to order and units); $domain$ = arbitrary integral domains
 (nonzero, no zero divisors). These are nested classes of increasing generality.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each double arrow $\Rightarrow$ means ``every ring in the class on the
 left belongs to the class on the right.'' They are logical implications, not ring
 homomorphisms. There is no formula; the arrow records a strict containment of classes.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is a linear chain, not a square, so there is no commutativity
 condition. The content is: $ED\RightarrowPID\RightarrowUFD\Rightarrow
 domain$, and all implications are strict (none reverses).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $ED\RightarrowPID$: the Division Algorithm forces every
 ideal to be generated by the element of minimal norm (proved in this section).
 $PID\RightarrowUFD$: in a PID every irreducible is prime (an irreducible
 generates a maximal ideal, and maximal ideals are prime), giving unique factorization. $UFD\Rightarrowdomain$: the
 definition of UFD already assumes the ring is an integral domain.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} Placed at the very opening of Section 8.1, the chain orients
 the entire chapter. Section 8.1 proves the leftmost implication; Sections 8.2--8.3 fill
 in the rest and supply counterexamples showing each arrow is strict.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $Z$ is an ED ($\Nm(n)=|n|$), hence a PID (every ideal $nZ$), hence
 a UFD (prime factorization), hence an integral domain. $Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID
 (since $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is not principal), showing UFD $\not\Rightarrow$ PID.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read $\Rightarrow$ as an isomorphism or a ring map.
 These arrows say nothing about maps between individual rings; they record class
 containments. Also, the diagram does not assert $domain\RightarrowUFD$;
 that arrow is absent on purpose.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the four principal classes of integral
 domains form a strict left-to-right hierarchy, and Section 8.1 focuses on Euclidean
 domains because they sit at the strongest (leftmost) rung.
\end{dgx}

Title: Norm
Content:
\begin{definition}[Norm]
Let $R$ be an integral domain. A norm on $R$ is any function
$\Nm\colon R\toZ_{\ge0}$ with $\Nm(0)=0$. The norm is positive if in addition
$\Nm(a)>0$ for all $a\neq0$. (No multiplicativity or other property is assumed; a norm is
just a way to measure ``size'' by a nonnegative integer.)
\end{definition}

Title: Euclidean domain
Content:
\begin{definition}[Euclidean domain]
An integral domain $R$ is a Euclidean domain (ED) if there is a norm $\Nm$ on $R$
admitting a Division Algorithm: for every $a,b\in R$ with $b\neq0$ there exist
$q,r\in R$ with
\[
a = qb + r,\qquad where r=0 \ or \ \Nm(r)<\Nm(b).
\]
We call $q$ the quotient and $r$ the remainder. Uniqueness of $q,r$ is
not required.
\end{definition}

Title: Flagship examples
Content:
\begin{definition}[Flagship examples]
Each of the following is a Euclidean domain.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $Z$, with $\Nm(n)=|n|$. Division with remainder is grade-school division.
\item[(b)] Any field $\F$, with $\Nm(a)=0$ for all $a$ (or $\Nm(a)=1$ for $a\neq0$): for
$b\neq0$ take $q=ab^{-1}$, $r=0$. Fields are (degenerately) Euclidean.
\item[(c)] $\F[x]$ for a field $\F$, with $\Nm(f)=\deg f$ (and $\Nm(0)=0$). This is
polynomial long division; it works precisely because the leading coefficient of $b$ is a
unit. (Theorem~ [REF:thm:fxeuclid@c8] below.)
\item[(d)] $Z[i]=\{a+bi : a,b\inZ\}$, the Gaussian integers, with
$\Nm(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$. Division is ``divide in $C$, then round to the nearest lattice
point'' (Theorem~ [REF:thm:zieuclid@c8] below).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Has a norm'' is not the same as ``is Euclidean.'' Every integral domain carries
the trivial norm $\Nm(a)=0$. Being Euclidean is about the existence of a norm for which
the Division Algorithm holds. Conversely a ring can fail to be Euclidean for
every possible norm (Section 8.2: $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2]$); the tool for proving
such a thing is the universal side divisor, below.
\end{pitfall}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > The Euclidean algorithm and Bezout
Type: theorem
Title: Euclidean Algorithm
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Euclidean Algorithm]
Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain and $a,b\in R$ with $b\neq0$. Apply the Division Algorithm
repeatedly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a &= q_0 b + r_0, & \Nm(r_0)&<\Nm(b),\\
b &= q_1 r_0 + r_1, & \Nm(r_1)&<\Nm(r_0),\\
r_0 &= q_2 r_1 + r_2, & \Nm(r_2)&<\Nm(r_1),\\
&\ \vdots\\
r_{k-2} &= q_k r_{k-1} + r_k, & \Nm(r_k)&<\Nm(r_{k-1}),\\
r_{k-1} &= q_{k+1} r_k + 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remainders have strictly decreasing nonnegative-integer norms, so the process
terminates with a zero remainder. The last nonzero remainder $r_k$ is a gcd of $a$ and $b$. (If already $r_0=0$, then
$b\mid a$ and $b$ itself is a gcd.)
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-c5adb0968b6e7c38bc7e
Content:
\begin{proof}
Termination: $\Nm(r_0)>\Nm(r_1)>\cdots\ge0$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers, hence finite. Let $r_k$ be the last nonzero remainder. Reading the
last equation $r_{k-1}=q_{k+1}r_k$ gives $r_k\mid r_{k-1}$. Substituting upward,
$r_k\mid r_{k-2}=q_kr_{k-1}+r_k$, then $r_k\mid r_{k-3}$, $\dots$, and finally
$r_k\mid b$ and $r_k\mid a$. So $r_k$ is a common divisor. Conversely, if
$d'\mid a$ and $d'\mid b$, then reading the equations downward,
$d'\mid r_0=a-q_0b$, then $d'\mid r_1$, $\dots$, $d'\mid r_k$. Hence $r_k$ is a
greatest common divisor.
\end{proof}

Title: Bezout / $(a,b)=(d)$ in an ED
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Bezout / $(a,b)=(d)$ in an ED]
Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain and $a,b\in R$ not both zero, with gcd $d$. Then
$\langle d\rangle=\langle a,b\rangle$ as ideals; equivalently there exist $x,y\in R$ with
\[
d = ax + by .
\]
\end{theorem}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > The Euclidean algorithm and Bezout
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-6156e11f534a63766f38
Content:
\begin{proof}
Back-substitute the Euclidean Algorithm. From $r_k=r_{k-2}-q_kr_{k-1}$, and recursively
expressing each $r_j$ as an $R$-combination of $a,b$, we obtain $d=r_k=ax+by$ for some
$x,y\in R$. Thus $d\in\langle a,b\rangle$, so $\langle d\rangle\subseteq\langle a,b\rangle$. The reverse inclusion is
$d\mid a$ and $d\mid b$, i.e.\ $a,b\in\langle d\rangle$. Hence $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > The Euclidean algorithm and Bezout
Type: method
Title: Division / Euclidean / Bezout recipe
Content:
\begin{method}{Division / Euclidean / Bezout recipe}
Trigger. You are in $Z$, $\F[x]$, or $Z[i]$ (anything with a stated norm and
Division Algorithm) and you need to (a) divide with remainder, (b) compute a gcd, or
(c) write the gcd as a linear combination.
\begin{enumerate}
\item One division. To compute $q,r$ in $a=qb+r$:
 \begin{itemize}
 \item $Z$: $q=\lfloor a/b\rfloor$ (or nearest integer), $r=a-qb$.
 \item $\F[x]$: long division; cancel the leading term repeatedly until $\deg r<\deg b$.
 \item $Z[i]$: form $a/b=\frac{a\overline b}{\Nm(b)}\inQ(i)$, round each coordinate to
 the nearest integer to get $q$, set $r=a-qb$.
 \end{itemize}
\item gcd. Iterate: replace $(a,b)\mapsto(b,r)$ until $r=0$. The last nonzero
remainder is the gcd (unique up to a unit multiple).
\item Bezout. Solve each division equation for its remainder and back-substitute
from the bottom up, eliminating intermediate remainders, until only $a,b$ remain.
\item Check. Recompute $ax+by$ and confirm it equals $d$; confirm $d\mid a$
and $d\mid b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

embedding_text:

Type: example
Title: Euclidean algorithm in $Z$ with Bezout
Content:
\begin{wex}{Euclidean algorithm in $Z$ with Bezout}
Compute $\gcd(3220,2299)$ in $Z$ and write it as $3220x+2299y$.
\wrec This is $Z$ with $\Nm(n)=|n|$, an ED; the Euclidean Algorithm gives the gcd and
back-substitution gives Bezout.
\wsol
Divisions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
3220 &= 1\cdot 2299 + 921,\\
2299 &= 2\cdot 921 + 457,\\
921 &= 2\cdot 457 + 7,\\
457 &= 65\cdot 7 + 2,\\
7 &= 3\cdot 2 + 1,\\
2 &= 2\cdot 1 + 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Last nonzero remainder: $\gcd=1$, so $3220,2299$ are coprime. Back-substitute:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &= 7 - 3\cdot 2\\
 &= 7 - 3(457 - 65\cdot 7) = 196\cdot 7 - 3\cdot 457\\
 &= 196(921 - 2\cdot 457) - 3\cdot 457 = 196\cdot 921 - 395\cdot 457\\
 &= 196\cdot 921 - 395(2299 - 2\cdot 921) = 986\cdot 921 - 395\cdot 2299\\
 &= 986(3220 - 2299) - 395\cdot 2299 = 986\cdot 3220 - 1381\cdot 2299.
\end{aligned}
\]
Check. $986\cdot 3220 = 3{,}174{,}920$ and $1381\cdot 2299 = 3{,}174{,}919$, so
$986\cdot 3220 - 1381\cdot 2299 = 1$. Thus $x=986$, $y=-1381$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-coprime gcd in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-coprime gcd in $Z$}
Compute $\gcd(252,198)$ and a Bezout expression.
\wrec Same machine; here the gcd exceeds $1$, so it shows up as the last nonzero remainder
$>1$.
\wsol
\[
252 = 1\cdot 198 + 54,\qquad 198 = 3\cdot 54 + 36,\qquad 54 = 1\cdot 36 + 18,\qquad 36 = 2\cdot 18 + 0.
\]
So $\gcd(252,198)=18$. Back-substitute:
\[
18 = 54 - 36 = 54 - (198 - 3\cdot 54) = 4\cdot 54 - 198 = 4(252-198) - 198 = 4\cdot 252 - 5\cdot 198 .
\]
Check. $4\cdot 252 = 1008$, $5\cdot 198 = 990$, difference $18$. And
$252=18\cdot 14$, $198=18\cdot 11$, confirming $18\mid 252,198$.
\end{wex}

Title: {$\F[x]$ is Euclidean}
Label: thm:fxeuclid@c8
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$\F[x]$ is Euclidean}] 
If $\F$ is a field then $\F[x]$ with $\Nm(f)=\deg f$ is a Euclidean domain: for
$a,b\in\F[x]$ with $b\neq0$ there are unique $q,r$ with $a=qb+r$ and $r=0$ or
$\deg r<\deg b$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:fxeuclid@c8

title: {$\F[x]$ is Euclidean}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Division in $\F[x]$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-abdbcae70b7543687bf9
Content:
\begin{proof}
Existence by induction on $\deg a$. If $a=0$ or $\deg a<\deg b$, take $q=0$, $r=a$.
Otherwise let $a=\alpha x^n+\cdots$ and $b=\beta x^m+\cdots$ with $n\ge m$. Because $\F$ is
a field, $\beta^{-1}$ exists, so $a':=a-\alpha\beta^{-1}x^{n-m}b$ kills the leading term and
has $\deg a'<\deg a$. By induction $a'=q'b+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg b$; then
$a=(\alpha\beta^{-1}x^{n-m}+q')b+r$. Uniqueness: if $q_1b+r_1=q_2b+r_2$ then
$(q_1-q_2)b=r_2-r_1$; if $q_1\neq q_2$ the left side has degree $\ge\deg b$ while the right
has degree $<\deg b$, a contradiction. So $q_1=q_2$ and $r_1=r_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{pitfall}
The leading coefficient of $b$ must be a unit. Over $Z$ (not a field) you cannot
divide $x$ by $2x$ inside $Z[x]$ with a smaller-degree remainder, and indeed $Z[x]$ is
not a Euclidean domain (it is not even a PID, since $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is not principal).
The field hypothesis is what makes $\F[x]$ Euclidean.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: Long division in $Q[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Long division in $Q[x]$}
Divide $a=x^4-3x^3+2x^2+4x-1$ by $b=x^2-x+1$ in $Q[x]$.
\wrec $Q$ is a field, so $Q[x]$ is Euclidean with $\Nm=\deg$; perform long division until
the remainder has degree $<2$.
\wsol
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^4-3x^3+2x^2+4x-1 &= (x^2)(x^2-x+1) + (-2x^3+x^2+4x-1)\\
&= (x^2-2x)(x^2-x+1) + (-x^2+6x-1)\\
&= (x^2-2x-1)(x^2-x+1) + 5x.
\end{aligned}
\]
So $q=x^2-2x-1$ and $r=5x$, with $\deg r=1<2=\deg b$.
Check. $(x^2-2x-1)(x^2-x+1)=x^4-3x^3+2x^2-x-1$; adding $5x$ gives
$x^4-3x^3+2x^2+4x-1=a$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Division over a finite field $\F_2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Division over a finite field $\F_2$}
Divide $a=x^4+x^3+1$ by $b=x^2+x+1$ in $\F_2[x]$ (coefficients mod $2$).
\wrec $\F_2=Z/(2)Z$ is a field, so $\F_2[x]$ is Euclidean; reduce every coefficient mod $2$
as you go.
\wsol
Subtract (=\,add, in characteristic $2$) leading terms. First $(x^2)(x^2+x+1)=x^4+x^3+x^2$,
and $a$ minus this is $(x^4+x^3+1)-(x^4+x^3+x^2)=x^2+1$ (in $\F_2$, $-x^2=x^2$):
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^4+x^3+1 &= (x^2)(x^2+x+1) + (x^2+1)\\
&= (x^2+1)(x^2+x+1) + x.
\end{aligned}

cancel), and adding the remainder $x$ recovers $x^4+x^3+1$. So $q=x^2+1$, $r=x$,
$\deg r=1<2$. Check. $a-qb=x$, degree $1<2$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{gcd in $\F[x]$ via the Euclidean algorithm}
Compute $\gcd(x^3-1,\ x^2-1)$ in $Q[x]$ and express it as a combination.
\wrec Two polynomials over a field: iterate division. The (monic) last nonzero remainder is
the gcd.
\wsol
\[
x^3-1 = x\,(x^2-1) + (x-1),\qquad x^2-1 = (x+1)(x-1) + 0 .
\]
Last nonzero remainder $x-1$, so $\gcd=x-1$. Bezout from the first line:
\[
x-1 = (x^3-1) - x\,(x^2-1),
\]
i.e.\ the coefficients are $1$ and $-x$. Check. $x-1\mid x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ and
$x-1\mid x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {$Z[i]$ is Euclidean}
Label: thm:zieuclid@c8
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$Z[i]$ is Euclidean}] 
The Gaussian integers $Z[i]$ with $\Nm(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$ form a Euclidean domain. Concretely,
for $\alpha,\beta\inZ[i]$ with $\beta\neq0$ there exist $q,r\inZ[i]$ with
$\alpha=q\beta+r$ and $\Nm(r)\le\tfrac12\Nm(\beta)<\Nm(\beta)$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:zieuclid@c8

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Division in the Gaussian integers $Z[i]$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-e063ae449ae4a608465f
Content:
\begin{proof}
Compute the exact quotient in $Q(i)$:
$\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac{\alpha\overline\beta}{\Nm(\beta)}=s+ti$ with $s,t\inQ$. Pick
integers $m,n$ nearest to $s,t$, so $|s-m|\le\tfrac12$ and $|t-n|\le\tfrac12$, and set
$q=m+ni$, $r=\alpha-q\beta$. Then $\frac{r}{\beta}=(s-m)+(t-n)i$, so
\[
\Nm(r)=\Nm(\beta)\bigl((s-m)^2+(t-n)^2\bigr)\le \Nm(\beta)\bigl(\tfrac14+\tfrac14\bigr)
=\tfrac12\Nm(\beta)<\Nm(\beta).
\]
Since $r=\alpha-q\beta\inZ[i]$, this is a valid division step.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}
$\Nm$ on $Z[i]$ is multiplicative: $\Nm(\alpha\beta)=\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)$ (it is
$|\alpha|^2$). Consequently the units of $Z[i]$ are exactly the elements of norm $1$,
namely $\units{Z[i]}=\{\pm1,\pm i\}$, and $\beta\mid\alpha$ forces
$\Nm(\beta)\mid\Nm(\alpha)$ in $Z$ -- a powerful divisibility test.
\end{remark}

Content:
\begin{method}{Dividing in $Z[i]$ (round to nearest lattice point)}
Trigger. You must divide, gcd, or factor in $Z[i]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Multiply numerator and denominator by $\overline\beta$:
$\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}=\dfrac{\alpha\overline\beta}{\Nm(\beta)}=s+ti$.
\item Round: $m=\operatorname{round}(s)$, $n=\operatorname{round}(t)$; set $q=m+ni$.
\item Remainder $r=\alpha-q\beta$. It automatically satisfies $\Nm(r)<\Nm(\beta)$.
\item For a gcd, iterate $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(\beta,r)$. For factoring, use
multiplicativity: if $\Nm(\alpha)=p$ is a prime in $Z$, then $\alpha$ is irreducible in
$Z[i]$; factor $\Nm(\alpha)$ in $Z$ first to know what norms to look for.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: One division step in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{One division step in $Z[i]$}
Divide $\alpha=4+5i$ by $\beta=1+2i$.
\wrec $Z[i]$, $\Nm=a^2+b^2$: rationalize and round to the nearest Gaussian integer.
\wsol
$\Nm(\beta)=1^2+2^2=5$ and $\overline\beta=1-2i$, so
\[
\frac{4+5i}{1+2i}=\frac{(4+5i)(1-2i)}{5}=\frac{4-8i+5i+10}{5}=\frac{14-3i}{5}=2.8-0.6i.
\]
Round $2.8\to3$ and $-0.6\to-1$, so $q=3-i$. Then
\[
r=\alpha-q\beta=(4+5i)-(3-i)(1+2i)=(4+5i)-(3+6i-i+2)=(4+5i)-(5+5i)=-1.
\]
So $4+5i=(3-i)(1+2i)+(-1)$ with $\Nm(r)=1<5=\Nm(\beta)$.
Check. $(3-i)(1+2i)=5+5i$, and $5+5i-1=4+5i=\alpha$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Euclidean algorithm in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Euclidean algorithm in $Z[i]$}
Compute a gcd of $\alpha=11+3i$ and $\beta=1+8i$.
\wrec Iterate Gaussian division; the last nonzero remainder (up to a unit) is the gcd.
\wsol
Step 1. $\Nm(1+8i)=65$, $\dfrac{11+3i}{1+8i}=\dfrac{(11+3i)(1-8i)}{65}=\dfrac{35-85i}{65}
=0.54-1.31i$, round to $q=1-i$:
\[
r_0=(11+3i)-(1-i)(1+8i)=(11+3i)-(9+7i)=2-4i,\quad \Nm=20<65.
\]
Step 2. Divide $1+8i$ by $2-4i$: $\Nm(2-4i)=20$,
$\dfrac{(1+8i)(2+4i)}{20}=\dfrac{-30+20i}{20}=-1.5+i$, round to $q=-2+i$:
\[
r_1=(1+8i)-(-2+i)(2-4i)=(1+8i)-(0+10i)=1-2i,\quad \Nm=5<20.
\]
Step 3. Divide $2-4i$ by $1-2i$: $\dfrac{(2-4i)(1+2i)}{5}=\dfrac{10}{5}=2$, so $q=2$,
$r_2=(2-4i)-2(1-2i)=0$. The last nonzero remainder is $\gcd=1-2i$.
Check. $(1-2i)(1+5i)=11+3i$ and $(1-2i)(-3+2i)=1+8i$, so $1-2i$ divides both;
$\Nm(1-2i)=5$ divides $\Nm(11+3i)=130$ and $\Nm(1+8i)=65$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Factoring a Gaussian integer
Content:
\begin{wex}{Factoring a Gaussian integer}
Factor $\alpha=4+7i$ into irreducibles in $Z[i]$.
\wrec Multiplicativity of $\Nm$: factor $\Nm(\alpha)$ in $Z$, then split each rational
prime into Gaussian primes and match.
\wsol
$\Nm(4+7i)=4^2+7^2=65=5\cdot 13$. In $Z[i]$, $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ and $13=(3+2i)(3-2i)$, and each
factor has prime norm ($5$ resp.\ $13$), hence is irreducible. Since
$\Nm(\alpha)=5\cdot13$, $\alpha$ is a product of one norm-$5$ and one norm-$13$ irreducible.
Try $(2+i)(3+2i)=6+4i+3i-2=4+7i$. Hit.
\[
4+7i=(2+i)(3+2i),\qquad \Nm: 65 = 5\cdot 13.
\]
Check. $(2+i)(3+2i)=6+4i+3i+2i^2=6+7i-2=4+7i$. \checkmark Each factor has prime
norm so is irreducible; the factorization is complete (up to units $\pm1,\pm i$).
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A norm divisibility test
Content:
\begin{wex}{A norm divisibility test}
Show $1+2i$ does not divide $1+3i$ in $Z[i]$, but $1+2i$ does divide $5$.
\wrec $\beta\mid\alpha\Rightarrow\Nm(\beta)\mid\Nm(\alpha)$ in $Z$; if the norm
fails, divisibility fails. When the norm passes, finish by exact division.
\wsol
$\Nm(1+2i)=5$. For $1+3i$: $\Nm(1+3i)=10$, and $5\mid 10$, so the norm test is
inconclusive -- do the division:
$\dfrac{1+3i}{1+2i}=\dfrac{(1+3i)(1-2i)}{5}=\dfrac{7+i}{5}=1.4+0.2i\notinZ[i]$.
So $1+2i$ does not divide $1+3i$: the norm test passed but the quotient is not a
Gaussian integer. (Moral: a divisible norm is necessary, not sufficient.)
For $5$: $\dfrac{5}{1+2i}=\dfrac{5(1-2i)}{5}=1-2i\inZ[i]$, so $1+2i\mid5$ with
$5=(1+2i)(1-2i)$. Check. $(1+2i)(1-2i)=1+4=5$. \checkmark
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A norm divisibility test}
Show $1+2i$ does \emph{not} divide $1+3i$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, but $1+2i$ \emph{does} divide $5$.
\wrec $\beta\mid\alpha\Rightarrow\Nm(\beta)\mid\Nm(\alpha)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$; if the norm
fails, divisibility fails. When the norm passes, finish by exact division.
\wsol
$\Nm(1+2i)=5$. For $1+3i$: $\Nm(1+3i)=10$, and $5\mid 10$, so the norm test is
inconclusive -- do the division:
$\dfrac{1+3i}{1+2i}=\dfrac{(1+3i)(1-2i)}{5}=\dfrac{7+i}{5}=1.4+0.2i\notin\mathbb{Z}[i]$.
So $1+2i$ does \emph{not} divide $1+3i$: the norm test passed but the quotient is not a
Gaussian integer. (Moral: a divisible norm is necessary, not sufficient.)
For $5$: $\dfrac{5}{1+2i}=\dfrac{5(1-2i)}{5}=1-2i\in\mathbb{Z}[i]$, so $1+2i\mid5$ with
$5=(1+2i)(1-2i)$. \textit{Check.} $(1+2i)(1-2i)=1+4=5$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{proposition}[ED $\Rightarrow$ PID]
Every ideal in a Euclidean domain $R$ is principal. More precisely, if $I\neq(0)$ then
$I=\langle d\rangle$ where $d$ is any nonzero element of $I$ of minimal norm.
\end{proposition}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-d37749c5ce09bb7dcb55
Content:
\begin{proof}
The zero ideal is $(0)=\langle 0\rangle$. Let $I\neq(0)$. The set $\{\Nm(a):a\in I,\ a\neq0\}$ is a
nonempty subset of $Z_{\ge0}$, so by well-ordering it has a least element; choose $d\in I$,
$d\neq0$, achieving it, i.e.\ $\Nm(d)$ is minimal. Clearly $\langle d\rangle\subseteq I$. Conversely,
take any $a\in I$ and divide: $a=qd+r$ with $r=0$ or $\Nm(r)<\Nm(d)$. Now
$r=a-qd\in I$ (as $a,qd\in I$). If $r\neq0$ then $\Nm(r)<\Nm(d)$ contradicts the
minimality of $\Nm(d)$ among nonzero elements of $I$. Hence $r=0$, so $a=qd\in\langle d\rangle$.
Therefore $I\subseteq\langle d\rangle$, giving $I=\langle d\rangle$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: The inclusion is strict elsewhere
Content:
\begin{remark}[The inclusion is strict elsewhere]
This is exactly the ED $\Rightarrow$ PID arrow of the hierarchy. The remaining arrows
(PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD, and the strictness of every inclusion) are Sections 8.2--8.3. For
context: $Z[x]$ is a UFD that is not a PID (so UFD $\not\Rightarrow$ PID), and
$Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2]$ is a PID that is not Euclidean (so PID $\not\Rightarrow$
ED). The latter is proved using universal side divisors.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
ED \arrow[r, Rightarrow, "{Sec. 8.1}"] & PID \arrow[r, Rightarrow, "{Sec. 8.3}"] & UFD
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three classes of integral domains: $ED$ (Euclidean domains),
 $PID$ (principal ideal domains), $UFD$ (unique factorization domains).
 Unlike the opening diagram, this version omits the bare ``domain'' node and carries
 explicit reference labels, serving as a precise theorem-map.
\dgi{Arrows:} Two labeled double implications. The label ``Sec.\ 8.1'' on the first arrow
 points to this section, where it is proved that every ED is a PID, witnessed by the minimal-norm
 generator argument. The label ``Sec.\ 8.3'' on the second arrow refers to Section 8.3, where
 the PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD implication is established. Neither arrow represents a ring
 homomorphism; both are logical entailments between domain classes.
\dgi{What commutes:} Again a linear chain; the relevant statement is the transitivity
 $ED\RightarrowUFD$, which follows by composing the two labeled arrows.
 Neither implication reverses: $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID but not an ED;
 $Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Prop.\ 8.1 (proved just above): take $d\in I$ of minimal norm;
 the Division Algorithm forces every other element of $I$ to be a multiple of $d$, so
 $I=\langle d\rangle$. Section 8.2 then uses PID to get irreducible $\Leftrightarrow$
 prime, which yields unique factorization.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This annotated version of the opening diagram closes the
 remark that justifies why each arrow is strict. By attaching theorem numbers, it lets
 the reader immediately locate the proof of each step, making the chapter's logical
 structure self-documenting.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $Z[i]$ (Gaussian integers) is an ED (proved in this section via
 the rounding argument), hence a PID (Prop.\ 8.1), hence a UFD (Section 8.3). The chain
 is witnessed concretely: $\langle 11+3i, 1+8i\rangle = \langle 1-2i\rangle$ in $Z[i]$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Seeing ``Prop.\ 8.1'' on the first arrow, students sometimes think
 the proposition is the implication diagram. The diagram is a schematic summary;
 the proposition is the actual proof that every ideal of an ED has a minimal-norm
 generator. The diagram does not prove the result---it just records where it lives.

Type: example
Title: Reading off the generator from minimal norm in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading off the generator from minimal norm in $Z$}
Use the proposition to find a generator of $I=\langle 12,30\rangle\subseteqZ$.
\wrec $Z$ is Euclidean; the generator is the nonzero element of $I$ of least absolute
value, which the Euclidean algorithm produces as $\gcd$.
\wsol
$I=\langle 12,30\rangle=\{12s+30t:s,t\inZ\}$. The smallest positive element is $\gcd(12,30)$:
$30=2\cdot 12+6$, $12=2\cdot 6+0$, so $\gcd=6$ and $6=30-2\cdot 12\in I$. By the
proposition $I=\langle 6\rangle$. Check. $12=6\cdot 2$, $30=6\cdot 5\in\langle 6\rangle$, and
$6\in I$, so $\langle 12,30\rangle=\langle 6\rangle$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Principal ideal in $Q[x]$}
Show $I=\langle x^3-1,\ x^2-1\rangle\subseteqQ[x]$ is principal and find a generator.
\wrec $Q[x]$ is Euclidean ($\Nm=\deg$); the generator is the nonzero element of least
degree in $I$, i.e.\ the $\gcd$.
\wsol
From the earlier worked example $\gcd(x^3-1,x^2-1)=x-1$ and
$x-1=(x^3-1)-x(x^2-1)\in I$. Both generators lie in $\langle x-1\rangle$ since
$x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$ and $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$. Hence $I=\langle x-1\rangle$.
Check. $x-1\in I$ and $I\subseteq\langle x-1\rangle$, so equality. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A principal ideal in $Z[i]$}
Show $I=\langle 11+3i,\ 1+8i\rangle\subseteqZ[i]$ is principal and find a generator.
\wrec $Z[i]$ is Euclidean; the generator is a Gaussian gcd of the two elements.
\wsol
From the Gaussian Euclidean algorithm above, $\gcd(11+3i,1+8i)=1-2i$, with
$11+3i=(1-2i)(1+5i)$ and $1+8i=(1-2i)(-3+2i)$. Hence both generators lie in $\langle 1-2i\rangle$,

quotients $1+5i$ and $-3+2i$ confirm divisibility. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Universal side divisors: a non-Euclidean test
Type: definition
Title: Universal side divisor
Content:
\begin{definition}[Universal side divisor]
Let $R$ be an integral domain and $\tilde R=\units R\cup\{0\}$. A nonzero nonunit
$u\in R$ is a universal side divisor if for every $x\in R$ there is some
$z\in\tilde R$ with $u\mid (x-z)$ in $R$ -- i.e.\ $u$ divides $x$ ``up to a unit or
zero.'' Equivalently, $u$ divides $x-z$ for some $z$ that is $0$ or a unit.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Universal side divisors: a non-Euclidean test
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-97591a3a862c23d3cf0d
Content:
\begin{proof}
Choose $u$ a nonzero nonunit of minimal norm among all nonzero nonunits (such $u$
exists by well-ordering of norms; the set is nonempty as $R$ is not a field). For any
$x\in R$ divide: $x=qu+r$ with $r=0$ or $\Nm(r)<\Nm(u)$. If $r=0$ then $u\mid x$, take
$z=0$. If $r\neq0$ then $\Nm(r)<\Nm(u)$ forces $r$ to be a unit (by minimality of $\Nm(u)$
among nonzero nonunits, anything of strictly smaller positive norm is a unit). Then
$u\mid (x-r)$ with $r\in\units R$, so $z=r$ works. Hence $u$ is a universal side
divisor.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Euclidean Domains > Universal side divisors: a non-Euclidean test
Type: method
Title: Proving ``not Euclidean'' via side divisors
Content:
\begin{method}{Proving ``not Euclidean'' via side divisors}
Trigger. You suspect a domain $R$ (not a field) is not Euclidean and want a proof
that rules out all norms.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Identify $\units R$ (often just $\{\pm1\}$), so $\tilde R=\units R\cup\{0\}$ is small.
\item Find all candidate universal side divisors by applying the definition to one
well-chosen $x$: a universal side divisor $u$ divides $x-z$ for some $z\in\tilde R$, so it is a
nonunit divisor of one of these finitely many elements (e.g.\ for $x=2$ and $\tilde R=\{0,\pm1\}$:
a divisor of $2$ or $3$). Do not simply take the elements of smallest field norm: the norm in
the Proposition is an unknown Euclidean norm, not the field norm.
\item For each candidate $u$, exhibit an $x$ such that $u\nmid(x-z)$ for every
$z\in\tilde R$. This kills $u$.
\item If no universal side divisor exists, the contrapositive of the Proposition shows
$R$ is not Euclidean (for any norm).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
One shows $\units R=\{\pm1\}$, so $\tilde R=\{0,\pm1\}$. If $R$ were Euclidean it would have a
universal side divisor $u$. Taking $x=2$ in the definition, $u$ divides $2$, $1$ or $3$, and
$u\nmid 1$ since $u$ is not a unit. The field norm $\Nm(a+b\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2)=a^2+ab+5b^2$
never equals $2$ or $3$, so $2$ and $3$ are irreducible in $R$ and $u\in\{\pm2,\pm3\}$. But
neither $\pm2$ nor $\pm3$ is a universal side divisor: taking $x=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2$, one checks $u\nmid(x-z)$ for
$z\in\{0,1,-1\}$ in each case (the relevant norm equations have no solution in $R$). With no
universal side divisor, the Proposition forces $R$ non-Euclidean. That $R$ is nonetheless a
PID is shown by a Dedekind--Hasse style norm argument; the details are in Section 8.2.
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Not Euclidean'' is a strong claim: it must hold for every possible norm, not just
the obvious field norm. That is exactly why the universal side divisor (a norm-free
condition) is the right tool -- ruling out one norm proves nothing, but the absence of a
universal side divisor rules out all norms at once.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: $Z$ has a universal side divisor
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z$ has a universal side divisor}
Exhibit a universal side divisor in $Z$.
\wrec $Z$ is a non-field ED, so one must exist; the Proposition says to take a nonzero
nonunit of minimal norm.
\wsol
Units are $\pm1$, so $\tildeZ=\{0,1,-1\}$. The nonzero nonunits of least $|\cdot|$ are
$\pm2$; take $u=2$. For any $x\inZ$, divide by $2$: the remainder is $0$ or $1$, i.e.\
$x\equiv 0$ or $1\pmod 2$. If $x$ even, $2\mid(x-0)$; if $x$ odd, $2\mid(x-1)$.
Since $0,1\in\tildeZ$, $u=2$ is a universal side divisor.
Check. Every residue mod $2$ is $0$ or a unit ($1$), exactly as the Proposition
predicts. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}$ has a universal side divisor}
Exhibit a universal side divisor in $\mathbb{Z}$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ is a non-field ED, so one must exist; the Proposition says to take a nonzero
nonunit of minimal norm.
\wsol
Units are $\pm1$, so $\tilde\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1,-1\}$. The nonzero nonunits of least $|\cdot|$ are
$\pm2$; take $u=2$. For any $x\in\mathbb{Z}$, divide by $2$: the remainder is $0$ or $1$, i.e.\
$x\equiv 0$ or $1\pmod 2$. If $x$ even, $2\mid(x-0)$; if $x$ odd, $2\mid(x-1)$.
Since $0,1\in\tilde\mathbb{Z}$, $u=2$ is a universal side divisor.
\textit{Check.} Every residue mod $2$ is $0$ or a unit ($1$), exactly as the Proposition
predicts. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A universal side divisor in $Q[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A universal side divisor in $Q[x]$}
Find a universal side divisor in $Q[x]$.
\wrec Non-field ED; minimal-norm nonzero nonunit means least positive degree, i.e.\
degree $1$.
\wsol
$\units{Q[x]}=Q^\times$ (nonzero constants), so $\tilde R=Q^\times\cup\{0\}=Q$. Take
$u=x$. For any $f\inQ[x]$, divide by $x$: $f=x\,g + f(0)$ with remainder the constant
$f(0)\inQ=\tilde R$. Thus $x\mid(f-f(0))$, so $u=x$ is a universal side divisor.
Check. The remainder $f(0)$ is always $0$ or a unit (a nonzero constant), matching
the definition. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Find a universal side divisor in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
\wrec Non-field ED; minimal-norm nonzero nonunit means least positive degree, i.e.\
degree $1$.
\wsol
$\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}=\mathbb{Q}^\times$ (nonzero constants), so $\tilde R=\mathbb{Q}^\times\cup\{0\}=\mathbb{Q}$. Take

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item For each of the following five pairs of integers $a$ and $b$, determine their greatest common divisor $d$ and write $d$ as a linear combination $ax + by$ of $a$ and $b$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $a = 20$, $b = 13$.
\item[(b)] $a = 69$, $b = 372$.
\item[(c)] $a = 11391$, $b = 5673$.
\item[(d)] $a = 507885$, $b = 60808$.
\item[(e)] $a = 91442056588823$, $b = 779086434385541$ (the Euclidean Algorithm requires only 7 steps for these integers).
\end{enumerate}

\item For each of the following pairs of integers $a$ and $n$, show that $a$ is relatively prime to $n$ and determine the inverse of $a$ mod $n$ (cf.\ D\&F, Section 0.3).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $a = 13$, $n = 20$.
\item[(b)] $a = 69$, $n = 89$.
\item[(c)] $a = 1891$, $n = 3797$.
\item[(d)] $a = 6003722857$, $n = 77695236973$ (the Euclidean Algorithm requires only 3 steps for these integers).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean Domain. Let $m$ be the minimum integer in the set of norms of nonzero elements of $R$. Prove that every nonzero element of $R$ of norm $m$ is a unit. Deduce that a nonzero element of norm zero (if such an element exists) is a unit.

\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean Domain.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that if $(a, b) = 1$ and $a$ divides $bc$, then $a$ divides $c$. More generally, show that if $a$ divides $bc$ with nonzero $a$, $b$ then $\frac{a}{(a,b)}$ divides $c$.
\item[(b)] Consider the Diophantine Equation $ax + by = N$ where $a$, $b$ and $N$ are integers and $a$, $b$ are nonzero. Suppose $x_0$, $y_0$ is a solution: $ax_0 + by_0 = N$. Prove that the full set of solutions to this equation is given by
\[ x = x_0 + \frac{b}{(a,b)} t \qquad y = y_0 - \frac{a}{(a,b)} t \]
as $t$ ranges over the integers. [If $x$, $y$ is a solution to $ax + by = N$, show that $a(x - x_0) = b(y_0 - y)$ and use (a).]
\end{enumerate}

\item Determine all integer solutions of the following equations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $2x + 4y = 5$
\item[(b)] $17x + 29y = 31$
\item[(c)] $85x + 145y = 505$.
\end{enumerate}

\item ({\it The Postage Stamp Problem}) Let $a$ and $b$ be two relatively prime positive integers. Prove that every sufficiently large positive integer $N$ can be written as a linear combination $ax + by$ of $a$ and $b$ where $x$ and $y$ are both nonnegative, i.e., there is an integer $N_0$ such that for all $N \geq N_0$ the equation $ax + by = N$ can be solved with both $x$ and $y$ nonnegative integers. Prove in fact that the integer $ab - a - b$ cannot be written as a nonnegative integer combination of $a$ and $b$ but that every integer greater than $ab - a - b$ is a nonnegative integer combination of $a$ and $b$ (so every ``postage'' greater than $ab - a - b$ can be obtained using only stamps in denominations $a$ and $b$).

\item Find a generator for the ideal $(85, 1 + 13i)$ in $Z[i]$, i.e., a greatest common divisor for $85$ and $1 + 13i$, by the Euclidean Algorithm. Do the same for the ideal $(47 - 13i, 53 + 56i)$.

\item Let $F = Q(\sqrt{D})$ be a quadratic field ($D\neq 0,1$ a squarefree integer) with associated quadratic integer ring $O=Z[\omega]$, where $\omega=\sqrt{D}$ if $D\equiv 2,3\pmod 4$ and $\omega=\frac{1+\sqrt{D}}{2}$ if $D\equiv 1\pmod 4$, and field norm $N(a+b\sqrt{D})=(a+b\sqrt{D})(a-b\sqrt{D})=a^2-Db^2$ ($a,b\inQ$), as in D\&F, Section 7.1.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $D$ is $-1$, $-2$, $-3$, $-7$ or $-11$. Prove that $O$ is a Euclidean Domain with respect to $N$. [Modify the proof for $Z[i]$ ($D = -1$) in the text. For $D = -3, -7, -11$ prove that every element of $F$ differs from an element in $O$ by an element whose norm is at most $(1 + |D|)^2/(16|D|)$, which is less than $1$ for these values of $D$. Plotting the points of $O$ in $C$ may be helpful.]
\item[(b)] Suppose that $D = -43$, $-67$, or $-163$. Prove that $O$ is not a Euclidean Domain with respect to any norm. [Apply the same proof as for $D = -19$ in the text.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that the ring of integers $O=Z[\sqrt{2}]$ in the quadratic field $Q(\sqrt{2})$ is a Euclidean Domain with respect to the norm given by the absolute value of the field norm $N(a+b\sqrt{2})=a^2-2b^2$ (cf. the previous exercise).

\item Prove that the quotient ring $Z[i]/I$ is finite for any nonzero ideal $I$ of $Z[i]$. [Use the fact that $I = (\alpha)$ for some nonzero $\alpha$ and then use the Division Algorithm in this Euclidean Domain to see that every coset of $I$ is represented by an element of norm less than $N(\alpha)$.]
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Use the Euclidean algorithm in $Z$ to compute $\gcd(2024, 748)$, and express it in
the form $2024s + 748t$ with $s, t \in Z$.

\item Use the Euclidean algorithm in $Z$ to compute $\gcd(1573, 308)$, and write it as an
integer combination of $1573$ and $308$.

\item In $Q[x]$, compute $\gcd\bigl(x^3 + 2x^2 - x - 2,\ x^3 - x^2 - 4x + 4\bigr)$
(normalized to be monic) and express it as
$a(x)\bigl(x^3 + 2x^2 - x - 2\bigr) + b(x)\bigl(x^3 - x^2 - 4x + 4\bigr)$.

\item In $\F_5[x]$, divide $x^4 + 3x^2 + 1$ by $x^2 + x + 1$, finding the quotient $q$ and
remainder $r$, and verify that $\deg r < \deg(x^2 + x + 1)$. (Reduce every coefficient mod
$5$ as you go, and confirm $q\,(x^2+x+1) + r = x^4 + 3x^2 + 1$ in $\F_5[x]$.)

\item In $Z[i]$, divide $\alpha = 11 + 7i$ by $\beta = 3 + i$: find $q, r \in Z[i]$ with
$\alpha = q\beta + r$ and $\Nm(r) < \Nm(\beta)$. What does the value of $r$ tell you about a
gcd of $\alpha$ and $\beta$?

\item Use the Euclidean algorithm in $Z[i]$ to compute a gcd of $\alpha = 8 + 6i$ and
$\beta = 5 - 15i$, giving your answer up to a unit of $Z[i]$.

\item In $Z$, exhibit explicit integers $x, y$ with $\gcd(240, 46) = 240x + 46y$, obtained
by back-substitution in the Euclidean algorithm.

\item In the Euclidean domain $Z[i]$, find a gcd of $\alpha = 7 + i$ and $\beta = 4 - 3i$,
and express it as a $Z[i]$-linear combination $\mu\alpha + \nu\beta$.

\item Prove that every field $F$ is a Euclidean domain with the norm $\Nm(a) = 0$ for all
$a \in F$ (equivalently, any constant norm on $F \setminus \{0\}$). Conclude that the only
nonzero ideal of $F$ is $F$ itself, and that it is principal.

\item Find a universal side divisor in $\F_2[x]$ and a universal side divisor in $\F_3[x]$.
(In each case identify $\tilde R = \units R \cup \{0\}$ first, then verify the defining
divisibility condition.)
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain with norm $\Nm$. Prove that if $a \in R$ is a nonzero
nonunit and $\Nm(a)$ is minimal among the norms of all nonzero nonunits of $R$, then $a$ is
irreducible. (If $a=bc$, divide $b$ by $a$: $b=qa+r$ with $r=0$ or
$\Nm(r)<\Nm(a)$. By minimality $r$ is $0$ or a unit, and $r=b(1-qc)$; conclude that $c$ or $b$ is
a unit.)

\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain and $a, b \in R$ not both zero. Prove that any two
greatest common divisors of $a$ and $b$ are associates, and conversely that any associate of
a gcd of $a, b$ is again a gcd. (Use $\langle a,b\rangle = \langle d\rangle$ for a gcd $d$, together with the
mutual-divisibility characterization of associates.)

\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain whose norm $\Nm$ satisfies $\Nm(a)\le\Nm(ab)$ for all nonzero
$a,b\in R$ (as $|\cdot|$ on $Z$, $\deg$ on $\F[x]$ and $\Nm(c+di)=c^2+d^2$ on $Z[i]$ do). Prove the
divisibility lemma: if $a$ divides $b$ and $b \neq 0$, then $\Nm(a) \le \Nm(b)$. Deduce that two nonzero
elements $a, b \in R$ are associates if and only if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$. Show that the
hypothesis on $\Nm$ is needed: on $Z$, the norm with $\Nm(2)=100$ and $\Nm(n)=|n|$ for $n\neq 2$
admits a Division Algorithm, yet $2\mid 4$ and $\Nm(2)>\Nm(4)$.

\item Let $F$ be a field. Prove that every nonzero ideal $I$ of $F[x]$ is generated by a
unique monic polynomial $g \in F[x]$, namely the monic polynomial of least degree in
$I$. (Use that $F[x]$ is a Euclidean domain with $\Nm = \deg$: pick a least-degree nonzero
element of $I$, divide an arbitrary element of $I$ by it, and rescale to make it monic;
then argue uniqueness of the monic generator.)
\end{exers}

Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain and $a, b \in R$ with gcd $d$. Justify both inclusions of
the ideal diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\langle a,b\rangle \arrow[r, equal] & \langle d\rangle
\end{tikzcd}
\]
by proving $\langle d\rangle \subseteq \langle a,b\rangle$ and $\langle a,b\rangle \subseteq \langle d\rangle$, naming the
property of $R$ used for each inclusion.

\item In $Z[i]$, with $a = 2 + 2i$ and $b = 5 + i$, compute a gcd $d$ and fill in $d$ to make
the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\langle 2+2i,\ 5+i\rangle \arrow[r, equal] & \langle d\rangle
\end{tikzcd}
\]
an honest equality of ideals; verify that your $d$ divides both generators and is a
$Z[i]$-linear combination of them.

\item Diagram the halting of the Euclidean algorithm in $Z$ for $a = 803$, $b = 154$: draw
one arrow per division step
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
(803,\,154) \arrow[r] & (154,\,33) \arrow[r] & (33,\,22) \arrow[r] & (22,\,11) \arrow[r] & (11,\,0)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
labelling each arrow with its $(q, r)$ and confirming $\Nm(r) < \Nm(b)$ at every step. Read
off the generator of $\langle 803, 154\rangle$ from the last nonzero remainder, and explain how the
strictly decreasing norms force the process to halt.

\item Draw the one-arrow refinement ladder
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em]
field \arrow[r, Rightarrow, "{trivially Euclidean}"] & ED
\end{tikzcd}
\]
and locate on it a field, $Z$, and $Z[i]$, indicating for each which side of the arrow it
sits on. Explain, via the universal-side-divisor proposition, why ``ED'' is the relevant rung
for the Division Algorithm: every non-field ED has a universal side divisor (e.g.\ $2$ in $Z$,
$x$ in $Q[x]$), a norm-free certificate that a generic domain need not possess. Note also why
the arrow does not reverse, citing $Z$ as an ED that is not a field.
\end{exers}

Content:
Recall (8.1) that a Euclidean domain (ED) is an integral domain $R$ equipped with a norm $N\colon R\toZ_{\ge 0}$ (with $N(0)=0$) such that for all $a,b\in R$ with $b\neq 0$ there exist $q,r\in R$ with
\[
a = qb + r,\qquad r=0 \ or \ N(r)<N(b).
\]
The division algorithm is exactly what lets us run the Euclidean algorithm to compute gcds. We now isolate the purely ideal-theoretic consequence that makes the machinery work, and find that it is strictly weaker than possessing a division algorithm.

Title: Principal ideal, principal ideal domain
Content:
\begin{definition}[Principal ideal, principal ideal domain]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. An ideal $I\subseteq R$ is principal if $I=\langle a\rangle=aR$ for some single element $a\in R$. A principal ideal domain (PID) is an integral domain in which every ideal is principal.
\end{definition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > Principal ideal domains
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-e1e26d04b4ddf6cb799f
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain with norm $N$, and let $I\subseteq R$ be an ideal. If $I=\langle 0\rangle$ it is principal, so assume $I\neq\langle 0\rangle$. Among the nonzero elements of $I$, choose $d\in I$ of minimal norm $N(d)$ (possible since $N$ takes values in $Z_{\ge 0}$, a well-ordered set). Clearly $\langle d\rangle\subseteq I$. Conversely take any $a\in I$ and divide: write $a=qd+r$ with $r=0$ or $N(r)<N(d)$. Then $r=a-qd\in I$. If $r\neq 0$ then $N(r)<N(d)$ contradicts the minimality of $N(d)$ among nonzero elements of $I$. Hence $r=0$, so $a=qd\in\langle d\rangle$. Therefore $I=\langle d\rangle$ is principal.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > Principal ideal domains
Type: example
Title: $\F[x]$ is a PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\F[x]$ is a PID}
Let $\F$ be a field. Show $\F[x]$ is a PID and identify the generator of an arbitrary nonzero ideal.
\wrec ED $\Longrightarrow$ PID: $\F[x]$ carries the degree norm, so it is Euclidean, hence a PID. The generator-of-minimal-norm in the proof becomes the monic polynomial of least degree.
\wsol The map $N(f)=\deg f$ (for $f\neq 0$) makes $\F[x]$ Euclidean: polynomial long division over a field gives $f=qg+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$ (the leading coefficient of $g$ is a unit, so division never stalls). Hence $\F[x]$ is a PID by the theorem. Concretely, given an ideal $I\neq\langle 0\rangle$, pick $d\in I$ of least degree; rescaling by the inverse of its leading coefficient we may take $d$ monic, and the ED proof gives $I=\langle d\rangle$ with $d$ the unique monic generator. Check. Two monic generators $d_1,d_2$ of $I$ satisfy $d_1\mid d_2$ and $d_2\mid d_1$, so they are associates; the only monic associate of a monic polynomial is itself, so the monic generator is unique.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Generator of $(f,g)$ in $Q[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Generator of $(f,g)$ in $Q[x]$}
In $R=Q[x]$ find a generator of $I=\langle f,g\rangle$ with $f=x^3-1$, $g=x^2-1$.
\wrec In a PID $\langle f,g\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ where $d=\gcd(f,g)$, computed by the Euclidean algorithm (the division algorithm of the ED).
\wsol Run the Euclidean algorithm. Divide $f$ by $g$:
\[
x^3-1 = x\,(x^2-1) + (x-1),\qquad r_1=x-1.
\]
Divide $g$ by $r_1$:
\[
x^2-1 = (x+1)(x-1) + 0,\qquad r_2=0.
\]
The last nonzero remainder is $x-1$, so $\gcd(f,g)=x-1$ (already monic) and $I=\langle x-1\rangle$. Check. $x-1\mid x^3-1$ since $x=1$ is a root of $x^3-1$, and $x-1\mid x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$. And $x-1$ is a $Q[x]$-combination: from the first equation $x-1=(x^3-1)-x(x^2-1)$, so $x-1\in I$. Both inclusions hold, confirming $\langle f,g\rangle=\langle x-1\rangle$.
\end{wex}

Title: Generator of $(a,b)$ in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Generator of $(a,b)$ in $Z$}
In $Z$ find a generator of $I=\langle 1755,1599\rangle$.
\wrec $Z$ is Euclidean (norm $|\cdot|$), hence a PID; $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$, and the gcd is a $Z$-linear combination (Bezout).
\wsol Euclidean algorithm:
\[
1755 = 1\cdot 1599 + 156,\quad 1599 = 10\cdot 156 + 39,\quad 156 = 4\cdot 39 + 0.
\]
Last nonzero remainder $39$, so $\gcd=39$ and $I=\langle 39\rangle$. Check. $1755=39\cdot 45$, $1599=39\cdot 41$, so $39$ divides both. Back-substitute for Bezout: $39=1599-10\cdot 156=1599-10(1755-1599)=11\cdot 1599-10\cdot 1755$. Indeed $11\cdot 1599-10\cdot 1755=17589-17550=39$. Thus $39\in I$ and $I=\langle 39\rangle$.
\end{wex}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > Gcds in a PID and the structure of ideals
Type: theorem
Title: gcd as ideal generator
Content:
\begin{theorem}[gcd as ideal generator]
Let $R$ be a PID and $a,b\in R$ not both zero. Write $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ (possible since $R$ is a PID). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $d$ is a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$: $d\mid a$, $d\mid b$, and if $e\mid a$ and $e\mid b$ then $e\mid d$.
\item $d=ax+by$ for some $x,y\in R$ (a linear combination of $a,b$).
\item $d$ is unique up to multiplication by a unit (i.e. up to associates).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-67a7681ac640e24e0305
Content:
\begin{proof}
Since $a,b\in\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ we have $d\mid a$ and $d\mid b$. Since $d\in\langle a,b\rangle=aR+bR$, there are $x,y\in R$ with $d=ax+by$, giving (2). If $e\mid a$ and $e\mid b$ then $e$ divides $ax+by=d$, proving $d$ is greatest and giving (1). For (3): if $\langle d\rangle=\langle d'\rangle$ then $d\mid d'$ and $d'\mid d$, so $d'=ud$ with $u\in\units{R}$. In a domain such $d,d'$ are associates.
\end{proof}

In a general UFD gcds exist but need not be linear combinations; the linear-combination property is special to PIDs (it is equivalent to being a Bezout domain).

Title: Finding the generator of a sum of ideals $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$
Content:
\begin{method}{Finding the generator of a sum of ideals $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$}
Trigger. You see $\langle a,b\rangle$, $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$, or ``the ideal generated by $a$ and $b$'' in a PID and want a single generator.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Compute $d=\gcd(a,b)$ (Euclidean algorithm if a norm is available).
\item Then $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$. Dually, $\langle a\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle=\langle \operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\rangle$.
\item Normalize: in $Z$ take $d>0$; in $\F[x]$ take $d$ monic. This pins down the generator exactly.
\item Sanity check by back-substitution: write $d=ax+by$ to confirm $d\in\langle a,b\rangle$, and check $d\mid a,\ d\mid b$ to confirm $\langle a,b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Nonzero prime ideals are maximal in a PID
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Nonzero prime ideals are maximal in a PID]
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain. Then every nonzero prime ideal of $R$ is maximal.
\end{theorem}

Type: corollary
Content:
\begin{corollary}
In a PID $R$, a nonzero element $p$ is prime if and only if it is irreducible, and the quotient $R/\langle p\rangle$ is a field for every irreducible $p$.
\end{corollary}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > Gcds in a PID and the structure of ideals
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-bb3e5e89530d00ddd330
Content:
\begin{proof}
$p$ prime $\Longleftrightarrow$ $\langle p\rangle$ nonzero prime $\Longleftrightarrow$ (by the theorem) $\langle p\rangle$ maximal $\Longleftrightarrow$ $R/\langle p\rangle$ a field. In any domain prime $\Longrightarrow$ irreducible. For the reverse, let $p$ be irreducible. Then $\langle p\rangle\neq\langle 0\rangle$ and $\langle p\rangle\neq R$, and $\langle p\rangle$ is contained in some maximal ideal $\langle m\rangle$. From $\langle p\rangle\subseteq\langle m\rangle$ we get $p=mr$; irreducibility forces $m$ or $r$ to be a unit, and $m$ is not a unit (else $\langle m\rangle=R$), so $r\in\units{R}$ and $\langle p\rangle=\langle m\rangle$ is maximal, hence prime.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Prime $=$ maximal applied to $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Prime $=$ maximal applied to $Z$}
Show that in $Z$ the nonzero prime ideals are precisely the maximal ideals, and list both.
\wrec $Z$ is a PID, so the theorem applies: every nonzero prime ideal is maximal.
\wsol The ideals of $Z$ are $\langle n\rangle$, $n\ge 0$. The ideal $\langle n\rangle$ is prime iff $n=0$ or $n=p$ prime. The nonzero primes are exactly $\langle p\rangle$ for $p$ a rational prime, and each is maximal because $Z/\langle p\rangle=\F_p$ is a field. The ideal $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime (since $Z$ is a domain) but not maximal --- this is the unique nonmaximal prime, and the theorem only claims maximality for nonzero primes. Check. $\langle 6\rangle$ is not prime ($2\cdot 3\in\langle 6\rangle$ but $2,3\notin\langle 6\rangle$), consistent with $6$ not being a rational prime; $Z/\langle 6\rangle\congZ/2\timesZ/3$ is not a field.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Prime $=$ maximal applied to $\F[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Prime $=$ maximal applied to $\F[x]$}
Show every nonzero prime ideal of $Q[x]$ is maximal, and decide whether $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ and $\langle x^2-1\rangle$ are maximal.
\wrec $Q[x]$ is a PID, so nonzero primes are maximal; primality of $\langle f\rangle$ is irreducibility of $f$.
\wsol Nonzero prime ideals of $Q[x]$ are $\langle p(x)\rangle$ with $p$ irreducible, and each is maximal with $Q[x]/\langle p\rangle$ a field. Now $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $Q$ (no rational root, degree $2$), so $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is maximal and $Q[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle\congQ(i)$, a field. But $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is reducible, so $\langle x^2-1\rangle$ is not prime, hence not maximal. Check. $Q[x]/\langle x^2-1\rangle\congQ[x]/\langle x-1\rangle\timesQ[x]/\langle x+1\rangle\congQ\timesQ$ by CRT --- a product of two fields, not a field, so indeed not maximal.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The zero ideal can be a nonmaximal prime
Content:
\begin{wex}{The zero ideal can be a nonmaximal prime}
In $R=Q[x]$, is $\langle 0\rangle$ prime? Maximal? Reconcile with the theorem.
\wrec The theorem restricts to nonzero prime ideals; $\langle 0\rangle$ is exempt.
\wsol $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime since $R$ is a domain ($fg=0\Longrightarrow f=0$ or $g=0$). It is not maximal: $\langle 0\rangle\subsetneq\langle x\rangle\subsetneq R$. So $\langle 0\rangle$ is a prime that is not maximal, and there is no contradiction --- the theorem only promotes nonzero primes to maximal. Check. $R/\langle 0\rangle=R=Q[x]$ is a domain but not a field ($x$ has no inverse), confirming $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime but not maximal.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: PID $\Longrightarrow$ Noetherian
Content:
\begin{theorem}[PID $\Longrightarrow$ Noetherian]
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain. Then $R$ satisfies the ascending chain condition (ACC) on ideals: every chain
\[
I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq I_3\subseteq\cdots
\]
of ideals stabilizes, i.e. there is $n$ with $I_n=I_{n+1}=\cdots$. Equivalently, every nonempty collection of ideals has a maximal element. (Such a ring is called Noetherian.)
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > Noetherian: the ascending chain condition
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-20d3aa1c2ad1a18ebbe0
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots$ be an ascending chain. Put $I=\bigcup_{k\ge 1} I_k$. This is an ideal: if $a,b\in I$ then $a\in I_j,\ b\in I_k$ for some $j,k$, so both lie in $I_{\max(j,k)}$ (the chain is nested), hence $a-b\in I$ and $ra\in I$ for all $r\in R$. Since $R$ is a PID, $I=\langle d\rangle$ for some $d$. Now $d\in I=\bigcup_k I_k$, so $d\in I_n$ for some $n$. Then
\[
\langle d\rangle\subseteq I_n\subseteq I_{n+1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq I=\langle d\rangle,
\]
forcing $I_n=I_{n+1}=\cdots=\langle d\rangle$. The chain stabilizes at stage $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
ACC is exactly the finiteness needed to prove existence of irreducible factorizations: if some element had no factorization into irreducibles, one could build a strictly ascending chain of ideals, contradicting ACC. Type: example
Title: ACC fails in a non-PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{ACC fails in a non-PID}
Exhibit an ascending chain in $R=Q[x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots]$ (infinitely many variables) that never stabilizes, illustrating that non-PIDs can fail ACC.
\wrec ACC is a theorem for PIDs; a ring that violates ACC therefore cannot be a PID. We build a strictly increasing chain.
\wsol Let $I_k=\langle x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k\rangle$. Then $I_1\subsetneq I_2\subsetneq I_3\subsetneq\cdots$ since $x_{k+1}\in I_{k+1}\setminus I_k$ (no $R$-combination of $x_1,\dots,x_k$ produces $x_{k+1}$: evaluate at $x_1=\cdots=x_k=0$, $x_{k+1}=1$, which kills every element of $I_k$ but sends $x_{k+1}$ to $1$). This chain never stabilizes, so $R$ is not Noetherian and a fortiori not a PID. Check. Indeed $I_k=\langle x_1,\dots,x_k\rangle$ needs $k$ generators and is not principal for $k\ge 2$, consistent with $R$ failing to be a PID.
\end{wex}

Title: {$Z[x]$ is not a PID}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$Z[x]$ is not a PID}]
The ideal $I=\langle 2,x\rangle\subseteqZ[x]$ is not principal. Hence $Z[x]$ is an integral domain that is not a PID. (More generally, if $R$ is not a field then $R[x]$ is not a PID.)
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > $Z[x]$ is not a PID
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-978ce175291cf45864f6
Content:
\begin{proof}
First identify $I$ concretely: $\langle 2,x\rangle=\{\,f\inZ[x] : f(0)\ is even\,\}$. Indeed every element $2g+xh$ has constant term $2g(0)$, which is even; conversely if $f(0)=2c$ then $f=2c+(f-2c)$ where $f-2c$ has zero constant term, hence is $x\cdot(poly)\in\langle x\rangle$, so $f\in\langle 2,x\rangle$. In particular $I\neqZ[x]$ because $1\notin I$ ($1(0)=1$ is odd).

Suppose for contradiction $I=\langle p\rangle$ for some $p\inZ[x]$. Since $2\in I=\langle p\rangle$, we have $p\mid 2$ in $Z[x]$. The divisors of the constant $2$ in $Z[x]$ are units $\pm 1$ and $\pm 2$ (a degree argument: $2=pq$ forces $\deg p=\deg q=0$, so $p\inZ$ and $p\mid 2$ in $Z$).
\begin{itemize}
\item If $p=\pm 1$ then $\langle p\rangle=Z[x]\neq I$ (we showed $1\notin I$). Contradiction.
\item If $p=\pm 2$ then $\langle p\rangle=\langle 2\rangle$ consists of polynomials with all coefficients even; but $x\in I$ has an odd coefficient, so $x\notin\langle 2\rangle=\langle p\rangle$, contradicting $x\in I$.
\end{itemize}
No choice of $p$ works, so $I$ is not principal and $Z[x]$ is not a PID.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Why non-principal $\langle 2,x\rangle$ kills PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why non-principal $\langle 2,x\rangle$ kills PID}
Spell out the logical step: how does $\langle 2,x\rangle$ not being principal prove $Z[x]$ is not a PID?
\wrec Definition unpacking: a PID requires every ideal principal, so one non-principal ideal is a counterexample.
\wsol A PID is defined as an integral domain in which every ideal is principal. $Z[x]$ is an integral domain (it is a subring of $Q[x]$, itself a domain; equivalently the product of two nonzero polynomials is nonzero by adding leading degrees). The previous proposition exhibits a single ideal, $\langle 2,x\rangle$, that is not principal. The universal quantifier ``every ideal is principal'' is therefore false for $Z[x]$, so $Z[x]$ fails the definition of PID. Check. No contradiction with $Z[x]$ being a UFD --- being a UFD does not require all ideals principal; indeed $Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID, so the inclusion PID $\subset$ UFD is strict, witnessed precisely by $Z[x]$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > $Z[x]$ is not a PID
Type: example
Title: $\langle 2,x\rangle$ has no gcd-style single generator
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\langle 2,x\rangle$ has no gcd-style single generator}
Confirm directly that $2$ and $x$ have gcd $1$ in $Z[x]$ yet $\langle 2,x\rangle\neq\langle 1\rangle$, so the ``$\gcd$ generates'' theorem really needs the PID hypothesis.
\wrec Contrast with the PID gcd theorem: there $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$. Failure here pinpoints why $Z[x]$ is not a PID.
\wsol In $Z[x]$ the only common divisors of $2$ and $x$ are units $\pm 1$ (a divisor of $x$ is $\pm 1$ or $\pm x$ up to units; $\pm x\nmid 2$), so $\gcd(2,x)=1$. If $Z[x]$ were a PID we would get $\langle 2,x\rangle=\langle \gcd(2,x)\rangle=\langle 1\rangle=Z[x]$, i.e. $1=2f+xg$ for some $f,g\inZ[x]$. Evaluate at $x=0$: $1=2f(0)$, impossible in $Z$ (left side odd, right side even). Check. So $1\notin\langle 2,x\rangle$, $\langle 2,x\rangle\subsetneqZ[x]$, and the gcd $1$ fails to generate the ideal --- exactly the PID property that breaks. This is the same obstruction as the non-principality computation, viewed through Bezout.
\end{wex}

Title: $\F[x,y]$ is not a PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\F[x,y]$ is not a PID}
Show $R=Q[x,y]$ is not a PID using the ideal $\langle x,y\rangle$.
\wrec Same non-principal-ideal strategy; $\langle x,y\rangle$ is the ``functions vanishing at the origin'' ideal and needs two generators.
\wsol $\langle x,y\rangle=\{f\inQ[x,y] : f(0,0)=0\}$, a maximal ideal with $R/\langle x,y\rangle\congQ$. Suppose $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle p\rangle$. Then $p\mid x$ and $p\mid y$. Divisors of $x$ in $Q[x,y]$ are (up to units) $1$ and $x$; the only common divisor of $x$ and $y$ is a unit, so $p\inQ^\times$, giving $\langle p\rangle=R$. But $\langle x,y\rangle\neq R$ since $1\notin\langle x,y\rangle$ ($1(0,0)=1\neq 0$). Contradiction, so $R$ is not a PID. Check. Consistent with $Q[x,y]=Q[x][y]$ being $S[y]$ for $S=Q[x]$ a non-field, so $\langle x,y\rangle$ behaves just like $\langle 2,x\rangle$ did in $Z[x]$; and $Q[x,y]$ is still a UFD.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Two generators does not mean non-principal. Writing an ideal as $\langle a,b\rangle$ does not by itself prove it is non-principal --- in a PID every $\langle a,b\rangle$ collapses to $\langle d\rangle$. E.g. $\langle 6,9\rangle=\langle 3\rangle$ in $Z$. To prove non-principality you must show no single element generates it, as in $\langle 2,x\rangle$. Conversely, do not conclude $Z[x]$ is ``not a UFD'' from this; it is a UFD. Only the PID property fails.
\end{pitfall}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Prime ideal is maximal'' needs nonzero AND PID. The theorem is false without both hypotheses. In $Z$, $\langle 0\rangle$ is prime but not maximal (the nonzero hypothesis matters). In $Z[x]$ (not a PID), $\langle x\rangle$ is prime ($Z[x]/\langle x\rangle\congZ$ is a domain) but not maximal, since $\langle x\rangle\subsetneq\langle 2,x\rangle\subsetneqZ[x]$. So $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle\congZ$ is a domain that is not a field --- exactly the failure of ``prime $=$ maximal'' in a non-PID.

Title: {A PID that is not Euclidean}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{A PID that is not Euclidean}]
Let $\omega=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}$ and $R=Z[\omega]$, the ring of integers of $Q(\sqrt{-19})$, with field norm $\Nm(a+b\omega)=a^2+ab+5b^2$. Then $R$ is a principal ideal domain, but $R$ is not a Euclidean domain (for any norm whatsoever). Hence the inclusion $\{ED\}\subsetneq\{PID\}$ is strict.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Indication]
Not Euclidean. The key is the notion of a universal side divisor: in any Euclidean domain that is not a field, there exists a nonzero nonunit $u$ such that for every $x\in R$ there is $z\in\{0\}\cup\units{R}$ with $u\mid (x-z)$ --- equivalently every residue class of $R/\langle u\rangle$ is represented by $\{0\}\cup\units{R}$. For $R=Z[\omega]$ one checks $\units{R}=\{\pm 1\}$ (the norm form $a^2+ab+5b^2$ equals $1$ only at $(\pm 1,0)$). Taking $x=2$, a universal side divisor $u$ divides $2-0$, $2-1$ or $2+1$, i.e.\ $2$, $1$ or $3$, and $u\nmid 1$ since $u$ is not a unit. For $b\neq 0$ the norm form equals $(a+\tfrac b2)^2+\tfrac{19}{4}b^2\ge 5$, and for $b=0$ it is $a^2$, so it never takes the values $2$ or $3$; hence $2$ and $3$ are irreducible in $R$ and the only candidates are $u=\pm 2$ and $u=\pm 3$. Testing them shows neither is a universal side divisor: $R/\langle 2\rangle$ and $R/\langle 3\rangle$ have order $\Nm(2)=4$ and $\Nm(3)=9$ respectively, too large to be covered by the three residues $\{0,\pm 1\}$. Hence $R$ has no universal side divisor, so $R$ is not Euclidean for any norm.

Is a PID. One uses the Dedekind--Hasse criterion: an integral domain $R$ is a PID iff there is a function $N\colon R\toZ_{\ge 0}$ (a Dedekind--Hasse norm) with $N(a)>0$ for $a\neq 0$ such that for all nonzero $a,b\in R$, either $a\in\langle b\rangle$ or there is a nonzero $r\in\langle a,b\rangle$ with $N(r)<N(b)$. The field norm $\Nm$ is shown to be a Dedekind--Hasse norm on $Z[\omega]$ by a direct (case) verification: given $a,b$, the quotient $a/b\inQ(\sqrt{-19})$ can be approximated by an element of $R$ closely enough (or, when it cannot, one multiplies by a small element) to produce such an $r$. This makes every ideal principal, so $R$ is a PID. Full details are in Dummit \& Foote, $\S$8.1--8.2.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The strict hierarchy]
We have proper containments
\[
\{fields\}\subsetneq\{Euclidean domains\}\subsetneq\{PIDs\}\subsetneq\{UFDs\}\subsetneq\{integral domains\}.
\]
Witnesses for strictness: $Z$ is a non-field ED; $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a non-Euclidean PID; $Z[x]$ is a non-PID UFD; $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a non-UFD domain (e.g. $6=2\cdot 3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ are two essentially different factorizations into irreducibles).
\end{corollary}

\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
fields \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & ED \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & PID \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & UFD \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & domain
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is a class of commutative rings (or integral domains): fields, Euclidean domains (ED), principal ideal domains (PID), unique factorization domains (UFD), and general integral domains. The arrow direction runs from more structured to less structured.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each double arrow ($\Rightarrow$) is a logical implication between ring classes: fields $\Rightarrow$ ED means every field is a Euclidean domain (the trivial norm $N(a)=0$ for all $a\neq 0$ works, or simply every nonzero ideal is $R$ so division is trivial); ED $\Rightarrow$ PID is the theorem proved in this section; PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD is stated in the remark and proved in the next section; UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain is definitional (UFDs are defined to be integral domains).
\dgi{What commutes:} The chain is a transitive sequence: fields $\Rightarrow$ ED $\Rightarrow$ PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain. By transitivity, fields $\Rightarrow$ domain (every field is an integral domain), and every ED is a UFD, etc. All six composite implications hold (ten implications in all, counting the four arrows).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Each implication is strict one-way. The chain is linear, not a square, so ``commutativity'' here means transitivity: if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow C$ then $A\Rightarrow C$ by chaining. No nontrivial reverse implication holds, as the witnesses in the corollary show.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram crystallizes the cumulative work of Section 8.2: every theorem in this section either proves one of the forward arrows (ED $\Rightarrow$ PID was the first theorem) or exhibits a witness showing the arrow cannot be reversed. It is the organizing spine of the section.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $Z$ is an ED (norm $|\cdot|$) but not a field ($2$ is not invertible). $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID but not an ED (no universal side divisor). $Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID ($\langle 2,x\rangle$ is non-principal). $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain but not a UFD ($6=2\cdot 3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read $\Rightarrow$ as $\Leftrightarrow$, concluding, e.g., that every PID must be Euclidean. The corollary's list of witnesses is precisely to block this: each arrow is strict, so the reverse implication fails for an explicit ring.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the five standard classes of integral domains form a strict linear hierarchy of inclusions, with each arrow forward proved and each reversal blocked by a concrete example.
\end{dgx}

\end{tikzcd}\]

The next diagram records, inside a PID, the coincidence of nonzero primes with maximal ideals and the gcd computation $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=normal, column sep=0pt]
\langle a\rangle \arrow[dr, phantom, "\subseteq"] & & \langle b\rangle \arrow[dl, phantom, "\supseteq"] \\
& \langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle \arrow[d, "{if d prime}"] & \\
& \langle d\rangle\ maximal &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four ideal-nodes inside a fixed PID $R$. Top row: $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle$, the principal ideals generated by individual elements $a,b\in R$. Middle: $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$, the sum of those two ideals, which collapses to a single principal ideal because $R$ is a PID; $d$ is the gcd, well-defined up to a unit. Bottom: $\langle d\rangle$ labeled maximal, active only when $d$ is a prime element.
\dgi{Arrows:} The phantom arrows from $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle$, labeled $\subseteq$ and $\supseteq$ (each symbol opens toward the larger ideal), record containments: $\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle a,b\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle\subseteq\langle a,b\rangle$ (each generator belongs to the larger ideal). The vertical arrow from $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ to $\langle d\rangle\ maximal$ is a conditional logical step: when $d$ is a prime element, the theorem ``nonzero prime ideals are maximal in a PID'' promotes $\langle d\rangle$ from merely principal to maximal.
\dgi{What commutes:} No closed square, so the relevant equalities are: (1) $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ as ideals (PID gives every two-generator ideal a single generator, namely the gcd); (2) $\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$ names that generator as the gcd; (3) when $d$ is prime, $\langle d\rangle$ is maximal (the nonzero-prime-is-maximal theorem).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $d$: different choices of gcd are associates ($d'=ud$, $u\in\units{R}$), so $\langle d'\rangle=\langle d\rangle$; the ideal is independent of the choice of associate. The equality $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ follows because $d\mid a$ and $d\mid b$ give $\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$, hence $\langle a,b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$; and $d=ax+by\in\langle a,b\rangle$ gives the reverse.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is a visual summary of two payoffs of the PID axiom proved in this section: ideal-sums compress to a gcd generator, and prime generators produce maximal ideals (hence fields as quotients). It shows the student what ``every ideal is principal'' buys in one picture.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $Z$: $a=12$, $b=8$, $d=\gcd(12,8)=4$, so $\langle 12,8\rangle=\langle 4\rangle$. If $d=5$ (prime), $\langle 5\rangle$ is maximal and $Z/\langle 5\rangle=\F_5$ is a field. In $Q[x]$: $a=x^3-1$, $b=x^2-1$, $d=x-1$, $\langle x^3-1,x^2-1\rangle=\langle x-1\rangle$; since $x-1$ is irreducible (prime in a PID), $\langle x-1\rangle$ is maximal and $Q[x]/\langle x-1\rangle\congQ$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the middle equality $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ as saying $a=d$ or $b=d$; in fact $d$ is a new element (the gcd), generally different from $a$ and $b$, and the equality is of ideals, not elements. Also, the bottom node $\langle d\rangle\ maximal$ applies only when $d$ is prime; if $d=4$ in $Z$, $\langle 4\rangle$ is not maximal ($\langle 4\rangle\subsetneq\langle 2\rangle\subsetneqZ$).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that in a PID the two-generator ideal $\langle a,b\rangle$ automatically collapses to the principal ideal $\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$, and if that gcd happens to be prime the ideal is moreover maximal, linking the gcd computation directly to the prime-equals-maximal theorem.
\end{dgx}

Type: remark
Title: Summary of what the PID axiom buys
Content:
\begin{remark}[Summary of what the PID axiom buys]
Every ideal principal $\Longrightarrow$ (i) gcds exist and are Bezout combinations $d=ax+by$; (ii) every nonzero prime ideal is maximal, and prime $=$ irreducible; (iii) ACC holds, so factorizations into irreducibles exist. Together (ii) and (iii) give the next section's theorem PID $\Longrightarrow$ UFD. None of these uses a division algorithm directly --- which is why a non-Euclidean ring like $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ can still enjoy all of them.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Principal Ideal Domains > ED $\subset$ PID is strict: $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Prove that in a Principal Ideal Domain two ideals $(a)$ and $(b)$ are comaximal (cf. Section 7.6) if and only if a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ is $1$ (in which case $a$ and $b$ are said to be coprime or relatively prime).

\item Prove that any two nonzero elements $a,b$ of a P.I.D. have a least common multiple, i.e., an element $e$ with $a\mid e$ and $b\mid e$ such that $e\mid e'$ whenever $a\mid e'$ and $b\mid e'$ (cf. D\&F, Exercise 11 of Section 8.1).

\item Prove that a quotient of a P.I.D. by a prime ideal is again a P.I.D.

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain. Prove that if the following two conditions hold then $R$ is a Principal Ideal Domain:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] any two nonzero elements $a$ and $b$ in $R$ have a greatest common divisor which can be written in the form $ra + sb$ for some $r, s \in R$, and
\item[(ii)] if $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ are nonzero elements of $R$ such that $a_{i+1} \mid a_i$ for all $i$, then there is a positive integer $N$ such that $a_n$ is a unit times $a_N$ for all $n \geq N$.
\end{itemize}

\item Let $R$ be the quadratic integer ring $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$. Define the ideals $I_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, $I_3 = (3, 2 + \sqrt{-5})$, and $I_3' = (3, 2 - \sqrt{-5})$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I_2$, $I_3$, and $I_3'$ are nonprincipal ideals in $R$. [D\&F prove this for $I_3$ in Section 8.1 (Example 2 following Proposition 1) by comparing norms.]
\item[(b)] Prove that the product of two nonprincipal ideals can be principal by showing that $I_2^2$ is the principal ideal generated by $2$, i.e., $I_2^2 = (2)$.
\item[(c)] Prove similarly that $I_2 I_3 = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ and $I_2 I_3' = (1 + \sqrt{-5})$ are principal. Conclude that the principal ideal $(6)$ is the product of $4$ ideals: $(6) = I_2^2 I_3 I_3'$.
\end{itemize}

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain and suppose that every prime ideal in $R$ is principal. This exercise proves that every ideal of $R$ is principal, i.e., $R$ is a P.I.D.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Assume that the set of ideals of $R$ that are not principal is nonempty and prove that this set has a maximal element under inclusion (which, by hypothesis, is not prime). [Use Zorn's Lemma.]
\item[(b)] Let $I$ be an ideal which is maximal with respect to being nonprincipal, and let $a, b \in R$ with $ab \in I$ but $a \notin I$ and $b \notin I$. Let $I_a = (I, a)$ be the ideal generated by $I$ and $a$, let $I_b = (I, b)$ be the ideal generated by $I$ and $b$, and define $J = \{r \in R \mid rI_a \subseteq I\}$. Prove that $I_a = (\alpha)$ and $J = (\beta)$ are principal ideals in $R$ with $I \subseteq I_b \subseteq J$ and $I_a J = (\alpha\beta) \subseteq I$.
\item[(c)] If $x \in I$ show that $x = s\alpha$ for some $s \in J$. Deduce that $I = I_a J$ is principal, a contradiction, and conclude that $R$ is a P.I.D.
\end{itemize}

\item An integral domain $R$ in which every ideal generated by two elements is principal (i.e., for every $a, b \in R$, $(a, b) = (d)$ for some $d \in R$) is called a Bezout Domain. [cf. also Exercise 11 in Section 3.]
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Prove that the integral domain $R$ is a Bezout Domain if and only if every pair of elements $a, b$ of $R$ has a g.c.d. $d$ that can be written as an $R$-linear combination of $a$ and $b$, i.e., $d = ra + sb$ for some $r, s \in R$.
\item[(b)] Prove that every finitely generated ideal of a Bezout Domain is principal. [cf. the exercises in Sections 9.2 and 9.3 for Bezout Domains in which not every ideal is principal.]
\item[(c)] Let $F$ be the fraction field of the Bezout Domain $R$. Prove that every element of $F$ can be written in the form $a/b$ with $a$ and $b$ relatively prime elements of $R$ (cf. Exercise 1).
\end{itemize}

\item Prove that if $R$ is a Principal Ideal Domain and $D$ is a multiplicatively closed subset of $R$ with $0\notin D$, then $D^{-1}R$ is also a P.I.D. (cf. Section 7.5).
\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Show directly that every ideal of $Z$ is principal: given a nonzero ideal $I\subseteqZ$, prove that $I=\langle d\rangle$, where $d$ is the least positive element of $I$. (Hint: well-ordering produces $d$; for $a\in I$ divide $a=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$ and rule out $r>0$.)

\item In a PID, prove that a nonzero element $p$ is prime if and only if it is irreducible. (You may use: every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal, and in a PID nonzero primes are maximal.)

\item In a PID $R$, suppose $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle=R$ (so $a,b$ are comaximal). Prove the Chinese Remainder Theorem in this setting: the natural map
\[
R/\langle ab\rangle\longrightarrow R/\langle a\rangle\times R/\langle b\rangle,\qquad x+\langle ab\rangle\mapsto\bigl(x+\langle a\rangle,\,x+\langle b\rangle\bigr),
\]
is a ring isomorphism. (Hint: surjectivity uses $1=ax+by$; for injectivity show $\langle a\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle=\langle ab\rangle$ when $a,b$ are comaximal.)

\item Use the ascending chain condition in a PID to prove existence of factorizations: every nonzero nonunit of a PID is a finite product of irreducible elements. (Hint: if some $a$ had no such factorization, build a strictly ascending chain $\langle a\rangle\subsetneq\langle a_1\rangle\subsetneq\langle a_2\rangle\subsetneq\cdots$ of ideals by repeatedly splitting off a proper non-unit factor, contradicting ACC.)

\item Prove that a PID satisfies the ascending chain condition on ideals (so PID $\Longrightarrow$ Noetherian): every chain $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq I_3\subseteq\cdots$ of ideals stabilizes. (Hint: the union $I=\bigcup_k I_k$ is an ideal, hence $I=\langle d\rangle$; locate $d$ in some $I_n$.)

\item In $Z$ compute $\gcd(85,49)$ by the Euclidean algorithm, and then either find the inverse of $49$ in $Z/(85)Z$ using Bezout or show no inverse exists.

\item Determine, with proof, whether $\langle 7,\,3+\sqrt{-5}\rangle$ is a principal ideal in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, where $\Nm(a+b\sqrt{-5})=a^2+5b^2$. (Hint: if the ideal were $\langle d\rangle$, then $\Nm(d)$ divides both $\Nm(7)=49$ and $\Nm(3+\sqrt{-5})=14$; rule out $\Nm(d)=7$ by checking $a^2+5b^2=7$ has no solution, and show $1$ is not in the ideal.)
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that in a PID every nonzero prime ideal is maximal. Then give an integral domain having a nonzero prime ideal that is not maximal, exhibiting where the PID hypothesis is needed. (Hint: in $Z[x]$, the ideal $\langle x\rangle$ is prime since $Z[x]/\langle x\rangle\congZ$ is a domain, but $\langle x\rangle\subsetneq\langle 2,x\rangle\subsetneqZ[x]$.)

\item Let $R$ be a PID and $p\in R$ irreducible. Prove that the only ideals of $R$ containing $\langle p^2\rangle$ are $\langle 1\rangle=R$, $\langle p\rangle$, and $\langle p^2\rangle$, and deduce that $R/\langle p^2\rangle$ is a local ring whose unique maximal ideal is $\langle p\rangle/\langle p^2\rangle$. (Hint: an ideal containing $\langle p^2\rangle$ is $\langle d\rangle$ with $d\mid p^2$; the divisors of $p^2$ up to units are $1,p,p^2$.)

\item Let $\omega=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}$ and $R=Z[\omega]$, with field norm $\Nm(a+b\omega)=a^2+ab+5b^2$. Prove that $R$ has no universal side divisor, hence is not a Euclidean domain for any norm; you may use that $\units{R}=\{\pm1\}$ and that $R$ is a PID (via the Dedekind--Hasse criterion). Conclude that $\{ED\}\subsetneq\{PID\}$ is strict. (Hint: taking $x=2$ shows that a universal side divisor divides $2$ or $3$; since $a^2+ab+5b^2$ never equals $2$ or $3$, it must be $\pm2$ or $\pm3$. But $|R/\langle 2\rangle|=\Nm(2)=4$ and $|R/\langle 3\rangle|=\Nm(3)=9$ exceed the three residues $\{0,\pm1\}$.)

\item Let $\F$ be a field. Show that the formal power series ring $\F[[x]]$ is a PID whose only nonzero proper ideals are $\langle x^n\rangle$ for $n\ge1$, and identify $\units{\F[[x]]}$. (Hint: a power series is a unit iff its constant term is nonzero; for a nonzero ideal let $n$ be the minimal order of its elements and show the ideal equals $\langle x^n\rangle$.)
\end{exers}
