\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item In $Z$, consider the divisor lattice of $12$ under reverse divisibility ($\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle b\rangle$ iff $b\mid a$):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=normal, column sep=large]
& \langle 1\rangle=Z & \\
\langle 2\rangle \arrow[ur, hook] & & \langle 3\rangle \arrow[ul, hook'] \\
\langle 4\rangle \arrow[u, hook] & & \langle 6\rangle \arrow[u, hook'] \arrow[ull, hook', crossing over] \\
& \langle 12\rangle \arrow[ul, hook'] \arrow[ur, hook] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
Interpret each edge as a divisibility relation, identify which of $\langle 2\rangle,\langle 3\rangle,\langle 4\rangle,\langle 6\rangle,\langle 12\rangle$ are prime (hence maximal in $Z$), and state $\langle 2\rangle\cap\langle 3\rangle$ and $\langle 2\rangle+\langle 3\rangle$ as principal ideals.

\item In $Z$, fill in the PID gcd diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\langle a\rangle \arrow[r, hook] & \langle a,b\rangle \arrow[r, equal] & \langle d\rangle & \langle b\rangle \arrow[l, hook']
\end{tikzcd}\]
for $a=1240$, $b=962$: compute $d=\gcd(a,b)$ by the Euclidean algorithm, exhibit Bezout coefficients $x,y$ with $d=ax+by$, and verify both inclusions $\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$.

\item Let $R$ be a PID and $p\in R$ irreducible. Using that $\langle p\rangle$ is maximal, explain why in the diagram
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & R/\langle p\rangle
\end{tikzcd}\]
the surjection $\pi$ has $\ker\pi=\langle p\rangle$ and the target $R/\langle p\rangle$ is a field. Then specialize to $R=Q[x]$, $p=x^2+1$, and identify the field $Q[x]/\langle x^2+1\rangle$.

\item In $R=Z$, complete the gcd--lcm diamond
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=small]
& \langle d\rangle & \\
\langle a\rangle \arrow[ur, hook] & & \langle b\rangle \arrow[ul, hook'] \\
& \langle m\rangle \arrow[ul, hook] \arrow[ur, hook'] &
\end{tikzcd}\]
for $a=12$, $b=18$: fill in $d=\gcd(a,b)$ and $m=\lcm(a,b)$, label each edge with the divisibility it encodes, state $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$ and $\langle a\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle$ as principal ideals, and verify $\langle d\rangle\langle m\rangle=\langle ab\rangle$ (i.e.\ $dm$ and $ab$ are associates).
\end{exers}

Type: definition
Title: Associates
Content:
\begin{definition}[Associates]
Two elements $a, b \in R$ are associates, written $a \sim b$, if $a = ub$ for some unit $u \in \units{R}$. Equivalently (in a domain), $a \sim b$ iff $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$, iff $\langle a\rangle = \langle b\rangle$ as principal ideals.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Characterizations of associates
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Characterizations of associates]
In an integral domain, for $a, b \in R$ the following are equivalent: (i) $a = ub$ for a unit $u$; (ii) $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$; (iii) $\langle a\rangle = \langle b\rangle$.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f9a259a1074be3694612
Content:
\begin{proof}
We verify the three characterizations agree. If $a = ub$ with $u$ a unit, then $b \mid a$, and $b = u^{-1} a$ gives $a \mid b$; conversely $\langle a\rangle \subseteq \langle b\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle \subseteq \langle a\rangle$, so $\langle a\rangle = \langle b\rangle$. If instead $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$, write $b = xa$ and $a = yb$. Then $a = yxa$, so $a(1 - yx) = 0$. If $a = 0$ then $b = 0$ and they are trivially associates; if $a \neq 0$, since $R$ is a domain $1 = yx$, so $y$ is a unit and $a = yb$. Finally $\langle a\rangle = \langle b\rangle \Longrightarrow a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$ directly. So all three are equivalent.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Associate is an equivalence relation. In $Z$ the units are $\{\pm 1\}$, so $a \sim b \Longleftrightarrow b = \pm a$; the associate classes of nonzero elements are $\{n, -n\}$. In a field every nonzero element is a unit, so all nonzero elements are associates of $1$. In $Z[i]$ the units are $\{\pm 1, \pm i\}$, so each nonzero $\alpha$ has four associates $\pm\alpha, \pm i\alpha$.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: Irreducible, prime
Content:
\begin{definition}[Irreducible, prime]
Let $r \in R$ be nonzero and not a unit.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $r$ is irreducible if whenever $r = ab$ with $a, b \in R$, then $a$ or $b$ is a unit. (It cannot be written as a product of two nonunits.)
\item[(ii)] $r$ is prime if the ideal $\langle r\rangle$ is a nonzero prime ideal; equivalently, $r \neq 0$, $r$ is not a unit, and $r \mid ab \Longrightarrow r \mid a$ or $r \mid b$.
\end{enumerate}
An element with a nontrivial factorization $r = ab$ (both nonunits) is reducible.
\end{definition}

Type: method
Title: Deciding irreducible vs.\ reducible, and prime
Content:
\begin{method}{Deciding irreducible vs.\ reducible, and prime}
Trigger. You are handed a specific nonzero nonunit $r$ in a concrete domain and asked whether it is irreducible and/or prime.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Irreducible test (norm method). If a multiplicative norm $\Nm \colon R \to Z_{\geq 0}$ is available with $\Nm(\alpha\beta) = \Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)$ and $\Nm(\alpha) = 1 \Longleftrightarrow \alpha \in \units{R}$, then in any factorization $r = ab$ we get $\Nm(r) = \Nm(a)\Nm(b)$. If $\Nm(r)$ is prime in $Z$, one factor has norm $1$ and is a unit, so $r$ is irreducible. (The converse can fail.)
\item Reducible. Exhibit one factorization $r = ab$ with $\Nm(a), \Nm(b) > 1$.
\item Prime test. Find $a, b$ with $r \mid ab$ but $r \nmid a$ and $r \nmid b$ to show not prime; or prove $R / \langle r\rangle$ is a domain to show prime.
\item Shortcut. Prime always implies irreducible (Proposition below). In a UFD the two notions coincide, so the norm test settles both.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8eb49e59168f1885bbc3
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $p$ be prime and suppose $p = ab$. Then $p \mid ab$, so by primality $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $p \mid a$, write $a = px$. Then $p = ab = pxb$, so $p(1 - xb) = 0$; since $p \neq 0$ and $R$ is a domain, $xb = 1$, so $b$ is a unit. Thus in any factorization $p = ab$ one factor is a unit, i.e.\ $p$ is irreducible.
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The converse fails in general: irreducible does not imply prime in an arbitrary domain. The standard counterexample is $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ (worked below), where $2$ is irreducible but $2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ while $2$ divides neither factor. The notions coincide in every UFD; conversely, a domain in which every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducibles and every irreducible is prime is a UFD (see the additional exercises).
\end{pitfall}

Title: Prime implies irreducible, by hand in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Prime implies irreducible, by hand in $Z$}
\wrec In $Z$, verify directly that the prime $5$ is irreducible using only the definition, to see the general proof concretely.
\wsol Suppose $5 = ab$ with $a, b \in Z$. Then $5 \mid ab$; since $5$ is prime in the usual sense, $5 \mid a$ or $5 \mid b$, say $5 \mid a$, so $a = 5x$. Then $5 = 5xb \Longrightarrow xb = 1 \Longrightarrow b \in \{\pm 1\} = \units{Z}$. So one factor is a unit and $5$ is irreducible. Check. The only factorizations of $5$ are $5 = 1 \cdot 5 = (-1)(-5)$, each with a unit factor; consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: An irreducible that is not prime in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{An irreducible that is not prime in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
\wrec We want a domain where unique factorization fails; the norm $\Nm(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$ flags two genuinely different factorizations of the same element.
\wsol In $R = Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the norm $\Nm(a+b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$ is multiplicative, and $\units{R} = \{\pm 1\}$ since $\Nm(\alpha) = 1 \Longrightarrow a^2 + 5b^2 = 1 \Longrightarrow b = 0,\ a = \pm 1$. Consider
\[
6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}).
\]
$2$ is irreducible: $\Nm(2) = 4$. If $2 = \alpha\beta$ with both nonunits then $\Nm(\alpha) = \Nm(\beta) = 2$, but $a^2 + 5b^2 = 2$ has no integer solution. So no such factorization exists; $2$ is irreducible. (Same argument: $3$ has $\Nm = 9$, and $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ is unsolvable, so $3$ is irreducible; $1 \pm \sqrt{-5}$ each have $\Nm = 6$, and $\Nm = 2$ or $3$ are both unsolvable, so they are irreducible too.)
$2$ is not prime: $2 \mid 6 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$. But $2 \nmid (1 \pm \sqrt{-5})$: if $1 + \sqrt{-5} = 2(a + b\sqrt{-5})$ then $2b = 1$, impossible in $Z$. So $2$ divides the product but neither factor: $2$ is irreducible but not prime.
Check. The two factorizations of $6$ use irreducibles $\{2, 3\}$ versus $\{1+\sqrt{-5}, 1-\sqrt{-5}\}$, and $2 \not\sim 1 \pm \sqrt{-5}$ (different norms $4$ vs $6$), so factorization into irreducibles is not unique. Hence $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Irreducibility via prime norm in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Irreducibility via prime norm in $Z[i]$}
\wrec Whenever $\Nm(\alpha)$ is a rational prime, the norm test instantly forces $\alpha$ irreducible.
\wsol In $Z[i]$, $\Nm(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$ is multiplicative and $\units{Z[i]} = \{\pm 1, \pm i\}$ (the norm-$1$ elements). Take $\alpha = 2 + i$: $\Nm(2+i) = 4 + 1 = 5$, a prime. If $2 + i = \beta\gamma$ then $5 = \Nm(\beta)\Nm(\gamma)$, so one of $\Nm(\beta), \Nm(\gamma)$ equals $1$, i.e.\ is a unit. Hence $2 + i$ is irreducible. Likewise $2 - i$ ($\Nm = 5$), $1 + i$ ($\Nm = 2$), and $3$ ($\Nm = 9$, but $a^2 + b^2 = 3$ unsolvable, so $3$ stays irreducible in $Z[i]$) are all irreducible. Check. The splitting $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$ has consistent norms, since $\Nm(2+i)\Nm(2-i) = 5 \cdot 5 = 25 = \Nm(5)$, matching $\Nm(5) = 5^2 = 25$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Factoring rational primes in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Factoring rational primes in $Z[i]$}
\wrec $Z[i]$ is a UFD (it is Euclidean), so each integer prime $p$ either stays irreducible or splits; the splitting is governed by $p \bmod 4$ and read off the norm.
\wsol (a) $5$ splits. $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$. Check: $(2+i)(2-i) = 4 - i^2 = 4 + 1 = 5$. Both factors have norm $5$ (prime), hence irreducible; $5$ is a product of two nonassociate irreducibles.
(b) $2$ ramifies. $2 = -i(1+i)^2$. Check: $(1+i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i$, and $-i \cdot 2i = -2i^2 = 2$. Here $1 + i$ is irreducible ($\Nm = 2$) and $-i$ is a unit, so $2$ is (a unit times) the square of one irreducible.
(c) $3$ is inert. $\Nm(3) = 9$; a proper factor would need norm $3$, but $a^2 + b^2 = 3$ has no integer solution, so $3$ remains irreducible in $Z[i]$.
Check. Norms multiply correctly: (a) $5 \cdot 5 = 25 = \Nm(5)$; (b) $\Nm((1+i)^2) = 2^2 = 4 = \Nm(2)$ and the unit $-i$ has norm $1$; (c) $9$ has no factorization $9 = 3 \cdot 3$ realized by norm-$3$ Gaussian integers. All consistent with $Z[i]$ being a UFD.
\end{wex}

\begin{theorem}[In a UFD, irreducible $\Longleftrightarrow$ prime]
In a unique factorization domain $R$, an element is prime if and only if it is irreducible.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Unique Factorization Domains > Unique factorization domains
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-540cd25ce1b61e3eb9b9
Content:
\begin{proof}
Prime $\Longrightarrow$ irreducible holds in any domain. For the converse, let $p$ be irreducible and suppose $p \mid ab$, say $ab = pc$. If $a$ is a unit then $b = a^{-1} p c$, so $p \mid b$; symmetrically if $b$ is a unit then $p \mid a$. So assume $a$ and $b$ are nonzero nonunits (if $a = 0$ then $p \mid a$ trivially, similarly for $b$). Factor $a = \prod_i p_i$ and $b = \prod_j q_j$ into irreducibles, and factor $c$ into irreducibles (absorbing any unit). Then
\[
\Big(\prod_i p_i\Big)\Big(\prod_j q_j\Big) = p \cdot \prod_k r_k
\]
are two factorizations of $ab$ into irreducibles. By uniqueness, the irreducible $p$ on the right is an associate of some factor on the left, i.e.\ $p \sim p_i$ for some $i$ (so $p \mid a$) or $p \sim q_j$ for some $j$ (so $p \mid b$). Hence $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$, and $p$ is prime.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Using uniqueness to prove irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime
Content:
\begin{wex}{Using uniqueness to prove irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime}
\wrec In a UFD the only way an irreducible can divide a product is to appear (up to associates) in the factorization of one of the factors.
\wsol Work in $Z$ (a UFD). Let $p = 7$ (irreducible) and suppose $7 \mid ab$ with $a = 2^2 \cdot 7 = 28$, $b = 15 = 3 \cdot 5$. Then $ab = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$. The irreducible $7$ appears in this unique factorization; tracing it back, $7$ came from $a = 28$, so $7 \mid a$. In general the prime $7$ must show up in the merged factorization of $ab$, and uniqueness pins it to a factor of $a$ or of $b$. Check. Indeed $7 \mid 28 = a$, and $7 \nmid 15 = b$; the conclusion ``$7 \mid a$'' is exactly what primality predicts.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: gcds exist in a UFD
Content:
\begin{theorem}[gcds exist in a UFD]
Let $R$ be a UFD. Write the distinct irreducibles (up to associates) appearing in $a$ and $b$ as $p_1, \dots, p_k$, so
\[
a = u \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,e_i}, \qquad b = v \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,f_i} \qquad (u, v \in \units{R},\ e_i, f_i \geq 0).
\]
Then $d = \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,\min(e_i, f_i)}$ is a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ (unique up to associates), and $\ell = \prod_i p_i^{\,\max(e_i,f_i)}$ is a least common multiple.
\end{theorem}

$d \mid a$ since $\min(e_i, f_i) \leq e_i$, and likewise $d \mid b$. If $c \mid a$ and $c \mid b$, then in the factorization of $c$ each irreducible (an associate of some $p_i$, since $c$ divides $a$) appears to a power $\leq e_i$ and $\leq f_i$, hence $\leq \min(e_i, f_i)$; so $c \mid d$. Type: example
Title: gcd via factorizations in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{gcd via factorizations in $Z$}
\wrec Both numbers factor into the same set of primes; take the minimum exponent prime-by-prime.
\wsol $a = 360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$, $b = 84 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$. Common primes $2, 3$ (and $5, 7$ with exponent $0$ in the other). Minima: $2^{\min(3,2)} = 2^2$, $3^{\min(2,1)} = 3^1$, $5^{\min(1,0)} = 5^0$, $7^{\min(0,1)} = 7^0$. So $\gcd = 2^2 \cdot 3 = 12$. Check. $12 \mid 360$ ($360/12 = 30$) and $12 \mid 84$ ($84/12 = 7$), and $\gcd(30, 7) = 1$, so $12$ is greatest. Also $\operatorname{lcm} = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 2520$, and $12 \cdot 2520 = 30240 = 360 \cdot 84$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{gcd via factorizations in $Z[i]$}
\wrec $Z[i]$ is a UFD, so the same min-exponent recipe works once we factor into Gaussian irreducibles.
\wsol Compute $\gcd(2+i, 5)$ in $Z[i]$. Factor: $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$ and $2+i$ is irreducible ($\Nm = 5$). Writing both over the irreducibles $\{2+i, 2-i\}$: $\;2+i = (2+i)^1(2-i)^0$, $\;5 = (2+i)^1(2-i)^1$. Minima: $(2+i)^{\min(1,1)}(2-i)^{\min(0,1)} = (2+i)^1$. So $\gcd(2+i, 5) = 2+i$ (up to a unit). Check. $2+i \mid 5$ since $5/(2+i) = 5(2-i)/\Nm(2+i) = 5(2-i)/5 = 2-i \in Z[i]$, and $2+i \mid 2+i$ trivially; nothing of larger norm divides $2+i$, so $2+i$ is the gcd. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Unique Factorization Domains > The implication chain: ED $\Longrightarrow$ PID $\Longrightarrow$ UFD
Type: proof
Title: Proof sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-39d8ba2730ad70c03c9d
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Two ingredients. Existence: a PID is Noetherian, so the ascending chain condition holds on (principal) ideals. If some nonzero nonunit had no factorization into irreducibles, one builds a strictly increasing chain $\langle a_1\rangle \subsetneq \langle a_2\rangle \subsetneq \cdots$ by repeatedly splitting a non-factorable factor, contradicting ACC; hence every element factors into irreducibles. Uniqueness: in a PID every irreducible $p$ is prime, because $\langle p\rangle$ is maximal (if $\langle p\rangle \subseteq \langle m\rangle \subseteq R$ then $p = mb$, and irreducibility forces $m$ a unit or $b$ a unit, i.e.\ $\langle m\rangle = R$ or $\langle m\rangle = \langle p\rangle$), and maximal ideals are prime. With ``irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime'' available, the standard cancellation argument shows any two irreducible factorizations match up to order and associates. The strictness of the inclusions: $Z[i]$ is Euclidean; $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID that is not Euclidean (next box); $Z[x]$ is a UFD that is not a PID (e.g.\ $\langle 2, x\rangle$ is not principal); $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain that is not a UFD.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Unique Factorization Domains > The implication chain: ED $\Longrightarrow$ PID $\Longrightarrow$ UFD
Type: prose
Part: 1/2
Content:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
ED \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & PID \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & UFD \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & domain
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four classes of integral domains, listed left to right in strictly increasing generality:
 Euclidean domains (ED), principal ideal domains (PID), unique factorization domains (UFD),
 and arbitrary integral domains (domain). Each node represents a class of rings, not a single ring.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each double arrow $\Rightarrow$ is a class inclusion: every ED is a PID,
 every PID is a UFD, every UFD is an integral domain. There are no arrows going right to left,
 signalling that each inclusion is strict.
\dgi{What commutes:} The chain is a linear sequence, not a square, so commutativity is trivial:
 the unique path from ED to domain passes through PID and UFD. What matters is the direction
 and the absence of reverse arrows.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} ED $\Rightarrow$ PID: in a nonzero ideal $I$ a nonzero element $d$ of minimal norm
 generates $I$ (dividing $a\in I$ by $d$ leaves a remainder in $I$ of smaller norm, hence $0$). PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD: in a PID, ACC on principal ideals gives existence of
 irreducible factorizations, and every irreducible is prime (because $\langle p\rangle$ is maximal hence
 prime), giving uniqueness. UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain: a UFD is by definition a domain.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the structural punchline of the section. After
 proving prime $\Rightarrow$ irreducible (always), irreducible $\Rightarrow$ prime (in a UFD), and
 every PID is a UFD, the diagram collects those implications into a single memorable hierarchy,
 and the proof-sketch above has just verified each implication.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $Z[i]$ (Gaussian integers) is Euclidean via the norm, hence a PID,
 hence a UFD. $Z[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID but not Euclidean (no Euclidean function).
 $Z[x]$ is a UFD (since $Z$ is) but not a PID ($\langle 2,x\rangle$ is not principal).
 $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain but not a UFD (the element $6$ has two genuinely different
 irreducible factorizations).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the implication chain as ``every UFD has a
 Euclidean algorithm'' or conflate PID and UFD. Neither reverse arrow exists: each class
 is genuinely more restrictive than the one to its right. In particular, having unique factorization does
 not by itself guarantee that every ideal is principal.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the standard classes of ``nice'' domains form a
 strict linear hierarchy, and each step genuinely loses structure, as witnessed by concrete
 examples sitting in each gap.
\end{dgx}

\]

Inside the world of elements, the dual picture is the relation between prime and irreducible:

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=huge]
\{prime\} \arrow[r, hook, "{always}"] & \{irreducible\} \arrow[l, bend left=25, dashed, "{in a UFD}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two subsets of the nonzero nonunits of an integral domain $R$: the set of prime
 elements $\{prime\}$ and the set of irreducible elements $\{irreducible\}$.
 Both live inside the same domain; the diagram compares them as subsets.
\dgi{Arrows:} The solid hooked arrow $\hookrightarrow$ labelled ``always'' is a set inclusion:
 every prime element is irreducible, in any integral domain, with no extra hypotheses. The
 dashed arrow going back, labelled ``in a UFD,'' is a conditional inclusion: in a UFD (and only
 in a UFD, among the named classes) every irreducible is also prime, so the two sets coincide.
 The dashed style signals that this reverse arrow does not exist in general.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no square to commute; the diagram expresses set-containment.
 The solid arrow means $\{prime\} \subseteq \{irreducible\}$ in every domain.
 Together with the dashed arrow in a UFD, the conclusion is
 $\{prime\} = \{irreducible\}$ inside any UFD.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Solid arrow: if $p$ is prime and $p = ab$, then $p \mid ab$, so
 $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $p \mid a$, write $a = px$; then $p(1-xb) = 0$ and
 $p \neq 0$ forces $xb = 1$, so $b$ is a unit. Dashed arrow (in a UFD only): if $p$ is
 irreducible and $p \mid ab$, factor $a$ and $b$ into irreducibles; unique factorization
 forces $p$ to be an associate of some factor in $a$ or in $b$, giving $p \mid a$ or
 $p \mid b$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The two diagrams together (the domain-class chain and this
 element-level diagram) explain why UFDs are the right setting for unique factorization:
 uniqueness requires cancellation, which requires that irreducibles generate prime ideals, which
 is exactly the dashed arrow. The failure of the dashed arrow in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ (where $2$ is
 irreducible but not prime) is what breaks unique factorization there.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $Z$ (a UFD) every irreducible is $\pm p$ for a rational prime $p$,
 and every such $p$ is prime: both arrows hold and the sets are equal. In $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ (not
 a UFD) the element $2$ is irreducible but $2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}) = 6$ while
 $2$ divides neither factor, so $2$ is not prime: the dashed reverse arrow fails.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often assume the dashed arrow is ``obvious'' and apply it outside
 UFDs. Checking that an element is irreducible (no factorization into nonunits) does not
 automatically make it prime (divides a product implies divides a factor); the extra hypothesis
 of unique factorization is essential and cannot be dropped.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that prime and irreducible coincide in every UFD,
 and that in a domain where factorizations into irreducibles exist (such as $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$) the
 failure of this coincidence is exactly what makes it not a UFD: it is the mechanism by which
 unique factorization breaks down.
\end{dgx}

Title: The PID-not-Euclidean example, stated
Content:
\begin{remark}[The PID-not-Euclidean example, stated]
The ring $R = Z\!\left[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}\right]$ (the ring of integers of $Q(\sqrt{-19})$) is a principal ideal domain but admits no Euclidean function whatsoever. D\&F prove it is not Euclidean by showing it has no ``universal side divisor'' (the field norm rules out small remainders), yet a careful argument with the Dedekind--Hasse criterion shows every ideal is principal. So the inclusion ED $\subsetneq$ PID is strict.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: Content, primitive
Content:
\begin{definition}[Content, primitive]
Let $R$ be a UFD with fraction field $\Frac(R)$. For a nonzero $f = \sum a_i x^i \in R[x]$, the content $\cont(f)$ is a gcd of the coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_n$ (well-defined up to a unit). Call $f$ primitive if $\cont(f)$ is a unit, i.e.\ the coefficients have no common irreducible factor.
\end{definition}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Unique Factorization Domains > Gauss's lemma and polynomials over a UFD
Type: theorem
Title: Gauss's Lemma, stated
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Gauss's Lemma, stated]
Let $R$ be a UFD with fraction field $F = \Frac(R)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The product of two primitive polynomials in $R[x]$ is primitive; more generally $\cont(fg) \sim \cont(f)\cont(g)$.
\item[(ii)] If $f \in R[x]$ factors as $f = AB$ with $A, B \in F[x]$ nonconstant, then $f = ab$ for some $a, b \in R[x]$ with $\deg a = \deg A$, $\deg b = \deg B$. Hence a nonconstant $f \in R[x]$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ iff it is primitive and irreducible in $F[x]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Relation: proof_of=unit-bce63b34f37603a46e86
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
(i) Suppose $f, g$ primitive but $fg$ not, so some irreducible (hence prime, $R$ a UFD) $p$ divides every coefficient of $fg$. Reduce mod $p$: in the domain $(R/\langle p\rangle)[x]$ we get $\bar f \bar g = 0$, forcing $\bar f = 0$ or $\bar g = 0$, i.e.\ $p \mid \cont(f)$ or $p \mid \cont(g)$, contradicting primitivity. The content formula follows by pulling out contents. (ii) Clear denominators and contents from an $F[x]$-factorization and apply (i) to descend the factorization to $R[x]$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$R$ a UFD $\Longrightarrow R[x]$ a UFD, stated}]
If $R$ is a UFD then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is a UFD. By induction $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is a UFD; in particular $Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and $\F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ are UFDs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Sketch]
The irreducibles of $R[x]$ are exactly (a) the irreducibles of $R$ (as constant polynomials) and (b) primitive polynomials that are irreducible in $F[x]$, where $F = \Frac(R)$. Existence of factorizations: split off the content (factored in the UFD $R$) and factor the primitive part using that $F[x]$ is a PID, hence a UFD, then descend via Gauss's Lemma. Uniqueness: Gauss's Lemma transfers the unique factorization in $F[x]$ back to $R[x]$, matched with unique factorization of the content in $R$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: $Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID}
\wrec Inheritance gives the UFD property; a single non-principal ideal blocks the PID property, witnessing strictness of PID $\subsetneq$ UFD.
\wsol Since $Z$ is a UFD, $Z[x]$ is a UFD by the theorem above. But $Z[x]$ is not a PID: the ideal $\langle 2, x\rangle$ (all polynomials with even constant term) is not principal. If $\langle 2, x\rangle = \langle d\rangle$, then $d \mid 2$ forces $d \in \{\pm 1, \pm 2\}$, and $d \mid x$ forces $\deg d = 0$ with $d$ dividing the leading coefficient $1$, so $d \in \{\pm 1\}$; but then $\langle d\rangle = Z[x] \neq \langle 2, x\rangle$ (the constant $1 \notin \langle 2,x\rangle$). Contradiction. Check. $\langle 2,x\rangle$ is a maximal ideal with $Z[x]/\langle 2,x\rangle \cong \F_2$, yet it needs two generators, confirming $Z[x]$ is a UFD that is not a PID.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Irreducibility in $Z[x]$ via Gauss's Lemma
Content:
\begin{wex}{Irreducibility in $Z[x]$ via Gauss's Lemma}
\wrec Gauss's Lemma reduces irreducibility over $Z$ to: primitive plus irreducible over $Q$.
\wsol Let $f(x) = x^2 - 2 \in Z[x]$. Content: $\gcd(1, 0, -2) = 1$, so $f$ is primitive. Over $Q$, $f$ has no rational root ($\sqrt 2 \notin Q$, and a degree-$2$ polynomial with no root in a field is irreducible there), so $f$ is irreducible in $Q[x]$. By Gauss's Lemma (ii), $f$ is irreducible in $Z[x]$. Check. Any factorization $x^2 - 2 = (ax+b)(cx+d)$ over $Z$ needs $ac = 1$, $bd = -2$, $ad + bc = 0$; $a = c = 1$ forces $b + d = 0$ and $bd = -2$, so $b, -b$ with $-b^2 = -2$, i.e.\ $b^2 = 2$, impossible in $Z$. Irreducible, as predicted.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Irreducible over $Z$'' is not the same as ``irreducible over $Q$'' for imprimitive polynomials. The polynomial $2x + 4 = 2(x+2)$ is reducible in $Z[x]$ (the constant $2$ is a nonunit irreducible factor) but is a unit times an irreducible in $Q[x]$, where $2$ is a unit. Gauss's Lemma compares the two worlds only after you strip the content, i.e.\ for primitive polynomials.
\end{pitfall}

Type: remark
Title: Summary of the logic
Content:
\begin{remark}[Summary of the logic]
The whole section threads one chain of implications: a multiplicative norm certifies irreducibles; prime $\Longrightarrow$ irreducible always; the reverse irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime is exactly the property that makes factorizations unique, and it holds in every PID (because irreducibles generate maximal ideals there). Thus ED $\Longrightarrow$ PID $\Longrightarrow$ UFD, while $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ shows a domain can fail to be a UFD precisely by having an irreducible that is not prime.
\end{remark}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $G = Q^{\times}$ be the multiplicative group of nonzero rational numbers. If $a = p/q \in G$, where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime integers, let $\varphi : G \to G$ be the map which interchanges the primes $2$ and $3$ in the prime factorizations of $p$ and $q$ (so, for example, $\varphi(2^4 3^{11} 5^1 13^2) = 3^4 2^{11} 5^1 13^2$, $\varphi(3/16) = \varphi(3/2^4) = 2/3^4 = 2/81$, and $\varphi$ is the identity on all rational numbers with numerators and denominators relatively prime to $2$ and to $3$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\varphi$ is a group isomorphism.
\item[(b)] Prove that there are infinitely many isomorphisms of the group $G$ to itself.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $a$ and $b$ be nonzero elements of the Unique Factorization Domain $R$. Prove that $a$ and $b$ have a least common multiple (cf. Exercise 11 of Section 1) and describe it in terms of the prime factorizations of $a$ and $b$ in the same fashion that Proposition 13 describes their greatest common divisor.

\item Determine all the representations of the integer $2130797 = 17^2 \cdot 73 \cdot 101$ as a sum of two squares.

\item Prove that if an integer is the sum of two rational squares, then it is the sum of two integer squares (for example, $13 = (1/5)^2 + (18/5)^2 = 2^2 + 3^2$).

\item Let $R = Z[\sqrt{-n}]$ where $n$ is a squarefree integer greater than $3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $2$, $\sqrt{-n}$ and $1 + \sqrt{-n}$ are irreducibles in $R$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $R$ is not a U.F.D. Conclude that the quadratic integer ring $O$ is not a U.F.D. for $D \equiv 2, 3 \bmod 4$, $D < -3$ (so also not Euclidean and not a P.I.D.). [Show that either $\sqrt{-n}$ or $1 + \sqrt{-n}$ is not prime.]
\item[(c)] Give an explicit ideal in $R$ that is not principal. [Using $(b)$ consider a maximal ideal containing the nonprime ideal $(\sqrt{-n})$ or $(1 + \sqrt{-n})$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that the quotient ring $Z[i]/(1 + i)$ is a field of order $2$.
\item[(b)] Let $q \in Z$ be a prime with $q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$. Prove that the quotient ring $Z[i]/(q)$ is a field with $q^2$ elements.
\item[(c)] Let $p \in Z$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \bmod 4$ and write $p = \pi \overline{\pi}$ as in Proposition 18. Show that the hypotheses for the Chinese Remainder Theorem (Theorem 17 in Section 7.6) are satisfied and that $Z[i]/(p) \cong Z[i]/(\pi) \times Z[i]/(\overline{\pi})$ as rings. Show that the quotient ring $Z[i]/(p)$ has order $p^2$ and conclude that $Z[i]/(\pi)$ and $Z[i]/(\overline{\pi})$ are both fields of order $p$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $\pi$ be an irreducible element in $Z[i]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For any integer $n \geq 0$, prove that $(\pi^{n+1}) = \pi^{n+1}Z[i]$ is an ideal in $(\pi^n) = \pi^n Z[i]$ and that multiplication by $\pi^n$ induces an isomorphism $Z[i]/(\pi) \cong (\pi^n)/(\pi^{n+1})$ as additive abelian groups.
\item[(b)] Prove that $|Z[i]/(\pi^n)| = |Z[i]/(\pi)|^n$.
\item[(c)] Prove for any nonzero $\alpha$ in $Z[i]$ that the quotient ring $Z[i]/(\alpha)$ has order equal to $N(\alpha)$. [Use $(b)$ together with the Chinese Remainder Theorem and the results of the previous exercise.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R$ be the quadratic integer ring $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ and define the ideals $I_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, $I_3 = (3, 2 + \sqrt{-5})$, and $I_3' = (3, 2 - \sqrt{-5})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $2$, $3$, $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ and $1 - \sqrt{-5}$ are irreducibles in $R$, no two of which are associate in $R$, and that $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5}) \cdot (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ are two distinct factorizations of $6$ into irreducibles in $R$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $I_2$, $I_3$, and $I_3'$ are prime ideals in $R$. [One approach: for $I_3$, observe that $R/I_3 \cong (R/(3))/(I_3/(3))$ by the Third Isomorphism Theorem for Rings. Show that $R/(3)$ has $9$ elements, $(I_3/(3))$ has $3$ elements, and $R/I_3 \cong Z/3Z$ as an additive abelian group. Conclude that $I_3$ is a maximal (hence prime) ideal and that $R/I_3 \cong Z/3Z$ as rings.]
\item[(c)] Show that the factorizations in $(a)$ imply the equality of ideals $(6) = (2)(3)$ and $(6) = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$. Show that these two ideal factorizations give the same factorization of the ideal $(6)$ as the product of prime ideals (cf. Exercise 5 in Section 2).
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose that the quadratic integer ring $O$ is a P.I.D. Prove that the absolute value of the field norm $N$ on $O$ (here $D\neq 0,1$ is a squarefree integer, $O=Z[\omega]$, where $\omega=\sqrt{D}$ if $D\equiv 2,3\pmod 4$ and $\omega=\frac{1+\sqrt{D}}{2}$ if $D\equiv 1\pmod 4$, and $N(a+b\sqrt{D})=(a+b\sqrt{D})(a-b\sqrt{D})=a^2-Db^2$ for $a,b\inQ$, as in D\&F, Section 7.1) is a Dedekind--Hasse norm on $O$. Conclude that if the quadratic integer ring $O$ possesses any Dedekind--Hasse norm, then in fact the absolute value of the field norm on $O$ already provides a Dedekind--Hasse norm on $O$. [If $\alpha, \beta \in O$ then $(\alpha, \beta) = (\gamma)$ for some $\gamma \in O$. Show that if $\beta$ does not divide $\alpha$ then $0 < |N(\gamma)| < |N(\beta)|$ --- use the fact that the units in $O$ are precisely the elements whose norm is $\pm 1$.]

\item ($k$-stage Euclidean Domains) Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $N : R \to Z^+ \cup \{0\}$ be a norm on $R$.

Content:
The ring $R$ is Euclidean with respect to $N$ if for any $a, b \in R$ with $b \neq 0$ there exist elements $q$ and $r$ in $R$ with
\[
a = qb + r \qquad with r = 0 or N(r) < N(b).
\]
Suppose now that this condition is weakened, namely that for any $a, b \in R$ with $b \neq 0$ there exist elements $q, q'$ and $r, r'$ in $R$ with
\[
a = qb + r, \qquad b = q'r + r' \qquad with r' = 0 or N(r') < N(b),
\]
i.e., the remainder after two divisions is smaller. Call such a domain a $2$-stage Euclidean Domain.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that iterating the divisions in a $2$-stage Euclidean Domain produces a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ which is a linear combination of $a$ and $b$. Conclude that every finitely generated ideal of a $2$-stage Euclidean Domain is principal. (There are $2$-stage Euclidean Domains that are not P.I.D.s, however.) [Imitate the proof of Theorem 4.]
\item[(b)] Prove that a $2$-stage Euclidean Domain in which every nonzero nonunit can be factored into a finite number of irreducibles is a Unique Factorization Domain. [Prove first that irreducible elements are prime, as follows: If $p$ is irreducible and $p \mid ab$ with $p$ not dividing $a$, use part $(a)$ to write $px + ay = 1$ for some $x, y$. Multiply through by $b$ to conclude that $p \mid b$, so $p$ is prime. Now follow the proof of uniqueness in Theorem 14.]
\item[(c)] Make the obvious generalization to define the notion of a $k$-stage Euclidean Domain for any integer $k \geq 1$. Prove that statements $(a)$ and $(b)$ remain valid if ``$2$-stage Euclidean'' is replaced by ``$k$-stage Euclidean.''
\end{enumerate}

\item (Characterization of P.I.D.s) Prove that $R$ is a P.I.D. if and only if $R$ is a U.F.D. that is also a Bezout Domain (cf. Exercise 7 in Section 2). [One direction is given by Theorem 14. For the converse, let $a$ be a nonzero element of the ideal $I$ with a minimal number of irreducible factors. Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Factor $85$ into irreducibles in $Z[i]$, using the norm $\Nm(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$. (Hint: $85 = 5 \cdot 17$.)

Answer. Both $5$ and $17$ are $\equiv 1 \bmod 4$, hence split: $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$ and $17 = (4+i)(4-i)$. Each factor has prime norm ($\Nm(2 \pm i) = 5$, $\Nm(4 \pm i) = 17$), so each is irreducible. Thus, up to units,
\[
85 = (2+i)(2-i)(4+i)(4-i).
\]
Check. $\Nm(2+i)\Nm(2-i)\Nm(4+i)\Nm(4-i) = 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 17 \cdot 17 = 25 \cdot 289 = 7225 = 85^2 = \Nm(85)$. Consistent.

\item Determine whether $1 + 3i$ is irreducible in $Z[i]$, using the norm $\Nm(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$.

Answer. $\Nm(1+3i) = 1 + 9 = 10 = 2 \cdot 5$, which is not a rational prime, so the prime-norm shortcut does not apply and $1+3i$ may well be reducible. Seek a factor of norm $2$ or $5$: the norm-$2$ element $1+i$ divides $1+3i$, since
\[
(1+i)(2+i) = 2 + i + 2i + i^2 = 1 + 3i.
\]
Both $1+i$ ($\Nm = 2$) and $2+i$ ($\Nm = 5$) have prime norm, hence are irreducible nonunits. So $1 + 3i = (1+i)(2+i)$ is reducible. Check. $\Nm(1+i)\Nm(2+i) = 2 \cdot 5 = 10 = \Nm(1+3i)$. Consistent. (Contrast: a Gaussian integer of prime norm is forced to be irreducible; composite norm leaves the question open until you exhibit a proper factor.)

\item Prove that in any integral domain every prime element is irreducible. (Reproduce the one-line argument.)

Answer. Let $p$ be prime and write $p = ab$. Then $p \mid ab$, so $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $p \mid a$, $a = px$. Then $p = pxb$, so $p(1 - xb) = 0$. Since $R$ is a domain and $p \neq 0$, $xb = 1$, so $b$ is a unit. Thus in any factorization one factor is a unit, and $p$ is irreducible.

\item Show that $3$ is irreducible but not prime in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ by exhibiting two factorizations of $9$. (Use $\Nm(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$.)

Answer. Two factorizations:
\[
9 = 3 \cdot 3 = (2+\sqrt{-5})(2-\sqrt{-5}), \qquad \Nm(2 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 4 + 5 = 9.
\]
$3$ irreducible: $\Nm(3) = 9$, so a proper factor would have norm $3$, but $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ has no integer solution; hence $3$ is irreducible. $3$ not prime: $3 \mid 9 = (2+\sqrt{-5})(2-\sqrt{-5})$, but $3 \nmid 2 + \sqrt{-5}$ (would force $3 \mid 2$ in $Z$) and $3 \nmid 2 - \sqrt{-5}$. So $3$ is irreducible but not prime, and $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.

\item In $\F_3[x]$, decide whether $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible; if reducible, factor it.

Answer. Test for roots in $\F_3$: $0^2 + 1 = 1$, $1^2 + 1 = 2$, $2^2 + 1 = 5 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. No root, and a degree-$2$ polynomial over a field with no root is irreducible. So $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible in $\F_3[x]$. (Contrast: over $\F_2$, $x^2 + 1 = (x+1)^2$; over $\F_5$, $x^2 + 1 = (x+2)(x-2)$. The $\F_3$ case is inert.)

\item In $Z$, factor $a = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2$ and $b = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$, and read off $\gcd$ and $\lcm$ by taking $\min/\max$ exponents.

Answer. Here $a = 600$, $b = 630$.
\[
\gcd(a,b) = 2^{\min(3,1)} 3^{\min(1,2)} 5^{\min(2,1)} 7^{\min(0,1)} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 30,
\]
\[
\lcm(a,b) = 2^{3} 3^{2} 5^{2} 7^{1} = 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 25 \cdot 7 = 12600.
\]
Check. $\gcd \cdot \lcm = 30 \cdot 12600 = 378000 = 600 \cdot 630 = ab$. Consistent.

\item Suppose $R$ is a UFD and $p$ is irreducible. Prove $p$ is prime, appealing to uniqueness of factorization.

Answer. Suppose $p \mid ab$, say $ab = pc$. If $a$ or $b$ is $0$ or a unit, then $p$ divides $a$ or $b$ directly (e.g.\ $b = a^{-1} pc$ if $a$ is a unit). Otherwise factor $a$, $b$, and $c$ into irreducibles, absorbing $c$ into $p$ if $c$ is a unit. Then
\[
\Big(\prod_i p_i\Big)\Big(\prod_j q_j\Big) = p \cdot \prod_k r_k
\]
are two irreducible factorizations of $ab$. By uniqueness the irreducible $p$ on the right is an associate of some factor on the left, so $p \sim p_i$ for some $i$ (whence $p \mid a$) or $p \sim q_j$ for some $j$ (whence $p \mid b$). Hence $p$ is prime.

\item In $Z[i]$, list the associates of $1 + i$, show $1 - i$ is among them, and deduce $2 = -i(1+i)^2$.

Answer. $\units{Z[i]} = \{1, -1, i, -i\}$, so the associates of $1+i$ are
\[
1+i,\quad -(1+i) = -1-i,\quad i(1+i) = -1+i,\quad -i(1+i) = 1-i.
\]
Thus $1 - i = -i(1+i)$ is an associate of $1+i$. Then
\[
2 = (1+i)(1-i) = (1+i)\big(-i(1+i)\big) = -i(1+i)^2,
\]
with $1+i$ irreducible ($\Nm(1+i) = 2$), so $2$ ramifies. Check. $(1+i)^2 = 2i$ and $-i \cdot 2i = 2$. Consistent.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that an integral domain $R$ is a UFD if and only if every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducibles and every irreducible element of $R$ is prime.

Answer. $(\Rightarrow)$ In a UFD factorizations exist by definition, and irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime holds (the uniqueness axiom forces it). $(\Leftarrow)$ Existence is the first hypothesis. For uniqueness, suppose $p_1 \cdots p_n = q_1 \cdots q_m$ with all factors irreducible, hence prime. Then $p_1 \mid q_1 \cdots q_m$, so $p_1 \mid q_j$ for some $j$; since $q_j$ is irreducible, $q_j \sim p_1$. Cancel (valid in a domain) and induct on $n$. Thus $n = m$ and the factors match up to associates and order, so $R$ is a UFD.

\item Show $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD by exhibiting an element with two essentially different irreducible factorizations, proving each factor irreducible by the norm.

Answer. Take
\[
21 = 3 \cdot 7 = (1+2\sqrt{-5})(1-2\sqrt{-5}),
\]
with $\Nm(3) = 9$, $\Nm(7) = 49$, $\Nm(1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}) = 1 + 20 = 21$. Each factor is irreducible: $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ and $a^2 + 5b^2 = 7$ are unsolvable in $Z$, so $3$ and $7$ are irreducible; a proper factor of $1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}$ would have norm $3$ or $7$, impossible, so $1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}$ are irreducible. No factor on the left is an associate of one on the right: the units are only $\pm 1$, and the norms $9, 49$ on the left differ from $21, 21$ on the right. Hence the two factorizations of $21$ are essentially different, and $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.

\item Prove Gauss's Lemma: with $R$ a UFD, the product of two primitive polynomials in $R[x]$ is primitive (so $\cont(fg) \sim \cont(f)\cont(g)$). State where content is used.

Answer. Let $f, g \in R[x]$ be primitive. If $fg$ were not primitive, some irreducible $p$ (hence prime, since $R$ is a UFD) would divide every coefficient of $fg$. Reduce mod $p$: in $(R/\langle p\rangle)[x]$, an integral domain, $\bar f \, \bar g = 0$, so $\bar f = 0$ or $\bar g = 0$, i.e.\ $p \mid \cont(f)$ or $p \mid \cont(g)$, contradicting primitivity. For the general formula, write $f = \cont(f) f_0$, $g = \cont(g) g_0$ with $f_0, g_0$ primitive; then $fg = \cont(f)\cont(g)\, f_0 g_0$ with $f_0 g_0$ primitive by the first part, so $\cont(fg) \sim \cont(f)\cont(g)$. Content enters twice: to reduce the general claim to the primitive case, and to make $R/\langle p\rangle$ a domain by invoking the primality of the irreducible $p$.

\item Let $p$ be a rational prime with $p \equiv 1 \bmod 4$. Using that $p$ is a sum of two squares, show $p$ is reducible in $Z[i]$ and describe its factorization up to units.

Answer. Since $p \equiv 1 \bmod 4$, $p = a^2 + b^2 = (a+bi)(a-bi)$. Now $\Nm(a+bi) = p$ is prime, so $a+bi$ and $a-bi$ are irreducible; they are non-associate, since their ratio is not a unit (a unit multiple would force $a = \pm b$ or $ab = 0$, making $p = a^2 + b^2$ degenerate, not an odd prime). Thus $p$ splits into two non-associate irreducibles, hence is reducible in $Z[i]$, with $p = \pi \overline{\pi}$ up to units. Example: $13 = 3^2 + 2^2 = (3+2i)(3-2i)$.

\item Give a domain with a nonzero nonunit having no factorization into irreducibles, showing existence can fail without an ascending-chain hypothesis. Use $R = Z + xQ[x]$.

Answer. Let $R = Z + xQ[x]$ (polynomials with integer constant term and rational higher coefficients). The element $x$ is a nonzero nonunit. But $x = 2 \cdot \tfrac{x}{2}$ with $\tfrac{x}{2} \in R$, and $\tfrac{x}{2} = 2 \cdot \tfrac{x}{4}$, etc., giving an infinite chain of proper divisors $x, \tfrac{x}{2}, \tfrac{x}{4}, \dots$. Equivalently the principal ideals ascend without stabilizing,
\[
\langle x\rangle \subsetneq \langle \tfrac{x}{2}\rangle \subsetneq \langle \tfrac{x}{4}\rangle \subsetneq \cdots,
\]
so ACC on principal ideals fails. This chain alone does not rule out a factorization of $x$, so argue directly: the units of $R$ are $\pm 1$, and a nonzero $f \in R$ with constant term $0$ is never irreducible, since $f = 2 \cdot \tfrac{f}{2}$ with $2$ and $\tfrac{f}{2}$ nonunits of $R$. So every irreducible of $R$ has nonzero constant term, hence so does every product of irreducibles, while $x$ has constant term $0$. Hence $x$ admits no finite factorization into irreducibles, and existence of irreducible factorizations is not automatic in a domain; UFDs must assume it.
\end{exers}

\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & R/\langle p\rangle
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad \ker\pi = \langle p\rangle,\quad R/\langle p\rangle\ a domain
\]

\{prime\} \arrow[r, hook, "{always}"] & \{irreducible\} \arrow[l, bend left=25, dashed, "{in a UFD}"]

\end{tikzcd}
\]

Type: prose
Content:
We have seen that the ring of Gauss integers $Z[i]=\{\,a+bi\st a,b\inZ\,\}$ is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID and a UFD: every nonzero nonunit is a product of prime elements, called Gauss primes, unique up to units and order. The units are $\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$. Our goal is to classify the Gauss primes by relating them to the rational primes $2,3,5,7,\dots$ of $Z$, and to harvest from that classification Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares.

The whole story is governed by the multiplicative norm
\[
\Nm(a+bi)=(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^2+b^2=\abs{a+bi}^2\inZ_{\ge 0},
\]
which satisfies $\Nm(\alpha\beta)=\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)$. A Gauss integer $\alpha$ is a unit iff $\Nm(\alpha)=1$. We write $\overline{\alpha}=a-bi$ for the complex conjugate, so $\Nm(\alpha)=\alpha\overline{\alpha}$.

Type: lemma
Title: Divisibility by rational integers
Content:
\begin{lemma}[Divisibility by rational integers]
Let $d\inZ$ and $a+bi\inZ[i]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A Gauss integer that is a real number is an ordinary integer.
\item $d$ divides $a+bi$ in $Z[i]$ if and only if $d$ divides both $a$ and $b$ in $Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Gauss Primes and Sums of Two Squares > The classification theorem
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-81d016c78974cd48f1f7
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) Let $\pi=a+bi$ and factor the positive integer $\Nm(\pi)=a^2+b^2=p_1\cdots p_k$ into rational primes. This same equation $\pi\overline{\pi}=p_1\cdots p_k$ holds in $Z[i]$, but the right side need not be a prime factorization there. Continue factoring each $p_j$ in $Z[i]$ to reach a Gauss-prime factorization. By unique factorization in $Z[i]$, the Gauss primes obtained must be associates of the two factors $\pi$ and $\overline{\pi}$. Hence at most two prime factors occur, so $\Nm(\pi)$ is either a rational prime or a product of two rational primes; in the latter case matching $\pi,\overline{\pi}$ against the factors forces the two to be equal, so $\Nm(\pi)=p^2$.

(b) A rational prime $p$ is not a unit of $Z[i]$, so some Gauss prime $\pi$ divides $p$. Then $\overline{\pi}$ divides $\overline{p}=p$ as well, so $\Nm(\pi)=\pi\overline{\pi}$ divides $p^2$ in $Z[i]$ and (being a positive integer) in $Z$. Thus $\Nm(\pi)\in\{p,p^2\}$. If $\Nm(\pi)=p^2$ then $\pi$ and $p$ are associates and $p$ is itself a Gauss prime; if $\Nm(\pi)=p$ then $p=\pi\overline{\pi}$ splits.

(d) We show (i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iii), (i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv), and (ii)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv); part (c) then follows since the inert primes are precisely those that are not of the split type.

(i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iii). If $p=\pi\overline{\pi}$ with $\pi=a+bi$ a Gauss prime, then $p=a^2+b^2$ is a sum of two squares. Conversely if $p=a^2+b^2$, then $p=(a-bi)(a+bi)$ factors in $Z[i]$, and by (a) each factor has norm $p$, hence is a Gauss prime; so $p$ is a product of conjugate Gauss primes.

(i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv). The quotient $R=Z[i]/(p)$ may be built in two steps from $Z[x]$. Killing $x^2+1$ first yields $Z[i]$, then killing $p$ yields $R$; killing $p$ first yields $\F_p[x]$, then killing $x^2+1$ yields $R$ again. So $R\cong\F_p[x]/(x^2+1)$. Now $(p)$ is a maximal ideal of $Z[i]$ iff $p$ is a Gauss prime; equivalently $R$ is a field iff $x^2+1$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$. Thus $p$ is inert iff $x^2+1$ is irreducible mod $p$, i.e. iff $-1$ is not a square mod $p$. Negating, $p$ splits iff $-1$ is a square mod $p$, which is (iv). (For $p=2$, $x^2+1=(x+1)^2$ in $\F_2[x]$ and $-1\equiv 1$ is a square; $2=-i(1+i)^2$ is ramified.)

(ii)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv). It is clear that $-1$ is a square modulo $2$. For odd $p$, the multiplicative group $\F_p^\times$ is cyclic of order $p-1$. An element $\overline a$ solves $x^2\equiv -1$ iff $\overline a$ has order $4$ (its square then has order $2$, and $-1$ is the unique element of order $2$). And $\F_p^\times$ contains an element of order $4$ iff $4\mid p-1$, i.e. iff $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$. Hence $-1$ is a square mod $p$ iff $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ (or $p=2$), which is (ii).
\end{proof}

Title: Fermat's two-squares theorem
Label: art:gauss_primes:fermat@c8
Content:
\begin{corollary}[Fermat's two-squares theorem] 
A rational prime $p$ is a sum of two integer squares, $p=a^2+b^2$, if and only if $p=2$ or $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$. No prime $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ is a sum of two squares.
\end{corollary}
label: art:gauss_primes:fermat@c8

Content:
\begin{remark}
The arithmetic obstruction for $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ is visible mod $4$ directly: every square is $\equiv 0$ or $1\pmod 4$, so $a^2+b^2\in\{0,1,2\}\pmod 4$ and can never be $\equiv 3$. The deeper content of the theorem is the converse --- that $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ always is a sum of two squares --- which is exactly the splitting of $p$ in the UFD $Z[i]$.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Deciding how a rational prime $p$ factors in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{method}{Deciding how a rational prime $p$ factors in $Z[i]$}
Trigger. You must factor a rational prime in the Gauss integers, or test whether $x^2+1$ factors mod $p$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Reduce $p$ modulo $4$.
\item If $p=2$: ramified, $2=-i(1+i)^2$, with $\Nm(1+i)=2$.
\item If $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$: split. Solve $a^2+b^2=p$ (equivalently find $c$ with $c^2\equiv -1\bmod p$, then $\gcd_{Z[i]}(p,\,c+i)$ gives the factor). Then $p=(a+bi)(a-bi)$ with both factors Gauss primes of norm $p$.
\item If $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$: inert, $p$ stays a Gauss prime, $\Nm(p)=p^2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: The split primes $5,13,17$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The split primes $5,13,17$}
Factor $5$, $13$, and $17$ into Gauss primes.
\wrec All three are $\equiv 1\pmod 4$ ($5,13,17$), so by Theorem~ [REF:art:gauss_primes:main@c8] (d) each splits as a product of conjugate Gauss primes; find $a,b$ with $a^2+b^2=p$.
\wsol $5=4+1=2^2+1^2$, so $5=(2+i)(2-i)$. $13=9+4=3^2+2^2$, so $13=(3+2i)(3-2i)$. $17=16+1=4^2+1^2$, so $17=(4+i)(4-i)$. In each case both factors have norm $p$ (a rational prime), hence are Gauss primes by part~(a). Check. $(2+i)(2-i)=4-i^2=5$; $(3+2i)(3-2i)=9-4i^2=13$; $(4+i)(4-i)=16-i^2=17$. Correspondingly $-1$ is a QR: $2^2\equiv -1\ (5)$, $5^2=25\equiv -1\ (13)$, $4^2=16\equiv -1\ (17)$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The ramified prime $2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The ramified prime $2$}
Factor $2$ in $Z[i]$ and explain why it is special.
\wrec $2$ is the unique prime where the two conjugate factors are associates rather than distinct --- the ramified case.
\wsol $2=1+1=1^2+1^2=(1+i)(1-i)$. Here $1-i=-i(1+i)$ (since $-i(1+i)=-i-i^2=1-i$), so the two factors are associates of the single Gauss prime $\pi=1+i$, with $\Nm(1+i)=2$. Thus $2=(1+i)(1-i)=-i(1+i)^2$ is, up to a unit, the square of one Gauss prime. Check. $-i(1+i)^2=-i(1+2i+i^2)=-i(2i)=-2i^2=2$. Unlike $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ where $2+i$ and $2-i$ are non-associate, here both ``factors'' are $\pm i$-multiples of $1+i$, which is what ramified means.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The inert primes $3,7,11$}
Show $3$, $7$, and $11$ remain prime in $Z[i]$, and connect to $x^2+1$ mod $p$.
\wrec All are $\equiv 3\pmod 4$ ($3,7,11$), so by Theorem~ [REF:art:gauss_primes:main@c8] (c) they are inert: $p$ stays a Gauss prime, equivalently $x^2+1$ is irreducible mod $p$ and $-1$ is a non-residue.
\wsol Suppose $3=\alpha\beta$ with neither a unit. Taking norms, $9=\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)$ with $\Nm(\alpha),\Nm(\beta)>1$, forcing $\Nm(\alpha)=3$. But $\Nm(a+bi)=a^2+b^2=3$ has no integer solution (squares are $0,1,4,9,\dots$; no two sum to $3$). So $3$ has no proper factor and is a Gauss prime. The same norm argument kills $7$ ($a^2+b^2=7$ unsolvable: $0,1,4$ give sums $0,1,2,4,5,8$, never $7$) and $11$ ($a^2+b^2=11$ unsolvable). Check. Consistently, $-1$ is a non-residue: mod $3$ the squares are $\{0,1\}$, mod $7$ they are $\{0,1,2,4\}$, mod $11$ they are $\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}$ --- none contains $p-1\equiv -1$. So $x^2+1$ is irreducible in each $\F_p[x]$ and $\F_p[x]/(x^2+1)=\F_{p^2}$ is a field, matching $Z[i]/(p)$ being a field.
\end{wex}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Gauss Primes and Sums of Two Squares > The classification theorem
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Split factors are not always associates --- only $2$ ramifies. For $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ the conjugates $a+bi$ and $a-bi$ are non-associate Gauss primes (e.g. $2+i$ and $2-i$ are not $\pm 1,\pm i$ multiples of each other). Only $p=2$ has its two factors associate, because $(1+i)/(1-i)=i$ is a unit. Calling $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ ``ramified'' is the common slip; $5$ is split, $2$ is ramified.
\end{pitfall}

Section: Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs > Gauss Primes and Sums of Two Squares > The Gauss-prime lattice in the plane
Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Reading the diagram: the orange point $1+i$ (and its three unit-multiples) is the lone ramified prime, nearest the origin off the axes. The blue points are split primes, each appearing as a conjugate pair $a\pm bi$ symmetric across the real axis, together with their $i$-rotations --- e.g. $2\pm i,\,1\pm 2i$ above $5$, and $3\pm 2i,\,2\pm 3i$ above $13$. The red points $\pm 3,\pm 3i$ are inert: the rational prime $3$ and its unit multiples, sitting squarely on the axes because $\Nm=9$ cannot be written $a^2+b^2$ with both $a,b$ nonzero small. The eightfold symmetry of the whole picture is the action of the units $\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$ together with complex conjugation.
\end{remark}

\item [DF 8.1.3] Let $R$ be a Euclidean Domain and $m$ the minimum norm of a nonzero element. Prove every nonzero element of norm $m$ is a unit, and deduce a nonzero element of norm zero (if any) is a unit.
\item [DF 8.1.4] In a Euclidean Domain: (a) if $(a,b)=1$ and $a\mid bc$ then $a\mid c$, and more generally $\frac{a}{(a,b)}\mid c$; (b) describe the full solution set of $ax+by=N$ given one solution.
\item [DF 8.1.9] Prove the ring of integers $O$ in $Q(\sqrt{2})$ is a Euclidean Domain with respect to the absolute value of the field norm.
\item [DF 8.1.10] Prove $Z[i]/I$ is finite for any nonzero ideal $I$ of $Z[i]$, using $I=(\alpha)$ and the Division Algorithm.
\item [DF 8.2.1] Prove that in a PID two ideals $(a),(b)$ are comaximal iff a gcd of $a$ and $b$ is $1$.
\item [DF 8.2.2] Prove any two nonzero elements of a PID have a least common multiple.
\item [DF 8.2.3] Prove that a quotient of a PID by a prime ideal is again a PID.
\item [DF 8.2.7] (Bezout Domains) Prove an integral domain $R$ is a Bezout Domain iff every pair $a,b$ has a gcd of the form $ra+sb$; that every finitely generated ideal is principal; and that every element of $\Frac(R)$ is $a/b$ with $a,b$ coprime.
\item [DF 8.2.8] Prove that if $R$ is a PID and $D$ a multiplicatively closed subset with $0\notin D$, then $D^{-1}R$ is a PID.
\item [DF 8.3.1] For $G=\units{Q}$ and the map $\varphi$ swapping the primes $2,3$ in prime factorizations: (a) prove $\varphi$ is a group isomorphism; (b) prove there are infinitely many isomorphisms $G\to G$.

\item [DF 8.3.4] Prove that if an integer is a sum of two rational squares, then it is a sum of two integer squares.
\item [DF 8.3.6] (a) Prove $Z[i]/(1+i)$ is a field of order $2$; (b) for a prime $q\equiv 3\ (4)$ prove $Z[i]/(q)$ is a field with $q^2$ elements; (c) for $p\equiv 1\ (4)$ with $p=\pi\overline{\pi}$, apply CRT to show $Z[i]/(p)\congZ[i]/(\pi)\timesZ[i]/(\overline{\pi})$ and each factor is a field of order $p$.
\item [Artin 1.1] Prove a positive integer that is not a perfect square is not the square of a rational number.
\item [Artin 1.3] (CRT) For coprime $n,m$ and arbitrary $a,b$, prove $x\equiv a\ (m)$, $x\equiv b\ (n)$ has a solution, and determine all solutions.
\item [Artin 1.5] For coprime integers $a,b$, prove there are integers $m,n$ with $a^m+b^n\equiv 1\ (ab)$.
\item [Artin 2.4] Adapt Euclid's argument to prove that for any field $F$ there are infinitely many monic irreducible polynomials in $F[x]$.
\item [Artin 2.6] Prove the rings (a) $Z[\omega]$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, and (b) $Z[\sqrt{-2}]$ are Euclidean domains.
\item [Artin 2.7] Prove the gcd of two integers in $Z$ equals their gcd in the ring of Gauss integers.
\item [Artin 2.9] Prove the ring $F[x,x^{-1}]$ of Laurent polynomials over a field $F$ is a PID.
\item [Artin 2.10] Prove the ring $R[[t]]$ of formal power series is a UFD.
\item [Artin 3.1] For $\varphi:Z[x]\toC$ with (a) $\varphi(x)=1+\sqrt{2}$, (b) $\varphi(x)=\tfrac12+\sqrt{2}$: is $\ker\varphi$ principal, and if so find a generator.
\item [Artin 3.2] Prove two integer polynomials are relatively prime in $Q[x]$ iff the ideal they generate in $Z[x]$ contains a nonzero integer.
\item [Artin 3.6] For $\alpha\inC$, prove the kernel of the substitution map $Z[x]\toC$, $x\mapsto\alpha$, is a principal ideal and describe its generator.
\item [Artin 4.3] Decide whether $x^4+6x^3+9x+3$ generates a maximal ideal in $Q[x]$.
\item [Artin 4.4] Factor $x^5+2x^4+3x^3+3x+5$ modulo $2$, modulo $3$, and in $Q$.
\item [Artin 4.5] Which of $x^2+27x+213$, $8x^3-6x+1$, $x^3+6x^2+1$, $x^5-3x^4+3$ are irreducible in $Q[x]$?
\item [Artin 4.6] Factor $x^5+5x+5$ into irreducibles in $Q[x]$ and in $F_2[x]$.
\item [Artin 4.8] How can $f(x)=x^4+bx^2+c$ factor over a field $F$?

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Polynomial Rings > Definitions and Basic Properties > The polynomial ring $R[x]$
Type: definition
Title: The polynomial ring in one variable
Content:
\begin{definition}[The polynomial ring in one variable]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The polynomial ring $R[x]$ is the set of all formal
finite sums
\[
f(x)=a_n x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_1 x + a_0,\qquad a_i\in R,
\]
where the coefficient $a_i$ lies in $R$ for each $i$ and only finitely many are
nonzero. If $a_n\neq 0$ we call $n=\deg f$ the degree of $f$, $a_n$ the
leading coefficient $\LC(f)$, and $a_n x^n$ the leading term. A polynomial
is monic if $\LC(f)=1$. The zero polynomial has, by convention, $\deg 0=-\infty$
(equivalently, undefined); it has no leading term. Polynomials of degree $0$ together with
$0$ are the constants $R\subseteq R[x]$.

Addition and multiplication are: with $f=\sum_i a_i x^i$ and $g=\sum_j b_j x^j$,
\[
f+g=\sum_k (a_k+b_k)\,x^k,\qquad
fg=\sum_k\Big(\textstyle\sum_{i+j=k} a_i b_j\Big)x^k .
\]
\end{definition}

Content:
\begin{remark}
The coefficient of $x^k$ in $fg$ is the convolution $c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j$. Two
polynomials are equal iff all corresponding coefficients are equal; $R[x]$ is a commutative
ring with identity $1\in R$, and $R\hookrightarrow R[x]$ as the constants makes $R$ a
subring.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Computing $f+g$ and $fg$ by hand
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $f+g$ and $fg$ by hand}
Trigger. You must add or multiply concrete polynomials, possibly over a ring with
zero divisors or characteristic $n$.\\[2pt]
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Align by power. Write each polynomial with explicit $x^k$ slots; treat
 missing powers as coefficient $0$.
 \item Add: add coefficients slot by slot in $R$ (reduce mod $n$ in
 $Z/(n)Z$).
 \item Multiply: for each output power $k$, sum $a_ib_j$ over all $i+j=k$
 (convolution); reduce each coefficient in $R$.
 \item Read off the leading term last; in $Z/(n)Z$ a top coefficient can vanish,
 so recompute $\deg$ after reducing.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Multiplying in $Z/(3)Z[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Multiplying in $Z/(3)Z[x]$}
Compute $(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)$ in $Z/(3)Z[x]$.
\wrec Convolution multiplication with coefficient arithmetic done mod $3$.
\wsol
Expand, then reduce each coefficient mod $3$:
\[
(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)=2x^3+4x^2+x^2+2x+x+2=2x^3+5x^2+3x+2 .
\]
Reduce mod $3$: $5\equiv 2$, $3\equiv 0$, so
\[
(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)=2x^3+2x^2+2 \in Z/(3)Z[x].
\]
Check (convolution by slots). $a=(1,1,2)$ for $(a_0,a_1,a_2)$, $b=(2,1)$.
$c_0=1\cdot2=2$; $c_1=1\cdot2+1\cdot1=3\equiv0$; $c_2=2\cdot2+1\cdot1=5\equiv2$;
$c_3=2\cdot1=2$. Coefficients $(2,0,2,2)$ match. $\deg=3=2+1$, as expected since
$Z/(3)Z$ is a field (a domain), so no degree drop. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Degree can drop in $Z/(4)Z[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Degree can drop in $Z/(4)Z[x]$}
In $Z/(4)Z[x]$ compute $(2x+1)^2$ and report its degree.
\wrec $Z/(4)Z$ has the zero divisor $2$ ($2\cdot2=4\equiv0$); the top coefficient of a
product may vanish.
\wsol
\[
(2x+1)^2=4x^2+4x+1 .
\]
Reduce mod $4$: $4\equiv0$, $4\equiv0$, so $(2x+1)^2=1$ in $Z/(4)Z[x]$.
Check. The leading coefficients multiply to $2\cdot2=4\equiv0$, so the $x^2$ term
dies and the $x$ term dies too. Result is the constant $1$, of degree $0$, while
$\deg(2x+1)+\deg(2x+1)=1+1=2$. Hence $\deg(fg)<\deg f+\deg g$. This is impossible over an
integral domain, but $Z/(4)Z$ is not a domain. As a bonus, $2x+1$ is a unit of
$Z/(4)Z[x]$ with inverse itself. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\wrec $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ has the zero divisor $2$ ($2\cdot2=4\equiv0$); the top coefficient of a
product may vanish.

Reduce mod $4$: $4\equiv0$, $4\equiv0$, so $(2x+1)^2=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

\begin{wex}{Adding and multiplying in $Z/(5)Z[x]$}
In $Z/(5)Z[x]$, let $f=3x^2+4$ and $g=2x+3$. Compute $f+g$ and $fg$.
\wrec Slot addition and convolution, all coefficients mod $5$.
\wsol
$f=3x^2+0\cdot x+4$, $g=0\cdot x^2+2x+3$.
\[
f+g=3x^2+2x+7\equiv 3x^2+2x+2 .
\]
For $fg$: $c_0=4\cdot3=12\equiv2$; $c_1=4\cdot2=8\equiv3$; $c_2=3\cdot3=9\equiv4$;
$c_3=3\cdot2=6\equiv1$. So
\[
fg=x^3+4x^2+3x+2 \inZ/(5)Z[x].
\]
Check. $Z/(5)Z$ is a field, so $\deg(fg)=2+1=3$ and $\LC(fg)=3\cdot2=6\equiv1$,
matching the $x^3$ coefficient. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A product over $Z$ with telescoping middle terms
Content:
\begin{wex}{A product over $Z$ with telescoping middle terms}
Compute $(x^2+x+1)(x-1)$ in $Z[x]$.
\wrec Ordinary convolution over the domain $Z$; watch cancellation in the interior
coefficients.
\wsol
\[
(x^2+x+1)(x-1)=x^3+x^2+x-x^2-x-1=x^3-1 .
\]
Check. $c_0=1\cdot(-1)=-1$; $c_1=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$;
$c_2=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$; $c_3=1\cdot1=1$. So $x^3-1$. Interior cancellation does
not lower the degree because the top coefficient $1\cdot1=1\neq0$. \checkmark
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A product over $\mathbb{Z}$ with telescoping middle terms}
Compute $(x^2+x+1)(x-1)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Ordinary convolution over the domain $\mathbb{Z}$; watch cancellation in the interior
coefficients.
\wsol
\[
(x^2+x+1)(x-1)=x^3+x^2+x-x^2-x-1=x^3-1 .
\]
\textit{Check.} $c_0=1\cdot(-1)=-1$; $c_1=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$;
$c_2=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$; $c_3=1\cdot1=1$. So $x^3-1$. Interior cancellation does
\emph{not} lower the degree because the top coefficient $1\cdot1=1\neq0$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Degree of a product is the sum of degrees'' is only guaranteed when $R$ is an integral
domain. Over $Z/(4)Z$, $Z/(6)Z$, or any ring with zero divisors the leading coefficients
can multiply to $0$ and the degree drops (or the product becomes a unit/constant). Always
reduce coefficients before reading off the degree.
\end{pitfall}

Type: definition
Title: Polynomials in several variables, by iteration
Content:
\begin{definition}[Polynomials in several variables, by iteration]
Define $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ recursively by
\[
R[x_1,\dots,x_n]:=\big(R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]\big)[x_n].
\]
Concretely an element is a finite sum of monomials
$a\,x_1^{d_1}x_2^{d_2}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ with $a\in R$. The (total) degree of such a
monomial is $d_1+\dots+d_n$, and the total degree of $f\neq 0$ is the maximum total
degree of a monomial appearing with nonzero coefficient. A polynomial is homogeneous
of degree $d$ if every monomial has total degree $d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
Iteration means a polynomial in $Z[x,y]$ may be read as a polynomial in $y$ whose
coefficients lie in $Z[x]$, or vice versa. For instance
$x^2y+xy+3y+x^2 = (x^2+x+3)\,y + x^2 \in (Z[x])[y]$, a degree-$1$ polynomial in $y$.

Title: $Z[x,y]$ and its total degree
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z[x,y]$ and its total degree}
Let $f=x^2y+3xy^2+y+5\inZ[x,y]$. Find the total degree of $f$, view $f$ in
$(Z[x])[y]$, and compute $f\cdot y$.
\wrec Total degree counts the largest $d_x+d_y$; iteration groups by powers of $y$.
\wsol
Monomial total degrees: $x^2y\!:2{+}1{=}3$; $3xy^2\!:1{+}2{=}3$; $y\!:1$; $5\!:0$. So
$\deg f=3$. As an element of $(Z[x])[y]$:
\[
f=(3x)\,y^2+(x^2+1)\,y+5,\qquad \deg_y f=2,\ \LC_y(f)=3x .
\]
Multiplying by $y$ shifts every $y$-power up by one:
\[
f\cdot y=x^2y^2+3xy^3+y^2+5y,\qquad \deg(f\cdot y)=4 .
\]
Check. $3x\cdot y^2\cdot y=3xy^3$ has total degree $1+3=4$, the new maximum;
since $Z$ is a domain, $\deg(f\cdot y)=\deg f+\deg y=3+1=4$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-ed40eb4f1d14906d4a7c
Content:
\begin{proof}
Write $f=a_mx^m+\cdots$, $g=b_nx^n+\cdots$ with $a_m=\LC(f)\neq0$, $b_n=\LC(g)\neq0$.
The coefficient of $x^{m+n}$ in $fg$ is $a_mb_n$. Since $R$ is a domain and
$a_m,b_n\neq0$, we have $a_mb_n\neq0$. No monomial of higher degree can occur, so $fg\neq0$,
$\deg(fg)=m+n$, and $\LC(fg)=a_mb_n$. This proves (1) and shows $R[x]$ has no zero divisors,
i.e.\ (3).

For (2): if $u\in\units{R}$ then $u$ is a unit in $R[x]$, so $\units{R}\subseteq\units{R[x]}$.
Conversely, suppose $fg=1$ in $R[x]$. Taking degrees and using (1),
$\deg f+\deg g=\deg 1=0$, and since degrees are nonnegative integers, $\deg f=\deg g=0$.
Thus $f,g\in R$ and $fg=1$ in $R$, so $f\in\units{R}$. Hence
$\units{R[x]}\subseteq\units{R}$.
\end{proof}

$\deg(fg)=m+n$, and $\LC(fg)=a_mb_n$. This proves (1) and shows $R[x]$ has no zero divisors,
i.e.\ (3).

For (2): if $u\in\units{R}$ then $u$ is a unit in $R[x]$, so $\units{R}\subseteq\units{R[x]}$.
Conversely, suppose $fg=1$ in $R[x]$. Taking degrees and using (1),
$\deg f+\deg g=\deg 1=0$, and since degrees are nonnegative integers, $\deg f=\deg g=0$.
Thus $f,g\in R$ and $fg=1$ in $R$, so $f\in\units{R}$. Hence
$\units{R[x]}\subseteq\units{R}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{method}{Degree arguments}
Trigger. You must show a product is nonzero, identify the units of $R[x]$, prove an
element is irreducible by degree count, or rule out a factorization.\\[2pt]
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Confirm the base ring is a domain. Only then is $\deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g$
 and $\LC(fg)=\LC(f)\LC(g)$ valid.
 \item Take degrees of the hypothesized identity (e.g.\ $fg=1$, or $fg=h$).
 \item Solve the integer equation in nonnegative degrees; small/forced solutions
 pin down $\deg f,\deg g$.
 \item Translate back to a statement about constants/leading coefficients in $R$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: Units of $Z[x]$ versus $Q[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Units of $Z[x]$ versus $Q[x]$}
Determine $\units{Z[x]}$ and $\units{Q[x]}$.
\wrec $Z$ and $Q$ are integral domains, so $\units{R[x]}=\units{R}$.
\wsol
$Z$ is a domain with $\units{Z}=\{\pm1\}$, so by Prop.\ 4(2),
$\units{Z[x]}=\{\,1,\,-1\,\}$. In particular $x$, $2$, and $x+1$ are non-units in $Z[x]$.
$Q$ is a field, so $\units{Q}=Q\setminus\{0\}$ and
$\units{Q[x]}=Q\setminus\{0\}$, the nonzero constants; e.g.\ $\tfrac12$ is a unit but $x$
is not.
Check (degree argument). If $fg=1$ in $Z[x]$ then $\deg f=\deg g=0$, so $f,g\inZ$
with $fg=1$, forcing $f=\pm1$. The same argument over $Q$ gives nonzero rationals.
\checkmark
\end{wex}

Determine $\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}$ and $\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}$.

$\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain with $\units{\mathbb{Z}}=\{\pm1\}$, so by Prop.\ 4(2),
$\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}=\{\,1,\,-1\,\}$. In particular $x$, $2$, and $x+1$ are non-units in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
$\mathbb{Q}$ is a field, so $\units{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ and
$\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}=\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$, the nonzero constants; e.g.\ $\tfrac12$ is a unit but $x$
is not.
\textit{Check (degree argument).} If $fg=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ then $\deg f=\deg g=0$, so $f,g\in\mathbb{Z}$
with $fg=1$, forcing $f=\pm1$. The same argument over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives nonzero rationals.

Title: $2x+1$ is a unit in $Z/(4)Z[x]$ but the proposition does not apply
Content:
\begin{wex}{$2x+1$ is a unit in $Z/(4)Z[x]$ but the proposition does not apply}
Show $2x+1\in\units{Z/(4)Z[x]}$, and explain why this does not contradict Prop.\ 4(2).
\wrec A degree-$1$ unit can only exist when the base ring is not a domain.
\wsol
$(2x+1)(2x+1)=4x^2+4x+1=1$ in $Z/(4)Z[x]$ (computed earlier), so $2x+1$ is its own inverse,
hence a unit of degree $1$.
Check. Prop.\ 4 requires $R$ to be an integral domain; $Z/(4)Z$ is not
($2\cdot2=0$), so $\units{Z/(4)Z[x]}\neq(Z/(4)Z)^{\times}$. Indeed the nilpotent $2$ produces
the non-constant unit $1+2x$ (a unit because $2$ is nilpotent: $(1+2x)(1-2x)=1-4x^2=1$).
\checkmark
\end{wex}

\wrec A degree-$1$ unit can only exist when the base ring is \emph{not} a domain.
\wsol
$(2x+1)(2x+1)=4x^2+4x+1=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ (computed earlier), so $2x+1$ is its own inverse,
hence a unit of degree $1$.
\textit{Check.} Prop.\ 4 requires $R$ to be an integral domain; $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ is not
($2\cdot2=0$), so $\units{\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]}\neq(\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. Indeed the nilpotent $2$ produces

Type: example
Title: No nontrivial factorization of a linear polynomial over a domain
Content:
\begin{wex}{No nontrivial factorization of a linear polynomial over a domain}
Over the domain $Z$, show $x$ cannot be written as a product of two non-units of $Z[x]$.
\wrec Pure degree count plus $\units{Z[x]}=\{\pm1\}$.
\wsol
Suppose $x=fg$ with $f,g\inZ[x]$. By additivity $\deg f+\deg g=\deg x=1$, so one factor,
say $g$, has degree $0$: $g=c\inZ$. Then $f=ax+b$ and $cf=x$ forces $ca=1$, $cb=0$, so
$c\in\{\pm1\}$, i.e.\ $c$ is a unit. Hence any factorization of $x$ has a unit factor; $x$ is
irreducible in $Z[x]$.
Check. The leading coefficient equation $\LC(f)\LC(g)=1$ in $Z$ forces a unit
leading coefficient. \checkmark
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{No nontrivial factorization of a linear polynomial over a domain}
Over the domain $\mathbb{Z}$, show $x$ cannot be written as a product of two non-units of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Pure degree count plus $\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}=\{\pm1\}$.
\wsol
Suppose $x=fg$ with $f,g\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. By additivity $\deg f+\deg g=\deg x=1$, so one factor,
say $g$, has degree $0$: $g=c\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then $f=ax+b$ and $cf=x$ forces $ca=1$, $cb=0$, so
$c\in\{\pm1\}$, i.e.\ $c$ is a unit. Hence any factorization of $x$ has a unit factor; $x$ is
irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\textit{Check.} The leading coefficient equation $\LC(f)\LC(g)=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ forces a unit
leading coefficient. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Title: $R[x]$ inherits domain-ness, but a quotient need not
Content:
\begin{wex}{$R[x]$ inherits domain-ness, but a quotient need not}
Decide whether $Z[x]$ is a domain and whether $Z/(6)Z[x]$ is a domain.
\wrec $R$ a domain $\Rightarrow R[x]$ a domain; $R$ with zero divisors $\Rightarrow R[x]$
has them too.
\wsol
$Z$ is a domain, so $Z[x]$ is a domain by Prop.\ 4(3). $Z/(6)Z$ is not a domain
($2\cdot3=0$), and these zero divisors persist as constants in $Z/(6)Z[x]$:
$\bar2\cdot\bar3=\bar0$ with $\bar2,\bar3\neq0$. So $Z/(6)Z[x]$ is not a domain.
Check. $\deg$ additivity fails in $Z/(6)Z[x]$, e.g.\ $(3x+1)(2x)=6x^2+2x=2x$ drops
from degree $2$ to degree $1$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Decide whether $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain and whether $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain.
\wrec $R$ a domain $\Rightarrow R[x]$ a domain; $R$ with zero divisors $\Rightarrow R[x]$
has them too.
\wsol
$\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain, so $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain by Prop.\ 4(3). $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} a domain
($2\cdot3=0$), and these zero divisors persist as constants in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$:
$\bar2\cdot\bar3=\bar0$ with $\bar2,\bar3\neq0$. So $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not a domain.

Type: proposition
Title: D\&F 9.1, Prop.\ 2
Content:
\begin{proposition}[D\&F 9.1, Prop.\ 2]
Let $I$ be an ideal of the commutative ring $R$, and let
\[
I[x]:=\{\,f\in R[x]\ \st\ every coefficient of f lies in I\,\}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[(1)] $I[x]$ is an ideal of $R[x]$;
 \item[(2)] $R[x]/I[x]\cong (R/I)[x]$;
 \item[(3)] if $I$ is a prime ideal of $R$, then $I[x]$ is a prime ideal of $R[x]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Polynomial Rings > Definitions and Basic Properties > Ideal extension $I[x]$, the quotient $R[x]/I[x]$, and primeness
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-1fb4f4a024094e973eb3
Content:
\begin{proof}
Consider the reduction-of-coefficients map. Reducing each coefficient mod $I$ via
$R\twoheadrightarrow R/I$, $a\mapsto\bar a$, induces a ring homomorphism
\[
\varphi: R[x]\longrightarrow (R/I)[x],\qquad
\varphi\Big(\textstyle\sum_i a_i x^i\Big)=\textstyle\sum_i \bar a_i\, x^i .
\]
It is a homomorphism because reduction mod $I$ respects the coefficient formulas for sums
($\overline{a_k+b_k}=\bar a_k+\bar b_k$) and products
($\overline{\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j}=\sum_{i+j=k}\bar a_i\bar b_j$). It is surjective since any
$\sum \bar c_i x^i$ is hit by $\sum c_i x^i$. Its kernel is exactly the polynomials all of
whose coefficients reduce to $0$, i.e.\ all of whose coefficients lie in $I$:
$\ker\varphi=I[x]$. In particular $I[x]$ is an ideal (a kernel), proving (1), and the
First Isomorphism Theorem gives
\[
R[x]/I[x]\;\cong\;(R/I)[x],
\]
proving (2). For (3): if $I$ is prime then $R/I$ is an integral domain, so by Prop.\ 4(3)
$(R/I)[x]$ is an integral domain; hence $R[x]/I[x]\cong(R/I)[x]$ is a domain, which says
exactly that $I[x]$ is a prime ideal of $R[x]$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: {The reduction map $Z[x]\to\F_p[x]$}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{The reduction map $Z[x]\to\F_p[x]$}]
The most important instance is $R=Z$, $I=(p)$ for a prime $p$. Then $Z/(p)=\F_p$ and
Prop.\ 2 gives the surjective reduction mod $p$ homomorphism with kernel $(p)[x]=(p)$
(the polynomials with all coefficients divisible by $p$):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
Z[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "\bmod p"] & \F_p[x]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $Z[x]$ is the polynomial ring over the integers, a commutative domain. $\F_p[x]$ is the polynomial ring over the prime field $\F_p = Z/(p)$, also a commutative domain (in fact a Euclidean domain, since $\F_p$ is a field).
\dgi{Arrows:} The single arrow is the reduction-mod-$p$ ring homomorphism $\varphi: Z[x] \to \F_p[x]$ defined by $\varphi(\sum_i a_i x^i) = \sum_i \bar{a}_i x^i$, where $\bar{a}_i = a_i \bmod p$. It is surjective (every polynomial in $\F_p[x]$ is hit by any lift of its coefficients to $Z$), hence the double-head arrow.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is a single arrow, so there is no path equality to verify. The key identity is $\ker \varphi = (p)[x] = (p)$, the set of polynomials all of whose coefficients are divisible by $p$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism because coefficient-reduction mod $p$ is itself a ring homomorphism $Z \to \F_p$, and polynomial arithmetic (sum and convolution formulas) is defined coefficient-by-coefficient, so $\varphi(f+g) = \varphi(f)+\varphi(g)$ and $\varphi(fg) = \varphi(f)\varphi(g)$ follow termwise.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The surjectivity and kernel computation give, by the First Isomorphism Theorem, $Z[x]/(p) \cong \F_p[x]$. Since $\F_p[x]$ is a domain, $(p)$ is prime in $Z[x]$. This single arrow is the engine of the reduction-mod-$p$ irreducibility test: if $f$ is monic and $\varphi(f)$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$, then $f$ is irreducible in $Z[x]$. (Monic cannot be dropped: $f=3x+3=3(x+1)$ is reducible in $Z[x]$, yet $\varphi(f)=x+1$ is irreducible in $\F_2[x]$.)
\dgi{Concrete example:} With $p=3$: $\varphi(2x^2 + 3x + 7) = 2x^2 + 0\cdot x + 1 = 2x^2 + 1 \in \F_3[x]$. The polynomial $3x \in \ker\varphi$ since all coefficients are divisible by $3$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\varphi$ sends $x \mapsto p$ or changes the variable; it does not. Only the coefficients are reduced; the indeterminate $x$ is unchanged. Also, surjectivity does not mean $\varphi$ has a ring-homomorphism section: the map $\F_p[x] \to Z[x]$ sending $\bar{a}_i \mapsto a_i$ (any lift) is a set map but not a ring map.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that reducing coefficients mod a prime $p$ gives a surjective ring homomorphism from $Z[x]$ onto the simpler Euclidean domain $\F_p[x]$, whose kernel is exactly the ideal $(p)$, proving $(p)$ prime and enabling the reduction-mod-$p$ irreducibility criterion.
\end{dgx}
so $Z[x]/(p)\cong\F_p[x]$. Because $(p)$ is prime in $Z$, $(p)$ is prime in $Z[x]$ and
$\F_p[x]$ is an integral domain. This is the engine behind the reduction-mod-$p$
irreducibility test of \S9.4.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Recognizing and using $I[x]$ / reduction quotients
Content:
\begin{method}{Recognizing and using $I[x]$ / reduction quotients}
Trigger. You see a quotient $R[x]/J$ where $J$ is ``coefficients in some ideal,''
or you want to reduce a polynomial problem to a simpler ring.\\[2pt]
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Spot $I[x]$: $J$ consists of all polynomials whose coefficients lie in an
 ideal $I\subseteq R$ (e.g.\ $J=(p)$ in $Z[x]$ means ``all coefficients divisible by
 $p$'').
 \item Quotient downstairs first: replace $R$ by $R/I$ coefficientwise; the
 quotient is $(R/I)[x]$.
 \item Test primeness: $I[x]$ is prime $\iff$ $R/I$ is a domain $\iff$ $I$ is
 prime in $R$.
 \item To kill a variable too, quotient additionally by $(x)$ (or $(x-a)$): use
 evaluation $x\mapsto 0$ (or $x\mapsto a$).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}
