Title: $M/\ker\cong\im$ for a concrete map
Content:
\begin{wex}{$M/\ker\cong\im$ for a concrete map}
Let $\varphi\colonZ^2\toZ$ be the $Z$-linear map $\varphi(a,b)=2a-4b$. Identify $\ker\varphi$, $\im\varphi$, and verify the First Isomorphism Theorem.
\wrec $\varphi$ is $Z$-linear (additive, and $Z$-scalars come from additivity). Recognition: ``compute a quotient by realizing it as the kernel of an explicit map'' $=$ apply $M/\ker\cong\im$.
\wsol Image: $\im\varphi=\{2a-4b:a,b\inZ\}=2Z$ since $\gcd(2,4)=2$ and $2a-4b$ ranges over all multiples of $2$ (take $a=1,b=0$ to get $2$). Kernel: $2a-4b=0\iff a=2b$, so $\ker\varphi=\{(2b,b):b\inZ\}=Z\cdot(2,1)$, a rank-$1$ free submodule. First Theorem: $Z^2/Z(2,1)\cong 2Z\congZ$. Check via a basis: $\{(2,1),(1,0)\}$ is a $Z$-basis of $Z^2$ (the matrix with these as columns has determinant $2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1=-1$, a unit), so modding by $Z(2,1)$ leaves the free rank-$1$ quotient generated by the image of $(1,0)$, i.e.\ $Z$. Consistent with $2Z\congZ$.
\end{wex}

Title: $\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(m)Z)\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(m)Z)\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$}
Prove $\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(m)Z)\congZ/(d)Z$ where $d=\gcd(m,n)$, as abelian groups.
\wrec Maps out of the cyclic module $Z/(n)Z$ are determined by the image of $\bar 1$; the set of valid images is itself a subgroup of $Z/(m)Z$. Recognition: ``$\Hom$ out of a cyclic group'' $=$ annihilator subgroup of the codomain.
\wsol By the previous analysis, $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(\bar 1)$ is a map $\Theta\colon\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(m)Z)\toZ/(m)Z$, and it is an injective group homomorphism: $\Theta(\varphi+\psi)=(\varphi+\psi)(\bar 1)=\varphi(\bar 1)+\psi(\bar 1)$, and $\varphi$ is recovered from $\varphi(\bar 1)$. Its image is $\{\bar a\inZ/(m)Z: m\mid na\}=\{\bar a: \tfrac{m}{d}\mid a\}=\tfrac{m}{d}Z/(m)Z=\langle \overline{m/d}\rangle$. This is the unique subgroup of $Z/(m)Z$ of order $d$, which is cyclic, hence $\congZ/(d)Z$. Therefore $\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(m)Z)\congZ/(d)Z$. Check. $n=4,m=6$ gives $d=2$ and $\Hom\congZ/(2)Z$ (the two homs of the first example, $\bar 0$ and $\bar 3$, with $\bar 3=\overline{6/2}$ generating the order-$2$ subgroup inside $Z/(6)Z$). $n=m$ gives $d=n$ and $\Hom_Z(Z/(n)Z,Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$, matching $\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\Hom_R(R,M)\cong M$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Hom_R(R,M)\cong M$}
For any $R$-module $M$, show evaluation at $1$ gives an isomorphism $\Hom_R(R,M)\cong M$ (of $R$-modules when $R$ is commutative).
\wrec $R$ is the free module on one generator $1$; a hom out of it is determined by $\varphi(1)$, with no relations. Recognition: ``$\Hom$ out of the free rank-$1$ module'' $=$ evaluation at the basis element.
\wsol Define $\Phi\colon\Hom_R(R,M)\to M$ by $\Phi(\varphi)=\varphi(1)$. Homomorphism of abelian groups: $\Phi(\varphi+\psi)=(\varphi+\psi)(1)=\varphi(1)+\psi(1)$. Injective: if $\varphi(1)=0$ then $\varphi(r)=\varphi(r\cdot 1)=r\varphi(1)=0$ for all $r$, so $\varphi=0$. Surjective: given $m\in M$, define $\varphi_m(r)=rm$; this is $R$-linear since $\varphi_m(r r'+r'')=(rr'+r'')m=r(r'm)+r''m=r\varphi_m(r')+\varphi_m(r'')$, and $\Phi(\varphi_m)=\varphi_m(1)=m$. Hence $\Phi$ is a bijective homomorphism. When $R$ is commutative, $\Hom_R(R,M)$ is an $R$-module (see below) and $\Phi(s\varphi)=(s\varphi)(1)=s\,\varphi(1)=s\Phi(\varphi)$, so $\Phi$ is $R$-linear. Check. For $R=M=Z$, $\Hom_Z(Z,Z)\congZ$ (each hom is ``multiply by $\varphi(1)$''), as expected.
\end{wex}

Title: $F[x]$-module homs are operator-commuting linear maps
Content:
\begin{wex}{$F[x]$-module homs are operator-commuting linear maps}
Let $V,W$ be $F[x]$-modules, i.e.\ $F$-vector spaces with linear operators $T\colon V\to V$ (action of $x$ on $V$) and $S\colon W\to W$ (action of $x$ on $W$). Show $\Hom_{F[x]}(V,W)$ is exactly the set of $F$-linear maps $\varphi\colon V\to W$ with $\varphi\circ T=S\circ\varphi$.
\wrec $F[x]$ is generated as an $F$-algebra by $F$ and $x$; an $F[x]$-hom must be $F$-linear and respect multiplication by $x$. Recognition: ``module hom over $F[x]$'' $=$ intertwiner of the two operators.
\wsol An $F[x]$-linear $\varphi$ is in particular $F$-linear (restrict scalars to $F\subseteq F[x]$). The scalar rule on the generator $x$ reads $\varphi(x\cdot v)=x\cdot\varphi(v)$, i.e.\ $\varphi(Tv)=S\varphi(v)$, the intertwining relation $\varphi T=S\varphi$. Conversely, if $\varphi$ is $F$-linear and $\varphi T=S\varphi$, then for any $p(x)=\sum c_i x^i\in F[x]$ we have $p(x)\cdot v=p(T)v$ and
\[
\varphi(p(x)\cdot v)=\varphi\!\Big(\textstyle\sum_i c_i T^i v\Big)=\sum_i c_i\,\varphi(T^i v)=\sum_i c_i\,S^i\varphi(v)=p(S)\varphi(v)=p(x)\cdot\varphi(v),
\]
where $\varphi(T^i v)=S^i\varphi(v)$ follows by iterating $\varphi T=S\varphi$. So $\varphi$ is $F[x]$-linear. The intertwining condition is exactly commutativity of
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
V \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, "T"'] & W \arrow[d, "S"] \\
V \arrow[r, "\varphi"'] & W
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four copies of two $F$-vector spaces: $V$ appears at upper-left and lower-left, $W$ appears at upper-right and lower-right. Each space carries the structure of an $F[x]$-module: $V$ is equipped with the linear operator $T$ (multiplication by $x$ on $V$), and $W$ is equipped with $S$ (multiplication by $x$ on $W$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\varphi\colon V \to W$ (top and bottom, the $F$-linear map being tested); it appears twice because the square depicts the two ways of composing with the operators. $T\colon V \to V$ (left side, the operator on $V$, i.e.\ the action of $x$ on $V$). $S\colon W \to W$ (right side, the operator on $W$, the action of $x$ on $W$).
\dgi{What commutes:} The square commutes iff $S \circ \varphi = \varphi \circ T$: applying $\varphi$ then $S$ (top-then-right) equals applying $T$ then $\varphi$ (left-then-bottom). This is exactly the intertwining relation.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take $v \in V$. Right-then-down: $v \xmapsto{\varphi} \varphi(v) \xmapsto{S} S(\varphi(v))$. Down-then-right: $v \xmapsto{T} Tv \xmapsto{\varphi} \varphi(Tv)$. These agree iff $\varphi(Tv) = S\varphi(v)$ for all $v$, which is exactly the condition that $\varphi$ is $F[x]$-linear (respects multiplication by $x$). No well-definedness issue arises since $\varphi$ is an ordinary $F$-linear map; the content is purely the commutativity condition.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The worked example has just shown that $F[x]$-linearity of $\varphi$ is equivalent to commutativity of this square. This repackages the algebraic condition $\varphi(x \cdot v) = x \cdot \varphi(v)$ into a visual that makes the intertwining requirement impossible to misstate.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Let $V = W = F^2$, $T = S = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (the nilpotent Jordan block). The $F[x]$-module homs $\varphi$ are exactly the $F$-linear maps whose matrix $A$ satisfies $AS = SA$, i.e.\ matrices commuting with $T$. These are scalar multiples of $I$ and $T$ plus their span: $A = aI + bT$ for $a,b \in F$, giving a $2$-dimensional commutant.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the diagram as saying $\varphi = T$ or $\varphi = S$; in fact $\varphi$ goes between different spaces (or between two copies of the same space with possibly different operators) and the arrows $T,S$ represent the module structure, not the map being studied. Also, commutativity of the square is a condition on $\varphi$, not a conclusion that follows for free.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that an $F[x]$-module homomorphism is precisely an $F$-linear map $\varphi$ that intertwines the two operators, $\varphi\circ T=S\circ\varphi$ ($\varphi$ need not be invertible, so it need not conjugate $T$ into $S$), making the representation-theory notion of ``intertwiner'' identical to the module-homomorphism notion.
\end{dgx}
Check. If $V=W=F^2$ with $T=S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, then the $\varphi$ commuting with $T$ are exactly the matrices $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ ($a,b\in F$), a $2$-dimensional space, consistent with $\End_{F[x]}(V)$ being the commutant of $T$.
\end{wex}

Title: Quotient by a relation: $F[x]/(x^2)$ as a module map
Content:
\begin{wex}{Quotient by a relation: $F[x]/(x^2)$ as a module map}
Let $R=F[x]$ and $M=F[x]$. Consider $\pi\colon F[x]\to F[x]/(x^2)$, the projection. Use the First Theorem to identify the quotient, and find $\im$ and $\ker$ of multiplication-by-$x$ on $F[x]/(x^2)$.
\wrec Projection onto a quotient ring viewed as a module: $\ker=(x^2)$. Multiplication by $x$ is an $F[x]$-endomorphism. Recognition: ``identify a quotient module'' $=$ exhibit it as $\im$ of a surjection.
\wsol The projection $\pi\colon F[x]\to F[x]/(x^2)$ is surjective $F[x]$-linear with $\ker\pi=(x^2)$, so by Theorem~ [REF:thm:first@c10] , $F[x]/(x^2)\cong\im\pi=F[x]/(x^2)$ (tautologically), and as an $F$-vector space it has basis $\{\bar 1,\bar x\}$. Now let $\mu_x\colon F[x]/(x^2)\to F[x]/(x^2)$, $\mu_x(\bar f)=x\bar f$. Then $\mu_x(\bar 1)=\bar x$ and $\mu_x(\bar x)=\overline{x^2}=\bar 0$. So $\im\mu_x=F\bar x=(x)/(x^2)$ and $\ker\mu_x=F\bar x=(x)/(x^2)$ as well. By the First Theorem applied to $\mu_x$: $\big(F[x]/(x^2)\big)/\ker\mu_x\cong\im\mu_x$, i.e.\ $\big(F[x]/(x^2)\big)\big/\big((x)/(x^2)\big)\cong (x)/(x^2)$; both sides are $1$-dimensional over $F$, consistent. Check. $\dim_F\ker\mu_x+\dim_F\im\mu_x=1+1=2=\dim_F F[x]/(x^2)$ (rank--nullity).
\end{wex}

Title: Second and Third Theorems in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Second and Third Theorems in $Z$}
Inside $M=Z$, take $A=4Z$ and $B=6Z$. Verify the Second Isomorphism Theorem; then with $A=12Z\sgr B=4Z\sgrZ$, verify the Third.
\wrec Submodules of $Z$ are the ideals $nZ$; sums and intersections are computed by $\gcd$ and $\operatorname{lcm}$. Recognition: ``check an isomorphism theorem on a concrete lattice.''
\wsol Second: $A+B=4Z+6Z=\gcd(4,6)Z=2Z$ and $A\cap B=4Z\cap 6Z=\operatorname{lcm}(4,6)Z=12Z$. The theorem predicts $(A+B)/B\cong A/(A\cap B)$, i.e.\ $2Z/6Z\cong 4Z/12Z$. Both are cyclic of order $3$: $2Z/6Z=\{\bar 0,\bar 2,\bar 4\}\congZ/(3)Z$ and $4Z/12Z=\{\bar 0,\bar 4,\bar 8\}\congZ/(3)Z$. Confirmed. Third: with $12Z\sgr 4Z\sgrZ$, the theorem gives $(Z/12Z)/(4Z/12Z)\congZ/4Z$. Now $Z/12Z$ has order $12$, $4Z/12Z$ has order $3$, so the quotient has order $12/3=4$, matching $|Z/4Z|=4$. Confirmed.
\end{wex}

\begin{proposition}[$\Hom_R(M,N)$ is an abelian group] 
Let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. Define $(\varphi+\psi)(m)=\varphi(m)+\psi(m)$. Then $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is an abelian group with this addition, identity the zero map, and inverse $(-\varphi)(m)=-\varphi(m)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[$\Hom_R(M,N)$ is an $R$-module when $R$ is commutative] 
Suppose $R$ is commutative. For $r\in R$ and $\varphi\in\Hom_R(M,N)$ define $(r\varphi)(m)=r\big(\varphi(m)\big)$. Then $r\varphi\in\Hom_R(M,N)$ and this makes $\Hom_R(M,N)$ an $R$-module.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
If $R$ is not commutative, $(r\varphi)(m)=r\varphi(m)$ generally fails to be $R$-linear: the computation above breaks at $rs=sr$. So in general $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is only an abelian group, not an $R$-module. (It does carry actions by the center of $R$ and by $\End_R$, but not by $R$ itself in general.)
\end{pitfall}

Title: $\End_R(M)$ is a ring
Label: thm:endring@c10
Content:
\begin{theorem}[$\End_R(M)$ is a ring] 
$\End_R(M)=\Hom_R(M,M)$ is a ring with $1$ under pointwise addition and composition as multiplication; the identity is $\id_M$. When $R$ is commutative, $\End_R(M)$ is an $R$-algebra, and $M$ is naturally a left $\End_R(M)$-module via $\varphi\cdot m=\varphi(m)$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:endring@c10

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-dea3be14e20b62d07826
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Proposition~ [REF:prop:homgroup@c10] , $(\End_R(M),+)$ is an abelian group. Composition of $R$-linear maps is $R$-linear and associative, with two-sided identity $\id_M$. Distributivity: $(\varphi\circ(\psi+\chi))(m)=\varphi(\psi(m)+\chi(m))=\varphi\psi(m)+\varphi\chi(m)$ (using additivity of $\varphi$), and $((\psi+\chi)\circ\varphi)(m)=\psi\varphi(m)+\chi\varphi(m)$. Hence $\End_R(M)$ is a ring with $1=\id_M$. When $R$ is commutative, $r\mapsto r\cdot\id_M$ maps $R$ into the center of $\End_R(M)$ (since $r\,\id_M$ commutes with every $R$-linear $\varphi$: $\varphi(rm)=r\varphi(m)$), making $\End_R(M)$ an $R$-algebra. The action $\varphi\cdot m=\varphi(m)$ satisfies $(\varphi\psi)\cdot m=\varphi(\psi(m))=\varphi\cdot(\psi\cdot m)$ and $\id_M\cdot m=m$, so $M$ is a left $\End_R(M)$-module.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Recognizing $\End_R(M)$
Content:
\begin{method}{Recognizing $\End_R(M)$}
Trigger. Asked to compute or describe $\End_R(M)$ for a specific module.
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $R$ is commutative and $M=R^n$ is free, $\End_R(R^n)\cong M_n(R)$ (matrices acting on column vectors). For noncommutative $R$, left multiplication by a matrix is not $R$-linear: the $R$-linear maps of the left module $R^n$ (row vectors) are $v\mapsto vB$, and $\End_R(R^n)\cong M_n(R^{op})$, where the opposite ring $R^{op}$ is $R$ with the product $a*b=ba$ (so $\End_R(R)\cong R^{op}$).
\item If $M$ is an $F[x]$-module $(V,T)$, $\End_{F[x]}(V)$ is the commutant of $T$: all $F$-linear maps commuting with $T$.
\item If $M=Z/(n)Z$ over $Z$, $\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$ (each endomorphism is multiplication by a residue).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$ as a ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$ as a ring}
Show $\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)\congZ/(n)Z$ as rings.
\wrec Endomorphisms of the cyclic group $Z/(n)Z$ are determined by the image of $\bar 1$, which can be any element. Recognition: ``endomorphism ring of a cyclic module.''
\wsol By the analysis of homs out of cyclic modules with $m=n$ (so $d=\gcd(n,n)=n$), every $\bar a\inZ/(n)Z$ arises as $\varphi(\bar 1)$, giving $\varphi_a(\bar k)=k\bar a=\overline{ka}$. The map $\bar a\mapsto\varphi_a$ is a bijection $Z/(n)Z\to\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)$. It respects addition: $\varphi_a+\varphi_b=\varphi_{a+b}$. It respects multiplication via composition: $(\varphi_a\circ\varphi_b)(\bar 1)=\varphi_a(\bar b)=\overline{ab}=\varphi_{ab}(\bar 1)$, so $\varphi_a\circ\varphi_b=\varphi_{ab}$. And $\varphi_1=\id$. Hence $\bar a\mapsto\varphi_a$ is a ring isomorphism $Z/(n)Z\cong\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)$. Check. Units of $\End_Z(Z/(n)Z)$ $=$ automorphisms $\operatorname{Aut}(Z/(n)Z)\cong(Z/(n)Z)^\times$, matching the units on the ring side. For $n=6$: $|(Z/(6)Z)^\times|=\phi(6)=2$, and indeed $\operatorname{Aut}(Z/(6)Z)$ has order $2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\Hom$ is additive: $\Hom_R(M,N_1\oplus N_2)\cong\Hom_R(M,N_1)\oplus\Hom_R(M,N_2)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Hom$ is additive: $\Hom_R(M,N_1\oplus N_2)\cong\Hom_R(M,N_1)\oplus\Hom_R(M,N_2)$}
Establish the natural isomorphism of abelian groups (of $R$-modules if $R$ commutative).
\wrec A map into a direct sum is the same as a pair of maps into the factors, via the projections. Recognition: ``$\Hom$ into a direct sum splits.''
\wsol Let $p_i\colon N_1\oplus N_2\to N_i$ be the projections. Define $\Theta(\varphi)=(p_1\varphi,p_2\varphi)$. This is an additive map $\Hom_R(M,N_1\oplus N_2)\to\Hom_R(M,N_1)\oplus\Hom_R(M,N_2)$. Inverse: given $(\alpha,\beta)$, set $\Psi(\alpha,\beta)(m)=(\alpha(m),\beta(m))$, which is $R$-linear into $N_1\oplus N_2$. Then $\Theta\Psi(\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,\beta)$ and $\Psi\Theta(\varphi)=\varphi$ since $\varphi(m)=(p_1\varphi(m),p_2\varphi(m))$. Hence $\Theta$ is an isomorphism. Check. $\Hom_Z(Z,Z/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z)\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$, matching $\Hom_Z(Z,Z/(6)Z)\congZ/(6)Z$ and the CRT $Z/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\congZ/(6)Z$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-example, then repaired to a linear map
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-example, then repaired to a linear map}
Decide whether $\varphi\colonR^2\toR$, $\varphi(x,y)=x^2+y$, is an $R$-module homomorphism; then repair it.
\wrec Test the two axioms; squaring destroys additivity/scaling. Recognition: ``is this a module map?'' $=$ check linearity, do not assume.
\wsol Scalar test: $\varphi(r(x,y))=\varphi(rx,ry)=(rx)^2+ry=r^2x^2+ry$, whereas $r\varphi(x,y)=r(x^2+y)=rx^2+ry$. These differ (e.g.\ $r=2,(x,y)=(1,0)$: $\varphi(2,0)=4$ but $2\varphi(1,0)=2$). So $\varphi$ is not $R$-linear. Repair: drop the square: $\psi(x,y)=ax+by$ for fixed $a,b\inR$ is $R$-linear, and these are all of $\Hom_R(R^2,R)$ (the dual space), since $\psi$ is determined by $\psi(e_1)=a$, $\psi(e_2)=b$. Check. $\Hom_R(R^2,R)\congR^2$ as $R$-modules, consistent with $\Hom_R(R^2,M)\cong M^2$ at $M=R$.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Use the submodule criterion to show that kernels and images of $R$-module homomorphisms are submodules.

\item Show that the relation ``is $R$-module isomorphic to'' is an equivalence relation on any set of $R$-modules.

\item Give an explicit example of a map from one $R$-module to another which is not an $R$-module homomorphism but which is a homomorphism of the groups involved (i.e., is a $Z$-module homomorphism).

\item Let $A$ be any $Z$-module, let $a$ be any element of $A$ and let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that the map $\varphi_a : Z/(n)Z \to A$ given by $\varphi_a(\bar{k}) = ka$ is a well defined $Z$-module homomorphism if and only if $na = 0$. Prove that $\Hom_{Z}(Z/(n)Z, A) \cong A_n$, where $A_n = \{ a \in A \mid na = 0 \}$ (so $A_n$ is the annihilator in $A$ of the ideal $(n)$ of $Z$, cf. Exercise 10, Section 1).

\item Exhibit all $Z$-module homomorphisms from $Z/(3)Z$ to $Z/(9)Z$.

\item Prove that $\Hom_{Z}(Z/(n)Z, Z/(m)Z) \cong Z/((n,m))Z$.

\item Let $z$ be a fixed element of the center of $R$. Prove that the map $m \mapsto zm$ is an $R$-module homomorphism from $M$ to itself. Show that for a commutative ring $R$ the map from $R$ to $\End_R(M)$ given by $r \mapsto r\,\id_M$ is a ring homomorphism (where $\id_M$ is the identity endomorphism).

\item Let $\varphi : M \to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism. Prove that $\varphi(\Tor(M)) \subseteq \Tor(N)$ (cf. Exercise 8 in Section 1).

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Prove that $\Hom_R(R, M)$ and $M$ are isomorphic as left $R$-modules. [Show that each element of $\Hom_R(R, M)$ is determined by its value on the identity of $R$.]

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Prove that $\Hom_R(R, R)$ and $R$ are isomorphic as rings.

\item Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be $R$-modules and let $B_i$ be a submodule of $A_i$ for each $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. Prove that
\[ (A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n)/(B_1 \times \cdots \times B_n) \cong (A_1/B_1) \times \cdots \times (A_n/B_n). \]
[Recall Exercise 14 in Section 5.1.]

\item Let $I$ be a left ideal of $R$ and let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove
\[ R^n / I R^n \cong \underbrace{R/IR \times \cdots \times R/IR}_{n} \]
where $I R^n$ is defined as in Exercise 5 of Section 1. [Use the preceding exercise.]

\item Let $I$ be a nilpotent ideal in a commutative ring $R$ (cf. Exercise 37, Section 7.3), let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules and let $\varphi : M \to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism. Show that if the induced map $\bar{\varphi} : M/IM \to N/IN$ is surjective, then $\varphi$ is surjective.

\item Let $R = Z[x]$ be the ring of polynomials in $x$ and let $A = Z[\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots]$ be the ring of polynomials in independent indeterminates $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots$. Define an action of $R$ on $A$ as follows: (1) let $1 \in R$ act on $A$ as the identity, (2) for $n \geq 1$ let $x^n \circ 1 = \theta_n$, let $x^n \circ \theta_i = \theta_{n+i}$ for all $i \geq 1$, and let $x^n$ act as $0$ on every monomial of total degree at least $2$, and (3) extend $Z$-linearly in both variables, i.e., $(f+g) \circ a = f \circ a + g \circ a$ and $f \circ (a + b) = f \circ a + f \circ b$ for all $f, g \in R$ and $a, b \in A$. \\
(a) Show that $x^{p+q} \circ a = x^p \circ (x^q \circ a)$ for all $p, q \geq 0$ and every monomial $a$ (the key case is $x^{p+q} \circ \theta_i = \theta_{p+q+i}$), and deduce that $A$ is a (unital) $R$-module under this action. \\
(b) Show that the map $\varphi\colon R \to A$, $\varphi(r) = r \circ 1$, is an $R$-module homomorphism with $\varphi(1) = 1$, but is not a ring homomorphism.

\item Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Prove that if $R$ is a commutative ring then $\Hom_R(M, M)$ is an $R$-module. [Show how an element $r$ acting on the map $\varphi$ gives a map $r\varphi$, and that this map is again an $R$-module homomorphism.]

\item For any left ideal $I$ of $R$ define
\[ IM = \left\{ \sum_{finite} a_i m_i \mid a_i \in I, \; m_i \in M \right\} \]
to be the collection of all finite sums of elements of the form $am$ where $a \in I$ and $m \in M$. Prove that $IM$ is a submodule of $M$.
\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Show that the map $\varphi\colon M\to M$ defined by $\varphi(m)=rm$ for a fixed central element $r$ (i.e.\ $rs=sr$ for all $s\in R$) is an $R$-module homomorphism. Give an example with $R$ noncommutative and $r$ not central where $\varphi$ fails to be a homomorphism.

\item Let $N\sgr M$ be a submodule. Verify directly from the axioms that the quotient $M/N$ is a left $R$-module under $r(m+N)=rm+N$, including a check that this action is well defined.

\item Let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism. Prove that $\ker\varphi\sgr M$ and $\im\varphi\sgr N$, and that $\varphi$ is injective if and only if $\ker\varphi=0$.

\item Regard $Z/12Z$ as a $Z$-module. List all of its submodules, and for each submodule $N$ identify the quotient $(Z/12Z)/N$ up to isomorphism.

\item Let $R=Z$ and let $\varphi\colon Z^2\toZ$ be given by $\varphi(a,b)=2a-3b$. Compute $\ker\varphi$ and $\im\varphi$, and describe $Z^2/\ker\varphi$.

\item Let $V=R^2$ be viewed as an $R[x]$-module via the linear operator $T(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,-x_1)$ (so $x$ acts as $T$). Determine all $R[x]$-submodules of $V$. (Hint: these are the $T$-invariant subspaces.)

\item Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and let $A\subseteq M$ be any subset. Show that
\[
RA=\Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^k r_i a_i : k\inZ_{\ge 0},\ r_i\in R,\ a_i\in A\Bigr\}
\]
is the smallest submodule of $M$ containing $A$.

\item Let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism and let $L\sgr N$. Prove that $\varphi^{-1}(L)=\{m\in M : \varphi(m)\in L\}$ is a submodule of $M$ containing $\ker\varphi$.

\item Show that the map $\Hom_R(R,M)\to M$ sending $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(1)$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups, where $R$ is viewed as a left $R$-module over itself.

\item Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules. Prove that $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is an abelian group under pointwise addition. If $R$ is commutative, show that $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is itself an $R$-module via $(r\varphi)(m)=r\,\varphi(m)$, and explain where commutativity is used.

\item Let $R$ be commutative and let $M=R^n$ be the free module of rank $n$. Prove that $\End_R(M)=\Hom_R(M,M)$ is isomorphic to the ring $M_n(R)$ of $n\times n$ matrices over $R$.

\item Let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be a surjective $R$-module homomorphism. Establish a bijection between the submodules of $N$ and the submodules of $M$ that contain $\ker\varphi$, and show this bijection preserves inclusions.

\item Let $A,B\sgr M$. Prove the Second Isomorphism Theorem for modules:
\[
(A+B)/B \;\cong\; A/(A\cap B).
\]

\item Let $N\sgr L\sgr M$. Prove the Third Isomorphism Theorem for modules:
\[
(M/N)/(L/N)\;\cong\;M/L.
\]

\item Let $\varphi\colon Z/6Z\toZ/6Z$ be a $Z$-module homomorphism with $\varphi(\bar 1)=\bar 4$. Compute $\ker\varphi$ and $\im\varphi$ explicitly, and decide whether $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. Show that a left $R$-module $M$ is the same data as an abelian group $M$ together with a ring homomorphism $R\to\End_Z(M)$ that sends $1_R$ to $\id_M$ (this is where (M4) enters).

\end{exers}

\item Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules. Prove that $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is an abelian group under pointwise addition. If $R$ is commutative, show that $\Hom_R(M,N)$ is itself an $R$-module via $(r\varphi)(m)=r\,\varphi(m)$, and explain where commutativity is used.

\item Let $R$ be commutative and let $M=R^n$ be the free module of rank $n$. Prove that $\End_R(M)=\Hom_R(M,M)$ is isomorphic to the ring $M_n(R)$ of $n\times n$ matrices over $R$.

\item Let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be a surjective $R$-module homomorphism. Establish a bijection between the submodules of $N$ and the submodules of $M$ that contain $\ker\varphi$, and show this bijection preserves inclusions.

\item Let $A,B\sgr M$. Prove the Second Isomorphism Theorem for modules:
\[
(A+B)/B \;\cong\; A/(A\cap B).
\]

\item Let $N\sgr L\sgr M$. Prove the Third Isomorphism Theorem for modules:
\[
(M/N)/(L/N)\;\cong\;M/L.
\]

\item Let $\varphi\colon \mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-module homomorphism with $\varphi(\bar 1)=\bar 4$. Compute $\ker\varphi$ and $\im\varphi$ explicitly, and decide whether $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. Show that a left $R$-module $M$ is the same data as an abelian group $M$ together with a ring homomorphism $R\to\End_\mathbb{Z}(M)$ that sends $1_R$ to $\id_M$ (this is where (M4) enters).

\end{exers}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be commutative and $M$ an $R$-module. Recall $\ann_R(M)=\{r\in R : rm=0 for all m\in M\}$. Show $\ann_R(M)$ is a two-sided ideal of $R$, and that $M$ is naturally a module over $R/\ann_R(M)$. If $M=Z/4Z\oplusZ/6Z$ as a $Z$-module, compute $\ann_Z(M)$.

\item Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. An element $m\in M$ is a torsion element if $rm=0$ for some nonzero $r\in R$. Suppose $R$ is an integral domain. Prove that the set $\Tor(M)$ of torsion elements is a submodule of $M$, and that $M/\Tor(M)$ is torsion-free. Show by example that $\Tor(M)$ need not be a submodule when $R$ has zero divisors.

\item Let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism and suppose there exists an $R$-module homomorphism $\psi\colon N\to M$ with $\varphi\circ\psi=\id_N$. Prove that $M\cong\ker\varphi\oplus\im\psi$, and that $\psi$ is injective with $\im\psi$ a complement to $\ker\varphi$.

\item Let $R$ be commutative with $1\ne 0$. Prove that any two bases of the free module $R^n$ have the same cardinality (so $\rank$ is well defined), by reducing modulo a maximal ideal $m$ of $R$ and using dimension over the field $R/m$.

\item Let $M$ be an $R$-module generated by a single element, say $M=Rm$. Prove that $M\cong R/\ann_R(m)$ as $R$-modules, where $\ann_R(m)=\{r\in R : rm=0\}$. Conclude that every cyclic abelian group is $\congZ/nZ$ for some $n\ge 0$.

\item Let $R$ be a ring and let $0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi} B\xrightarrow{\varphi} C\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that the following are equivalent: (i) there is $s\colon C\to B$ with $\varphi\circ s=\id_C$; (ii) there is $r\colon B\to A$ with $r\circ\psi=\id_A$; (iii) $B\cong A\oplus C$ compatibly with $\psi,\varphi$.

\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item (Universal property of the quotient.) Let $N\sgr M$ and let $\pi\colon M\to M/N$ be the canonical projection. Prove that for every $R$-module homomorphism $f\colon M\to L$ with $N\subseteq\ker f$ there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\bar f\colon M/N\to L$ making the diagram commute:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & M/N \arrow[d, dashed, "{\exists!\,\bar f}"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item (Free module / universal property.) Let $A$ be a set, $R^{(A)}$ the free $R$-module on $A$, and $\iota\colon A\to R^{(A)}$ the inclusion of basis. Given an $R$-module $M$ and any set map $f\colon A\to M$, show there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\Phi\colon R^{(A)}\to M$ with $\Phi\circ\iota=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, dashed, "{\exists!\,\Phi}"] \\
& M
\end{tikzcd}\]
Deduce that every $R$-module is a quotient of a free $R$-module.

\item (Factoring a homomorphism.) Let $f\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-module homomorphism. Using the universal property of the quotient, construct the canonical factorization through $\bar f$ and prove $\bar f$ is injective:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[rr, bend left=30, "f"] & M/\ker f \arrow[r, dashed, hook, "\bar f"'] & N
\end{tikzcd}\]
Conclude the First Isomorphism Theorem $M/\ker f\cong\im f$.

\item (Lifting against a surjection.) Suppose
\[\begin{tikzcd}
& M \arrow[d, "f"] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
is given with $g$ surjective and $M$ free on a basis $\{e_i\}$. Construct a homomorphism $\tilde f\colon M\to B$ with $g\circ\tilde f=f$ by choosing preimages of $f(e_i)$, and explain which property of free modules makes the lift exist. Is $\tilde f$ unique?

\item (The five lemma.) Consider a commutative diagram of $R$-modules with exact rows
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
A_1 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "f_1"] & A_2 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "f_2"] & A_3 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "f_3"] & A_4 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "f_4"] & A_5 \arrow[d, "f_5"] \\
B_1 \arrow[r] & B_2 \arrow[r] & B_3 \arrow[r] & B_4 \arrow[r] & B_5
\end{tikzcd}\]
Prove the Five Lemma: if $f_1$ is surjective, $f_5$ is injective, and $f_2,f_4$ are isomorphisms, then $f_3$ is an isomorphism. (Do an honest diagram chase, surjectivity of $f_3$ first, then injectivity.)

\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Generation of Modules, Direct Sums, and Free Modules > Generating submodules, direct sums, and free modules
Type: definition
Title: Submodule generated by a subset
Content:
\begin{definition}[Submodule generated by a subset]
Let $M$ be an $R$-module and $A\subseteq M$ a subset.
\begin{itemize}
\item $RA \;=\; \{\, r_1a_1+\cdots+r_na_n \;:\; n\inZ_{\ge 0},\ r_i\in R,\ a_i\in A \,\}$ is the set of all (finite) $R$-linear combinations of elements of $A$ (with the empty sum equal to $0$). This is the submodule generated by $A$; it is the smallest submodule of $M$ containing $A$, and equals the intersection of all submodules containing $A$.
\item If $RA=M$ we say $A$ generates $M$, or $A$ is a set of generators.
\item $M$ is finitely generated if $M=RA$ for some finite set $A$.
\item $M$ is cyclic if $M=Rm=\{rm:r\in R\}$ for a single $m\in M$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Cyclic modules are quotients of $R$: $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Cyclic modules are quotients of $R$: $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$]
Let $M$ be an $R$-module and $m\in M$. Define $\pi:R\to M$ by $\pi(r)=rm$. Then $\pi$ is an $R$-module homomorphism with image $Rm$, and
\[
\ker\pi=\ann(m):=\{r\in R: rm=0\},
\]
which is a left ideal of $R$. Hence
\[
Rm \;\cong\; R/\ann(m)
\]
as left $R$-modules. In particular $M$ is cyclic iff $M\cong R/I$ for some left ideal $I$ of $R$.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-6c70674ac2e587565bfa
Content:
\begin{proof}
For $r,s\in R$ and the module axioms, $\pi(r+s)=(r+s)m=rm+sm=\pi(r)+\pi(s)$ and $\pi(sr)=(sr)m=s(rm)=s\,\pi(r)$, so $\pi$ is an $R$-module map (here $R$ is viewed as a left module over itself). Its image is $\{rm:r\in R\}=Rm$. Its kernel is $\{r:rm=0\}=\ann(m)$, a submodule of the left $R$-module $R$, i.e.\ a left ideal. The First Isomorphism Theorem for modules gives $R/\ker\pi\cong\im\pi$, that is $R/\ann(m)\cong Rm$. If $M=Rm$ then $M\cong R/\ann(m)$; conversely if $M\cong R/I$ then the image of $1$ generates, so $M$ is cyclic.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Identifying and analyzing $RA$, finitely generated, cyclic
Content:
\begin{method}{Identifying and analyzing $RA$, finitely generated, cyclic}
Trigger. You are asked what a subset generates, whether a module is finitely generated/cyclic, or to identify a cyclic module up to isomorphism.
\begin{enumerate}
\item To compute $RA$: take all finite $R$-linear combinations $\sum r_ia_i$. Verify it is closed under $+$ and under $R$-scaling (it is, by construction).
\item ``Cyclic'' means one generator $m$: then $M=Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$. Compute $\ann(m)=\{r:rm=0\}$ as a left ideal; read off the quotient.
\item ``Finitely generated'' means some finite $A$ works; to disprove, show no finite set generates (e.g.\ a divisibility/denominator obstruction).
\item Over a field $R=F$: modules are vector spaces; ``finitely generated'' $=$ ``finite-dimensional'', ``cyclic'' $=$ ``dimension $\le 1$''.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Cyclic $Z$-modules: $Z m\cong Z/\ann(m)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cyclic $Z$-modules: $Z m\cong Z/\ann(m)$}
Let $M=Z/(12)Z$ as a $Z$-module and $m=\overline{8}$. Identify the cyclic submodule $Z m$ and write it as $Z/\ann(m)$.
\wrec The rule $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$ with $R=Z$, $M=Z/(12)Z$: compute $\ann(\overline 8)$ as an ideal of $Z$.
\wsol $\ann(\overline 8)=\{k\inZ: 8k\equiv 0 \pmod{12}\}$. Now $8k\equiv 0\pmod{12}$ iff $12\mid 8k$ iff $3\mid 2k$ iff $3\mid k$. So $\ann(\overline 8)=3Z$, and
\[
Z\,\overline 8 \;\cong\; Z/3Z=Z/(3)Z.
\]
Concretely $Z\overline8=\{\overline0,\overline8,\overline4\}$ (since $2\cdot\overline8=\overline{16}=\overline4$, $3\cdot\overline8=\overline{24}=\overline0$), a $3$-element submodule. Check. $|Z\overline8|=12/\gcd(8,12)=12/4=3$, matching $|Z/(3)Z|=3$. Consistent.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Cyclic $\mathbb{Z}$-modules: $\mathbb{Z} m\cong \mathbb{Z}/\ann(m)$}
Let $M=\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module and $m=\overline{8}$. Identify the cyclic submodule $\mathbb{Z} m$ and write it as $\mathbb{Z}/\ann(m)$.
\wrec The rule $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$ with $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M=\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$: compute $\ann(\overline 8)$ as an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol $\ann(\overline 8)=\{k\in\mathbb{Z}: 8k\equiv 0 \pmod{12}\}$. Now $8k\equiv 0\pmod{12}$ iff $12\mid 8k$ iff $3\mid 2k$ iff $3\mid k$. So $\ann(\overline 8)=3\mathbb{Z}$, and
\[
\mathbb{Z}\,\overline 8 \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Concretely $\mathbb{Z}\overline8=\{\overline0,\overline8,\overline4\}$ (since $2\cdot\overline8=\overline{16}=\overline4$, $3\cdot\overline8=\overline{24}=\overline0$), a $3$-element submodule. \textit{Check.} $|\mathbb{Z}\overline8|=12/\gcd(8,12)=12/4=3$, matching $|\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}|=3$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A cyclic module over a polynomial ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{A cyclic module over a polynomial ring}
Let $R=\F[x]$ where $\F$ is a field, and let $M=R$, $m=x^2-1\in R$. Describe $Rm$ and its annihilator. Then redo with $M=R/(x^2-1)$ and $m=\overline{x}$.
\wrec $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$. In an integral domain $\ann$ of a nonzero element is $0$; in a quotient ring use the quotient law.
\wsol (a) $R=\F[x]$ is a domain, so $\ann_R(x^2-1)=\{f: f\cdot(x^2-1)=0\}=0$. Hence $R(x^2-1)\cong R/0\cong R$, the principal ideal $(x^2-1)$, a free rank-$1$ submodule. (b) In $M=R/(x^2-1)$, $\ann_M(\overline x)=\{f:\ f\,\overline x=\overline 0\}=\{f:\ (x^2-1)\mid xf\}$. Since $\gcd(x,x^2-1)=1$, $(x^2-1)\mid xf$ iff $(x^2-1)\mid f$, so $\ann(\overline x)=(x^2-1)$ and $R\overline x\cong R/(x^2-1)=M$; thus $\overline x$ generates $M$ and $M$ is cyclic. Check. $\dim_\F M=2$ with basis $\overline1,\overline x$; and $\overline x\cdot\overline x=\overline{x^2}=\overline1$, so $R\overline x\supseteq\{\overline1,\overline x\}$ spans, confirming $M=R\overline x$.
\end{wex}

Title: Cyclic over a noncommutative ring: $\ann$ is only a left ideal
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cyclic over a noncommutative ring: $\ann$ is only a left ideal}
Let $R=M_2(\F)$ (a noncommutative ring) acting on the column space $M=\F^2$. Take $m=\binom{1}{0}$. Show $M=Rm$ and compute $\ann(m)$.
\wrec $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$ where $\ann(m)$ is a left ideal (not two-sided when $R$ is noncommutative).
\wsol For $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{psmallmatrix}$, $Am=\binom{a}{c}$ ranges over all of $\F^2$ as $a,c$ vary, so $Rm=\F^2=M$ (cyclic). And $\ann(m)=\{A:Am=0\}=\{A:a=c=0\}=\left\{\begin{psmallmatrix}0&b\\0&d\end{psmallmatrix}\right\}$, the matrices with zero first column. Check. This set is closed under left multiplication: $B\begin{psmallmatrix}0&b\\0&d\end{psmallmatrix}$ again has zero first column, confirming it is a left ideal. It is not a right ideal (multiplying on the right by a permutation can move the nonzero column), as expected.
\end{wex}

Title: Generators need not be unique or minimal
Content:
\begin{wex}{Generators need not be unique or minimal}
In $M=Z/(6)Z$ (a $Z$-module), show $A=\{\overline2,\overline3\}$ generates $M$ but $M$ is also cyclic.
\wrec $RA$ is all $Z$-combinations; cyclic means a single generator suffices.
\wsol $Z\{\overline2,\overline3\}\ni \overline3-\overline2=\overline1$, and $\overline1$ generates $Z/(6)Z$, so $A$ generates $M$. But also $M=Z\overline1$ is cyclic with the single generator $\overline1$. Thus $\{\overline2,\overline3\}$ is a (non-minimal) generating set. Check. $\ann(\overline1)=6Z$ so $Z\overline1\congZ/6Z=M$; the two-element set is genuinely redundant.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: External direct sum
Content:
\begin{definition}[External direct sum]
Given $R$-modules $M_1,\dots,M_n$, their (external) direct sum is the Cartesian product
\[
M_1\oplus\cdots\oplus M_n=\{(m_1,\dots,m_n):m_i\in M_i\}
\]
with componentwise operations $(m_i)+(m_i')=(m_i+m_i')$ and $r(m_i)=(rm_i)$. For an arbitrary index set, the direct sum $\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i$ consists of tuples with finitely many nonzero entries (inside the direct product $\prod_{i\in I}M_i$).
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Internal direct sum criterion
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Internal direct sum criterion]
Let $N_1,\dots,N_k$ be submodules of an $R$-module $M$. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] The map $\pi:N_1\oplus\cdots\oplus N_k\to M$, $\pi(a_1,\dots,a_k)=a_1+\cdots+a_k$, is an isomorphism (onto $M$).
\item[(2)] $M=N_1+\cdots+N_k$ and for each $i$,
\[
N_i\cap\Big(\sum_{j\neq i}N_j\Big)=0.
\]
\item[(3)] Every $m\in M$ is written uniquely as $m=a_1+\cdots+a_k$ with $a_i\in N_i$.
\end{enumerate}
When these hold we write $M=N_1\oplus\cdots\oplus N_k$ and call it the internal direct sum.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\pi$ is always an $R$-module homomorphism, and $\im\pi=N_1+\cdots+N_k$; so $\pi$ is surjective iff $M=\sum N_i$. It remains to relate injectivity of $\pi$ to (2) and to (3). Injectivity is equivalent to: the only way to write $0=a_1+\cdots+a_k$ with $a_i\in N_i$ is $a_i=0$ for all $i$. If some $a_i\neq 0$ with $\sum a_j=0$, then $a_i=-\sum_{j\neq i}a_j\in N_i\cap\sum_{j\neq i}N_j$, a nonzero element; conversely a nonzero element of $N_i\cap\sum_{j\neq i}N_j$ produces a nontrivial relation. Hence injectivity $\Longleftrightarrow$ (2). Finally, two representations $m=\sum a_i=\sum a_i'$ differ by a representation of $0$, so uniqueness in (3) is exactly injectivity of $\pi$ together with surjectivity. Thus (1)$\Longleftrightarrow$(2)$\Longleftrightarrow$(3).
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
For three or more submodules, pairwise trivial intersection $N_i\cap N_j=0$ ($i\neq j$) is not enough for a direct sum. The correct condition is $N_i\cap\big(\sum_{j\neq i}N_j\big)=0$ for each $i$. Example in $M=R^2$: lines $N_1=R(1,0)$, $N_2=R(0,1)$, $N_3=R(1,1)$ meet pairwise in $0$, yet $N_3\subseteq N_1+N_2$, so $N_3\cap(N_1+N_2)=N_3\neq 0$ and the sum is not direct.
\end{pitfall}

Type: method
Title: Recognizing a direct sum
Content:
\begin{method}{Recognizing a direct sum}
Trigger. You must decide whether $M$ splits as $N_1\oplus\cdots\oplus N_k$, or build a module out of pieces.
\begin{enumerate}
\item External: just form tuples with componentwise structure; this always exists.
\item Internal (two summands): check $M=N_1+N_2$ and $N_1\cap N_2=0$.
\item Internal ($k\ge 3$): check $M=\sum N_i$ and $N_i\cap\sum_{j\neq i}N_j=0$ for every $i$ (NOT just pairwise).
\item Equivalent shortcut: show unique representation $m=\sum a_i$. Existence $\Rightarrow$ spanning; uniqueness $\Rightarrow$ the intersection condition.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ as $Z$-modules (CRT)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ as $Z$-modules (CRT)}
Show $Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ as $Z$-modules, both externally (via a map) and internally (via submodules).
\wrec Internal direct sum criterion plus the cyclic isomorphism $Rm\cong R/\ann(m)$; $Z$-module $=$ abelian group.
\wsol External map. Define $\varphi:Z\toZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ by $\varphi(k)=(k\bmod 2,\ k\bmod 3)$, a $Z$-module homomorphism. $\ker\varphi=\{k:2\mid k and 3\mid k\}=6Z$ (since $\gcd(2,3)=1$). It is surjective: $|Z/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z|=6=[Z:6Z]$ and injectivity on the quotient forces a bijection. So $Z/6Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$, i.e.\ $Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$.

Internal. In $M=Z/(6)Z$ set $N_1=Z\overline3=\{\overline0,\overline3\}$ and $N_2=Z\overline2=\{\overline0,\overline2,\overline4\}$. Then $\ann(\overline3)=2Z$ so $N_1\congZ/(2)Z$; $\ann(\overline2)=3Z$ so $N_2\congZ/(3)Z$. Also $N_1\cap N_2=\{\overline0\}$ (orders $2$ and $3$ are coprime) and $N_1+N_2\ni\overline3+\overline2=\overline5$ and $\overline3+\overline4=\overline1$, so $N_1+N_2=M$. By the two-summand criterion $M=N_1\oplus N_2\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$. Check. $\overline1=\overline3+\overline4=\overline3+2\cdot\overline2$ uniquely splits as $(\overline3,\ \overline4)\in N_1\times N_2$; orders multiply $2\cdot3=6$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Title: Splitting a $Z$-module: $Z/(30)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\oplusZ/(5)Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Splitting a $Z$-module: $Z/(30)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\oplusZ/(5)Z$}
Decompose $Z/(30)Z$ as an internal direct sum of cyclic $Z$-modules.
\wrec Iterated CRT via the internal criterion for three submodules.
\wsol Let $N_1=Z\overline{15}\congZ/(2)Z$, $N_2=Z\overline{10}\congZ/(3)Z$, $N_3=Z\overline6\congZ/(5)Z$ (annihilators $2Z,3Z,5Z$ respectively). Their orders $2,3,5$ are pairwise coprime, so $N_i\cap\sum_{j\neq i}N_j$ has order dividing both $|N_i|$ and $|\sum_{j\neq i}N_j|$ (orders dividing $15,10,6$ respectively, since $N_j+N_k$ is the image of $N_j\oplus N_k$), and $\gcd$ forces $0$ in each case. Sum: $\overline{15}+\overline{10}+\overline6=\overline{31}=\overline1$ generates, so $\sum N_i=M$. Hence $Z/(30)Z=N_1\oplus N_2\oplus N_3\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\oplusZ/(5)Z$. Check. $2\cdot3\cdot5=30=|M|$. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: Free module on a set
Content:
\begin{definition}[Free module on a set]
Let $A$ be a set. The free $R$-module on $A$ is
\[
R^{(A)}=\bigoplus_{a\in A}R,
\]
the set of finitely-supported functions $A\to R$, written as formal finite sums $\sum_{a\in A}r_a\,a$ with $r_a\in R$ (almost all $0$). There is a canonical injection $\iota:A\to R^{(A)}$, $\iota(a)=1\cdot a$, identifying $A$ with the standard basis $\{e_a\}_{a\in A}$. When $A=\{1,\dots,n\}$ we write $R^n$. A module $M$ is free (with basis $\iota(A)$) if $M\cong R^{(A)}$ for some $A$.
\end{definition}

Type: theorem
Title: Universal property of the free module
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Universal property of the free module]
Let $A$ be a set and $\iota:A\to R^{(A)}$ the canonical inclusion. For every $R$-module $M$ and every set map $f:A\to M$, there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\Phi:R^{(A)}\to M$ with $\Phi\circ\iota=f$, namely $\Phi\big(\sum_a r_a\,a\big)=\sum_a r_a\,f(a)$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& M
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $A$ is a plain set (no module structure); $R^{(A)}$ is the free left $R$-module on $A$, consisting of formal finite $R$-linear combinations of elements of $A$; $M$ is an arbitrary left $R$-module.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota: A \to R^{(A)}$ is the canonical set-map sending $a \mapsto 1\cdot a$, i.e.\ the inclusion of $A$ as the standard basis of $R^{(A)}$. $f: A \to M$ is any set-map (no linearity required). $\Phi: R^{(A)} \to M$ is the unique $R$-module homomorphism extending $f$; its existence and uniqueness are what the theorem asserts, hence the dashed arrow labelled $\exists!\,\Phi$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\Phi \circ \iota = f$. That is, for every $a \in A$, $\Phi(\iota(a)) = f(a)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $a \in A$. Along the top-then-down path: $a \xmapsto{\iota} 1\cdot a \xmapsto{\Phi} \Phi(1\cdot a) = 1\cdot f(a) = f(a)$. Along the diagonal: $a \xmapsto{f} f(a)$. Both give $f(a)$ because $\Phi$ is defined by $R$-linear extension of $f$ on basis elements, and $\iota(a)$ is exactly the basis element corresponding to $a$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the precise statement of the universal property of the free module. It says that $R^{(A)}$ is the ``most efficient'' module receiving $A$: every set-map out of $A$ into any $R$-module lifts to a unique $R$-module map out of $R^{(A)}$. The uniqueness (expressed by the dashed arrow) distinguishes this from mere existence of some extension.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R = Z$, $A = \{e_1, e_2\}$, $R^{(A)} = Z^2$, $M = Z/6Z$, $f(e_1) = \overline{2}$, $f(e_2) = \overline{3}$. The unique extension is $\Phi(a,b) = \overline{2a+3b}$, and $\Phi \circ \iota(e_1) = \overline{2} = f(e_1)$, confirming commutativity.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\Phi$ is the same as $f$; in fact $f$ is a set-map on $A$ while $\Phi$ is an $R$-module map on all of $R^{(A)}$, a much larger domain. The diagram emphasizes this by drawing $f$ and $\iota$ separately.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that specifying an $R$-module map out of $R^{(A)}$ is exactly the same data as specifying a set-map out of $A$, so there are no relations to check when building maps from free modules.
\end{dgx}
Equivalently, restriction $\Hom_R(R^{(A)},M)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,M)$, $g\mapsto g\circ\iota$, is a bijection.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Existence. Define $\Phi(\sum_a r_a a)=\sum_a r_a f(a)$ (a finite sum). This is well defined because each element of $R^{(A)}$ has a unique finitely-supported expression $\sum r_a a$. It is additive and $R$-linear because the operations on $R^{(A)}$ are componentwise, and $\Phi(\iota(a))=\Phi(1\cdot a)=f(a)$. Uniqueness. Any $R$-map $\Psi$ with $\Psi\iota=f$ must satisfy $\Psi(\sum_a r_a a)=\sum_a r_a\Psi(a)=\sum_a r_a f(a)=\Phi(\sum r_a a)$, since $\{a\}$ generates $R^{(A)}$ and $\Psi$ respects $R$-linear combinations. So $\Psi=\Phi$.
\end{proof}

Type: corollary
Title: Every module is a quotient of a free module
Content:
\begin{corollary}[Every module is a quotient of a free module]
Every $R$-module $M$ is a quotient of a free module. If $A\subseteq M$ generates $M$ (e.g.\ $A=M$), the universal map $\Phi:R^{(A)}\to M$ determined by $a\mapsto a$ is surjective, giving a short exact sequence
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \ker\Phi \arrow[r, hook] & R^{(A)} \arrow[r, two heads, "\Phi"] & M \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\qquadand\qquad
M\cong R^{(A)}/\ker\Phi .
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $0$ denotes the trivial module; $\ker\Phi$ is the kernel of $\Phi$, a submodule of $R^{(A)}$ (explicitly, the set of formal combinations $\sum r_a a$ that map to $0$ under $\Phi$); $R^{(A)}$ is the free module on the generating set $A$; $M$ is the given $R$-module being presented.
\dgi{Arrows:} The left $0 \to \ker\Phi$ is the zero map (inclusion of the trivial module). The map $\ker\Phi \to R^{(A)}$ is the inclusion of the kernel as a submodule. The map $\Phi: R^{(A)} \twoheadrightarrow M$ (double-headed arrow) is the surjection induced by $a \mapsto a$, the universal map extending the inclusion $A \hookrightarrow M$. The right $M \to 0$ is the zero map.
\dgi{What commutes:} The sequence is exact: (i) $\operatorname{im}(0 \to \ker\Phi) = 0 = \ker(\ker\Phi \to R^{(A)})$; (ii) $\operatorname{im}(\ker\Phi \to R^{(A)}) = \ker\Phi = \ker\Phi$, the kernel of $\Phi$; (iii) $\operatorname{im}(\Phi) = M = \ker(M \to 0)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Condition (ii) is the definition of $\ker\Phi$: the inclusion picks out exactly those elements sent to $0$ by $\Phi$. Condition (iii) is surjectivity of $\Phi$: since $A$ generates $M$, every element of $M$ is an $R$-linear combination of elements of $A$, hence in the image of $\Phi$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This short exact sequence encodes the presentation of $M$ as a quotient of a free module. The kernel $\ker\Phi$ records exactly the relations among the generators in $A$. The isomorphism $M \cong R^{(A)}/\ker\Phi$ displayed alongside is the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to $\Phi$. This is the foundation for the theory of module presentations and resolutions.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M = Z/6Z$, $A = M$ (all elements), $R^{(A)}$ free of rank $6$. Alternatively, take $A = \{1\}$, $R^{(A)} = Z$, $\Phi(n) = \overline{n}$; then $\ker\Phi = 6Z$ and the sequence is $0 \to 6Z \to Z \to Z/6Z \to 0$, the standard presentation of $Z/6Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The sequence tells you $M \cong R^{(A)}/\ker\Phi$, but this does not mean $R^{(A)} \cong \ker\Phi \oplus M$ in general. A short exact sequence splits only when $M$ is projective (e.g., free), which is not guaranteed here.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that every module, however complicated, can be described by generators and relations---the free module supplies the generators and its kernel under $\Phi$ records all the relations.
\end{dgx}
Moreover $M$ is finitely generated iff $M$ is a quotient of some $R^n$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, hook, "\subseteq"'] & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, two heads, "\Phi"] \\
& M
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $A$ is a generating subset of $M$ (a set, not a module); $R^{(A)}$ is the free module on $A$; $M$ is the $R$-module being presented as a quotient.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota: A \to R^{(A)}$ is the standard basis inclusion $a \mapsto 1\cdot a$. The hooked diagonal arrow $A \hookrightarrow M$ is the set-theoretic inclusion of $A$ as a subset of $M$ (the map $f = \operatorname{incl}$ in the universal property). $\Phi: R^{(A)} \twoheadrightarrow M$ (double-headed arrow) is the unique $R$-module surjection extending the inclusion; it is surjective precisely because $A$ generates $M$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\Phi \circ \iota = \operatorname{incl}$, i.e.\ for every $a \in A$, $\Phi(1\cdot a) = a$. This is the defining property of $\Phi$ as the universal extension of the inclusion $f = \operatorname{incl}$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness: different choices of representative within the basis element $1\cdot a$ do not arise since the free module has a canonical basis. Commutativity follows directly: $\Phi(\iota(a)) = \Phi(1\cdot a) = 1\cdot \operatorname{incl}(a) = a$, matching the diagonal arrow. No coset ambiguity arises because the domain is free.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram instantiates the universal property in the specific case $f = \operatorname{incl}$ (when $A \subseteq M$), yielding a canonical surjection. It visually separates the generating role of $A$ (diagonal arrow into $M$) from the free extension role of $R^{(A)}$ (vertical arrow), making clear that the surjection is induced, not assumed.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $M = Z/nZ$, $A = \{\overline{1}\}$, $R^{(A)} = Z$, $\iota(1) = 1 \in Z$, $\Phi(k) = \overline{k}$. The diagram says $\Phi(\iota(1)) = \overline{1}$, which is the inclusion of the generator; $\Phi$ surjects because $\overline{1}$ generates $Z/nZ$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse this triangle with the one in the theorem statement. There, $f: A \to M$ was an arbitrary set-map and $\Phi$ was merely asserted to exist. Here, $f$ is specifically the inclusion $A \subseteq M$ and surjectivity of $\Phi$ follows from the generating hypothesis---this is the application, not the definition, of the universal property.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that when $A$ generates $M$, the universal property of $R^{(A)}$ immediately produces a surjection $R^{(A)} \twoheadrightarrow M$, so every module is a quotient of a free module with no additional construction needed.
\end{dgx}
\end{corollary}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-b4ed75ab94803e6ec506
Content:
\begin{proof}
Take $A$ a generating set and $f:A\hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion. The induced $\Phi$ has image $\Phi(R^{(A)})=R\cdot A=M$, so $\Phi$ is onto. By the First Isomorphism Theorem $M\cong R^{(A)}/\ker\Phi$. If $M$ is finitely generated, choose $A$ finite of size $n$; then $R^{(A)}=R^n$ surjects onto $M$. Conversely a quotient of $R^n$ is generated by the $n$ images of the standard basis.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Rank of a free module is well defined over a commutative ring
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Rank of a free module is well defined over a commutative ring]
Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring. If $R^m\cong R^n$ as $R$-modules, then $m=n$. Thus the rank of a free module $R^n$ is a well-defined invariant.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-99ff5fe0b70fbafa3ce7
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $m$ be a maximal ideal of $R$ (exists since $R\neq 0$), and let $k=R/m$, a field. Tensoring with $k$, $k\otimes_R R^n\cong k^n$ as $k$-vector spaces (tensor commutes with finite direct sums and $k\otimes_R R\cong k$). An isomorphism $R^m\cong R^n$ of $R$-modules induces an isomorphism $k^m\cong k^n$ of $k$-vector spaces, so $m=\dim_k k^m=\dim_k k^n=n$ by uniqueness of dimension over a field.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Using the universal property to define a map out of $R^{(A)}$
Content:
\begin{method}{Using the universal property to define a map out of $R^{(A)}$}
Trigger. You must construct an $R$-homomorphism whose domain is free (or $R^n$), or prove two maps out of a free module agree.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Specify the map only on the basis: choose any $f(a)\in M$ for each basis element $a$. No relations to check --- a free module has none.
\item Extend $R$-linearly: $\Phi(\sum r_a a)=\sum r_a f(a)$. The theorem guarantees this is a well-defined homomorphism and is the unique extension.
\item To prove $\Phi=\Psi$ on $R^{(A)}$, check only $\Phi(a)=\Psi(a)$ on basis elements.
\item To present a module: pick generators $A$, get $\Phi:R^{(A)}\twoheadrightarrow M$, then $M\cong R^{(A)}/\ker\Phi$ and $\ker\Phi$ records the relations.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Build a map out of a free module via the universal property
Content:
\begin{wex}{Build a map out of a free module via the universal property}
Construct the $Z$-module homomorphism $\Phi:Z^2\toZ/(6)Z$ with $\Phi(e_1)=\overline2$, $\Phi(e_2)=\overline3$, and identify $\im\Phi$ and $\ker\Phi$.
\wrec Universal property of $R^{(A)}=Z^2$: a map is determined by its values on the basis $\{e_1,e_2\}$.
\wsol By the universal property $\Phi(a,b)=a\,\overline2+b\,\overline3=\overline{2a+3b}$. Image: $2a+3b$ realizes $\overline1=\overline3-\overline2$ (take $a=-1,b=1$), so $\im\Phi=Z/(6)Z$ (surjective). Kernel: $(a,b)\in\ker\Phi$ iff $2a+3b\equiv0\pmod6$. Reduce: mod $2$, $3b\equiv b\equiv0$, so $b$ is even; mod $3$, $2a\equiv -a\equiv0$, so $a$ is divisible by $3$. These two congruences are independent and together necessary and sufficient, so $\ker\Phi=3Z\oplus2Z=Z(3,0)+Z(0,2)$. Check. $\Phi(3,0)=\overline6=\overline0$, $\Phi(0,2)=\overline6=\overline0$. Index: $[Z^2:\ker\Phi]=\det\begin{psmallmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{psmallmatrix}=6=|\im\Phi|$, confirming $Z^2/\ker\Phi\congZ/(6)Z$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Free of rank $2$: a basis and coordinates
Content:
\begin{wex}{Free of rank $2$: a basis and coordinates}
In $M=Z^2$, let $v_1=(2,1)$ and $v_2=(1,1)$. Decide whether $\{v_1,v_2\}$ is a basis of $Z^2$, and if so give the coordinates of $(3,2)$.
\wrec A free module of rank $2$: $\{v_1,v_2\}$ is a basis iff the change-of-basis matrix is invertible over $R=Z$ (determinant a unit).
\wsol Form $B=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ with columns $v_1,v_2$. $\det B=2\cdot1-1\cdot1=1\in\units{Z}=\{\pm1\}$, so $B$ is invertible over $Z$ with $B^{-1}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{psmallmatrix}$. Hence $\{v_1,v_2\}$ is a $Z$-basis. Coordinates of $w=(3,2)$: solve $Bc=w$, $c=B^{-1}w=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}3\\2\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1\\1\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $(3,2)=1\cdot v_1+1\cdot v_2$. Check. $1\cdot(2,1)+1\cdot(1,1)=(3,2)$. Correct, and integer coordinates confirm $w\inZ^2$ exactly.
\end{wex}

Title: A determinant that is not a unit: NOT a basis
Content:
\begin{wex}{A determinant that is not a unit: NOT a basis}
In $M=Z^2$, is $\{(2,0),(0,3)\}$ a basis?
\wrec Same criterion: over $Z$ a generating square matrix must have determinant $\pm1$.
\wsol $\det\begin{psmallmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{psmallmatrix}=6\notin\units{Z}$. The set is $Z$-linearly independent (no nontrivial integer relation $a(2,0)+b(0,3)=0$ except $a=b=0$), but it does not span: $(1,0)\notinZ(2,0)+Z(0,3)$. So it is independent but not a basis. Check. $Z(2,0)+Z(0,3)=2Z\oplus3Z$ has index $6$ in $Z^2$, so it is a proper submodule; over a field this could not happen, but over $Z$ independence does not give spanning.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Q$ is not a free $Z$-module
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q$ is not a free $Z$-module}
Show the $Z$-module $Q$ is not free; in particular it has no basis and is not finitely generated.
\wrec Free $=R^{(A)}$ with a basis; over $Z$, freeness forces a $Z$-independent generating set. Find an obstruction (any two elements are $Z$-dependent).
\wsol Any two nonzero elements $\tfrac{a}{b},\tfrac{c}{d}\inQ$ ($a,b,c,d\neq0$) satisfy the nontrivial $Z$-relation $(cb)\tfrac{a}{b}-(ad)\tfrac{c}{d}=ca-ca=0$ with integer coefficients $cb,\,ad$ not both zero. So any $Z$-linearly independent subset of $Q$ has at most one element. Thus a basis would be a single element $\{q\}$, giving $Q=Z q\congZ$ --- false, since $Z$ is not a divisible group ($\tfrac q2\inQ$ but $\tfrac q2\notinZ q$ for $q\neq0$). Hence $Q$ has no basis and is not free. It is also not finitely generated: a finite set $\{\tfrac{a_1}{b_1},\dots,\tfrac{a_n}{b_n}\}$ generates a subgroup inside $\tfrac1{b_1\cdots b_n}Z\neqQ$. Check. Divisibility is the obstruction: $Q$ is divisible, $Z^{(A)}$ is not (for $A\neq\varnothing$), so $Q\not\congZ^{(A)}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Uniqueness in the universal property forces a relation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Uniqueness in the universal property forces a relation}
Suppose $R=\F[x]$ and $M$ is the $R$-module $\F^2$ where $x$ acts as the matrix $T=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. Use the universal property of $R^1=R$ to find $\ann_R(v)$ for $v=e_1$ and identify $Rv$.
\wrec Free module $R=\F[x]$ on one generator; map $1\mapsto v$ extends uniquely to $\Phi:R\to M$, $\Phi(f)=f(T)v$, and $\ker\Phi=\ann(v)$.
\wsol $\Phi:R\to M$, $f\mapsto f(T)e_1$. Compute the orbit: $1\cdot e_1=e_1$, $x\cdot e_1=Te_1=e_2$, $x^2\cdot e_1=T^2e_1=-e_1$. So $\{e_1,xe_1\}=\{e_1,e_2\}$ spans $M$, hence $\Phi$ is onto and $Rv=M$. The relation $x^2 e_1=-e_1$ means $(x^2+1)e_1=0$, so $x^2+1\in\ann(v)$. Since $\F[x]$ is a PID and $\dim_\F M=2$ forces $\deg$ of the generator $=2$, $\ann(v)=(x^2+1)$. Thus $Rv\cong\F[x]/(x^2+1)$. Check. $\dim_\F \F[x]/(x^2+1)=2=\dim_\F M$, and $T^2+I=0$ confirms $x^2+1$ annihilates. Consistent.
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The universal property characterizes $R^{(A)}$ up to unique isomorphism: any module $F$ with a map $\iota:A\to F$ having the same universal extension property is canonically isomorphic to $R^{(A)}$. This is the module-theoretic instance of ``free objects are unique,'' and is the template for the analogous characterizations of the tensor product and of projective/injective modules later in the chapter.
\end{remark}

\item Prove that if $A$ and $B$ are sets of the same cardinality, then the free modules $F(A)$ and $F(B)$ are isomorphic.

Exercise 17 in Section 5.1) with the action of $R$ componentwise multiplication. In other words, the direct sum of the $M_i$'s is the subset of the direct product, $\prod_{i \in I} M_i$, which consists of all elements $\prod_{i \in I} m_i$ such that only finitely many of the components $m_i$ are nonzero; the action of $R$ on the direct product or direct sum is given by $r \prod_{i \in I} m_i = \prod_{i \in I} r m_i$ (cf. Appendix I for the definition of Cartesian products of infinitely many sets). The direct sum will be denoted by $\bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Prove that the direct product of the $M_i$'s is an $R$-module and the direct sum of the $M_i$'s is a submodule of their direct product.
\item[(b)] Show that if $R = Z$, $I = Z^+$ and $M_i$ is the cyclic group of order $i$ for each $i$, then the direct sum of the $M_i$'s is not isomorphic to their direct product. [Look at torsion.]
\end{itemize}

\item Let $I$ be a nonempty index set and for each $i \in I$ let $N_i$ be a submodule of $M$. Prove that the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] the map from the (external) direct sum $\bigoplus_{i \in I} N_i$ to the submodule of $M$ generated by all the $N_i$'s sending a tuple to the sum of its components is an isomorphism (cf. Exercise 20)
\item[(ii)] if $\{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_k\}$ is any finite subset of $I$ then $N_{i_1} \cap (N_{i_2} + \cdots + N_{i_k}) = 0$
\item[(iii)] if $\{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_k\}$ is any finite subset of $I$ then $N_{i_1} + \cdots + N_{i_k} = N_{i_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus N_{i_k}$
\item[(iv)] for every element $x$ of the submodule of $M$ generated by the $N_i$'s there are unique elements $a_i \in N_i$ for all $i \in I$ such that all but a finite number of the $a_i$ are zero and $x$ is the (finite) sum of the $a_i$.
\end{itemize}

\item Let $R$ be a Principal Ideal Domain, let $M$ be a torsion $R$-module (cf. Exercise 4) and let $p$ be a prime in $R$ (do not assume $M$ is finitely generated, hence it need not have a nonzero annihilator --- cf. Exercise 5). The $p$-primary component of $M$ is the set of all elements of $M$ that are annihilated by some positive power of $p$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Prove that the $p$-primary component is a submodule. [See Exercise 13 in Section 1.]
\item[(b)] Prove that this definition of $p$-primary component agrees with the one given in Exercise 18 when $M$ has a nonzero annihilator.
\item[(c)] Prove that $M$ is the (possibly infinite) direct sum of its $p$-primary components, as $p$ runs over all primes of $R$.
\end{itemize}

\item Show that any direct sum of free $R$-modules is free.

\item (An arbitrary direct product of free modules need not be free) For each positive integer $i$ let $M_i$ be the free $Z$-module $Z$, and let $M$ be the direct product $\prod_{i \in Z^+} M_i$ (cf. Exercise 20). Each element of $M$ can be written uniquely in the form $(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots)$ with $a_i \in Z$ for all $i$. Let $N$ be the submodule of $M$ consisting of all such tuples with only finitely many nonzero $a_i$. Assume $M$ is a free $Z$-module with basis $B$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Show that $N$ is countable.
\item[(b)] Show that there is some countable subset $B_1$ of $B$ such that $N$ is contained in the submodule, $N_1$, generated by $B_1$. Show also that $N_1$ is countable.
\item[(c)] Let $\overline{M} = M/N_1$. Show that $\overline{M}$ is a free $Z$-module. Deduce that if $\overline{x}$ is any nonzero element of $\overline{M}$ then there are only finitely many distinct positive integers $k$ such that $\overline{x} = k\overline{m}$ for some $m \in \overline{M}$ (depending on $k$).
\item[(d)] Let $S = \{(b_1, b_2, b_3, \ldots) \mid b_i = \pm i! for all i\}$. Prove that $S$ is uncountable. Deduce that there is some $s \in S$ with $s \notin N_1$.
\item[(e)] Show that the assumption $M$ is free leads to a contradiction: By (d) we may choose $s \in S$ with $s \notin N_1$. Show that for each positive integer $k$ there is some $m \in \overline{M}$ and $\overline{s} = k\overline{m}$, contrary to (c). [Use the fact that $N \subseteq N_1$.]
\end{itemize}

\item In the construction of direct limits, Exercise 8 of Section 7.6, show that if all $A_i$ are $R$-modules and the maps $\rho_{ij}$ are $R$-module homomorphisms, then the direct limit $A = \varinjlim A_i$ may be given the structure of an $R$-module in a natural way such that the maps $\rho_i : A_i \to A$ are all $R$-module homomorphisms. Verify the corresponding universal property (part (e)) for $R$-module homomorphisms $\varphi_i : A_i \to C$ commuting with the $\rho_{ij}$.

\item Carry out the analysis of the preceding exercise corresponding to inverse limits to show that an inverse limit of $R$-modules is an $R$-module satisfying the appropriate universal property (cf. Exercise 10 of Section 7.6).

\item (Free modules over noncommutative rings need not have a unique rank) Let $M$ be the $Z$-module $Z \times Z \times \cdots$ of Exercise 24 and let $R$ be its endomorphism ring, $R = \End_{Z}(M)$ (cf. Exercises 29 and 30 in Section 7.1). Define $\varphi_1, \varphi_2 \in R$ by
\[
\varphi_1(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots) = (a_1, a_3, a_5, \ldots) \qquad \varphi_2(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots) = (a_2, a_4, a_6, \ldots).
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\{\varphi_1, \varphi_2\}$ is a free basis of the left $R$-module $R$. [Define the maps $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ by $\psi_1(a_1, a_2, \ldots) = (a_1, 0, a_2, 0, \ldots)$ and $\psi_2(a_1, a_2, \ldots) = (0, a_1, 0, a_2, \ldots)$. Verify that $\varphi_i \psi_i = 1$, $\varphi_1 \psi_2 = 0 = \varphi_2 \psi_1$ and $\psi_1 \varphi_1 + \psi_2 \varphi_2 = 1$.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Generation of Modules, Direct Sums, and Free Modules > Generating submodules, direct sums, and free modules
Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Show that the
subset $N$ of $M$ consisting of all $R$-linear combinations of a fixed set
$A\subseteq M$ equals the intersection of all submodules of $M$ containing $A$.
Conclude that $RA=\langle A\rangle$.

\item In the $Z$-module $Z$, find a generating set of size $1$. Show that the
single element $2$ does not generate $Z$ as a $Z$-module (since
$Z\cdot 2=2Z\neZ$), but that $\{2,3\}$ does generate $Z$ as a
$Z$-module because $\gcd(2,3)=1$. Identify a minimal generating set of the
$Z$-module $Z$.

\item Let $M=Z/6Z$ as a $Z$-module. List all submodules, and for each give a
single generator. Which elements of $M$ generate $M$?

\item Show that $Q$ is not a finitely generated $Z$-module. (Hint: a finite
generating set has a common denominator.)

\item Let $R$ be a ring and let $M_1,\dots,M_k$ be submodules of a module $M$.
Prove that the sum $M_1+\cdots+M_k=\{m_1+\cdots+m_k \st m_i\in M_i\}$ is a
submodule, and that it is the smallest submodule containing every $M_i$.

\item Give an explicit isomorphism $Z/6Z\cong Z/2Z\oplusZ/3Z$ of
$Z$-modules, and verify it is a bijective $R$-homomorphism. Explain why
$Z/4Z\not\congZ/2Z\oplusZ/2Z$.

\item Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules. Show that the external direct sum
$M\oplus N$ together with the maps $\iota_M\colon m\mapsto(m,0)$ and
$\pi_M\colon(m,n)\mapsto m$ satisfies $\pi_M\iota_M=\id_M$, $\pi_N\iota_N=\id_N$,
and $\iota_M\pi_M+\iota_N\pi_N=\id_{M\oplus N}$.

\item Prove that for $R$-modules $A,B,C$ there is a natural isomorphism
$\Hom_R(A\oplus B,\,C)\cong \Hom_R(A,C)\oplus\Hom_R(B,C)$.

\item Let $F$ be the free $Z$-module on the set $A=\{x,y,z\}$. Write down the
element $3x-2y+5z$ as a function $A\toZ$ with finite support, and compute the
image of this element under the unique homomorphism $F\toZ/4Z$ sending
$x\mapsto 1,\ y\mapsto 1,\ z\mapsto 2$.

\item Suppose $R$ is a nonzero commutative ring and $R^m\cong R^n$ as
$R$-modules. Use the fact that $R$ has a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and reduce
modulo $\mathfrak m$ to prove $m=n$ (so free rank is well defined over a nonzero
commutative ring).

\item Let $V$ be the $\F[x]$-module given by $V=\F^2$ with $x$ acting as the
matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ over $\F=R$. Determine whether
$V$ is generated by a single element as an $\F[x]$-module, and if so exhibit a
generator.

\item Let $N\sgr M$ be $R$-modules. Prove that if $M/N$ and $N$ are both finitely
generated, then $M$ is finitely generated. Give generators of $M$ explicitly in
terms of generators of $N$ and lifts of generators of $M/N$.

\item Show that a finitely generated module over a field $\F$ (i.e.\ a finite
dimensional vector space) is free, and that its rank equals its dimension.

\item Let $R=Z$ and consider the submodule $N=\langle (2,0),(0,3)\rangle\sgr Z^2$.
Compute the quotient $Z^2/N$ as an explicit direct sum of cyclic groups.

\item Prove that an $R$-module $M$ is generated by a single element if and only
if $M\cong R/I$ for some left ideal $I$ of $R$. Identify $I$ as an annihilator.

\end{exers}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Generation of Modules, Direct Sums, and Free Modules > Generating submodules, direct sums, and free modules
Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and suppose the left $R$-module $R$ has a
proper submodule that is also a direct summand, say $R=I\oplus J$ with $I,J$
nonzero left ideals. Prove that $1=e+f$ with $e\in I$, $f\in J$, that $e,f$ are
orthogonal idempotents, and that $I=Re$, $J=Rf$.

\item Show that $Q$ is not a projective $Z$-module. (Hint: $Q$ is not free
since it is not finitely generated and any free $Z$-module of rank $\ge 2$ has
linearly independent elements, while any two elements of $Q$ are $Z$-linearly
dependent; then argue that a projective module is a direct summand of a free
module, and a nonzero divisible submodule of a free $Z$-module must be $0$.)

\item Let $A$ be an infinite set and $R$ a nonzero ring. Prove that the free
module $R^{(A)}$ (finite support) is not isomorphic to the direct product
$R^A$ when $R$ is a field and $A$ is countably infinite, by a cardinality /
dimension argument.

\item Let $M$ be an $R$-module with submodules $N_1,N_2$ such that $M=N_1+N_2$
and $N_1\cap N_2=0$. Prove $M\cong N_1\oplus N_2$ via $n_1+n_2\mapsto(n_1,n_2)$,
and show by example over $R=Z$ that $M=N_1+N_2$ alone is insufficient.

\item Prove that a finitely generated module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$
cannot be generated by fewer than $n$ elements if $M/\mathfrak m M$ has dimension
$n$ over $R/\mathfrak m$ for some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ (Nakayama-style
lower bound). State precisely the version of Nakayama's lemma you use.

\item Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules with
$C$ free. Prove the sequence splits, so $B\cong A\oplus C$.

\end{exers}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Generation of Modules, Direct Sums, and Free Modules > Generating submodules, direct sums, and free modules
Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}

\item (Universal property of free modules.) Let $A$ be a set, $R^{(A)}$ the free
module with basis map $\iota\colon A\to R^{(A)}$, $M$ any $R$-module, and
$f\colon A\to M$ any set map. State and prove the universal property by
constructing the unique $R$-homomorphism $\Phi$ making the triangle commute:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, dashed, "{\exists!\,\Phi}"] \\
 & M
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then prove that this universal property characterizes $R^{(A)}$ up to unique
isomorphism.

\item (Projectivity via lifting.) Call $P$ projective if for every surjection
$g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ and every $f\colon P\to C$ there is
$\tilde f\colon P\to B$ with $g\tilde f=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 & P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "{\exists\,\tilde f}"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
Using the universal property of free modules from the previous exercise, prove
that every free module is projective.

\item (Splitting a short exact sequence.) Given
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
prove the equivalence of: (a) there is $s\colon C\to B$ with $\varphi s=\id_C$;
(b) there is $r\colon B\to A$ with $r\psi=\id_A$; (c) $B\cong A\oplus C$
compatibly with $\psi,\varphi$. Draw the maps $s$ and $r$ on the diagram and
verify each implication.

\item (Pullback of generators.) Let $\pi\colon R^{(A)}\twoheadrightarrow M$ be
the surjection induced by a generating set $\{m_a\}_{a\in A}$ of $M$, with kernel
$K$. Display the short exact sequence
$0\to K\to R^{(A)}\xrightarrow{\pi} M\to 0$ and prove that $M$ is finitely
generated iff $A$ may be chosen finite. Show $K$ is the module of relations among
the $m_a$.

\item (Hom is left exact.) Given an exact sequence
$0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C$ of $R$-modules and an
$R$-module $D$, prove the induced sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(D,A) \arrow[r, "\psi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,B) \arrow[r, "\varphi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,C)
\end{tikzcd}\]
is exact, and give an example with $D=Z/2Z$ over $R=Z$ showing $\varphi_*$
need not be surjective even when $\varphi$ is.

\end{exers}

Type: definition
Title: $R$-balanced map
Content:
\begin{definition}[$R$-balanced map]
A map $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ into an abelian group $L$ is $R$-balanced (or middle linear) if for all $m,m'\in M$, $n,n'\in N$, $r\in R$:
\[
\varphi(m+m',\,n)=\varphi(m,n)+\varphi(m',n),\quad
\varphi(m,\,n+n')=\varphi(m,n)+\varphi(m,n'),\quad
\varphi(mr,\,n)=\varphi(m,\,rn).
\]
The first two say $\varphi$ is biadditive; the third lets scalars ``slide across'' the $\times$.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: Tensor product $M\otimes_R N$
Content:
\begin{definition}[Tensor product $M\otimes_R N$]
The tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$ is the abelian group
\[
M\otimes_R N \;=\; F\big/H,
\]
where $F$ is the free abelian group $Z^{(M\times N)}$ on the set $M\times N$, and $H$ is the subgroup generated by all elements
\[
(m+m',n)-(m,n)-(m',n),\quad (m,n+n')-(m,n)-(m,n'),\quad (mr,n)-(m,rn),
\]
for $m,m'\in M$, $n,n'\in N$, $r\in R$. The image of $(m,n)$ in $M\otimes_R N$ is the simple tensor $m\otimes n$. Every element of $M\otimes_R N$ is a finite sum $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i$.
\end{definition}

By construction the relations defining $H$ become, in $M\otimes_R N$, exactly the bilinearity identities:
\[
(m+m')\otimes n = m\otimes n + m'\otimes n,\qquad
m\otimes(n+n') = m\otimes n + m\otimes n',\qquad
mr\otimes n = m\otimes rn.
\]
Useful consequences: $0\otimes n = m\otimes 0 = 0$ and $(-m)\otimes n = -(m\otimes n) = m\otimes(-n)$, since $0\otimes n=(0+0)\otimes n=0\otimes n+0\otimes n$.

Type: theorem
Title: Universal property of $\otimes$
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Universal property of $\otimes$]
The canonical map $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, is $R$-balanced, and it is universal: for every $R$-balanced map $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ there is a unique group homomorphism $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$ with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$, i.e. $\varphi=\Phi\circ\iota$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
Thus $\{R-balanced maps M\times N\to L\}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\{group homs M\otimes_R N\to L\}$, naturally in $L$.
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects. Top-left: the Cartesian product $M\times N$, a set (not a module), where $M$ is a right $R$-module and $N$ is a left $R$-module. Top-right: the tensor product $M\otimes_R N$, an abelian group, constructed as the free abelian group on $M\times N$ modulo the balanced relations. Bottom: an arbitrary abelian group $L$, the target of any $R$-balanced map.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, is the canonical $R$-balanced map whose existence is the whole point of the construction. (2) $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ is an arbitrary $R$-balanced map. (3) The dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$ is the unique group homomorphism induced by $\varphi$ via the universal property; it satisfies $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$, i.e., for every $(m,n)\in M\times N$, $\Phi(\iota(m,n))=\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Start with $(m,n)\in M\times N$. Along the top-then-down path: $\iota$ sends $(m,n)$ to $m\otimes n$, then $\Phi$ sends $m\otimes n$ to $\varphi(m,n)$---that is exactly how $\Phi$ is defined on simple tensors. Along the diagonal: $\varphi$ sends $(m,n)$ directly to $\varphi(m,n)$. Both paths produce $\varphi(m,n)$. Well-definedness: $\Phi$ is defined first on the free group $F$ by $\tilde\varphi(m,n)=\varphi(m,n)$, then one checks $\tilde\varphi$ kills the subgroup $H$ of balanced relations (possible exactly because $\varphi$ is balanced), so $\Phi$ descends to $F/H=M\otimes_R N$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the raison d'etre of the tensor product: it converts the non-additive data of a balanced map into a clean group homomorphism. The theorem is placed here immediately after defining $M\otimes_R N$ to show that the messy quotient construction is the right object: one never has to return to the quotient; one just works with balanced maps.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M=Z/(m)Z$, $N=Z/(n)Z$, $L=Z/(d)Z$ ($d=\gcd(m,n)$), and $\varphi(\bar a,\bar b)=\overline{ab}$. This is $Z$-balanced and well defined on cosets; the induced $\Phi\colonZ/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\toZ/(d)Z$ is an isomorphism, recovering $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(d)Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students try to define $\Phi$ directly by ``$\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$'' without first verifying $\varphi$ is balanced. This is circular: the universal property only hands you $\Phi$ after the balanced-axiom check. Skipping that check means $\Phi$ may not be well defined on the tensor product (different representatives of a simple tensor could give different outputs).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the tensor product $M\otimes_R N$ is precisely the abelian group that linearizes balanced maps---every balanced map out of $M\times N$ corresponds uniquely to a group homomorphism out of $M\otimes_R N$.
\end{dgx}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Sketch (existence/uniqueness)]
$\iota$ is balanced because the three defining families of relations in $H$ are killed in the quotient. Given a balanced $\varphi$, define a group hom $\tilde\varphi\colon F\to L$ on the free generators by $\tilde\varphi(m,n)=\varphi(m,n)$. Balancedness says $\tilde\varphi$ vanishes on every generator of $H$, hence on $H$, so $\tilde\varphi$ factors through $F/H=M\otimes_R N$ to give $\Phi$ with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$. Uniqueness: the simple tensors $m\otimes n$ generate $M\otimes_R N$, so a homomorphism is determined by its values on them, and $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$ is forced. (This is the precise sense in which $M\otimes_R N$ is the ``most general'' target receiving a balanced map.)
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The universal property characterizes $M\otimes_R N$ up to a unique isomorphism: any abelian group $T$ with a balanced $\iota'\colon M\times N\to T$ through which all balanced maps factor uniquely is canonically isomorphic to $M\otimes_R N$. This is why, to compute a tensor product, one almost never returns to the quotient construction --- one identifies a group with the right universal property.
\end{remark}
