Title: $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$}
Compute $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z$ as an abelian group; deduce $Z/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ/(3)Z$.
\wrec Here $R=Z$, so balanced $=$ $Z$-bilinear; both sides are cyclic, generated by $\bar1\otimes\bar1$. Use the slide relation with integer scalars to force the order.
\wsol Let $d=\gcd(m,n)$. The group $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z$ is generated by $\bar1\otimes\bar1$ since $\bar a\otimes\bar b=ab(\bar1\otimes\bar1)$. So it is cyclic. Now
\[
m(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\overline{m}\otimes\bar1=\bar0\otimes\bar1=0,\qquad
n(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar1\otimes\overline{n}=\bar1\otimes\bar0=0,
\]
so the order of $\bar1\otimes\bar1$ divides both $m$ and $n$, hence divides $d=\gcd(m,n)$. Thus there is a surjection $Z/(d)Z\twoheadrightarrow Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z$. For the reverse, the map $\varphi\colonZ/(m)Z\timesZ/(n)Z\toZ/(d)Z$, $\varphi(\bar a,\bar b)=\overline{ab}$, is well defined ($Z/(d)Z$ is a quotient of both $Z/(m)Z$ and $Z/(n)Z$) and $Z$-bilinear, so by the UP it induces $\Phi\colon Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\toZ/(d)Z$ with $\bar1\otimes\bar1\mapsto\bar1$, a generator. A surjection $Z/(d)Z\to G\toZ/(d)Z$ sending generator to generator forces $|G|=d$, so $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(d)Z$. Check. $Z/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ/(3)Z\congZ/(\gcd(2,3))Z=Z/(1)Z=0$. Sanity: $\bar1\otimes\bar1=3(\bar1\otimes\bar1)-2(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar1\otimes\bar3-\bar2\otimes\bar1=0-0=0$. Every simple tensor is $0$, so the group is $0$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z=0$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z=0$}
Show $Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z=0$ for every $n\ge1$.
\wrec A torsion module tensored with a divisible group: clear the torsion by absorbing $n$ into a denominator using the slide $qr\otimes x=q\otimes rx$.
\wsol Take a simple tensor $q\otimes\bar a$ with $q\inQ$, $\bar a\inZ/(n)Z$. Write $q=\frac{q}{n}\cdot n$. Then
\[
q\otimes\bar a=\Big(\tfrac{q}{n}\cdot n\Big)\otimes\bar a=\tfrac{q}{n}\otimes (n\cdot\bar a)=\tfrac{q}{n}\otimes\bar 0=0.
\]
(Here $\frac qn\inQ$ is a legitimate scalar; the slide moves the integer $n$ from the $Q$-side to the $Z/(n)Z$-side, where it annihilates.) Every simple tensor is $0$ and simple tensors generate, so $Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z=0$. Check. Consistency with the previous example via $Z/(n)Z$ being torsion --- a divisible group tensored with finite torsion vanishes. E.g. $Q\otimes_ZZ/(5)Z$: $q\otimes\bar a=\frac q5\otimes\overline{5a}=\frac q5\otimes\bar0=0$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $R\otimes_R N\cong N$ (unit object)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$R\otimes_R N\cong N$ (unit object)}
For a left $R$-module $N$ (with $R$ a right module over itself), prove $R\otimes_R N\cong N$ as abelian groups, naturally.
\wrec $R$ is the multiplicative ``unit'' for $\otimes$; expect $r\otimes n\mapsto rn$, with inverse $n\mapsto 1\otimes n$.
\wsol Forward. Define $\varphi\colon R\times N\to N$ by $\varphi(r,n)=rn$. Biadditive in each slot, and balanced: $\varphi(rs,n)=(rs)n=r(sn)=\varphi(r,sn)$. By the UP, get $\Phi\colon R\otimes_R N\to N$, $\Phi(r\otimes n)=rn$. Backward. Define $\Psi\colon N\to R\otimes_R N$ by $\Psi(n)=1\otimes n$; it is a group hom. Inverse check. $\Phi\Psi(n)=\Phi(1\otimes n)=1\cdot n=n$. And on a simple tensor, $\Psi\Phi(r\otimes n)=\Psi(rn)=1\otimes rn=1\cdot r\otimes n=r\otimes n$ (slide $1r\otimes n=1\otimes rn$ read backwards). Since simple tensors generate, $\Psi\Phi=\id$. Hence $R\otimes_R N\cong N$. Check. With $R=Z$, $Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(n)Z$, consistent with the $\gcd$ formula at $m=0$ read as $\gcd(0,n)=n$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: A bilinear map factoring through $\otimes$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A bilinear map factoring through $\otimes$}
Let $V=W=R^2$ over $R=R$. The determinant-style map $\beta\colon R^2\timesR^2\toR$, $\beta\big((a,b),(c,d)\big)=ad-bc$, is $R$-bilinear. Realize it as a homomorphism out of $R^2\otimes_RR^2$.
\wrec ``$R$-bilinear map into a group'' is exactly the UP trigger: it must factor uniquely through $\otimes$.
\wsol Check $\beta$ is balanced over $R$: additive in each argument (determinant expansion is linear in each row), and for $\lambda\inR$, $\beta(\lambda u,v)=\lambda\beta(u,v)=\beta(u,\lambda v)$. (Over the commutative ring $R$, an $R$-bilinear map is in particular balanced, and $\lambda$ slides freely.) By the UP there is a unique $R$-linear $B\colonR^2\otimes_RR^2\toR$ with $B(u\otimes v)=ad-bc$. On the basis $\{e_1\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_2,e_2\otimes e_1,e_2\otimes e_2\}$ of $R^2\otimes_RR^2\congR^4$, $B$ takes values $0,1,-1,0$. Check. $B(e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1)=1-(-1)=2$; directly $\beta(e_1,e_2)-\beta(e_2,e_1)=1-(-1)=2$. Note $e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1\neq0$ is not a simple tensor (it is the alternating combination $\det$ detects). Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Symmetry and a vanishing simple tensor
Content:
\begin{wex}{Symmetry and a vanishing simple tensor}
In $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(10)Z$, evaluate $\bar3\otimes\bar5$ and $\bar2\otimes\bar5$, and identify the whole group.
\wrec Cyclic generator argument plus slide relations to test individual simple tensors.
\wsol $\gcd(6,10)=2$, so $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(10)Z\congZ/(2)Z$, generated by $\bar1\otimes\bar1$ of order $2$. Now
\[
\bar3\otimes\bar5=15(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\overline{15}\cdot(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar1\cdot(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar1\otimes\bar1\neq0,
\]
since $15\equiv1\pmod2$. And
\[
\bar2\otimes\bar5=10(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar0,
\]
since $10\equiv0\pmod2$ (equivalently $\bar2\otimes\bar5=\bar1\otimes\overline{10}=\bar1\otimes\bar0=0$). Check. Both $\bar2$ and $\bar5$ are nonzero, yet $\bar2\otimes\bar5=0$ --- a concrete instance of ``$m\otimes n=0$ with $m,n\neq0$''. The image of $\bar a\otimes\bar b$ is $\overline{ab}\inZ/(2)Z$, matching $\bar3\otimes\bar5\mapsto\overline{15}=\bar1$ and $\bar2\otimes\bar5\mapsto\overline{10}=\bar0$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Extension of scalars / induced module
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Extension of scalars / induced module]
Let $R\subseteq S$ be a subring (with $1_R=1_S$) and $N$ a left $R$-module. Regard $S$ as an $(S,R)$-bimodule (left $S$-action by multiplication, right $R$-action by multiplication). Then
\[
S\otimes_R N
\]
is a left $S$-module via $s'\cdot(s\otimes n)=(s's)\otimes n$, extended additively. Moreover $\iota\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $\iota(n)=1\otimes n$, is an $R$-module homomorphism, and the pair $(S\otimes_R N,\iota)$ is universal for $R$-maps into $S$-modules:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & S\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,F"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
i.e. for every $S$-module $L$ and $R$-module hom $f\colon N\to L$ there is a unique $S$-module hom $F\colon S\otimes_R N\to L$ with $F\circ\iota=f$ (so $F(s\otimes n)=s\,f(n)$).
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Top-left: $N$, a left $R$-module (living at the smaller scalar level). Top-right: $S\otimes_R N$, the extended module, a left $S$-module formed by tensoring over $R$ with the $(S,R)$-bimodule $S$; simple tensors $s\otimes n$ span it, with $S$-action $s'(s\otimes n)=(s's)\otimes n$. Bottom: $L$, an arbitrary left $S$-module serving as target.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $\iota(n)=1\otimes n$, is the canonical $R$-module map from $N$ into the extended module, given by tensoring with the identity $1\in S$; it need not be injective (e.g.\ for $Z\subseteqQ$, $\iota\colonZ/(2)Z\toQ\otimes_ZZ/(2)Z=0$). \begin{wex}{Complexification $C\otimes_RR^n\congC^n$}

Check. $\dim_C(C\otimes_RR^n)=n$ while $\dim_R(C\otimes_RR^n)=2n$, matching $\dim_RC^n=2n$. For $n=1$: $C\otimes_RR\congC$ (a special case of $R\otimes_R N\cong N$, with $R=R$, $N=C$ and the two factors interchanged). Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $Q\otimes_Z M$ kills torsion
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q\otimes_Z M$ kills torsion}
Let $M$ be an abelian group ($Z$-module) and $T(M)$ its torsion subgroup. Show extension of scalars to $Q$ annihilates torsion: $Q\otimes_Z M\congQ\otimes_Z(M/T(M))$, and $Q\otimes_Z M=0$ iff $M$ is torsion.
\wrec Same denominator trick as $Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z$, applied element-by-element to torsion.
\wsol If $x\in M$ is torsion, say $kx=0$ with $k\ge1$, then for any $q\inQ$,
\[
q\otimes x=\Big(\tfrac qk\cdot k\Big)\otimes x=\tfrac qk\otimes(kx)=\tfrac qk\otimes 0=0.
\]
So every simple tensor with torsion right entry vanishes; hence the quotient map $M\to M/T(M)$ induces an isomorphism $Q\otimes_Z M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Q\otimes_Z(M/T(M))$ (its kernel is generated by tensors $q\otimes t$, $t\in T(M)$, all $0$). In particular, if $M=T(M)$ is all torsion then $Q\otimes_Z M=0$. Conversely if $M$ has an element $x$ of infinite order, $Z x\congZ$ embeds and (since $Q$ is flat / $Q\otimes_ZZ=Q$) contributes a nonzero $Q$ inside $Q\otimes_Z M$. Check. $Q\otimes_ZZ\congQ$ (rank $1$), $Q\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z=0$ (torsion), and $Q\otimes_Z(Z\oplusZ/(n)Z)\congQ\oplus0=Q$. The dimension equals the free rank of $M$. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Extending scalars on a free module: $S\otimes_R R^k\cong S^k$}

\end{wex}

Title: Reduction mod $p$: $Z/(p)Z\otimes_Z M\cong M/pM$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reduction mod $p$: $Z/(p)Z\otimes_Z M\cong M/pM$}
For $R=Z$, $S=Z/(p)Z$ is a quotient ring; show $Z/(p)Z\otimes_Z M\cong M/pM$ for any abelian group $M$.
\wrec Tensoring with a cyclic quotient ring $Z/pZ=Z/(p)$; expect to mod out by $p$.
\wsol Define $\varphi\colonZ/(p)Z\times M\to M/pM$ by $\varphi(\bar a,m)=\overline{am}$. Well defined: if $a\equiv a'\pmod p$ then $am-a'm=(a-a')m\in pM$. It is $Z$-balanced (biadditive; $\varphi(\bar a r,m)=\overline{arm}=\varphi(\bar a,rm)$ for $r\inZ$). The UP gives $\Phi\colonZ/(p)Z\otimes_Z M\to M/pM$, $\bar a\otimes m\mapsto\overline{am}$. Inverse: $\Psi\colon M/pM\toZ/(p)Z\otimes_Z M$, $\Psi(\bar m)=\bar1\otimes m$, well defined since $\bar1\otimes pm=\bar p\otimes m=\bar0\otimes m=0$. They invert each other on generators. Check. $Z/(p)Z\otimes_ZZ\congZ/pZ$ ($M=Z$), and $Z/(p)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(n)Z/pZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(p,n))Z$, agreeing with the $\gcd$ formula. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: $\otimes$ over a commutative ring
Content:
\begin{proposition}[$\otimes$ over a commutative ring]
Let $R$ be commutative and $M,N$ be $R$-modules (a right module is a left module via $mr:=rm$). Then $M\otimes_R N$ is an $R$-module via
\[
r\cdot(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn),
\]
extended additively, and this action is well defined. The canonical map $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$ is $R$-bilinear, and $M\otimes_R N$ is universal among $R$-modules receiving an $R$-bilinear map: every $R$-bilinear $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ into an $R$-module $L$ factors uniquely through an $R$-module hom $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi\ (R-bilinear)"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi\ (R-linear)"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Top-left: the Cartesian product $M\times N$ of two $R$-modules (here $R$ is commutative, so left and right actions coincide). Top-right: $M\otimes_R N$, now an $R$-module (not just an abelian group), via $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$. Bottom: $L$, an arbitrary $R$-module serving as target.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, the canonical map, now $R$-bilinear (not merely balanced) because $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$ in the $R$-module $M\otimes_R N$. (2) $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$, any $R$-bilinear map. (3) The dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$, the unique $R$-module homomorphism with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$; this upgrades the abelian-group UP to the $R$-module level.
\dgi{What commutes:} $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$: for every $(m,n)$, $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The abelian-group universal property already gives a unique group hom $\Phi$ with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$. One then checks $\Phi$ is $R$-linear: $\Phi(r(m\otimes n))=\Phi((rm)\otimes n)=\varphi(rm,n)=r\varphi(m,n)=r\Phi(m\otimes n)$, using $R$-linearity of $\varphi$ in the first argument. Commutativity of $R$ is used to make $(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$ a single well-posed relation rather than two separate axioms.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This proposition is placed here to show that, over a commutative ring, the tensor product is the universal $R$-module for bilinear maps---it lives in the category of $R$-modules, not just abelian groups. This is the natural setting for all subsequent applications (direct-sum decompositions, rank computation, symmetry $M\otimes_R N\cong N\otimes_R M$).
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=R$, $M=N=R^2$, $L=R$, $\varphi=\det$ (the determinant, which is $R$-bilinear). The unique $\Phi\colonR^2\otimes_RR^2\toR$ sends $e_i\otimes e_j\mapsto\det(e_i,e_j)$. Here $\Phi$ is an $R$-linear map between $R$-modules (not just an abelian-group hom).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Over a non-commutative ring $R$, $M\otimes_R N$ is only an abelian group, not an $R$-module (there is no canonical way to make the scalar action well defined without commutativity). Students sometimes write $r(m\otimes n)$ for general $R$ without checking; this is only valid when $R$ is commutative (or $M$/$N$ are bimodules).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that over a commutative ring the universal property of the tensor product holds in the richer category of $R$-modules, so $R$-bilinear maps correspond bijectively to $R$-linear maps out of $M\otimes_R N$---not just group homomorphisms.
\end{dgx}
\end{proposition}

Here $\Phi$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map between $\mathbb{R}$-modules (not just an abelian-group hom).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Over a non-commutative ring $R$, $M\otimes_R N$ is only an abelian group, not an $R$-module (there is no canonical way to make the scalar action well defined without commutativity). Students sometimes write $r(m\otimes n)$ for general $R$ without checking; this is only valid when $R$ is commutative (or $M$/$N$ are bimodules).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that over a commutative ring the universal property of the tensor product holds in the richer category of $R$-modules, so $R$-bilinear maps correspond bijectively to $R$-linear maps out of $M\otimes_R N$---not just group homomorphisms.
\end{dgx}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Sketch]
For fixed $r$, $(m,n)\mapsto (rm)\otimes n$ is $R$-balanced (using commutativity: $(mr')\mapsto r(mr')\otimes n=(mr')\otimes rn$ etc.), so $r\cdot(-)$ is a well-defined endomorphism; commutativity gives $(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$. Content:
\begin{remark}
Over commutative $R$, every $R$-bilinear map is $R$-balanced (not conversely: $(u,v)\mapsto\overline{uv}$, the complex conjugate of $uv$, is a $C$-balanced map $C\timesC\toC$ that is not $C$-bilinear), and one writes $r(m\otimes n)$ unambiguously. The earlier examples $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$, $R^2\otimes_RR^2\congR^4$, $C\otimes_RR^n\congC^n$ are all instances. Tensor distributes over direct sums: $M\otimes_R\big(\bigoplus_i N_i\big)\cong\bigoplus_i(M\otimes_R N_i)$, which together with $R\otimes_R N\cong N$ and $R/(a)\otimes_R R/(b)\cong R/(a,b)$ computes all tensor products of finitely generated modules over a PID.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: A PID tensor over $F[x]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A PID tensor over $F[x]$}
Let $R=F[x]$ ($F$ a field). Compute $\big(R/(x)\big)\otimes_R\big(R/(x^2)\big)$ and $\big(R/(x)\big)\otimes_R\big(R/(x-1)\big)$.
\wrec Cyclic-over-cyclic blocks over the PID $F[x]$: answer is $R/(\gcd)$.
\wsol By the block formula $R/(a)\otimes_R R/(b)\cong R/(\gcd(a,b))$. First, $\gcd(x,x^2)=x$, so
\[
\big(F[x]/(x)\big)\otimes_{F[x]}\big(F[x]/(x^2)\big)\cong F[x]/(x)\cong F.
\]
Second, $\gcd(x,\,x-1)=1$ (they are coprime: $1\cdot x-1\cdot(x-1)=1$), so
\[
\big(F[x]/(x)\big)\otimes_{F[x]}\big(F[x]/(x-1)\big)\cong F[x]/(1)=0.
\]
Check. The second is the $F[x]$-analogue of $Z/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ/(3)Z=0$ (coprime annihilators $\Rightarrow$ tensor $0$). For the first, $1\otimes 1$ generates and $x(1\otimes1)=\bar x\otimes1=0\otimes 1=0$, so the module is killed by $x$ and is $1$-dimensional over $F$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Direct sums: a $2\times2$ block computation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Direct sums: a $2\times2$ block computation}
Over $R=Z$, compute $(Z/(4)Z\oplusZ/(6)Z)\otimes_ZZ/(9)Z$.
\wrec Distribute $\otimes$ over $\oplus$, then apply the $\gcd$ rule to each block.
\wsol
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Z/(4)Z\oplusZ/(6)Z)\otimes_ZZ/(9)Z
&\cong(Z/(4)Z\otimes_ZZ/(9)Z)\oplus(Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(9)Z)\\
&\congZ/(\gcd(4,9))Z\oplusZ/(\gcd(6,9))Z=Z/(1)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z\congZ/(3)Z.
\end{aligned}
\]
Check. $\gcd(4,9)=1\Rightarrow$ first block $0$; $\gcd(6,9)=3\Rightarrow$ second block $Z/(3)Z$. The generator $(\bar0,\bar1)\otimes\bar1$ has order $3$ (it corresponds to the generator $\bar1\otimes\bar1\neq0$ of the block $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(9)Z\congZ/(3)Z$, and $3\cdot\big((\bar0,\bar1)\otimes\bar1\big)=(\bar0,\bar3)\otimes\bar1$ corresponds to $\bar3\otimes\bar1=3(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=0$). Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Free $\otimes$ free: $R^m\otimes_R R^n\cong R^{mn}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Free $\otimes$ free: $R^m\otimes_R R^n\cong R^{mn}$}
For commutative $R$, show $R^m\otimes_R R^n\cong R^{mn}$ and exhibit a basis.
\wrec Both factors free; distribute over $\oplus$ and use $R\otimes_R R\cong R$.
\wsol
\[
R^m\otimes_R R^n\cong\Big(\bigoplus_{i=1}^m R\Big)\otimes_R\Big(\bigoplus_{j=1}^n R\Big)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\bigoplus_{j=1}^n (R\otimes_R R)\cong\bigoplus_{i,j}R=R^{mn},
\]
with $R$-basis $\{e_i\otimes f_j: 1\le i\le m,\ 1\le j\le n\}$. Check. Ranks multiply: $\operatorname{rank}=mn$. For $R=R$, $m=n=2$ recovers $R^2\otimes_RR^2\congR^4$ with basis $e_1\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_2,e_2\otimes e_1,e_2\otimes e_2$, consistent with the determinant example. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Scalars commute past $\otimes$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Scalars commute past $\otimes$}
Over commutative $R=Z$, verify directly in $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(10)Z$ that $3\cdot(\bar1\otimes\bar1)$ can be computed on either factor.
\wrec Proposition: $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$ over commutative $R$.
\wsol Compute three ways: $3\cdot(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar3\otimes\bar1$ (act on the left factor) $=\bar1\otimes\bar3$ (act on the right factor) $=3(\bar1\otimes\bar1)$ again. In $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(10)Z\congZ/(2)Z$ (from $\gcd(6,10)=2$), the generator $\bar1\otimes\bar1$ has order $2$, so $3(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=1\cdot(\bar1\otimes\bar1)=\bar1\otimes\bar1$. Check. $\bar3\otimes\bar1\mapsto\overline{3}=\bar1\inZ/(2)Z$ and $\bar1\otimes\bar3\mapsto\overline{3}=\bar1\inZ/(2)Z$ under the iso $\bar a\otimes\bar b\mapsto\overline{ab}$; both equal $\bar1\otimes\bar1$. The action is consistent on both factors, as the Proposition guarantees. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: remark
Title: Summary of the universal pictures
Content:
\begin{remark}[Summary of the universal pictures]
The three universal properties in this section are the same diagram with different decorations:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "balanced \varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\ & L
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
N \arrow[r, "1\otimes-"] \arrow[dr, "R-map f"'] & S\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,S-map F"] \\ & L
\end{tikzcd}\]
Left: ordinary tensor product (balanced maps $\leftrightarrow$ group homs). Right: extension of scalars (induction $\dashv$ restriction). In each case the dashed arrow exists and is unique --- that uniqueness is what makes ``define a map on simple tensors'' legitimate after verifying balancedness.
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left diagram --- same three objects as the original tensor UP: $M\times N$ (Cartesian product, not a module), $M\otimes_R N$ (abelian group, or $R$-module when $R$ is commutative), and $L$ (an abelian group). This is the balanced-map / tensor-product universal property.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, canonical balanced map (top). $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$, any balanced map (diagonal). Dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$, unique group hom with $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$ (vertical, induced).
\dgi{What commutes:} $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$: both paths $(m,n)\to L$ agree.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $\Phi$ is defined on generators $m\otimes n$ by $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$; well-defined because $\varphi$ is balanced and therefore kills all relations in $H$. The summary presents this schematically to contrast it with the right-hand diagram.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark is placed after all three UP results to make visible that the same categorical pattern governs ordinary tensor products, extension of scalars, and the commutative-ring case. The left diagram encodes: to get a map out of $M\otimes_R N$, supply a balanced map and the UP does the rest.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $M=Z/(m)Z$, $N=Z/(n)Z$, $L=Z/(\gcd(m,n))Z$, $\varphi(\bar a,\bar b)=\overline{ab}$; the induced $\Phi$ is the isomorphism $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students reading the summary in isolation may think the two diagrams describe different objects. They describe the same shape (a universal triangle) applied to two different situations; the objects and arrow-types differ in each.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the tensor-product UP and the extension-of-scalars UP share the same universal-triangle shape, so mastering the pattern in one context immediately transfers to the other.
\end{dgx}
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Right diagram --- $N$ (a left $R$-module, the module before extension), $S\otimes_R N$ (the extended left $S$-module), and $L$ (an arbitrary left $S$-module).
\dgi{Arrows:} $1\otimes -\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $n\mapsto 1\otimes n$, the canonical $R$-module map (top; not injective in general). $f\colon N\to L$, any $R$-module homomorphism (diagonal). Dashed $F\colon S\otimes_R N\to L$, unique $S$-module homomorphism extending $f$ via $F(s\otimes n)=s\,f(n)$ (vertical).
\dgi{What commutes:} $F\circ(1\otimes -)=f$: $F(1\otimes n)=1\cdot f(n)=f(n)$ for every $n\in N$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $F$ relies on the $R$-balanced check $(s,n)\mapsto s\,f(n)$: the relation $(sr)\otimes n\mapsto (sr)f(n)=s\,f(rn)$ holds because $f$ is $R$-linear. Thus the balanced map induces $F$ as a group hom; it is $S$-linear by the $S$-action on $S\otimes_R N$. The uniqueness in the ``induction $\dashv$ restriction'' adjunction means any $R$-map $N\to L$ extends to a unique $S$-map $S\otimes_R N\to L$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The right diagram records that extension of scalars is the left adjoint to restriction of scalars: $\operatorname{Hom}_S(S\otimes_R N,L)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,L)$, a bijection natural in $L$. Placing it beside the tensor UP makes clear that both are instances of a single ``represent a functor by a universal object'' construction.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=R$, $S=C$, $N=R^2$, $L=C^3$, $f\colonR^2\toC^3$ an $R$-linear embedding. The unique $C$-linear extension is $F\colonC\otimes_RR^2\congC^2\toC^3$, $F(z\otimes v)=zf(v)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Thinking $F$ is the same map as $f$. They differ: $f$ is only $R$-linear into $L$, while $F$ is $S$-linear out of the larger module $S\otimes_R N$. The canonical map $\iota=1\otimes -$ is the bridge between them.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the extension-of-scalars construction $S\otimes_R N$ is the universal way to convert an $R$-linear map into an $S$-linear one, exhibiting the adjunction between induction and restriction of scalars.
\end{dgx}
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $f:R\to S$ be a ring homomorphism from the ring $R$ to the ring $S$ with $f(1_R)=1_S$. Verify the details that $sr=sf(r)$ defines a right $R$-action on $S$ under which $S$ is an $(S,R)$-bimodule.

\item Show that the element ``$2\otimes 1$'' is $0$ in $Z\otimes_{Z}Z/2Z$ but is nonzero in $2Z\otimes_{Z}Z/2Z$.

\item Show that $C\otimes_{R}C$ and $C\otimes_{C}C$ are both left $R$-modules but are not isomorphic as $R$-modules.

\item Show that $Q\otimes_{Z}Q$ and $Q\otimes_{Q}Q$ are isomorphic left $Q$-modules. [Show they are both $1$-dimensional vector spaces over $Q$.]

\item If $R$ is any integral domain with quotient field $Q$, prove that $(Q/R)\otimes_{R}(Q/R)=0$.

\item Let $I=(2,x)$ be the ideal generated by $2$ and $x$ in the ring $R=Z[x]$.

The ring $Z/2Z=R/I$ is naturally an $R$-module annihilated by both $2$ and $x$. \\ (a) Show that the map $\varphi:I\times I\toZ/2Z$ defined by $\varphi(a_{0}+a_{1}x+\cdots+a_{n}x^{n},b_{0}+b_{1}x+\cdots+b_{m}x^{m})=\frac{a_{0}}{2}b_{1}\bmod 2$ is $R$-bilinear. \\ (b) Show that there is an $R$-module homomorphism from $I\otimes_{R}I\toZ/2Z$ mapping $p(x)\otimes q(x)$ to $\frac{p(0)}{2}q'(0)$ where $q'$ denotes the usual polynomial derivative of $q$. \\ (c) Show that $2\otimes x\neq x\otimes 2$ in $I\otimes_{R}I$.

\item Suppose $I$ is a principal ideal in the integral domain $R$. Prove that the $R$-module $I\otimes_{R}I$ has no nonzero torsion elements (i.e., $rm=0$ with $0\neq r\in R$ and $m\in I\otimes_{R}I$ implies that $m=0$).

\item Let $I=(2,x)$ be the ideal generated by $2$ and $x$ in the ring $R=Z[x]$ as in Exercise 17. Show that the nonzero element $2\otimes x-x\otimes 2$ in $I\otimes_{R}I$ is a torsion element. Show in fact that $2\otimes x-x\otimes 2$ is annihilated by both $2$ and $x$ and that the submodule of $I\otimes_{R}I$ generated by $2\otimes x-x\otimes 2$ is isomorphic to $R/I$.

\item Let $I=(2,x)$ be the ideal generated by $2$ and $x$ in the ring $R=Z[x]$. Show that the element $2\otimes 2+x\otimes x$ in $I\otimes_{R}I$ is not a simple tensor, i.e., cannot be written as $a\otimes b$ for some $a,b\in I$.

\item Suppose $R$ is commutative and let $I$ and $J$ be ideals of $R$. \\ (a) Show there is a surjective $R$-module homomorphism from $I\otimes_{R}J$ to the product ideal $IJ$ mapping $i\otimes j$ to the element $ij$. \\ (b) Give an example to show that the map in (a) need not be injective (cf. Exercise 17).

\item Suppose that $M$ is a left and a right $R$-module such that $rm=mr$ for all $r\in R$ and $m\in M$. Show that the elements $r_{1}r_{2}$ and $r_{2}r_{1}$ act the same on $M$ for every $r_{1},r_{2}\in R$. (This explains why the assumption that $R$ is commutative in the definition of an $R$-algebra is a fairly natural one.)

\item Verify the details that the multiplication in Proposition 21 makes $A\otimes_{R}B$ into an $R$-algebra.

\item Prove that the extension of scalars from $Z$ to the Gaussian integers $Z[i]$ of the ring $R$ is isomorphic to $C$ as a ring: $Z[i]\otimes_{Z}R\congC$ as rings.

\item Let $S$ be a commutative ring containing $R$ (with $1_{S}=1_{R}$) and let $x$ be an indeterminate over $S$. Prove that $S[x]$ and $S\otimes_{R}R[x]$ are isomorphic as $S$-algebras.

\item Let $S$ be a commutative ring containing $R$ (with $1_{S}=1_{R}$) and let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ be independent indeterminates over the ring $S$. Show that for every ideal $I$ in the polynomial ring $R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ that $S\otimes_{R}(R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/I)\cong S[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/IS[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ as $S$-algebras.

\item (a) Write down a formula for the multiplication of two elements $a\cdot 1+b\cdot e_{2}+c\cdot e_{3}+d\cdot e_{4}$ and $a'\cdot 1+b'\cdot e_{2}+c'\cdot e_{3}+d'\cdot e_{4}$ in the example $A=C\otimes_{R}C$ following Proposition 21 (where $1=1\otimes 1$ is the identity of $A$). \\ (b) Let $\epsilon_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(1\otimes 1+i\otimes i)$ and $\epsilon_{2}=\frac{1}{2}(1\otimes 1-i\otimes i)$. Show that $\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}=0$, $\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}=1$, and $\epsilon_{j}^{2}=\epsilon_{j}$ for $j=1,2$ ($\epsilon_{1}$ and $\epsilon_{2}$ are called orthogonal idempotents in $A$). Deduce that $A$ is isomorphic as a ring to the direct product of two principal ideals: $A\cong A\epsilon_{1}\times A\epsilon_{2}$ (cf. Exercise 1, Section 7.6). \\ (c) Prove that the map $\varphi:C\timesC\toC\timesC$ by $\varphi(z_{1},z_{2})=(z_{1}z_{2},z_{1}\overline{z_{2}})$, where $\overline{z_{2}}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_{2}$, is an $R$-bilinear map. \\ (d) Let $\Phi$ be the $R$-module homomorphism from $A$ to $C\timesC$ obtained from $\varphi$ in (c). Show that $\Phi(\epsilon_{1})=(0,1)$ and $\Phi(\epsilon_{2})=(1,0)$. Show also that $\Phi$ is $C$-linear, where the action of $C$ is on the left tensor factor in $A$ and on both factors in $C\timesC$. Deduce that $\Phi$ is surjective. Show that $\Phi$ is a $C$-algebra isomorphism.
\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R = Z$. Compute $Z/(4)Z \otimes_{Z} Z/(6)Z$ explicitly, identifying it with $Z/(d)Z$ for the appropriate $d$, and write down the image of $\bar 1 \otimes \bar 1$.

\item Show that $Q \otimes_{Z} Z/(n)Z = 0$ for every $n \geq 1$. (Hint: write $\frac{a}{b} \otimes \bar x = \frac{a}{bn} \otimes n\bar x$.)

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-module. Construct a natural isomorphism $R \otimes_R M \cong M$ of $R$-modules, and verify it sends $r \otimes m \mapsto rm$.

\item Prove that $Z/(m)Z \otimes_{Z} Z/(n)Z \cong Z/(\gcd(m,n))Z$ for all positive integers $m, n$.

\item Let $V, W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $\F$ with $\dim_\F V = p$ and $\dim_\F W = q$. Prove $\dim_\F (V \otimes_\F W) = pq$ by exhibiting a basis of the tensor product in terms of bases of $V$ and $W$.

\item Let $R$ be commutative and let $M, N$ be $R$-modules. Prove the commutativity isomorphism $M \otimes_R N \cong N \otimes_R M$ as $R$-modules, sending $m \otimes n \mapsto n \otimes m$. Explain where you use the balanced (middle-linear) property.

\item Let $A$ be a nonzero finite abelian group. Show $A \otimes_{Z} Q = 0$ but $A \otimes_{Z} A$ need not vanish; illustrate with $A = Z/(2)Z$.

\item Let $f \colon M \to M'$ and $g \colon N \to N'$ be $R$-module homomorphisms ($R$ commutative). Define $f \otimes g \colon M \otimes_R N \to M' \otimes_R N'$ on simple tensors and verify it is a well-defined $R$-module homomorphism.

\item Compute $Z/(n)Z \otimes_{Z} Q/Z$ and determine whether it is zero. Justify.

\item Let $I, J$ be ideals of a commutative ring $R$. Prove $R/I \otimes_R R/J \cong R/(I+J)$ as $R$-modules.

\item Let $R = Z$ and consider the free module $Z^2$. Compute $Z^2 \otimes_{Z} Z/(3)Z$ and identify it as an abelian group; state its order.

\item For $R$ commutative, prove the associativity isomorphism $(M \otimes_R N) \otimes_R L \cong M \otimes_R (N \otimes_R L)$, sending $(m \otimes n) \otimes \ell \mapsto m \otimes (n \otimes \ell)$.

\item Let $S$ be a commutative ring containing the commutative ring $R$ as a subring (so $S$ is an $R$-algebra). For the $R$-module $R^n$, compute the $S$-module $S \otimes_R R^n$ obtained by extension of scalars and identify it as a free $S$-module of a stated rank.

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item State and prove the universal property of the tensor product: for every $R$-balanced (middle-linear) map $\varphi \colon M \times N \to L$ there is a unique group homomorphism $\Phi$ making the diagram commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\otimes"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
Verify that this universal property characterizes $M \otimes_R N$ up to unique isomorphism.

\item Recall the lifting property of projective modules. Use it together with the right-exactness of $- \otimes_R N$ to prove that if $P$ is projective then $P \otimes_R N$ is a direct summand of a free-module tensor, and that $- \otimes_R P$ takes the surjection $g$ to a surjection in the diagram below.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
& P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]

\item Let $R$ be commutative and let
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that for any $R$-module $N$ the induced sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
A \otimes_R N \arrow[r, "\psi \otimes 1"] & B \otimes_R N \arrow[r, "\varphi \otimes 1"] & C \otimes_R N \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
is exact (right-exactness), and give an explicit example with $R = Z$, $N = Z/(n)Z$ showing $\psi \otimes 1$ need not be injective.

\item Define an $R$-module $N$ to be flat if $- \otimes_R N$ is exact. Show that in the diagram of exercise 3, $N$ is flat iff $\psi \otimes 1$ is injective for every injection $\psi$, and use this criterion to verify that every free $R$-module is flat.

\item Consider a commutative diagram of $R$-modules with exact rows
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
& A \arrow[r, "\psi"] \arrow[d, "a"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, "b"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "c"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A' \arrow[r, hook, "\psi'"] & B' \arrow[r, "\varphi'"] & C'
\end{tikzcd}\]
Using the snake lemma, derive the exact sequence relating $\ker a, \ker b, \ker c$ and $\coker a, \coker b, \coker c$, then specialize to the rows obtained by applying $- \otimes_R N$ to a short exact sequence to interpret the connecting map.

\end{exers}

Throughout, $R$ is a ring with $1$ and modules are left $R$-modules unless noted. The
organizing idea of this section is to track when applying a functor (taking $\Hom$, or
tensoring) to a sequence of modules preserves the property ``image $=$ kernel at every
spot.'' Three classes of modules are exactly the ones that make a given functor preserve
exactness: projective for $\Hom_R(P,-)$, injective for $\Hom_R(-,Q)$, and flat for
$M\otimes_R-$.

Type: definition
Title: Exact sequence
Content:
\begin{definition}[Exact sequence]
A pair of $R$-module homomorphisms $X\xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ }Y\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }Z$ is
exact at $Y$ if $\im\alpha=\ker\beta$. A (finite or infinite) sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
\cdots \arrow[r] & X_{n+1} \arrow[r, "\alpha_{n+1}"] & X_n \arrow[r, "\alpha_n"] & X_{n-1} \arrow[r] & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each $X_n$ is an $R$-module (a term in the sequence). The dots indicate the sequence may extend infinitely in either direction. The subscript tracks position: $X_{n+1}$ feeds into $X_n$, which feeds into $X_{n-1}$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\alpha_{n+1}\colon X_{n+1}\to X_n$ and $\alpha_n\colon X_n\to X_{n-1}$ are $R$-module homomorphisms. The entire collection $\{\alpha_n\}$ is the chain of maps whose image-kernel relations the definition controls.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is an exact sequence, not a commutative square, so the relevant condition is not a path equality but the exactness conditions: $\operatorname{im}\alpha_{n+1} = \operatorname{ker}\alpha_n$ at every interior term $X_n$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Exactness at $X_n$ has two parts. First, $\alpha_n\circ\alpha_{n+1}=0$ (the composite vanishes), giving $\operatorname{im}\alpha_{n+1}\subseteq\operatorname{ker}\alpha_n$. Second, the reverse inclusion: every element of $\operatorname{ker}\alpha_n$ is in the image of $\alpha_{n+1}$. Together these force $\operatorname{im}=\operatorname{ker}$ at $X_n$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram introduces the definition of an exact sequence in full generality. The image-kernel condition is the single organizing equation that makes the whole theory of projective, injective, and flat modules meaningful.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $\cdots\toZ\xrightarrow{\times2}Z\xrightarrow{\pi}Z/(2)Z\to0\to\cdots$; exactness at the middle $Z$ says $\operatorname{im}(\times2)=2Z=\operatorname{ker}\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse $\alpha_n\circ\alpha_{n+1}=0$ (the composite kills everything) with full exactness; the first condition gives only $\subseteq$, not equality. A chain complex satisfies only the first; an exact sequence needs equality at every term.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that exactness at each node is the precise local condition image-equals-kernel, and the full sequence is exact when this holds simultaneously at every interior term.
\end{dgx}
is exact if it is exact at every interior $X_n$, i.e. $\im\alpha_{n+1}=\ker\alpha_n$
for all $n$.
\end{definition}

Type: prose
Content:
Two boundary cases pin down the language. With $0$ the zero module:
\begin{itemize}
\item $0\xrightarrow{\ }A\xrightarrow{\ \psi\ }B$ is exact at $A$ $\iff$ $\ker\psi=0$ $\iff$ $\psi$ is injective.
\item $B\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }C\xrightarrow{\ }0$ is exact at $C$ $\iff$ $\im\varphi=C$ $\iff$ $\varphi$ is surjective.
\end{itemize}

Type: definition
Title: Short exact sequence
Content:
\begin{definition}[Short exact sequence]
A short exact sequence (SES) is an exact sequence of the form
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $0$ is the zero module (placed at both ends). $A$, $B$, $C$ are $R$-modules. The zero modules bookend the sequence to enforce injectivity at the left and surjectivity at the right.
\dgi{Arrows:} The map $0\to A$ is forced to be the zero map. $\psi\colon A\to B$ is an $R$-module homomorphism required to be injective (exactness at $A$). $\varphi\colon B\to C$ is an $R$-module homomorphism required to be surjective (exactness at $C$). The map $C\to 0$ is also forced.
\dgi{What commutes:} Three exactness conditions hold simultaneously: (i) $\operatorname{ker}\psi=0$ so $\psi$ is injective; (ii) $\operatorname{im}\varphi=C$ so $\varphi$ is surjective; (iii) $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$ in the middle.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Condition (i) follows from exactness at $A$: $\operatorname{im}(0\to A)=0=\operatorname{ker}\psi$. Condition (ii) follows from exactness at $C$: $\operatorname{ker}(C\to0)=C=\operatorname{im}\varphi$. Condition (iii) is exactness at $B$. Together they say $\psi$ identifies $A$ as a submodule of $B$ and $\varphi$ exhibits $C$ as the quotient $B/\operatorname{im}\psi$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The SES is the standard package for encoding a submodule--quotient relationship. It unifies injectivity, surjectivity, and the image-kernel equation into a single compact object that is the building block for all splitting, projectivity, and injectivity arguments that follow.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $0\to nZ\hookrightarrowZ\xrightarrow{\pi}Z/(n)Z\to0$, with $\psi$ the inclusion and $\varphi=\pi$ the quotient map. Then $\operatorname{im}\psi=nZ=\operatorname{ker}\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read a SES as saying $B\cong A\oplus C$; this is the split case only. The sequence records the relationship $C\cong B/A$ but says nothing about a complementary copy of $C$ inside $B$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a short exact sequence packages the three conditions -- $\psi$ injective, $\varphi$ surjective, $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$ -- into one object that describes $B$ as an extension of $C$ by $A$.
\end{dgx}
Exactness at all three interior spots means precisely: $\psi$ is injective, $\varphi$ is
surjective, and $\im\psi=\ker\varphi$. Thus $\psi$ embeds $A$ as a submodule of $B$ and
$\varphi$ induces an isomorphism $B/\im\psi\cong C$, i.e. $C\cong B/A$.
\end{definition}

It unifies injectivity, surjectivity, and the image-kernel equation into a single compact object that is the building block for all splitting, projectivity, and injectivity arguments that follow.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $0\to n\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\to0$, with $\psi$ the inclusion and $\varphi=\pi$ the quotient map. Then $\operatorname{im}\psi=n\mathbb{Z}=\operatorname{ker}\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read a SES as saying $B\cong A\oplus C$; this is the split case only. The sequence records the relationship $C\cong B/A$ but says nothing about a complementary copy of $C$ inside $B$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a short exact sequence packages the three conditions -- $\psi$ injective, $\varphi$ surjective, $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$ -- into one object that describes $B$ as an extension of $C$ by $A$.
\end{dgx}
Exactness at all three interior spots means precisely: $\psi$ is injective, $\varphi$ is
surjective, and $\im\psi=\ker\varphi$. Thus $\psi$ embeds $A$ as a submodule of $B$ and
$\varphi$ induces an isomorphism $B/\im\psi\cong C$, i.e. $C\cong B/A$.
\end{definition}

Type: method
Title: Testing exactness of a (short) sequence
Content:
\begin{method}{Testing exactness of a (short) sequence}
Trigger. You are handed a chain of maps and asked whether it is exact, or whether
the two end zeros are legitimate. Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item At each interior node $Y$ with incoming $\alpha$ and outgoing $\beta$, first check
$\beta\circ\alpha=0$ (this gives $\im\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$ for free).
\item Then check the reverse $\ker\beta\subseteq\im\alpha$: take $y\in\ker\beta$ and exhibit a preimage under $\alpha$.
\item Leftmost zero $\Rightarrow$ check the first nonzero map is injective; rightmost zero $\Rightarrow$ check the last nonzero map is surjective.
\item For a SES, equivalently verify: $\psi$ injective, $\varphi$ surjective, $\im\psi=\ker\varphi$; often it is fastest to use the dimension/order count $|B|=|A|\cdot|C|$ (finite case) or $\rank$ count as a sanity check.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: An exact sequence of abelian groups
Content:
\begin{wex}{An exact sequence of abelian groups}
Problem. Show $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\ \times 3\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }Z/(3)Z\to0$ is exact,
where $\pi$ is reduction mod $3$.
\wrec A length-$5$ sequence with end zeros is a SES; check injective, surjective, and
$\im=\ker$ in the middle.
\wsol Left: $\times3\colon n\mapsto 3n$ has kernel $\{n:3n=0\}=0$, so it is
injective; exact at the left $Z$. Right: $\pi$ is surjective onto $Z/(3)Z$; exact at
$Z/(3)Z$. Middle: $\im(\times3)=3Z$ and $\ker\pi=\{n:3\mid n\}=3Z$, so
$\im(\times3)=\ker\pi$; exact at the middle $Z$. Hence exact everywhere.
Check. $Z/3Z\congZ/(3)Z$, consistent with $C\cong B/A$, and the first isomorphism
theorem gives $Z/\ker\pi=Z/3Z\cong\im\pi=Z/(3)Z$. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{An exact sequence of abelian groups}
Problem. Show $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times 3\ }\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is exact,
where $\pi$ is reduction mod $3$.
\wrec A length-$5$ sequence with end zeros is a SES; check injective, surjective, and
$\im=\ker$ in the middle.
\wsol \emph{Left:} $\times3\colon n\mapsto 3n$ has kernel $\{n:3n=0\}=0$, so it is
injective; exact at the left $\mathbb{Z}$. \emph{Right:} $\pi$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$; exact at
$\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. \emph{Middle:} $\im(\times3)=3\mathbb{Z}$ and $\ker\pi=\{n:3\mid n\}=3\mathbb{Z}$, so
$\im(\times3)=\ker\pi$; exact at the middle $\mathbb{Z}$. Hence exact everywhere.
\textit{Check.} $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$, consistent with $C\cong B/A$, and the first isomorphism
theorem gives $\mathbb{Z}/\ker\pi=\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\cong\im\pi=\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. Correct.

Title: A four-term sequence that fails exactness
Content:
\begin{wex}{A four-term sequence that fails exactness}
Problem. Is $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }Z\to0$ exact?
\wrec Same SES test; watch the middle composite and the surjectivity.
\wsol Compose the two middle maps: $n\mapsto 2n\mapsto 4n$, which is not zero, so
$\im(\times2)=2Z\not\subseteq\ker(\times2)=0$. Already exactness at the middle fails.
Also the right map $\times2\colonZ\toZ$ has image $2Z\neqZ$, so it is not surjective and
the rightmost zero is illegitimate.
Check. A SES with $A=C=Z$ would force $B$ to be an extension of $Z$ by $Z$ with
$B/A\cong C=Z$; that is possible (e.g. $B=Z^2$ with the maps being inclusion of the first
factor and projection to the second), but here the chosen maps simply fail the equalities.
Not exact.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A four-term sequence that fails exactness}
Problem. Is $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }\mathbb{Z}\to0$ exact?
\wrec Same SES test; watch the middle composite and the surjectivity.
\wsol Compose the two middle maps: $n\mapsto 2n\mapsto 4n$, which is \emph{not} zero, so
$\im(\times2)=2\mathbb{Z}\not\subseteq\ker(\times2)=0$. Already exactness at the middle fails.
Also the right map $\times2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ has image $2\mathbb{Z}\neq\mathbb{Z}$, so it is not surjective and
the rightmost zero is illegitimate.
\textit{Check.} A SES with $A=C=\mathbb{Z}$ would force $B$ to be an extension of $\mathbb{Z}$ by $\mathbb{Z}$ with
$B/A\cong C=\mathbb{Z}$; that is possible (e.g. $B=\mathbb{Z}^2$ with the maps being inclusion of the first
factor and projection to the second), but here the chosen maps simply fail the equalities.
Not exact.
\end{wex}

Title: Exactness with a direct sum in the middle
Content:
\begin{wex}{Exactness with a direct sum in the middle}
Problem. For $R$-modules $A,C$, show $0\to A\xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }A\oplus
C\xrightarrow{\ p\ }C\to0$ is exact, where $\iota(a)=(a,0)$ and $p(a,c)=c$.
\wrec ``Inclusion then projection'' is the prototype SES; check the three conditions.
\wsol $\iota$ is injective since $\iota(a)=(0,0)\Rightarrow a=0$. $p$ is surjective since
$p(0,c)=c$. Middle: $\im\iota=\{(a,0)\}=A\oplus0$ and $\ker p=\{(a,c):c=0\}=A\oplus0$, equal.
Exact. Check. $(A\oplus C)/(A\oplus0)\cong C$, matching $C\cong B/A$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Exact. \textit{Check.} $(A\oplus C)/(A\oplus0)\cong C$, matching $C\cong B/A$. Correct.

Title: Kernel--cokernel exact sequence
Content:
\begin{wex}{Kernel--cokernel exact sequence}
Problem. Given any $R$-homomorphism $f\colon M\to N$, build a four-term exact sequence
recording $\ker f$ and $\coker f=N/\im f$.
\wrec Any single map spawns a canonical exact sequence through its kernel and cokernel.
\wsol Take $0\to\ker f\xrightarrow{\ \subseteq\ }M\xrightarrow{\ f\ }N\xrightarrow{\
q\ }\coker f\to0$, with $q$ the quotient map. Exact at $\ker f$: inclusion is injective.
At $M$: image of inclusion is $\ker f$. At $N$: $\im f=\ker q$ by definition of the
quotient $N/\im f$. At $\coker f$: $q$ is surjective. Check. $f$ injective $\iff
\ker f=0$ (left three terms collapse to a SES) and $f$ surjective $\iff\coker f=0$. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:

Title: A vector-space exact sequence and dimension count
Content:
\begin{wex}{A vector-space exact sequence and dimension count}
Problem. Over $\F=Q$, is $0\toQ^2\xrightarrow{\ A\ }Q^3\xrightarrow{\ B\ }Q\to0$ exact
for $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$?
\wrec For vector spaces, exactness of a SES is equivalent to the rank--nullity count
$\dim B=\dim A+\dim C$ together with $\im=\ker$.
\wsol $A$ has rank $2$, so injective; exact at $Q^2$. $B$ has rank $1$, so surjective onto
$Q$; exact at $Q$. Middle: $\im A=\{(x,y,0)\}$ and $\ker B=\{(x,y,z):z=0\}=\{(x,y,0)\}$,
equal. Exact. Check. $\dimQ^3=3=2+1=\dimQ^2+\dimQ$, consistent. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A vector-space exact sequence and dimension count}
Problem. Over $\F=\mathbb{Q}$, is $0\to\mathbb{Q}^2\xrightarrow{\ A\ }\mathbb{Q}^3\xrightarrow{\ B\ }\mathbb{Q}\to0$ exact
for $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$?
\wrec For vector spaces, exactness of a SES is equivalent to the rank--nullity count
$\dim B=\dim A+\dim C$ together with $\im=\ker$.
\wsol $A$ has rank $2$, so injective; exact at $\mathbb{Q}^2$. $B$ has rank $1$, so surjective onto
$\mathbb{Q}$; exact at $\mathbb{Q}$. Middle: $\im A=\{(x,y,0)\}$ and $\ker B=\{(x,y,z):z=0\}=\{(x,y,0)\}$,
equal. Exact. \textit{Check.} $\dim\mathbb{Q}^3=3=2+1=\dim\mathbb{Q}^2+\dim\mathbb{Q}$, consistent. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Split SES; splitting and retraction]
A SES $0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ is split if there is an
$R$-homomorphism $s\colon C\to B$ (a splitting / section) with $\varphi\circ
s=\id_C$; equivalently, if there is an $R$-homomorphism $t\colon B\to A$ (a
retraction) with $t\circ\psi=\id_A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
$(1)\Rightarrow(3)$: Given $s$, set $K=\im s$. For $b\in B$, write
$b=(b-s\varphi(b))+s\varphi(b)$. Now $\varphi(b-s\varphi(b))=\varphi(b)-\varphi
s\varphi(b)=\varphi(b)-\varphi(b)=0$, so $b-s\varphi(b)\in\ker\varphi=\im\psi$. Thus
$B=\im\psi+K$. If $x\in\im\psi\cap K$, then $x=s(c)$ and $\varphi(x)=0$, but
$\varphi(x)=\varphi s(c)=c$, so $c=0$ and $x=0$; the sum is direct. The map
$\varphi|_K\colon K\to C$ has inverse $s$, so it is an isomorphism.
$(3)\Rightarrow(2)$: With $B=\im\psi\oplus K$, define $t\colon B\to A$ by
$t(\psi(a)+k)=a$ (well defined since $\psi$ is injective). Then $t\psi=\id_A$.
$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$: Given $t$, restrict $\varphi$ to $\ker t$; one checks
$\varphi|_{\ker t}$ is an isomorphism whose inverse is a splitting $s$. Concretely, for
$c\in C$ pick $b$ with $\varphi(b)=c$ and set $s(c)=b-\psi t(b)$; this is independent of the
choice of $b$ and satisfies $\varphi s=\id_C$. Finally, in every case the assignment
$a+c\mapsto\psi(a)+s(c)$ gives an isomorphism $A\oplus C\xrightarrow{\cong}B$.
\end{proof}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Exact Sequences --- Projective, Injective, and Flat Modules > Split short exact sequences
Type: method
Title: Deciding whether a SES splits
Content:
\begin{method}{Deciding whether a SES splits}
Trigger. You have a SES and want to know if $B\cong A\oplus C$, or you must build
a splitting. Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Try to define a section $s\colon C\to B$ by sending generators of $C$ to chosen
preimages that respect all relations; if the relations can be honored, $s$ exists
and the sequence splits.
\item Equivalently hunt for a retraction $t\colon B\to A$ fixing the copy of $A$.
\item To prove non-splitting, show $B\not\cong A\oplus C$ as $R$-modules (compare
torsion, order of elements, number of elements of a given order, etc.).
\item Special automatic case: if $C$ is projective (e.g. free), the sequence always splits.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Title: The classic non-split SES $0\toZ\xrightarrow{2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The classic non-split SES $0\toZ\xrightarrow{2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$}
Problem. Show $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }Z/(2)Z\to0$ is exact but
does not split.
\wrec A SES of abelian groups; non-splitting is detected by comparing $B$ with $A\oplus C$.
\wsol Exact: $\times2$ injective, $\pi$ surjective, $\im(\times2)=2Z=\ker\pi$. Suppose a
splitting $s\colonZ/(2)Z\toZ$ existed. Then $s(\bar1)\inZ$ must satisfy $2\cdot
s(\bar1)=s(2\cdot\bar1)=s(\bar0)=0$, forcing $s(\bar1)=0$, so $s=0$ and $\pi s=0\neq\id$.
No splitting exists. Equivalently $B=Z$ is torsion-free while
$A\oplus C=Z\oplusZ/(2)Z$ has a nonzero element of order $2$, so $Z\not\congZ\oplusZ/(2)Z$.
Check. $|A|\cdot|C|$ as orders matches the index $[Z:2Z]=2=|Z/(2)Z|$; the order
count passes yet the sequence still fails to split, confirming the order count is not
sufficient.
\end{wex}

Problem. Show $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times2\ }\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is exact but
does \emph{not} split.
\wrec A SES of abelian groups; non-splitting is detected by comparing $B$ with $A\oplus C$.
\wsol Exact: $\times2$ injective, $\pi$ surjective, $\im(\times2)=2\mathbb{Z}=\ker\pi$. Suppose a
splitting $s\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ existed. Then $s(\bar1)\in\mathbb{Z}$ must satisfy $2\cdot
s(\bar1)=s(2\cdot\bar1)=s(\bar0)=0$, forcing $s(\bar1)=0$, so $s=0$ and $\pi s=0\neq\id$.
No splitting exists. Equivalently $B=\mathbb{Z}$ is torsion-free while
$A\oplus C=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ has a nonzero element of order $2$, so $\mathbb{Z}\not\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$.

count passes yet the sequence still fails to split, confirming the order count is not
sufficient.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A split SES of abelian groups}
Problem. Show $0\toZ/(2)Z\xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }Z/(6)Z\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }Z/(3)Z\to0$ splits,
where $\iota(\bar1)=\bar3$ and $\varphi$ is reduction mod $3$.
\wrec Build a section sending the generator of $Z/(3)Z$ to a compatible preimage in $Z/(6)Z$.
\wsol Exact: $\iota(\bar1)=\bar3$ has order $2$ in $Z/(6)Z$, injective; $\ker\varphi=\{\bar0,\bar3\}=\im\iota$;
$\varphi$ surjective. Define $s\colonZ/(3)Z\toZ/(6)Z$ by $s(\bar1)=\bar4$. Check well defined:
$3\cdot\bar4=\bar{12}=\bar0$ in $Z/(6)Z$, so the relation $3\bar1=0$ is honored. Then
$\varphi(s(\bar1))=\varphi(\bar4)=\bar1$, so $\varphi s=\id$. Splits, and indeed
$Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ by CRT. Check. $|Z/(6)Z|=6=2\cdot3=|Z/(2)Z|\cdot|Z/(3)Z|$ and the
direct sum decomposition exists. Correct.
\end{wex}

\wrec Build a section sending the generator of $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ to a compatible preimage in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol Exact: $\iota(\bar1)=\bar3$ has order $2$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$, injective; $\ker\varphi=\{\bar0,\bar3\}=\im\iota$;
$\varphi$ surjective. Define $s\colon\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ by $s(\bar1)=\bar4$. Check well defined:
$3\cdot\bar4=\bar{12}=\bar0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$, so the relation $3\bar1=0$ is honored. Then
$\varphi(s(\bar1))=\varphi(\bar4)=\bar1$, so $\varphi s=\id$. Splits, and indeed
$\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ by CRT. \textit{Check.} $|\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}|=6=2\cdot3=|\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}|\cdot|\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}|$ and the
direct sum decomposition exists. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Surjection onto a free module always splits
Content:
\begin{wex}{Surjection onto a free module always splits}
Problem. Show every SES $0\to A\to B\xrightarrow{\varphi}R^n\to0$ of $R$-modules splits.
\wrec The right-hand term is free; lift a basis to define a section.
\wsol Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be the standard basis of $R^n$. Since $\varphi$ is surjective,
pick $b_i\in B$ with $\varphi(b_i)=e_i$. Define $s\colon R^n\to B$ by
$s(\sum r_ie_i)=\sum r_ib_i$; this is well defined precisely because $R^n$ is free on the
$e_i$ (no relations to honor). Then $\varphi s(e_i)=\varphi(b_i)=e_i$, so $\varphi
s=\id_{R^n}$. Splits. Check. Consequently $B\cong A\oplus R^n$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-split SES of $\F[x]$-modules
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-split SES of $\F[x]$-modules}
Problem. Let $R=\F[x]$ and let $V=R/(x^2)$ with $A=(x)/(x^2)\cong R/(x)=\F$,
$C=R/(x)=\F$. Show $0\to A\to V\to C\to0$ is non-split.
\wrec An $\F[x]$-module is a vector space with operator $x$; non-splitting shows up as a
single Jordan block rather than two.
\wsol Here $x$ acts on $V=R/(x^2)$ as the nilpotent operator with $x\cdot\bar1=\bar x\neq0$
but $x\cdot\bar x=0$ -- a single $2\times2$ Jordan block for eigenvalue $0$. A splitting
would give $V\cong A\oplus C$ with $x$ acting as $0$ on each summand, i.e. $x\cdot v=0$ for
all $v$. But $x\cdot\bar1=\bar x\neq0$, contradiction. Non-split. Check. As
$\F$-spaces $\dim V=2=\dim A+\dim C$, so the order/dimension count passes while the operator
structure forbids splitting. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
``$|B|=|A|\cdot|C|$, so $B\cong A\oplus C$'' is false. The order/dimension count is a
necessary consequence of a SES but says nothing about splitting:
$0\toZ\xrightarrow{2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ passes the count yet does not split, and
$0\toZ/(2)Z\toZ/(4)Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ has $|B|=4=2\cdot2$ but $Z/(4)Z\not\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(2)Z$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: definition
Title: Projective module
Content:
\begin{definition}[Projective module]
An $R$-module $P$ is projective if for every surjection $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow
C$ and every homomorphism $f\colon P\to C$ there is a (not necessarily unique) lift
$\tilde f\colon P\to B$ with $g\circ\tilde f=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 & P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $P$ is the module being tested for projectivity. $B$ and $C$ are $R$-modules. The diagram encodes a universal lifting problem: can every map out of $P$ be routed through $B$ instead of going directly to $C$?
\dgi{Arrows:} $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ is a surjective $R$-module homomorphism (the twoheads notation). $f\colon P\to C$ is an arbitrary $R$-homomorphism. The dashed arrow $\tilde f\colon P\to B$ is the asserted lift, with $\exists$ indicating it need not be unique.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $g\circ\tilde f = f$. That is, the two paths from $P$ to $C$ agree: going directly via $f$ equals going via $\tilde f$ and then $g$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} By definition, $P$ is projective precisely when such a $\tilde f$ always exists. The surjectivity of $g$ guarantees enough elements in $B$ to hit any $f(p)$; projectivity says a coherent (homomorphism) choice of preimages can always be made.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the definition of projectivity. It asserts that $P$ is ``free enough'' to lift maps through any surjection, and it is the precise condition that later characterizes free modules and direct summands of free modules, and makes $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ exact.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $P=Z$, $g\colonZ\twoheadrightarrowZ/(5)Z$ (reduction mod 5), $f\colonZ\toZ/(5)Z$ with $f(1)=\bar3$. Lift: $\tilde f(1)=3\inZ$; then $g(\tilde f(1))=\bar3=f(1)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow is not unique in general; the definition asks only for existence. Also the diagram requires $g$ to be surjective: if $g$ is merely an arbitrary homomorphism, the lift need not exist even for free $P$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $P$ is projective when every map from $P$ into a quotient can be lifted to a map into the module above it, making $P$ ``resolution-proof'' against surjections.
\end{dgx}
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: In $0\to A\to B\xrightarrow{g}P\to0$ apply lifting to $f=\id_P$ and
the surjection $g$; the lift $\tilde f\colon P\to B$ satisfies $g\tilde f=\id_P$, a
splitting. $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$: Every module is a quotient of a free module, so there is a
SES $0\to Q\to F\xrightarrow{\,p\,}P\to0$ with $F$ free. By $(2)$ it splits, so
$F\cong P\oplus Q$. $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$: Free modules lift (Worked Ex.\ ``free $\Rightarrow$
projective'' below), and a direct summand of a lifter lifts: given $f\colon P\to C$ and
$g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$, extend $f$ by $0$ on $Q$ to get $F=P\oplus Q\to C$, lift
that to $B$ since $F$ is free, then restrict to $P$. $(1)\iff(4)$: $\Hom_R(P,-)$ is always
left exact (Thm.~ [REF:thm:homexact@c10] ); it is exact iff it preserves surjections, which is
exactly the lifting property.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Recognizing / using projectivity
Content:
\begin{method}{Recognizing / using projectivity}
Trigger. You must lift a map through a surjection, split a SES whose quotient is
$P$, or certify a module is projective. Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $P$ is free, it is projective -- lift by sending a basis to chosen preimages.
\item To show $P$ projective, exhibit a free $F$ with $F\cong P\oplus Q$ (find a complementary summand).
\item Over $Z/(n)Z$ with $n=ab$, $\gcd(a,b)=1$: $Z/(n)Z\congZ/(a)Z\oplusZ/(b)Z$, so each factor is a projective $Z/(n)Z$-module.
\item To use projectivity, invoke the lift $\tilde f$ or the automatic splitting of $0\to A\to B\to P\to0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Free $\Rightarrow$ projective
Content:
\begin{wex}{Free $\Rightarrow$ projective}
Problem. Show every free $R$-module $F=R^{(A)}$ is projective.
\wrec Lifting on a free module is determined freely by where the basis goes.
\wsol Let $\{e_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a basis, $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ surjective,
$f\colon F\to C$. For each $a$ pick $b_a\in B$ with $g(b_a)=f(e_a)$ (possible by
surjectivity). Define $\tilde f\colon F\to B$ on the basis by $\tilde f(e_a)=b_a$ and extend
$R$-linearly; this is well defined since $F$ is free. Then $g\tilde f(e_a)=g(b_a)=f(e_a)$
for all $a$, so $g\tilde f=f$. Check. The diagram commutes on a generating set, hence
everywhere. Correct.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "{\tilde f\,:\,e_a\mapsto b_a}"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R^{(A)}$ is the free $R$-module on index set $A$ with basis $\{e_a\}_{a\in A}$. $B$ and $C$ are arbitrary $R$-modules. This is the same lifting triangle as in the definition of projective, now specialized to a free module.
\dgi{Arrows:} $f\colon R^{(A)}\to C$ is the map to be lifted. $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ is a surjection. The dashed $\tilde f\colon R^{(A)}\to B$ is the explicit lift constructed by sending $e_a\mapsto b_a$ where $g(b_a)=f(e_a)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $g\circ\tilde f = f$. Concretely $g(\tilde f(e_a))=g(b_a)=f(e_a)$ for all $a\in A$, and since $\{e_a\}$ is a basis this forces $g\tilde f=f$ everywhere.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The key is that $R^{(A)}$ is free: defining a homomorphism on a free module requires only a choice of images for each basis element with no relations to satisfy. Surjectivity of $g$ supplies the needed $b_a$, and freeness lets the formula $\tilde f(\sum r_ae_a)=\sum r_ab_a$ extend consistently.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram provides the base case (free $\Rightarrow$ projective) for the whole theory. All other projectivity proofs either cite this directly or use summand arguments that reduce to it.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R^{(A)}=Z$, $g\colonZ\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$, $f\colonZ\toZ/(n)Z$ with $f(1)=\bar k$. Pick any $b_1\inZ$ with $g(b_1)=\bar k$, e.g. $b_1=k$; then $\tilde f(n)=kn$ lifts $f$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The lift $\tilde f$ depends on the choice of preimages $b_a$ and is not unique. Students sometimes think the diagram forces a canonical lift; it does not. What freeness guarantees is only that some consistent choice always works.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a free module lifts every map through every surjection because its basis elements can be sent independently to any chosen preimages, with no relations obstructing the construction.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}

Title: $Z/(2)Z$ is a projective $Z/(6)Z$-module
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(2)Z$ is a projective $Z/(6)Z$-module}
Problem. Show $Z/(2)Z$ is projective as a $Z/(6)Z$-module.
\wrec Direct summand of a free module $\Rightarrow$ projective; use CRT to split the free
module $Z/(6)Z$.
\wsol By the Chinese Remainder Theorem $Z/(6)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ as rings and as
$Z/(6)Z$-modules. The free rank-$1$ module $F=Z/(6)Z$ thus decomposes as
$F\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$, exhibiting $Z/(2)Z$ as a direct summand of the free module $Z/(6)Z$. By
Thm.~ [REF:thm:proj@c10] $(3)$, $Z/(2)Z$ is projective. Check. The complementary summand is
$Q=Z/(3)Z$, and $Z/(2)Z\oplusZ/(3)Z$ has order $6=|Z/(6)Z|$. Note $Z/(2)Z$ is not free over
$Z/(6)Z$ (it has $2$ elements, not a multiple of $6$), so projective $\not\Rightarrow$
free in general. Correct.
\end{wex}

Problem. Show $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is projective as a $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$-module.
\wrec Direct summand of a free module $\Rightarrow$ projective; use CRT to split the free
module $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol By the Chinese Remainder Theorem $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ as rings and as
$\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$-modules. The free rank-$1$ module $F=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ thus decomposes as
$F\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$, exhibiting $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ as a direct summand of the free module $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$. By

\begin{wex}{$Z/(2)Z$ is NOT projective over $Z/(4)Z$}
Problem. Show $Z/(2)Z$ is not a projective $Z/(4)Z$-module.
\wrec If projective, the surjection $Z/(4)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(2)Z$ would split.
\wsol Consider $0\toZ/(2)Z\xrightarrow{\times2}Z/(4)Z\xrightarrow{\pi}Z/(2)Z\to0$ (with
$\times2\colon\bar1\mapsto\bar2$). If $Z/(2)Z$ were projective, this SES would split, giving
$Z/(4)Z\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(2)Z$. But $Z/(4)Z$ has an element of order $4$ while
$Z/(2)Z\oplusZ/(2)Z$ has exponent $2$. Contradiction. Check. Equivalently no section
$s\colonZ/(2)Z\toZ/(4)Z$ with $\pi s=\id$ exists: $s(\bar1)$ would need odd value, but
$2s(\bar1)=s(\bar2)=s(\bar0)=0$ forces $s(\bar1)\in\{\bar0,\bar2\}$, both even,
contradiction. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Lifting a map using projectivity of $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Lifting a map using projectivity of $Z$}
Problem. Let $g\colonZ\twoheadrightarrowZ/(5)Z$ be reduction and $f\colonZ\toZ/(5)Z$ be
$f(1)=\bar3$. Lift $f$ through $g$.
\wrec $Z$ is free, hence projective; lift by choosing one preimage of $f$ of a generator.
\wsol Choose $b\inZ$ with $g(b)=\bar3$, e.g. $b=3$. Define $\tilde f\colonZ\toZ$ by
$\tilde f(1)=3$, i.e. $\tilde f(n)=3n$. Then $g\tilde f(1)=g(3)=\bar3=f(1)$, so $g\tilde
f=f$. Check. Any $b\in 3+5Z$ also works (lifts are non-unique), confirming the lift
need not be unique. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Lifting a map using projectivity of $\mathbb{Z}$}
Problem. Let $g\colon\mathbb{Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ be reduction and $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ be
$f(1)=\bar3$. Lift $f$ through $g$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ is free, hence projective; lift by choosing one preimage of $f$ of a generator.
\wsol Choose $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $g(b)=\bar3$, e.g. $b=3$. Define $\tilde f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ by
$\tilde f(1)=3$, i.e. $\tilde f(n)=3n$. Then $g\tilde f(1)=g(3)=\bar3=f(1)$, so $g\tilde
f=f$. \textit{Check.} Any $b\in 3+5\mathbb{Z}$ also works (lifts are non-unique), confirming the lift
need not be unique. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Direct sum of projectives is projective
Content:
\begin{wex}{Direct sum of projectives is projective}
Problem. Show $P_1\oplus P_2$ is projective whenever $P_1,P_2$ are.
\wrec Lift on each summand separately and combine; or use that a summand-of-free plus
summand-of-free is a summand of free.
\wsol Given $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ and $f\colon P_1\oplus P_2\to C$, restrict to
$f_i=f|_{P_i}$. Lift each to $\tilde f_i\colon P_i\to B$ with $g\tilde f_i=f_i$. Define
$\tilde f(p_1,p_2)=\tilde f_1(p_1)+\tilde f_2(p_2)$. Then $g\tilde
f(p_1,p_2)=g\tilde f_1(p_1)+g\tilde f_2(p_2)=f_1(p_1)+f_2(p_2)=f(p_1,p_2)$.
Check. If $F_i\cong P_i\oplus Q_i$ are free then $F_1\oplus F_2$ is free and
$\cong(P_1\oplus P_2)\oplus(Q_1\oplus Q_2)$, re-deriving projectivity via
Thm.~ [REF:thm:proj@c10] $(3)$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Problem. Show $P_1\oplus P_2$ is projective whenever $P_1,P_2$ are.
\wrec Lift on each summand separately and combine; or use that a summand-of-free plus

Type: definition
Title: Injective module
Content:
\begin{definition}[Injective module]
An $R$-module $Q$ is injective if for every injection $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow
B$ and every homomorphism $f\colon A\to Q$ there is an extension $\tilde f\colon B\to Q$
with $\tilde f\circ\iota=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[d, "f"'] & B \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"] \\
 & Q &
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $A$ and $B$ are $R$-modules with $A$ a submodule of $B$ (witnessed by $\iota$). $Q$ is the module being tested for injectivity. The $0$ at the left signals that $\iota$ is injective (the sequence $0\to A\to B$ is exact at $A$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$ is an injection. $f\colon A\to Q$ is an arbitrary $R$-homomorphism from the submodule. The dashed $\tilde f\colon B\to Q$ is the asserted extension of $f$ past the inclusion, with $\exists$ indicating it need not be unique.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\tilde f\circ\iota = f$. That is, the two paths from $A$ to $Q$ agree: the direct map $f$ equals the composition $\tilde f$ followed back along $\iota$, i.e. $\tilde f$ restricted to $A$ is $f$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $Q$ is injective precisely when such a $\tilde f$ always exists. This is the dual of projectivity: instead of lifting through a surjection on the output side, we extend along an injection on the input side. Divisibility over $Z$ supplies the solutions needed to make the extension a homomorphism.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the definition of injectivity. It is the categorical dual of the projective lifting diagram, and it encodes the precise condition that makes $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ exact: every map into $Q$ from a submodule extends to the whole ambient module.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $A=2Z\subset B=Z$, $f\colon2Z\toQ$ with $f(2)=3$. Since $Q$ is divisible, extend: $\tilde f(1)=3/2$ and $\tilde f(n)=3n/2$; then $\tilde f(2)=3=f(2)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse the direction of duality: in the projective diagram $P$ maps into a surjection; in the injective diagram $Q$ is the target and the extension goes from $B$ to $Q$. The arrows run opposite to each other.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $Q$ is injective when any map into $Q$ defined on a submodule can always be extended to the entire ambient module, making $Q$ ``absorption-proof'' against injections.
\end{dgx}
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: extend $\id_Q$ along $Q\hookrightarrow B$ to get a retraction $B\to
Q$, which splits the sequence (Prop.~ [REF:prop:split@c10] ). $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$ and the link
to exactness of $\Hom_R(-,Q)$ follow from the long-exactness machinery; $\Hom_R(-,Q)$ is
always left exact (Thm.~ [REF:thm:homexact@c10] ), and injectivity is exactly the statement that
it carries injections $A\hookrightarrow B$ to surjections $\Hom_R(B,Q)\twoheadrightarrow
\Hom_R(A,Q)$, i.e. every $f\colon A\to Q$ extends to $B$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Baer's Criterion
Label: thm:baer@c10
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Baer's Criterion] 
An $R$-module $Q$ is injective if and only if for every left ideal $I\subseteq R$, every
$R$-homomorphism $g\colon I\to Q$ extends to an $R$-homomorphism $\tilde g\colon R\to Q$.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:baer@c10

Title: Proof sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-0b19d3c3672045ace293
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) is the extension property applied to $I\hookrightarrow R$. ($\Leftarrow$)
Given $f\colon A\to Q$ with $A\subseteq B$, use Zorn's Lemma on the poset of partial
extensions $(A',f')$ with $A\subseteq A'\subseteq B$ and $f'|_A=f$. A maximal element
$(A^*,f^*)$ must have $A^*=B$: if some $b\in B\smallsetminus A^*$, the set $I=\{r\in
R:rb\in A^*\}$ is a left ideal, $r\mapsto f^*(rb)$ defines $g\colon I\to Q$, and the
hypothesis extends $g$ to $R$, which lets us extend $f^*$ to $A^*+Rb$, contradicting
maximality. Hence $f^*\colon B\to Q$ extends $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Divisible module]
An abelian group (i.e. $Z$-module) $D$ is divisible if for every $d\in D$ and every
nonzero $n\inZ$ there exists $d'\in D$ with $nd'=d$.

\end{definition}

Label: cor:divisible@c10
Content:
\begin{corollary} 
A $Z$-module is injective if and only if it is divisible. In particular $Q$, $Q/Z$, and
$R/Z$ are injective $Z$-modules, while $Z$ and $Z/(n)Z$ ($n\geq2$) are not.
\end{corollary}
label: cor:divisible@c10

\begin{proof}
By Baer's Criterion over $R=Z$ it suffices to extend maps from ideals $I=nZ$ to $Z$. A
map $g\colon nZ\to D$ is determined by $g(n)=d\in D$; an extension $\tilde g\colonZ\to D$
exists iff there is $d'=\tilde g(1)$ with $nd'=g(n)=d$, i.e. iff $D$ is divisible.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Showing a module is (not) injective
Content:
\begin{method}{Showing a module is (not) injective}
Trigger. Certify injectivity, or extend a map past an inclusion.
Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Over $Z$: injective $\iff$ divisible -- check $nd'=d$ solvable for all $n\neq0$, $d$.
\item General ring: use Baer -- only need to extend maps $I\to Q$ from ideals $I$ to $R$.
\item To extend a concrete $f\colon A\to Q$, push along $A\hookrightarrow B$ by choosing images of new generators consistently (divisibility supplies the needed solutions).
\item To prove not injective, exhibit an inclusion $A\hookrightarrow B$ and $f\colon A\to Q$ admitting no extension (often a torsion/divisibility obstruction).
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $Q/Z$ is injective (divisible)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q/Z$ is injective (divisible)}
Problem. Show $Q/Z$ is an injective $Z$-module.
\wrec Over $Z$, injective $=$ divisible; verify $n$-divisibility of every coset.
\wsol Take $\bar a=a+Z\inQ/Z$ with $a\inQ$, and $n\geq1$. Set $\bar a'=(a/n)+Z$. Then
$n\bar a'=(n\cdot a/n)+Z=a+Z=\bar a$. So every element is $n$-divisible; $Q/Z$ is
divisible, hence injective by Cor.~ [REF:cor:divisible@c10] . Check. Concretely
$2\cdot(\tfrac14+Z)=\tfrac12+Z$ and $3\cdot(\tfrac1{12}+Z)=\tfrac14+Z$, illustrating
solvability. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is injective (divisible)}
Problem. Show $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module.
\wrec Over $\mathbb{Z}$, injective $=$ divisible; verify $n$-divisibility of every coset.
\wsol Take $\bar a=a+\mathbb{Z}\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $a\in\mathbb{Q}$, and $n\geq1$. Set $\bar a'=(a/n)+\mathbb{Z}$. Then
$n\bar a'=(n\cdot a/n)+\mathbb{Z}=a+\mathbb{Z}=\bar a$. So every element is $n$-divisible; $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is
divisible, hence injective by Cor.~\ref{cor:divisible@c10}. \textit{Check.} Concretely
$2\cdot(\tfrac14+\mathbb{Z})=\tfrac12+\mathbb{Z}$ and $3\cdot(\tfrac1{12}+\mathbb{Z})=\tfrac14+\mathbb{Z}$, illustrating
solvability. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Q$ is injective; extend a map
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q$ is injective; extend a map}
Problem. Let $f\colon2Z\toQ$ be $f(2)=3$. Extend $f$ to $Z\toQ$ (witnessing injectivity
of $Q$).
\wrec $Q$ is divisible, so by Baer extend from the ideal $2Z$ to $Z$.
\wsol $f$ is determined by $f(2)=3$. An extension $\tilde f\colonZ\toQ$ needs $\tilde
f(1)=q$ with $2q=f(2)=3$, so $q=\tfrac32$. Define $\tilde f(n)=\tfrac32 n$. Then $\tilde
f(2)=3=f(2)$ and $\tilde f|_{2Z}=f$. Check. $\tilde f(4)=6=2f(2)=2\cdot3$, agrees
with $f(4)=6$. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Q}$ is injective; extend a map}
Problem. Let $f\colon2\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ be $f(2)=3$. Extend $f$ to $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ (witnessing injectivity
of $\mathbb{Q}$).
\wrec $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible, so by Baer extend from the ideal $2\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol $f$ is determined by $f(2)=3$. An extension $\tilde f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ needs $\tilde
f(1)=q$ with $2q=f(2)=3$, so $q=\tfrac32$. Define $\tilde f(n)=\tfrac32 n$. Then $\tilde
f(2)=3=f(2)$ and $\tilde f|_{2\mathbb{Z}}=f$. \textit{Check.} $\tilde f(4)=6=2f(2)=2\cdot3$, agrees
with $f(4)=6$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z$ is NOT injective
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z$ is NOT injective}
Problem. Show $Z$ is not an injective $Z$-module.
\wrec Injective over $Z$ means divisible; $Z$ is not divisible.
\wsol $Z$ is not divisible: $1\inZ$ is not divisible by $2$ (no integer $m$ with
$2m=1$). Concretely take $\id\colonZ\toZ$ and the inclusion
$Z\xrightarrow{\times2}Z$; an extension $\tilde f\colonZ\toZ$ of $\id$ along $\times2$
would need $\tilde f(\times2\cdot1)=\tilde f(2)$ to equal $\id(1)=1$, i.e. $2\tilde
f(1)=1$, impossible in $Z$. So no extension; $Z$ is not injective. Check.
Consistent with Cor.~ [REF:cor:divisible@c10] , since $Z$ is non-divisible. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z/(n)Z$ is not injective over $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(n)Z$ is not injective over $Z$}
Problem. Show $Z/(4)Z$ is not an injective $Z$-module.
\wrec Finite nonzero groups are never divisible.
\wsol If $Z/(4)Z$ were divisible, then for $\bar1$ and $n=4$ there would be $\bar x$ with
$4\bar x=\bar1$. But $4\bar x=\bar0$ for every $\bar x\inZ/(4)Z$, so $\bar0=\bar1$ is forced,
false. Not divisible, hence not injective. Check. Any finite group $G$ with $|G|=m>1$
fails $m$-divisibility, so no nonzero finite abelian group is injective over $Z$. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:

Problem. Show $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ is not an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module.
\wrec Finite nonzero groups are never divisible.
\wsol If $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ were divisible, then for $\bar1$ and $n=4$ there would be $\bar x$ with

false. Not divisible, hence not injective. \textit{Check.} Any finite group $G$ with $|G|=m>1$

Type: example
Title: A direct product of injectives is injective
Content:
\begin{wex}{A direct product of injectives is injective}
Problem. Show $\prod_{i}Q_i$ is injective if each $Q_i$ is.
\wrec Extension into a product is extension coordinatewise.
\wsol Given $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$ and $f\colon A\to\prod_iQ_i$, write
$f=(f_i)$ with $f_i=\pi_i\circ f\colon A\to Q_i$. Each $f_i$ extends to $\tilde f_i\colon
B\to Q_i$ by injectivity of $Q_i$. Set $\tilde f=(\tilde f_i)\colon B\to\prod_iQ_i$. Then
$\pi_i\tilde f\iota=\tilde f_i\iota=f_i=\pi_i f$ for all $i$, so $\tilde f\iota=f$.
Check. The universal property of the product makes the coordinatewise map a genuine
homomorphism. Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{A direct product of injectives is injective}
Problem. Show $\prod_{i}Q_i$ is injective if each $Q_i$ is.
\wrec Extension into a product is extension coordinatewise.
\wsol Given $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$ and $f\colon A\to\prod_iQ_i$, write
$f=(f_i)$ with $f_i=\pi_i\circ f\colon A\to Q_i$. Each $f_i$ extends to $\tilde f_i\colon
B\to Q_i$ by injectivity of $Q_i$. Set $\tilde f=(\tilde f_i)\colon B\to\prod_iQ_i$. Then
$\pi_i\tilde f\iota=\tilde f_i\iota=f_i=\pi_i f$ for all $i$, so $\tilde f\iota=f$.
\textit{Check.} The universal property of the product makes the coordinatewise map a genuine
homomorphism. Correct.

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Injectivity is not the same as ``$f$ is injective.'' An injective module is a target
$Q$ with the extension property; it has nothing to do with any one map being one-to-one.
Likewise ``divisible $\Rightarrow$ injective'' is a theorem only over special rings ($Z$, PIDs, and more
generally Dedekind domains); over a general ring use Baer's Criterion.
\end{pitfall}
