Title: Left exactness of $\Hom$
Label: thm:homexact@c10
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Left exactness of $\Hom$] 
Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ be a SES of $R$-modules and $D$
any $R$-module. Then the induced sequences
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(D,A) \arrow[r, hook, "\psi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,B) \arrow[r, "\varphi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,C)
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is a Hom-set: $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)$ is the abelian group of all $R$-module homomorphisms from $D$ to $A$, and similarly for $B$ and $C$. The fixed module $D$ is the source; applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ to the SES $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ produces this three-term sequence.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\psi_*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)$ is post-composition with $\psi$: $\psi_*(h)=\psi\circ h$. $\varphi_*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,C)$ is post-composition with $\varphi$: $\varphi_*(h)=\varphi\circ h$. The leading $0$ forces $\psi_*$ to be injective.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness holds at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)$: $\psi_*$ is injective (if $\psi h=0$ then $h=0$ since $\psi$ is mono). Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)$: $\operatorname{im}\psi_*=\operatorname{ker}\varphi_*$, i.e. a map $h\colon D\to B$ satisfies $\varphi(h(d))=0$ for all $d$ iff $h$ factors through $\psi$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For $\operatorname{ker}\varphi_*\subseteq\operatorname{im}\psi_*$: if $\varphi\circ h=0$ then $\operatorname{im}h\subseteq\operatorname{ker}\varphi=\operatorname{im}\psi$, so $h$ factors as $h=\psi\circ h'$ for a unique $h'\colon D\to A$ (injectivity of $\psi$ makes $h'$ unique). The right end need not be exact: a map $D\to C$ need not lift to $D\to B$ unless $D$ is projective.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the covariant left-exactness theorem, the foundational algebraic fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ does not destroy exactness at the left, but the right end may fail. The extent of that failure is measured by $\operatorname{Ext}^1$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ and $D=Z/(2)Z$. Then $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z/(2)Z,Z)=0$ (no nonzero map), $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z/(2)Z,Z)=0$, $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z/(2)Z,Z/(2)Z)=Z/(2)Z$. The right arrow cannot be surjective since there is no lift $Z/(2)Z\toZ$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students forget the sequence is only three terms long and not right-exact. Writing $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,C)\to0$ is wrong in general; the terminal $0$ requires $D$ projective.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ to a SES preserves the left two exactness conditions but can fail to be surjective at the right, with projectivity of $D$ being exactly the condition that restores full exactness.
\end{dgx}
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(C,D) \arrow[r, hook, "\varphi^*"] & \Hom_R(B,D) \arrow[r, "\psi^*"] & \Hom_R(A,D)
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is again a Hom-set, but now the fixed module $D$ is the target and the source varies. $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,D)$ are abelian groups. Applying the contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,D)$ reverses the order of the original $A\to B\to C$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\varphi^*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$ is pre-composition with $\varphi$: $\varphi^*(h)=h\circ\varphi$. $\psi^*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,D)$ is pre-composition with $\psi$: $\psi^*(h)=h\circ\psi$. Note the arrows in the Hom sequence run opposite to the original SES.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)$: $\varphi^*$ is injective (if $h\circ\varphi=0$ and $\varphi$ is surjective then $h=0$). Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$: $\operatorname{im}\varphi^*=\operatorname{ker}\psi^*$, since $h\circ\psi=0$ iff $h$ kills $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$, iff $h$ factors through $C=B/\operatorname{ker}\varphi$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For $\operatorname{ker}\psi^*\subseteq\operatorname{im}\varphi^*$: if $h\circ\psi=0$ then $\operatorname{ker}\varphi=\operatorname{im}\psi\subseteq\operatorname{ker}h$, so $h$ factors through $B/\operatorname{im}\psi\cong C$ via the map induced by $\varphi$, i.e. $h=h'\circ\varphi=\varphi^*(h')$. The right end need not be surjective unless $D$ is injective.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the contravariant left-exactness result, the dual partner of the covariant sequence above. Together they establish that both Hom functors are left exact but generally not right exact, with the two possible failures governed by injectivity (contravariant) and projectivity (covariant).
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ and $D=Z$. Then $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z/(2)Z,Z)=0$, $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z,Z)=Z$, and $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z,Z)=Z$. The map $\psi^*$ is $\times2\colonZ\toZ$, which is not surjective (the identity $\id\colonZ\toZ$ has no preimage), showing the right end can fail.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Contravariance flips the arrows: the sequence runs $C\to B\to A$ in the Hom-sequence even though the original ran $A\to B\to C$.

Title: Right exactness of $\otimes$
Label: thm:tensorexact@c10
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Right exactness of $\otimes$] 
Let $A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ be exact (right exact) and $M$ a right
$R$-module. Then
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
M\otimes_R A \arrow[r, "1\otimes\psi"] & M\otimes_R B \arrow[r, two heads, "1\otimes\varphi"] & M\otimes_R C \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $M\otimes_R A$, $M\otimes_R B$, $M\otimes_R C$ are tensor products of the right $R$-module $M$ with left $R$-modules $A$, $B$, $C$ respectively. The terminal $0$ signals right-exactness: the last map is surjective.
\dgi{Arrows:} $1\otimes\psi\colon M\otimes_R A\to M\otimes_R B$ is the map induced on simple tensors by $m\otimes a\mapsto m\otimes\psi(a)$. $1\otimes\varphi\colon M\otimes_R B\to M\otimes_R C$ is $m\otimes b\mapsto m\otimes\varphi(b)$. The trailing $0$ says $1\otimes\varphi$ is surjective.
\dgi{What commutes:} Three exactness conditions: (i) $1\otimes\varphi$ is surjective (exactness at $M\otimes_R C$); (ii) $\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)\subseteq\operatorname{ker}(1\otimes\varphi)$ since $\varphi\circ\psi=0$; (iii) $\operatorname{ker}(1\otimes\varphi)=\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$ (exactness at $M\otimes_R B$). The left map $1\otimes\psi$ need not be injective.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Surjectivity of $1\otimes\varphi$: every simple tensor $m\otimes c$ with $c=\varphi(b)$ equals $(1\otimes\varphi)(m\otimes b)$. For exactness at $M\otimes_R B$: the identification $M\otimes_R C\cong(M\otimes_R B)/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$ follows from the universal property of the tensor product applied to the composite $M\times C\to M\otimes_R B/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This theorem draws the dividing line between flat and non-flat modules. Right-exactness is free; left-exactness (injectivity of $1\otimes\psi$) is the flatness condition on $M$. The diagram organizes what tensor always preserves versus what it can destroy.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M=Z/(2)Z$, $A\xrightarrow{\times2}B=Z$ (injective). Then $1\otimes(\times2)\colonZ/(2)Z\toZ/(2)Z$ sends $\bar a\mapsto\overline{2a}=\bar0$, the zero map; left-exactness fails. But the surjection $Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ is preserved: $Z/(2)Z\otimesZ/(2)Z\to0$ remains exact.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students assume tensor preserves injectivity as well as surjectivity, writing $0\to M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to\cdots$ without checking flatness. The left $0$ is wrong unless $M$ is flat.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that tensoring with $M$ always preserves the right end of an exact sequence (surjections become surjections) but can destroy the left end (injections may become non-injective), with flatness of $M$ being the exact condition that restores full exactness.
\end{dgx}

\end{theorem}

For exactness at $M\otimes_R B$: the identification $M\otimes_R C\cong(M\otimes_R B)/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$ follows from the universal property of the tensor product applied to the composite $M\times C\to M\otimes_R B/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This theorem draws the dividing line between flat and non-flat modules. Right-exactness is free; left-exactness (injectivity of $1\otimes\psi$) is the flatness condition on $M$. The diagram organizes what tensor always preserves versus what it can destroy.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M=\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, $A\xrightarrow{\times2}B=\mathbb{Z}$ (injective). Then $1\otimes(\times2)\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ sends $\bar a\mapsto\overline{2a}=\bar0$, the zero map; left-exactness fails. But the surjection $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is preserved: $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ remains exact.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students assume tensor preserves injectivity as well as surjectivity, writing $0\to M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to\cdots$ without checking flatness. The left $0$ is wrong unless $M$ is flat.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that tensoring with $M$ always preserves the right end of an exact sequence (surjections become surjections) but can destroy the left end (injections may become non-injective), with flatness of $M$ being the exact condition that restores full exactness.
\end{dgx}
is exact. The functor $M\otimes_R-$ is in general \emph{not} left exact: $1\otimes\psi$ need
not be injective even when $\psi$ is. $M$ is called \emph{flat} when $M\otimes_R-$ also
preserves injections (equivalently, is exact).
\end{theorem}

Type: definition
Title: Flat module
Content:
\begin{definition}[Flat module]
A right $R$-module $M$ is flat if the functor $M\otimes_R-$ preserves injections:
for every injection $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$ of left $R$-modules,
$1\otimes\iota\colon M\otimes_R A\to M\otimes_R B$ is injective. Equivalently (with right
exactness), $M\otimes_R-$ is exact.
\end{definition}

Label: prop:flat@c10
Content:
\begin{proposition} 
Free modules are flat; more generally projective modules are flat; and a direct sum
$\bigoplus_i M_i$ is flat iff each $M_i$ is flat. Over $Z$, a module is flat iff it is
torsion-free.
\end{proposition}
label: prop:flat@c10

Type: method
Title: Detecting flatness / failure of left-exactness
Content:
\begin{method}{Detecting flatness / failure of left-exactness}
Trigger. You tensor an injection and ask if it stays injective, or must certify a
module flat. Recipe.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Free or projective $\Rightarrow$ flat (safe default).
\item Over $Z$ (or a PID): flat $\iff$ torsion-free. So $Q,Z,Z^n$ are flat;
$Z/(n)Z$ ($n\geq2$) is not.
\item To show non-flatness, tensor the injection $Z\xrightarrow{\times n}Z$ with the
module and find a nonzero kernel.
\item Right-exactness always holds: only the left end ($1\otimes\psi$ injective) is at stake.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: $Z/(2)Z$ is not flat: $\times2$ becomes zero
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z/(2)Z$ is not flat: $\times2$ becomes zero}
Problem. Tensor the injection $Z\xrightarrow{\times2}Z$ with $Z/(2)Z$ and show injectivity is
lost.
\wrec Tensoring with a torsion module can kill an injection -- compute the induced map on
simple tensors.
\wsol The map $1\otimes(\times2)\colonZ/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ\toZ/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ$ sends
$\bar a\otimes n\mapsto\bar a\otimes 2n$. Using $Z/(2)Z\otimes_ZZ\congZ/(2)Z$ (via $\bar
a\otimes n\mapsto\overline{an}$), the map becomes $\bar a\mapsto\overline{2a}=\bar0$ in
$Z/(2)Z$. So $1\otimes(\times2)=0$ is the zero map, hence not injective although
$\times2$ is. Therefore $Z/(2)Z$ is not flat. Check. Consistent with
Prop.~ [REF:prop:flat@c10] : $Z/(2)Z$ has torsion (every element killed by $2$). Correct.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is not flat: $\times2$ becomes zero}
Problem. Tensor the injection $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Z}$ with $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ and show injectivity is
lost.
\wrec Tensoring with a torsion module can kill an injection -- compute the induced map on
simple tensors.
\wsol The map $1\otimes(\times2)\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}$ sends
$\bar a\otimes n\mapsto\bar a\otimes 2n$. Using $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ (via $\bar
a\otimes n\mapsto\overline{an}$), the map becomes $\bar a\mapsto\overline{2a}=\bar0$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$. So $1\otimes(\times2)=0$ is the zero map, hence \emph{not} injective although
$\times2$ is. Therefore $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is not flat. \textit{Check.} Consistent with
Prop.~\ref{prop:flat@c10}: $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ has torsion (every element killed by $2$). Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Q$ is flat over $Z$ (torsion-free) and restores exactness
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q$ is flat over $Z$ (torsion-free) and restores exactness}
Problem. Tensor $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ with $Q$ and identify the result.
\wrec $Q$ is torsion-free over $Z$, hence flat; tensoring should keep the left injection
injective.
\wsol Using $Q\otimes_ZZ\congQ$ and $Q\otimes_ZZ/(2)Z\cong0$ (since $q\otimes\bar
a=\tfrac{q}{2}\cdot2\otimes\bar a=\tfrac q2\otimes 2\bar a=\tfrac q2\otimes\bar0=0$), the
sequence becomes
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & Q \arrow[r, "\times2", "\cong"'] & Q \arrow[r] & 0 \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The four nodes after the initial $0$ arise from tensoring $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times2}Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ with $Q$. The left two nodes are $Q\otimes_ZZ\congQ$; the third is $Q\otimes_ZZ/(2)Z=0$; the final $0$ is $Q\otimes_Z0=0$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The map $\times2\colonQ\toQ$ is $1\otimes(\times2)$, i.e. $q\mapsto2q$. The subsequent arrow $Q\to0$ is the zero map. The initial $0\toQ$ says the left map is injective.
\dgi{What commutes:} The sequence is exact at all spots: $0\toQ\xrightarrow{\times2}Q\to0\to0$. Exactness at the left $Q$: $\times2$ is injective (kernel is $\{q\inQ:2q=0\}=0$). Exactness at the right $Q$: $\times2$ is surjective (bijection on $Q$). The middle term $0$ causes no issue.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Flatness of $Q$ over $Z$ (it is torsion-free, hence flat by the PID criterion) means $1\otimes(\times2)$ inherits the injectivity of $\times2\colonZ\toZ$. The collapse $Q\otimes_ZZ/(2)Z=0$ occurs because $q\otimes\bar a=\tfrac{q}{2}\otimes2\bar a=\tfrac{q}{2}\otimes\bar0=0$ for all $q,\bar a$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the worked demonstration of flatness at work: tensoring the non-split SES with a flat module produces a fully exact (even split) sequence where the torsion term has been annihilated. It contrasts sharply with the $Z/(2)Z$ computation that precedes it.
\dgi{Concrete example:} This diagram is the concrete example, but note the phenomenon more sharply: $\times2\colonQ\toQ$ has the inverse $\times\tfrac12$, so the tensored sequence is not merely exact but actually has $\times2$ as an isomorphism, making the sequence split.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students may think that when the right-hand term becomes $0$ after tensoring, something went wrong. In fact $Q\otimes_ZZ/(2)Z=0$ is correct and expected: $Q$ is divisible, and any torsion module tensored with $Q$ collapses to zero.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that tensoring a SES with a flat module such as $Q$ preserves full exactness, here visibly converting the original non-split sequence into a fully exact sequence with the torsion term annihilated.
\end{dgx}
Here $\times2\colonQ\toQ$ is a bijection (invert by $\times\tfrac12$), so the sequence is
exact at every spot. Flatness of $Q$ kept the left map injective, and indeed exact.
Check. $Q\otimesZ/(2)Z=0$ matches $Q$ being divisible (multiplication by $2$
surjective), so the cokernel collapses; consistent. Correct.
\end{wex}

\end{dgx}

\begin{wex}{$Z^n$ is flat}
Problem. Show $Z^3$ is a flat $Z$-module.
\wrec Free $\Rightarrow$ flat; tensoring with a free module is taking direct sums of copies.
\wsol For any injection $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$, $Z^3\otimes_Z A\cong A^3$ and
$Z^3\otimes_Z B\cong B^3$, with $1\otimes\iota$ becoming $\iota^3=(\iota,\iota,\iota)$,
which is injective since each coordinate $\iota$ is. So $Z^3$ is flat. Check.
$Z^3$ is torsion-free, matching the PID criterion. Correct.
\end{wex}

Title: Tensoring computes $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Tensoring computes $Z/(m)Z\otimes_ZZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$}
Problem. Compute $Z/(6)Z\otimes_ZZ/(4)Z$ and use it to see non-flatness in action.
\wrec Right-exactness of tensor: present $Z/(4)Z$ as $Z\xrightarrow{\times4}Z\toZ/(4)Z\to0$
and tensor.
\wsol Tensoring the presentation with $Z/(6)Z$ gives, by right exactness,
$Z/(6)Z\xrightarrow{\times4}Z/(6)Z\toZ/(6)Z\otimesZ/(4)Z\to0$, so $Z/(6)Z\otimesZ/(4)Z\congZ/(6)Z/4Z/(6)Z$.
In $Z/(6)Z$, $4Z/(6)Z=\{\bar0,\bar4,\bar2\}=2Z/(6)Z$ has order $3$, so $Z/(6)Z/4Z/(6)Z$ has order $2$,
i.e. $\congZ/(2)Z$. Since $\gcd(6,4)=2$, this matches $Z/(\gcd(6,4))Z=Z/(2)Z$. Check. The
formula $Z/(m)Z\otimesZ/(n)Z\congZ/(\gcd(m,n))Z$ gives $Z/(2)Z$, agreeing. The very fact that
tensoring with $Z/(6)Z$ turned the injection $\times4$ into a non-injection on a torsion
quotient again shows $Z/(6)Z$ is not flat ($Z/(4)Z$ is not flat either, by the torsion criterion of Prop.~ [REF:prop:flat@c10] ). Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Failure then repair of left-exactness}
Problem. Contrast tensoring $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times3}Z\toZ/(3)Z\to0$ with $M=Z/(3)Z$ versus
$M=Q$.
\wrec Same SES, two coefficient modules: torsion $Z/(3)Z$ breaks injectivity, flat $Q$
preserves it.
\wsol With $M=Z/(3)Z$: $1\otimes(\times3)\colonZ/(3)Z\toZ/(3)Z$ is $\bar a\mapsto\overline{3a}=\bar0$,
the zero map -- not injective, so left-exactness fails; the full tensored sequence
$Z/(3)Z\xrightarrow{0}Z/(3)Z\toZ/(3)Z\otimesZ/(3)Z\to0$ has $Z/(3)Z\otimesZ/(3)Z\congZ/(3)Z$.
With $M=Q$: $1\otimes(\times3)\colonQ\toQ$ is multiplication by $3$, a bijection, so the
left map stays injective; and $Q\otimesZ/(3)Z=0$, yielding the exact
$0\toQ\xrightarrow{\times3}Q\to0$. Check. $Z/(3)Z$ has torsion (non-flat),
$Q$ is torsion-free (flat), exactly predicting the two behaviors. Correct.
\end{wex}

\wrec Same SES, two coefficient modules: torsion $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ breaks injectivity, flat $\mathbb{Q}$

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Tensoring is only right exact: $1\otimes\psi$ may fail to be injective even when
$\psi$ is. Do not assume $M\otimes_R(-)$ preserves submodules -- e.g. $Z\subsetZ$ via
$\times2$ tensored with $Z/(2)Z$ collapses to the zero map. The fix is exactly flatness of
$M$. Dually, $\Hom$ is only left exact, with the right-hand surjectivity governed by
projectivity (covariant slot) or injectivity (contravariant slot).
\end{pitfall}

\begin{pitfall}
Tensoring is only \emph{right} exact: $1\otimes\psi$ may fail to be injective even when
$\psi$ is. Do not assume $M\otimes_R(-)$ preserves submodules -- e.g. $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ via
$\times2$ tensored with $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ collapses to the zero map. The fix is exactly flatness of
$M$. Dually, $\Hom$ is only \emph{left} exact, with the right-hand surjectivity governed by
projectivity (covariant slot) or injectivity (contravariant slot).
\end{pitfall}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Exact Sequences --- Projective, Injective, and Flat Modules > Flat modules
Type: remark
Title: The three dictionaries
Content:
\begin{remark}[The three dictionaries]
Projective, injective, flat are the modules that ``correct'' the one-sided exactness of the
three basic functors:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=large]
P projective \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & \Hom_R(P,-) exact \\
Q injective \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & \Hom_R(-,Q) exact \\
M flat \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & M\otimes_R- exact
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left column lists module-theoretic properties: $P$ projective, $Q$ injective, $M$ flat. The right column lists the corresponding functor-exactness properties for $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$, and $M\otimes_R-$, each of which is only partially exact in general.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each horizontal double-headed arrow $\leftrightarrow$ denotes a biconditional (if and only if). The three rows are three separate equivalences, not a commutative diagram in the traditional sense: no path-composition is being equated. Rather, this is a correspondences table displayed diagrammatically.
\dgi{What commutes:} The three equivalences hold simultaneously and independently: (i) $P$ projective $\iff$ $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ carries every surjection to a surjection (i.e. is exact); (ii) $Q$ injective $\iff$ $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ carries every injection to a surjection (i.e. is exact); (iii) $M$ flat $\iff$ $M\otimes_R-$ carries every injection to an injection (i.e. is exact).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Each iff was established in the section: (i) the lifting property of $P$ is equivalent to exactness of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ because lifting is exactly preserving surjections. (ii) The extension property of $Q$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ preserving injections-to-surjections. (iii) The definition of flat is directly that $M\otimes_R-$ preserves injections.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the organizational capstone of the entire section. It collects the three module classes and their functor-exactness characterizations into one unified picture, clarifying that projective, injective, and flat are each the ``right'' hypothesis to add to the base functor to make it fully exact.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Over $Z$: $Z$ is projective (free) and flat (torsion-free); $\operatorname{Hom}_Z(Z,-)=\operatorname{id}$ is trivially exact. $Q/Z$ is injective (divisible). $Z/(2)Z$ is neither projective, injective, nor flat, and all three functors applied to it can fail exactness.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The implications run only one way downward: free $\Rightarrow$ projective $\Rightarrow$ flat, but not conversely in general. Students sometimes read the triple list as saying projective, injective, and flat are equivalent to each other; they are not -- they correspond to three different functors.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that projective, injective, and flat modules are precisely the three module classes that upgrade their associated functor from one-sided exact to fully exact, organizing the entire theory around a single unifying principle.
\end{dgx}
Implications: free $\Rightarrow$ projective $\Rightarrow$ flat (none reversible in general),
and over $Z$: projective $=$ free for finitely generated, injective $=$ divisible,
flat $=$ torsion-free.
\end{remark}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exact sequences and splitting.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exact sequences and splitting.}
\item Determine whether $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times6}Z\xrightarrow{\pi}Z/(6)Z\to0$ is exact,
where $\pi$ is reduction mod $6$; if so, decide whether it splits.
\item Show $0\toZ/(3)Z\xrightarrow{\iota}Z/(12)Z\xrightarrow{\varphi}Z/(4)Z\to0$ is a split SES,
where $\iota(\bar1)=\bar4$ and $\varphi$ is reduction mod $4$; exhibit a section.
\item For an $R$-homomorphism $f\colon M\to N$, prove the sequence
$0\to\ker f\to M\xrightarrow{f}\im f\to0$ is exact, and give an example over $R=Z$ where it
does not split.
\item Prove that $0\toZ/(2)Z\toZ/(4)Z\toZ/(2)Z\to0$ does not split, and conclude
$Z/(4)Z\not\congZ/(2)Z\oplusZ/(2)Z$.

\end{exers}
latex:
\begin{exers}{Exact sequences and splitting.}
\item Determine whether $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times6}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is exact,
where $\pi$ is reduction mod $6$; if so, decide whether it splits.
\item Show $0\to\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\iota}\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is a split SES,
where $\iota(\bar1)=\bar4$ and $\varphi$ is reduction mod $4$; exhibit a section.
\item For an $R$-homomorphism $f\colon M\to N$, prove the sequence
$0\to\ker f\to M\xrightarrow{f}\im f\to0$ is exact, and give an example over $R=\mathbb{Z}$ where it
does not split.
\item Prove that $0\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ does not split, and conclude
$\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\not\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$.

\end{exers}

Title: Projective, injective, flat.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Projective, injective, flat.}
\item Show $Z/(3)Z$ is a projective $Z/(12)Z$-module but is not free over $Z/(12)Z$.
\item Using Baer's Criterion, decide whether $Z$ is an injective module over itself, and
whether $Q$ is.
\item Prove that $Q/Z$ is divisible, and deduce that it is an injective $Z$-module.
\item Show that a finite direct sum of flat modules is flat, and that $Z/(n)Z$ ($n\geq2$) is
never flat over $Z$.

\end{exers}

\item Using Baer's Criterion, decide whether $\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective module over itself, and

Type: exercise_set
Title: Hom and tensor computations.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Hom and tensor computations.}
\item Compute $\Hom_Z(Z/(4)Z,Z/(6)Z)$ and $\Hom_Z(Z/(6)Z,Z/(4)Z)$, and verify each has order
$\gcd(4,6)=2$.
\item Compute $Z/(4)Z\otimes_ZZ/(6)Z$ and $Q\otimes_ZZ/(5)Z$ from presentations, identifying
each result.
\item For a left $R$-module $M$, prove $R\otimes_R M\cong M$ and use it to show $R$ is a
flat module over itself.
\item Tensor the SES $0\toZ\xrightarrow{\times5}Z\toZ/(5)Z\to0$ with $M=Z/(10)Z$ and exhibit
explicitly the failure of injectivity at the left end.

\end{exers}
latex:
\begin{exers}{Hom and tensor computations.}
\item Compute $\Hom_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z})$ and $\Hom_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z})$, and verify each has order
$\gcd(4,6)=2$.
\item Compute $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ from presentations, identifying
each result.
\item For a left $R$-module $M$, prove $R\otimes_R M\cong M$ and use it to show $R$ is a
flat module over itself.
\item Tensor the SES $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times5}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ with $M=\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z}$ and exhibit
explicitly the failure of injectivity at the left end.

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Suppose that
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[r, "\psi"] \arrow[d, "\alpha"] & B \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, "\beta"] & C \arrow[d, "\gamma"] \\
A' \arrow[r, "\psi'"] & B' \arrow[r, "\varphi'"] & C'
\end{tikzcd}
\]
is a commutative diagram of groups and the rows are exact. Prove that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] if $\varphi$ and $\alpha$ are surjective, and $\beta$ is injective then $\gamma$ is injective. [If $c \in \ker\gamma$, show there is a $b \in B$ with $\varphi(b) = c$. Show that $\varphi'(\beta(b)) = 0$ and deduce that $\beta(b) = \psi'(a')$ for some $a' \in A'$. Show there is an $a \in A$ with $\alpha(a) = a'$ and that $\beta(\psi(a)) = \beta(b)$. Conclude that $b = \psi(a)$ and hence $c = \varphi(b) = 0$.]
\item[(b)] if $\psi'$, $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ are injective, then $\beta$ is injective,
\item[(c)] if $\varphi$, $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ are surjective, then $\beta$ is surjective,
\item[(d)] if $\beta$ is injective, $\alpha$ and $\varphi$ are surjective, then $\gamma$ is injective,
\item[(e)] if $\beta$ is surjective, $\gamma$ and $\psi'$ are injective, then $\alpha$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
\item Suppose
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\alpha"] & B \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\beta"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\gamma"] & D \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\delta"] & E \arrow[d, "\varepsilon"] \\
A' \arrow[r] & B' \arrow[r] & C' \arrow[r] & D' \arrow[r] & E'
\end{tikzcd}
\]
is a commutative diagram of groups, and the rows are exact. Prove that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] if $\alpha$ is surjective, and $\beta, \delta$ are injective, then $\gamma$ is injective,
\item[(b)] if $\varepsilon$ is injective, and $\beta, \delta$ are surjective, then $\gamma$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be $R$-modules. Prove that $P_1 \oplus P_2$ is a projective $R$-module if and only if both $P_1$ and $P_2$ are projective.
\item Let $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ be $R$-modules. Prove that $Q_1 \oplus Q_2$ is an injective $R$-module if and only if both $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are injective.
\item Let $A_1$ and $A_2$ be $R$-modules. Prove that $A_1 \oplus A_2$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if both $A_1$ and $A_2$ are flat. More generally, prove that an arbitrary direct sum $\sum_i A_i$ of $R$-modules is flat if and only if each $A_i$ is flat. (Use the fact that tensor product commutes with arbitrary direct sums.)
\item Prove that the following are equivalent for a ring $R$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Every $R$-module is projective.
\item[(ii)] Every $R$-module is injective.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $A$ be a nonzero finite abelian group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $A$ is not a projective $Z$-module.
\item[(b)] Prove that $A$ is not an injective $Z$-module.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $Q$ be a nonzero divisible $Z$-module. Prove that $Q$ is not a projective $Z$-module. Deduce that the rational numbers $Q$ is not a projective $Z$-module. [Show first that if $F$ is any free module then $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} nF = 0$ (use a basis of $F$ to prove this). Now suppose to the contrary that $Q$ is projective and derive a contradiction from Proposition 30(4).]
\item Assume $R$ is commutative with $1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that the tensor product of two free $R$-modules is free. (Use the fact that tensor products commute with direct sums.)
\item[(b)] Use (a) to prove that the tensor product of two projective $R$-modules is a projective $R$-module.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $R$ and $S$ be rings with $1$ and let $M$ and $N$ be left $R$-modules. Assume also that $M$ is an $(R,S)$-bimodule.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For $s \in S$ and for $\varphi \in \Hom_R(M,N)$ define $s\varphi : M \to N$ by $(s\varphi)(m) = \varphi(ms)$. Prove that $s\varphi$ is a homomorphism of left $R$-modules, and that this action of $S$ on $\Hom_R(M,N)$ makes it into a left $S$-module.
\item[(b)] Let $S = R$ and let $M = R$ (as an $(R,R)$-bimodule by left and right ring multiplication on itself). For each $n \in N$ define $\varphi_n \in \Hom_R(R,N)$ by $\varphi_n(r) = rn$, i.e., $\varphi_n$ is the unique $R$-module homomorphism mapping $1_R$ to $n$. Show that $s\varphi_n$ as defined in (a) is the homomorphism $\varphi_{sn}$. Deduce that the map $n \mapsto \varphi_n$ is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules: $N \cong \Hom_R(R,N)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $R$ and $S$ be rings with $1$ and let $M$ and $N$ be left $R$-modules. Assume also that $N$ is an $(R,S)$-bimodule.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For $s \in S$ and for $\varphi \in \Hom_R(M,N)$ define $\varphi s : M \to N$ by $(\varphi s)(m) = \varphi(m)s$. Prove that $\varphi s$ is a homomorphism of left $R$-modules, and that this action of $S$ on $\Hom_R(M,N)$ makes it into a right $S$-module.
\item[(b)] Let $N = R$ as an $(R,R)$-bimodule as above. Deduce that $\Hom_R(M,R)$ is a right $R$-module --- called the dual module to $M$.

Part: 2/3
Content:
Exercise 10).
\item Let $A$ be a finitely generated abelian group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $A$ is projective if and only if $A$ is a free $Z$-module.
\item[(b)] Prove that $A$ is injective if and only if $A = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $0 \to L \xrightarrow{\;\psi\;} M \xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;} N \to 0$ be a sequence of $R$-modules.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that the associated sequence
\[
0 \to \Hom_R(D,L) \xrightarrow{\;\psi'\;} \Hom_R(D,M) \xrightarrow{\;\varphi'\;} \Hom_R(D,N) \to 0
\]
is a short exact sequence of abelian groups for all $R$-modules $D$ if and only if the original sequence is a split short exact sequence. [To show the sequence splits, take $D = N$ and show the lift of the identity map in $\Hom_R(N,N)$ to $\Hom_R(N,M)$ is a splitting homomorphism for $\varphi$.]
\item[(b)] Prove that the associated sequence
\[
0 \to \Hom_R(N,D) \xrightarrow{\;\varphi'\;} \Hom_R(M,D) \xrightarrow{\;\psi'\;} \Hom_R(L,D) \to 0
\]
is a short exact sequence of abelian groups for all $R$-modules $D$ if and only if the original sequence is a split short exact sequence.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $M$ be a left $Z$-module and let $R$ be a ring with $1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\Hom_{Z}(R,M)$ is a left $R$-module under the action $(r\varphi)(r') = \varphi(r'r)$ (see Exercise 10).
\item[(b)] Suppose that $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\;\psi\;} B$ is an exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that if every $Z$-module homomorphism $f$ from $A$ to $M$ lifts to a $Z$-module homomorphism $F$ from $B$ to $M$ with $f = F \circ \psi$, then every $R$-module homomorphism $f'$ from $A$ to $\Hom_{Z}(R,M)$ lifts to an $R$-module homomorphism $F'$ from $B$ to $\Hom_{Z}(R,M)$ with $f' = F' \circ \psi$. [Given $f'$, show that $f(a) = f'(a)(1)$ defines a $Z$-module homomorphism of $A$ to $M$. If $F$ is a lift of $f$ to $B$, show that $F'(b)(r) = F(rb)$ defines an $R$-module homomorphism from $B$ to $\Hom_{Z}(R,M)$ that lifts $f'$.]
\item[(c)] Prove that if $Q$ is an injective $Z$-module then $\Hom_{Z}(R,Q)$ is an injective $R$-module. (cf. Exercise 19.)
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $J$ be an $(R,R)$-bimodule, let $A$ be a left $R$-module and let $M = \Hom_R(J,A)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For $r \in R$ and for $\varphi \in \Hom_R(J,A)$ define $r\varphi$ by $(r\varphi)(j) = \varphi(jr)$. Prove that $r\varphi$ is a homomorphism of left $R$-modules, and that this action of $R$ on $\Hom_R(J,A)$ makes it into a left $R$-module. (cf. Exercise 10.)
\item[(b)] If $A$ is an injective $R$-module and $J$ is flat as a right $R$-module, prove that $M = \Hom_R(J,A)$ is an injective $R$-module. [Use the natural isomorphism $\Hom_R(X,M)\cong\Hom_R(J\otimes_R X,A)$ for left $R$-modules $X$. Flatness cannot be dropped: $\Hom_{Z}(Z/(2)Z,Q/Z)\congZ/(2)Z$ is not an injective $Z$-module.]
\end{enumerate}
\item Show that if $R$ is a Noetherian ring (cf. Exercise 14 in Section 10.3) and $Q$ is an injective $R$-module then any direct sum of copies of $Q$ is also an injective $R$-module. [Use Baer's Criterion, Proposition 36.]
\item This exercise proves that $Q/Z$ is an injective $Z$-module (cf. Corollary 35).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that a quotient of a divisible group is again divisible.
\item[(b)] Prove that $Q/Z$ is a divisible group, hence is an injective $Z$-module.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $M$ be any left $R$-module. This exercise proves that $M$ may be embedded in an injective $R$-module.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $M$ is contained in an injective $Z$-module $Q$ (cf. Exercise 18 and Corollary~ [REF:cor:divisible@c10] ).
\item[(b)] Show that $\Hom_R(R,M) \subseteq \Hom_{Z}(R,M) \subseteq \Hom_{Z}(R,Q)$ as $R$-modules, and that $\Hom_{Z}(R,Q)$ is an injective $R$-module by Exercise 15.
\item[(c)] Deduce that $M$ is contained in an injective $R$-module. [Use the $R$-module isomorphism $M \cong \Hom_R(R,M)$ of Exercise 10.]
\end{enumerate}
\item This exercise completes the proof of Proposition 34. Suppose that $Q$ is an $R$-module with the property that every short exact sequence $0 \to Q \to M_1 \to M_2 \to 0$ splits and suppose that the sequence $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\;\psi\;} B$ is exact. Prove that every $R$-module homomorphism $f$ from $A$ to $Q$ lifts to an $R$-module homomorphism $F$ from $B$ to $Q$ with $f = F \circ \psi$ (i.e., $Q$ has the injective property with respect to all injections). [Imitate the proof of Proposition 34 (and use the previous exercise) to embed $Q$ into an injective module $I$. Then the splitting property together with Exercise 4 using Exercise 1(b) gives an isomorphism from $Q$ to a direct summand of $I$. Use the fact that the property in Proposition 36 holds for injective modules.]
\item Prove that the injective hull of the $Z$-module $Z$ is $Q$ and that $Q$ contains an isomorphic copy of $Z$ as an essential submodule.
\item Prove that the injective hull of the $Z$-module $Z/p^nZ$ is the injective hull of $Z/pZ$ and deduce that $Z/p^nZ$ has the Pr\"ufer group $Z[1/p]/Z$ (the $p$-primary part of $Q/Z$), not $Q/Z$ itself, as its injective hull.
\item If $F$ is a field, prove that the injective hull of $F[x]$ is the rational function field $F(x)$.

Content:
If $M$ is flat over $R$ and $N$ is flat as an $S$-module then prove that $M \otimes_R N$ is flat as a right $S$-module.
\item Suppose that $R$ is a commutative ring and that $M$ and $N$ are flat $R$-modules. Prove that $M \otimes_R N$ is a flat $R$-module. (See the previous exercise.)
\item Prove that the (right) module $M \otimes_R S$ obtained by changing the base from the ring $R$ to the ring $S$ by some homomorphism $f : R \to S$ with $f(1_R) = 1_S$ (cf. Example 6 following Corollary 12 in Section 4) of the flat (right) $R$-module $M$ is the flat (right) $S$-module $M \otimes_R S$.
\item Prove that $A$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$ the map from $A \otimes_R I$ to $A \otimes_R R \cong A$ induced by the inclusion $I \subseteq R$ is injective. [The image of $A \otimes_R I$ in $A \otimes_R R = A$ is $AI$, so this is equivalent to showing that the natural map $A \otimes_R I \to AI$ is injective.]
\item (A Flatness Criterion) Parts (a)--(c) of this exercise prove that $A$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if (I) for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$, the map from $A \otimes_R I \to A$ given by $a \otimes i \mapsto ai$ is injective (cf. the preceding exercise). By the previous two exercises it suffices to prove that (I) implies $A$ is flat, i.e., that $A \otimes_R B \to A \otimes_R C$ is injective for every injection of (left) $R$-modules $\iota : B \to C$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose that $L_2 \subseteq L_1$ are two left ideals of $R$. Show that if (I) is satisfied for both $L_1$ and $L_2$ then (I) is satisfied for $L_1/L_2$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $D_1 \subseteq D_2 \subseteq \cdots$ is an ascending chain of left ideals of $R$ and let $D = \bigcup_i D_i$. Show that if (I) is satisfied for each $D_i$ then (I) is satisfied for $D$.
\item[(c)] Use Zorn's Lemma to prove that (I) is satisfied for every left ideal of $R$. Prove that this implies $A$ is flat as follows. Let $B$ be a submodule of the $R$-module $C$. By the previous exercises it suffices to consider the case where $C = R^n$ is a finitely generated free module; use induction on $n$, the case $n = 1$ being the assumption that (I) holds, together with parts (a) and (b), to complete the proof. [Use the commutative diagram with exact rows obtained from $0 \to K \to R^n \to R \to 0$, where $K = R^{n-1}$, and apply the snake lemma.]
\end{enumerate}
\item (A Flatness Criterion for quotients) Suppose $A = F/K$ where $F$ is flat (e.g., if $F$ is free) and $K$ is an $R$-submodule of $F$. Show that $A = F/K$ is flat if and only if $K \cap FI = KI$ for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$. (Use the flatness criterion in the preceding exercise.) [Use the previous exercise. Since $F$ is flat, $F \otimes I \cong FI$, and the image of $K \otimes I$ in $FI$ is $KI$; tensoring $0 \to K \to F \to A \to 0$ with $I$ gives $A \otimes I \cong FI/KI$. Under this identification the map $A \otimes I \to A = F/K$ is $FI/KI \to F/K$, whose kernel is $(K \cap FI)/KI$.]
\item Let $M$ and $N$ be submodules of the $R$-module $L$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $\alpha : A \to M$ and $\beta : A \to N$ are $R$-module homomorphisms. Prove that $X = \{(\alpha(a), -\beta(a)) \mid a \in A\}$ is an $R$-submodule of the direct sum $M \oplus N$ and prove that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ factor through the quotient $(M \oplus N)/X$ (called the pushout or fiber sum of $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and that there is a commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[r, "\beta"] \arrow[d, "\alpha"'] & N \arrow[d, "\pi_2"] \\
M \arrow[r, "\pi_1"'] & P
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ are the natural maps to the quotient induced by the maps into the first and second components.
\item[(b)] Suppose $f : M \to D$ and $g : N \to D$ are $R$-module homomorphisms with $f \circ \alpha = g \circ \beta$. Prove that there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism from the pushout $P$ to $D$ making the natural diagram commute.
\item[(c)] If $M$ and $N$ are submodules of an $R$-module $L$, show that the pushout of the inclusion maps $M \cap N \hookrightarrow M$ and $M \cap N \hookrightarrow N$ is isomorphic to the submodule $M + N$ of $L$.
\end{enumerate}
\item (Schanuel's Lemma) If $0 \to K \to P \xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;} M \to 0$ and $0 \to K' \to P' \xrightarrow{\;\varphi'\;} M \to 0$ are exact sequences of $R$-modules where $P$ and $P'$ are projective, prove that $K \oplus P' \cong K' \oplus P$ as $R$-modules. [Show that there is an exact sequence $0 \to \ker \pi \to X \xrightarrow{\;\pi\;} P \to 0$ where $X = \{(x,y) \in P \oplus P' \mid \varphi(x) = \varphi'(y)\}$ is the submodule that is the pullback (or fiber product) of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$, and the map $\pi$ is the natural projection onto the first component. Show that $\ker \pi \cong K'$ and that this sequence splits since $P$ is projective. Deduce that $X \cong K' \oplus P$. Show similarly that $X \cong K \oplus P'$.] The $R$-modules $M$ and $N$ are said to be projectively equivalent if $M \oplus P \cong N \oplus Q$ for some projective $R$-modules $P$ and $Q$. Similarly, $M$ and $N$ are injectively equivalent if $M \oplus Q \cong N \oplus Q'$ for some injective modules $Q$, $Q'$. This exercise shows $K$ and $K'$ are projectively equivalent.
\end{exers}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Exact Sequences --- Projective, Injective, and Flat Modules > Exercises
Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Show that a sequence $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B$ of $R$-modules is exact (at $A$) if and only if $\psi$ is injective. Dually, show that $B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ is exact (at $C$) if and only if $\varphi$ is surjective.

\item Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that $C \cong B/\psi(A)$ as $R$-modules.

\item Determine whether the sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] 0 \arrow[r] & Z \arrow[r, "2"] & Z \arrow[r] & Z/(2)Z \arrow[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd}\]
of $Z$-modules is exact, where the first map is multiplication by $2$ and the second is reduction mod $2$. Justify exactness at each of the three middle positions.

\item Consider the $Z$-module homomorphisms in
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] Z \arrow[r, "f"] & Z \oplus Z \arrow[r, "g"] & Z \end{tikzcd}\]
where $f(n) = (n, -n)$ and $g(a,b) = a + b$. Verify that $\im f = \ker g$, i.e.\ the sequence is exact at $Z \oplus Z$.

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. Prove that the free $R$-module $R^n$ is projective. More generally, prove that every free $R$-module is projective.

\item Prove that a finite direct sum $P_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus P_n$ of $R$-modules is projective if and only if each $P_i$ is projective.

\item Show that $Z/(2)Z$ is a projective $Z/(6)Z$-module by exhibiting a $Z/(6)Z$-module $Q$ with $Z/(2)Z \oplus Q$ free. Conclude $Z/(2)Z$ is projective but not free over $Z/(6)Z$.

\item Show that $Z/(2)Z$ is not a projective $Z/(4)Z$-module. (Show the surjection $Z/(4)Z \to Z/(2)Z$ does not split, i.e.\ the identity map $Z/(2)Z \to Z/(2)Z$ does not lift through it.)

\item Prove that the short exact sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] 0 \arrow[r] & Z \arrow[r, hook, "2"] & Z \arrow[r, two heads] & Z/(2)Z \arrow[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd}\]
of $Z$-modules does not split. Compare with problem 8.

\item Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove the following are equivalent: (a) the sequence splits; (b) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\lambda : B \to A$ with $\lambda \circ \psi = \id_A$; (c) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\mu : C \to B$ with $\varphi \circ \mu = \id_C$. In each splitting case prove $B \cong A \oplus C$.

\item Prove that an $R$-module $P$ is projective if and only if every short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to P \to 0$ of $R$-modules splits.

\item Show that $Q$ is an injective $Z$-module. (Use the criterion that a $Z$-module $Q$ is injective if and only if it is divisible, i.e.\ $nQ = Q$ for every nonzero integer $n$.)

\item Show that $Z$ is not an injective $Z$-module by exhibiting an injection $Z \to Q$ and a homomorphism $Z \to Z$ that does not extend to $Q$.

\item Compute the following tensor products of $Z$-modules, identifying each as a familiar abelian group:
\[ Z/(4)Z \otimes_Z Z/(6)Z, \qquad Z/(m)Z \otimes_Z Z/(n)Z, \qquad Q \otimes_Z Z/(n)Z \ (n > 0), \qquad Q \otimes_Z Q. \]

\item Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and let $I, J \sgr R$ be ideals. Prove that there is an $R$-module isomorphism $R/I \otimes_R R/J \cong R/(I+J)$.

\item Prove that every free $R$-module $R^{(A)}$ is flat. Deduce that every projective $R$-module is flat. (You may use that a direct summand of a flat module is flat.)

\end{exers}

Prove the following are equivalent: (a) the sequence splits; (b) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\lambda : B \to A$ with $\lambda \circ \psi = \id_A$; (c) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\mu : C \to B$ with $\varphi \circ \mu = \id_C$. In each splitting case prove $B \cong A \oplus C$.

\item Prove that an $R$-module $P$ is projective if and only if every short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to P \to 0$ of $R$-modules splits.

\item Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module. (Use the criterion that a $\mathbb{Z}$-module $Q$ is injective if and only if it is divisible, i.e.\ $nQ = Q$ for every nonzero integer $n$.)

\item Show that $\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module by exhibiting an injection $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q}$ and a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ that does not extend to $\mathbb{Q}$.

\item Compute the following tensor products of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, identifying each as a familiar abelian group:
\[ \mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}, \qquad \mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}, \qquad \mathbb{Q} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z} \ (n > 0), \qquad \mathbb{Q} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Q}. \]

\item Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and let $I, J \sgr R$ be ideals. Prove that there is an $R$-module isomorphism $R/I \otimes_R R/J \cong R/(I+J)$.

\item Prove that every free $R$-module $R^{(A)}$ is flat. Deduce that every projective $R$-module is flat. (You may use that a direct summand of a flat module is flat.)

\end{exers}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item (Five Lemma) Suppose the diagram of $R$-modules
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
A_1 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\alpha_1"] & A_2 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\alpha_2"] & A_3 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\alpha_3"] & A_4 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\alpha_4"] & A_5 \arrow[d, "\alpha_5"] \\
B_1 \arrow[r] & B_2 \arrow[r] & B_3 \arrow[r] & B_4 \arrow[r] & B_5
\end{tikzcd}\]
has exact rows and is commutative. Prove that if $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_4, \alpha_5$ are isomorphisms then $\alpha_3$ is an isomorphism. (Prove the stronger statement: $\alpha_3$ injective when $\alpha_2, \alpha_4$ injective and $\alpha_1$ surjective; $\alpha_3$ surjective when $\alpha_2, \alpha_4$ surjective and $\alpha_5$ injective.)

\item Prove that an $R$-module $P$ is projective if and only if $P$ is a direct summand of a free module. (Show every module is a quotient of a free module, then use the lifting property to split the resulting surjection onto $P$.)

\item Let $R$ be a PID and let $P$ be a finitely generated projective $R$-module. Prove that $P$ is free. (Use the structure theorem: a finitely generated module over a PID that is a submodule of a free module is free.)

\item (Flatness via Tor) Show that the $Z$-module $Z/(n)Z$ is not flat for $n > 1$ by tensoring the exact sequence $0 \to Z \xrightarrow{n} Z \to Z/(n)Z \to 0$ with $Z/(n)Z$ and exhibiting where left-exactness fails. Identify $\Tor_1^Z(Z/(n)Z, Z/(n)Z)$.

\item Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and $S$ a multiplicatively closed subset. Prove that the localization $S^{-1}R$ is a flat $R$-module, i.e.\ $S^{-1}R \otimes_R (-)$ is exact. (You may take as known that localization is an exact functor.)

\item (Schanuel's Lemma) Suppose $0 \to K_1 \to P_1 \to M \to 0$ and $0 \to K_2 \to P_2 \to M \to 0$ are short exact sequences of $R$-modules with $P_1, P_2$ projective. Prove $K_1 \oplus P_2 \cong K_2 \oplus P_1$.

\end{exers}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Exact Sequences --- Projective, Injective, and Flat Modules > Exercises
Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item (Lifting property of projectives) Let $P$ be a projective $R$-module, let $g : B \to C$ be a surjection of $R$-modules, and let $f : P \to C$ be any homomorphism. State and prove the existence of the dashed lift in
\[\begin{tikzcd}
& P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then show by example (over $R = Z$) that the lift $\tilde f$ need not be unique.

\item (Extension property of injectives) Let $Q$ be an injective $R$-module, let $\iota : A \to B$ be an injection of $R$-modules, and let $f : A \to Q$ be any homomorphism. Prove the existence of the dashed extension $F$ making
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & B \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists\,F"] \\
& Q
\end{tikzcd}\]
commute. Using this with $A = Z \hookrightarrow B = Q = Q$, find all extensions of $f = \id_Z$.

\item (Universal property of tensor product) Let $M, N, L$ be $R$-modules over a commutative ring $R$ and let $\varphi : M \times N \to L$ be $R$-bilinear. State the universal property realized by
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\otimes"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
and use it to prove the canonical isomorphism $R \otimes_R N \cong N$ as $R$-modules.

\item (Snake Lemma) Given a commutative diagram of $R$-modules with exact rows
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
& A \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "a"] & B \arrow[r, two heads] \arrow[d, "b"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "c"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A' \arrow[r, hook] & B' \arrow[r] & C' &
\end{tikzcd}\]
state the snake lemma (the existence of the connecting map $\delta : \ker c \to \coker a$ and the resulting six-term exact sequence $\ker a \to \ker b \to \ker c \xrightarrow{\delta} \coker a \to \coker b \to \coker c$), and prove that $\delta$ is well defined.

\item (Splitting via a section) Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Suppose a homomorphism $\mu : C \to B$ exists with $\varphi \circ \mu = \id_C$, as in
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[l, dashed, bend left, "\mu"] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
Prove that $B = \psi(A) \oplus \mu(C)$ and hence $B \cong A \oplus C$.

\end{exers}

Section: Introduction to Module Theory > Graded Problem Bank > Easy
Type: exercise_set
Content:
\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 10.1.1] Prove that $0m = 0$ and $(-1)m = -m$ for all $m$ in an $R$-module $M$.
\item [DF 10.1.2] Prove that $\units{R}$ and $M$ satisfy the two group-action axioms for the action of the multiplicative group $\units{R}$ on the set $M$.
\item [DF 10.1.3] If $rm = 0$ for some $r \in R$ and some $m \neq 0$, prove that $r$ has no left inverse in $R$.
\item [DF 10.1.6] Show that the intersection of any nonempty collection of submodules of an $R$-module is a submodule.
\item [DF 10.1.7] If $N_1 \subseteq N_2 \subseteq \cdots$ is an ascending chain of submodules of $M$, prove that $\bigcup_i N_i$ is a submodule.
\item [DF 10.1.9] If $N \le M$, prove that the annihilator $\ann_R(N) = \{r \in R \mid rn = 0\ \forall n \in N\}$ is a two-sided ideal of $R$.
\item [DF 10.1.10] If $I$ is a right ideal of $R$, prove that the annihilator of $I$ in $M$, namely $\{m \in M \mid am = 0\ \forall a \in I\}$, is a submodule of $M$.
\item [DF 10.1.11] For $M = Z/(24)Z \times Z/(15)Z \times Z/(50)Z$ as a $Z$-module, find a generator of the annihilator of $M$ in $Z$, and describe the annihilator of $I = 2Z$ in $M$ as a direct product of cyclic groups.
\item [DF 10.1.15] If $M$ is a finite abelian group, hence a $Z$-module, can this action be extended to make $M$ into a $Q$-module?
\item [DF 10.2.1] Use the submodule criterion to show that kernels and images of $R$-module homomorphisms are submodules.
\item [DF 10.2.2] Show that ``is $R$-module isomorphic to'' is an equivalence relation on any set of $R$-modules.
\item [DF 10.2.3] Give an explicit map between $R$-modules that is a $Z$-module homomorphism but not an $R$-module homomorphism.
\item [DF 10.2.5] Exhibit all $Z$-module homomorphisms from $Z/(3)Z$ to $Z/(9)Z$.
\item [DF 10.3.4] Prove that every finite abelian group is a torsion $Z$-module, and give an example of an infinite abelian group that is a torsion $Z$-module.
\item [DF 10.3.6] Prove that a quotient of an $R$-module generated by $n$ elements is generated by $n$ or fewer elements; deduce that quotients of cyclic modules are cyclic.
\item [DF 10.4.2] Show that $2 \otimes 1$ is $0$ in $Z \otimes_{Z} Z/(2)Z$ but nonzero in $2Z \otimes_{Z} Z/(2)Z$.
\item [DF 10.4.4] Show that $Q \otimes_{Z} Q$ and $Q \otimes_{Q} Q$ are isomorphic left $Q$-modules, each being a $1$-dimensional $Q$-vector space.
\item [DF 10.4.11] For a basis $\{e_1, e_2\}$ of $R^2$, show that $e_1 \otimes e_2 + e_2 \otimes e_1$ in $R^2 \otimes_{R} R^2$ is not a simple tensor $v \otimes w$.
\item [DF 10.4.13] Prove that the usual dot product $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\cdot(b_1,\ldots,b_n) = a_1 b_1 + \cdots + a_n b_n$ is a bilinear map $R^n \times R^n \to R$.
\item [DF 10.4.23] Prove the ring isomorphism $Z[i] \otimes_{Z} R \cong C$.
\item [DF 10.5.3] Prove that $P_1 \oplus P_2$ is a projective $R$-module if and only if both $P_1$ and $P_2$ are projective.
\item [DF 10.5.4] Prove that $Q_1 \oplus Q_2$ is an injective $R$-module if and only if both $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are injective.
\item [Artin 1.1] Let $R$ be a ring and $V = R$ the $R$-module $R$. Determine all $R$-module homomorphisms $\varphi : V \to V$.
\item [Artin 1.2] Let $V$ be an abelian group. Prove that if $V$ admits a $Q$-module structure compatible with its given addition, then that structure is uniquely determined.
\item [Artin 1.3] Let $R = Z[\alpha]$ where $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer. Prove that for any nonzero integer $m$ the quotient $R/mR$ is finite, and determine its order.
\item [Artin 2.1] For $R = C[x,y]$, let $M$ be the ideal generated by $x$ and $y$. Is $M$ a free $R$-module?
\item [Artin 5.2] Identify the abelian group presented by the integer matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 6 \end{psmallmatrix}$.
\item [Artin 7.1] Find a direct sum of cyclic groups isomorphic to the abelian group with presentation matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}$.
\item [Artin 7.2] Write the abelian group generated by $x, y$ with the single relation $3x + 4y = 0$ as a direct sum of cyclic groups.
\item [Artin 7.5] Determine the number of isomorphism classes of abelian groups of order $400$.
\item [Artin 8.1] For the operator $T$ on $C^2$ with matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}$, decide whether the corresponding $C[t]$-module is cyclic.
\item [Artin M.1] In how many ways can the additive group $Z/(5)Z$ be given the structure of a module over the Gaussian integers $Z[i]$?
\item [Artin M.2] Classify the finitely generated modules over the ring $Z/(6)Z$.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{}
\item [DF 10.1.4] For $M = R^n$ and left ideals $I_1, \ldots, I_n$ of $R$, prove that $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \mid x_i \in I_i\}$ and $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \mid x_i \in R,\ \sum x_i = 0\}$ are submodules of $M$.
\item [DF 10.1.5] For a left ideal $I$ of $R$, prove that $IM = \{\sum_{finite} a_i m_i \mid a_i \in I,\ m_i \in M\}$ is a submodule of $M$.
\item [DF 10.1.8] Prove that if $R$ is an integral domain then $\Tor(M)$ is a submodule; give a ring $R$ and module $M$ with $\Tor(M)$ not a submodule; and show that if $R$ has zero divisors then every nonzero $R$-module has nonzero torsion.
\item [DF 10.1.12] Prove that the annihilator in $M$ of $\ann_R(N)$ contains $N$ (with an example of strict containment), and that the annihilator in $R$ of $\ann_M(I)$ contains $I$ (with an example of strict containment).
\item [DF 10.1.13] For an ideal $I$ of $R$, let $M'$ be the elements of $M$ annihilated by some power $I^k$. Prove that $M'$ is a submodule of $M$.

\item [Artin 7.8] For $F = F_p$, determine for which primes $p$ the additive group $F^1$ admits a $Z[i]$-module structure, and likewise for $F^2$.
\item [Artin 7.9] Show that a $Z[i]$-module is equivalent to an abelian group $V$ together with a homomorphism $\varphi : V \to V$ satisfying $\varphi \circ \varphi = -\,id$.
\item [Artin 8.2] For a $C[t]$-module of the form $C[t]/(t-a)^n$, show there is a $C$-basis in which the matrix of the corresponding linear operator is a Jordan block.
\item [Artin 8.3] For $R = F[x]$ and $V$ the $R$-module on a generator $v$ with relation $(x^3 + 3x + 2)v = 0$, choose an $F$-basis and find the matrix of multiplication by $x$.
\item [Artin 8.4] For an $F[t]$-module $V$ with $F$-basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ and $B$ the matrix of $T$, prove $A = tI - B$ is a presentation matrix for the module.
\item [Artin 8.6] Classify finitely generated modules over the ring $C[\epsilon]$ where $\epsilon^2 = 0$.
\item [Artin 9.2] Prove that the $C[x,y]$-module with generators $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$ and relations $v_1 + yv_2 + xv_3 + x^2v_4 = 0$, $xv_1 + (x+3)v_2 + yv_3 + y^2v_4 = 0$ is free by exhibiting a basis.
\item [Artin M.3] For a finite abelian group $A$ and a nontrivial homomorphism $\varphi : A \to C^\times$, prove that $\sum_{a \in A} \varphi(a) = 0$.
\item [Artin M.4] When an integer $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ is diagonalized as $Q^{-1} A P$, determine how unique the matrices $P$ and $Q$ are.

\item [DF 10.3.20] For a PID $R$, a torsion $R$-module $M$, and a prime $p$, prove the $p$-primary component is a submodule, agrees with the earlier definition when $M$ has nonzero annihilator, and that $M$ is the (possibly infinite) direct sum of its $p$-primary components.

Type: prose
Content:
Throughout, $F$ denotes a field; its elements are called scalars. A vector space over $F$ is, axiomatically, just a unital module over $F$ (D\&F Chapter 10), but because $F$ is a field every such module behaves far better than a general module: it always has a basis, its ``size'' is a single well-defined number, and a linear map is pinned down by its action on a basis. The whole of linear algebra is the unwinding of these facts.

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The familiar cancellations $0v=0$, $\alpha 0=0$, and $(-1)v=-v$ hold by the module arguments: $0v=(0+0)v=0v+0v$; $\alpha 0=\alpha(0+0)=\alpha 0+\alpha 0$; and $0=0v=(1+(-1))v=v+(-1)v$. Over a field there is one more, decisive consequence: if $\alpha v=0$ then either $\alpha=0$ or $v=0$. Indeed if $\alpha\neq 0$ then $v=1v=(\alpha^{-1}\alpha)v=\alpha^{-1}(\alpha v)=\alpha^{-1}0=0$. This ``no zero divisors for scalar action'' is exactly what fails for modules over a ring with zero divisors, and it is the engine behind every uniqueness statement below.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: Subspace
Content:
\begin{definition}[Subspace]
A subset $W\subseteq V$ is a subspace (written $W\sgr V$) if $W$ is nonempty and closed under addition and scalar multiplication: for all $\alpha\in F$ and $w_1,w_2\in W$, both $w_1+w_2\in W$ and $\alpha w_1\in W$. Equivalently, $W\neq\varnothing$ and $\alpha w_1+w_2\in W$ for all $\alpha\in F$, $w_1,w_2\in W$. A subspace is itself a vector space under the restricted operations.
\end{definition}

Type: example
Title: The one-step subspace test on $R^3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The one-step subspace test on $R^3$}
Decide whether $W=\{(x,y,z)\inR^3 : x-2y+z=0\}$ is a subspace of $R^3$, and whether $U=\{(x,y,z): x-2y+z=1\}$ is.
\wrec Use the one-step test: a nonempty subset is a subspace iff it is closed under $\alpha w_1+w_2$. A defining equation that is homogeneous (right side $0$) survives this closure; an inhomogeneous one (right side $1$) does not, because it fails to contain $0$.
\wsol $W$ contains $0=(0,0,0)$ since $0-0+0=0$, so $W\neq\varnothing$. If $w_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$, $w_2=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ lie in $W$ and $\alpha\inR$, then the coordinate satisfying the test is
\[
(x_1-2y_1+z_1)\alpha+(x_2-2y_2+z_2)=\alpha\cdot 0+0=0,
\]
so $\alpha w_1+w_2\in W$. Hence $W\sgrR^3$. For $U$: $0\notin U$ because $0-0+0=1$ is false, so $U$ is not even nonempty-with-zero; concretely $(1,0,0)\in U$ but $2\cdot(1,0,0)=(2,0,0)$ has $2-0+0=2\neq 1$, so $U$ is not closed. Check. $W$ is the kernel of the linear functional $(x,y,z)\mapsto x-2y+z$, a plane through the origin --- exactly the shape a subspace of $R^3$ should have.
\end{wex}

Title: Subspaces of $\Hom$ and a non-subspace
Content:
\begin{wex}{Subspaces of $\Hom$ and a non-subspace}
Inside $\End_R(R^2)\cong \Mat_2(R)$, show the symmetric matrices $S=\{A : A\trans=A\}$ form a subspace, and the invertible matrices do not.
\wrec One-step test again, now in a function/matrix space; transpose is $R$-linear, so the symmetry condition is homogeneous. ``Invertible'' is multiplicative, not additive, so expect failure.
\wsol $S\neq\varnothing$ (it contains $0$). If $A\trans=A$, $B\trans=B$, $\alpha\inR$, then $(\alpha A+B)\trans=\alpha A\trans+B\trans=\alpha A+B$, so $S$ is a subspace; in fact $S=\Span(E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}+E_{21})$ has dimension $3$. The invertible matrices fail closure under addition: $I$ and $-I$ are invertible but $I+(-I)=0$ is not. Check. A subspace must contain $0$; the zero matrix is never invertible, so the invertible set can never be a subspace --- consistent with the failure we found.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: Intersections and sums
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Intersections and sums]
Let $\{W_i\}_{i\in I}$ be a family of subspaces of $V$. Then $\bigcap_{i\in I}W_i$ is a subspace. The sum $W_1+\cdots+W_k=\{w_1+\cdots+w_k : w_j\in W_j\}$ is a subspace, and is the smallest subspace containing every $W_j$. (The union of subspaces is in general not a subspace.)
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each contains $0$, hence is nonempty. For the intersection, if $v,w\in\bigcap W_i$ and $\alpha\in F$, then $\alpha v+w\in W_i$ for every $i$ since each $W_i$ is a subspace; thus $\alpha v+w\in\bigcap W_i$. For the sum, given two elements $\sum_j w_j$ and $\sum_j w_j'$ and $\alpha\in F$, the combination $\alpha\sum_j w_j+\sum_j w_j'=\sum_j(\alpha w_j+w_j')$ has $j$-th term in $W_j$, so lies in the sum. Any subspace containing all $W_j$ must contain all such finite sums, so the sum is the smallest such subspace.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Title: Linear combination and span
Content:
\begin{definition}[Linear combination and span]
Let $A\subseteq V$. A linear combination of $A$ is a vector $\alpha_1 v_1+\cdots+\alpha_n v_n$ with $n\geq 0$, $v_i\in A$, $\alpha_i\in F$. The span of $A$,
\[
\Span(A)=\{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i v_i : n\geq 0,\ v_i\in A,\ \alpha_i\in F\},
\]
is the set of all linear combinations of finitely many elements of $A$; it is the smallest subspace of $V$ containing $A$ (the empty combination gives $0$, so $\Span(\varnothing)=\{0\}$). We say $A$ spans (or generates) $V$ if $\Span(A)=V$.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: Linear dependence and independence
Content:
\begin{definition}[Linear dependence and independence]
A set $A\subseteq V$ is linearly dependent if there exist distinct $v_1,\dots,v_n\in A$ and scalars $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in F$ not all zero with $\alpha_1 v_1+\cdots+\alpha_n v_n=0$. Otherwise $A$ is linearly independent: the only way to write $0$ as a finite combination of distinct elements of $A$ is with all coefficients $0$.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Independence is exactly a uniqueness of representation statement: $A$ is independent iff every vector in $\Span(A)$ is a linear combination of elements of $A$ in at most one way. Indeed if $\sum\alpha_i v_i=\sum\beta_i v_i$ then $\sum(\alpha_i-\beta_i)v_i=0$, so independence forces $\alpha_i=\beta_i$; conversely a nontrivial relation gives two representations of $0$.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Independence over $R$ via a determinant
Content:
\begin{wex}{Independence over $R$ via a determinant}
Are $v_1=(1,2,1)$, $v_2=(2,1,0)$, $v_3=(1,-1,1)$ linearly independent in $R^3$?
\wrec In $F^n$ with $n$ vectors, independence is equivalent to the matrix with these columns being invertible, i.e.\ having nonzero determinant: $\det\neq 0\iff$ independent.
\wsol Form $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2&1\\2&1&-1\\1&0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ (columns $v_1,v_2,v_3$). Expanding along the bottom row,
\[
\det A=1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix}-0+1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{psmallmatrix}=1(-2-1)+1(1-4)=-3-3=-6\neq 0.
\]
So the only solution of $\alpha_1 v_1+\alpha_2 v_2+\alpha_3 v_3=0$ is $\alpha=0$, and the set is independent. Check. Since $\det A=-6\neq 0$, $A$ is invertible, so the three columns also span $R^3$; three independent vectors in a $3$-dimensional space ought to be a basis, as the next subsection confirms.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Dependence over $\F_2$ that would be independence over $Q$}
In $\F_2^{\,3}$ ($\F_2=Z/2Z$) consider $v_1=(1,1,0)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, $v_3=(1,0,1)$. Are they independent?
\wrec The field matters: solve $\alpha_1 v_1+\alpha_2 v_2+\alpha_3 v_3=0$ with $\alpha_i\in\F_2$. A relation valid mod $2$ need not be valid over $Q$, and vice versa.
\wsol Try $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha_3=1$:
\[
v_1+v_2+v_3=(1{+}0{+}1,\;1{+}1{+}0,\;0{+}1{+}1)=(0,0,0)\ in \F_2.
\]
This is a nontrivial relation (coefficients all $1\neq 0$), so the set is dependent over $\F_2$. Check. Over $Q$ the same three vectors give $v_1+v_2+v_3=(2,2,2)\neq 0$, and one checks $\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{psmallmatrix}=2\neq 0$, so they are independent over $Q$. The dependence appeared precisely because $2\equiv 0$ in $\F_2$ --- a vivid reminder that (in)dependence is relative to $F$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Functions: $\{1,\cos^2 x,\cos 2x\}$ in the space of real functions
Content:
\begin{wex}{Functions: $\{1,\cos^2 x,\cos 2x\}$ in the space of real functions}
Show $\{1,\cos^2 x,\cos 2x\}$ is linearly dependent in the $R$-vector space $C(R)$ of continuous functions, while $\{1,\cos x,\cos 2x\}$ is independent.
\wrec A relation among functions must hold for every input $x$. Use a known identity to exhibit dependence; to prove independence, evaluate at enough points to force the coefficients to $0$.
\wsol The identity $\cos 2x=2\cos^2 x-1$ rearranges to $1\cdot 1-2\cdot\cos^2 x+1\cdot\cos 2x=0$ for all $x$ --- a nontrivial relation, so $\{1,\cos^2 x,\cos 2x\}$ is dependent. For $\{1,\cos x,\cos 2x\}$, suppose $a+b\cos x+c\cos 2x=0$ for all $x$. Evaluate at $x=0$: $a+b+c=0$; at $x=\pi$: $a-b+c=0$; at $x=\pi/2$: $a-c=0$. From the first two, $b=0$; then $a=-c$ and $a=c$, forcing $a=c=0$. So all coefficients vanish and the set is independent. Check. The dependence used a genuine identity (true for all $x$), whereas the independence argument only needed three sample points to pin down three unknowns --- exactly the count one expects.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Basis]
A subset $B\subseteq V$ is a basis of $V$ if $B$ is linearly independent and $\Span(B)=V$. Equivalently, every $v\in V$ is a linear combination of elements of $B$ in exactly one way.

Type: proposition
Title: Universal property of a basis
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Universal property of a basis]
Let $B=\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$ be a basis of $V$ and let $W$ be any $F$-vector space. For every function $f\colonB\to W$ there is a unique $F$-linear map $T\colon V\to W$ with $T(e_i)=f(e_i)$ for all $i$. Pictorially, writing $\iota\colonB\hookrightarrow V$ for the inclusion:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
B \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & V \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,T"] \\
& W
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $B$ is the basis (a set, not yet a vector space); $V$ is the $F$-vector space spanned by $B$; $W$ is an arbitrary $F$-vector space. These are the two categories in play: on top sits the set-theoretic datum $f$, and below sits the linear-algebraic world where $T$ must live.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colonB\hookrightarrow V$ is the set-inclusion, not a linear map (its domain is a set, not a vector space). $f\colonB\to W$ is any set-function, the freely chosen target values. $T\colon V\to W$ (dashed) is the unique $F$-linear map whose existence the proposition asserts; it is not given but constructed.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $T\circ\iota = f$, i.e.\ $T(e_i)=f(e_i)$ for every $e_i\inB$. This single equation, stated for set-elements of $B$, determines $T$ on all of $V$ by linearity.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take any $v\in V$; write $v=\sum_i\alpha_i e_i$ (unique, since $B$ is a basis). Then $T(v)=\sum_i\alpha_i T(e_i)=\sum_i\alpha_i f(e_i)$. Along the top-then-down path, $e_i\xrightarrow{\iota} e_i\xrightarrow{T} T(e_i)=f(e_i)$ by this formula, which is the value of the diagonal arrow $f$. Well-definedness (the reason $T$ is a genuine function): the coefficients $\alpha_i$ are unique by linear independence, so the formula $T(v)=\sum\alpha_i f(e_i)$ depends only on $v$, not on any choice of representative.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the engine of all linear algebra: it says the set-function $f$ on the basis is the only data needed to pin down the linear map $T$ on all of $V$. Every matrix calculation, every change-of-basis argument, and every representation-theoretic construction reduces to specifying a map on a basis and invoking this universal property.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $B=\{e_1,e_2\}$ standard basis of $R^2$, $W=R^3$, $f(e_1)=(1,0,-1)$, $f(e_2)=(2,1,0)$. The unique linear $T$ sends $(a,b)\mapsto a(1,0,-1)+b(2,1,0)$, i.e.\ the matrix with columns $f(e_i)$; this is the worked example immediately following.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\iota$ is a linear map and that the diagram is a composition of linear maps on the top edge. It is not: $\iota$ is a set inclusion and $f$ is a set-function; only the dashed $T$ is linear. The diagram lives in two categories simultaneously, and that is its whole point.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that specifying a linear map out of $V$ is equivalent to specifying a set-function out of any basis of $V$, with uniqueness guaranteed by independence and existence guaranteed by spanning.
\end{dgx}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Existence. Each $v\in V$ has a unique expression $v=\sum_i\alpha_i e_i$ (finite sum) by the basis property; set $T(v)=\sum_i\alpha_i f(e_i)$. This is well defined precisely because the $\alpha_i$ are unique, and linearity is immediate from the coordinatewise definition. Uniqueness. Type: example
Title: Building a linear map from its values on a basis
Content:
\begin{wex}{Building a linear map from its values on a basis}
Let $B=\{e_1,e_2\}$ be the standard basis of $R^2$ and define $T\colonR^2\toR^3$ by $T(e_1)=(1,0,-1)$, $T(e_2)=(2,1,0)$. Compute $T(3,-2)$ and the matrix of $T$.
\wrec By the universal property, naming $T$ on a basis determines $T$ everywhere; just expand the input in the basis and push the coefficients through.
\wsol Write $(3,-2)=3e_1-2e_2$. Then
\[
T(3,-2)=3T(e_1)-2T(e_2)=3(1,0,-1)-2(2,1,0)=(3-4,\,0-2,\,-3-0)=(-1,-2,-3).
\]
The matrix (columns $=T(e_j)$) is $\bigl[\,T\,\bigr]=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, and indeed $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}3\\-2\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}-1\\-2\\-3\end{psmallmatrix}$. Check. The two outputs agree, confirming the map computed abstractly equals the matrix computed concretely.
\end{wex}

Type: lemma
Title: Replacement / Exchange Lemma
Content:
\begin{lemma}[Replacement / Exchange Lemma]
Suppose $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_m\}\subseteq V$ is linearly independent and $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$ spans $V$. Then $m\leq n$, and one may reorder $S$ so that $\{a_1,\dots,a_m,s_{m+1},\dots,s_n\}$ still spans $V$. In words: an independent set is never larger than a spanning set, and its members can be swapped in for spanning vectors one at a time.
\end{lemma}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Definitions and Basic Theory > Bases, the replacement lemma, and dimension
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-809ebecde6525d16167a
Content:
\begin{proof}
We exchange $a_1,\dots,a_m$ into $S$ inductively, maintaining a spanning set of size $n$. Suppose for some $0\leq k<m$ we have a spanning set $\{a_1,\dots,a_k,s_{k+1},\dots,s_n\}$ (the case $k=0$ is $S$). Since this set spans, write $a_{k+1}=\sum_{i\leq k}\beta_i a_i+\sum_{j>k}\gamma_j s_j$. Not all $\gamma_j$ are $0$: otherwise $a_{k+1}\in\Span(a_1,\dots,a_k)$, contradicting independence of $A$. Reorder so $\gamma_{k+1}\neq 0$; then $s_{k+1}=\gamma_{k+1}^{-1}\bigl(a_{k+1}-\sum_{i\leq k}\beta_i a_i-\sum_{j>k+1}\gamma_j s_j\bigr)$, so $s_{k+1}\in\Span(a_1,\dots,a_{k+1},s_{k+2},\dots,s_n)$, and replacing $s_{k+1}$ by $a_{k+1}$ keeps the set spanning. This requires a fresh $s_j$ at each step, so we can never run out before exhausting $A$; hence $m\leq n$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Invariance of dimension
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Invariance of dimension]
If $V$ has a finite basis, then any two bases of $V$ have the same number of elements. This common number is the dimension $\dim_F V$. More generally (using the lemma in the infinite case via Zorn) any two bases of $V$ have the same cardinality.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-580ca050fb2d993cc9a5
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $B=\{e_1,\dots,e_n\}$ be a finite basis and $B'$ any basis. Every finite subset of $B'$ is independent and $B$ spans, so by the Replacement Lemma every finite subset of $B'$ has at most $n$ elements; hence $B'$ is finite, say $B'=\{f_1,\dots,f_m\}$, and $m\leq n$. Symmetrically ($B$ independent, $B'$ spanning) $n\leq m$. Hence $n=m$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Existence of a basis, via Zorn's Lemma
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Existence of a basis, via Zorn's Lemma]
Every vector space $V$ has a basis. More precisely, every linearly independent subset $A\subseteq V$ is contained in a basis, and every spanning set contains a basis.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Definitions and Basic Theory > Bases, the replacement lemma, and dimension
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-afc7e96bce755113dfdf
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $P$ be the set of linearly independent subsets of $V$ containing $A$, partially ordered by inclusion; $P\neq\varnothing$ since $A\inP$. Given a chain $C\subseteqP$, its union $U=\bigcupC$ is independent: any finite relation involves finitely many vectors, all lying in a single member of the chain (chains are totally ordered), which is independent; so $U\inP$ is an upper bound. By Zorn's Lemma $P$ has a maximal element $B\supseteq A$. If $B$ failed to span, some $v\notin\Span(B)$ would make $B\cup\{v\}$ independent (a relation $\alpha v+\sum\alpha_i e_i=0$ forces $\alpha=0$ by $v\notin\SpanB$, then the rest $=0$ by independence of $B$), contradicting maximality. So $B$ is a basis containing $A$. For the last assertion, let $S$ span $V$ and run the same argument with $P$ the set of independent subsets of $S$ (and $A=\varnothing$): a maximal one $B\subseteq S$ contains every $s\in S$ in its span (otherwise $B\cup\{s\}$ would be a larger independent subset of $S$), so $\Span(B)\supseteq\Span(S)=V$ and $B\subseteq S$ is a basis.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Extending an independent set to a basis
Content:
\begin{wex}{Extending an independent set to a basis}
Extend $\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}$ to a basis of $R^3$.
\wrec By the existence theorem an independent set extends to a basis; concretely, adjoin standard vectors and test independence by a determinant until it is nonzero.
\wsol The two vectors are independent (neither is a scalar multiple of the other). Try adjoining $e_1=(1,0,0)$ and form
\[
\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&0\end{psmallmatrix}=1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}-0+1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}=0+1\cdot 1=1\neq 0.
\]
So $\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,0)\}$ is independent, and being three independent vectors in $R^3$ it is a basis. Check. $\dim_RR^3=3$, and we produced exactly $3$ independent vectors --- the count matches, confirming we have a genuine basis.
\end{wex}

Section: Vector Spaces > Definitions and Basic Theory > Bases, the replacement lemma, and dimension
Type: example
Title: Dimension counts over different fields
Content:
\begin{wex}{Dimension counts over different fields}
Compute $\dim$ in each case: $\Mat_2(\F_2)$ over $\F_2$; $C$ over $R$; $R$ over $Q$; and the space $P_3$ of real polynomials of degree $\leq 3$, over $R$.
\wrec Find an explicit basis and count it; invariance of dimension guarantees the count is independent of the basis chosen.
\wsol $\Mat_2(\F_2)$ has basis $\{E_{11},E_{12},E_{21},E_{22}\}$, so $\dim_{\F_2}\Mat_2(\F_2)=4$ (and the space has $2^4=16$ elements). $C=R\cdot 1\oplusR\cdot i$ has basis $\{1,i\}$, so $\dim_RC=2$. $P_3$ has basis $\{1,x,x^2,x^3\}$, so $\dim_R P_3=4$. Finally $\dim_QR=\infty$: a finite basis would make $R$ countable (finitely many rational coordinates), but $R$ is uncountable. Check. For $\Mat_2(\F_2)$, $\abs{\Mat_2(\F_2)}=\abs{\F_2}^{\dim}=2^4=16$, matching the direct count of $2\times 2$ binary matrices.
\end{wex}

Type: corollary
Content:
\begin{corollary}
Let $\dim_F V=n<\infty$. Then: (i) any independent set has $\leq n$ elements, with equality iff it is a basis; (ii) any spanning set has $\geq n$ elements, with equality iff it is a basis; (iii) any $n$ vectors that are independent, or that span, form a basis.
\end{corollary}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Definitions and Basic Theory > Bases, the replacement lemma, and dimension
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-942e0354c2e7e881e5a6
Content:
\begin{proof}
Both bounds are the Replacement Lemma applied against a fixed basis of size $n$. If an independent set has exactly $n$ elements but failed to span, it would extend (by the existence theorem) to a strictly larger independent set, exceeding $n$ --- impossible; so it is a basis. Dually, a spanning set of exactly $n$ elements that were dependent would contain a basis of size $<n$, contradicting invariance. Part (iii) is the equality cases of (i),(ii).
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Classification by dimension
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Classification by dimension]
Two $F$-vector spaces $V,W$ are isomorphic ($V\cong W$) if and only if $\dim_F V=\dim_F W$. In particular every $n$-dimensional space is isomorphic to $F^n$ via a choice of basis.
\end{theorem}
