\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Prove that if $M$ is a cyclic $R$-module then $T(M)=S(M)$, i.e., the tensor algebra $T(M)$ is commutative.

\item Fill in the details for the proof of Proposition 33 that $S/I=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\infty} S_k/I_k$. [Show first that $S_kI_j\subseteq I_{k+j}$. Use this to show that the multiplication $(S_i/I_i)(S_j/I_j)\subseteq S_{i+j}/I_{i+j}$ is well defined, and then check the ring axioms and verify the statements made in the proof of Proposition 33.]

\item Show that the image of the map $Sym_2$ for the $Z$-module $Z$ consists of the $2$-tensors $a(1\otimes 1)$ where $a$ is an even integer. Conclude in particular that the symmetric tensor $1\otimes 1$ in $Z\otimes_{Z}Z$ is not contained in the image of the map $Sym_2$.

\item Prove that $m\wedge n_1\wedge n_2\wedge\cdots\wedge n_k=(-1)^k(n_1\wedge n_2\wedge\cdots\wedge n_k\wedge m)$. In particular, $x\wedge(y\wedge z)=(y\wedge z)\wedge x$ for all $x,y,z\in M$.

\item Prove that if $M$ is a free $R$-module of rank $n$ then $\extp^i(M)$ is a free $R$-module of rank $\binom{n}{i}$ for $i=0,1,2,\dots$.

\item If $A$ is an $R$-algebra and $\varphi\colon M\to A$ is an $R$-module homomorphism with $\varphi(m)^2=0$ for all $m\in M$, prove there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $\Phi\colon\extp(M)\to A$ such that $\Phi|_M=\varphi$.

\item Let $R=Z[x,y]$ and $I=(x,y)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that if $ax+by=a'x+b'y$ in $R$ then $a'=a+yf$ and $b'=b-xf$ for some polynomial $f(x,y)\in R$.
\item[(b)] Prove the map $\varphi(ax+by,\,cx+dy)=ad-bc \bmod (x,y)$ in the example following Corollary 37 is a well defined alternating $R$-bilinear map from $I\times I$ to $R/I$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $F$ be its field of fractions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Considering $F$ as an $R$-module, prove that $\extp^2 F=0$.
\item[(b)] Let $I$ be an $R$-submodule of $F$ (for example, any ideal in $R$). Prove that $\extp^i I$ is a torsion $R$-module for $i\ge 2$ (i.e., for every $x\in\extp^i I$ there is some nonzero $r\in R$ with $rx=0$).
\item[(c)] Give an example of an integral domain $R$ and $R$-module $I$ in $F$ with $\extp^i I\ne 0$ for every $i\ge 0$ (cf. the example following Corollary 37).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R=Z[G]$ be the group ring of the group $G=\{1,\sigma\}$ of order $2$. Let $M=Z e_1\oplusZ e_2$ be a free $Z$-module of rank $2$ with basis $e_1$ and $e_2$. Define $\sigma(e_1)=e_1+2e_2$ and $\sigma(e_2)=-e_2$. Prove that this makes $M$ into an $R$-module and that the $R$-module $\extp^2 M$ is a group of order $2$ with $e_1\wedge e_2$ as generator.

\item Prove that $z-\tfrac{1}{k!}Alt(z)=\tfrac{1}{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}\bigl(z-\epsilon(\sigma)\,\sigma z\bigr)$ for any $k$-tensor $z$ and use this to prove that the kernel of the $R$-module homomorphism $\tfrac{1}{k!}Alt$ in Proposition 40 is $A^k(M)$.

\item Suppose that $-1\ne 1$ in $F$. Prove that the image of $Alt_k$ is the unique largest subspace of $T^k(V)$ on which each permutation $\sigma$ in the symmetric group $S_k$ acts as multiplication by the scalar $\epsilon(\sigma)$.

\item \leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that if $f(x,y)$ is an alternating bilinear map on $V$ (i.e., $f(x,x)=0$ for all $x\in V$) then $f(x,y)=-f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in V$.
\item[(b)] Suppose that $-1\ne 1$ in $F$. Prove that if $f(x,y)$ is a bilinear map on $V$ with $f(x,y)=-f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in V$ then $f$ is alternating (i.e., $f(x,x)=0$ for all $x\in V$).
\item[(c)] Suppose that $-1=1$ in $F$. Prove that every alternating bilinear form $f(x,y)$ on $V$ is symmetric (i.e., $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in V$). Prove that there is a symmetric bilinear map on $V$ that is not alternating. [One approach: show that $C^2(V)\subseteqA^2(V)$ and $C^2(V)\neA^2(V)$ by counting dimensions. Alternatively, construct an explicit symmetric map that is not alternating.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $F$ be any field in which $-1\ne 1$ and let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. Prove that $V\otimes_F V=S^2(V)\oplus\extp^2(V)$, i.e., that every $2$-tensor can be written uniquely as a sum of a symmetric and an alternating tensor.

\item Prove that if $M$ is an $R$-module direct factor of the $R$-module $N$ then $T(M)$ (respectively, $S(M)$ and $\extp(M)$) is an $R$-subalgebra of $T(N)$ (respectively, $S(N)$ and $\extp(N)$).

\end{exers}

Prove that there is a symmetric bilinear map on $V$ that is not alternating. [One approach: show that $C^2(V)\subseteq\mathcal{A}^2(V)$ and $C^2(V)\ne\mathcal{A}^2(V)$ by counting dimensions. Alternatively, construct an explicit symmetric map that is not alternating.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $F$ be any field in which $-1\ne 1$ and let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. Prove that $V\otimes_F V=S^2(V)\oplus\extp^2(V)$, i.e., that every $2$-tensor can be written uniquely as a sum of a symmetric and an alternating tensor.

\item Prove that if $M$ is an $R$-module direct factor of the $R$-module $N$ then $T(M)$ (respectively, $S(M)$ and $\extp(M)$) is an $R$-subalgebra of $T(N)$ (respectively, $S(N)$ and $\extp(N)$).

\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\F$ with $\dim V = n$. Compute $\dim V^{\otimes k}$ in terms of $n$ and $k$, and explain why $T(V) = \bigoplus_{k \geq 0} V^{\otimes k}$ is infinite-dimensional whenever $n \geq 1$.

\item Let $V$ have ordered basis $\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}$. Inside the symmetric algebra $S(V)$, write down a basis for the degree-$2$ component $S^2(V)$ and verify directly that $\dim S^2(V) = \binom{n+k-1}{k}$ with $n = 3$, $k = 2$.

\item With $V$ as in the previous problem, list a basis for $\extp^2(V)$ and for $\extp^3(V)$, and confirm the formula $\dim \extp^k(V) = \binom{n}{k}$. What is $\extp^k(V)$ for $k > 3$, and why?

\item In the exterior algebra $\extp(V)$, prove that $v \extp v = 0$ for every $v \in V$, and deduce that $w \extp z = -\, z \extp w$ for all $w, z \in V$. (Begin from the defining relations of $\extp(V)$.)

\item Let $V = \F^2$ with basis $\{e_1, e_2\}$. Compute the product $(2e_1 + 3e_2) \extp (e_1 - e_2)$ in $\extp^2(V)$, expressing the answer as a scalar multiple of $e_1 \extp e_2$.

\item Let $\varphi \colon V \to V$ be the linear map given on the basis $\{e_1, e_2\}$ of $V = \F^2$ by $\varphi(e_1) = e_1 + 2e_2$ and $\varphi(e_2) = 3e_1 + 4e_2$. The induced map $\extp^2(\varphi) \colon \extp^2(V) \to \extp^2(V)$ acts on the one-dimensional space $\extp^2(V)$ as multiplication by a scalar. Compute that scalar and identify it as $\det$ of a matrix.

\item Show that the tensor algebra $T(V)$, the symmetric algebra $S(V)$, and the exterior algebra $\extp(V)$ are all graded $\F$-algebras: in each case exhibit the grading and verify that the product of a degree-$i$ element with a degree-$j$ element lands in degree $i + j$.

\item Let $\dim V = n$. Prove that the top exterior power $\extp^n(V)$ is one-dimensional, and that a linear map $\varphi \in \End(V)$ induces multiplication by $\det \varphi$ on $\extp^n(V)$. Use this to give a basis-free proof that $\det(\psi \varphi) = \det(\psi)\det(\varphi)$.

\item Describe explicitly the surjective algebra homomorphisms $T(V) \twoheadrightarrow S(V)$ and $T(V) \twoheadrightarrow \extp(V)$, and identify the two-sided ideals that are their kernels. State which ideal is generated by elements $v \otimes w - w \otimes v$ and which by elements $v \otimes v$.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $\dim V = n$. Compute $\sum_{k=0}^{m} \dim S^k(V)$, the dimension of the part of $S(V)$ of degree at most $m$ (note $\dim S(V)=\infty$ for $n\ge 1$), i.e.\ give a closed form for $\sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{n+k-1}{k}$, and prove that $\dim \extp(V) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} = 2^n$.

\item Let $W \subseteq V$ be a subspace with $\dim W = r$ and $\dim V = n$. Prove that the inclusion $W \hookrightarrow V$ induces an injective algebra homomorphism $\extp(W) \to \extp(V)$, and that $\extp^r(W) \to \extp^r(V)$ is injective onto a one-dimensional subspace. Interpret a nonzero element of $\extp^r(W)$ as encoding the subspace $W$.

\item Prove that vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k \in V$ are linearly independent if and only if $v_1 \extp v_2 \extp \cdots \extp v_k \neq 0$ in $\extp^k(V)$. Use this to characterize when an element $v_1 \extp \cdots \extp v_n \in \extp^n(V)$ is a basis of $\extp^n(V)$.

\item Suppose $\F$ has characteristic $0$. Construct an explicit $\F$-linear injection $S^k(V) \to V^{\otimes k}$ (a symmetrization splitting of the projection $V^{\otimes k} \to S^k(V)$) and verify on $S^2(V)$ with $\dim V = 2$ that your map is a section of the canonical projection.

\item Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ with $\dim V = n$. Show that $\tr\bigl(\extp^k(\varphi)\bigr)$ equals the $k$-th elementary symmetric function of the eigenvalues of $\varphi$ (over $C$), and in particular recover $\tr(\extp^1(\varphi)) = \tr(\varphi)$ and $\tr(\extp^n(\varphi)) = \det(\varphi)$.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item State and prove the universal property of the tensor algebra by completing the diagram below: given any $\F$-algebra $A$ and any $\F$-linear map $f \colon V \to A$, show there is a unique algebra homomorphism $\tilde{f}$ making the triangle commute, where $\iota \colon V \to T(V)$ is the canonical inclusion.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
V \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & T(V) \arrow[d, dashed, "\tilde{f}"] \\
& A
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\item The symmetric algebra solves a mapping problem into commutative algebras. Let $A$ be a commutative $\F$-algebra and $f \colon V \to A$ linear. Show the dashed arrow $\bar{f}$ exists uniquely and that the lower triangle commutes, where $\pi \colon T(V) \to S(V)$ is the canonical projection and $\tilde{f}$ is from the previous exercise.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large]
V \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[drr, bend right=15, "f"'] & T(V) \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, "\tilde{f}"] & S(V) \arrow[d, dashed, "\bar{f}"] \\
& & A
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State the analogous universal property for $\extp(V)$ (replacing commutative algebras by algebras in which every $f(v)$ squares to $0$).

\item Functoriality. Let $\varphi \colon V \to W$ be linear. Show that $\varphi$ induces algebra homomorphisms making each square below commute, where the vertical maps are the canonical projections, and conclude that $\extp$ is a functor (i.e.\ $\extp(\psi \varphi) = \extp(\psi)\,\extp(\varphi)$ and $\extp(\id_V) = \id$).
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
T(V) \arrow[r, "T(\varphi)"] \arrow[d, "\pi_V"'] & T(W) \arrow[d, "\pi_W"] \\
\extp(V) \arrow[r, "\extp(\varphi)"'] & \extp(W)
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\item Let $0 \to U \xrightarrow{\,i\,} V \xrightarrow{\,p\,} Q \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of finite-dimensional vector spaces, with $\dim U = r$ and $\dim Q = s$. Fix a linear section $\sigma\colon Q\to V$ of $p$ ($p\sigma=\id_Q$) and let the diagonal arrow be $\mu_\sigma(w\otimes\eta)=w\extp\extp^s(\sigma)(\eta)$; this map depends on $\sigma$. Establish the canonical isomorphism on top exterior powers indicated by the dashed arrow (show that $\mu_\sigma\circ(\extp^r(i)\otimes\id)$ is independent of $\sigma$ and bijective), and use the diagram to prove $\extp^{r+s}(V) \cong \extp^r(U) \otimes \extp^s(Q)$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\extp^r(U) \otimes \extp^s(Q) \arrow[r, dashed, "\sim"] \arrow[d, "\extp^r(i)\,\otimes\,\id"'] & \extp^{r+s}(V) \\
\extp^r(V) \otimes \extp^s(Q) \arrow[ur, "\mu_\sigma"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\item Connect the top exterior power to the determinant via naturality. For $\varphi \in \End(V)$ with $\dim V = n$, show the square below commutes, where the vertical arrows are the canonical identification of $\extp^n(V)$ with $\F$ after choosing a basis $e_1 \extp \cdots \extp e_n$, and conclude that the scalar by which $\extp^n(\varphi)$ acts is independent of that choice and equals $\det \varphi$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\extp^n(V) \arrow[r, "\extp^n(\varphi)"] \arrow[d, "\sim"'] & \extp^n(V) \arrow[d, "\sim"] \\
\F \arrow[r, "\cdot\,\det\varphi"'] & \F
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
The abstract picture of \S11.1--11.2 --- vector spaces, linear maps, rank and nullity --- has a thoroughly concrete shadow: once bases are fixed, a linear map $T\colon F^n\to F^m$ is an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, and the equation $T(x)=b$ is the linear system $AX=B$. Artin develops the computational side first (Chapter 1), and it is worth having in hand as the algorithmic complement to the structure theory. The single tool that does everything below --- solving systems, deciding consistency, computing $\rank$, inverting a matrix --- is row reduction by elementary matrices.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: definition
Title: Elementary matrices and row operations
Content:
\begin{definition}[Elementary matrices and row operations]
Let $F$ be a field. An elementary matrix is an $n\times n$ matrix obtained from the identity $I_n$ by one of three modifications, and left multiplication $X\mapsto EX$ performs the corresponding elementary row operation on $X$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Transvection. Put a scalar $a$ in the $(i,j)$ position ($i\neq j$) of $I_n$. Then $EX$ adds $a\cdot(row j)$ to (row $i$).
\item[(ii)] Swap. Exchange rows $i$ and $j$ of $I_n$ (zeros on the $(i,i),(j,j)$ diagonal, ones in the $(i,j),(j,i)$ slots). Then $EX$ interchanges (row $i$) and (row $j$).
\item[(iii)] Scaling. Replace one diagonal entry of $I_n$ by a nonzero scalar $c$. Then $EX$ multiplies (row $i$) by $c$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

Type: lemma
Title: Elementary matrices are invertible
Content:
\begin{lemma}[Elementary matrices are invertible]
Each elementary matrix $E$ is invertible, and $E^{-1}$ is again elementary of the same type. A finite product of elementary matrices is therefore invertible.
\end{lemma}

Content:
\begin{proof}
The inverse operation is itself elementary: ``subtract $a\cdot(row j)$ from (row $i$)'' undoes type (i), the swap undoes itself (type (ii)), and ``multiply (row $i$) by $c^{-1}$'' undoes type (iii). The matrix of the inverse operation is $E^{-1}$. A product of invertibles is invertible.
\end{proof}

Row reduction of a matrix $M$ means producing $M'=E_k\cdots E_2E_1\,M$ for some sequence of elementary matrices, i.e.\ applying row operations until no further simplification is useful. Setting $P=E_k\cdots E_1$ (an invertible matrix), we have $M'=PM$; this $P$ records the whole reduction.

Type: theorem
Title: Existence of a row echelon form
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Existence of a row echelon form]
Every matrix $M$ can be carried to a matrix in row echelon form by a finite sequence of elementary row operations. The resulting echelon form is uniquely determined by $M$.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-74242fcbe8aec720bee1
Content:
\begin{proof}
Induct on the number of rows. If $M=0$ it is already echelon. Otherwise let column $p$ be the first nonzero column. Use a type (ii) swap to bring a nonzero entry of column $p$ to the top row, then a type (iii) scaling to normalize it to $1$: this is the first pivot. Type (i) operations clear all other entries of column $p$. The matrix now has block form $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&*\\0&D\end{psmallmatrix}$ with a smaller matrix $D$ below-right; since the columns left of $D$ are zero, operating on $D$ leaves the rest untouched. By induction $D$ reduces to echelon form, after which type (i) operations clear the entries above the new pivots. The four conditions then hold. Uniqueness (which we use but do not prove here) follows because the pivot columns and the coordinates of the free columns are determined by the linear dependencies among the columns of $M$, which row operations preserve.
\end{proof}

Title: Row operations preserve the solution set
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Row operations preserve the solution set]
If $M=[A\mid B]$ is the augmented matrix of the system $AX=B$ and $M'=[A'\mid B']=PM$ with $P$ invertible, then $AX=B$ and $A'X=B'$ have exactly the same solutions.
\end{proposition}

Because $P$ is invertible and $[A'\mid B']=[PA\mid PB]$: if $AX=B$ then $A'X=PAX=PB=B'$; conversely if $A'X=B'$ then $AX=P^{-1} A'X=P^{-1} B'=B$. The two equations are interchanged by the invertible $P$, hence have identical solution sets.
\end{proof}

Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: theorem
Title: Solving $AX=B$ from echelon form
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Solving $AX=B$ from echelon form]
Let $[A'\mid B']$ be the row echelon form of the augmented matrix of $AX=B$, with $B'$ a single column.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] The system is consistent (has a solution) if and only if the last column $B'$ contains no pivot --- equivalently, there is no row of the form $[\,0\ \cdots\ 0\mid 1\,]$, which would read $0=1$.
\item[(2)] When consistent, the free variables (those whose columns carry no pivot) may be assigned arbitrary values, and the pivot variables are then determined uniquely.
\end{enumerate}
In particular a consistent system has a unique solution iff every column of $A'$ is a pivot column.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-a1cf38523d15afadafc7
Content:
\begin{proof}
A pivot in the last column gives an equation $0\cdot x_1+\cdots+0\cdot x_n=1$, impossible, so consistency forces no such pivot. Conversely, if no pivot sits in column $B'$, solve from the bottom up: each nonzero row has its pivot in some column of $A'$, expressing that pivot variable in terms of the free variables to its right; assigning the free variables any values determines the pivot variables in turn. Uniqueness holds exactly when there are no free variables, i.e.\ when every column of $A'$ is a pivot column.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Title: Rank via echelon form
Content:
\begin{definition}[Rank via echelon form]
The rank $\rank A$ is the number of pivots (equivalently, of nonzero rows) in any row echelon form of $A$. For $A$ the matrix of $T\colon F^n\to F^m$ this agrees with $\dim\im T$, and $\nullity A=n-\rank A=\dim\ker T$ counts the free variables --- the concrete face of rank--nullity from \S11.2.
\end{definition}

Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: example
Title: An underdetermined (consistent) system
Content:
\begin{wex}{An underdetermined (consistent) system}
Solve the system over $Q$
\[
x_1+x_2+2x_3+x_4=5,\qquad x_1+x_2+2x_3+6x_4=10,\qquad x_1+2x_2+5x_3+2x_4=7.
\]
\wrec This is Artin's system (1.2.11): three equations, four unknowns. Reduce the augmented matrix to echelon form; with fewer pivots than unknowns expect a one-parameter family.
\wsol Augment and reduce:
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c}1&1&2&1&5\\1&1&2&6&10\\1&2&5&2&7\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow[R_3-R_1]{R_2-R_1}
\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c}1&1&2&1&5\\0&0&0&5&5\\0&1&3&1&2\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{R_2\leftrightarrow R_3}
\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c}1&1&2&1&5\\0&1&3&1&2\\0&0&0&5&5\end{array}\right].
\]
Scale $R_3$ by $\tfrac15$, then clear above each pivot ($R_1-R_2$, then eliminate column $4$):
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c}1&0&-1&0&3\\0&1&3&0&1\\0&0&0&1&1\end{array}\right].
\]
Pivots sit in columns $1,2,4$; column $3$ is free. Setting $x_3=c$,
\[
x_1=3+c,\quad x_2=1-3c,\quad x_4=1,\quad x_3=c\qquad(c\inQ\ arbitrary).
\]
Check. Substitute into the first equation: $(3+c)+(1-3c)+2c+1=5$ for all $c$. The last column carries no pivot, so the system is consistent; $\rank=3<4$, giving $4-3=1$ free parameter --- exactly the line of solutions found.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: An inconsistent system
Content:
\begin{wex}{An inconsistent system}
Decide whether $AX=B$ is solvable, where
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&6&0&1\\0&0&1&2\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\wrec Here $A$ is already in echelon form; consistency is decided purely by whether a pivot lands in the augmented (last) column.
\wsol Form the augmented matrix
\[
[A\mid B]=\left[\begin{array}{cccc|c}1&6&0&1&1\\0&0&1&2&3\\0&0&0&0&1\end{array}\right].
\]
The bottom row reads $0x_1+0x_2+0x_3+0x_4=1$, i.e.\ $0=1$, which no $X$ can satisfy. A pivot has appeared in the last column, so the system is inconsistent: there is no solution. Check. Replacing $B$ by $B'=(1,3,0)\trans$ removes the offending pivot; then with $x_2=s$, $x_4=t$ free, $x_1=1-6s-t$ and $x_3=3-2t$ solve it. Consistency is a property of $B$ relative to the column space of $A$, detected by the last-column pivot test.
\end{wex}

Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: method
Title: Inverting a matrix by reduction
Content:
\begin{method}{Inverting a matrix by reduction}
To compute $A^{-1}$ for an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A$, row reduce the augmented block $[\,A\mid I_n\,]$ until the left block becomes $I_n$. The right block is then $A^{-1}$. (If the left block instead develops a zero row, $A$ is not invertible.) Reason: the operations multiply by $P=E_k\cdots E_1$ with $PA=I$, so $P=A^{-1}$; the same $P$ applied to $I$ on the right yields $PI=A^{-1}$.
\end{method}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-7fa6df0a501209522543
Content:
\begin{proof}
A square echelon matrix is either $I$ (when it has $n$ pivots, one per column) or has a zero bottom row (fewer than $n$ pivots).

(a)$\Rightarrow$(b): if $E_k\cdots E_1A=I$ then $A=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}$, a product of elementary matrices since each $E_i^{-1}$ is elementary.
(b)$\Rightarrow$(c): a product of invertibles is invertible.
(c)$\Rightarrow$(a): if $A$ is invertible so is its echelon form $A'=PA$; an invertible matrix has no zero row, so by the dichotomy $A'=I$.
(c)$\Rightarrow$(d): $X=A^{-1} B$ is a solution, and if $AX=AX'$ then $X=X'$ after multiplying by $A^{-1}$.
(d)$\Rightarrow$(e): the case $B=0$ has the solution $X=0$, which is then the unique one.
(e)$\Rightarrow$(c): if $AX=0$ forces $X=0$ there are no free columns, so the echelon form has $n$ pivots and equals $I$, putting us back at (a)$\Rightarrow$(c).
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: One-sided inverses suffice
Content:
\begin{remark}[One-sided inverses suffice]
A useful consequence: if a square $A$ has a right inverse $B$ (so $AB=I$) it is invertible with $A^{-1}=B$. Indeed reducing $A$ gives $A'=PA$ in echelon form, whence $A'B=PAB=P$; since $P$ is invertible its bottom row is nonzero, so $A'$ has no zero row and thus $A'=I$, making $P$ a left inverse of $A$. Now $A$ has both a left and a right inverse, and these coincide ($L=L(AB)=(LA)B=B$). The symmetric argument handles a left inverse.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Computing an inverse over $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Computing an inverse over $Q$}
Invert $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\2&6\end{pmatrix}$ by reduction (Artin's Example 1.2.18).
\wrec Augment with $I_2$ and drive the left block to $I_2$; whatever the right block becomes is $A^{-1}$.
\wsol
\[
[A\mid I]=\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&5&1&0\\2&6&0&1\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{R_2-2R_1}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&5&1&0\\0&-4&-2&1\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{-\frac14 R_2}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&5&1&0\\0&1&\tfrac12&-\tfrac14\end{array}\right].
\]
Clear above the second pivot with $R_1-5R_2$:
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1&0&-\tfrac32&\tfrac54\\0&1&\tfrac12&-\tfrac14\end{array}\right],
\qquadso\qquad A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac32&\tfrac54\\[2pt]\tfrac12&-\tfrac14\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Check. The $2\times2$ formula gives $\det A=6-10=-4$ and $A^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{-4}\begin{psmallmatrix}6&-5\\-2&1\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}-3/2&5/4\\1/2&-1/4\end{psmallmatrix}$, matching. And $AA^{-1}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&5\\2&6\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}-3/2&5/4\\1/2&-1/4\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$.
\end{wex}

Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Matrices, row reduction, and linear systems
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The last-column pivot test decides consistency, not uniqueness. A system can be consistent yet have infinitely many solutions (free columns of $A'$, as in the underdetermined example), and can be inconsistent regardless of how many free columns $A'$ has. Keep the two columns of bookkeeping separate: a pivot in $B'$ kills all solutions; a free column in $A'$ multiplies the solutions. Also: over a ring that is not a field do not ``divide'' carelessly --- type (iii) scaling requires the pivot entry to be a unit, which is automatic in a field but fails for matrices over a mere ring.
\end{pitfall}

Content:
\begin{remark}[Bridge to the abstract chapter]
Theorem~ [REF:art:matrices:invtfae@c11] is the matrix incarnation of the isomorphism criterion: $A$ invertible $\iff$ the map $T=L_A$ is bijective $\iff$ $\ker T=0$ $\iff$ $\im T=F^n$, the $\dim V=n$ case of rank--nullity. The factorization $A=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}$ says $\GL_n(F)$ is generated by elementary matrices, the computational shadow of the structure of $\GL_n$ studied later. Thus the algorithm of this section and the structure theory of \S11.1--11.2 are two views of one object.
\end{remark}

Type: prose
Content:
A permutation of the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a bijection $p\colon\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,n\}$. The set of all such permutations is the symmetric group $\Sym_n$ (Artin writes $S_n$). The advantage of viewing a permutation as a map --- rather than as a reordered list --- is that two permutations compose as functions: the product $qp$ means $q\circ p$, ``first do $p$, then $q$.''

Type: definition
Title: Cycle notation
Content:
\begin{definition}[Cycle notation]
A cycle $(c_1\,c_2\,\cdots\,c_r)$ denotes the permutation that sends $c_1\mapsto c_2$, $c_2\mapsto c_3$, \dots, $c_{r-1}\mapsto c_r$, and $c_r\mapsto c_1$, fixing all unlisted indices. A $2$-cycle is a transposition. Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles; one omits $1$-cycles (fixed points), and writes the identity as $1$.
\end{definition}

Type: prose
Content:
For example, Artin's permutation $p$ with $p(1)=3,\,p(2)=5,\,p(3)=4,\,p(4)=1,\,p(5)=2$ has cycle form
\[
p=(1\,3\,4)(2\,5).
\]
Cycle notation is not unique: $(1\,3\,4)=(3\,4\,1)=(4\,1\,3)$, and disjoint cycles may be reordered, so $p=(2\,5)(1\,3\,4)$ as well.

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Because $qp=q\circ p$ is read right-to-left, composing cycles takes practice. With $q=(1\,4\,5\,2)$ and $p=(1\,3\,4)(2\,5)$ one follows each index through $p$ first, then $q$: $3\xmapsto{p}4\xmapsto{q}5$, so $qp$ sends $3\mapsto 5$; tracking all indices gives $qp=(1\,3\,5)$, while $pq=(2\,3\,4)$. Composition is not commutative.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Multiplying permutations in cycle notation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Multiplying permutations in cycle notation}
With $p=(1\,3\,4)(2\,5)$ and $q=(1\,4\,5\,2)$ in $\Sym_5$, compute $qp$ and confirm $pq\ne qp$.
\wrec Product means compose right-to-left ($qp=q\circ p$); chase each index through $p$ then through $q$.
\wsol Apply $p$ then $q$ to each index: $1\xmapsto{p}3\xmapsto{q}3$; $3\xmapsto{p}4\xmapsto{q}5$; $5\xmapsto{p}2\xmapsto{q}1$; and $2\xmapsto{p}5\xmapsto{q}2$, $4\xmapsto{p}1\xmapsto{q}4$ are fixed. So $qp=(1\,3\,5)$. Reversing the order, $pq$: $1\xmapsto{q}4\xmapsto{p}1$ fixed; $2\xmapsto{q}1\xmapsto{p}3$; $3\xmapsto{q}3\xmapsto{p}4$; $4\xmapsto{q}5\xmapsto{p}2$; so $pq=(2\,3\,4)$. Check. $qp=(1\,3\,5)$ moves $1$, but $pq=(2\,3\,4)$ fixes $1$; the two products differ, so $\Sym_5$ is non-abelian.
\end{wex}

Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > The sign of a permutation
Type: definition
Title: Permutation matrix
Content:
\begin{definition}[Permutation matrix]
The permutation matrix $P=P_p$ of $p\in\Sym_n$ is the matrix that permutes coordinates by $p$ under left multiplication. In terms of the matrix units $e_{ij}$ (a single $1$ in position $i,j$),
\[
P_p=\sum_{i=1}^n e_{p(i),\,i},
\]
so $P_p$ has a single $1$ in each row and each column. Equivalently $P_p\,x$ moves the $i$th entry of $x$ to position $p(i)$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: Permutation matrices, Artin 1.5.10
Label: art:perm_det:permmat@c11
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Permutation matrices, Artin 1.5.10] 
Let $p,q\in\Sym_n$ with matrices $P,Q$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A matrix is a permutation matrix iff it has exactly one $1$ in each row and column and $0$ elsewhere.
\item[(b)] $\det P=\pm1$.
\item[(c)] $P_{pq}=P_p P_q$, so $p\mapsto P_p$ is a group homomorphism $\Sym_n\to\GL_n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
label: art:perm_det:permmat@c11

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8528c00becf9cee7c00c
Content:
\begin{proof}
Part (a) is immediate from $P_p=\sum_i e_{p(i),i}$ and the bijectivity of $p$. For (c), using $e_{ij}e_{k\ell}=\delta_{jk}e_{i\ell}$,
\[
P_pP_q=\Bigl(\sum_i e_{p(i),i}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_j e_{q(j),j}\Bigr)=\sum_{i,j}\delta_{i,\,q(j)}\,e_{p(i),\,j}=\sum_j e_{p(q(j)),\,j}=P_{pq},
\]
the surviving terms being those with $i=q(j)$. For (b): a transposition's matrix is an elementary row-swap matrix, with determinant $-1$; since every permutation is a product of transpositions, $\det P=(-1)^{(\# swaps)}=\pm1$ by multiplicativity of $\det$ (and part (c)).
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Title: Sign
Content:
\begin{definition}[Sign]
The sign of $p$ is $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=\det P_p\in\{+1,-1\}$. A permutation is even if $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=+1$ and odd if $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=-1$.
\end{definition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > The sign of a permutation
Type: prose
Content:
By Proposition~ [REF:art:perm_det:permmat@c11] (c) and multiplicativity of the determinant, $\operatorname{sgn}$ is a homomorphism: $\operatorname{sgn}(qp)=\operatorname{sgn}(q)\operatorname{sgn}(p)$. A transposition is odd ($\operatorname{sgn}=-1$), so if $p=\tau_1\cdots\tau_k$ is any factorization into transpositions then $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=(-1)^k$; in particular the parity of $k$ is an invariant of $p$, even though $k$ itself is not. An $r$-cycle is a product of $r-1$ transpositions, $(c_1\cdots c_r)=(c_1\,c_r)\cdots(c_1\,c_3)(c_1\,c_2)$, so $\operatorname{sgn}$ of an $r$-cycle is $(-1)^{r-1}$.

The sign can also be read from inversions: an inversion of $p$ is a pair $i<j$ with $p(i)>p(j)$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=(-1)^{\#inversions}$. (Each adjacent transposition changes the inversion count by $\pm1$, matching the row-swap computation of $\det P_p$.)

Type: example
Title: Sign by three routes
Content:
\begin{wex}{Sign by three routes}
Compute $\operatorname{sgn}(p)$ for $p=(1\,3\,4)(2\,5)\in\Sym_5$ using transpositions, cycle lengths, and inversions.
\wrec $\operatorname{sgn}$ is multiplicative; an $r$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{r-1}$; or count inversions of the one-line image.
\wsol Transpositions: $(1\,3\,4)=(1\,4)(1\,3)$ (two transpositions, even) and $(2\,5)$ is one transposition (odd), so $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=(+1)(-1)=-1$. Cycle lengths: a $3$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{2}=+1$, a $2$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{1}=-1$; product $=-1$. Inversions: the one-line image is $(p(1),\dots,p(5))=(3,5,4,1,2)$; counting pairs $i<j$ with $p(i)>p(j)$ gives $7$ inversions, namely $(1,4),(1,5),(2,3),(2,4),(2,5),(3,4),(3,5)$, and $(-1)^7=-1$. Check. All three routes give $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=-1$, so $p$ is odd.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: Complete expansion, Artin 1.6.4
Label: art:perm_det:leibniz@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Complete expansion, Artin 1.6.4] 
For an $n\times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$,
\[
\det A=\sum_{p\in\Sym_n}\operatorname{sgn}(p)\,a_{1,p(1)}\,a_{2,p(2)}\cdots a_{n,p(n)}.
\]
\end{theorem}
label: art:perm_det:leibniz@c11

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > The complete (Leibniz) expansion of the determinant
Type: proof
Title: Proof sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-1c6be46207e3eb8b058e
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write the $i$th row as $A_i=\sum_{j}a_{ij}e_j$ (here $e_j$ is the $j$th standard row vector). Because $\det$ is linear in each row separately (Artin 1.4.7), expanding all $n$ rows gives
\[
\det A=\sum_{j_1,\dots,j_n}a_{1j_1}\cdots a_{nj_n}\,\det\bigl[e_{j_1};\dots;e_{j_n}\bigr],
\]
a sum over all functions $i\mapsto j_i$. A determinant of standard basis rows vanishes when two rows coincide (alternating property), so only the choices where $i\mapsto j_i=p(i)$ is a permutation survive. For such a $p$, $\det[e_{p(1)};\dots;e_{p(n)}]=\det P_p^{\trans}=\det P_p=\operatorname{sgn}(p)$. Collecting the surviving terms yields the stated formula.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: Relation to the exterior-algebra determinant of \S11.5
Content:
\begin{remark}[Relation to the exterior-algebra determinant of \S11.5]
This is the same number produced by the top exterior power. If $V=\F^n$ has basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$, then $\extp^n(V)$ is $1$-dimensional, spanned by $e_1\extp\cdots\extp e_n$. Feeding the columns $A_1,\dots,A_n$ of $A$ into the universal alternating $n$-linear map gives
\[
A_1\extp\cdots\extp A_n=(\det A)\;e_1\extp\cdots\extp e_n,
\]
which defines $\det A$ intrinsically. Reordering basis wedges with the anticommutativity $e_i\extp e_j=-e_j\extp e_i$ produces exactly the sign $\operatorname{sgn}(p)$ on the term indexed by $p$, recovering Theorem~ [REF:art:perm_det:leibniz@c11] . Thus ``alternating $n$-linear, normalized to $1$ on $I$'' (Artin's defining properties 1.4.7) and ``the coefficient on the top wedge'' are two faces of one object.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: Expansion by minors, Artin 1.6.1--1.6.2
Label: art:perm_det:laplace@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Expansion by minors, Artin 1.6.1--1.6.2] 
Let $A_{ij}$ be the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$. Then for any fixed row $i$ or any fixed column $j$,
\[
\det A=\sum_{v=1}^{n}(-1)^{i+v}a_{iv}\det A_{iv}\qquad(along row $i$),
\]
\[
\det A=\sum_{v=1}^{n}(-1)^{v+j}a_{vj}\det A_{vj}\qquad(along column $j$).
\]
The signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ form a checkerboard pattern.
\end{theorem}
label: art:perm_det:laplace@c11

Type: proof
Title: Proof sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-1cf9605c8778b384a1f5
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Group the $n!$ terms of Theorem~ [REF:art:perm_det:leibniz@c11] by the value $v=p(i)$ in the chosen row $i$. Factoring out $a_{iv}$ from each group, what remains is a signed sum over permutations of the remaining indices --- precisely $(-1)^{i+v}\det A_{iv}$, the cofactor. (The sign $(-1)^{i+v}$ records the transpositions needed to move entry $(i,v)$ into the corner before deleting its row and column.) Summing over $v$ recovers $\det A$. Applying the result to $A^{\trans}$, whose determinant equals $\det A$, gives the column version.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The $i,j$ entry of the cofactor matrix is $\operatorname{cof}(A)_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det A_{ji}$ (note the transposed indices: it is the $(j,i)$ cofactor $(-1)^{j+i}\det A_{ji}$ in the sense of the proof above). Artin uses the cofactor matrix to write the inverse: $A^{-1}=\det(A)^{-1}\operatorname{cof}(A)$ when $\det A\ne0$. For hand computation, expand along whichever row or column has the most zeros.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: A $3\times3$ determinant, two ways
Content:
\begin{wex}{A $3\times3$ determinant, two ways}
Compute $\det A$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\0&2&1\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}$ by complete expansion and by cofactors.
\wrec Both Theorem~ [REF:art:perm_det:leibniz@c11] and Theorem~ [REF:art:perm_det:laplace@c11] apply; the row with a zero ($a_{21}=0$) makes cofactor expansion along row $2$ cheapest.
\wsol Complete expansion (1.6.5):
\[
\det A=(1)(2)(2)+(1)(1)(1)+(2)(0)(0)-(1)(1)(0)-(1)(0)(2)-(2)(2)(1)=4+1+0-0-0-4=1.
\]
Cofactor along row $2$ (signs $-,+,-$):
\[
\det A=-0\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&2\end{pmatrix}+2\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&2\end{pmatrix}-1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=0+2(0)-1(-1)=1.
\]
Check. Both methods give $\det A=1$, so $A$ is invertible over $Q$ (indeed over $Z$, since $\det=\pm1$ would even give $A^{-1}\in\Mat_3(Z)$).
\end{wex}

\end{wex}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Matrices, Row Reduction, and Explicit Determinants > Cofactor (Laplace) expansion
Type: example
Title: The $3\times3$ Vandermonde determinant
Content:
\begin{wex}{The $3\times3$ Vandermonde determinant}
Show $\det V=(b-a)(c-a)(c-b)$ for $V=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&a^2\\1&b&b^2\\1&c&c^2\end{pmatrix}$, and read off when the rows are dependent.
\wrec Use cofactor expansion, or column operations followed by expansion; the answer must vanish exactly when two of $a,b,c$ coincide (two equal rows).
\wsol Subtract row $1$ from rows $2$ and $3$ (this leaves $\det$ unchanged) to get
\[
\det V=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&a&a^2\\0&b-a&b^2-a^2\\0&c-a&c^2-a^2\end{pmatrix}
=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}b-a&b^2-a^2\\c-a&c^2-a^2\end{pmatrix},
\]
expanding along column $1$. Factor $b^2-a^2=(b-a)(b+a)$ and $c^2-a^2=(c-a)(c+a)$, then pull $(b-a)$ from row $1$ and $(c-a)$ from row $2$:
\[
\det V=(b-a)(c-a)\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&b+a\\1&c+a\end{pmatrix}=(b-a)(c-a)\bigl((c+a)-(b+a)\bigr)=(b-a)(c-a)(c-b).
\]
Check. Setting $a=b$ makes the first factor $0$ and indeed rows $1,2$ of $V$ coincide; the determinant vanishes exactly when two of $a,b,c$ are equal, matching the alternating property of $\det$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Sign from the complete expansion of a single term
Content:
\begin{wex}{Sign from the complete expansion of a single term}
In a $4\times4$ matrix, the complete expansion contains the term $a_{1,2}a_{2,4}a_{3,1}a_{4,3}$. Determine its sign.
\wrec By Theorem~ [REF:art:perm_det:leibniz@c11] the coefficient is $\operatorname{sgn}(p)$ where $p$ is the permutation with $p(i)$ equal to the second index of $a_{i,\cdot}$.
\wsol The column indices give $p(1)=2,\,p(2)=4,\,p(3)=1,\,p(4)=3$, i.e.\ $p=(1\,2\,4\,3)$, a single $4$-cycle. A $4$-cycle is a product of $3$ transpositions, so $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=(-1)^{3}=-1$. (Inversion check on $(2,4,1,3)$: pairs $(2,1),(4,1),(4,3)$ are inverted, $3$ inversions, $(-1)^3=-1$.) Check. Both the cycle-length rule and the inversion count give $\operatorname{sgn}(p)=-1$, so this term appears with a minus sign in $\det A$.
\end{wex}

\begin{remark}
The complete expansion is mostly of theoretical value: with $n!$ terms it is impractical for large $n$, but it exhibits $\det A$ as a polynomial in the $n^2$ entries with coefficients $\pm1$. Hence if each $a_{ij}(t)$ is a differentiable (or polynomial, or continuous) function of a parameter $t$, so is $\det A(t)$ --- a fact used repeatedly when $A$ varies, e.g.\ in computing characteristic polynomials.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: Invariant subspace, eigenvector, eigenvalue
Content:
\begin{definition}[Invariant subspace, eigenvector, eigenvalue]
A subspace $W\subseteq V$ is $T$-invariant if $T(W)\subseteq W$; then $T$ restricts to an operator $T|_W$ on $W$. A nonzero vector $v\in V$ is an eigenvector of $T$ if
\[
T(v)=\lambda v\qquadfor some scalar \lambda\in F,
\]
and the scalar $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue attached to $v$. A nonzero column vector $X$ is an eigenvector of a square matrix $A$ when $AX=\lambda X$, i.e.\ $AX$ is a scalar multiple of $X$.
\end{definition}
latex:
\begin{definition}[Invariant subspace, eigenvector, eigenvalue]
A subspace $W\subseteq V$ is \textbf{$T$-invariant} if $T(W)\subseteq W$; then $T$ restricts to an operator $T|_W$ on $W$. A nonzero vector $v\in V$ is an \textbf{eigenvector} of $T$ if
\[
T(v)=\lambda v\qquad\text{for some scalar }\lambda\in F,
\]
and the scalar $\lambda$ is the \textbf{eigenvalue} attached to $v$. A nonzero column vector $X$ is an eigenvector of a square matrix $A$ when $AX=\lambda X$, i.e.\ $AX$ is a scalar multiple of $X$.
\end{definition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Eigenvectors and invariant subspaces
Type: prose
Content:
An eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$ is a fixed vector; one with eigenvalue $0$ is a nonzero element of the nullspace. Over $V=F^n$, a nonzero $v$ is an eigenvector exactly when $v$ and $T(v)$ are parallel. The link to invariant subspaces is immediate: the line $F v$ spanned by an eigenvector is $T$-invariant, because $T(cv)=c\lambda v\in F v$; conversely a $T$-invariant line is spanned by an eigenvector. An eigenvector is precisely a basis of a one-dimensional invariant subspace.

If $W$ is $T$-invariant and we extend a basis $(w_1,\dots,w_k)$ of $W$ to a basis $B$ of $V$, the matrix of $T$ acquires the block form
\[
[T]_B=\begin{pmatrix} A & B'\\ 0 & D\end{pmatrix},
\]
where $A$ is the $k\times k$ matrix of $T|_W$. The case $k=1$ (an eigenvector $v_1$ placed first) gives the first column $(\lambda,0,\dots,0)^{\trans}$.

\begin{proposition}[Similar matrices share eigenvalues] 
If $A'=P^{-1} A P$ for an invertible $P$, then $A$ and $A'$ have the same eigenvalues.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-a5e48e83b5eef6ef2047
Content:
\begin{proof}
Similar matrices represent the same operator $T$ in different bases, and the eigenvalues are an intrinsic feature of $T$: if $A X=\lambda X$ then $A'(P^{-1} X)=P^{-1} A P P^{-1} X=P^{-1}(AX)=\lambda(P^{-1} X)$, and $P^{-1} X\neq 0$. So every eigenvalue of $A$ is one of $A'$, and symmetrically.
\end{proof}

Title: Diagonal matrix $=$ basis of eigenvectors
Label: art:eigen:diagbasis@c11
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Diagonal matrix $=$ basis of eigenvectors] 
The matrix of $T$ in a basis $B=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ is diagonal if and only if each $v_j$ is an eigenvector. Equivalently, $A\in\Mat_n(F)$ is similar to a diagonal matrix iff $F^n$ has a basis of eigenvectors of $A$.
\end{proposition}
label: art:eigen:diagbasis@c11

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-2d5cc448f527b0d38572
Content:
\begin{proof}
If $T(v_j)=\lambda_j v_j$ for all $j$, the $j$th column of $[T]_B$ is $\lambda_j$ in row $j$ and $0$ elsewhere, so $[T]_B=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$. Conversely, if $[T]_B$ is diagonal with entries $\lambda_j$, then reading off column $j$ gives $T(v_j)=\lambda_j v_j$, so each $v_j$ is an eigenvector. The matrix statement is the same fact applied to $T=$ left multiplication by $A$, with $P=[B]$ the change-of-basis matrix.
\end{proof}

Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > The characteristic polynomial
Type: prose
Content:
To find eigenvectors one first finds eigenvalues. Rewrite $T(v)=\lambda v$ as $(\lambda I-T)(v)=0$: a nonzero $v$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$ iff $v$ lies in the kernel of $\lambda I-T$. Hence $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue iff $\lambda I-T$ is singular, iff $\det(\lambda I-A)=0$. Replacing the unknown $\lambda$ by an indeterminate $t$ turns this into a polynomial condition.

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > The characteristic polynomial
Type: proposition
Title: Basic facts
Label: art:eigen:charpoly@c11
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Basic facts] 
Let $p(t)=\det(tI-A)$ for an $n\times n$ matrix $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $p(t)$ is a monic polynomial of degree $n$, and the eigenvalues of $T$ are exactly the roots of $p(t)$ in $F$.
\item[(b)] $p(t)$ does not depend on the choice of basis; it is an invariant of $T$.
\item[(c)] $p(t)=t^n-(\tr A)\,t^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^n\det A$, where $\tr A$ is the sum of the diagonal entries.
\item[(d)] If $A$ is upper or lower triangular with diagonal entries $a_{11},\dots,a_{nn}$, then $p(t)=(t-a_{11})\cdots(t-a_{nn})$; the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
label: art:eigen:charpoly@c11

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > The characteristic polynomial
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-802ecc8574e27bc41d79
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) The complete expansion of $\det(tI-A)$ is a sum of products, one entry from each row and column; the leading term comes from the diagonal $(t-a_{11})\cdots(t-a_{nn})$, giving degree $n$ and leading coefficient $1$. The eigenvalue criterion is the singularity computation above together with $\det(\lambda I-A)=p(\lambda)$.

(b) A change of basis replaces $A$ by $A'=P^{-1} A P$, and
\[
tI-A'=tI-P^{-1} A P=P^{-1}(tI-A)P,
\]
so $\det(tI-A')=\det(P^{-1})\det(tI-A)\det(P)=\det(tI-A)$.

(c) The $t^n$ and $t^{n-1}$ terms of the expansion come only from the diagonal product $(t-a_{11})\cdots(t-a_{nn})$, whose expansion contributes $t^n-(a_{11}+\cdots+a_{nn})t^{n-1}+\cdots$; the constant term is $p(0)=\det(-A)=(-1)^n\det A$.

(d) If $A$ is triangular, so is $tI-A$, with diagonal entries $t-a_{ii}$, and the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > The characteristic polynomial
Type: corollary
Title: Existence over $C$; trace and determinant
Label: art:eigen:exist@c11
Content:
\begin{corollary}[Existence over $C$; trace and determinant] 
Let $T$ act on a finite-dimensional space $V\neq\{0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $T$ has at most $n=\dim V$ eigenvalues.
\item[(b)] If $F=C$, then $T$ has at least one eigenvalue, hence at least one eigenvector.
\item[(c)] If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the eigenvalues of a complex $n\times n$ matrix $A$ (with multiplicity), then $\det A=\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n$ and $\tr A=\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}
label: art:eigen:exist@c11

Type: proof

Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) Eigenvalues are roots of $p(t)$, which has degree $n$, hence at most $n$ roots. (b) By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra every complex polynomial of positive degree has a root, so $p(t)$ has a root $\lambda\inC$, and $\lambda I-A$ is then singular. (c) Over $C$, $p(t)=(t-\lambda_1)\cdots(t-\lambda_n)$; comparing with the form in Proposition~ [REF:art:eigen:charpoly@c11] (c), the coefficient of $t^{n-1}$ gives $\tr A=\sum\lambda_i$ and the constant term gives $(-1)^n\det A=(-1)^n\prod\lambda_i$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: A diagonalizable $2\times 2$ matrix
Content:
\begin{wex}{A diagonalizable $2\times 2$ matrix}
Diagonalize $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}3&2\\1&4\end{psmallmatrix}$ over $R$.
\wrec Two distinct eigenvalues will force a basis of eigenvectors (Proposition~ [REF:art:eigen:diagbasis@c11] ); compute $p(t)$, then solve $(\lambda I-A)X=0$.
\wsol $p(t)=t^2-(\tr A)t+\det A=t^2-7t+10=(t-5)(t-2)$, so the eigenvalues are $5$ and $2$. For $\lambda=5$: $(5I-A)=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&-2\\-1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ kills $v_1=(1,1)^{\trans}$. For $\lambda=2$: $(2I-A)=\begin{psmallmatrix}-1&-2\\-1&-2\end{psmallmatrix}$ kills $v_2=(2,-1)^{\trans}$. With $P=[\,v_1\ v_2\,]=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix}$ we get $P^{-1} A P=\begin{psmallmatrix}5&0\\0&2\end{psmallmatrix}$. Check. $A v_1=(5,5)^{\trans}=5v_1$ and $A v_2=(4,-2)^{\trans}=2v_2$; also $\tr A=7=5+2$ and $\det A=10=5\cdot 2$, matching Corollary~ [REF:art:eigen:exist@c11] (c).
\end{wex}

Title: A non-diagonalizable $2\times 2$ matrix
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-diagonalizable $2\times 2$ matrix}
Show the shear $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ is not diagonalizable over any field.
\wrec $A$ is triangular, so its eigenvalues are read off the diagonal (Proposition~ [REF:art:eigen:charpoly@c11] (d)); diagonalizability needs a full basis of eigenvectors (Proposition~ [REF:art:eigen:diagbasis@c11] ).
\wsol Here $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, so the only eigenvalue is $\lambda=1$ (a double root). The eigenvectors solve $(I-A)X=0$, i.e.\ $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}X=0$, forcing the second coordinate to vanish: the eigenspace is the single line $F\cdot(1,0)^{\trans}$, dimension $1$. There is no basis of eigenvectors, so $A$ is not similar to a diagonal matrix. Check. If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(1,1)P^{-1}$ held, then $A=I$, which is false. So a repeated eigenvalue with a deficient eigenspace genuinely blocks diagonalization.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Eigenvalues of a triangular $3\times 3$ matrix}
Read off the eigenvalues and find an eigenvector of $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&5&-1\\0&3&4\\0&0&2\end{psmallmatrix}$.
\wrec For a triangular matrix the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues, with no determinant expansion needed (Proposition~ [REF:art:eigen:charpoly@c11] (d)).
\wsol The diagonal gives $p(t)=(t-2)^2(t-3)$, so the eigenvalues are $2$ (multiplicity $2$) and $3$. Check. $A e_1=(2,0,0)^{\trans}=2e_1$, and $\tr A=2+3+2=7=2+2+3$ matches the eigenvalue sum.
\end{wex}

Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Triangular and diagonal forms
Type: theorem
Title: Triangularization over $C$
Label: art:eigen:triangular@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Triangularization over $C$] 
Let $T$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$. Then there is a basis of $V$ in which the matrix of $T$ is upper triangular. Equivalently, every complex $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is similar to an upper triangular matrix: there is $P\in\GL_n(C)$ with $P^{-1} A P$ upper triangular.
\end{theorem}
label: art:eigen:triangular@c11

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Triangular and diagonal forms
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-83965b02fdf3e7253316
Content:
\begin{proof}
Induct on $n=\dim V$, the case $n=1$ being trivial. By Corollary~ [REF:art:eigen:exist@c11] (b), $A$ has an eigenvector $v_1$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Extend to a basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$; in this basis (equivalently, after conjugating $A$ by $P=[\,v_1\ \cdots\ v_n\,]$) the matrix takes the block form
\[
A'=P^{-1} A P=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda & * \\ 0 & D\end{pmatrix},
\]
where $D$ is $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ (the first column is $(\lambda,0,\dots,0)^{\trans}$ because $A v_1=\lambda v_1$). By induction there is $Q\in\GL_{n-1}(C)$ with $Q^{-1} D Q$ upper triangular. Set $Q_1=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&Q\end{psmallmatrix}$. Then
\[
Q_1^{-1} A' Q_1=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda & * \\ 0 & Q^{-1} D Q\end{pmatrix}
\]
is upper triangular, and it equals $(PQ_1)^{-1} A (PQ_1)$. Listing the basis in reverse order yields a lower-triangular form instead.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}
The only feature of $C$ used is that the characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors. Hence the same induction proves: over any field $F$, if the characteristic polynomial of $A$ is a product of linear factors in $F$, then $A$ is similar over $F$ to an upper (or lower) triangular matrix. In the induction step one checks that the characteristic polynomial of the block $D$ is $p(t)/(t-\lambda)$, so the splitting hypothesis passes from $A$ to $D$.
\end{remark}

Title: Distinct eigenvalues give independence
Label: art:eigen:indep@c11
Content:
\begin{proposition}[Distinct eigenvalues give independence] 
Eigenvectors $v_1,\dots,v_r$ of $T$ belonging to distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$ are linearly independent.
\end{proposition}
label: art:eigen:indep@c11

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Triangular and diagonal forms
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f5947a54980c56b225f6
Content:
\begin{proof}
Induct on $r$; the case $r=1$ holds because an eigenvector is nonzero. Suppose $a_1 v_1+\cdots+a_r v_r=0$. Applying $T$ gives a second relation $a_1\lambda_1 v_1+\cdots+a_r\lambda_r v_r=0$. Multiply the first relation by $\lambda_r$ and subtract the second:
\[
a_1(\lambda_r-\lambda_1)v_1+\cdots+a_{r-1}(\lambda_r-\lambda_{r-1})v_{r-1}=0.
\]
By induction $v_1,\dots,v_{r-1}$ are independent, so each $a_i(\lambda_r-\lambda_i)=0$ for $i<r$; since the $\lambda_i$ are distinct, $\lambda_r-\lambda_i\neq 0$, forcing $a_1=\cdots=a_{r-1}=0$. The original relation collapses to $a_r v_r=0$, and $v_r\neq 0$ gives $a_r=0$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: Diagonalizability criterion
Label: art:eigen:diag@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Diagonalizability criterion] 
Let $T$ act on an $n$-dimensional space $V$ over $F$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $T$ is diagonalizable iff $V$ has a basis of eigenvectors of $T$.
\item[(b)] If the characteristic polynomial of $T$ has $n$ distinct roots in $F$, then $T$ is diagonalizable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: art:eigen:diag@c11

\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Triangular and diagonal forms
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Distinct eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary for diagonalizability: the identity $I_n$ has the single eigenvalue $1$ yet is already diagonal. The sharp statement (over a field where the characteristic polynomial splits) is that $T$ is diagonalizable iff its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct linear factors. Conversely, the shear $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ has minimal polynomial $(t-1)^2$, with a repeated factor, and is not diagonalizable.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Cayley--Hamilton
Label: art:eigen:ch@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Cayley--Hamilton] 
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: if $p(t)=\det(tI-A)$, then $p(A)=0$.
\end{theorem}
label: art:eigen:ch@c11

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Cayley--Hamilton
Type: proof
Title: Proof via triangularization
Relation: proof_of=unit-ff81ce06ee33dae2ee92
Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof via triangularization]
Work over $C$ (the general case follows because $p(A)=0$ is a system of polynomial identities in the entries of $A$, and the complex case implies it formally over any field). By Theorem~ [REF:art:eigen:triangular@c11] write $A=P U P^{-1}$ with $U$ upper triangular, diagonal entries $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$; these are the eigenvalues, and $p(t)=(t-\lambda_1)\cdots(t-\lambda_n)$. Since $p(A)=P\,p(U)\,P^{-1}$, it suffices to show $p(U)=(U-\lambda_1 I)\cdots(U-\lambda_n I)=0$.

Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be the standard basis and $W_k=\Span(e_1,\dots,e_k)$. Because $U$ is upper triangular, $U(W_k)\subseteq W_k$, and moreover $(U-\lambda_k I)$ sends $W_k$ into $W_{k-1}$ (the $k$th column of $U-\lambda_k I$ has a $0$ in position $k$, so $U e_k-\lambda_k e_k\in W_{k-1}$). Hence the product $(U-\lambda_1 I)\cdots(U-\lambda_n I)$, applied right-to-left, drives $W_n\to W_{n-1}\to\cdots\to W_0=\{0\}$. Therefore $p(U)=0$, and $p(A)=0$.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Cayley--Hamilton
Type: remark
Title: The continuity / diagonalizable-dense argument
Content:
\begin{remark}[The continuity / diagonalizable-dense argument]
Here is a second proof over $C$. Matrices with $n$ distinct eigenvalues are dense in $\Mat_n(C)$: the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial is a polynomial in the entries that is not identically zero, so its non-vanishing locus is dense. For such a diagonalizable $A$, Cayley--Hamilton is immediate --- in an eigenbasis $A$ is $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ and $p(A)=\operatorname{diag}(p(\lambda_1),\dots,p(\lambda_n))=0$ since each $\lambda_i$ is a root of $p$. The map $A\mapsto p_A(A)$ is a polynomial (hence continuous) function of the entries of $A$, and it vanishes on the dense diagonalizable set, so it vanishes everywhere.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Eigenvalues, Characteristic Polynomials, and Triangular Form > Cayley--Hamilton
Type: example
Title: Cayley--Hamilton on a $2\times 2$ matrix
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cayley--Hamilton on a $2\times 2$ matrix}
Verify $p(A)=0$ for $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}3&2\\1&4\end{psmallmatrix}$, and use it to express $A^{-1}$.
\wrec By Theorem~ [REF:art:eigen:ch@c11] , $A$ kills $p(t)=t^2-7t+10$; the constant term lets us solve for $A^{-1}$.
\wsol $A^2=\begin{psmallmatrix}11&14\\7&18\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $A^2-7A+10I=\begin{psmallmatrix}11&14\\7&18\end{psmallmatrix}-\begin{psmallmatrix}21&14\\7&28\end{psmallmatrix}+\begin{psmallmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. From $A^2-7A+10I=0$ we get $A(7I-A)=10I$, hence $A^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{10}(7I-A)=\tfrac{1}{10}\begin{psmallmatrix}4&-2\\-1&3\end{psmallmatrix}$. Check. $A\cdot\tfrac{1}{10}\begin{psmallmatrix}4&-2\\-1&3\end{psmallmatrix}=\tfrac{1}{10}\begin{psmallmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{psmallmatrix}=I$. Correct.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
Throughout this section the field of scalars is $R$, and vectors are real column vectors. The dot product of $X=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\trans$ and $Y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\trans$ in $R^n$ is
\[
(X\cdot Y)=x_1y_1+\dots+x_ny_n=X\trans Y,
\]
the matrix product of a row and a column. The length of $X$ is $\abs{X}$ with $\abs{X}^2=(X\cdot X)=X\trans X$, and $X$ is orthogonal to $Y$, written $X\perp Y$, when $(X\cdot Y)=0$. The dot product is what an orthogonal matrix is built to protect.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Orthogonal Matrices, Rotations, and the Matrix Exponential > Orthogonal matrices and rotations
Type: definition
Title: Orthogonal matrix
Content:
\begin{definition}[Orthogonal matrix]
A real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is orthogonal if $A\trans A=I$; equivalently $A$ is invertible with $A^{-1}=A\trans$. The orthogonal matrices form a subgroup $O(n)\sgr\GL_n(R)$, the orthogonal group; those with $\det=1$ form the special orthogonal group $SO(n)\norO(n)$, of index $2$.
\end{definition}

Type: lemma
Title: Columns are orthonormal
Content:
\begin{lemma}[Columns are orthonormal]
A matrix $A$ is orthogonal if and only if its columns $A_1,\dots,A_n$ form an orthonormal basis of $R^n$, i.e.\ $(A_i\cdot A_j)=\delta_{ij}$.
\end{lemma}

Content:
\begin{proof}
The $(i,j)$ entry of $A\trans A$ is $A_i\trans A_j=(A_i\cdot A_j)$. Thus $A\trans A=I$ if and only if $(A_i\cdot A_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for all $i,j$, which says exactly that the columns are mutually orthogonal unit vectors.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Orthogonal Matrices, Rotations, and the Matrix Exponential > Orthogonal matrices and rotations
Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Two consequences are immediate. First, $\det(A\trans A)=(\det A)^2=\det I=1$, so $\det A=\pm1$ for every orthogonal $A$; this is what cuts $O(n)$ into the two cosets $SO(n)$ and its complement. Second, a linear operator $T$ on $R^n$ preserves the dot product (a so-called orthogonal operator) if and only if its standard matrix $A$ is orthogonal, because
\[
(TX\cdot TY)=(AX)\trans(AY)=X\trans(A\trans A)Y,
\]
and this equals $X\trans Y=(X\cdot Y)$ for all $X,Y$ exactly when $A\trans A=I$. Preserving the dot product is the same as preserving all lengths, since $(X\cdot Y)$ is recovered from lengths by polarization.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Orthogonal Matrices, Rotations, and the Matrix Exponential > The $2\times2$ case: $SO(2)$ and $O(2)$
Type: theorem
Title: Classification of $2\times2$ orthogonal matrices
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Classification of $2\times2$ orthogonal matrices]
Let $A\inO(2)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\det A=1$, then $A=R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}c&-s\\ s&c\end{pmatrix}$ with $c=\cos\theta$, $s=\sin\theta$, for some angle $\theta$. This is counterclockwise rotation through $\theta$; these matrices are $SO(2)$.
\item If $\det A=-1$, then $A=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ s&-c\end{pmatrix}$. Such an $A$ is the reflection of the plane across the line through the origin making angle $\theta/2$ with the $x$-axis.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Vector Spaces > Orthogonal Matrices, Rotations, and the Matrix Exponential > The $2\times2$ case: $SO(2)$ and $O(2)$
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-d7fc4ba708469c252e78
Content:
\begin{proof}
The first column of $A$ is a unit vector, so it equals $(c,s)\trans=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\trans$ for some $\theta$. The second column is a unit vector orthogonal to the first, and in $R^2$ there are exactly two such: $(-s,c)\trans$ and $(s,-c)\trans$. The first choice gives $R_\theta$, with $\det R_\theta=c^2+s^2=1$; the second gives $\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ s&-c\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $-c^2-s^2=-1$. This exhausts $O(2)$ and separates the two cases by the sign of the determinant.

For the rotation, $R_\theta(1,0)\trans=(c,s)\trans$ and $R_\theta(0,1)\trans=(-s,c)\trans$ are the standard basis turned counterclockwise by $\theta$. For the reflection $S=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ s&-c\end{pmatrix}$ the characteristic polynomial is $t^2-1$, so the eigenvalues are $+1$ and $-1$ with orthogonal eigenvectors; writing a unit vector as $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\trans$ one finds $S(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\trans=(\cos(\theta-\alpha),\sin(\theta-\alpha))\trans$, which is fixed exactly when $\alpha=\theta/2$. So $S$ fixes the line at angle $\theta/2$ and negates its perpendicular: a reflection across that line.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}
The map $\theta\mapsto R_\theta$ is a homomorphism $R\toSO(2)$ with $R_\theta R_\phi=R_{\theta+\phi}$ and kernel $2\piZ$, so $SO(2)\congR/2\piZ$ is the circle group: rotations add their angles. A product of two reflections has determinant $(-1)(-1)=1$, hence is a rotation; this is the algebra behind ``two mirrors make a turn.''
\end{remark}

\begin{wex}{Reading a $2\times2$ orthogonal matrix}
Classify $A=\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\sqrt3\\ \sqrt3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&\sqrt3\\ \sqrt3&-1\end{pmatrix}$.
\wrec Check $\det$: $+1$ means a rotation $R_\theta$ (read $\theta$ off $\cos\theta,\sin\theta$); $-1$ means a reflection (fixed line at angle $\theta/2$).
\wsol For $A$, $\det A=\tfrac14(1+3)=1$, so $A=R_\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $\sin\theta=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, giving $\theta=60^\circ$: rotation by $60^\circ$. For $B$, $\det B=\tfrac14(-1-3)=-1$, a reflection; here $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $\sin\theta=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so $\theta=60^\circ$ and the mirror line sits at $\theta/2=30^\circ$ to the $x$-axis. Check: $A\trans A=I$ since the columns are orthonormal, and $B^2=I$ as every reflection squares to the identity.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Composing two reflections is a rotation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Composing two reflections is a rotation}
Let $F_0$ be reflection across the $x$-axis and $F_\beta$ be reflection across the line at angle $\beta$. Show $F_\beta F_0$ is a rotation and find its angle.
\wrec Each reflection has $\det=-1$, so the product has $\det=+1$ and lies in $SO(2)$; multiply the matrices.
\wsol With $c=\cos2\beta$, $s=\sin2\beta$ the reflection matrices are $F_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $F_\beta=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ s&-c\end{pmatrix}$. Then
\[
F_\beta F_0=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ s&-c\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c&-s\\ s&c\end{pmatrix}=R_{2\beta}.
\]
So the composite is rotation by $2\beta$, twice the angle between the mirrors. Check: $\det(F_\beta F_0)=(-1)(-1)=1$ and $\tr=2\cos2\beta=2c$, consistent with $R_{2\beta}$.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: Rotation of $R^3$
Content:
\begin{definition}[Rotation of $R^3$]
A rotation of $R^3$ about the origin is a linear operator $\rho$ that fixes a unit vector $u$ (a pole) and rotates the $2$-dimensional subspace $W=u^\perp$. The line $R u$ is the axis. With $u=e_1$ and an orthonormal basis $(e_2,e_3)$ of $W$, the matrix has the block form
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ 0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose lower-right $2\times2$ block is the planar rotation $R_\theta$. The pair $(u,\theta)$ is the spin; note $(u,\theta)$ and $(-u,-\theta)$ give the same rotation.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rotation of $\mathbb{R}^3$]
A \emph{rotation} of $\mathbb{R}^3$ about the origin is a linear operator $\rho$ that fixes a unit vector $u$ (a \emph{pole}) and rotates the $2$-dimensional subspace $W=u^\perp$. The line $\mathbb{R} u$ is the \emph{axis}. With $u=e_1$ and an orthonormal basis $(e_2,e_3)$ of $W$, the matrix has the block form
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ 0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose lower-right $2\times2$ block is the planar rotation $R_\theta$. The pair $(u,\theta)$ is the \emph{spin}; note $(u,\theta)$ and $(-u,-\theta)$ give the same rotation.
\end{definition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-67048df9db2a011ddb74
Content:
\begin{proof}
It suffices to show $\det(M-I)=0$. For $3\times3$ matrices $\det(-B)=(-1)^3\det B=-\det B$, so $\det(I-M)=-\det(M-I)$. Using $\det M=1$ and $M\trans M=I$,
\[
\det(M-I)=\det(M-I)\trans=\det M\cdot\det(M-I)\trans=\det\!\big(M(M\trans-I)\big)=\det(I-M).
\]
Hence $\det(M-I)=\det(I-M)=-\det(M-I)$, forcing $\det(M-I)=0$. So $M-I$ is singular and $1$ is an eigenvalue, with a unit eigenvector $u$: a candidate pole.
\end{proof}

Title: Euler's theorem
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Euler's theorem]
The $3\times3$ rotation matrices are exactly the orthogonal $3\times3$ matrices of determinant $1$; that is, the rotations of $R^3$ are precisely the elements of $SO(3)$.
\end{theorem}

Section: Vector Spaces > Orthogonal Matrices, Rotations, and the Matrix Exponential > Rotations of $R^3$ and Euler's theorem
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-541cddc2f54ee39b149a
Content:
\begin{proof}
$(\Rightarrow)$ If $\rho$ is a rotation with spin $(u,\theta)$, build an orthonormal basis $B$ by appending to $u$ an orthonormal basis of $W=u^\perp$. In this basis $\rho$ has the block matrix $M'$ above, which is orthogonal with $\det M'=\det R_\theta=1$. The change-of-basis matrix $P=[B]$ has orthonormal columns, so $P$ is orthogonal, and $M=PM'P^{-1}$ is therefore orthogonal with $\det M=\det M'=1$.

$(\Leftarrow)$ Conversely let $M\inSO(3)$ and let $T$ be multiplication by $M$. By the lemma there is a unit eigenvector $u$ with $Tu=u$. Let $W=u^\perp$, a $2$-dimensional space. Since $T$ is orthogonal it preserves the dot product, so it sends $W$ to $W$: for $w\in W$, $(Tw\cdot u)=(Tw\cdot Tu)=(w\cdot u)=0$. The restriction $T|_W$ is again orthogonal in dimension $2$, hence by the planar classification it is a rotation or a reflection. A reflection on $W$ has $\det=-1$, and combined with $T u=u$ would give $\det M=-1$, contradiction. So $T|_W$ is a rotation: $T$ fixes $u$ and rotates $W=u^\perp$, which is exactly a rotation of $R^3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Trace gives the angle; composites are rotations]
If $M\inSO(3)$ represents the rotation with spin $(u,\theta)$, then
\[
\tr M=1+2\cos\theta.
\]
Moreover the composition of any two rotations of $R^3$ is again a rotation about some axis.
\end{corollary}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-5b9bd3abb61e3200edd4
Content:
\begin{proof}
Choose an orthonormal basis $(u,v_2,v_3)$; in it $M$ is similar to the block matrix $M'$, whose trace is $1+\cos\theta+\cos\theta=1+2\cos\theta$. Trace is similarity-invariant, so $\tr M=1+2\cos\theta$. For the second statement, $SO(3)$ is a group, so a product of two of its elements is again in $SO(3)$, hence a rotation by Euler's theorem. (Geometrically this is not at all obvious: two spins about different axes compose to a single spin about a third.)
\end{proof}

Title: Axis and angle of a $3\times3$ rotation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Axis and angle of a $3\times3$ rotation}
Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Confirm $M\inSO(3)$, then find its axis and angle.
\wrec Verify $M\trans M=I$ and $\det M=1$; the axis is the $+1$-eigenvector, and $\theta$ comes from $\tr M=1+2\cos\theta$.
\wsol The columns are $e_2,e_3,e_1$, an orthonormal basis, so $M\trans M=I$; this is an even permutation (a $3$-cycle), so $\det M=1$ and $M\inSO(3)$. For the axis solve $Mu=u$: the system makes all coordinates equal, so $u=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)\trans$. For the angle, $\tr M=0=1+2\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$ and $\theta=120^\circ$. Check: $M$ cyclically permutes $e_1\to e_2\to e_3\to e_1$, and $M^3=I$, consistent with a $120^\circ$ turn about the main diagonal $(1,1,1)$.
\end{wex}

Title: Reconstructing a rotation matrix from spin
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reconstructing a rotation matrix from spin}
Find the matrix of the rotation about $u=e_3=(0,0,1)\trans$ through $\theta=90^\circ$, and verify the trace formula.
\wrec The axis is $e_3$, so the fixed direction is the third coordinate; put the planar rotation $R_{90^\circ}$ in the top-left $2\times2$ block acting on $e_1,e_2$.
\wsol With $\cos90^\circ=0$, $\sin90^\circ=1$,
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Indeed $Me_3=e_3$ and the upper-left block rotates the $xy$-plane by $90^\circ$. Check: $\det M=1$ and $\tr M=0+0+1=1=1+2\cos90^\circ$, since $\cos90^\circ=0$. Also $M^4=I$, as a quarter turn must satisfy.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Recovering the angle but not the axis sign
Content:
\begin{wex}{Recovering the angle but not the axis sign}
A matrix $M\inSO(3)$ has $\tr M=2$. What is its rotation angle, and why is the axis not pinned down by the trace alone?
\wrec Use $\tr M=1+2\cos\theta$ to solve for $\cos\theta$; remember the spin $(u,\theta)$ equals $(-u,-\theta)$.
\wsol $2=1+2\cos\theta$ gives $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, so $\theta=\pm60^\circ$. The trace is a similarity invariant and depends only on $\cos\theta$, so it cannot distinguish $\theta$ from $-\theta$ nor select between the two poles $\pm u$; the unsigned angle $60^\circ$ is all the trace sees. Check: rotations by $+60^\circ$ about $u$ and by $-60^\circ$ about $u$ (equivalently $+60^\circ$ about $-u$) both have trace $2$ but are inverse to each other, confirming the trace alone is blind to orientation. To fix the axis one solves $Mu=u$.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The trace gives only $\cos\theta$, hence the angle up to sign. Orthogonality alone is weaker still: $\det=-1$ orthogonal matrices (improper rotations, reflections, rotary reflections) are not rotations. Always check $\det=+1$ before invoking Euler's theorem, and find the axis by solving $(M-I)u=0$ rather than guessing from the trace.
\end{pitfall}

Type: prose
Content:
The scalar differential equation $\frac{dx}{dt}=ax$ has solutions $x(t)=ce^{at}$, and the entire theory rests on the single fact that $\frac{d}{dt}e^{at}=ae^{at}$. To solve a coupled first-order system $\frac{dX}{dt}=AX$ with $A$ a constant $n\times n$ matrix, we manufacture the same machine one dimension up: a matrix-valued function $e^{tA}$ with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}$. Building it, proving it works, and computing it are the content of this section. Throughout, $A\in\Mat_n(C)$, and derivatives of vector- or matrix-valued functions of the real variable $t$ are taken entrywise.

Type: definition
Title: Matrix exponential
Content:
\begin{definition}[Matrix exponential]
For $A\in\Mat_n(C)$ the exponential of $A$ is the matrix obtained by substituting $A$ for $x$ and $\id$ for $1$ in the Taylor series of $e^x$:
\[
e^{A}=\id+\frac{A}{1!}+\frac{A^2}{2!}+\frac{A^3}{3!}+\cdots=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k}{k!}.
\]
More usefully we exponentiate $tA$ to get the matrix-valued function
\[
e^{tA}=\id+\frac{tA}{1!}+\frac{t^2A^2}{2!}+\frac{t^3A^3}{3!}+\cdots=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.
\]
\end{definition}

Title: Convergence and derivative; Artin 5.4.4
Label: art:matexp:main@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Convergence and derivative; Artin 5.4.4] 
Let $A\in\Mat_n(C)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The series for $e^{tA}$ converges absolutely, and uniformly on every bounded set of $t$.
\item[(b)] $e^{tA}$ is a differentiable function of $t$, with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$.
\item[(c)] If $A,B\in\Mat_n(C)$ commute, $AB=BA$, then $e^{A+B}=e^{A}e^{B}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
label: art:matexp:main@c11

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-c774c312de23eac0158d
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) The $k=0$ term is the constant matrix $\id$, which does not affect convergence. For $k\ge1$ bound the $(i,j)$ entry of the degree-$k$ term: $\abs{\tfrac{t^k(A^k)_{ij}}{k!}}\le\frac{\abs{t}^k\,\lVert A^k\rVert}{k!}\le\frac{\abs{t}^k\,n^{k-1}\lVert A\rVert^k}{k!}=\frac1n\cdot\frac{(n\abs{t}\,\lVert A\rVert)^k}{k!}$. For $\abs{t}\le r$ these are dominated by the constants $m_k=\frac1n\cdot\frac{(nr\lVert A\rVert)^k}{k!}$, and $\sum_k m_k=\frac1n e^{\,nr\lVert A\rVert}<\infty$ by the ratio test. By the Weierstrass $M$-test each entry series converges absolutely and uniformly on $\abs{t}\le r$.

(b) Each entry of $e^{tA}$ is a power series in $t$ whose term-by-term derivative is again uniformly convergent (same $M$-test, shifted index), so we may differentiate term by term:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{kt^{k-1}A^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{t^{k-1}A^{k}}{(k-1)!}=A\sum_{j\ge 0}\frac{t^{j}A^{j}}{j!}=Ae^{tA},
\]
and the $A$ may be pulled out on either side since it commutes with every $A^j$, giving also $e^{tA}A$.

(c) When $AB=BA$ the binomial theorem holds: $(A+B)^k=\sum_{i+j=k}\binom{k}{i}A^iB^j$. Substituting and reindexing the absolutely convergent double sum,
\[
e^{A+B}=\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{(A+B)^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac1{k!}\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{k!}{i!\,j!}A^iB^j=\Bigl(\sum_{i\ge 0}\frac{A^i}{i!}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge 0}\frac{B^j}{j!}\Bigr)=e^{A}e^{B}.
\]
Absolute convergence is what licenses the rearrangement (Cauchy product), which needs no commutativity; $AB=BA$ is used only in the binomial expansion of $(A+B)^k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
(a) The $k=0$ term is the constant matrix $\id$, which does not affect convergence. For $k\ge1$ bound the $(i,j)$ entry of the degree-$k$ term: $\abs{\tfrac{t^k(A^k)_{ij}}{k!}}\le\frac{\abs{t}^k\,\lVert A^k\rVert}{k!}\le\frac{\abs{t}^k\,n^{k-1}\lVert A\rVert^k}{k!}=\frac1n\cdot\frac{(n\abs{t}\,\lVert A\rVert)^k}{k!}$. For $\abs{t}\le r$ these are dominated by the constants $m_k=\frac1n\cdot\frac{(nr\lVert A\rVert)^k}{k!}$, and $\sum_k m_k=\frac1n e^{\,nr\lVert A\rVert}<\infty$ by the ratio test. By the Weierstrass $M$-test each entry series converges absolutely and uniformly on $\abs{t}\le r$.

(b) Each entry of $e^{tA}$ is a power series in $t$ whose term-by-term derivative is again uniformly convergent (same $M$-test, shifted index), so we may differentiate term by term:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{kt^{k-1}A^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{t^{k-1}A^{k}}{(k-1)!}=A\sum_{j\ge 0}\frac{t^{j}A^{j}}{j!}=Ae^{tA},
\]
and the $A$ may be pulled out on either side since it commutes with every $A^j$, giving also $e^{tA}A$.

(c) When $AB=BA$ the binomial theorem holds: $(A+B)^k=\sum_{i+j=k}\binom{k}{i}A^iB^j$. Substituting and reindexing the absolutely convergent double sum,
\[
e^{A+B}=\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{(A+B)^k}{k!}=\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac1{k!}\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{k!}{i!\,j!}A^iB^j=\Bigl(\sum_{i\ge 0}\frac{A^i}{i!}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge 0}\frac{B^j}{j!}\Bigr)=e^{A}e^{B}.
\]
Absolute convergence is what licenses the rearrangement (Cauchy product), which needs no commutativity; $AB=BA$ is used only in the binomial expansion of $(A+B)^k$.
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The law $e^{A+B}=e^{A}e^{B}$ requires $AB=BA$. For $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ one has $AB\ne BA$, and indeed $e^{A}e^{B}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, whereas $e^{B}e^{A}=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{psmallmatrix}$, so the two products even disagree with each other --- neither can equal the symmetric quantity $e^{A+B}$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: theorem
Title: Fundamental matrix; Artin 5.4.9
Label: art:matexp:basis@c11
Content:
\begin{theorem}[Fundamental matrix; Artin 5.4.9] 
Let $A\in\Mat_n(C)$. The columns of $e^{tA}$ form a basis of the solution space of $\frac{dX}{dt}=AX$. Equivalently, every solution is $X(t)=e^{tA}C$ for a unique constant vector $C\inC^n$; the initial condition $X(0)=X_0$ forces $C=X_0$.
\end{theorem}
label: art:matexp:basis@c11

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-f734746d068c873b9ea9
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~ [REF:art:matexp:main@c11] (b) the matrix $e^{tA}$ satisfies $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}$, so each column solves the system; thus $X(t)=e^{tA}C$ is a solution for every constant $C$. Conversely let $X(t)$ be any solution. Differentiate $e^{-tA}X(t)$ by the product rule, using that $A$ and $e^{-tA}$ commute:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(e^{-tA}X(t)\bigr)=(-A\,e^{-tA})X(t)+e^{-tA}\bigl(AX(t)\bigr)=e^{-tA}(-A+A)X(t)=0.
\]
Hence $e^{-tA}X(t)$ is a constant vector $C$, and $X(t)=e^{tA}C$. Setting $t=0$ gives $X(0)=e^{0}C=C$, so $C$ is uniquely determined (and equals the initial value). The columns are independent because $e^{tA}$ is invertible (its determinant never vanishes).
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Computing $e^{tA}$.
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $e^{tA}$.}
The series is rarely summed directly. Instead:
\begin{itemize}
\item Diagonal: if $A=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ then $e^{tA}=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_1 t},\dots,e^{\lambda_n t})$, read straight off the series.
\item Diagonalizable: if $P^{-1}AP=D$ is diagonal, then $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$, so $e^{tA}=Pe^{tD}P^{-1}$. (Conjugation commutes with the whole series.)
\item Jordan block: if $A=\lambda\id+N$ with $N$ nilpotent ($N^k=0$), then since $\lambda\id$ and $N$ commute, $e^{tA}=e^{\lambda t}e^{tN}$ and $e^{tN}=\id+tN+\cdots+\frac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}N^{k-1}$ is a finite sum.
\item Complex eigenvalues: a pair $\lambda=r\pm si$ contributes real solutions through $e^{(r+si)t}=e^{rt}(\cos st+i\sin st)$; take real and imaginary parts.
\end{itemize}
\end{method}
