Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Field automorphisms and the group $\Aut(K/F)$
Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
Let $K/F$ be a field extension. An automorphism $\sigma$ of $K$ is said to fix $F$ (or fix $F$ pointwise) if $\sigma(a)=a$ for every $a\in F$. The collection of such automorphisms is
\[
\Aut(K/F)=\{\sigma\in\Aut(K):\sigma(a)=a\ for all a\in F\},
\]
a subgroup of $\Aut(K)$. We call $\sigma$ an $F$-automorphism of $K$.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Field automorphisms and the group $\Aut(K/F)$
Type: prose
Content:
Two structural facts make the group manageable. First, an $F$-automorphism is $F$-linear: it fixes $F$ and respects addition and scalar multiplication, so $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$ is a linear transformation of the $F$-vector space $K$. Second, every field $K$ contains a unique smallest subfield, its prime field $P$ ($\congQ$ if $\charac K=0$, $\cong\F_p$ if $\charac K=p$), and every automorphism fixes $P$ pointwise. Hence $\Aut(K)=\Aut(K/P)$: the unqualified automorphism group is automorphisms over the prime field.

Title: {an $F$-automorphism is determined by its values on generators}

\begin{lemma}[{an $F$-automorphism is determined by its values on generators}]
If $K=F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ and $\sigma,\tau\in\Aut(K/F)$ satisfy $\sigma(\alpha_i)=\tau(\alpha_i)$ for all $i$, then $\sigma=\tau$. In particular $\sigma=\id$ iff $\sigma$ fixes a generating set.
\end{lemma}

Type: example
Title: Reading an automorphism off a single generator
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading an automorphism off a single generator}
Show that any $\sigma\in\Aut(Q(\sqrt2)/Q)$ is determined by the single value $\sigma(\sqrt2)$, and list the only possible values.
\wrec By the lemma, $\sigma$ is determined by its action on the generator $\sqrt2$ of $Q(\sqrt2)$ over $Q$; the value must itself be a root of the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt2$ (next subsection).
\wsol A general element is $a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\inQ$, and $\sigma(a+b\sqrt2)=a+b\,\sigma(\sqrt2)$ because $\sigma$ fixes $Q$. So $\sigma$ is pinned down by $\sigma(\sqrt2)$. Applying $\sigma$ to $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ gives $\sigma(\sqrt2)^2=\sigma(2)=2$, so $\sigma(\sqrt2)=\pm\sqrt2$. Thus there are at most two automorphisms. Sanity check: both candidates are realizable -- $\sigma(\sqrt2)=\sqrt2$ gives the identity, and $\sigma(\sqrt2)=-\sqrt2$ gives a well-defined ring map since $Q(\sqrt2)\congQ[x]/(x^2-2)$ and $-\sqrt2$ is also a root of $x^2-2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Complex conjugation as an automorphism
Content:
\begin{wex}{Complex conjugation as an automorphism}
Verify that $\tau:C\toC$, $\tau(a+bi)=a-bi$, is an element of $\Aut(C/R)$, and find its order.
\wrec An $R$-automorphism is a bijective ring map fixing $R$; conjugation visibly fixes $R$ ($b=0$) and is its own inverse.
\wsol For $z=a+bi,\ w=c+di$: $\tau(z+w)=(a+c)-(b+d)i=\tau(z)+\tau(w)$, and $\tau(zw)=\tau((ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i)=(ac-bd)-(ad+bc)i=(a-bi)(c-di)=\tau(z)\tau(w)$. Also $\tau(1)=1$ and $\tau$ fixes every real number, so $\tau\in\Aut(C/R)$. Finally $\tau^2(a+bi)=\tau(a-bi)=a+bi$, so $\tau^2=\id$ and $\tau\neq\id$, giving $\ord{\tau}=2$. Sanity check: $[C:R]=2$, and $\Aut(C/R)=\{\id,\tau\}\congZ/(2)Z$ has order equal to the degree -- exactly what the bound below predicts for this (Galois) extension.
\end{wex}

Content:
The single most useful fact in the section is that $F$-automorphisms cannot move a root of an $F$-polynomial to a non-root. This is what makes $\Aut(K/F)$ finite and computable when $K/F$ is a finite extension: it embeds into a permutation group of finitely many roots.

Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Automorphisms permute roots
Type: proposition
Title: {$\sigma$ permutes the roots of an $F$-polynomial}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$\sigma$ permutes the roots of an $F$-polynomial}]
Let $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$ and let $p(x)\in F[x]$. If $\alpha\in K$ is a root of $p$, then $\sigma(\alpha)$ is also a root of $p$. Consequently $\sigma$ permutes the set of roots of $p$ lying in $K$, and if $p$ is irreducible over $F$ then $\sigma$ sends each root of $p$ to another root of $p$.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Write $p(x)=\sum_i c_i x^i$ with $c_i\in F$. Applying $\sigma$ to the equation $\sum_i c_i\alpha^i=0$ and using $\sigma(c_i)=c_i$ (since $c_i\in F$) and the multiplicativity/additivity of $\sigma$ gives $\sum_i c_i\,\sigma(\alpha)^i=0$, i.e.\ $p(\sigma(\alpha))=0$. So $\sigma$ maps roots to roots; being injective on the finite root set of $p$ in $K$, it permutes them.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The proposition explains the asymmetry between abstract and embedded roots. An automorphism may only send $\alpha$ to a conjugate that actually lies in $K$. If $K$ contains some but not all roots of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$, the missing roots are simply unavailable as targets, and $\Aut(K/F)$ is smaller than the degree. This is precisely the failure of normality, seen below for $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: The only roots available may be the obvious ones
Content:
\begin{wex}{The only roots available may be the obvious ones}
For $K=Q(\sqrt[4]2)$, show that an automorphism over $Q$ can send $\sqrt[4]2$ only to $\pm\sqrt[4]2$, not to the complex roots $\pm i\sqrt[4]2$.
\wrec $\sqrt[4]2$ has minimal polynomial $x^4-2$ over $Q$ (Eisenstein at $2$); by the proposition $\sigma(\sqrt[4]2)$ is a root of $x^4-2$ lying in $K$.
\wsol The four roots of $x^4-2$ are $\pm\sqrt[4]2,\ \pm i\sqrt[4]2$. But $K=Q(\sqrt[4]2)\subsetR$, so the non-real roots $\pm i\sqrt[4]2$ do not lie in $K$. Hence $\sigma(\sqrt[4]2)\in\{\sqrt[4]2,-\sqrt[4]2\}$, giving at most two automorphisms. Both occur: $\sqrt[4]2\mapsto-\sqrt[4]2$ extends $\sqrt2\mapsto\sqrt2$ (since $(-\sqrt[4]2)^2=\sqrt2$), so $\Aut(Q(\sqrt[4]2)/Q)\congZ/(2)Z$. Sanity check: $[Q(\sqrt[4]2):Q]=4$ but only $2$ automorphisms appear, so this real extension is not Galois -- two of the four conjugates escaped the field.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Automorphisms of $Q(\sqrt[4]2)/Q(\sqrt2)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Automorphisms of $Q(\sqrt[4]2)/Q(\sqrt2)$}
Determine $\Aut(Q(\sqrt[4]2)/Q(\sqrt2))$ explicitly.
\wrec Now $\sqrt2$ is fixed, so $\sigma(\sqrt[4]2)$ must be a root of the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[4]2$ over the larger base $Q(\sqrt2)$, namely $x^2-\sqrt2$.
\wsol Over $Q(\sqrt2)$ the element $\beta=\sqrt[4]2$ satisfies $\beta^2=\sqrt2$, and $x^2-\sqrt2$ is its minimal polynomial (degree $2=[Q(\sqrt[4]2):Q(\sqrt2)]$). Its roots are $\pm\sqrt[4]2$, both in $K$. So $\sigma(\sqrt[4]2)=\pm\sqrt[4]2$, giving $\Aut(Q(\sqrt[4]2)/Q(\sqrt2))=\{\id,\ \sqrt[4]2\mapsto-\sqrt[4]2\}\congZ/(2)Z$. Sanity check: $[Q(\sqrt[4]2):Q(\sqrt2)]=2$ and we found $2$ automorphisms, so this degree-$2$ step is Galois (both roots of the quadratic live in $K$).
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{definition}
Let $H\subseteq\Aut(K)$ be any subset (most often a subgroup). The fixed field of $H$ is
\[
\Fix(H)=\{\alpha\in K:\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha\ for all \sigma\in H\},
\]
a subfield of $K$. If $H=\Aut(K/F)$ then $F\subseteq\Fix(H)$, since every $\sigma\in H$ fixes $F$ by definition.
\end{definition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Fixed fields and the bound $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\le[K:F]$
Type: theorem
Title: {the degree bound and the linear independence of characters}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{the degree bound and the linear independence of characters}]
Let $K/F$ be a finite extension. Then
\[
\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\ \le\ [K:F].
\]
More generally, distinct automorphisms $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m$ of $K$ are linearly independent over $K$ as functions $K^{\times}\to K$ (Dedekind's lemma), and if $G\le\Aut(K)$ is a finite subgroup of order $m$ with $\Fix(G)=F$, then $[K:F]=m$.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Fixed fields and the bound $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\le[K:F]$
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-7646e344af50e4f1d0b9
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Dedekind's lemma: a minimal-length nontrivial $K$-linear relation $\sum_i a_i\sigma_i(x)=0$ (all $x$) is impossible -- pick $y$ with $\sigma_1(y)\neq\sigma_2(y)$, substitute $xy$, and subtract $\sigma_1(y)$ times the original to get a shorter relation, a contradiction. For the bound: if $[K:F]=n$, with $F$-basis $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n$, and there were $n+1$ distinct $F$-automorphisms $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n+1}$, the homogeneous $K$-linear system $\sum_j\sigma_j(\omega_i)x_j=0$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) of $n$ equations in $n+1$ unknowns would have a nonzero solution $x\in K^{n+1}$; by $F$-linearity $\sum_j x_j\sigma_j$ then vanishes on all of $K$, a nontrivial $K$-dependence among the $\sigma_j$, contradicting independence. The equality $[K:\Fix(G)]=\abs G$ is the quantitative converse, proved by the same independence input (Artin's theorem).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
Build automorphisms by the isomorphism-extension theorem. Type: example
Title: Counting embeddings to realize all $[K:F]$ automorphisms
Content:
\begin{wex}{Counting embeddings to realize all $[K:F]$ automorphisms}
For the splitting field $K$ of $f(x)=(x^2-2)(x^2-3)$ over $Q$, count $\Aut(K/Q)$ by extending one root choice at a time.
\wrec $f$ is separable (four distinct roots $\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt3$), so by the corollary $\abs{\Aut(K/Q)}=[K:Q]$; count by isomorphism-extension across the tower $Q\subsetQ(\sqrt2)\subsetQ(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$.
\wsol Adjoin $\sqrt2$: the irreducible $x^2-2$ has $2$ roots in $K$, so an embedding of $Q(\sqrt2)$ extends in $2$ ways ($\sqrt2\mapsto\pm\sqrt2$). Over $Q(\sqrt2)$, $\sqrt3$ still has minimal polynomial $x^2-3$ (degree $2$, $\sqrt3\notinQ(\sqrt2)$), with $2$ roots $\pm\sqrt3$ in $K$, doubling each choice. Total $2\cdot2=4$ automorphisms, and $[K:Q]=2\cdot2=4$. Sanity check: the four maps are the independent sign choices $(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\mapsto(\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt3)$; they meet the degree bound exactly, confirming separability gives equality.
\end{wex}

Title: When the bound is strict: a tell-tale gap
Content:
\begin{wex}{When the bound is strict: a tell-tale gap}
Without listing automorphisms, predict whether $\abs{\Aut(Q(\sqrt[3]2)/Q)}$ equals $[Q(\sqrt[3]2):Q]=3$.
\wrec Equality requires $K$ to contain all roots of the minimal polynomials of its generators (normality) and those polynomials to be separable; check whether all roots of $x^3-2$ lie in $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$.
\wsol The roots of $x^3-2$ are $\sqrt[3]2,\ \zeta_3\sqrt[3]2,\ \zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]2$ with $\zeta_3=e^{2\pi i/3}$ non-real. But $Q(\sqrt[3]2)\subsetR$, so two of the three roots are absent. Any $\sigma$ must send $\sqrt[3]2$ to a root in $K$, leaving only $\sigma(\sqrt[3]2)=\sqrt[3]2$, the identity. So $\abs{\Aut(Q(\sqrt[3]2)/Q)}=1<3$: the bound is strict. Sanity check: this matches the degree bound (a number $\le3$) and confirms a strict gap exactly where roots escape, anticipating the detailed count in the next subsection.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
A finite extension $K/F$ is Galois if $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=[K:F]$, equivalently (by the theorem above) if $\Fix(\Aut(K/F))=F$. When $K/F$ is Galois we write
\[
\Gal(K/F)=\Aut(K/F),
\]
the Galois group of the extension. By the corollary and its converse (proved in Section 14.2), $K/F$ is Galois precisely when $K$ is the splitting field over $F$ of some separable polynomial; equivalently $K/F$ is normal and separable.
\end{definition}

Section: Galois Theory > Basic Definitions > Galois extensions and the Galois group
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Degree $[K:F]$ many automorphisms require BOTH normality (all conjugates of each generator lie in $K$) and separability (those conjugates are distinct). Degree alone is no guarantee: $Q(\sqrt[3]2)/Q$ has degree $3$ but only the identity automorphism, since the field is real while two of the three cube roots of $2$ are complex. It fails normality: $x^3-2$ does not split in $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$. (In characteristic $p$ one can instead fail separability, e.g.\ $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$, where $x^p-t=(x-t^{1/p})^p$ has a single repeated root.)
\end{pitfall}

\wrec By the root-permutation proposition, $\sigma(\sqrt[3]2)$ is a root of $x^3-2$ in $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2)\subsetR$; the other two roots are non-real.
\wsol The roots of $x^3-2$ are $\sqrt[3]2,\ \zeta_3\sqrt[3]2,\ \zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]2$; only $\sqrt[3]2$ is real, hence the only root in $K$. So $\sigma(\sqrt[3]2)=\sqrt[3]2$, forcing $\sigma=\id$ by the generator lemma. Thus $\Aut(Q(\sqrt[3]2)/Q)=\{\id\}$, $\abs{\Aut}=1<3=[K:Q]$, and $\Fix(\{\id\})=K=Q(\sqrt[3]2)\supsetneqQ$. Sanity check: both Galois criteria fail in agreement -- the order is $1\neq3$, and the fixed field is all of $K$ rather than $Q$. The extension is separable (char $0$) but not normal.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{The splitting field $Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)/Q$ is Galois with group $S_3$}
Show the splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $Q$ is Galois of degree $6$ with $\Gal\cong S_3$.
\wrec $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)$ is the splitting field of the separable $x^3-2$, hence Galois with $\abs{\Gal}=[K:Q]$; the group acts faithfully by permuting the $3$ roots, so embeds in $S_3$.
\wsol Degree: $[Q(\sqrt[3]2):Q]=3$ and $[Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3):Q(\sqrt[3]2)]=2$ (since $\zeta_3$ satisfies $x^2+x+1$, irreducible over the real field $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$), so $[K:Q]=6$. Thus $\abs{\Gal(K/Q)}=6$. Every automorphism permutes the three roots $\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]2$, giving an injection $\Gal(K/Q)\hookrightarrow S_3$; as both have order $6$ it is an isomorphism, $\Gal(K/Q)\cong S_3$. Sanity check: $\abs{S_3}=6=[K:Q]$, and the extension is normal (all roots of $x^3-2$ are now present) and separable, so it is genuinely Galois -- contrast the non-Galois subextension $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$. Concretely $\sigma:\sqrt[3]2\mapsto\zeta_3\sqrt[3]2,\ \zeta_3\mapsto\zeta_3$ has order $3$ and $\tau:\zeta_3\mapsto\zeta_3^2$ (complex conjugation) has order $2$, with $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}=\sigma^{-1}$, the defining $S_3$ relation.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q$ is Galois with the Klein four-group
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q$ is Galois with the Klein four-group}
Determine $\Gal(Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q)$.
\wrec Splitting field of the separable $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)$, so Galois of degree $4$; automorphisms are the independent sign choices on $\sqrt2,\sqrt3$.
\wsol The four automorphisms send $(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ to $(\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt3)$; call them $\id,\ \sigma:(\!-\!\sqrt2,\sqrt3),\ \tau:(\sqrt2,-\sqrt3),\ \sigma\tau:(\!-\!\sqrt2,-\sqrt3)$. Each non-identity element has order $2$ ($\sigma^2$ sends $\sqrt2\mapsto\sqrt2$, etc.), and $\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma$, so the group is $Z/(2)Z\timesZ/(2)Z$, the Klein four-group $V_4$. Sanity check: $\abs{V_4}=4=[Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3):Q]$; the three order-$2$ subgroups fix the three quadratic subfields $Q(\sqrt3),Q(\sqrt2),Q(\sqrt6)$ respectively, and $\Fix(V_4)=Q$, confirming the Galois condition. The lattice anti-correspondence:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3) \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
Q(\sqrt2) \arrow[dr,dash] & Q(\sqrt3) \arrow[d,dash] & Q(\sqrt6) \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& Q &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& 1 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\langle \tau\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & \langle \sigma\rangle \arrow[d,dash] & \langle \sigma\tau\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& V_4 &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left lattice has five field objects: the top node $Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ is the degree-$4$ Galois extension $K$; the three middle nodes $Q(\sqrt2)$, $Q(\sqrt3)$, $Q(\sqrt6)$ are the three degree-$2$ intermediate fields; the bottom node $Q$ is the base field $F$. The right lattice has five subgroup objects: the top node $1$ is the trivial subgroup of $V_4 = \Gal(K/Q)$; the three middle nodes $\gen\tau$, $\gen\sigma$, $\langle \sigma\tau\rangle$ are the three order-$2$ subgroups; the bottom node $V_4$ is the full Galois group.
\dgi{Arrows:} Every dash in both lattices is an inclusion. In the field lattice each dash from $Q$ to a middle field is a degree-$2$ inclusion of fields; each dash from a middle field to $K$ is another degree-$2$ inclusion. In the subgroup lattice each dash from $1$ to a middle subgroup is subgroup inclusion, and each dash from a middle subgroup down to $V_4$ records the same. The horizontal $\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }$ arrow is the Galois correspondence: a subgroup $H \le V_4$ maps to its fixed field $\Fix(H) = \{\alpha \in K : \sigma(\alpha) = \alpha for all \sigma \in H\}$, and an intermediate field $E$ maps to $\Gal(K/E) \le V_4$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The diagram records an order-reversing bijection, not path-commutativity. The key equalities are $\Fix(1) = K$, $\Fix(V_4) = Q$, $\Fix(\gen\sigma) = Q(\sqrt3)$, $\Fix(\gen\tau) = Q(\sqrt2)$, $\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle) = Q(\sqrt6)$. Containment reverses: $\gen\sigma \le V_4$ on the right corresponds to $Q \subseteq Q(\sqrt3)$ on the left, so a larger subgroup fixes a smaller field.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase $\gen\sigma$ explicitly. Since $\sigma$ sends $\sqrt2 \mapsto -\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3 \mapsto \sqrt3$, a general element $a + b\sqrt2 + c\sqrt3 + d\sqrt6 \in K$ is fixed by $\sigma$ iff $b = 0$ and $d = 0$, leaving $a + c\sqrt3 \in Q(\sqrt3)$. So $\Fix(\gen\sigma) = Q(\sqrt3)$. Similarly $\tau(\sqrt3 \mapsto -\sqrt3,\ \sqrt2 \mapsto \sqrt2)$ fixes only $Q(\sqrt2)$, and $\sigma\tau(\sqrt6 = \sqrt2\cdot\sqrt3 \mapsto (-\sqrt2)(-\sqrt3) = \sqrt6)$ fixes only $Q(\sqrt6)$. These are genuine fixed-field computations, not just index counting.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The worked example has just established $\Gal(Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q) \cong V_4$ and verified the Galois condition $\abs{\Gal} = [K:F] = 4$. The diagram is an explicit preview of the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory (Section 14.2): it shows the promised anti-isomorphism between the lattice of intermediate fields and the lattice of subgroups, making abstract theory concrete and checkable for this small but complete example.
\dgi{Concrete example:} The index $[\gen\sigma : 1] = 2$ in the right lattice corresponds to the degree $[K : Q(\sqrt3)] = 2$ in the left lattice. The subgroup $\gen\sigma$ has index $2$ in $V_4$, so its fixed field $Q(\sqrt3)$ has degree $2$ over $Q$, exactly matching. Every index-to-degree correspondence in the diagram works out this cleanly, which is characteristic of a Galois extension where the theorem applies with full strength.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the lattices as going in the same direction and conclude that $Q$ (at the bottom left) corresponds to $1$ (at the top right). The anti-isomorphism goes the other way: $Q$ at the bottom of the field lattice corresponds to $V_4$ at the bottom of the subgroup lattice (a larger subgroup fixes a smaller field). Separately, because all three intermediate subgroups have the same order $2$, you cannot identify which subgroup corresponds to which intermediate field by order alone; the explicit fixed-field calculation above is necessary.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that for a Galois extension with Galois group $V_4$, the lattice of intermediate fields and the lattice of subgroups are in perfect order-reversing bijection via the fixed-field map $\Fix$, so the two diamond-shaped lattices are mirror images of each other.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{The cyclotomic extension $Q(\zeta_5)/Q$}
Identify $\Gal(Q(\zeta_5)/Q)$ where $\zeta_5=e^{2\pi i/5}$.
\wrec $Q(\zeta_5)$ is the splitting field of the separable $x^5-1$ (roots the distinct $5$th roots of unity), hence Galois; $\zeta_5$ has minimal polynomial the cyclotomic $\Phi_5(x)=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$.
\wsol $\Phi_5$ is irreducible over $Q$ (Eisenstein at $5$ after $x\mapsto x+1$), so $[Q(\zeta_5):Q]=4$ and $\abs{\Gal}=4$. An automorphism $\sigma$ sends $\zeta_5$ to another primitive $5$th root, $\zeta_5^a$ with $a\in\{1,2,3,4\}$; the rule $\sigma_a:\zeta_5\mapsto\zeta_5^a$ gives $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\sigma_{ab\bmod5}$, so $\Gal(Q(\zeta_5)/Q)\cong(Z/(5)Z)^{\times}=(Z/5Z)^{\times}$, cyclic of order $4$. Sanity check: $(Z/(5)Z)^{\times}=\langle 2\rangle$ since $2^1,2^2,2^3,2^4=2,4,3,1\pmod5$ runs through all units, so the group is $Z/(4)Z$, and $\abs{(Z/(5)Z)^{\times}}=\varphi(5)=4=[Q(\zeta_5):Q]$, meeting the bound.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The fixed field of complex conjugation on $C$}

\wrec $\Fix(H)$ collects the elements moved by no element of $H$; for $\tau:a+bi\mapsto a-bi$ this is the equation $a+bi=a-bi$.
\wsol $\tau(a+bi)=a+bi$ iff $-bi=bi$ iff $b=0$ iff $a+bi\inR$. So $\Fix(\gen\tau)=R$. Since $\gen\tau=\{\id,\tau\}$ has order $2=[C:R]$ and fixes exactly $R$, the extension $C/R$ is Galois with $\Gal(C/R)=\{\id,\tau\}\congZ/(2)Z$. Sanity check: $[C:R]=2$ equals $\abs{\gen\tau}$, and the fixed field equals the base field $R$ -- both Galois criteria confirmed.
\end{wex}

Title: Distinguishing $Q(\sqrt2)$ from $Q(\sqrt3)$ via automorphisms
Content:
\begin{wex}{Distinguishing $Q(\sqrt2)$ from $Q(\sqrt3)$ via automorphisms}
Show $Q(\sqrt2)$ and $Q(\sqrt3)$ are not isomorphic as fields.
\wrec An isomorphism of fields preserves which elements are squares; the existence of $\sqrt2$ as a square is an isomorphism invariant.
\wsol Any field isomorphism $\varphi:Q(\sqrt2)\toQ(\sqrt3)$ fixes $Q$ (it fixes $1$, hence $Z$, hence $Q$). Then $\varphi(\sqrt2)^2=\varphi(2)=2$, so $Q(\sqrt3)$ would contain an element squaring to $2$. But elements of $Q(\sqrt3)$ are $a+b\sqrt3$ with $(a+b\sqrt3)^2=a^2+3b^2+2ab\sqrt3=2$ forcing $ab=0$ and $a^2+3b^2=2$, which has no rational solution ($a^2=2$ or $3b^2=2$, neither solvable in $Q$). So no such $\varphi$ exists. Sanity check: equivalently $2$ is a square in $Q(\sqrt2)$ but not in $Q(\sqrt3)$, an isomorphism-invariant property, so the fields differ -- consistent with their distinct (though both order-$2$) automorphism groups acting on different generators.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {isomorphism-extension counts embeddings}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{isomorphism-extension counts embeddings}]
Let $\varphi:F\to F'$ be a field isomorphism, $K/F$ finite, and $L$ a field containing $\varphi(F)=F'$. The number of embeddings $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow L$ extending $\varphi$ is at most $[K:F]$, with equality when $L$ contains a splitting field over $F'$ of the (image under $\varphi$ of the) minimal polynomials of a generating set and every such minimal polynomial is separable. Taking $F'=F$, $\varphi=\id$, and $L=K$ a splitting field recovers $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\le[K:F]$ with equality in the separable normal case.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Induct on $[K:F]$. Write $K=F(\alpha)(\dots)$ and let $m_\alpha$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$, of degree $d=[F(\alpha):F]$. An extension of $\varphi$ to $F(\alpha)$ is determined by sending $\alpha$ to a root in $L$ of $\varphi(m_\alpha)$; there are at most $d$ such roots, exactly $d$ distinct ones when $\varphi(m_\alpha)$ is separable and splits in $L$. Each choice fixes a new base isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\alpha')$, and the inductive hypothesis multiplies in the remaining $[K:F(\alpha)]$ extensions. Multiplying degree by degree up the tower gives the bound and the equality criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{wex}{Embedding count up a tower for $Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)$}
Recount $\abs{\Aut(Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)/Q)}$ purely as a product of per-step embedding counts.
\wrec Embeddings multiply along a tower: (number of roots of each minimal polynomial available in $K$) at each adjunction; separability and normality make every factor maximal.
\wsol Step $1$, adjoin $\sqrt[3]2$ with minimal polynomial $x^3-2$: in $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)$ all $3$ roots $\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]2$ are present, so $3$ extensions. Step $2$, adjoin $\zeta_3$ with minimal polynomial $x^2+x+1$ over $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$: both roots $\zeta_3,\zeta_3^2$ lie in $K$, so $2$ extensions each. Total $3\cdot2=6=[K:Q]$. Sanity check: this product equals the group order $\abs{S_3}=6$ found earlier; had a root been missing (as in $Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ alone) a factor would have dropped below the degree and the bound would be strict.
\end{wex}

Title: Finite-field cross-reference: Frobenius realizes the bound
Content:
\begin{wex}{Finite-field cross-reference: Frobenius realizes the bound}
For $K=\F_{p^n}$ over $F=\F_p$, identify the automorphism that achieves $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=[K:F]=n$, and point to where the lattice is worked out.
\wrec $\F_{p^n}/\F_p$ is the splitting field of the separable $x^{p^n}-x$, so by the corollary it is Galois of degree $n$; the group is generated by Frobenius (Section 14.3).
\wsol The map $\Frob_p:\alpha\mapsto\alpha^p$ is an $\F_p$-automorphism (it fixes $\F_p$ by Fermat: $a^p=a$), and $\langle \Frob_p\rangle=\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)\congZ/(n)Z$ has order $n=[\F_{p^n}:\F_p]$, meeting the bound. The full subfield/subgroup correspondence -- subfields $\F_{p^d}$ for $d\mid n$ matched with $\langle \Frob_p^{d}\rangle$ -- is developed in Section 14.3. Sanity check: $\Frob_p^n(\alpha)=\alpha^{p^n}=\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in\F_{p^n}$, while for $0<k<n$ the polynomial $x^{p^k}-x$ has at most $p^k<p^n$ roots, so $\Frob_p^k\neq\id$; hence $\ord{\Frob_p}=n$, and the extension is normal (a splitting field) and separable, hence genuinely Galois, exactly the equality case of the bound.
\end{wex}

Title: Strictness from inseparability in characteristic $p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Strictness from inseparability in characteristic $p$}
Show $K=\F_p(t^{1/p})$ over $F=\F_p(t)$ has degree $p$ but only the trivial automorphism group, so equality fails for the separability reason.
\wrec Here normality holds but separability fails: the minimal polynomial of $t^{1/p}$ is $x^p-t=(x-t^{1/p})^p$, a single root of multiplicity $p$.
\wsol $x^p-t$ is irreducible over $F=\F_p(t)$ (Eisenstein at the prime $t$ in $\F_p[t]$), so $[K:F]=p$. Over $K$ it factors as $(x-t^{1/p})^p$, so $t^{1/p}$ is the only root. Any $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$ must fix $t$ and send $t^{1/p}$ to a root of $x^p-t$ in $K$, i.e.\ to $t^{1/p}$ itself; hence $\sigma=\id$ and $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=1<p$. Sanity check: the bound $\abs{\Aut}\le[K:F]=p$ holds, but is strict; the failure here is inseparability ($x^p-t$ has a repeated root), complementing the normality failure of $Q(\sqrt[3]2)/Q$. Both reasons must be excluded for an extension to be Galois.
\end{wex}

 \begin{enumerate}
 \item[(a)] Show that if the field $K$ is generated over $F$ by the elements $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ then an automorphism $\sigma$ of $K$ fixing $F$ is uniquely determined by $\sigma(\alpha_1), \ldots, \sigma(\alpha_n)$. In particular show that an automorphism fixes $K$ if and only if it fixes a set of generators for $K$.
 \item[(b)] Let $G \le \Gal(K/F)$ be a subgroup of the Galois group of the extension $K/F$ and suppose $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k$ are generators for $G$. Show that the subfield $E/F$ is fixed by $G$ if and only if it is fixed by the generators $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k$.
 \end{enumerate}

 \item Let $\tau$ be the map $\tau : C \to C$ defined by $\tau(a+bi) = a - bi$ (complex conjugation). Prove that $\tau$ is an automorphism of $C$.

 \item Determine the fixed field of complex conjugation on $C$.

 \item Prove that $Q(\sqrt{2})$ and $Q(\sqrt{3})$ are not isomorphic.

 \item Determine the automorphisms of the extension $Q(\sqrt[4]{2})/Q(\sqrt{2})$ explicitly.

 \item Let $k$ be a field.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item[(a)] Show that the mapping $\varphi : k[t] \to k[t]$ defined by $\varphi(f(t)) = f(at+b)$ for fixed $a, b \in k$, $a \ne 0$ is an automorphism of $k[t]$ which is the identity on $k$.
 \item[(b)] Conversely, let $\varphi$ be an automorphism of $k[t]$ which is the identity on $k$. Prove that there exist $a, b \in k$ with $a \ne 0$ such that $\varphi(f(t)) = f(at+b)$ as in (a).
 \end{enumerate}

 \item This exercise determines $Aut(R/Q)$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item[(a)] Prove that any $\sigma \in Aut(R/Q)$ takes squares to squares and takes positive reals to positive reals. Conclude that $a < b$ implies $\sigma a < \sigma b$ for every $a, b \in R$.
 \item[(b)] Prove that $-\dfrac{1}{m} < a - b < \dfrac{1}{m}$ implies $-\dfrac{1}{m} < \sigma a - \sigma b < \dfrac{1}{m}$ for every positive integer $m$. Conclude that $\sigma$ is a continuous map on $R$.
 \item[(c)] Prove that any continuous map on $R$ which is the identity on $Q$ is the identity map, hence $Aut(R/Q) = 1$.
 \end{enumerate}

 \item Prove that the automorphisms of the rational function field $k(t)$ which fix $k$ are precisely the fractional linear transformations determined by $t \mapsto \dfrac{at+b}{ct+d}$ for $a, b, c, d \in k$, $ad - bc \ne 0$ (so $f(t) \in k(t)$ maps to $f\!\left(\dfrac{at+b}{ct+d}\right)$) (cf. Exercise 18 of Section 13.2).

 \item Determine the fixed field of the automorphism $t \mapsto t+1$ of $k(t)$.

 \item Let $K$ be an extension of the field $F$. Let $\varphi : K \to K'$ be an isomorphism of $K$ with a field $K'$ which maps $F$ to the subfield $F'$ of $K'$. Prove that the map $\sigma \mapsto \varphi \sigma \varphi^{-1}$ defines a group isomorphism $Aut(K/F) \stackrel{\sim}{\to} Aut(K'/F')$.
\end{exers}

Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt5)$. Compute $\Aut(K/Q)$ explicitly by determining the possible values of $\sigma(\sqrt5)$, exhibit the fixed field $\Fix(\Aut(K/Q))$, and decide whether $K/Q$ is Galois.
\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt[3]7)$ and $L=Q(\sqrt[3]7,\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Compute $\abs{\Aut(K/Q)}$ and $\abs{\Aut(L/Q)}$, and in each case compare with the degree $[K:Q]$, $[L:Q]$ to say which extension is Galois.
\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt5)$. Show $[K:Q]=8$, prove $K/Q$ is Galois, and describe $\Gal(K/Q)$ as an abstract group by giving its action on the three generators.
\item For each of the following automorphisms of the rational function field $Q(t)$, verify it lies in $\Aut(Q(t)/Q)$ and compute its order: (a) $\sigma:t\mapsto -t$; (b) $\tau:t\mapsto 1-t$; (c) $\rho:t\mapsto 1/t$.
\item Let $\zeta_7=e^{2\pi i/7}$ and $K=Q(\zeta_7)$. Show $K/Q$ is Galois of degree $6$, prove $\Gal(K/Q)\cong(Z/(7)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic, and exhibit a generator $\sigma_a:\zeta_7\mapsto\zeta_7^a$ by finding a primitive root $a$ modulo $7$.
\item Let $G=\{\id,\sigma\}$ where $\sigma\in\Aut(Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q)$ is the map $\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2,\ \sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3$. Compute $\Fix(G)$ directly from the action on a $Q$-basis of $Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$, and verify $[Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3):\Fix(G)]=\abs{G}$.
\item Let $K/F$ be a finite extension and let $\alpha\in K$ have minimal polynomial $m_{\alpha,F}(x)$ of degree $d$. Suppose $K$ contains exactly $r$ of the $d$ roots of $m_{\alpha,F}$. Prove that $\abs{\{\sigma(\alpha):\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)\}}\le r$, and exhibit an explicit $\alpha$ and $K$ for which this bound is strict (fewer images than available roots).
\item Let $F=Z/(p)Z(t)$ be the rational function field over $Z/(p)Z$ and $K=Z/(p)Z(t^{1/p})$. Show $[K:F]=p$ but $\Aut(K/F)=\{\id\}$, and explain in one sentence which of the two Galois conditions (normality or separability) fails here.
\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $K/F$ be a finite extension and $G=\Aut(K/F)$. Prove that $F\subseteq\Fix(G)$ always holds, and that $K/F$ is Galois if and only if $\Fix(G)=F$. Then give an explicit non-Galois extension $K/Q$ for which $\Fix(\Aut(K/Q))$ is strictly larger than $Q$, and identify that fixed field.
\item Let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m$ be distinct automorphisms of a field $K$. Use Dedekind's lemma (linear independence of characters) to prove that no nontrivial relation $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\,\sigma_i(x)=0$ (for all $x\in K^{\times}$) with $a_i\in K$ can hold. Then deduce the bound $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\le[K:F]$ for $K/F$ finite, sketching how independence forces it.
\item Let $\alpha=\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}$. Show $[Q(\alpha):Q]=4$, that $Q(\alpha)/Q$ is Galois, and that $\Gal(Q(\alpha)/Q)\congZ/(4)Z$ is cyclic (not $V_4$); produce a generator by computing its action on $\alpha$. (Hint: relate $\alpha^2-2$ to $\sqrt2$ and find the conjugate $\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}$ inside $Q(\alpha)$.)
\item Let $K$ be the splitting field of $f(x)=x^4-2$ over $Q$. Show $[K:Q]=8$, prove $K/Q$ is Galois, and prove $\Gal(K/Q)\cong D_8$ (the dihedral group of order $8$) by exhibiting an order-$4$ element and an order-$2$ element with the dihedral relation.
\item Let $K/F$ be finite and let $H\le\Aut(K/F)$ be a finite subgroup. Prove Artin's equality $[K:\Fix(H)]=\abs{H}$ in the special case $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$, $H=\langle \sigma\rangle$ for the order-$2$ map $\sigma:(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\mapsto(-\sqrt2,-\sqrt3)$, by computing $\Fix(H)$ and its degree explicitly, and confirm $\Fix(H)=Q(\sqrt6)$.
\end{exers}

Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ with $\Gal(K/Q)=V_4=\{\id,\sigma,\tau,\sigma\tau\}$ where $\sigma:(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\mapsto(-\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ and $\tau:(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\mapsto(\sqrt2,-\sqrt3)$. Complete the subfield lattice on the left and the subgroup lattice on the right, and prove the two are matched by $\Fix$ (each intermediate field is the fixed field of the indicated subgroup):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& K \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
Q(\sqrt2) \arrow[dr,dash] & {?} \arrow[d,dash] & Q(\sqrt6) \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& Q &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& 1 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\langle \tau\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & {?} \arrow[d,dash] & \langle \sigma\tau\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& V_4 &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Fill in both ``$?$'' nodes, and for each of the three middle fields verify directly that it equals $\Fix$ of the subgroup placed opposite it.
\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)$ be the splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $Q$, with $\Gal(K/Q)\cong S_3$. Draw the full lattice of subgroups of $S_3$ and, opposite it, the lattice of intermediate fields between $Q$ and $K$; complete the skeleton below and prove that the order-$3$ subgroup corresponds to $Q(\zeta_3)$ while the three order-$2$ subgroups correspond to the three fields $Q(\sqrt[3]2),\ Q(\zeta_3\sqrt[3]2),\ Q(\zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]2)$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.2em]
& &[-1em] K \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] &[-1em] & \\
Q(\sqrt[3]2) \arrow[drr,dash] & Q(\zeta_3\sqrt[3]2) \arrow[dr,dash] &[-1em] &[-1em] {?} \arrow[dl,dash] & Q(\zeta_3) \arrow[dll,dash] \\
& &[-1em] Q &[-1em] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State, for each intermediate field, whether it is Galois over $Q$, and prove your claim using normality of the corresponding subgroup in $S_3$.
\item Let $\varphi:K\to K'$ be a field isomorphism carrying the subfield $F\subseteq K$ onto $F'\subseteq K'$. Prove that conjugation $\sigma\mapsto\varphi\,\sigma\,\varphi^{-1}$ is a group isomorphism $\Aut(K/F)\cong\Aut(K'/F')$ by showing the square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
K \arrow[r,"\sigma"] \arrow[d,"\varphi"'] & K \arrow[d,"\varphi"] \\
K' \arrow[r,"\varphi\sigma\varphi^{-1}"'] & K'
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes for every $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$. Verify that $\varphi\sigma\varphi^{-1}$ does fix $F'$ pointwise, and that the assignment respects composition.
\item Let $K/F$ be finite with $G=\Aut(K/F)$, and let $E=\Fix(G)$. Construct the diagram of inclusions
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
F \arrow[r,hook,"\iota"] & E \arrow[r,hook,"j"] & K
\end{tikzcd}
\]
and prove that $K/E$ is Galois with $\Gal(K/E)=G$, while $E/F$ carries only the trivial automorphism group ``visible from $G$.'' Conclude that $K/F$ is Galois if and only if the middle node collapses, i.e.\ $E=F$, and illustrate with $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, $F=Q$ by identifying $E$ explicitly.
\end{exers}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory > Linear independence of characters
Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
A character of a group $G$ with values in a field $L$ is a group homomorphism $\chi\colon G\to L^{\times}$. Characters $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$ are linearly independent over $L$ if no relation $a_1\chi_1+\cdots+a_n\chi_n=0$ holds with $a_i\in L$ not all zero, where equality means $\sum_i a_i\chi_i(g)=0$ for every $g\in G$.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: theorem
Title: {linear independence of characters (Dedekind--Artin)}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{linear independence of characters (Dedekind--Artin)}]
If $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$ are distinct characters of a group $G$ with values in a field $L$, then they are linearly independent over $L$. In particular, distinct field embeddings $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n\colon K\to L$ are linearly independent as $L$-valued functions on $K^{\times}$.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-60142105feebf5a8c38d
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Suppose not, and take a dependence relation $\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i\chi_i=0$ with the fewest nonzero coefficients; clearly $m\ge2$ and all $a_i\neq0$. Since $\chi_1\neq\chi_m$ there is $g_0\in G$ with $\chi_1(g_0)\neq\chi_m(g_0)$. Evaluate the relation at $g_0g$ and use $\chi_i(g_0g)=\chi_i(g_0)\chi_i(g)$ to get a second relation $\sum_i a_i\chi_i(g_0)\chi_i=0$. Subtract $\chi_m(g_0)$ times the original from this: the $\chi_m$ term cancels, leaving a shorter nontrivial relation (its $\chi_1$ coefficient $a_1(\chi_1(g_0)-\chi_m(g_0))$ is nonzero), contradicting minimality.
\end{proof}

The single most important consequence: an automorphism group cannot collapse the dimension count. If $G=\{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n\}$ is a finite set of distinct automorphisms of $K$, the linear system over $K$ that would force $K^{G}$ to have small codimension is incompatible with independence. \begin{corollary}[{nonzero trace}]
If $K/F$ is a finite Galois extension with $G=\Gal(K/F)$, then the trace map $\Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)=\sum_{\sigma\in G}\sigma(\alpha)$ is not identically zero; some $\alpha\in K$ has $\Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)\neq0$.
\end{corollary}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$\Tr_{K/F}=\sum_{\sigma\in G}\sigma$ is exactly an $F$-linear combination (all coefficients $1$) of the distinct embeddings $\sigma$. If it were the zero function, that would be a nontrivial linear dependence among distinct characters $K^{\times}\to K^{\times}$, contradicting the theorem.

Type: example
Title: Three embeddings of a number field are independent
Content:
\begin{wex}{Three embeddings of a number field are independent}
Let $K=Q(\theta)$ with $\theta=2^{1/3}$ embedded in $C$, and let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\colon K\toC$ send $\theta$ to $\theta,\ \omega\theta,\ \omega^2\theta$ ($\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$). Show no $a_i\inC$ with $\sum a_i\sigma_i=0$ exist unless all $a_i=0$.
\wrec These are three distinct embeddings of a field into $C$, so the theorem on independence of characters applies directly.
\wsol Evaluate $\sum_i a_i\sigma_i$ at $1,\theta,\theta^2$. Since each $\sigma_j$ fixes $Q$, at $1$ we get $a_1+a_2+a_3=0$. At $\theta$ we get $a_1\theta+a_2\omega\theta+a_3\omega^2\theta=0$, i.e.\ $a_1+a_2\omega+a_3\omega^2=0$. At $\theta^2$ we get $a_1+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^4=a_1+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega=0$. The coefficient matrix is the Vandermonde matrix on $1,\omega,\omega^2$, which is invertible (distinct entries), forcing $a_1=a_2=a_3=0$. Sanity check: the Vandermonde determinant is $\prod_{i<j}(\omega^{j}-\omega^{i})\neq0$ precisely because $1,\omega,\omega^2$ are distinct, which is the same nonvanishing that drives the general proof.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {Artin}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Artin}]
Let $G$ be a finite group of automorphisms of a field $K$, and let $F=K^{G}=\Fix(G)=\{\alpha\in K:\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha\ for all\ \sigma\in G\}$ be its fixed field. Then $K/F$ is a finite extension with
\[
[K:F]=\abs{G},
\]
and $K/F$ is Galois with $\Gal(K/F)=G$.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-53e43c463e32ff8d4f19
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Write $G=\{\sigma_1=\id,\dots,\sigma_n\}$, $n=\abs{G}$. First $[K:F]\le n$: if $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{n+1}\in K$ were $F$-linearly independent, the $n\times(n+1)$ system $\sum_j x_j\sigma_i(\alpha_j)=0$ has a nonzero solution $x\in K^{n+1}$; choosing one with fewest nonzero entries and averaging over $G$ produces (via independence of characters) a nontrivial $F$-relation among the $\alpha_j$, a contradiction. Conversely $[K:F]\ge n$: the $n$ distinct automorphisms $\sigma_i$ are $F$-linear maps $K\to K$, and by independence of characters they are linearly independent in the $F$-vector space $\Hom_F(K,K)$, which has dimension $[K:F]^2$ over $F$, but more sharply they restrict to distinct embeddings, forcing $[K:F]\ge n$. Hence $[K:F]=n$. Since $G\subseteq\Aut(K/F)$ and $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}\le[K:F]=n=\abs{G}$ always, we get $\Aut(K/F)=G$ of order $[K:F]$, which makes $K/F$ Galois with $\Gal(K/F)=G$.
\end{proof}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-4fe6d7c63a845201494a
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$: a normal separable extension is the splitting field of the product of the (separable) minimal polynomials of a set of generators. $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$: counting embeddings of a splitting field, separability makes every root simple so all $[K:F]$ extensions of the identity exist as automorphisms. $(3)\Rightarrow(4)$: if $F_0=\Fix(\Aut(K/F))\supseteq F$, then by Artin $[K:F_0]=\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=[K:F]$, forcing $F_0=F$. $(4)\Rightarrow(1)$: by Artin $K/F$ is Galois with $\Gal=\Aut(K/F)$, and a Galois extension is normal (the orbit of any root under the group gives all conjugates inside $K$) and separable (distinct conjugates, no repeated roots).
\end{proof}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Normality and separability are independent conditions and both are needed. $Q(2^{1/3})/Q$ is separable (characteristic $0$) but not normal -- it omits the complex roots $\omega2^{1/3},\omega^22^{1/3}$ -- so $\abs{\Aut(Q(2^{1/3})/Q)}=1<3=[Q(2^{1/3}):Q]$ and the extension is not Galois. Over $\F_p(t)$ the extension $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$ is normal (it is the splitting field of $x^p-t=(x-t^{1/p})^p$) but inseparable, again failing $(3)$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: $Q(2^{1/3})/Q$ is not Galois
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q(2^{1/3})/Q$ is not Galois}
Show $\abs{\Aut(Q(2^{1/3})/Q)}=1$ and conclude the extension is not Galois.
\wrec Use characterization (3): an automorphism must send $2^{1/3}$ to another root of its minimal polynomial $x^3-2$ lying in the field.
\wsol The minimal polynomial of $\theta=2^{1/3}$ over $Q$ is $x^3-2$, with roots $\theta,\omega\theta,\omega^2\theta$. But $Q(\theta)\subsetR$, while $\omega\theta,\omega^2\theta\notinR$, so the only root inside $Q(\theta)$ is $\theta$ itself. Any $\sigma\in\Aut(Q(\theta)/Q)$ is determined by $\sigma(\theta)$, which must be a root of $x^3-2$ in $Q(\theta)$, hence $\sigma(\theta)=\theta$ and $\sigma=\id$. So $\abs{\Aut}=1\neq3=[Q(\theta):Q]$. Sanity check: characterization (4) agrees -- $\Fix(\Aut)=\Fix(\{\id\})=Q(\theta)\neqQ$, so $K/F$ fails the fixed-field test as well.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q$ is Galois by all four tests
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q$ is Galois by all four tests}
Verify the four characterizations for $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ over $Q$.
\wrec $K$ is the splitting field of $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)$, a separable polynomial in characteristic $0$; this is characterization (2).
\wsol The polynomial $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)$ has roots $\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt3$, all distinct, and $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ contains all of them, so $K$ is its splitting field: (2) holds, hence (1) normal+separable. The four automorphisms send $\sqrt2\mapsto\pm\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3\mapsto\pm\sqrt3$ independently, so $\abs{\Aut(K/Q)}=4=[K:Q]$: (3) holds. Finally any element fixed by all four sign-changes lies in $Q$, giving $\Fix(\Aut)=Q$: (4) holds. Sanity check: $[K:Q]=[K:Q(\sqrt2)]\cdot[Q(\sqrt2):Q]=2\cdot2=4$, matching $\abs{\Aut(K/Q)}=4$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Recovering the base field as a fixed field
Content:
\begin{wex}{Recovering the base field as a fixed field}
With $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ and $\sigma\colon\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2,\sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3$, identify $\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)$.
\wrec By Artin, $[K:\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)]=\abs{\langle \sigma\rangle}=2$, so $\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)$ is a degree-$2$ subfield -- one of the quadratic subfields.
\wsol $\sigma$ fixes $\sqrt3$ and negates $\sqrt2$, so it fixes $Q(\sqrt3)$ pointwise; since $[K:Q(\sqrt3)]=2=\abs{\langle \sigma\rangle}$, Artin forces $\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)=Q(\sqrt3)$. Sanity check: $\sigma(\sqrt6)=\sigma(\sqrt2)\sigma(\sqrt3)=-\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt3=-\sqrt6$, so $\sqrt6\notin\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)$, consistent with $\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)=Q(\sqrt3)$ not containing $\sqrt6$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory > The fundamental theorem of Galois theory
Type: theorem
Title: {the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory}]
Let $K/F$ be a finite Galois extension with $G=\Gal(K/F)$. The maps
\[
H\ \longmapsto\ \Fix(H)=K^{H},\qquad E\ \longmapsto\ \Gal(K/E)
\]
are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections between the set of subgroups $H\sgr G$ and the set of intermediate fields $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item (Degrees.) If $E=\Fix(H)$ then $[K:E]=\abs{H}$ and $[E:F]=[G:H]$.
\item (Conjugacy.) For $\sigma\in G$, $\Fix(\sigma H\sigma^{-1})=\sigma(\Fix(H))$; conjugate subgroups correspond to conjugate (i.e.\ $F$-isomorphic) intermediate fields.
\item (Normality.) $E/F$ is Galois $\iff$ $H=\Gal(K/E)$ is normal in $G$, and then restriction induces an isomorphism
\[
\Gal(E/F)\ \cong\ G/H.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\item (Normality.) $E/F$ is Galois $\iff$ $H=\Gal(K/E)$ is normal in $G$, and then restriction induces an isomorphism
\[

\]

Section: Galois Theory > The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory > The fundamental theorem of Galois theory
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-445e171dcda51f891ad9
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
That the maps are inverse bijections is Artin run in both directions: for any subgroup $H$, $K/\Fix(H)$ is Galois with group exactly $H$ (so $\Gal(K/\Fix(H))=H$), and for any intermediate $E$, $K/E$ is Galois (it is a splitting field of the same separable polynomial), so $\Fix(\Gal(K/E))=E$. Inclusion reversal is immediate: a bigger group fixes fewer elements. (1) is the degree formula $[K:F]=[K:E][E:F]$ combined with $\abs{G}=[K:F]$, $\abs{H}=[K:E]$. For (2), $\tau\in\sigma H\sigma^{-1}$ fixes $\sigma(\alpha)$ iff $\sigma^{-1}\tau\sigma\in H$ fixes $\alpha$, giving $\Fix(\sigma H\sigma^{-1})=\sigma\Fix(H)$. For (3), $E=\Fix(H)$ is stable under all of $G$ (i.e.\ $\sigma(E)=E$ for all $\sigma$, equivalently $E/F$ normal) iff $\sigma H\sigma^{-1}=H$ for all $\sigma$ by (2), i.e.\ $H\nor G$; the restriction map $G\to\Gal(E/F)$ is then onto with kernel exactly $H$, so $\Gal(E/F)\cong G/H$.
\end{proof}

Type: proposition
Title: {the $V_4$ correspondence}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{the $V_4$ correspondence}]
Let $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$, $G=\Gal(K/Q)=\{\id,\sigma,\tau,\sigma\tau\}$ where
\[
\sigma\colon\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2,\ \sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3,\qquad
\tau\colon\sqrt2\mapsto\sqrt2,\ \sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3.
\]
Then $G\cong V_4$, and its three order-$2$ subgroups $\langle \tau\rangle,\langle \sigma\rangle,\langle \sigma\tau\rangle$ correspond to the three quadratic subfields $Q(\sqrt2),Q(\sqrt3),Q(\sqrt6)$ respectively. Every subgroup is normal, so every intermediate field is Galois over $Q$.
\end{proposition}

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& G \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\langle \tau\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & \langle \sigma\tau\rangle \arrow[d,dash] & \langle \sigma\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& 1 &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& Q \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
Q(\sqrt2) \arrow[dr,dash] & Q(\sqrt6) \arrow[d,dash] & Q(\sqrt3) \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& K &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left Hasse diagram: five groups -- the full Galois group $G=V_4$ (top node), the three
 order-$2$ subgroups $\langle \tau\rangle,\langle \sigma\tau\rangle,\langle \sigma\rangle$ (middle row), and the trivial group $1$
 (bottom node). Right Hasse diagram: five fields -- $Q$ (top node), the three quadratic intermediate
 fields $Q(\sqrt2),Q(\sqrt6),Q(\sqrt3)$ (middle row), and the top field $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$
 (bottom node). All edges are inclusion lines (dashes), not arrows with direction.
\dgi{Arrows:} The two Hasse diagrams are linked by the correspondence arrow $\xleftrightarrow{\Fix}$
 between them. Within each diagram, the edges record containment: on the left, $1\subset\langle \cdot\rangle\subset G$;
 on the right, $Q\subsetQ(\sqrt{d})\subset K$. The $\Fix$ arrow itself is the Galois correspondence map
 $H\mapsto K^H$, and its inverse is $E\mapsto\Gal(K/E)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is not a commutative square but a bijection of posets. The key content is the
 order-reversal: $H_1\subset H_2$ in the left diagram if and only if $\Fix(H_2)\subset\Fix(H_1)$ in the
 right. Concretely: $1\subset\langle \tau\rangle\subset G$ on the left maps to $K\supsetQ(\sqrt2)\supsetQ$ on the
 right; similarly for the other two chains.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Artin's theorem guarantees $K/\Fix(H)$ is Galois with group exactly $H$, and
 $\Fix(\Gal(K/E))=E$ for every intermediate $E$. Inclusion reversal holds because a larger group fixes
 fewer elements: if $H_1\subset H_2$ then every element fixed by $H_2$ is also fixed by $H_1$, giving
 $\Fix(H_2)\subset\Fix(H_1)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the first visual summary of the Fundamental Theorem applied to the
 $V_4$ example. It shows concretely that the three subgroups and three intermediate fields are in
 bijection via $\Fix$, and the upside-down relationship between the two lattices encodes the
 inclusion-reversing nature of the Galois correspondence.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $\langle \sigma\tau\rangle$ consists of $\id$ and the automorphism $c\colon\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2,\sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3$.
 Then $\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)=\{r\in K: c(r)=r\}$. Since $c(\sqrt6)=(-\sqrt2)(-\sqrt3)=\sqrt6$, we get
 $Q(\sqrt6)\subseteq\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)$; degree count gives equality. This matches the middle entry of
 the right diagram paired with the middle subgroup.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the Hasse diagrams as having the same orientation and are surprised
 that the bigger group $G$ at the top of the left diagram pairs with the smaller field $Q$ at the top of the
 right diagram. The lattices are mirror images vertically: ``top'' in the group lattice (big group) pairs with
 ``top'' in the field lattice (small field), because more symmetry means fewer fixed elements.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the Galois correspondence turns the subgroup lattice of $V_4$
 upside-down to produce the intermediate-field lattice of $Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/Q$, with each subgroup
 paired to its fixed field; since the field lattice is drawn inverted, each pair sits at the same height.
\end{dgx}
Note that the field diagram is drawn upside down (larger fields lower), so the two diagrams have the same shape: the top group $G$ matches the top field $Q$, the bottom group $1$ matches the bottom field $K$, and each order-$2$ subgroup in the middle row sits opposite the quadratic field it fixes.

Title: Computing $\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)=Q(\sqrt6)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Computing $\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)=Q(\sqrt6)$}
Verify that the diagonal subgroup $\langle \sigma\tau\rangle$ fixes $Q(\sqrt6)$ and nothing larger.
\wrec By Artin $[K:\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)]=\abs{\langle \sigma\tau\rangle}=2$, so the fixed field is quadratic; find an explicit fixed element.
\wsol $\sigma\tau$ sends $\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3$, hence $\sqrt6=\sqrt2\sqrt3\mapsto(-\sqrt2)(-\sqrt3)=\sqrt6$. So $Q(\sqrt6)\subseteq\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)$; both have degree $2$ over $Q$ (the latter by Artin), so they are equal. Sanity check: $\sigma\tau(\sqrt2)=-\sqrt2\neq\sqrt2$, so $\sqrt2\notin\Fix(\langle \sigma\tau\rangle)$, confirming the fixed field is $Q(\sqrt6)$ and not all of $K$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: All subfields of the splitting field of $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)(x^2-5)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{All subfields of the splitting field of $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)(x^2-5)$}
Find $\Gal(K/Q)$ and count the intermediate fields for $K=Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt5)$.
\wrec Independent square roots give $G\cong V_4\timesZ/(2)Z\cong(Z/(2)Z)^3$ by the biquadratic principle; subfields correspond to subgroups of $(Z/(2)Z)^3$.
\wsol Each generator independently sends $\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt5$ to $\pm$ themselves, so $\abs{G}=8$ and $G\cong(Z/(2)Z)^3$, with $[K:Q]=8$. The number of subgroups of $(Z/(2)Z)^3$ by order: one trivial, $7$ of order $2$ (one per nonzero vector), $7$ of order $4$ (one per $2$-dimensional subspace, equivalently per nonzero linear functional), one of order $8$, total $16$. Hence $16$ intermediate fields: $Q$ itself, $7$ quadratic fields $Q(\sqrt{d})$ for $d\in\{2,3,5,6,10,15,30\}$, $7$ biquadratic fields of degree $4$, and $K$. Sanity check: the $7$ quadratics correspond to the $7$ subgroups of index $2$ (order $4$), and the $7$ degree-$4$ fields to the $7$ subgroups of order $2$ -- the order-reversal swaps the two counts, both equal to $2^3-1=7$.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: {$\Gal(Q(2^{1/4},i)/Q)\cong D_8$}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$\Gal(Q(2^{1/4},i)/Q)\cong D_8$}]
Let $\theta=2^{1/4}$ (real positive) and $K=Q(\theta,i)$, the splitting field of $x^4-2$ over $Q$. Then $[K:Q]=8$ and $G=\Gal(K/Q)\cong D_8$, generated by
\[
\sigma\colon\theta\mapsto i\theta,\ i\mapsto i,\qquad
\tau\colon\theta\mapsto\theta,\ i\mapsto-i\ (complex conjugation),
\]
with relations $\sigma^4=\tau^2=\id$ and $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}=\sigma^{-1}$.
\end{proposition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory > Showcase II: the splitting field of $x^4-2$, group $D_8$
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-57acf7876ab7077a649d
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The four roots of $x^4-2$ are $\theta,i\theta,-\theta,-i\theta=i^k\theta$, so $K=Q(\theta,i)$. Now $[Q(\theta):Q]=4$ (Eisenstein at $2$) and $\theta\inR$ while $i\notinR$, so $[K:Q(\theta)]=2$, giving $[K:Q]=8$. The extension is Galois (splitting field of a separable polynomial), so $\abs{G}=8$. The map $\sigma$ permutes the roots cyclically and fixes $i$; computing $\sigma^2(\theta)=i^2\theta=-\theta$, $\sigma^4=\id$, so $\ord\sigma=4$. Complex conjugation $\tau$ fixes $\theta$ and inverts $i$, $\ord\tau=2$. Finally $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}(\theta)=\tau\sigma(\theta)=\tau(i\theta)=-i\theta=\sigma^3(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}(\theta)$ and both fix $i$, so $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}=\sigma^{-1}$: these are the dihedral relations, $G\cong D_8$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: $\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)=Q(\theta)$ is not Galois over $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)=Q(\theta)$ is not Galois over $Q$}
Identify the fixed field of complex conjugation $\tau$ and explain why it is not normal over $Q$.
\wrec $\tau$ fixes $\theta=2^{1/4}\inR$; by Artin $[K:\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)]=2$, so $\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)$ is a degree-$4$ field. Non-normality of $\langle \tau\rangle$ in $G$ predicts the field is not Galois over $Q$.
\wsol $\tau$ fixes $\theta$ and $Q$, so $Q(\theta)\subseteq\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)$; since $[Q(\theta):Q]=4=[G:\langle \tau\rangle]$, equality holds, $\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle)=Q(\theta)$. Now $\langle \tau\rangle$ is not normal: $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}$ sends $\theta\mapsto\sigma\tau(-i\theta)=\sigma(i\theta)=-\theta$ and $i\mapsto-i$, so $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\sigma^2\tau$ and $\sigma\langle \tau\rangle\sigma^{-1}=\langle \sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}\rangle=\langle \sigma^2\tau\rangle\neq\langle \tau\rangle$. Correspondingly $Q(\theta)$ contains only the real roots $\pm\theta$ of $x^4-2$, not the conjugates $i\theta,-i\theta$, so it is not a splitting field and not normal over $Q$. Sanity check: $\abs{\Aut(Q(\theta)/Q)}=2$ (only $\theta\mapsto\pm\theta$ stay in the real field $Q(\theta)$) while $[Q(\theta):Q]=4$, so by characterization (3) it is indeed not Galois.
\end{wex}

Title: $\Fix(\langle \sigma^2\rangle)=Q(i,\sqrt2)$ is Galois over $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Fix(\langle \sigma^2\rangle)=Q(i,\sqrt2)$ is Galois over $Q$}
Find the fixed field of the center $\langle \sigma^2\rangle$ and identify $\Gal$ of that field over $Q$.
\wrec $\langle \sigma^2\rangle$ is the center of $D_8$, hence normal; its fixed field is degree $[G:\langle \sigma^2\rangle]=4$ and Galois over $Q$ with group $G/\langle \sigma^2\rangle$.
\wsol $\sigma^2$ sends $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ and fixes $i$, so it fixes $\theta^2=\sqrt2$ and $i$; thus $Q(i,\sqrt2)\subseteq\Fix(\langle \sigma^2\rangle)$, and both are degree $4$ over $Q$, so equal. Since $\langle \sigma^2\rangle\nor G$, the field $Q(i,\sqrt2)$ is Galois over $Q$ with $\Gal\cong G/\langle \sigma^2\rangle$. As $D_8/Z(D_8)\cong V_4$, we get $\Gal(Q(i,\sqrt2)/Q)\cong V_4$. Sanity check: $Q(i,\sqrt2)$ is itself a biquadratic field $Q(\sqrt{-1},\sqrt2)$ whose group is visibly $V_4$ (independent sign changes on $i,\sqrt2$), agreeing with $D_8/Z\cong V_4$.
\end{wex}

Title: The three quadratic subfields and which subgroups give them
Content:
\begin{wex}{The three quadratic subfields and which subgroups give them}
Determine the three quadratic subfields of $K=Q(\theta,i)$ and the subgroups they correspond to.
\wrec Quadratic subfields $\leftrightarrow$ index-$2$ (order-$4$) subgroups of $G$; there are exactly three subgroups of order $4$ in $D_8$.
\wsol The order-$4$ subgroups are $\langle \sigma\rangle$ (cyclic), $\langle \sigma^2,\tau\rangle$, and $\langle \sigma^2,\sigma\tau\rangle$. Their fixed fields: $\Fix(\langle \sigma\rangle)=Q(i)$ (since $\sigma$ fixes $i$ and moves $\theta$); $\Fix(\langle \sigma^2,\tau\rangle)=Q(\sqrt2)$ (both fix $\theta^2=\sqrt2$, and $\tau$ moves $i$); $\Fix(\langle \sigma^2,\sigma\tau\rangle)=Q(\sqrt{-2})$ (one checks $\sigma\tau$ fixes $i\theta^2=i\sqrt2$, and $\sigma^2$ fixes it too, with $(i\sqrt2)^2=-2$). All three are normal, so all three quadratics are Galois over $Q$. Sanity check: the three quadratic subfields of any field containing $Q(\sqrt2,i)$ that are $Q(\sqrt d)$ must have $d\in\{2,-1,-2\}$ up to squares, and indeed $2\cdot(-1)=-2$, so $\{Q(\sqrt2),Q(i),Q(\sqrt{-2})\}$ is exactly the $V_4$ family of quadratics inside $Q(i,\sqrt2)$.
\end{wex}

Title: A non-normal reflection subgroup and its conjugate field
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-normal reflection subgroup and its conjugate field}
Show $\langle \tau\rangle$ and $\langle \sigma^2\tau\rangle$ are conjugate in $D_8$ and that their fixed fields $Q(\theta),Q(i\theta)$ are $Q$-isomorphic but distinct.
\wrec Part (2) of the Fundamental Theorem: conjugate subgroups have conjugate (hence $F$-isomorphic) fixed fields, and a non-normal subgroup gives a non-Galois, hence properly conjugated, field.
\wsol Compute $\sigma\langle \tau\rangle\sigma^{-1}=\langle \sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}\rangle$. Since $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\sigma^2\tau$ (from $\tau\sigma=\sigma^{-1}\tau$, so $\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma^{-1}$ and $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\tau\sigma^{-2}=\tau\sigma^2=\sigma^2\tau$ using $\tau\sigma^2=\sigma^{-2}\tau=\sigma^2\tau$), we get $\sigma\langle \tau\rangle\sigma^{-1}=\langle \sigma^2\tau\rangle$. Hence by (2), $\sigma(\Fix(\langle \tau\rangle))=\Fix(\langle \sigma^2\tau\rangle)$, i.e.\ $\sigma(Q(\theta))=Q(\sigma\theta)=Q(i\theta)$. The two fields $Q(\theta)$ and $Q(i\theta)$ are distinct (one is real, the other is not) but $\sigma$ is a $Q$-isomorphism between them. Sanity check: both are roots-of-$x^4-2$ adjunctions, $[Q(\theta):Q]=[Q(i\theta):Q]=4$, and neither is normal over $Q$ (each contains only one root pair of $x^4-2$), exactly as predicted for fixed fields of non-normal subgroups.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {$Q(\zeta_p)/Q$ is cyclic of order $p-1$}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$Q(\zeta_p)/Q$ is cyclic of order $p-1$}]
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $\zeta_p=e^{2\pi i/p}$ a primitive $p$-th root of unity. Then $Q(\zeta_p)/Q$ is Galois with
\[
\Gal(Q(\zeta_p)/Q)\ \cong\ (Z/(p)Z)^{\times}\ \cong\ Z/((p-1))Z,
\]
cyclic of order $p-1$. The automorphism $\sigma_a$ is given by $\sigma_a(\zeta_p)=\zeta_p^{a}$ for $a\in(Z/(p)Z)^{\times}$. For each divisor $d\mid p-1$ there is a unique intermediate field of degree $d$ over $Q$, namely $\Fix$ of the unique subgroup of index $d$.
\end{theorem}
latex:
\begin{theorem}[{$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}$ is cyclic of order $p-1$}]
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $\zeta_p=e^{2\pi i/p}$ a primitive $p$-th root of unity. Then $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with
\[
\Gal(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})\ \cong\ (\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\ \cong\ \mathbb{Z}/((p-1))\mathbb{Z},
\]
cyclic of order $p-1$. The automorphism $\sigma_a$ is given by $\sigma_a(\zeta_p)=\zeta_p^{a}$ for $a\in(\mathbb{Z}/(p)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. For each divisor $d\mid p-1$ there is a \emph{unique} intermediate field of degree $d$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, namely $\Fix$ of the unique subgroup of index $d$.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-1e8c09f1d29ebe24a951
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The minimal polynomial of $\zeta_p$ over $Q$ is the $p$-th cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_p(x)=x^{p-1}+\cdots+x+1$, irreducible (Eisenstein after $x\mapsto x+1$), so $[Q(\zeta_p):Q]=p-1$. The extension is the splitting field of $x^p-1$ (separable, since $p\neq0$ in $Q$), hence Galois. An automorphism must send $\zeta_p$ to another primitive root $\zeta_p^a$ with $a\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$, and $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\sigma_{ab}$, giving $\Gal\cong(Z/(p)Z)^{\times}$, which is cyclic of order $p-1$ because $(Z/(p)Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic for $p$ prime. Subgroups of a cyclic group are unique of each order, so intermediate fields are unique of each degree.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
The subgroup/subfield correspondence for $Q(\zeta_p)$ is an order anti-isomorphism between the (totally ordered, when $p-1$ is a prime power, otherwise a divisor lattice) subgroup lattice of $Z/((p-1))Z$ and the subfield lattice. We illustrate with $p=13$, where $p-1=12$ reproduces the divisor lattice of $12$ from the finite-fields section.

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& \langle \sigma\rangle \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\langle \sigma^{2}\rangle \arrow[d,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & \langle \sigma^{3}\rangle \arrow[d,dash] \\
\langle \sigma^{4}\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & & \langle \sigma^{6}\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& 1 &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.4em]
& Q \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
E_2 \arrow[d,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & E_3 \arrow[d,dash] \\
E_4 \arrow[dr,dash] & & E_6 \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& Q(\zeta_{13}) &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left diagram: the subgroup lattice of $\Gal(Q(\zeta_{13})/Q)\congZ/(12)Z$, a cyclic group
 of order $12$. Nodes are the six subgroups of $Z/(12)Z$: the full group $\langle \sigma\rangle$ (order $12$, top),
 then $\langle \sigma^2\rangle$ (order $6$), $\langle \sigma^3\rangle$ (order $4$), $\langle \sigma^4\rangle$ (order $3$),
 $\langle \sigma^6\rangle$ (order $2$), and $1$ (order $1$, bottom). Right diagram: the corresponding subfield
 lattice of $Q(\zeta_{13})/Q$. Nodes are $Q$ (top), $E_2$ (degree $2$), $E_3$ (degree $3$), $E_4$
 (degree $4$), $E_6$ (degree $6$), and $Q(\zeta_{13})$ (degree $12$, bottom).
\dgi{Arrows:} The edges in both diagrams encode inclusion (of subgroups on the left, of fields on the
 right). The $\xleftrightarrow{\Fix}$ link between the two diagrams records the Galois correspondence
 $\langle \sigma^m\rangle\mapsto E_{12/ord(\langle \sigma^m\rangle)}$: a subgroup of order $k$ corresponds to a
 subfield of degree $12/k$ over $Q$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The order anti-isomorphism: $\langle \sigma^a\rangle\subset\langle \sigma^b\rangle$ iff
 $E_{12/ord(\langle \sigma^b\rangle)}\subset E_{12/ord(\langle \sigma^a\rangle)}$. In the displayed case,
 $\langle \sigma^4\rangle$ (order $3$) $\subset$ $\langle \sigma^2\rangle$ (order $6$) corresponds to $E_4\supset E_2$.
 Every subgroup is normal (the group is cyclic, hence abelian), so every $E_d$ is Galois over $Q$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Because $Z/(12)Z$ is cyclic, its subgroups are exactly the cyclic subgroups
 $\langle \sigma^d\rangle$ for $d\mid 12$, one of each order $12/d$, and the unique subgroup of each given order
 means there is exactly one intermediate field of each degree dividing $12$. The correspondence maps
 $\langle \sigma^d\rangle\mapsto\Fix(\langle \sigma^d\rangle)$, a subfield of degree $[Z/(12)Z:\langle \sigma^d\rangle]=d$ over $Q$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This paired diagram specializes the Fundamental Theorem to the cyclotomic
 case $p=13$, showing visually that the divisor lattice of $12$ governs both sides. The unique-subfield
 property (one per divisor of $p-1$) and the abelian/normal property (every subfield is Galois over $Q$)
 are both immediately visible from the diagram.
\dgi{Concrete example:} The subgroup $\langle \sigma^6\rangle\congZ/(2)Z$ (order $2$, generated by complex
 conjugation $\sigma_{-1}\colon\zeta_{13}\mapsto\zeta_{13}^{-1}$) corresponds to $E_6=\Fix(\langle \sigma^6\rangle)$,
 the maximal real subfield $Q(\zeta_{13}+\zeta_{13}^{-1})=Q(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{13})$, of degree $6$ over $Q$.
 This sits in row $E_6$ of the right diagram, paired with $\langle \sigma^6\rangle$ at the same level on the left.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse the degree of $E_d$ with the order of the corresponding
 subgroup. The correspondence swaps these: the subfield $E_d$ has degree $d$ over $Q$, but the
 corresponding subgroup $\langle \sigma^{d}\rangle$ has order $12/d$, not $d$. The formula is
 $[E_d:Q]=[Z/(12)Z:subgroup]=12/(subgroup order)$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the divisor lattice of $p-1=12$ simultaneously organizes
 the subgroups of the cyclic Galois group and the intermediate subfields of $Q(\zeta_{13})/Q$, with
 the correspondence reversing the order so that a larger subgroup gives a smaller fixed field.
\end{dgx}
Here $E_d=\Fix$ of the subgroup of order $12/d$ is the unique subfield with $[E_d:Q]=d$; the subgroup $\langle \sigma^{m}\rangle$ has order $12/\gcd(12,m)$. Since $\langle \sigma\rangle\congZ/(12)Z$ is abelian, every subgroup is normal, so every subfield $E_d$ is Galois over $Q$ (cyclic, in fact).

Title: The unique quadratic subfield of $Q(\zeta_p)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The unique quadratic subfield of $Q(\zeta_p)$}
Show $Q(\zeta_p)$ contains a unique quadratic subfield, and identify it as $Q(\sqrt{p^{*}})$ with $p^{*}=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$.
\wrec Cyclic group of order $p-1$ (even) has a unique subgroup of index $2$, hence a unique degree-$2$ subfield; the quadratic Gauss sum pins it down.
\wsol $\Gal\congZ/((p-1))Z$ has a unique subgroup of index $2$ (the squares in $(Z/(p)Z)^{\times}$), so by the Fundamental Theorem a unique quadratic subfield $E_2=\Fix(squares)$. The quadratic Gauss sum $g=\sum_{a=1}^{p-1}\bigl(\tfrac{a}{p}\bigr)\zeta_p^{a}$ satisfies $g^2=p^{*}=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$ and lies in $Q(\zeta_p)$, so $E_2=Q(g)=Q(\sqrt{p^{*}})$. Sanity check: for $p=5$, $p^{*}=(-1)^2\cdot5=5$, and indeed $Q(\zeta_5)\supsetQ(\sqrt5)$ (the real subfield $Q(\cos72^\circ)=Q(\tfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{4})$); for $p=3$, $p^{*}=(-1)^1\cdot3=-3$ and $Q(\zeta_3)=Q(\sqrt{-3})$, matching $\zeta_3=\tfrac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}$.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Subfields of $Q(\zeta_7)$}
List all subfields of $Q(\zeta_7)$ and their degrees over $Q$.
\wrec $\Gal(Q(\zeta_7)/Q)\congZ/(6)Z$, cyclic; subfields correspond to divisors of $6$, one per divisor.
\wsol Divisors of $6$ are $1,2,3,6$, so there are subfields of degrees $1,2,3,6$: $Q$; the unique quadratic $Q(\sqrt{-7})$ (since $7^{*}=(-1)^3\cdot7=-7$); the unique cubic $E_3=\Fix(the order-2 subgroup)$, which is the real subfield $Q(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1})=Q(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{7})$; and $Q(\zeta_7)$ itself. Sanity check: $4$ divisors of $6$ give $4$ subfields; the cubic $Q(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{7})$ is real of degree $3$ (it is $\Fix$ of complex conjugation $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{-1}$, the unique order-$2$ subgroup), and $[Q(\zeta_7):Q(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{7})]=2$ as it adjoins back the non-real $\zeta_7$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The fixed field of complex conjugation in $Q(\zeta_p)$}
Identify $\Fix(\langle c\rangle)$ where $c\colon\zeta_p\mapsto\zeta_p^{-1}$ is complex conjugation.
\wrec $c=\sigma_{-1}$ has order $2$ in the cyclic group $\Gal$; its fixed field has degree $(p-1)/2$ and is the maximal real subfield.
\wsol Complex conjugation fixes $\eta=\zeta_p+\zeta_p^{-1}=2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{p}\inR$, and $Q(\eta)$ is real of degree $(p-1)/2$ over $Q$. Since $\langle c\rangle$ has order $2$, Artin gives $[Q(\zeta_p):\Fix(\langle c\rangle)]=2$, so $[\Fix(\langle c\rangle):Q]=(p-1)/2=[Q(\eta):Q]$, forcing $\Fix(\langle c\rangle)=Q(\eta)=Q(\zeta_p)\capR$. Sanity check: $\langle c\rangle$ is normal (the group is abelian), so $Q(\eta)$ is Galois over $Q$ of degree $(p-1)/2$ with group $\Gal/\langle c\rangle\congZ/(((p-1)/2))Z$, cyclic -- the maximal totally real subfield, as expected.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Galois over an intermediate field that is not Galois over the base}
In $K=Q(\theta,i)$ with $\theta=2^{1/4}$, show $K/Q(\theta)$ is Galois even though $Q(\theta)/Q$ is not.
\wrec ``Galois'' is relative: $K/E$ is always Galois for any intermediate $E$ (it is the splitting field of the same separable polynomial over $E$), but $E/F$ is Galois only when $\Gal(K/E)\nor\Gal(K/F)$.
\wsol Over $E=Q(\theta)$, the polynomial $x^4-2=(x-\theta)(x+\theta)(x^2+\theta^2)$ has $K=E(i)$ as splitting field, separable, so $K/E$ is Galois with $\Gal(K/E)=\langle \tau\rangle$ of order $2$. But $\langle \tau\rangle$ is not normal in $D_8$, so $E/Q$ is not Galois -- consistent with $Q(\theta)$ containing only the two real roots $\pm\theta$ of $x^4-2$. Sanity check: $[K:E]=2=\abs{\langle \tau\rangle}$ confirms $K/E$ Galois by (3); and the failure of normality of $\langle \tau\rangle$ in $G$ is exactly the obstruction (3) of the Fundamental Theorem to $E/Q$ being Galois.
\end{wex}

\begin{remark}
The relativity in the last example is the most common source of confusion. Being Galois is a property of a pair of fields, never of a single field. In a tower $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$ with $K/F$ Galois, $K/E$ is automatically Galois, but $E/F$ is Galois precisely when the corresponding subgroup is normal. The Fundamental Theorem is what converts the field-theoretic question (is $E/F$ normal?) into a finite group-theoretic one (is $\Gal(K/E)\nor\Gal(K/F)$?).
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Determine the minimal polynomial over $Q$ for the element $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5}$.

\item Determine the minimal polynomial over $Q$ for the element $1+\sqrt[3]{2}+\sqrt[3]{4}$.

\item Determine the Galois group of $(x^2-2)(x^2-3)(x^2-5)$. Determine all the subfields of the splitting field of this polynomial.

\item Let $p$ be a prime. Determine the elements of the Galois group of $x^p-2$.

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^p-2$ for $p$ a prime is isomorphic to the group of matrices $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ where $a,b\inF_p$, $a\neq 0$.

\item Let $K=Q(\sqrt[8]{2},i)$ and let $F_1=Q(i)$, $F_2=Q(\sqrt{2})$, $F_3=Q(\sqrt{-2})$. Prove that $\Gal(K/F_1)\cong Z_8$, $\Gal(K/F_2)\cong D_8$, $\Gal(K/F_3)\cong Q_8$.

\item Determine all the subfields of the splitting field of $x^8-2$ which are Galois over $Q$.

In particular show that $N_{K/F}(a)=a^n$ and $Tr_{K/F}(a)=na$ for all $a\in F$.

\item With notation as in the previous problems show more generally that $\prod_\sigma(x-\sigma(\alpha))=(m_\alpha(x))^{n/d}$.

\item Use the linear independence of characters to show that for any Galois extension $K$ of $F$ there is an element $\alpha\in K$ with $Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)\neq 0$.

\item Suppose $K/F$ is a Galois extension and let $\sigma$ be an element of the Galois group.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $\alpha\in K$ is of the form $\alpha=\dfrac{\beta}{\sigma\beta}$ for some nonzero $\beta\in K$. Prove that $N_{K/F}(\alpha)=1$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $\alpha\in K$ is of the form $\alpha=\beta-\sigma\beta$ for some $\beta\in K$. Prove that $Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)=0$.
\end{enumerate}

\item (Hilbert's Theorem 90) Let $K$ be a Galois extension of $F$ with cyclic Galois group of order $n$ generated by $\sigma$. Suppose $\alpha\in K$ has $N_{K/F}(\alpha)=1$. Prove that $\alpha$ is of the form $\alpha=\dfrac{\beta}{\sigma\beta}$ for some nonzero $\beta\in K$. [By the linear independence of characters show there exists some $\theta\in K$ such that
\[
\beta=\theta+\alpha\sigma(\theta)+(\alpha\,\sigma\alpha)\sigma^2(\theta)+\cdots+(\alpha\,\sigma\alpha\cdots\sigma^{n-2}\alpha)\sigma^{n-1}(\theta)
\]
is nonzero. Compute $\dfrac{\beta}{\sigma\beta}$ using the fact that $\alpha$ has norm 1 to $F$.]

\item Prove that the rational solutions $a,b\inQ$ of Pythagoras' equation $a^2+b^2=1$ are of the form $a=\dfrac{s^2-t^2}{s^2+t^2}$ and $b=\dfrac{2st}{s^2+t^2}$ for some $s,t\inQ$ and hence show that any right triangle with integer sides has sides of lengths $((m^2-n^2)d,2mnd,(m^2+n^2)d)$ for some integers $m,n,d$. [Note that $a^2+b^2=1$ is equivalent to $N_{Q(i)/Q}(a+ib)=1$, then use Hilbert's Theorem 90 above with $\beta=s+it$.]

\item Generalize the previous problem to determine all the rational solutions of the equation $a^2+Db^2=1$ for $D\inZ$, $D>0$, $D$ not a perfect square in $Z$.

\item (Additive Hilbert's Theorem 90) Let $K$ be a Galois extension of $F$ with cyclic Galois group of order $n$ generated by $\sigma$. Suppose $\alpha\in K$ has $Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)=0$. Prove that $\alpha$ is of the form $\alpha=\beta-\sigma\beta$ for some $\beta\in K$. [Let $\theta\in K$ be an element with $Tr_{K/F}(\theta)\neq 0$ by a previous exercise, let
\[
\beta=\frac{1}{Tr_{K/F}(\theta)}[\alpha\sigma(\theta)+(\alpha+\sigma\alpha)\sigma^2(\theta)+\cdots+(\alpha+\sigma\alpha+\cdots+\sigma^{n-2}\alpha)\sigma^{n-1}(\theta)]
\]
and compute $\beta-\sigma\beta$.]

\item Let $\alpha=\sqrt{(2+\sqrt{2})(3+\sqrt{3})}$ (positive real square roots) and consider the extension $E=Q(\alpha)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $a=(2+\sqrt{2})(3+\sqrt{3})$ is not a square in $F=Q(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$. [If $a=c^2$, $c\in F$, then also $a\varphi(a)=(2+\sqrt{2})^2\cdot 6=(c\varphi c)^2$ for the automorphism $\varphi\in\Gal(F/Q)$ fixing $Q(\sqrt{2})$. Since $c\varphi c=N_{F/Q(\sqrt{2})}(c)\inQ(\sqrt{2})$ conclude that this implies $\sqrt{6}\inQ(\sqrt{2})$, a contradiction.]
\item[(b)] Conclude from (a) that $[E:Q]=8$. Prove that the roots of the minimal polynomial over $Q$ for $\alpha$ are the 8 elements $\pm\sqrt{(2\pm\sqrt{2})(3\pm\sqrt{3})}$.
\item[(c)] Let $\beta=\sqrt{(2-\sqrt{2})(3+\sqrt{3})}$. Show that $\alpha\beta=\sqrt{2}(3+\sqrt{3})\in F$ so that $\beta\in E$. Show similarly that the other roots are also elements of $E$ so that $E$ is a Galois extension of $Q$. Show that the elements of the Galois group are precisely the maps determined by mapping $\alpha$ to one of the eight elements in (b).
\item[(d)] Let $\sigma\in\Gal(E/Q)$ be the automorphism which maps $\alpha$ to $\beta$. Show that since $\sigma(\alpha^2)=\beta^2$ that $\sigma(\sqrt{2})=-\sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma(\sqrt{3})=\sqrt{3}$. From $\alpha\beta=\sqrt{2}(3+\sqrt{3})$ conclude that $\sigma(\alpha\beta)=-\alpha\beta$ and hence $\sigma(\beta)=-\alpha$. Show that $\sigma$ is an element of order 4 in $\Gal(E/Q)$.
\item[(e)] Show similarly that the map $\tau$ defined by $\tau(\alpha)=\sqrt{(2+\sqrt{2})(3-\sqrt{3})}$ is an element of order 4 in $\Gal(E/Q)$. Prove that $\sigma$ and $\tau$ generate the Galois group, $\sigma^4=\tau^4=1$, $\sigma^2=\tau^2$ and that $\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma^3$.
\item[(f)] Conclude that $\Gal(E/Q)\cong Q_8$, the quaternion group of order 8.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $f(x)\in F[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ over the field $F$, let $L$ be the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $F$ and let $\alpha$ be a root of $f(x)$ in $L$. If $K$ is any Galois extension of $F$ contained in $L$, show that the polynomial $f(x)$ splits into a product of $m$ irreducible polynomials each of degree $d$ over $K$, where $m=[F(\alpha)\cap K:F]$ and $d=[K(\alpha):K]$ (cf.\ also the generalization in Exercise 4 of Section 4). [If $H$ is the subgroup of the Galois group of $L$ over $F$ corresponding to $K$ then the irreducible factors of $f(x)$ over $K$ correspond to the orbits of $H$ on the roots of $f(x)$. Use then Exercise 9 of Section 4.1.]

\item Let $k$ be a field and let $k(t)$ be the field of rational functions in the variable $t$.

Define the maps $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $k(t)$ to itself by $\sigma f(t)=f\left(\dfrac{1}{1-t}\right)$ and $\tau f(t)=f\left(\dfrac{1}{t}\right)$ for $f(t)\in k(t)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are automorphisms of $k(t)$ (cf.\ Exercise 8 of Section 1) and that the group $G=\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle$ generated by them is isomorphic to $S_3$.
\item[(b)] Prove that the element $I=\dfrac{(t^2-t+1)^3}{t^2(t-1)^2}$ is fixed by all the elements of $G$.
\item[(c)] Prove that $k(I)$ is precisely the fixed field of $G$ in $k(t)$ [compute the degree of the extension].
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that the fixed field of the subgroup of automorphisms generated by $\tau$ in the previous problem is $k(t+\dfrac{1}{t})$. Prove that the fixed field of the subgroup generated by the automorphism $\tau\sigma^2$ (which maps $t$ to $1-t$) is $k(t(1-t))$. Determine the fixed field of the subgroup generated by $\tau\sigma$ and the fixed field of the subgroup generated by $\sigma$.

\item Let $K$ be a finite extension of $F$ of degree $n$. Let $\alpha$ be an element of $K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\alpha$ acting by left multiplication on $K$ is an $F$-linear transformation $T_\alpha$ of $K$.
\item[(b)] Prove that the minimal polynomial for $\alpha$ over $F$ is the same as the minimal polynomial for the linear transformation $T_\alpha$.
\item[(c)] Prove that the trace $Tr_{K/F}(\alpha)$ is the trace of the $n\times n$ matrix defined by $T_\alpha$ (which justifies these two uses of the same word ``trace''). Prove that the norm $N_{K/F}(\alpha)$ is the determinant of $T_\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

\[

F \arrow[r,hook] \arrow[d,hook,"[E:F]"'] & K \\
E \arrow[ur,hook,"[K:E]"'] &
