Type: example
Title: Why no general quintic formula can exist
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why no general quintic formula can exist}
Deduce that there is no formula in radicals for the roots of the ``generic'' quintic.
\wrec The generic polynomial $x^5-t_1x^4+\cdots\pm t_5$ over the field $Q(t_1,\dots,t_5)$ of its coefficients has Galois group exactly $S_5$; insolvability of $S_5$ then applies.
\wsol Over $F=Q(t_1,\dots,t_5)$ with the $t_i$ the elementary symmetric functions of independent transcendentals $x_1,\dots,x_5$, the splitting field is $Q(x_1,\dots,x_5)$ and $\Gal=S_5$ (it permutes the $x_i$ and fixes the symmetric functions $t_i$). Since $S_5$ is not solvable, Galois's criterion says the generic quintic is not solvable by radicals: there is no universal radical formula in the coefficients. The explicit $x^5-6x+3$ shows this already fails over $Q$, not merely generically. Sanity check: the same argument gives $\Gal=S_n$ for the generic degree-$n$ polynomial, solvable iff $n\le4$ -- recovering the classical existence of quadratic/cubic/quartic formulas and the nonexistence for all $n\ge5$.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 1/3
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Use Cardano's Formulas to solve the equation $x^3 + x^2 - 2 = 0$. In particular show that the equation has the real root
\[
\frac{1}{3}\bigl(\sqrt[3]{26 + 15\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt[3]{26 - 15\sqrt{3}} - 1\bigr).
\]
Show directly that the roots of this cubic are $1$, $-1 \pm i$. Explain this by proving that
\[
\sqrt[3]{26 + 15\sqrt{3}} = 2 + \sqrt{3} \qquad \sqrt[3]{26 - 15\sqrt{3}} = 2 - \sqrt{3}
\]
so that
\[
\sqrt[3]{26 + 15\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt[3]{26 - 15\sqrt{3}} = 4.
\]

\item Let $\zeta_7$ be a primitive $7^{th}$ root of unity and let $\alpha = \zeta_7 + \zeta_7^{-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\zeta_7$ is a root of the quadratic $z^2 - \alpha z + 1$ over $Q(\alpha)$.
\item[(b)] Show using the minimal polynomial for $\zeta_7$ that $\alpha$ is a root of the cubic $x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1$.
\item[(c)] Use (a) and (b) together with the explicit solution of the cubic in (b) in the text to express $\zeta_7$ in terms of radicals similar to the expressions given earlier for the other roots of unity of small order. (The complicated nature of the expression explains why we did not include $\zeta_7$ earlier in our list of explicit roots of unity.)
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $\neq 2$. State and prove a necessary and sufficient condition on $a, b \in F$ so that $F(\sqrt{a}) = F(\sqrt{b})$. Use this to determine whether $Q(\sqrt{1 - \sqrt{2}}) = Q(i, \sqrt{2})$.

\item Let $K = Q(\sqrt[n]{a})$, where $a \in Q$, $a > 0$ and suppose $[K : Q] = n$ (i.e., $x^n - a$ is irreducible). Let $E$ be any subfield of $K$ and let $[E : Q] = d$. Prove that $E = Q(\sqrt[d]{a})$. [Consider $N_{K/E}(\sqrt[n]{a}) \in E$.]

\item Let $K$ be as in the previous exercise. Prove that if $n$ is odd then $K$ has no nontrivial subfields which are Galois over $Q$ and if $n$ is even then the only nontrivial subfield of $K$ which is Galois over $Q$ is $Q(\sqrt{a})$.

\item Let $L$ be the Galois closure of $K$ in the previous two exercises (i.e., the splitting field of $x^n - a$). Prove that $[L : Q] = n\varphi(n)$ or $\frac{1}{2}n\varphi(n)$. [Note that $Q(\zeta_n) \cap K$ is a Galois extension of $Q$.]

\item (Kummer Generators for Cyclic Extensions) Let $F$ be a field of characteristic not dividing $n$ containing the $n^{th}$ roots of unity and let $K$ be a cyclic extension of degree $d$ dividing $n$. \item[(d)] Prove that $\tau g = g$ if $\tau \in H$ and $\tau g = -g$ if $\tau \notin H$. Conclude that $[Q(g) : Q] = 2$. Recall that complex conjugation is the automorphism $\sigma_{-1}$ on $K$ (cf. Exercise 7 of Section 5). Conclude that $\bar{g} = g$ if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\bar{g} = -g$ if $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$; with $g\bar{g} = p$ from (e) this makes $g$ a square root of $p$ (i.e., $g^2 = p$) if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and a square root of $-p$ (i.e., $g^2 = -p$) if $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, where $\bar{g}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $g$.
\item[(e)] Prove that $g^2 = \pm p$. [The complex conjugate of a root of unity is its reciprocal. $\bar{g} = \sum_{i=0}^{p-2} (-1)^i (\sigma^i(\zeta_p))^{-1}$ gives
\[
g\bar{g} = \sum_{i,j=0}^{p-2} (-1)^i (-1)^j \frac{\sigma^i(\zeta_p)}{\sigma^j(\zeta_p)} = \sum_{i,j=0}^{p-2} (-1)^{i-j} \sigma^j\Bigl(\frac{\sigma^{i-j}(\zeta_p)}{\zeta_p}\Bigr)
\]
\[
= \sum_{k=0}^{p-2} (-1)^k \sum_{j=0}^{p-2} \sigma^j \frac{\sigma^k(\zeta_p)}{\zeta_p}
\]
where $k = i - j$. If $k = 0$ the element $\frac{\sigma^k(\zeta_p)}{\zeta_p}$ is 1, and if $k \neq 0$ then this is a primitive $p^{th}$ root of unity. Use the previous exercise to conclude that the inner sum is $p - 1$ when $k = 0$ and is $-1$ otherwise.]
\item[(f)] Conclude that $g^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p$ and that $Q(\sqrt{(-1)^{(p-1)/2} p})$ is the unique quadratic subfield of $Q(\zeta_p)$. (Cf. also Exercise 33 of Section 6.)
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $L$ be the Galois closure of the finite extension $Q(\alpha)$ of $Q$. For any prime $p$ dividing the order of $\Gal(L/Q)$ prove there is a subfield $F$ of $L$ with $[L : F] = p$ and $L = F(\alpha)$.

\item Let $F$ be a subfield of the real numbers $R$. Let $a$ be an element of $F$ and let $K = F(\sqrt[n]{a})$ where $\sqrt[n]{a}$ denotes any real $n^{th}$ root of $a$. Prove that if $L$ is any Galois extension of $F$ contained in $K$ then $[L : F] \leq 2$.

\item This exercise shows that in general it is necessary to use complex numbers when expressing real roots in terms of radicals and generalizes the Casus irreducibilis of cubic equations. Let $f(x) \in Q[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial all of whose roots are real. Suppose further that one of the roots, $\alpha$, of $f(x)$ can be expressed in terms of real radicals (i.e., there is a root extension of real fields $Q = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m$ with $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$, $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m - 1$, for some integers $n_i$ and some $a_i \in K_i$ and $\alpha \in K_m$). Prove that the Galois group of $f(x)$ is a 2-group. Conclude in particular that the degree of $f(x)$ is a power of 2 and that the real roots of such a polynomial can be expressed entirely in terms of real radicals if and only if these roots can be constructed by straightedge and compass. [The argument is similar to the case of cubics. Let $L \subseteq R$ be the Galois closure of $Q(\alpha)$ and suppose the order of $\Gal(L/Q)$ is divisible by some odd prime $p$. Let $F$ be a subfield of $L$ with $[L : F] = p$ and $L = F(\alpha)$ by Exercise 12 and consider the composite fields $K_i' = F K_i$, $i = 0, 1, \ldots, m$. These are again real radical extensions and by the argument in the text for the Casus irreducibilis, we may assume each $[K_{i+1}' : K_i']$ is a prime. Since $\alpha \notin F = F K_0$, there is an integer $s$ with $\alpha \notin K_s'$, $\alpha \in K_{s+1}'$. Since the extensions are of prime degree, we have $K_{s+1}' = K_s'(\alpha)$. Since $L = F(\alpha)$ is a Galois extension of degree $p$, $K_{s+1}'$ is a Galois extension of $K_s'$ of degree $p$, contradicting the previous exercise.]

\item (`Cardano's Formulas' for a Cubic in Characteristic 2) Suppose $f(x) = x^3 + px + q$ is an irreducible cubic over a field of characteristic 2. Let $\rho$ be a primitive $3^{rd}$ root of unity and let $\theta, \theta'$ be the roots of the quadratic $x^2 + qx + (p^3 + q^2)$, cf. Exercise 50 of Section 6. Let $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be cube roots of $\rho q + \theta$ and $\rho q + \theta'$, respectively, where the cube roots are chosen so that $\theta_1\theta_2 = p$. Show that the roots of $f(x)$ are given by $\alpha = \theta_1 + \theta_2$, $\beta = \rho\alpha + \theta_1$, and $\gamma = \rho\alpha + \theta_2 = \alpha + \beta$.

\item Let $a$ be a nonzero rational number.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Determine when the extension $Q(\sqrt{ai})$ $(i^2 = -1)$ is of degree 4 over $Q$.
\item[(b)] When $K = Q(\sqrt{ai})$ is of degree 4 over $Q$ show that $K$ is Galois over $Q$ with the Klein 4-group as Galois group. In this case determine the quadratic extensions of $Q$ contained in $K$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $D$ be a squarefree integer and let $a \in Q$ be a nonzero rational number. Show that $Q(\sqrt{a\sqrt{D}})$ cannot be a cyclic extension of degree 4 over $Q$.

\item Let $D \neq 1$ be a squarefree integer and let $a \in Q$ be a nonzero rational number.

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 3/3
Content:
Prove that if $Q(\sqrt{a\sqrt{D}})$ is Galois over $Q$ then $D = -1$.

\item Let $D \in Z$ be a squarefree integer and let $K = Q(\sqrt{D})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that if $D = s^2 + t^2$ is the sum of two rational squares then there exists an extension $L/Q$ containing $K$ which is Galois over $Q$ with a cyclic Galois group of order 4. [Consider the extension $Q(\sqrt{D + s\sqrt{D}})$.] (Note also that $D$ is the sum of two rational squares if and only if $D$ is also the sum of two integer squares, so one may assume $s$ and $t$ are integral without loss.)
\item[(b)] Prove conversely that if $K$ can be embedded in a cyclic extension $L$ of degree 4 as in (a) then $D$ is the sum of two squares. [One approach: (i) observe first that $L$ is quadratic over $K$, so $L = K(\sqrt{a + b\sqrt{D}})$ for some $a, b \in Q$. (ii) show that $L$ contains the quadratic subfield $Q(\sqrt{a^2 - b^2 D})$, which must be $Q(\sqrt{D})$ if $L/Q$ is cyclic, see Exercise 7.]
\item[(c)] Conclude in particular that $Q(\sqrt{3})$ is not a subfield of any cyclic extension of degree 4 over $Q$. Similarly conclude that the fields $Q(\sqrt{D})$ for squarefree integers $D < 0$ are never contained in cyclic extensions of degree 4 over $Q$ (this gives an alternate proof for Exercise 19, Section 6).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $p$ be a prime. Show that any solvable subgroup of $S_p$ of order divisible by $p$ is contained in the normalizer of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S_p$ (a Frobenius group of order $p(p - 1)$). Conclude that an irreducible polynomial $f(x) \in Q[x]$ of degree $p$ is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is contained in the Frobenius group of order $p(p - 1)$. [Let $G \le S_p$ be a solvable subgroup of order divisible by $p$. Then $G$ contains a $p$-cycle, hence a transitive on $\{1, 2, \ldots, p\}$. Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Exhibit an explicit radical tower $Q=K_0\subseteq K_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq K_m=K$ realizing the splitting field $K$ of $x^4-2$ over $Q$, giving each generator $\alpha_{i+1}$ and the element $\alpha_{i+1}^{\,n_{i+1}}\in K_i$ of which it is a root. Compute $[K:Q]$ and identify $\Gal(K/Q)$.
\item Let $F=Q(\zeta_7)$ and $a=3$. Determine $[F(\sqrt[7]{3}):F]$, prove that $F(\sqrt[7]{3})/F$ is cyclic, and find the order of $3$ in the group $F^{\times}/(F^{\times})^{7}$. Describe a generator $\sigma$ of $\Gal(F(\sqrt[7]{3})/F)$ by its effect on $\sqrt[7]{3}$.
\item Let $K/F$ be cyclic of degree $4$ with $\Gal(K/F)=\langle \sigma\rangle$, and suppose $\zeta=\zeta_4=i\in F$. For $\theta\in K$ form the Lagrange resolvent $(\theta,\zeta)=\theta+\zeta\,\sigma(\theta)+\zeta^2\sigma^2(\theta)+\zeta^3\sigma^3(\theta)$. Prove that $\sigma\bigl((\theta,\zeta)\bigr)=\zeta^{-1}(\theta,\zeta)$ and deduce that $(\theta,\zeta)^4\in F$.
\item Decide, with full justification, whether each of the following is solvable by radicals over $Q$: (a) $x^4-10x^2+1$; (b) $x^5-1$; (c) $x^6+3$; (d) $x^3-3x-1$. For each, name the Galois group (up to isomorphism) and explain why it is or is not solvable.
\item Determine which of the symmetric groups $S_2,S_3,S_4,S_5,S_6$ are solvable, exhibiting a subnormal series with abelian quotients in each solvable case and naming the nonabelian simple composition factor in each non-solvable case.
\item Show that $f(x)=x^5-4x^4+2$ is irreducible over $Q$, has exactly three real roots, and conclude that $\Gal(f/Q)\cong S_5$, so $f$ is not solvable by radicals. (Use $f'$ to count real roots.)
\item Let $F$ have characteristic $5$ and consider the Artin--Schreier polynomial $g(x)=x^5-x-a$ for $a\in F$. Prove that $g$ is either split over $F$ or irreducible over $F$, that in the irreducible case $F(\alpha)/F$ is cyclic of degree $5$ for any root $\alpha$, and describe a generator of $\Gal(F(\alpha)/F)$ by its effect on $\alpha$.
\item Let $a\inQ^{\times}$ and let $K$ be the splitting field of $x^p-a$ over $Q$, where $p$ is an odd prime and $x^p-a$ is irreducible. Show that $\Gal(K/Q)$ is isomorphic to the group of affine maps $x\mapsto ux+v$ on $Z/(p)Z$ with $u\in(Z/(p)Z)^{\times}$, $v\inZ/(p)Z$, and prove directly from this description that $\Gal(K/Q)$ is solvable.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $F$ contain a primitive $n$th root of unity, and let $a,b\in F^{\times}$. Prove that $F(\sqrt[n]{a})=F(\sqrt[n]{b})$ if and only if $a$ and $b$ generate the same cyclic subgroup of $F^{\times}/(F^{\times})^{n}$. Use this to count the distinct fields among $F(\sqrt[5]{a})$ as $a$ ranges over a system of representatives when $\abs{F^{\times}/(F^{\times})^{5}}$ has order $5$.
\item Let $f(x)\inQ[x]$ be irreducible of prime degree $p$. Prove that $f$ is solvable by radicals if and only if its splitting field is generated over $Q$ by any two of its roots. (One direction: use that a transitive solvable subgroup of $S_p$ lies in the affine group $\operatorname{AGL}_1(Z/(p)Z)$ of order $p(p-1)$, in which a point stabilizer acts freely on the remaining points.)
\item Let $K/F$ be a radical Galois extension in characteristic $0$. Prove that $\Gal(K/F)$ is solvable without invoking the full solvability criterion, by induction on $[K:F]$: adjoin a suitable root of unity, peel off the bottom cyclic step via Kummer theory, and apply the closure properties of solvable groups to the quotient.
\item Construct an irreducible quintic $f(x)\inQ[x]$ whose Galois group is the dihedral group $D_{10}$ of order $10$ (so $f$ is solvable by radicals), and prove that your $f$ has exactly one real root. Explain why the number of real roots is consistent with $\Gal(f)\le F_{20}$, and why exactly three real roots would be incompatible with $\Gal(f)\le F_{20}$. (One real root does not rule out $S_5$: $x^5-x-1$ has one real root and group $S_5$.)
\item Let $p$ be a prime and let $F$ have characteristic $0$ and contain a primitive $p$th root of unity. Suppose $K/F$ is Galois with $\Gal(K/F)$ a nonabelian group of order $p^3$. Prove that $K/F$ is a radical extension, and exhibit a chain of subfields corresponding to a composition series of $\Gal(K/F)$ in which every successive step is a degree-$p$ Kummer extension $F_i(\sqrt[p]{a_i})$.
\end{exers}

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=3.2em]

Section: Galois Theory > Computation of Galois Groups over $Q$ > Reduction mod $p$ and Dedekind's theorem
Type: prose
Content:
Let $f(x)\inZ[x]$ be monic, separable, of degree $n$, with splitting field $K$ over $Q$ and Galois group $G=\Gal(K/Q)$. Labelling the $n$ distinct roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ identifies $G$ with a subgroup of $S_n$ (every automorphism permutes the roots, and is determined by that permutation). The central computational problem of the section is to locate this subgroup of $S_n$ exactly. The single most powerful tool is to reduce $f$ modulo a prime and read the resulting factorization as a permutation.

Write $\overline{f}\in\F_p[x]$ for the reduction of $f$ mod $p$, and recall $\disc(f)\inZ$, the discriminant. A prime $p$ is unramified for $f$ when $p\nmid\disc(f)$; then $\overline{f}$ is still separable (its discriminant $\overline{\disc(f)}\neq0$ in $\F_p$), so $\overline{f}$ factors into distinct irreducibles over $\F_p$.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Computation of Galois Groups over $Q$ > Reduction mod $p$ and Dedekind's theorem
Type: theorem
Title: {Dedekind's theorem}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Dedekind's theorem}]
Let $f\inZ[x]$ be monic and separable, and let $p$ be a prime with $p\nmid\disc(f)$. Suppose
\[
\overline{f}=\overline{g_1}\,\overline{g_2}\cdots\overline{g_k}\quadin \F_p[x],
\]
a product of distinct monic irreducibles with $\deg\overline{g_i}=d_i$. Then $\Gal(f/Q)$, viewed in $S_n$, contains a permutation whose cycle type is $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Computation of Galois Groups over $Q$ > Reduction mod $p$ and Dedekind's theorem
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-96f0f4f405636e3a08a2
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Each prime $\mathfrak p$ of the splitting-field ring lying over $p$ has a Frobenius automorphism $\Frob_{\mathfrak p}\in G$, characterized by $\Frob_{\mathfrak p}(x)\equiv x^p\pmod{\mathfrak p}$. Because $p$ is unramified, reduction mod $\mathfrak p$ is a bijection between the roots of $f$ in characteristic $0$ and the roots of $\overline f$ in $\overline{\F_p}$. Frobenius acts on the latter as $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^p$, and on the roots of a single irreducible factor $\overline{g_i}$ of degree $d_i$ it acts as a single $d_i$-cycle (the roots of an irreducible over $\F_p$ form one Frobenius orbit, of size equal to the degree). Pulling this back through the bijection, $\Frob_{\mathfrak p}$ is an element of $G$ with cycle type $(d_1,\dots,d_k)$.
\end{proof}

Section: Galois Theory > Computation of Galois Groups over $Q$ > Reduction mod $p$ and Dedekind's theorem
Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Dedekind's theorem only ever produces lower bounds: each prime hands us one cycle type known to occur in $G$. It never certifies that a cycle type is absent. So the method is to collect cycle types from several primes and ask which transitive subgroup of $S_n$ is forced to contain all of them. The discriminant test and resolvents supply the complementary upper bounds.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: A 4-cycle and a transposition from two primes
Content:
\begin{wex}{A 4-cycle and a transposition from two primes}
For $f(x)=x^4-x-1$, find primes exhibiting a $4$-cycle and a transposition in $\Gal(f/Q)$.
\wrec By Dedekind's theorem an irreducible reduction $\overline f$ of degree $4$ gives a $4$-cycle, and a factorization of type $2+1+1$ gives a transposition; we just factor mod small primes.
\wsol Mod $2$: $x^4-x-1\equiv x^4+x+1$, which is irreducible over $\F_2$ (no root since $0,1$ both give $1$; and the only way a rootless quartic could factor is as a product of two irreducible quadratics, but the unique irreducible quadratic over $\F_2$ is $x^2+x+1$, whose square $(x^2+x+1)^2=x^4+x^2+1\neq x^4+x+1$). Hence $\overline f$ is irreducible mod $2$, giving both transitivity (so $f$ is irreducible over $Q$) and a $\mathbf 4$-cycle. So $G$ is a transitive subgroup of $S_4$ containing a $4$-cycle: $G\in\{C_4,D_8,S_4\}$. The discriminant is $\disc(f)=-283$, which is negative and hence not a perfect square, so $G\not\subseteq A_4$ (this is automatic here, since a $4$-cycle is already odd). Mod $17$: $x^4-x-1$ factors as a product of two linear factors and one irreducible quadratic (cycle type $2+1+1$), giving a transposition in $G$. This alone does not force $S_4$: $D_8$ also contains transpositions (e.g.\ $\langle (1\,2\,3\,4),(1\,3)\rangle=D_8$). Mod $7$: $\overline f=(x+4)(x^3+3x^2+2x+5)$ with the cubic irreducible (cycle type $3+1$), giving a $3$-cycle; then $3\mid\abs G$, which rules out $C_4$ and $D_8$, so $G=S_4$. Sanity check: $-283<0$ is certainly not a square, consistent with the odd $4$-cycle (and the transposition) lying in $G$; and $\abs G$ is divisible by $4$ and by $3$ while $G$ contains odd permutations, so $G\neq A_4$ and $\abs G=24$.
\end{wex}

Type: proposition
Title: {transitivity from irreducibility}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{transitivity from irreducibility}]
$f\inQ[x]$ is irreducible if and only if $G=\Gal(f/Q)$ acts transitively on the roots. In particular an irreducible $f$ of degree $n$ has $n\mid\abs{G}$.
\end{proposition}

Type: theorem
Title: {the discriminant test}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{the discriminant test}]
Let $f\inQ[x]$ be separable of degree $n$ with roots $\alpha_i$ and $\disc(f)=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$. Then $\sqrt{\disc(f)}\inQ$ if and only if $G\subseteq A_n$. Equivalently, for monic $f\inZ[x]$ with squarefree-checked discriminant, $G\subseteq A_n\iff\disc(f)$ is a perfect square in $Q$.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-bbafc2b7d10aac02ecbd
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The element $\delta=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$ satisfies $\delta^2=\disc(f)\inQ$, and any $\sigma\in G$ sends $\delta\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\delta$. Thus $\delta$ is fixed by all of $G$ (hence $\delta\inQ$ and $\disc f$ is a square) exactly when every $\sigma\in G$ is even, i.e.\ $G\subseteq A_n$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Pinning down $\Gal(f/Q)$ for irreducible $f\inZ[x]$ of degree $n$.
Content:
\begin{method}{Pinning down $\Gal(f/Q)$ for irreducible $f\inZ[x]$ of degree $n$.}
\textup{(1)} Confirm $f$ is irreducible over $Q$, so $G$ is a transitive subgroup of $S_n$.
\textup{(2)} Compute $\disc(f)$; decide whether it is a perfect square. If yes, $G\subseteq A_n$; if no, $G\not\subseteq A_n$.
\textup{(3)} Factor $\overline f$ for several primes $p\nmid\disc(f)$, recording cycle types via Dedekind.
\textup{(4)} Intersect the constraints with the (short) list of transitive subgroups of $S_n$. A single cycle type often eliminates all but one candidate.
\textup{(5)} If two candidates survive, one inside the other, cycle types can never rule out the larger one (e.g.\ $C_4\le D_8$ when no transposition has appeared, or the solvable groups $C_5\le D_{10}\le F_{20}$ in $S_5$); separate them with a resolvent polynomial.
\end{method}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Reduction mod $p$ never proves a cycle type is missing from $G$, so you cannot conclude $G\neq S_n$ just because you have not seen a transposition. Likewise a square discriminant only says $G\subseteq A_n$; it does not by itself distinguish, say, $V_4$ from $A_4$ inside $S_4$, nor $A_n$ from a proper transitive subgroup of $A_n$. Always pair cycle-type evidence with the discriminant and, when needed, a resolvent.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: Discriminant forces $S_3$ vs.\ $A_3$ for a cubic
Content:
\begin{wex}{Discriminant forces $S_3$ vs.\ $A_3$ for a cubic}
Show $f(x)=x^3-x-1$ has Galois group $S_3$.
\wrec For an irreducible cubic, $G$ is transitive in $S_3$, so $G\in\{A_3,S_3\}$; the discriminant test decides which, since $\disc=-4a^3-27b^2$ for $x^3+ax+b$.
\wsol $f$ is irreducible over $Q$ (no rational root: $\pm1$ give $-1,-1$). Here $a=-1,b=-1$, so $\disc(f)=-4(-1)^3-27(-1)^2=4-27=-23$. Since $-23$ is negative it is not a perfect square in $Q$, so $G\not\subseteq A_3$, forcing $G=S_3$. Sanity check: mod $2$, $\overline f=x^3+x+1$ is irreducible, giving a $3$-cycle; mod $5$, $f(2)=8-2-1=5\equiv0$, so $x\equiv2$ is a root and $\overline f=(x-2)(x^2+2x-2)$ splits as (linear)(irreducible quadratic), a transposition. A $3$-cycle and a transposition generate $S_3$, confirming $G=S_3$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: An $S_4$ quartic via discriminant and a 4-cycle
Content:
\begin{wex}{An $S_4$ quartic via discriminant and a 4-cycle}
Prove $f(x)=x^4+x+1$ has Galois group $S_4$.
\wrec Irreducible quartic gives transitive $G\sgr S_4$; a non-square discriminant rules out $A_4$ and $V_4$ (the transitive subgroups inside $A_4$), and a mod-$p$ $4$-cycle plus a $3$-cycle pin $S_4$.
\wsol Irreducibility over $Q$: no rational roots ($\pm1$ give $3,1$), and $x^4+x+1$ is not a product of two rational quadratics (matching coefficients $x^4+x+1=(x^2+bx+c)(x^2-bx+d)$ forces $c+d-b^2=0,\ b(d-c)=1,\ cd=1$, which has no rational solution). So $G$ is transitive in $S_4$. Discriminant of $x^4+px+q$ is $-27p^4+256q^3$; with $p=q=1$ this is $-27+256=229$, which is prime, hence not a perfect square: $G\not\subseteq A_4$. Mod $2$: $x^4+x+1$ is irreducible over $\F_2$, giving a $4$-cycle. The transitive subgroups of $S_4$ are $C_4,V_4,D_8,A_4,S_4$; those containing a $4$-cycle are $C_4,D_8,S_4$. Of these, only $S_4$ contains an element of order $3$ ($\abs{C_4}=4$ and $\abs{D_8}=8$ are not divisible by $3$), so a $3$-cycle will pin down $S_4$. Mod $5$: testing residues, $f(0)=1,f(1)=3,f(2)=16+2+1=19\equiv4,f(3)=81+3+1=85\equiv0$, so $x\equiv3$ is a root mod $5$ and $\overline f=(x-3)\cdot(cubic)$; that cubic is irreducible mod $5$ (it has no root among the remaining residues), giving cycle type $3+1$, a $3$-cycle. A $4$-cycle and a $3$-cycle generate $S_4$, so $G=S_4$. Sanity check: $\abs{S_4}=24$ is divisible by $4$ (transitivity) and by $3$ (the $3$-cycle); and $229$ not a square is consistent with the odd permutation (the $4$-cycle) lying in $G$.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
When $\disc(f)$ is a square the discriminant test only narrows $G$ to a subgroup of $A_n$, and for $n=4$ several such subgroups can share cycle types. The resolvent cubic resolves them. For a quartic
\[
f(x)=x^4+px^2+qx+r\quad(depressed; remove the cubic term first),
\]
with roots $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4$, the three quantities
\[
\beta_1=\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4,\quad
\beta_2=\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4,\quad
\beta_3=\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3
\]
are permuted by $S_4$ through the quotient $S_4/V_4\cong S_3$. Their elementary symmetric functions are polynomials in $p,q,r$, giving the resolvent cubic
\[
g(x)=x^3-p\,x^2-4r\,x+(4pr-q^2).
\]

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Computation of Galois Groups over $Q$ > The resolvent cubic and the quartic playbook
Type: theorem
Title: {quartic Galois groups via the resolvent}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{quartic Galois groups via the resolvent}]
Let $f\inQ[x]$ be an irreducible quartic with resolvent cubic $g$, and let $G=\Gal(f/Q)\sgr S_4$. Then, writing $D=\disc(f)=\disc(g)$:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
G\cong S_4 & \iff g is irreducible and D is not a square;\\
G\cong A_4 & \iff g is irreducible and D is a square;\\
G\cong V_4 & \iff g splits completely over Q;\\
G\cong C_4 or D_8 & \iff g has exactly one rational root.
\end{array}
\]
In the last case $C_4$ and $D_8$ are separated by whether $f$ remains irreducible over $Q(\sqrt D)$: $C_4$ if $f$ becomes reducible there, $D_8$ if it stays irreducible.
\end{theorem}

Let $f\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ be an irreducible quartic with resolvent cubic $g$, and let $G=\Gal(f/\mathbb{Q})\sgr S_4$. Then, writing $D=\disc(f)=\disc(g)$:

\begin{wex}{A $V_4$ quartic: square discriminant, split resolvent}
Determine $\Gal(f/Q)$ for $f(x)=x^4+1$.
\wrec Irreducible quartic; compute $\disc$ and the resolvent cubic. A completely split resolvent signals $V_4$.
\wsol $x^4+1=\Phi_8(x)$ is irreducible over $Q$ (the $8$th cyclotomic polynomial). It is already depressed with $p=0,q=0,r=1$. Resolvent: $g(x)=x^3-0\cdot x^2-4x+0=x^3-4x=x(x-2)(x+2)$, which splits completely over $Q$. By the theorem $G\cong V_4$. Sanity check: $Q(\zeta_8)$ has degree $\varphi(8)=4$ over $Q$ with abelian Galois group $(Z/(8)Z)^{\times}\congZ/2\timesZ/2\cong V_4$, matching exactly; and $\disc(x^4+1)=256=16^2$ is a perfect square, consistent with $V_4\subseteq A_4$.
\end{wex}

Title: $A_4$ vs.\ $V_4$ when the discriminant is a square
Content:
\begin{wex}{$A_4$ vs.\ $V_4$ when the discriminant is a square}
Show $f(x)=x^4+8x+12$ has Galois group $A_4$.
\wrec Square discriminant puts $G\sgr A_4$, so $G\in\{V_4,A_4\}$; the resolvent cubic being irreducible (not split) selects $A_4$.
\wsol $f$ is irreducible over $Q$ (no rational roots by the rational-root test on divisors of $12$, and no rational quadratic factorization). It is depressed: $p=0,q=8,r=12$. Discriminant of $x^4+qx+r$ is $-27q^4+256r^3=-27\cdot4096+256\cdot1728=-110592+442368=331776=576^2$, a perfect square, so $G\sgr A_4$. Resolvent cubic: $g(x)=x^3-0\cdot x^2-4(12)x+(0-64)=x^3-48x-64$. This is irreducible over $Q$: a rational root would be an integer dividing $64$; for $\abs x\ge16$ we have $\abs{x^3-48x}=\abs x\,(x^2-48)>64$, and testing $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8$ gives no zero (e.g.\ $g(8)=512-384-64=64\neq0$, $g(-4)=-64+192-64=64\neq0$). Since $g$ is irreducible and $D$ is a square, $G\cong A_4$. Sanity check: $\sqrt D=576\inQ$ matches $G\subseteq A_4$; an irreducible resolvent means $\Gal(g/Q)=S_3$ or $A_3=C_3$, and $\disc(g)=\disc(f)$ is a square so $\Gal(g/Q)=C_3$, hence $G/(G\cap V_4)\cong C_3$, giving $\abs G=12$, i.e.\ $A_4$.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{$C_4$ vs.\ $D_8$: one rational resolvent root}
Identify $\Gal(f/Q)$ for $f(x)=x^4+5x^2+5$.
\wrec One rational resolvent root signals $C_4$ or $D_8$; the tiebreak is whether $f$ stays irreducible over $Q(\sqrt D)$.
\wsol By the rational root test and Eisenstein at $5$, $f=x^4+5x^2+5$ is irreducible over $Q$. Depressed with $p=5,q=0,r=5$. Resolvent: $g(x)=x^3-5x^2-20x+(4\cdot25-0)=x^3-5x^2-20x+100=(x-5)(x^2-20)$. So $g$ has exactly one rational root $x=5$ (since $x^2-20$ is irreducible over $Q$), placing $G\in\{C_4,D_8\}$. Discriminant: $f$ is biquadratic, $x^2=\tfrac{-5\pm\sqrt5}{2}$, so the splitting field is $Q\bigl(\sqrt{\tfrac{-5+\sqrt5}{2}}\bigr)$, which contains $\sqrt5$; one computes $D=\disc(f)=2000=400\cdot5$, so $\sqrt D=20\sqrt5$ and $Q(\sqrt D)=Q(\sqrt5)$. Over $Q(\sqrt5)$ the quartic factors as $\bigl(x^2-\tfrac{-5+\sqrt5}{2}\bigr)\bigl(x^2-\tfrac{-5-\sqrt5}{2}\bigr)$, i.e.\ $f$ becomes reducible, so $G\cong C_4$. Sanity check: a biquadratic $x^4+px^2+r$ with $\sqrt r=\sqrt5$ irrational but $\sqrt{p^2-4r}=\sqrt{25-20}=\sqrt5$ relating the two radicals is the classic $C_4$ pattern (Galois group cyclic of order $4$), and indeed $\abs{Q(\zeta):Q}$-type cyclic structure gives $\abs G=4$ with a single $4$-cycle generator.
\end{wex}

Title: Reading the resolvent backwards
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading the resolvent backwards}
Given that an irreducible quartic $f$ has resolvent cubic $g$ with $\disc(g)$ a non-square and $g$ irreducible, name $G$.
\wrec $g$ irreducible means $\Gal(g/Q)$ is transitive in $S_3$; a non-square $\disc(g)=\disc(f)$ means $G\not\subseteq A_4$.
\wsol Irreducible $g$ with non-square discriminant has $\Gal(g/Q)=S_3$, so $G/(G\cap V_4)\cong S_3$ has order $6$; since $G$ is transitive, $4\mid\abs G=6\,\abs{G\cap V_4}$, so $12\mid\abs G$; and $G\neq A_4$, because the image of $A_4$ in $S_4/V_4\cong S_3$ is only $A_3$. Hence $\abs G=24$, giving $G\cong S_4$. Sanity check: this is exactly the first row of the table ($g$ irreducible, $D$ not a square $\Rightarrow S_4$), and $\abs{S_4}=24=6\cdot4$ matches $\abs{S_3}\cdot\abs{V_4}$.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
The resolvent cubic is one instance of a general device. Given $f$ of degree $n$ and a polynomial expression $\theta(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ whose $S_n$-orbit has size $m$, the resolvent
\[
R(x)=\prod_{\sigma\in S_n/\operatorname{Stab}(\theta)}\bigl(x-\sigma\cdot\theta\bigr)\inQ[x]
\]
has degree $m$ and rational coefficients (symmetric in the $\alpha_i$). The factorization pattern of $R$ over $Q$ reflects the orbits of $G$ on the cosets $S_n/\operatorname{Stab}(\theta)$: when $R$ has distinct roots, a rational root of $R$ corresponds to a $G$-fixed coset $\tau\operatorname{Stab}(\theta)$, i.e.\ to $G\sgr\tau\operatorname{Stab}(\theta)\tau^{-1}$. This separates transitive subgroups that Dedekind cannot, since cycle types only exhibit elements of $G$ and can never show that $G$ lies in a smaller group.

\begin{remark}
The canonical pair Dedekind cannot tell apart in $S_5$ is the cyclic $C_5$, the dihedral $D_{10}$, the Frobenius group $F_{20}$, and $A_5,S_5$: the transitive subgroups of $S_5$ are exactly $C_5\psgr D_{10}\psgr F_{20}\psgr S_5$ together with $A_5$. Each of $C_5,D_{10},F_{20}$ contains $5$-cycles, and cycle types alone (constrained also by the discriminant, which is a square iff $G\sgr A_5$) leave genuine ambiguity. A degree-$6$ sextic resolvent is built from a polynomial expression $\theta$ in the roots whose stabilizer in $S_5$ is exactly $F_{20}$ (order $20$, index $6$), so that $S_5$ permutes the six conjugates of $\theta$ through $S_5/F_{20}$; this resolvent has a rational root precisely when $G$ fixes one of the six cosets, i.e.\ when $G$ is conjugate into $F_{20}$, separating the solvable groups $C_5,D_{10},F_{20}$ from $A_5,S_5$.
\end{remark}

Title: The low-degree playbook.
Content:
\begin{method}{The low-degree playbook.}
\textup{Cubics ($n=3$):} irreducible $\Rightarrow G\in\{A_3,S_3\}$; $\disc$ a square $\iff A_3=C_3$, else $S_3$.
\textup{Quartics ($n=4$):} transitive subgroups $C_4,V_4,D_8,A_4,S_4$; use the resolvent cubic table above.
\textup{Quintics ($n=5$):} transitive subgroups $C_5,D_{10},F_{20},A_5,S_5$. First, $\disc$ a square $\iff G\sgr A_5$, separating $\{C_5,D_{10},A_5\}$ (square) from $\{F_{20},S_5\}$ (non-square). Then a transposition (cycle type $2+1+1+1$) or a single $2$-cycle from Dedekind forces $G=S_5$; a $5$-cycle is automatic from transitivity; an element of cycle type $2+2+1$ lies in $A_5$ and (with the discriminant) helps separate $C_5,D_{10},A_5$. The sextic resolvent separates the solvable trio $\{C_5,D_{10},F_{20}\}$ (rational root) from $\{A_5,S_5\}$ (no rational root).
\end{method}

Title: $x^5-x-1$ has Galois group $S_5$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$x^5-x-1$ has Galois group $S_5$}
Prove the irreducible quintic $f(x)=x^5-x-1$ has $\Gal(f/Q)=S_5$.
\wrec Irreducible quintic is transitive in $S_5$; by the playbook, exhibiting a $5$-cycle, an element of order $6$ (type $2+3$), and a transposition forces $S_5$, since $S_5$ is the only transitive subgroup of $S_5$ containing a transposition.
\wsol Irreducibility over $Q$: mod $3$, $f(x)=x^5-x-1\equiv x^5+2x+2$. Testing $0,1,2$: $f(0)=2,f(1)=1+2+2=5\equiv2,f(2)=32-2-1=29\equiv2\pmod3$, no linear factor; one checks it has no quadratic factor either, so $\overline f$ is irreducible over $\F_3$ (a known irreducible quintic mod $3$). Hence $f$ is irreducible over $Q$ and $\overline f$ irreducible mod $3$ gives a $5$-cycle. Mod $2$: $x^5-x-1\equiv x^5+x+1=(x^2+x+1)(x^3+x^2+1)$ over $\F_2$ (both factors irreducible: the quadratic is the unique irreducible one, and the cubic has no root in $\F_2$). This gives cycle type $2+3$, an element of order $\lcm(2,3)=6$. Its cube, $((2-cycle)(3-cycle))^3$, equals the $2$-cycle (the $3$-cycle cubes to identity), so $G$ contains a transposition. The only transitive subgroup of $S_5$ that contains a transposition is $S_5$ itself (a transitive subgroup generated by transpositions and acting transitively is all of $S_5$; more directly, a transposition together with a $5$-cycle generates $S_5$). Hence $G=S_5$. Sanity check: $\disc(x^5-x-1)=2869=19\cdot151$, which is not a perfect square, so $G\not\subseteq A_5$, fully consistent with the odd transposition lying in $G$; and a $5$-cycle plus a transposition is the textbook generating set for $S_5$.
\end{wex}

Title: $x^5+20x+16$ lands in $A_5$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$x^5+20x+16$ lands in $A_5$}
Show $f(x)=x^5+20x+16$ has Galois group $A_5$ (not $S_5$).
\wrec Square discriminant forces $G\sgr A_5$; combined with transitivity (a $5$-cycle) and a $3$-cycle (an even element of order $3$), which rules out the solvable groups $C_5,D_{10}$, we get $G=A_5$.
\wsol $f$ is irreducible over $Q$ (Eisenstein fails at $2$ since $4\mid16$; instead reduce mod $3$: $x^5+20x+16\equiv x^5+2x+1$, irreducible over $\F_3$, so $f$ is irreducible over $Q$). The mod-$3$ irreducibility gives a $\mathbf 5$-cycle. Discriminant: for $x^5+ax+b$, $\disc=4^4a^5+5^5b^4=256a^5+3125b^4$; with $a=20,b=16$ this is $256\cdot20^5+3125\cdot16^4$. Now $20^5=3.2\times10^6=3200000$, so $256\cdot3200000=819200000$; and $16^4=65536$, so $3125\cdot65536=204800000$; sum $=1024000000=32000^2$, a perfect square. So $G\sgr A_5$, i.e.\ $G\in\{C_5,D_{10},A_5\}$. Mod $7$: $x^5+20x+16\equiv(x+2)(x+3)(x^3+2x^2-2x-2)$ over $\F_7$, cycle type $3+1+1$, a $3$-cycle (an even permutation), forcing $3\mid\abs G$. Since $3\nmid\abs{C_5}=5$ and $3\nmid\abs{D_{10}}=10$, neither $C_5$ nor $D_{10}$ can contain a $3$-cycle, so the only remaining even transitive group is $A_5$ ($\abs{A_5}=60$). Hence $G=A_5$. Sanity check: $1024000000=(32000)^2$ is a clean square, matching $G\subseteq A_5$; and $\abs{A_5}=60$ is divisible by $5$ (transitivity) and by $3$ (the $3$-cycle), exactly the primes our cycle types demanded, while $\abs{C_5}=5,\abs{D_{10}}=10$ both fail the divisibility-by-$3$ test. (One can also confirm an even $2+2+1$ element appears, e.g.\ mod $23$, consistent with $G\subseteq A_5$.)
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Two primes already forcing $S_n$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Two primes already forcing $S_n$}
Explain why for $f(x)=x^6+24x-20$ a transposition plus a reduction of type $5+1$ would force $S_6$, and contrast with the actual answer $A_6$.
\wrec If Dedekind ever delivers a transposition and (via another prime) a $p$-cycle on $n-1$ or all $n$ points appropriately, transitivity plus a transposition can force $S_n$; a square discriminant blocks any transposition, redirecting to $A_n$.
\wsol For a transitive $G\sgr S_n$, possessing a transposition and an $(n-1)$-cycle (with the fixed point disjoint) generates $S_n$; even just a transposition together with an $n$-cycle when $n$ is prime generates $S_n$. So, once $f$ is known to be irreducible, two well-chosen primes -- one giving cycle type $(n-1)+1$ (an $(n-1)$-cycle; when $n$ is prime an irreducible $\overline f$, i.e.\ an $n$-cycle, also works) and one giving cycle type $2+1+\cdots+1$ (a transposition) -- already force $G=S_n$. (For composite $n$ an $n$-cycle does not suffice: $\langle (1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6),(1\,4)\rangle$ is transitive of order only $24$.) For $f=x^6+24x-20$, however, $\disc(f)$ turns out to be a perfect square, so $G\subseteq A_6$ and no prime can ever produce a transposition (a single $2$-cycle is odd). Thus the transposition route is unavailable; instead one collects even cycle types (e.g.\ a $5$-cycle from an irreducible-quintic-times-linear reduction, type $5+1$, which is even; and a $3$-cycle, type $3+1+1+1$) and shows the only transitive even subgroup of $S_6$ generated by them is $A_6$. Sanity check: $5+1$ and $3+1+1+1$ are both even permutations (a $5$-cycle and a $3$-cycle), consistent with $G\subseteq A_6$; and a $5$-cycle together with a $3$-cycle inside a transitive group on $6$ points generates a large group, with $A_6$ the smallest containing both while respecting the square-discriminant constraint.
\end{wex}

Title: Subfields forced by the $A_4$ identification
Content:
\begin{wex}{Subfields forced by the $A_4$ identification}
For an irreducible quartic with $G\cong A_4$, list the degrees of the intermediate fields and the unique proper subfield that is normal over $Q$ of small degree.
\wrec Intermediate fields correspond to subgroups of $A_4$; degrees over $Q$ equal indices $[A_4:H]$. The only normal subgroup giving a small abelian quotient is $V_4\nor A_4$.
\wsol $\abs{A_4}=12$, so $[K:Q]=12$. Subgroups of $A_4$: the trivial group, three subgroups of order $2$ (each $\langle (ab)(cd)\rangle$), one $V_4$ of order $4$, four $C_3$'s of order $3$, and $A_4$. The corresponding subfield degrees $[\,\cdot:Q]=[A_4:H]$ are $12$ (top $K$), $6$ (from the order-$2$ subgroups), $3$ (from $V_4$), $4$ (from the $C_3$'s), and $1$ (base). The normal subgroup $V_4\nor A_4$ has quotient $A_4/V_4\cong C_3$, so $\Fix(V_4)$ is a cyclic cubic field normal over $Q$ -- the splitting field of the (irreducible, square-discriminant) resolvent cubic. Sanity check: $A_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$ (a classical fact), so there is no intermediate field of degree $2$ over $Q$; consistent with the resolvent test for $A_4$ requiring $g$ irreducible (no rational/quadratic resolvent root), hence no quadratic subfield other than $Q$ itself -- indeed $\disc$ being a square means $Q(\sqrt D)=Q$.
\end{wex}

Title: Residue degrees as cycle lengths
Content:
\begin{wex}{Residue degrees as cycle lengths}
With $f=x^4+x+1$ ($G=S_4$) and $p=5$, interpret the factorization $\overline f=(x-3)(irreducible cubic)$ in terms of primes of $K$ above $5$.
\wrec The degrees of the irreducible factors of $\overline f$ over $\F_p$ are the residue degrees $f(\mathfrak p\mid p)$ of the primes $\mathfrak p$ of (the ring of integers of) the root field $Q(\alpha)$ lying over $p$, and they form the cycle type of a Frobenius element; every prime of $K$ over $p$ has residue degree equal to the order of that Frobenius.
\wsol Mod $5$, $\overline f=(x-3)(x^3+\cdots)$ has factor degrees $1$ and $3$, so the Frobenius at $5$ has cycle type $(1,3)$ -- a $3$-cycle fixing one root. Correspondingly, in the field $Q(\alpha)=Q[x]/(f)$ the prime $5$ splits as $\mathfrak p_1\mathfrak p_2$ with residue degrees $1$ and $3$ (and ramification $1$, since $5\nmid\disc f=229$). In the full splitting field $K$ the prime $5$ is unramified with Frobenius conjugacy class equal to that of a $(1,3)$-element of $S_4$. Sanity check: the residue degrees sum to $1+3=4=\deg f=[Q(\alpha):Q]$, as required for an unramified prime; and a $3$-cycle is an even permutation, while the existence (at other primes) of odd permutations is what makes $G=S_4\not\subseteq A_4$.
\end{wex}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $p$ be a prime. Prove that the polynomial $x^4+1$ splits mod $p$ either into two irreducible quadratics or into 4 linear factors using Corollary 41 together with the knowledge that the Galois group of this polynomial is the Klein 4-group.

\item (Cf. Exercise 48 of Section 6.)
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Let $K$ be the splitting field of $x^6-2x^3-2$. Prove that if $[K:Q]=12$ then $K=Q(\sqrt[3]{2}\cdot i,\sqrt{3})$ and $K$ is generated over the biquadratic field $F=Q(i,\sqrt{3})$ by $\alpha=\sqrt[3]{1+\sqrt{3}}$ and $\beta=\sqrt[3]{1-\sqrt{3}}$. Conclude that any element of $\Gal(K/Q)$ of order 3 maps $\alpha$ to another cube root of $1+\sqrt{3}$ and $\beta$ to another cube root of $1-\sqrt{3}$, and if it is the identity on $\alpha$ or $\beta$ then it is the identity on all of $K$.
\item[(b)] Show that the factorization of $f(x)$ into irreducibles over $F_{13}$ is $(x-7)(x-8)(x-11)(x^3+3)$ and use Corollary 41 to show that $[K:Q]=36$.
\item[(c)] Knowing that $G=\Gal(K/Q)$ is of order 36 determine all the elements of $G$ explicitly when the group $G$ is isomorphic to $S_3\times S_3$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^5+20x+16$ is $A_5$.

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^5+x^4-4x^3-3x^2+3x+1$ is cyclic of order 5. [Show this is the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_{11}+\zeta_{11}^{-1}$.]

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^5+11x+44$ is the dihedral group $D_{10}$ (cf. Exercise 21 of Section 7).

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^5+15x+12$ is $F_{20}$, the Frobenius group of order 20 (cf. Exercise 21 of Section 7).

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^6+24x-20$ is $A_6$.

\item Prove that the Galois group of $x^7+7x^4+14x+3$ is $A_7$.

\item Determine a polynomial of degree 7 whose Galois group is cyclic of order 7.

\item Determine the probable Galois group of $x^7-7x+3$.
\end{exers}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $f(x)=x^3+x^2-2x-1\inQ[x]$. Show $f$ is irreducible over $Q$, compute $\disc(f)$, and use the discriminant test to prove $\Gal(f/Q)\congZ/(3)Z$ (the cyclic group $A_3$). [This is the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1}$.]
\item Use Dedekind's theorem to determine $\Gal(f/Q)$ for $f(x)=x^3-2$. Reduce mod a prime giving an irreducible cubic and a prime giving cycle type $2+1$, and confirm the result against $\disc(x^3+b)=-27b^2$.
\item For $f(x)=x^4-2x^2-2$ (Eisenstein at $2$), form the resolvent cubic $g(x)=x^3-px^2-4rx+(4pr-q^2)$, factor $g$ over $Q$, and identify $\Gal(f/Q)$ among $\{C_4,V_4,D_8,A_4,S_4\}$. If you land in the $C_4$-vs-$D_8$ case, carry out the tiebreak using irreducibility of $f$ over $Q(\sqrt{\disc f})$.
\item Let $f(x)=x^4+3x+3$. Verify $f$ is irreducible over $Q$, compute $\disc(x^4+qx+r)=-27q^4+256r^3$ for this $f$, and decide whether $\Gal(f/Q)\subseteq A_4$. Then factor $\overline f$ modulo two unramified primes to find a $4$-cycle and a transposition in $G$, and pin down $G$ with the resolvent cubic (cycle types alone can never rule out $S_4$).
\item Let $f\inZ[x]$ be monic, separable, of degree $7$, with $\overline f$ irreducible mod $11$ and $\overline f$ of cycle type $2+5$ mod $13$ (both primes unramified). Prove that $\Gal(f/Q)=S_7$. State precisely which two group-theoretic facts about transitive subgroups of $S_7$ you are using.
\item Suppose $f\inZ[x]$ is monic separable of degree $5$ and that, over several unramified primes, the cycle types $5$, $2+2+1$, and $5$ all occur, while $\disc(f)$ is a perfect square. Show these data force $G\in\{D_{10},A_5\}$ (the element of type $2+2+1$ already rules out $C_5$) but cannot by themselves distinguish these two, and describe what additional computation (a resolvent of which degree) would separate the solvable case $D_{10}$ from $A_5$.
\item Let $\zeta_{13}$ be a primitive $13$th root of unity and $f(x)$ the minimal polynomial of $\alpha=\zeta_{13}+\zeta_{13}^{-1}$ over $Q$. Determine $\deg f$, prove $\Gal(f/Q)$ is cyclic, and give its order. [Use $\Gal(Q(\zeta_{13})/Q)\cong(Z/(13)Z)^{\times}$ and the order-$2$ subgroup $\{\pm1\}$ (of index $6$).]
\item Let $f(x)=x^4+1$ and let $p$ be an odd prime. Using the fact that $\Gal(f/Q)\cong V_4$, show via Dedekind's theorem that $\overline f$ can never have an irreducible quartic factor mod $p$, and conclude that $\overline f$ factors mod every odd $p$ as a product of linear and/or quadratic factors. Relate the three possible factorization patterns to the three index-$2$ subgroups of $V_4$.
\end{exers}

Then factor $\overline f$ modulo two unramified primes to find a $4$-cycle and a transposition in $G$, and pin down $G$ with the resolvent cubic (cycle types alone can never rule out $S_4$).
\item Let $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be monic, separable, of degree $7$, with $\overline f$ irreducible mod $11$ and $\overline f$ of cycle type $2+5$ mod $13$ (both primes unramified). Prove that $\Gal(f/\mathbb{Q})=S_7$. State precisely which two group-theoretic facts about transitive subgroups of $S_7$ you are using.
\item Suppose $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is monic separable of degree $5$ and that, over several unramified primes, the cycle types $5$, $2+2+1$, and $5$ all occur, while $\disc(f)$ is a perfect square. Show these data force $G\in\{D_{10},A_5\}$ (the element of type $2+2+1$ already rules out $C_5$) but cannot by themselves distinguish these two, and describe what additional computation (a resolvent of which degree) would separate the solvable case $D_{10}$ from $A_5$.
\item Let $\zeta_{13}$ be a primitive $13$th root of unity and $f(x)$ the minimal polynomial of $\alpha=\zeta_{13}+\zeta_{13}^{-1}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Determine $\deg f$, prove $\Gal(f/\mathbb{Q})$ is cyclic, and give its order. [Use $\Gal(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{13})/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/(13)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and the order-$2$ subgroup $\{\pm1\}$ (of index $6$).]
\item Let $f(x)=x^4+1$ and let $p$ be an odd prime. Using the fact that $\Gal(f/\mathbb{Q})\cong V_4$, show via Dedekind's theorem that $\overline f$ can never have an irreducible quartic factor mod $p$, and conclude that $\overline f$ factors mod every odd $p$ as a product of linear and/or quadratic factors. Relate the three possible factorization patterns to the three index-$2$ subgroups of $V_4$.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $f(x)=x^4-2$ with splitting field $K=Q(\sqrt[4]{2},i)$, so $G=\Gal(K/Q)\cong D_8$ (the dihedral group of order $8$, realized as a transitive subgroup of $S_4$). Complete the subgroup lattice of $D_8$ on the left and the corresponding subfield lattice on the right, labelling each field with its degree over $Q$ and proving the indicated correspondence is order-reversing:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.3em]
& D_8 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
H_1 \arrow[dr,dash] & \langle r\rangle\congZ/(4)Z \arrow[d,dash] & H_2 \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& \langle r^2\rangle \arrow[d,dash] & \\
& 1 &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.3em]
& Q \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
Q(\sqrt2) \arrow[dr,dash] & Q(i) \arrow[d,dash] & Q(\sqrt{-2}) \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& Q(\sqrt2,i) \arrow[d,dash] & \\
& K &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Here $H_1,H_2$ are the two Klein-four subgroups of $D_8$. Identify $H_1,H_2$ as concrete subgroups of $S_4$, verify $\Fix(\langle r^2\rangle)=Q(\sqrt2,i)$, and explain why $\langle r\rangle$ corresponds to the quadratic field $Q(i)$, while the field $Q(\sqrt{\disc f})=Q(\sqrt{-2})$ cut out by the discriminant ($\disc f=-2^{11}$) corresponds to $H_2=D_8\cap A_4$.
\item Let $f$ be an irreducible quartic with $G=\Gal(f/Q)\cong A_4$ and splitting field $K$. The resolvent cubic $g$ is irreducible with square discriminant, so its splitting field $M=\Fix(V_4)$ is a cyclic cubic over $Q$. Draw the diagram exhibiting $M$ as the fixed field of $V_4\nor A_4$ and prove $\Gal(M/Q)\cong A_4/V_4\congZ/(3)Z$ by completing the quotient square:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A_4 \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"q"] \arrow[d,equal] & A_4/V_4 \arrow[d,"\cong"] \\
\Gal(K/Q) \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"res"'] & \Gal(M/Q)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State why $A_4$ has no subgroup of index $2$, and conclude that $K$ has no quadratic subfield over $Q$ (so the only proper normal subextension of small degree is the cyclic cubic $M$).
\item Let $L/Q$ be Galois with $\Gal(L/Q)\cong S_3$, arising as the splitting field of an irreducible cubic $h$ with non-square discriminant $D$. Complete the lattice below, where $Q(\sqrt D)=\Fix(A_3)$ is the unique quadratic subfield and $Q(\theta_i)=\Fix(\langle \tau_i\rangle)$ are the three conjugate non-normal cubic root fields, and prove that exactly one of the four proper intermediate fields is normal over $Q$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.2em]
& & 1 \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & \\
\langle \tau_1\rangle \arrow[drr,dash] & \langle \tau_2\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & & \langle \tau_3\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] & A_3 \arrow[dll,dash] \\
& & S_3 & &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.2em]
& & L \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & \\
Q(\theta_1) \arrow[drr,dash] & Q(\theta_2) \arrow[dr,dash] & & Q(\theta_3) \arrow[dl,dash] & Q(\sqrt D) \arrow[dll,dash] \\
& & Q & &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Show $[Q(\theta_i):Q]=3$ and $[Q(\sqrt D):Q]=2$, and explain via the Galois correspondence why the cubic fields are not normal over $Q$ while $Q(\sqrt D)$ is.
\item Let $K$ be the splitting field of a monic separable $f\inZ[x]$ and let $p\nmid\disc(f)$ with Frobenius $\Frob_p\in\Gal(K/Q)$ acting on the roots with cycle type $(d_1,\dots,d_k)$. For each fixed-point-free arrangement, draw the diagram relating the decomposition group $D_{\mathfrak p}=\langle \Frob_p\rangle$ at a prime $\mathfrak p\mid p$ of $K$ to the factorization of $p$ in the root field $Q(\alpha)=\Fix(G_\alpha)$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
D_{\mathfrak p}=\langle \Frob_p\rangle \arrow[r,"\Fix"] \arrow[d,dash] & K^{D_{\mathfrak p}} \arrow[d,dash] \\
G \arrow[r,"\Fix"] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove that the residue degrees of the primes of $Q(\alpha)$ above $p$ equal the lengths $d_i$ of the orbits of $\langle \Frob_p\rangle$ on the cosets $G/G_\alpha$, and confirm $\sum_i d_i=\deg f$.
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Algebraic independence and transcendence degree
Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
A subset $S=\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}\subseteq K$ is algebraically independent over $F$ if there is no nonzero polynomial $g\in F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $g(t_1,\dots,t_n)=0$; equivalently, the evaluation map $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to K$ is injective. A maximal algebraically independent subset of $K$ is a transcendence basis of $K/F$, and its cardinality is the transcendence degree $\operatorname{trdeg}_F K$. The extension is purely transcendental if $K=F(S)$ for some algebraically independent $S$, so that $K$ is $F$-isomorphic to a rational function field $F(x_1,\dots,x_n)$.
\end{definition}

Content:
A single element $t$ is algebraically independent over $F$ precisely when it is transcendental over $F$ in the old sense (no $g(t)=0$ for $g\ne0$ in one variable). The leap is that algebraic independence is exactly the field-theoretic analogue of linear independence: it satisfies an exchange property, so all maximal independent sets have the same size, just as for a vector-space basis.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Algebraic independence and transcendence degree
Type: theorem
Title: {the exchange lemma and well-definedness of transcendence degree}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{the exchange lemma and well-definedness of transcendence degree}]
Algebraic dependence is a matroid (it satisfies the Steinitz exchange axiom). Consequently any two transcendence bases of $K/F$ have the same cardinality, so $\operatorname{trdeg}_F K$ is well defined. Moreover $\operatorname{trdeg}$ is additive in towers: for $F\subseteq L\subseteq K$,
\[
\operatorname{trdeg}_F K=\operatorname{trdeg}_F L+\operatorname{trdeg}_L K .
\]
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Algebraic independence and transcendence degree
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-e0914e94c0dba866402a
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Call $\alpha$ dependent on a set $T$ if $\alpha$ is algebraic over $F(T)$. The Steinitz exchange axiom says: if $\alpha$ is dependent on $T\cup\{\beta\}$ but not on $T$, then $\beta$ is dependent on $T\cup\{\alpha\}$ -- this follows by clearing denominators in the polynomial relation witnessing the dependence and solving for $\beta$, which now appears to positive degree. Exchange forces all maximal independent sets to be equinumerous by the usual replacement argument (replace the elements of one basis one at a time by elements of another). Additivity in towers: concatenate a transcendence basis $S$ of $L/F$ with a transcendence basis $T$ of $K/L$. The union is algebraically independent over $F$: a relation $g(S,T)=0$ with $g$ over $F$, read as a polynomial in the elements of $T$ with coefficients in $F[S]\subseteq L$, has all these coefficients equal to $0$ because $T$ is independent over $L$, and then each coefficient is the zero polynomial because $S$ is independent over $F$. Maximality follows from transitivity of ``algebraic over'': $K$ is algebraic over $L(T)$, which is algebraic over $F(S\cup T)$ because $L$ is algebraic over $F(S)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{wex}{Transcendence degree of a rational function field}
Show $\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x,y)=2$, where $x,y$ are independent transcendentals.
\wrec By definition $x,y$ independent means no nonzero $g\in F[X,Y]$ has $g(x,y)=0$; this is exactly the statement that $\{x,y\}$ is algebraically independent, and it is maximal because $F(x,y)$ is algebraic over itself.
\wsol The set $\{x,y\}$ is algebraically independent over $F$ by hypothesis, so $\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x,y)\ge2$. It is maximal: any third element $z\in F(x,y)$ is a rational function $z=p(x,y)/q(x,y)$, hence satisfies $q(x,y)\,z-p(x,y)=0$, a nonzero polynomial relation among $x,y,z$ over $F$. So $\{x,y\}$ is a transcendence basis and $\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x,y)=2$. Sanity check: additivity gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x,y)=\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x)+\operatorname{trdeg}_{F(x)}F(x)(y)=1+1=2$, since $y$ is transcendental over $F(x)$.
\end{wex}

Title: A dependent set and a transcendence basis inside $F(x)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A dependent set and a transcendence basis inside $F(x)$}
Show $\{x^2,x^3\}$ is not algebraically independent over $F$, while $\{x\}$ is a transcendence basis of $F(x)/F$.
\wrec Algebraic independence of $\{a,b\}$ fails as soon as one nonzero $g\in F[X,Y]$ kills $(a,b)$; here a single relation between $x^2$ and $x^3$ is visible.
\wsol Put $a=x^2,\ b=x^3$. Then $a^3=x^6=b^2$, so $g(X,Y)=X^3-Y^2$ is a nonzero polynomial with $g(a,b)=0$. Hence $\{x^2,x^3\}$ is algebraically dependent; its transcendence degree is only $1$ (both lie in $F(x)$, which has transcendence degree $1$). On the other hand $\{x\}$ is algebraically independent (a single transcendental) and maximal, because every element of $F(x)$ is algebraic -- indeed rational -- over $F(x)$. So $\operatorname{trdeg}_F F(x)=1$. Sanity check: $F(x^2,x^3)=F(x)$ since $x=x^3/x^2$, so adjoining the dependent pair recovers the whole field, confirming both generate a transcendence-degree-$1$ extension, not $2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Transcendence degree is insensitive to algebraic extensions
Content:
\begin{wex}{Transcendence degree is insensitive to algebraic extensions}
Let $K=F(x,y)$ and let $L=K(\sqrt{x})=F(\sqrt{x},y)$. Compute $\operatorname{trdeg}_F L$.
\wrec Adjoining an algebraic element changes the algebraic part of an extension but not its transcendence degree, by additivity in the tower $F\subseteq K\subseteq L$ with $\operatorname{trdeg}_K L=0$.
\wsol Let $u=\sqrt{x}$, so $u^2=x$ and $u$ is algebraic over $K$. Then $L=K(u)$ is algebraic over $K$, giving $\operatorname{trdeg}_K L=0$. By additivity $\operatorname{trdeg}_F L=\operatorname{trdeg}_F K+\operatorname{trdeg}_K L=2+0=2$. A transcendence basis is $\{u,y\}$: indeed $x=u^2\in F(u,y)$ and $L=F(u,y)$ is purely transcendental of degree $2$ in $u,y$. Sanity check: $\{x,y\}$ and $\{u,y\}$ are both transcendence bases of $L$, each of size $2$, consistent with well-definedness; the only change is that $L/F(u,y)$ is trivial whereas $L/F(x,y)$ is algebraic of degree $2$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Algebraic independence and transcendence degree
Type: example
Title: An elliptic relation: a non-purely-transcendental extension
Content:
\begin{wex}{An elliptic relation: a non-purely-transcendental extension}
Show $Q\bigl(k,\sqrt{k^3-k}\bigr)$ has transcendence degree $1$ over $Q$ but is not purely transcendental.
\wrec Transcendence degree is computed by a greedy basis; pure transcendentality is a finer property that can fail even at degree $1$, detected by an irreducible relation of the wrong shape (an elliptic curve has genus $1$, not $0$).
\wsol Let $y=\sqrt{k^3-k}$, so $y^2=k^3-k$ with $k$ transcendental over $Q$. Then $\{k\}$ is a transcendence basis: $y$ is algebraic of degree $2$ over $Q(k)$, so $\operatorname{trdeg}_QQ(k,y)=1$. It is not purely transcendental: a purely transcendental degree-$1$ field is $Q(z)$, a rational function field, whose associated curve has genus $0$, whereas $y^2=k^3-k$ defines a smooth cubic (an elliptic curve) of genus $1$; a field of genus $1$ cannot equal one of genus $0$. Concretely, no rational parametrization $k=\phi(z),\ y=\psi(z)$ with $\phi$ nonconstant exists: it would identify $Q(k,y)$ with a subfield of $Q(z)$ strictly containing $Q$, and by L\"uroth's theorem every such subfield is again a rational function field $Q(w)$, of genus $0$. The obstruction is the genus, not a lack of rational points: the curve contains $(0,0)$, $(\pm1,0)$ and the rational point $[0:1:0]$ at infinity. Sanity check: contrast with $y^2=k^2-k$, which factors via $y=k\sqrt{1-1/k}$ -- a conic, genus $0$, which is rational; the cubic's nonzero discriminant $\disc(k^3-k)=-4(-1)^3=4\neq0$ confirms $y^2=k^3-k$ is genuinely elliptic, not a degenerate conic.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}
A transcendence basis $S$ of $K/F$ is a separating transcendence basis if $K$ is a (finite) separable algebraic extension of $F(S)$. When such a basis exists, $K/F$ is called separably generated.
\end{definition}

Type: example
Title: A separating transcendence basis exists
Content:
\begin{wex}{A separating transcendence basis exists}
Let $K=\F_p(t)(\alpha)$ where $\alpha^2-\alpha-t=0$ and $p$ is odd. Exhibit a separating transcendence basis.
\wrec An Artin--Schreier-type relation $\alpha^2-\alpha-t=0$ is separable when its derivative in $\alpha$ is nonzero; we look for a transcendental base leaving a separable residual extension.
\wsol Here $\{t\}$ is a transcendence basis and $\alpha$ is algebraic over $\F_p(t)$ with minimal polynomial $f(x)=x^2-x-t$. Its derivative $f'(x)=2x-1$ is nonzero ($p$ odd), and $\gcd(f,f')=1$, so $f$ is separable and $K/\F_p(t)$ is separable. Thus $\{t\}$ is a separating transcendence basis. Sanity check: alternatively take $\{\alpha\}$ as the basis -- then $t=\alpha^2-\alpha\in\F_p(\alpha)$ so $K=\F_p(\alpha)$ is purely transcendental in $\alpha$, hence trivially separable over $\F_p(\alpha)$; either basis separates.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: No separating transcendence base: infinitely many $p$-power roots
Content:
\begin{wex}{No separating transcendence base: infinitely many $p$-power roots}
Let $K=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\F_p\bigl(t^{1/p^k}\bigr)$, the field obtained from $\F_p(t)$ by adjoining all $p$-power roots of $t$. Show $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\F_p}K=1$ but $K/\F_p$ has no separating transcendence base.
\wrec Transcendence degree counts independent transcendentals; a separating base would make $K$ separable over a rational function field, but every element here has a $p$-th root in $K$, an obstruction to separability.
\wsol Each $t^{1/p^k}$ is transcendental over $\F_p$, and any two of them are algebraically dependent ($t^{1/p^k}=(t^{1/p^{k+1}})^p$), so $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\F_p}K=1$; e.g.\ $\{t\}$ is a transcendence basis. Suppose $\{u\}$ were a separating transcendence base, so $K/\F_p(u)$ is separable algebraic. Every element of $K$ is a $p$-th power in $K$: if $a=r(t^{1/p^k})$ with $r\in\F_p(X)$, then $a=\bigl(r(t^{1/p^{k+1}})\bigr)^p$, since the Frobenius fixes the coefficients of $r$. In particular $v=u^{1/p}\in K$. But $v$ is a root of $x^p-u=(x-v)^p$, which is irreducible over $\F_p(u)$ because the transcendental $u$ is not a $p$-th power in $\F_p(u)$; so $v$ is inseparable over $\F_p(u)$, a contradiction. Hence no separating base exists. Sanity check: $K$ being closed under $p$-th roots means $K=K^{1/p}$, the exact failure of separable generation; this matches that $K$ is not finitely generated over $\F_p$, the hypothesis under which separating bases are guaranteed over perfect fields.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
Let $K/F$ be finite and fix an algebraic closure $\overline F\supseteq K$. The separable degree $[K:F]_s$ is the number of $F$-embeddings $K\hookrightarrow\overline F$. The inseparable degree is the quotient $[K:F]_i=[K:F]/[K:F]_s$.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Separable and inseparable degree
Type: theorem
Title: {multiplicativity and the degree factorization}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{multiplicativity and the degree factorization}]
For finite extensions $F\subseteq L\subseteq K$:
\[
[K:F]_s=[K:L]_s\,[L:F]_s,\qquad
[K:F]=[K:F]_s\,[K:F]_i,
\]
and $[K:F]_i$ is always a power of $p=\charac F$ (and $=1$ in characteristic $0$). The extension $K/F$ is separable iff $[K:F]_s=[K:F]$, equivalently $[K:F]_i=1$.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Separable and inseparable degree
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-67a9fff176632ae882f2
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
For a simple extension $F(\alpha)/F$ with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$, the $F$-embeddings into $\overline F$ are in bijection with the distinct roots of $m_\alpha$, so $[F(\alpha):F]_s$ counts distinct roots while $[F(\alpha):F]=\deg m_\alpha$ counts roots with multiplicity. In characteristic $p$, $m_\alpha(x)=g(x^{p^e})$ for a separable $g$, and every root has the same multiplicity $p^e$, so $[F(\alpha):F]_i=p^e$. Multiplicativity of $[\cdot:\cdot]_s$ comes from extending embeddings step by step through a tower (each of the $[L:F]_s$ embeddings of $L$ extends in exactly $[K:L]_s$ ways to $K$). Dividing the multiplicative relation for ordinary degree by that for separable degree gives multiplicativity of the inseparable degree, hence $[K:F]_i$ is a product of prime-power local inseparable degrees, a power of $p$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Separable degree equals degree for a separable extension
Content:
\begin{wex}{Separable degree equals degree for a separable extension}
Compute $[Q(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega):Q]_s$, where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$.
\wrec In characteristic $0$ every extension is separable, so $[K:F]_s=[K:F]$ and $[K:F]_i=1$; we only need the ordinary degree.
\wsol $K=Q(\sqrt[3]2,\omega)$ is the splitting field of $x^3-2$, with $[K:Q]=6$. Since $\characQ=0$, $K/Q$ is separable, so $[K:Q]_s=6$ and $[K:Q]_i=1$. Sanity check: $K/Q$ is Galois with $\Gal(K/Q)\cong S_3$ of order $6$, and the number of $Q$-embeddings of a Galois extension into $\overlineQ$ equals $\abs{\Gal(K/Q)}=6=[K:Q]_s$, exactly as the separable degree should.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Separable and inseparable degree
Type: example
Title: A mixed example: computing $[K:F]_s$ and $[K:F]_i$
Content:
\begin{wex}{A mixed example: computing $[K:F]_s$ and $[K:F]_i$}
Let $p$ be a prime, $F=\F_p(s,t)$ with $s,t$ independent transcendentals, and $K=F(\alpha,\beta)$ where $\alpha^p=s$ and $\beta^2-\beta-t=0$ (take $p$ odd). Find $[K:F]$, $[K:F]_s$, $[K:F]_i$.
\wrec Factor through the tower $F\subseteq F(\alpha)\subseteq K$. The first step $x^p-s$ is purely inseparable (one repeated root), contributing to $[\cdot:\cdot]_i$; the second step $x^2-x-t$ is separable, contributing to $[\cdot:\cdot]_s$.
\wsol Step one: $x^p-s$ is irreducible over $F$ (Eisenstein at the prime $s$ in $\F_p[s][t]$-localized, or since $s$ is not a $p$-th power in $F$) and equals $(x-\alpha)^p$ over $\overline F$, so $[F(\alpha):F]=p$ with a single root: $[F(\alpha):F]_s=1$, $[F(\alpha):F]_i=p$. Step two: $x^2-x-t$ has derivative $2x-1\ne0$, hence is separable of degree $2$ over $F(\alpha)$: $[K:F(\alpha)]=[K:F(\alpha)]_s=2$, $[K:F(\alpha)]_i=1$. Multiplying: $[K:F]=p\cdot2=2p$, $[K:F]_s=1\cdot2=2$, $[K:F]_i=p\cdot1=p$. Sanity check: $[K:F]_s\cdot[K:F]_i=2\cdot p=2p=[K:F]$, and $[K:F]_i=p$ is a power of $p$, both as required.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Separable and inseparable degree each equal $p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Separable and inseparable degree each equal $p$}
Let $K=\F_p(x,y)$ with $x,y$ independent transcendentals and $F=\F_p(x^p-x,\ y^p-x)$. Show $[K:F]=p^2$ with $[K:F]_s=[K:F]_i=p$.
\wrec Write $s=x^p-x$ and $t=y^p-x$. Then $x$ is a root of a separable polynomial over $F$, while $y$ is a $p$-th root, the inseparable layer; build the tower so each layer's type is visible.
\wsol Over $F=\F_p(s,t)$, the element $x$ satisfies $x^p-x-s=0$, an Artin--Schreier polynomial: separable (derivative $px^{p-1}-1=-1\ne0$) and irreducible of degree $p$, so $[F(x):F]=[F(x):F]_s=p$ with $[F(x):F]_i=1$. Now over $F(x)$ we have $y^p=t+x$, i.e.\ $y$ is a root of $z^p-(t+x)=(z-y)^p$: purely inseparable of degree $p$, so $[K:F(x)]=[K:F(x)]_i=p$, $[K:F(x)]_s=1$. Hence $[K:F]=p\cdot p=p^2$, $[K:F]_s=p\cdot1=p$, $[K:F]_i=1\cdot p=p$. Sanity check: $[K:F]_s\,[K:F]_i=p\cdot p=p^2=[K:F]$; and $s-t=(x^p-x)-(y^p-x)=x^p-y^p=(x-y)^p\in F$, so $E=F(x-y)$ is a $p$-th root extension realizing the purely inseparable degree-$p$ piece, consistent with $[K:F]_i=p$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
An algebraic extension $K/F$ of characteristic $p$ is purely inseparable if every $\alpha\in K$ has $\alpha^{p^k}\in F$ for some $k\ge0$; equivalently the minimal polynomial of each $\alpha$ over $F$ has the form $x^{p^k}-a$. Then $[K:F]_s=1$, so $K/F$ admits only the identity embedding and $\Aut(K/F)=1$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {purely inseparable means trivial separable degree}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{purely inseparable means trivial separable degree}]
A finite extension $K/F$ is purely inseparable iff $[K:F]_s=1$, iff $[K:F]=[K:F]_i$. In that case $[K:F]$ is a power of $p$ and $\Aut(K/F)=\{\id\}$.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-9306656091b571a53f29
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
If $\alpha^{p^k}=a\in F$ then $m_\alpha\mid x^{p^k}-a=(x-\alpha)^{p^k}$, so $\alpha$ is the only root: one embedding. Conversely if $[K:F]_s=1$ each generator has a single root in $\overline F$, forcing minimal polynomials of the shape $(x-\alpha)^{p^k}$, i.e.\ $x^{p^k}-\alpha^{p^k}$ with $\alpha^{p^k}\in F$. Finally, every $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$, followed by the inclusion $K\subseteq\overline F$, is an $F$-embedding $K\hookrightarrow\overline F$; the inclusion is the only one, so $\sigma=\id$ and $\Aut(K/F)=1$.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
A field $F$ is perfect if every algebraic extension of $F$ is separable. Characteristic $0$ fields are perfect; a characteristic $p$ field $F$ is perfect iff the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ is surjective, i.e.\ $F=F^p$. Finite fields and algebraically closed fields are perfect.
\end{definition}

Type: example
Title: The purely inseparable extension $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$ of degree $p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The purely inseparable extension $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$ of degree $p$}
Show $K=\F_p(t^{1/p})$ is purely inseparable of degree $p$ over $F=\F_p(t)$ with $\Aut(K/F)=1$, even though $K/F$ is normal.
\wrec $t$ is not a $p$-th power in $F=\F_p(t)$, so $x^p-t$ is irreducible; in characteristic $p$ it factors as $(x-t^{1/p})^p$, the signature of pure inseparability.
\wsol Let $\theta=t^{1/p}$, so $\theta^p=t$. Over $F$, $x^p-t=(x-\theta)^p$ has $\theta$ as its only root, with multiplicity $p$. The polynomial is irreducible (Eisenstein at $t$ in $\F_p[t]$), so $[K:F]=p$, $[K:F]_s=1$, $[K:F]_i=p$: purely inseparable. Any $\sigma\in\Aut(K/F)$ must send $\theta$ to a root of $x^p-t$, but $\theta$ is the only root, so $\sigma(\theta)=\theta$ and $\sigma=\id$. Thus $\Aut(K/F)=1$. Yet $K/F$ is normal: $K$ is the splitting field of $x^p-t$ (it splits completely, as $(x-\theta)^p$). Sanity check: $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=1\ne p=[K:F]$, so the would-be ``Galois group'' is too small -- this is precisely why normal $+$ inseparable is not Galois; the count $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=[K:F]$ holds only when $K/F$ is also separable.
\end{wex}

Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > Purely inseparable extensions and perfect fields
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Normal'' does not imply ``Galois.'' The extension $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$ is normal (it is a splitting field) but $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=1<p=[K:F]$. Galois requires normal and separable; equivalently $\abs{\Aut(K/F)}=[K:F]$, which forces $[K:F]_s=[K:F]$. Whenever an extension has nontrivial inseparable degree, its automorphism group is strictly too small to ``see'' the whole extension.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: A perfect field: $F=F^p$ for finite fields
Content:
\begin{wex}{A perfect field: $F=F^p$ for finite fields}
Verify that $\F_q$ ($q=p^n$) is perfect by checking Frobenius is surjective.
\wrec A characteristic-$p$ field is perfect iff $x\mapsto x^p$ is onto; on a finite field an injective endomorphism is automatically onto.
\wsol Frobenius $\phi:\F_q\to\F_q$, $\phi(a)=a^p$, is a field homomorphism, hence injective (its kernel is $0$). An injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective, so $\phi$ is onto: $\F_q=\F_q^p$. Therefore $\F_q$ is perfect and every algebraic extension of $\F_q$ is separable. Sanity check: concretely in $\F_p$, $a^p=a$ for all $a$ (Fermat), so $\phi=\id$ is trivially surjective; and there are no purely inseparable extensions of a finite field, consistent with $\overline{\F_p}/\F_p$ being separable.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: An imperfect field and its separable closure
Content:
\begin{wex}{An imperfect field and its separable closure}
Show $F=\F_p(t)$ is not perfect, and describe the separable closure of $F$ inside a purely inseparable extension.
\wrec $F$ imperfect means $F\ne F^p$: some element is not a $p$-th power. The separable closure $F^{sep}$ of $F$ in $\overline F$ collects all elements separable over $F$; purely inseparable elements lie outside it.
\wsol In $F=\F_p(t)$, the element $t$ is not a $p$-th power: if $t=g(t)^p$ for $g\in F$, comparing degrees forces $1=p\deg g$, impossible. So $F\ne F^p$ and $F$ is imperfect. Inside $\overline F$, $F^{sep}=\{\alpha\in\overline F:\alpha separable over F\}$ is a field (the separable elements form a subfield), and $\overline F/F^{sep}$ is purely inseparable. The element $t^{1/p}$ is not in $F^{sep}$: its minimal polynomial $x^p-t=(x-t^{1/p})^p$ is inseparable. Sanity check: $[F^{sep}:F]=[\overline F:F]_s$ and $[\overline F:F^{sep}]=[\overline F:F]_i$, factoring the closure into its separable-then-purely-inseparable layers; over the perfect field $\F_p$ this inseparable layer is trivial, matching the previous example.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Every purely inseparable extension is normal
Content:
\begin{wex}{Every purely inseparable extension is normal}
Prove that a purely inseparable extension $K/F$ is normal.
\wrec Normal means every irreducible polynomial over $F$ with a root in $K$ splits in $K$. For purely inseparable $K/F$ the minimal polynomials have the single-root form $(x-\alpha)^{p^k}$, which trivially splits once it has one root.
\wsol Let $\alpha\in K$ with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha\in F[x]$. By pure inseparability $\alpha^{p^k}=a\in F$ for some $k$, so $m_\alpha\mid x^{p^k}-a=(x-\alpha)^{p^k}$; being irreducible and monic, $m_\alpha=(x-\alpha)^{p^j}$ for some $j\le k$. This polynomial splits completely in $K$ (all roots equal $\alpha\in K$). Since every such $m_\alpha$ splits in $K$, the extension $K/F$ is normal. Sanity check: this matches the example $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$, which we already saw is a splitting field (of $x^p-t$), hence normal -- normality holds despite the trivial automorphism group.
\end{wex}

Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > The Krull topology and profinite Galois groups
Type: definition
Content:
\begin{definition}
Let $K/F$ be Galois, possibly infinite. The Krull topology on $G=\Gal(K/F)$ has, as a base of open neighborhoods of $\id$, the subgroups $\Gal(K/E)$ where $E/F$ ranges over the finite Galois subextensions $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$. These subgroups are normal of finite index, and $G$ becomes a Hausdorff, compact, totally disconnected topological group.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > The Krull topology and profinite Galois groups
Type: theorem
Title: {$\Gal(K/F)$ is profinite}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$\Gal(K/F)$ is profinite}]
For $K/F$ Galois, $\Gal(K/F)$ is the inverse limit of the finite Galois groups of its finite subextensions:
\[
\Gal(K/F)\ \cong\ \varprojlim_{E}\ \Gal(E/F),
\]
the limit taken over finite Galois $E/F$ inside $K$, with transition maps the restriction homomorphisms $\Gal(E'/F)\twoheadrightarrow\Gal(E/F)$ for $E\subseteq E'$. The Krull topology coincides with the inverse-limit (subspace of product) topology, making $G$ a profinite group: compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-7322cfc4f0167e11d7fe
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
An automorphism $\sigma\in\Gal(K/F)$ is determined by its restrictions $\sigma|_E$ to all finite Galois $E/F$, and these restrictions are compatible: $(\sigma|_{E'})|_E=\sigma|_E$ for $E\subseteq E'$. This is exactly the data of an element of the inverse limit, giving an injective homomorphism $\sigma\mapsto(\sigma|_E)_E$. It is surjective because a compatible system glues to a well-defined automorphism of $K=\bigcup_E E$. The product $\prod_E\Gal(E/F)$ of finite (discrete) groups is compact by Tychonoff; the inverse limit is a closed subset, hence compact, and the subspace topology is the Krull topology.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > The Krull topology and profinite Galois groups
Type: theorem
Title: {Fundamental Theorem for infinite Galois extensions}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Fundamental Theorem for infinite Galois extensions}]
Let $K/F$ be Galois with group $G=\Gal(K/F)$ carrying the Krull topology. Then
\[
\{closed subgroups H\sgr G\}\ \xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\ \{intermediate fields F\sgr E\sgr K\}
\]
is an inclusion-reversing bijection, $H\mapsto\Fix(H)$ and $E\mapsto\Gal(K/E)$. Under it:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item open subgroups correspond to finite-degree subextensions $E/F$;
\item closed normal subgroups correspond to Galois subextensions $E/F$, with $\Gal(E/F)\cong G/\Gal(K/E)$.
\end{enumerate}
Every open subgroup is closed of finite index, but not every (abstract) finite-index subgroup is open; the correspondence sees only closed subgroups.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-74e6b5d190099c90dedb
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The finite case applies to each finite Galois layer $E/F$; passing to the limit, $\Gal(K/E)$ is closed (the intersection, over all $\alpha\in E$, of the open subgroups $\Gal(K/F(\alpha))$; $E/F$ need not be finitely generated). Closedness of $H$ is exactly the condition $H=\Gal(K/\Fix(H))$, i.e.\ that no extra automorphisms ``approximate'' $H$ in the Krull topology. For closed $H$: open $\iff$ finite index $\iff$ contains some $\Gal(K/E)$ with $E/F$ finite, which translates to $\Fix(H)/F$ finite. Normality and the quotient identification descend from the finite layers.
\end{proof}
