Type: example
Title: The absolute Galois group of a finite field is $\widehat{Z}$
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{wex}{The absolute Galois group of a finite field is $\widehat{Z}$}
Identify $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$ as a profinite group and locate the Frobenius.
\wrec $\overline{\F_p}=\bigcup_n\F_{p^n}$ with each $\F_{p^n}/\F_p$ finite Galois cyclic of order $n$; the absolute group is the inverse limit of these $Z/(n)Z$ under restriction, which is $\widehatZ=\varprojlimZ/(n)Z$.
\wsol The finite Galois subextensions of $\overline{\F_p}/\F_p$ are the $\F_{p^n}$, with $\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)\congZ/(n)Z$ generated by the Frobenius $\Frob_p:x\mapsto x^p$. For $n\mid m$, restriction $\Gal(\F_{p^m}/\F_p)\to\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)$ is the natural surjection $Z/(m)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$ sending Frobenius to Frobenius. Hence
\[
\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)\ \cong\ \varprojlim_{n}Z/(n)Z\ =\ \widehatZ,
\]
topologically generated by $\Frob_p=(\,1\bmod n\,)_n$: the closure of $\langle \Frob_p\rangle$ is all of $\widehatZ$. The inverse system of restriction maps is:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.6em]
& Z/(12)Z \arrow[dl,twoheadrightarrow]\arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow] & \\
Z/(4)Z \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] & & Z/(6)Z \arrow[dll,twoheadrightarrow]\arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] \\
Z/(2)Z \arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow] & & Z/(3)Z \arrow[dl,twoheadrightarrow] \\
& Z/(1)Z &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Gal(\,\cdot\,/\F_p)\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.6em]
& \F_{p^{12}} \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\F_{p^{4}} \arrow[d,dash] & & \F_{p^{6}} \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[d,dash] \\
\F_{p^{2}} \arrow[dr,dash] & & \F_{p^{3}} \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& \F_{p} &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left diagram contains finite cyclic groups $Z/(n)Z$ for various $n$ (here
$n\in\{1,2,3,4,6,12\}$), each of which is the Galois group $\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)$ of a finite
subextension; each node is a finite group, a quotient of $\widehatZ$. The right diagram contains finite fields $\F_{p^n}$ arranged by inclusion; each node is a finite
field extension of $\F_p$ of degree $n$. The two lattices are placed in bijective correspondence by the Galois pairing: groups on the left,
fields on the right.

\dgi{Arrows:} Left side: every arrow $Z/(m)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$ (when $n\mid m$) is the
restriction homomorphism $\Gal(\F_{p^m}/\F_p)\to\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)$, concretely the reduction
map sending $[k\bmod m]\mapsto[k\bmod n]$; it is surjective (indicated by the double-headed arrow). Right side: each dash-arrow $\F_{p^n}\to\F_{p^m}$ (when $n\mid m$) is the unique field
inclusion $\F_{p^n}\hookrightarrow\F_{p^m}$; these are the transition maps going in the opposite
direction from the group maps. The horizontal double-arrow $\xleftrightarrow{\ \Gal(\,\cdot\,/\F_p)\ }$ records that the two lattices are matched
node by node by $\F_{p^n}\mapsto\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)\cong\widehatZ/n\widehatZ$. This is not the Galois correspondence
itself: $H\mapsto\Fix(H)$, $E\mapsto\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/E)$ pairs $\F_{p^n}$ with the closed subgroup
$n\widehatZ=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^n})$, the kernel of $\widehatZ\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$.

\dgi{What commutes:} The diagram encodes compatibility of restrictions: for $n\mid m\mid r$,
the composite restriction $Z/(r)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(m)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$ equals the
direct restriction $Z/(r)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$, i.e.\ reduction mod $r$ then mod $m$ then
mod $n$ equals reduction mod $r$ then mod $n$ directly, because $n\mid m\mid r$ makes
$k\bmod n = (k\bmod m)\bmod n$. This is the inverse-system compatibility condition whose limit defines $\widehatZ$.

\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generator: the Frobenius $\Frob_p$ corresponds to $1$ in each
$Z/(n)Z$. Along the path $Z/(12)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(4)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(2)Z$, the element
$1\inZ/(12)Z$ maps to $1\inZ/(4)Z$ then to $1\inZ/(2)Z$. Along the direct path $Z/(12)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(2)Z$, $1$ maps to $1\inZ/(2)Z$ immediately. Both give $1\inZ/(2)Z$ because $1\bmod 4 = 1$ and $1\bmod 2 = 1$; reduction is transitive. The right-hand inclusion lattice commutes for the dual reason: $\F_{p^2}\subseteq\F_{p^4}\subseteq\F_{p^{12}}$
and $\F_{p^2}\subseteq\F_{p^{12}}$ are the same inclusion.

\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the key visual for why $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)\cong\widehatZ$:
it shows that the entire absolute Galois group is completely controlled by the finite pieces $Z/(n)Z$
and their compatible restriction maps. An element of $\widehatZ$ is precisely a compatible system of residues $(a_n\inZ/(n)Z)_n$ with
$a_n\equiv a_m\pmod{n}$ for $n\mid m$, which is exactly what Frobenius gives:
$a_n = 1\bmod n$ for all $n$. The paired lattice also makes the Fundamental Theorem for $\overline{\F_p}/\F_p$ visible in one picture:
larger quotients $Z/(n)Z$ on the left sit beside larger fields $\F_{p^n}$ on the right, while the closed
subgroups $n\widehatZ$ fixing these fields get smaller (fewer automorphisms fix more elements).

\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $n=2$, $m=6$: $Z/(6)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(2)Z$ sends $[1]\mapsto[1]$,
$[2]\mapsto[0]$, $[3]\mapsto[1]$, etc.\ (reduce mod $2$), and the corresponding field inclusion is
$\F_{p^2}\hookrightarrow\F_{p^6}$.

$a_n = 1\bmod n$ for all $n$. The paired lattice also makes the Fundamental Theorem for $\overline{\F_p}/\F_p$ visible in one picture:
larger quotients $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ on the left sit beside larger fields $\F_{p^n}$ on the right, while the closed
subgroups $n\widehat\mathbb{Z}$ fixing these fields get smaller (fewer automorphisms fix more elements).

\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $n=2$, $m=6$: $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ sends $[1]\mapsto[1]$,
$[2]\mapsto[0]$, $[3]\mapsto[1]$, etc.\ (reduce mod $2$), and the corresponding field inclusion is
$\F_{p^2}\hookrightarrow\F_{p^6}$.

Title: The absolute Galois group of a finite field is $\widehat{Z}$
Part: 2/2
Content:
The Frobenius $\Frob_p\in\Gal(\F_{p^6}/\F_p)\congZ/(6)Z$ restricts to $\Frob_p\in\Gal(\F_{p^2}/\F_p)\congZ/(2)Z$:
the $p$-th power map on $\F_{p^6}$ restricts to the $p$-th power map on the subfield $\F_{p^2}$, and $[1\bmod6]$ maps to
$[1\bmod2]$, consistently.

\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the arrows as going in the same direction on both sides. They do not: group restriction maps $Z/(m)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$ go from larger group to smaller
(decreasing $m\to n$ with $n\mid m$), while field inclusions go from smaller field to larger
($\F_{p^n}\hookrightarrow\F_{p^m}$). This reversal is the inclusion-reversing nature of the Galois correspondence; missing it leads to
thinking $\F_{p^{12}}$ is ``killed'' by the largest group, when in fact $\F_{p^{12}}$ is fixed
by the smallest group $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^{12}})$. Also: $\widehatZ$ itself does not appear as a node in the left lattice -- the lattice only shows
the finite quotients; $\widehatZ$ is the limit of the whole diagram, not a single term.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the infinite profinite group $\widehatZ=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$
is completely and faithfully encoded by the finite data on the left -- the lattice of cyclic groups
$Z/(n)Z$ connected by surjective reduction maps -- which is paired arrow-by-arrow with the lattice
of finite fields on the right by $\F_{p^n}\mapsto\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)$.
\end{dgx}
On the left the maps $Z/(m)Z\twoheadrightarrowZ/(n)Z$ (for $n\mid m$) are reduction-of-residues; the limit over all $n$ is $\widehatZ\cong\prod_\ellZ_\ell$. On the right, larger fields sit higher: $\F_{p^n}=\Fix\bigl(\,\overline{\langle \Frob_p^{\,n}\rangle}\,\bigr)$, the closed subgroup $n\widehatZ$. Sanity check: $\widehatZ$ is uncountable and compact, whereas $\langle \Frob_p\rangle\congZ$ is countable -- so Frobenius generates $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$ only topologically (its closure is everything), never as an abstract group; this is exactly the gap between abstract and closed subgroups that the Krull topology fixes.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: An open subgroup and its finite subextension
Content:
\begin{wex}{An open subgroup and its finite subextension}
In $G=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)=\widehatZ$, identify the open subgroup corresponding to $\F_{p^n}$ and its index.
\wrec Open subgroups $\leftrightarrow$ finite-degree subextensions; the subgroup fixing $\F_{p^n}$ is $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^n})$, the closed (and open) subgroup $n\widehatZ\sgr\widehatZ$.
\wsol The intermediate field $\F_{p^n}$ has $[\F_{p^n}:\F_p]=n<\infty$, so it corresponds to an open subgroup $H=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^n})$. As a subgroup of $\widehatZ$ this is $n\widehatZ=\overline{\langle \Frob_p^{\,n}\rangle}$, with $[\widehatZ:n\widehatZ]=n$. Indeed $H\cong\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^n})\cong\widehatZ$ again (generated by $\Frob_{p^n}=\Frob_p^{\,n}$), since $\overline{\F_p}/\F_{p^n}$ has the same shape. Sanity check: the index $n$ equals $[\F_{p^n}:\F_p]=\abs{G/H}$, matching that $G/H\cong\Gal(\F_{p^n}/\F_p)\congZ/(n)Z$ -- the open subgroup has finite index exactly equal to the finite degree it fixes.
\end{wex}

Title: A closed-but-not-open subgroup
Content:
\begin{wex}{A closed-but-not-open subgroup}
Exhibit in $\widehatZ=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$ a closed subgroup of infinite index, and name its fixed field.
\wrec Closed subgroups $\leftrightarrow$ all intermediate fields; an infinite-index closed subgroup fixes an infinite-degree subextension. The $\ell$-part of $\widehatZ$ gives one.
\wsol Fix a prime $\ell$ and let $H=\prod_{q\ne\ell}Z_q\sgr\widehatZ=\prod_qZ_q$ (drop the $\ell$-component). Then $H$ is closed (a product of closed factors), and $[\widehatZ:H]$ is infinite (the quotient is $Z_\ell$, infinite). Its fixed field $\Fix(H)=\bigcup_k\F_{p^{\ell^k}}$ is the union of all $\F_{p^{\ell^k}}$, an infinite algebraic extension of $\F_p$ with $\Gal\congZ_\ell$. This $H$ is not open: open subgroups have finite index. Sanity check: $\Fix(H)/\F_p$ being infinite matches $H$ being closed but not open (item (1) of the Fundamental Theorem); and $\widehatZ/H\congZ_\ell$ is itself profinite, consistent with $\Fix(H)/\F_p$ being Galois with group $Z_\ell$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The motivating open problem: $\Gal(\overlineQ/Q)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The motivating open problem: $\Gal(\overlineQ/Q)$}
Frame the absolute Galois group of $Q$ as an inverse limit and state why it is hard.
\wrec Every finite Galois $E/Q$ gives a finite quotient $\Gal(E/Q)$; the absolute group is their inverse limit, but unlike the finite-field case the finite quotients are not all cyclic and are far from understood.
\wsol Set $G_Q=\Gal(\overlineQ/Q)=\varprojlim_E\Gal(E/Q)$ over finite Galois $E/Q$, a profinite group under the Krull topology. By the Fundamental Theorem, closed subgroups of $G_Q$ correspond to subfields of $\overlineQ$, and open subgroups to number fields (finite-degree $E/Q$). Unlike $\widehatZ=G_{\F_p}$, which is abelian and topologically cyclic, $G_Q$ is highly nonabelian, and which finite groups arise as quotients $\Gal(E/Q)$ is the unsolved Inverse Galois Problem. Sanity check: the abelianization $G_Q^{ab}=\Gal(Q^{ab}/Q)\cong\widehatZ^\times$ is known (Kronecker--Weber: $Q^{ab}=Q(\mu_\infty)$ is generated by all roots of unity), so even the abelian part already requires the full profinite machinery of this section -- the nonabelian part remains open.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Prove that every purely inseparable extension is normal.

\item Let $p$ be a prime and let $K = F_p(x, y)$ with $x$ and $y$ independent transcendentals over $F_p$. Let $F = F_p(x^p - x, y^p - x)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $[K : F] = p^2$ and the separable degree and inseparable degree of $K/F$ are each $p$.
\item[(b)] Prove that there is a subfield $E$ of $K$ containing $F$ which is purely inseparable over $F$ of degree $p$ (so then $K$ is a separable extension of $E$ of degree $p$). [Let $s = x^p - x$ and $t = y^p - x$ and consider $s - t$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $s$ and $t$ be independent transcendentals over $F_p$, and let $F$ be the field $F_p(s, t)$. Let $\beta$ be a root of $x^2 - sx + t = 0$ and let $\alpha$ be a root of $x^p - \beta = 0$ (in some algebraic closure of $F$). Set $E = F(\beta)$ and $K = F(\alpha)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $E$ is a Galois extension of $F$ of degree 2 and that $K$ is a purely inseparable extension of $E$ of degree $p$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $K$ is not a normal extension of $F$. [If it were, conjugate $\beta$ over $F$ to show that $K$ would contain a $p^{th}$ root of $s$ and then also a $p^{th}$ root of $t$, so that $[K : F] \geq p^2$, a contradiction.]
\item[(c)] Prove that there is no field $K_0$ such that $F \subseteq K_0 \subseteq K$ with $K_0/F$ purely inseparable and $K/K_0$ separable. [If there were such a field, use Exercise 1 and the fact that the composite of two normal extensions is again normal to show that $K$ would be a normal extension of $F$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Under the notation of the previous exercise prove that $\alpha, s$ is a separating transcendence base for $K$ over $F_p$.

\item Let $p$ be a prime, let $t$ be transcendental over $F_p$ and let $K$ be obtained by adjoining to $F_p(t)$ all $p$-power roots of $t$. Prove that $K$ has transcendence degree 1 over $F_p$ and has no separating transcendence base.

\item Show that if $k$ is transcendental over $Q$ then $Q(k, \sqrt{k^3 - k})$ is not a purely transcendental extension of $Q$. (This is an example of what is called an elliptic function field.)

\item Let $k$ be the field with 4 elements, $t$ transcendental over $k$, $F = k(t^4 + t)$ and $K = k(t)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $[K : F] = 4$.
\item[(b)] Show that $K$ is separable over $F$.
\item[(c)] Show that $K$ is Galois over $F$.
\item[(d)] Describe the lattice of subgroups of the Galois group and the corresponding lattice of subfields of $K$, giving each subfield in the form $k(r)$, for some rational function $r$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$ and let $t$ be transcendental over $k$. Suppose $F$ is a degree 2 field extension of $k(t)$. Show that $F$ can be written in the form $k(t, y)$, for some $y \in F$ with $y^2 \in k(t)$ and $y$ transcendental over $k$. If $y^2 = 4t^3 - t - 1$, find $[F : k(y)]$ and determine if $k(t) \cap k(y)$ is the field $k$.

\item Let $t$ be transcendental over $F_3$, let $K = F_3(t)$, let $G = Aut(K/F_3)$ and let $F$ be the fixed field of $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove $G \cong S_4$ and deduce that there is a unique field $E$ with $F \subseteq E \subseteq K$ and $[E : F] = 2$. [Recall that $G \cong PGL_2(F_3)$; show that $GL_2(F_3)$ permutes the 4 lines in a 2-dimensional vector space over $F_3$ and the kernel of this permutation representation is the scalar matrices.]
\item[(b)] Complete the description of the lattice of subfields of $K$ containing $E$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.3em, column sep=0.9em]
& & & K \arrow[ddlll,dash]\arrow[ddll,dash]\arrow[ddl,dash]\arrow[dd,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[drr,dash]\arrow[drrr,dash] & & & \\[1.2em]
& & & & \square \arrow[ddr,dash] & \square \arrow[dd,dash] & F_3\!\left(\dfrac{t^2 + 1}{t + 1}\right) \arrow[ddl,dash] \\
F_3(t^3 - t) \arrow[ddrrr,dash] & \square \arrow[ddrr,dash] & \square \arrow[ddr,dash] & F_3\!\left(\dfrac{t^2 + t}{(t - 1)^3}\right) \arrow[dd,dash] & & & \\
& & & & & \square \arrow[dll,dash] & \\
& & & F_3\!\left(\dfrac{(t^6 + t^4 + t^2 + 1)^2}{(t^3 - t)^3}\right) & & &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Give each subfield in the form $E(r)$ for some rational function $r$. (The lattice of subgroups of $A_4$ appears in Section 3.5).
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that a purely transcendental proper extension of a field is never algebraically closed.

\item Let $S$ be a set of independent transcendentals over a field $F$ and let $\Omega$ be an algebraic closure of $F(S)$. Prove that any permutation on $S$ extends to an element of $Aut(F(S)/F)$. Prove that any such automorphism of $F(S)$ extends to an automorphism of $\Omega$. Deduce that $C$ has infinitely many automorphisms.

\item Let $K$ be a subfield of $C$ maximal with respect to the property ``$\sqrt{2} \notin K$.''
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show such a field $K$ exists.
\item[(b)] Show that $C$ is algebraic over $K$.
\item[(c)] Prove that every finite extension of $K$ in $C$ is Galois with Galois group a cyclic 2-group.
\item[(d)] Deduce that $[C : K]$ is countable (and not finite).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $K$ be the fixed field in $C$ of an automorphism of $C$. Prove that every finite extension of $K$ in $C$ is cyclic.

\item Let $K_n$ be the splitting field of $(x^2 - p_1)(x^2 - p_2)\cdots(x^2 - p_n)$ over $Q$, where $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ are the first $n$ primes.

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Transcendental Extensions, Inseparable Extensions, Infinite Galois Groups > The Krull topology and profinite Galois groups
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (from the text).
Part: 2/2
Content:
Prove that the Galois group of $K_n/Q$ is an elementary abelian 2-group of order $2^n$.

\item Let $K_0 = Q$ and for $n \geq 0$ define the field $K_{n+1}$ as the extension of $K_n$ obtained by adjoining to $K_n$ all roots of all cubic polynomials over $K_n$. Let $K$ be the union of the subfields $K_n$, $n \geq 0$. Prove that $K$ is a Galois extension of $Q$. Prove that every cubic polynomial over $K$ splits completely over $K$. Prove that there are nontrivial abelian extensions of $K$.

\item Let $F$ be the composite of all the splitting fields of irreducible cubics over $Q$. Prove that $F$ does contain all quadratic extensions of $Q$. [One way is to consider the polynomials $x^3 + 3ax + 2a$ for $a \in Z^+$.]

\item Let $K_0 = Q$ and for $n \geq 0$ define the field $K_{n+1}$ as the extension of $K_n$ obtained by adjoining to $K_n$ all radicals of elements in $K_n$. Let $K$ be the union of the subfields $K_n$, $n \geq 0$. Prove that $K$ is a Galois extension of $Q$. Prove that there are no nontrivial solvable Galois extensions of $K$. Prove that there are nontrivial Galois extensions of $K$.

\item Let $F_0 = Q$ and for $n \geq 0$ define the field $F_{n+1}$ as the extension of $F_n$ obtained by adjoining to $F_n$ all real radicals of elements in $F_n$. Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $x,y,z$ be independent transcendentals over a field $F$. For each of the following subsets of $F(x,y,z)$, decide whether it is algebraically independent over $F$ and compute the transcendence degree of the subfield it generates: (a) $\{x+y,\ x-y\}$; (b) $\{x^2,\ xy,\ y^2\}$; (c) $\{x,\ y,\ xy+z\}$.
\item Let $K=F(x,y)$ with $x,y$ independent transcendentals and let $L=F(x)\subseteq K$. Using additivity of transcendence degree in the tower $F\subseteq L\subseteq K$, compute $\operatorname{trdeg}_F K$, $\operatorname{trdeg}_F L$, and $\operatorname{trdeg}_L K$, and exhibit a transcendence basis of $K/F$ that contains a transcendence basis of $L/F$.
\item Let $p$ be a prime, $F=\F_p(t)$, and $K=F(\alpha)$ where $\alpha^p=t$. Compute $[K:F]$, $[K:F]_s$, and $[K:F]_i$, and write down the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$ together with its factorization in $\overline{F}[x]$.
\item Let $p$ be an odd prime, $F=\F_p(s,t)$ with $s,t$ independent transcendentals, and $K=F(\alpha,\beta)$ where $\alpha^p=s$ and $\beta^p=t$. Show $[K:F]=p^2$ and determine $[K:F]_s$ and $[K:F]_i$. Prove that $K/F$ is purely inseparable and that $\Aut(K/F)=1$.
\item Decide whether each extension is separable, purely inseparable, or neither, with justification: (a) $\F_p(t^{1/p})/\F_p(t)$; (b) $\F_p(t)(\alpha)/\F_p(t)$ where $\alpha^2-\alpha-t=0$ and $p$ is odd; (c) $K=\F_p(t^{1/p},u)$ over $F=\F_p(t,u)$, where $u$ is a further transcendental, independent of $t$.
\item Show that the Frobenius endomorphism $\varphi\colon a\mapsto a^p$ of $F=\F_p(t)$ is injective but not surjective, exhibit an element of $F$ not in the image $F^p$, and conclude that $F$ is not a perfect field.
\item Let $G=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)\cong\widehat{Z}$ with topological generator the Frobenius $\Frob_p\colon x\mapsto x^p$. For $n=12$, list all intermediate fields $\F_p\subseteq E\subseteq\F_{p^{12}}$, and for each give the corresponding subgroup of $\Gal(\F_{p^{12}}/\F_p)\congZ/(12)Z$ as the subgroup generated by a power of $\Frob_p$, so that $E$ is its $\Fix$. State which of these $E$ are Galois over $\F_p$.
\item In $G=\widehat{Z}=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$, decide for each subgroup whether it is open, closed-but-not-open, or neither, and name its fixed field when it is closed: (a) $n\widehat{Z}$ for a fixed integer $n\ge1$; (b) $\prod_{q\neq\ell}Z_q$ for a fixed prime $\ell$; (c) the abstract subgroup $\langle \Frob_p\rangle\congZ$ generated by Frobenius.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $p$ be a prime, $F=\F_p(s,t)$, and let $K=F(x,y)$ where $x^p-x=s$ (Artin--Schreier) and $y^p=t+x$. Compute $[K:F]$, $[K:F]_s$, and $[K:F]_i$ by passing through the tower $F\subseteq F(x)\subseteq K$, identifying which step is separable and which is purely inseparable. Then exhibit an element $w\in K$ with $w^p\in F$ but $w\notin F$, and describe the maximal purely inseparable subextension of $K/F$.
\item Prove the multiplicativity of separable degree in a tower: for finite extensions $F\subseteq L\subseteq K$, show $[K:F]_s=[K:L]_s\,[L:F]_s$ by counting extensions of $F$-embeddings $L\hookrightarrow\overline{F}$ to $F$-embeddings $K\hookrightarrow\overline{F}$. Deduce that $[K:F]_i$ is multiplicative as well, and hence is always a power of $\charac F$ when positive.
\item Let $K/F$ be a finite extension in characteristic $p$. Let $K_{sep}$ be the separable closure of $F$ in $K$ (the set of elements of $K$ separable over $F$). Prove $K_{sep}$ is a field with $F\subseteq K_{sep}\subseteq K$, that $[K_{sep}:F]=[K:F]_s$, and that $K/K_{sep}$ is purely inseparable with $[K:K_{sep}]=[K:F]_i$. Illustrate with $F=\F_p(s,t)$, $K=F(\alpha,\beta)$ where $\alpha^p-\alpha=s$ and $\beta^p=t$, by naming $K_{sep}$ explicitly.
\item Let $K/F$ be a (possibly infinite) Galois extension with $G=\Gal(K/F)$ under the Krull topology. Prove that for every intermediate field $E$ with $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$ the subgroup $\Gal(K/E)$ is closed, and that $\Fix(\Gal(K/E))=E$. Then exhibit, for $K=\overline{\F_p}$ over $F=\F_p$, an abstract subgroup of $G$ that is not closed, and identify the closed subgroup it determines via $H\mapsto\Gal(K/\Fix(H))$.
\item Prove that $\widehat{Z}\cong\prod_{\ell}Z_\ell$, the product over all primes $\ell$, by combining the Chinese Remainder isomorphisms $Z/(n)Z\cong\prod_{\ell}Z/(\ell^{v_\ell(n)})Z$ in the inverse limit $\widehat{Z}=\varprojlim_nZ/(n)Z$. Using this, show $\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$ has, for each prime $\ell$, a unique closed subgroup with quotient $Z_\ell$, and name its fixed field as a union of finite fields.
\end{exers}

Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $p$ be an odd prime, $F=\F_p(s,t)$, and $K=F(\alpha,\beta)$ where $\alpha^p=s$ (purely inseparable, degree $p$) and $\beta^2-\beta-t=0$ (separable, degree $2$). Complete the Galois/degree lattice below, labelling each edge with its degree and marking each as separable (s) or purely inseparable (i):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=2.6em]
& K=F(\alpha,\beta) & \\
F(\alpha) \arrow[ur,dash] & & F(\beta) \arrow[ul,dash] \\
& F \arrow[ul,dash]\arrow[ur,dash] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify which intermediate field is $K_{sep}$, prove $F(\beta)/F$ is Galois, and show $K/F$ is neither separable nor purely inseparable by computing $[K:F]_s$ and $[K:F]_i$.
\item For $G=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)\cong\widehat{Z}$, complete the two mutually corresponding lattices below for the layer $\F_{p^{18}}/\F_p$ (so $n=18$): on the left the subgroups of $Z/(18)Z$, on the right the intermediate fields. Fill in every node on the right, write each subgroup on the left as $\langle \Frob_p^{\,18/m}\rangle$ (the node $Z/(m)Z$ stands for the unique subgroup of order $m$, and each edge is an inclusion of subgroups), then state the $\Fix$ correspondence between them.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.8em, column sep=1.8em]
& Z/(18)Z \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
Z/(9)Z \arrow[d,dash] & & Z/(6)Z \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[d,dash] \\
Z/(3)Z \arrow[dr,dash] & & Z/(2)Z \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& Z/(1)Z &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.8em, column sep=1.8em]
& \F_{p} \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
\square \arrow[d,dash] & & \square \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[d,dash] \\
\square \arrow[dr,dash] & & \square \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& \F_{p^{18}} &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove that the correspondence is inclusion-reversing and that every subextension here is Galois over $\F_p$ with cyclic Galois group, identifying $\Gal(\F_{p^d}/\F_p)$ for each divisor $d$ of $18$.
\item Let $K/F$ be Galois with $G=\Gal(K/F)$ profinite, and let $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$ be a finite Galois subextension. Show that restriction fits into the commutative diagram of profinite groups
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=2.6em]
G=\Gal(K/F) \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"\rho"] \arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow,"\operatorname{res}_E"'] & G/\Gal(K/E) \arrow[d,"\cong"] \\
& \Gal(E/F)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $\rho$ is the quotient map and $\operatorname{res}_E$ is restriction to $E$. Prove $\Gal(K/E)$ is open and normal in $G$, that the vertical map is the canonical isomorphism, and that $\operatorname{res}_E$ is a continuous open surjection.
\item In $G=\widehat{Z}=\Gal(\overline{\F_p}/\F_p)$, fix a prime $\ell$ and let $H=\prod_{q\neq\ell}Z_q$. Complete and justify the diagram exhibiting $\Fix(H)=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\F_{p^{\ell^k}}$ as an infinite Galois extension of $\F_p$ with group $\widehat{Z}/H\congZ_\ell$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.0em, column sep=2.4em]
\widehat{Z} \arrow[d,phantom,"\Fix"description] & H \arrow[l,hook'] \arrow[d,phantom,"\Fix"description] \\
\F_p \arrow[r,hook] & \Fix(H)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Show $H$ is closed but not open, that $[\widehat{Z}:H]$ is infinite, and conclude that $\Fix(H)/\F_p$ is an infinite-degree subextension corresponding (by item (1) of the infinite Fundamental Theorem) to a closed non-open subgroup.
\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
A permutation $\sigma$ of the indices $\{1,\dots,n\}$ acts on the polynomial ring $R[u]=R[u_1,\dots,u_n]$ by permuting the variables: for $f=f(u_1,\dots,u_n)$ we set $(\sigma f)(u_1,\dots,u_n)=f(u_{\sigma 1},\dots,u_{\sigma n})$. Since $\sigma$ fixes the constants, it is an $R$-algebra automorphism, and the symmetric group $\Sym_n$ acts on $R[u]$ by $R$-automorphisms. A polynomial is symmetric if it is fixed by every permutation.

\begin{definition}[Symmetric polynomial]
$g\in R[u_1,\dots,u_n]$ is symmetric if $\sigma g=g$ for all $\sigma\in\Sym_n$, i.e.\ $g(u_{\sigma 1},\dots,u_{\sigma n})=g(u_1,\dots,u_n)$. The symmetric polynomials form a subring of $R[u]$. Equivalently, $g$ is symmetric iff any two monomials in the same $\Sym_n$-orbit (e.g.\ $u_1^2u_2$ and $u_2u_3^2$) occur with the same coefficient; the sum of the monomials in one orbit is an orbit sum, and the orbit sums form an $R$-basis of the symmetric polynomials.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: Elementary symmetric polynomials
Content:
\begin{definition}[Elementary symmetric polynomials]
The elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1,\dots,e_n$ in $u_1,\dots,u_n$ are the orbit sums of the squarefree monomials:
\[
e_1=\sum_i u_i,\qquad e_2=\sum_{i<j}u_iu_j,\qquad e_3=\sum_{i<j<k}u_iu_ju_k,\qquad\dots,\qquad e_n=u_1u_2\cdots u_n.
\]
Thus $e_k$ is the orbit sum of $u_1u_2\cdots u_k$; it is the sum of all $\binom nk$ squarefree degree-$k$ monomials. (Artin writes these $s_1,\dots,s_n$; we use $e_k$ here.)
\end{definition}

Content:
The $e_k$ arise as the coefficients of the polynomial with roots $u_1,\dots,u_n$. Expanding $P(x)=(x-u_1)\cdots(x-u_n)$ and collecting by degree gives Vieta's formulas with alternating signs:
\[
P(x)=(x-u_1)(x-u_2)\cdots(x-u_n)=x^n-e_1x^{n-1}+e_2x^{n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^n e_n.
\]
For $n=2$ this is $x^2-(u_1+u_2)x+u_1u_2$; for $n=3$ it is $x^3-(u_1+u_2+u_3)x^2+(u_1u_2+u_1u_3+u_2u_3)x-u_1u_2u_3$. Following Artin, we therefore label undetermined coefficients of a monic degree-$n$ polynomial in the matching alternating form
\[
f(x)=x^n-a_1x^{n-1}+a_2x^{n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^n a_n .
\]

Title: {coefficients are the elementary symmetric functions of the roots}

Content:
\begin{lemma}[{coefficients are the elementary symmetric functions of the roots}]
 
If $f(x)=x^n-a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^n a_n$ splits as $f(x)=(x-\alpha_1)\cdots(x-\alpha_n)$ in a field $K$, then $a_k=e_k(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ for each $k$. That is, the coefficients are obtained by evaluating the elementary symmetric functions at the roots.
\end{lemma}
label: art:symmetric:vieta@c14

Type: theorem
Title: {Fundamental (Symmetric Functions) Theorem}
Label: art:symmetric:fund@c14
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Fundamental (Symmetric Functions) Theorem}]
 
Let $R$ be any commutative ring. Every symmetric polynomial $g(u_1,\dots,u_n)\in R[u]$ can be written as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions, and in exactly one way: there is a unique polynomial $G(z_1,\dots,z_n)\in R[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ in new variables such that
\[
g(u_1,\dots,u_n)=G\bigl(e_1,\dots,e_n\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, $R[e_1,\dots,e_n]$ is the full ring of symmetric polynomials, and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are algebraically independent over $R$.
\end{theorem}
label: art:symmetric:fund@c14

\]

\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Existence, by induction (Artin's reduction)
Relation: proof_of=unit-65cf818c4076a5a2aca3
Content:
\begin{proof}[Existence, by induction (Artin's reduction)]
Induct on $n$; the case $n=1$ is trivial since $u_1=e_1$. Assume the theorem for $n-1$ variables. Given a symmetric $g$ in $u_1,\dots,u_n$, substitute $u_n=0$ to get $g^{0}(u_1,\dots,u_{n-1})=g(u_1,\dots,u_{n-1},0)$, which is symmetric in $u_1,\dots,u_{n-1}$. Under $u_n=0$ the elementary symmetric functions specialize to $e_1^{0},\dots,e_{n-1}^{0}$ (those in $u_1,\dots,u_{n-1}$) while $e_n\mapsto 0$. By the induction hypothesis $g^{0}=Q(e_1^{0},\dots,e_{n-1}^{0})$ for some polynomial $Q$.

Now set $p=g-Q(e_1,\dots,e_{n-1})$, a difference of symmetric polynomials, hence symmetric. Setting $u_n=0$ gives $p|_{u_n=0}=g^{0}-Q(e_1^{0},\dots,e_{n-1}^{0})=0$, so $u_n\mid p$. Because $p$ is symmetric, every $u_i$ divides $p$, and therefore the product $e_n=u_1\cdots u_n$ divides $p$. Write $p=e_n\,h$ with $h$ symmetric; comparing degrees, $\deg h=\deg p-n<\deg g$. A second induction, on the degree, expresses $h$ as a polynomial in the $e_i$, hence so is $p$, hence so is
\[
g=Q(e_1,\dots,e_{n-1})+e_n\,h .
\]
Uniqueness (algebraic independence of the $e_i$) is checked by tracking the lexicographically leading term in the algorithm below: distinct monomials $e_1^{b_1}\cdots e_n^{b_n}$ have distinct leading monomials $u_1^{b_1+\cdots+b_n}u_2^{b_2+\cdots+b_n}\cdots u_n^{b_n}$, each with coefficient $1$; so if $G\ne0$, the largest leading monomial among the $e$-monomials occurring in $G$ appears in $G(e)$ with the nonzero coefficient it has in $G$, and $G\mapsto G(e)$ is injective.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Lexicographic leading-term algorithm: reduce a symmetric $g$ to a polynomial in the $e_i$.
Content:
\begin{method}{Lexicographic leading-term algorithm: reduce a symmetric $g$ to a polynomial in the $e_i$.}
Order monomials lexicographically by exponent ($u_1>u_2>\cdots>u_n$). Let the leading monomial of $g$ be $c\,u_1^{a_1}u_2^{a_2}\cdots u_n^{a_n}$; symmetry forces $a_1\ge a_2\ge\cdots\ge a_n$. Subtract
\[
c\;e_1^{\,a_1-a_2}\,e_2^{\,a_2-a_3}\cdots e_{n-1}^{\,a_{n-1}-a_n}\,e_n^{\,a_n},
\]
whose own leading monomial is exactly $c\,u_1^{a_1}\cdots u_n^{a_n}$ (since $e_k$ leads with $u_1\cdots u_k$). The difference is symmetric with a strictly smaller leading monomial. Repeat; the process terminates because the leading exponent vector decreases in a well-ordering. The accumulated subtractions reassemble $g$ as a polynomial $G(e_1,\dots,e_n)$.
\end{method}

Title: The power sum $\sum u_i^2$ in the $e_i$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The power sum $\sum u_i^2$ in the $e_i$}
Express the symmetric polynomial $p_2=u_1^2+u_2^2+\cdots+u_n^2$ as a polynomial in $e_1,\dots,e_n$.
\wrec $p_2$ is symmetric of degree $2$, so it is a linear combination of the degree-$2$ products $e_1^2$ and $e_2$ (the only weight-$2$ monomials in the $e_i$). Find the coefficients by undetermined coefficients, evaluating at special values (Artin's method) or by direct expansion.
\wsol Write $p_2=c_1e_1^2+c_2e_2$. Evaluate at $u=(1,0,\dots,0)$: then $e_1=1$, $e_2=0$, $p_2=1$, giving $c_1=1$. Evaluate at $u=(1,-1,0,\dots,0)$: then $e_1=0$, $e_2=-1$, $p_2=2$, giving $-c_2=2$, so $c_2=-2$. Hence
\[
u_1^2+\cdots+u_n^2=e_1^2-2e_2 .
\]
Check. Directly, $e_1^2=(\sum_i u_i)^2=\sum_i u_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}u_iu_j=p_2+2e_2$, so $p_2=e_1^2-2e_2$, matching.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{The power sum $\sum u_i^3$ in the $e_i$}
Express $p_3=u_1^3+u_2^3+\cdots+u_n^3$ in terms of $e_1,e_2,e_3$.
\wrec $p_3$ is symmetric of degree $3$, hence a combination of the weight-$3$ monomials $e_1^3,\ e_1e_2,\ e_3$. Pin the three coefficients by special substitutions, or apply Newton's identity below.
\wsol Write $p_3=c_1e_1^3+c_2e_1e_2+c_3e_3$. At $u=(1,0,\dots)$: $e_1=1$, $e_2=e_3=0$, $p_3=1\Rightarrow c_1=1$. At $u=(1,1,0,\dots)$: $e_1=2$, $e_2=1$, $e_3=0$, $p_3=2$, so $8c_1+2c_2=2$, i.e.\ $8+2c_2=2\Rightarrow c_2=-3$. At $u=(1,1,1,0,\dots)$: $e_1=3$, $e_2=3$, $e_3=1$, $p_3=3$, so $27c_1+9c_2+c_3=3$, i.e.\ $27-27+c_3=3\Rightarrow c_3=3$. Hence
\[
u_1^3+\cdots+u_n^3=e_1^3-3e_1e_2+3e_3 .

Title: {Newton's identities}
Label: art:symmetric:newton@c14
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Newton's identities}]
 
With $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$, the power sums and elementary symmetric functions satisfy, for every $k\ge 1$,
\[
p_k-e_1p_{k-1}+e_2p_{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}e_{k-1}p_1+(-1)^k k\,e_k=0 .
\]
In particular $p_1=e_1$, $p_2=e_1p_1-2e_2=e_1^2-2e_2$, and $p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=e_1^3-3e_1e_2+3e_3$.
\end{proposition}
label: art:symmetric:newton@c14

Type: proof
Title: Sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-6a1c35e13b44300e161c
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
Form the generating identity $\prod_i(1-u_i t)=\sum_{k\ge 0}(-1)^k e_k t^k$. Take the logarithmic derivative in $t$:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\log\prod_i(1-u_it)=\sum_i\frac{-u_i}{1-u_it}=-\sum_i\sum_{k\ge 1}u_i^{\,k}t^{k-1}=-\sum_{k\ge 1}p_k\,t^{k-1}.
\]
Writing $E(t)=\sum_k(-1)^k e_k t^k$, the left side equals $E'(t)/E(t)$, so $-\bigl(\sum_{k\ge1}p_kt^{k-1}\bigr)E(t)=E'(t)$. Multiplying out and equating the coefficient of $t^{k-1}$ on both sides yields exactly the stated identity for each $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{wex}{Algorithmic reduction of a degree-three symmetric polynomial}
Reduce the orbit sum
\[
g=u_1^2u_2+u_1^2u_3+u_2^2u_1+u_2^2u_3+u_3^2u_1+u_3^2u_2
\]
in three variables (the orbit of $u_1^2u_2$) to a polynomial in $e_1,e_2,e_3$, following Artin's set-$u_3=0$ reduction.
\wrec $g$ is symmetric of degree $3$. Use the inductive reduction: set $u_3=0$, solve in two variables, then correct by a multiple of $e_3$ to repair the three-variable case (Lemma in the proof of the Fundamental Theorem).
\wsol Step 1. Set $u_3=0$. Then $g^{0}=u_1^2u_2+u_2^2u_1=u_1u_2(u_1+u_2)=e_2^{0}\,e_1^{0}$, where $e_1^{0}=u_1+u_2$, $e_2^{0}=u_1u_2$ are the two-variable elementary symmetric functions. So the two-variable answer is $e_1^{0}e_2^{0}$.

Step 2. Compare $g$ with the three-variable $e_1e_2=(u_1+u_2+u_3)(u_1u_2+u_1u_3+u_2u_3)$. This product has nine terms; six of them are exactly the orbit sum $g$ (each $u_i^2u_j$ appears once), and the remaining three terms are each $u_1u_2u_3=e_3$. Thus $e_1e_2=g+3e_3$, giving
\[
g=e_1e_2-3e_3 .
\]
This matches the leading-term algorithm too: $g$ leads with $u_1^2u_2$ (exponents $(2,1,0)$), and the prescribed subtraction is $e_1^{2-1}e_2^{1-0}e_3^{0}=e_1e_2$, leaving $-3e_3$. Check. At $u=(1,1,1)$, $g=6$ while $e_1e_2-3e_3=3\cdot3-3\cdot1=6$; at $u=(1,1,0)$, $g=2$ while $e_1e_2-3e_3=2\cdot1-0=2$. Both agree.
\end{wex}

Title: {symmetric functions of roots stay in the base field}
Label: art:symmetric:rational@c14
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{symmetric functions of roots stay in the base field}]
 
Let $f(x)=x^n-a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^n a_n\in F[x]$ split completely in an extension $K/F$ with roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$. If $g(u_1,\dots,u_n)$ is any symmetric polynomial with coefficients in $F$, then $g(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)\in F$.
\end{corollary}
label: art:symmetric:rational@c14

Relation: proof_of=unit-e851bf3d8187c295fbd6
Content:
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~ [REF:art:symmetric:fund@c14] , $g=G(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ with $G$ having coefficients in $F$. Evaluating at $u_i=\alpha_i$ and using Lemma~ [REF:art:symmetric:vieta@c14] , $e_k(\alpha)=a_k\in F$. Hence $g(\alpha)=G(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ is a polynomial expression in the $a_k\in F$ with coefficients in $F$, so it lies in $F$. For instance $\alpha_1^k+\cdots+\alpha_n^k\in F$ for every $k$, even when no individual root lies in $F$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Corollary~ [REF:art:symmetric:rational@c14] is the bridge to Galois theory: the coefficients $a_k$ are the elementary symmetric functions of the roots, so any quantity invariant under permuting the roots is already expressible in the $a_k$ and therefore rational over $F$. The Galois group acts on the roots by permutations, and the symmetric (fully invariant) functions are precisely the ones fixed by the whole symmetric group -- the bottom of the fixed-field correspondence.
\end{remark}

Type: prose
Content:
The chain of subrings underlying the theorem is best seen as a tower: the full polynomial ring sits above its symmetric subring, which is freely generated by the $e_i$, and specializing the variables to the roots $u_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ sends those generators to the coefficients of $f$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=3.0em]
R[u_1,\dots,u_n] \arrow[d,dash] & \\
R[e_1,\dots,e_n]=R[u]^{\Sym_n} \arrow[d,dash] \arrow[r, "u_i\,\mapsto\,\alpha_i"] & F[a_1,\dots,a_n] \\
R \arrow[r, equal] & R
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five nodes arranged as a lopsided tower.
 Upper-left: $R[u_1,\dots,u_n]$, the full polynomial ring in $n$ indeterminates over a commutative ring $R$.
 Middle-left: $R[e_1,\dots,e_n]=R[u]^{\Sym_n}$, the subring of symmetric polynomials; by the Fundamental Theorem it equals the polynomial ring in the elementary symmetric functions $e_1,\dots,e_n$, which are algebraically independent over $R$.
 Bottom-left: $R$, the base ring (constant polynomials).
 Middle-right: $F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$, the polynomial ring (actually a subring of $F$) generated by the coefficients $a_k$ of $f$; since the $a_k\in F$, this is just $F$ itself in the splitting situation, but writing it this way highlights the parallelism with the left column.
 Bottom-right: $R$ again (identifying the two copies by the ``equal'' sign).
\dgi{Arrows:} Four arrows.
 (1) Upper vertical edge: inclusion $R[u]^{\Sym_n}\hookrightarrow R[u_1,\dots,u_n]$, inserting the symmetric subring into the full ring.
 (2) Lower vertical edge: inclusion $R\hookrightarrow R[u]^{\Sym_n}$, viewing $R$ as constant symmetric polynomials.
 (3) Horizontal middle: the evaluation/specialization map $\operatorname{ev}_\alpha\colon R[u]^{\Sym_n}\to F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ defined by $u_i\mapsto\alpha_i$; since $e_k(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)=a_k$ by Vieta (Lemma~ [REF:art:symmetric:vieta@c14] ), this carries $e_k\mapsto a_k$ and is a ring homomorphism.
 (4) Bottom horizontal: the identity/equality $R\xrightarrow{=}R$.
 Well-definedness of $\operatorname{ev}_\alpha$: a polynomial map $u_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ is always a ring homomorphism and needs no coset check; the point is merely that symmetric polynomials evaluated at the roots stay in $F$ (proved in Corollary~ [REF:art:symmetric:rational@c14] ).
\dgi{What commutes:} The square formed by arrows (2), (3), (4), and the inclusion $R\hookrightarrow F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ commutes: going right-then-up ($R\to R\to F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$: arrow (4), then the inclusion) and going up-then-right ($R\to R[u]^{\Sym_n}\to F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$: arrows (2) and (3)) both land a constant $r\in R$ at $r\in F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$.
 The upper-left triangle is not a commuting square but an inclusion chain: $R\subseteq R[u]^{\Sym_n}\subseteq R[u_1,\dots,u_n]$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Take a constant $r\in R$.
 Along the up-then-right path: $r$ is already in $R[u]^{\Sym_n}$ (constant polynomial), and $\operatorname{ev}_\alpha(r)=r\in F$.
 Along the right-then-up path: $r\mapsto r$ by the equality arrow, then $r\mapsto r$ by the inclusion.
 These agree because evaluating a constant polynomial at any point returns that constant; no $u_i$ are substituted.
 The key nontrivial commutativity is $\operatorname{ev}_\alpha(e_k)=a_k$, which is exactly Vieta's theorem: the coefficient of $x^{n-k}$ in $\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)$ is $(-1)^k e_k(\alpha)=(-1)^k a_k$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the geometric summary of Corollary~ [REF:art:symmetric:rational@c14] and the Fundamental Theorem together.
 It shows that the specialization $u_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ does not leave the base field: any symmetric polynomial (left column) maps to a polynomial in the $a_k$ (right column), which lie in $F$.
 The author places it here to make visible why ``symmetric functions of roots are rational'': the horizontal evaluation map is the concrete realization of the abstract isomorphism $R[u]^{\Sym_n}\cong R[e_1,\dots,e_n]$, and it lands in $F$ because $a_k\in F$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R=F=Q$, $n=2$, $f(x)=x^2-3x+1$ (roots $\alpha_1,\alpha_2=\tfrac{3\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$, which are irrational).
 $e_1(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=\alpha_1+\alpha_2=3=a_1\inQ$.
 $e_2(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=\alpha_1\alpha_2=1=a_2\inQ$.
 The power sum $p_2=\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2=e_1^2-2e_2=9-2=7\inQ$, even though $\alpha_i\notinQ$.
 The horizontal arrow in the diagram sends $e_1\mapsto 3$, $e_2\mapsto 1$, entirely within $Q$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students read the horizontal arrow as an isomorphism $R[u]^{\Sym_n}\cong F[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ and conclude the two rings are the same.
 They are not in general isomorphic as abstract rings; the arrow is an evaluation homomorphism, not an isomorphism: in the basic case $R=F$ it is onto $F[a_1,\dots,a_n]=F$, and its kernel is the maximal ideal $(e_1-a_1,\dots,e_n-a_n)$ of the polynomial ring $F[e_1,\dots,e_n]$ -- never zero, and consisting exactly of the relations forced by $f$.
 What matters is the image: every symmetric combination of the roots is a polynomial in the $a_k$, hence in $F$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the Fundamental Theorem converts the abstract statement ``symmetric functions of roots are rational'' into a concrete factorization: every such function factors through the elementary symmetric functions $e_k$, which are sent to the coefficients $a_k\in F$ by Vieta, so the result lands in $F$ automatically.
\end{dgx}
The left edges are the inclusions $R\subseteq R[u]^{\Sym_n}\subseteq R[u]$, with $R[u]^{\Sym_n}$ free on $e_1,\dots,e_n$; the horizontal map is evaluation at the roots, carrying $e_k\mapsto a_k$.

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The theorem expresses symmetric polynomials in the $e_i$ with coefficients in $R$ only; it does not let you divide. Newton's identity $p_k+\cdots+(-1)^k k\,e_k=0$ solves for $p_k$ in terms of lower data without dividing, but solving for $e_k$ in terms of the $p_j$ introduces the factor $\tfrac1k$. Hence the change of generators from $e$'s to power sums $p$'s is valid only when $1,2,\dots,n$ are invertible in $R$ (e.g.\ over a field of characteristic $0$, or any characteristic exceeding $n$), and can fail in small positive characteristic.
\end{pitfall}

\begin{definition}[discriminant]
The discriminant of $f$ is

\disc(f)=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2

Content:
\begin{proposition}[the discriminant is a polynomial in the coefficients] 
$\disc(f)$ is a symmetric polynomial in $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ with integer coefficients. Consequently, by the Symmetric Functions Theorem, it is an integer polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions $s_1,\dots,s_n$; writing $A(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ for that polynomial,
\[
\disc(f)=A(s_1,\dots,s_n)\in F
\]
whenever $f\in F[x]$. In particular the discriminant of $f$ lies in the base field $F$, even though it is defined through the roots.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-392d06c82af7387ec9ff
Content:
\begin{proof}
A permutation $\tau\in\Sym_n$ of the variables sends each factor $(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ to another factor $(\alpha_{\tau(i)}-\alpha_{\tau(j)})^2$ of the same product: since $(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)^2=(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$, the squaring kills the sign that the transposition would otherwise introduce, so $\tau$ merely permutes the $\binom{n}{2}$ factors among themselves and fixes their product. Thus $\disc(f)$ is symmetric. The Symmetric Functions Theorem then writes any symmetric integer polynomial uniquely as an integer polynomial $A(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ in the elementary symmetric functions. When the $\alpha_i$ are the roots of $f\in F[x]$, the $s_i$ are (up to sign) the coefficients of $f$, hence lie in $F$, so $\disc(f)=A(s_1,\dots,s_n)\in F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[discriminant of a depressed cubic] 
Over a field of characteristic $\ne2,3$,
\[
\disc(x^3+px+q)=-4p^3-27q^2 .
\]
\end{theorem}
label: art:discriminant:cubic@c14

Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ be the roots of $g(x)=x^3+px+q$, so $g'(x)=3x^2+p$. From $g(x)=\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)$ one gets $g'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$, and multiplying over $i$ yields the resultant identity
\[
\prod_{i}g'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{i\ne j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)=(-1)^{\binom{3}{2}}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=-\disc(g).
\]
Now evaluate $\prod_i g'(\alpha_i)=\prod_i(3\alpha_i^2+p)$ using $\alpha_i^3=-p\alpha_i-q$. Expanding the symmetric product $\prod_i(3\alpha_i^2+p)$ and rewriting in the elementary symmetric functions $s_1=0,\ s_2=p,\ s_3=-q$ of the depressed cubic gives $\prod_i g'(\alpha_i)=4p^3+27q^2$. Hence $\disc(g)=-(4p^3+27q^2)=-4p^3-27q^2$.
\end{proof}

Title: Discriminant of $x^3+3x+1$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Discriminant of $x^3+3x+1$}
Compute $\disc(x^3+3x+1)$.
\wrec Already depressed ($p=3,\ q=1$); apply Theorem~ [REF:art:discriminant:cubic@c14] directly.
\wsol $\disc=-4(3)^3-27(1)^2=-4\cdot27-27=-108-27=-135=-5\cdot3^3$. Check. $-135<0$, and for a real cubic a negative discriminant signals one real and two complex-conjugate roots; here $x^3+3x+1$ is strictly increasing ($g'(x)=3x^2+3>0$), so it has exactly one real root, consistent with $\disc<0$.
\end{wex}

\wrec Depressed with $p=-3,\ q=1$; use $\disc=-4p^3-27q^2$.
\wsol $\disc=-4(-3)^3-27(1)^2=-4(-27)-27=108-27=81=3^4$. Check. $81=9^2$ is a perfect square in $Q$. Also $81>0$, predicting three distinct real roots; indeed $g(x)=x^3-3x+1=2\cos3\theta$-type behavior gives $g(-2)<0<g(-1)$, $g(0)>0>g(1)$, $g(1)<0<g(2)$, three real roots. Both checks agree.

\begin{wex}{Reduce a non-depressed cubic first}
Compute $\disc(x^3-3x^2+1)$.
\wrec Not depressed; substitute $x=y+1$ (i.e.\ $x=y-a/3$ with $a=-3$) to remove the $x^2$ term, then apply the formula.
\wsol $x=y+1$: $(y+1)^3-3(y+1)^2+1=y^3+3y^2+3y+1-3y^2-6y-3+1=y^3-3y-1$, so $p=-3,\ q=-1$. Then $\disc=-4(-3)^3-27(-1)^2=108-27=81=3^4$. Check. Translation by $1$ does not move root differences, so the answer must match a depressed cubic with the same differences; $y^3-3y-1$ has the same discriminant $81$ as $y^3-3y+1$ since $\disc$ depends on $q$ only through $q^2$.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
The discriminant is a perfect square as a function of the roots:
\[
\delta:=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j),\qquad \disc(f)=\delta^2 .
\]
The element $\delta$ lies in the splitting field $K$, is nonzero when the roots are distinct, and a permutation $\sigma$ of the roots multiplies it by the sign:
\[
\sigma(\delta)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\delta .
\]
This single transformation rule is the bridge between the discriminant and the Galois group.

\begin{theorem}[discriminant criterion] 
Let $f\in F[x]$ be separable with splitting field $K$, $\operatorname{char}F\ne2$, and view $G=\Gal(K/F)$ as a subgroup of $\Sym_n$ via its action on the roots. Then
\[
\disc(f)\ is a square in F\iff G\sgrA_n .
\]
\end{theorem}
label: art:discriminant:An@c14

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8eaeaeb34902562b26cc
Content:
\begin{proof}
Since $\disc(f)=\delta^2\in F$, we have $\delta\in F$ if and only if $\disc(f)$ is a square in $F$. Now $\delta\in F$ iff $\delta$ is fixed by every $\sigma\in G$ (Galois). But $\sigma(\delta)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\delta$ and $\delta\ne0$, so $\sigma(\delta)=\delta$ iff $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=1$, i.e.\ iff $\sigma\inA_n$. Hence $\delta\in F$ iff every element of $G$ is even, i.e.\ iff $G\sgrA_n$. (Characteristic $\ne2$ guarantees $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=-1$ is genuinely distinct from $+1$.)
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[Galois theory for a cubic] 
Let $f$ be an irreducible cubic over $F$ ($\operatorname{char}F\ne2,3$) with splitting field $K$ and $G=\Gal(K/F)$, and let $D=\disc(f)$.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
\item If $D$ is a square in $F$, then $G=A_3$ and $[K:F]=3$.
\item If $D$ is not a square in $F$, then $G=\Sym_3$ and $[K:F]=6$.
\end{itemize}
\end{corollary}
label: art:discriminant:cubicgal@c14

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-e70c1d768016b80118db
Content:
\begin{proof}
Because $f$ is irreducible of degree $3$, $G$ is a transitive subgroup of $\Sym_3$, hence $G=A_3$ or $G=\Sym_3$. By Theorem~ [REF:art:discriminant:An@c14] , $G\sgrA_3$ exactly when $D$ is a square in $F$; the only transitive subgroup of $\Sym_3$ contained in $A_3$ is $A_3$ itself. So $D$ square gives $G=A_3$ with $[K:F]=|A_3|=3$, and $D$ non-square gives $G=\Sym_3$ with $[K:F]=6$.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
When $G=\Sym_3$ the proper intermediate fields are exactly the four predicted by the four nontrivial proper subgroups of $\Sym_3$: the three fields $F(\alpha_1),F(\alpha_2),F(\alpha_3)$ (each fixed by a transposition) and the quadratic field $F(\delta)$ fixed by $A_3$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& 1 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[ddr,dash,out=0,in=0,looseness=1.6] & \\
\langle (2\,3)\rangle \arrow[dr,dash] & \langle (1\,3)\rangle \arrow[d,dash] & \langle (1\,2)\rangle \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& \Sym_3 & A_3 \arrow[l,dash]
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& K \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash]\arrow[ddr,dash,out=0,in=0,looseness=1.6] & \\
F(\alpha_1) \arrow[dr,dash] & F(\alpha_2) \arrow[d,dash] & F(\alpha_3) \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& F & F(\delta) \arrow[l,dash]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left lattice: subgroups of $\Sym_3$ under inclusion -- the trivial group $1$ at the top, the three order-$2$ cyclic subgroups $\langle (2\,3)\rangle$, $\langle (1\,3)\rangle$, $\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ in the middle, and at the bottom $\Sym_3$ itself alongside $A_3$ (the unique index-$2$ normal subgroup, order $3$). Right lattice: intermediate fields of the splitting extension $K/F$ -- the full splitting field $K$ at the top, the three cubic subfields $F(\alpha_1)$, $F(\alpha_2)$, $F(\alpha_3)$ in the middle, and at the bottom $F$ alongside the quadratic subfield $F(\delta)=F(\sqrt{D})$. Both lattices are ordered by inclusion (subgroups) and by containment (fields); the dash edges record these inclusions.
\dgi{Arrows:} The double-headed arrow $\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }$ between the two lattices is the Galois correspondence: to each subgroup $H \leq \Sym_3$ it assigns the fixed field $\Fix(H) = \{x\in K : \sigma(x)=x for all \sigma\in H\}$; to each intermediate field $L$ it assigns $\Gal(K/L)$. Every dash edge in both diagrams is an inclusion; no edge carries an explicit formula because the correspondence is the conceptual content, not element-level maps.
\dgi{What commutes:} The correspondence reverses inclusion: if $H_1 \leq H_2$ then $\Fix(H_2) \subseteq \Fix(H_1)$. Concretely, $1 \leq \langle (i\,j)\rangle \leq \Sym_3$ maps to $K \supseteq F(\alpha_k) \supseteq F$, and $1 \leq A_3 \leq \Sym_3$ maps to $K \supseteq F(\delta) \supseteq F$. Every containment on the left reverses to a containment on the right: this order-reversal is the defining ``commuting'' property of the Galois correspondence.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Suppose $H_1 \subseteq H_2$ and $x\in\Fix(H_2)$. Every $\sigma \in H_1$ lies in $H_2$ and therefore fixes $x$, so $x\in\Fix(H_1)$; that is, $\Fix(H_2) \subseteq \Fix(H_1)$. The inclusion flips because a larger group imposes more conditions $\sigma(x)=x$, so fewer elements satisfy all of them -- a direct consequence of the definition of fixed field, no element-chasing beyond this.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the payoff of Corollary~ [REF:art:discriminant:cubicgal@c14] : once we know $G=\Sym_3$, it displays all proper intermediate fields in one picture, including the distinguished quadratic field $F(\delta)$ fixed by $A_3$. The position of $A_3$ in the left lattice (index $2$ in $\Sym_3$, containing none of the index-$3$ subgroups $\langle (i\,j)\rangle$) explains why $F(\delta)$ is a degree-$2$ extension of $F$ and is contained in none of the cubic fields $F(\alpha_k)$ (a degree-$2$ subfield cannot lie in a degree-$3$ extension of $F$).
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $f(x)=x^3-3x+1$ over $Q$, where $\disc=81=9^2$ and $G=A_3$. In that case the left lattice collapses: only $1 \leq A_3$ survive as subgroups, and the right lattice collapses to $K \supseteq Q$ with $F(\delta)=Q(9)=Q$. Contrast with $f(x)=x^3+3x+1$ ($\disc=-135$, $G=\Sym_3$): the full diagram applies, $F(\delta)=Q(\sqrt{-135})$ is genuinely quadratic, and each $Q(\alpha_i)$ is a distinct cubic subfield of the degree-$6$ splitting field.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} $A_3$ is drawn in the same row as $\Sym_3$ only to keep the picture compact; the two are comparable, $A_3 \subsetneq \Sym_3$ (the horizontal edge), and correspondingly $F \subsetneq F(\delta)$, with $F=\Fix(\Sym_3)$ the fixed field of the full Galois group. What $A_3$ is incomparable with are the three order-$2$ subgroups (it contains none of them and lies in none of them), which is why $F(\delta)$ neither contains nor is contained in any $F(\alpha_k)$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the Galois correspondence turns the subgroup lattice of $\Sym_3$ upside-down into the field lattice of $K/F$, making the distinguished quadratic subfield $F(\sqrt{D})$ visible as the fixed field of the unique index-$2$ subgroup $A_3$, so reading off all intermediate fields reduces to reading off all subgroups of the Galois group.
\end{dgx}
The larger subgroup $A_3$ (order $3$, index $2$) corresponds to the smaller field $F(\delta)=F(\sqrt{D})$, a quadratic over $F$; the small subgroups $\langle (i\,j)\rangle$ (order $2$, index $3$) correspond to the larger cubic fields $F(\alpha_k)$.

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
``Square in $F$'' is essential -- the discriminant is computed in $F$, but whether it is a square depends on $F$. Over $Q$, $\disc(x^3-3x+1)=81$ is a square and the group is $A_3$; but $-135$ being negative is automatically a non-square in $Q$, while over $C$ every element is a square, so this criterion is only informative over fields with genuine non-squares. Also remember $D=\delta^2$ is the square; the field-theoretic content lives in $\delta=\sqrt{D}$, not in $D$.
\end{pitfall}

Let $f(x)=x^3-c_1x^2+c_2x-c_3$ be an irreducible cubic over a field $F$ (characteristic $\neq 2,3$), and let $K$ be a splitting field of $f$ over $F$, with roots $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\in K$, so
\[
f(x)=(x-\alpha_1)(x-\alpha_2)(x-\alpha_3)\in K[x].
\]
Because $c_1=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3\in F$, the third root lies in the field generated by the first two: $F(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=F(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=K$. Setting $L=F(\alpha_1)$, irreducibility gives $[L:F]=3$, and over $L$ the cubic factors as $f(x)=(x-\alpha_1)q(x)$ with $q$ the quadratic whose roots are $\alpha_2,\alpha_3$. Thus $K$ is obtained from $L$ by adjoining a root of a quadratic, and there are exactly two cases:
\[
[K:F]=
\begin{cases}
6, & q irreducible over L\ \ (then [K:L]=2),\\
3, & q splits over L\ \ (then K=L).
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{remark}
Acting on the three roots, $\Gal(K/F)$ embeds as a transitive subgroup of $S_3$. The only transitive subgroups of $S_3$ are $S_3$ itself and $A_3=\langle (1\,2\,3)\rangle$, the cyclic group of order $3$. Type: proof

Content:
\begin{proof}
We have $\delta^2=D$, so $D$ is a square in $F$ exactly when $\delta\in F$. A permutation of the roots multiplies $\delta$ by its sign, so $\delta$ is fixed by every even element of $G$ and negated by every odd one. If $\delta\in F$ then $\delta$ is fixed by all of $G$; hence $G$ contains no odd permutation, forcing $G\le A_3$. As $G$ is transitive this gives $G=A_3$ and $[K:F]=3$. If $\delta\notin F$ then $\delta$ is moved by some element of $G$, so $G$ contains an odd permutation; a transitive subgroup of $S_3$ with an odd permutation must be all of $S_3$, so $G=S_3$ and $[K:F]=6$.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
For a depressed cubic $x^3+px+q$ (the $x^2$ term cleared by $x\mapsto x+c_1/3$), the discriminant simplifies to
\[
D=-4p^3-27q^2.
\]
The subfield lattice mirrors the subgroup lattice of $G$. When $G=A_3$ there are no proper intermediate fields (degree $3$ is prime); when $G=S_3$ the four nontrivial proper subgroups give four proper intermediate fields, $F(\alpha_1),F(\alpha_2),F(\alpha_3)$ and $F(\delta)=F(\sqrt{D})$.

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.5em]
& & K \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & \\
F(\alpha_1)\arrow[drr,dash] & F(\alpha_2)\arrow[dr,dash] & F(\alpha_3)\arrow[d,dash] & & F(\sqrt{D})\arrow[dll,dash] \\
& & F & &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.5em]
& & S_3 \arrow[dll,dash]\arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash]\arrow[drr,dash] & & \\
\langle (2\,3)\rangle\arrow[drr,dash] & \langle (1\,3)\rangle\arrow[dr,dash] & \langle (1\,2)\rangle\arrow[d,dash] & & A_3\arrow[dll,dash] \\
& & 1 & &
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left diagram: six nodes arranged as a lattice of subfields of the splitting field $K$
over $F$. Top node is $K$ (the full splitting field, degree $6$ over $F$ when $G = S_{3}$). The four
middle nodes are $F(\alpha_{1})$, $F(\alpha_{2})$, $F(\alpha_{3})$ (each of degree $3$ over $F$, generated by
one root) and $F(\sqrt{D})$ (degree $2$ over $F$, the fixed field of $A_{3}$). Bottom node is $F$ (the base
field). Right diagram: six nodes arranged as the subgroup lattice of $S_{3}$. Top is $S_{3}$
itself, the four middle nodes are $\langle (2\,3)\rangle$, $\langle (1\,3)\rangle$, $\langle (1\,2)\rangle$ (order-$2$ transpositions),
and $A_{3}$ (index-$2$ normal subgroup of order $3$), and the bottom node is the trivial subgroup $1$.
\dgi{Arrows:} All edges are drawn as unlabelled dashes, indicating containment (field inclusions on
the left; subgroup inclusions on the right). The horizontal double arrow $\xleftrightarrow{\ \Fix\ }$
between the two diagrams is the Galois correspondence: it sends each subgroup $H \leq S_{3}$ to its fixed
field $\Fix(H) = \{ x \in K : \sigma(x) = x for all \sigma \in H \}$, and in the other direction
sends each intermediate field $E$ to $\Gal(K/E)$. The correspondence reverses inclusion: larger
subgroups correspond to smaller (lower) subfields.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no loop to chase here; instead the key equalities are the index--degree
pairings. For each pair $(E, H)$ matched by $\Fix$: $[K:E] = |H|$ and $[E:F] = [S_{3}:H]$.
Concretely: $\Fix(\langle (2\,3)\rangle) = F(\alpha_{1})$ because $(2\,3)$ swaps $\alpha_{2}$ and $\alpha_{3}$ while
fixing $\alpha_{1}$; $\Fix(A_{3}) = F(\sqrt{D})$ because the even permutations fix $\delta = \sqrt{D}$;
$\Fix(1) = K$ and $\Fix(S_{3}) = F$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory guarantees the correspondence is an
inclusion-reversing bijection between the lattice of intermediate fields $F \subseteq E \subseteq K$
and the lattice of subgroups $H \leq G = S_{3}$, because $K/F$ is a finite Galois extension ($K$ is a
splitting field of a separable polynomial). The sign-of-permutation argument from the proof shows $\delta$
is fixed exactly by even permutations, placing $F(\sqrt{D})$ opposite $A_{3}$; and $\alpha_{i}$ is fixed by
the unique transposition that fixes index $i$, placing $F(\alpha_{i})$ opposite $\langle (the other two)\rangle$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the payoff of Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:main@c14] . It makes
visible, simultaneously, (a) the degree formula $[K:F] = |G| = 6$, (b) why $F(\sqrt{D})$ is the
unique degree-$2$ intermediate field (corresponding to the unique index-$2$ subgroup $A_{3}$), and
(c) why the three fields $F(\alpha_{i})$ are conjugate (corresponding to the three conjugate order-$2$
subgroups). A student who only sees the algebraic statement gains this geometric picture of the full
intermediate-field structure at a glance.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $F = Q$ and $f(x) = x^{3} + 3x + 1$ (Worked Example above, $D = -135$,
not a square, $G = S_{3}$, $[K:Q] = 6$). The four proper intermediate fields are $Q(\alpha_{1})$,
$Q(\alpha_{2})$, $Q(\alpha_{3})$ (each of degree $3$ and generated by a single root: one of them by the real root, the other two by the two non-real, complex-conjugate roots) and $Q(\sqrt{-135}) = Q(\sqrt{-15})$ (degree $2$).
Matching to the right diagram: $\Gal(K/Q(\alpha_{i})) = \langle (transposition fixing i)\rangle$ and
$\Gal(K/Q(\sqrt{-15})) = A_{3}$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the correspondence as order-preserving, thinking a
larger subgroup corresponds to a larger subfield. It is order-reversing: the biggest
proper subgroup $A_{3}$ (order $3$) corresponds to the smallest proper intermediate field
$F(\sqrt{D})$ (degree $2$ over $F$, degree $3$ below $K$). Also, the diagram applies only to the
$G = S_{3}$ case ($D$ not a square); when $G = A_{3}$ the lattices collapse to two-node chains ($F\subset K$ and $1<A_{3}$) with no
proper intermediate fields.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the Galois correspondence turns the abstract group-theoretic
structure of $S_{3}$ (four nontrivial proper subgroups in two conjugacy classes) into a concrete map of all intermediate
fields between $F$ and its cubic splitting field, with the discriminant field $F(\sqrt{D})$ sitting at the
unique degree-$2$ level.
\end{dgx}

Title: $x^3+3x+1$ has Galois group $S_3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$x^3+3x+1$ has Galois group $S_3$}
Show $f(x)=x^3+3x+1$ is irreducible over $Q$ and determine $\Gal(K/Q)$ and $[K:Q]$.
\wrec The cubic is already depressed ($p=3,q=1$); use the rational root test for irreducibility, then Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:main@c14] via $D=-4p^3-27q^2$.
\wsol A cubic is reducible over $Q$ iff it has a rational root; the only candidates are $\pm1$, and $f(1)=5\neq0$, $f(-1)=-3\neq0$, so $f$ is irreducible. The discriminant is
\[
D=-4(3)^3-27(1)^2=-108-27=-135=-5\cdot 3^3.
\]
This is negative, hence not a square in $Q$, so by Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:main@c14] we get $G=S_3$ and $[K:Q]=6$. Geometrically $f'(x)=3x^2+3>0$ everywhere, so $f$ is strictly increasing with a single real root; the splitting field also contains the two complex roots, confirming $[K:Q]>3$. Check. $D<0$ means exactly one real root and a non-real conjugate pair, the signature of an $S_3$ cubic over $Q$.
\end{wex}

Concretely, if $\alpha_1$ is a root then $\alpha_2=\alpha_1^2-2$ is another root: indeed $g(\alpha_1^2-2)=(\alpha_1^2-2)^3-3(\alpha_1^2-2)+1$ reduces to $0$ after using $\alpha_1^3=3\alpha_1-1$. Check. $\delta=\sqrt{81}=9\inQ$, so no automorphism can negate $\delta$; $G$ contains only even permutations, i.e.\ $G=A_3$, consistent with $K=Q(\alpha_1)$ being all of the splitting field.

f(x)=x^3+3px+2q,\qquad s_1=0,\ s_2=3p,\ s_3=-2q,\qquad D=-2^2 3^3(q^2+p^3),

\[
z=m_1+\omega m_2+\omega^2 m_3,\qquad z'=m_1+\omega^2 m_2+\omega m_3.
\]

Following Artin's normalization, write the cubic as
\[
f(x)=x^3+3px+2q,\qquad s_1=0,\ s_2=3p,\ s_3=-2q,\qquad D=-2^2 3^3(q^2+p^3),
\]
with roots $m_1,m_2,m_3$ (numbered arbitrarily). Set the two resolvents
\[
z=m_1+\omega m_2+\omega^2 m_3,\qquad z'=m_1+\omega^2 m_2+\omega m_3.
\]

Title: {resolvents are eigenvectors}
Label: art:cubic:resolvent@c14
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{resolvents are eigenvectors}] 
For $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)$ one has $\sigma(z)=\omega^{-1}z$ and $\sigma(z')=\omega z'$. Consequently $z^3$ and $z'^3$ are fixed by $\sigma$, hence lie in $F$, and
\[
m_1=\tfrac13(s_1+z+z')=\tfrac13(z+z').
\]
\end{proposition}
label: art:cubic:resolvent@c14

Type: proof

Content:
\begin{proof}
The automorphism $\sigma$ permutes the roots cyclically, $m_1\mapsto m_2\mapsto m_3\mapsto m_1$, and fixes $\omega\in F$. Therefore
\[
\sigma(z)=m_2+\omega m_3+\omega^2 m_1=\omega^2(m_1+\omega m_2+\omega^2 m_3)=\omega^2 z=\omega^{-1}z,
\]
using $\omega^3=1$. The same computation with $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ swapped gives $\sigma(z')=\omega z'$. Cubing, $\sigma(z^3)=(\omega^{-1})^3z^3=z^3$ and likewise $\sigma(z'^3)=z'^3$; since $\sigma$ generates $G$, both $z^3,z'^3$ lie in the fixed field $F$. Finally $z+z'=(m_1+m_1)+(\omega+\omega^2)m_2+(\omega^2+\omega)m_3=2m_1-m_2-m_3$, and adding $s_1=m_1+m_2+m_3=0$ gives $z+z'=3m_1$, i.e.\ $m_1=\tfrac13(z+z')$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
By Proposition~ [REF:art:cubic:resolvent@c14] , $z^3$ and $z'^3$ are the two roots of a quadratic over $F$ -- the resolvent quadratic -- whose coefficients are symmetric in the $m_i$ up to $\delta$. Carrying out the elimination using $A-B=\delta$ and $A+B=6q$ shows
\[
z^3,\ z'^3 = 27\bigl(-q\pm\sqrt{q^2+p^3}\bigr),
\]
so $z=3\sqrt[3]{-q+\sqrt{q^2+p^3}}$ and $z'=3\sqrt[3]{-q-\sqrt{q^2+p^3}}$. Substituting into $m_1=\tfrac13(z+z')$ yields the stated sum of cube roots. The product constraint $zz'=9\sqrt[3]{q^2-(q^2+p^3)}=-9p$ (equivalently the cube-root product $=-p$) selects the three correct pairings out of the nine formal ones, giving exactly the three roots $m_1,m_2,m_3$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The formula is genuinely ambiguous if read naively: the inner square root has two values, and each cube root has three, so the right-hand term can be read six ways, as can the other -- yet $f$ has only three roots. The product condition $zz'=-9p$ (cube roots multiplying to $-p$) is what cuts the $9$ formal pairings down to the $3$ true roots. This is why a radical expression for a root, on its own, is of limited practical use.
\end{remark}

Title: Cardano on $x^3+3x+2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cardano on $x^3+3x+2$}
Use Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:cardano@c14] to write a root of $f(x)=x^3+3x+2$ in radicals.
\wrec Match $x^3+3px+2q$: here $3p=3$ and $2q=2$, so $p=1,q=1$; then plug into the boxed formula.
\wsol With $p=q=1$ we get $q^2+p^3=1+1=2$, so
\[
m_1=\sqrt[3]{\,-1+\sqrt2\,}+\sqrt[3]{\,-1-\sqrt2\,}.
\]
The discriminant is $D=-2^2 3^3(q^2+p^3)=-4\cdot27\cdot2=-216<0$, not a square, so $G=S_3$ over $Q$ and the two cube-root terms are genuinely needed (one real root, two complex). Check. Numerically $-1+\sqrt2\approx0.4142$ and $-1-\sqrt2\approx-2.4142$, with real cube roots $\approx0.7454$ and $\approx-1.3415$; their sum $\approx-0.596$ satisfies $(-0.596)^3+3(-0.596)+2\approx-0.21-1.79+2\approx0$. The cube roots' product is $\sqrt[3]{(-1)^2-2}=\sqrt[3]{-1}=-1=-p$, as required.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Deriving a root of $x^3-3x+1$ through the resolvent
Content:
\begin{wex}{Deriving a root of $x^3-3x+1$ through the resolvent}
For $g(x)=x^3-3x+1$ (the $A_3$ cubic above), set up the resolvent and read off $m_1=\tfrac13(z+z')$.
\wrec Write $g$ as $x^3+3px+2q$: then $3p=-3$ and $2q=1$, so $p=-1$, $q=\tfrac12$; apply Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:cardano@c14] with these values, working over $F=Q(\omega)$ so that $z,z'$ exist.
\wsol Here $q^2+p^3=\tfrac14-1=-\tfrac34$, so the inner square root is $\sqrt{-3/4}=\tfrac{\sqrt{-3}}{2}$, which lies in $Q(\omega)$ since $\sqrt{-3}=\omega-\omega^2\inQ(\omega)$. Then
\[
z^3=27\bigl(-\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt{-3}}{2}\bigr)=27\,\omega,\qquad z'^3=27\bigl(-\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt{-3}}{2}\bigr)=27\,\omega^2,
\]
because $-\tfrac12\pm\tfrac{\sqrt{-3}}{2}=\omega,\omega^2$ exactly. Choosing $z=3\sqrt[3]{\omega}$ and $z'=3\sqrt[3]{\omega^2}$ with $zz'=-9p=9$, a root is
\[
m_1=\tfrac13(z+z')=\sqrt[3]{\omega}+\sqrt[3]{\omega^2}=2\cos\!\Bigl(\tfrac{2\pi}{9}\Bigr)\approx 1.532.
\]
Check. $D=81=9^2$ is a square, confirming $G=A_3$; the resolvent cubes $z^3=27\omega$ and $z'^3=27\omega^2$ are $27$ times the primitive cube roots of unity, so $z^3z'^3=27^2$ matches $(zz')^3=9^3=729=27^2$. Numerically $g(1.532)\approx 3.596-4.596+1\approx0$.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The clean cube-root form requires $\omega\in F$. The discriminant test (Theorem~ [REF:art:cubic:main@c14] ) lives over the original $F$, but the Lagrange resolvent only diagonalizes $\sigma$ after adjoining $\omega$. For an $A_3$ cubic over $Q$ such as $x^3-3x+1$, the splitting field $K=Q(\alpha_1)$ is real and does not contain $\omega$; Cardano's formula then expresses the real root as a sum of cube roots of complex numbers (the casus irreducibilis), even though the root itself is real. The detour through non-real numbers is unavoidable: in the casus irreducibilis no expression of the root by real radicals exists.
\end{pitfall}

Section: Galois Theory > Quartic Equations and the Resolvent Cubic > Quartic equations and the resolvent cubic
Type: prose
Content:
For a quartic the Galois group is hard to pin down by degree alone. Throughout this section $F$ is a field of characteristic $\neq2$. Let $f(x)\in F[x]$ be an irreducible separable quartic with (distinct) roots $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4$ in a splitting field $K$. Acting on the four roots represents $G=\Gal(K/F)$ as a transitive subgroup of $S_4$, and there are only five such up to conjugacy:
\[
S_4,\quad A_4,\quad D_4,\quad C_4,\quad V_4 .
\]
Here $D_4$ is the dihedral group of order $8$ (this is D\&F's $D_8$), realized as the symmetries of the square $1\,2\,3\,4$; there are three conjugate copies of $D_4$ and three of $C_4$. The group $V_4=\{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is the Klein four-group of double transpositions -- a normal subgroup of $S_4$ (Artin writes it $D_2$). The orders are $\ord{S_4}=24$, $\ord{A_4}=12$, $\ord{D_4}=8$, $\ord{C_4}=\ord{V_4}=4$, so $\ord{G}=[K:F]$ already separates $S_4,A_4,D_4$ but leaves the pair $\{C_4,V_4\}$ of order $4$ undecided -- and the order is itself awkward to compute. To resolve everything Artin uses two auxiliary quantities built from the roots: the square root of the discriminant, and Lagrange's resolvent cubic.

Type: definition

\begin{definition}
The discriminant of $f$ is $D=\delta^2$, where
\[
\delta=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)=(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)(\alpha_1-\alpha_3)(\alpha_1-\alpha_4)(\alpha_2-\alpha_3)(\alpha_2-\alpha_4)(\alpha_3-\alpha_4).
\]
The roots being distinct, $\delta\neq0$. A permutation $\sigma$ of the roots multiplies $\delta$ by $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$: even permutations fix $\delta$, odd permutations negate it.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Galois Theory > Quartic Equations and the Resolvent Cubic > Quartic equations and the resolvent cubic
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-ceae2085a9528d9c0bc8
Content:
\begin{proof}
$D=\delta^2$ is a square in $F$ exactly when $\delta\in F$, i.e.\ when $\delta$ is fixed by every element of $G$. The permutations fixing $\delta$ are precisely the even ones, so $D$ is a square iff $G\sgr A_4$. Among the five transitive subgroups, those lying in $A_4$ are $A_4$ itself and $V_4$ (its elements $(ij)(kl)$ are even); the ones containing an odd permutation are $S_4$, $D_4$ (which contains $4$-cycles and transpositions, both odd), and $C_4$ (a $4$-cycle is odd). Reading off the list of five transitive subgroups above gives the two cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
With the roots numbered $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_4$, form the three sums of opposite root-pairs
\[
\beta_1=\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4,\qquad
\beta_2=\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4,\qquad
\beta_3=\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3,
\]
and set
\[
g(x)=(x-\beta_1)(x-\beta_2)(x-\beta_3).
\]
This $g$ is the resolvent cubic of $f$.
\end{definition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-b97fbe9fdad23c265484
Content:
\begin{proof}
Let $B=\{\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\}$, a set of size $3$ by the Lemma. The action of $S_4$ on $B$ is transitive with kernel $V_4$, giving $\varphi\colon S_4\to S_3$. The roots of $g$ are the $\beta_i$, so $g$ splits in $F$ iff $G$ fixes every $\beta_i$, i.e.\ iff $G\sgr\ker\varphi=V_4$; since $G$ is a transitive subgroup, this forces $G=V_4$.

If $g$ is irreducible over $F$, then $G$ acts transitively on its roots $B$, so $\varphi(G)$ is a transitive subgroup of $S_3$ and $3\mid\ord{\varphi(G)}\mid\ord G$. Conversely, if $3\mid\ord G$ then $G$ contains an element $\rho$ of order $3$ (Cauchy); $\rho\notin V_4=\ker\varphi$, so $\varphi(\rho)$ is a $3$-cycle permuting $B$ cyclically, whence $G$ acts transitively on $B$ and $g$ is irreducible. The transitive subgroups with $3\mid\ord G$ are exactly $S_4$ and $A_4$. The remaining case -- $g$ has one root in $F$ and the other two are conjugate over a quadratic -- leaves $G$ of order divisible by $2$ but not $3$ and not all of $V_4$, which by the list of five transitive subgroups means $G=D_4$ or $C_4$.
\end{proof}

Type: method
Title: Identifying $\Gal(f/F)$ for an irreducible quartic.
Content:
\begin{method}{Identifying $\Gal(f/F)$ for an irreducible quartic.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Compute the discriminant $D$ and decide whether it is a square in $F$.
\item Form the resolvent cubic $g$ and find its factorization type over $F$ (split / one root / irreducible).
\item Read off $G$ from the table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & D a square & D not a square\\\hline
g reducible & V_4 & D_4 or C_4\\
g irreducible & A_4 & S_4
\end{array}
\]
\end{enumerate}
The one residual ambiguity ($D_4$ vs.\ $C_4$, when $D$ is not a square and $g$ has a single root in $F$) is not resolved by any symmetric expression in the roots; one decides it directly, e.g.\ by checking whether $f$ stays irreducible over $F(\sqrt D)$, or whether a product like $\alpha_i\alpha_j$ lies in the relevant quadratic field.
\end{method}

Type: prose
Content:
The homomorphism $\varphi\colon S_4\to S_3$ underlying the whole method is best pictured as a quotient lattice, with $V_4=\ker\varphi$ at the bottom:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.6em]
& S_4 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
A_4 \arrow[dr,dash] & & D_4 \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash] \\
& V_4 \arrow[d,dash] & C_4 \arrow[dl,dash] \\
& 1 &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }
\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.6em]
S_3 \arrow[d,dash] \\
A_3 \arrow[d,dash] \\
1
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Under $\varphi$: $S_4\twoheadrightarrow S_3$, $A_4\twoheadrightarrow A_3=C_3$, while $D_4,C_4,V_4$ all map into a single transposition-or-trivial image, which is why $g$ fails to be irreducible exactly for these.

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left lattice has six nodes: the group $S_4$ (order 24) at the top; its subgroups $A_4$ (order 12, alternating) and $D_4$ (order 8, dihedral, one of three conjugate copies); then the Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ (order 4, normal in $S_4$) and the cyclic $C_4$ (order 4); and the trivial group $1$ at the bottom. The right lattice has three nodes: $S_3$ (order 6) at top, $A_3 = C_3$ (order 3, even permutations of the $\beta_i$) in the middle, and $1$ at the bottom. The horizontal arrow $\varphi$ between the two lattices is the surjective group homomorphism induced by the action of $S_4$ on $\{\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\}$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Dashes in both lattices are inclusion arrows (subgroup containment), pointing downward by convention. The arrow $\xrightarrow{\varphi}$ between the diagrams is the surjection $\varphi\colon S_4\twoheadrightarrow S_3$ sending each $\sigma\in S_4$ to the permutation it induces on the resolvent roots $\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3$; this is an induced map, and its kernel is precisely $V_4$ (the elements fixing all $\beta_i$).
\dgi{What commutes:} This is not a commutativity diagram but a correspondence diagram: the left lattice restricted to $G = \Gal(f/F) \le S_4$ maps via $\varphi$ onto a subgroup $\varphi(G) \le S_3$, with $G \cap V_4 = \ker(\varphi|_G)$, yielding an isomorphism $G/(G \cap V_4) \cong \varphi(G)$. The key containments: $\varphi(S_4) = S_3$, $\varphi(A_4) = A_3$, $\varphi(V_4) = 1$, and $\varphi(D_4) = \varphi(C_4)$ is a subgroup of order $2$ generated by a transposition (not all of $S_3$).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\varphi$: we need $\sigma(\beta_i)$ to depend only on $\sigma$ and not on a choice of representative, which is automatic since $\sigma$ acts on roots directly. The key check is that $V_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$: any conjugate of an element of $V_4$ is again a double transposition, so $V_4$ is normal and $S_4/V_4 \cong S_3$ is a genuine quotient. For $\sigma \in D_4$ or $C_4$: these groups intersect $V_4$ in a subgroup of order $\ge 2$, so $\varphi(\sigma)$ generates a proper subgroup of $S_3$ -- it cannot act transitively on $\{\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\}$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} Immediately after the classification method, this diagram explains why the resolvent cubic $g$ detects $3 \mid |G|$: $g$ is irreducible iff $G$ acts transitively on $\{\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\}$ iff $\varphi(G)$ is transitive in $S_3$ iff $3 \mid |\varphi(G)|$ iff $3 \mid |G|$. The lattice picture makes visible exactly which of the five transitive subgroups of $S_4$ have $3$-power in their image.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G = A_4$. Its image $\varphi(A_4) = A_3 = C_3$ is transitive (order 3), so $g$ is irreducible. Take $G = V_4$: $\varphi(V_4) = \{e\}$ (all elements are double transpositions fixing every $\beta_i$), so $g$ splits completely. Take $G = D_4$: $\varphi(D_4)$ is generated by a single transposition, a subgroup of order 2 in $S_3$; transitivity fails, so $g$ has exactly one rational root. These match the three rows of the classification table.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read the left lattice as a single subgroup chain $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset 1$ and ignore $D_4$ and $C_4$. But the whole point of the diagram is that $D_4$ and $C_4$ do not contain $A_4$; they sit on a separate branch on the right, where $D_4$ contains $V_4$ but $C_4\le D_4$ does not. Collapsing $D_4$ and $C_4$ into the $A_4$-chain gives the wrong lattice and misses the $D_4/C_4$ ambiguity entirely.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the surjection $\varphi\colon S_4\twoheadrightarrow S_3$ with kernel $V_4$ converts the question ``which of the five transitive Galois groups does $f$ have?'' into the question ``where does $G$ sit in $S_3$?'', and the resolvent cubic $g$ reads off exactly that image by whether it is irreducible, has one root, or splits.
\end{dgx}
