Type: example
Title: Radical of a principal ideal in $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Radical of a principal ideal in $Z$}
Compute $\rad(180)$ in $Z$ and identify the primes over $(180)$.
\wrec In a U.F.D., if $a=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$ then $\rad(a)=(p_1\cdots p_r)$; the minimal primes over $(a)$ are the $(p_i)$ (in $Z$ these are all the primes over $(a)$).
\wsol Factor $180=2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5$, so the distinct prime divisors are $2,3,5$ and $\rad(180)=(2\cdot3\cdot5)=(30)$. The primes containing $(180)$ are $(2),(3),(5)$, and $(2)\cap(3)\cap(5)=(\lcm(2,3,5))=(30)$, matching the theorem. Sanity check: $30^2=900=5\cdot180\in(180)$ so $30\in\rad(180)$; and $\rad(180)$ is itself radical since $30=2\cdot3\cdot5$ is squarefree, so $\rad\rad(180)=(30)$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A radical ideal need not be prime
Content:
\begin{wex}{A radical ideal need not be prime}
In $k[x,y]$ show $\rad(xy)=(xy)$ is radical but not prime.
\wrec An ideal is radical iff the quotient has no nilpotents; it is prime iff the quotient is a domain.
\wsol Since $xy$ is squarefree (product of the distinct irreducibles $x,y$), $(xy)=(x)\cap(y)$ and $\rad(xy)=(x)\cap(y)=(xy)$, a radical ideal. But it is not prime: $x\cdot y\in(xy)$ while neither $x$ nor $y$ lies in $(xy)$ (degree reasons). Sanity check: $k[x,y]/(xy)$ has no nilpotents (a polynomial whose square is divisible by $xy$ is itself divisible by both $x$ and $y$ off the axes), confirming radical, yet it has the zero divisors $\bar x,\bar y$, confirming non-prime.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Nilradical of $Z/12Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Nilradical of $Z/12Z$}
Find the nilpotent elements of $R=Z/12Z$ and exhibit $\nil(R)$ as an intersection of primes.
\wrec $\nil(R)=\rad(0)=\bigcap\fp$; in $Z/nZ$ the primes are $(p)/nZ$ for $p\mid n$.
\wsol $12=2^2\cdot3$, so $\rad(0)$ in $Z$ pulled to the quotient is $(6)/12Z=\{0,6\}$. Indeed $6^2=36\equiv0$, while $2,3,4$ are not nilpotent ($2^k$ cycles through $2,4,8,4,\dots$). The primes of $Z/12Z$ are $(2)$ and $(3)$, and $(2)\cap(3)=(6)$. Sanity check: $\{0,6\}$ is closed under addition and absorbs multiplication, and $(\bar6)^2=\bar0$, so it is the nilradical; the quotient $Z/12Z$ is not reduced precisely because $12$ is not squarefree.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The radical of an ideal; reduced rings
Type: example
Title: Powers of the radical: the Noetherian case
Content:
\begin{wex}{Powers of the radical: the Noetherian case}
If $R$ is Noetherian, show some power of $\rad\fa$ lies in $\fa$; deduce the nilradical is nilpotent.
\wrec In a Noetherian ring $\rad\fa$ is finitely generated, so finitely many of its generators' powers land in $\fa$.
\wsol Write $\rad\fa=(a_1,\dots,a_m)$ with $a_i^{k_i}\in\fa$, and put $k=\max_i k_i$. Then $(\rad\fa)^{km}$ is generated by products $a_1^{d_1}\cdots a_m^{d_m}$ with $\sum d_i=km$, and by pigeonhole some $d_i\ge k$, so each generator has a factor $a_i^{d_i}\in\fa$; hence $(\rad\fa)^{km}\subseteq\fa$. Taking $\fa=0$ gives $\nil(R)^{km}=0$. Sanity check: in $Z/p^eZ$ the nilradical is $(p)$ and $(p)^e=0$, exactly a finite power vanishing; over a non-Noetherian ring this can fail, e.g.\ $k[x_1,x_2,\dots]/(x_1,x_2^2,x_3^3,\dots)$ has a non-nilpotent nilradical.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}
For an ideal $\fa\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ (or any subset of polynomials), the zero set (variety) is
\[
V(\fa)=\{P\in\Aff^n : f(P)=0\ for all f\in\fa\}.
\]
For a subset $A\subseteq\Aff^n$, the ideal of $A$ is
\[
I(A)=\{f\in k[x_1,\dots,x_n] : f(P)=0\ for all P\in A\}.
\]
A subset of the form $V(\fa)$ is an affine algebraic set.
\end{definition}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The maps $I(\cdot)$ and $V(\cdot)$: a Galois connection
Type: proposition
Title: {the Galois connection}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{the Galois connection}]
The maps $V$ and $I$ are inclusion-reversing and satisfy, for all ideals $\fa$ and subsets $A$,
\[
\fa\subseteq I(V(\fa)),\qquad A\subseteq V(I(A)),\qquad V(I(V(\fa)))=V(\fa),\qquad I(V(I(A)))=I(A).
\]
Consequently $V$ and $I$ restrict to mutually inverse, order-reversing bijections between the algebraic sets $V(\fa)$ and the ideals of the form $I(A)$. Moreover $I(A)$ is always a radical ideal.
\end{proposition}

Type: example
Title: $V$ collapses an ideal and its radical
Content:
\begin{wex}{$V$ collapses an ideal and its radical}
Show $V(\fa)=V(\rad\fa)$ for every ideal $\fa$, with the explicit case $\fa=(x^2)$ in $k[x]$.
\wrec A point kills $f$ iff it kills $f^k$; so passing to radicals does not change zero sets.
\wsol If $a\in\rad\fa$ then $a^k\in\fa$, and $a^k(P)=0$ on $V(\fa)$ gives $a(P)^k=0$, hence $a(P)=0$; so $V(\fa)\subseteq V(\rad\fa)$, and the reverse holds since $\fa\subseteq\rad\fa$ reverses. For $(x^2)\subseteq k[x]$: $\rad(x^2)=(x)$ and $V(x^2)=V(x)=\{0\}$. Sanity check: the ``double point'' $(x^2)$ and the reduced point $(x)$ have the same underlying set $\{0\}$; the radical forgets the multiplicity, exactly the redundancy the radical was invented to remove.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $I$ of a finite point set
Content:
\begin{wex}{$I$ of a finite point set}
With $k$ infinite, compute $I(\{(0,0),(1,0)\})$ in $k[x,y]$.
\wrec $I(A)$ is the set of polynomials vanishing at every listed point; for finitely many points it is an intersection of the corresponding maximal ideals.
\wsol A point $(a,b)$ has $I(\{(a,b)\})=(x-a,y-b)$, the maximal ideal of functions vanishing there. So $I(\{(0,0),(1,0)\})=(x,y)\cap(x-1,y)$. A polynomial lies here iff it vanishes at both points; one checks this intersection equals $(y,\ x^2-x)=(y,\ x(x-1))$. Sanity check: $y$ vanishes on both, and $x(x-1)$ vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=1$; conversely modulo $(y,x(x-1))$ every class is represented by $c_0+c_1x$, a $2$-dimensional $k$-space, matching the $2$ points -- the coordinate ring of two reduced points is $k\times k$.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {irreducible $\Longleftrightarrow$ prime; unique decomposition}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{irreducible $\Longleftrightarrow$ prime; unique decomposition}]
Let $V$ be a nonempty algebraic set in $\Aff^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $V$ is irreducible if and only if $I(V)$ is a prime ideal; equivalently iff $k[V]$ is an integral domain.
\item $V$ has a unique irredundant decomposition $V=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_q$ into varieties with $V_i\not\subseteq V_j$ for $i\ne j$. The $V_i$ are the irreducible components of $V$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) If $V=V_1\cup V_2$ properly, pick $f_1\in I(V_1)\setminus I(V)$ and $f_2\in I(V_2)\setminus I(V)$; then $f_1f_2$ vanishes on $V$ so $f_1f_2\in I(V)$ with neither factor in $I(V)$, so $I(V)$ is not prime. Conversely if $f_1f_2\in I(V)$ with $f_i\notin I(V)$, set $V_i=V\cap V(f_i)$: both are proper closed subsets and $V=V_1\cup V_2$, so $V$ is reducible. The translation to $k[V]$ is the standard fact that $R/\fp$ is a domain iff $\fp$ is prime. (2) Existence: were the family of algebraic sets with no finite decomposition into varieties nonempty, a maximal $I(V_0)$ (Noetherian!) gives a minimal bad $V_0$ which, being reducible, splits into strictly smaller pieces that do decompose -- contradiction. Uniqueness: intersect one decomposition against the other and use irreducibility to match components.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the order-reversing bijection of the Galois connection made precise on the irreducible level: varieties in $\Aff^n$ correspond to prime ideals that arise as $I(V)$. It refines the radical theorem -- writing a radical ideal as $\bigcap\fp$ over its minimal primes is the algebraic shadow of decomposing $V$ into components. (The general module/ideal version, primary decomposition, is developed in Section~6.)

\begin{definition}
For a variety $V$ the domain $k[V]$ has a fraction field $k(V)$, the field of rational functions on $V$. The dimension of $V$ is $\dim V=\trdeg_k k(V)$.
\end{definition}

Type: example
Title: The cuspidal cubic is a variety
Content:
\begin{wex}{The cuspidal cubic is a variety}
With $k$ infinite, show $V=V(y^2-x^3)\subseteq\Aff^2$ is irreducible and compute its coordinate ring and dimension.
\wrec $V$ is a variety iff $I(V)$ is prime iff $k[V]$ is a domain; $\dim V=\trdeg_k k(V)$.
\wsol $y^2-x^3$ is irreducible in $k[x,y]$ (it is monic of degree $2$ in $y$ with no root in $k[x]$, as $x^3$ is not a square), so $(y^2-x^3)$ is prime. It equals $I(V)$: if $f$ vanishes on $V$, write $f\equiv a(x)+y\,b(x)\pmod{y^2-x^3}$; then $a(t^2)+t^3b(t^2)=0$ for every $t$ in the infinite field $k$, so this polynomial in $t$ is $0$, and comparing even and odd powers of $t$ gives $a=b=0$. Then $k[V]=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ is a domain, so $V$ is a variety. Setting $t=y/x$ in $k(V)$ gives $x=t^2,\ y=t^3$, so $k(V)=k(t)$ and $\dim V=\trdeg_k k(t)=1$. Sanity check: $V$ is the image of the parametrization $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$, a curve, consistent with dimension $1$; the cusp at the origin does not affect irreducibility or dimension.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A union of axes is reducible
Content:
\begin{wex}{A union of axes is reducible}
With $k$ infinite, decompose $V(xy)\subseteq\Aff^2$ into components and read off the coordinate ring's defect.
\wrec $V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g)$; the components are the $V(\fp_i)$ for the minimal primes $\fp_i$ over $I(V)$.
\wsol $V(xy)=V(x)\cup V(y)$, the union of the two coordinate axes. Since $(xy)=(x)\cap(y)$ with $(x),(y)$ prime and incomparable, the irredundant decomposition is into the $y$-axis $V(x)$ and the $x$-axis $V(y)$. The coordinate ring $k[x,y]/(xy)$ has the zero divisors $\bar x\bar y=0$, so it is not a domain -- exactly why $V(xy)$ is not a variety. Sanity check: two distinct minimal primes $(x),(y)$ over the radical ideal $(xy)$ give exactly two components; the ring is reduced (radical ideal) but not a domain (reducible).
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Points are zero-dimensional varieties
Content:
\begin{wex}{Points are zero-dimensional varieties}
Show a single point $P=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ is a variety and $\dim\{P\}=0$.
\wrec $I(\{P\})=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$ is maximal, hence prime; dimension is the transcendence degree of the residue field.
\wsol The ideal $\fm_P=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$ is maximal with $k[x]/\fm_P\cong k$, so it is prime and $\{P\}$ is irreducible. Then $k[\{P\}]=k$ and $k(\{P\})=k$, giving $\dim=\trdeg_k k=0$. Sanity check: a finite set $\{P_1,\dots,P_r\}$ decomposes into its singletons, each a $0$-dimensional component, and its coordinate ring is $k^r$ -- $r$ minimal primes, $r$ points, dimension $0$.
\end{wex}

Title: Linear subspaces are varieties
Content:
\begin{wex}{Linear subspaces are varieties}
With $k$ infinite, show the zero set $V$ of linear polynomials $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_m$, when nonempty, is a variety.
\wrec An ideal generated by linear forms (after translating to the origin) has domain quotient -- a polynomial ring in the remaining coordinates.
\wsol After an affine change of coordinates, $V$ is the linear subspace $x_{d+1}=\cdots=x_n=0$, with $I(V)=(x_{d+1},\dots,x_n)$, a prime ideal (the quotient is the domain $k[x_1,\dots,x_d]$). So $V$ is a variety with $k[V]\cong k[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ and $\dim V=\trdeg_k k(x_1,\dots,x_d)=d$. Sanity check: $\dim V=d$ matches the geometric dimension of a $d$-plane, and $k(V)=k(x_1,\dots,x_d)$ is a rational function field, the prototype of dimension $d$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The hyperbola and its rational function field
Content:
\begin{wex}{The hyperbola and its rational function field}
With $k$ infinite, show $V=V(xy-1)\subseteq\Aff^2$ is a variety with $k[V]\cong k[x,x^{-1}]$.
\wrec $V(xy-1)$ is a variety iff $xy-1$ is irreducible; the coordinate ring is the localization adjoining $x^{-1}$.
\wsol $xy-1$ is irreducible (degree $1$ in $y$, primitive), so $(xy-1)$ is prime. It equals $I(V)$: if $f$ vanishes on $V$ then $f(t,t^{-1})=0$ for the infinitely many $t\in k^\times$, so $f(x,x^{-1})=0$ in $k[x,x^{-1}]$, i.e.\ $f\in\ker\bigl(k[x,y]\to k[x,x^{-1}],\ y\mapsto x^{-1}\bigr)=(xy-1)$. Hence $V$ is a variety. On $V$, $y=x^{-1}$, so $k[V]=k[x,y]/(xy-1)\cong k[x,x^{-1}]$, a domain. Its fraction field is $k(x)$, so $\dim V=1$. Sanity check: every point of $V$ has $x\ne0$, consistent with inverting $x$; and although over $R$ the hyperbola has two visible ``branches,'' they are not subvarieties -- the Zariski topology cannot separate them since $V$ is irreducible.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The Zariski topology, closure, and density
Type: proposition
Title: {algebraic sets form the closed sets of a topology}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{algebraic sets form the closed sets of a topology}]
On $\Aff^n$ the collection of affine algebraic sets satisfies the closed-set axioms:
\[
V(\fa)\cap V(\fb)=V(\fa+\fb)\ (arbitrary intersections),\quad V(\fa)\cup V(\fb)=V(\fa\fb)=V(\fa\cap\fb),\quad \varnothing=V(1),\ \Aff^n=V(0).
\]
The resulting topology is the Zariski topology. The same construction with $k[V]$ in place of $k[\Aff^n]$ topologizes any algebraic set $V$, intrinsically (independent of the embedding) and agreeing with the subspace topology.
\end{proposition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The Zariski topology is coarse and almost never Hausdorff. On $\Aff^1$ over an infinite field the only proper closed sets are the finite ones, so any two nonempty opens meet; points are closed ($T_1$) but no two points are separated by disjoint opens. This coarseness is the source of the slogan ``nonempty open $\Rightarrow$ dense'' and is why irreducibility (a topological condition) is so strong. In Section~8 the same topology is placed on $\Spec R$, with prime ideals as points; the present picture is its $k$-rational shadow.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The Zariski topology, closure, and density
Type: proposition
Title: {Zariski closure}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Zariski closure}]
For any subset $A\subseteq\Aff^n$ the Zariski closure (smallest algebraic set containing $A$) is $\overline{A}=V(I(A))$. Hence $A$ is dense in a variety $V$ iff $V(I(A))=V$.
\end{proposition}

Title: The Zariski closure of the parabola-points

\begin{wex}{The Zariski closure of the parabola-points}
Over $R$, find the Zariski closure of $A=\{(a,a^2):a\inR\}\subseteq\Aff^2$.
\wrec $\overline A=V(I(A))$; compute $I(A)$ as the polynomials vanishing along the parametrized set.
\wsol A polynomial $f$ vanishes on $A$ iff $f(a,a^2)=0$ for all $a$, i.e.\ $f(x,y)\equiv0\pmod{y-x^2}$ since substituting $y=x^2$ kills it for the infinitely many $a$ (and $R$ is infinite). So $I(A)=(y-x^2)$ and $\overline A=V(y-x^2)$, the whole parabola. Sanity check: $y-x^2$ is irreducible, so $\overline A$ is a variety of dimension $1$; the infinite set $A$ is Zariski dense in it, illustrating that an infinite subset of a curve already determines the curve.
\end{wex}

Title: Zariski versus Euclidean closed sets
Content:
\begin{wex}{Zariski versus Euclidean closed sets}
Over $R$, show the interval $[0,1]\subseteq\Aff^1$ is Euclidean-closed but not Zariski-closed.
\wrec Zariski-closed sets in $\Aff^1$ over an infinite field are only $\varnothing$, all of $\Aff^1$, and finite sets.
\wsol $[0,1]$ is infinite but is not all of $\Aff^1$, so it is not a Zariski-closed set; its Zariski closure is $V(I([0,1]))=V(0)=\Aff^1$, since the only polynomial vanishing on an infinite set is $0$. Yet $[0,1]$ is closed in the Euclidean topology. Sanity check: this confirms the Euclidean topology is strictly finer; every Zariski-closed set (finite, or all of $R$) is Euclidean-closed, but not conversely.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The Zariski topology, closure, and density
Type: example
Title: Nonempty open sets are dense in a variety
Content:
\begin{wex}{Nonempty open sets are dense in a variety}
Let $V$ be a variety and $U_1,U_2$ nonempty Zariski-open subsets of $V$. Show $U_1\cap U_2\ne\varnothing$, hence every nonempty open is dense.
\wrec Irreducibility says $V$ is not a union of two proper closed sets; complements translate this to opens.
\wsol If $U_1\cap U_2=\varnothing$ then $V=(V\setminus U_1)\cup(V\setminus U_2)$ writes $V$ as a union of two closed sets, each proper since $U_i\ne\varnothing$. This contradicts irreducibility. Taking $U_2$ arbitrary nonempty open shows $U_1$ meets every nonempty open, i.e.\ $\overline{U_1}=V$. Sanity check: on $\Aff^1$ over $R$ a nonempty open is $R$ minus finitely many points; any two such overlap in cofinitely many points, exactly density. Reducible sets fail this: on $V(xy)$ the punctured axes give disjoint nonempty opens.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{An irreducible set is connected}
Deduce that a variety is connected in the Zariski topology.
\wrec Connected means not a disjoint union of two nonempty opens; use that nonempty opens are dense.
\wsol If $V=U_1\sqcup U_2$ with both $U_i$ nonempty open and disjoint, then $U_1\cap U_2=\varnothing$ contradicts the previous example. So no such splitting exists and $V$ is connected. Sanity check: connectedness is weaker than irreducibility -- $V(xy)$ is connected (the axes meet at the origin) but reducible -- so irreducible $\Rightarrow$ connected is the expected one-way implication.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The Nullstellensatz: closing the dictionary
Type: theorem
Title: {Hilbert's Nullstellensatz}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Hilbert's Nullstellensatz}]
Let $E$ be an algebraically closed field. For every ideal $\fa$ of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$,
\[
I(V(\fa))=\rad\fa.
\]
Consequently $V$ and $I$ are mutually inverse, order-reversing bijections
\[
\{affine algebraic sets in \Aff^n_E\}\ \xleftrightarrow[\ V\ ]{\ I\ }\ \{radical ideals of E[x_1,\dots,x_n]\},
\]
under which varieties correspond to prime ideals and points to maximal ideals.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Radicals and Affine Varieties > The Nullstellensatz: closing the dictionary
Type: prose
Content:
The dictionary is now complete over $E=\overline E$: containment of algebraic sets is reverse-containment of radical ideals; irreducible components are minimal primes; the coordinate ring $E[V]=E[x]/I(V)$ is a reduced finitely generated $E$-algebra whose maximal ideals are the points of $V$.

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=2.0em]
\{varieties\} \arrow[r,leftrightarrow,"I"] \arrow[d,phantom,"\rotatebox{90}{$\subseteq$}"] & \{primes\} \arrow[d,phantom,"\rotatebox{90}{$\supseteq$}"] \\
\{points\} \arrow[r,leftrightarrow,"I"'] & \{maximal ideals\}
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four collections, each a node. Top-left: the set of affine varieties in $\Aff^n_E$ (irreducible algebraic sets, i.e.\ algebraic sets whose ideal is prime). Top-right: the set of prime ideals of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ that arise as $I(V)$ for some variety $V$ -- over $E=\overline{E}$ these are exactly all prime ideals by the Nullstellensatz. Bottom-left: the set of closed points, i.e.\ individual points $P=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\Aff^n_E$. Bottom-right: the set of maximal ideals of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, which by the weak Nullstellensatz are exactly the $\fm_P=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The top horizontal double arrow is the bijection $I\colon\{varieties\}\leftrightarrow\{prime ideals\}$ given by $V\mapsto I(V)$ and $\fp\mapsto V(\fp)$; it reverses containment. The bottom horizontal double arrow is the same map $I$ restricted to points and maximal ideals: $P\mapsto\fm_P$ and $\fm\mapsto V(\fm)$, again a bijection by the weak Nullstellensatz. The left vertical symbol records that a point lies in a variety, $\{P\}\subseteq V$ (a single point is itself a $0$-dimensional variety, so as collections $\{points\}\subseteq\{varieties\}$). The right vertical symbol records the reversed containment of the corresponding ideals, $I(V)\subseteq\fm_P$: the maximal ideal below contains the prime above. (As collections the inclusion goes the other way: maximal ideals are special primes, $\{maximal ideals\}\subseteq\{prime ideals\}$.) Neither vertical relation is a ring map.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no composite of two arrows to equate in the usual sense; the diagram records that the bijection $I$ on the top row restricts to the bijection $I$ on the bottom row. Precisely: if $P\in\Aff^n_E$ is a point (bottom-left), its image under the bottom $I$ is $\fm_P$ (bottom-right), and $\fm_P$ is also what the top $I$ sends the variety $\{P\}$ to; so the two rows are compatible: $I(\{P\})=\fm_P$ is both a prime (top-right entry) and a maximal ideal (bottom-right entry). Diagram compatibility: a point lying in a variety on the left, $\{P\}\subseteq V$, corresponds under the order-reversing bijection $I$ to the maximal ideal containing the prime on the right, $I(V)\subseteq\fm_P$.

Title: Testing equality of algebraic sets and ideals over $\overline{E}$.

\begin{method}{Testing equality of algebraic sets and ideals over $\overline{E}$.}
To decide whether $V(\fa)=V(\fb)$, compare radicals: $V(\fa)=V(\fb)\iff\rad\fa=\rad\fb$. To decide whether a function $g$ vanishes on $V(\fa)$, test whether $g\in\rad\fa$ (e.g.\ via a Gr\"obner-basis radical-membership computation, or by exhibiting $g^N\in\fa$). To find the components of $V(\fa)$, compute the minimal primes over $\rad\fa$.
\end{method}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The Nullstellensatz requires $E$ algebraically closed. Over $R$ or $Q$ it fails: $(x^2+1)$ is its own radical yet $I(V(x^2+1))=R[x]\ne(x^2+1)$. Also, $V(\fa)\ne\varnothing$ for proper $\fa$ uses algebraic closure: the weak Nullstellensatz gives a common zero precisely because $\rad\fa\ne(1)$.
\end{pitfall}

Title: Reading off components via the Nullstellensatz
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading off components via the Nullstellensatz}
Over $C$, find the irreducible components of $V(xz,yz)\subseteq\Aff^3$.
\wrec Components $\leftrightarrow$ minimal primes over $\rad(xz,yz)$; compute the radical and factor it as an intersection of primes.
\wsol $(xz,yz)=(z)\cap(x,y)$: a polynomial vanishing wherever $z=0$ or $x=y=0$ lies in this intersection, and both $(z)$ and $(x,y)$ are prime. The ideal is already radical (intersection of primes), with minimal primes $(z)$ and $(x,y)$, which are incomparable. So $V(xz,yz)=V(z)\cup V(x,y)$ is the union of the plane $z=0$ and the $z$-axis. Sanity check: the $z=0$ plane has dimension $2$ and the $z$-axis dimension $1$; they are the two components, meeting in the origin -- an embedded incidence but two genuine top-level components since neither prime contains the other.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Radical membership decides vanishing
Content:
\begin{wex}{Radical membership decides vanishing}
Over $C$, does $g=x^2y$ vanish on $V(\fa)$ for $\fa=(x^3,\,xy^2)$? Compute $I(V(\fa))$.
\wrec By the Nullstellensatz $g$ vanishes on $V(\fa)$ iff $g\in\rad\fa$; find $\rad\fa$ as an intersection of primes.
\wsol $V(\fa)=V(x^3)\cap V(xy^2)=V(x)$, the $y$-axis (the line $x=0$ in $\Aff^2$). So $I(V(\fa))=I(V(x))=(x)=\rad\fa$ (indeed $x\in\rad\fa$ since $x^3\in\fa$). Now $g=x^2y\in(x)$, so $g$ vanishes on $V(\fa)$. Sanity check: directly, every point of $V(\fa)$ has $x=0$, so $x^2y=0$ there; and $\rad(x^3,xy^2)=(x)$ because $x^3\in\fa$ gives $x\in\rad\fa$, while $\fa\subseteq(x)$ gives $\rad\fa\subseteq\rad(x)=(x)$.
\end{wex}

Title: Maximal ideals are points over $C$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Maximal ideals are points over $C$}
Over $C$, identify the maximal ideals of $C[x,y]$ and the corresponding algebraic sets.
\wrec The weak Nullstellensatz: every maximal ideal of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $E=\overline E$ is $\fm_P=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$.
\wsol Each point $P=(a,b)\in\Aff^2_C$ gives the maximal ideal $\fm_P=(x-a,y-b)$ with $C[x,y]/\fm_P\congC$, and $V(\fm_P)=\{P\}$. Conversely every maximal ideal arises this way, so maximal ideals $\leftrightarrow$ points bijectively. Sanity check: this is the bottom row of the dictionary square; over $R$ it fails, since $(x^2+1)\subseteqR[x]$ is maximal but is no point's ideal -- a maximal ideal with empty zero set, impossible over $C$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The radical ideal $\leftrightarrow$ algebraic set bijection in action
Content:
\begin{wex}{The radical ideal $\leftrightarrow$ algebraic set bijection in action}
Over $C$, verify $V$ and $I$ are inverse on $\fa=(x^2-y)$ and on the set $A=V(\fa)$.
\wrec Check $I(V(\fa))=\rad\fa$ and $V(I(A))=A$ for a specific prime (hence radical) ideal.
\wsol $x^2-y$ is irreducible, so $(x^2-y)$ is prime, hence radical, and $A=V(x^2-y)$ is the parabola $y=x^2$. Then $I(A)=(x^2-y)$ by the Nullstellensatz (it equals $\rad(x^2-y)=(x^2-y)$), and $V(I(A))=V(x^2-y)=A$. Sanity check: $(x^2-y)$ prime $\Rightarrow A$ a variety; the round trips $\fa\mapsto V(\fa)\mapsto I(V(\fa))=\fa$ and $A\mapsto I(A)\mapsto V(I(A))=A$ both close, exactly the bijection the Nullstellensatz asserts.
\end{wex}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 1/4
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Prove (3) of Corollary 22 directly by considering the collection $S$ of ideals that do not contain a finite product of prime ideals. [If $I$ is a maximal element in $S$, show that since $I$ is not prime there are ideals $J, K$ properly containing $I$ (hence not in $S$) with $JK \subseteq I$.]

\item Let $I$ and $J$ be ideals in the ring $R$. Prove the following statements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $I^k \subseteq J$ for some $k \geq 1$ then $\rad I \subseteq \rad J$.
\item[(b)] If $I^k \subseteq J \subseteq I$ for some $k \geq 1$ then $\rad I = \rad J$.
\item[(c)] $\rad(IJ) = \rad(I \cap J) = \rad I \cap \rad J$.
\item[(d)] $\rad(\rad I) = \rad I$.
\item[(e)] $\rad I + \rad J \subseteq \rad(I + J)$ and $\rad(I + J) = \rad(\rad I + \rad J)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that the intersection of two radical ideals is again a radical ideal.

\item Let $I = \fm_1 \fm_2$ be the product of the ideals $\fm_1 = (x, y)$ and $\fm_2 = (x - 1, y - 1)$ in $\F_2[x, y]$. Prove that $I$ is a radical ideal. Prove that the ideal $(x^3 - y^2)$ is a radical ideal in $\F_2[x, y]$.

\item If $I = (xy, (x - y)z) \subseteq k[x, y, z]$ prove that $\rad I = (xy, xz, yz)$. For this ideal prove directly that $Z(I) = Z(\rad I)$, that $Z(I)$ is not irreducible, and that $\rad I$ is not prime.

\item Give an example to show that over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed the containment $I \subseteq I(Z(I))$ can be proper even when $I$ is a radical ideal.

\item Suppose $R$ and $S$ are rings and $\varphi : R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism. If $I$ is an ideal of $R$ show that $\varphi(\rad I) \subseteq \rad(\varphi(I))$. If in addition $\varphi$ is surjective and $I$ contains the kernel of $\varphi$ show that $\varphi(\rad I) = \rad(\varphi(I))$.

\item Suppose the prime ideal $\fp$ contains the ideal $I$. Prove that $\fp$ contains the radical of $I$.

\item Prove that for any field $k$ the map $Z$ in the Nullstellensatz is always surjective and the map $I$ in the Nullstellensatz is always injective. [Use property (10) of the maps $Z$ and $I$ in Section 1.] Give examples (over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed) where $Z$ is not injective and $I$ is not surjective.

\item Prove that for $k$ a finite field the Zariski topology is the same as the discrete topology: every subset is closed (and open).

\item Let $V$ be a variety in $\Aff^n$ and let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be two subsets of $\Aff^n$ that are open in the Zariski topology. Prove that if $V \cap U_1 \neq \emptyset$ and $V \cap U_2 \neq \emptyset$ then $V \cap U_1 \cap U_2 \neq \emptyset$. Conclude that any nonempty open subset of a variety is everywhere dense in the Zariski topology (i.e., its closure is all of $V$).

\item Use the fact that nonempty open sets of an affine variety are everywhere dense to prove that an affine variety is connected in the Zariski topology. (A topological space is connected if it is not the union of two disjoint, proper, open subsets.)

\item Let $V$ be a nonempty affine algebraic set. Prove that if $k[V]$ is a direct sum of two nonzero ideals, then $V$ is not connected in the Zariski topology, and prove the converse when $k$ is algebraically closed. [Use the weak form of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.] Give a counterexample to the converse over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed.

\item Prove that if $k$ is an infinite field, then the varieties in $\Aff^1$ are the whole space and the one point subsets. What are the varieties in $\Aff^1$ in the case of a finite field $k$?

\item Suppose $V$ is a hypersurface in $\Aff^n$ and $I(V) = (f)$ for some nonconstant polynomial $f \in k[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]$. Prove that $V$ is a variety if and only if $f$ is irreducible.

\item Suppose $V \subseteq \Aff^n$ is an affine variety and $f \in k[V]$. Prove that the graph of $f$ (cf. Exercise 25 in Section 1) is an affine variety.

\item Prove that any permutation of the elements of a field $k$ is a continuous map from $\Aff^1$ to itself in the Zariski topology on $\Aff^1$. Deduce that if $k$ is an infinite field, there are Zariski continuous maps from $\Aff^1$ to itself that are not polynomials.

\item Let $V$ be an affine algebraic set in $\Aff^n$ over $k = C$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that morphisms of algebraic sets over $C$ are continuous in the Euclidean topology (the topology on $C^n$ obtained by identifying $C^n$ with $R^{2n}$ with its usual Euclidean topology).
\item[(b)] Prove that $V$ is a closed set in the Euclidean topology on $C^n$ (so the Zariski closed sets of $\Aff^n$ over $C$ are also Euclidean closed).
\item[(c)] Give an example of a set that is closed in the Euclidean topology but is not closed in the Zariski topology, i.e., is not an affine algebraic set (so the Euclidean topology is ``finer'' than the Zariski topology).
\end{enumerate}

\item Give an example of an injective $k$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi} : k[W] \to k[V]$ whose associated morphism $\varphi : V \to W$ is not surjective.

\item Suppose $\varphi : V \to W$ is a surjective morphism of affine algebraic sets. Prove that if $V$ is a variety then $W$ is a variety.

\item Let $V$ be an algebraic set in $\Aff^n$ and let $f \in k[V]$. Define $V_f = \{v \in V \mid f(v) \neq 0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $V_f$ is a Zariski open set in $V$ (called a principal open set in $V$).
\item[(b)] Let $J$ be the ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_{n+1}]$ generated by $I(V)$ and $x_{n+1} f - 1$, and let $W = Z(J) \subseteq \Aff^{n+1}$.

\item Prove that a prime ideal $\fp$ contains the ideal $I$ if and only if $\fp$ contains one of the associated primes of a minimal primary decomposition of $I$. [Use Exercise 3 and Exercise 11 in Section 7.4.]

\item Show that every associated prime ideal for a radical ideal is isolated. [Suppose that $\fp_2 = \rad Q_2 \subseteq \fp_1 = \rad Q_1$ in the decomposition of Theorem 21 for the radical ideal $I$. Show that if $a \in Q_2 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ ($\subseteq \fp_2 \subseteq \fp_1$) then $a^n \in I$ for some $n \geq 1$, conclude that $a \in Q_1$ and derive a contradiction to the minimality of the primary decomposition.]

\item Fix an element $a$ in the ring $R$. For any ideal $I$ in the ring $R$ let $I_a = \{r \in R \mid ar \in I\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I_a$ is an ideal and $I_a = R$ if and only if $a \in I$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $(I \cap J)_a = I_a \cap J_a$ for ideals $I$ and $J$.
\item[(c)] Suppose that $Q$ is a $\fp$-primary ideal and that $a \notin Q$. Prove that $Q_a$ is a $\fp$-primary ideal and that $Q_a = Q$ if $a \notin \fp$.
\end{enumerate}

\item With notation as in the previous exercise, suppose $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ is a minimal primary decomposition of the ideal $I$ and let $\fp_i$ be the prime ideal associated to $Q_i$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I_a = (Q_1)_a \cap \cdots \cap (Q_m)_a$ and that $\rad(I_a) = \rad((Q_1)_a) \cap \cdots \cap \rad((Q_m)_a)$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $\rad(I_a)$ is the intersection of the prime ideals $\fp_i$ for which $a \notin Q_i$. [Use the previous exercise.]
\item[(c)] Prove that if $\rad(I_a)$ is a prime ideal then $\rad(I_a) = \fp_j$ for some $j$. [Use the fact that prime ideals are irreducible.]
\item[(d)] For each $i = 1, \ldots, m$, prove that $\rad(I_a) = \fp_i$ for some $a \in R$. [Show there exists an $a \in R$ with $a \notin Q_i$ but $a \in Q_j$ for all $j \neq i$.]
\item[(e)] Show from (c) and (d) that the associated primes for a minimal primary decomposition are precisely the collection of prime ideals among the ideals $\rad(I_a)$ for $a \in R$, and conclude that they are uniquely determined by $I$ independent of the minimal primary decomposition.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $\fp_1, \ldots, \fp_m$ be the associated prime ideals of the ideal $(0)$ in the Noetherian ring $R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\fp_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fp_m$ is the collection of nilpotent elements in $R$. [Apply Corollary 22 to $I = (0)$.]
\item[(b)] Show that $\fp_1 \cup \cdots \cup \fp_m$ is the collection of zero divisors in $R$. [Let $I = (0)$ in the previous exercise and show that the set of zero divisors is given by the set $\bigcup_{a \in R - \{0\}} (0)_a = \bigcup_{a \in R - \{0\}} \rad((0)_a)$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $R$ is a Noetherian ring. Prove that $R$ is either an integral domain, has nonzero nilpotent elements, or has at least two minimal prime ideals. [Use the previous exercise.]

\item Prove that the ideal $I$ in the Noetherian ring $R$ is radical if and only if the primary components of a minimal primary decomposition are all prime ideals, and conclude that in this case the minimal primary decomposition is unique. [If $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ is radical with $Q_i$ a $\fp_i$-primary component of a minimal decomposition, show that if $a \in \fp_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fp_m$ then some power of $a$ is in $I$, hence $a \in I$ since $I$ is radical. Deduce that $I = \fp_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fp_m$ and show that this is also a minimal primary decomposition, i.e., for any $i$ there exists $b$ with $b \notin \fp_i$, but $b \in \fp_j$ for $j \neq i$. If $a \in \fp_i$, show that $ab \in Q_i$, and that $a \in Q_i$. Conclude that $Q_i = \fp_i$.]

\item Prove that a Noetherian integral domain $R$ is a U.F.D. if and only if for every $a \in R$ the isolated primes associated to the principal ideal $(a)$ are principal ideals. [See Example 2 following Corollary 22. To prove $R$ is a U.F.D., show that an irreducible $a \in R$ is prime and then follow the proof of Theorem 14 in Section 8.3.]

\item Let $R$ be the ring of all real valued functions on the open interval $(-1, 1)$ that have derivatives of all orders (the ring of $C^{\infty}$ functions). Let
\[
F(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-1/x^4} & if x \neq 0 \\ 0 & if x = 0 \end{cases}
\]
(you may assume $F \in R$ and $F^{(n)}(0) = 0$ for all $n \geq 0$). Let $(F)$ be the principal ideal generated by $F$ and let $A = \rad((F))$. Let $\fm$ be the (maximal) ideal of all functions in $R$ that are zero at $x = 0$ and let $\fp = \bigcap_{n \geq 1} \fm^n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\fm = (x)$ is the ideal generated by the function $x$ in $R$ and that $\fm^n = (x^n)$ consists of the functions $f$ with $f(0) = f'(0) = \cdots = f^{(n-1)}(0) = 0$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $R$ is not Noetherian (compare Exercise 33 in Section 7.4). [One approach is the following: Let $G(x)$ be the function that is $0$ for $x < 0$ and is equal to $F(x)$ for $x \geq 0$. Let $I_n$ be the ideal of functions in $R$ vanishing for all $x \leq 1/n$. Use translates of $G(x)$ to show that $I_1 \subset I_2 \subset I_3 \subset \cdots$ is an infinite ascending chain.]
\item[(c)] Prove that $\fp$ consists of the functions all of whose derivatives are zero at $x = 0$ (i.e., the functions whose associated Taylor series at $x = 0$ is identically zero), and that $\fp$ is a prime ideal.
\item[(d)] Prove that $F \in \fp$ and deduce that $A \subseteq \fp$.
\item[(e)] Prove that $A \neq \fp$. [Let $G(x) = e^{-1/x^2}$ when $x \neq 0$ and $G(0) = 0$. Show that $G \in \fp$ but $G \notin A$.]
\item[(f)] Show that there is a prime ideal $\fq$ containing $(F)$ with $\fq \neq \fp, \fm$.

[One approach is the following: Let $G(x)$ be the function that is $0$ for $x < 0$ and is equal to $F(x)$ for $x \geq 0$. Let $I_n$ be the ideal of functions in $R$ vanishing for all $x \leq 1/n$. Use translates of $G(x)$ to show that $I_1 \subset I_2 \subset I_3 \subset \cdots$ is an infinite ascending chain.]
\item[(c)] Prove that $\fp$ consists of the functions all of whose derivatives are zero at $x = 0$ (i.e., the functions whose associated Taylor series at $x = 0$ is identically zero), and that $\fp$ is a prime ideal.
\item[(d)] Prove that $F \in \fp$ and deduce that $A \subseteq \fp$.
\item[(e)] Prove that $A \neq \fp$. [Let $G(x) = e^{-1/x^2}$ when $x \neq 0$ and $G(0) = 0$. Show that $G \in \fp$ but $G \notin A$.]
\item[(f)] Show that there is a prime ideal $\fq$ containing $(F)$ with $\fq \neq \fp, \fm$.

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 4/4
Content:
Prove that $\fq \subset \fp$, i.e., there are nonzero prime ideals properly contained in $\fp$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $A$ be any ideal in $R = k[x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\rad(A \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]) = \rad A \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $(f_1, \ldots, f_s)$ is an ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Let $F_1, \ldots, F_t$ be generators for the radical of $(f_1, \ldots, f_s)$, computed in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Suppose $J$ is an ideal in $R$ and let $A = J + (f_1, \ldots, f_s)$, $B = J + (F_1, \ldots, F_t)$ as ideals in $R$. Prove that $\rad A = \rad B$.
\item[(c)] Conclude from (a) and (b) that $A = (y_1 - x_1, \ldots, y_m - x_m, f_1, \ldots, f_s) \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$ and $B = (y_1 - x_1, \ldots, y_m - x_m, F_1, \ldots, F_t) \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$ have the same zero sets over an algebraically closed field $k$. [Use Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Determine the Zariski closure in $C^3$ of the points on the curve $\{(a^2, a^3, a^4) \mid a \in C\}$.

\item Show that $Z(x^3 - xyz + z^2)$ is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $\{(st, s + t, s^2 t) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Show that $Z(x^3 z^2 - 3xy^2 z^2 - y^6 - z^4)$ is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $\{(s^2 + t^2, st, s^3) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Find equations defining the Zariski closure of the set of points $\{(s^4, s^3 t, st^3, t^4) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Show that $V = Z(x^2 - y^2 z)$ (the Whitney umbrella surface) is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $S = \{(st, s, t^2) \mid s, t \in R\}$. Show that $S$ is not Zariski closed in $V$ (the missing points explain the name for the surface). Do the same over $C$, but show that in this case $S = V$ is closed.

\item Let $V = Z(xz^2 - w^3, \; xw^2 - y^4, \; y^4 z^2 - w^5) \subseteq C^4$. Determine the Zariski closure of the image of $V$ under the projection $\pi((x, y, z, w)) = (x, y, z)$.

\item Let $V = Z(xy - 1)$ in $\Aff^2$ and let $S$ be the projection of $V$ onto the $x$-axis in $\Aff^1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $k = R$, show that $I(V) = (xy - 1) \subseteq R[x, y]$ and that $(u - x, xy - 1) \cap R[u] = 0$ in $R[x, y, u]$. Use Propositions 8 and 16 to conclude that the Zariski closure of $S$ is $\Aff^1$ and show that $S$ is not itself closed.
\item[(b)] If $k = \F_3$, show that $I(V) = (xy - 1, x^3 - x, y^3 - y) \subseteq \F_3[x, y]$ and that $(u - x, xy - 1, x^3 - x, y^3 - y) \cap \F_3[u] = (u^2 - 1)$ in $\F_3[x, y, u]$. Use Propositions 8 and 16 to conclude that $S$ is Zariski closed in $\Aff^1$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Recall the ideal quotient $(I : J) = \{r \in R \mid rJ \subseteq I\}$ of two ideals $I, J$ in a ring $R$ (cf. Exercise 34 ff. in Section 9.6). Clearly $I \subseteq (I : J)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $Z(I) - Z(J)$, the set of elements of $Z(I)$ not lying in $Z(J)$, is contained in $Z((I : J))$ and conclude that the Zariski closure of $Z(I) - Z(J)$ is contained in $Z((I : J))$.
\item[(b)] Show that if $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is a radical ideal then $Z((I : J))$ is precisely the Zariski closure of $Z(I) - Z(J)$.
\item[(c)] Show that if $V$ and $W$ are affine algebraic sets then $(I(V) : I(W)) = I(V - W)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $\fa,\fb$ be ideals of a commutative ring $R$. Prove $\rad(\fa\fb)=\rad(\fa\cap\fb)=\rad\fa\cap\rad\fb$, and prove $\rad(\fa+\fb)=\rad(\rad\fa+\rad\fb)$. Give an example in $k[x,y]$ where $\rad\fa+\rad\fb\subsetneq\rad(\fa+\fb)$.
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Prove that an element $u\in R$ is a unit if and only if its image is a unit in the reduced ring $R/\nil(R)$. Deduce that $R$ is local if and only if $R/\nil(R)$ is local, and that the two rings have the same maximal ideals under the correspondence of the Lattice Isomorphism Theorem.
\item Let $V\subseteq\Aff^n$ be an affine variety over an algebraically closed field $E$ and let $f,g\in E[V]$. Prove that $V_f\cap V_g\ne\varnothing$ whenever $f\ne0$ and $g\ne0$, where $V_h=\{P\in V:h(P)\ne0\}$, and conclude that $E[V]$ is an integral domain. (Use that nonempty opens are dense in an irreducible space.)
\item Let $E$ be algebraically closed and $\fa$ a proper ideal of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Prove that $V(\fa)$ is a finite set if and only if $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]/\rad\fa$ is a finite-dimensional $E$-vector space, and that in that case $\abs{V(\fa)}=\dim_E\bigl(E[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(\fa))\bigr)$.
\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Prove that $R$ is reduced and has exactly one minimal prime ideal if and only if $R$ is an integral domain. Then give, for each $m\ge1$, a reduced ring with exactly $m$ minimal primes, and identify its minimal primes geometrically as the components of an algebraic set.
\end{exers}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Over $C$, let $\fa=(xy,\,xz,\,yz)\subseteqC[x,y,z]$, whose zero set is the union of the three coordinate axes. Complete the lattice of minimal primes over $\fa$ and the matching diagram of irreducible components (ordered by inclusion), and prove the labelled correspondence is the order-reversing bijection of the Nullstellensatz:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
(x,y) & (x,z) & (y,z) \\
& (xy,xz,yz) \arrow[ul,dash] \arrow[u,dash] \arrow[ur,dash] &
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xleftrightarrow{\ V\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& V(xy,xz,yz) & \\
V(x,y) \arrow[ur,dash] & V(x,z) \arrow[u,dash] & V(y,z) \arrow[ul,dash]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify each $V(\fp_i)$ as one of the coordinate axes, verify $\fa=\rad\fa=(x,y)\cap(x,z)\cap(y,z)$, and state the dimension of each component.
\item Let $E$ be algebraically closed and $\varphi:E[y_1,\dots,y_m]\to E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ an $E$-algebra homomorphism, inducing the polynomial map $\varphi^\ast:\Aff^n\to\Aff^m$ on points. Prove the square below commutes (top is $\fb\mapsto V(\fb)$ in $\Aff^m$, bottom is $\fa\mapsto V(\fa)$ in $\Aff^n$, left is extension $\fb\mapsto\varphi(\fb)E[x]$, right is preimage under $\varphi^\ast$), and deduce that $\overline{\varphi^\ast(\Aff^n)}=V(\ker\varphi)$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\{ideals of E[y]\} \arrow[r,"V"] \arrow[d,"{\fb\mapsto\varphi(\fb)E[x]}"'] & \{closed sets of \Aff^m\} \arrow[d,"(\varphi^\ast)^{-1}"] \\
\{ideals of E[x]\} \arrow[r,"V"'] & \{closed sets of \Aff^n\}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Conclude that a polynomial map has Zariski-dense image exactly when the comorphism $\varphi$ is injective.
\item Over an algebraically closed field $E$, let $\fa\subseteq\fb$ be radical ideals of $E[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, so $W=V(\fb)\subseteq V(\fa)=V$ is a closed algebraic subset. Writing $E[V]=E[x]/\fa$, complete the diagram relating coordinate rings to ideals and prove every arrow is the natural one and the square is a pushout of rings, $E[W]\cong E[V]\otimes_{E[x]}E[x]/\fb$ (it is not a pullback unless $\fa=0$):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
E[x] \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] & E[V] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] \\
E[x]/\fb \arrow[r,equal] & E[W]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the kernel of $E[V]\twoheadrightarrow E[W]$ as $\fb/\fa$, prove it is a radical ideal of $E[V]$, and state the resulting inclusion-reversing bijection between closed algebraic subsets of $V$ and radical ideals of $E[V]$ (under which the closed subvarieties correspond to the prime ideals).
\item Over $C$, let $\fa=(x^2-y)\subseteqC[x,y]$ and let $\fm_P=(x-a,\,y-a^2)$ for a point $P=(a,a^2)\in V(\fa)$. Complete the diagram exhibiting the quotient $C[x,y]\toC[V(\fa)]\toC[V(\fa)]/(\fm_P/\fa)\congC$ and prove the composite is evaluation at $P$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
C[x,y] \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi"] \arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow,"\operatorname{ev}_P"'] & C[V(\fa)] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"\overline{\operatorname{ev}_P}"] \\
& C
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Verify $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_P)=\fm_P$, that $\fm_P\supseteq\fa$, and that the maximal ideals of $C[V(\fa)]$ are exactly the $\fm_P/\fa$ for $P\in V(\fa)$, so they biject with the points of the parabola.
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Modules, Tensor Products, and Nakayama's Lemma > Modules: the common generalization
Type: prose
Content:
Atiyah and Macdonald open their chapter on modules with a slogan worth keeping in front of us: working with modules rather than just ideals gives extra ``elbow-room'', and with it greater clarity and simplicity. A vector space is a module over a field; an abelian group is a module over $Z$; an ideal of a ring $A$ is a module over $A$; the ring $A$ itself is a module over $A$. The single notion of module unifies all of these, and -- crucially for the geometric program -- it is the right home for the functorial operations (quotient, localization, tensor, completion) that we will use to ``concentrate near a point''.

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Modules, Tensor Products, and Nakayama's Lemma > Modules: the common generalization
Type: definition
Title: {$A$-module}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{$A$-module}]
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with $1$. An $A$-module is an abelian group $(M,+)$ together with a scalar multiplication $A\times M\to M$, $(a,x)\mapsto ax$, satisfying for all $a,b\in A$ and $x,y\in M$:
\[
a(x+y)=ax+ay,\quad (a+b)x=ax+bx,\quad (ab)x=a(bx),\quad 1x=x.
\]
Equivalently, giving an $A$-module structure on the abelian group $M$ is the same as giving a ring homomorphism $A\to\End(M)$ into the (in general noncommutative) ring $\End(M)$ of abelian-group endomorphisms of $M$: the image of $a$ is the map $x\mapsto ax$.
\end{definition}

Content:
\begin{remark}
The endomorphism-ring viewpoint is the conceptual core. A module is a ring acting on an abelian group; a representation of $A$. When $A=k[G]$ is the group ring of a finite group $G$ over a field $k$, an $A$-module is exactly a $k$-linear representation of $G$ -- so representation theory is a chapter of module theory. When $A=k[x]$, an $A$-module is a $k$-vector space equipped with a single distinguished endomorphism (the action of $x$); the structure theory of such modules is the theory of rational/Jordan canonical forms in D\&F Chapter 12.
\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: {submodule, quotient, homomorphism}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{submodule, quotient, homomorphism}]
A submodule $M'\subseteq M$ is a subgroup closed under the $A$-action; the quotient group $M/M'$ then inherits an $A$-action $a(x+M')=ax+M'$ and is the quotient module. An $A$-module homomorphism (or $A$-linear map) $f:M\to N$ is an additive map with $f(ax)=a\,f(x)$ for all $a\in A$, $x\in M$. Its kernel $\ker f=\{x:f(x)=0\}$ is a submodule of $M$, its image $\im f=f(M)$ a submodule of $N$, and its cokernel $\coker f=N/\im f$ a quotient of $N$. The set $\Hom_A(M,N)$ of all $A$-linear maps is itself an $A$-module under $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ and $(af)(x)=a\,f(x)$.
\end{definition}

Title: Building and recognizing modules
Content:
\begin{method}{Building and recognizing modules}
To produce an $A$-module: take an abelian group on which $A$ acts, or a quotient/submodule/$\Hom$/direct sum of known modules. To recognize the action concretely, find the ring homomorphism $A\to\End(M)$. To verify a subset is a submodule, check it is a nonempty subgroup stable under multiplication by every $a\in A$ (it suffices to test the scalars in a ring-generating set of $A$, since stability propagates through sums and products of scalars; testing only the module generators is not enough -- stability is required for all scalars).
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Ideals and quotients as modules
Content:
\begin{wex}{Ideals and quotients as modules}
Show that an ideal $\fa\subseteq A$ and the quotient $A/\fa$ are $A$-modules, and identify $\Hom_A(A/\fa,M)$.
\wrec An ideal is exactly an additive subgroup stable under multiplication by all of $A$ -- precisely a submodule of $A$. The quotient module $A/\fa$ then carries the induced action.
\wsol $\fa$ is a subgroup of $(A,+)$ and $a\cdot x\in\fa$ for $a\in A$, $x\in\fa$ by the ideal axiom, so $\fa$ is a submodule of the $A$-module $A$. Hence $A/\fa$ is a quotient module; its $A$-action is $a(b+\fa)=ab+\fa$. An $A$-linear map $f:A/\fa\to M$ is determined by $m:=f(1+\fa)$, and is well defined iff $\fa$ annihilates $m$, i.e.\ $\fa m=0$. Thus
\[
\Hom_A(A/\fa,M)\ \cong\ \{m\in M:\fa m=0\}=(0:_M\fa),
\]
the submodule of $M$ killed by $\fa$. Sanity check: with $\fa=0$ this recovers $\Hom_A(A,M)\cong M$; with $A=Z$, $\fa=nZ$, $M=Z/mZ$ it gives the $n$-torsion of $Z/mZ$, of order $\gcd(n,m)$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The annihilator and faithful modules
Content:
\begin{wex}{The annihilator and faithful modules}
Define $\Ann(M)$ and show $M$ is naturally a faithful module over $A/\Ann(M)$.
\wrec The annihilator $\Ann(M)=\{a\in A:aM=0\}$ measures ``how much of $A$ acts trivially''; quotienting it out makes the action faithful.
\wsol $\Ann(M)=\{a\in A:ax=0\ \forall x\in M\}$ is an ideal: if $a,b$ kill $M$ so does $a-b$, and if $a$ kills $M$ then so does $ca$ for any $c$. The action factors through $A/\Ann(M)$ because $a\in\Ann(M)$ acts as $0$; the induced module is faithful, meaning $\Ann_{A/\Ann(M)}(M)=0$, since by construction nothing outside $\Ann(M)$ kills all of $M$. Sanity check: for $M=Z/nZ$ over $A=Z$ we get $\Ann(M)=nZ$ and $M$ is faithful over $Z/nZ$; for a finite-dimensional $k[x]$-module, $\Ann(M)=(m(x))$ is generated by the minimal polynomial.
\end{wex}

Title: $\Hom$ functoriality
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Hom$ functoriality}
For $u:M'\to M$ and $v:N\to N''$, describe the induced maps on $\Hom$ and their variance.
\wrec $\Hom_A(-,N)$ is contravariant and $\Hom_A(M,-)$ is covariant; precomposition reverses arrows, postcomposition preserves them.
\wsol Given $u:M'\to M$, define $\bar u:\Hom_A(M,N)\to\Hom_A(M',N)$ by $\bar u(f)=f\circ u$ (contravariant). Given $v:N\to N''$, define $\bar v:\Hom_A(M,N)\to\Hom_A(M,N'')$ by $\bar v(f)=v\circ f$ (covariant). Both are $A$-linear. Sanity check: identities go to identities and $\overline{u_1u_2}=\bar u_2\bar u_1$ (order reversed) while $\overline{v_1v_2}=\bar v_1\bar v_2$ (order preserved), the signature of contra- vs.\ covariance.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
A sequence of $A$-modules and homomorphisms $\cdots\to M_{i-1}\xrightarrow{f_{i-1}}M_i\xrightarrow{f_i}M_{i+1}\to\cdots$ is exact at $M_i$ if $\im f_{i-1}=\ker f_i$, and exact if exact everywhere. The atomic cases:
\[
0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\ exact\iff f\ injective,\qquad
M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0\ exact\iff g\ surjective,
\]
and a short exact sequence
\[
0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0
\]
is exact iff $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective, and $g$ induces an isomorphism $\coker f=M/f(M')\cong M''$. Every long exact sequence splices together from short ones.

M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0\ \text{exact}\iff g\ \text{surjective},
\]
and a \emph{short exact sequence}
\[
0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0
\]
is exact iff $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective, and $g$ induces an isomorphism $\coker f=M/f(M')\cong M''$. Every long exact sequence splices together from short ones.

Type: proposition
Title: {left-exactness of $\Hom$}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{left-exactness of $\Hom$}]
Let $M'\xrightarrow{u}M\xrightarrow{v}M''\to0$ be a sequence of $A$-modules. It is exact iff for every $A$-module $N$ the sequence
\[
0\to\Hom_A(M'',N)\xrightarrow{\bar v}\Hom_A(M,N)\xrightarrow{\bar u}\Hom_A(M',N)
\]
is exact. Dually, $0\to N'\xrightarrow{u}N\xrightarrow{v}N''$ is exact iff $0\to\Hom_A(M,N')\to\Hom_A(M,N)\to\Hom_A(M,N'')$ is exact for all $M$.
\end{proposition}

\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-0697310743852a89d6fa
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
These are pure diagram chases. For the first: a map $M''\to N$ pulls back along $v$ to a map $M\to N$ killing $\im u=\ker v$, and conversely a map $M\to N$ that kills $\ker v$ descends through the surjection $v$. Injectivity of $\bar v$ is surjectivity of $v$; exactness in the middle is $\im u=\ker v$. Note the right end is not surjective in general: not every $M'\to N$ extends. So $\Hom$ is only left-exact -- the failure of right-exactness is measured by the $\Ext$ functors.
\end{proof}

Type: proposition
Title: {snake lemma}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{snake lemma}]
Given a commutative diagram with exact rows
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
0\arrow[r] & M'\arrow[r,hook,"u"]\arrow[d,"f'"] & M\arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"v"]\arrow[d,"f"] & M''\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f''"] & 0\\
0\arrow[r] & N'\arrow[r,hook,"u'"] & N\arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"v'"] & N''\arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Six $A$-modules arranged in two horizontal short exact sequences. Top row: $0$, $M'$, $M$, $M''$, $0$. Bottom row: $0$, $N'$, $N$, $N''$, $0$. Three vertical maps connect the rows: $f':M'\to N'$, $f:M\to N$, $f'':M''\to N''$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Horizontal arrows $u:M'\hookrightarrow M$ and $v:M\twoheadrightarrow M''$ form the top short exact sequence; $u':N'\hookrightarrow N$ and $v':N\twoheadrightarrow N''$ form the bottom one. The vertical maps $f'$, $f$, $f''$ are $A$-module homomorphisms (not assumed injective or surjective); they carry information about how the two sequences relate.
\dgi{What commutes:} The left square commutes: $f\circ u = u'\circ f'$, i.e.\ mapping $M'$ to $M$ then down equals mapping $M'$ down then to $N$. The right square commutes: $f''\circ v = v'\circ f$, i.e.\ mapping $M$ to $M''$ then down equals mapping $M$ down then to $N''$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic $m'\in M'$: along the top-left square, $u(m')$ maps to $f(u(m'))$; along the bottom-left square, $f'(m')$ maps to $u'(f'(m'))$; these agree by hypothesis (commutativity is given as data, not derived). The diagram is a hypothesis of the snake lemma, not a conclusion.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This commutative diagram is the input to the snake lemma. The two paths through each square being equal is exactly the condition that lets the connecting homomorphism $\delta:\ker f''\to\coker f'$ be built by the ``lift, apply, pull back'' procedure described in the proof. Without commutativity, the lift would be ambiguous and $\delta$ would not be well defined.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $A=Z$, both rows equal $0\toZ\xrightarrow{n}Z\toZ/n\to0$, and $f'=f=f''$ each equal to multiplication by $2$. The left square: $f(n\cdot m')=2nm'=n\cdot(2m')=u'(f'(m'))$. The connecting map $\delta:\ker(2:Z/n\toZ/n)\to\coker(2:Z\toZ)=Z/2$ records the $2$-torsion of $Z/n$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often think the vertical maps must be injections or surjections. They need not be; the snake lemma extracts exact information from $\ker$ and $\coker$ of arbitrary $f'$, $f$, $f''$ as long as the squares commute and the rows are exact.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that commutativity of the two squares, together with exactness of the rows, is precisely the data needed to define the connecting homomorphism $\delta$ and produce the six-term exact sequence on kernels and cokernels.
\end{dgx}
there is a natural connecting homomorphism $\delta:\ker f''\to\coker f'$ fitting into an exact sequence
\[
0\to\ker f'\to\ker f\to\ker f''\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }\coker f'\to\coker f\to\coker f''\to0.
\]
\end{proposition}

Type: proposition
Title: {five lemma}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{five lemma}]
In a commutative diagram with exact rows
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.4em]
M_1\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f_1"] & M_2\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f_2"] & M_3\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f_3"] & M_4\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f_4"] & M_5\arrow[d,"f_5"]\\
N_1\arrow[r] & N_2\arrow[r] & N_3\arrow[r] & N_4\arrow[r] & N_5
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Ten $A$-modules, $M_1,\dots,M_5$ forming the top exact row and $N_1,\dots,N_5$ forming the bottom exact row. Five vertical maps $f_i:M_i\to N_i$ ($i=1,\dots,5$) connect corresponding positions.
\dgi{Arrows:} The horizontal arrows (unlabelled in this diagram) form two five-term exact sequences. The vertical arrows $f_i$ are $A$-module homomorphisms with given properties: $f_1$ surjective, $f_5$ injective, $f_2$ and $f_4$ isomorphisms. The arrow $f_3$ is the one whose isomorphism the lemma concludes.
\dgi{What commutes:} Every square commutes: for each $i$, the horizontal map $M_i\to M_{i+1}$ followed by $f_{i+1}$ equals $f_i$ followed by the horizontal map $N_i\to N_{i+1}$. Exactness means $\operatorname{im}(M_{i-1}\to M_i)=\operatorname{ker}(M_i\to M_{i+1})$ at each $M_i$, and likewise for the $N$-row.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Commutativity of each square is given as hypothesis. The argument for $f_3$ being an isomorphism is a four-step diagram chase: surjectivity of $f_1$ and injectivity of $f_2$ and $f_4$ give injectivity of $f_3$ (``four-lemma''); surjectivity of $f_2$ and $f_4$ and injectivity of $f_5$ give surjectivity of $f_3$ (the other four-lemma). A generic element in $\ker f_3$ is chased left to show it must be zero; a generic element in the image is lifted from the $N$-row upward.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The five lemma is the standard tool for proving that a map between two exact sequences is an isomorphism by bootstrapping from known isomorphisms at adjacent positions. In this chapter it is used again for completions, to show that the natural map $\widehat R\otimes_R M\to\widehat M$ is an isomorphism for a finitely generated module $M$ over a Noetherian ring $R$ (Proposition~ [REF:prop:flat@c15] ).
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take both rows to be $Z\xrightarrow{2}Z\toZ/2\to0\to0$ and $f_1=f_2=f_4=f_5=\id$, $f_3$ the induced map $Z/2\toZ/2$. Then $f_3$ is an isomorphism (the identity), consistent with the lemma.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The hypothesis on $f_1$ is surjectivity, not injectivity, and on $f_5$ is injectivity, not surjectivity. Swapping these weakens the conclusion. Also, the lemma applies to two exact sequences of the same length five, not to arbitrary diagrams; adding or removing terms changes what is provable.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that knowing the four outer vertical maps are (nearly) isomorphisms forces the middle vertical map to be an isomorphism, with the proof being a purely formal element chase using exactness and commutativity.
\end{dgx}

Type: example
Title: Splicing a long exact sequence into short ones
Content:
\begin{wex}{Splicing a long exact sequence into short ones}
Given an exact sequence $\cdots\to M_{i-1}\to M_i\to M_{i+1}\to\cdots$, exhibit the short exact sequences whose images are the $\im f_i$.
\wrec Set $N_i=\im f_i=\ker f_{i+1}$; exactness says each map factors surjection-then-inclusion through these images.
\wsol Each $f_i:M_i\to M_{i+1}$ factors as $M_i\twoheadrightarrow N_i\hookrightarrow M_{i+1}$ with $N_i=\im f_i$. Exactness at $M_i$ is $N_{i-1}=\ker f_i$, so
\[
0\to N_{i-1}\to M_i\to N_i\to0
\]
is short exact for every $i$. Sanity check: reading $\dim$ (over a field) gives $\dim M_i=\dim N_{i-1}+\dim N_i$, which telescopes to the alternating-sum relation used next.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Additive functions on short exact sequences
Content:
\begin{wex}{Additive functions on short exact sequences}
Let $\lambda$ be a $Z$-valued function on a class $\mathcal C$ of modules, additive on short exact sequences whose terms lie in $\mathcal C$. Prove $\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\lambda(M_i)=0$ for an exact sequence $0\to M_0\to\cdots\to M_n\to0$ in which all the $M_i$ and all the kernels of the maps lie in $\mathcal C$.
\wrec Additivity means $\lambda(M)=\lambda(M')+\lambda(M'')$ for $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$; this is the abstract Euler characteristic / dimension count.
\wsol Splice into short exact sequences $0\to N_{i-1}\to M_i\to N_i\to0$ with $N_{-1}=0=N_n$ (A\&M Prop.\ 2.11). Additivity gives $\lambda(M_i)=\lambda(N_{i-1})+\lambda(N_i)$. Form $\sum(-1)^i\lambda(M_i)=\sum(-1)^i\bigl(\lambda(N_{i-1})+\lambda(N_i)\bigr)$; the $N$-terms telescope and cancel because each $N_i$ appears once with sign $(-1)^i$ and once with $(-1)^{i+1}$, leaving $0$. Sanity check: for $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ this is just additivity; for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces $\lambda=\dim$ recovers rank--nullity $\dim M=\dim\ker+\dim\im$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The connecting map in a concrete snake
Content:
\begin{wex}{The connecting map in a concrete snake}
Compute $\delta$ for multiplication by $2$ on $0\toZ\toZ\toZ/2\to0$.
\wrec The snake's $\delta:\ker f''\to\coker f'$ is built by lift-apply-pull back; here all three vertical maps are multiplication by $2$.
\wsol Apply the snake to the commutative diagram whose two identical rows are $0\toZ\xrightarrow{n}Z\toZ/n\to0$ and whose three vertical maps are all $\times2$. On the two copies of $Z$ the map $\times2$ is injective, so $\ker f'=\ker f=0$, while $\ker f''=(Z/n)[2]$ is the $2$-torsion of $Z/n$; the cokernels are $\coker f'=\coker f=Z/2$ and $\coker f''=(Z/n)/2(Z/n)$. The snake sequence is therefore
\[
0\to0\to0\to(Z/n)[2]\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }Z/2\toZ/2\to(Z/n)/2(Z/n)\to0.
\]
Sanity check: with $n=2$ the $2$-torsion $(Z/2)[2]=Z/2$ maps isomorphically by $\delta$ onto $\coker f'=Z/2$, since exactness at $\ker f''$ with $\ker f=0$ forces $\delta$ injective, and a count of orders ($2=2$) then makes it onto.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {direct sum and product}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{direct sum and product}]
For a family $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ of $A$-modules, the direct product $\prod_{i\in I}M_i$ is the set of all families $(x_i)$ with the componentwise operations; the direct sum $\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i$ is the submodule of families $(x_i)$ with $x_i=0$ for all but finitely many $i$. For finite $I$ the two coincide. A free module is one isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{i\in I}A$, written $A^{(I)}$; the finite free modules are $A^n$.
\end{definition}

Type: prose
Content:
A module $M$ is finitely generated (f.g.) if there exist $x_1,\dots,x_n\in M$ with $M=Ax_1+\cdots+Ax_n$, equivalently if there is a surjection $A^n\twoheadrightarrow M$, equivalently if $M\cong A^n/K$ for some submodule $K$ and some $n$ (A\&M Prop.\ 2.3). Generation by $n$ elements is captured by the surjection $A^n\twoheadrightarrow M$; if its kernel is also finitely generated (automatic when $A$ is Noetherian), $M$ has a finite presentation $A^m\to A^n\to M\to0$.

Type: example
Title: $\Hom$ and direct sums vs.\ products
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Hom$ and direct sums vs.\ products}
Establish $\Hom_A\bigl(\bigoplus_i M_i,N\bigr)\cong\prod_i\Hom_A(M_i,N)$ and $\Hom_A\bigl(N,\prod_i M_i\bigr)\cong\prod_i\Hom_A(N,M_i)$.
\wrec A map out of a direct sum is a tuple of maps on the summands (universal property of $\oplus$); a map into a product is a tuple of maps to the factors (universal property of $\prod$).
\wsol For the first, restrict $f:\bigoplus M_i\to N$ to each summand to get $(f|_{M_i})_i$; conversely glue $(f_i)$ by $f((x_i))=\sum_i f_i(x_i)$ -- a finite sum since $(x_i)\in\bigoplus$. These are mutually inverse $A$-isomorphisms. For the second, post-compose $g:N\to\prod M_i$ with the projections $\pi_i$ to get $(\pi_i g)_i$; conversely assemble. Sanity check: with $M_i=A$ for $i\in I$ we get $\Hom_A(A^{(I)},N)\cong N^I=\prod_I N$, the ``dual of free is product'' statement; for finite $I$ both sides are $N^{|I|}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Quotient of $A$ by an ideal as a sum decomposition (CRT)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Quotient of $A$ by an ideal as a sum decomposition (CRT)}
For coprime ideals show $A/(\fa\cap\fb)\cong A/\fa\oplus A/\fb$ as $A$-modules.
\wrec When $\fa+\fb=A$ the Chinese Remainder map is an isomorphism; this is a module (indeed ring) decomposition.
\wsol The map $A\to A/\fa\oplus A/\fb$, $x\mapsto(x+\fa,x+\fb)$, is $A$-linear with kernel $\fa\cap\fb$. Coprimality $\fa+\fb=A$ gives surjectivity (pick $e\in\fa$, $f\in\fb$ with $e+f=1$; then $f\equiv1,\ e\equiv0\pmod{\fa}$ and vice versa, so any target $(\bar s,\bar t)$ is hit by $sf+te$). Hence $A/(\fa\cap\fb)\cong A/\fa\oplus A/\fb$, and $\fa\cap\fb=\fa\fb$ in this case. Sanity check: $A=Z$, $\fa=3Z$, $\fb=5Z$ gives $Z/15\congZ/3\oplusZ/5$, the classical CRT, an isomorphism of $Z$-modules of order $15$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Free of rank determined: $A^m\cong A^n\Rightarrow m=n$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Free of rank determined: $A^m\cong A^n\Rightarrow m=n$}
Show that over a nonzero commutative ring, free modules have a well-defined rank.
\wrec Pass to a residue field: tensoring (or quotienting) by a maximal ideal turns $A^n$ into a vector space of dimension $n$, and dimension is an invariant.
\wsol Let $\fm$ be a maximal ideal of $A$, $k=A/\fm$. An isomorphism $A^m\cong A^n$ induces, after reducing mod $\fm$ (i.e.\ applying $A/\fm\otimes_A-$, see below), an isomorphism of $k$-vector spaces $k^m\cong k^n$. Hence $m=\dim_k k^m=\dim_k k^n=n$. Sanity check: the argument needs $A\neq0$ so that a maximal ideal exists; over the zero ring $A^m=0=A^n$ for all $m,n$ and rank is meaningless, consistent with the hypothesis.
\end{wex}

\begin{proposition}[{determinant trick, A\&M 2.4}]
Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module, $\fa\subseteq A$ an ideal, and $\phi:M\to M$ an $A$-endomorphism with $\phi(M)\subseteq\fa M$. Then $\phi$ satisfies an equation
\[
\phi^n+a_1\phi^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\qquad(a_i\in\fa)
\]
as an endomorphism of $M$.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-67dfcabd3d24cb775003
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Pick generators $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $M$. Since $\phi(x_i)\in\fa M$, write $\phi(x_i)=\sum_j a_{ij}x_j$ with $a_{ij}\in\fa$. Then $\sum_j(\delta_{ij}\phi-a_{ij})x_j=0$, i.e.\ the matrix $\Phi=(\delta_{ij}\phi-a_{ij})$ over the commutative ring $A[\phi]$ kills the vector $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$. Multiply by the adjugate: $\operatorname{adj}(\Phi)\Phi=\det(\Phi)\cdot I$, so $\det(\delta_{ij}\phi-a_{ij})$ annihilates every $x_j$, hence all of $M$. Expanding the determinant gives the monic equation with coefficients in $\fa$. This is literally Cayley--Hamilton with entries in $A[\phi]$.
\end{proof}

Title: {Nakayama's lemma}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Nakayama's lemma}]
Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module and $\fa\subseteq\Jac(A)$ an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical. If $\fa M=M$ then $M=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
By the corollary there is $x=1+a$ with $a\in\fa\subseteq\Jac(A)$ and $xM=0$. But $\Jac(A)$ is characterized as $\{a:1+ab\in\units{A}\ \forall b\}$, so $x=1+a$ is a unit. Multiplying $xM=0$ by $x^{-1}$ gives $M=0$. The finite-generation hypothesis is essential (see the pitfall).
\end{proof}

Title: {local form, A\&M 2.6--2.8}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{local form, A\&M 2.6--2.8}]
Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a local ring with maximal ideal $\fm$ and residue field $k=A/\fm$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item If $N\subseteq M$ is a submodule with $N+\fm M=M$, then $N=M$.
\item Elements $x_1,\dots,x_n\in M$ generate $M$ as an $A$-module iff their images $\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_n$ span the $k$-vector space $M/\fm M$. In particular the images of a minimal generating set form a basis of $M/\fm M$, so every minimal generating set has the same size $\dim_k M/\fm M$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) Apply Nakayama to $M/N$, which is f.g.\ with $\fm(M/N)=M/N$, forcing $M/N=0$. (2) The $\bar x_i$ span $M/\fm M$ iff $\sum Ax_i+\fm M=M$ iff (by (1)) $\sum Ax_i=M$; and a spanning set of the vector space $M/\fm M$ is a basis iff it is minimal. The point: over a local ring, counting minimal generators of a f.g.\ module is linear algebra over the residue field.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Nakayama fails without finite generation. Take $A=Z_{(p)}$ (local, $\fm=pZ_{(p)}$) and $M=Q$. Then $\fm M=pQ=Q=M$ but $M\neq0$. The determinant trick needs a finite generating set to form the matrix; $Q$ is not finitely generated over $Z_{(p)}$. Likewise the hypothesis $\fa\subseteq\Jac(A)$ cannot be dropped: $\fa=A$ trivially has $\fa M=M$ for every $M$.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: Cayley--Hamilton recovered
Content:
\begin{wex}{Cayley--Hamilton recovered}
Recover the classical Cayley--Hamilton theorem from A\&M 2.4.
\wrec Take $A=$ the base ring, $M=A^n$ free with the standard basis, $\fa=A$, and $\phi$ a given matrix; the trick produces the characteristic-polynomial equation.
\wsol Let $T\in\Mat_n(A)$ act on $M=A^n$. With $\fa=A$ and generators the standard basis, the matrix in the proof is $tI-T$ evaluated at $t=\phi=T$, and $\det(tI-T)=\chi_T(t)$ is the characteristic polynomial. The determinant trick gives $\chi_T(T)=0$. Sanity check: for $n=1$, $T=(a)$, $\chi_T(t)=t-a$ and $\chi_T(T)=T-aI=0$; the general statement is exactly Cayley--Hamilton.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Surjective endomorphism of a f.g.\ module is injective
Content:
\begin{wex}{Surjective endomorphism of a f.g.\ module is injective}
Show every surjective $A$-endomorphism $\phi$ of a finitely generated $A$-module $M$ is an isomorphism.
\wrec View $M$ as a module over $B=A[t]$ with $t$ acting as $\phi$; surjectivity says $tM=M$ over the ideal $(t)$, and a Nakayama-style argument applies.
\wsol Regard $M$ as an $A[t]$-module via $t\cdot x=\phi(x)$; $M$ is f.g.\ over $A[t]$ (already over $A$). Surjectivity of $\phi$ means $(t)M=M$ where $(t)\subseteq A[t]$. By the determinant trick (A\&M 2.4 with $\fa=(t)$ and the identity endomorphism) there is $x=1+t\,h(t)$ with $xM=0$, i.e.\ $\bigl(1+t\,h(t)\bigr)M=0$. Reading off in terms of $\phi$: $\id=-\phi\,h(\phi)$ on $M$, so $\phi$ has the two-sided inverse $-h(\phi)$, hence is injective and an isomorphism. Sanity check: this fails for non-f.g.\ modules -- the shift $\phi(a_0,a_1,\dots)=(a_1,a_2,\dots)$ on $A^{(\Zpos)}$ is surjective but not injective.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Minimal generators of a module over a local ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{Minimal generators of a module over a local ring}
Let $A=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$, $\fm=(x,y)$, and $M=\fm$. Compute the minimal number of generators of $M$.
\wrec Over a local ring this number is $\dim_k M/\fm M$ by the local Nakayama corollary.
\wsol Here $M=\fm=(x,y)$ and $\fm M=\fm^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)$. So $M/\fm M=\fm/\fm^2$ has $k$-basis the images of $x,y$, giving $\dim_k\fm/\fm^2=2$. Hence the minimal number of generators of $\fm$ is $2$, realized by $\{x,y\}$. Sanity check: any single element $f\in\fm$ has $f\in\fm^2+kx+ky$ but cannot span $\fm/\fm^2$ (dimension $2$), so $\fm$ is not principal -- correctly, the maximal ideal of a $2$-dimensional regular local ring needs exactly $2$ generators.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $N+\fm M=M\Rightarrow N=M$ in practice
Content:
\begin{wex}{$N+\fm M=M\Rightarrow N=M$ in practice}
With $A=Z_{(2)}$, $M=A^2$, $N=A\cdot(1,1)+A\cdot(0,2)$, decide whether $N=M$.
\wrec Reduce mod $\fm=2A$: $N=M$ iff the images of the generators span $M/\fm M=k^2$, $k=\F_2$.
\wsol Mod $2$, the generators become $(1,1)$ and $(0,0)$, spanning only a $1$-dimensional subspace of $\F_2^2$. So $N+\fm M\neq M$, and indeed $N\neq M$ (e.g.\ $(1,0)\notin N$, since $a(1,1)+b(0,2)=(a,a+2b)=(1,0)$ forces $a=1$, $1+2b=0$, impossible in $Z_{(2)}$). Sanity check: had we used $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$, the reductions $(1,1),(0,1)$ span $\F_2^2$, and then Nakayama gives $N=M$ -- which one verifies directly since $(1,0)=(1,1)-(0,1)\in N$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Modules, Tensor Products, and Nakayama's Lemma > Tensor products and the universal property
Type: theorem
Title: {tensor product, A\&M 2.12}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{tensor product, A\&M 2.12}]
There is a pair $(T,g)$ -- an $A$-module $T=M\otimes_A N$ and an $A$-bilinear map $g:M\times N\to T$, $g(x,y)=x\otimes y$ -- with the universal property: for every $A$-module $P$ and every $A$-bilinear $f:M\times N\to P$ there is a unique $A$-linear $f':T\to P$ with $f=f'\circ g$. The pair is unique up to unique isomorphism.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-23033d8f5170cc84fa2a
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Existence: form the free module $C=A^{(M\times N)}$ on symbols $(x,y)$, and quotient by the submodule $D$ generated by all
\[
(x+x',y)-(x,y)-(x',y),\ (x,y+y')-(x,y)-(x,y'),\ (ax,y)-a(x,y),\ (x,ay)-a(x,y).
\]
Set $T=C/D$ and let $x\otimes y$ be the image of $(x,y)$; the relations are exactly bilinearity. An $A$-bilinear $f$ extends to an $A$-linear map on $C$ that kills $D$, hence factors through $T$ uniquely. Uniqueness is the usual universal-property argument. The elements $x\otimes y$ (the simple or decomposable tensors) generate $T$ but are not all of $T$; a general element is a finite sum $\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{pitfall}
The notation $x\otimes y$ is ambiguous about the ambient tensor product, and ``$x\otimes y=0$'' can change meaning under enlargement. Over $A=Z$, take $M=Z$, $N=Z/2$. In $Z\otimesZ/2$ the element $2\otimes x$ equals $1\otimes 2x=1\otimes0=0$. But the same symbol inside $2Z\otimesZ/2$ need not vanish (A\&M, Remark ii after 2.12; cf.\ Cor.\ 2.13: if $\sum x_i\otimes y_i=0$ in $M\otimes N$ it already vanishes in $M_0\otimes N_0$ for some finitely generated submodules). Always name the tensor product you are in.
\end{pitfall}

Type: proposition
Title: {canonical isomorphisms, A\&M 2.14}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{canonical isomorphisms, A\&M 2.14}]
There are unique $A$-isomorphisms
\[
M\otimes N\xrightarrow{\cong}N\otimes M,\quad
(M\otimes N)\otimes P\xrightarrow{\cong}M\otimes(N\otimes P),\quad
(M\oplus N)\otimes P\xrightarrow{\cong}(M\otimes P)\oplus(N\otimes P),\quad
A\otimes M\xrightarrow{\cong}M,
\]
sending $x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x$; $(x\otimes y)\otimes z\mapsto x\otimes(y\otimes z)$; distributing over the sum; and $a\otimes x\mapsto ax$.
\end{proposition}

Type: example
Title: $A\otimes_A M\cong M$ and $A/\fa\otimes_A M\cong M/\fa M$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$A\otimes_A M\cong M$ and $A/\fa\otimes_A M\cong M/\fa M$}
Prove the unit law and the base-change-to-a-quotient formula.
\wrec Both follow from the universal property: a bilinear map out of $A\times M$ is determined by the action $a\cdot(-)$, and tensoring with $A/\fa$ imposes exactly the relations $\fa M=0$.
\wsol For $A\otimes_A M\cong M$: the bilinear map $(a,x)\mapsto ax$ induces $A\otimes M\to M$, $a\otimes x\mapsto ax$, with inverse $x\mapsto1\otimes x$; these compose to identities. For $A/\fa\otimes_A M$: apply $-\otimes_A M$ to $0\to\fa\to A\to A/\fa\to0$ (right-exactness, below) to get $\fa\otimes M\to M\to A/\fa\otimes M\to0$. The image of $\fa\otimes M\to M$ is $\fa M$, so $A/\fa\otimes_A M\cong M/\fa M$. Sanity check: $Z/n\otimes_ZZ/m\cong(Z/m)/n(Z/m)\congZ/\gcd(n,m)$ -- e.g.\ $Z/2\otimesZ/3=0$ and $Z/2\otimesZ/4\congZ/2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Tensor of free modules
Content:
\begin{wex}{Tensor of free modules}
Show $A^m\otimes_A A^n\cong A^{mn}$, with basis $e_i\otimes f_j$.
\wrec Tensor distributes over direct sums and $A\otimes A\cong A$, so a free-times-free is free of the product rank.
\wsol Using distributivity and $A\otimes A\cong A$:
\[
A^m\otimes A^n=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i=1}^m A\Bigr)\otimes\Bigl(\bigoplus_{j=1}^n A\Bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{i,j}(A\otimes A)\cong\bigoplus_{i,j}A=A^{mn}.
\]
A basis is $\{e_i\otimes f_j\}$. Sanity check: a bilinear map $A^m\times A^n\to P$ is the same as an $m\times n$ array of elements of $P$, i.e.\ an element of $P^{mn}$, matching $\Hom_A(A^{mn},P)\cong P^{mn}$ -- exactly the universal property.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Tensor product of homomorphisms
Content:
\begin{wex}{Tensor product of homomorphisms}
For $f:M\to M'$ and $g:N\to N'$, construct $f\otimes g:M\otimes N\to M'\otimes N'$ and verify functoriality.
\wrec The map $(x,y)\mapsto f(x)\otimes g(y)$ is bilinear, so it induces a unique linear map on the tensor product.
\wsol Bilinearity of $(x,y)\mapsto f(x)\otimes g(y)$ gives a well-defined $A$-linear $f\otimes g$ with $(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=f(x)\otimes g(y)$. Since simple tensors generate, $f\otimes g$ is unique. Functoriality $(f'\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ g)=(f'\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes g)$ holds on simple tensors, hence everywhere. Sanity check: $\id_M\otimes\id_N=\id_{M\otimes N}$, and $f\otimes g=0$ whenever $f=0$ or $g=0$, consistent with $(0\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=0\otimes g(y)=0$.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {restriction and extension of scalars}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{restriction and extension of scalars}]
Restriction: a $B$-module $N$ becomes an $A$-module by $a\cdot x:=f(a)x$. Extension (base change): an $A$-module $M$ becomes a $B$-module $M_B:=B\otimes_A M$, with $B$ acting on the left factor, $b'(b\otimes x)=b'b\otimes x$. These are adjoint: $\Hom_B(B\otimes_A M,N)\cong\Hom_A(M,N)$ naturally (extension is left adjoint to restriction).
\end{definition}

Title: {right-exactness of tensor, A\&M 2.18}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{right-exactness of tensor, A\&M 2.18}]
For any $A$-module $N$, the functor $-\otimes_A N$ is right-exact: if $M'\xrightarrow{u}M\xrightarrow{v}M''\to0$ is exact, then
\[
M'\otimes N\xrightarrow{u\otimes1}M\otimes N\xrightarrow{v\otimes1}M''\otimes N\to0
\]
is exact. There is a canonical adjunction isomorphism $\Hom_A(M\otimes N,P)\cong\Hom_A\bigl(M,\Hom_A(N,P)\bigr)$, so $-\otimes N$ is a left adjoint and hence right-exact.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Adjunction: an $A$-bilinear map $M\times N\to P$ is the same as an $A$-linear $M\to\Hom_A(N,P)$ (curry the second variable), which is the same as an $A$-linear $M\otimes N\to P$. So $T(-)=-\otimes N$ is left adjoint to $\Hom_A(N,-)$. Left adjoints preserve cokernels (right-exactness): apply the left-exact $\Hom(-,\Hom(N,P))$ and the left-exactness of $\Hom(T(-),P)$ to deduce exactness of $T$ on the right end, for all $P$. Tensoring need not preserve injections on the left.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Title: {flat module}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{flat module}]
An $A$-module $N$ is flat if $-\otimes_A N$ is exact, equivalently (A\&M 2.19) if tensoring any injection $M'\hookrightarrow M$ with $N$ stays injective; it suffices to test injections $\fa\hookrightarrow A$ with $\fa$ finitely generated. Free modules are flat; localizations $S^{-1} A$ are flat (Section~15.5); over a PID, flat $=$ torsion-free.
\end{definition}
