Title: Tensor is not left-exact: a witness
Content:
\begin{wex}{Tensor is not left-exact: a witness}
Exhibit an injection that fails to stay injective after tensoring.
\wrec Right-exactness can drop an injection to a non-injection; the standard witness is multiplication by $2$ tensored with $Z/2$.
\wsol Take $0\toZ\xrightarrow{2}Z$ over $A=Z$ and tensor with $N=Z/2$. The map becomes $Z/2\xrightarrow{\,\overline{2}\,}Z/2$, which is multiplication by $2=0$ on $Z/2$, the zero map -- not injective, although the original was. So $-\otimesZ/2$ is not exact and $Z/2$ is not a flat $Z$-module. Sanity check: $Z/2$ has $2$-torsion, and over the PID $Z$ ``flat $=$ torsion-free'' predicts non-flatness; the right-exact sequence $Z\xrightarrow{2}Z\toZ/2\to0$ tensored with $Z/2$ correctly gives $Z/2\xrightarrow{0}Z/2\toZ/2\to0$, exact only on the right.
\end{wex}

Title: Free modules are flat
Content:
\begin{wex}{Free modules are flat}
Show $A^n$ (and more generally any free module) is flat.
\wrec Tensoring with $A$ is the identity functor, and tensoring with a direct sum is the direct sum of the tensors; direct sums of exact sequences are exact.
\wsol For an injection $M'\hookrightarrow M$, tensoring with $A$ gives $M'\hookrightarrow M$ unchanged (since $A\otimes-\cong\id$), still injective. Tensoring with $A^{(I)}=\bigoplus_I A$ gives $\bigoplus_I M'\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_I M$, injective because a direct sum of injections is injective. Hence every free module is flat. Sanity check: $Z^n$ is torsion-free, consistent with flat $=$ torsion-free over $Z$; and the failure example above used the non-free $Z/2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Extension of scalars preserves finite generation
Content:
\begin{wex}{Extension of scalars preserves finite generation}
If $M$ is generated by $x_1,\dots,x_n$ over $A$, show $M_B=B\otimes_A M$ is generated by $1\otimes x_1,\dots,1\otimes x_n$ over $B$.
\wrec Simple tensors $b\otimes x$ generate $M_B$, and $b\otimes x$ rewrites in terms of the $1\otimes x_i$ using bilinearity.
\wsol Any element of $M_B$ is a finite sum $\sum b_j\otimes m_j$. Writing $m_j=\sum_i a_{ij}x_i$ with $a_{ij}\in A$ and pulling scalars across, $b_j\otimes m_j=\sum_i b_j\otimes a_{ij}x_i=\sum_i(b_j f(a_{ij}))(1\otimes x_i)$. So everything is a $B$-combination of the $1\otimes x_i$. Sanity check (A\&M 2.16--2.17): if moreover $B$ is f.g.\ as an $A$-module by $y_1,\dots,y_m$, then the $mn$ products $y_k x_i$ generate $N$ over $A$ whenever $N$ is f.g.\ over $B$ -- the tower-of-generators principle.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A torsion-free non-flat module needs a non-PID
Content:
\begin{wex}{A torsion-free non-flat module needs a non-PID}
Over $A=k[x,y]$ show the ideal $\fm=(x,y)$ is torsion-free but not flat.
\wrec Over a non-PID, torsion-free no longer forces flat; test flatness by tensoring the inclusion $\fm\hookrightarrow A$ or by finding a nonzero element of $\Tor_1$.
\wsol $\fm$ is a submodule of the domain $A$, hence torsion-free. But consider the relation $y\cdot x-x\cdot y=0$ among the generators $x,y$ of $\fm$. In $\fm\otimes_A\fm$ the element $x\otimes y-y\otimes x$ is nonzero (it spans the kernel $\Tor_1^A(A/\fm,\fm)\cong\Tor_2^A(A/\fm,A/\fm)\cong k$ of $\fm\otimes_A\fm\to\fm$), so $-\otimes_A\fm$ does not stay injective on $\fm\hookrightarrow A$: the induced $\fm\otimes\fm\to A\otimes\fm=\fm$ kills $x\otimes y-y\otimes x\neq0$. Hence $\fm$ is not flat. Sanity check: this is impossible over a PID, matching that $k[x,y]$ is not a PID; the obstruction lives exactly where $\fm$ fails to be free (it is not, by the local computation above needing $2$ generators).
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {$A$-algebra}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{$A$-algebra}]
An $A$-algebra is a ring $B$ together with a ring homomorphism $f:A\to B$; equivalently, a ring $B$ that is also an $A$-module with compatible multiplication. An $A$-algebra homomorphism $h:B\to C$ is a ring map commuting with the structure maps, $h\circ f=g$. $B$ is finite over $A$ if it is f.g.\ as an $A$-module, and of finite type (finitely generated as an algebra) if $B=A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ for finitely many $x_i$, i.e.\ a quotient of a polynomial ring $A[t_1,\dots,t_n]\twoheadrightarrow B$.
\end{definition}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
This is where arithmetic and geometry merge in the A\&M sense. Every ring is uniquely a $Z$-algebra (the map $n\mapsto n\cdot1$), so commutative-ring theory is the theory of $Z$-algebras. Geometrically, when $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is prime, a finite-type $k$-algebra $B=k[t_1,\dots,t_n]/I$ is the coordinate ring of the affine variety $V(I)\subseteq\Aff^n_k$; an $A$-algebra map is a morphism of the associated $\Spec$'s in the opposite direction (Section~15.8). The two readings of $\Spec A$ -- ``primes of arithmetic'' for $A=Z$ and ``points of geometry'' for $A=k[t_1,\dots,t_n]/I$ -- are the same construction applied to two flavors of algebra.
\end{remark}

Type: proposition
Title: {tensor product of algebras}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{tensor product of algebras}]
Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:A\to C$ be $A$-algebras. Then $D=B\otimes_A C$ is an $A$-algebra with multiplication determined by
\[
(b\otimes c)(b'\otimes c')=bb'\otimes cc',
\]
and $D$ is the coproduct (pushout) of $B$ and $C$ over $A$: there are $A$-algebra maps $u:B\to D$, $u(b)=b\otimes1$, and $v:C\to D$, $v(c)=1\otimes c$, universal among pairs of $A$-algebra maps out of $B$ and $C$ to a common target.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
A\arrow[r,"g"]\arrow[d,"f"'] & C\arrow[d,"v"]\\
B\arrow[r,"u"'] & B\otimes_A C
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four $A$-algebras at the corners of a commutative square: $A$ (the base ring, top-left), $C$ (top-right), $B$ (bottom-left), and $B\otimes_A C$ (bottom-right, the coproduct/pushout). Every arrow is a ring homomorphism that is also $A$-linear.
\dgi{Arrows:} $g:A\to C$ is the structure map making $C$ an $A$-algebra. $f:A\to B$ is the structure map making $B$ an $A$-algebra. $v:C\to B\otimes_A C$ is the canonical map $c\mapsto 1\otimes c$. $u:B\to B\otimes_A C$ is the canonical map $b\mapsto b\otimes 1$. Both $u$ and $v$ are $A$-algebra homomorphisms into the tensor product algebra.
\dgi{What commutes:} The square commutes: $v\circ g = u\circ f$. Concretely, for $a\in A$: along the top-right path, $a\mapsto g(a)\mapsto 1\otimes g(a)$; along the bottom-left path, $a\mapsto f(a)\mapsto f(a)\otimes 1$. These are equal in $B\otimes_A C$ because $f(a)\otimes 1=1\otimes g(a)$ is the defining relation of the tensor product over $A$ (the scalar $a$ can be moved across the $\otimes$ symbol).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $B\otimes_A C$ as an $A$-module means $f(a)b\otimes c = b\otimes g(a)c$ for all $a\in A$. Setting $b=1$, $c=1$: $f(a)\otimes 1=1\otimes g(a)$, exactly the relation $u\circ f=v\circ g$. The key is that both $f(a)$ (as a left $B$-scalar) and $g(a)$ (as a left $C$-scalar) come from the same element $a\in A$, and the tensor product identifies them.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram encodes the universal property of the coproduct (pushout) of $A$-algebras: $B\otimes_A C$ is the initial $A$-algebra equipped with maps from both $B$ and $C$ that agree on the common subalgebra $A$. Any pair of $A$-algebra maps $B\to E$ and $C\to E$ factors uniquely through $B\otimes_A C$. The diagram is placed here to show that the tensor product of algebras is not just an $A$-module but satisfies the correct universal property in the category of $A$-algebras.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $A=R$, $B=R[x]$, $C=R[y]$; then $B\otimes_R C\congR[x,y]$, $u$ sends $x\mapsto x\otimes 1=x$, $v$ sends $y\mapsto 1\otimes y=y$, and $f=g$ are both the inclusion $R\hookrightarrowR[x]$ (resp.\ $R[y]$). The square says the inclusion $R\hookrightarrowR[x,y]$ via $x$ or via $y$ agrees on scalars, i.e.\ $R$ sits inside $R[x,y]$ by a single canonical map.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read $u$ and $v$ as inclusions and assume $B$ and $C$ are subobjects of $B\otimes_A C$; in general they need not be injective (if $B$ or $C$ is not flat over $A$ the maps can have nontrivial kernel). Also, the multiplication rule $(b\otimes c)(b'\otimes c')=bb'\otimes cc'$ (which makes $B\otimes_A C$ a commutative ring) requires checking it is well defined on equivalence classes, which is the ``only subtle point'' cited in the proof.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $B\otimes_A C$ is the pushout of $B$ and $C$ over $A$ in the category of commutative $A$-algebras, making the square commute and satisfying the universal property that any compatible pair of $A$-algebra maps out of $B$ and $C$ factors uniquely through $B\otimes_A C$.
\end{dgx}
\end{proposition}

Type: example
Title: Polynomial rings tensor to polynomial rings
Content:
\begin{wex}{Polynomial rings tensor to polynomial rings}
Compute $A[x]\otimes_A A[y]$.
\wrec Tensor product of free algebras adds variables; the universal property says a map out is a choice of images for $x$ and $y$.
\wsol $A[x]\otimes_A A[y]\cong A[x,y]$ via $x\otimes1\mapsto x$, $1\otimes y\mapsto y$. As $A$-modules both sides are free on the monomials $x^i y^j$, and the multiplications match by the algebra-tensor rule $(x\otimes1)(1\otimes y)=x\otimes y\mapsto xy$. Sanity check: this is the pushout/coproduct statement -- $A[x,y]$ is the free $A$-algebra on $\{x,y\}$, exactly the coproduct of the free algebras on $\{x\}$ and $\{y\}$; geometrically $\Aff^1\times_{\Spec A}\Aff^1=\Aff^2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Base change of a quotient algebra
Content:
\begin{wex}{Base change of a quotient algebra}
For an ideal $I\subseteq A[x]$, compute $B\otimes_A\bigl(A[x]/I\bigr)$.
\wrec Extension of scalars commutes with quotients (right-exactness) and with adjoining variables, so it turns $A[x]/I$ into $B[x]/I^e$.
\wsol Right-exactness applied to $0\to I\to A[x]\to A[x]/I\to0$ tensored with $B$ gives $B\otimes_A(A[x]/I)\cong(B\otimes_A A[x])/(image of B\otimes I)\cong B[x]/I^e$, where $I^e=I\cdot B[x]$ is the extension. Sanity check: $R\otimes_RR[x]/(x^2+1)\congR[x]/(x^2+1)\congC$, while $C\otimes_RR[x]/(x^2+1)\congC[x]/(x^2+1)\congC[x]/((x-i)(x+i))\congC\timesC$ -- the extension splits, the geometric fibre over $\SpecR$ acquires two points after base change to $C$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A tensor product of fields that is not a field
Content:
\begin{wex}{A tensor product of fields that is not a field}
Show $C\otimes_RC\congC\timesC$.
\wrec Write one factor as $R[x]/(x^2+1)$ and base-change; the quadratic splits over $C$, so the tensor product breaks into a product.
\wsol $C\otimes_RC\congC\otimes_RR[x]/(x^2+1)\congC[x]/(x^2+1)\congC[x]/(x-i)\timesC[x]/(x+i)\congC\timesC$ by CRT (the factors $(x-i),(x+i)$ are coprime in $C[x]$). Sanity check: as $R$-vector spaces both sides have dimension $4$; and $C\otimes_RC$ has nonzero zero-divisors (the idempotents $\tfrac12(1\otimes1\mp i\otimes i)$), so it is not a field even though both factors are -- tensor of fields over a subfield need not be a field. Geometrically $\Spec(C\otimes_RC)$ is two points: the two ways to embed $C$ into $C$ over $R$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Localization as base change and its flatness
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localization as base change and its flatness}
Realize the ring of fractions $S^{-1} M$ as $S^{-1} A\otimes_A M$, anticipating Section~15.5.
\wrec Localization is extension of scalars along $A\to S^{-1} A$; the resulting functor is exact, which is the flatness of $S^{-1} A$.
\wsol For a multiplicative set $S\subseteq A$, there is a natural isomorphism $S^{-1} A\otimes_A M\cong S^{-1} M$, $(\tfrac{a}{s})\otimes x\mapsto\tfrac{ax}{s}$ (Section~15.5 makes this precise). Because localizing is exact -- it preserves injections, surjections, kernels -- $S^{-1} A$ is a flat $A$-module, and $-\otimes_A S^{-1} A=S^{-1}(-)$ is an exact functor. Sanity check: exactness is visible on the witness above -- tensoring $0\toZ\xrightarrow{2}Z$ with the flat module $Z_{(3)}=S^{-1}Z$ ($S=Z\setminus3Z$) keeps $2$ a unit times an injection, so injectivity survives, unlike tensoring with $Z/2$. This interaction of tensor and localization is the technical bridge to the next section.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Modules, Tensor Products, and Nakayama's Lemma > Algebras and tensor products of algebras
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Part: 1/3
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).}
\item Show that $(Z/mZ) \otimes_{Z} (Z/nZ) = 0$ if $m, n$ are coprime.

\item Let $A$ be a ring, $\fa$ an ideal, $M$ an $A$-module. Show that $(A/\fa) \otimes_A M$ is isomorphic to $M/\fa M$.
[Tensor the exact sequence $0 \to \fa \to A \to A/\fa \to 0$ with $M$.]

\item Let $A$ be a local ring, $M$ and $N$ finitely generated $A$-modules. Prove that if $M \otimes_A N = 0$, then $M = 0$ or $N = 0$.
[Let $\fm$ be the maximal ideal, $k = A/\fm$ the residue field. Let $M_k = k \otimes_A M \cong M/\fm M$ by Exercise 2. By Nakayama's lemma, $M_k = 0 \Rightarrow M = 0$. But $M \otimes_A N = 0 \Rightarrow (M \otimes_A N)_k = 0 \Rightarrow M_k \otimes_k N_k = 0 \Rightarrow M_k = 0$ or $N_k = 0$, since $M_k$, $N_k$ are vector spaces over a field.]

\item Let $M_i$ ($i \in I$) be any family of $A$-modules, and let $M$ be their direct sum. Prove that $M$ is flat $\iff$ each $M_i$ is flat.

\item Let $A[x]$ be the ring of polynomials in one indeterminate over a ring $A$. Prove that $A[x]$ is a flat $A$-algebra. [Use Exercise 4.]

\item For any $A$-module $M$, let $M[x]$ denote the set of all polynomials in $x$ with coefficients in $M$, that is to say expressions of the form
\[
m_0 + m_1 x + \cdots + m_r x^r \qquad (m_i \in M).
\]
Defining the product of an element of $A[x]$ and an element of $M[x]$ in the obvious way, show that $M[x]$ is an $A[x]$-module. Show that $M[x] \cong A[x] \otimes_A M$.

\item Let $\fp$ be a prime ideal in $A$. Show that $\fp[x]$ is a prime ideal in $A[x]$. If $\fm$ is a maximal ideal in $A$, is $\fm[x]$ a maximal ideal in $A[x]$?

\item i) If $M$ and $N$ are flat $A$-modules, then so is $M \otimes_A N$.
ii) If $B$ is a flat $A$-algebra and $N$ is a flat $B$-module, then $N$ is flat as an $A$-module.

\item Let $0 \to M' \to M \to M'' \to 0$ be an exact sequence of $A$-modules. If $M'$ and $M''$ are finitely generated, then so is $M$.

\item Let $A$ be a ring, $\fa$ an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$; let $M$ be an $A$-module and $N$ a finitely generated $A$-module, and let $u : M \to N$ be a homomorphism. If the induced homomorphism $M/\fa M \to N/\fa N$ is surjective, then $u$ is surjective.

\item Let $A$ be a ring $\neq 0$. Show that $A^m \cong A^n \Rightarrow m = n$.
[Let $\fm$ be a maximal ideal of $A$ and let $\phi : A^m \to A^n$ be an isomorphism. Then $1 \otimes \phi : (A/\fm) \otimes A^m \to (A/\fm) \otimes A^n$ is an isomorphism between vector spaces of dimensions $m$ and $n$ over the field $k = A/\fm$. Hence $m = n$.] (Cf. Chapter 3, Exercise 15.)
If $\phi : A^m \to A^n$ is surjective, then $m \geq n$. If $\phi : A^m \to A^n$ is injective, is it always the case that $m \leq n$?

\item Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module and $\phi : M \to A^n$ a surjective homomorphism. Show that $\Ker(\phi)$ is finitely generated.
[Let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be a basis of $A^n$ and choose $u_i \in M$ such that $\phi(u_i) = e_i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$). Show that $M$ is the direct sum of $\Ker(\phi)$ and the submodule generated by $u_1, \ldots, u_n$.]

Content:
Define $i \leq j$ to mean $M_i \subseteq M_j$ and let $\mu_{ij} : M_i \to M_j$ be the embedding of $M_i$ in $M_j$. Show that
\[
\varinjlim M_i = \sum M_i = \bigcup_i M_i.
\]
In particular, any $A$-module is the direct limit of its finitely generated submodules.

\item Let $M = (M_i, \mu_{ij})$, $N = (N_i, \nu_{ij})$ be direct systems of $A$-modules over the same directed set. Let $M$, $N$ be the direct limits and $\mu_i : M_i \to M$, $\nu_i : N_i \to N$ the associated homomorphisms. A homomorphism $\Phi : M \to N$ is by definition a family of $A$-module homomorphisms $\phi_i : M_i \to N_i$ such that $\phi_j \circ \mu_{ij} = \nu_{ij} \circ \phi_i$ whenever $i \leq j$. Show that $\Phi$ defines a unique homomorphism $\phi = \varinjlim \phi_i : M \to N$ such that $\phi \circ \mu_i = \nu_i \circ \phi_i$ for all $i \in I$.

\item A sequence of direct systems and homomorphisms
\[
M \to N \to P
\]
is exact if the corresponding sequence of modules and module homomorphisms is exact for each $i \in I$. Show that the sequence $M \to N \to P$ of direct limits is then exact. [Use Exercise 15.]

\noindentTensor products commute with direct limits

\item Keeping the same notation as in Exercise 14, let $N$ be any $A$-module. Then $(M_i \otimes N, \mu_{ij} \otimes 1)$ is a direct system; let $P = \varinjlim (M_i \otimes N)$ be its direct limit. For each $i \in I$ we have a homomorphism $\mu_i \otimes 1 : M_i \otimes N \to M \otimes N$, hence by Exercise 16 a homomorphism $\psi : P \to M \otimes N$. Show that $\psi$ is an isomorphism, so that
\[
\varinjlim (M_i \otimes N) \cong (\varinjlim M_i) \otimes N.
\]
[For each $i \in I$ let $g_i : M_i \times N \to M_i \otimes N$ be the canonical bilinear mapping. Passing to the limit we obtain a mapping $g : M \times N \to P$. Show that $g$ is $A$-bilinear and hence define a homomorphism $\phi : M \otimes N \to P$. Verify that $\phi \circ \psi$ and $\psi \circ \phi$ are identity mappings.]

\item Let $(A_i, \alpha_{ij})$ be a direct system of rings indexed by a directed set $I$, and for each $i \leq j$ in $I$ let $\alpha_{ij} : A_i \to A_j$ be a ring homomorphism, satisfying conditions (1) and (2) of Exercise 14. Regarding each $A_i$ as a $Z$-module we can then form the direct limit $A = \varinjlim A_i$. Show that $A$ inherits a ring structure from the $A_i$ so that the mappings $A_i \to A$ are ring homomorphisms. The ring $A$ is the direct limit of the system $(A_i, \alpha_{ij})$. If $A = 0$ prove that $A_i = 0$ for some $i \in I$. [Remember that all rings have identity elements!]

\item Let $(A_i, \alpha_{ij})$ be a direct system of rings and let $N_i$ be the nilradical of $A_i$. Show that $\varinjlim N_i$ is the nilradical of $\varinjlim A_i$. If each $A_i$ is an integral domain, then $\varinjlim A_i$ is an integral domain.

\item Let $(B_\lambda)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ be a family of $A$-algebras. For each finite subset $J$ of $\Lambda$ let $B_J$ denote the tensor product (over $A$) of the $B_\lambda$ for $\lambda \in J$. If $J'$ is another finite subset of $\Lambda$ and $J \subseteq J'$, there is a canonical $A$-algebra homomorphism $B_J \to B_{J'}$. Let $B$ denote the direct limit of the rings $B_J$ as $J$ runs through all finite subsets of $\Lambda$. The ring $B$ has a natural $A$-algebra structure for which the homomorphisms $B_J \to B$ are $A$-algebra homomorphisms. The $A$-algebra $B$ is the tensor product of the family $(B_\lambda)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$.

\noindentFlatness and the Tor functor

\item In these Exercises it will be assumed that the reader is familiar with the definition and basic properties of the Tor functor. If $M$ is an $A$-module, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] $M$ is flat;
\item[ii)] $\operatorname{Tor}_n^A(M, N) = 0$ for all $n > 0$ and all $A$-modules $N$;
\item[iii)] $\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(M, N) = 0$ for all $A$-modules $N$.
\end{enumerate}
[To show that (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii), take a free resolution of $N$ and tensor it with $M$. Since $M$ is flat, the resulting sequence is exact and therefore its homology groups, which are the $\operatorname{Tor}_n^A(M, N)$, are zero for $n > 0$. To show that (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), for the exact sequence
\[
0 \to N' \to N \to N'' \to 0
\]
take the Tor exact sequence
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1(M, N'') \to M \otimes N' \to M \otimes N \to M \otimes N'' \to 0:
\]
since $\operatorname{Tor}_1(M, N'') = 0$ it follows that $M$ is flat.]

\item Let $0 \to N' \to N \to N'' \to 0$ be an exact sequence, with $N''$ flat. Then $N'$ is flat $\iff N$ is flat. [Use Exercise 24 and the Tor exact sequence.]

\item Let $N$ be an $A$-module. Then $N$ is flat $\iff \operatorname{Tor}_1(A/\fa, N) = 0$ for all finitely generated ideals $\fa$.
[Show first that $\operatorname{Tor}_1(M, N) = 0$ for all finitely generated $A$-modules $M$, then for all $A$-modules $M$. If $M$ is finitely generated, let $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ be a set of generators of $M$, and let $M_i$ be the submodule generated by $x_1, \ldots, x_i$. By considering the successive quotients $M_i/M_{i-1}$ and using Exercise 25, deduce that $\operatorname{Tor}_1(M, N) = 0$ whenever $\operatorname{Tor}_1(A/\fa, N) = 0$ for all ideals $\fa$ (each $M_i/M_{i-1}$ is cyclic, hence isomorphic to some $A/\fa$). So that $N$ is flat $\iff \operatorname{Tor}_1(A/\fa, N) = 0$ for all finitely generated ideals $\fa$. Finally use (2.19) to reduce to the case where $\fa$ is a finitely generated ideal.]

\item A ring $A$ is absolutely flat if every $A$-module is flat. Prove that the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] $A$ is absolutely flat;
\item[ii)] Every principal ideal is idempotent;
\item[iii)] Every finitely generated ideal is a direct summand of $A$.
\end{enumerate}
[i) $\Rightarrow$ ii). Let $x \in A$.

the mapping $i^*$ is injective. Hence $\operatorname{Im}(p) = 0$ (as $i^*\circ p$ is the zero map $(x)\to A/(x)$), so $(x)\otimes A/(x)\cong(x)/(x^2)$ is $0$, i.e.\ $(x) = (x^2)$.

\item A Boolean ring is absolutely flat. The ring of Chapter 1, Exercise 7 is absolutely flat. Every homomorphic image of an absolutely flat ring is absolutely flat. If a local ring is absolutely flat, then it is a field. If $A$ is absolutely flat, every non-unit in $A$ is a zero-divisor.

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Over $A=Z$, compute the abelian group $Z/12\otimes_ZZ/18$ and identify it as $Z/(d)Z$ for the correct $d$; then compute $\Hom_Z(Z/12,Z/18)$ and verify that it too is cyclic of order $\gcd(12,18)=6$, so that the two groups are (non-canonically) isomorphic, and exhibit an explicit isomorphism.
\item Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $A$-module. Compute $\Ann(M\oplus N)$ in terms of $\Ann(M)$ and $\Ann(N)$, and show by example over $A=Z$ that $\Ann(M\otimes_A N)$ can be strictly larger than $\Ann(M)+\Ann(N)$. (Try $M=Q$, $N=Z/2$.)
\item Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be a local ring and $M$ a finitely generated $A$-module with $\dim_k(M/\fm M)=3$. Decide, with proof, which of the following must hold: (a) $M$ is generated by exactly $3$ elements and no fewer; (b) every generating set of $M$ has at least $3$ elements; (c) $M\cong A^3$. Give a counterexample to any that fails.
\item Take $A=Z$ and the short exact sequence $0\toZ\xrightarrow{6}Z\toZ/6\to0$. Apply $-\otimes_ZZ/4$ and write out the resulting right-exact sequence with all maps computed; identify the kernel of the leftmost map and explain why it is exactly $\Tor_1^{Z}(Z/6,Z/4)$.
\item Let $\phi:M\to M$ be an $A$-endomorphism of a finitely generated $A$-module with $\phi(M)\subseteq\fa M$ for an ideal $\fa$, and let $\phi^n+a_1\phi^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0$ ($a_i\in\fa$) be the relation given by the determinant trick. Writing $\phi=\id_M-\psi$, show that $\psi\,q(\psi)=-(1+a_1+\cdots+a_n)\id_M$ for some $q\in A[t]$, and deduce that if the coefficient sum $1+a_1+\cdots+a_n$ is a unit (for instance if $\fa\subseteq\Jac(A)$) then $\id_M-\phi$ is an automorphism of $M$, whereas $\phi$ itself need not be injective (take $\phi=0$ and $M\neq0$). When $M=A^r$ ($r\ge1$) is free, show also that $\det(\phi)\in\fa$.
\item Over $A=k[t]$, regard a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$ with a linear operator $T$ as an $A$-module $M_T$. Show $M_T\otimes_{k[t]}k[t]/(t-\lambda)\cong V/(T-\lambda)V$ and identify this quotient with the cokernel of $T-\lambda$; deduce that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ iff this tensor product is nonzero.
\item Let $f:A\to B$ be a ring homomorphism and $M$ an $A$-module. Prove the projection formula in the special case: for an ideal $\fa\subseteq A$, $B\otimes_A(M/\fa M)\cong (B\otimes_A M)/\fa^e(B\otimes_A M)$ where $\fa^e=\fa B$. Verify it on $A=Z$, $B=Z/4$, $M=Z$, $\fa=2Z$.
\item Show that $Q\otimes_ZQ\congQ$ as $Q$-vector spaces and as rings, but that $Q\otimes_Z(Z/n)=0$ for every $n\ge1$. Conclude that $Q$ is a flat but not faithfully flat $Z$-module by exhibiting a nonzero module killed by $Q\otimes_Z-$.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $M$ a finitely presented $A$-module: $A^m\xrightarrow{\psi}A^n\to M\to0$ exact. Prove that for any flat $A$-module $F$, the natural map $F\otimes_A\Hom_A(M,A)\to\Hom_A(M,F)$ is an isomorphism: first when $M$ is finite free, then in general by applying $\Hom_A(-,A)$, $F\otimes_A-$ and $\Hom_A(-,F)$ to the presentation. State precisely where finite presentation and flatness enter, give the map explicitly, and show that the map need not be an isomorphism when $F$ is not flat (take $A=Z$, $M=F=Z/2$).
\item Let $(A,\fm,k)$ be local and $u:M\to N$ a homomorphism of finitely generated $A$-modules. Prove that $u$ is surjective iff the induced map $\bar u:M/\fm M\to N/\fm N$ of $k$-vector spaces is surjective. Then show by example that the analogous statement for injectivity is false (find local $A$ and an injective $\bar u$ with $u$ not injective).
\item Let $N$ be an $A$-module. Prove that $N$ is flat iff for every relation $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=0$ with $a_i\in A$, $x_i\in N$, there exist $y_1,\dots,y_m\in N$ and $b_{ij}\in A$ with $x_i=\sum_j b_{ij}y_j$ and $\sum_i a_i b_{ij}=0$ for all $j$ (the equational criterion for flatness). Use this to re-derive that $Z/2$ is not a flat $Z$-module from the relation $2\cdot\bar1=0$.
\item Let $B$ and $C$ be $A$-algebras with $A$ a field $k$. Prove that $\dim_k(B\otimes_k C)=(\dim_k B)(\dim_k C)$ when both are finite-dimensional, and that $B\otimes_k C$ is reduced when $B,C$ are reduced and $k$ is perfect; give a counterexample over an imperfect field $k=\F_p(t)$ with $B=C=k(t^{1/p})$ showing the tensor product can have nonzero nilpotents.
\item Let $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ be a short exact sequence of $A$-modules with $M''$ flat. Prove that for every $A$-module $N$ the sequence $0\to M'\otimes N\to M\otimes N\to M''\otimes N\to0$ is exact (i.e. flatness of $M''$ makes the sequence universally left-exact too), and deduce that an extension of a flat module by a flat module is flat.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item For a ring map $f:A\to B$, extension of scalars $M\mapsto B\otimes_A M$ is left adjoint to restriction. Complete the naturality square below for an $A$-linear map $g:M\to M'$ (vertical maps are the unit $\eta_M:M\to B\otimes_A M$, $x\mapsto1\otimes x$, of the adjunction; horizontal maps are $g$ and $1\otimes g$), prove it commutes, and prove the universal property $\Hom_B(B\otimes_A M,N)\cong\Hom_A(M,N)$ for a $B$-module $N$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
M \arrow[r,"g"] \arrow[d,"\eta_M"'] & M' \arrow[d,"\eta_{M'}"] \\
B\otimes_A M \arrow[r,"1\otimes g"'] & B\otimes_A M'
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify, in the universal property, the unique $B$-linear map induced by a given $A$-linear $M\to N$.
\item Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:A\to C$ be $A$-algebras. Complete the pushout square exhibiting $B\otimes_A C$ as the coproduct of $B$ and $C$ in the category of $A$-algebras, fill in the dashed universal arrow to an arbitrary $A$-algebra $E$ receiving maps $\beta:B\to E$, $\gamma:C\to E$, and prove the induced map is the unique $A$-algebra homomorphism making both triangles commute:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
A \arrow[r,"g"] \arrow[d,"f"'] & C \arrow[d,"v"] \arrow[ddr,bend left,"\gamma"] & \\
B \arrow[r,"u"'] \arrow[drr,bend right,"\beta"'] & B\otimes_A C \arrow[dr,dashed,"\exists!\,h"] & \\
& & E
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Specialize to $A=R$, $B=C=C$ and identify $h$ when $E=C\timesC$.
\item Let $\fa\subseteq A$ be an ideal and $M$ an $A$-module. Complete the diagram below, in which the top row is the defining presentation of $A/\fa\otimes_A M$ obtained by tensoring $0\to\fa\to A\to A/\fa\to0$ with $M$, and prove the induced isomorphism $A/\fa\otimes_A M\cong M/\fa M$ (identify the dashed vertical isomorphism and show the right square commutes):

\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]

\]

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Multiplicatively closed sets and the ring of fractions
Type: prose
Content:
The construction of fractions is the algebraist's tool for inverting a chosen set of elements. The model is the passage from $Z$ to $Q$: there one inverts every nonzero integer. The general construction lets us invert only a prescribed family $S$, and -- crucially -- it works even when $R$ is not a domain. Atiyah and Macdonald frame the whole chapter geometrically: $\Spec R$ is a space whose points are the prime ideals of $R$, and forming fractions concentrates attention near a point or on an open set. This is the algebraic shadow of localizing a function $f(x)$ near a point of the real line in order to study its differentiability.

Title: {multiplicatively closed set}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{multiplicatively closed set}]
A subset $S\subseteq R$ of a commutative ring with $1$ is multiplicatively closed (a multiplicative set) if $1\in S$ and $a,b\in S\implies ab\in S$. (D\&F write $D$ for this set; A\&M write $S$. We use $S$.)
\end{definition}

Type: theorem
Title: {ring of fractions and its universal property}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{ring of fractions and its universal property}]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $S\subseteq R$ multiplicatively closed. There is a commutative ring $S^{-1}R$ and a ring homomorphism $\pi\colon R\to S^{-1}R$, $\pi(r)=r/1$, with the following universal property: for every ring homomorphism $\psi\colon R\to T$ (sending $1$ to $1$) such that $\psi(s)$ is a unit in $T$ for all $s\in S$, there is a unique ring homomorphism $\Psi\colon S^{-1}R\to T$ with $\Psi\circ\pi=\psi$. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\ker\pi=\{r\in R:\ sr=0 for some s\in S\}$; thus $\pi$ is injective iff $S$ contains no zero divisor of $R$.
\item $S^{-1}R=0$ iff $0\in S$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
On $R\times S$ put $(r,s)\sim(r',s')$ iff $x(s'r-sr')=0$ for some $x\in S$. The extra factor $x$ -- absent in the domain case -- is exactly what repairs transitivity when $R$ has zero divisors. Write $r/s$ for the class, set
\[
\frac rs+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{s'r+sr'}{ss'},\qquad \frac rs\cdot\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'},
\]
and check these are well defined; $1=1/1$, and each $s/1$ is a unit with inverse $1/s$. Given $\psi$ with $\psi(S)\subseteq T^{\times}$, the only possible extension is $\Psi(r/s)=\psi(r)\psi(s)^{-1}$; one checks it is well defined and a homomorphism, and uniqueness is forced because every element of $S^{-1}R$ is $(r/1)(s/1)^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: {philosophy: $\Spec$ and concentration}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{philosophy: $\Spec$ and concentration}]
The universal property says $S^{-1}R$ is the universal (initial) $R$-algebra in which the elements of $S$ become invertible. Geometrically, the map $\pi^{*}\colon\Spec(S^{-1}R)\to\Spec R$ realizes $\Spec(S^{-1}R)$ as the subset of points (primes) that ``survive'' inverting $S$ -- those missing $S$. Inverting $f$ keeps the open set where $f\ne0$; inverting $R\setminus\fp$ keeps only the primes contained in $\fp$, i.e.\ concentrates on an infinitesimal neighborhood of the point $\fp$. This is the recurring A\&M slogan: the prime ideal is the common generalization of a prime of arithmetic and a point of geometry, and localization concentrates near such a point.
\end{remark}

Type: method
Title: Computing in $S^{-1}R$
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing in $S^{-1}R$}
To test $r/s=r'/s'$, clear denominators with a slack factor: find $x\in S$ with $x(s'r-sr')=0$. To test $r/s=0$, find $s'\in S$ with $s'r=0$. To invert: $s/1$ has inverse $1/s$. Never assume $R\hookrightarrow S^{-1}R$ -- that holds only when $S$ has no zero divisors.
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: The slack factor is necessary
Content:
\begin{wex}{The slack factor is necessary}
In $R=k[x,y]/(xy)$ with $S=\{1,x,x^2,\dots\}$, show $y/1=0$ in $S^{-1}R=R_x$.
\wrec Use $\ker\pi=\{r:\ sr=0,\ s\in S\}$; here $x\cdot y=0$ in $R$ and $x\in S$.
\wsol Since $xy=0$ in $R$ and $x\in S$, the element $y$ lies in $\ker\pi$, so $y/1=0/1$ in $R_x$. Concretely $y=xy/x=0/x=0$. Hence $\pi\colon R\to R_x$ is not injective: $x$ is a zero divisor of $R$. In fact $\pi(R)=k[x]$ and $R_x=k[x,x^{-1}]$, the Laurent polynomials. Sanity check: the only obstruction $0\in S$ would force $R_x=0$; but $x$ is not nilpotent, so $R_x\ne0$, and indeed $k[x,x^{-1}]\ne0$.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Multiplicatively closed sets and the ring of fractions
Type: example
Title: $R_f\cong R[t]/(tf-1)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$R_f\cong R[t]/(tf-1)$}
For $f\in R$ and $S=\{f^n\}$, identify $R_f$ with a quotient of a polynomial ring.
\wrec Inverting $f$ means adjoining a formal inverse $t$ with $tf=1$; the universal property pins down the isomorphism.
\wsol Let $T=R[t]/(tf-1)$, with $\bar t$ the class of $t$, so $\bar t\,f=1$ in $T$: thus $f$ is a unit in $T$. The map $R\to T$ inverts $f$, so by the universal property factors uniquely through $R_f\to T$, $1/f\mapsto\bar t$. Conversely $R\to R_f$ sends $f$ to a unit, so $R[t]\to R_f$, $t\mapsto1/f$, kills $tf-1$ and factors through $T\to R_f$. These are mutually inverse, so $R_f\cong R[t]/(tf-1)$. Sanity check: if $f$ is nilpotent, $f^n=0\in S$ forces $R_f=0$; correspondingly $T=R[t]/(tf-1)$ collapses, since in $T$ we have $1=(tf)^n=t^n f^n=t^n\cdot0=0$, so $R[t]/(tf-1)=0$, matching.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Z_{(p)}$ and $Z[1/p]$: localizing at vs.\ away from $(p)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z_{(p)}$ and $Z[1/p]$: localizing at vs.\ away from $(p)$}
Describe $S^{-1}Z$ for $S=Z\setminus(p)$, and for $S=\{1,p,p^2,\dots\}$.
\wrec $\fp=(p)$ is prime, so $S=Z\setminus(p)$ is multiplicative; localizing at it inverts every integer not divisible by $p$. Inverting the powers of $p$ does the opposite.
\wsol $Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\inQ:\ p\nmid b\}$: the rationals with denominator prime to $p$. Its unique maximal ideal is $pZ_{(p)}=\{a/b:\ p\mid a,\ p\nmid b\}$, and every $b$ with $p\nmid b$ is a unit. By contrast $Z[1/p]=\{a/p^n\}$ inverts $p$ and keeps all primes $\ne(p)$. Sanity check: $(p)$ is the only prime meeting $S=\{p^n\}$, so $\SpecZ[1/p]$ is $\SpecZ$ minus the point $(p)$; whereas $\SpecZ_{(p)}=\{(0),(p)\}$, the two primes contained in $(p)$ -- concentration near the point $(p)$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Localizing a ring of functions at a point
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing a ring of functions at a point}
Let $R$ be a ring of $k$-valued functions on a set $V$ containing the constants, and for $a\in V$ let $\fm_a=\{f:\ f(a)=0\}$. Identify $R_{\fm_a}$.
\wrec Evaluation at $a$ is a surjection $R\to k$ with kernel $\fm_a$, so $\fm_a$ is maximal; $S=R\setminus\fm_a$ consists of functions nonvanishing at $a$.
\wsol $R_{\fm_a}=\{f/g:\ f,g\in R,\ g(a)\ne0\}$. Each such fraction has a well-defined value $(f/g)(a)=f(a)/g(a)\in k$ independent of representative, so $R_{\fm_a}$ is a ring of ``rational functions defined at $a$.'' Sanity check: the residue field is $R_{\fm_a}/\fm_a R_{\fm_a}\cong k$ via $f/g\mapsto f(a)/g(a)$ -- evaluation at the point survives localization, which is precisely the meaning of ``germ at $a$.''
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {module of fractions}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{module of fractions}]
Let $M$ be an $R$-module. On $S\times M$ put $(s,m)\sim(s',m')$ iff $x(s'm-sm')=0$ for some $x\in S$. Writing $m/s$ for the class, the set $S^{-1}M$ of classes is an $S^{-1}R$-module under
\[
\frac ms+\frac{m'}{s'}=\frac{s'm+sm'}{ss'},\qquad \frac rs\cdot\frac m{s'}=\frac{rm}{ss'}\quad(r/s\in S^{-1}R).
\]
There is an $R$-homomorphism $\pi\colon M\to S^{-1}M$, $m\mapsto m/1$, with $\ker\pi=\{m:\ sm=0 for some s\in S\}$. When $S=R\setminus\fp$ we write $M_{\fp}$; when $S=\{f^n\}$ we write $M_f$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {$S^{-1}M\cong S^{-1}R\otimes_R M$}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$S^{-1}M\cong S^{-1}R\otimes_R M$}]
For any $R$-module $M$ there is a natural isomorphism of $S^{-1}R$-modules
\[
S^{-1}M\ \cong\ S^{-1}R\otimes_R M,\qquad m/s\ \longleftrightarrow\ (1/s)\otimes m.
\]
Thus $S^{-1}M$ is obtained from $M$ by extension of scalars along $\pi\colon R\to S^{-1}R$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
The map $S^{-1}R\times M\to S^{-1}M$, $(r/s,m)\mapsto rm/s$, is $R$-bilinear, inducing $S^{-1}R\otimes_R M\to S^{-1}M$; the rule $m/s\mapsto(1/s)\otimes m$ is a well-defined inverse (one checks independence of representative using the slack factor). Both directions are $S^{-1}R$-linear, so they are mutually inverse isomorphisms.
\end{proof}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Modules of fractions and exactness
Type: theorem
Title: {exactness of localization; $S^{-1}R$ is flat}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{exactness of localization; $S^{-1}R$ is flat}]
The functor $M\mapsto S^{-1}M$ is exact: if $0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0$ is a short exact sequence of $R$-modules, then
\[
0\to S^{-1}M'\xrightarrow{S^{-1}f}S^{-1}M\xrightarrow{S^{-1}g}S^{-1}M''\to0
\]
is exact. Equivalently, $S^{-1}R$ is a flat $R$-module, and $S^{-1}(\cdot)=S^{-1}R\otimes_R(\cdot)$ preserves injections.
\end{theorem}

\[
0\to S^{-1}M'\xrightarrow{S^{-1}f}S^{-1}M\xrightarrow{S^{-1}g}S^{-1}M''\to0
\]
is exact. Equivalently, $S^{-1}R$ is a \emph{flat} $R$-module, and $S^{-1}(\cdot)=S^{-1}R\otimes_R(\cdot)$ preserves injections.
\end{theorem}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Modules of fractions and exactness
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-b7eea7aa78149221838e
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
It suffices (A\&M 3.3) to show $S^{-1}$ preserves exactness at a single spot: if $M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}M''$ is exact at $M$ then so is the localized sequence. ``$\supseteq$'': $g f=0$ gives $S^{-1}g\,S^{-1}f=0$. ``$\subseteq$'': if $(S^{-1}g)(m/s)=g(m)/s=0$, then $t\,g(m)=0=g(tm)$ for some $t\in S$, so $tm=f(m')$ by exactness, whence $m/s=f(m')/(ts)=(S^{-1}f)(m'/ts)$. Applying this to $0\to M'\to M$ shows $S^{-1}f$ is injective, giving full short-exactness; flatness is the tensor restatement.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: {why flatness matters}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{why flatness matters}]
Flatness is exactly the statement that localizing never creates spurious relations: a relation among fractions can always be cleared (multiply by a common $s\in S$) back to a relation in $M$. This is the technical engine behind every local-global principle below. A\&M emphasize that flatness, injectivity of a map, and being zero are all properties that can be checked locally.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Localization kills $S$-torsion
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localization kills $S$-torsion}
Show $S^{-1}M=0$ iff every $m\in M$ is annihilated by some $s\in S$ (i.e.\ $M$ is $S$-torsion).
\wrec $m/1=0$ in $S^{-1}M$ iff $sm=0$ for some $s\in S$; $S^{-1}M=0$ means every $m/1$, hence every $m/t$, is zero.
\wsol If $S^{-1}M=0$ then $m/1=0$ for all $m$, so each $m$ has $s_m\in S$ with $s_m m=0$. Conversely if each $m$ is $S$-torsion, then any $m/t=0$ since $s_m(m)=0$. Sanity check: for $R=Z$, $M=Z/6Z$, $S=Z\setminus(2)$: every element is killed by $3\in S$? No -- $3\cdot\bar1=\bar3\ne0$, but $3\cdot\bar2=\bar0$; the $2$-torsion-free part dies. Indeed $M_{(2)}=Z/2Z\ne0$, consistent with $M$ not being $S$-torsion. (Compare the next example.)
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Modules of fractions and exactness
Type: example
Title: Localizing a finite abelian group at a prime
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing a finite abelian group at a prime}
For $M=Z/6Z$ as a $Z$-module, compute $M_{(p)}$ for each prime $p$ and $M_{(0)}$.
\wrec $M_{(p)}$ inverts all integers prime to $p$; this projects $M$ onto its $p$-primary component (Sylow $p$-subgroup).
\wsol $Z/6Z\congZ/2Z\oplusZ/3Z$. Inverting $S=Z\setminus(2)$ makes $3$ a unit, so the $Z/3Z$ summand (killed by $3\in S$) dies: $M_{(2)}\congZ/2Z$. Symmetrically $M_{(3)}\congZ/3Z$. For $p\notin\{2,3\}$, both $2,3\in S$ are units, so all of $M$ is $S$-torsion and $M_{(p)}=0$. At $\fp=(0)$, $S=Z\setminus\{0\}$ inverts everything, killing the entire torsion group: $M_{(0)}=0$. Sanity check: $M_{(p)}$ is the $p$-primary component, nonzero only for $p\in\{2,3\}$, exactly the primes dividing $6$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Localization commutes with direct sums and quotients
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localization commutes with direct sums and quotients}
Verify $S^{-1}(M\oplus N)\cong S^{-1}M\oplus S^{-1}N$ and $S^{-1}(M/N)\cong S^{-1}M/S^{-1}N$.
\wrec Both follow from exactness (or from $S^{-1}R\otimes_R(\cdot)$ commuting with $\oplus$ and right-exactness).
\wsol For sums: $(m,n)/s\mapsto(m/s,n/s)$ is an $S^{-1}R$-isomorphism. For quotients: apply the exact functor $S^{-1}$ to $0\to N\to M\to M/N\to0$, getting $0\to S^{-1}N\to S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}(M/N)\to0$, so $S^{-1}(M/N)\cong S^{-1}M/S^{-1}N$ with $S^{-1}N\subseteq S^{-1}M$ a submodule. Sanity check: take $R=Z$, $M=Z$, $N=6Z$, $S=Z\setminus(2)$. Then $S^{-1}M=Z_{(2)}$, $S^{-1}N=6Z_{(2)}=2Z_{(2)}$ (since $3$ is a unit), and $Z_{(2)}/2Z_{(2)}\congZ/2Z\cong(Z/6Z)_{(2)}$, matching.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $S^{-1}(\Ann M)=\Ann(S^{-1}M)$ for finitely generated $M$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$S^{-1}(\Ann M)=\Ann(S^{-1}M)$ for finitely generated $M$}
Show that for finitely generated $M$, localization commutes with the annihilator.
\wrec For a single generator $\Ann(Rm)$ this is clear; reduce a finite generating set via $\Ann(M+N)=\Ann M\cap\Ann N$ and the fact that $S^{-1}$ commutes with finite intersections.
\wsol If $M=Rm$ then $\Ann(S^{-1}M)=\{r/s:\ (r/s)(m/1)=0\}=\{r/s:\ s'rm=0\}=S^{-1}\Ann(M)$. For $M=\sum_{i=1}^n Rm_i$, write $\Ann M=\bigcap_i\Ann(Rm_i)$; since $S^{-1}$ commutes with finite intersections, $S^{-1}\Ann M=\bigcap_i S^{-1}\Ann(Rm_i)=\bigcap_i\Ann(S^{-1}Rm_i)=\Ann(S^{-1}M)$. Sanity check: finiteness is needed -- for $M=\bigoplus_{p}Z/pZ$ over $Z$, $\Ann M=0$ but $S^{-1}M$ can have nonzero annihilator after localizing away infinitely many torsion pieces.
\end{wex}

Title: {extension/contraction under $S^{-1}$}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{extension/contraction under $S^{-1}$}]
With the notation above:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Every ideal $\fb$ of $S^{-1}R$ is extended: $\fb=(\fb^{c})^{e}$. Hence distinct ideals of $S^{-1}R$ have distinct contractions.
\item For an ideal $\fa$ of $R$, the contraction of its extension is the saturation
\[
\fa^{ec}=\bigcup_{s\in S}(\fa:s)=\{r\in R:\ sr\in\fa for some s\in S\}.
\]
Moreover $\fa^{e}=S^{-1}R$ (the whole ring) iff $\fa\cap S\ne\varnothing$.
\item $S^{-1}$ commutes with finite sums, finite intersections, products and radicals of ideals; and $S^{-1}R/S^{-1}\fa\cong S^{-1}(R/\fa)$.
\item If $R$ is Noetherian (resp.\ Artinian), so is $S^{-1}R$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-a972ff47fe025a9c17f1
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) Given $a/s\in\fb$, also $a/1=s(a/s)\in\fb$, so $a\in\fb^{c}$ and $a/s\in(\fb^{c})^{e}$; the reverse inclusion is clear. (2) $r\in\fa^{ec}\iff r/1\in S^{-1}\fa\iff r/1=a/s$ with $a\in\fa\iff x(sr-a)=0$ some $x\in S\iff (xs)r\in\fa$, i.e.\ $r\in(\fa:xs)$. (3) Sums/intersections/products: clear denominators with a common $s$. Radicals: $(a/s)^n=a^n/s^n\in S^{-1}\fa\iff t a^n\in\fa$ some $t\iff(ta)^n\in\fa\iff ta\in\rad\fa$, giving $\rad(S^{-1}\fa)=S^{-1}(\rad\fa)$. The quotient formula is exactness applied to $0\to\fa\to R\to R/\fa\to0$. (4) Chains in $S^{-1}R$ contract (injectively, by (1)) to chains in $R$.
\end{proof}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Extension and contraction of ideals
Type: remark
Title: {saturation, geometrically}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{saturation, geometrically}]
Loosely, $\fa^{ec}$ collects the elements that would lie in $\fa$ if denominators from $S$ were allowed. Ideals meeting $S$ ``blow up'' to the unit ideal -- they vanish from $\Spec(S^{-1}R)$ -- while primes disjoint from $S$ are the ones localization remembers (a non-prime ideal disjoint from $S$ can still grow under $\fa\mapsto\fa^{ec}$, as the next example shows). This is why A\&M say localization cuts out the part of $\Spec R$ disjoint from $S$.
\end{remark}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Extension and contraction of ideals
Type: example
Title: Saturation that strictly enlarges $\fa$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Saturation that strictly enlarges $\fa$}
In $R=Z$, $S=Z\setminus(2)$, compute the saturation of $\fa=(12)$.
\wrec $\fa^{ec}=\{r:\ sr\in(12),\ s\in S\}$; inverting odd numbers should strip the odd part $3$ from $12=2^2\cdot3$.
\wsol With $s=3\in S$ and $r=4$: $3\cdot4=12\in(12)$, so $4\in\fa^{ec}$, though $4\notin(12)$. In general $r\in\fa^{ec}\iff$ some odd multiple of $r$ is divisible by $12=2^2\cdot3\iff 4\mid r$ (the odd factor $3$ is absorbed by $S$). Hence $\fa^{ec}=(4)$, the $2$-primary part of $(12)$. Sanity check: in $Z_{(2)}$, $3$ is a unit, so $(12)^e=(4\cdot3)^e=(4)^e$, and contracting $(4)Z_{(2)}$ gives back $(4)$ -- exactly the saturation.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Extension and contraction of ideals
Type: example
Title: An ideal that becomes the whole ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{An ideal that becomes the whole ring}
With $R=Z$, $S=Z\setminus(2)$, show $(3)^{e}=Z_{(2)}$.
\wrec $\fa^{e}=S^{-1}R$ iff $\fa\cap S\ne\varnothing$; here $3\in(3)\cap S$.
\wsol Since $3\in(3)$ and $3\in S=Z\setminus(2)$, we have $3\in(3)\cap S$, so $(3)^{e}$ contains the unit $3/1$, forcing $(3)^{e}=Z_{(2)}$. Sanity check: $(3)$ corresponds to the point $(3)\in\SpecZ$, which is not contained in $(2)$, so it disappears when we concentrate near $(2)$ -- its extension is the unit ideal.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Extension and contraction of ideals
Type: example
Title: Localization commutes with radicals
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localization commutes with radicals}
In $R=k[x,y]$, $S=\{1,y,y^2,\dots\}$, verify $\rad((x^2)^e)=((x))^e$ in $R_y$.
\wrec $S^{-1}(\rad\fa)=\rad(S^{-1}\fa)$; here $\rad(x^2)=(x)$ in $k[x,y]$.
\wsol In $R$, $\rad(x^2)=(x)$. Extending: $\rad((x^2)^e)=(\rad(x^2))^e=(x)^e$ in $R_y=k[x,y,y^{-1}]$. Directly: $(x/1)^2=x^2/1$ generates $(x^2)^e$, and its radical is generated by $x/1$. Sanity check: $y$ is a unit in $R_y$ and $y\notin(x)$, so the extension is a proper prime ideal (it is $(x)R_y$, with quotient $R_y/(x)R_y\cong k[y,y^{-1}]$, a domain), confirming $(x)^e$ is radical (indeed prime).
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: prose
Content:
The deepest structural fact is that localization sorts the primes: $\Spec(S^{-1}R)$ is exactly the part of $\Spec R$ disjoint from $S$. Specializing $S=R\setminus\fp$ produces a local ring whose single closed point is $\fp$ -- the algebraic ``germ'' at the point $\fp\in\Spec R$.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: theorem
Title: {prime correspondence}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{prime correspondence}]
Extension and contraction are mutually inverse, inclusion-preserving bijections
\[
\{primes \fq of R with \fq\cap S=\varnothing\}\ \xrightleftharpoons[\ c\ ]{\ e\ }\ \{primes of S^{-1}R\}.
\]
A prime $\fq$ disjoint from $S$ extends to the prime $S^{-1}\fq$; conversely every prime of $S^{-1}R$ contracts to such a $\fq$, and $\fq^{ec}=\fq$. Primary ideals correspond to primary ideals under the same maps.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-8bed4b56d29f9d33e0b5
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The contraction of a prime is always prime, and lands in a prime disjoint from $S$ (else its extension is the unit ideal). For $\fq$ prime with $\fq\cap S=\varnothing$: if $(a/s)(b/t)\in S^{-1}\fq$, clear denominators to get $x\,ab\in\fq$ for some $x\in S$; since $x\notin\fq$ and $\fq$ is prime, $ab\in\fq$, hence $a\in\fq$ or $b\in\fq$, so $a/s$ or $b/t\in S^{-1}\fq$ -- thus $S^{-1}\fq$ is prime. Finally $\fq^{ec}=\fq$ by the saturation formula and primality.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: theorem
Title: {$R_{\fp}$ is a local ring}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$R_{\fp}$ is a local ring}]
Let $\fp$ be a prime of $R$ and $S=R\setminus\fp$. Then $R_{\fp}=S^{-1}R$ is a local ring: it has a unique maximal ideal, namely $\fp^{e}=S^{-1}\fp=\{a/s:\ a\in\fp,\ s\notin\fp\}$. Its residue field is
\[
R_{\fp}/\fp R_{\fp}\ \cong\ \Frac(R/\fp),
\]
the field of fractions of the domain $R/\fp$. The primes of $R_{\fp}$ correspond bijectively to the primes of $R$ contained in $\fp$.
\end{theorem}

\]

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-c0388bce6e46fe32d519
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
A prime $\fq$ is disjoint from $S=R\setminus\fp$ iff $\fq\subseteq\fp$. Among these, $\fp$ itself is the largest, so $S^{-1}\fp$ is the largest -- hence unique maximal -- ideal of $R_{\fp}$. Equivalently, every $a/s$ with $a\notin\fp$ has $a\in S$, so $a/s$ is a unit; the nonunits are exactly $S^{-1}\fp$, which is therefore an ideal (Prop.\ on local rings). The residue field statement is the quotient formula $R_{\fp}/\fp R_{\fp}\cong S^{-1}(R/\fp)=\Frac(R/\fp)$.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: remark
Title: {the local ring is the germ at a point}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{the local ring is the germ at a point}]
$\Spec R_{\fp}$ is the set of primes $\subseteq\fp$ -- the points of $\Spec R$ that specialize to $\fp$, i.e.\ an infinitesimal neighborhood of the point $\fp$. The closed point is $\fp R_{\fp}$, the generic point is $(0)$ when $R$ is a domain. The residue field $\Frac(R/\fp)$ is the field of values ``at the point.'' This is the precise sense in which $R_{\fp}$ is the ring of germs of functions near $\fp$.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: example
Title: $\Spec R_{\fp}$ for $R=k[x,y]$, $\fp=(x)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Spec R_{\fp}$ for $R=k[x,y]$, $\fp=(x)$}
Identify the primes of the local ring $R_{(x)}$ and its residue field.
\wrec Primes of $R_{\fp}\leftrightarrow$ primes $\fq\subseteq\fp=(x)$ of $k[x,y]$.
\wsol The primes of $k[x,y]$ contained in $(x)$ are $(0)$ and $(x)$ itself (a prime $\fq$ with $(0)\subsetneq\fq\subsetneq(x)$ would give $\hgt(x)\ge2$, but $(x)$ has height $1$). So $\Spec R_{(x)}=\{(0)\subsetneq(x)R_{(x)}\}$, a chain of length one. The residue field is $R_{(x)}/(x)R_{(x)}\cong\Frac(k[x,y]/(x))=\Frac(k[y])=k(y)$. Sanity check: $\dim R_{(x)}=\hgt(x)=1$, matching the length-one chain of primes; the residue field $k(y)$ records the coordinate $y$ left free along the line $x=0$ (the transverse coordinate $x$ vanishes there).
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: example
Title: Localizing at a maximal ideal: residue field $k$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing at a maximal ideal: residue field $k$}
For $R=k[x,y]$ ($k=\bar k$) and $\fm=(x-a,y-b)$, compute the residue field of $R_{\fm}$.
\wrec $\fm$ is maximal with $R/\fm\cong k$ (evaluation at $(a,b)$); localizing keeps the functions defined at the point $(a,b)$.
\wsol $R_{\fm}=\{f/g:\ g(a,b)\ne0\}$ is the ring of rational functions regular at $(a,b)$. Its maximal ideal is $\fm R_{\fm}=\{f/g:\ f(a,b)=0\}$ and the residue field is $R_{\fm}/\fm R_{\fm}\cong\Frac(R/\fm)=\Frac(k)=k$. Sanity check: evaluation $f/g\mapsto f(a,b)/g(a,b)\in k$ is a surjective ring map with kernel $\fm R_{\fm}$, and over $k=\bar k$ the residue field at a closed point is $k$ itself (Nullstellensatz).
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: example
Title: Prime correspondence for $R_f$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Prime correspondence for $R_f$}
With $R=k[x]$, $f=x$, list the primes of $R_x=k[x,x^{-1}]$.
\wrec Primes of $R_f\leftrightarrow$ primes $\fq$ with $\fq\cap\{1,x,x^2,\dots\}=\varnothing$, i.e.\ primes not containing $x$.
\wsol Primes of $k[x]$ are $(0)$ and the maximals $(p(x))$ for monic irreducible $p$. Those meeting $S=\{x^n\}$ are exactly the ones containing $x$, namely $(x)$. So $\Spec R_x=\{(0)\}\cup\{(p(x)):\ p\ne x\}$ -- all primes except $(x)$. Sanity check: geometrically $\Spec k[x,x^{-1}]=\Aff^1\setminus\{0\}$, the punctured line; removing the origin $(x)$ is exactly inverting $x$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The prime correspondence and localization at a prime
Type: example
Title: A localization with a unique nonzero prime
Content:
\begin{wex}{A localization with a unique nonzero prime}
If $\fp$ is a height-one prime of a domain $R$ that is minimal among nonzero primes, show $R_{\fp}$ has exactly one nonzero prime.
\wrec Primes of $R_{\fp}\leftrightarrow$ primes $\subseteq\fp$; minimality of $\fp$ over $(0)$ leaves only $(0)$ and $\fp$.
\wsol The primes of $R$ contained in $\fp$ are $(0)$ (since $R$ is a domain) and $\fp$ (if $\fp$ is minimal nonzero, nothing sits strictly between). Hence $\Spec R_{\fp}=\{(0),\fp R_{\fp}\}$, so $R_{\fp}$ has the single nonzero prime $\fp R_{\fp}$, which is also maximal. Sanity check: $R=Z$, $\fp=(p)$ gives $R_{\fp}=Z_{(p)}$, a DVR with the unique nonzero prime $(p)Z_{(p)}$ -- the prototypical local ring of dimension one.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The local-global principle
Type: prose
Content:
The payoff of all the above is a dictionary: many properties of a module or a map hold globally iff they hold at every localization. ``Being zero,'' injectivity, surjectivity, and flatness are all local properties. This is the technique A\&M call passing between local and global, and it underlies essentially all of dimension theory.

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-e814bdc6fc8f4cb0ff56
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$(1)\!\Rightarrow\!(2)\!\Rightarrow\!(3)$ are trivial. For $(3)\!\Rightarrow\!(1)$: if $0\ne m\in M$, then $\Ann(m)$ is a proper ideal, so it lies in some maximal $\fm$. In $M_{\fm}$, the class $m/1=0$ would give $s m=0$ for some $s\notin\fm$ -- but then $s\in\Ann(m)\subseteq\fm$, a contradiction. So $M_{\fm}\ne0$, against (3). Hence $M=0$.
\end{proof}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The local-global principle
Type: corollary
Title: {injectivity and surjectivity are local}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{injectivity and surjectivity are local}]
An $R$-module map $\varphi\colon M\to N$ is injective (resp.\ surjective, resp.\ an isomorphism) iff $\varphi_{\fm}\colon M_{\fm}\to N_{\fm}$ is injective (resp.\ surjective, iso) for every maximal ideal $\fm$.
\end{corollary}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
By exactness, $(\ker\varphi)_{\fm}=\ker(\varphi_{\fm})$ and $(\coker\varphi)_{\fm}=\coker(\varphi_{\fm})$. Apply the theorem to $\ker\varphi$ (resp.\ $\coker\varphi$): it is $0$ iff all its localizations vanish iff each $\varphi_{\fm}$ is injective (resp.\ surjective).
\end{proof}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > The local-global principle
Type: remark
Title: {flatness is local too}
Content:
\begin{remark}[{flatness is local too}]
A\&M record (3.10) that flatness of $M$ is equivalent to flatness of every $M_{\fp}$, equivalently every $M_{\fm}$. The proof is the same localize-the-kernel argument applied to the criterion ``$N\to P$ injective $\Rightarrow M\otimes N\to M\otimes P$ injective,'' using that $\otimes$ commutes with localization. The pattern -- a property is global iff local at every maximal ideal -- is the organizing principle of commutative algebra.
\end{remark}

Title: {a domain is the intersection of its localizations}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{a domain is the intersection of its localizations}]
If $R$ is an integral domain with fraction field $F$, then inside $F$,
\[
R=\bigcap_{\fp}R_{\fp}=\bigcap_{\fm}R_{\fm},
\]
the intersection over all primes, equivalently over all maximal ideals.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Clearly $R\subseteq\bigcap_{\fm}R_{\fm}$. If $a\in F$ lies in every $R_{\fm}$, set $\fa=\{d\in R:\ da\in R\}$, an ideal with $a\in R\iff\fa=R$. If $\fa\ne R$, pick a maximal $\fm\supseteq\fa$; since $a\in R_{\fm}$, $a=r/d$ with $d\notin\fm$, so $d\in\fa\setminus\fm$, contradiction. Hence $\fa=R$ and $a\in R$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Detecting $M=0$ locally
Content:
\begin{wex}{Detecting $M=0$ locally}
Let $R=Z$ and $M$ an abelian group with $M_{(p)}=0$ for all primes $p$ and $M_{(0)}=0$. Conclude $M=0$.
\wrec The local-global principle: $M=0\iff M_{\fm}=0$ for all maximal $\fm$; the maximal ideals of $Z$ are the $(p)$.
\wsol Every maximal ideal of $Z$ is $(p)$ for a prime $p$, and by hypothesis each $M_{(p)}=0$. By the theorem, $M=0$. Sanity check: contrapositively, if $M\ne0$ pick $0\ne m$; $\Ann(m)=(n)$ for some $n\ge0$; choose a prime $p\mid n$ (or $p$ arbitrary if $n=0$) with $(p)\supseteq\Ann(m)$ -- then $m/1\ne0$ in $M_{(p)}$, contradicting $M_{(p)}=0$.
\end{wex}

\wsol At $(2)$: $\varphi_{(2)}\colonZ_{(2)}\toZ_{(2)}$ is multiplication by $2$, injective on the domain $Z_{(2)}$ (no zero divisors). At $(p)$, $p\ne2$: $2$ is a unit in $Z_{(p)}$, so $\varphi_{(p)}$ is an isomorphism, hence injective. At $(0)$: multiplication by $2$ on $Q$ is injective. All localizations injective $\Rightarrow\varphi$ injective. Sanity check: $\coker\varphi=Z/2Z$ is not zero, so $\varphi$ is not surjective -- and indeed $\coker(\varphi_{(2)})=Z_{(2)}/2Z_{(2)}\congZ/2Z\ne0$, correctly detecting non-surjectivity at the single prime $(2)$.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z=\bigcap_pZ_{(p)}$ concretely
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z=\bigcap_pZ_{(p)}$ concretely}
Verify that a rational $a/b$ (in lowest terms) lies in every $Z_{(p)}$ iff $a/b\inZ$.
\wrec $Z=\bigcap_{\fm}Z_{(\fm)}$; $a/b\inZ_{(p)}\iff p\nmid b$.
\wsol If $a/b$ in lowest terms has $b>1$, take a prime $p\mid b$; then $a/b\notinZ_{(p)}$, so $a/b$ fails to be in the intersection. If $b=1$, then $a/b=a\inZ\subseteqZ_{(p)}$ for all $p$. Hence $\bigcap_pZ_{(p)}=Z$. Sanity check: $1/6\notinZ_{(2)}$ and $\notinZ_{(3)}$ (caught at the primes dividing the denominator), but $1/6\inZ_{(5)}$ -- so $1/6$ is excluded from the intersection exactly because it is not an integer.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Normality is local
Content:
\begin{wex}{Normality is local}
State and use the criterion: a domain $R$ is integrally closed iff every $R_{\fm}$ is.
\wrec Like $M=0$, integral closure is detected at maximal ideals, via $R=\bigcap_{\fm}R_{\fm}$.
\wsol If $R$ is normal and $y\in F$ is integral over $R_{\fp}$, clearing the (finitely many) denominators $d_i\notin\fp$ shows $y'=y(d_0\cdots d_{n-1})^n$ is integral over $R$, hence $y'\in R$, hence $y\in R_{\fp}$: so $R_{\fp}$ is normal. Conversely if each $R_{\fm}$ is normal and $y\in F$ is integral over $R$, then $y$ is integral over each $R_{\fm}$, so $y\in R_{\fm}$ for all $\fm$, whence $y\in\bigcap_{\fm}R_{\fm}=R$: $R$ is normal. Sanity check: $R=k[t^2,t^3]$ is not normal; its non-normality localizes to the single maximal ideal $\fm=(t^2,t^3)$, where $R_{\fm}$ fails to be integrally closed ($t=t^3/t^2$ is integral but not in $R_{\fm}$), pinpointing the singular point.
\end{wex}

Content:

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r,"\pi_f"] \arrow[d,"\pi_{\fp}"'] & R_f \arrow[d,"localize at \fp R_f"] \\
R_{\fp} \arrow[r,equal] & (R_f)_{\fp R_f}
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\xrightarrow{\ \Spec\ }\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\Spec R & D(f) \arrow[l,hook'] \\
\{\fq\subseteq\fp\} \arrow[u,hook] & \{\fq\subseteq\fp\} \arrow[l,equal]\arrow[u,hook']
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} There are two paired diagrams. In the ring square (left): $R$ is the base commutative ring;
 $R_f = S^{-1}R$ with $S = \{f^n\}$ is the localization inverting $f$; $R_{\fp} = (R \setminus \fp)^{-1}R$
 is the localization at the prime $\fp$; $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ is $R_f$ further localized at the prime
 $\fp R_f$ of $R_f$ (the image of $\fp$ in $R_f$, which is prime because $f \notin \fp$ ensures
 $\fp$ survives to $R_f$). In the Spec square (right): $\Spec R$ is the full prime spectrum; $D(f)$ is
 the distinguished open set $\{\fq \in \Spec R : f \notin \fq\}$, the image of $\Spec R_f$; the two
 copies of $\{\fq \subseteq \fp\}$ are the Spec of $R_{\fp}$, the set of primes contained in $\fp$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Ring square: $\pi_f \colon R \to R_f$, $r \mapsto r/1$, is the canonical localization map
 inverting $f$; $\pi_{\fp} \colon R \to R_{\fp}$, $r \mapsto r/1$, is the canonical localization map
 inverting $R \setminus \fp$; the right vertical arrow localizes $R_f$ at $\fp R_f$, sending
 $r/f^n \mapsto (r/f^n)/1$; the bottom equality asserts the two iterated localizations coincide.
 Spec square: $D(f) \hookrightarrow \Spec R$ is the open immersion, the injection on spectra induced
 by $\pi_f$; the left vertical inclusion $\{\fq \subseteq \fp\} \hookrightarrow \Spec R$ is the
 injection on spectra induced by $\pi_{\fp}$; the equality on the bottom says $\Spec R_{\fp}$
 is the same subset whether reached via $R$ or via $R_f$ first; the right vertical inclusion
 $\{\fq \subseteq \fp\} \hookrightarrow D(f)$ holds because any $\fq \subseteq \fp$ satisfies
 $f \notin \fq$ (since $f \in \fq$ would give $f \in \fq \subseteq \fp$,
 contradicting $f \notin \fp$).
\dgi{What commutes:} In the ring square, down-then-right equals right-then-down:
 $(localize at \fp R_f) \circ \pi_f = \pi_{\fp}$, i.e., $(R_f)_{\fp R_f} = R_{\fp}$
 as $R$-algebras. Concretely: any $r/s$ with $s \notin \fp$ can be reached from $R$ either by
 first inverting $f$ (giving $r/1$ and $s/1$ in $R_f$) then localizing at $\fp R_f$, where $s/1$ becomes a unit, or directly as $r/s$
 in $R_{\fp}$. In the Spec square, both paths from the lower-right corner to the upper-left corner
 $\Spec R$ give the same inclusion: the primes $\subseteq \fp$ that miss $f$ sit inside $D(f)$
 inside $\Spec R$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic element $r/s \in R_{\fp}$ (so $r \in R$, $s \notin \fp$).
 Via the right-then-down path: first map $r$ to $r/1 \in R_f$, then to $(r/1)/1 \in (R_f)_{\fp R_f}$;
 $s$ maps to $s/1 \in R_f$, which is a unit in $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ because $s \notin \fp$ means
 $s/1 \notin \fp R_f$, so $(r/1)/(s/1) = r/s$ in $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$. Via the left-then-bottom path:
 the canonical map $R \to R_{\fp}$ sends $r \mapsto r/s \cdot s/1$; inverting $s$ gives $r/s$.
 The universal property of localization ensures uniqueness: both $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ and $R_{\fp}$
 invert exactly $R \setminus \fp$, so by universality there is a unique isomorphism between them
 compatible with the maps from $R$. Well-definedness of the induced map $(R_f)_{\fp R_f} \to R_{\fp}$
 requires checking that a fraction $r/s$ with $s/1 \in \fp R_f$ cannot arise when $s \notin \fp$
 -- indeed $s/1 \in \fp R_f$ iff $s \in \fp$, so the condition exactly matches.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram crystallizes the synthesis paragraph's key claim: localizing
 at a prime $\fp$ is a two-step process -- first restrict to the open set $D(f)$ containing $\fp$
 (by inverting $f$), then localize the resulting ring at its prime $\fp R_f$. It shows that the
 global prime $\fp$ and the local prime $\fp R_f$ encode the same data, and that the local ring
 $R_{\fp}$ (with residue field $\kappa(\fp) = \Frac(R/\fp)$) is the common value at the bottom of both paths. The Spec dual
 makes the geometric content visible: the infinitesimal neighborhood $\{\fq \subseteq \fp\}$
 of the point $\fp$ is equally well described as the intersection $D(f) \cap \Spec R_{\fp}$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R = Z$, $\fp = (2)$, $f = 3$. Then $R_f = Z[1/3]$ and
 $\fp R_f = 2Z[1/3]$. Localizing at $\fp R_f$: $(Z[1/3])_{(2)} = \{a/b \in Q : b odd\}
 = Z_{(2)}$, which equals $R_{\fp} = Z_{(2)}$ directly. Spec side: $D(3) = \Spec Z \setminus
 \{(3)\}$ contains $(2)$, and $\Spec Z_{(2)} = \{(0),(2)\} \subseteq D(3) \subseteq \Spec Z$,
 with all three inclusions matching the diagram.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often think $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ is a further localization that
 strictly enlarges $R_{\fp}$, inverting more elements. In fact it inverts exactly the same
 set $R \setminus \fp$ as $R_{\fp}$ does, so both sides are the same ring by the universal property.
 The equality arrow on the bottom of the ring square is a genuine identity of $R$-algebras, not
 merely a map -- do not treat it as an inclusion or an approximation.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that localizing at a prime $\fp$ factors through any
 distinguished open $D(f)$ containing $\fp$, so $R_{\fp}$ can be computed in stages, and the
 geometric picture (an infinitesimal neighborhood of $\fp$ inside $\Spec R$) is faithfully
 captured by either route.
\end{dgx}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Localization: Rings and Modules of Fractions > Synthesis: localization as a map of spectra
Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Localization need not be surjective on rings (e.g.\ $Z\toZ_{(2)}$ misses $1/3$) and need not be injective: $R\to S^{-1}R$ has kernel the $S$-torsion. And ``local property'' is one-directional in subtlety: $M=0$, injectivity, flatness localize correctly, but properties like ``$R$ is a domain'' do not -- every $R_{\fm}$ can be a domain while $R$ is not (e.g.\ $R=Z/6Z$: $R_{(2)}\congZ/2Z$ and $R_{(3)}\congZ/3Z$ are fields, yet $R$ has zero divisors). Always check whether the property you want is genuinely local.
\end{pitfall}

Type: example
Title: Reading the spectrum of $R_f$ as a distinguished open
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading the spectrum of $R_f$ as a distinguished open}
For $R=k[x,y]$, $f=x$, describe $\Spec R_x$ as an open subset of $\Spec R$ and find its dimension.
\wrec $\Spec R_f=D(f)=\{\fq:\ f\notin\fq\}$; inverting $x$ removes exactly the primes containing $x$.
\wsol The primes containing $x$ are those of $k[x,y]$ with $x\in\fq$, i.e.\ the primes of $k[x,y]/(x)\cong k[y]$ pulled back -- the line $V(x)$. So $\Spec R_x=\Spec k[x,y]\setminus V(x)=\Aff^2\setminus\{x=0\}$, the complement of a line. Its dimension is still $2$ (an open dense subset of the plane). Sanity check: $\dim R_x\le\dim k[x,y]=2$ because the primes of $R_x$ correspond to primes of $k[x,y]$ (preserving inclusions), and the chain $(0)\subsetneq(y)\subsetneq(x-1,y)$ of primes not containing $x$ gives $\dim R_x\ge2$; so $\dim R_x=2$. (For a general domain, inverting one nonzero element can lower the dimension: $\dimZ_{(2)}=1$ but $Z_{(2)}[1/2]=Q$ has dimension $0$.)
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Factoring $R_{\fp}$ through $R_f$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Factoring $R_{\fp}$ through $R_f$}
Show that for $f\notin\fp$, $R_{\fp}=(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$, i.e.\ localizing at $\fp$ is unchanged by first inverting an $f\notin\fp$.
\wrec Both rings invert exactly $R\setminus\fp$: in $R_f$, the prime $\fp R_f$ has complement $S_f=\{g/f^n:\ g\notin\fp\}$, and re-localizing inverts these.
\wsol The composite $R\to R_f\to(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ inverts every element of $R\setminus\fp$ (since $f\notin\fp$ is already inverted, and everything outside $\fp R_f$ is inverted in the second step). By the universal property there is a unique map $R_{\fp}\to(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$; conversely $(R_f)_{\fp R_f}$ inverts only elements that are units in $R_{\fp}$, giving the inverse. Hence the two coincide. Sanity check: take $R=Z$, $\fp=(2)$, $f=3$. Then $R_f=Z[1/3]$ and $(Z[1/3])_{(2)}=\{a/b:\ b odd\}=Z_{(2)}$, since inverting $3$ then localizing at $2$ recovers exactly the integers localized at $2$. Matches.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Primary ideals under localization
Content:
\begin{wex}{Primary ideals under localization}
Let $\fq$ be $\fp$-primary in $R$ and $S$ a multiplicative set. Describe $S^{-1}\fq$ in the two cases $S\cap\fp=\varnothing$ and $S\cap\fp\ne\varnothing$.
\wrec Primary ideals correspond to primary ideals when their radical misses $S$; if the radical meets $S$, the extension is the whole ring.
\wsol If $S\cap\fp\ne\varnothing$, pick $s\in S\cap\fp$; some power $s^n\in\fq$ (as $\fp=\rad\fq$), and $s^n\in S$, so $S^{-1}\fq=S^{-1}R$. If $S\cap\fp=\varnothing$, then $S^{-1}\fp$ is prime and $S^{-1}\fq$ is $S^{-1}\fp$-primary with contraction back to $R$ equal to $\fq$ (using that $dr\in\fq$, $d\notin\fp$ force $r\in\fq$ by primariness). Sanity check: $R=Z$, $\fq=(4)$ (which is $(2)$-primary), $S=Z\setminus(2)$ gives $S^{-1}(4)=4Z_{(2)}$, still $(2)Z_{(2)}$-primary, contracting to $(4)$; whereas $S=Z\setminus(3)$ meets $(2)$ at $2$, and $2\in S$ inverts, so $S^{-1}(4)=Z_{(3)}$, the whole ring.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Localization and minimal primary decomposition}
For a minimal primary decomposition $\fa=\fq_1\cap\dots\cap\fq_m$ in a Noetherian $R$ with $\fq_i$ being $\fp_i$-primary, describe $S^{-1}\fa$ when $S$ misses $\fp_1,\dots,\fp_t$ and meets $\fp_{t+1},\dots,\fp_m$.
\wrec $S^{-1}$ commutes with finite intersection; components whose radical meets $S$ extend to the unit ideal and drop out.
\wsol Since $S^{-1}(\fq_i)=S^{-1}R$ for $i>t$ (their primes meet $S$) and these are units in the intersection, $S^{-1}\fa=S^{-1}\fq_1\cap\dots\cap S^{-1}\fq_t$, a minimal primary decomposition in $S^{-1}R$ with $S^{-1}\fq_i$ being $S^{-1}\fp_i$-primary. Contracting back, $(S^{-1}\fa)^c=\fq_1\cap\dots\cap\fq_t$. Sanity check: taking $S=R\setminus\fp$ for a minimal prime $\fp$ of $\fa$ keeps only the single component $\fq$ belonging to $\fp$, which proves the primary component at an isolated prime is uniquely determined by $\fa$ -- the local characterization of the isolated components.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 1/4
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Suppose $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. Prove that $D^{-1}M = 0$ if and only if $dM = 0$ for some $d \in D$.

\item Let $I$ be an ideal in $R$, let $D$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $R$ with ring of fractions $D^{-1}R$, and let $c(eI)$ be the saturation of $I$ with respect to $D$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $c(eI) = R$ if and only if $eI = D^{-1}R$ if and only if $I \cap D \neq \emptyset$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $I = c(eI)$ is saturated if and only if for every $d \in D$, if $da \in I$ then $a \in I$.
\item[(c)] Prove that extension and contraction define inverse bijections between the ideals of $R$ saturated with respect to $D$ and the ideals of $D^{-1}R$.
\item[(d)] Let $I = (2x, 3y) \subseteq Z[x, y]$. Show the saturation of $I$ with respect to $Z - \{0\}$ is $(x, y)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item If $I$ is an ideal in the commutative ring $R$ let $\varphi : R[x_1, \ldots, x_n] \to (R/I)[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ be the ring homomorphism with kernel $I[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ given by reducing coefficients modulo $I$. If $\overline{A}$ is an ideal in $(R/I)[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$, let $A$ denote the inverse image of $\overline{A}$ under $\varphi$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For any $i \geq 1$ show that the inverse image under $\varphi$ of the subring $(R/I)[x_1, \ldots, x_i]$ is $R[x_1, \ldots, x_i] + I[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $\varphi(A \cap R[x_1, \ldots, x_i]) = \overline{A} \cap (R/I)[x_1, \ldots, x_i]$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $f = y^5 - z^4$, viewed as a polynomial in $y$ with coefficients in $Q[z]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $f$ has no roots in $Q[z]$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $f = (y^2 + ay + b)(y^3 + cy^2 + dy + e)$. Show that $a, b, c, d, e$ satisfy the system of equations
\[
a + c = 0, \quad ac + b + d = 0, \quad ad + bc + e = 0, \quad ae + bd = 0, \quad be + z^4 = 0.
\]
Deduce that $e^5 = -z^{12}$ and conclude that $f$ is irreducible in $Q[y, z]$. [Use elimination.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $R$ is a U.F.D. with field of fractions $F$ and $p \in R[x]$ is a monic polynomial.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that the ideal $pR[x]$ generated by $p$ in $R[x]$ is prime if and only if the ideal $pF[x]$ generated by $p$ in $F[x]$ is prime. [Use Gauss' Lemma.]
\item[(b)] Show that $pR[x]$ is saturated, i.e., that $pF[x] \cap R[x] = pR[x]$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Show that $I = (y^3 - xz, xy^2 - z^2)$ is not a prime ideal in $Q[x, y, z]$ and find explicit elements $a, b \in Q[x, y, z]$ with $ab \in I$ but $a \notin I$ and $b \notin I$.

\item Show that $P = (y^3 - xz, xy^2 - z^2, x^2 - yz)$ is a prime ideal in $Q[x, y, z]$.

\item Show that $P = (x^2 - yz, w^2 - x^4 z)$ is a prime ideal in $Q[x, y, z, w]$.

\item Show that $P = (xz^2 - w^3, xw^2 - y^4, y^4 z^2 - w^5)$ is a prime ideal in $Q[x, y, z, w]$.

\item Show that $I = (xy - w^3, y^2 - zw)$ is not a prime ideal in $Q[x, y, z, w]$ and find $a, b$ with $ab \in I$ but $a, b \notin I$.

\item Let $R_P$ be the localization of $R$ at the prime $P$. Prove that if $Q$ is a $P$-primary ideal of $R$ then $Q = c(eQ)$ with respect to the extension and contraction of $Q$ to $R_P$. Show the same result holds if $Q$ is $P'$-primary for some prime $P'$ contained in $P$.

\item Let $R = R[x, y, z]/(xy - z^2)$, let $P = (\bar{x}, \bar{z})$ be the prime ideal generated by the images of $x$ and $z$ in $R$, and let $R_P$ be the localization of $R$ at $P$. Prove that $P^2 R_P \cap R = (\bar{x})$ and is strictly larger than $P^2$.

\item Prove that if $N$ and $N'$ are two $R$-submodules of an $R$-module $M$ with $N_P = N'_P$ in the localization $M_P$ for every prime ideal $P$ of $R$ (or just for every maximal ideal) then $N = N'$.

\item Suppose $\varphi : M \to N$ is an $R$-module homomorphism. Prove that $\varphi$ is injective (respectively, surjective) if and only if the induced $R_P$-module homomorphism $\varphi : M_P \to N_P$ is injective (respectively, surjective) for every prime ideal $P$ of $R$ (or just for every maximal ideal of $R$).

\item Let $R = Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ be the ring of integers in the quadratic field $Q(\sqrt{-5})$ and let $I$ be the prime ideal $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$ of $R$ generated by $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ (cf. Exercise 5, Section 8.2).
