Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Prove (3) of Corollary 22 directly by considering the collection $S$ of ideals that do not contain a finite product of prime ideals. [If $I$ is a maximal element in $S$, show that since $I$ is not prime there are ideals $J, K$ properly containing $I$ (hence not in $S$) with $JK \subseteq I$.]

\item Let $I$ and $J$ be ideals in the ring $R$. Prove the following statements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $J^k \subseteq I$ for some $k \geq 1$ then $\rad I \supseteq \rad J$.
\item[(b)] If $I^k \subseteq J \subseteq I$ for some $k \geq 1$ then $\rad I = \rad J$.
\item[(c)] $\rad(IJ) = \rad(I \cap J) = \rad I \cap \rad J$.
\item[(d)] $\rad(\rad I) = \rad I$.
\item[(e)] $\rad I + \rad J \subseteq \rad(I + J)$ and $\rad(I + J) = \rad(\rad I + \rad J)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that the intersection of two radical ideals is again a radical ideal.

\item Let $I = \fm_1 \fm_2$ be the product of the ideals $\fm_1 = (x, y)$ and $\fm_2 = (x - 1, y - 1)$ in $\F_2[x, y]$. Prove that $I$ is a radical ideal. Prove that the ideal $(x^3 - y^2)$ is a radical ideal in $\F_2[x, y]$.

\item If $I = (xy, (x - y)z) \subseteq k[x, y, z]$ prove that $\rad I = (xy, xz, yz)$. For this ideal prove directly that $Z(I) = Z(\rad I)$, that $Z(I)$ is not irreducible, and that $\rad I$ is not prime.

\item Give an example to show that over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed the containment $I \subseteq I(Z(I))$ can be proper even when $I$ is a radical ideal.

\item Suppose $R$ and $S$ are rings and $\varphi : R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism. If $I$ is an ideal of $R$ show that $\varphi(\rad I) \subseteq \rad(\varphi(I))$. If in addition $\varphi$ is surjective and $I$ contains the kernel of $\varphi$ show that $\varphi(\rad I) = \rad(\varphi(I))$.

\item Suppose the prime ideal $P$ contains the ideal $I$. Prove that $P$ contains the radical of $I$.

\item Prove that for any field $k$ the map $Z$ in the Nullstellensatz is always surjective and the map $I$ in the Nullstellensatz is always injective. [Use property (10) of the maps $Z$ and $I$ in Section 1.] Give examples (over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed) where $Z$ is not injective and $I$ is not surjective.

\item Prove that for $k$ a finite field the Zariski topology is the same as the discrete topology: every subset is closed (and open).

\item Let $V$ be a variety in $\Aff^n$ and let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be two subsets of $\Aff^n$ that are open in the Zariski topology. Prove that if $V \cap U_1 \neq \emptyset$ and $V \cap U_2 \neq \emptyset$ then $V \cap U_1 \cap U_2 \neq \emptyset$. Conclude that any nonempty open subset of a variety is everywhere dense in the Zariski topology (i.e., its closure is all of $V$).

\item Use the fact that nonempty open sets of an affine variety are everywhere dense to prove that an affine variety is connected in the Zariski topology. (A topological space is connected if it is not the union of two disjoint, proper, open subsets.)

\item Let $V$ be a nonempty affine algebraic set. Prove that if $k[V]$ is a direct sum of two nonzero ideals, then $V$ is not connected in the Zariski topology, and prove the converse when $k$ is algebraically closed. [Use the weak form of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.] Give a counterexample to the converse over a field $k$ that is not algebraically closed.

\item Prove that if $k$ is an infinite field, then the varieties in $\Aff^1$ are the whole space and the one point subsets. What are the varieties in $\Aff^1$ in the case of a finite field $k$?

\item Suppose $V$ is a hypersurface in $\Aff^n$ and $I(V) = (f)$ for some nonconstant polynomial $f \in k[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]$. Prove that $V$ is a variety if and only if $f$ is irreducible.

\item Suppose $V \subseteq \Aff^n$ is an affine variety and $f \in k[V]$. Prove that the graph of $f$ (cf. Exercise 25 in Section 1) is an affine variety.

\item Prove that any permutation of the elements of a field $k$ is a continuous map from $\Aff^1$ to itself in the Zariski topology on $\Aff^1$. Deduce that if $k$ is an infinite field, there are Zariski continuous maps from $\Aff^1$ to itself that are not polynomials.

\item Let $V$ be an affine algebraic set in $\Aff^n$ over $k = C$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that morphisms of algebraic sets over $C$ are continuous in the Euclidean topology (the topology on $C^n$ obtained by identifying $C^n$ with $R^{2n}$ with its usual Euclidean topology).
\item[(b)] Prove that $V$ is a closed set in the Euclidean topology on $C^n$ (so the Zariski closed sets of $\Aff^n$ over $C$ are also Euclidean closed).
\item[(c)] Give an example of a set that is closed in the Euclidean topology but is not closed in the Zariski topology, i.e., is not an affine algebraic set (so the Euclidean topology is ``finer'' than the Zariski topology).
\end{enumerate}

\item Give an example of an injective $k$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi} : k[W] \to k[V]$ whose associated morphism $\varphi : V \to W$ is not surjective.

\item Suppose $\varphi : V \to W$ is a surjective morphism of affine algebraic sets. Prove that if $V$ is a variety then $W$ is a variety.

\item Let $V$ be an algebraic set in $\Aff^n$ and let $f \in k[V]$. Define $V_f = \{v \in V \mid f(v) \neq 0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $V_f$ is a Zariski open set in $V$ (called a principal open set in $V$).
\item[(b)] Let $J$ be the ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_{n+1}]$ generated by $I(V)$ and $x_{n+1} f - 1$, and let $W = Z(J) \subseteq \Aff^{n+1}$.

Show that $J = I(W)$ and that the map $\pi : \Aff^{n+1} \to \Aff^n$ by projection onto the first $n$ coordinates is a Zariski continuous bijection from $W$ onto $V_f$ (so the principal open set $V_f$ in $V$ may be embedded as a closed set in some (larger) affine space).
\item[(c)] If $U$ is any open set in $V$ show that $U = V_{f_1} \cup \cdots \cup V_{f_m}$ for some $f_1, \ldots, f_m \in k[V]$. (This shows that the principal open sets form a base for the Zariski topology.)
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that $\GL_n(k)$ is an open affine algebraic set in $\Aff^{n^2}$ and can be embedded as a closed affine algebraic set in $\Aff^{n^2 + 1}$. In particular, deduce that the set $k^\times$ of nonzero elements in $\Aff^1$ embeds into $\Aff^2$ as the hyperbola $xy = 1$. [Use the preceding exercise.]

\item Show that if $k$ is infinite then $\{(a, a^2, a^3) \mid a \in k\} \subseteq \Aff^3$ is an affine algebraic variety. If $k$ is finite show that this set is always reducible.

\item Let $V = Z(xz - y^2, yz - x^3, z^2 - x^2 y) \subseteq \Aff^3$. Show that if $k$ is infinite then $V$ is an affine variety. [Use Exercise 26 of Section 1 and Exercise 20.]

\item Suppose $f(x) = x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c$ is an irreducible cubic in $Q[x]$ of discriminant $D$. Let $I = (x + y + z + a, \; xy + xz + yz - b, \; xyz + c)$ in $Q[x, y, z]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I$ is a prime ideal if and only if $D$ is not a square in $Q$, in which case $I$ is a maximal ideal and $Q[x, y, z]/I$ is a splitting field for $f(x)$ over $Q$.
\item[(b)] If $D = r^2$, prove that the primary decomposition of $I$ is $I = Q_+ \cap Q_-$ where $Q_\pm = (I, \; (x - y)(x - z)(y - z) \mp r)$. Prove $Q_+$ and $Q_-$ are maximal ideals, and $Q[x, y, z]$ modulo $Q_+$ or $Q_-$ is a splitting field for $f(x)$ over $Q$.
\end{enumerate}

\item A topological space $X$ is called quasicompact if whenever any collection of closed subsets $V_i$ of $X$ has empty intersection, then some finite number of these also has empty intersection, i.e.,
\[
whenever \bigcap_i V_i = \emptyset there exists V_{i_1}, V_{i_2}, \ldots, V_{i_N} such that \bigcap_{j=1}^{N} V_{i_j} = \emptyset.
\]
Prove that every affine algebraic set is quasicompact. [Translate the definition into a property of ideals in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$.] (A quasicompact and Hausdorff space is called compact.)

\item When $k$ is an infinite field prove that the Zariski topology on $k^2$ is not the same as taking the Zariski topology on $k$ and then forming the product topology on $k \times k$. [By Exercise 14 of Section 1, in the product topology on $k \times k$ the Zariski closed sets in $k \times k$ are finite unions of sets of the form $\{a\} \times \{b\}$, $\{a\} \times k$ and $k \times \{b\}$, for any $a, b \in k$.]

\item Prove that each of the following rings have infinitely many minimal prime ideals, and that $(0)$ is not the intersection of any finite number of these (so $(0)$ does not have a primary decomposition in these rings):
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] the infinite direct product ring $Z/2Z \times Z/2Z \times \cdots$ (which is a Boolean ring, cf. Exercise 23 in Section 7.4).
\item[(b)] $k[x_1, x_2, \ldots]/(x_1 x_2, x_3 x_4, \ldots, x_{2i-1} x_{2i}, \ldots)$, where $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ are independent variables over the field $k$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are ideals with $AB \subseteq Q$ for a primary ideal $Q$. Prove that if $A \not\subseteq Q$ then $B \subseteq \rad Q$.

\item Let $Q$ be a $P$-primary ideal and suppose $A$ is an ideal not contained in $Q$. Define $A' = \{r \in R \mid rA \subseteq Q\}$ to be the elements of $R$ that when multiplied by elements of $A$ give elements of $Q$. Prove that $A'$ is a $P$-primary ideal.

\item Prove that if $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to the same prime ideal $P$, then $Q_1 \cap Q_2$ is a primary ideal belonging to $P$. Conclude that a finite intersection of $P$-primary ideals is again $P$-primary.

\item Prove that if $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to the same maximal ideal $M$, then $Q_1 + Q_2$ and $Q_1 Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to $M$. Conclude that finite sums and finite products of $M$-primary ideals are again $M$-primary.

\item Let $I = (x^2, xy, xz, yz)$ in $k[x, y, z]$. Prove that a primary decomposition of $I$ is $I = (x, y) \cap (x, z) \cap (x, y, z)^2$, determine the isolated and embedded primes of $I$, and find $\rad I$.

\item Suppose $\varphi : R \to S$ is a surjective ring homomorphism. Prove that an ideal $Q$ in $R$ containing the kernel of $\varphi$ is primary if and only if $\varphi(Q)$ is primary in $S$, and when this is the case the prime associated to $\varphi(Q)$ is the image $\varphi(P)$ of the prime $P$ associated to $Q$.

\item Suppose $\varphi : R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $I$ is an ideal of $R$ containing $\ker \varphi$ with minimal primary decomposition $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ with $\rad Q_i = P_i$. If $\varphi$ is a surjective homomorphism prove that $\varphi(I) = \varphi(Q_1) \cap \cdots \cap \varphi(Q_m)$, where $\rad \varphi(Q_i)$ is given by $\varphi(P_i)$, is a minimal primary decomposition of $\varphi(I)$. [Use the previous exercise.]
\item[(b)] Suppose $I$ is an ideal of $S$ with minimal primary decomposition $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ with $\rad Q_i = P_i$. Prove that $\varphi^{-1}(I) = \varphi^{-1}(Q_1) \cap \cdots \cap \varphi^{-1}(Q_m)$, where $\rad \varphi^{-1}(Q_i)$ is given by $\varphi^{-1}(P_i)$, is a primary decomposition of $\varphi^{-1}(I)$, and is minimal if $\varphi$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I = (xy, x - yz)$ in $k[x, y, z]$.

\item Prove that if $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to the same prime ideal $P$, then $Q_1 \cap Q_2$ is a primary ideal belonging to $P$. Conclude that a finite intersection of $P$-primary ideals is again $P$-primary.

\item Prove that if $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to the same maximal ideal $M$, then $Q_1 + Q_2$ and $Q_1 Q_2$ are primary ideals belonging to $M$. Conclude that finite sums and finite products of $M$-primary ideals are again $M$-primary.

\item Let $I = (x^2, xy, xz, yz)$ in $k[x, y, z]$. Prove that a primary decomposition of $I$ is $I = (x, y) \cap (x, z) \cap (x, y, z)^2$, determine the isolated and embedded primes of $I$, and find $\rad I$.

\item Suppose $\varphi : R \to S$ is a surjective ring homomorphism. Prove that an ideal $Q$ in $R$ containing the kernel of $\varphi$ is primary if and only if $\varphi(Q)$ is primary in $S$, and when this is the case the prime associated to $\varphi(Q)$ is the image $\varphi(P)$ of the prime $P$ associated to $Q$.

\item Suppose $\varphi : R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $I$ is an ideal of $R$ containing $\ker \varphi$ with minimal primary decomposition $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ with $\rad Q_i = P_i$. If $\varphi$ is a surjective homomorphism prove that $\varphi(I) = \varphi(Q_1) \cap \cdots \cap \varphi(Q_m)$, where $\rad \varphi(Q_i)$ is given by $\varphi(P_i)$, is a minimal primary decomposition of $\varphi(I)$. [Use the previous exercise.]
\item[(b)] Suppose $I$ is an ideal of $S$ with minimal primary decomposition $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ with $\rad Q_i = P_i$. Prove that $\varphi^{-1}(I) = \varphi^{-1}(Q_1) \cap \cdots \cap \varphi^{-1}(Q_m)$, where $\rad \varphi^{-1}(Q_i)$ is given by $\varphi^{-1}(P_i)$, is a primary decomposition of $\varphi^{-1}(I)$, and is minimal if $\varphi$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I = (xy, x - yz)$ in $k[x, y, z]$.

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 3/4
Content:
Prove that $(x, z) \cap (y^2, x - yz)$ is a minimal primary decomposition of $I$. [Consider the ring homomorphism $\varphi : k[x, y, z] \to k[y, z]$ given by mapping $x$ to $yz$, $y$ to $y$, and $z$ to $z$ and use the previous exercise.]

\item Prove that a prime ideal $P$ contains the ideal $I$ if and only if $P$ contains one of the associated primes of a minimal primary decomposition of $I$. [Use Exercise 3 and Exercise 11 in Section 7.4.]

\item Show that every associated prime ideal for a radical ideal is isolated. [Suppose that $P_2 = \rad Q_2 \subseteq P_1 = \rad Q_1$ in the decomposition of Theorem 21 for the radical ideal $I$. Show that if $a \in Q_2 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ ($\subseteq P_2 \subseteq P_1$) then $a^n \in I$ for some $n \geq 1$, conclude that $a \in Q_1$ and derive a contradiction to the minimality of the primary decomposition.]

\item Fix an element $a$ in the ring $R$. For any ideal $I$ in the ring $R$ let $I_a = \{r \in R \mid ar \in I\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I_a$ is an ideal and $I_a = R$ if and only if $a \in I$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $(I \cap J)_a = I_a \cap J_a$ for ideals $I$ and $J$.
\item[(c)] Suppose that $Q$ is a $P$-primary ideal and that $a \notin Q$. Prove that $Q_a$ is a $P$-primary ideal and that $Q_a = Q$ if $a \notin P$.
\end{enumerate}

\item With notation as in the previous exercise, suppose $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ is a minimal primary decomposition of the ideal $I$ and let $P_i$ be the prime ideal associated to $Q_i$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I_a = (Q_1)_a \cap \cdots \cap (Q_m)_a$ and that $\rad(I_a) = \rad((Q_1)_a) \cap \cdots \cap \rad((Q_m)_a)$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $\rad(I_a)$ is the intersection of the prime ideals $P_i$ for which $a \notin Q_i$. [Use the previous exercise.]
\item[(c)] Prove that if $\rad(I_a)$ is a prime ideal then $\rad(I_a) = P_j$ for some $j$. [Use the fact that prime ideals are irreducible.]
\item[(d)] For each $i = 1, \ldots, m$, prove that $\rad(I_a) = P_i$ for some $a \in R$. [Show there exists an $a \in R$ with $a \notin Q_i$ but $a \in Q_j$ for all $j \neq i$.]
\item[(e)] Show from (c) and (d) that the associated primes for a minimal primary decomposition are precisely the collection of prime ideals among the ideals $\rad(I_a)$ for $a \in R$, and conclude that they are uniquely determined by $I$ independent of the minimal primary decomposition.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $P_1, \ldots, P_m$ be the associated prime ideals of the ideal $(0)$ in the Noetherian ring $R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $P_1 \cap \cdots \cap P_m$ is the collection of nilpotent elements in $R$. [Apply Corollary 22 to $I = (0)$.]
\item[(b)] Show that $P_1 \cup \cdots \cup P_m$ is the collection of zero divisors in $R$. [Let $I = (0)$ in the previous exercise and show that the set of zero divisors is given by the set $\bigcup_{a \in R - \{0\}} (0)_a = \bigcup_{a \in R - \{0\}} \rad((0)_a)$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $R$ is a Noetherian ring. Prove that $R$ is either an integral domain, has nonzero nilpotent elements, or has at least two minimal prime ideals. [Use the previous exercise.]

\item Prove that the ideal $I$ in the Noetherian ring $R$ is radical if and only if the primary components of a minimal primary decomposition are all prime ideals, and conclude that in this case the minimal primary decomposition is unique. [If $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_m$ is radical with $Q_i$ a $P_i$-primary component of a minimal decomposition, show that if $a \in P_1 \cap \cdots \cap P_m$ then some power of $a$ is in $I$, hence $a \in I$ since $I$ is radical. Deduce that $I = P_1 \cap \cdots \cap P_m$ and show that this is also a minimal primary decomposition, i.e., for any $i$ there exists $b$ with $b \notin P_i$, but $b \in P_j$ for $j \neq i$. If $a \in P_i$, show that $ab \in Q_i$, and that $a \in Q_i$. Conclude that $Q_i = P_i$.]

\item Prove that a Noetherian integral domain $R$ is a U.F.D. if and only if for every $a \in R$ the isolated primes associated to the principal ideal $(a)$ are principal ideals. [See Example 2 following Corollary 22. To prove $R$ is a U.F.D., show that an irreducible $a \in R$ is prime and then follow the proof of Theorem 14 in Section 8.3.]

\item Let $R$ be the ring of all real valued functions on the open interval $(-1, 1)$ that have derivatives of all orders (the ring of $C^\infty$ functions). Let
\[
F(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-1/x^4} & if x \neq 0 \\ 0 & if x = 0 \end{cases}
\]
(you may assume $F \in R$ and $F^{(n)}(0) = 0$ for all $n \geq 0$). Let $(F)$ be the principal ideal generated by $F$ and let $A = \rad((F))$. Let $M$ be the (maximal) ideal of all functions in $R$ that are zero at $x = 0$ and let $P = \bigcap_{n \geq 1} M^n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $M = (x)$ is the ideal generated by the function $x$ in $R$ and that $M^n = (x^n)$ consists of the functions $f$ with $f(0) = f'(0) = \cdots = f^{(n-1)}(0) = 0$.
\item[(b)] Prove that $R$ is not Noetherian (compare Exercise 33 in Section 7.4). [One approach is the following: Let $G(x)$ be the function that is $0$ for $x < 0$ and is equal to $F(x)$ for $x \geq 0$. Let $I_n$ be the ideal of functions in $R$ vanishing for all $x \leq 1/n$. Use translates of $G(x)$ to show that $I_1 \subset I_2 \subset I_3 \subset \cdots$ is an infinite ascending chain.]
\item[(c)] Prove that $P$ consists of the functions all of whose derivatives are zero at $x = 0$ (i.e., the functions whose associated Taylor series at $x = 0$ is identically zero), and that $P$ is a prime ideal.
\item[(d)] Prove that $F \in P$ and deduce that $A \subseteq P$.
\item[(e)] Prove that $A \neq P$. [Let $G(x) = e^{-1/x^2}$ when $x \neq 0$ and $G(0) = 0$. Show that $G \in P$ but $G \notin A$.]
\item[(f)] Show that there is a prime ideal $Q$ containing $(F)$ with $Q \neq P, M$.

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Primary Decomposition > Existence in Noetherian rings; Supp, Ass, and symbolic powers
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 4/4
Content:
Prove that $Q \subset P$, i.e., there are nonzero prime ideals properly contained in $P$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $A$ be any ideal in $R = k[x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $\rad(A \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]) = \rad A \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $(f_1, \ldots, f_s)$ is an ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Let $F_1, \ldots, F_t$ be generators for the radical of $(f_1, \ldots, f_s)$, computed in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Suppose $J$ is an ideal in $R$ and let $A = J + (f_1, \ldots, f_s)$, $B = J + (F_1, \ldots, F_t)$ as ideals in $R$. Prove that $\rad A = \rad B$.
\item[(c)] Conclude from (a) and (b) that $A = (y_1 - x_1, \ldots, y_m - x_m, f_1, \ldots, f_s) \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$ and $B = (y_1 - x_1, \ldots, y_m - x_m, F_1, \ldots, F_t) \cap k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$ have the same zero sets over an algebraically closed field $k$. [Use Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Determine the Zariski closure in $C^3$ of the points on the curve $\{(a^2, a^3, a^4) \mid a \in C\}$.

\item Show that $Z(x^3 - xyz + z^2)$ is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $\{(st, s + t, s^2 t) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Show that $Z(x^3 z^2 - 3xy^2 z^2 - y^6 - z^4)$ is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $\{(s^2 + t^2, st, s^3) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Find equations defining the Zariski closure of the set of points $\{(s^4, s^3 t, s t^3, t^4) \mid s, t \in R\}$.

\item Show that $V = Z(x^2 - y^2 z)$ (the Whitney umbrella surface) is the smallest algebraic set in $R^3$ containing the points $S = \{(st, s, t^2) \mid s, t \in R\}$. Show that $S$ is not Zariski closed in $V$ (the missing points explain the name for the surface). Do the same over $C$, but show that in this case $S = V$ is closed.

\item Let $V = Z(xz^2 - w^3, \; xw^2 - y^4, \; y^4 z^2 - w^5) \subseteq C^4$. Determine the Zariski closure of the image of $V$ under the projection $\pi((x, y, z, w)) = (x, y, z)$.

\item Let $V = Z(xy - 1)$ in $\Aff^2$ and let $S$ be the projection of $V$ onto the $x$-axis in $\Aff^1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $k = R$, show that $I(V) = (xy - 1) \subseteq R[x, y]$ and that $(u - x, xy - 1) \cap R[u] = 0$ in $R[x, y, u]$. Use Propositions 8 and 16 to conclude that the Zariski closure of $S$ is $\Aff^1$ and show that $S$ is not itself closed.
\item[(b)] If $k = \F_3$, show that $I(V) = (xy - 1, x^3 - x, y^3 - y) \subseteq \F_3[x, y]$ and that $(u - x, xy - 1, x^3 - x, y^3 - y) \cap \F_3[u] = (u^2 - 1)$ in $\F_3[x, y, u]$. Use Propositions 8 and 16 to conclude that $S$ is Zariski closed in $\Aff^1$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Recall the ideal quotient $(I : J) = \{r \in R \mid rJ \subseteq I\}$ of two ideals $I, J$ in a ring $R$ (cf. Exercise 34 ff. in Section 9.6). Clearly $I \subseteq (I : J)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $Z(I) - Z(J)$, the set of elements of $Z(I)$ not lying in $Z(J)$, is contained in $Z((I : J))$ and conclude that the Zariski closure of $Z(I) - Z(J)$ is contained in $Z((I : J))$.
\item[(b)] Show that if $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is a radical ideal then $Z((I : J))$ is precisely the Zariski closure of $Z(I) - Z(J)$.
\item[(c)] Show that if $V$ and $W$ are affine algebraic sets then $(I(V) : I(W)) = I(V - W)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Primary Decomposition > Existence in Noetherian rings; Supp, Ass, and symbolic powers
Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).}
\item If an ideal $\fa$ has a primary decomposition, then $\Spec(A/\fa)$ has only finitely many irreducible components.

\item If $\fa = \rad(\fa)$, then $\fa$ has no embedded prime ideals.

\item If $A$ is absolutely flat, every primary ideal is maximal.

\item In the polynomial ring $Z[t]$, the ideal $\fm = (2, t)$ is maximal and the ideal $\fq = (4, t)$ is $\fm$-primary, but is not a power of $\fm$.

\item In the polynomial ring $K[x, y, z]$ where $K$ is a field and $x, y, z$ are independent indeterminates, let $\fp_1 = (x, y)$, $\fp_2 = (x, z)$, $\fm = (x, y, z)$; $\fp_1$ and $\fp_2$ are prime, and $\fm$ is maximal. Let $\fa = \fp_1 \fp_2$. Show that $\fa = \fp_1 \cap \fp_2 \cap \fm^2$ is a reduced primary decomposition of $\fa$. Which components are isolated and which are embedded?

\item Let $X$ be an infinite compact Hausdorff space, $C(X)$ the ring of real-valued continuous functions on $X$ (Chapter 1, Exercise 26). Is the zero ideal decomposable in this ring?

\item Let $A$ be a ring and let $A[x]$ denote the ring of polynomials in one indeterminate over $A$. For each ideal $\fa$ of $A$, let $\fa[x]$ denote the set of all polynomials in $A[x]$ with coefficients in $\fa$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] $\fa[x]$ is the extension of $\fa$ to $A[x]$.
\item[ii)] If $\fp$ is a prime ideal in $A$, then $\fp[x]$ is a prime ideal in $A[x]$.
\item[iii)] If $\fq$ is a $\fp$-primary ideal in $A$, then $\fq[x]$ is a $\fp[x]$-primary ideal in $A[x]$. [Use Chapter 1, Exercise 2.]
\item[iv)] If $\fa = \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} \fq_i$ is a minimal primary decomposition in $A$, then $\fa[x] = \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} \fq_i[x]$ is a minimal primary decomposition in $A[x]$.
\item[v)] If $\fp$ is a minimal prime ideal of $\fa$, then $\fp[x]$ is a minimal prime ideal of $\fa[x]$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $k$ be a field. Show that in the polynomial ring $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ the ideals $\fp_i = (x_1, \ldots, x_i)$ $(1 \leq i \leq n)$ are prime and all their powers are primary. [Use Exercise 7.]

\item In a ring $A$, let $D(A)$ denote the set of prime ideals $\fp$ which satisfy the following condition: there exists $a \in A$ such that $\fp$ is minimal in the set of prime ideals containing $(0 : a)$. Show that $x \in A$ is a zero-divisor $\Leftrightarrow x \in \fp$ for some $\fp \in D(A)$. Let $S$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$, and identify $\Spec(S^{-1}A)$ with its image in $\Spec(A)$ (Chapter 3, Exercise 21). Show that
\[
D(S^{-1}A) = D(A) \cap \Spec(S^{-1}A).
\]
If the zero ideal has a primary decomposition, show that $D(A)$ is the set of associated prime ideals of $0$.

\item For any prime ideal $\fp$ in a ring $A$, let $S_\fp(0)$ denote the kernel of the homomorphism $A \to A_\fp$. Prove that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] $S_\fp(0) \subseteq \fp$.
\item[ii)] $\rad(S_\fp(0)) = \fp \Leftrightarrow \fp$ is a minimal prime ideal of $A$.
\item[iii)] If $\fp \supseteq \fp'$, then $S_\fp(0) \subseteq S_{\fp'}(0)$.
\item[iv)] $\bigcap_{\fp \in D(A)} S_\fp(0) = 0$, where $D(A)$ is defined in Exercise 9.
\end{enumerate}

\item If $\fp$ is a minimal prime ideal of a ring $A$, show that $S_\fp(0)$ (Exercise 10) is the smallest $\fp$-primary ideal. Let $\fa$ be the intersection of the ideals $S_\fp(0)$ as $\fp$ runs through the minimal prime ideals of $A$. Show that $\fa$ is contained in the nilradical of $A$. Suppose that the zero ideal is decomposable. Prove that $\fa = 0$ if and only if every prime ideal of $0$ is isolated.

\item Let $A$ be a ring, $S$ a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$. For any ideal $\fa$, let $S(\fa)$ denote the contraction of $S^{-1}\fa$ in $A$. The ideal $S(\fa)$ is called the saturation of $\fa$ with respect to $S$. Prove that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] $S(\fa) \cap S(\fb) = S(\fa \cap \fb)$.
\item[ii)] $S(\rad(\fa)) = \rad(S(\fa))$.
\item[iii)] $S(\fa) = (1) \Leftrightarrow \fa$ meets $S$.
\item[iv)] $S_1(S_2(\fa)) = (S_1 S_2)(\fa)$.
\end{enumerate}
If $\fa$ has a primary decomposition, prove that the set of ideals $S(\fa)$ (where $S$ runs through all multiplicatively closed subsets of $A$) is finite.

Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Part: 2/2
Content:
By Exercise 11 (applied in $A/\fa$) the ideal $\fq_1 = S_{\fp_1}(\fa)$ is $\fp_1$-primary, and by (L1) $\fq_1 = (\fa : x)$ for some $x \notin \fp_1$. Check that $\fa = \fq_1 \cap (\fa + (x))$. By Zorn's lemma choose $\fa_1 \supseteq \fa + (x)$ maximal among the ideals $\fb \supseteq \fa$ with $\fq_1 \cap \fb = \fa$; since $x \in \fa_1$, $\fa_1 \not\subseteq \fp_1$. Repeat the construction with $\fa_1$ in place of $\fa$, and so on: after $n$ steps $\fa = \fq_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fq_n \cap \fa_n$, where each $\fq_i$ is $\fp_i$-primary, $\fa_{n-1} = \fq_n \cap \fa_n$ and $\fa_n \not\subseteq \fp_n$. If some $\fa_n = (1)$, the process stops and $\fa$ is a finite intersection of primary ideals; otherwise continue by transfinite induction, noting that each $\fa_n$ strictly contains $\fa_{n-1}$.]

\item Consider the following condition on a ring $A$:
\begin{quote}
(L2) Given an ideal $\fa$ and a descending chain $S_1 \supseteq S_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq S_n \supseteq \cdots$ of multiplicatively closed subsets of $A$, there exists an integer $n$ such that $S_n(\fa) = S_{n+1}(\fa) = \cdots$.
\end{quote}
Prove that the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] Every ideal in $A$ has a primary decomposition;
\item[ii)] $A$ satisfies (L1) and (L2).
\end{enumerate}
[For i) $\Rightarrow$ ii), use Exercises 12 and 15. For ii) $\Rightarrow$ i), in the notation of the hint to Exercise 17 put $S_n = S_{\fp_1} \cap \cdots \cap S_{\fp_n}$; since $\fa_n \supseteq \fa_i \not\subseteq \fp_i$ for $i \le n$, $S_n$ meets $\fa_n$ (prime avoidance), so $S_n(\fa_n) = (1)$ and therefore $S_n(\fa) = \fq_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fq_n$. Now use (L2) to show that the construction must terminate after a finite number of steps.]

\item Let $A$ be a ring and $\fp$ a prime ideal of $A$. Show that every $\fp$-primary ideal contains $S_\fp(0)$, the kernel of the canonical homomorphism $A \to A_\fp$. Suppose that $A$ satisfies the following condition: for every prime ideal $\fp$, the intersection of all $\fp$-primary ideals of $A$ is equal to $S_\fp(0)$. (Noetherian rings satisfy this condition: see Chapter 10.) Let $\fp_1, \ldots, \fp_n$ be distinct prime ideals, none of which is a minimal prime ideal of $A$. Then there exists an ideal $\fa$ in $A$ whose associated prime ideals are $\fp_1, \ldots, \fp_n$.

[Proof by induction on $n$. The case $n = 1$ is trivial (take $\fa = \fp_1$). Suppose $n > 1$ and let $\fp_n$ be maximal in the set $\{\fp_1, \ldots, \fp_n\}$. By the inductive hypothesis there exists an ideal $\fb$ and a minimal primary decomposition $\fb = \fq_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fq_{n-1}$, where $\fq_i$ is $\fp_i$-primary. If $\fb \subseteq S_{\fp_n}(0)$, let $\fp$ be a minimal prime ideal of $A$ contained in $\fp_n$. Then $S_{\fp_n}(0) \subseteq S_\fp(0)$, hence $\fb \subseteq S_\fp(0)$. Taking radicals and using Exercise 10, we have $\fp_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fp_{n-1} \subseteq \fp$, hence (since $\fp$ is a prime ideal) $\fp_i \subseteq \fp$ for some $i$, hence $\fp_i = \fp$ since $\fp$ is minimal. This is a contradiction since no $\fp_i$ is minimal. Hence $\fb \not\subseteq S_{\fp_n}(0)$ and therefore there exists a $\fp_n$-primary ideal $\fq_n$ such that $\fb \not\subseteq \fq_n$. Show that $\fa = \fq_1 \cap \cdots \cap \fq_n$ has the required properties.]

\item Let $M$ be a fixed $A$-module, $N$ a submodule of $M$. The radical of $N$ in $M$ is defined to be
\[
r_M(N) = \{x \in A \mid x^q M \subseteq N for some q > 0\}.
\]
Show that $r_M(N) = r(N : M) = r(\Ann(M/N))$. In particular, $r_M(N)$ is an ideal. State and prove the formulas for $r_M(N)$ analogous to (1.13).

\item An element $x \in A$ defines an endomorphism $\phi_x$ of $M$, namely $m \mapsto xm$. The element $x$ is said to be a zero-divisor (resp. nilpotent) in $M$ if $\phi_x$ is not injective (resp. is nilpotent). A submodule $Q$ of $M$ is primary in $M$ if $Q \neq M$ and every zero-divisor in $M/Q$ is nilpotent. Show that if $Q$ is primary in $M$, then $(Q : M)$ is a primary ideal and hence $r_M(Q)$ is a prime ideal $\fp$. We say that $Q$ is $\fp$-primary (in $M$). Prove the analogues of (4.3) and (4.4).

\item A primary decomposition of $N$ in $M$ is a representation of $N$ as an intersection
\[
N = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_n
\]
of primary submodules of $M$; it is a minimal primary decomposition if the ideals $\fp_i = r_M(Q_i)$ are all distinct and if none of the components $Q_i$ can be omitted from the intersection, that is if $Q_i \not\supseteq \bigcap_{j \neq i} Q_j$ $(1 \leq i \leq n)$. Prove the analogue of (4.5), that the prime ideals $\fp_i$ depend only on $N$ (and $M$). They are called the prime ideals belonging to $N$ in $M$. Show that they are also the prime ideals belonging to $0$ in $M/N$.

\item State and prove the analogues of (4.6)--(4.11) inclusive. (There is no loss of generality in taking $N = 0$.)
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item In $Z$ give the minimal primary decomposition of the ideal $(360)$, identify the prime belonging to each component, and verify that $\rad(360)$ is the squarefree radical of $360$. Then decide which (if any) of the associated primes are embedded.
\item In $k[x,y]$ let $\fq=(x^3,\,xy,\,y^2)$. Compute the quotient ring $k[x,y]/\fq$ explicitly as a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, give a basis, and use the description ``every zero-divisor is nilpotent'' to decide whether $\fq$ is primary. If it is, name the prime $\fp=\rad\fq$ to which it belongs.
\item Let $R=k[x,y,z]$ and $\fa=(xy,\,yz,\,zx)$. Show $\fa=(x,y)\cap(y,z)\cap(z,x)$, conclude that $\fa$ is radical, and list the minimal primes of $\fa$. Describe $Z(\fa)\subseteq\Aff^3$ as a union of irreducible components and match each component to its prime.
\item Let $\fq$ be a $\fp$-primary ideal and let $x\in R$ with $x\notin\fp$. Using only the definition of primary, prove directly that the colon ideal $(\fq\colonid x)$ equals $\fq$. Then exhibit, in $k[x,y]$ with $\fq=(x^2,y)$, an element $f\in\fq$ for which $(\fq\colonid f)=R$.
\item In $R=k[x,y]$ consider $\fa=(x^2,\,xy^2)$. Find a minimal primary decomposition of $\fa$ with exactly two components, identify the isolated and embedded primes, and compute $\rad\fa$. Confirm your decomposition by checking that each given generator of $\fa$ lies in both primary components.
\item Let $\fp=(x,z)$ in $R=k[x,y,z]/(z^2-x^2 y)$ (the Whitney-umbrella coordinate ring). Show $\fp$ is prime by exhibiting $R/\fp$ as a polynomial ring, and decide whether $\fp^2$ is primary by testing the relation $\bar z^2=\bar x^2\bar y$ against the primary definition.
\item Let $A=Z/12Z$ regarded as a $Z$-module. Compute $\Ass_Z(A)$ by finding, for each prime $p\mid 12$, an element of $A$ whose annihilator is $(p)$. Then reconcile your answer with the minimal primary decomposition of the ideal $(12)\subseteqZ$.
\item Let $\fq_1,\dots,\fq_r$ all be $\fp$-primary in a ring $R$. Prove that $\fq_1\cap\cdots\cap\fq_r$ is again $\fp$-primary, and give an example in $k[x,y]$ of two distinct $(x,y)$-primary ideals whose intersection is strictly smaller than either.
\end{exers}

\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $\fa=(x)\cap(x,y)^2$ in $R=k[x,y]$, with associated primes $\fp_1=(x)$ (isolated) and $\fp_2=(x,y)$ (embedded). On the prime spectrum draw the inclusion poset of closed sets and prove the indicated containment. Complete the skeleton, labelling each arrow with the inclusion of vanishing loci, and prove that $V(\fp_2)\subseteq V(\fp_1)$ so the embedded point adds no new support:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.8em, column sep=2.0em]
\fp_1=(x) \arrow[r,hook] & \fp_2=(x,y) \\
V(\fp_1) & V(\fp_2) \arrow[l,hook']
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Conclude that $\Supp(R/\fa)=V(\fa)=V(\fp_1)=V(\fp_1)\cup V(\fp_2)$ and explain why $\Ass(\fa)$ nonetheless records both primes.
\item Let $\fp$ be a minimal (isolated) prime of a decomposable ideal $\fa$, and put $S=R\setminus\fp$. The second uniqueness theorem says the isolated component is $\fq_\fp=(S^{-1}\fa)^c$. Complete the localization square below (horizontal maps are the localization $R\to S^{-1}R$, vertical maps the quotients by $\fa$ and its extension), prove it commutes, and prove that contracting $S^{-1}\fa$ back to $R$ kills every component $\fq_j$ with $\fp_j\not\subseteq\fp$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r,"\lambda"] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] & S^{-1}R \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow] \\
R/\fa \arrow[r,"\overline{\lambda}"'] & S^{-1}R\,/\,S^{-1}\fa
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Deduce that $\fq_\fp$ depends only on $\fa$ and $\fp$, not on the chosen minimal decomposition.
\item Let $R$ be Noetherian and $\fp\in\Spec R$. Complete the inverse-limit tower of symbolic powers and the parallel tower of ordinary powers, with horizontal maps the natural surjections $R/\fp^{(n+1)}\twoheadrightarrow R/\fp^{(n)}$ (and $R/\fp^{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow R/\fp^{n}$) and the vertical maps $R/\fp^n\to R/\fp^{(n)}$ induced by $\fp^n\subseteq\fp^{(n)}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=1.8em]
\cdots \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp^{(3)} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp^{(2)} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp^{(1)} \\
\cdots \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp^3 \arrow[u]\arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp^2 \arrow[u]\arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & R/\fp \arrow[u,equal]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove each vertical map is well defined, that the rightmost map is an isomorphism (so $\fp^{(1)}=\fp$), and give a prime $\fp$ in some $R$ for which the map $R/\fp^2\to R/\fp^{(2)}$ is not injective.
\end{exers}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Integral Dependence, Valuation Rings, and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz > Integral elements: the geometry of a ramified cover
Type: prose
Content:
In classical algebraic geometry one frequently studies a curve as a (ramified) covering of the line: a finite map $C\to\Aff^1$ presenting the function field of $C$ as a finite extension of $k(t)$. Algebraically this is the relation between a ring and a subring expressed by integral dependence. Integrality is to ring extensions what algebraicity is to field extensions, with one crucial sharpening: we demand a monic equation, not merely a nonzero one. This single adjustment -- forcing the leading coefficient to be $1$ -- is what makes the theory control prime ideals so tightly (Lying Over, Going Up, Going Down), and it is the algebraic engine behind Hilbert's Nullstellensatz: the dictionary between the geometry of points in $\Aff^n$ and the maximal ideals of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.

Throughout, $A\subseteq B$ are commutative rings with $1\in A$. We freely identify ``$A$ a subring of $B$'' with the inclusion homomorphism; the general statements about a homomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ follow by replacing $A$ with $\varphi(A)$.

Type: definition
Title: integral element, integral extension, integral closure
Content:
\begin{definition}[integral element, integral extension, integral closure]
Let $A\subseteq B$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item An element $x\in B$ is integral over $A$ if $x$ is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$:
\[
x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0=0,\qquad a_i\in A.
\]
\item $B$ is integral over $A$ (an integral extension) if every $x\in B$ is integral over $A$.
\item The integral closure of $A$ in $B$ is $\overline{A}=\{x\in B:x integral over A\}$. If $\overline{A}=A$, then $A$ is integrally closed in $B$.
\item For a domain $A$ with fraction field $K=\Frac(A)$, the integral closure of $A$ in $K$ is the normalization of $A$; $A$ is integrally closed (or normal) if it equals its normalization.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Integral Dependence, Valuation Rings, and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz > Integral elements: the geometry of a ramified cover
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-5f74ccee2b11a0fab239
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): the monic relation lets one rewrite $x^n$, hence every $x^{n+r}$, as an $A$-combination of $1,x,\dots,x^{n-1}$, so $A[x]=A1+Ax+\cdots+Ax^{n-1}$. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): take $C=A[x]$. (iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv): take $M=C$, faithful because $1\in C$. (iv)$\Rightarrow$(i) is the determinant trick: multiplication by $x$ on the finitely generated module $M=Av_1+\cdots+Av_n$ gives $xv_i=\sum_j a_{ij}v_j$, so $(xI-(a_{ij}))v=0$; multiplying by the adjugate yields $\det(xI-(a_{ij}))\cdot v_i=0$ for all $i$. Faithfulness forces $\det(xI-(a_{ij}))=0$, a monic equation for $x$ over $A$.
\end{proof}

Type: corollary
Title: {the integral closure is a ring; transitivity; A\&M 5.2--5.6}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{the integral closure is a ring; transitivity; A\&M 5.2--5.6}]
Let $A\subseteq B$ and $x,y\in B$ integral over $A$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $x\pm y$ and $xy$ are integral over $A$; hence $\overline{A}$ is a subring of $B$ containing $A$.
\item (Tower / finite type $+$ integral $=$ finite.) If $B=A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with each $x_i$ integral over $A$, then $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module.
\item (Transitivity.) If $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ with $C$ integral over $B$ and $B$ integral over $A$, then $C$ is integral over $A$.
\item $\overline{A}$ is integrally closed in $B$ (the closure stops after one step).
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

Title: A\&M's slogan
Content:
\begin{remark}[A\&M's slogan]
Corollary~(2) is the identity finite type $+$ integral $=$ finite: a ring extension that is both finitely generated as an algebra and integral is finitely generated as a module. This is the precise sense in which a ramified cover $C\to\Aff^1$ is ``finite over the base.''
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: $\sqrt2$ is an algebraic integer; $1/2$ is not
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\sqrt2$ is an algebraic integer; $1/2$ is not}
Decide which of $\sqrt2,\ \tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\ \tfrac12\inQ$ are integral over $Z$.
\wrec An element of $Q$ is integral over the UFD $Z$ iff it lies in $Z$ (rational root test); for irrationals, exhibit a monic integer equation.
\wsol $\sqrt2$ satisfies $x^2-2=0$, monic over $Z$, so it is integral. The golden ratio $\tau=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ satisfies $x^2-x-1=0$, monic over $Z$, so it is integral. But $\tfrac12$ is integral over $Z$ iff $\tfrac12\inZ$ (since $Z$ is a UFD, hence integrally closed): if $(1/2)^n+a_{n-1}(1/2)^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0$ then clearing denominators gives $1=-2(a_{n-1}+\cdots+2^{n-1}a_0)$, forcing $2\mid1$, impossible. Sanity check: the minimal polynomial of $\tfrac12$ over $Q$ is $x-\tfrac12$, not monic over $Z$, matching Proposition~28 of D\&F that $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer iff $m_{\alpha,Q}\inZ[x]$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Integral closure need not equal the subring: the cuspidal cubic
Content:
\begin{wex}{Integral closure need not equal the subring: the cuspidal cubic}
Let $R=k[x,y]/(x^2-y^3)=k[\bar x,\bar y]$. Show $R$ is not integrally closed in its fraction field.
\wrec Look for an element of $\Frac(R)$ satisfying a monic equation over $R$ but lying outside $R$; the cusp at the origin is the geometric obstruction.
\wsol In $\Frac(R)$ set $t=\bar x/\bar y$. Then $t^2=\bar x^2/\bar y^2=\bar y^3/\bar y^2=\bar y$, so $t$ satisfies the monic equation $T^2-\bar y=0$ over $R$; hence $t$ is integral over $R$. But $t=\bar x/\bar y\notin R$: the parametrization $\bar x\mapsto s^3,\ \bar y\mapsto s^2$ identifies $R$ with $k[s^2,s^3]\subseteq k[s]$, and $t\mapsto s\notin k[s^2,s^3]$. The normalization is $k[s]=k[t]$, the smooth line resolving the cusp. Sanity check: $t$ also satisfies $T^3-\bar x=0$ (since $t^3=\bar x^3/\bar y^3=\bar x^3/\bar x^2=\bar x$), a second monic witness; and $R$ being non-normal forces it to be a non-UFD, consistent with $\bar x^2=\bar y^3$ giving two distinct factorizations of the same element.
\end{wex}

Content:
\begin{wex}{Every UFD is integrally closed}
Show that a UFD $A$ is integrally closed in $\Frac(A)$.
\wrec Use the rational root argument: a fraction in lowest terms satisfying a monic equation must have unit denominator.
\wsol Let $a/b\in\Frac(A)$ in lowest terms ($\gcd(a,b)=1$) satisfy $(a/b)^n+r_{n-1}(a/b)^{n-1}+\cdots+r_0=0$ with $r_i\in A$. Clearing $b^n$: $a^n=-b(r_{n-1}a^{n-1}+\cdots+r_0b^{n-1})$, so every irreducible dividing $b$ divides $a^n$, hence divides $a$. Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, $b$ has no irreducible factors, i.e.\ $b$ is a unit and $a/b\in A$. Sanity check: $Z$, $k[x]$, and $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ are all UFDs, hence all integrally closed -- recovering Example~(1) above and the normality of polynomial rings used in the Nullstellensatz.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The ring of integers of $Q(\sqrt D)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The ring of integers of $Q(\sqrt D)$}
For squarefree $D$, compute the normalization of $Z$ in $Q(\sqrt D)$.
\wrec Test $\alpha=a+b\sqrt D$ ($a,b\inQ$): integral iff its $Q$-minimal polynomial $x^2-2ax+(a^2-b^2D)$ has integer coefficients.
\wsol Integrality forces $2a\inZ$ and $a^2-b^2D\inZ$; then $(2b)^2D=(2a)^2-4(a^2-b^2D)\inZ$, and as $D$ is squarefree this forces $2b\inZ$. Writing $a=x/2,\ b=y/2$ with $x,y\inZ$ gives $x^2-y^2D\equiv0\pmod4$. As squares are $0,1\bmod4$ and $D$ is squarefree, either $D\equiv2,3\pmod4$ with $x,y$ both even (so $a,b\inZ$), or $D\equiv1\pmod4$ with $x,y$ of equal parity. Hence
\[
\mathcal O_{Q(\sqrt D)}=\begin{cases}Z[\sqrt D],&D\equiv2,3\pmod4,\\[2pt]Z\!\left[\tfrac{1+\sqrt D}{2}\right],&D\equiv1\pmod4.\end{cases}
\]
Sanity check: for $D=5$, $\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ is integral (Worked Example above), so $Z[\sqrt5]\subsetneq\mathcal O_{Q(\sqrt5)}$ -- $Z[\sqrt5]$ is the non-maximal, non-integrally-closed order, and adjoining the golden ratio normalizes it.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
A\&M's central philosophy is that a prime ideal is the common generalization of ``a prime of arithmetic'' and ``a point of geometry,'' and that a ring map $A\to B$ is to be read geometrically as a map of spaces $\Spec B\to\Spec A$, $\fq\mapsto\fq\cap A$ (contraction). For a finite (integral, finite-type) map this is the algebra of a ramified cover, and the three classical theorems say the fibers and chains behave as a covering should: every point of the base is hit (Lying Over), chains lift upward (Going Up), and -- when the base is normal -- chains lift downward (Going Down). We write $\fq\cap A$ for the contraction $\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$ when $A\subseteq B$.

Type: theorem
Title: {integral extensions: field, Lying Over, Going Up, Going Down; D\&F 26}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{integral extensions: field, Lying Over, Going Up, Going Down; D\&F 26}]
Let $A\subseteq B$ be commutative rings with $B$ integral over $A$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item (Fields together.) If $B$ is a domain, then $A$ is a field iff $B$ is a field.
\item (Lying Over.) For every prime $\fp\subseteq A$ there is a prime $\fq\subseteq B$ with $\fq\cap A=\fp$. Moreover $\fp$ is maximal iff $\fq$ is maximal.
\item (Going Up.) A chain $\fp_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\fp_n$ of primes of $A$, partially lifted to $\fq_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\fq_m$ in $B$ ($m<n$, $\fq_i\cap A=\fp_i$), can be completed to $\fq_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\fq_n$ with $\fq_i\cap A=\fp_i$.
\item (Going Down.) If in addition $B$ is a domain and $A$ is integrally closed in its fraction field (i.e.\ $A$ is normal), then a descending chain $\fp_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\fp_n$ partially lifted to $\fq_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\fq_m$ ($m<n$) can be completed downward.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-6b6c38fbe39244c18a9d
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1): if $A$ is a field and $0\neq s\in B$ satisfies a monic equation with nonzero constant term $a_0$, then $s\cdot(-a_0^{-1})(s^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1)=1$ gives $s^{-1}\in B$. Conversely if $B$ is a field and $0\neq r\in A$, then $r^{-1}\in B$ is integral, and its monic equation rearranges to express $r^{-1}$ as an $A$-combination of nonnegative powers of $r$, so $r^{-1}\in A$. (2): reduce mod the primes -- $B/\fq$ is integral over $A/(\fq\cap A)$, so (1) gives the maximality statement; existence of some $\fq$ is the localization argument $S^{-1} A\subseteq S^{-1} B$ at $S=A\setminus\fp$ (a maximal ideal $\fn$ of $S^{-1} B$ contracts, by the maximality statement applied to the integral extension $S^{-1} A\subseteq S^{-1} B$, to the maximal ideal $\fp S^{-1} A$ of the local ring $S^{-1} A$, so the contraction of $\fn$ to $B$ is a prime of $B$ lying over $\fp$). (3) is an induction reducing to $n=2$, $m=1$: pass to $\overline A=A/\fp_1\subseteq\overline B=B/\fq_1$, apply Lying Over to $\fp_2/\fp_1$, and pull back. (4) is A\&M 5.16: reduce to $n=2$, $m=1$; since $A$ is integrally closed, A\&M 5.15 is used to show that $\fp_2B$ does not meet the multiplicative set $(A\setminus\fp_2)(B\setminus\fq_1)$, and an ideal of $B$ maximal among those containing $\fp_2B$ and disjoint from this set is a prime $\fq_2\subseteq\fq_1$ with $\fq_2\cap A=\fp_2$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: contraction is a continuous map of spectra
Content:
\begin{remark}[contraction is a continuous map of spectra]
The assignment $\fq\mapsto\fq\cap A$ is the continuous map $\Spec B\to\Spec A$ induced by $A\hookrightarrow B$. Lying Over says it is surjective; Going Up says it is a closed map (A\&M Ex.~5.1); Going Down says the generizations lift, which geometrically forbids the cover from ``jumping'' to a lower-dimensional sheet. For finite $B$ over $A$, the fibers are finite and nonempty -- a genuine branched covering of $\Spec A$.
\end{remark}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[{finitely many primes over a maximal ideal; D\&F 27}]
If $B$ is integral and finitely generated as a ring over $A$, and $\fm\subseteq A$ is maximal, then the set of maximal ideals $\fq\subseteq B$ with $\fq\cap A=\fm$ is finite and nonempty.
\end{corollary}

Type: example
Title: $Z\subseteqZ[i]$: primes lying over $(p)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z\subseteqZ[i]$: primes lying over $(p)$}
Describe the primes of $Z[i]$ lying over the rational primes $(2),(5),(7)$.
\wrec $Z[i]$ is integral over $Z$ (each $a+bi$ satisfies a monic quadratic); Lying Over guarantees a prime over each $(p)$, and the splitting type is read from $x^2+1\bmod p$.
\wsol Since $Z[i]\congZ[x]/(x^2+1)$, primes over $(p)$ correspond to irreducible factors of $x^2+1$ in $\F_p[x]$. Over $(5)$: $x^2+1=(x-2)(x+2)$, so $(5)$ splits: two primes $(2+i),(2-i)$ lie over it. Over $(2)$: $x^2+1=(x+1)^2$, so $(2)$ ramifies: the single prime $(1+i)$ lies over it with $(2)=(1+i)^2$ up to a unit. Over $(7)$: $x^2+1$ is irreducible mod $7$ ($-1$ is a non-residue), so $(7)$ is inert: $(7)$ stays prime in $Z[i]$. Sanity check: each fiber is finite and nonempty (Corollary), and $\fq\capZ=(p)$ is maximal iff $\fq$ is maximal -- indeed all three primes $(1+i),(2+i),(7)$ are maximal in the Dedekind domain $Z[i]$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Lying Over can fail without monic: $Z\subseteqQ$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Lying Over can fail without monic: $Z\subseteqQ$}
Show $Q$ is not integral over $Z$, and that contraction $\SpecQ\to\SpecZ$ is not surjective.
\wrec Integrality is essential in Lying Over; drop it and surjectivity dies.
\wsol $Q$ is the localization $S^{-1}Z$ at $S=Z\setminus\{0\}$, a non-integral extension ($\tfrac12$ is not integral, Worked Example above). $\SpecQ=\{(0)\}$ has one point, and contraction sends it to $(0)\subseteqZ$; no rational prime $(p)$ is hit. Sanity check: this matches the general principle that localization removes the closed points $V(p)$ -- ``concentrating near the generic point'' -- whereas integral extensions, by contrast, hit every point of the base.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $A$ field iff $B$ field, in action
Content:
\begin{wex}{$A$ field iff $B$ field, in action}
Let $A=k$ a field and $B$ a domain integral over $k$. Show $B$ is a field.
\wrec Apply the direction ``$A$ a field $\Rightarrow$ $B$ a field'' of part~(1) of the theorem; it is the converse direction that kills the polynomial ring inside the Nullstellensatz proof.
\wsol By (1), $A=k$ a field and $B$ a domain integral over $A$ forces $B$ to be a field. Concretely, each $0\neq b\in B$ satisfies $b^n+a_{n-1}b^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0$ with $a_i\in k$; we may take $a_0\neq0$ (cancel powers of $b$ in the domain $B$), and then $b^{-1}=-a_0^{-1}(b^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1)\in B$. Sanity check: if instead $B=k[y]$ (a polynomial ring), then $y$ is transcendental over $k$, so it satisfies no monic equation over $k$ and $k[y]$ is not integral over $k$; correspondingly $B=k[y]$ is not a field -- consistent with the theorem, since its hypothesis fails. The contrapositive ``$B$ not a field $\Rightarrow$ $B$ not integral over the field $k$'' is the direction shown here; what forces $q=0$ in the proof of Zariski's Lemma below is the converse direction of (1): a field that is integral over a subring forces that subring to be a field.
\end{wex}

Content:
To prove the Nullstellensatz we need two algebraic facts. Noether Normalization says every finitely generated algebra over a field is a finite (integral) module over a polynomial subring -- the algebraic form of ``project a variety onto a coordinate subspace as a ramified cover.'' Zariski's Lemma (A\&M Corollary~5.24) says a field that is finitely generated as an algebra over a subfield is finite as an extension, i.e.\ algebraic. Type: definition
Title: algebraic independence
Content:
\begin{definition}[algebraic independence]
Elements $y_1,\dots,y_q$ of a $k$-algebra are algebraically independent over $k$ if no nonzero polynomial $p\in k[X_1,\dots,X_q]$ has $p(y_1,\dots,y_q)=0$; equivalently $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]\cong k[X_1,\dots,X_q]$ as $k$-algebras.
\end{definition}

Title: {Noether Normalization Lemma; D\&F 30}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Noether Normalization Lemma; D\&F 30}]
Let $k$ be a field and $A=k[r_1,\dots,r_m]$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Then there exist $0\le q\le m$ and algebraically independent $y_1,\dots,y_q\in A$ such that $A$ is integral over the polynomial subring $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$.
\end{theorem}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Integral Dependence, Valuation Rings, and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz > Noether normalization and Zariski's lemma
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-ca93e333b2bb805ddc02
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Induct on $m$. If the $r_i$ are algebraically independent, take $y_i=r_i$. Otherwise a nonzero relation $f(r_1,\dots,r_m)=0$ holds. The key move is a change of variables $X_i=x_i-x_m^{\alpha_i}$ with $\alpha_i=(1+d)^i$ (where $d=\deg f$): in base $b=d+1$ the exponents separate, so $g(X_1,\dots,X_{m-1},x_m)=f(X_1+x_m^{\alpha_1},\dots,x_m)$ has a single highest pure power $cx_m^N$. Dividing by $c$ makes $r_m$ monic, hence integral, over $B=k[s_1,\dots,s_{m-1}]$ where $s_i=r_i-r_m^{\alpha_i}$; each $r_i$ ($i<m$) is then integral over $B[r_m]$, so $A$ is integral over $B$ by transitivity. As $B$ is generated by $m-1$ elements, induction finishes.
\end{proof}

Title: {Zariski's Lemma; A\&M Cor.~5.24}

\begin{theorem}[{Zariski's Lemma; A\&M Cor.~5.24}]
Let $k$ be a field and let $L\supseteq k$ be a field that is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra. Then $L$ is a finite (hence algebraic) field extension of $k$.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
By Noether Normalization, $L=k[r_1,\dots,r_m]$ is integral over a polynomial ring $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$. By the ``fields together'' theorem (part~1), since $L$ is a field and integral over the domain $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$, that subring must be a field too. But a polynomial ring in $q\ge1$ variables is never a field. Hence $q=0$, so $L$ is integral over $k$, i.e.\ algebraic, and being finitely generated and algebraic it is finite over $k$.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: A\&M's transcendence-degree proof
Content:
\begin{remark}[A\&M's transcendence-degree proof]
A\&M reach Zariski's Lemma without normalization, via Proposition~5.23 (extending homomorphisms to $\Omega$): if $A\subseteq B$ are domains with $B$ finitely generated over $A$, then there is $0\neq u\in A$ such that, for any algebraically closed $\Omega$, every homomorphism $\varphi:A\to\Omega$ with $\varphi(u)\neq0$ extends to $B$. Applied with $A=k$ and $B=L$ (A\&M Corollary~5.24), the inclusion $k\hookrightarrow\overline k$ extends to a homomorphism $L\to\overline k$, which is injective because $L$ is a field; so $L$ is algebraic over $k$. Both routes deliver the same arithmetic-geometry payoff.
\end{remark}

Title: Normalizing $k[x,y]/(xy-1)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Normalizing $k[x,y]/(xy-1)$}
Exhibit a Noether normalization of $A=k[x,y]/(xy-1)$ (the hyperbola, $\cong k[t,t^{-1}]$).
\wrec Find one algebraically independent element over which $A$ is integral; the relation $xy=1$ must be turned into a monic equation.
\wsol Here $\bar x,\bar y$ satisfy $\bar x\bar y=1$, so they are algebraically dependent ($q<2$). Set $u=\bar x+\bar y$. Then $\bar x,\bar y$ are the two roots of $T^2-uT+1=0$ (since $\bar x+\bar y=u$, $\bar x\bar y=1$), a monic equation over $k[u]$; hence $A=k[u][\bar x]$ is integral over $k[u]$, and $u$ is algebraically independent (transcendental) over $k$. So $q=1$ and $k[u]\hookrightarrow A$ is a normalization. Sanity check: $\dim A=1$ matches $q=1$ (the number of normalizing parameters equals the Krull dimension); and $A=k[t,t^{-1}]$ is indeed integral over $k[t+t^{-1}]$, so the hyperbola is finite over the line with coordinate $u=\bar x+\bar y$ -- but not over the $x$-axis, since $\bar y=\bar x^{-1}$ is not integral over the integrally closed ring $k[\bar x]$.
\end{wex}

Title: Why a polynomial ring is never a field
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why a polynomial ring is never a field}
Verify the step ``$q\ge1\Rightarrow k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$ not a field'' used in Zariski's Lemma.
\wrec A field has every nonzero element invertible; produce a non-invertible element of the polynomial ring.
\wsol In $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$ with $q\ge1$, the element $y_1$ is nonzero but not a unit: if $y_1\cdot g=1$ then comparing degrees gives $1+\deg g=0$, impossible. So $k[y_1,\dots,y_q]$ is not a field. Sanity check: this is precisely why $q=0$ is forced, collapsing $L$ to an algebraic extension of $k$ -- the linchpin of the weak Nullstellensatz.
\end{wex}

Title: Noether normalization of a hypersurface
Content:
\begin{wex}{Noether normalization of a hypersurface}
Normalize $A=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3-x)$ over an infinite field $k$.
\wrec After a linear change ensuring the top-degree form is monic in one variable, that variable becomes integral over the others.
\wsol The relation $y^2=x^3+x$ is monic in $y$ over $k[x]$ ($y^2-(x^3+x)=0$), so $\bar y$ is integral over $k[\bar x]$, and $\bar x$ is transcendental over $k$ (no relation in $x$ alone). Thus $A=k[\bar x][\bar y]$ is integral over $k[\bar x]$ with $q=1$. Sanity check: $A$ is a free $k[\bar x]$-module on $\{1,\bar y\}$ of rank $2$ -- for $\charac k\neq2$ the elliptic curve presents itself as a degree-$2$ ramified cover of the $x$-line, branched where $x^3+x=0$, exactly the ``ramified covering'' picture A\&M opens the chapter with.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {Nullstellensatz, Weak Form; D\&F 31}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Nullstellensatz, Weak Form; D\&F 31}]
Let $k$ be algebraically closed. The maximal ideals of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ are exactly
\[
\fm=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n),\qquad (a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\Aff^n,
\]
so $Z,I$ give a bijection $\{points of \Aff^n\}\longleftrightarrow\{maximal ideals of k[\Aff^n]\}$. Moreover every proper ideal $I$ has $Z(I)\neq\varnothing$.
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-28d145ce180dd94e3b69
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Each $(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$ is maximal (the quotient is $k$). Conversely, for maximal $\fm$, the field $E=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/\fm$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra, so by Zariski's Lemma $E$ is algebraic over $k$; as $k=\overline k$, $E=k$. Thus each $x_i$ maps to some $a_i\in k$, giving $x_i-a_i\in\fm$, whence $\fm=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$. For the last clause, a proper $I$ lies in a maximal $\fm=(x_i-a_i)$, so $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in Z(I)$.
\end{proof}

Title: {Nullstellensatz, Strong Form; D\&F 32}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Nullstellensatz, Strong Form; D\&F 32}]
Let $k$ be algebraically closed. Then for every ideal $I\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$,
\[
I\bigl(Z(I)\bigr)=\rad I,
\]
and $Z,I$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections
\[
\{affine algebraic sets in \Aff^n\}\ \xleftrightarrow[\ Z\ ]{\ I\ }\ \{radical ideals of k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$\rad I\subseteq I(Z(I))$ is clear. For the reverse, the Rabinowitsch trick: given $g\in I(Z(I))$ with $I=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$, the ideal $I'=(f_1,\dots,f_m,x_{n+1}g-1)$ in $k[x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}]$ has empty zero set (wherever the $f_i$ vanish, $g$ vanishes, so $x_{n+1}g-1$ cannot). By the Weak Form, $1\in I'$; writing $1=\sum a_if_i+a_{m+1}(x_{n+1}g-1)$, substituting $x_{n+1}=1/g$ and clearing denominators yields $g^N\in I$, i.e.\ $g\in\rad I$.
\end{proof}

Title: the geometric dictionary, completed
Content:
\begin{remark}[the geometric dictionary, completed]
Combined with $\S15.2$: points $\leftrightarrow$ maximal ideals; irreducible algebraic sets $\leftrightarrow$ prime ideals; algebraic sets $\leftrightarrow$ radical ideals; and unique decomposition of an algebraic set into irreducible components mirrors the unique writing of a radical ideal as an irredundant intersection of finitely many primes (its minimal primes). The Nullstellensatz is the statement that $k[\Aff^n]\rightsquigarrow\Aff^n$ loses no information when $k=\overline k$: geometry and the algebra of $k[\Aff^n]$ are the same subject. The variant for arbitrary $k$ (D\&F Cor.~33) recovers $I_k(Z_{\overline k}(I))=\rad I$ by base-changing to $\overline k$.
\end{remark}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Integral Dependence, Valuation Rings, and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz > Hilbert's Nullstellensatz: the dictionary points $\leftrightarrow$ ideals
Type: prose
Content:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=2.0em]
\{maximal ideals\} \arrow[r,dash] \arrow[d,dash] & \{points of \Aff^n\} \arrow[d,dash] \\
\{prime ideals\} \arrow[r,dash] \arrow[d,dash] & \{irreducible sets\} \arrow[d,dash] \\
\{radical ideals\} \arrow[r,dash,"{Z,\,I}"'] & \{algebraic sets\}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left column lists three nested classes of ideals in $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ ($k$
algebraically closed): maximal ideals $\subseteq$ prime ideals $\subseteq$ radical ideals.
The right column lists the corresponding nested classes of subsets of $\Aff^n$: closed points
$\subseteq$ irreducible closed sets $\subseteq$ arbitrary algebraic sets. Each row is a single
class on each side; the vertical inclusions on both sides record the containment
maximal $\subseteq$ prime $\subseteq$ radical and point $\subseteq$ irreducible $\subseteq$
algebraic set.

\dgi{Arrows:} Every horizontal dash in the diagram stands for the mutually inverse bijections
$Z: I \mapsto \{a\in\Aff^n : f(a)=0 for all f\in I\}$ (zero-set) and
$I: S \mapsto \{f\in k[x_1,\dots,x_n] : f(a)=0 for all a\in S\}$ (ideal of a set).
The label $Z,\,I$ on the bottom horizontal dash makes this explicit.
The vertical dashes are the forgetful inclusions: a maximal ideal is in particular a prime ideal
(a prime ideal is in particular a radical ideal); a point is in particular an irreducible set.
No arrow is an isomorphism of rings or a group homomorphism; each dash is a set-theoretic
bijection between the indicated collections.

\dgi{What commutes:} The diagram commutes in the sense that the bijections $Z$ and $I$ are
compatible with the vertical inclusions: if $\fm$ is a maximal ideal corresponding to
the point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ under the bijection, then reading $\fm$ as a prime ideal
corresponds, under the prime-to-irreducible bijection, to the same point viewed as an
irreducible set; and reading it as a radical ideal corresponds to the same point viewed as an
algebraic set. Concretely: $Z(\fm) = \{(a_1,\dots,a_n)\}$ and
$Z(\fm) = Z(\fm)$ as an algebraic set -- the maps on each row restrict and agree across rows.

\dgi{Why it commutes:} For the top row, the Nullstellensatz Weak Form gives
$\fm = (x_1 - a_1,\dots, x_n - a_n)$ and $Z(\fm) = \{(a_1,\dots,a_n)\}$,
a single point. A single point is irreducible (its ideal is prime) and is an algebraic set
(it is closed), so the single point sits in all three right-column classes. The vertical
nesting is preserved because the three horizontal bijections are restrictions of a single one:
by the Strong Form, $Z$ and $I$ are mutually inverse bijections between radical ideals and
algebraic sets, and under this bijection the maximal ideals correspond to the points (Weak Form)
and the prime ideals to the irreducible sets (a radical ideal is prime iff its zero set is
irreducible).

\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the payoff of the entire section. It records,
in one picture, the two-sided Nullstellensatz dictionary: the Weak Form identifies the top
row (points $\leftrightarrow$ maximal ideals), the remark on irreducible components extends
it to the middle row (irreducible sets $\leftrightarrow$ prime ideals), and the Strong Form
($I(Z(I)) = \rad I$) closes the bottom row. It also shows that $Z$ and $I$ are not
just a random pair of maps but a hierarchy-preserving correspondence -- the geometry of
$\Aff^n$ and the algebra of $k[\Aff^n]$ are the same ordered structure.

\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $n=1$, $k=C$. Maximal ideals of $C[x]$: $(x-a)$ for $a\inC$;
corresponding points: $\{a\} \subset \Aff^1$. Prime ideals: $(0)$ and $(x-a)$; irreducible
sets: $\Aff^1$ itself (corresponding to $(0)$, the generic point) and individual points.
Radical ideals: $(0)$ and the ideals $((x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_r))=(x-a_1)\cap\cdots\cap(x-a_r)$
with $a_1,\dots,a_r$ distinct ($r=0$ giving $(1)$); algebraic sets: $\Aff^1=Z((0))$ and the finite
subsets $\{a_1,\dots,a_r\}$ of $C$. In each row $Z$ and $I$ are mutually inverse, and the vertical
inclusions on both sides are the natural ones.

\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the dashes as isomorphisms of rings, or think
$Z$ is a ring map. It is not: $Z$ sends ideals to sets of points, and $I$ sends sets
to ideals, so the bijections live at the level of collections of subsets, not ring
homomorphisms. A second pitfall: the middle row (prime $\leftrightarrow$ irreducible) is
not stated in the two Nullstellensatz theorems above; it follows from combining the
Strong Form with the general fact that a radical ideal is prime iff the algebraic set is
irreducible. Do not cite the Nullstellensatz alone for the prime/irreducible bijection.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the Nullstellensatz makes the entire
three-level hierarchy of ideals (maximal, prime, radical) in $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ mirror-image
the entire three-level hierarchy of geometric objects (points, irreducible varieties,
algebraic sets) in $\Aff^n$, with $Z$ and $I$ as the explicit, mutually inverse dictionaries.
\end{dgx}

Title: Maximal ideals of $C[x,y]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Maximal ideals of $C[x,y]$}
List the maximal ideals of $C[x,y]$ and identify the one at the origin.
\wrec $C$ is algebraically closed, so the Weak Nullstellensatz applies: maximal ideals are points.
\wsol Every maximal ideal of $C[x,y]$ has the form $(x-a,y-b)$ for a unique $(a,b)\inC^2$, with quotient $C[x,y]/(x-a,y-b)\congC$ via $x\mapsto a,\ y\mapsto b$. The origin corresponds to $(x,y)$. Sanity check: $(x-a,y-b)$ is the kernel of evaluation $\operatorname{ev}_{(a,b)}:C[x,y]\toC$, a surjection onto a field, so the kernel is maximal; and distinct points give distinct kernels, so the correspondence is a bijection.
\end{wex}

Title: Weak Form fails over $R$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Weak Form fails over $R$}
Show $(x^2+1)\subseteqR[x]$ is maximal but not of the form $(x-a)$.
\wrec Algebraic closure is essential; over $R$, $E=R[x]/\fm$ may be a proper algebraic extension of $R$.
\wsol $R[x]/(x^2+1)\congC$ is a field, so $(x^2+1)$ is maximal, yet it is not $(x-a)$ for any $a\inR$ (it has no real root). The Weak Nullstellensatz fails because $R\neq\overlineR$: here $E=C$ is algebraic over $R$ of degree $2$ but $\neqR$. Sanity check: over $C$, $x^2+1=(x-i)(x+i)$ factors and the two maximal ideals $(x-i),(x+i)$ are points -- the obstruction is purely the failure of $R$ to be algebraically closed.
\end{wex}

Title: $I(Z(I))=\rad I$ on a concrete ideal
Content:
\begin{wex}{$I(Z(I))=\rad I$ on a concrete ideal}
For $I=(x^2,y)\subseteqC[x,y]$, compute $Z(I)$, $I(Z(I))$, and $\rad I$, and check equality.
\wrec Compute the zero set, take the ideal of that set, and independently compute the radical; the Strong Form predicts they match.
\wsol $Z(I)=\{(x,y):x^2=0,\ y=0\}=\{(0,0)\}$, the origin. Then $I(Z(I))=I(\{(0,0)\})=(x,y)$, the maximal ideal at the origin. Independently $\rad(x^2,y)=(x,y)$: $x\in\rad I$ since $x^2\in I$, and $(x,y)$ is already prime (quotient $\congC$) hence radical, and contains $I$. So $I(Z(I))=(x,y)=\rad I$. Sanity check: $I=(x^2,y)\subsetneq(x,y)=\rad I$ is a strict containment -- the non-reducedness $x^2$ (a ``double point'' / embedded thickening) is invisible to $Z$, exactly what passing to the radical erases.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
A\&M's deepest structural result here is that the integral closure of a domain $A$ in a field $K$ is the intersection of all valuation rings of $K$ containing $A$. Valuation rings are the maximal local rings under dominance, the local incarnation of ``a point on a curve,'' and they encode orders of vanishing. This section develops them and closes the circle back to $\S15.2$'s geometry: a Noetherian normal domain is the ring of functions regular at every codimension-one point.

Type: definition
Title: valuation ring; dominance
Content:
\begin{definition}[valuation ring; dominance]
Let $K$ be a field. A subring $B\subseteq K$ is a valuation ring of $K$ if for every $0\neq x\in K$, at least one of $x,\ x^{-1}$ lies in $B$. Given local rings $A\subseteq B$ with maximal ideals $\fm_A,\fm_B$, we say $B$ dominates $A$ if $A\subseteq B$ and $\fm_B\cap A=\fm_A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
(i): if $x,y$ are non-units, then $x/y$ or $y/x\in B$, say $x/y\in B$, whence $x+y=(1+x/y)y\in By\subseteq\fm$; and $ax\in\fm$ for $a\in B$; so $\fm$ is an ideal, the unique maximal one. (ii): immediate from the definition, since $x$ or $x^{-1}$ already lies in $B\subseteq B'$. (iii): if $x\in K$ is integral over $B$, $x^n+b_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+b_0=0$; if $x\notin B$ then $x^{-1}\in B$, and multiplying by $x^{-(n-1)}$ gives $x=-(b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}x^{-1}+\cdots+b_0x^{-(n-1)})\in B$, a contradiction. So $x\in B$.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: {maximal dominated rings are valuation rings; A\&M 5.19--5.21}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{maximal dominated rings are valuation rings; A\&M 5.19--5.21}]
Let $K$ be a field, $\Omega$ an algebraically closed field, and let $\Sigma$ be the set of pairs $(A,f)$ with $A$ a subring of $K$ and $f:A\to\Omega$ a homomorphism, ordered by extension. A maximal element $(B,g)\in\Sigma$ has $B$ a valuation ring of $K$, with maximal ideal $\ker g$. Equivalently: the rings dominating a given local subring of $K$ have, among them, valuation rings as the maximal elements under dominance.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Zorn's Lemma gives a maximal $(B,g)$; $\fm=\ker g$ is prime in $B$ since $g(B)\subseteq\Omega$ is a domain inside a field; $g$ extends to $B_\fm$, so maximality forces $B=B_\fm$, a local ring with maximal ideal $\fm$ (Lemma 5.19). For $x\neq0$ in $K$, comparing the extensions of $\fm$ in $B[x]$ and $B[x^{-1}]$ shows at least one is proper, so $g$ extends to $B[x]$ or $B[x^{-1}]$ (Lemma 5.20); maximality forces $x\in B$ or $x^{-1}\in B$. Hence $B$ is a valuation ring.
\end{proof}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Integral Dependence, Valuation Rings, and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz > Valuation rings and the integral closure as an intersection
Type: theorem
Title: {integral closure $=$ intersection of valuation rings; A\&M 5.22}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{integral closure $=$ intersection of valuation rings; A\&M 5.22}]
Let $A$ be a subring of a field $K$. Then the integral closure $\overline A$ of $A$ in $K$ is the intersection of all valuation rings of $K$ that contain $A$:
\[
\overline A=\bigcap_{\substack{B\ valuation ring of K\\ A\subseteq B}}B.
\]
In particular, $A$ is integrally closed in $K$ iff $A$ is an intersection of valuation rings.
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
($\subseteq$) Every valuation ring $B\supseteq A$ is integrally closed (Prop.~5.18(iii)) and contains $A$, hence contains $\overline A$. ($\supseteq$) If $x\in K$ is not integral over $A$, then $x^{-1}$ is a non-unit in $A'=A[x^{-1}]$, so $x^{-1}$ lies in a maximal ideal $\fm'$; extending the residue map $A'\to A'/\fm'\hookrightarrow\Omega$ to a maximal pair gives a valuation ring $B\supseteq A$ with $x^{-1}\in\fm_B$, so $x\notin B$. Thus anything in every such $B$ is integral.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Title: orders of vanishing; tie-back to $\S15.2$
Content:
\begin{remark}[orders of vanishing; tie-back to $\S15.2$]
A valuation ring of $k(C)$ (the function field of a curve) records, at a chosen point $P$, the order of vanishing of a rational function: $B=\{f:\operatorname{ord}_P(f)\ge0\}$ with maximal ideal $\{f:\operatorname{ord}_P(f)>0\}$. Dominance ``$B$ dominates the local ring $\mathcal O_{C,P}$'' is the algebraic statement ``the valuation is centered at $P$.'' The theorem then reads: a function is integral over the coordinate ring iff it has nonnegative order at every point -- i.e.\ regular functions are those with no poles, the bridge from this section's integrality to the $\S15.2$ geometry of $Z(\cdot)$ and normal varieties.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: $Z_{(p)}$ is a valuation ring of $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z_{(p)}$ is a valuation ring of $Q$}
Show the localization $Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\inQ:p\nmid b\}$ is a valuation ring of $Q$, and identify its valuation.
\wrec Check the defining dichotomy $x$ or $x^{-1}\in B$ via the $p$-adic valuation $v_p$.
\wsol Write $0\neq x=p^n\cdot u$ with $u\inQ^\times$ a unit at $p$ (numerator and denominator prime to $p$); set $v_p(x)=n$. Then $x\inZ_{(p)}\iff v_p(x)\ge0$, and $x^{-1}$ has $v_p(x^{-1})=-n$, so exactly one of $v_p(x),v_p(x^{-1})$ is $\ge0$ (both if $n=0$). Hence $x$ or $x^{-1}\inZ_{(p)}$: it is a valuation ring. Its maximal ideal is $pZ_{(p)}=\{x:v_p(x)>0\}$. Sanity check: $Z_{(p)}$ is local with residue field $\F_p$, and it is integrally closed (it is a localization of the UFD $Z$), matching Prop.~5.18(iii). The ``point'' it centers on is the prime $(p)\in\SpecZ$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $k[x]_{(x)}$ as order of vanishing at $0$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$k[x]_{(x)}$ as order of vanishing at $0$}
Identify the valuation ring $k[x]_{(x)}\subseteq k(x)$ and its valuation geometrically.
\wrec The local ring of the line at the origin records vanishing order at $x=0$.
\wsol $B=k[x]_{(x)}=\{f/g:g(0)\neq0\}$. For $0\neq h\in k(x)$ write $h=x^n\cdot(p/q)$ with $p(0),q(0)\neq0$; then $\operatorname{ord}_0(h)=n$ and $h\in B\iff n\ge0$. So $h$ or $h^{-1}\in B$ always, and $B$ is the valuation ring of order-of-vanishing at the origin, with maximal ideal $(x)$ and residue field $k$. Sanity check: a rational function lies in $B$ iff it has no pole at $0$ -- ``regular at the origin'' -- the local-ring picture from $\S15.5$ realized as a valuation; and $\bigcap_{a\in k}k[x]_{(x-a)}\supseteq k[x]$ recovers global regularity as ``regular at every point.''
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-valuation subring
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-valuation subring}
Show $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is local but not a valuation ring of $k(x,y)$.
\wrec Test the dichotomy on $x/y$: a valuation ring must contain $x/y$ or $y/x$.
\wsol The element $x/y\in k(x,y)$ is not in $B=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ (its denominator $y$ vanishes at the maximal ideal's point), and neither is $y/x$. So $B$ fails the valuation dichotomy: $B$ is a local ring that is not a valuation ring. Sanity check: this reflects that the local ring of the plane at the origin has dimension $2$, whereas a rank-one (discrete) valuation records only codimension-one (order-one) data; one must blow up or pass to a curve through the origin to obtain an honest valuation dominating $B$ -- consistent with A\&M~5.21, where valuation rings arise as maximal dominating rings, not arbitrary local rings.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $Z$ as an intersection of valuation rings
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z$ as an intersection of valuation rings}
Express $Z$ as an intersection of valuation rings of $Q$, illustrating Theorem 5.22.
\wrec $Z$ is integrally closed in $Q$ (it is a UFD), so it must equal an intersection of valuation rings; the $Z_{(p)}$ are the natural candidates.
\wsol $\bigcap_{p\ prime}Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\inQ:p\nmid b for all p\}=\{a/b:b=\pm1\}=Z$. Each $Z_{(p)}$ is a valuation ring containing $Z$ (previous Worked Example), and an element of $Q$ lies in all of them iff its reduced denominator has no prime factor, i.e.\ is a unit. Sanity check: this is Theorem 5.22 with $A=K\capZ=Z$ already integrally closed -- $\overlineZ=Z=\bigcap_pZ_{(p)}$ -- and geometrically it says ``an integer is a rational function on $\SpecZ$ with no poles at any prime,'' the arithmetic analogue of a regular function on a curve.
\end{wex}

Title: Going Down over a normal base, in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Going Down over a normal base, in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Illustrate that normality of the base is what powers Going Down, using $Z\subseteqZ[\sqrt{-5}]$.
\wrec Going Down needs $A$ integrally closed in its fraction field (normal), not in $B$; $Z$ is normal, so chains descend.
\wsol $Z$ is integrally closed (UFD), and $Z[\sqrt{-5}]=\mathcal O_{Q(\sqrt{-5})}$ (here $-5\equiv3\bmod4$) is integral over $Z$. Take the chain $(2)\supseteq(0)$ in $Z$ and a prime $\fq_1=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ over $(2)$. Going Down completes it downward: there is $\fq_2\subseteq\fq_1$ with $\fq_2\capZ=(0)$, namely $\fq_2=(0)$ itself (a prime of the domain $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ contracting to $(0)$). Sanity check: had $A$ been non-normal the descent could fail in general, but for this short chain the lower prime is automatic -- $\fq_2=(0)$ lies over $(0)$ simply because $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain -- and no valuation ring is involved; the hypothesis ``$A$ integrally closed'' of A\&M's Theorem~5.16 enters the general proof through A\&M 5.15. Note $\fq_1^2=(2)$ here since $(2)$ ramifies as $(2)=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})^2$, consistent with $2$ being a ramified (non-split) prime.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Integral closure of $k[x^2,x^3]$ via the valuation criterion
Content:
\begin{wex}{Integral closure of $k[x^2,x^3]$ via the valuation criterion}
Confirm the normalization of $A=k[x^2,x^3]$ is $k[x]$ using Theorem 5.22's ``no poles'' reading.
\wrec An element of $k(x)=\Frac(A)$ is in $\overline A$ iff it lies in every valuation ring of $k(x)$ containing $A$; equivalently, it is a polynomial (no poles).
\wsol $\Frac(A)=k(x)$ since $x=x^3/x^2\in\Frac(A)$. The nontrivial valuation rings of $k(x)/k$ are the localizations $k[x]_{(p)}$ at the monic irreducibles $p\in k[x]$ (the finite places, of which the $k[x]_{(x-a)}$ are the degree-one ones) together with the order-at-infinity ring $\{f/g:\deg f\le\deg g\}$; an element regular at every finite place and at infinity is a constant, but the ring at infinity does not contain $A$ ($x^2$ has a pole at infinity), so the valuation rings containing $A$ are $k(x)$ and the finite ones, leaving exactly the polynomials regular at all finite places: $\overline A=\bigcap_{p\ monic\ irred.}k[x]_{(p)}=k[x]$. Indeed $x=x^3/x^2$ is integral over $A$ ($x$ satisfies $T^2-x^2=0$). Sanity check: $A=k[x^2,x^3]=k[s,t]/(t^2-s^3)$ is the cusp again; its normalization $k[x]$ smooths the cusp, matching the earlier direct computation and the geometric slogan ``normalize $=$ remove the singularity by demanding no poles.''
\end{wex}
