Title: Algebraic integers form a ring -- without finding a formula
Content:
\begin{wex}{Algebraic integers form a ring -- without finding a formula}
Show $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ is an algebraic integer, using the ``integral closure is a ring'' corollary rather than computing a minimal polynomial by hand first.
\wrec Sums and products of integral elements are integral (Corollary), so it suffices that $\sqrt2,\sqrt3$ are integral.
\wsol $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3$ are integral over $Z$ (roots of $x^2-2,\ x^2-3$), and the integral closure $\overlineZ$ in $\overlineQ$ is a ring, so $\sqrt2+\sqrt3\in\overlineZ$ is an algebraic integer. To exhibit a witness: $\alpha=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ gives $\alpha^2=5+2\sqrt6$, so $(\alpha^2-5)^2=24$, i.e.\ $\alpha^4-10\alpha^2+1=0$, monic over $Z$. Sanity check: the abstract closure-is-a-ring argument predicts integrality before any computation; the explicit quartic $x^4-10x^2+1$ confirms it and is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ over $Q$, with integer coefficients as Proposition~28 demands.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 1/3
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Use the fact that a U.F.D. is integrally closed to prove that the Gaussian integers $Z[i]$ is the ring of integers in $Q(i)$.

\item Suppose $k$ is a field and let $t = x/y$ in the field of fractions of the integral domain $R = k[x,y]/(x^2 - y^3)$. Prove that $K = k(t)$ is the fraction field of $R$ and $k[t]$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $K$.

\item Suppose $k$ is a field and $i$ and $j$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find the normalization of the integral domain $R = k[x,y]/(x^i - y^j)$ (cf.\ Exercise 14, Section 9.1).

\item Suppose $k$ is a field and let $P$ be the ideal $(y^2 - x^3 - x^2)$ in the polynomial ring $k[x,y]$. Prove that $P$ is a prime ideal and find the normalization of the integral domain $R = k[x,y]/P$. [To prove $P$ is prime, show that $y^2 - x^3 - x^2$ is irreducible in the U.F.D.\ $k[x,y]$. Then consider $t = y/x$ in the field of fractions of $R$.]

\item If $R$ is an integral domain with field of fractions $F$, show that $F$ is a finitely generated $R$-module if and only if $R = F$.

\item For each of the following give specific rings $R \subseteq S$ and explicit ideals in these rings that exhibit the specified relation:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] an ideal $I$ of $R$ such that $I \neq IS \cap R$ (so the contraction of the extension of an ideal $I$ need not equal $I$);
\item[(b)] a prime ideal $P$ of $R$ such that there is no prime ideal $Q$ of $S$ with $P = Q \cap R$;
\item[(c)] a maximal ideal $M$ of $S$ such that $M \cap R$ is not maximal in $R$;
\item[(d)] a prime ideal $P$ of $R$ whose extension $PS$ to $S$ is not a prime ideal in $S$;
\item[(e)] an ideal $J$ of $S$ such that $J \neq (J \cap R)S$ (so the extension of the contraction of an ideal $J$ need not equal $J$).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $O_K$ be the ring of integers in a number field $K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose that every nonzero ideal $I$ of $O_K$ can be written as the product of powers of prime ideals. Prove that an ideal $Q$ of $O_K$ is $P$-primary if and only if $Q = P^m$ for some $m \geq 1$. [Show first that since nonzero primes in $O_K$ are maximal that $P_1^{m_1} \subseteq P_2^{m_2}$ for distinct nonzero primes $P_1, P_2$ implies $P_1 = P_2$.]
\item[(b)] Suppose that an ideal $Q$ of $O_K$ is $P$-primary if and only if $Q = P^m$ for some $m \geq 1$. Assuming all of Theorem 21, prove that every nonzero ideal $I$ of $O_K$ can be written uniquely as the product of powers of prime ideals. [Prove that $P_1^{m_1}$ and $P_2^{m_2}$ are comaximal ideals if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are distinct nonzero prime ideals and use the Chinese Remainder Theorem.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that if $s_1, \ldots, s_n \in S$ are integral over $R$, then the ring $R[s_1, \ldots, s_n]$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.

\item Suppose that $S$ is integral over $R$ and that $P$ is a prime ideal in $R$. Prove that every element $s$ in the ideal $PS$ generated by $P$ in $S$ satisfies an equation $s^n + a_{n-1}s^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1 s + a_0 = 0$ where the coefficients $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ are elements of $P$. [If $s = p_1 s_1 + \cdots + p_m s_m \in PS$, show that $T = R[s_1, \ldots, s_m]$ satisfies the hypotheses in Proposition 23(3). Follow the proof in Proposition 23 that $s$ is integral, noting that $s \in PT$ so that the $a_{ij}$ are elements of $P$.]

\item Prove the following generalization of Proposition 28: Suppose $R$ is an integrally closed integral domain with field of fractions $k$ and $\alpha$ is an element of an extension field $K$ of $k$. Show that $\alpha$ is integral over $R$ if and only if $\alpha$ is algebraic over $k$ and the minimal polynomial $m_{\alpha,k}(x)$ for $\alpha$ over $k$ has coefficients in $R$. [If $\alpha$ is integral prove the conjugates of $\alpha$, i.e., the roots of $m_{\alpha,k}(x)$, are also integral, so the elementary symmetric functions of the conjugates are elements of $k$ that are integral over $R$.]

\item Suppose $R$ is an integrally closed integral domain with field of fractions $k$ and $p(x) \in R[x]$ is a monic polynomial. Show that if $p(x) = a(x)b(x)$ with monic polynomials $a(x), b(x) \in k[x]$ then $a(x), b(x) \in R[x]$ (compare to Gauss' Lemma, Proposition 5, Section 9.3). [See the previous exercise.]

\item Suppose $S$ is an integral domain that is integral over a ring $R$ as in the previous exercise. If $P$ is a prime ideal in $R$, let $s$ be any element in the ideal $PS$ generated by $P$ in $S$. Prove that, with the exception of the leading term, the coefficients of the minimal polynomial $m_{s,k}(x)$ for $s$ over $k$ are elements of $P$. [By Exercise 10, $m_{s,k}(x) \in R[x]$. Exercise 9 shows that $s$ is a root of a monic polynomial $p(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_0$ with $a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1} \in P$. Use the previous exercise to show that $p(x) = m_{s,k}(x)b(x)$ with $b(x)$ in $R[x]$, and consider this equation in the integral domain $(R/P)[x]$.]

\item Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $A$ be a subring of $K$ maximal with respect to $1/2 \notin A$. (Such $A$ exists by Zorn's Lemma.) Let $F$ be the field of fractions of $A$ in $K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $K$ is algebraic over $F$. [If $t$ is transcendental over $F$, show that $1/2 \notin A[t]$.]
\item[(b)] Show that $A$ is integrally closed in $K$. [Show that $1/2$ is not in the integral closure of $A$ in $K$.]
\item[(c)] Deduce from (a) and (b) that $K = F$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Show that a field $K$ is the field of fractions of some proper subring of $K$ if and only if $K$ is not a subfield of the algebraic closure of a finite field. [If $K$ contains $t$ transcendental over $\F_p$ argue as in the preceding exercise with $1/t$ in place of $1/2$ to show that $K$ is the quotient field of some proper subring.]

\item Let $V$ be an affine algebraic set over an algebraically closed field $k$.

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 2/3
Content:
Prove that for some $n$ there is a surjective morphism from $V$ onto $\Aff^n$ with finite fibers, and that if $V$ is a variety, then $n$ can be taken to be the dimension of $V$. [By Noether's Normalization Lemma the finitely generated $k$-algebra $S = k[V]$ contains a polynomial subalgebra $R = k[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]$ such that $S$ is integral over $R$. Apply Theorem 6 to the inclusion of $R$ in $S$ to obtain a morphism $\varphi$ from $V$ to $\Aff^n$. To see that $\varphi$ is surjective with finite fibers, apply Corollary 27 to the maximal ideal $(x_1 - a_1, \ldots, x_n - a_n)$ of $R$ corresponding to a point $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ of $\Aff^n$.]

\item Let $V$ be an affine algebraic set in $C^n$. Prove that $V$ is compact in the Euclidean topology (i.e., closed and bounded) if and only if it is finite. [Use Exercise 18 in Section 2, the previous exercise, and the behavior of compact sets with respect to continuous functions.]

\item Let $R$ be a subring of the commutative ring $S$ with $1_S \in R$ and suppose that $S$ is integral over $R$. This exercise proves that $R$ and $S$ have the same Krull dimension, cf.\ Section 16.1.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $P_1 \subset P_2 \subset \cdots \subset P_n$ is a chain of distinct prime ideals in $R$ prove that there is a chain $Q_1 \subset Q_2 \subset \cdots \subset Q_n$ of distinct prime ideals in $S$ with $Q_i \cap R = P_i$.
\item[(b)] Prove conversely that if $Q_1 \subset Q_2 \subset \cdots \subset Q_n$ is a chain of distinct prime ideals in $S$ and $P_i = Q_i \cap R$ then $P_1 \subset P_2 \subset \cdots \subset P_n$ is a chain of distinct prime ideals in $R$. [To prove the $P_i$ are distinct, pass to a quotient and reduce the problem to showing that if $Q$ is a nonzero prime ideal in the integral domain $S$ then $Q \cap R$ is a nonzero prime ideal in $R$. In this case, if $s \in Q$ is nonzero, show that the constant coefficient of a polynomial of minimal degree in $R[x]$ satisfied by $s$ is a nonzero element in $Q \cap R$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $V = Z(I)$ and $W = Z(J)$ where $I$ is the ideal $(uv + v) \subseteq C[u,v]$ and $J$ is the ideal $(-2y - y^2 + 2z + z^2,\ 2x - yz - z^2) \subseteq C[x,y,z]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $I$ and $J$ are radical ideals that are not prime. Conclude that $I = I(V)$ and $J = I(W)$ and that $V$ and $W$ are reducible algebraic sets.
\item[(b)] Show that the map $\varphi : V \to W$ defined by $\varphi((a_1, a_2)) = (a_1^2 + a_2,\ a_1 + a_2,\ a_1 - a_2)$ is an isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I = (x^3 + y^3 + z^3,\ x^2 + y^2 + z^2,\ (x + y + z)^3) \subseteq k[x,y,z]$. Use Grobner bases to show that $x, y, z \in \rad I$ if $\charac(k) \neq 2, 3$.

\item Let $I = (x^3 + y^3 + z^3,\ xy + xz + yz,\ xyz) \subseteq k[x,y,z]$. Use Grobner bases to show that $x, y, z \in \rad I$.

\item Let $I = (x^4 + y^4 + z^4,\ x + y + z) \subseteq k[x,y,z]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Use Grobner bases to show that $xy + xz + yz \in \rad I$ if $\charac(k) \neq 2$ and determine the smallest power of $xy + xz + yz$ contained in $I$. Show that none of $x$, $y$ or $z$ is contained in $\rad I$.
\item[(b)] If $J = (x^4 + y^4 + z^4,\ x + y + z,\ xy + xz + yz)$ show that the reduced Grobner basis of $J$ relative to the lexicographic ordering $x > y > z$ is $\{x + y + z,\ y^2 + yz + z^2\}$. Deduce that $k[x,y,z]/J \cong k[y,z]/(y^2 + yz + z^2)$ and that $J$ is radical if $\charac(k) \neq 3$.
\item[(c)] If $\charac(k) \neq 2, 3$, show that $\rad I = J$.
\item[(d)] If $\charac(k) = 3$, show that $\rad I = (x - y,\ y - z)$.
\item[(e)] If $\charac(k) = 2$, show that $I = (x + y + z)$ is a prime, hence radical, ideal.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I = (x^2 y + z^3,\ x + y^3 - z,\ 2y^4 z - yz^2 - z^3) \subseteq k[x,y,z]$. Use Grobner bases to show that $x, y, z \in \rad I$ and conclude that $\rad I = (x, y, z)$. Show that $x^9, y^7, z^9$ are the smallest powers of $x$, $y$, $z$, respectively, lying in $I$.

\item Let $V = Z(x^3 - x^2 z - y^2 z)$ and $W = Z(x^2 + y^2 - z^2)$ in $C^3$. Show that $I(V) = (x^3 - x^2 z - y^2 z)$ and $I(W) = (x^2 + y^2 - z^2)$ in $C[x,y,z]$.

\item Let $V = Z(x^3 + y^3 + 7z^3) \subseteq C^3$. Show that $I(V) = (x^3 + y^3 + 7z^3)$ in $C[x,y,z]$.

\item Let $I = (xz + y^2 + z^2,\ xy - xz + yz - 2z^2)$ and let $K = I + (x^2 - 3y^2 + yz) \subseteq C[x,y,z]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] By Exercise 46 in Section 1, there is an injective $C$-algebra homomorphism from $C[x,y,z]/K$ to $C[u,v]/(u^3 - uv^2 + v^3)$. Use this together with the example preceding Proposition 34 to prove that $K$ is a radical ideal and deduce that $\rad I \subseteq K$.
\item[(b)] Show that $\rad I \subseteq (y, z)$.
\item[(c)] Show that $K \cap (y, z) = I$ and deduce that $I$ is radical, so that $I(V) = I$ if $V = Z(I)$.
\item[(d)] Show that $y(x^2 - 3y^2 + yz)$ and $z(x^2 - 3y^2 + yz)$ are elements of $I$ but none of $y$, $z$, or $x^2 - 3y^2 + yz$ is contained in $I$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $I$ be an ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Prove that the following are equivalent (an ideal satisfying any of these conditions is called a zero-dimensional ideal because of (d)):
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The quotient $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/I$ has finite dimension as a vector space over $k$.
\item[(b)] $I \cap k[x_i] \neq 0$ for each $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.
\item[(c)] If $G$ is any reduced Grobner basis for $I$ then for each $i = 1, \ldots, n$, there is a $g_i \in G$ with leading term $x_i^{n_i}$ for some $n_i \geq 1$.
\item[(d)] The set of common zeros $Z_{\bar{k}}(I)$ of the polynomials in $I$ in an algebraic closure $\bar{k}$ of $k$ is finite.
\end{enumerate}
[For (a) implies (b) use the injection $k[x_i]/(I \cap k[x_i]) \to k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/I$. For (b) implies (c) note some $LT(g_i)$ divides the leading term of a generator for $I \cap k[x_i]$.

\begin{enumerate}

\item[(b)] If $J = (x^4 + y^4 + z^4,\ x + y + z,\ xy + xz + yz)$ show that the reduced Grobner basis of $J$ relative to the lexicographic ordering $x > y > z$ is $\{x + y + z,\ y^2 + yz + z^2\}$. Deduce that $k[x,y,z]/J \cong k[y,z]/(y^2 + yz + z^2)$ and that $J$ is radical if $\charac(k) \neq 3$.
\item[(c)] If $\charac(k) \neq 2, 3$, show that $\rad I = J$.
\item[(d)] If $\charac(k) = 3$, show that $\rad I = (x - y,\ y - z)$.
\item[(e)] If $\charac(k) = 2$, show that $I = (x + y + z)$ is a prime, hence radical, ideal.

\item Let $I = (xz + y^2 + z^2,\ xy - xz + yz - 2z^2)$ and let $K = I + (x^2 - 3y^2 + yz) \subseteq \mathbb{C}[x,y,z]$.

For (c) implies (a) use Exercise 37 in Section 9.6. Show (b) implies (d). For (d) implies (b) show the product $m_{a_1,k}(x_i) \cdots m_{a_N,k}(x_i)$ of the minimal polynomials of the $i$th coordinates $a_1, \ldots, a_N$ of the points in $Z_{\bar{k}}(I)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $I(Z_{\bar{k}}(I))$ and apply Corollary 33.]

\item Let $I$ be a zero-dimensional ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ and let $I'$ be the ideal generated by $I$ in $\bar{k}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ where $\bar{k}$ is the algebraic closure of $k$. Let $Z(I)$ be the zero set of $I$ in $k^n$ and let $Z_{\bar{k}}(I)$ be the zero set of $I$ (equivalently, of $I'$) in $\bar{k}^n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $\abs{Z_{\bar{k}}(I)} = \dim_{\bar{k}} \bar{k}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/\rad I'$. [Show that $\rad I'$ is the product of the maximal ideals corresponding to the points in $Z_{\bar{k}}$ and use the Chinese Remainder Theorem.]
\item[(b)] Show $\abs{Z(I)} \leq \dim_k k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/I$. [One approach: use Exercise 43 in Section 1 and observe that $\dim_{\bar{k}} \bar{k}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/\rad I' \leq \dim_{\bar{k}} \bar{k}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/I'$.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $I$ is a zero-dimensional ideal in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$, and suppose $I \cap k[x_i]$ is generated by the nonzero polynomial $h_i$ (cf.\ Exercise 26). Let $r_i$ be the product of the irreducible factors of $h_i$ (the `squarefree part' of $h_i$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $I + (r_1, \ldots, r_n) \subseteq \rad I$.
\item[(b)] (Radicals of zero-dimensional ideals for perfect fields) If $k$ is a perfect field, prove that $\rad I = I + (r_1, \ldots, r_n)$. [Use induction on $n$. Write $r_1 = p_1 \cdots p_\ell$ with distinct irreducibles $p_i$ in $k[x_1]$. If $J = I + (r_1, \ldots, r_n)$ show that $J = J_1 \cap \cdots \cap J_\ell$ where $J_i = I + (p_i)$. Show for each $i$ that reduction modulo $p_i$ induces an isomorphism $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/J_i \cong K[x_2, \ldots, x_n]/J_i'$ where $K$ is the extension field $k[x]/(p_i)$ and $J_i' \subseteq K[x_2, \ldots, x_n]$ is the reduction of the ideal $J_i$ modulo $(p_i)$. Use Exercise 11 of Section 13.5 to show that the image of $r_j$ in $J_i' \cap K[x_j]$ remains a nonzero squarefree polynomial for each $j = 2, \ldots, n$ since $k$ is perfect. Conclude by induction that $J_i'$ is a radical ideal. Deduce that $J_i$ is a radical ideal, and finally that $J$ is a radical ideal.]
\item[(c)] Find the radicals of $(x^7 + x + y^3,\ x^4 + y^3 + y)$, $(x^3 - xy^2 + x,\ x^2 y + y^3)$, and $(x^4 + y^3,\ x^3 - xy + y^2)$ in $Q[x,y]$ and of $(x^2 + y^2 z,\ x^2 y^2 + z^3,\ y^2 + z^2)$ in $Q[x,y,z]$.
\item[(d)] Let $k = \F_p(t)$. Show that $I = (x^p + t,\ y^p - t)$ is a zero-dimensional ideal in $k[x,y]$ such that both $I \cap k[x]$ and $I \cap k[y]$ contain nonzero squarefree polynomials, but that $I$ is not a radical ideal (so the result in (b) need not hold if $k$ is not perfect). [Show that $x + y \in \rad I$ but $x + y \notin I$.]
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).}
\item Let $f : A \to B$ be an integral homomorphism of rings. Show that $f^* : \Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ is a closed mapping, i.e.\ that it maps closed sets to closed sets. (This is a geometrical equivalent of (5.10).)

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a ring $B$ such that $B$ is integral over $A$, and let $f : A \to \Omega$ be a homomorphism of $A$ into an algebraically closed field $\Omega$. Show that $f$ can be extended to a homomorphism of $B$ into $\Omega$. [Use (5.10).]

\item Let $f : B \to B'$ be a homomorphism of $A$-algebras, and let $C$ be an $A$-algebra. If $f$ is integral, prove that $f \otimes 1 : B \otimes_A C \to B' \otimes_A C$ is integral. (This includes (5.6)(ii) as a special case.)

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a ring $B$ such that $B$ is integral over $A$. Let $\fn$ be a maximal ideal of $B$ and let $\fm = \fn \cap A$ be the corresponding maximal ideal of $A$. Is $B_{\fn}$ necessarily integral over $A_{\fm}$? [Consider the subring $k[x^2 - 1]$ of $k[x]$, where $k$ is a field, and let $\fn = (x - 1)$. Can the localization $1/(x + 1)$ be integral?]

\item Let $A \subseteq B$ be rings, $B$ integral over $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If $x \in A$ is a unit in $B$ then it is a unit in $A$.
\item[(ii)] The Jacobson radical of $A$ is the contraction of the Jacobson radical of $B$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ be integral $A$-algebras. Show that $\prod_{i=1}^{n} B_i$ is an integral $A$-algebra.

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a ring $B$, such that the set $B - A$ is closed under multiplication. Show that $A$ is integrally closed in $B$.

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Let $A$ be a subring of an integral domain $B$, and let $C$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. Let $f, g$ be monic polynomials in $B[x]$ such that $fg \in C[x]$. Then $f, g$ are in $C[x]$. [Take a field containing $B$ in which the polynomials $f, g$ split into linear factors: say $f = \prod_i (x - \xi_i)$, $g = \prod_j (x - \eta_j)$. Each $\xi_i$ and each $\eta_j$ is a root of $fg$, hence is integral over $C$. Hence the coefficients of $f$ and $g$ are integral over $C$.]
\item[(ii)] Prove the same result without assuming that $B$ (or $A$) is an integral domain.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a ring $B$ and let $C$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. Prove that $C[x]$ is the integral closure of $A[x]$ in $B[x]$. [If $f \in B[x]$ is integral over $A[x]$, then
\[
f^m + g_1 f^{m-1} + \cdots + g_m = 0 \qquad (g_i \in A[x]).
\]
Let $r$ be an integer larger than the degrees of $f, g_1, \ldots, g_m$ (so that $-f_1$ below is monic), and let $f_1 = f - x^r$, so that
\[
(f_1 + x^r)^m + g_1 (f_1 + x^r)^{m-1} + \cdots + g_m = 0,
\]
or say
\[
f_1^m + h_1 f_1^{m-1} + \cdots + h_m = 0,
\]
where $h_m = (x^r)^m + g_1 (x^r)^{m-1} + \cdots + g_m \in A[x]$. Now apply Exercise 8 to the polynomials $-f_1$ and $f_1^{m-1} + h_1 f_1^{m-2} + \cdots + h_{m-1}$.]

\item A ring homomorphism $f : A \to B$ is said to have the going-up property (resp.\ the going-down property) if the conclusion of the going-up theorem (5.11) (resp.\ the going-down theorem (5.16)) holds for $B$ and its subring $f(A)$. Let $f^* : \Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ be the mapping associated with $f$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Consider the following three statements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $f^*$ is a closed mapping.
\item[(b)] $f$ has the going-up property.
\item[(c)] Let $\fq$ be any prime ideal of $B$ and let $\fp = \fq^c$. Then $f^* : \Spec(B/\fq) \to \Spec(A/\fp)$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
Prove that (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c). (See also Chapter 6, Exercise 11.)
\item[(ii)] Consider the following three statements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a$'$)] $f^*$ is an open mapping.
\item[(b$'$)] $f$ has the going-down property.
\item[(c$'$)] For any prime ideal $\fq$ of $B$, if $\fp = \fq^c$, then $f^* : \Spec(B_{\fq}) \to \Spec(A_{\fp})$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
Prove that (a$'$) $\Rightarrow$ (b$'$) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c$'$). (See also Chapter 7, Exercise 23.) [To prove that (a$'$) $\Rightarrow$ (c$'$), observe that $B_{\fq}$ is the direct limit of the rings $B_t$ where $t \in B - \fq$; hence, by Chapter 3, Exercise 26, we have $f^*(\Spec(B_{\fq})) = \bigcap_t f^*(\Spec(B_t)) = \bigcap_t f^*(Y_t)$. \end{enumerate}

\item Let $f : A \to B$ be a flat homomorphism of rings. Then $f$ has the going-down property. [Chapter 3, Exercise 18.]

\item Let $G$ be a finite group of automorphisms of a ring $A$, and let $A^G$ denote the subring of $G$-invariants, that is of all $x \in A$ such that $\sigma(x) = x$ for all $\sigma \in G$. Show that the action of $G$ on $A$ extends to an action on $S^{-1}A$, and that $(S^G)^{-1} A^G \cong (S^{-1}A)^G$.

\item In the situation of Exercise 12, let $\fp$ be a prime ideal of $A^G$, and let $P$ be the set of prime ideals of $A$ whose contraction is $\fp$. Show that $G$ acts transitively on $P$. In particular, $P$ is finite.

\item Let $A$ be an integrally closed domain, $K$ its field of fractions and $L$ a finite normal separable extension of $K$. Let $G$ be the Galois group of $L$ over $K$ and let $B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $L$. Show that $\sigma(B) = B$ for all $\sigma \in G$, and that $A = B^G$.

\item Let $A, B, L$ be as in Exercise 14, but let $L$ be any finite extension field of $K$, and let $B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $L$.

Content:
Show that, if $\fp$ is any prime ideal of $A$, then the set of prime ideals $\fq$ of $B$ which contract to $\fp$ is finite (in other words, $\Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ has finite fibers). [Reduce to the two cases (a) $L$ separable over $K$ and (b) $L$ purely inseparable over $K$. In case (a), embed $L$ in a finite normal separable extension of $K$, and use Exercises 13 and 14. In case (b), if $\fq$ is a prime ideal of $B$ such that $\fq \cap A = \fp$, show that $\fq$ is the set of all $x \in B$ such that $x^{p^m} \in \fp$ for some $m \geq 0$, where $p$ is the characteristic of $K$, and hence that $\Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ is bijective in this case.]

\item Let $k$ be a field and let $A \neq 0$ be a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Then there exist elements $y_1, \ldots, y_r \in A$ which are algebraically independent over $k$ and such that $A$ is integral over $k[y_1, \ldots, y_r]$. We shall sketch a proof in which $k$ is infinite. (The result is still true if $k$ is finite, but a different proof is needed.) Let $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ generate $A$ as a $k$-algebra. We can renumber the $x_i$ so that $x_1, \ldots, x_r$ are algebraically independent over $k$ and each of $x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_n$ is algebraic over $k[x_1, \ldots, x_r]$. Now proceed by induction on $n$. If $n = r$ there is nothing to do, so suppose $n > r$ and the result true for $n - 1$ generators. The generator $x_n$ is algebraic over $k[x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}]$, hence there exists a polynomial $f \neq 0$ in $n$ variables such that $f(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}, x_n) = 0$. Let $F$ be the homogeneous part of highest degree in $f$. Since $k$ is infinite, there exist $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1} \in k$ such that $F(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1}, 1) \neq 0$. Put $x_i' = x_i - \lambda_i x_n$ $(1 \leq i \leq n - 1)$. Show that $x_n$ is integral over the ring $A' = k[x_1', \ldots, x_{n-1}']$, and hence that $A$ is integral over $A'$. Then apply the inductive hypothesis to $A'$ to complete the proof. From the proof it follows that $y_1, \ldots, y_r$ may be chosen to be linear combinations of $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. This has the following geometrical interpretation: if $k$ is algebraically closed and $X$ is an affine algebraic variety in $k^n$ with coordinate ring $A \neq 0$, then there exists a linear subspace $L$ of dimension $r$ in $k^n$ and a linear mapping of $k^n$ onto $L$ which maps $X$ onto $L$. [Use Exercise 2.]

\item Deduce from Exercise 16 a proof of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (over an algebraically closed field $k$) in the following form: if $X$ is an affine algebraic variety in $k^n$, and $I(X)$ is the ideal of $X$ in the polynomial ring $k[t_1, \ldots, t_n]$ (Chapter 1, Exercise 27), then $I(X) \neq (1)$ implies $X$ is not empty. [Let $A = k[t_1, \ldots, t_n]/I(X)$ be the coordinate ring of $X$. Then $A \neq 0$, hence by Exercise 16 there exists a linear subspace $L$ of dimension $\geq 0$ in $k^n$ and a mapping of $X$ onto $L$. Hence $X \neq \varnothing$.]

\item Let $k$ be a field and $B$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Suppose that $B$ is a field. Then $B$ is a finite algebraic extension of $k$. (This is another version of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz. The following proof is due to Zariski. For other proofs, see (5.24), (7.9).)

Let $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ generate $B$ as a $k$-algebra. The proof is by induction on $n$. If $n = 1$ the result is clearly true, so assume $n > 1$. Let $A = k[x_1]$ and let $K = k(x_1)$ be the field of fractions of $A$. By the inductive hypothesis, $B$ is a finite algebraic extension of $K$, hence each of $x_2, \ldots, x_n$ satisfies a monic polynomial equation with coefficients in $K$, that is coefficients of the form $a/b$ where $a$ and $b$ are in $A$. If $f$ is the product of the denominators of all these coefficients, then each of $x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is integral over $A_f$. Hence $B$ and therefore $K$ is integral over $A_f$. Suppose $x_1$ is transcendental over $k$. Then $A$ is integrally closed, because it is a unique factorization domain. Hence $A_f$ is integrally closed (5.12), and therefore $A_f = K$, which is clearly absurd. Hence $x_1$ is algebraic over $k$, hence $K$ (and therefore $B$) is a finite extension of $k$.

\item Deduce the result of Exercise 17 from Exercise 18.

\item Let $A$ be a subring of an integral domain $B$ such that $B$ is finitely generated over $A$. Show that there exists $s \neq 0$ in $A$ and elements $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ in $B$, algebraically independent over $A$ and such that $B_s$ is integral over $B_s'$, where $B' = A[y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. [Let $S = A - \{0\}$ and let $K = S^{-1}A$, the field of fractions of $A$. Then $S^{-1}B$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra and therefore by the normalization lemma (Exercise 16) there exist $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in S^{-1}B$, algebraically independent over $K$ and such that $S^{-1}B$ is integral over $K[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Let $z_1, \ldots, z_m$ generate $B$ as an $A$-algebra. Then each $z_j$ (regarded as an element of $S^{-1}B$) is integral over $K[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. By writing an equation of integral dependence for each $z_j$, show that there exists $s \in S$ such that $x_i = y_i/s$ $(1 \leq i \leq n)$ with $y_i \in B$, and such that each $sz_j$ is integral over $B'$. Deduce that this $s$ satisfies the conditions stated.]

\item Let $A, B$ be as in Exercise 20. Show that there exists $s \neq 0$ in $A$ such that, if $\Omega$ is an algebraically closed field and $f : A \to \Omega$ is a homomorphism for which $f(s) \neq 0$, then $f$ can be extended to a homomorphism $B \to \Omega$. [With the notation of Exercise 20, $f$ can be extended first of all to $B'$, for example by mapping each $y_i$ to $0$; then to $B_s'$ (because $f(s) \neq 0$), and finally to $B_s$ (by Exercise 2, because $B_s$ is integral over $B_s'$).]

Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Part: 4/4
Content:
Show that $v(x + y) \geq \min(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K^*$.

\item Conversely, let $\Gamma$ be a totally ordered abelian group (written additively), and let $K$ be a field. A valuation of $K$ with values in $\Gamma$ is a mapping $v : K^* \to \Gamma$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $v(xy) = v(x) + v(y)$,
\item[(2)] $v(x + y) \geq \min(v(x), v(y))$,
\end{enumerate}
for all $x, y \in K^*$. Show that the set consisting of $0$ and the elements $x \in K^*$ such that $v(x) \geq 0$ is a valuation ring of $K$. This ring is called the valuation ring of $v$, and the subgroup $v(K^*)$ of $\Gamma$ is the value group of $v$. Thus the concepts of valuation ring and valuation are essentially equivalent.

\item Let $\Gamma$ be a totally ordered abelian group. A subgroup $\Delta$ of $\Gamma$ is isolated in $\Gamma$ if, whenever $0 \leq \beta \leq \alpha$ and $\alpha \in \Delta$, we have $\beta \in \Delta$. Let $A$ be a valuation ring of a field $K$, with value group $\Gamma$ (Exercise 31). If $\fp$ is a prime ideal of $A$, show that $v(A - \fp)$ is the set of elements $\geq 0$ in an isolated subgroup $\Delta$ of $\Gamma$, and that the mapping so defined of $\Spec(A)$ into the set of isolated subgroups of $\Gamma$ is bijective. If $\fp$ is a prime ideal of $A$ and $\Delta$ is the corresponding isolated subgroup, show that the value groups of the valuation rings $A/\fp$ and $A_{\fp}$ are $\Delta$ and $\Gamma/\Delta$ respectively (up to isomorphism of ordered groups).

\item Let $\Gamma$ be a totally ordered abelian group. We shall show how to construct a field $K$ and a valuation $v$ of $K$ with $\Gamma$ as value group. Let $k$ be any field and let $A = k[\Gamma]$ be the group algebra of $\Gamma$ over $k$. By definition, $A$ is freely generated as a $k$-vector space by elements $x_\alpha$ $(\alpha \in \Gamma)$ such that $x_\alpha x_\beta = x_{\alpha + \beta}$. Show that $A$ is an integral domain. If $u = \lambda_1 x_{\alpha_1} + \cdots + \lambda_n x_{\alpha_n}$ is any non-zero element of $A$, where the $\lambda_i$ are all $\neq 0$ and $\alpha_1 < \cdots < \alpha_n$, define $v_0(u)$ to be $\alpha_1$. Show that the mapping $v_0 : A - \{0\} \to \Gamma$ satisfies conditions (1) and (2) of Exercise 31. Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $A$. Show that $v_0$ can be uniquely extended to a valuation $v$ of $K$, and that the value group of $v$ is $\Gamma$.

\item Let $A$ be a valuation ring and $K$ its field of fractions. Let $f : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism such that $f^* : \Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ is a closed mapping. Then if $g : B \to K$ is any $A$-algebra homomorphism (i.e., if $g \circ f$ is the embedding of $A$ in $K$) we have $g(B) = A$. [Let $C = g(B)$; obviously $C \supseteq A$. Let $\fn$ be a maximal ideal of $C$. Since $f^*$ is closed, $\fm = \fn \cap A$ is a maximal ideal of $A$, whence $A_{\fm} = A$. Also the local ring $C_{\fn}$ dominates $A_{\fm}$. Hence by Exercise 27 we have $C_{\fn} = A$ and therefore $C \subseteq A$.]

\item From Exercises 1 and 3 it follows that, if $f : A \to B$ is integral and $C$ is any $A$-algebra, then the mapping $(f \otimes 1)^* : \Spec(B \otimes_A C) \to \Spec(C)$ is a closed map. Conversely, suppose that $f : A \to B$ has this property and that $B$ is an integral domain. Then $f$ is integral. [Replacing $A$ by its image in $B$, reduce to the case where $A \subseteq B$ and $f$ is the injection. Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $B$ and let $A'$ be a valuation ring of $K$ containing $A$. By (5.22) it is enough to show that $A'$ contains $B$. By hypothesis $\Spec(B \otimes_A A') \to \Spec(A')$ is a closed map. Apply the result of Exercise 34 to the homomorphism $B \otimes_A A' \to K$ defined by $b \otimes a' \mapsto ba'$. It follows that $ba' \in A'$ for all $b \in B$ and all $a' \in A'$; taking $a' = 1$, we have what we want.]

Show that the result just proved remains valid if $B$ is a ring with only finitely many minimal prime ideals (e.g., if $B$ is Noetherian). [Let $\fp_i$ be the minimal prime ideals. Then each composite homomorphism $A \to B \to B/\fp_i$ is integral, hence $A \to \prod_i (B/\fp_i)$ is integral, hence $A \to B/\fN$ is integral (where $\fN$ is the nilradical of $B$), hence finally $A \to B$ is integral.]
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Decide which of $\sqrt[3]{5},\ \tfrac{3+\sqrt{13}}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\sqrt{13}}{2},\ \tfrac{7}{3}$ are integral over $Z$. For each integral element exhibit an explicit monic equation over $Z$, and for each non-integral element give the obstruction (use that $Z$ is integrally closed).

\item Let $R=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^5)$ with $\bar x,\bar y$ the images of $x,y$. Set $t=\bar y/\bar x^2\in\Frac(R)$. Show that $t$ is integral over $R$, that $t\notin R$, and that the normalization of $R$ is $k[t]$. Identify the parametrization $\bar x\mapsto s^2,\ \bar y\mapsto s^5$ and locate the singular point geometrically.

\item Compute the normalization of $Z$ in $Q(\sqrt{-3})$, and verify directly that $\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}$ satisfies a monic quadratic over $Z$ while $\sqrt{-3}$ alone generates a strictly smaller, non-normal order. Conclude $Z[\sqrt{-3}]\subsetneq\mathcal O_{Q(\sqrt{-3})}$.

\item In $Z[i]$, determine the splitting type (split, inert, or ramified) of the rational primes $(3),(13),(2)$ by factoring $x^2+1$ modulo each, and list the prime(s) of $Z[i]$ lying over each. Verify that every fiber is finite and nonempty, as Lying Over and the finite-fiber corollary require.

\item Let $A=k[x,y]/(xy-x)$ with $k$ a field. Show that $A$ is not a domain by exhibiting zero divisors, and find a Noether normalization: produce an algebraically independent set $\{y_1,\dots,y_q\}$ over which $A$ is integral, and identify $q$.

\item Let $A=k[x,y,z]/(z^2-xy)$ over an infinite field $k$. Show that $\bar z$ is integral over $k[\bar x,\bar y]$, that $\bar x,\bar y$ are algebraically independent over $k$, and hence that $A$ is integral over the polynomial ring $k[\bar x,\bar y]$ with $q=2$. Exhibit $A$ as a finitely generated $k[\bar x,\bar y]$-module and give a generating set.

\item Show that $B=\{a/b\inQ:b odd\}=Z_{(2)}$ is a valuation ring of $Q$ by verifying the dichotomy $x\in B$ or $x^{-1}\in B$ via the $2$-adic valuation $v_2$. Identify its maximal ideal, its units, and its residue field.

\item For the ideal $I=(x^3,xy)\subseteqC[x,y]$ compute $Z(I)$, then $I(Z(I))$, and independently $\rad I$, and confirm the Strong Nullstellensatz prediction $I(Z(I))=\rad I$. Identify which generator records non-reducedness invisible to $Z$.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $A\subseteq B$ with $B$ integral over $A$, and let $x\in A$. Prove that if $x$ is a unit in $B$ then $x$ is a unit in $A$. Deduce that the Jacobson radical of $A$ is the contraction $\Jac(B)\cap A$ of the Jacobson radical of $B$. [Use that $x^{-1}\in B$ is integral over $A$.]

\item Let $A$ be an integrally closed domain with fraction field $K$, let $K\subseteq L$ be a field extension, and let $\alpha\in L$ be algebraic over $K$ with minimal polynomial $m_{\alpha,K}(x)$. Prove that $\alpha$ is integral over $A$ if and only if $m_{\alpha,K}(x)\in A[x]$. [If $\alpha$ is integral, show every conjugate of $\alpha$ is integral, so the elementary symmetric functions -- the coefficients of $m_{\alpha,K}$ -- are integral elements of $K$, hence in $A$.]

\item Let $B$ be a valuation ring of a field $K$ with maximal ideal $\fm$. Prove that for any two ideals $\fa,\fb$ of $B$ either $\fa\subseteq\fb$ or $\fb\subseteq\fa$ (the ideals are totally ordered by inclusion). Deduce that $B$ is integrally closed in $K$ and that every finitely generated ideal of $B$ is principal.

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a field $K$ and let $\overline A$ be its integral closure in $K$. Prove that $x\in K$ fails to be integral over $A$ if and only if there is a valuation ring $B$ of $K$ with $A\subseteq B$ and $x\notin B$. Conclude $\overline A=\bigcap_{B}B$, the intersection over all valuation rings $B$ of $K$ containing $A$. [For one direction, if $x$ is not integral, $x^{-1}$ is a non-unit of $A[x^{-1}]$; extend a residue homomorphism to a maximal pair.]

\item Let $k$ be a field and let $B$ be a finitely generated $k$-algebra that happens to be a field. Prove (Zariski's Lemma) that $B$ is a finite, hence algebraic, extension of $k$. Then deduce the Weak Nullstellensatz: if $k=\overline k$, every maximal ideal of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has the form $(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$. [Use Noether Normalization and the ``fields together'' theorem to force the polynomial subring to have $q=0$.]
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $A=Z$ and $B=Z[i]$, with the inclusion inducing the contraction map $\Spec B\to\Spec A$. Complete the diagram below recording the fibers over $(2),(5),(7)$, label each vertical edge with its splitting type (ramified, split, inert), and prove that each contracts to the correct rational prime:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.0em, column sep=1.4em]
(1+i) \arrow[d,dash] & (2+i)\ \ (2-i) \arrow[d,dash] & (7) \arrow[d,dash] \\
(2) & (5) & (7)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove that $\fq\mapsto\fq\capZ$ is surjective onto $\SpecZ$ (Lying Over) and that each fiber shown is finite and nonempty. State which primes are maximal.

\item Let $A$ be a normal domain with fraction field $K$, let $A\subseteq B$ with $B$ a domain integral over $A$, and let $\fp_1\supseteq\fp_2$ be primes of $A$ with a chosen $\fq_1$ over $\fp_1$. Complete the Going-Down square below (vertical arrows are the inclusions $A\hookrightarrow B$, horizontal arrows the localizations at $A\setminus\fp_2$) and prove there is a prime $\fq_2\subseteq\fq_1$ of $B$ with $\fq_2\cap A=\fp_2$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
A \arrow[r,"\ell_A"] \arrow[d,hook] & A_{\fp_2} \arrow[d,hook] \\
B \arrow[r,"\ell_B"'] & (A\setminus\fp_2)^{-1} B
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify where normality of $A$ enters the argument, and explain via the valuation-ring criterion (integral closure $=$ intersection of valuation rings) why dropping normality can break the descent.

\item Let $A$ be a subring of a field $K$ and $\Omega$ an algebraically closed field. Complete the extension diagram below, where $(B,g)$ is a maximal element (under extension of homomorphisms $A'\to\Omega$, $A\subseteq A'\subseteq K$) and the dashed arrow is the extension to be constructed:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
A \arrow[r,hook] \arrow[dr,"f"'] & B \arrow[d,dashed,"g"] \arrow[r,hook] & K \\
& \Omega &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove that $B$ is a valuation ring of $K$ with maximal ideal $\ker g$, and that $\overline A=\bigcap_B B$ over all such valuation rings. Conclude that $A$ is integrally closed in $K$ if and only if $A$ is an intersection of valuation rings of $K$.

\item Let $k=\overline k$ and let $V=Z(I)\subseteq\Aff^n$ be an affine algebraic set with coordinate ring $A=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/\rad I$ (recall $I(V)=I(Z(I))=\rad I$). Complete the dictionary diagram below and prove that the labelled correspondence is an inclusion-reversing bijection on the indicated classes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=2.2em]
\{points of V\} \arrow[r,dash,"{Z,\,I}"] \arrow[d,dash] & \{maximal ideals of A\} \arrow[d,dash] \\
\{irreducible subsets of V\} \arrow[r,dash] \arrow[d,dash] & \{prime ideals of A\} \arrow[d,dash] \\
\{closed subsets of V\} \arrow[r,dash,"{Z,\,I}"'] & \{radical ideals of A\}
\end{tikzcd}

Type: prose
Content:
Throughout, ``ring'' means commutative ring with $1$ and every homomorphism $\varphi\colon R\to S$ sends $1_R$ to $1_S$. The previous sections built a dictionary between an affine algebraic set $V$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ and its coordinate ring $k[V]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V)$: by the Nullstellensatz the points of $V$ are the maximal ideals $\fm=I(v)$ of $k[V]$, and a morphism $V\to W$ is a $k$-algebra map $k[W]\to k[V]$. We now reverse the arrow. Starting from any commutative ring $R$ we manufacture a space whose ``functions'' are the elements of $R$.

The first guess -- take the maximal ideals as ``points'' -- fails functorially: the preimage of a maximal ideal under a ring map need not be maximal (e.g.\ under $Z\hookrightarrowQ$ the maximal ideal $(0)$ of $Q$ pulls back to $(0)$, which is not maximal in $Z$). But the preimage of a prime ideal is always prime. This forces the right definition.

Title: {prime and maximal spectrum}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{prime and maximal spectrum}]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. The prime spectrum (or spectrum) of $R$ is the set
\[
\Spec R=\{\fp\subseteq R : \fp is a prime ideal\}.
\]
The maximal spectrum $\mSpec R=\{\fm : \fm maximal\}$ is the subset of maximal ideals. A prime $\fp$ is to be thought of as a ``point'' of the geometric object attached to $R$.
\end{definition}

Type: prose
Content:
This is the central object of Atiyah--Macdonald's geometric program: a prime ideal is the common generalization of a prime of arithmetic (the points $(p)$ of $\SpecZ$) and a point of geometry (the maximal ideals $(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$ of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$). The single set $\Spec R$ houses both kinds of object and, crucially, also the ``subvariety'' points (non-maximal primes) that the classical picture suppressed.

Type: definition
Title: {value of a function at a point}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{value of a function at a point}]
For $f\in R$ and $\fp\in\Spec R$, the value of $f$ at $\fp$ is the residue
\[
f(\fp)=\overline{f}\in R/\fp,\qquadan element of the integral domain R/\fp.
\]
Thus $f$ is a function on $\Spec R$ whose values at different points lie in different domains. Two elements $f,g$ have equal values at every $\fp$ iff $f-g$ lies in every prime, i.e.\ iff $f-g\in\nil(R)$ (the nilradical). So an element of $R$ is determined by its values only up to the nilradical.
\end{definition}

Type: example
Title: $\Spec$ of a field and of $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Spec$ of a field and of $Z$}
Describe $\Spec R$ and $\mSpec R$ for $R$ a field and for $R=Z$.
\wrec A field has a unique prime $(0)$; $Z$ is a PID, so its nonzero primes are the $(p)$.
\wsol If $R$ is a field then $(0)$ is its only proper ideal that is prime (it is even maximal), so $\Spec R=\mSpec R=\{(0)\}$, a one-point space. For $R=Z$: the primes are $(0)$ together with $(p)$ for each rational prime $p>0$. The maximal ideals are exactly the $(p)$, so $\mSpecZ=\SpecZ\setminus\{(0)\}$. Sanity check: $(0)$ is prime because $Z$ is a domain but not maximal because $Z$ is not a field; each $(p)$ is maximal since $Z/pZ=\F_p$ is a field. The lone non-maximal prime $(0)$ is the ``generic point'' we meet below.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > The Prime Spectrum and the Zariski Topology > From points to primes: the spectrum as a set
Type: example
Title: $\SpecZ[x]$: the four families of primes
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\SpecZ[x]$: the four families of primes}
List the prime ideals of $Z[x]$ and identify the maximal ones.
\wrec $Z[x]$ has Krull dimension $2$; primes come in chains of length $\le2$ governed by ``which integer prime, which polynomial mod it.''
\wsol The primes of $Z[x]$ are: (a) $(0)$; (b) $(p)$ for a rational prime $p$; (c) $(f)$ where $f$ has content $1$ and is irreducible in $Q[x]$; (d) $(p,g)$ where $p$ is prime and $g$ is monic and irreducible modulo $p$. Only the type-(d) ideals are maximal: $Z[x]/(p,g)\cong\F_p[x]/(\overline g)$ is a finite field. Sanity check on dimension: a maximal chain is $(0)\subsetneq(p)\subsetneq(p,g)$ of length $2$, matching $\dimZ[x]=\dimZ+1=2$; and $(0)\subsetneq(f)\subsetneq(p,g)$ when $g\mid f\bmod p$ gives another length-$2$ chain.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[{$V(\fa)$ and the Zariski topology}]
For a subset $E\subseteq R$ let
\[
V(E)=\{\fp\in\Spec R : E\subseteq\fp\}\subseteq\Spec R .
\]
Since $E\subseteq\fp\iff(E)\subseteq\fp$, we may and do assume $E=\fa$ is an ideal; $V(\fa)$ is the set of points at which every $f\in\fa$ vanishes. For $Y\subseteq\Spec R$ set $I(Y)=\bigcap_{\fp\in Y}\fp$. The sets $V(\fa)$ are the closed sets of the Zariski topology on $\Spec R$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {axioms for the closed sets; the $V$--$I$ correspondence}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{axioms for the closed sets; the $V$--$I$ correspondence}]
Let $R$ be a ring.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $V(0)=\Spec R$, $V(R)=\varnothing$; $V(\fa)=V(\rad\fa)$ and $I(V(\fa))=\rad\fa$.
\item $V(\fa\cap\fb)=V(\fa\fb)=V(\fa)\cup V(\fb)$.
\item For any family $\{\fa_i\}$, $V\bigl(\sum_i\fa_i\bigr)=\bigcap_i V(\fa_i)$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence $\{V(\fa)\}$ is closed under finite unions and arbitrary intersections, defining a topology. The maps $V,I$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections
\[
\{Zariski-closed subsets of \Spec R\}\ \xrightleftharpoons[\ V\ ]{\ I\ }\ \{radical ideals of R\}.
\]
Closed points correspond to maximal ideals; irreducible closed sets correspond to prime ideals.
\end{proposition}

Type: definition
Title: {basic open sets}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{basic open sets}]
For $f\in R$ let
\[
D(f)=\Spec R\setminus V(f)=\{\fp : f\notin\fp\}=\{\fp : f(\fp)\neq0\},
\]
the set of points where $f$ is nonzero. These basic (or principal) open sets form a basis for the Zariski topology: every open set is a union of $D(f)$'s, since the complement of $V(\fa)$ is $\bigcup_{f\in\fa}D(f)$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {calculus of basic opens}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{calculus of basic opens}]
Let $f,g,g_1,\dots,g_n\in R$, $X=\Spec R$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $D(f)=X\iff f$ is a unit; $D(f)=\varnothing\iff f$ is nilpotent.
\item $D(f)\cap D(g)=D(fg)$.
\item $D(f)\subseteq D(g_1)\cup\dots\cup D(g_n)\iff f\in\rad(g_1,\dots,g_n)$; in particular $D(f)=D(g)\iff\rad(f)=\rad(g)$.
\item The natural map $R\to R_f$ induces a homeomorphism $\Spec R_f\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D(f)$.
\item $\Spec R$ is quasi-compact; hence each $D(f)$ is quasi-compact.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) $f$ a unit $\iff$ no prime contains it; $f$ nilpotent $\iff$ every prime contains it ($\nil R=\bigcap\fp$). (3) $D(f)\subseteq\bigcup D(g_i)$ says every prime containing $(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ contains $f$, i.e.\ $f\in\bigcap_{(g_i)\subseteq\fp}\fp=\rad(g_1,\dots,g_n)$. (4) Localization $R\to R_f$ gives a bijection of primes of $R_f$ with primes of $R$ missing $\{1,f,f^2,\dots\}$, i.e.\ with $D(f)$, and it is bicontinuous. (5) Quasi-compactness: if $X=\bigcup_i D(g_i)$ then $(g_i)=R$ (no prime contains all $g_i$), so $1=\sum_{j=1}^m a_jg_{i_j}$ is a finite relation, and the corresponding $D(g_{i_1}),\dots,D(g_{i_m})$ already cover $X$.
\end{proof}

Title: Reading $\Spec$ from the ideal theory of $R$

\begin{method}{Reading $\Spec$ from the ideal theory of $R$}
To analyze $\Spec R$ as a space: (i) closed points $=$ maximal ideals; (ii) the closure of $\{\fp\}$ is $V(\fp)=\{\fq:\fq\supseteq\fp\}$, so smaller primes are ``more generic''; (iii) $X$ irreducible $\iff\nil R$ prime; irreducible components $\leftrightarrow$ minimal primes of $R$; (iv) test separation/connectedness via idempotents and basic opens; (v) compute fibers of $\varphi^*\colon\Spec S\to\Spec R$ over $\fp$ by factoring in $S\otimes_R\kappa(\fp)$, where $\kappa(\fp)=\Frac(R/\fp)$.
\end{method}

Title: Closure of a point; closed points are maximal
Content:
\begin{wex}{Closure of a point; closed points are maximal}
Compute the closure $\overline{\{\fp\}}$ of a point, and show $\fp$ is closed iff $\fp$ is maximal.
\wrec The smallest closed set containing $\fp$ is $V(\fp)$; a point is closed iff it equals its closure.
\wsol The closed sets containing $\fp$ are the $V(\fa)$ with $\fa\subseteq\fp$, the smallest being $V(\fp)=\{\fq:\fq\supseteq\fp\}$. Hence $\overline{\{\fp\}}=V(\fp)$. So $\{\fp\}$ is closed $\iff V(\fp)=\{\fp\}\iff$ no prime strictly contains $\fp$ $\iff\fp$ is maximal. Sanity check: in $\SpecZ$, $\overline{\{(0)\}}=V((0))=\SpecZ$ (so $(0)$ is dense), while $\overline{\{(p)\}}=\{(p)\}$ since $(p)$ is maximal. The topology is generally not $T_1$ (non-closed points exist) but it is always $T_0$.
\end{wex}

Show any two distinct points of $\Spec R$ are topologically distinguishable, yet $\SpecZ$ is not Hausdorff.
\wrec $T_0$ means: for $\fp\ne\fq$ some open set contains one but not the other. Hausdorff fails because of the generic point.
\wsol If $\fp\ne\fq$, say $f\in\fp\setminus\fq$; then $D(f)$ contains $\fq$ but not $\fp$, giving $T_0$. For $Z$: any nonempty open set is the complement of a finite set of closed points (since proper closed sets $V(\fa)$, $\fa\ne0$, are finite), so any two nonempty opens meet -- no disjoint neighborhoods exist, hence not Hausdorff. Sanity check: in $\SpecZ$ every nonempty open contains $(0)$, the generic point, so opens can never be disjoint.
\end{wex}

Title: Quasi-compact but not compact: an infinite cover with no finite subcover of an open subset
Content:
\begin{wex}{Quasi-compact but not compact: an infinite cover with no finite subcover of an open subset}
Show $\Spec R$ is quasi-compact, but exhibit an open subset of some $\Spec R$ whose cover has no finite subcover.
\wrec $\Spec R$ itself is always quasi-compact by the unit-relation argument; non-quasi-compact open subsets arise in non-Noetherian rings.
\wsol Quasi-compactness of $X$ was proved above. For the failure on an open subset, take $R=k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ (infinitely many variables) and $U=\bigcup_{i\ge1}D(x_i)$, the complement of the closed set $V(x_1,x_2,\dots)$. Given any finite subfamily $D(x_{i_1}),\dots,D(x_{i_m})$, consider the prime $\fp=(x_{i_1},\dots,x_{i_m})$ (prime since $R/\fp\cong k[x_k:k\notin\{i_1,\dots,i_m\}]$ is a domain). It contains each $x_{i_j}$, so $\fp\notin D(x_{i_j})$ for every $j$; yet $\fp\in U$, since it omits any $x_k$ with $k\notin\{i_1,\dots,i_m\}$, whence $\fp\in D(x_k)\subseteq U$. Thus the finite union fails to cover $U$, and no finite subcover exists. Sanity check: $U$ is quasi-compact iff it is a finite union of basic opens (Section~15.8, Exercise 12); here it is genuinely infinite, consistent with $R$ non-Noetherian.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > The Prime Spectrum and the Zariski Topology > Irreducibility, components, and the nilradical
Type: theorem
Title: {irreducible closed sets $\leftrightarrow$ primes; components $\leftrightarrow$ minimal primes}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{irreducible closed sets $\leftrightarrow$ primes; components $\leftrightarrow$ minimal primes}]
Let $R$ be a ring, $X=\Spec R$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item A closed set $V(\fa)$ is irreducible $\iff\rad\fa=I(V(\fa))$ is prime. Thus the irreducible closed subsets of $X$ are exactly the $V(\fp)=\overline{\{\fp\}}$ for $\fp\in\Spec R$, and $\fp$ is the unique generic point of $V(\fp)$.
\item $X$ is irreducible $\iff\nil R$ is prime.
\item The irreducible components of $X$ are the closures $V(\fp)$ of the minimal primes $\fp$ of $R$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) If $\rad\fa=\fp$ is prime and $V(\fp)=V(\fb)\cup V(\fc)=V(\fb\cap\fc)$, then $\fp=\rad(\fb\cap\fc)\supseteq\fb\fc$, so $\fp\supseteq\fb$ or $\fp\supseteq\fc$, forcing $V(\fp)$ equal to one piece. Conversely if $\rad\fa$ is not prime, pick $fg\in\rad\fa$ with $f,g\notin\rad\fa$; then $V(\fa)=V(\fa+(f))\cup V(\fa+(g))$ is a proper decomposition. (2) is (1) with $\fa=0$. (3) An irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed set $=V(\fp)$ with $\fp$ minimal, since $V(\fp)\subseteq V(\fq)\iff\fq\subseteq\fp$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[{$\Spec R$ and $\Spec R_{red}$ coincide}]
Let $\nil R$ be the nilradical and $R_{red}=R/\nil R$ the associated reduced ring. The canonical surjection $R\to R_{red}$ induces a homeomorphism
\[
\Spec R_{red}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Spec R .

Topologically, nilpotents are invisible.
\end{theorem}

Title: $\SpecZ/12Z$ and the nilradical
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\SpecZ/12Z$ and the nilradical}
Compute $\Spec(Z/12Z)$ as a topological space and verify it equals $\Spec$ of its reduction.
\wrec $Z/12Z$ is Artinian; its primes are the maximal ideals coming from the prime divisors of $12$. The nilradical kills the square factor.
\wsol $12=2^2\cdot3$, so $Z/12Z\congZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ by CRT. Its primes are $(2)/(12)$ and $(3)/(12)$ -- two points, both closed (maximal), with the discrete topology. The nilradical is $(6)/(12)$ (since $6^2=36\equiv0$), and $R_{red}=Z/12Z/(6)\congZ/6Z\cong\F_2\times\F_3$, which again has exactly the two points $(2),(3)$. Sanity check: $\abs{\Spec}=2=$ number of distinct prime divisors of $12$; squaring the $2$ (from $4$) added nilpotents but no new points, confirming $\Spec R=\Spec R_{red}$.
\end{wex}

Title: Generic point of $\Spec k[x,y]$ and the curve points
Content:
\begin{wex}{Generic point of $\Spec k[x,y]$ and the curve points}
With $R=k[x,y]$ ($k$ algebraically closed), identify the generic point and describe the closure of $(f)$.
\wrec Primes are $(0)$, the $(f)$ for $f$ irreducible, and the maximals $(x-a,y-b)$; closure of $\fp$ is $V(\fp)$.
\wsol $(0)$ is prime (the domain $k[x,y]$), and $\overline{\{(0)\}}=V(0)=\Spec R$, so $(0)$ is the generic point of the irreducible space $\Spec k[x,y]$ ($=$ the plane $\Aff^2$). For an irreducible $f$, $\overline{\{(f)\}}=V(f)=\{(f)\}\cup\{(x-a,y-b):f(a,b)=0\}$: the point $(f)$ itself together with exactly the closed points lying on the curve $f=0$. Sanity check: $V(f)$ is irreducible because $(f)$ is prime; its generic point $(f)$ is the curve ``as a whole,'' its closed points are the geometric points on it -- precisely the classical picture of Section~15.3 with one extra generic dot.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: An irreducible component count: $\Spec k[x,y]/(xy)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{An irreducible component count: $\Spec k[x,y]/(xy)$}
Show $X=\Spec k[x,y]/(xy)$ is connected but reducible, with two irreducible components.
\wrec $(xy)=(x)\cap(y)$ is radical but not prime; minimal primes give components.
\wsol In $S=k[x,y]/(xy)$ the minimal primes are $(x)$ and $(y)$ (since $(xy)=(x)\cap(y)$ and $x\cdot y=0$). Their closures $V(x)$ and $V(y)$ are the two coordinate axes, each homeomorphic to $\Spec k[x]\cong\Aff^1$. So $X=V(x)\cup V(y)$ is reducible with two components. It is connected because the two axes meet at the origin $(x,y)/(xy)$. Sanity check: $\nil S=0$ (the ring is reduced) yet $\nil S$ is not prime, matching ``$X$ irreducible $\iff\nil$ prime''; two minimal primes $=$ two components.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\Spec R$ connected $\iff$ no nontrivial idempotent
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Spec R$ connected $\iff$ no nontrivial idempotent}
Show $\Spec R$ is disconnected iff $R\cong R_1\times R_2$ with $R_i\ne0$ iff $R$ has an idempotent $e\ne0,1$.
\wrec A clopen decomposition of $X$ corresponds to a product decomposition of $R$ via an idempotent.
\wsol If $R=R_1\times R_2$ then $X=\Spec R$ is the disjoint union $V(0\times R_2)\sqcup V(R_1\times0)$ of two nonempty clopen pieces $\cong\Spec R_1,\Spec R_2$ (a prime of a product lives in one factor). Conversely a disconnection $X=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$ into clopen sets gives complementary idempotents: $Y_i=D(e_i)=V(1-e_i)$ with $e_1+e_2=1$, $e_1e_2=0$, so $e=e_1$ is a nontrivial idempotent and $R\cong Re_1\times Re_2$. Sanity check: a local ring or a domain has only the idempotents $0,1$, so its spectrum is connected -- e.g.\ $\SpecZ$ is connected, with generic point $(0)$ gluing all closed points together.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {$\Spec$ is a contravariant functor to $Top$}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$\Spec$ is a contravariant functor to $Top$}]
Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring homomorphism. Then $\fq\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$ defines a map
\[
\varphi^{*}\colon\Spec S\longrightarrow\Spec R,\qquad\varphi^{*}(\fq)=\varphi^{-1}(\fq),
\]
which is continuous for the Zariski topologies. Concretely:
\[
(\varphi^{*})^{-1}\bigl(V(\fa)\bigr)=V\bigl(\varphi(\fa)S\bigr),\qquad
(\varphi^{*})^{-1}\bigl(D(f)\bigr)=D\bigl(\varphi(f)\bigr).
\]
Moreover $(\psi\circ\varphi)^{*}=\varphi^{*}\circ\psi^{*}$ and $\id^{*}=\id$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
This is exactly why primes, not maximals, are the right ``points.'' Over an algebraically closed $k$, a $k$-algebra map between affine $k$-algebras does pull maximal ideals back to maximal ideals (Nullstellensatz), so for the geometric points the classical and the schematic pictures agree; but the spectrum also carries the non-closed primes corresponding to the subvarieties of $V$, and on those the functoriality is genuinely needed. The pair $(\mSpec R,R)$ is the ``canonical model''; the equivalence of categories
\[
\{affine algebraic sets/k\}\ \xleftrightarrow{\ \ }\ \{affine k-algebras\},\qquad
V\mapsto k[V],\quad R\mapsto\mSpec R,
\]
upgrades, for arbitrary rings, to the affine-scheme correspondence of Theorem~ [REF:thm:scheme@c15] below.
\end{remark}

Title: The inclusion $Z\hookrightarrowZ[i]$ and its fibers
Content:
\begin{wex}{The inclusion $Z\hookrightarrowZ[i]$ and its fibers}
Describe $\varphi^{*}\colon\SpecZ[i]\to\SpecZ$ for $\varphi\colonZ\hookrightarrowZ[i]$, computing the fiber over each $(p)$.
\wrec Fibers of $\varphi^{*}$ over $(p)$ are read off from the factorization of $p$ in the Gaussian integers, i.e.\ from $p\bmod4$.
\wsol The fiber over $(p)$ is $\{\fq\in\SpecZ[i]:\fq\capZ=(p)\}$, the primes of $Z[i]$ above $p$. By the theory of $Z[i]$ (a PID): if $p=2$, $2=-i(1+i)^2$ is ramified, one point $(1+i)$; if $p\equiv3\pmod4$, $p$ is inert, one point $(p)$; if $p\equiv1\pmod4$, $p=\pi\overline\pi$ splits, two points $(\pi),(\overline\pi)$. Over $(0)$ lies the single generic point $(0)$. Sanity check: the residue field $Z[i]/\fq$ has order $p^f$ with $f=1$ (split/ramified) or $f=2$ (inert), and $\sum_{\fq\mid p}e_\fq f_\fq=2=[Q(i):Q]$ in each case ($e=2,f=1$ ramified; $e=f=1$ twice split; $e=1,f=2$ inert).
\end{wex}

Title: The projection $k[x]\hookrightarrow k[x,y]$ and vertical-line fibers
Content:
\begin{wex}{The projection $k[x]\hookrightarrow k[x,y]$ and vertical-line fibers}
For $k$ algebraically closed and $\varphi\colon k[x]\hookrightarrow k[x,y]$, describe $\varphi^{*}\colon\Spec k[x,y]\to\Spec k[x]$ and the fiber over $(x-a)$.
\wrec $\varphi^{*}$ is the projection $\Aff^2\to\Aff^1$; the fiber over a point of the line is the vertical line above it (plus its generic point).
\wsol $\varphi^{*}(\fq)=\fq\cap k[x]$. Over the closed point $(x-a)\in\Spec k[x]$ the fiber consists of the primes $\fq$ of $k[x,y]$ with $\fq\cap k[x]=(x-a)$: these are the maximal ideals $(x-a,y-b)$ for $b\in k$ together with the height-$1$ prime $(x-a)$ itself (the whole vertical line, its generic point). Over $(0)$ the fiber adds the generic point $(0)$ of the plane and all the ``slanted'' curve primes $(f)$ with $f\notin k[x]$. Sanity check: setting $x=a$, the fiber ring is $k[x,y]/(x-a)\cong k[y]$, whose spectrum is the $y$-line $\{(y-b)\}\cup\{(0)\}$ -- exactly the points found.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Localization as an open immersion: $\Spec R_f\hookrightarrow\Spec R$}
Show the localization map $R\to R_f$ realizes $\Spec R_f$ as the open set $D(f)$.
\wrec Primes of $R_f$ correspond to primes of $R$ not containing $f$; that set is $D(f)$.
\wsol The map $R\to R_f$ inverts $f$, so $\fq\mapsto\fq\cap R$ is a bijection $\Spec R_f\to\{\fp:f\notin\fp\}=D(f)$, bicontinuous since every ideal of $R_f$ is extended. Thus localization at $f$ is the algebraic operation realizing the open subset $D(f)$, dual to quotient realizing the closed subset $V(\fa)$. Sanity check: $R=Z$, $f=6$ gives $R_6=Z[1/6]$ and $D(6)=\SpecZ\setminus\{(2),(3)\}=\{(0)\}\cup\{(p):p\ne2,3\}$ -- precisely the primes missing $2$ and $3$, the points where $6$ is invertible.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {$\mSpec$ and the points of a variety}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{$\mSpec$ and the points of a variety}]
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and $R=k[V]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V)$ an affine $k$-algebra (finitely generated, reduced). Then by the Nullstellensatz:
\[
\mSpec R\ \xleftrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ V,\qquad (x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)\bmod I(V)\ \longleftrightarrow\ (a_1,\dots,a_n)\in V,
\]
and $\Spec R\leftrightarrow\{subvarieties of V\}$ (irreducible closed subsets via their generic primes). For a maximal ideal $\fm$, the residue field is $R/\fm\cong k$, so a closed point is a genuine $k$-valued point.
\end{theorem}

Type: theorem
Title: {the structure sheaf and affine schemes}
Label: thm:scheme@c15
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{the structure sheaf and affine schemes}] 
Let $X=\Spec R$. For an open $U\subseteq X$ let $\mathcal O_X(U)$ be the ring of functions $s\colon U\to\coprod_{\fp\in U}R_\fp$ with $s(\fp)\in R_\fp$ and $s$ locally a fraction: each point has a basic neighborhood $D(g)\subseteq U$ on which $s=a/g^{n}$ for fixed $a\in R$, $n\ge0$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\mathcal O_X(D(f))\cong R_f$; in particular the global sections are $\mathcal O_X(X)\cong R$.
\item The stalk at $\fp$ is the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,\fp}\cong R_\fp$, with maximal ideal $\fp R_\fp$ and residue field $\kappa(\fp)=\Frac(R/\fp)$.
\end{enumerate}
The pair $(\Spec R,\mathcal O_{\Spec R})$ is an affine scheme. Every ring map $\varphi\colon R\to S$ induces a morphism of affine schemes $(\varphi^{*},\varphi^{\#})\colon(\Spec S,\mathcal O_{\Spec S})\to(\Spec R,\mathcal O_{\Spec R})$, where on stalks $\varphi^{\#}\colon R_{\fp}\to S_{\fq}$ is a local homomorphism; conversely every such morphism arises from a unique ring map. Thus
\[
\{commutative rings\}\ \xleftrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \{affine schemes\}\quad(contravariant),
\]
the founding equivalence of scheme theory.
\end{theorem}
label: thm:scheme@c15

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-1e26d4a095ed96aeae6a
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$\mathcal O_X(D(f))\cong R_f$ is a sheaf-gluing computation: a locally-fraction section on $D(f)$ is patched from compatible fractions $a_i/g_i^{n}$ on a finite cover $D(g_i)$ (using quasi-compactness), and the identities $f^{N}=\sum b_ig_i^{n}$ assemble a single global $a/f^{M}$. The stalk is the direct limit $\varinjlim_{\fp\in D(f)}\mathcal O_X(D(f))=\varinjlim_{f\notin\fp}R_f=R_\fp$. The local-homomorphism condition is forced because $\varphi^{-1}(\fq)=\fp$ means $\varphi_\fp^{-1}(\fq S_\fq)=\fp R_\fp$; the example $Z_{(2)}\hookrightarrowQ$ shows a non-local map of stalks does not come from a ring map of the right spectra.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The terminology is geometric: above each point $\fp$ sits the local ring $R_\fp$ -- the ``stalk'' (as of wheat) -- and a section over $U$ is a choice of germ at each point, locally given by one fraction; the totality is the ``sheaf'' (bundle) of stalks. Localization is literally ``concentrating near a point'': $R_\fp$ is the ring of rational functions defined in some Zariski neighborhood of $\fp$, and $\kappa(\fp)$ is the field of values at the generic point of $V(\fp)$. A scheme is glued from affine charts $(\Spec R_i,\mathcal O)$ exactly as a manifold is glued from Euclidean charts.
\end{remark}

Title: Structure sheaf on $\SpecZ$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Structure sheaf on $\SpecZ$}
Compute $\mathcal O(D(n))$, the global sections, and the stalks for $X=\SpecZ$.
\wrec $Z$ is a PID, so every open is basic: $D(n)=\{\fp:n\notin\fp\}$, and $\mathcal O(D(n))=Z_n=Z[1/n]$.
\wsol For $n\ge1$, $D(n)=\{(p):p\nmid n\}\cup\{(0)\}$ and $\mathcal O(D(n))=Z[1/n]=\{a/b\inQ:p\mid b\Rightarrow p\mid n\}$. Global sections: $\mathcal O(X)=\mathcal O(D(1))=Z$. Stalks: $\mathcal O_{(p)}=Z_{(p)}$ (rationals with denominator prime to $p$) and $\mathcal O_{(0)}=Z_{(0)}=Q$ at the generic point. All restriction maps are the evident inclusions inside $Q$. Sanity check: $\mathcal O(X)=Z$ recovers ``functions regular everywhere $=$ the ring,'' the arithmetic analogue of ``polynomial functions on $\Aff^n$ regular everywhere are polynomials.''
\end{wex}

Title: Values, the nilradical, and functions not determined pointwise
Content:
\begin{wex}{Values, the nilradical, and functions not determined pointwise}
In $R=k[x]/(x^2)$ show two distinct elements have identical values at every point of $\Spec R$.
\wrec $\Spec R$ is a single point; values lie in $R/\fp$, and the difference of equal-valued elements lies in $\nil R$.
\wsol $R=k[x]/(x^2)$ is local with unique prime $\fp=(x)$ (the nilradical), $R_{red}=k$. So $\Spec R=\{(x)\}$ is one point and $\kappa(\fp)=R/(x)=k$. The elements $0$ and $\overline x$ are distinct in $R$ but both have value $0$ in $R/(x)=k$, since $\overline x\in\nil R$. Sanity check: $f,g$ agree at all points $\iff f-g\in\nil R$; here $\overline x-0=\overline x$ is nilpotent ($\overline x^2=0$), so the two functions are pointwise equal yet algebraically different -- the nilpotent ``thickening'' invisible to $\Spec$ but recorded in $\mathcal O$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\SpecZ[x]$ fibered over $\SpecZ$ via a cubic
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\SpecZ[x]$ fibered over $\SpecZ$ via a cubic}
For $f=x^3+x+1$, locate the closed points of $V(f)\subseteq\SpecZ[x]$ in the fibers over $(2),(3),(5)$.
\wrec Closed points of $V(f)$ over $(p)$ are the maximals $(p,g)$ with $g\mid\overline f$ in $\F_p[x]$, one per irreducible factor.
\wsol Reduce $f$ modulo each prime: $f\equiv x^3+x+1\pmod2$ is irreducible (no root in $\F_2$, since $f(0)=f(1)=1$), giving one closed point $(2,x^3+x+1)$; modulo $3$ the only root is $x=1$ ($f(0)=1$, $f(1)=0$, $f(2)=2$), so $f\equiv(x-1)(x^2+x+2)\pmod3$ with $x^2+x+2$ irreducible over $\F_3$, giving the two points $(3,x-1)$ and $(3,x^2+x+2)$; modulo $5$, $f$ has no root ($f(0),\dots,f(4)=1,3,1,1,4$), so as a rootless cubic it is irreducible, giving one closed point $(5,x^3+x+1)$. Sanity check: the number of closed points over $(p)$ equals the number of distinct irreducible factors of $f\bmod p$ ($1,2,1$ respectively), and the splitting type is governed by the Galois group of $f$ over $Q$ acting on the roots ($f$ is irreducible over $Q$, as it has no rational root).
\end{wex}

Title: $\Spec k[x]$ over an algebraically closed $k$, and a non-closed comparison
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\Spec k[x]$ over an algebraically closed $k$, and a non-closed comparison}
Describe $\Spec k[x]$ for $k$ algebraically closed, and contrast with $\SpecR[x]$.
\wrec Over $\overline k$ every nonzero prime of $k[x]$ is $(x-a)$; over $R$ there are also degree-$2$ primes.
\wsol For $k=\overline k$: $\Spec k[x]=\{(0)\}\cup\{(x-a):a\in k\}$, the generic point plus the affine line $\Aff^1(k)=\mSpec$. For $R=R[x]$: primes are $(0)$, the $(x-a)$ with $a\inR$ (residue field $R$), and the $(x^2+bx+c)$ with negative discriminant (residue field $C$); the latter ``hide'' a conjugate pair of complex points. Sanity check: $\SpecR[x]=\{(0)\}\sqcup\mSpecR[x]$, where $\mSpecR[x]=R\sqcup\{conjugate pairs in C\setminusR\}$ is in bijection with $C/(complex conjugation)$ -- exactly the failure of $k$ not being algebraically closed, and the reason the Nullstellensatz bijection $\mSpec\leftrightarrow$ points needs $k=\overline k$.
\end{wex}

Type: prose
Content:
A single diagram records the contravariant dictionary at the heart of the section: the algebraic operations on $R$ on the left, their geometric meaning on $\Spec R$ on the right, with quotients giving closed pieces and localizations giving open pieces.

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=2.0em]
R/\fa \arrow[d,dash] & R \arrow[l,twoheadrightarrow,"quotient"'] \arrow[r,"localize"] \arrow[d,dash] & R_f \arrow[d,dash] \\
V(\fa)\ (closed) & \Spec R & D(f)\ (open)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.6em, column sep=2.2em]
\Spec S \arrow[r,"\varphi^{*}"] \arrow[d,dash] & \Spec R \arrow[d,dash] \\
\fq \arrow[r,mapsto] & \varphi^{-1}(\fq)
\end{tikzcd}
\]

The left square shows the two ways to ``cut out'' a chart -- closed via $R\twoheadrightarrow R/\fa$ realizing $V(\fa)$, open via $R\to R_f$ realizing $D(f)$ -- while the right square shows that a ring map runs functions backward (contravariance), the engine of the affine-scheme equivalence of Theorem~ [REF:thm:scheme@c15] .

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left square, top row: $R$ (the base commutative ring), $R/\fa$ (the quotient ring by an ideal $\fa\subseteq R$), and $R_f$ (the localization at a single element $f\in R$). Bottom row: $\Spec R$ (the full prime spectrum), $V(\fa)\subseteq\Spec R$ (the Zariski-closed set of primes containing $\fa$), and $D(f)\subseteq\Spec R$ (the basic open set of primes missing $f$). Right square: $\Spec S$ and $\Spec R$ are topological spaces (prime spectra of rings $S$ and $R$ linked by $\varphi\colon R\to S$); the bottom row displays generic elements $\fq\in\Spec S$ and its image $\varphi^{-1}(\fq)\in\Spec R$.
\dgi{Arrows:} In the left square: $R\twoheadrightarrow R/\fa$ is the surjective quotient map (kills $\fa$); $R\to R_f$ is the localization map (inverts powers of $f$); the three vertical undirected solid lines are not maps of rings but the dictionary correspondences linking each algebraic object to its geometric counterpart. In the right square: $\varphi^{*}\colon\Spec S\to\Spec R$ is the induced continuous map of spaces, sending $\fq$ to its contraction $\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$; the bottom horizontal arrow records the same assignment at the element level via $\mapsto$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The left square is a correspondence table, not a commutative square of ring maps: each algebraic operation (quotient by $\fa$, localize at $f$) produces exactly one geometric piece ($V(\fa)$ closed, $D(f)$ open), with $\Spec R$ in the center mediating both. The right square does commute as a diagram of spaces: the top arrow $\varphi^{*}$ and the bottom element-level arrow agree, i.e.\ $\varphi^{*}(\fq)=\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$ for every $\fq\in\Spec S$, making the square a definition diagram rather than a commutativity condition to verify.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For the right square, well-definedness of $\varphi^{*}$ is the key: if $\fq$ is prime in $S$ and $ab\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$, then $\varphi(a)\varphi(b)\in\fq$, so $\varphi(a)\in\fq$ or $\varphi(b)\in\fq$ (since $\fq$ is prime), hence $a\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$ or $b\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$: the preimage of a prime is prime. For the left correspondence: $\pi^{*}(\fq)=\pi^{-1}(\fq)$ for $\pi\colon R\to R/\fa$ lands in $V(\fa)$ because $\fa\subseteq\pi^{-1}(\fq)$ always; and the primes of $R_f$ biject with primes of $R$ not containing $f$, i.e.\ with $D(f)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} These two panels summarize the entire section in one picture. Every algebraic operation studied -- quotient (closed immersion), localization (open immersion), ring map (continuous pullback) -- has now been given a geometric meaning. The author places this diagram at the close of the section as a unified dictionary: the left panel shows how algebra carves out geometry, and the right panel shows how algebra maps run backward geometrically, which is the content of the contravariant functor $\Spec$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R=Z$, $\fa=(6)$, $f=5$, and $\varphi\colonZ\hookrightarrowZ[i]$. Left panel: $R/\fa=Z/6Z$ corresponds to $V(6)=\{(2),(3)\}$ (closed, two points); $R_f=Z[1/5]$ corresponds to $D(5)=\SpecZ\setminus\{(5)\}$ (open). Right panel: $\varphi^{*}((2+i)Z[i])=(2+i)Z[i]\capZ=(5)$; $\varphi^{*}(3Z[i])=(3)$; $\varphi^{*}(0)=(0)$ -- primes of $Z[i]$ pull back to the primes of $Z$ they lie over.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often confuse the vertical solid lines in the left panel with ring homomorphisms, reading ``$R/\fa\to V(\fa)$'' as a map between algebraic and geometric objects of the same type. They are a dictionary correspondence, not a morphism; the actual maps are $\pi^{*}\colon\Spec(R/\fa)\xrightarrow{\sim}V(\fa)$ and $\iota^{*}\colon\Spec R_f\xrightarrow{\sim}D(f)$, which are homeomorphisms of topological spaces, not ring maps. Collapsing this distinction causes confusion when one later writes $\mathcal O(V(\fa))$ versus $R/\fa$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two fundamental algebraic operations -- quotienting and localizing -- are precisely the operations that carve out closed and open subsets of $\Spec R$, while any ring map $\varphi$ automatically produces a continuous map of spectra running in the opposite direction, assembling algebra and geometry into a single contravariant dictionary.
\end{dgx}

\dgi{Why it commutes:} For the right square, well-definedness of $\varphi^{*}$ is the key: if $\fq$ is prime in $S$ and $ab\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$, then $\varphi(a)\varphi(b)\in\fq$, so $\varphi(a)\in\fq$ or $\varphi(b)\in\fq$ (since $\fq$ is prime), hence $a\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$ or $b\in\varphi^{-1}(\fq)$: the preimage of a prime is prime. For the left correspondence: $\pi^{*}(\fq)=\pi^{-1}(\fq)$ for $\pi\colon R\to R/\fa$ lands in $V(\fa)$ because $\fa\subseteq\pi^{-1}(\fq)$ always; and the primes of $R_f$ biject with primes of $R$ not containing $f$, i.e.\ with $D(f)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} These two panels summarize the entire section in one picture. Every algebraic operation studied -- quotient (closed immersion), localization (open immersion), ring map (continuous pullback) -- has now been given a geometric meaning. The author places this diagram at the close of the section as a unified dictionary: the left panel shows how algebra carves out geometry, and the right panel shows how algebra maps run backward geometrically, which is the content of the contravariant functor $\Spec$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $\fa=(6)$, $f=5$, and $\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}[i]$. Left panel: $R/\fa=\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ corresponds to $V(6)=\{(2),(3)\}$ (closed, two points); $R_f=\mathbb{Z}[1/5]$ corresponds to $D(5)=\Spec\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{(5)\}$ (open). Right panel: $\varphi^{*}((2+i)\mathbb{Z}[i])=(2+i)\mathbb{Z}[i]\cap\mathbb{Z}=(5)$; $\varphi^{*}(3\mathbb{Z}[i])=(3)$; $\varphi^{*}(0)=(0)$ -- primes of $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ pull back to the primes of $\mathbb{Z}$ they lie over.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often confuse the vertical solid lines in the left panel with ring homomorphisms, reading ``$R/\fa\to V(\fa)$'' as a map between algebraic and geometric objects of the same type. They are a dictionary correspondence, not a morphism; the actual maps are $\pi^{*}\colon\Spec(R/\fa)\xrightarrow{\sim}V(\fa)$ and $\iota^{*}\colon\Spec R_f\xrightarrow{\sim}D(f)$, which are homeomorphisms of topological spaces, not ring maps. Collapsing this distinction causes confusion when one later writes $\mathcal O(V(\fa))$ versus $R/\fa$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two fundamental algebraic operations -- quotienting and localizing -- are precisely the operations that carve out closed and open subsets of $\Spec R$, while any ring map $\varphi$ automatically produces a continuous map of spectra running in the opposite direction, assembling algebra and geometry into a single contravariant dictionary.
\end{dgx}
