Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 1/3
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item If $\fN$ is the nilradical of $R$, prove that $\Spec R$ and $\Spec R/\fN$ are homeomorphic. [Show that the natural homomorphism from $R$ to $R/\fN$ induces a Zariski continuous isomorphism from $\Spec R/\fN$ to $\Spec R$.]

\item Let $I$ be an ideal in the ring $R$. Prove that the continuous map from $\Spec R/I$ to $\Spec R$ induced by the canonical projection homomorphism $R \to R/I$ maps $\Spec R/I$ homeomorphically onto the closed set $Z(I)$ in $\Spec R$.

\item Prove that two elements $f, g \in R$ have the same values at all elements $P$ in $\Spec R$ if and only if $f - g$ is contained in the nilradical of $R$. In particular, prove that an element in an affine $k$-algebra is uniquely determined by its values.

\item Let $k$ be an arbitrary field, not necessarily algebraically closed. Prove that the prime ideals in $k[x, y]$ (i.e., the elements of $\Spec k[x, y]$) are
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(0)$,
\item[(ii)] $(f)$ where $f$ is an irreducible polynomial in $k[x, y]$, and
\item[(iii)] $(p(x), g(x, y))$ where $p(x)$ is an irreducible polynomial in $k[x]$ and $g(x, y)$ is a polynomial in $k[x, y]$ that is irreducible modulo $p(x)$, i.e., $g(x, y)$ remains irreducible in the quotient $k[x, y]/(p(x))$.
\end{enumerate}
Prove that $\mSpec k[x, y]$ consists of the primes in (iii). [Use Exercise 20 in Section 1.]

\item Let $\fm = (p(x), g(x, y))$ be a maximal ideal in $k[x, y]$ as in the previous exercise. Show that $K = k[x, y]/\fm$ is an algebraic field extension of $k$, so that $k[x, y]$ can also be viewed as a subring of $K[x, y]$. If $x, y$ are mapped to $\alpha, \beta \in K$, respectively, under the canonical homomorphism $k[x, y] \to k[x, y]/\fm$, prove that $\fm = k[x, y] \cap (x - \alpha, y - \beta) \subseteq K[x, y]$.

\item Describe the elements in $\Spec R[x]$ and $\Spec C[x]$. Describe the elements in $\Spec Z_{(2)}[x]$ where $Z_{(2)} = \{a/b \in Q \mid b is odd\}$ is the localization of $Z$ at the prime $(2)$.

\item Let $(f) = (x^5 + x + 1)$ in $\Spec Z[x]$ viewed as fibered over $\Spec Z$ as in Example 3 following Proposition 55. Show that there are two closed points in the fiber over $(2)$, three closed points in the fiber over $(5)$, four closed points in the fiber over $(19)$, and five closed points in the fiber over $(211)$.

\item Let $(f) = (x^4 + 1)$ in $\Spec Z[x]$ viewed as fibered over $\Spec Z$ as in Example 3 following Proposition 55. Prove that there is one closed point in the fiber over $(2)$, four closed points in the fiber over $p$ for $p$ odd, $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, and two closed points in the fiber over $p$ for all other odd primes $p$ (cf. Corollary 16 in Section 3 of Chapter 14).

\item Prove that the elements in the fiber over $(p)$ of the Zariski continuous map from $\Spec Z[x]$ to $\Spec Z$ are homeomorphic with the elements in $\Spec(Z[x] \otimes_{Z} \F_p)$.

\item Let $X = \Spec R$ and let $X_f$ be the principal open set corresponding to $f \in R$. Prove that $X_f \cap X_g = X_{fg}$. Prove that $X_f = X$ if and only if $f$ is a unit in $R$, and that $X_f = \varnothing$ if and only if $f$ is nilpotent.

\item If $X_f$ and $X_g$ are principal open sets in $X = \Spec R$, prove that the open set $X_f \cup X_g$ is the complement of the closed set $Z(I)$ where $I = (f, g)$ is the ideal in $R$ generated by $f$ and $g$.

\item Prove that a Zariski open subset $U$ of $X = \Spec R$ is quasicompact if and only if $U$ is a finite union of principal open subsets. Give an example of a ring $R$, a Zariski open subset $U$ of $\Spec R$, and a Zariski open covering of $U$ that cannot be reduced to a finite subcovering.

\item Let $\varphi : R \to S$ be a homomorphism of rings. Prove that under the induced map $\varphi^*$ from $Y = \Spec S$ to $X = \Spec R$ the full preimage of the principal open set $X_f$ in $X$ is the principal open set $Y_{\varphi(f)}$ in $Y$.

\item Suppose that $R = R_1 \times R_2$ is the direct product of the rings $R_1$ and $R_2$. Prove that $X = \Spec R$ is the disjoint union of open subspaces $X_1, X_2$ (which are therefore also closed), where $X_1$ is homeomorphic to $\Spec R_1$ and $X_2$ is homeomorphic to $\Spec R_2$.

\item Prove that $X = \Spec R$ is not connected if and only if $R$ is the direct product of two nonzero rings if and only if $R$ contains an idempotent $e$ with $e \neq 0, 1$ (cf. the previous exercise).

\item Prove that $X = \Spec R$ is irreducible (i.e., any two nonempty open subsets have a nontrivial intersection) if and only if $X_f \cap X_g \neq \varnothing$ for any two nonempty principal open sets $X_f$ and $X_g$. Deduce that $X = \Spec R$ is irreducible if and only if the nilradical of $R$ is a prime ideal. [Use Exercise 10.]

\item Let $G = \langle a\rangle$ be a group of order 2, let $R = Z[G] = \{m + na \mid m, n \in Z\}$ be the corresponding group ring, and let $X = \Spec R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that the nilradical of $R$ is $(0)$ but is not a prime ideal. Prove that $X = X^{+} \cup X^{-}$ where $X^{+} = Z(1 - a)$ and $X^{-} = Z(1 + a)$. [Use $(1 + a)(1 - a) = 0$.]
\item[(b)] Prove that the homomorphism $Z[G] \to Z$ defined by mapping $a$ to $1$ induces a homeomorphism of $X^{+}$ with $\Spec Z$, and the homomorphism mapping $a$ to $-1$ induces a homeomorphism of $X^{-}$ with $\Spec Z$.
\item[(c)] Prove that $X^{+} \cap X^{-}$ consists of the single element $\fm = (1 + a, 1 - a) = (2, 1 - a)$ and that this is a closed point in $X$.
\item[(d)] Show that $(1 - a)$ and $(1 + a)$ are the unique non-closed points in $X$, with closures $X^{+}$ and $X^{-}$, respectively.

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 2/3
Content:
Describe the closed points, $\mSpec R$, in $X$ and prove that $\Spec Z[\langle a\rangle]$ can be pictured as fibered over $\Spec Z$ with $X^{-}$ containing $(1 + a), \fm, (3, 1 + a), (5, 1 + a), \ldots$ and $X^{+}$ containing $(1 - a), \fm, (3, 1 - a), (5, 1 - a), \ldots$ lying over the primes $(0), (2), (3), (5), \ldots$ of $\Spec Z$ (the two lines cross at $\fm$).
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $O$ be the structure sheaf on $X = \Spec R$, let $U$ be an open set in $X$, and suppose $s, t \in O(U)$. If $s = a/f_1^n$ on $X_{f_1}$ and $t = b/f_2^m$ on $X_{f_2}$, show that
\[
st = (ab f_1^m f_2^n)/(f_1 f_2)^{n+m} \quad and \quad s + t = (a f_1^m f_2^{m+n} + b f_1^{m+n} f_2^n)/(f_1 f_2)^{n+m}
\]
on $X_{f_1 f_2}$. Deduce that $O(U)$ is a commutative ring with identity.

\item Let $O$ be the structure sheaf on $X = \Spec R$, let $V \subseteq U$ be open sets in $X$, and let $s \in O(U)$. Suppose $P \in V$ and that $s = a/f^n$ on $X_f \subseteq U$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that there is a principal open set $X_{f'} \subseteq V \cap X_f$ containing $P$.
\item[(b)] Show that $(f')^m = bf$ for some $b \in R$.
\item[(c)] Show that $s = (ab^n)/(f')^{mn}$ on $X_{f'}$ and conclude that restricting $s$ to $V$ gives a well defined ring homomorphism from $O(U)$ to $O(V)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $\varphi : R \to S$ be a homomorphism of rings, let $X = \Spec R$, $Y = \Spec S$, and let $V \subseteq U$ be Zariski open subsets of $X$. Set $V' = (\varphi^*)^{-1}(V)$ and $U' = (\varphi^*)^{-1}(U)$, the corresponding Zariski open subsets of $Y$ with respect to the continuous map $\varphi^* : Y \to X$ induced by $\varphi$. Prove that the induced map $\varphi^{\#} : O_X(U) \to O_Y(U')$ on sections is a ring homomorphism. Prove that $V' \subseteq U'$ and that $\varphi^{\#}$ is compatible with restriction, i.e., that the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
O_X(U) \arrow[r, "\varphi^{\#}"] \arrow[d] & O_Y(U') \arrow[d] \\
O_X(V) \arrow[r, "\varphi^{\#}"'] & O_Y(V')
\end{tikzcd}
\]
is commutative, where the vertical maps are the restriction homomorphisms.

\item Suppose $D$ is a multiplicatively closed subset of $R$. Show that the localization homomorphism $R \to D^{-1}R$ induces a homeomorphism from $\Spec(D^{-1}R)$ to the collection of prime ideals $P$ of $R$ with $P \cap D = \varnothing$.

\item Show that $\Spec k[x, y]/(xy)$ is connected but is the union of two proper closed subsets each homeomorphic to $\Spec k[x]$, hence is not irreducible (cf. Exercise 16).

\item For each of the following rings $R$ exhibit the elements of $\Spec R$, the open sets $U$ in $\Spec R$, the sections $O(U)$ of the structure sheaf for $\Spec R$ for each open $U$, and the stalks $O_P$ at each point $P \in \Spec R$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $Z/4Z$,
\item[(b)] $Z/6Z$,
\item[(c)] $Z/2Z \times Z/3Z$,
\item[(d)] $Z/2Z \times Z/2Z \times Z/2Z$.
\end{enumerate}

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If every ideal of $R$ is principal, show every open set in $\Spec R$ is a principal open set.
\item[(b)] Show that if $R = Z[x]/(4, x^2)$ then $R$ contains a nonprincipal ideal, but every open set in $\Spec R$ is a principal open set.
\end{enumerate}

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $M$ is an $R$-module prove that $\Supp(M)$ is the union of the Zariski closed sets $Z(P)$, $P\in\Supp(M)$. [Use Exercise 33 of Section 4.] Show that $\Supp(M)$ need not be Zariski closed (consider the $Z$-module $\bigoplus_pZ/pZ$).
\item[(b)] If $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module prove that $\Supp(M) = Z(\Ann(M)) \subseteq \Spec R$. [Use Exercise 34 of Section 4.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $M$ is a finitely generated module over the Noetherian ring $R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that there are finitely many minimal primes $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ containing $\Ann(M)$. [Use Corollary 22.]
\item[(b)] Prove that $\{P_1, \ldots, P_n\}$ is also the set of minimal primes in $\Ass_R(M)$ and that $\Supp(M)$ is the union of the Zariski closed sets $Z(P_1), \ldots, Z(P_n)$ in $\Spec R$. [Use the previous exercise and Exercise 40 in Section 4.]
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R = k[x, y]$ and let $M$ be the ideal $(x, y)$ in $R$. Prove that $\Supp(M) = \Spec R$ and $\Ass_R(M) = \{0\}$.

\item This exercise proves that the ideal $Q$ in a Noetherian ring $R$ is $P$-primary if and only if $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $Q$ is a $P$-primary ideal and let $M$ be the $R$-module $R/Q$. If $0 \neq m \in M$, show that $Q \subseteq \Ann(m) \subseteq P$ and that $\rad \Ann(m) = P$. Deduce that if $\Ann(m)$ is a prime ideal then it is equal to $P$ and hence that $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$. [Use Exercise 33 in Section 1.]
\item[(b)] For any ideal $Q$ of $R$, let $0 \neq M \subseteq R/Q$. Prove that the radical of $\Ann(M)$ is the intersection of the prime ideals in $\Supp(M)$. [Use Proposition 12 and Exercise 25.]
\item[(c)] For $M$ as in (b), prove that the radical of $\Ann(M)$ is also the intersection of the prime ideals in $\Ass_R(M)$. [Use Exercise 26(b).]
\item[(d)] If $Q$ is an ideal of $R$ with $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$ prove that $\rad Q = P$. [Use the fact that $Q = \Ann(R/Q)$ and (c).]
\item[(e)] If $Q$ is an ideal of $R$ with $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$ prove that $Q$ is $P$-primary. [If $ab \in Q$ with $a \notin Q$ consider $0 \neq M = (Ra + Q)/Q \subseteq R/Q$ and show that $b$ is contained in $\Ann(M) \subseteq \rad \Ann(M)$.

\item[(a)] $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$,
\item[(b)] $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$,
\item[(c)] $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$,
\item[(d)] $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If every ideal of $R$ is principal, show every open set in $\Spec R$ is a principal open set.
\item[(b)] Show that if $R = \mathbb{Z}[x]/(4, x^2)$ then $R$ contains a nonprincipal ideal, but every open set in $\Spec R$ is a principal open set.
\end{enumerate}

\item[(a)] If $M$ is an $R$-module prove that $\Supp(M)$ is the union of the Zariski closed sets $Z(P)$, $P\in\Supp(M)$. [Use Exercise 33 of Section 4.] Show that $\Supp(M)$ need not be Zariski closed (consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\bigoplus_p\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$).
\item[(b)] If $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module prove that $\Supp(M) = Z(\Ann(M)) \subseteq \Spec R$. [Use Exercise 34 of Section 4.]

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that there are finitely many minimal primes $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ containing $\Ann(M)$. [Use Corollary 22.]
\item[(b)] Prove that $\{P_1, \ldots, P_n\}$ is also the set of minimal primes in $\Ass_R(M)$ and that $\Supp(M)$ is the union of the Zariski closed sets $Z(P_1), \ldots, Z(P_n)$ in $\Spec R$. [Use the previous exercise and Exercise 40 in Section 4.]
\end{enumerate}

\item This exercise proves that the ideal $Q$ in a Noetherian ring $R$ is $P$-primary if and only if $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $Q$ is a $P$-primary ideal and let $M$ be the $R$-module $R/Q$. If $0 \neq m \in M$, show that $Q \subseteq \Ann(m) \subseteq P$ and that $\rad \Ann(m) = P$. Deduce that if $\Ann(m)$ is a prime ideal then it is equal to $P$ and hence that $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$. [Use Exercise 33 in Section 1.]
\item[(b)] For any ideal $Q$ of $R$, let $0 \neq M \subseteq R/Q$. Prove that the radical of $\Ann(M)$ is the intersection of the prime ideals in $\Supp(M)$. [Use Proposition 12 and Exercise 25.]
\item[(c)] For $M$ as in (b), prove that the radical of $\Ann(M)$ is also the intersection of the prime ideals in $\Ass_R(M)$. [Use Exercise 26(b).]
\item[(d)] If $Q$ is an ideal of $R$ with $\Ass_R(R/Q) = \{P\}$ prove that $\rad Q = P$. [Use the fact that $Q = \Ann(R/Q)$ and (c).]

\end{enumerate}

\item The subspace of $\Spec(A)$ consisting of the maximal ideals of $A$, with the induced topology, is called the maximal spectrum of $A$ and is denoted by $\operatorname{Max}(A)$. For arbitrary commutative rings it does not have the nice functorial properties of $\Spec(A)$ (see Exercise 21), because the inverse image of a maximal ideal under a ring homomorphism need not be maximal. Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space and let $C(X)$ denote the ring of all real-valued continuous functions on $X$. For each $x \in X$, let $\fm_x$ be the set of all $f \in C(X)$ such that $f(x) = 0$. The ideal $\fm_x$ is maximal, because it is the kernel of the (surjective) homomorphism $C(X) \to R$ which takes $f$ to $f(x)$. If $\overline{X}$ denotes $\operatorname{Max}(C(X))$, we have therefore defined a mapping $\mu : X \to \overline{X}$, namely $x \mapsto \fm_x$. Show that $\mu$ is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto $\overline{X}$. Thus $X$ can be reconstructed from the ring of functions $C(X)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Let $\fm$ be any maximal ideal of $C(X)$, and let $V = V(\fm)$ be the set of common zeros of the functions in $\fm$: that is, $V = \{x \in X \mid f(x) = 0 for all f \in \fm\}$. Suppose that $V$ is empty. Then for each $x \in X$ there exists $f_x \in \fm$ such that $f_x(x) \neq 0$. Since $f_x$ is continuous, there is an open neighborhood $U_x$ of $x$ in $X$ on which $f_x$ does not vanish. By compactness a finite number of the neighborhoods, say $U_{x_1}, \ldots, U_{x_n}$, cover $X$. Let
\[
f = f_{x_1}^2 + \cdots + f_{x_n}^2.
\]
Then $f$ does not vanish at any point of $X$, hence is a unit in $C(X)$. But this contradicts $f \in \fm$, hence $V$ is non-empty. Let $x$ be a point of $V$. Then $\fm \subseteq \fm_x$, hence $\fm = \fm_x$ because $\fm$ is maximal. Hence $\mu$ is surjective.
\item[(ii)] By Urysohn's lemma (this is the only non-trivial fact required in the argument) the continuous functions separate the points of $X$. Hence $x \neq y \Rightarrow \fm_x \neq \fm_y$ and therefore $\mu$ is injective.
\item[(iii)] Let $f \in C(X)$; let $U_f = \{x \in X \mid f(x) \neq 0\}$ and let $\overline{U}_f = \{\fm \in \overline{X} \mid f \notin \fm\}$. Show that $\mu(U_f) = \overline{U}_f$. The open sets $U_f$ (resp.\ $\overline{U}_f$) form a basis of the topology of $X$ (resp.\ $\overline{X}$) and therefore $\mu$ is a homeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Let $R = k[x,y,z]/(xy, xz)$ with $k$ a field. Compute the minimal primes of $R$, describe the irreducible components of $X = \Spec R$ geometrically (as a union of a plane and a line meeting at the origin), and decide whether $X$ is connected and whether it is irreducible. Identify the unique generic point of each component.

\item In $R = Z/180Z$ list every element of $\Spec R$, compute the nilradical $\nil R$, exhibit $R_{red}$ explicitly as a product of finite fields, and confirm that $\Spec R$ and $\Spec R_{red}$ have the same underlying set with the discrete topology. State $\abs{\Spec R}$ and explain why it equals the number of distinct prime divisors of $180$.

\item For $R = k[x,y]$ and $f = x^2 - y^3$, decide whether $(f)$ is prime, identify the closure $\overline{\{(f)\}}$ as a closed subset of $\Spec R$, and determine the closed points of $V(f)$ when $k$ is algebraically closed. Is $(f)$ a closed point of $\Spec R$? Justify using the closure-of-a-point computation.

\item Let $X = \Spec R$ and let $f, g \in R$. Prove directly from the definitions that $D(f) \subseteq D(g)$ if and only if $f \in \rad(g)$, and that $D(f) = D(f^2)$ for every $f$. Deduce that the map $\rad(g) \mapsto D(g)$ is well defined on radicals, and use this to show $D(6) = D(12)$ in $\Spec Z$ while $D(6) \neq D(2)$.

\item Consider the localization map $\varphi\colon Z \to Z[1/10]$. Describe $\varphi^{*}\colon \Spec Z[1/10] \to \Spec Z$ as a subset of $\Spec Z$, identify which primes $(p)$ lie in the image, and verify that the image equals the basic open set $D(10)$. State the global sections $O_{\SpecZ}(D(10))$ and the stalk at $(7)$.

\item Let $\varphi\colon R \to S$ be a ring homomorphism with induced map $\varphi^{*}\colon \Spec S \to \Spec R$. Prove that if $\varphi$ is surjective then $\varphi^{*}$ is a homeomorphism of $\Spec S$ onto the closed set $V(\ker\varphi) \subseteq \Spec R$, and that if $\varphi$ is the localization $R \to R_f$ then $\varphi^{*}$ is a homeomorphism of $\Spec R_f$ onto the open set $D(f)$. Contrast the two cases (closed immersion versus open immersion).

\item In $R = k[x]/(x^2)$ (the dual numbers), show that $\Spec R$ is a single point $\fp = (\overline{x})$, compute the value $f(\fp) \in R/\fp$ of $f = a + b\overline{x}$, and exhibit two distinct elements of $R$ with identical values at every point of $\Spec R$. Identify $\nil R$ and $R_{red}$, and explain what topological information about $R$ is lost on passing to $\Spec R$.

\item Let $R = \prod_{i=1}^{n} k_i$ be a finite product of fields. Prove that $\Spec R$ is a discrete space on $n$ points, exhibit the nontrivial idempotents witnessing the total disconnection, and show that the basic open set $D(e_i)$ for the standard idempotent $e_i$ is the single point corresponding to the $i$th factor.
\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that for ideals $\fa, \fb$ of a ring $R$ one has $V(\fa) \subseteq V(\fb)$ if and only if $\rad\fb \subseteq \rad\fa$, and that $V(\fa) = V(\fb)$ if and only if $\rad\fa = \rad\fb$. Conclude that $V$ and $I$ restrict to mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections between the Zariski-closed subsets of $\Spec R$ and the radical ideals of $R$.

\item Let $X = \Spec R$. Prove that a closed set $V(\fa)$ is irreducible if and only if $\rad\fa$ is a prime ideal, and deduce that the irreducible components of $X$ are exactly the closures $V(\fp)$ of the minimal primes $\fp$ of $R$. Apply this to $R = k[x,y]/(x^2 y, x y^2)$ to list the irreducible components.

\item Let $\fp$ be a prime of $R$ and let $\kappa(\fp) = \Frac(R/\fp)$ be its residue field. For a ring map $\varphi\colon R \to S$, prove that the fiber $(\varphi^{*})^{-1}(\fp) \subseteq \Spec S$ is canonically homeomorphic to $\Spec\bigl(S \otimes_R \kappa(\fp)\bigr)$. Use this to compute the number of points in the fiber of $\Spec Z[x]/(f) \to \Spec Z$ over $(p)$ for $f = x^2 + 1$ when $p = 2$, $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

\item Prove that $X = \Spec R$ is quasi-compact: every open cover by basic open sets $\{D(g_i)\}_{i \in I}$ admits a finite subcover, by showing that $X = \bigcup_i D(g_i)$ forces $(g_i : i \in I) = R$ and extracting a finite unit relation $1 = \sum_{j} a_j g_{i_j}$. Then exhibit a non-Noetherian ring $R$ and an open subset $U \subseteq \Spec R$ that is not quasi-compact.

\item Prove that $\Spec R$ is disconnected if and only if $R$ contains an idempotent $e$ with $e \neq 0, 1$, by showing that a clopen decomposition $\Spec R = D(e) \sqcup D(1-e)$ corresponds to a ring decomposition $R \cong Re \times R(1-e)$. Deduce that the spectrum of any local ring or any integral domain is connected.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a ring and $\fa$ an ideal, with quotient $\pi\colon R \twoheadrightarrow R/\fa$ and localization $\lambda\colon R \to R_f$. Complete the diagram below, in which the bottom row records the geometric pieces of $\Spec R$ cut out by these two algebraic operations. Prove that $\pi^{*}$ is a homeomorphism onto the closed set $V(\fa)$ and that $\lambda^{*}$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $D(f)$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.8em, column sep=2.2em]
R/\fa \arrow[d,dash] & R \arrow[l,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi"'] \arrow[r,"\lambda"] \arrow[d,dash] & R_f \arrow[d,dash] \\
V(\fa) \arrow[r,hook,"\pi^{*}"'] & \Spec R & D(f) \arrow[l,hook',"\lambda^{*}"']
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Label the horizontal maps of the bottom row as closed immersion and open immersion respectively, and state the image of each.

\item For ring maps $\varphi\colon R \to S$ and $\psi\colon S \to T$, complete the triangle of induced spectrum maps below and prove that $\Spec$ is a contravariant functor, i.e.\ that $(\psi \circ \varphi)^{*} = \varphi^{*} \circ \psi^{*}$ and $\id^{*} = \id$. Prove also that each arrow is continuous by showing $(\varphi^{*})^{-1}(D(f)) = D(\varphi(f))$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=2.6em]
\Spec T \arrow[r,"\psi^{*}"] \arrow[dr,"(\psi\circ\varphi)^{*}"'] & \Spec S \arrow[d,"\varphi^{*}"] \\
& \Spec R
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Verify the identity explicitly for $R = Z \hookrightarrow S = Z[i] \hookrightarrow T = Z[i,1/(1+i)]$ by tracing the point $(0) \in \Spec T$.

\item Let $\fp \in \Spec R$ and consider the localization $R \to R_\fp$ together with the residue field $\kappa(\fp) = R_\fp / \fp R_\fp = \Frac(R/\fp)$. Complete the square below relating the two ways of forming the residue field at $\fp$ (localize then quotient, versus quotient then localize), and prove it commutes; conclude that both routes produce the same field $\kappa(\fp)$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r,"localize at \fp"] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"quotient by \fp"'] & R_\fp \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"quotient by \fp R_\fp"] \\
R/\fp \arrow[r,"localize at (0)"'] & \kappa(\fp)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the stalk $O_{\Spec R, \fp}$ of the structure sheaf at $\fp$ with $R_\fp$, and verify the diagram for $R = Z$, $\fp = (5)$, computing $\kappa((5))$ and $O_{\SpecZ,(5)}$.

\item Let $f = x^3 - x - 1 \in Z[x]$ and view $V(f) \subseteq \Spec Z[x]$ as fibered over $\Spec Z$ via the inclusion $Z \hookrightarrow Z[x]$. Complete the diagram below, in which the fiber over $(p)$ is identified with $\Spec\bigl(\F_p[x]/(\overline{f})\bigr)$, and prove the induced map is a homeomorphism onto the fiber. Use it to count the closed points of the fiber over $(2)$, $(3)$, and $(23)$ from the factorization type of $\overline{f}$ in $\F_p[x]$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\Spec\bigl(\F_p[x]/(\overline{f})\bigr) \arrow[r,hook] \arrow[d] & \Spec\bigl(Z[x]/(f)\bigr) \arrow[d,"\varphi^{*}"] \\
\Spec \F_p \arrow[r,hook] & \Spec Z
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State the number of distinct irreducible factors of $\overline{f}$ over each of $\F_2, \F_3, \F_{23}$ and confirm it equals the number of closed points in the corresponding fiber.
\end{exers}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Filtrations and the topology they generate
Type: prose
Content:
Completion, like localization, is a device for simplifying a ring near a point. Localization concentrates near a prime by inverting everything outside it; completion concentrates near an ideal $\fa$ by remembering an element only through its successive residues modulo $\fa, \fa^2, \fa^3, \dots$. Geometrically this is the passage from a polynomial to its Taylor expansion at a point; arithmetically it is the passage from an integer to its base-$p$ digits, i.e.\ to its image in all the rings $Z/p^nZ$. Atiyah--Macdonald's organizing slogan is that the prime ideal is the common generalization of "a point of geometry" and "a prime of arithmetic," and the $\fa$-adic completion treats both uniformly: the local ring of a nonsingular point of an $n$-dimensional variety completes to the power series ring $k[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$, while $Z$ completed at $(p)$ gives the $p$-adic integers $Z_p$.

The technical engine is a filtration: a descending chain of subgroups that we declare to be a fundamental system of neighborhoods of $0$.

Type: definition
Title: {topology from a filtration of subgroups}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{topology from a filtration of subgroups}]
Let $G$ be an abelian group equipped with a descending chain of subgroups
\[
G=G_0\supseteq G_1\supseteq G_2\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_n\supseteq\cdots .
\]
Declare the cosets $\{g+G_n:g\in G,\ n\ge0\}$ to be a base of open sets. This makes $G$ a topological abelian group: $0$ has the $G_n$ as a fundamental system of neighborhoods, and addition and negation are continuous. Each $G_n$ is simultaneously open (it is a neighborhood of each of its points $g$, since $g+G_n\subseteq G_n$) and closed (its complement is the union of the open cosets $h+G_n$, $h\notin G_n$).
\end{definition}

Title: {$\fa$-adic topology}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{$\fa$-adic topology}]
Let $R$ be a ring and $\fa\subseteq R$ an ideal. The $\fa$-adic filtration is $G_n=\fa^n$ (with $\fa^0=R$); the resulting topology is the $\fa$-adic topology on $R$. For an $R$-module $M$, the $\fa$-adic topology on $M$ comes from the filtration $G_n=\fa^n M$. An element is "small" when it lies in a high power of $\fa$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
Continuity of the group operations gives (i). For (ii), $x\in\overline{\{0\}}$ iff every neighborhood $x+G_n$ of $x$ meets $\{0\}$, i.e.\ $-x\in G_n$ for all $n$, i.e.\ $x\in H$. Since the cosets of $H$ are exactly the closures of points, they are all closed in $G/H$, so $G/H$ is Hausdorff, giving (iii); and (iv) is (iii) read at $H=0$.
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: The $p$-adic topology on $Z$ is Hausdorff
Content:
\begin{wex}{The $p$-adic topology on $Z$ is Hausdorff}
For a prime $p$ show that the $(p)$-adic topology on $Z$ satisfies $\bigcap_n p^nZ=0$, hence is Hausdorff.
\wrec Hausdorff $\iff\bigcap_n G_n=0$ with $G_n=p^nZ$; reduce to: no nonzero integer is divisible by every power of $p$.
\wsol If $m\in\bigcap_n p^nZ$ then $p^n\mid m$ for all $n$. A nonzero integer has finitely many prime factors with finite multiplicities, so $p^n\nmid m$ once $p^n>\abs m$. Hence $m=0$ and $\bigcap_n p^nZ=0$, so the topology is Hausdorff by Lemma~ [REF:lem:intersection@c15] (iv). Sanity check: the distance $\abs{m}_p=p^{-v_p(m)}$ is a genuine metric precisely because $v_p(m)<\infty$ for $m\neq0$, matching the vanishing intersection.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-Hausdorff adic topology
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-Hausdorff adic topology}
Let $R=k[x]_{(x)}\times k$ with $\fa=\fm\times k$ where $\fm=xk[x]_{(x)}$. Exhibit $\bigcap_n\fa^n\neq0$.
\wrec Hausdorffness can fail when $\fa$ contains an idempotent-like direction killing no power; the intersection $\bigcap\fa^n$ measures the failure.
\wsol With $\fa=\fm\times k$ we have $\fa^n=\fm^n\times k$ (since $k\cdot k=k$), so $\bigcap_n\fa^n=\bigl(\bigcap_n\fm^n\bigr)\times k=0\times k\neq0$. The topology is not Hausdorff: the whole subgroup $0\times k$ is in the closure of $0$. Sanity check: the offending factor $k$ is a field on which $\fa$ acts as the unit ideal, so no power of $\fa$ shrinks it -- exactly the obstruction Krull's theorem (below) rules out under Jacobson-radical hypotheses.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {inverse limit and completion}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{inverse limit and completion}]
An inverse system of abelian groups is a sequence $(A_n)_{n\ge0}$ with homomorphisms $\theta_{n+1}\colon A_{n+1}\to A_n$. Its inverse limit is
\[
\varprojlim A_n=\{(a_n)\in\textstyle\prod_n A_n:\ \theta_{n+1}(a_{n+1})=a_n\ for all n\},
\]
the group of coherent sequences. For a filtered group $G$ with the system $G/G_{n+1}\to G/G_n$ (the natural surjections), the completion is
\[
\widehat G\;=\;\varprojlim_n G/G_n .
\]
For a ring $R$ with $G_n=\fa^n$ this is the ring $\widehat R=\varprojlim R/\fa^n$; for a module, $\widehat M=\varprojlim M/\fa^n M$, an $\widehat R$-module.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Completion as an inverse limit
Type: prose
Content:
The tower of quotients whose limit is the completion is the central diagram of the whole section:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.0em, row sep=3.2em]
\cdots \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & |[alias=A]| R/\fa^{n+1} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"\theta_{n+1}"] & |[alias=B]| R/\fa^{n} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"\theta_{n}"] & \cdots \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & |[alias=C]| R/\fa^{2} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"\theta_2"] & |[alias=D]| R/\fa \\
& & |[alias=H]| \widehat R=\varprojlim R/\fa^n \arrow[to=A,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi_{n+1}"]\arrow[to=B,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi_n"',near end]\arrow[to=C,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi_2"]\arrow[to=D,twoheadrightarrow,"\pi_1"',end anchor=south west]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Each $\theta_{n+1}$ is the reduction $R/\fa^{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow R/\fa^n$ (a surjective system), and $\widehat R$ sits over the tower compatibly with all projections $\pi_n\colon\widehat R\to R/\fa^n$. A point of $\widehat R$ is precisely a system of "residues to every order" that fit together.

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The top row consists of a tower of quotient rings $R/\fa^n$ for $n=1,2,\dots$ (each is a ring, not merely a set; it records the residue of every element modulo $\fa^n$). The bottom vertex is $\widehat R = \varprojlim R/\fa^n$, the $\fa$-adic completion of $R$: it is also a ring (the inverse limit inherits the ring structure coordinatewise from the product $\prod_n R/\fa^n$). These are connected in a directed fan: one row going right, one vertex projecting up.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each horizontal arrow $\theta_{n+1}\colon R/\fa^{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow R/\fa^n$ is the natural surjective ring homomorphism (reduction mod $\fa^n$): it sends $a + \fa^{n+1}$ to $a + \fa^n$, which is well-defined since $\fa^{n+1}\subseteq\fa^n$. Each $\pi_n\colon\widehat R\to R/\fa^n$ is the projection onto the $n$-th stage: it sends the coherent sequence $(a_m)_{m\ge1}$ to $a_n$. These are the canonical maps from the inverse limit to its factors.
\dgi{What commutes:} For every $n$, the triangle $\widehat R \xrightarrow{\pi_{n+1}} R/\fa^{n+1} \xrightarrow{\theta_{n+1}} R/\fa^n$ commutes with the projection $\pi_n$: $$\theta_{n+1}\circ\pi_{n+1} = \pi_n.$$ In other words, reducing a coherent sequence one level and then projecting equals projecting directly. This is not one equation but a whole compatible family, one for each consecutive pair $(n,n+1)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Let $(a_m)\in\widehat R$ be a coherent sequence, so $\theta_{m+1}(a_{m+1})=a_m$ for all $m$. Following the first path: $\pi_{n+1}(a_m)=a_{n+1}$, then $\theta_{n+1}(a_{n+1})=a_n$. Following $\pi_n$: $(a_m)\mapsto a_n$. Both give $a_n$. The equality holds by the definition of a coherent sequence: the coherence condition $\theta_{n+1}(a_{n+1})=a_n$ is exactly what living in the inverse limit means. No separate argument is needed; the commutativity is built into the membership criterion of $\varprojlim R/\fa^n$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the definition made visual. The text has just defined $\widehat R$ as the subgroup of $\prod R/\fa^n$ consisting of coherent sequences; the diagram encodes the universal property of $\varprojlim$: every ring fitting over the entire tower compatibly maps uniquely into $\widehat R$ compatibly with the projections, which determines $\widehat R$ up to unique isomorphism. Every subsequent result in this section -- exactness of completion, flatness of $\widehat R$, and Noetherianity -- is proved by leveraging this tower structure and the surjectivity of the system $(\theta_{n+1})$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R=Z$ and $\fa=(p)$. Then $R/\fa^n=Z/p^nZ$, each $\theta_{n+1}$ reduces a residue mod $p^{n+1}$ to a residue mod $p^n$ (drop the top digit in base $p$), and $\widehat R=Z_p$ is the ring of $p$-adic integers. A point of $Z_p$ is a coherent sequence $(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots)$ with $a_n\inZ/p^nZ$ and $a_{n+1}\equiv a_n\pmod{p^n}$, exactly a formal series $\sum_{k\ge0}c_k p^k$. The projections $\pi_n$ send this series to its partial sum mod $p^n$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read $\widehat R$ as sitting below the tower because the arrows $\pi_n$ point upward in the diagram, and conclude that $\widehat R$ is a quotient of the $R/\fa^n$. It is the opposite: $\widehat R$ is a subring of $\prod R/\fa^n$, with each $\pi_n$ a surjection onto $R/\fa^n$ (not an injection). Concretely, $Z_p\twoheadrightarrowZ/p^nZ$ is onto with kernel $p^nZ_p$ -- information is lost by projection, never gained.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the completion $\widehat R$ is not merely the limit of an algebraic process but the universal ring sitting compatibly over the entire tower of finite-order approximations $R/\fa^n$, so that knowing $\widehat R$ is equivalent to knowing all residues of every element to every order simultaneously.
\end{dgx}

The projections $\pi_n$ send this series to its partial sum mod $p^n$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often read $\widehat R$ as sitting \emph{below} the tower because the arrows $\pi_n$ point upward in the diagram, and conclude that $\widehat R$ is a quotient of the $R/\fa^n$. It is the opposite: $\widehat R$ is a \emph{subring} of $\prod R/\fa^n$, with each $\pi_n$ a surjection onto $R/\fa^n$ (not an injection). Concretely, $\mathbb{Z}_p\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ is onto with kernel $p^n\mathbb{Z}_p$ -- information is \emph{lost} by projection, never gained.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the completion $\widehat R$ is not merely the limit of an algebraic process but the universal ring sitting compatibly over the entire tower of finite-order approximations $R/\fa^n$, so that knowing $\widehat R$ is equivalent to knowing all residues of every element to every order simultaneously.
\end{dgx}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The inverse-limit description does not depend on a metric and is manifestly functorial: a filtration-compatible homomorphism $f\colon G\to H$ (with $f(G_n)\subseteq H_n$) induces $\widehat f\colon\widehat G\to\widehat H$ on coherent sequences, and $\widehat{g\circ f}=\widehat g\circ\widehat f$. The only drawback is that this description presupposes a choice of filtration $(G_n)$; the completion itself depends only on the topology, since two filtrations defining the same topology are cofinal in each other and so have the same inverse limit (for instance all stable $\fa$-filtrations, Lemma~ [REF:lem:stable@c15] below).
\end{remark}

Title: The $p$-adic integers $Z_p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The $p$-adic integers $Z_p$}
Identify $\widehatZ=\varprojlimZ/p^nZ$ and describe its elements.
\wrec $\widehatZ$ is the inverse limit of the tower $\cdots\toZ/p^3\toZ/p^2\toZ/p$; an element is a coherent sequence of residues.
\wsol An element of $Z_p:=\varprojlimZ/p^nZ$ is a sequence $(a_n)$ with $a_n\inZ/p^nZ$ and $a_{n+1}\equiv a_n\pmod{p^n}$. Writing $a_n$ in base $p$, coherence means the digits stabilize, so each element is a formal series $\sum_{k\ge0}c_kp^k$ with $0\le c_k<p$ -- a "$p$-adic integer." Addition and multiplication carry as in base-$p$ arithmetic. Sanity check: the constant sequences embed $Z\hookrightarrowZ_p$ (injective since $\bigcap p^nZ=0$), and $1+p+p^2+\cdots$ converges to $(1-p)^{-1}$ because $(1-p)\sum_{k=0}^N p^k=1-p^{N+1}\to1$ in the $p$-adic topology.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Formal power series $k[[x]]$ as a completion
Content:
\begin{wex}{Formal power series $k[[x]]$ as a completion}
For $R=k[x]$ and $\fa=(x)$, identify $\widehat R$.
\wrec $\widehat R=\varprojlim k[x]/(x^n)$; a coherent sequence is a polynomial specified to all orders, i.e.\ a power series.
\wsol $k[x]/(x^n)$ is the ring of polynomials of degree $<n$ (truncation), and the maps drop the top term. A coherent sequence assigns to each $n$ a polynomial $\bmod\,x^n$ with the lower terms agreeing, hence a formal series $\sum_{k\ge0}a_kx^k$. Thus $\widehat{k[x]}=k[[x]]$, the ring of formal power series. Sanity check: $\bigcap_n(x)^n=0$ in $k[x]$ (a nonzero polynomial has finite order of vanishing), so $k[x]\hookrightarrow k[[x]]$ injectively, and $1-x$ is a unit in $k[[x]]$ with inverse $\sum x^k$, mirroring $(1-p)^{-1}$ above.
\end{wex}

Title: Completion of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ at the origin

\begin{wex}{Completion of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ at the origin}
Compute $\widehat R$ for $R=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, $\fa=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$.
\wrec The geometric picture: completing the polynomial ring at the maximal ideal of the origin should give multivariate Taylor expansions.
\wsol $R/\fa^m$ is spanned by monomials of total degree $<m$, and the system truncates total degree. A coherent sequence is a formal sum of monomials of all degrees, so $\widehat R=k[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$, the formal power series ring in $n$ variables. Sanity check: this matches the slogan that the local ring of a smooth point of an $n$-dimensional variety completes to $k[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$; here the "variety" is $\Aff^n$ and the point is the origin, smooth of dimension $n$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $\widehat R$ over the completion functor is functorial and forgets nothing finite
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\widehat R$ over the completion functor is functorial and forgets nothing finite}
Show $\pi_n\colon\widehat R\to R/\fa^n$ is surjective with kernel $\widehat{\fa^n}=\ker(\widehat R\to R/\fa^n)$, and $\widehat R/\widehat{\fa^n}\cong R/\fa^n$.
\wrec Surjectivity of an inverse limit onto a finite stage uses that the system $R/\fa^{m}\to R/\fa^n$ ($m\ge n$) is surjective; the kernel is the coherent sequences vanishing $\bmod\,\fa^n$.
\wsol Given $\bar a\in R/\fa^n$, lift it to $a\in R$; its constant coherent sequence projects to $\bar a$, so $\pi_n$ is onto. The kernel consists of coherent sequences $(a_m)$ with $a_n=0$, which is exactly $\widehat{\fa^n}$. Hence $\widehat R/\widehat{\fa^n}\cong R/\fa^n$. Sanity check: with $R=Z$, $\fa=(p)$ this says $Z_p/p^nZ_p\congZ/p^nZ$ -- completing does not change any finite-order residue information.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Exactness of completion and flatness
Type: prose
Content:
The reason completion is a powerful tool is that, restricted to finitely generated modules over a Noetherian ring, it is exact, and the functor $M\mapsto\widehat M$ is realized by tensoring with the flat algebra $\widehat R$. This is the analogue, for completion, of the fact that localization $S^{-1}(-)$ is exact and flat. The proof rests on a structural property of surjective inverse systems and on the Artin--Rees lemma.

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Exactness of completion and flatness
Type: proposition
Title: {exactness for surjective systems}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{exactness for surjective systems}]
If $0\to(A_n)\to(B_n)\to(C_n)\to0$ is an exact sequence of inverse systems (compatible exact sequences at each level), then
\[
0\to\varprojlim A_n\to\varprojlim B_n\to\varprojlim C_n
\]
is always exact. If moreover $(A_n)$ is a surjective system (each $\theta_{n+1}\colon A_{n+1}\to A_n$ is onto), then $\varprojlim A_n\to\varprojlim B_n\to\varprojlim C_n\to0$ is exact too, so the whole sequence of limits is short exact.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Assemble the levelwise maps into $d^A\colon\prod A_n\to\prod A_n$, $d^A(a_n)=a_n-\theta_{n+1}(a_{n+1})$; then $\varprojlim A_n=\ker d^A$ and $\coker d^A=\varprojlim^1 A_n$. The snake lemma applied to the commutative ladder gives the six-term sequence $0\to\varprojlim A\to\varprojlim B\to\varprojlim C\to\varprojlim^1\!A\to\cdots$. When $(A_n)$ is surjective, $d^A$ is onto, so $\varprojlim^1 A_n=0$ and right-exactness follows. The filtration systems $R/\fa^n$ are surjective, so this case always applies.
\end{proof}

Title: {$\fa$-adic completion is exact on f.g.\ modules over Noetherian $R$}

Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$\fa$-adic completion is exact on f.g.\ modules over Noetherian $R$}] 
Let $R$ be Noetherian and let $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ be exact with all modules finitely generated. Then the sequence of $\fa$-adic completions
\[
0\to\widehat{M'}\to\widehat M\to\widehat{M''}\to0
\]
is exact.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
The filtration $\{(\fa^n M)\cap M'\}$ on $M'$ is, by Artin--Rees (below), a stable $\fa$-filtration of $M'$, hence equivalent to $\{\fa^n M'\}$ and giving the same completion $\widehat{M'}$. With this identification the systems $(M'/(\fa^nM\cap M'))$, $(M/\fa^nM)$, $(M''/\fa^nM'')$ form a short exact sequence of inverse systems whose left term is surjective, so taking $\varprojlim$ is exact by the previous proposition.
\end{proof}

Type: proposition
Title: {$\widehat R$ is flat}
Label: prop:flat@c15
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{$\widehat R$ is flat}] 
Let $R$ be Noetherian, $\widehat R$ its $\fa$-adic completion. For every finitely generated $R$-module $M$ the natural map $\widehat R\otimes_R M\to\widehat M$ is an isomorphism, and consequently $\widehat R$ is a flat $R$-module.
\end{proposition}
label: prop:flat@c15

A finite presentation $R^p\to R^q\to M\to0$ gives, after applying the right-exact $\widehat R\otimes_R(-)$ and the exact $\widehat{(-)}$ (Proposition~ [REF:prop:exact@c15] ), a diagram whose first two vertical maps are isomorphisms; the five lemma makes $\widehat R\otimes_R M\to\widehat M$ an isomorphism. Flatness then follows because $\widehat{(-)}$ is exact on finitely generated modules and the comparison is natural.
\end{proof}

Title: Completion of an ideal versus the completed ideal
Content:
\begin{wex}{Completion of an ideal versus the completed ideal}
For $R$ Noetherian and an ideal $\fb\subseteq R$, show $\widehat{\fb}\cong\widehat R\otimes_R\fb\cong\widehat R\,\fb$, the ideal of $\widehat R$ generated by $\fb$.
\wrec Apply flatness (Proposition~ [REF:prop:flat@c15] ) to the finitely generated module $\fb$ and the inclusion $\fb\hookrightarrow R$.
\wsol Tensoring $0\to\fb\to R$ with the flat $\widehat R$ keeps it injective, so $\widehat R\otimes_R\fb\hookrightarrow\widehat R$ has image the $\widehat R$-submodule generated by $\fb$, i.e.\ $\widehat R\fb$. By Proposition~ [REF:prop:flat@c15] , $\widehat R\otimes_R\fb\cong\widehat{\fb}$. Hence $\widehat{\fb}=\widehat R\fb$. Sanity check: with $R=Z$, $\fb=(p^k)$, $\fa=(p)$ this reads $\widehat{(p^k)}=p^kZ_p$, and indeed the completion of $p^kZ$ is the elements of $Z_p$ divisible by $p^k$.
\end{wex}

Title: $\widehat{\fa^n}=\widehat{\fa}^{\,n}$ and the topology of $\widehat R$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\widehat{\fa^n}=\widehat{\fa}^{\,n}$ and the topology of $\widehat R$}
For $R$ Noetherian, show $(\fa^n)\widehat{\ } =\widehat\fa^{\,n}$ and that $\widehat R$ is $\widehat\fa$-adically complete with $\bigcap_n\widehat\fa^{\,n}=0$.
\wrec Use flatness/identities $\widehat{\fa^n}=\widehat R\fa^n=(\widehat R\fa)^n=\widehat\fa^{\,n}$, then $\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}\cong R/\fa^n$.
\wsol By the previous example $\widehat{\fa^n}=\widehat R\fa^n=(\widehat R\fa)^n=\widehat\fa^{\,n}$. Since $\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}=\widehat R/\widehat{\fa^n}\cong R/\fa^n$, the completion of $\widehat R$ for its $\widehat\fa$-topology is $\varprojlim\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}=\varprojlim R/\fa^n=\widehat R$, so $\widehat R$ is complete. And $\bigcap_n\widehat\fa^{\,n}=\ker(\widehat R\to\varprojlim R/\fa^n)=0$, so $\widehat R$ is Hausdorff. Sanity check: $\widehat R$ is its own completion (idempotence of completion), exactly as $Z_p$ completed at $p$ is again $Z_p$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: definition
Title: {$\fa$-filtration, stable}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{$\fa$-filtration, stable}]
An $\fa$-filtration of an $R$-module $M$ is a chain $M=M_0\supseteq M_1\supseteq\cdots$ with $\fa M_n\subseteq M_{n+1}$ for all $n$. It is stable if $\fa M_n=M_{n+1}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. The $\fa$-adic filtration $M_n=\fa^n M$ is stable.
\end{definition}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: lemma
Title: {stable filtrations have bounded difference}
Label: lem:stable@c15
Content:
\begin{lemma}[{stable filtrations have bounded difference}] 
Any two stable $\fa$-filtrations $(M_n),(M_n')$ of $M$ have bounded difference: there is $n_0$ with $M_{n+n_0}\subseteq M_n'$ and $M_{n+n_0}'\subseteq M_n$ for all $n\ge0$. In particular all stable $\fa$-filtrations determine the same topology -- the $\fa$-adic topology -- and hence the same completion.
\end{lemma}
label: lem:stable@c15

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: theorem
Title: {Artin--Rees lemma}
Label: thm:ar@c15
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Artin--Rees lemma}] 
Let $R$ be Noetherian, $\fa\subseteq R$ an ideal, $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module with a stable $\fa$-filtration $(M_n)$, and $M'\subseteq M$ a submodule. Then $(M'\cap M_n)$ is a stable $\fa$-filtration of $M'$. Equivalently, there is an integer $k$ with
\[
(\fa^n M)\cap M'=\fa^{n-k}\bigl((\fa^k M)\cap M'\bigr)\qquadfor all n\ge k.
\]
\end{theorem}
label: thm:ar@c15

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-7900c0918c624f674c4c
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
Form the Rees algebra $R^\ast=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\fa^n=R[\fa t]\subseteq R[t]$; since $R$ is Noetherian and $\fa$ finitely generated, $R^\ast$ is Noetherian. The stable filtration makes $M^\ast=\bigoplus_n M_n$ a finitely generated graded $R^\ast$-module, and $(M'\cap M_n)$ defines a graded $R^\ast$-submodule of $M^\ast$. A submodule of a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is finitely generated, and for graded modules finite generation is equivalent to the filtration being stable (Lemma~ [REF:lem:Mstar@c15] ). Hence $(M'\cap M_n)$ is stable.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[{topology comparison}]
With $R,\fa,M$ as above and $M'\subseteq M$ finitely generated, the filtrations $(\fa^n M')$ and $(\fa^n M\cap M')$ of $M'$ have bounded difference. In particular the $\fa$-adic topology of $M'$ coincides with the subspace topology induced from the $\fa$-adic topology of $M$.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: example
Title: Artin--Rees fails without Noetherian: a non-stable intersection
Content:
\begin{wex}{Artin--Rees fails without Noetherian: a non-stable intersection}
Illustrate that, over a non-Noetherian ring, $(\fa^n M\cap M')$ need not be $\fa$-stable, by recalling A\&M's $C^\infty$ example in spirit.
\wrec Artin--Rees needs $R$ Noetherian (to make the Rees algebra Noetherian); drop it and the comparison of topologies can break.
\wsol Let $R$ be the ring of $C^\infty$ functions on $R$ and $\fa$ the ideal of functions vanishing at $0$. Take $M=R$ and $M'=(h)$ with $h=e^{-1/x^2}$ (extended by $0$). Since $\fa=(x)$ (Hadamard's lemma, see below) and $h=x^n\cdot(h/x^n)$ with $h/x^n$ again smooth, $h\in\fa^n$ for every $n$, so $\fa^n\cap M'=M'$ for all $n$ (in particular $\bigcap_n\fa^n\neq0$: the $\fa$-adic topology is not Hausdorff). If this filtration were $\fa$-stable we would get $\fa M'=M'$, i.e.\ $h=xgh$ for some $g\in R$; then $g(x)=1/x$ wherever $h(x)\neq0$, i.e.\ for all $x\neq0$, which is unbounded near $0$ -- impossible. So $(\fa^n\cap M')$ is not stable, and the subspace topology on $M'$ (indiscrete) differs from its $\fa$-adic topology ($h\notin\fa M'$). Non-Hausdorffness alone would not show this: $E=\bigcap_n\fa^n$ satisfies $\fa E=E$, since a flat $f$ equals $x\cdot(f/x)$ with $f/x$ again flat. Sanity check: $R/\fa\congR$ shows $\fa$ is maximal (and by Hadamard's lemma even principal, $\fa=(x)$), yet $R$ is not Noetherian -- e.g.\ the ideal of functions flat at $0$ is not finitely generated -- so the Noetherian hypothesis of Theorem~ [REF:thm:ar@c15] fails and the Artin--Rees comparison is unavailable.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: example
Title: Artin--Rees on $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Artin--Rees on $Z$}
For $R=Z$, $\fa=(p)$, $M=Z$, $M'=(m)$ with $p\nmid m$, find $k$ in the Artin--Rees identity.
\wrec Compute $(p^nZ)\cap mZ$ and compare with $p^{n-k}\bigl((p^kZ)\cap mZ\bigr)$.
\wsol Since $\gcd(p^n,m)=1$, $(p^nZ)\cap mZ=p^n mZ=\operatorname{lcm}(p^n,m)Z$. Then $p^{n-k}\bigl((p^kZ)\cap mZ\bigr)=p^{n-k}\cdot p^k mZ=p^n mZ$, which agrees for every $n\ge k$ already with $k=0$. Sanity check: when $\fa$ and $M'$ are "transverse" ($\fa^k M\cap M'=\fa^k M'$ at $k=0$) the filtration $(M'\cap\fa^n M)=(\fa^n M')$ exactly, the cleanest possible case of bounded difference.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Stable filtrations and the Artin--Rees lemma
Type: example
Title: A nontrivial Artin--Rees constant
Content:
\begin{wex}{A nontrivial Artin--Rees constant}
In $R=k[x,y]$, $\fa=(x,y)$, $M=R$, $M'=(x)$, compare $(\fa^n)\cap(x)$ with $\fa^{n-1}\bigl(\fa\cap(x)\bigr)$.
\wrec $(x)$ is generated by the degree-$1$ element $x$; intersecting with $\fa^n$ should recover $x\cdot\fa^{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$.
\wsol An element of $(\fa^n)\cap(x)$ is $x\cdot g$ lying in $\fa^n=(x,y)^n$. Since $x$ has degree $1$, $xg\in\fa^n\iff g\in\fa^{n-1}$ (as $(x,y)$ is graded and $x$ is a nonzerodivisor of degree $1$). Hence $(\fa^n)\cap(x)=x\,\fa^{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. In particular $\fa\cap(x)=x\,\fa^0=xR=(x)$ (taking $n=1$), since $(x)\subseteq\fa$. With $k=1$ the Artin--Rees identity reads $(\fa^n)\cap(x)=\fa^{n-1}\bigl((\fa)\cap(x)\bigr)=\fa^{n-1}(x)=x\,\fa^{n-1}$, valid for all $n\ge1$. The constant $k=0$ does not work: $\fa^{n}\bigl((\fa^0)\cap(x)\bigr)=\fa^n(x)=x\,\fa^n\neq x\,\fa^{n-1}$, so $k=1$ is the smallest admissible Artin--Rees constant here. Sanity check: degrees match -- $(\fa^n)\cap(x)$ is spanned by $x\cdot(monomials of degree\ge n-1)$, exactly $x\,\fa^{n-1}$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: definition
Title: {graded ring/module, associated graded}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{graded ring/module, associated graded}]
A graded ring is $A=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}A_n$ with $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$; then $A_0$ is a subring and each $A_n$ an $A_0$-module. A graded $A$-module is $M=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}M_n$ with $A_mM_n\subseteq M_{m+n}$. For a ring $R$ and ideal $\fa$, the associated graded ring is
\[
\gr_\fa(R)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\fa^n/\fa^{n+1}\qquad(\fa^0=R),
\]
with multiplication $(\bar x_m)(\bar y_n)=\overline{x_my_n}\in\fa^{m+n}/\fa^{m+n+1}$. For a filtered module $(M_n)$, $\gr(M)=\bigoplus_n M_n/M_{n+1}$ is a graded $\gr_\fa(R)$-module.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {Noetherianity of $\gr_\fa(R)$ and a graded criterion}
Label: prop:grnoeth@c15
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Noetherianity of $\gr_\fa(R)$ and a graded criterion}] 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item A graded ring $A$ is Noetherian $\iff$ $A_0$ is Noetherian and $A$ is a finitely generated $A_0$-algebra.
\item If $R$ is Noetherian and $\fa\subseteq R$ an ideal, then $\gr_\fa(R)$ is Noetherian.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
label: prop:grnoeth@c15

Type: proof

Relation: proof_of=unit-354a1c1d98aaa825db4c
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
For (i): if $A$ is Noetherian then $A_0=A/A_+$ is Noetherian and $A_+=\bigoplus_{n>0}A_n$ is finitely generated by homogeneous $x_1,\dots,x_s$, which then generate $A$ over $A_0$; conversely Hilbert's basis theorem gives Noetherianity. For (ii): $\gr_\fa(R)$ has degree-zero part $R/\fa$ (Noetherian) and is generated over it by the finitely many generators of $\fa$ read in $\fa/\fa^2$, so (i) applies.
\end{proof}

Title: {$M^\ast$ finitely generated $\iff$ filtration stable}
Label: lem:Mstar@c15
Content:
\begin{lemma}[{$M^\ast$ finitely generated $\iff$ filtration stable}] 
Let $R$ be Noetherian, $\fa$ an ideal, $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module, $(M_n)$ an $\fa$-filtration. Form $A^\ast=\bigoplus_n\fa^n=R[\fa t]$ (Noetherian) and the graded $A^\ast$-module $M^\ast=\bigoplus_n M_n$. Then $M^\ast$ is a finitely generated $A^\ast$-module $\iff$ the filtration $(M_n)$ is stable.
\end{lemma}
label: lem:Mstar@c15

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-f37a410bae0a052f3174
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
The truncations $Q_n=\bigoplus_{r\le n}M_r$ are finitely generated; $M^\ast$ is finitely generated iff the ascending chain of $A^\ast$-submodules generated by the $Q_n$ stabilizes, i.e.\ iff $M^\ast=A^\ast\!\cdot Q_{n_0}$ for some $n_0$, i.e.\ iff $M_{n_0+r}=\fa^r M_{n_0}$ for all $r$ -- precisely stability. This lemma supplies the proof of Artin--Rees (Theorem~ [REF:thm:ar@c15] ).
\end{proof}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-97825a3faa24a49d6dcb
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
By Artin--Rees the filtration $(\fa^n M\cap E)$ is stable, but $\fa^n M\cap E=E$ for all $n$, so stability forces $\fa E=\fa^n M\cap E$ to equal $E$ from some point on, i.e.\ $\fa E=E$. Now $E$ is a finitely generated module with $\fa E=E$, so by the determinant trick (Cayley--Hamilton form of Nakayama) some $x\equiv1\pmod\fa$ kills $E$. If $\fa\subseteq\Jac(R)$ then $x=1-a$ with $a\in\Jac(R)$ is a unit, forcing $E=0$, giving (1) and its special case (2). If $R$ is a domain and $\fa\neq(1)$, then $1+\fa$ contains no zero-divisors and $x\neq0$, so again $E=0$, giving (3).
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Both Krull's theorem and the exactness of completion are downstream of Artin--Rees, which is why A\&M give that lemma the central role. The hypotheses cannot be dropped: over the non-Noetherian $C^\infty$ ring the maximal ideal $\fa$ at $0$ has $\bigcap_n\fa^n\neq0$ (the flat function $e^{-1/x^2}$), and no element of $1+\fa$ kills $e^{-1/x^2}$ (such an element $u$ would vanish at every $x\neq0$, hence at $0$ by continuity, while $u(0)=1$), so Krull's conclusion fails -- the obstruction is exactly non-Noetherianity.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: Krull intersection in a Noetherian local domain
Content:
\begin{wex}{Krull intersection in a Noetherian local domain}
Let $(R,\fm)$ be a Noetherian local domain. Show $\bigcap_n\fm^n=0$.
\wrec $\fm\subseteq\Jac(R)=\fm$ (local), and $R$ is a domain, so Theorem~ [REF:thm:krull@c15] (2)/(3) applies.
\wsol Put $E=\bigcap_n\fm^n$. By Krull $\fm E=E$ with $E$ finitely generated, so Nakayama (with $\fm\subseteq\Jac R$) gives $E=0$. Sanity check: in $R=k[x]_{(x)}$, $\fm=(x)$, indeed $\bigcap_n(x)^n=0$ -- a germ vanishing to all orders is the zero germ; and the completion $\widehat R=k[[x]]$ is Hausdorff, consistent with $E=0$.
\end{wex}

title: Krull intersection in a Noetherian local domain

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: example
Title: Krull's theorem can fail for non-domains without the radical hypothesis
Content:
\begin{wex}{Krull's theorem can fail for non-domains without the radical hypothesis}
Show $\bigcap_n\fa^n\neq0$ is possible when $\fa\not\subseteq\Jac(R)$, using $R=Z/6Z$, $\fa=(2)$.
\wrec Theorem~ [REF:thm:krull@c15] (1) needs $\fa\subseteq\Jac(R)$; in a product of fields $\Jac(R)=0$, so the conclusion is not guaranteed.
\wsol In $R=Z/6Z\congZ/2Z\timesZ/3Z$, the ideal $\fa=(2)$ corresponds to $0\timesZ/3Z$, which is idempotent: $\fa^2=\fa$. Hence $\bigcap_n\fa^n=\fa\neq0$. Here $\Jac(R)=0$ (a product of fields), so $\fa\not\subseteq\Jac(R)$ and Krull(1) does not apply. The element of $1+\fa$ annihilating $E=\fa$: take $1+2=3$, and indeed $3\cdot\fa=3\cdot(0\timesZ/3Z)=0$, so $\fa E=E$ with annihilator $3\in1+\fa$, consistent with the theorem's $\fa E=E$ conclusion. Sanity check: the theorem's true assertion ($\fa E=E$) holds; only the stronger $E=0$ fails, exactly because the radical hypothesis is absent.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The associated graded of $Z$ at $(p)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The associated graded of $Z$ at $(p)$}
Compute $\gr_{(p)}(Z)$.
\wrec $\gr_\fa(R)=\bigoplus_n\fa^n/\fa^{n+1}$; here $\fa^n=p^nZ$.
\wsol Each graded piece $p^nZ/p^{n+1}Z\congZ/pZ=\F_p$, generated by the class $\bar p^{\,n}$ of $p^n$. Multiplication sends $\bar p^{\,m}\cdot\bar p^{\,n}\mapsto\bar p^{\,m+n}$, so $\gr_{(p)}(Z)\cong\F_p[t]$ with $t=\bar p$ the class of $p$ in degree $1$. Sanity check: $\F_p[t]$ is a Noetherian domain (matching Proposition~ [REF:prop:grnoeth@c15] (ii)); its degree-$0$ part $\F_p=Z/pZ=R/\fa$, as required.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: example
Title: The associated graded of a regular local ring is a polynomial ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{The associated graded of a regular local ring is a polynomial ring}
For $R=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{(x_1,\dots,x_n)}$, $\fm=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, identify $\gr_\fm(R)$.
\wrec $\gr_\fm(R)=\bigoplus_d\fm^d/\fm^{d+1}$; the $d$-th piece is the space of degree-$d$ forms in the $x_i$.
\wsol $\fm^d/\fm^{d+1}$ has basis the monomials of total degree $d$ in $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and the product respects degree, so $\gr_\fm(R)\cong k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ as a graded ring (a polynomial ring, $n$ variables in degree $1$). Sanity check: $\dim_k\fm^d/\fm^{d+1}=\binom{d+n-1}{n-1}$, the number of degree-$d$ monomials -- the Hilbert function of the tangent cone of the smooth point, which for a regular point is that of affine $n$-space, confirming the "tangent cone $=\Aff^n$" picture.
\end{wex}

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Completions, Filtrations, and Graded Rings > Graded rings, $\gr_\fa(R)$, and Krull's theorem
Type: example
Title: $\gr_\fa(R)\cong\gr_{\widehat\fa}(\widehat R)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$\gr_\fa(R)\cong\gr_{\widehat\fa}(\widehat R)$}
For $R$ Noetherian, show completion does not change the associated graded ring.
\wrec Use $\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}\cong R/\fa^n$, hence $\widehat\fa^{\,n}/\widehat\fa^{\,n+1}\cong\fa^n/\fa^{n+1}$.
\wsol From $\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}\cong R/\fa^n$ (earlier example) the short exact sequences $0\to\widehat\fa^{\,n}/\widehat\fa^{\,n+1}\to\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n+1}\to\widehat R/\widehat\fa^{\,n}\to0$ match those for $R$, giving $\widehat\fa^{\,n}/\widehat\fa^{\,n+1}\cong\fa^n/\fa^{n+1}$ in each degree, compatibly with products. Hence $\gr_{\widehat\fa}(\widehat R)\cong\gr_\fa(R)$. Sanity check: with $R=Z$, $\fa=(p)$: $\gr_{(p)}(Z)\cong\F_p[t]\cong\gr_{pZ_p}(Z_p)$ -- the graded ring sees only the finite residues $\fa^n/\fa^{n+1}$, which completion preserves.
\end{wex}

Type: lemma
Title: {filtered comparison}
Label: lem:filtcomp@c15
Content:
\begin{lemma}[{filtered comparison}] 
Let $\phi\colon A\to B$ be a homomorphism of filtered groups with $\phi(A_n)\subseteq B_n$, inducing $\gr(\phi)\colon\gr(A)\to\gr(B)$ and $\widehat\phi\colon\widehat A\to\widehat B$. If $A$ is complete, $B$ Hausdorff, and $\gr(\phi)$ is surjective (resp.\ injective), then $\widehat\phi$ -- equivalently $\phi$ under completeness -- is surjective (resp.\ injective).
\end{lemma}
label: lem:filtcomp@c15

\begin{proposition}[{Noetherian lifting}] 
Let $A$ be a filtered ring, complete and Hausdorff, with $\bigcap A_n=0$. If $\gr(A)$ is Noetherian, then $A$ is Noetherian.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{remark}
A\&M also record (Proposition 10.16) that if $(R,\fm)$ is Noetherian local then $\widehat R$ is again local with maximal ideal $\widehat\fm$ and residue field $\widehat R/\widehat\fm\cong R/\fm$. Completion thus preserves the local-ring structure while improving it: $\widehat R$ is complete, so Hensel's lemma is available.
\end{remark}

Type: theorem
Title: {Hensel's lemma, statement}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Hensel's lemma, statement}]
Let $(R,\fm)$ be a complete Noetherian local ring with residue field $k=R/\fm$, and let $f\in R[x]$ be monic. If $\bar f\in k[x]$ factors as $\bar f=\bar g\,\bar h$ with $\bar g,\bar h$ monic and coprime (in particular if $\bar a\in k$ is a simple root of $\bar f$, $\bar f'(\bar a)\neq0$), then the factorization lifts: there exist monic $g,h\in R[x]$ with $f=gh$, $\bar g,\bar h$ the given factors (in the simple-root case, a root $a\in R$ with $f(a)=0$ and $a\equiv\bar a$). The lift is unique.
\end{theorem}

Type: example
Title: $Z_p$ is a Noetherian complete DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z_p$ is a Noetherian complete DVR}
Confirm $Z_p$ is Noetherian and describe its ideals.
\wrec $Z_p$ is the $(p)$-adic completion of the Noetherian $Z$, so Theorem~ [REF:thm:noeth@c15] applies; locate its ideals via $\widehat{(p^k)}$.
\wsol By Theorem~ [REF:thm:noeth@c15] , $Z_p$ is Noetherian. Its nonzero ideals are $p^kZ_p=\widehat{(p^k)}$ for $k\ge0$, since every nonzero $x\inZ_p$ is $p^{v}\cdot u$ with $u$ a unit ($v=v_p(x)<\infty$ as $\bigcap p^nZ_p=0$). Thus $Z_p$ is a discrete valuation ring: local, with maximal ideal $pZ_p$, residue field $\F_p$, and $\gr_{(p)}(Z_p)\cong\F_p[t]$. Sanity check: the ideals of $Z_p$ form the single chain $Z_p\supset pZ_p\supset p^2Z_p\supset\cdots\supset0$; its only primes are $pZ_p$ and $0$, so the longest chain of primes is $0\subsetneq pZ_p$, matching $\dimZ_p=1$, and every ascending chain of ideals stops, matching the Noetherian conclusion.
\end{wex}

Title: $k[[x]]$ is a complete DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{$k[[x]]$ is a complete DVR}
Show $k[[x]]$ is Noetherian local with maximal ideal $(x)$, and identify its fraction field.
\wrec $k[[x]]$ is the $(x)$-adic completion of $k[x]$; apply Corollary~ [REF:cor:fps@c15] and the local-completion remark.
\wsol $k[[x]]$ is Noetherian by Corollary~ [REF:cor:fps@c15] . A series is a unit iff its constant term is nonzero, so the non-units form the maximal ideal $(x)$; every nonzero series is $x^v\cdot(unit)$, so the ideals are $(x^k)$ and $k[[x]]$ is a complete DVR. Its fraction field is the formal Laurent series field $k((x))=k[[x]][x^{-1}]$. Sanity check: $\bigcap_n(x)^n=0$ (a nonzero series has finite order), so $k[[x]]$ is Hausdorff and equals its own completion, as a complete DVR must.
\end{wex}

Title: Hensel: square roots in $Z_p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Hensel: square roots in $Z_p$}
For $p$ odd and $a\inZ$ with $p\nmid a$, show $a$ has a square root in $Z_p$ iff $a$ is a square mod $p$.
\wrec Apply Hensel to $f(x)=x^2-a$: a simple root mod $p$ (where $f'=2x\not\equiv0$ since $p$ odd) lifts to $Z_p$.
\wsol If $a\equiv b^2\pmod p$ with $p\nmid b$, then $\bar b$ is a root of $\bar f=x^2-\bar a$ and $\bar f'(\bar b)=2\bar b\neq0$ in $\F_p$ ($p$ odd, $p\nmid b$), a simple root. Hensel lifts it to $\alpha\inZ_p$ with $\alpha^2=a$. Conversely a square root in $Z_p$ reduces mod $p$ to a square root in $\F_p$. Sanity check: in $Z_7$, $2\equiv3^2=9\equiv2\pmod7$, so $\sqrt2\inZ_7$ exists; whereas $3$ is a nonsquare mod $7$ (squares are $1,2,4$), so $\sqrt3\notinZ_7$ -- exactly the quadratic-residue criterion.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Hensel: $(p-1)$-th roots of unity in $Z_p$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Hensel: $(p-1)$-th roots of unity in $Z_p$}
Show $Z_p$ contains $p-1$ distinct $(p-1)$-th roots of unity (the Teichmuller lifts).
\wrec Apply Hensel to $f(x)=x^{p-1}-1$; over $\F_p$ it splits into distinct linear factors (all simple roots) by Fermat.
\wsol Over $\F_p$, $x^{p-1}-1=\prod_{c\in\F_p^\times}(x-c)$ has $p-1$ distinct simple roots (each nonzero $c$ satisfies $c^{p-1}=1$ and $\bar f'(c)=(p-1)c^{p-2}\neq0$). Hensel lifts each to a unique $\omega_c\inZ_p$ with $\omega_c^{p-1}=1$ and $\omega_c\equiv c\pmod p$. These $p-1$ lifts are distinct (distinct residues), giving a cyclic group $\mu_{p-1}\subsetZ_p^\times$. Sanity check: the $\omega_c$ are the Teichmuller representatives, and $Z_p^\times\cong\mu_{p-1}\times(1+pZ_p)$, consistent with $\abs{(Z/p)^\times}=p-1$ on residues.
\end{wex}

Title: Completion of a Noetherian ring stays Noetherian: $Z[x]$ at $(p,x)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Completion of a Noetherian ring stays Noetherian: $Z[x]$ at $(p,x)$}
Identify the $(p,x)$-adic completion of $R=Z[x]$ and confirm Noetherianity.
\wrec $R=Z[x]$ is Noetherian; Theorem~ [REF:thm:noeth@c15] gives $\widehat R$ Noetherian, and concretely $\widehat R$ is a two-variable formal power series object.
\wsol With $\fa=(p,x)$, $R/\fa^n$ is residues mod $p$ and $x$ to total order $n$; the completion is $\widehat R=\varprojlimZ[x]/(p,x)^n\congZ_p[[x]]$, formal power series over $Z_p$. By Corollary~ [REF:cor:fps@c15] (with the Noetherian base $Z_p$) this is Noetherian. Sanity check: $\widehat R$ is local with maximal ideal $(p,x)\widehat R$ and residue field $\F_p$, and $\gr_{(p,x)}(Z[x])\cong\F_p[s,t]$ (with $s=\bar p,t=\bar x$), a Noetherian polynomial ring -- matching the lifting argument of Theorem~ [REF:thm:noeth@c15] .
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Flatness in action: $\widehat R$ detects intersections
Content:
\begin{wex}{Flatness in action: $\widehat R$ detects intersections}
Use flatness of $\widehat R$ over a Noetherian $R$ to show $\widehat{\fb\cap\fc}=\widehat\fb\cap\widehat\fc$ for ideals $\fb,\fc$.
\wrec A flat module preserves finite intersections of finitely generated submodules: $\widehat R\otimes(\fb\cap\fc)=(\widehat R\otimes\fb)\cap(\widehat R\otimes\fc)$ inside $\widehat R$.
\wsol Flatness applied to $0\to\fb\cap\fc\to\fb\oplus\fc\to\fb+\fc\to0$ (the Mayer--Vietoris sequence, with the last map $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$) stays exact after $\widehat R\otimes_R(-)$, identifying $\widehat{\fb\cap\fc}=\widehat R(\fb\cap\fc)=\widehat R\fb\cap\widehat R\fc=\widehat\fb\cap\widehat\fc$. Sanity check: with $R=Z$, $\fb=(4)$, $\fc=(6)$, $\fa=(2)$: $\fb\cap\fc=(12)$, and in $Z_2$, $4Z_2\cap6Z_2=4Z_2$ (since $6=2\cdot3$ with $3$ a unit, $6Z_2=2Z_2$, so $4Z_2\cap2Z_2=4Z_2$) -- and $\widehat{(12)}=12Z_2=4Z_2$ likewise (since $12=4\cdot3$, $3$ a unit), matching.
\end{wex}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).}
\item Let $\alpha_n \colon Z/pZ \to Z/p^nZ$ be the injection of abelian groups given by $\alpha_n(1) = p^{n-1}$, and let $\alpha \colon A \to B$ be the direct sum of all the $\alpha_n$ (where $A$ is a countable direct sum of copies of $Z/pZ$, and $B$ is the direct sum of the $Z/p^nZ$). Show that the $p$-adic completion of $A$ is just $A$ but that the completion of $A$ for the topology induced from the $p$-adic topology on $B$ is the direct product of the $Z/pZ$. Deduce that $p$-adic completion is not a right-exact functor on the category of all $Z$-modules.

\item In Exercise 1, let $A_n = \alpha^{-1}(p^n B)$, and consider the exact sequence
\[
0 \to A_n \to A \to A/A_n \to 0.
\]
Show that $\lim$ is not exact, and compute $\lim^1 A_n$.

\item Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $\fa$ an ideal and $M$ a finitely-generated $A$-module. Using Krull's Theorem and Exercise 14 of Chapter 3, prove that
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \fa^n M = \bigcap_{\fm \supseteq \fa} \operatorname{Ker}(M \to M_{\fm}),
\]
where $\fm$ runs over all maximal ideals containing $\fa$. Deduce that
\[
\widehat{M} = 0 \iff \operatorname{Supp}(M) \cap V(\fa) = \varnothing \quad (in \Spec(A)).
\]
[The reader should think of $\widehat{M}$ as the ``Taylor expansion'' of $M$ transversal to the subscheme $V(\fa)$: the above result then shows that $M$ is determined in a neighborhood of $V(\fa)$ by its Taylor expansion.]

\item Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $\fa$ an ideal in $A$, and $\widehat{A}$ the $\fa$-adic completion. For any $x \in A$, let $\widehat{x}$ be the image of $x$ in $\widehat{A}$. Show that
\[
x not a zero-divisor in A \implies \widehat{x} not a zero-divisor in \widehat{A}.
\]
Does this imply that
\[
A an integral domain \implies \widehat{A} an integral domain?
\]
[Apply the exactness of completion to the sequence $0 \to A \xrightarrow{x} A$.]

\item Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, let $\fa$, $\fb$ be ideals in $A$, and let $M$ be an $A$-module. Let $M^{\fa}$, $M^{\fb}$ denote the $\fa$-adic and $\fb$-adic completions respectively. If $M$ is finitely generated, prove that $(M^{\fa})^{\fb} \cong M^{\fa + \fb}$.

[Take the $\fa$-adic completion of the exact sequence
\[
0 \to \fb^n M \to M \to M/\fb^n M \to 0
\]
and apply (10.13). Thus use the isomorphism
\[
\varprojlim_n \left( \varprojlim_m M/(\fa^m M + \fb^n M) \right) \cong \varprojlim_p M/(\fa^p M + \fb^p M)
\]
and the inclusions $(\fa + \fb)^{2p} \subseteq \fa^p + \fb^p \subseteq (\fa + \fb)^p$.]

\item Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $\fa$ an ideal of $A$, $\widehat{A}$ the $\fa$-adic completion. For any $x \in A$ let $\widehat{x}$ be the image of $x$ in $\widehat{A}$. Prove that $\fa$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$ if and only if every maximal ideal of $A$ is closed for the $\fa$-topology. (A Noetherian topological ring in which the topology is defined by an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical is called a Zariski ring. Examples are local rings and ($\fa$-adic) completions.)

\item Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring, $\fa$ an ideal of $A$, and $\widehat{A}$ the $\fa$-adic completion. Prove that $\widehat{A}$ is faithfully flat over $A$ if and only if $A$ is a Zariski ring (for the $\fa$-topology). [Since $\widehat{A}$ is flat over $A$, it is enough (Chapter 3, Exercise 16) to show that $M \to \widehat{M}$ is injective for all finitely generated $M$ if and only if $A$ is a Zariski ring; now use (10.19) and Exercise 6.]

\item Let $A$ be the local ring of a point in $C^n$ (i.e., the ring of all rational functions $f/g \in C(z_1, \ldots, z_n)$ with $g(0) \neq 0$), let $B$ be the ring of power series in $z_1, \ldots, z_n$ which converge in some neighborhood of the origin, and let $C$ be the ring of formal power series in $z_1, \ldots, z_n$, so that $A \subseteq B \subseteq C$. Show that $B$ is a local ring and that its completion for the maximal ideal topology is $C$. Assuming that $B$ is Noetherian, prove that $B$ is $A$-flat. [Use Chapter 3, Exercise 17, and Exercise 7 above.]

\item Let $A$ be a local ring, $\fm$ its maximal ideal. Assume that $A$ is $\fm$-adically complete. For any polynomial $f(x) \in A[x]$, let $\bar{f}(x) \in (A/\fm)[x]$ denote its reduction mod $\fm$. Prove Hensel's lemma: if $f(x)$ is monic of degree $n$ and if there exist coprime monic polynomials $\bar{g}(x)$, $\bar{h}(x) \in (A/\fm)[x]$ of degrees $r$, $n - r$ with $\bar{f}(x) = \bar{g}(x)\bar{h}(x)$, then we can lift $\bar{g}(x)$, $\bar{h}(x)$ back to monic polynomials $g(x)$, $h(x) \in A[x]$ such that $f(x) = g(x)h(x)$.

[Assume inductively that we have constructed $g_k(x)$, $h_k(x) \in A[x]$ such that $g_k(x)h_k(x) - f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{\fm^k A[x]}$. Then use the fact that since $\bar{g}(x)$ and $\bar{h}(x)$ are coprime we can find $\bar{a}_p(x)$, $\bar{b}_p(x)$, of degrees $\leq n - r$, $r$ respectively, such that $x^p = \bar{a}_p(x)\bar{g}(x) + \bar{b}_p(x)\bar{h}(x)$, where $p$ is any integer such that $1 \leq p \leq n$. Finally, use the completeness of $A$ to show that the sequences $g_k(x)$, $h_k(x)$ converge to the required $g(x)$, $h(x)$.]

\item \begin{enumerate}
\item[i)] With the notation of Exercise 9, deduce from Hensel's lemma that if $\bar{f}(x)$ has a simple root $\alpha \in A/\fm$, then $f(x)$ has a simple root $a \in A$ such that $\alpha = a \bmod \fm$.
\item[ii)] Show that 2 is a square in the ring of 7-adic integers.
\item[iii)] Let $f(x, y) \in k[x, y]$, where $k$ is a field, and assume that $f(0, y)$ has $y = a_0$ as a simple root.

\item Show that the converse of (10.26) is false, even if we assume that $A$ is local and that $\widehat{A}$ is a finitely-generated $A$-module. [Take $A$ to be the ring of germs of $C^{\infty}$ functions of $x$ at $x = 0$, and use Borel's Theorem (every power series occurs as the Taylor expansion of some $C^{\infty}$ function).]

\item If $A$ is Noetherian, then $A[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]$ is a faithfully flat $A$-algebra. [Express $A \to A[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]$ as a composition of flat extensions, and use Exercise 5(v) of Chapter 1.]
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $G$ be a filtered abelian group with filtration $(G_n)$ and let $H=\bigcap_n G_n$. Prove that the completion map $\phi\colon G\to\widehat G$ factors as $G\twoheadrightarrow G/H\hookrightarrow\widehat G$, that $\widehat G\cong\widehat{G/H}$ for the quotient filtration, and conclude that completion depends only on the Hausdorff quotient. Deduce $\ker\phi=H$.
\item Let $R$ be Noetherian, $\fa\subseteq R$ an ideal, and $\widehat R$ the $\fa$-adic completion. Using flatness of $\widehat R$ over $R$ (Proposition on $\widehat R$ flat), prove that for finitely generated ideals $\fb,\fc$ one has $\widehat{(\fb:\fc)}=(\widehat\fb:\widehat\fc)$ in $\widehat R$, and that $\widehat{\Ann_R(M)}\subseteq\Ann_{\widehat R}(\widehat M)$ with equality when $M$ is finitely generated.
\item Let $(R,\fm)$ be a Noetherian local domain that is not a field, with $\dim_{R/\fm}(\fm/\fm^2)=1$. Prove that $\gr_\fm(R)\cong (R/\fm)[t]$ as graded rings, deduce that $\bigcap_n\fm^n=0$ via Krull, and conclude that $R$ is a discrete valuation ring. Show that $\widehat R\cong k[[t]]$ for $R=k[x]_{(x)}$, but that in general $\widehat R\not\cong(R/\fm)[[t]]$: for $R=Z_{(p)}$, $\widehat R=Z_p$ has characteristic $0$ while $\F_p[[t]]$ has characteristic $p$.
\item Let $R$ be Noetherian and $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ a short exact sequence of finitely generated $R$-modules. Prove that the associated graded sequence $0\to\gr(M')\to\gr(M)\to\gr(M'')\to0$ (for the $\fa$-adic filtrations, with $M'$ given the induced filtration $\fa^nM\cap M'$) is exact, and explain why this needs no Artin--Rees, while Artin--Rees is what shows that the induced filtration on $M'$ and the $\fa$-adic one have bounded difference (hence give the same topology and the same completion $\widehat{M'}$). Show by the example $M=k[x,y]$, $M'=(x,y^2)$, $\fa=(x,y)$ that the two graded modules $\gr(M')$ can nevertheless differ, even up to a shift.
\item Let $f(x)=x^3-x-1\inZ_3[x]$. Show that $\bar f\in\F_3[x]$ has no root in $\F_3$, hence Hensel's lemma gives no $3$-adic root, but that $f$ does acquire a root in the unramified extension of $Z_3$ with residue field $\F_{27}$. Contrast this with $g(x)=x^2-7$ over $Z_3$, and decide whether $g$ has a root in $Z_3$.
\end{exers}

R \arrow[r,"\phi^{\fa}"] \arrow[d,equal] & \widehat{R}^{\fa} \arrow[d,"\psi"] \\
R \arrow[r,"\phi^{\fb}"'] & \widehat{R}^{\fb}
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\item Let $R$ be Noetherian local with maximal ideal $\fm$. Complete the diagram exhibiting $\gr_\fm(R)\cong\gr_{\widehat\fm}(\widehat R)$ degree by degree, where the rows are the defining short exact sequences and the vertical isomorphisms come from $\widehat R/\widehat\fm^{\,n}\cong R/\fm^n$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & \fm^{n}/\fm^{n+1} \arrow[r,hook] \arrow[d,"\sim"'] & R/\fm^{n+1} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] \arrow[d,"\sim"'] & R/\fm^{n} \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\sim"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & \widehat\fm^{\,n}/\widehat\fm^{\,n+1} \arrow[r,hook] & \widehat R/\widehat\fm^{\,n+1} \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow] & \widehat R/\widehat\fm^{\,n} \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Prove the left vertical map is an isomorphism for every $n$, that these assemble into a graded ring isomorphism compatible with multiplication, and deduce that $\dim_{R/\fm}\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}=\dim_{R/\fm}\widehat\fm^{\,n}/\widehat\fm^{\,n+1}$ so that $R$ and $\widehat R$ have the same Hilbert function.

Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Dimension Theory > Krull dimension and height: chains of primes
Type: prose
Content:
The dimension of a ring is, before anything else, a measure of how long a chain of prime ideals can be. Atiyah--Macdonald open this chapter by insisting that dimension ``is essentially a local notion'': for a variety it counts the number of independent parameters near a point, and the algebraic stand-in for ``a point'' is a prime ideal. A chain of primes
\[
\fp_0\subsetneq\fp_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\fp_n
\]
is a strictly increasing sequence of primes; its length is $n$ (the number of strict inclusions, one less than the number of primes). This is the same convention used for the dimension of a variety as the number of strict inclusions in a longest chain of nested irreducible closed subsets.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Dimension Theory > Krull dimension and height: chains of primes
Type: definition
Title: {Krull dimension}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{Krull dimension}]
The Krull dimension $\dim A$ of a ring $A$ is the supremum of the lengths $n$ of chains of prime ideals $\fp_0\subsetneq\fp_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\fp_n$ in $A$. The height of a prime $\fp$, written $\hgt\fp$, is the supremum of the lengths of chains $\fp_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\fp_n=\fp$ descending from $\fp$; equivalently $\hgt\fp=\dim A_\fp$, the dimension of the local ring at $\fp$. Dually the coheight (or dimension of $\fp$) is the sup of lengths of chains ascending from $\fp$, equal to $\dim(A/\fp)$.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Commutative Rings and Algebraic Geometry > Dimension Theory > Krull dimension and height: chains of primes
Type: prose
Content:
The two halves of a prime split the ambient dimension: chains through $\fp$ are a descending chain (counted by $\hgt\fp=\dim A_\fp$) glued to an ascending one (counted by $\dim A/\fp$), so $\hgt\fp+\dim(A/\fp)\le\dim A$ always, with equality the typical ``catenary'' situation. Under the inclusion-preserving bijection $\fq\mapsto\fq A_\fp$ between primes contained in $\fp$ and primes of the localization $A_\fp$, height becomes ordinary dimension --- this is localization as ``concentrating near the point $\fp$''.
