Title: $k[x]/(f)$ as a product of Artinian local rings
Content:
\begin{wex}{$k[x]/(f)$ as a product of Artinian local rings}
With $f=(x-1)^2(x-2)^3\in k[x]$ ($\charac k\ne2,3$, $k$ containing $1,2$), decompose
$R=k[x]/(f)$.
\wrec $k[x]$ is a PID; CRT on the coprime prime-power factors of $f$ gives the local decomposition,
mirroring $Z/(n)Z$.
\wsol The factors $(x-1)^2$ and $(x-2)^3$ are coprime in $k[x]$, so
\[
R=k[x]/\bigl((x-1)^2(x-2)^3\bigr)\;\cong\;k[x]/(x-1)^2\;\times\;k[x]/(x-2)^3 .
\]
The first factor is Artinian local with maximal ideal $(\overline{x-1})$, square zero, of length $2$;
the second is Artinian local with maximal ideal $(\overline{x-2})$, cube zero, of length $3$. Sanity
check: $\dim_k R=\deg f=5=2+3$, and $\len_R(R)=2+3=5$; the nilradical (Jacobson radical) is generated
by the squarefree part $(x-1)(x-2)$, with $R/\Jac\cong k\times k$ -- two residue fields, one per root.
\end{wex}

Title: Idempotent lifting recovers the factors
Content:
\begin{wex}{Idempotent lifting recovers the factors}
For $R=Z/(12)Z$, find the nontrivial idempotents and match them to the product decomposition.
\wrec A product decomposition $R\cong A_1\times A_2$ corresponds to a pair of orthogonal idempotents
$e_1+e_2=1$; lift them from $R/\Jac=\prod k_i$.
\wsol $Z/(12)Z\congZ/(4)Z\timesZ/(3)Z$. The idempotents of the product are $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$;
pulled back by CRT these are $\bar9$ and $\bar4$ in $Z/(12)Z$ (since $9\equiv1\bmod4$, $9\equiv0\bmod3$
and $4\equiv0\bmod4$, $4\equiv1\bmod3$). Indeed $\bar9^2=\overline{81}=\bar9$ and
$\bar4^2=\overline{16}=\bar4$, with $\bar9+\bar4=\overline{13}=\bar1$ and $\bar9\cdot\bar4=\overline{36}=\bar0$.
The factor rings are $\bar9\,R\congZ/(4)Z$ and $\bar4\,R\congZ/(3)Z$. Sanity check: $\SpecZ/(12)Z$ is
disconnected into the two points $(\bar2)$ and $(\bar3)$ exactly because of the nontrivial idempotent
$\bar9$ ($\ne0,1$) -- a ring is a nontrivial product iff it has a nontrivial idempotent.
\end{wex}

For $R=\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$, find the nontrivial idempotents and match them to the product decomposition.
\wrec A product decomposition $R\cong A_1\times A_2$ corresponds to a pair of orthogonal idempotents
$e_1+e_2=1$; lift them from $R/\Jac=\prod k_i$.
\wsol $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. The idempotents of the product are $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$;
pulled back by CRT these are $\bar9$ and $\bar4$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ (since $9\equiv1\bmod4$, $9\equiv0\bmod3$
and $4\equiv0\bmod4$, $4\equiv1\bmod3$). Indeed $\bar9^2=\overline{81}=\bar9$ and
$\bar4^2=\overline{16}=\bar4$, with $\bar9+\bar4=\overline{13}=\bar1$ and $\bar9\cdot\bar4=\overline{36}=\bar0$.
The factor rings are $\bar9\,R\cong\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ and $\bar4\,R\cong\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$. Sanity check: $\Spec\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ is
disconnected into the two points $(\bar2)$ and $(\bar3)$ exactly because of the nontrivial idempotent

Title: Why the local factors must be local (no further splitting)
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why the local factors must be local (no further splitting)}
Show that $Z/(8)Z$ is indecomposable as a product, i.e.\ has no nontrivial idempotents.
\wrec An Artinian local ring has no idempotents other than $0,1$, because the maximal ideal is the
nilradical.
\wsol Suppose $e^2=e$ in $Z/(8)Z$. Then $e(e-1)=0$; since $Z/(8)Z$ is local with maximal ideal
$(\bar2)$ consisting of nilpotents, one of $e,e-1$ is a unit (anything outside $(\bar2)$ is a unit) and
the other is nilpotent. If $e$ is a unit, $e-1=0$ so $e=1$; if $e-1$ is a unit, $e$ is nilpotent and
idempotent, forcing $e=0$. So the only idempotents are $0,1$. Sanity check: $\SpecZ/(8)Z$ is a single
point $(\bar2)$ -- connected -- consistent with no nontrivial idempotent, and $Z/(8)Z$ is one of the
indecomposable local factors in any product it appears in.
\end{wex}

\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A finite-dimensional algebra is Artinian
Content:
\begin{wex}{A finite-dimensional algebra is Artinian}
Let $R$ be a $k$-algebra with $\dim_k R<\infty$. Show $R$ is Artinian, and bound its length.
\wrec Ideals are in particular $k$-subspaces, so chains of ideals have length bounded by $\dim_k R$.
\wsol Any descending chain of ideals $\fa_1\supseteq\fa_2\supseteq\cdots$ is a descending chain of
$k$-subspaces; their dimensions form a non-increasing sequence of non-negative integers bounded by
$\dim_k R$, so it stabilizes. Hence $R$ is Artinian, and $\len_R(R)\le\dim_k R$ (each simple factor has
$k$-dimension $\ge1$). Sanity check: for $R=k[x]/(f)$ with $f$ a product of linear factors over $k$, $\dim_k R=\deg f$ and $\len_R(R)=\deg f$ (length
equals $k$-dimension here since every residue field is $k$), so the bound is sharp; for a matrix
algebra such as $\Mat_2(k)$, $\dim_k=4$ but as a left module over itself it is the sum of its two
columns, a semisimple module of $\len=2$ (not simple), so the bound can be strict.
\end{wex}

Title: Spec of an Artinian ring is finite and discrete
Content:
\begin{wex}{Spec of an Artinian ring is finite and discrete}
Show that for an Artinian ring $R$, $\Spec R$ is a finite discrete topological space, and connect this
to the structure theorem.
\wrec Primes = maximals, finitely many; finitely many points each closed gives the discrete topology.
\wsol Every prime is maximal (dimension $0$) and there are only finitely many, say
$\fm_1,\dots,\fm_n$, so $\Spec R=\{\fm_1,\dots,\fm_n\}$ is finite. Each $\{\fm_i\}=V(\fm_i)$ is
closed (maximal ideals are closed points), and a finite $T_1$ space is discrete. Under the structure
theorem $R\cong\prod_i A_i$, the spectrum splits as the disjoint union $\Spec R=\coprod_i\Spec A_i$ with
$\Spec A_i=\{\fm_i\}$ a single point. Sanity check: a Noetherian ring has discrete $\Spec$ iff it is
Artinian; here the $n$ isolated points correspond exactly to the $n$ local factors $A_i$, the connected
components of $\Spec R$.
\end{wex}

Title: Krull dimension contrasts: Artinian vs.\ DVR vs.\ Dedekind
Content:
\begin{wex}{Krull dimension contrasts: Artinian vs.\ DVR vs.\ Dedekind}
Place $Z/(p^k)Z$, $Z_{(p)}$, and $Z$ on the dimension scale and say which are Artinian.
\wrec Artinian = Noetherian $+\dim0$; a DVR is a Noetherian local domain of $\dim1$ with principal
maximal ideal (equivalently a local PID that is not a field; it is integrally closed); a Dedekind domain is a Noetherian,
integrally closed domain of $\dim1$.
\wsol $Z/(p^k)Z$ is Artinian local: Noetherian (finite) with the single prime $(\bar p)$ maximal, so
$\dim=0$. The localization $Z_{(p)}$ is a DVR: Noetherian local with primes $(0)\subsetneq(p)$, so
$\dim=1$ -- not Artinian. And $Z$ is a Dedekind domain: Noetherian, integrally closed, of
$\dim1$ -- not Artinian. Sanity check: passing $Z\toZ/(p^k)$ collapses the chain $(0)\subsetneq(p)$
by killing $(0)$ (it becomes nilpotent), dropping the dimension from $1$ to $0$ and converting the
Dedekind/DVR world into the Artinian world -- the precise sense in which Artinian rings are
``dimension-zero'' fragments of the dimension-one theory developed next.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Krull dimension contrasts: Artinian vs.\ DVR vs.\ Dedekind}
Place $\mathbb{Z}/(p^k)\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, and $\mathbb{Z}$ on the dimension scale and say which are Artinian.
\wrec Artinian = Noetherian $+\dim0$; a DVR is a Noetherian local domain of $\dim1$ with principal
maximal ideal (equivalently a local PID that is not a field; it is integrally closed); a Dedekind domain is a Noetherian,
integrally closed domain of $\dim1$.
\wsol $\mathbb{Z}/(p^k)\mathbb{Z}$ is Artinian local: Noetherian (finite) with the single prime $(\bar p)$ maximal, so

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Do not conflate the module and ring statements. For modules, Artinian and Noetherian are
independent (the Prufer module $Z(p^\infty)$ is Artinian but not Noetherian). For commutative
rings, by contrast, Artinian implies Noetherian -- but only because the ring carries its own
ideal structure and dimension $0$. The implication is a theorem about rings, not a general fact about
modules, and it has no converse: $Z$ is Noetherian but not Artinian.
\end{pitfall}

ideal structure and dimension $0$. The implication is a theorem about rings, not a general fact about
modules, and it has no converse: $\mathbb{Z}$ is Noetherian but not Artinian.
\end{pitfall}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Suppose $R$ is an Artinian ring and $I$ is an ideal in $R$. Prove that $R/I$ is also Artinian.

\item Show that every finite commutative ring with $1$ is Artinian.

\item Prove that an integral domain of Krull dimension $0$ is a field.

\item Prove that an Artinian integral domain is a field.

\item Suppose $I$ is a nilpotent ideal in $R$ and $M = IM$ for some $R$-module $M$. Prove that $M = 0$.

\item Suppose that $0 \longrightarrow M' \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow M'' \longrightarrow 0$ is an exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that $M$ is an Artinian $R$-module if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are Artinian $R$-modules.

\item Suppose $R = F$ is a field. Prove that an $R$-module $M$ is Artinian if and only if it is Noetherian if and only if $M$ is a finite dimensional vector space over $F$.

\item Let $M$ be a maximal ideal of the ring $R$ and suppose that $M^n = 0$ for some $n \geq 1$. Prove that $R$ is Noetherian if and only if $R$ is Artinian. [Observe that each successive quotient $M^i/M^{i+1}$, $i = 0, \ldots, n-1$ in the filtration $R \supseteq M \supseteq M^2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq M^{n-1} \supseteq M^n = 0$ is a module over the field $F = R/M$. Then use the previous two exercises and Exercise 6 of Section 15.1.]

\item Let $M$ be a finitely generated $R$-module. Prove that if $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ are elements of $M$ whose images in $M/J M$ generate $M/J M$, then they generate $M$. Deduce that if $R$ is Noetherian and the images of $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ in $J/J^2$ generate $J/J^2$, then $J = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$. [Let $N$ be the submodule generated by $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and apply Nakayama's Lemma to the module $A = M/N$.]

\item Let $R = Z_{(2)}$ be the localization of $Z$ at the prime ideal $(2)$. Prove that $\Jac R = (2)$ is the ideal generated by $2$. If $M = Q$, prove that $M/2M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module but that $M$ is not finitely generated over $R$. Why doesn't this contradict the previous exercise? [Note the hypotheses in Nakayama's Lemma.]

\item Let $V$ be an affine variety over a field $k$ and let $R = k[V]$ be its coordinate ring. Let $d_1(R)$ denote the transcendence degree of the field of fractions $k(V)$ over $k$, and let $d_p(R)$ be the Krull dimension of $R$ defined in terms of chains of prime ideals. This exercise shows $d_1(R) = d_p(R)$. By Noether's Normalization Lemma there is a polynomial subring $R_1 = k[y_1, \ldots, y_m]$ of $R$ such that $R$ is integral over $R_1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $d_1(R_1) = d_1(R) = m$ and that $d_p(R_1) = d_p(R)$. Deduce that we may assume $R = R_1$. [Use the Going-up and Going-down Theorems (cf. Theorem 26, Section 15.3) to prove the second equality.]
\item[(b)] When $R = R_1$ show that $d_p(R) \geq d_1(R)$ by exhibiting an explicit chain of prime ideals of length $m$.
\item[(c)] When $R = R_1$ show that any nonzero prime ideal of $R$ contains an irreducible element $f$, and that $R/(f)$ is an integral domain whose field of fractions has transcendence degree $m-1$ over $k$. Use induction to show that $d_p(R) \leq d_1(R)$, and deduce that $d_p(R) = d_1(R)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R$ be a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $M$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The quotient $M/M^2$ is a module (i.e., vector space) over the field $R/M$. Prove that $d = \dim_{R/M}(M/M^2)$ is finite.
\item[(b)] Prove that $M$ can be generated as an ideal in $R$ by $d$ elements and by no fewer. [Use Exercise 9.]
\item[(c)] Let $R = k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]_{(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}$ be the localization of the polynomial ring $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ over the field $k$ at the maximal ideal $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, and let $M$ be the maximal ideal in $R$. Prove that $\dim_{R/M}(M/M^2) = n = \dim R$. [Cf. the previous exercise.]
\end{enumerate}

\item If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, prove that the Zariski topology on $\Spec R$ is discrete (i.e., every subset is Zariski open and also Zariski closed) if and only if $R$ is Artinian.

\item Suppose $I$ is the ideal $(x_1, x_2^2, x_3^3, \ldots)$ in the polynomial ring $k[x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots]$ where $k$ is a field and let $R$ be the quotient ring $k[x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots]/I$. Prove that the image of the ideal $(x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots)$ in $R$ is the unique prime ideal in $R$ but is not finitely generated. Deduce that $R$ is a local ring of Krull dimension $0$ but is not Artinian.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item For $R=Z/(200)Z$, decompose $R$ as a product of Artinian local rings, list its maximal ideals, identify $\Jac(R)$ and $\nil(R)$, and compute $\len_R(R)$.
\item In $R=k[x]/(x^4)$ ($k$ a field), write out the full descending chain of ideals, exhibit a composition series of $R$ over itself, and give $\len_R(R)$ together with $\dim_{R/\fm}(\fm/\fm^2)$ for the maximal ideal $\fm=(\bar x)$.
\item Let $R=k[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^2)$. Show $R$ is Artinian local, find its unique maximal ideal $\fm$, compute $\dim_k R$, $\dim_{R/\fm}(\fm/\fm^2)$, and $\len_R(R)$, and decide whether $\fm$ is principal.
\item Exhibit a strictly descending chain of ideals in $R=k[x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots]/(x_1^2,x_2^2,x_3^2,\dots)$ that never stabilizes, and conclude that $R$ is a local ring of Krull dimension $0$ that is not Artinian.
\item Compute $\len_Z(M)$ for the finite abelian group $M=Z/(4)Z\oplusZ/(18)Z\oplusZ/(75)Z$, and exhibit a composition series whose simple factors are the groups $Z/(p)Z$ that occur, with multiplicity.
\item Let $R=\F_2[x]/(x^6-1)$. Factor $x^6-1$ over $\F_2$, decompose $R$ as a product of local rings via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, state which factors are fields and which are Artinian local with nonzero nilradical, and compute $\len_R(R)$.
\item For the local ring $R=Z_{(3)}/(54)$, identify the maximal ideal $\fm$, show $\fm$ is nilpotent, give the smallest $k$ with $\fm^k=0$, and compute $\len_R(R)$.
\item In $R=Z/(12)Z$ find all idempotents, write the corresponding complete set of orthogonal idempotents $e_1+e_2=1$, and identify the two local factor rings $e_iR$ together with their residue fields.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that a commutative ring $R$ is Artinian if and only if $R$ is Noetherian and every prime ideal of $R$ is maximal. Then show by example that ``every prime ideal is maximal'' alone does not imply Artinian.
\item Let $R$ be Artinian with maximal ideals $\fm_1,\dots,\fm_n$ and let $\fN=\nil(R)$. Prove that $\fN=\Jac(R)$, that $\fN$ is nilpotent, and that $R/\fN\cong\prod_{i=1}^n R/\fm_i$ is a finite product of fields.
\item Let $A$ be an Artinian local ring with maximal ideal $\fm$. Prove that the following are equivalent: (i) every ideal of $A$ is principal; (ii) $\fm$ is principal; (iii) $\dim_{A/\fm}(\fm/\fm^2)\le 1$. Conclude that in case (iii) every nonzero ideal of $A$ equals some power $\fm^r$.
\item Let $R$ be a $k$-algebra with $\dim_k R<\infty$. Prove that $R$ is Artinian, that $\len_R(R)\le\dim_k R$, and that equality holds when every residue field $R/\fm_i$ equals $k$. Give an example where the inequality is strict.
\item Let $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules in which $M$ has finite length. Prove that $M'$ and $M''$ have finite length and that $\len_R(M)=\len_R(M')+\len_R(M'')$. Deduce that length is additive over finite direct sums.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $R=Z/(72)Z$, with $72=2^3\cdot3^2$. Complete the ideal-factorization lattice below (each node an ideal $(\bar d)$ for $d\mid 72$, edges drawn for divisibility/containment), label each edge with the $Z$-length of the corresponding successive quotient, and confirm that the total length down any maximal chain from $R$ to $0$ equals $\len_Z(R)=5$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.6em]
& R=(\bar1) \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & \\
(\bar2) \arrow[d,dash]\arrow[dr,dash] & & (\bar3) \arrow[dl,dash]\arrow[d,dash] \\
(\bar4) \arrow[d,dash] & (\bar6) & (\bar9) \\
(\bar8)\arrow[dr,dash] & & \\
& (\bar0) &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State which two nodes are the maximal ideals and verify $R/\Jac(R)\cong\F_2\times\F_3$.
\item Let $R=Z_{(p)}$ be the localization of $Z$ at $(p)$, a DVR with maximal ideal $\fm=(p)$, and for each $n\ge1$ let $R_n=R/(p^n)=Z/(p^n)Z$ be the Artinian local quotient. Complete the commuting square of the quotient maps and verify that the right-hand map $\rho$ is the canonical reduction with kernel $(p^{n-1})R_n$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r,twoheadrightarrow,"{\pi_n}"] \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{\pi_{n-1}}"'] & R_n=Z/(p^n)Z \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{\rho}"] \\
R_{n-1}=Z/(p^{n-1})Z \arrow[r,equal] & R/(p^{n-1})
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Show $\Ker(\rho)=(\overline{p^{n-1}})$, that $\Ker(\rho)$ is the unique minimal nonzero ideal of $R_n$, and that $\len_R(R_n)=n$.
\item Let $R$ be Artinian with maximal ideals $\fm_1,\dots,\fm_n$, and let $m$ satisfy $(\Jac R)^m=0$. The structure theorem gives $R\cong\prod_{i=1}^n A_i$ with $A_i=R/\fm_i^m$ local. Complete the diagram showing the projection onto a factor followed by reduction to the residue field, and identify each kernel:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
R \arrow[r,"\sim"] \arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow,"{q_i}"'] & \prod_{j=1}^n A_j \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{\operatorname{pr}_i}"] \\
& A_i \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{}"] \\
& A_i/\fm_iA_i\cong R/\fm_i
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Show $\Ker(\operatorname{pr}_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}A_j$, that $q_i$ is the localization map $R\to R_{\fm_i}=A_i$, and that the composite $R\twoheadrightarrow R/\fm_i$ is the $i$th factor of the corollary $R/\Jac(R)\cong\prod_i R/\fm_i$.
\item Let $A$ be an Artinian local ring with principal maximal ideal $\fm=(t)$, $\fm^k=0$ and $\fm^{k-1}\ne0$ -- the $0$-dimensional analogue of a DVR. Complete the chain of inclusions of its ideals (the full ideal lattice is a single chain) and label each arrow with the length of the successive quotient:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.2em]
0=(t^k) \arrow[r,hook] & (t^{k-1}) \arrow[r,hook] & \cdots \arrow[r,hook] & (t^2) \arrow[r,hook] & (t) \arrow[r,hook] & (t^0)=A
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Reading right to left as a descending chain, prove each successive quotient $(t^{r})/(t^{r+1})$ is a $1$-dimensional $A/\fm$-vector space, that $A$ has exactly $k+1$ ideals, and that $\len_A(A)=k$.
\end{exers}

R \arrow[r,"\sim"] \arrow[dr,twoheadrightarrow,"{q_i}"'] & \prod_{j=1}^n A_j \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{\operatorname{pr}_i}"] \\
& A_i \arrow[d,twoheadrightarrow,"{}"] \\
& A_i/\fm_iA_i\cong R/\fm_i
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Show $\Ker(\operatorname{pr}_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}A_j$, that $q_i$ is the localization map $R\to R_{\fm_i}=A_i$, and that the composite $R\twoheadrightarrow R/\fm_i$ is the $i$th factor of the corollary $R/\Jac(R)\cong\prod_i R/\fm_i$.
\item Let $A$ be an Artinian local ring with principal maximal ideal $\fm=(t)$, $\fm^k=0$ and $\fm^{k-1}\ne0$ -- the $0$-dimensional analogue of a DVR. Complete the chain of inclusions of its ideals (the full ideal lattice is a single chain) and label each arrow with the length of the successive quotient:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.2em]
0=(t^k) \arrow[r,hook] & (t^{k-1}) \arrow[r,hook] & \cdots \arrow[r,hook] & (t^2) \arrow[r,hook] & (t) \arrow[r,hook] & (t^0)=A
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Reading right to left as a descending chain, prove each successive quotient $(t^{r})/(t^{r+1})$ is a $1$-dimensional $A/\fm$-vector space, that $A$ has exactly $k+1$ ideals, and that $\len_A(A)=k$.
\end{exers}

Content:
Artinian rings were the Noetherian rings of dimension $0$. We now climb one rung and study the simplest Noetherian domains of dimension $1$. The local model for such a ring carries an extra, very concrete piece of data: a way to measure ``how divisible'' an element is by the maximal ideal. That measurement is a discrete valuation.

Type: example
Title: The $p$-adic valuation on $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The $p$-adic valuation on $Q$}
Verify that $v_p$ is a discrete valuation on $Q$ and identify its valuation ring.
\wrec Every nonzero rational has a unique form $p^n(a/b)$ with $p\nmid a$, $p\nmid b$; set $v_p=n$.
\wsol Write $x=p^n(a/b)\in\units{Q}$ with $a,b$ prime to $p$. Surjectivity is clear ($v_p(p^n)=n$). For (ii), if $x=p^m(a/b)$ and $y=p^n(c/d)$ then $xy=p^{m+n}(ac/bd)$ with $ac,bd$ prime to $p$, so $v_p(xy)=m+n=v_p(x)+v_p(y)$. For (iii), with $m\le n$, $x+y=p^m\bigl(a/b+p^{n-m}c/d\bigr)=p^m\cdot\tfrac{ad+p^{n-m}bc}{bd}$; the denominator is prime to $p$, the numerator may or may not be, so $v_p(x+y)\ge m=\min\{v_p(x),v_p(y)\}$. The valuation ring is $\{a/b:p\nmid b\}=Z_{(p)}$, the localization of $Z$ at $(p)$. Sanity check: $v_p(p)=1$ and $v_p(1/p)=-1$, so $p\inZ_{(p)}$ but $1/p\notinZ_{(p)}$, exactly the elements with nonnegative valuation.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The order valuation on a rational function field
Content:
\begin{wex}{The order valuation on a rational function field}
For $K=F(x)$ and an irreducible $f\in F[x]$, show $v_f$ is a discrete valuation and find its ring.
\wrec Each nonzero element of $F(x)$ is uniquely $f^n(a/b)$ with $f\nmid a$, $f\nmid b$.
\wsol The verification is identical to the $p$-adic case with the prime $p$ replaced by the irreducible $f$ and $Z$ replaced by the UFD $F[x]$: $v_f(gh)=v_f(g)+v_f(h)$ and the ultrametric inequality both follow from unique factorization. The valuation ring is the localization $F[x]_{(f)}$ of rational functions whose reduced denominator is not divisible by $f$. When $f=x-a$ has degree $1$, $v_f$ measures the order of vanishing at $x=a$: $v_f\ge0$ means defined at $a$, $v_f<0$ means a pole. Sanity check: $v_{x-a}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{x-a}\bigr)=-1$ (simple pole), $v_{x-a}\bigl((x-a)^2\bigr)=2$ (double zero), consistent with (ii).
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The valuation on formal Laurent series
Content:
\begin{wex}{The valuation on formal Laurent series}
Show the order map on $F((x))$ is a discrete valuation with ring $F[[x]]$.
\wrec A nonzero Laurent series $\sum_{i\ge n}a_ix^i$ with $a_n\neq0$ has order $n$.
\wsol Define $v\bigl(\sum_{i\ge n}a_ix^i\bigr)=n$ where $a_n\neq0$ is the lowest nonzero coefficient. Multiplying two series, the lowest terms multiply to give $a_nb_m x^{n+m}$ (nonzero, as $F$ is a domain), so $v$ is additive. For the sum, the lowest possible surviving term has exponent $\ge\min(n,m)$, giving (iii). The valuation ring $\{v\ge0\}\cup\{0\}$ is the power series ring $F[[x]]$. Sanity check: $v(x)=1$ and $v(x^{-1})=-1$, so $x\in F[[x]]$, $x^{-1}\notin F[[x]]$; and $F((x))=\Frac(F[[x]])$ since inverting $x$ recovers all Laurent series.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {uniformizer}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{uniformizer}]
If $R$ is a DVR with valuation $v$, an element $t\in R$ with $v(t)=1$ is a uniformizing parameter (or uniformizer, or local parameter). Such $t$ exists by surjectivity of $v$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {factorization in a DVR}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{factorization in a DVR}]
Let $R$ be a DVR with valuation $v$ and uniformizer $t$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item A nonzero $u\in R$ is a unit iff $v(u)=0$.
\item Every nonzero $r\in R$ is $r=u\,t^n$ for a unit $u$ and $n=v(r)\ge0$; every nonzero $x\in K$ is $x=u\,t^n$ for a unit $u$ and $n=v(x)\inZ$. The factorization is unique.
\item Every nonzero ideal of $R$ is $\fm^n=(t^n)$ for some $n\ge0$. In particular $R$ is Noetherian, indeed a PID.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) If $uw=1$ with $w\in R$ then $v(u)+v(w)=v(1)=0$ with both $\ge0$, forcing $v(u)=0$; conversely $v(u)=0$ gives $v(u^{-1})=0$, so $u^{-1}\in R$. (2) If $v(x)=n$ then $v(xt^{-n})=0$, so $xt^{-n}=u$ is a unit and $x=ut^n$. (3) For a nonzero ideal $I$ pick $r\in I$ of minimal valuation $n$; then $r=ut^n$ gives $t^n\in I$, so $(t^n)\subseteq I$, and any $a\in I$ has $v(a)\ge n$, whence $at^{-n}\in R$ and $a\in(t^n)$. So $I=(t^n)$.
\end{proof}

Type: corollary
Title: {ideal theory and spectrum}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{ideal theory and spectrum}]
Let $R$ be a DVR with maximal ideal $\fm=(t)=\{r:v(r)>0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $R$ is an integrally closed local ring; its nonzero ideals are exactly $\fm^n$, $n\ge0$, forming a single descending chain $R\supsetneq\fm\supsetneq\fm^2\supsetneq\cdots$.
\item $\Spec R=\{0,\fm\}$: the only primes are $(0)$ and $\fm$. Hence $\dim R=1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
A DVR is a PID, hence a UFD, hence integrally closed in its fraction field. Locality and the ideal description come from the previous proposition; the chain $\fm^n$ has trivial intersection $\bigcap_n\fm^n=0$ since $v$ of a nonzero element is finite. As every nonzero ideal is some $\fm^n$ and a prime containing $\fm^n$ contains $\fm$, the only nonzero prime is $\fm$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{method}{To produce a DVR by hand.} Exhibit a discrete valuation $v$ on a field $K$: typically $K$ is a UFD's fraction field and $v$ counts the multiplicity of a chosen prime/irreducible. Then $R=\{v\ge0\}\cup\{0\}$ is a DVR, a uniformizer is any element of valuation $1$ (the chosen prime itself), and the maximal ideal is $\{v>0\}$. To go the other way -- recognize an abstractly given ring as a DVR -- use the internal characterizations of the next subsection, which never mention $v$.\end{method}

Type: example
Title: Reading off the valuation in $Z_{(p)}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading off the valuation in $Z_{(p)}$}
In $R=Z_{(p)}$ with $p=5$, factor $r=\tfrac{50}{3}$ as $u\,t^n$ and identify the ideal it generates.
\wrec $t=p=5$ is a uniformizer; $v_5(r)=n$ and $u=r/5^n$ is a unit (valuation $0$).
\wsol $\tfrac{50}{3}=5^2\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}$, and $v_5(2/3)=0$ so $u=2/3$ is a unit in $Z_{(5)}$. Thus $r=u\,5^2$ with $n=v_5(r)=2$, and $(r)=(5^2)=\fm^2$. Sanity check: $2/3$ is a unit because both numerator and denominator are prime to $5$, so $(2/3)^{-1}=3/2\inZ_{(5)}$; and $(r)=(50/3)=(25)$ since $2/3$ is a unit, so $(r)=\fm^2$, which lies in $\fm^2$ but not in $\fm^3$ (as $v_5(r)=2$), exactly as the valuation predicts.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The residue field of a DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{The residue field of a DVR}
Compute the residue field $R/\fm$ for $Z_{(p)}$, $k[x]_{(x)}$, and $k[[t]]$.
\wrec $R/\fm$ is the field obtained by ``evaluating'' an element of valuation $0$; killing the uniformizer.
\wsol For $Z_{(p)}$, $\fm=(p)$ and $R/\fm=Z_{(p)}/(p)\congZ/pZ=\F_p$. For $k[x]_{(x)}$, $\fm=(x)$ and $R/\fm\cong k$ (set $x=0$). For $k[[t]]$, $\fm=(t)$ and $R/\fm\cong k$ (take the constant term). Sanity check: in each case the natural surjection $R\to R/\fm$ sends a unit (valuation $0$) to a nonzero residue and the uniformizer to $0$, and the kernel is exactly $\fm=\{v>0\}$, so the quotient is a field as $\fm$ is maximal.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The graded quotients $\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}$ are one-dimensional
Content:
\begin{wex}{The graded quotients $\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}$ are one-dimensional}
For a DVR $R$ with residue field $F=R/\fm$, show $\dim_F(\fm^n/\fm^{n+1})=1$.
\wrec $\fm^n=(t^n)$, so $\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}$ is generated over $F$ by the class of $t^n$.
\wsol Every element of $\fm^n$ is $r t^n$ with $r\in R$; modulo $\fm^{n+1}=(t^{n+1})$ it depends only on $r\bmod\fm$, giving an $F$-linear isomorphism $\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}\cong R/\fm=F$, $rt^n\mapsto\bar r$. Hence the dimension is $1$. Sanity check: the associated graded ring $\gr_\fm R=\bigoplus_n\fm^n/\fm^{n+1}\cong F[\bar t]$ is a polynomial ring in one variable over $F$, the algebraic shadow of ``$t$ is a single uniformizer.'' This $\dim=1$ is precisely the nonsingularity condition for curves at the end of the section.
\end{wex}

Type: theorem
Title: {equivalent characterizations of a DVR}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{equivalent characterizations of a DVR}]
For an integral domain $R$ that is not a field, with fraction field $K$, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $R$ is a discrete valuation ring.
\item $R$ is a PID with a unique nonzero prime ideal $\fp\neq0$.
\item $R$ is a UFD with a unique irreducible element up to associates.
\item $R$ is a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal $\fm$ is nonzero and principal.
\item $R$ is a Noetherian, integrally closed local domain of Krull dimension $1$; equivalently $\Spec R=\{0,\fm\}$ with $\fm\neq0$.
\item $R$ is a Noetherian local domain of dimension $1$ with $\dim_{R/\fm}(\fm/\fm^2)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
$(1)\Rightarrow$ everything: shown in the previous subsection. $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$: in a PID (hence UFD) the unique nonzero prime $\fp=(t)$ is generated by the unique irreducible $t$. $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$: unique factorization gives each nonzero element as $ut^n$ uniquely, and $v(ut^n)=n$ is a discrete valuation whose ring is $R$. $(4)\Rightarrow(2)$: write $\fm=(t)$; Krull's intersection / Nakayama gives $\bigcap\fm^i=0$, and any proper nonzero ideal $I$ sits in some $\fm^n\setminus\fm^{n+1}$, so $I=(t^n)$ -- every ideal is principal with a single prime $\fm$. The subtle implication is $(5)\Rightarrow(4)$: one must show $\fm$ is principal. Since $\fm=\Jac R\neq\fm^2$ (Nakayama), choose $t\in\fm\setminus\fm^2$. Dimension $1$ makes $\fm$ the radical of $(t)$, so $\fm^n\subseteq(t)$ for some $n$; take $n$ least and $x\in\fm^{n-1}\setminus(t)$, so that $x\fm\subseteq\fm^n\subseteq(t)$, and set $y=x/t\in K$. Then $y\notin R$ but $y\fm\subseteq R$. If $y\fm=R$ then $\fm=(t)$ after all; otherwise $y\fm\subseteq\fm$, so $y$ stabilizes the finitely generated faithful module $\fm$, forcing $y$ integral over $R$ (determinant trick), hence $y\in R$ by integral closure -- contradiction. So $\fm=(t)$. Finally $(4)\Leftrightarrow(6)$: by Nakayama a Noetherian local $\fm$ is principal iff $\dim_{R/\fm}\fm/\fm^2=1$ (the minimal number of generators of $\fm$ equals this dimension).
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[{localizing at a minimal prime gives a DVR}]
If $R$ is a Noetherian, integrally closed integral domain and $\fp$ is a minimal nonzero prime ideal, then the localization $R_\fp$ is a discrete valuation ring.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
Localization preserves all five hypotheses of characterization (5): $R_\fp$ is Noetherian, integrally closed, a domain, local with unique maximal ideal $\fp R_\fp$, and that ideal is the unique nonzero prime because $\fp$ was minimal -- so $\dim R_\fp=1$. By the theorem $R_\fp$ is a DVR. This is the bridge to the next section: it is exactly how a Dedekind domain breaks up into DVRs, one for each nonzero prime.

Type: example
Title: Why the local model must be one-dimensional
Content:
\begin{wex}{Why the local model must be one-dimensional}
Show that condition (5) genuinely needs $\dim R=1$: a dimension-$0$ Noetherian local domain is a field, hence not a DVR.
\wrec Dimension $0$ means every prime is maximal; the unique prime $(0)$ is then maximal.
\wsol If $R$ is a Noetherian local domain of dimension $0$, the zero ideal $(0)$ is prime (domain) and is the only prime, hence is maximal, so $\fm=(0)$ and $R$ is a field. A field $K$ is not the valuation ring of any discrete valuation on $K$ (a surjective $v$ takes negative values, so $\{v\ge0\}\cup\{0\}\ne K$), so it is excluded -- consistent with the theorem requiring ``$R$ is not a field.'' Sanity check: this is the Artinian boundary case from Section 16.1 (Noetherian $+$ dimension $0$), confirming DVRs sit one dimension above fields.
\end{wex}

Title: $Z_{(p)}$ satisfies characterization (2)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z_{(p)}$ satisfies characterization (2)}
Verify directly that $Z_{(p)}$ is a PID with a unique nonzero prime.
\wrec Localizing the PID $Z$ at $(p)$ keeps it a PID and isolates the single prime $(p)$.
\wsol Ideals of $Z_{(p)}$ correspond to ideals of $Z$ contained in $(p)$ together with extension; the primes surviving are exactly those $\subseteq(p)$, namely $(0)$ and $(p)$. Every nonzero ideal is $(p^n)Z_{(p)}$ since any rational $a/b$ ($p\nmid b$) is $p^{v_p}\cdotunit$. So $Z_{(p)}$ is a PID with unique nonzero prime $(p)$ -- characterization (2). Sanity check: $\dimZ_{(p)}=1$ matches the chain $0\subsetneq(p)$, and the unique irreducible (up to units) is $p$ itself, matching (3).
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $k[[t]]$ via characterization (4)
Content:
\begin{wex}{$k[[t]]$ via characterization (4)}
Show the power series ring $k[[t]]$ is a Noetherian local domain with principal maximal ideal, hence a DVR.
\wrec Units of $k[[t]]$ are the series with nonzero constant term; the non-units form the ideal $(t)$.
\wsol A series $\sum a_i t^i$ is a unit iff $a_0\neq0$ (invert by geometric series). Thus the non-units are exactly $(t)$, so $k[[t]]$ is local with maximal ideal $\fm=(t)$, principal and nonzero. It is a Noetherian domain (e.g.\ it is the $t$-adic completion of $k[t]$, or directly each ideal is $(t^n)$). By characterization (4) it is a DVR with uniformizer $t$. Sanity check: every nonzero series is $t^n\cdot(unit)$ where $n$ is the lowest exponent, giving the valuation $v=n$ and recovering characterization (1).
\end{wex}

Title: A non-example: $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is not a DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-example: $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is not a DVR}
Explain why the localization of $k[x,y]$ at the maximal ideal $(x,y)$ fails to be a DVR.
\wrec A DVR is dimension $1$ with a principal maximal ideal; here both fail.
\wsol The local ring $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ has $\dim R=2$ (chain $0\subsetneq(x)\subsetneq(x,y)$), violating characterization (5). Equivalently $\fm=(x,y)$ needs two generators: $\dim_{R/\fm}\fm/\fm^2=2\neq1$, violating (6). So $R$ is a regular local ring but of dimension $2$, not a DVR. Sanity check: $R$ is integrally closed and Noetherian, so it satisfies every condition except dimension $1$ / principal maximal ideal -- pinpointing exactly which hypotheses are doing the work.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A non-example: a non-integrally-closed dimension-$1$ local ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-example: a non-integrally-closed dimension-$1$ local ring}
Show $R=k[t^2,t^3]_{(t^2,t^3)}$ is a Noetherian local domain of dimension $1$ that is not a DVR.
\wrec Characterization (5) requires integral closure; the cusp coordinate ring fails it.
\wsol Let $A=k[t^2,t^3]\subseteq k[t]$, the coordinate ring of the cuspidal cubic $y^2=x^3$, and $R=A_\fm$ at $\fm=(t^2,t^3)$. Then $\dim R=1$ (it is a curve), $R$ is Noetherian and local. But $u=t^3/t^2=t\in K=\Frac(R)$ satisfies $u^2=t^2\in R$, so $u$ is integral over $R$ yet $u=t\notin R$. Thus $R$ is not integrally closed, so not a DVR. Sanity check: $\dim_{R/\fm}\fm/\fm^2=2$ here (generators $t^2,t^3$ are independent mod $\fm^2$), so (6) also fails -- the cusp is a singular point of the curve, the geometric face of ``not a DVR.''
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > The $p$-adic integers and completion
Type: definition
Title: {$v$-adic metric}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{$v$-adic metric}]
A discrete valuation $v$ on $K$ gives, for any fixed real $\beta>1$, an absolute value $\lVert a\rVert_v=\beta^{-v(a)}$ (with $\lVert0\rVert_v=0$) and metric $d_v(a,b)=\lVert a-b\rVert_v$. Axiom (iii) yields the ultrametric inequality $d_v(a,b)\le\max\{d_v(a,c),d_v(c,b)\}$. The completion $K_v$ is again a field with a discrete valuation extending $v$, and $\{v\ge0\}$ inside it is a complete DVR.
\end{definition}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > The $p$-adic integers and completion
Type: example
Title: The $p$-adic integers $Z_p$ as a DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{The $p$-adic integers $Z_p$ as a DVR}
Show $Z_p=\varprojlimZ/p^nZ$ is a DVR and identify its uniformizer and residue field.
\wrec $Z_p$ is the completion of $Z_{(p)}$; it is a PID with unique maximal ideal $pZ_p$.
\wsol Every nonzero $\alpha\inZ_p$ is uniquely $p^n u$ with $u\in\units{Z_p}$ a unit (constant $p$-adic digit nonzero), so $v_p(\alpha)=n$ is a discrete valuation and $Z_p$ is its ring -- a DVR by characterization (1). The uniformizer is $t=p$, the maximal ideal is $pZ_p$, and the residue field is $Z_p/pZ_p\cong\F_p$. Its fraction field is $Q_p$, in which every nonzero element is $p^n u$ with $n\inZ$. Sanity check: the sequence $1,p,p^2,\dots$ has $v_p\to+\infty$, so $\lVert p^k\rVert_p=p^{-k}\to0$; it converges to $0$ in the $p$-adic metric, the hallmark that ``divisible by a high power of $p$'' means ``small.''
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > The $p$-adic integers and completion
Type: example
Title: $Z_p$ as the completion of $Z_{(p)}$, and $Q_p$ from $Q$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z_p$ as the completion of $Z_{(p)}$, and $Q_p$ from $Q$}
Explain the sense in which $Z_p$ and $Q_p$ are completions, via $p$-adic Laurent expansions.
\wrec Completing $Q$ in the $p$-adic metric gives $Q_p$; each element has a digit expansion $\sum_{i\ge n_0}a_i p^i$.
\wsol Cauchy sequences in $(Q,d_{v_p})$ have limits represented as $\alpha=\sum_{i\ge n_0}a_i p^i$ with digits $a_i\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and $v_p(\alpha)=n_0$ when $a_{n_0}\neq0$. The subset with $n_0\ge0$ (no negative powers of $p$) is the completion of $Z$, namely $Z_p$; allowing finitely many negative powers gives $Q_p=\Frac(Z_p)$. This mirrors the power-series case $F[[x]]\subseteq F((x))$ exactly, with $p$ in place of $x$. Sanity check: truncating the series at $p^n$ recovers $Z/p^nZ$, so $Z_p=\varprojlimZ/p^nZ$ and $\bigcap_n p^nZ_p=0$, consistent with $v_p$ of a nonzero element being finite.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Laurent series as the completion of $k[x]_{(x)}$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Laurent series as the completion of $k[x]_{(x)}$}
Identify $\Frac(k[[x]])$ and relate $k[[x]]$ to the localization $k[x]_{(x)}$.
\wrec Completing $k(x)$ at the valuation $v_x$ (order at $x=0$) gives $k((x))$ with ring $k[[x]]$.
\wsol The valuation ring $k[x]_{(x)}$ (rational functions defined at $0$) is dense in its $v_x$-completion $k[[x]]$, and $\Frac(k[[x]])=k((x))$, the formal Laurent series. Every nonzero Laurent series is $x^n\cdot(unit)$, recovering $v_x=n$. Sanity check: $k[x]_{(x)}$ and $k[[x]]$ have the same residue field $k$ and the same uniformizer $x$, but only the completion is complete -- e.g.\ the partial sums of $\sum_{i\ge0}x^{i^2}$ form a Cauchy sequence in $k[x]_{(x)}$ with no limit there, since this series is not a rational function (its coefficients satisfy no linear recurrence), whereas $\sum_{i\ge0}x^i=1/(1-x)$ already lies in $k[x]_{(x)}$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The ultrametric inequality sharpened
Content:
\begin{wex}{The ultrametric inequality sharpened}
In a DVR's fraction field, prove that $v(x)<v(y)\Rightarrow v(x+y)=\min\{v(x),v(y)\}=v(x)$.
\wrec Equality holds in the ultrametric law whenever the two valuations differ; write $x+y=x(1+y/x)$.
\wsol Suppose $v(x)<v(y)$, so $v(y/x)=v(y)-v(x)>0$, i.e.\ $y/x\in\fm$. Then $1+y/x$ is a unit (it is $1$ plus a non-unit in a local ring), so $v(1+y/x)=0$, giving $v(x+y)=v(x)+v(1+y/x)=v(x)=\min\{v(x),v(y)\}$. Sanity check: in $Z_{(p)}$, $v_p(p+p^2)=v_p\bigl(p(1+p)\bigr)=1+0=1=\min(1,2)$; the only way the strict inequality $v(x+y)>\min$ can occur is when $v(x)=v(y)$ and leading terms cancel, e.g.\ $v_p(p-p)=+\infty$.
\end{wex}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > Fractional ideals and nonsingularity of curves
Type: definition
Title: {fractional ideal}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{fractional ideal}]
For a domain $R$ with fraction field $K$, a fractional ideal is a nonzero $R$-submodule $A\subseteq K$ with $dA\subseteq R$ for some nonzero $d\in R$ (equivalently $A=d^{-1} I$ for an ordinary ideal $I$). Products are defined by $AB=\{\sum a_ib_i\}$; $A$ is invertible if $AB=R$ for some fractional ideal $B$, necessarily $B=A^{-1}=\{x\in K:xA\subseteq R\}$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {DVRs via fractional ideals}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{DVRs via fractional ideals}]
Let $R$ be a local domain that is not a field. Then $R$ is a DVR if and only if every nonzero fractional ideal of $R$ is invertible.
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > Fractional ideals and nonsingularity of curves
Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-fce2ccf2469025022e44
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
If $R$ is a DVR with uniformizer $t$, every nonzero fractional ideal is $t^N R$ for some $N\inZ$ (clear denominators, then use that ordinary ideals are $\fm^n=(t^n)$), hence principal and invertible. Conversely, if every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible then every ideal is finitely generated (invertible $\Rightarrow$ finitely generated), so $R$ is Noetherian. With $\fm$ the maximal ideal, $\fm\neq\fm^2$ (else $\fm=0$ by Nakayama and $R$ is a field), so pick $t\in\fm\setminus\fm^2$. Then $t\fm^{-1}$ is a nonzero ideal of $R$; it cannot lie in $\fm$ (that would force $t\in\fm^2$), so $t\fm^{-1}=R$, i.e.\ $\fm=(t)$ is principal. By characterization (4), $R$ is a DVR.
\end{proof}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Discrete Valuation Rings > Fractional ideals and nonsingularity of curves
Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
Invertibility is the same as being projective: a nonzero fractional ideal $A$ of a domain is invertible iff $A$ is a projective $R$-module. Over a DVR every fractional ideal is even free of rank $1$ (it is principal), so the class group is trivial -- a DVR is a PID. Relaxing ``local'' while keeping ``every fractional ideal invertible'' gives, for domains that are not fields, exactly the Dedekind domains of the next section (Theorem~15(3) there; the definition itself is Noetherian, integrally closed, of dimension $1$); the class group then measures the failure to be a PID.
\end{remark}

Type: proposition
Title: {nonsingularity $=$ DVR}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{nonsingularity $=$ DVR}]
Let $C$ be an irreducible affine curve over an algebraically closed field $k$, and $v\in C$ a point with local ring $O_{v,C}$ and maximal ideal $\fm_v$. Then $C$ is nonsingular at $v$ (i.e.\ $\dim_k(\fm_v/\fm_v^2)=1$) if and only if $O_{v,C}$ is a discrete valuation ring.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
$O_{v,C}$ is a Noetherian local domain of dimension $1$ (the curve has $\trdeg_k k(C)=1$). Nonsingularity says $\dim_k(\fm_v/\fm_v^2)=1$, which by characterization (6) is exactly the DVR condition for a one-dimensional Noetherian local ring. The residue field is $k$ (Nullstellensatz, $k=\bar k$), so the $R/\fm$-dimension is the $k$-dimension.
\end{proof}

Title: {smoothness $=$ integral closure}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{smoothness $=$ integral closure}]
An irreducible affine curve $C$ over $k=\bar k$ is smooth (nonsingular at every point) iff its coordinate ring $k[C]$ is integrally closed.
\end{corollary}

Type: example
Title: Order of a zero/pole on a smooth curve
Content:
\begin{wex}{Order of a zero/pole on a smooth curve}
At a smooth point $v$ with uniformizer $t$, define and compute the order of $f$.
\wrec Every $f\inO_{v,C}$ (and every $f$ in the function field) is $u\,t^n$; set $ord_v(f)=n=v_v(f)$.
\wsol The valuation $v_v$ on $k(C)$ attached to the DVR $O_{v,C}$ assigns $ord_v(f)=n$ where $f=u\,t^n$, $u$ a unit. Then $n>0$ means a zero of order $n$, $n<0$ a pole of order $-n$, $n=0$ a nonzero finite value. For $C=\Aff^1$ with coordinate $x$ and $v$ the point $x=a$: $t=x-a$, and $f=(x-a)^2/(x-b)$ has $ord_v f=2$ at $a$ and $ord=-1$ at $b$. Sanity check: $ord_v(fg)=ord_v f+ord_v g$ by additivity of $v_v$, so orders add under multiplication and the ``divisor'' $\sum_vord_v(f)\cdot v$ is well defined -- the entry point to the theory of divisors on curves.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: A singular point fails to be a DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{A singular point fails to be a DVR}
For the cusp $C:\,y^2=x^3$ at the origin, show $\dim_k(\fm_v/\fm_v^2)=2$, hence singular.
\wrec Compute $\fm_v/\fm_v^2$ in $O_{0,C}$; if it has dimension $>1$ the local ring is not a DVR.
\wsol With $k[C]=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ and $\fm=(x,y)$ at the origin, in $\fm/\fm^2$ the relation $y^2=x^3$ lives in $\fm^3\subseteq\fm^2$ and imposes nothing, so $x,y$ are linearly independent mod $\fm^2$: $\dim_k(\fm/\fm^2)=2>1$. Hence $O_{0,C}$ is not a DVR and the origin is singular. Sanity check: this is the cusp $R=k[t^2,t^3]_{(t^2,t^3)}$ from earlier, where $t=y/x$ is integral but not in $R$ -- non-integral-closure and the dimension-$2$ cotangent space are two views of the same singularity.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Localizing a PID at a prime always gives a DVR
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing a PID at a prime always gives a DVR}
Show every localization $R_\fp$ of a PID $R$ at a nonzero prime $\fp=(p)$ is a DVR.
\wrec A PID is integrally closed (it is a UFD) and its nonzero primes are maximal, so the corollary on minimal primes applies.
\wsol $R$ is Noetherian, integrally closed, a domain; $\fp=(p)$ is a minimal nonzero prime (in a PID all nonzero primes are minimal $=$ maximal). By the corollary, $R_\fp$ is a DVR, with valuation $v_p(p^n a/b)=n$ for $a,b$ prime to $p$. This unifies the $Z_{(p)}$ and $F[x]_{(f)}$ examples. Sanity check: the fraction field of $R_\fp$ equals $\Frac(R)$, so each nonzero prime $p$ of $R$ yields one valuation on the common field $K$ -- exactly the family of DVRs that reassembles into the Dedekind domain $R$ in Section 16.3.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: From a Dedekind domain to its DVRs (forward link)
Content:
\begin{wex}{From a Dedekind domain to its DVRs (forward link)}
If $R$ is Noetherian, integrally closed, of dimension $1$, describe the family $\{R_\fp\}$ and why each is a DVR.
\wrec Each nonzero prime $\fp$ is minimal; localizing gives a one-dimensional integrally closed Noetherian local domain.
\wsol For each nonzero prime $\fp$ of $R$, the localization $R_\fp$ satisfies characterization (5): Noetherian, integrally closed, local with unique nonzero prime $\fp R_\fp$, dimension $1$. So $R_\fp$ is a DVR with a valuation $v_\fp$ on $K=\Frac(R)$, and the maximal ideals of $R$ are in bijection with these valuations. Sanity check: this is condition (2) of the upcoming Dedekind characterization ($R$ Noetherian with every $R_\fp$ a DVR), so a Dedekind domain is precisely a ``global'' object whose every local piece is a DVR -- the local-global principle that restores unique factorization at the level of ideals.
\end{wex}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item Suppose $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring with respect to the valuation $v$ on the fraction field $K$ of $R$. If $x, y \in K$ with $v(x) < v(y)$ prove that $v(x + y) = \min(v(x), v(y))$. [Note that $x + y = x(1 + y/x)$.]

\item Suppose $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring with unique maximal ideal $M$ and quotient $F = R/M$. For any $n \geq 0$ show that $M^n / M^{n+1}$ is a vector space over $F$ and that $\dim_F(M^n / M^{n+1}) = 1$.

\item Suppose $R$ is an integral domain that is also a local ring whose unique maximal ideal $M = (t)$ is nonzero and principal, and suppose that $\bigcap_{n \geq 1} (t^n) = 0$. Prove that $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring. [Show that every nonzero element in $R$ can be written in the form $u t^n$ for some unit $u \in R$ and some $n \geq 0$.]

\item Suppose $R$ is a Noetherian local ring whose unique maximal ideal $M = (t)$ is principal. Prove that either $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring or $t^n = 0$ for some $n \geq 0$. In the latter case show that $R$ is Artinian.

\item Suppose that $R$ is a Noetherian integral domain that is also a local ring of Krull dimension 1. Let $M$ be the unique maximal ideal of $R$ and let $F = R/M$, so that $M / M^2$ is a vector space over $F$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that if $\dim_F(M / M^2) = 1$ then $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring.
\item[(b)] If every nonzero ideal of $R$ is a power of $M$ prove that $R$ is a Discrete Valuation Ring.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$. Prove that every finitely generated $R$-submodule of $K$ is a fractional ideal of $R$. If $R$ is Noetherian, prove that $A$ is a fractional ideal of $R$ if and only if $A$ is a finitely generated $R$-submodule of $K$.

\item If $R$ is an integral domain and $A$ is a fractional ideal of $R$, prove that if $A$ is projective then $A$ is finitely generated. Conclude that every integral domain that is not Noetherian contains an ideal that is not projective.

\item Suppose $R$ is a Noetherian integral domain that is also a local ring with nonzero maximal ideal $M$. Prove that $R$ is a D.V.R. if and only if the only $M$-primary ideals in $R$ are the powers of $M$.

\item Let $C = Z(xz - y^2,\, yz - x^3,\, z^2 - x^2 y) \subset A^3$ over the algebraically closed field $k$. If $v = (0, 0, 0) \in C$, prove that $\dim_k(m_{v,C} / m_{v,C}^2) = 3$ so that $v$ is singular on $C$. Conclude that $k[C]$ is not integrally closed in $k(C)$ and determine its integral closure. [cf. Exercise 27, Section 15.4.]
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Practice problems.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item In $R=Z_{(7)}$ with uniformizer $t=7$, write each of $r_1=\tfrac{98}{15}$, $r_2=\tfrac{6}{343}$, and $r_3=\tfrac{21}{50}\cdot\tfrac{20}{63}$ in the form $u\,7^{\,n}$ with $u\in\units{R}$ and $n=v_7(r_i)\inZ$, and decide which $r_i$ lie in $R$.
\item Let $K=Q$ with the $5$-adic valuation $v_5$. Using only $v_5(x)<v_5(y)\Rightarrow v_5(x+y)=\min\{v_5(x),v_5(y)\}$ and additivity, compute $v_5\bigl(\tfrac{1}{25}+\tfrac{3}{10}\bigr)$ and $v_5\bigl(\tfrac{2}{5}+\tfrac{8}{5}\bigr)$, and explain why the second case can exceed the minimum.
\item In the power series DVR $R=\F_2[[t]]$, determine $v(f)$ and the unit part of $f=t^3+t^5+t^7$ and of $g=t^2(1+t)^{-1}$, then factor the product $fg$ as $u\,t^n$. Identify the ideal $(fg)$ as a power of $\fm=(t)$.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR and let $a,b\in R$ be nonzero with $v(a)=3$ and $v(b)=5$. Compute $v(a^2 b)$, decide whether $a\mid b$ in $R$, and determine the smallest $n$ with $\fm^n\subseteq (a)$ and the largest $m$ with $b\in\fm^m$.
\item For the localization $R=k[x]_{(x-2)}$ (rational functions defined at $x=2$), find the order $v_{x-2}(f)$ of $f=\dfrac{(x-2)^4(x+1)}{(x^2-4)}$ at $x=2$, give a uniformizer, and state the residue field $R/\fm$.
\item Let $\fm=(t)$ be the maximal ideal of a DVR $R$ with residue field $F$. Exhibit an explicit $F$-basis of the two-dimensional $F$-vector space $R/\fm^2$ when $R$ contains a field mapping isomorphically onto $F$ (e.g.\ $R=F[[t]]$), and explain why $R/\fm^2$ is a local ring that is not a domain.
\item In $Z_{(3)}$, list all ideals containing $(81)$, arrange them in their (totally ordered) chain, and for each quotient $\fm^i/\fm^{i+1}$ with $0\le i\le 3$ state its dimension over $F=\F_3$.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with valuation $v$ and let $x\in K$ satisfy $v(x)=-2$. Show $x\notin R$ but $x\in t^{-2}R$, find the least $N\ge0$ with $t^N x\in R$, and identify the fractional ideal $Rx$ as $\fm^{N'}$ for the appropriate $N'\inZ$.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with valuation $v$ and uniformizer $t$. Prove that an element $a\in R$ is irreducible if and only if $a$ is an associate of $t$, and deduce that $R$ has, up to associates, exactly one irreducible element. Conclude that $R$ is a UFD with this property and hence satisfies characterization (3) of a DVR.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with fraction field $K$. Prove that for any subring $S$ with $R\subseteq S\subseteq K$, either $S=R$ or $S=K$. [Show that if some $x\in S$ has $v(x)<0$ then $t^{-1}\in S$.] Conclude that $R$ is a maximal proper subring of $K$.
\item Let $v$ and $w$ be two discrete valuations on the same field $K$ having the same valuation ring $R$. Prove that $v=w$. [Compare uniformizers and use that every nonzero element is a unit times a power of a uniformizer.]
\item Let $R$ be a Noetherian local domain with principal maximal ideal $\fm=(t)\neq 0$, and suppose $R$ is not a field. Prove that $\bigcap_{n\ge1}\fm^n=0$ and deduce that every nonzero $x\in R$ has a well-defined largest $n$ with $x\in\fm^n$; use this to construct the valuation directly and prove $R$ is a DVR.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with fraction field $K$ and let $A\subseteq K$ be a nonzero fractional ideal. Prove that $A=t^N R$ for a unique $N\inZ$, that $A^{-1}=t^{-N}R$, and hence that the group of nonzero fractional ideals of $R$ under multiplication is infinite cyclic, generated by $\fm=(t)$ and isomorphic to $Z$ via $A\mapsto N$.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Commutative-diagram exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with uniformizer $t$. The nonzero ideals form the single descending chain below, with each quotient one-dimensional over $F=R/\fm$. Complete the diagram, label each downward edge with the codimension (the $F$-dimension of the corresponding quotient $\fm^i/\fm^{i+1}$), and prove $\len(R/\fm^n)=n$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=1.2em]
R \arrow[d,dash] \\
\fm=(t) \arrow[d,dash] \\
\fm^2=(t^2) \arrow[d,dash] \\
\vdots \arrow[d,dash] \\
\fm^n=(t^n)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Verify that the inclusions are strict and that $\bigcap_{n\ge0}\fm^n=0$.
\item Let $R$ be a Noetherian integrally closed domain and $\fp$ a minimal nonzero prime. The localization square below realizes the passage from the global domain to the local DVR. Prove the square commutes (horizontal maps are localization at $\fp$, vertical maps the inclusions $\fp\hookrightarrow R$ and $\fp R_\fp\hookrightarrow R_\fp$), and that $R_\fp$ is a DVR with maximal ideal $\fp R_\fp$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\fp \arrow[r] \arrow[d,hook] & \fp R_\fp \arrow[d,hook] \\
R \arrow[r,"\ell_\fp"'] & R_\fp
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the residue field $R_\fp/\fp R_\fp$ in terms of $\Frac(R/\fp)$, and explain why $\dim R_\fp=1$.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with fraction field $K$ and let $F$ denote the group of nonzero fractional ideals. The diagram exhibits the valuation as a group isomorphism. Complete it and prove every map shown is well-defined and that the square commutes (the left vertical map sends $x\mapsto Rx$, the right vertical map is the identity, the top map is $v$, the bottom map is $A\mapsto N$ where $A=t^N R$):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\units{K} \arrow[r,"v"] \arrow[d,"x\mapsto Rx"'] & Z \arrow[d,equal] \\
F \arrow[r,"A\mapsto N"'] & Z
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the kernel of $v:\units{K}\toZ$ as $\units{R}$, and conclude that $\units{K}/\units{R}\congZ\congF$.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with maximal ideal $\fm=(t)$ and residue field $F=R/\fm$. The diagram relates the quotient $R/\fm^2$ to its layers via the short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Complete it and prove the rows are exact, where $\pi$ is reduction mod $\fm$ and the left map is multiplication by $t$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & \fm/\fm^2 \arrow[r,hook] & R/\fm^2 \arrow[r,"\pi"] & R/\fm \arrow[r] & 0 \\
& F \arrow[u,"\cdot t","\cong"'] & & F \arrow[u,equal] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify both end terms with $F$, conclude $\len(R/\fm^2)=2$, and explain why the sequence does not split as $R$-modules unless $\fm^2=0$.
\end{exers}

\fm^2=(t^2) \arrow[d,dash] \\
\vdots \arrow[d,dash] \\
\fm^n=(t^n)
\end{tikzcd}

Prove the square commutes (horizontal maps are localization at $\fp$, vertical maps the inclusions $\fp\hookrightarrow R$ and $\fp R_\fp\hookrightarrow R_\fp$), and that $R_\fp$ is a DVR with maximal ideal $\fp R_\fp$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\fp \arrow[r] \arrow[d,hook] & \fp R_\fp \arrow[d,hook] \\
R \arrow[r,"\ell_\fp"'] & R_\fp
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the residue field $R_\fp/\fp R_\fp$ in terms of $\Frac(R/\fp)$, and explain why $\dim R_\fp=1$.

Complete it and prove every map shown is well-defined and that the square commutes (the left vertical map sends $x\mapsto Rx$, the right vertical map is the identity, the top map is $v$, the bottom map is $A\mapsto N$ where $A=t^N R$):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\units{K} \arrow[r,"v"] \arrow[d,"x\mapsto Rx"'] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[d,equal] \\
\mathcal{F} \arrow[r,"A\mapsto N"'] & \mathbb{Z}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify the kernel of $v:\units{K}\to\mathbb{Z}$ as $\units{R}$, and conclude that $\units{K}/\units{R}\cong\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathcal{F}$.
\item Let $R$ be a DVR with maximal ideal $\fm=(t)$ and residue field $F=R/\fm$. The diagram relates the quotient $R/\fm^2$ to its layers via the short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Complete it and prove the rows are exact, where $\pi$ is reduction mod $\fm$ and the left map is multiplication by $t$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & \fm/\fm^2 \arrow[r,hook] & R/\fm^2 \arrow[r,"\pi"] & R/\fm \arrow[r] & 0 \\
& F \arrow[u,"\cdot t","\cong"'] & & F \arrow[u,equal] &

Type: definition
Title: {fractional ideal}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{fractional ideal}]
A fractional ideal of $R$ is an $R$-submodule $A\subseteq K$ for which there is a nonzero $d\in R$ with $dA\subseteq R$. Equivalently, $A=d^{-1} I$ for some nonzero $d\in R$ and some (ordinary) ideal $I\subseteq R$. The ordinary ideals of $R$ are exactly the fractional ideals contained in $R$; to distinguish them we call them integral ideals. For $x\in K$ the cyclic module $Rx=\{rx:r\in R\}$ is the principal fractional ideal generated by $x$.
\end{definition}

Type: definition
Title: {product and inverse}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{product and inverse}]
If $A,B$ are fractional ideals their product $AB$ is the set of finite sums $\sum a_ib_i$ with $a_i\in A$, $b_i\in B$. If $A=d^{-1} I$ and $B=(d')^{-1} J$ then $AB=(dd')^{-1} IJ$, so $AB$ is again a fractional ideal. We call $A$ invertible if $AB=R$ for some fractional ideal $B$; such a $B$ is unique (if $AB=AC=R$ then $B=B(AC)=(BA)C=C$) and is written $A^{-1}$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {Prop.~9: the calculus of fractional ideals}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Prop.~9: the calculus of fractional ideals}]
Let $A$ be a fractional ideal of $R$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item A nonzero principal fractional ideal $A=xR$ is invertible, with $A^{-1}=x^{-1} R$.
\item If $A\ne0$ then $A'=(R:A)$ is a fractional ideal, $AA'\subseteq R$ always, and $AA'=R$ iff $A$ is invertible, in which case $A^{-1}=A'$.
\item An invertible fractional ideal is finitely generated.
\item The invertible fractional ideals form an abelian group under multiplication with identity $R$; the nonzero principal fractional ideals are a subgroup.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

If $AB=R$ then $B\subseteq A'$, whence $R=AB\subseteq AA'\subseteq R$, forcing $AA'=R$. Content:
Invertibility is closely tied to projectivity: a nonzero fractional ideal $A$ is invertible iff $A$ is projective as an $R$-module. Indeed from $\sum a_ia_i'=1$ one builds split maps $A\hookrightarrow R^n\twoheadrightarrow A$ exhibiting $A$ as a direct summand of a free module, and conversely a splitting produces dual elements $a_i'\in A'$ with $\sum a_ia_i'=1$. The bridge from local to global runs through the next fact.

\begin{proposition}[{Prop.~11: local invertibility detects a DVR}]
Let $R$ be a local domain, not a field. Then $R$ is a DVR iff every nonzero fractional ideal of $R$ is invertible.
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-8dc905aaf5c6da7912b6
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
If $R$ is a DVR with uniformizer $t$, every nonzero fractional ideal is $t^N R$ for some $N\inZ$, hence principal, hence invertible. Conversely, invertibility of ideals makes every ideal finitely generated (Prop.~9(3)), so $R$ is Noetherian; if $\fm$ is the maximal ideal then $\fm\ne\fm^2$ (else $\fm=0$ by Nakayama and $R$ is a field), so pick $t\in\fm\setminus\fm^2$. Then $t\fm^{-1}$ is an integral ideal; it cannot lie in $\fm$ (that would give $t\in\fm^2$), so $t\fm^{-1}=R$, i.e.\ $(t)=\fm$. A Noetherian local domain with principal maximal ideal is a DVR.
\end{proof}

Title: The standard fractional ideal $\tfrac12Z$ of $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The standard fractional ideal $\tfrac12Z$ of $Z$}
Exhibit $A=\tfrac12Z$ as a fractional ideal of $Z$ and compute $A'$ and $AA'$.
\wrec A fractional ideal of $Z$ is $d^{-1} I$ for an integer $d$ and ideal $I=(n)$; the inverse of a principal fractional ideal $xR$ is $x^{-1} R$.
\wsol Take $d=2$, $I=(1)=Z$: then $A=2^{-1}Z=\tfrac12Z$ is an $R$-submodule of $Q$ with $2A=Z\subseteqZ$, so it is fractional. It is principal, $A=(\tfrac12)Z$, so $A'=A^{-1}=2Z$ and $AA'=(\tfrac12\cdot2)Z=Z=R$. Sanity check: $A$ is invertible because every nonzero fractional ideal of the PID $Z$ is principal; here $A^{-1}=2Z$ and indeed $\tfrac12Z\cdot 2Z=Z$.
\end{wex}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Dedekind Domains > Fractional ideals and invertibility
Type: example
Title: A non-invertible fractional ideal in a non-normal ring
Content:
\begin{wex}{A non-invertible fractional ideal in a non-normal ring}
In $R=k[t^2,t^3]\subseteq k[t]$ (the cusp ring) let $\fm=(t^2,t^3)$. Show $\fm$ is not invertible.
\wrec For an integral ideal, $\fm$ invertible $\Rightarrow$ $\fm\fm'=R$; one tests whether $\fm'=(R:\fm)$ is large enough to recover $R$.
\wsol Here $K=k(t)$ and $\fm'=(R:\fm)=\{x\in K:x\fm\subseteq R\}$. The element $t=t^3/t^2$ satisfies $t\cdot t^2=t^3\in R$ and $t\cdot t^3=t^4=(t^2)^2\in R$, so $t\in\fm'$; thus $R[t]\subseteq\fm'$ and in fact $\fm'=k[t]$. Then $\fm\fm'=(t^2,t^3)k[t]=(t^2)k[t]=t^2k[t]$, which contains $t^2,t^3,t^4,\dots$ but not $1$, so $\fm\fm'\ne R$ and $\fm$ is not invertible. Sanity check: $R$ is not integrally closed ($t$ is integral over $R$ but $t\notin R$), so $R$ is not a Dedekind domain, and Theorem~15 below predicts that some ideal fails to be invertible -- exactly what we found.
\end{wex}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Dedekind Domains > Fractional ideals and invertibility
Type: example
Title: The inverse of $(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The inverse of $(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
In $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ let $\fp=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$. Verify $\fp$ is invertible by computing $\fp\fp'$.
\wrec In a Dedekind domain every nonzero ideal is invertible; one verifies it by producing $A'$ with $AA'=R$. Here $\fp'$ should be $\tfrac12\fp$ (the conjugate scaled).
\wsol Compute $\fp^2=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})^2$, generated by $4$, $2(1+\sqrt{-5})$, and $(1+\sqrt{-5})^2=-4+2\sqrt{-5}$. Each lies in $(2)$, so $\fp^2\subseteq(2)$. Conversely $\fp^2$ contains $4$ and $-4+2\sqrt{-5}$, hence their sum $2\sqrt{-5}$; and it contains $2(1+\sqrt{-5})=2+2\sqrt{-5}$, so $(2+2\sqrt{-5})-2\sqrt{-5}=2\in\fp^2$, giving $(2)\subseteq\fp^2$. Hence $\fp^2=(2)$, the statement that the prime $2$ is ramified with $N(\fp)=\abs{R/\fp}=2$. From $\fp^2=(2)$ we get $\fp\cdot\bigl(\tfrac12\fp\bigr)=\tfrac12\fp^2=\tfrac12(2)=R$, so $\fp$ is invertible with $\fp^{-1}=\tfrac12\fp$. Sanity check: $\fp$ is not principal (no element of $R$ has norm $2$, since $a^2+5b^2=2$ is insoluble), yet it is invertible -- the hallmark of a Dedekind domain that is not a PID, and the source of a nontrivial class group.
\end{wex}

Title: {Dedekind domain}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{Dedekind domain}]
A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian, integrally closed integral domain of Krull dimension $1$. Equivalently: $R$ is a Noetherian, integrally closed domain, not a field, in which every nonzero prime ideal is maximal.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}[Idea]
A PID is Noetherian, is integrally closed (being a UFD), and has every nonzero prime maximal. Type: theorem
Title: {Thm.~15 / A\&M Thm.~9.8: equivalent characterizations}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Thm.~15 / A\&M Thm.~9.8: equivalent characterizations}]
For an integral domain $R$ with fraction field $K\ne R$, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $R$ is Noetherian, integrally closed, and every nonzero prime is maximal \textup{(i.e.\ a Dedekind domain)}.
\item $R$ is Noetherian and for each nonzero prime $P$ the localization $R_P$ is a DVR.
\item Every nonzero fractional ideal of $R$ is invertible.
\item Every nonzero fractional ideal of $R$ is a projective $R$-module.
\item Every nonzero proper ideal $I$ factors as a product of prime ideals $I=P_1P_2\cdots P_n$; moreover the multiset $\{P_1,\dots,P_n\}$ is uniquely determined, so $I$ is uniquely a product of prime powers.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-6f41193bdf4c7ee4451c
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1)$\Rightarrow$(2): localizing preserves Noetherian, integrally closed, and dimension $1$, so $R_P$ is a local Noetherian integrally closed domain of dimension $1$, i.e.\ a DVR. (2)$\Rightarrow$(1): integral closure and "primes are maximal" are local properties, and a domain that is locally a DVR is integrally closed of dimension $1$. (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(3): invertibility $AA'=R$ is a local statement, $(AA')_P=A_P(A_P)'$; each $R_P$ being a DVR makes $A_P$ invertible (Prop.~11), so $AA'=R$ globally. Conversely invertible fractional ideals make $R$ Noetherian and each $R_P$ a local ring with all fractional ideals invertible, hence a DVR (Prop.~11). (3)$\Leftrightarrow$(4) is the projective $=$ invertible dictionary (the paragraph after Prop.~9). (1)$\Rightarrow$(5): a minimal primary decomposition $I=Q_1\cap\cdots\cap Q_n$ has pairwise comaximal radicals (primes are maximal), so $\bigcap Q_i=\prod Q_i$, and each $P$-primary $Q_i$ is a prime power $P_i^{m_i}$ because $R_{P_i}$ is a DVR. (5)$\Rightarrow$(3): one shows invertible primes are maximal and that the factorization forces every nonzero prime to be invertible, whence every ideal -- and then every fractional ideal -- is invertible. Uniqueness in (5) is the cancellation argument: in $P_1\cdots P_n=P_1'\cdots P_m'$ a minimal $P_1'$ contains some $P_i$, which in turn contains some $P_j'$; minimality of $P_1'$ forces $P_j'=P_i=P_1'$, allowing cancellation of the invertible $P_1'$.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{remark}
The logic of (5)$\Rightarrow$(3) is purely multiplicative and reverses the historical order. Dedekind defined his domains by property (5) -- unique factorization of ideals -- precisely to repair the failure of unique factorization of elements in rings of integers (Section 8.3). It was Noether who recognized the structural characterization (1). The two viewpoints, "ideals factor" and "Noetherian $+$ integrally closed $+$ dimension $1$," are the same world seen from arithmetic and from geometry respectively.
\end{remark}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[{Cor.~16: unique factorization in $\mathcal O_K$}]
If $\mathcal O_K$ is the ring of integers of a number field $K$ then every nonzero ideal $I$ factors uniquely as $I=P_1^{e_1}\cdots P_n^{e_n}$ with distinct primes $P_i$ and $e_i\ge1$.
\end{corollary}

Title: $Z$ as a Dedekind domain, all five conditions at once
Content:
\begin{wex}{$Z$ as a Dedekind domain, all five conditions at once}
Check that $Z$ satisfies each clause of Theorem~15 directly.
\wrec $Z$ is a PID, hence Dedekind; the five conditions should each be visible from elementary number theory.
\wsol (1) $Z$ is Noetherian, integrally closed (UFD), and its nonzero primes $(p)$ are maximal. (2) $Z_{(p)}$ is the DVR of $p$-adic valuation. (3) every fractional ideal is $\tfrac{a}{b}Z$, invertible with inverse $\tfrac{b}{a}Z$. (4) it is principal, hence free of rank $1$, hence projective. (5) $(n)=\prod(p_i)^{e_i}$ from $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$. Sanity check: the prime factorization of the integer $n$ and the prime-ideal factorization of $(n)$ literally coincide because $Z$ is a PID -- the class group is trivial.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Factoring an ideal in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Factoring an ideal in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Factor the ideal $(6)$ in $\mathcal O_K=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ into primes.
\wrec In a Dedekind domain $(6)=(2)(3)$ and each $(p)$ factors according to how $p$ splits; use norms to identify primes.
\wsol Set $\fp_2=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$, $\fp_3=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})$, $\fp_3'=(3,1-\sqrt{-5})$. One checks $(2)=\fp_2^2$ (ramified), $(3)=\fp_3\fp_3'$ (split). Hence
\[
(6)=(2)(3)=\fp_2^2\,\fp_3\,\fp_3'.
\]
Sanity check: this restores arithmetic to the famous failure $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ of unique factorization of elements: at the level of ideals, $(2)=\fp_2^2$, $(3)=\fp_3\fp_3'$, $(1+\sqrt{-5})=\fp_2\fp_3$, $(1-\sqrt{-5})=\fp_2\fp_3'$, and both decompositions of $(6)$ regroup the same four prime factors $\fp_2^2\fp_3\fp_3'$.
\end{wex}

Title: A nonzero prime that is maximal but not principal
Content:
\begin{wex}{A nonzero prime that is maximal but not principal}
Show $\fp_3=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})$ in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is maximal yet not principal.
\wrec Dimension $1$ forces every nonzero prime maximal; non-principality is detected by the norm ($N(\fp_3)=3$) against the absence of elements of norm $3$.
\wsol The quotient $\mathcal O_K/\fp_3\cong\F_3$ is a field, so $\fp_3$ is maximal. If $\fp_3=(\alpha)$ then $N(\alpha)=\abs{\mathcal O_K/\fp_3}=3$, i.e.\ $a^2+5b^2=3$ for integers $a,b$, which is impossible. Hence $\fp_3$ is not principal. Sanity check: consistent with dimension $1$ ($\fp_3$ is maximal) and with a nontrivial class group (a nonprincipal yet invertible prime), exactly as Theorem~15 allows.
\end{wex}

Title: Coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve is Dedekind
Content:
\begin{wex}{Coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve is Dedekind}
Let $C$ be a nonsingular irreducible affine curve over an algebraically closed field $k$. Show $k[C]$ is a Dedekind domain.
\wrec Use criterion (2): $k[C]$ is Noetherian of dimension $1$, and smoothness says each local ring $\mathcal O_{v,C}$ is a DVR.
\wsol $k[C]$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra and a domain, hence Noetherian; its dimension equals the transcendence degree of $k(C)$ over $k$, namely $1$. Smoothness at $v$ means $\dim_k(\fm_v/\fm_v^2)=1$, which for the Noetherian local ring $\mathcal O_{v,C}$ of dimension $1$ is exactly the DVR condition. So every localization at a closed point is a DVR; by (2), $k[C]$ is Dedekind. Sanity check: equivalently, $C$ is smooth iff $k[C]$ is integrally closed (normal), recovering criterion (1) -- "smooth curve $=$ normal one-dimensional ring."
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ is not Dedekind
Content:
\begin{wex}{$k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ is not Dedekind}
Show the cuspidal cubic coordinate ring $R=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ fails to be Dedekind.
\wrec A Dedekind domain is integrally closed; the cusp is a singular point, so normality fails.
\wsol Writing $t=y/x$ in the fraction field, $t^2=y^2/x^2=x^3/x^2=x$ and $t^3=tx=y$, so $t$ is integral over $R$ ($t^2-x=0$) but $t\notin R$. Thus $R$ is not integrally closed and not Dedekind; its integral closure is $k[t]$, the coordinate ring of the smooth normalization $\Aff^1$. Sanity check: this matches Worked Example~16.3.6 above, where $\fm=(x,y)$ was a non-invertible ideal -- non-invertibility of some ideal is exactly the failure of Theorem~15(3) caused by the singular point.
\end{wex}

Type: corollary
Title: {Cor.~9.9 / Exercise 6: the group of ideals is free}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{Cor.~9.9 / Exercise 6: the group of ideals is free}]
Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain. The nonzero fractional ideals form an abelian group $I(R)$ under multiplication. Every nonzero fractional ideal is uniquely $\prod_P P^{a_P}$ over the nonzero primes $P$, with $a_P\inZ$ and almost all $a_P=0$. Hence $I(R)$ is the free abelian group on the set of nonzero prime ideals.
\end{corollary}

Type: definition
Title: {ideal class group}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{ideal class group}]
The ideal class group of the Dedekind domain $R$ is the quotient
\[
\operatorname{Cl}(R)=I(R)/P(R).
\]
Its order $h_R=\abs{\operatorname{Cl}(R)}$ (when finite) is the class number. There is an exact sequence
\[
1\longrightarrow \units{R}\longrightarrow K^\times \xrightarrow{\ x\mapsto(x)\ } I(R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Cl}(R)\longrightarrow 1,
\]
identifying the kernel of $K^\times\to I(R)$ with the unit group $\units{R}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[{Cor.~20: $\operatorname{Cl}$ measures failure of UFD}]

Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
PID $\Leftrightarrow$ every ideal principal $\Leftrightarrow$ $P(R)=I(R)$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $\operatorname{Cl}(R)=1$. PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD always. For the converse, in a UFD a prime ideal $P$ contains an irreducible $a'$, and $P=(a')$ because $(a')$ is already a nonzero prime; since every ideal factors into primes, every ideal is principal.
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
For Dedekind domains arising in number theory the class group is a finite group: $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ is finite, its order $h_K$ being a central arithmetic invariant. The unit group is finitely generated by Dirichlet: $\units{\mathcal O_K}\cong\mu_K\timesZ^{r_1+r_2-1}$, where $r_1,r_2$ count real and complex-conjugate-pair embeddings. For general Dedekind domains finiteness can fail spectacularly: every abelian group $A$ (finite or infinite) is the class group of some Dedekind domain.
\end{remark}

Title: The class number of $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is $2$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The class number of $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is $2$}
Show $\operatorname{Cl}(Z[\sqrt{-5}])\congZ/(2)Z$ using the primes computed above.
\wrec Each ideal class is represented by an integral ideal of small norm; $\fp_2,\fp_3,\fp_3'$ are non-principal, and one checks the products that become principal.
\wsol The nonprincipal primes $\fp_2,\fp_3,\fp_3'$ all lie in one nontrivial class: $\fp_2\fp_3=(1+\sqrt{-5})$ and $\fp_2\fp_3'=(1-\sqrt{-5})$ are principal, so $[\fp_3]=[\fp_3']=[\fp_2]^{-1}=[\fp_2]$ (as $\fp_2^2=(2)$ is principal, $[\fp_2]$ has order $2$). Thus the class group is generated by $[\fp_2]$ with $[\fp_2]^2=1$, giving $\operatorname{Cl}\congZ/(2)Z$. Sanity check: $h=2\ne1$ certifies $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD, in exact agreement with $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ being two genuinely different element-factorizations.
\end{wex}

Title: Units of $Z[i]$ and the trivial class group
Content:
\begin{wex}{Units of $Z[i]$ and the trivial class group}
Identify $\units{Z[i]}$ and explain why $\operatorname{Cl}(Z[i])=1$.
\wrec $Z[i]$ is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID, hence a Dedekind domain with trivial class group; units are the elements of norm $1$.
\wsol $u\in\units{Z[i]}\Leftrightarrow N(u)=a^2+b^2=1\Leftrightarrow u\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}=\mu_4$. As a PID, $\operatorname{Cl}(Z[i])=1$ and $h=1$. Sanity check: here $K=Q(i)$ has $r_1=0$, $r_2=1$, so the Dirichlet rank is $r_1+r_2-1=0$ and $\units{Z[i]}$ is purely torsion -- exactly the $4$ roots of unity found.
\end{wex}

Title: Units of $Z[\sqrt2]$ are infinite, class number still $1$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Units of $Z[\sqrt2]$ are infinite, class number still $1$}
Describe $\units{Z[\sqrt2]}$ and its class group.
\wrec $Q(\sqrt2)$ is real quadratic; $Z[\sqrt2]$ is a PID (Euclidean), so $h=1$, but the unit group has positive rank.
\wsol $Z[\sqrt2]$ is Euclidean for the norm, so it is a PID and $\operatorname{Cl}=1$. The fundamental unit is $1+\sqrt2$ (norm $(1)^2-2(1)^2=-1$), and $\units{Z[\sqrt2]}=\{\pm(1+\sqrt2)^n:n\inZ\}\cong\{\pm1\}\timesZ$. \end{wex}

Title: Reading the exact sequence for $Z$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Reading the exact sequence for $Z$}
Interpret $1\to\units R\to K^\times\to I(R)\to\operatorname{Cl}(R)\to1$ for $R=Z$.
\wrec The maps are $\unitsZ\hookrightarrowQ^\times\to I(Z)\to\operatorname{Cl}(Z)$; identify each term.
\wsol $\unitsZ=\{\pm1\}$; $Q^\times\to I(Z)$ sends $x=\pm\prod p^{a_p}$ to the fractional ideal $\prod (p)^{a_p}$, with kernel $\{\pm1\}$; $I(Z)$ is free abelian on $\{(p)\}$; and $\operatorname{Cl}(Z)=1$ since $Z$ is a PID. Sanity check: the sequence collapses to $1\to\{\pm1\}\toQ^\times\to I(Z)\to1$, the statement that a positive rational is uniquely $\prod p^{a_p}$ -- the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, recast multiplicatively.
\end{wex}

Type: definition
Title: {divides}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{divides}]
For ideals $A,B$ of a domain $R$, say $B$ divides $A$ (written $B\mid A$) if $A=BC$ for some ideal $C$. Then $B\mid A\Rightarrow A\subseteq B$ always; in a Dedekind domain the converse holds: $A\subseteq B$ gives $C=AB^{-1}\subseteq BB^{-1}=R$, an integral ideal with $BC=A$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {Prop.~18: Chinese Remainder Theorem}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Prop.~18: Chinese Remainder Theorem}]
Let $R$ be Dedekind, $P_1,\dots,P_n$ distinct nonzero primes, $a_i\ge0$. Then
\[
R/(P_1^{a_1}\cdots P_n^{a_n})\ \cong\ R/P_1^{a_1}\times\cdots\times R/P_n^{a_n}.
\]
Equivalently, given $r_1,\dots,r_n\in R$ there is $r\in R$, unique modulo $P_1^{a_1}\cdots P_n^{a_n}$, with $r\equiv r_i\pmod{P_i^{a_i}}$ for each $i$.
\end{proposition}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[{Cor.~19: approximation and two-generation}]
Let $R$ be Dedekind, $I$ a nonzero ideal.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item There is an ideal $J$ coprime to $I$ with $IJ=(a)$ principal; $J$ lies in the inverse class $[I]^{-1}$.
\item Every ideal of $R/I$ is principal; equivalently, if $I_1\supseteq I$ then $I_1=I+Rb$ for some $b$.
\item Every ideal is generated by two elements: if $0\ne a\in I$ then $I=Ra+Rb$ for some $b\in I$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{wex}{CRT in $Z$ recovered}
Specialize Proposition~18 to $R=Z$ with $P_i=(p_i)$.
\wrec $Z$ is Dedekind; distinct primes $(p_i)$ are comaximal, so CRT for ideals is ordinary CRT for integers.
\wsol With $m=\prod p_i^{a_i}$, $Z/mZ\cong\prod_iZ/p_i^{a_i}Z$, the classical statement. Solving $x\equiv r_i\pmod{p_i^{a_i}}$ has a unique solution mod $m$. Sanity check: e.g.\ $Z/12Z\congZ/4Z\timesZ/3Z$ from $12=2^2\cdot3$, and $\abs{Z/12Z}=12=4\cdot3$ matches.

Type: example
Title: gcd of two ideals in $Z[i]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{gcd of two ideals in $Z[i]$}
Compute $(3+i)+(1+3i)$ and $(3+i)\cap(1+3i)$ in $Z[i]$ via factorization.
\wrec In the Dedekind (in fact principal) domain $Z[i]$, sum $=\gcd$ and intersection $=\operatorname{lcm}$, read off prime factorizations.
\wsol Norms: $N(3+i)=10=2\cdot5$, $N(1+3i)=10$. With $\pi_2=(1+i)$ ($N=2$) and the split primes over $5$, $\pi_5=(2+i),\bar\pi_5=(2-i)$, one finds $(3+i)=\pi_2\,(2-i)$ up to units and $(1+3i)=\pi_2\,(2+i)$. So $\gcd=(3+i)+(1+3i)=\pi_2=(1+i)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}=(3+i)\cap(1+3i)=\pi_2(2+i)(2-i)=(1+i)(5)=(5+5i)$ up to units. Sanity check: norms multiply correctly, $N(\gcd)\cdot N(\operatorname{lcm})=2\cdot 50=100=N(3+i)N(1+3i)=10\cdot10$, the ideal analogue of $\gcd\cdot\operatorname{lcm}=$ product.
\end{wex}
