Title: {Prop.~21: ideals as modules and the Steinitz class}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Prop.~21: ideals as modules and the Steinitz class}]
Let $R$ be Dedekind with fraction field $K$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For fractional ideals $I,J$: $I\cong J$ as $R$-modules iff $I=(a)J$ for some $a\in K^\times$, i.e.\ iff $[I]=[J]$ in $\operatorname{Cl}(R)$.
\item For nonzero fractional ideals, $I_1\oplus\cdots\oplus I_n\cong J_1\oplus\cdots\oplus J_m$ iff $n=m$ and $[I_1\cdots I_n]=[J_1\cdots J_m]$.
\item In particular $I_1\oplus\cdots\oplus I_n\cong R^{n-1}\oplus(I_1\cdots I_n)$, and $R^n\oplus I\cong R^n\oplus J\iff [I]=[J]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Relation: proof_of=unit-23427b7df044adefb256
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
(1) multiplication by $a$ is an isomorphism $J\to(a)J$; conversely an $R$-isomorphism $\varphi:I\to J$ is multiplication by the constant $c=\varphi(x)/x\in K^\times$ (since $x\varphi(y)=y\varphi(x)$), so $J=cI$, i.e.\ $I=(c^{-1})J$. The key reduction in (3) is the splitting $I\oplus J\cong R\oplus IJ$: replacing $I,J$ by coprime integral representatives, the sum map $I\oplus J\to I+J=R$ has kernel $I\cap J=IJ$, giving a short exact sequence $0\to IJ\to I\oplus J\to R\to0$ that splits because $R$ is free. Iterating gives (3); (2) follows by tracking the product class via a determinant.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: {Thm.~22: structure of f.g.\ modules over a Dedekind domain}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Thm.~22: structure of f.g.\ modules over a Dedekind domain}]
Let $M$ be a finitely generated module over the Dedekind domain $R$, of rank $n$, with torsion submodule $\Tor(M)$. Then
\[
M\ \cong\ R^{\,n-1}\oplus I\ \oplus\ \Tor(M)
\quad(when n=0 the free-and-Steinitz part is absent and M\cong\Tor(M)),
\]
for some nonzero ideal $I$, and
\[
\Tor(M)\ \cong\ R/P_1^{e_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus R/P_s^{e_s}
\]
for prime powers $P_i^{e_i}$. The prime powers $P_i^{e_i}$ are unique (the elementary divisors), and $I$ is unique up to its class $[I]\in\operatorname{Cl}(R)$ (the Steinitz class).
\end{theorem}

Type: proof
Title: Idea
Relation: proof_of=unit-04567a163e34ed4b6a93
Content:
\begin{proof}[Idea]
A finitely generated torsion-free $M$ embeds in $M\otimes_R K\cong K^n$; projecting to a last coordinate gives $0\to\ker\to M\to I_1\to0$ with $I_1$ a nonzero ideal, which splits because $I_1$ is projective (Theorem~15(4)). Induction yields $M\cong I_1\oplus\cdots\oplus I_n$, and Prop.~21(3) collapses this to $R^{n-1}\oplus(I_1\cdots I_n)$. For general $M$ the sequence $0\to\Tor(M)\to M\to M/\Tor(M)\to0$ splits (the quotient is torsion-free, hence projective). The torsion part is handled prime by prime: $\Tor(M)\cong\bigoplus N/P_i^{e_i}N$, and each piece, being a module over the DVR $R_{P_i}$, decomposes by the PID structure theorem.
\end{proof}

Content:
\begin{corollary}[{Cor.~23: projective $=$ torsion-free}]
A finitely generated module over a Dedekind domain is projective iff it is torsion-free. Moreover the class number is $1$ iff every finitely generated projective $R$-module is free.
\end{corollary}

\begin{wex}{A PID that is not a field is a Dedekind domain of class number $1$}
Show Theorem~22 reduces to the PID structure theorem when $\operatorname{Cl}(R)=1$.
\wrec If $h_R=1$ every ideal $I$ is principal, hence $I\cong R$ as a module, so the Steinitz class drops out.
\wsol When $\operatorname{Cl}(R)=1$, $[I]=[R]$ forces $I\cong R$, so $R^{n-1}\oplus I\cong R^n$ and $M\cong R^n\oplus\bigoplus R/P_i^{e_i}$ -- the elementary-divisor form of the PID theorem. Sanity check: for $R=Z$, $P_i=(p_i)$, this is $M\congZ^n\oplus\bigoplusZ/p_i^{e_i}Z$, the classification of finitely generated abelian groups.
\end{wex}

Title: A rank-one nonfree projective module
Content:
\begin{wex}{A rank-one nonfree projective module}
Exhibit a finitely generated projective module over $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ that is not free.
\wrec By Cor.~23, projective $=$ torsion-free; a non-principal ideal is torsion-free (projective) but not $\cong R$ (not free) when its class is nontrivial.
\wsol Take $M=\fp_2=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$. As a fractional ideal it is invertible, hence projective; it has rank $1$. It is not free: free of rank $1$ would mean $\fp_2\cong R$, i.e.\ $\fp_2$ principal, which it is not. Sanity check: $[\fp_2]\ne1$ in $\operatorname{Cl}(Z[\sqrt{-5}])\congZ/(2)Z$, so by the last clause of Cor.~23 not every projective is free, consistent with $h=2\ne1$.
\end{wex}

Title: Steinitz class detects a non-split direct sum
Content:
\begin{wex}{Steinitz class detects a non-split direct sum}
Decide whether $\fp_2\oplus\fp_2\cong R\oplus R$ over $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$.
\wrec Use Prop.~21(2)/(3): $\fp_2\oplus\fp_2\cong R\oplus\fp_2^2$, and $\fp_2^2=(2)$ is principal.
\wsol $\fp_2\oplus\fp_2\cong R\oplus(\fp_2\cdot\fp_2)=R\oplus\fp_2^2=R\oplus(2)\cong R\oplus R$, since $(2)\cong R$ as a module. So yes, $\fp_2\oplus\fp_2\cong R^2$. Sanity check: the Steinitz class is $[\fp_2^2]=[\fp_2]^2=1$ in $Z/(2)Z$, so the rank-$2$ projective is free even though each summand $\fp_2$ is not -- the class group is where the obstruction lives, and it vanishes after squaring.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Torsion module over a Dedekind domain}
Classify $M=R/\fp_2^3\oplus R/\fp_3$ as in Theorem~22 over $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$.
\wrec This is already in elementary-divisor form: the prime powers are $\fp_2^3$ and $\fp_3^1$, the module is pure torsion (rank $0$).

Sanity check: the two primes are distinct, so by CRT (Prop.~18) the summands are coprime and combine into the cyclic module $M\cong R/\fp_2^3\fp_3$ (the invariant-factor form); the elementary divisors $\{\fp_2^3,\fp_3\}$ are the unique invariants.
\end{wex}

Title: Quotient $R/I$ is Artinian
Content:
\begin{wex}{Quotient $R/I$ is Artinian}
Show that for a nonzero ideal $I$ of a Dedekind domain $R$, the ring $R/I$ is Artinian.
\wrec $R$ is Noetherian of dimension $1$; modding out a nonzero ideal kills the dimension, and Noetherian $+$ dimension $0$ $=$ Artinian.
\wsol Write $I=\prod P_i^{e_i}$. By CRT $R/I\cong\prod R/P_i^{e_i}$, and each $R/P_i^{e_i}\cong R_{P_i}/P_i^{e_i}R_{P_i}$ is a quotient of a DVR by a power of its maximal ideal, hence a local Artinian ring (a finite-length module over itself). A finite product of Artinian rings is Artinian. Sanity check: $R/I$ is Noetherian (quotient of Noetherian) with every prime maximal (dimension $0$), and Noetherian $+$ dimension $0$ is exactly Artinian -- the Akizuki--Hopkins criterion, tying back to Section 16.1.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: Localizing a Dedekind domain stays Dedekind
Content:
\begin{wex}{Localizing a Dedekind domain stays Dedekind}
If $R$ is Dedekind and $S\subseteq R$ is multiplicatively closed with $0\notin S$, show $S^{-1} R$ is Dedekind or a field.
\wrec Localization preserves Noetherian, integral closure, and can only lower dimension; the primes of $S^{-1} R$ are those of $R$ missing $S$.
\wsol $S^{-1} R$ is Noetherian (localization of Noetherian), integrally closed (integral closure commutes with localization), and a domain with fraction field $K$. Its nonzero primes correspond to nonzero primes of $R$ disjoint from $S$, each still maximal; so $\dim S^{-1} R\le1$. If some nonzero prime survives, $S^{-1} R$ is Dedekind; if all nonzero primes meet $S$, then $S^{-1} R=K$, a field. Sanity check: taking $S=R\setminus P$ recovers the localization $R_P$, which is a DVR -- a local Dedekind domain -- exactly criterion (2) of Theorem~15. The induced map on ideals $I(R)\to I(S^{-1} R)$ is the surjection sending the killed primes to $1$, so $\operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1} R)$ is a quotient of $\operatorname{Cl}(R)$.
\end{wex}

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 1/2
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).}
\item If $R$ is an integral domain, show that every fractional ideal of $R$ is invertible if and only if every integral ideal of $R$ is invertible.

\item Suppose $R$ is an integral domain with fraction field $K$ and $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ are fractional ideals of $R$ whose product is a nonzero principal fractional ideal: $A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n = Rx$ for some $0 \neq x \in K$. For each $i = 1, \ldots, n$ prove that $A_i$ is an invertible fractional ideal with inverse $(x^{-1}) A_1 \cdots A_{i-1} A_{i+1} \cdots A_n$.

\item Suppose $R$ is an integral domain with fraction field $K$ and $P$ is a nonzero prime ideal in $R$. Show that the fractional ideals of $R_P$ in $K$ are the $R_P$-modules of the form $A R_P$ where $A$ is a fractional ideal of $R$.

\item Suppose $R$ is an integral domain with fraction field $K$ and $A$ is a fractional ideal of $R$ in $K$. Let $A' = \{x \in K \mid xA \subseteq R\}$ as in Proposition 9.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For any prime ideal $P$ in $R$ prove that the localization $(A')_P$ of $A'$ at $P$ is a fractional ideal of $R_P$ in $K$.
\item[(b)] If $A$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, prove that $(A')_P = (A_P)'$ where $(A_P)'$ is the fractional $R_P$ ideal $\{x \in K \mid x A_P \subseteq R_P\}$ corresponding to the localization $A_P$.
\end{enumerate}

\item If $Q_1$ is a $P_1$-primary ideal and $Q_2$ is a $P_2$-primary ideal where $P_1$ and $P_2$ are comaximal ideals in a Noetherian ring $R$, prove that $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are also comaximal. [Use Proposition 14 in Section 15.2.]

\item Suppose $R$ is a Dedekind Domain with fraction field $K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that every nonzero fractional ideal of $R$ in $K$ can be written uniquely as the product of distinct prime powers $P_1^{a_1} \cdots P_n^{a_n}$ where the $a_i$ are nonzero integers, possibly negative.

Title: Exercises (Dummit \& Foote).
Part: 2/2
Content:
Explicitly exhibit $I$ as a direct summand of a free $R$-module to show that $I$ is projective. [Consider $I \oplus I^{-1}$ and use Proposition 21.]

\item Suppose $I$ and $J$ are two nonzero fractional ideals in the Dedekind Domain $R$ and that $I^n = J^n$ for some $n \neq 0$. Prove that $I = J$.

\item Suppose $K$ is an algebraic number field and $O_K$ is the ring of integers in $K$. If $P$ is a nonzero prime ideal in $O_K$ prove that $P = (p, \pi)$ for some prime $p \in Z$ and algebraic integer $\pi \in O_K$.

\item Suppose $K = Q(\sqrt{D})$ is a quadratic extension of $Q$ where $D$ is a square free integer and $O_K$ is the ring of integers in $K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $|O_K/(p)| = p^2$. [Observe that $O_K \cong Z^2$ as an abelian group.]
\item[(b)] Use Corollary 16 to show that there are 3 possibilities for the prime ideal factorization of $(p)$ in $O_K$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(p) = P$ is a prime ideal with $|O_K/P| = p^2$,
\item[(ii)] $(p) = P_1 P_2$ with distinct prime ideals $P_1, P_2$ and $|O_K/P_1| = |O_K/P_2| = p$,
\item[(iii)] $(p) = P^2$ for some prime ideal $P$ with $|O_K/P| = p$.
\end{enumerate}
(In cases (i), (ii), and (iii) the prime $p$ is said to be inert, split, or ramified in $O_K$, respectively. The set of ramified primes is finite: the primes $p$ dividing $D$ if $D \equiv 1, 2 \bmod 4$; $p = 2$ and the primes $p$ dividing $D$ if $D \equiv 3 \bmod 4$. Cf. Exercise 31 in Section 15.5.)
\item[(c)] Determine the prime ideal factorizations of the primes $p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11$ in the ring of integers $O_K = Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ of $K = Q(\sqrt{-5})$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $O$ be the ring of integers in the algebraic closure $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that the infinite sequence of ideals in $O$, $(2) \subseteq (\sqrt{2}) \subseteq (\sqrt[4]{2}) \subseteq (\sqrt[8]{2}) \subseteq \cdots$, is strictly increasing, and so $O$ is not Noetherian.
\item[(b)] Show that $O$ has Krull dimension 1. [Use Theorem 26 in Section 15.3.]
\item[(c)] Let $K$ be a number field and let $I$ be any ideal in $O_K$. Show that there is some finite extension $L$ of $K$ such that $I$ becomes principal when extended to $O_L$, i.e., the ideal $I O_L$ is principal (where $L$ depends on $I$)---you may use the theorem that the class group of $K$ is a finite group. [cf. Exercise 20.]
\item[(d)] Prove that $O$ is a Bezout Domain (cf. Section 8.1).
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $F$ and $K$ are algebraic number fields with $Q \subseteq F \subseteq K$, with rings of integers $O_F$ and $O_K$, respectively. Since $O_F \subseteq O_K$, the ring $O_K$ is naturally a module over $O_F$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove $O_K$ is a torsion free $O_F$-module of rank $n = [K : F]$. [Compute ranks over $Z$.] If $O_K$ is free over $O_F$ then $O_K$ is said to have a relative integral basis over $O_F$.
\item[(b)] Prove that if $F$ has class number 1 then $O_K$ has a relative integral basis over $O_F$. If $K = Q(\sqrt{-5}, \sqrt{2})$ then the ring of integers $O_K$ is given by $O_K = Z + Z\sqrt{-5} + Z\sqrt{-10} + Z\omega$ where $\omega = (\sqrt{-10} + \sqrt{2})/2$.
\item[(c)] If $F_1 = Q(\sqrt{2})$ prove that $O_K$ has a relative integral basis over $O_{F_1}$ and find an explicit basis $\{\alpha, \beta\}$: $O_K = O_{F_1} \cdot \alpha + O_{F_1} \cdot \beta$.
\item[(d)] If $F_2 = Q(\sqrt{-5})$, show that $P_3 = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5}) = (3, 5 + \sqrt{-5})$ is a prime ideal of $O_{F_2}$ that is not principal and that $O_K = O_{F_2} \cdot 1 + (1/3) P_3 \cdot \omega$. [Check that $\sqrt{-10} = (5 + \sqrt{-5})\omega/3$.] Conclude that the Steinitz class of $O_K$ as a module over $O_{F_2}$ is the nontrivial class of $P_3$ in the class group of $O_{F_2}$ and so there is no relative integral basis of $O_K$ over $O_{F_2}$.
\item[(e)] Determine whether $O_K$ has a relative integral basis over the ring of integers of the remaining quadratic subfield $F_3 = Q(\sqrt{-10})$ of $K$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Suppose $C$ is a nonsingular irreducible affine curve over an algebraically closed field $k$. Prove that the coordinate ring $k[C]$ is a Dedekind Domain.
\end{exers}

Type: exercise_set
Title: Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).
Content:
\begin{exers}{Exercises (Atiyah \& Macdonald).}
\item Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain, $S$ a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$. Show that $S^{-1}A$ is either a Dedekind domain or the field of fractions of $A$.

Suppose that $S \neq A - \{0\}$, and let $H$, $H'$ be the ideal class groups of $A$ and $S^{-1}A$ respectively. Show that extension of ideals induces a surjective homomorphism $H \to H'$.

\item Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain. If $f = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n$ is a polynomial with coefficients in $A$, the content of $f$ is the ideal $c(f) = (a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ in $A$. Prove Gauss's lemma that $c(fg) = c(f)c(g)$. [Localize at a maximal ideal.]

\item A valuation ring (other than a field) is Noetherian if and only if it is a discrete valuation ring.

\item Let $A$ be a local domain which is not a field and in which the maximal ideal $\fm$ is principal and $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \fm^n = 0$. Prove that $A$ is a discrete valuation ring.

\item Let $M$ be a finitely-generated module over a Dedekind domain. Prove that $M$ is flat $\Leftrightarrow M$ is torsion-free. [Use Chapter 3, Exercise 13 and Chapter 7, Exercise 16.]

\item Let $M$ be a finitely-generated torsion module ($T(M) = M$) over a Dedekind domain $A$. Prove that $M$ is uniquely representable as a finite direct sum of modules $A/\fp_i^{n_i}$, where $\fp_i$ are non-zero prime ideals of $A$. [For each $\fp \neq 0$, $M_\fp$ is a torsion $A_\fp$-module; use the structure theorem for modules over a principal ideal domain.]

\item Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain and $\fa \neq 0$ an ideal in $A$. Show that every ideal in $A/\fa$ is principal.

Deduce that every ideal in $A$ can be generated by at most 2 elements.

\item Let $\fa$, $\fb$, $\fc$ be three ideals in a Dedekind domain. Prove that
\[
\fa \cap (\fb + \fc) = (\fa \cap \fb) + (\fa \cap \fc)
\]
\[
\fa + (\fb \cap \fc) = (\fa + \fb) \cap (\fa + \fc).
\]
[Localize.]

\item (Chinese Remainder Theorem). Let $\fa_1, \ldots, \fa_n$ be ideals and let $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ be elements in a Dedekind domain $A$. Then the system of congruences $x \equiv x_i \pmod{\fa_i}$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) has a solution $x$ in $A$ $\Leftrightarrow x_i \equiv x_j \pmod{\fa_i + \fa_j}$ whenever $i \neq j$.

[This is equivalent to saying that the sequence of $A$-modules
\[
A \xrightarrow{\phi} \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} A/\fa_i \xrightarrow{\psi} \bigoplus_{i<j} A/(\fa_i + \fa_j)
\]
is exact, where $\phi$ and $\psi$ are defined as follows: $\phi(x) = (x + \fa_1, \ldots, x + \fa_n)$; $\psi(x_1 + \fa_1, \ldots, x_n + \fa_n)$ has $(i, j)$-component $x_i - x_j + \fa_i + \fa_j$. To show that this sequence is exact it is enough to show that it becomes exact when localized at any $\fp \neq 0$; in other words we may assume that $A$ is a discrete valuation ring, and then it is easy.]
\end{exers}

[For each $\fp \neq 0$, $M_\fp$ is a torsion $A_\fp$-module; use the structure theorem for modules over a principal ideal domain.]

\item Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain and $\fa \neq 0$ an ideal in $A$. Show that every ideal in $A/\fa$ is principal.

Deduce that every ideal in $A$ can be generated by at most 2 elements.

\item Let $\fa$, $\fb$, $\fc$ be three ideals in a Dedekind domain. Prove that
\[
\fa \cap (\fb + \fc) = (\fa \cap \fb) + (\fa \cap \fc)
\]
\[
\fa + (\fb \cap \fc) = (\fa + \fb) \cap (\fa + \fc).
\]
[Localize.]

\item (Chinese Remainder Theorem). Let $\fa_1, \ldots, \fa_n$ be ideals and let $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ be elements in a Dedekind domain $A$. Then the system of congruences $x \equiv x_i \pmod{\fa_i}$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) has a solution $x$ in $A$ $\Leftrightarrow x_i \equiv x_j \pmod{\fa_i + \fa_j}$ whenever $i \neq j$.

[This is equivalent to saying that the sequence of $A$-modules
\[
A \xrightarrow{\phi} \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} A/\fa_i \xrightarrow{\psi} \bigoplus_{i<j} A/(\fa_i + \fa_j)
\]
is exact, where $\phi$ and $\psi$ are defined as follows: $\phi(x) = (x + \fa_1, \ldots, x + \fa_n)$; $\psi(x_1 + \fa_1, \ldots, x_n + \fa_n)$ has $(i, j)$-component $x_i - x_j + \fa_i + \fa_j$. To show that this sequence is exact it is enough to show that it becomes exact when localized at any $\fp \neq 0$; in other words we may assume that $A$ is a discrete valuation ring, and then it is easy.]
\end{exers}

Title: Additional exercises.
Content:
\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $\fa,\fb$ nonzero integral ideals. Prove that $\fa\subseteq\fb$ if and only if $\fb\mid\fa$ (there is an integral ideal $\fc$ with $\fa=\fb\fc$), and deduce that $\fa$ is maximal among proper ideals if and only if $\fa$ is a nonzero prime.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and let $v_{\fp}\colon K^\times\toZ$ be the exponent of $\fp$ in the factorization of $(x)$. Prove that for all $x,y\in K^\times$ one has $v_{\fp}(xy)=v_{\fp}(x)+v_{\fp}(y)$ and $v_{\fp}(x+y)\ge\min\{v_{\fp}(x),v_{\fp}(y)\}$ whenever $x+y\ne0$, and conclude that $\{x\in K^\times:v_{\fp}(x)\ge0\}\cup\{0\}$ is the valuation ring $R_{\fp}$.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with only finitely many nonzero prime ideals. Prove that $R$ is a PID. [Use that for each prime $\fp$ one can find $x$ with $v_{\fp}(x)=1$ and $v_{\fq}(x)=0$ for the other primes $\fq$, via the Chinese Remainder Theorem.]
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $\fp$ a nonzero prime. Prove that the $R_{\fp}$-module $\fp^n R_{\fp}/\fp^{n+1}R_{\fp}$ is one-dimensional over the residue field $R/\fp$ for every $n\ge0$, and use this to compute $\len(R/\fp^m)$ as a module over $R$.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $I,J$ nonzero fractional ideals with $[I]=[J]$ in $\operatorname{Cl}(R)$. Prove $I\cong J$ as $R$-modules, and conversely that an $R$-module isomorphism $I\to J$ is multiplication by a fixed element of $K^\times$. Deduce that the assignment $[I]\mapsto$ (isomorphism class of $I$) is injective on $\operatorname{Cl}(R)$.
\end{exers}

Complete the divisibility (factorization) lattice below for the ideal $(6)=\fp_2^2\fp_3\fp_3'$, where an edge $\fa\,---\,\fb$ drawn upward means $\fa\mid\fb$ (equivalently $\fb\subseteq\fa$). Label each upward edge with the prime being adjoined and verify that "to contain is to divide" makes the diagram a sublattice of the divisor lattice:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.7em, column sep=1.4em]
& (6)=\fp_2^2\fp_3\fp_3' & \\
\fp_2^2\fp_3 \arrow[ur,dash] & \fp_2\fp_3\fp_3' \arrow[u,dash] & \fp_2^2\fp_3' \arrow[ul,dash] \\
\fp_2\fp_3 \arrow[u,dash]\arrow[ur,dash] & \fp_2^2 \arrow[ul,dash]\arrow[ur,dash] & \fp_2\fp_3' \arrow[ul,dash]\arrow[u,dash] \\
& R=(1) \arrow[ul,dash]\arrow[u,dash]\arrow[ur,dash] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
State which of the listed ideals is principal and identify $\gcd(\fp_2^2\fp_3,\fp_2\fp_3\fp_3')$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(\fp_2^2\fp_3,\fp_2\fp_3\fp_3')$ from the lattice.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $\fp$ a nonzero prime. The square below has horizontal maps the localization $R\to R_{\fp}$ (and its restriction to $\fp$) and vertical maps the inclusions. Prove the square commutes and that the induced map on quotients is an isomorphism $R/\fp\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R_{\fp}/\fp R_{\fp}$, exhibiting $R_{\fp}$ as a DVR with maximal ideal $\fp R_{\fp}$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
\fp \arrow[r] \arrow[d,hook] & \fp R_{\fp} \arrow[d,hook] \\
R \arrow[r,"\ell"'] & R_{\fp}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Identify a uniformizer of $R_{\fp}$ as the image of any $t\in\fp\setminus\fp^2$, and explain why the localization map sends the prime power $\fp^n$ to $(\ell(t))^n R_{\fp}$.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain. The diagram below is the defining exact sequence of the class group, with $\operatorname{div}\colon x\mapsto(x)$ and $\pi$ the quotient onto $\operatorname{Cl}(R)=I(R)/P(R)$. Prove exactness at every term and identify $\Ker(\operatorname{div})$ and $\Coker(\operatorname{div})$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=normal, column sep=2.2em]
1 \arrow[r] & \units R \arrow[r,hook] & K^\times \arrow[r,"\operatorname{div}"] & I(R) \arrow[r,"\pi"] & \operatorname{Cl}(R) \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Then, taking $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, label $I(R)$ as the free abelian group on the nonzero primes and locate the class $[\fp_2]$ of order $2$ as the image of $\pi$ on $\fp_2$.
\item Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $S\subseteq R$ multiplicatively closed with $0\notin S$. Extension of ideals $\fa\mapsto\fa S^{-1} R$ induces the homomorphisms in the square below, where the rows pass to class groups. Prove the square commutes and that the right-hand map $\operatorname{Cl}(R)\to\operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1} R)$ is surjective, with kernel generated by the classes of the primes $\fp$ meeting $S$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge]
I(R) \arrow[r,"\pi"] \arrow[d,"\cdot S^{-1} R"'] & \operatorname{Cl}(R) \arrow[d,"\overline{\cdot S^{-1} R}"] \\
I(S^{-1} R) \arrow[r,"\pi'"'] & \operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1} R)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Explain why a prime $\fp$ with $\fp\cap S\ne\varnothing$ maps to the unit ideal of $S^{-1} R$, and conclude that $\operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1} R)$ is a quotient of $\operatorname{Cl}(R)$.
\end{exers}

Type: prose
Content:
A complex number $\alpha$ is an algebraic number if it is a root of some nonzero
polynomial in $Q[x]$; the monic generator of the kernel of the substitution map
$Q[x]\toC$, $x\mapsto\alpha$, is its irreducible polynomial over $Q$. We call
$\alpha$ an algebraic integer when that irreducible polynomial has integer
coefficients. This is the number-theoretic shadow of the ring theory in this chapter: just as
$Z$ sits inside $Q$, a distinguished subring of algebraic integers sits inside every number
field, and for the quadratic fields it can be written down explicitly. The first surprise is
that the answer depends on a congruence mod $4$.

Type: definition
Title: {quadratic field}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{quadratic field}]
For a square-free integer $d\ne1$ (positive or negative, not a square in $Q$), the
quadratic number field is
\[
Q[\sqrt d]\;=\;\{a+b\sqrt d \st a,b\inQ\},
\]
real if $d>0$ and imaginary if $d<0$. Here $\sqrt d$ is the positive real root when $d>0$
and the positive imaginary root when $d<0$. Pulling square factors out of the radical lets us
always take $d$ square-free, so $d\equiv1,2,$ or $3\pmod4$ (never $0$, since $d$ is square-free).
\end{definition}

For a square-free integer $d\ne1$ (positive or negative, not a square in $\mathbb{Q}$), the

\[
\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt d]\;=\;\{a+b\sqrt d \st a,b\in\mathbb{Q}\},
\]

and the positive imaginary root when $d<0$. Pulling square factors out of the radical lets us
always take $d$ square-free, so $d\equiv1,2,$ or $3\pmod4$ (never $0$, since $d$ is square-free).
\end{definition}

conjugate is $\overline\alpha=a-b\delta$, and $\alpha,\overline\alpha$ are the two roots
of
\[
(x-\alpha)(x-\overline\alpha)\;=\;x^2-2a\,x+(a^2-b^2 d),
\]

$\alpha$ over $Q$. Reading off when its coefficients are integers gives the next two facts.

Title: {rational integers; integrality criterion}
Content:
\begin{lemma}[{rational integers; integrality criterion}]
A rational number is an algebraic integer if and only if it is an ordinary integer.
Consequently $\alpha=a+b\sqrt d$ (with $a,b\inQ$) is an algebraic integer if and only if
$2a\inZ$ and $a^2-b^2 d\inZ$.
\end{lemma}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Fields > Algebraic integers in a quadratic field
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-a441ec2fc826c3a597e0
Content:
\begin{proof}
A rational $a$ has irreducible polynomial $x-a$, which has integer coefficients exactly when
$a\inZ$. For the second statement, when $b\ne0$ the irreducible polynomial is
$x^2-2a\,x+(a^2-b^2 d)$, integral precisely when $2a$ and $a^2-b^2 d$ lie in $Z$; the case
$b=0$ is the first statement.
\end{proof}

Title: {ring of integers of $Q[\sqrt d]$; Artin 13.1.6}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{ring of integers of $Q[\sqrt d]$; Artin 13.1.6}]
Let $d$ be square-free and $\delta=\sqrt d$. The algebraic integers in $Q[\sqrt d]$ form a
ring $R$, the ring of integers, described by:
\[
R=\begin{cases}
Z[\sqrt d]=\{a+b\sqrt d\st a,b\inZ\}, & d\equiv 2,3\pmod4,\\[4pt]
Z[\eta]=\{a+b\eta\st a,b\inZ\},\quad \eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt d), & d\equiv 1\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
When $d\equiv1\pmod4$ the generator $\eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt d)$ is a root of the monic integer
polynomial $x^2-x+h$ with $h=(1-d)/4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[{ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt d]$; Artin 13.1.6}]
Let $d$ be square-free and $\delta=\sqrt d$. The algebraic integers in $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt d]$ form a
ring $R$, the \emph{ring of integers}, described by:
\[
R=\begin{cases}
\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]=\{a+b\sqrt d\st a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}, & d\equiv 2,3\pmod4,\\[4pt]
\mathbb{Z}[\eta]=\{a+b\eta\st a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\},\quad \eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt d), & d\equiv 1\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
When $d\equiv1\pmod4$ the generator $\eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt d)$ is a root of the monic integer
polynomial $x^2-x+h$ with $h=(1-d)/4$.
\end{theorem}

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Fields > Algebraic integers in a quadratic field
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-bb067ad36735186a3bee
Content:
\begin{proof}
Write $\alpha=a+b\delta$ and use the criterion: $2a\inZ$ and $a^2-b^2 d\inZ$. There are two
cases for $a$.

If $a\inZ$, then $a^2\inZ$ forces $b^2 d\inZ$; since $d$ is square-free it cannot cancel a
square in the denominator of $b^2$, so $b^2\inZ$ and hence $b\inZ$. (This square-free
cancellation is the lemma ``$r^2 d\inZ\Rightarrow r\inZ$''.)

If $a=m+\tfrac12$ is a half-integer ($m\inZ$), then $a^2=m^2+m+\tfrac14\inZ+\tfrac14$, so
integrality of $a^2-b^2 d$ puts $b^2 d\inZ+\tfrac14$. Then $4b^2 d\inZ$, so $2b\inZ$ by the
same square-free argument, i.e.\ $b$ is a half-integer. Writing $b=n+\tfrac12$, one checks
$b^2 d\inZ+\tfrac14$ holds if and only if $d\equiv1\pmod4$. Thus half-integer coordinates
occur exactly when $d\equiv1\pmod4$, and then $a,b$ are both half-integers; these are
precisely the elements $a'+b'\eta$ with $a',b'\inZ$. That $R$ is closed under multiplication
(hence a ring) is the direct computation $\eta^2=\eta-h$, or $\delta^2=d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Write $\alpha=a+b\delta$ and use the criterion: $2a\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $a^2-b^2 d\in\mathbb{Z}$. There are two
cases for $a$.

If $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, then $a^2\in\mathbb{Z}$ forces $b^2 d\in\mathbb{Z}$; since $d$ is square-free it cannot cancel a
square in the denominator of $b^2$, so $b^2\in\mathbb{Z}$ and hence $b\in\mathbb{Z}$. (This square-free
cancellation is the lemma ``$r^2 d\in\mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow r\in\mathbb{Z}$''.)

If $a=m+\tfrac12$ is a half-integer ($m\in\mathbb{Z}$), then $a^2=m^2+m+\tfrac14\in\mathbb{Z}+\tfrac14$, so

(hence a ring) is the direct computation $\eta^2=\eta-h$, or $\delta^2=d$.

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
For $d<0$ the ring $R$ is a lattice in $C$: rectangular when $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$
(basis $1,\delta$ with $\delta$ purely imaginary) and ``isosceles-triangular'' when
$d\equiv1\pmod4$ (basis $1,\eta$). Two famous cases: $d=-1$ gives the Gauss integers
$Z[i]$ on a square lattice, and $d=-3$ gives $Z[\eta]$ on an equilateral
triangular lattice. The geometry of $R$ as a lattice is what makes the imaginary case
tractable, and it drives the unit count below.
\end{remark}

Content:
From here we focus on the imaginary case $d<0$, where $R$ is a lattice; let $R$ denote the
ring of integers in $Q[\delta]$. The single tool that organizes factorization is the norm,
a multiplicative map to $\Zpos$ that turns questions about $R$ into questions about ordinary
integers.

Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Fields > The norm and the units
Type: definition
Title: {norm}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{norm}]
The norm of $\alpha=a+b\delta\in R$ is
\[
\Nm(\alpha)\;=\;\alpha\,\overline\alpha\;=\;a^2-b^2 d\;=\;\abs{\alpha}^2 .
\]
For $d<0$ this is a non-negative integer, and $\Nm(\alpha)=0$ only when $\alpha=0$; so
$\Nm(\alpha)$ is a positive integer for every $\alpha\ne0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[{multiplicativity}]
The norm is multiplicative: $\Nm(\beta\gamma)=\Nm(\beta)\,\Nm(\gamma)$ for all
$\beta,\gamma\in R$.
\end{proposition}

Course: abstract algebra notes

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-5a19ad9f4c00481c2090
Content:
\begin{proof}
Conjugation $\alpha\mapsto\overline\alpha$ is a ring homomorphism of $R$ (it is the restriction
of complex conjugation, and $\overline{\sqrt d}=-\sqrt d$ for $d<0$). Hence
$\Nm(\beta\gamma)=\beta\gamma\,\overline{\beta\gamma}=\beta\gamma\,\overline\beta\,\overline\gamma
=(\beta\overline\beta)(\gamma\overline\gamma)=\Nm(\beta)\Nm(\gamma)$.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
Multiplicativity is the lever: if $\alpha=\beta\gamma$ then $\Nm(\alpha)=\Nm(\beta)\Nm(\gamma)$
is a factorization in $Z$, so the only possible factors $\beta$ of $\alpha$ are those whose
norm divides $\Nm(\alpha)$. When $\Nm(\alpha)$ is small this is a finite, hand-checkable list.
The first dividend is a complete description of the units.

Type: theorem
Title: {units; Artin 13.2.2}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{units; Artin 13.2.2}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field $Q[\sqrt d]$, $d<0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\alpha\in R$ is a unit if and only if $\Nm(\alpha)=1$, and then
$\alpha^{-1}=\overline\alpha$.
\item The units are exactly $\{\pm1\}$, unless $d=-1$ or $d=-3$.
\item If $d=-1$ (the Gauss integers $Z[i]$), the units are the four powers of $i$:
$\{\pm1,\pm i\}$.
\item If $d=-3$, the units are the six powers of $\zeta_6=e^{2\pi i/6}=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-3})$,
namely the sixth roots of unity.
\end{enumerate}
In every case the units of an imaginary quadratic field are exactly the roots of unity it
contains.
\end{theorem}

Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt d]$, $d<0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\alpha\in R$ is a unit if and only if $\Nm(\alpha)=1$, and then

\item The units are exactly $\{\pm1\}$, \emph{unless} $d=-1$ or $d=-3$.
\item If $d=-1$ (the Gauss integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$), the units are the four powers of $i$:
$\{\pm1,\pm i\}$.
\item If $d=-3$, the units are the six powers of $\zeta_6=e^{2\pi i/6}=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-3})$,
namely the sixth roots of unity.
\end{enumerate}
In every case the units of an imaginary quadratic field are exactly the roots of unity it
contains.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Fields > The norm and the units
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-962129c7e5c530c6633e
Content:
\begin{proof}
(1) If $\alpha$ is a unit with inverse $\alpha^{-1}\in R$, then
$\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\alpha^{-1})=\Nm(1)=1$ with both factors positive integers, forcing
$\Nm(\alpha)=1$. Conversely $\Nm(\alpha)=\alpha\overline\alpha=1$ exhibits $\overline\alpha\in R$
as a two-sided inverse, so $\alpha$ is a unit and $\alpha^{-1}=\overline\alpha$.

(2)--(4) We solve $\Nm(\alpha)=1$ on the lattice. For $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$ with
$\alpha=a+b\delta$ ($a,b\inZ$), $\Nm(\alpha)=a^2-b^2 d=a^2+b^2\abs d=1$. If $\abs d\ge2$ this
forces $b=0,a=\pm1$, giving $\{\pm1\}$; the only escape is $d=-1$, where $a^2+b^2=1$ has the
four solutions $\pm1,\pm i$. For $d\equiv1\pmod4$ with $\alpha=a+b\eta$, the norm is the
positive-definite form $\Nm(a+b\eta)=a^2+ab+\tfrac{1-d}4\,b^2$; for $\abs d\ge7$ the
$b^2$-coefficient is $\ge2$ and again only $b=0,a=\pm1$ solve $=1$, while $d=-3$ gives
$a^2+ab+b^2=1$ with the six solutions that are the powers of $\zeta_6$. Geometrically, the unit
circle $\abs\alpha=1$ meets the lattice in just $\{\pm1\}$ except for the square lattice
($d=-1$, $4$ points) and the equilateral lattice ($d=-3$, $6$ points).
\end{proof}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The exceptional unit groups are exactly the lattice symmetries: $Z[i]$ on the square lattice
has the $4$ rotational symmetries $\{\pm1,\pm i\}$, and $Z[\eta]$ on the equilateral lattice
has the $6$ symmetries given by the powers of $\zeta_6$. Every other imaginary quadratic ring
has only $\{\pm1\}$.
\end{remark}

Title: {factorization terminates; Artin 13.2.3}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{factorization terminates; Artin 13.2.3}]
In the ring of integers $R$ of an imaginary quadratic field, every nonzero non-unit is a
product of finitely many irreducibles; factoring cannot continue forever.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Fields > The norm and the units
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-8b54a8b6874d7218d12f
Content:
\begin{proof}
If $\alpha=\beta\gamma$ is a proper factorization (neither factor a unit), then by part
(1) of the units theorem $\Nm(\beta),\Nm(\gamma)>1$, so $\Nm(\alpha)=\Nm(\beta)\Nm(\gamma)$ is
a proper factorization of the positive integer $\Nm(\alpha)$, and both factors are strictly
smaller. Thus each proper factorization strictly decreases the norm. A strictly
decreasing sequence of positive integers terminates, so after finitely many steps every factor
is irreducible. (This is the integrality of the norm doing the work of a well-ordering.)
\end{proof}

Type: example
Title: Units of the Gauss integers
Content:
\begin{wex}{Units of the Gauss integers}
Find all units of $R=Z[i]$ ($d=-1$) and confirm the count from the lattice.
\wrec A unit is exactly an element of norm $1$; here $\Nm(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$, so we solve
$a^2+b^2=1$ over $Z$.
\wsol The integer solutions of $a^2+b^2=1$ are $(\pm1,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$, i.e.\
$\{1,-1,i,-i\}$. These are the four powers of $i$: $i^0=1,\,i^1=i,\,i^2=-1,\,i^3=-i$, so
$\units{Z[i]}=\langle i\rangle$ is cyclic of order $4$. Check. The four points lie on the unit
circle at the $4$ lattice points nearest the origin -- the rotational symmetries of the square
lattice -- matching $\abs{\units{R}}=4$ for $d=-1$.
\end{wex}
latex:
\begin{wex}{Units of the Gauss integers}
Find all units of $R=\mathbb{Z}[i]$ ($d=-1$) and confirm the count from the lattice.
\wrec A unit is exactly an element of norm $1$; here $\Nm(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$, so we solve
$a^2+b^2=1$ over $\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol The integer solutions of $a^2+b^2=1$ are $(\pm1,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$, i.e.\
$\{1,-1,i,-i\}$. These are the four powers of $i$: $i^0=1,\,i^1=i,\,i^2=-1,\,i^3=-i$, so
$\units{\mathbb{Z}[i]}=\langle i\rangle$ is cyclic of order $4$. \textit{Check.} The four points lie on the unit
circle at the $4$ lattice points nearest the origin -- the rotational symmetries of the square
lattice -- matching $\abs{\units{R}}=4$ for $d=-1$.
\end{wex}

Title: Units when $d=-3$
Content:
\begin{wex}{Units when $d=-3$}
Show $\units R$ has order $6$ for $R=Z[\eta]$, $\eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-3})$.
\wrec Norm $1$ on the equilateral lattice; here $\Nm(a+b\eta)=a^2+ab+b^2$ (since
$h=(1-d)/4=1$), a positive-definite form.
\wsol Solve $a^2+ab+b^2=1$ over $Z$. Treating it as $a^2+ab+(b^2-1)=0$, the discriminant in
$a$ is $4-3b^2\ge0$ forces $b\in\{-1,0,1\}$; checking each gives the six solutions
\[
(a,b)\in\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1),(1,-1),(-1,1)\}.
\]
As elements these are $\pm1,\pm\eta,\pm(\eta-1)$, the six powers of
$\zeta_6=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-3})$. Check. $\zeta_6$ is a primitive $6$th root of unity, so
$\units R=\langle \zeta_6\rangle\congZ/(6)Z$, the $6$ rotational symmetries of the equilateral lattice.
\end{wex}

\]

$\zeta_6=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-3})$. \textit{Check.} $\zeta_6$ is a primitive $6$th root of unity, so
$\units R=\langle \zeta_6\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$, the $6$ rotational symmetries of the equilateral lattice.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $2$ is irreducible in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{$2$ is irreducible in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Let $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ ($d=-5\equiv3\bmod4$, units $\{\pm1\}$). Show $2$ is irreducible.
\wrec $\Nm(2)=4$; a proper factor would need norm $2$ (the only proper divisor of $4$ that is
$>1$ and $<4$), so check whether norm $2$ is attainable.
\wsol Here $\Nm(a+b\sqrt{-5})=a^2+5b^2$. Setting $a^2+5b^2=2$ has no integer solution: $b=0$
gives $a^2=2$ (impossible) and $\abs b\ge1$ gives $\ge5$. So no element has norm $2$. If
$2=\beta\gamma$ properly, then $4=\Nm(\beta)\Nm(\gamma)$ with both factors $>1$, forcing
$\Nm(\beta)=\Nm(\gamma)=2$ -- impossible. Hence $2$ is irreducible. Check. The same
computation shows $3$ is irreducible ($a^2+5b^2=3$ is unsolvable), and $1\pm\sqrt{-5}$ each have
norm $1+5=6$; these norms are exactly what powers the non-unique factorization next.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$: two factorizations
Content:
\begin{wex}{$6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$: two factorizations}
Exhibit $6$ as a product of irreducibles in $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ in two genuinely different ways,
and explain why $R$ is not a UFD.
\wrec Compare norms. The two products must use irreducibles (terminating factorization
guarantees an irreducible factorization exists); inequivalence is detected because the only
units are $\pm1$, so associates differ only by sign.
\wsol Compute norms: $\Nm(2)=4$, $\Nm(3)=9$, and
$\Nm(1\pm\sqrt{-5})=1^2+5\cdot1^2=6$. Both products give $6$:
\[
6\;=\;2\cdot3\;=\;(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}),
\qquad \Nm(6)=36=4\cdot9=6\cdot6 .
\]
Each of $2,3,1+\sqrt{-5},1-\sqrt{-5}$ is irreducible: norms $4,9,6,6$ would split only through a
factor of norm $2$ or $3$, and we saw $a^2+5b^2\in\{2,3\}$ is unsolvable. Now $2$ cannot be an
associate of $1\pm\sqrt{-5}$ -- the only units are $\pm1$, and $\pm(1\pm\sqrt{-5})\ne\pm2$ -- so
the two factorizations are not rearrangements of one another. Check. Multiplicativity is
consistent ($36=4\cdot9=6\cdot6$), yet $2$ divides $6=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ without
dividing either factor (that would need $\tfrac12(1\pm\sqrt{-5})\in R$, false for
$d\equiv3\bmod4$). So $2$ is irreducible but not prime: $R=Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a
unique factorization domain.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Irreducible is not the same as prime here. In $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the element $2$ is irreducible
(its norm $4$ admits no proper factor) yet not prime (it divides the product
$(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ but neither factor). Factorization into irreducibles always
terminates -- the norm descends -- but it need not be unique. Uniqueness is the
strictly stronger UFD condition, and Artin's theorem (13.2.5) records that for imaginary
$Q[\sqrt d]$ it holds for only nine values
$d=-1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163$. The repair, pursued next, is to factor ideals
rather than elements.
\end{pitfall}

Type: prose
Content:
Artin's route to ideal factorization in a quadratic ring is resolutely geometric: a nonzero ideal of $R=Z[\sqrt d]$ is first of all a lattice in $C$, a discrete rank-$2$ subgroup. The arithmetic that ordinary elements fail to provide -- unique factorization -- is then recovered at the level of these lattices. Throughout we take $d<0$ squarefree and $R$ the ring of integers in $F=Q(\sqrt d)$; for concreteness the running example is $\delta=\sqrt{-5}$, $\delta^2=-5$, where $d\equiv3\pmod4$ so $R=Z[\delta]$ with $Z$-basis $1,\delta$.

The arithmetic that ordinary elements fail to provide -- unique factorization -- is then recovered at the level of these lattices. Throughout we take $d<0$ squarefree and $R$ the ring of integers in $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$; for concreteness the running example is $\delta=\sqrt{-5}$, $\delta^2=-5$, where $d\equiv3\pmod4$ so $R=\mathbb{Z}[\delta]$ with $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $1,\delta$.

Type: definition
Title: {ideal as a sublattice}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{ideal as a sublattice}]
A nonzero subset $A\subseteq R$ is an ideal iff it is a subgroup closed under multiplication by every element of $R$. When $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$ (as in the running example), $R=Z\oplusZ\delta$ is a lattice in $C$, and any subgroup of $R$ closed under multiplication by $\delta$ is already an ideal: closure under $Z$ is automatic, and $a+b\delta$ then acts because $\delta$ does. (When $d\equiv1\pmod4$, $R=Z\oplusZ\eta$ and one tests closure under $\eta$ instead.)
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {Artin 13.3.1: every nonzero ideal is a full lattice}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Artin 13.3.1: every nonzero ideal is a full lattice}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field, $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$. Every nonzero ideal $A$ of $R$ is a sublattice of $R$ of full rank $2$. Conversely a sublattice $A\subseteq R$ is an ideal if and only if $\delta A\subseteq A$.
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Ideals as Lattices and Ideal Multiplication > Ideals as lattices in the complex plane
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-4371ebda85f70242883c
Content:
\begin{proof}
If $A\neq0$ pick $\alpha\in A$, $\alpha\neq0$; then $\{\alpha,\alpha\delta\}$ is $R$-independent (as $\delta\notinR$), so $A$ contains two independent vectors. Being a subgroup of the lattice $R$, $A$ is discrete, hence itself a lattice (a discrete subgroup containing two independent vectors is a full lattice). For the converse, a sublattice is closed under addition and under multiplication by $Z$ automatically; if in addition $\delta A\subseteq A$, then $A$ is closed under multiplication by every $a+b\delta\in R$, so $A$ is an ideal.
\end{proof}

Type: theorem
Title: {Artin 13.3.3: lattice basis of an ideal in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Artin 13.3.3: lattice basis of an ideal in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}]
Let $R=Z[\delta]$, $\delta^2=-5$, and let $A$ be a nonzero ideal. Let $\alpha\in A$ be nonzero of minimal absolute value. Then exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\{\alpha,\alpha\delta\}$ is a lattice basis for $A$, and $A=(\alpha)$ is principal; or
\item $\{\alpha,\tfrac12(\alpha+\alpha\delta)\}$ is a lattice basis for $A$, and $A$ is not principal.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Ideals as Lattices and Ideal Multiplication > Ideals as lattices in the complex plane
Type: proof
Title: Sketch, following Artin
Relation: proof_of=unit-0a506b7385348143dcde
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch, following Artin]
Since $\alpha\in A$, the principal ideal $(\alpha)\subseteq A$ has lattice basis $\{\alpha,\alpha\delta\}$. If $A=(\alpha)$ we are in case (i). Otherwise choose $\beta\in A\setminus(\alpha)$ lying in the fundamental rectangle of $(\alpha)$, i.e.\ $\beta=r\alpha+s\alpha\delta$ with $0\le r,s\le1$ (the rectangle, since $\delta$ is purely imaginary, has side ratio $1:\sqrt5$). The geometric lemma -- disks of radius $r=\abs{\alpha}$ about the four vertices together with disks of radius $\tfrac12 r$ about the three half-lattice points $\tfrac12\alpha\delta$, $\tfrac12(\alpha+\alpha\delta)$, $\alpha+\tfrac12\alpha\delta$ cover the rectangle, and the only lattice points interior to such disks are their centers -- forces $\beta$ to be one of the three half-lattice points. If $\beta=\alpha+\tfrac12\alpha\delta$ then $\tfrac12\alpha\delta\in A$, reducing to that case. If $\beta=\tfrac12\alpha\delta\in A$, multiplying by $\delta$ gives $\tfrac12\alpha\delta^2=-\tfrac52\alpha\in A$, and subtracting integer multiples of $\alpha$ shows $\tfrac12\alpha\in A$, contradicting minimality of $\abs\alpha$. The only survivor is $\beta=\tfrac12(\alpha+\alpha\delta)$, the rectangle center, giving case (ii); the resulting lattice is the non-principal shape.
\end{proof}

Type: definition
Title: {conjugate ideal}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{conjugate ideal}]
The conjugate of an ideal $A$ is $\overline A=\{\overline\alpha:\alpha\in A\}$, again an ideal of $R$. If $(\alpha,\beta)$ is a lattice basis for $A$, then $(\overline\alpha,\overline\beta)$ is a lattice basis for $\overline A$. The norm of $A$ is the lattice index $\Nm(A)=[R:A]$.
\end{definition}

Type: proposition
Title: {Artin 13.4.3: products via generators}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{Artin 13.4.3: products via generators}]
Let $A=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$ and $B=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)$ be ideals of a ring $R$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $AB$ is generated as an ideal by the $mn$ products $\alpha_i\beta_j$.
\item $(\alpha)(\beta)=(\alpha\beta)$: a product of principal ideals is principal.
\item If $A=(\alpha)$ is principal then $AB=\alpha B=\{\alpha\beta:\beta\in B\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Title: {Artin 13.4.8, Main Lemma}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Artin 13.4.8, Main Lemma}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field. For every nonzero ideal $A$,
\[
A\,\overline A=(n)=nR\qquadfor a positive integer n,
\]
and that integer is $n=\Nm(A)=[R:A]$.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Ideals as Lattices and Ideal Multiplication > The conjugate ideal and the main lemma
Type: proof
Title: Following Artin
Relation: proof_of=unit-bf20c359735341fe4c39
Content:
\begin{proof}[Following Artin]
Let $(\alpha,\beta)$ be a lattice basis for $A$, so $(\overline\alpha,\overline\beta)$ is one for $\overline A$. By Artin's Proposition 13.4.3(a), $A\overline A$ is generated by the four products $\alpha\overline\alpha,\ \alpha\overline\beta,\ \beta\overline\alpha,\ \beta\overline\beta$. Now $\alpha\overline\alpha=\abs\alpha^2$ and $\beta\overline\beta=\abs\beta^2$ and $\beta\overline\alpha+\alpha\overline\beta$ are each equal to their own complex conjugates, hence rational; being algebraic integers, they are ordinary integers. Let $n$ be their greatest common divisor in $Z$. As an integer combination of generators of $A\overline A$, we get $n\in A\overline A$, so $(n)\subseteq A\overline A$.

For the reverse inclusion it suffices to show $n$ divides each generator in $R$. It already divides $\alpha\overline\alpha$ and $\beta\overline\beta$ in $Z$. For the cross terms set $\gamma=\alpha\overline\beta/n$ and $\overline\gamma=\beta\overline\alpha/n$. These are the two roots of
\[
p(x)=x^2-\Bigl(\tfrac{\beta\overline\alpha+\alpha\overline\beta}{n}\Bigr)x+\tfrac{\alpha\overline\alpha\,\beta\overline\beta}{n^2},
\]
whose coefficients are integers because $n$ divides $\beta\overline\alpha+\alpha\overline\beta$, $\alpha\overline\alpha$, and $\beta\overline\beta$. Thus $\gamma,\overline\gamma$ are algebraic integers, hence lie in $R$, so $n$ divides $\alpha\overline\beta$ and $\beta\overline\alpha$ in $R$. Therefore $A\overline A\subseteq(n)$ and $A\overline A=(n)$. That $n=[R:A]$ follows because multiplication by $A$ scales lattice covolumes by $\Nm(A)$ and $A\overline A=(n)$ has index $n^2$, while $[R:A]=[R:\overline A]$.
\end{proof}

whose coefficients are integers because $n$ divides $\beta\overline\alpha+\alpha\overline\beta$, $\alpha\overline\alpha$, and $\beta\overline\beta$. Thus $\gamma,\overline\gamma$ are algebraic integers, hence lie in $R$, so $n$ divides $\alpha\overline\beta$ and $\beta\overline\alpha$ in $R$. Therefore $A\overline A\subseteq(n)$ and $A\overline A=(n)$. That $n=[R:A]$ follows because multiplication by $A$ scales lattice covolumes by $\Nm(A)$ and $A\overline A=(n)$ has index $n^2$, while $[R:A]=[R:\overline A]$.
\end{proof}

Title: {Artin 13.4.9: cancellation and ``to contain is to divide''}
Content:
\begin{corollary}[{Artin 13.4.9: cancellation and ``to contain is to divide''}]
For nonzero ideals $A,B,C$ of $R$: \textup{(a)} $AB=AC\iff B=C$, and $AB\subseteq AC\iff B\subseteq C$; \textup{(b)} $A\supseteq B$ if and only if $A$ divides $B$, i.e.\ $B=AC$ for some ideal $C$.
\end{corollary}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-59aabef1c2719250fe25
Content:
\begin{proof}
(a) If $AB=AC$, multiply by $\overline A$: by the Main Lemma $A\overline A=(n)$, so $nB=nC$, and dividing by $n$ gives $B=C$. (b) If a principal $(n)\supseteq B$ then $n$ divides every element of $B$, and $C=n^{-1}B$ is an ideal with $(n)C=B$. In general $A\supseteq B$ gives $(n)=A\overline A\supseteq\overline AB$, so $\overline AB=(n)C=A\overline AC$ for some $C$, and cancellation yields $B=AC$. Conversely $B=AC$ gives $B=AC\subseteq AR=A$.
\end{proof}

Title: {Artin 13.5.5: unique factorization of ideals}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{Artin 13.5.5: unique factorization of ideals}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field. Every nonzero proper ideal of $R$ is a product of nonzero prime (= maximal) ideals, and the factorization is unique up to the order of the factors.
\end{theorem}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Ideals as Lattices and Ideal Multiplication > Unique factorization of ideals
Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-bf613b4775aedb597dd1
Content:
\begin{proof}
Existence. If $B$ is maximal it is prime. Otherwise some ideal $A$ properly contains $B$; by Artin's Corollary 13.4.9(b), $A$ divides $B$, say $B=AC$, and cancellation forces $C\supsetneq B$ too. Since only finitely many ideals contain $B$ (each has $[R:B]<\infty$), recursively factoring $A$ and $C$ terminates with all factors maximal.

Uniqueness. Suppose $P_1\cdots P_r=Q_1\cdots Q_s$ with all $P_i,Q_j$ prime. Then $P_1\supseteq Q_1\cdots Q_s$, so by primeness $P_1\supseteq Q_j$ for some $j$, say $j=1$; as $Q_1$ is maximal, $P_1=Q_1$. Cancel $P_1$ (Artin's Corollary 13.4.9(a)) and induct.
\end{proof}

Title: The ideals over $2$ and $3$, and $A\overline A=(2)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The ideals over $2$ and $3$, and $A\overline A=(2)$}
With $A=(2,1+\delta)$, $\overline A=(2,1-\delta)$, $B=(3,1+\delta)$, $\overline B=(3,1-\delta)$, compute $A\overline A$.
\wrec Use Artin's Proposition 13.4.3(a): $A\overline A$ is generated by the four products of generators; then squeeze it between $(2)$ and itself.
\wsol The four products of $\{2,1+\delta\}$ and $\{2,1-\delta\}$ are
\[
A\overline A=\bigl(4,\ 2(1-\delta),\ 2(1+\delta),\ (1+\delta)(1-\delta)\bigr)=(4,\,2-2\delta,\,2+2\delta,\,6).
\]
Every generator is divisible by $2$, so $A\overline A\subseteq(2)$. Conversely $2=6-4\in A\overline A$, so $(2)\subseteq A\overline A$. Hence $A\overline A=(2)$. Check. The Main Lemma predicts $A\overline A=(\Nm A)$, and indeed $[R:A]=2$, so $n=2$ as found.
\end{wex}

Title: The split prime $3$ and the mixed products
Content:
\begin{wex}{The split prime $3$ and the mixed products}
Show $B\overline B=(3)$, and $A B=(1+\delta)$, $\overline A\,\overline B=(1-\delta)$.
\wrec Same generator-product computation; each product ideal turns out principal, generated by a shared divisor of all four generators.
\wsol For $B\overline B$ the four products are $9,\,3(1-\delta),\,3(1+\delta),\,6$, all divisible by $3$, and $3=9-6\in B\overline B$, so $B\overline B=(3)$. For $AB$ the four products of $\{2,1+\delta\}$, $\{3,1+\delta\}$ are $6,\,2(1+\delta),\,3(1+\delta),\,(1+\delta)^2$, each divisible by $1+\delta$; moreover $1+\delta=3(1+\delta)-2(1+\delta)\in AB$, so $AB=(1+\delta)$. Conjugating gives $\overline A\,\overline B=(1-\delta)$. Check. $\Nm(AB)=\abs{1+\delta}^2=6=[R:A][R:B]=2\cdot3$, consistent with norms being multiplicative.
\end{wex}

Title: The common refinement of $6=2\cdot3=(1+\delta)(1-\delta)$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The common refinement of $6=2\cdot3=(1+\delta)(1-\delta)$}
Express the principal ideal $(6)$ as a product of the prime ideals $A,\overline A,B,\overline B$ and reconcile the two element-factorizations.
\wrec Multiply the relations from the previous examples; both elementwise factorizations of $6$ must collapse to the same ideal factorization.
\wsol Using $A\overline A=(2)$, $B\overline B=(3)$, $AB=(1+\delta)$, $\overline A\,\overline B=(1-\delta)$,
\[
(6)=(2)(3)=(A\overline A)(B\overline B)=(AB)(\overline A\,\overline B)=(1+\delta)(1-\delta).
\]
The single ideal factorization $(6)=A\,\overline A\,B\,\overline B$ is the common refinement: regrouping $A\overline A\cdot B\overline B$ recovers $2\cdot3$, while regrouping $(AB)(\overline A\,\overline B)$ recovers $(1+\delta)(1-\delta)$. Check. Every factor is a genuine prime ideal ($\Nm A=\Nm\overline A=2$, $\Nm B=\Nm\overline B=3$, all prime), so this is the unique prime factorization of $(6)$ guaranteed by Artin's Theorem 13.5.5; the apparent non-uniqueness of element factorization was only a regrouping ambiguity among these prime factors. (Only three of them are distinct: $\overline A=A$, see the Remark below, so $(6)=A^2B\overline B$.)
\end{wex}

Restoring unique factorization at the level of ideals is exactly the order that the geometry of lattices recovers.

Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Splitting, Ramification, and Inert Primes > Splitting, ramifying, and inert primes
Type: prose
Content:
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic number field $Q[\sqrt{d}]$,
with $d<0$ squarefree. When $d\equiv2$ or $3\pmod 4$ we have $R=Z[\sqrt{d}]$, and when
$d\equiv1\pmod 4$ we have $R=Z[\eta]$ with $\eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{d})$. A rational prime
$p$ generates the ideal $(p)=pR$, but this ideal need not be prime in $R$. The central
question of this section is: how does the prime $p$ behave in $R$? Artin's answer is
that the behaviour of $(p)$ is governed entirely by how a single quadratic polynomial
factors modulo $p$ -- which, in turn, is read off from the Legendre symbol $\left(\tfrac{d}{p}\right)$.

Type: theorem
Title: {decomposition of a rational prime, Artin 13.6.1}
Content:
\begin{theorem}[{decomposition of a rational prime, Artin 13.6.1}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic number field, and let $p$ be a
rational prime.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For a nonzero prime ideal $P$ of $R$, write $P\overline{P}=(n)$ with $n$ a positive
integer. Then $n$ is either a rational prime or the square of a rational prime.
\item The ideal $(p)=pR$ is either a prime ideal, or the product $P\overline{P}$ of a prime
ideal and its conjugate.
\item If $d\equiv2$ or $3\pmod4$, then $(p)$ is prime if and only if $d$ is not a square
modulo $p$, equivalently if and only if $x^2-d$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$.
\item If $d\equiv1\pmod4$, put $h=\tfrac14(1-d)\inZ$. Then $(p)$ is prime if and only if
$x^2-x+h$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Content:
\begin{proof}[Proof of (c)]
Suppose $d\equiv2$ or $3\pmod4$, so $R=Z[\sqrt d]\congZ[x]/(x^2-d)$. The prime $p$ remains
prime in $R$ exactly when the quotient $\widetilde R=R/(p)$ is a field (a nonzero quotient of a
Dedekind domain by a maximal ideal). Reducing mod $p$ commutes with forming
$Z[x]/(x^2-d)$: the two ways of passing from $Z[x]$ to $\widetilde R$ -- first kill $x^2-d$
then reduce mod $p$, or first reduce mod $p$ then kill $x^2-d$ -- agree, giving
\[
\widetilde R \;=\; R/(p)\;\cong\;Z[x]/(x^2-d,\,p)\;\cong\;\F_p[x]/(x^2-d).
\]
This last ring is a field precisely when $x^2-d$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$. A monic quadratic
over a field is irreducible iff it has no root, and $x^2-d$ has a root in $\F_p$ iff $d$ is a
square modulo $p$. So $(p)$ is prime iff $d$ is not a square mod $p$; otherwise $x^2-d=(x-a)(x+a)$
splits and $(p)=P\overline P$ with $P=(p,\sqrt d-a)$. The proof of (d) is identical with
$x^2-x+h$, the minimal polynomial of $\eta$, in place of $x^2-d$. Parts (a) and (b) follow the
norm/unique-factorization argument of the Main Lemma and are taken as given here.
\end{proof}

Type: prose
Content:
The commuting reductions in the proof are exactly the square (13.6.3) in Artin: the two
routes from $Z[x]$ down to $\widetilde R$ must agree.

 
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
Z[x] \arrow[r, "x^2-d"] \arrow[d, "p"'] & Z[\sqrt d] \arrow[d, "p"] \\
\F_p[x] \arrow[r, "x^2-d"'] & \widetilde R=\F_p[x]/(x^2-d)
\end{tikzcd}
 

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four quotient rings arranged in a commutative square.
Upper-left: the polynomial ring $Z[x]$, the ambient free ring before imposing any relation.
Upper-right: $Z[\sqrt{d}] \cong Z[x]/(x^2-d)$, the ring of integers (when $d \equiv 2, 3 \pmod{4}$),
obtained by killing the relation $x^2 = d$.
Lower-left: $\F_p[x] = Z[x]/(p)$, polynomials over the prime field, obtained by reducing coefficients mod $p$.
Lower-right: $\widetilde{R} = \F_p[x]/(x^2-d) \cong R/(p)$, the target quotient that determines whether $p$ stays prime.
\dgi{Arrows:} The top horizontal arrow is the surjection $Z[x] \twoheadrightarrow Z[\sqrt{d}]$ with kernel $(x^2-d)$; it sends $x \mapsto \sqrt{d}$.
The left vertical arrow is the reduction $Z[x] \twoheadrightarrow \F_p[x]$ with kernel $(p)$; it reduces each coefficient mod $p$.
The right vertical arrow is the reduction $Z[\sqrt{d}] \twoheadrightarrow \widetilde{R} = Z[\sqrt{d}]/(p)$ with kernel $pZ[\sqrt{d}]$; it is a quotient of rings.
The bottom horizontal arrow is the surjection $\F_p[x] \twoheadrightarrow \F_p[x]/(x^2-d)$ killing $x^2-d$; it is well-defined because $x^2-d \in \F_p[x]$ (the relation descends from $Z[x]$).
\dgi{What commutes:} The two composites from upper-left to lower-right agree:
(top then right) $=$ (left then bottom), i.e.\ the map $Z[x] \to \widetilde{R}$ obtained by first

Type: method
Title: To decide the behaviour of an odd prime $p$ in $Z[\sqrt d]$ ($d\equiv2,3\bmod4$).
Content:
\begin{method}{To decide the behaviour of an odd prime $p$ in $Z[\sqrt d]$ ($d\equiv2,3\bmod4$).}
Compute the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)=+1$: $x^2-d$ has two roots mod $p$, so $p$ splits,
$(p)=P\overline P$ with $P=(p,\sqrt d-a)$ where $a^2\equiv d$.
\item $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)=0$ (i.e. $p\mid d$): $x^2-d=(x)^2$ has a double root, $p$
ramifies, $(p)=(p,\sqrt d)^2$. The prime $p=2$ is a separate ramification case.
\item $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)=-1$: $x^2-d$ is irreducible, so $p$ is inert and
$(p)$ stays prime.
\end{itemize}
\end{method}

Type: remark
Content:
\begin{remark}
The three behaviours are visible in the lattice of ideals between $(p)$ and $R$. By Artin's
Corollary 13.6.2, any proper ideal strictly larger than $(p)$ is prime, hence maximal. So the
interval $[(p),R]$ has at most one intermediate floor, and the trichotomy says how many distinct
primes sit on it: two when $p$ splits, one (doubled) when $p$ ramifies, none when $p$ is inert.
\end{remark}

Type: example
Title: The prime $2$ ramifies in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The prime $2$ ramifies in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Show that $(2)=A^2$ where $A=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$, so $2$ ramifies.
\wrec Here $p=2$, the degenerate case (note $2\nmid d=-5$; the prime $2$ ramifies whenever $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$): $x^2-d\equiv x^2+5\equiv x^2-1\equiv(x-1)^2\pmod2$ has a repeated root, signalling ramification. Compute $A\overline A$ directly.
\wsol Modulo $2$, $x^2+5\equiv x^2+1\equiv(x+1)^2$, a perfect square, so $2$ should ramify. Check it by hand: $\overline A=(2,1-\sqrt{-5})$, and $A\overline A$ is generated by the four products of generators,
\[
A\overline A=\big(4,\;2(1+\sqrt{-5}),\;2(1-\sqrt{-5}),\;(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})\big)=(4,\,2+2\sqrt{-5},\,2-2\sqrt{-5},\,6).
\]
Each generator is divisible by $2$, so $A\overline A\subseteq(2)$; conversely $2=6-4\in A\overline A$, so $(2)\subseteq A\overline A$. Hence $A\overline A=(2)$. But $A=\overline A$: complex conjugation sends $1+\sqrt{-5}\mapsto1-\sqrt{-5}=2-(1+\sqrt{-5})\in A$, so $\overline A\subseteq A$ and by symmetry $A=\overline A$. Therefore $(2)=A\overline A=A^2$, and $2$ ramifies.
Check. $N(A)=2$, so $N\big((2)\big)=N(A)^2=4=2^2$, matching the index $[R:(2)]=4$.
\end{wex}

Title: The prime $3$ splits in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The prime $3$ splits in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Show that $(3)=B\overline B$ with $B\neq\overline B$, so $3$ splits but does not ramify.
\wrec Check the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{-5}{3}\right)$: a value $+1$ predicts splitting. Then confirm $B\overline B=(3)$ and $B\neq\overline B$.
\wsol Modulo $3$, $-5\equiv1=1^2$, so $\left(\frac{-5}{3}\right)=+1$ and $x^2+5\equiv x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)\pmod3$ has two distinct roots: $3$ splits. Concretely $B=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})$ and $\overline B=(3,1-\sqrt{-5})$. The product $B\overline B$ is generated by
\[
\big(9,\;3(1-\sqrt{-5}),\;3(1+\sqrt{-5}),\;6\big),
\]
each divisible by $3$, so $B\overline B\subseteq(3)$; and $3=9-6\in B\overline B$, so $(3)\subseteq B\overline B$, giving $B\overline B=(3)$. Finally $B\neq\overline B$: if they were equal then $B$ would contain both $1+\sqrt{-5}$ and $1-\sqrt{-5}$, hence their difference $2\sqrt{-5}$ and (with $3\in B$) eventually $1\in B$, forcing $B=R$ -- but $N(B)=3\neq1$. So $B\neq\overline B$ and $3$ splits without ramifying.
Check. $\left(\frac{-5}{3}\right)=+1$ correctly predicted two prime factors, and $N(B)=3$ gives $N\big((3)\big)=9=3^2$.
\end{wex}

Title: The prime $7$ splits in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The prime $7$ splits in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Decide the behaviour of $7$ and exhibit a prime factor $P$ of $(7)$.
\wrec Reduce $d=-5$ mod $7$ and test whether it is a square: $\left(\frac{-5}{7}\right)=+1$ means split, $-1$ means inert.
\wsol Modulo $7$, $-5\equiv2$. The squares mod $7$ are $\{1,4,2,2,4,1\}=\{1,2,4\}$, and indeed $3^2=9\equiv2$, so $2$ is a square and $\left(\frac{-5}{7}\right)=+1$. Thus $x^2+5\equiv x^2-2\equiv(x-3)(x+3)\pmod7$ (check: $(x-3)(x+3)=x^2-9\equiv x^2-2$), so $7$ splits. A prime factor is
\[
P=(7,\;\sqrt{-5}-3),\qquad (7)=P\overline P,\quad \overline P=(7,\sqrt{-5}+3),
\]
following the recipe $P=(p,\sqrt d-a)$ with $a=3$, $a^2=9\equiv-5\pmod7$.
Check. $N(P)=7$ and $P\neq\overline P$ (a root $a=3\not\equiv-a=4\pmod7$ since $7\nmid 2a=6$), so $7$ splits, consistent with $\left(\frac{-5}{7}\right)=+1$.
\end{wex}

Title: The prime $11$ is inert in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
Content:
\begin{wex}{The prime $11$ is inert in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$}
Show that $(11)$ is a prime ideal of $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$.
\wrec Inertness is the case $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)=-1$: $x^2-d$ stays irreducible mod $p$, so $(p)$ is already maximal.
\wsol Modulo $11$, $-5\equiv6$. The nonzero squares mod $11$ are $\{1,4,9,5,3\}$, and $6$ is not among them, so $\left(\frac{-5}{11}\right)=-1$. Hence $x^2+5\equiv x^2-6$ has no root in $\F_{11}$ and is irreducible there, so by part (c) of the theorem $(11)=11R$ is prime in $Z[\sqrt{-5}]$: $11$ is inert.
Check. $R/(11)\cong\F_{11}[x]/(x^2-6)\cong\F_{121}$ is a field, confirming $(11)$ is maximal; the norm of the prime $(11)$ is $11^2=121$, the inert signature.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
The polynomial criterion in part (c) is stated for $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$ and for odd $p$. When
$d\equiv1\pmod4$ you must use $x^2-x+h$ (part (d)), not $x^2-d$: the ring is
$Z[\eta]$, not $Z[\sqrt d]$, and using the wrong polynomial can mispredict the prime $2$. The
Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)$ also says nothing directly at $p=2$; that prime is
handled by the root-count of the correct polynomial mod $2$, where a repeated root signals
ramification. (At an odd $p\mid d$ the symbol is $0$, and $p$ ramifies for every $d$.)
\end{pitfall}

\begin{pitfall}
The polynomial criterion in part (c) is stated for $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$ and for odd $p$. When
$d\equiv1\pmod4$ you must use $x^2-x+h$ (part (d)), \emph{not} $x^2-d$: the ring is
$\mathbb{Z}[\eta]$, not $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]$, and using the wrong polynomial can mispredict the prime $2$. The
Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{d}{p}\right)$ also says nothing directly at $p=2$; that prime is
handled by the root-count of the correct polynomial mod $2$, where a repeated root signals
ramification. (At an odd $p\mid d$ the symbol is $0$, and $p$ ramifies for every $d$.)
\end{pitfall}

\begin{remark}
Collecting the $d=-5$ data: $2$ ramifies, $3$ and $7$ split, $11$ is inert. For the split and ramified primes
$2,3,7$ the factorization $(p)=P\overline P$ (with $P=\overline P$ allowed) recovers $(p)$ on multiplying a
prime by its conjugate -- the ideal-theoretic shadow of the norm being multiplicative -- while the
inert $11$ generates a prime ideal $(11)$ of norm $121$. This is the
local mechanism behind the global factorization $(6)=A\overline A\,B\overline B=(2)(3)$ of
Artin's $(13.4.7)$: the rational primes dividing a norm split, ramify, or stay inert one at a time, and
their prime ideals reassemble into the unique factorization of any ideal of $R$.
\end{remark}

Type: prose
Content:
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic number field $Q[\sqrt d\,]$, $d$ a square-free negative integer. In Artin's development $R$ has unique factorization of ideals into primes, but typically fails unique factorization of elements; the class group is the precise algebraic gadget measuring that failure. We regard each nonzero ideal of $R$ as a lattice in $C$, and two such lattices are ``the same shape'' exactly when they differ by a complex scaling.

Type: definition
Title: {similar ideals, ideal classes}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{similar ideals, ideal classes}]
Two nonzero ideals $A,A'$ of $R$ are similar if $A'=\lambda A$ for some $\lambda\in\units{C}$. Similarity is an equivalence relation; its classes are the ideal classes. The class of $A$ is written $(A)$. Geometrically $A\sim A'$ iff, as lattices in $C$, they are orientation-preservingly similar figures (a rotation followed by a scaling), since a lattice looks the same at each point and the similarity may be assumed to carry $0\mapsto0$, i.e.\ to be multiplication by some $\lambda$.
\end{definition}

Title: {the class group}
Content:
\begin{proposition}[{the class group}]
The ideal classes form an abelian group $C$ under $(A)(B)=(AB)$, with identity $1=(R)$. It is the class group of $R$; its order is the class number $h$.
\end{proposition}

embedding_text:
Course: abstract algebra notes
Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Computing the Ideal Class Group > The finiteness bound and the algorithm
Type: proof
Title: Sketch
Relation: proof_of=unit-3ebd919550cc5ae03f85
Content:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
(a) The shortest-vector estimate (Minkowski) gives, in any nonzero ideal $A$, an element $\alpha\neq0$ with $\Nm(\alpha)\le\Nm(A)\,\mu$; here $\mu=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}A(R)$ where $A(R)$ is the covolume of $R$. Since $\alpha\in A$ we have $A\mid(\alpha)$, say $(\alpha)=AC$, so $\Nm(A)\Nm(C)=\Nm(\alpha)\le\Nm(A)\mu$ and hence $\Nm(C)\le\mu$. As $(\alpha)=AC$ is principal, $(C)=(A)^{-1}=(\overline A)$, and $\overline C$ then lies in the class $(A)$ with $\Nm(\overline C)=\Nm(C)\le\mu$.
(b) Factor such an $A$ into primes $A=P_1\cdots P_k$; then $\Nm(P_i)\le\Nm(A)\le\mu$. A prime ideal has norm $p$ or $p^2$; if $\Nm(P)=p^2$ then $P=(p)$ is principal with trivial class, so only primes of norm $p\le\mu$ matter.
(c) Only finitely many products of primes have norm $\le\mu$, and at most two primes lie over each integer, so finitely many ideals (hence classes) occur.
\end{proof}

Section: Artinian Rings, Discrete Valuation Rings, and Dedekind Domains > Computing the Ideal Class Group > The finiteness bound and the algorithm
Type: method
Title: Computing $C$ from the splitting of small primes.
Content:
\begin{method}{Computing $C$ from the splitting of small primes.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item Compute $\lfloor\mu\rfloor$ and list the primes $p\le\mu$.
\item Determine the splitting of each such $p$. For $d\equiv2,3\pmod 4$: $p=2$ and the odd $p\mid d$ ramify, $(p)=P\overline P$ with $P=\overline P$, so $(P)^2=1$ (order $\le2$); an odd $p\nmid d$ splits iff $x^2-d$ has a root in $\F_p$; if $p$ stays prime, $(p)$ has trivial class and is discarded. For each prime that splits or ramifies, include one prime factor's class as a generator.
\item Find relations by computing element norms: a factorization $\Nm(\alpha)=p^iq^js^k$, with $\alpha$ divisible by none of the integers $p,q,s$, yields an ideal relation $(\alpha)=P^i Q^j S^k$ (up to conjugates), hence a relation $(P)^i(Q)^j(S)^k=1$ in $C$.
\item Read off the group from generators and relations; a prime $P$ over $p$ is non-principal iff $p$ has no proper factor (norm-$p$ element) in $R$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

Type: example
Title: The class group for $d=-5$ ($h=2$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{The class group for $d=-5$ ($h=2$)}
Compute $C$ for $R=Z[\delta]$, $\delta=\sqrt{-5}$, and exhibit the non-trivial class.
\wrec $d=-5\equiv3\pmod4$, so $\mu=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\sqrt5\approx2.58$, $\lfloor\mu\rfloor=2$: only the prime $p=2$ need be examined.
\wsol The prime $2$ ramifies: $x^2-(-5)=x^2+5\equiv x^2+1\equiv(x+1)^2\pmod2$, and $(2)=A\overline A$ with $A=(2,\,1+\delta)$, $A=\overline A$. By the ramified-prime analysis $(A)$ has order $1$ or $2$, and order $1$ would make $A=(\alpha)$ with $\Nm(\alpha)=\Nm(A)=2$, i.e.\ $a^2+5b^2=2$ for integers $a,b$ -- impossible. So $(A)$ has order $2$. Every class is represented by an ideal of norm $\le2$; the ideals of norm $1$ form the class $1$ and the only ideal of norm $2$ is $A$, giving exactly two classes. Hence $C\congZ/2Z$, generated by $(A)$, and $R$ is not a UFD.

Check. The failure of unique factorization is visible directly: $6=2\cdot3=(1+\delta)(1-\delta)$ with all four factors irreducible, while at the ideal level $(6)=(2)(3)=A\overline A\,B\overline B$ refines both, where $B=(3,1+\delta)$, $A\overline A=(2)$, $B\overline B=(3)$, and $AB=(1+\delta)$ is principal -- confirming $(A)(B)=1$, i.e.\ $(B)=(A)^{-1}=(A)$, consistent with a group of order $2$.
\end{wex}

Type: example
Title: The class group for $d=-23$ ($h=3$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{The class group for $d=-23$ ($h=3$)}
Compute $C$ for the ring of integers of $Q[\sqrt{-23}\,]$.
\wrec $d=-23\equiv1\pmod4$, so $R=Z[\eta]$ with $\eta=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt{-23})$ and $\mu=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sqrt{23}\approx2.77$, $\lfloor\mu\rfloor=2$: examine $p=2$ only.
\wsol The minimal polynomial of $\eta$ is $x^2-x+6$. Modulo $2$, $x^2-x+6\equiv x^2+x=x(x+1)$ is reducible with distinct roots, so $2$ splits: $(2)=P\overline P$ with $P\neq\overline P$, $\Nm(P)=2$. So $C$ is generated by the single class $(P)$. To find its order, hunt for element norms that are powers of $2$. The norm form is $\Nm(a+b\eta)=(a+b\eta)(a+b\overline\eta)=a^2+ab+6b^2$ (since $\eta+\overline\eta=1$, $\eta\overline\eta=6$). Compute:
\[
\Nm(\eta)=6,\quad \Nm(1+\eta)=1+1+6=8=2^3 .
\]
The value $\Nm(1+\eta)=8=2^3$ gives the ideal relation $(1+\eta)=P^{\,3}$ or $\overline P^{\,3}$ (the conjugate splits the two prime factors of $(2)$, and $(1+\eta)\overline{(1+\eta)}=(P\overline P)^3=(2)^3$ with $2\nmid(1+\eta)$, so $(1+\eta)$ is one of $P^3,\overline P^3$). Either way $(P)^3=1$, so $(P)$ has order $1$ or $3$. Order $1$ would require a norm-$2$ element: $a^2+ab+6b^2=2$ has no integer solution ($b=0$ gives $a^2=2$; $b=\pm1$ gives $a^2\pm a+6=2$, i.e.\ $a^2\pm a+4=0$, discriminant $<0$; and $\abs b\ge2$ gives $a^2+ab+6b^2=(a+\tfrac b2)^2+\tfrac{23}4b^2\ge23$). So $P$ is non-principal and $(P)$ has order $3$. Hence $C\congZ/3Z$, generated by a prime over $2$.

Check. A cyclic group of order $3$ has no element of order $2$, consistent with $2$ splitting (not ramifying) -- a ramified $2$ would force an order-$2$ class and an even class number, contradicting $h=3$. The relation $\Nm(1+\eta)=2^3$ is exactly the ``$(P)^3=1$'' witness predicted by the norm lemma.
\end{wex}

Title: A larger run: $d=-14$ ($h=4$)
Content:
\begin{wex}{A larger run: $d=-14$ ($h=4$)}
Determine the structure of $C$ for $d=-14$.
\wrec $d=-14\equiv2\pmod4$, $\mu=\tfrac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{14}\approx4.32$, $\lfloor\mu\rfloor=4$: inspect $p=2,3$ (the prime $4$ is not prime).
\wsol Here $R=Z[\delta]$, $\delta=\sqrt{-14}$, $\Nm(a+b\delta)=a^2+14b^2$. The prime $2$ ramifies: $(2)=P\overline P$, $P=(2,\delta)$, $P=\overline P$, so $(P)^2=1$. For $3$: $x^2+14\equiv x^2+2\pmod3$ has roots $x=\pm1$ ($1+2=3\equiv0$), so $3$ splits, $(3)=Q\overline Q$, $\Nm(Q)=3$, contributing a generator $(Q)$. Now compute norms:
\[
\Nm(\delta)=14=2\cdot7,\quad \Nm(2+\delta)=4+14=18=2\cdot3^2,\quad \Nm(1+\delta)=1+14=15=3\cdot5 .
\]
From $\Nm(2+\delta)=2\cdot3^2$ we get $(2+\delta)=P\,Q^2$ (up to conjugating $Q$), so the relation $(P)(Q)^2=1$, i.e.\ $(P)=(Q)^{-2}=(Q)^2$. Thus every generator is a power of $(Q)$, and $C=\langle (Q)\rangle$ is cyclic. Moreover $P$ is non-principal: a generator would have norm $2$, and $a^2+14b^2=2$ is impossible. So $(P)=(Q)^2$ has order exactly $2$, and $(Q)$ has order $4$ (in particular $(Q)$ is non-principal, as also follows from $a^2+14b^2=3$ being impossible). Counting ideals of norm $\le4$ -- $R$, $P$, the two primes over $3$, and the only norm-$4$ ideal $P^2=(2)$ -- gives at most four classes, so $C=\langle (Q)\rangle\congZ/4Z$.

Check. $(Q)^2=(P)$ has order $2$ and $(Q)^4=(P)^2=1$, so the order of $(Q)$ is exactly $4$, matching the tabulated class group $C_4$ for $d=-14$. The single relation $(P)(Q)^2=1$ collapsing two generators to one cyclic generator is the typical end state of the algorithm.
\end{wex}

\wsol Here $R=\mathbb{Z}[\delta]$, $\delta=\sqrt{-14}$, $\Nm(a+b\delta)=a^2+14b^2$. The prime $2$ ramifies: $(2)=P\overline P$, $P=(2,\delta)$, $P=\overline P$, so $(P)^2=1$. For $3$: $x^2+14\equiv x^2+2\pmod3$ has roots $x=\pm1$ ($1+2=3\equiv0$), so $3$ splits, $(3)=Q\overline Q$, $\Nm(Q)=3$, contributing a generator $(Q)$. Now compute norms:
\[
\Nm(\delta)=14=2\cdot7,\quad \Nm(2+\delta)=4+14=18=2\cdot3^2,\quad \Nm(1+\delta)=1+14=15=3\cdot5 .
\]
From $\Nm(2+\delta)=2\cdot3^2$ we get $(2+\delta)=P\,Q^2$ (up to conjugating $Q$), so the relation $(P)(Q)^2=1$, i.e.\ $(P)=(Q)^{-2}=(Q)^2$. Thus every generator is a power of $(Q)$, and $C=\langle (Q)\rangle$ is cyclic. Moreover $P$ is non-principal: a generator would have norm $2$, and $a^2+14b^2=2$ is impossible. So $(P)=(Q)^2$ has order exactly $2$, and $(Q)$ has order $4$ (in particular $(Q)$ is non-principal, as also follows from $a^2+14b^2=3$ being impossible). Counting ideals of norm $\le4$ -- $R$, $P$, the two primes over $3$, and the only norm-$4$ ideal $P^2=(2)$ -- gives at most four classes, so $C=\langle (Q)\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$.

\textit{Check.} $(Q)^2=(P)$ has order $2$ and $(Q)^4=(P)^2=1$, so the order of $(Q)$ is exactly $4$, matching the tabulated class group $C_4$ for $d=-14$. The single relation $(P)(Q)^2=1$ collapsing two generators to one cyclic generator is the typical end state of the algorithm.
\end{wex}

Type: pitfall
Content:
\begin{pitfall}
Do not conflate the two norms. $\Nm(\alpha)=\alpha\overline\alpha$ is an integer attached to an element; $\Nm(A)=n$ where $A\overline A=(n)$ is attached to an ideal. They agree only on principal ideals, $\Nm((\alpha))=\Nm(\alpha)$. The algorithm works precisely by passing between them: a multiplicative element norm $\Nm(\alpha)=p^iq^js^k$, with $\alpha$ divisible by none of $p,q,s$, certifies a principal ideal $P^iQ^jS^k=(\alpha)$ (up to conjugates), hence a relation in $C$. Also, an integer prime $p$ with $\Nm(P)=p^2$ means $(p)=P$ stayed prime -- its class is trivial and must be discarded, not used as a generator.
\end{pitfall}

\end{remark}

Type: definition
Title: {the real embedding $R\toR^2$}
Content:
\begin{definition}[{the real embedding $R\toR^2$}]
Associate to $\alpha=a+b\sqrt d\in R$ the point
\[
\Phi(\alpha)=(u,v),\qquad u=a+b\sqrt d=\alpha,\quad v=a-b\sqrt d=\overline{\alpha}.
\]
These are the two ways the abstract field $Q[x]/(x^2-d)$ embeds in $R$, one sending the residue of $x$ to $+\sqrt d$ and the other to $-\sqrt d$. The image $\Phi(R)$ is a lattice in $R^2$ spanned by $\Phi(1)=(1,1)$ and $\Phi(\sqrt d)=(\sqrt d,-\sqrt d)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}

\end{remark}

\begin{wex}{Reading the norm as a product of coordinates}
For $\alpha=1+\sqrt2$ in $R=Z[\sqrt2]$, compute $\Phi(\alpha)$ and $\Nm(\alpha)$ and check the two agree.

\end{wex}

\begin{proposition}[{units have norm $\pm1$}]
An element $\alpha\in R$ is a unit if and only if $\Nm(\alpha)=\pm1$. Equivalently, $\Phi(\alpha)$ lies on one of the two hyperbolas
\[
uv=1\qquador\qquad uv=-1.
\]
\end{proposition}

Type: proof
Relation: proof_of=unit-6eb0b59a182c917d05dd
Content:
\begin{proof}
If $\alpha$ is a unit with inverse $\beta\in R$, then $\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)=\Nm(1)=1$ in $Z$, and both factors are integers, so $\Nm(\alpha)=\pm1$. Conversely, if $\Nm(\alpha)=\alpha\overline{\alpha}=\pm1$, then $\overline{\alpha}$ or $-\overline{\alpha}$ is an inverse of $\alpha$ lying in $R$ (the conjugate of an algebraic integer is again an algebraic integer in $R$), so $\alpha\in\units{R}$. The condition $\Nm(\alpha)=uv=\pm1$ is exactly membership of $\Phi(\alpha)$ in the two hyperbolas.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[{Dirichlet, rank one; Artin 13.9.9}]
Let $R$ be the ring of integers in a real quadratic field. The group of units $\units{R}$ is infinite. More precisely,
\[
\units{R}\;\cong\;\langle -1\rangle\times\langle \epsilon\rangle\;\cong\;Z/2Z\;\times\;Z,
\]
where $\epsilon>1$ is a uniquely determined fundamental unit.
\end{theorem}
